companyDescription: Allay Claims Limited is a claims management company acquired in 2015 that specialises in pursuing Personal Payment Insurance (PPI) tax refund claims on behalf of consumers. The company operates primarily through SMS marketing and online channels to identify and engage potential claimants.
companyLongDescription: Allay Claims Limited is a claims management company acquired in 2015 that specialises in pursuing Personal Payment Insurance (PPI) tax refund claims on behalf of consumers. The company operates primarily through SMS marketing and online channels to identify and engage potential claimants.
caseDescription: Allay Claims Limited sent 4.6 million unsolicited SMS marketing messages to consumers promoting PPI tax refund services between February 2023 and February 2024, without obtaining valid consent and failing to offer a simple means to opt out at the point of data collection. The company continued sending marketing messages even after the ICO's investigation commenced, resulting in a further 118,000+ complaints by January 2026.
violationSummary: The company engaged in systematic, large-scale collection and use of contact details for direct marketing without proper consent or opt-out mechanisms, fitting the surveillance category under Solove's framework. The deceptive representations about not using data for marketing exacerbate the surveillance aspect.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Allay Claims Limited sent 4,046,947 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to individuals between February 2023.
whyTheyWereWrong: Recipients received promotional SMS messages about PPI tax refunds they never agreed to, despite the company's own online guarantee stating 'We do not cold call.

claimsVsReality.claim: Allay's online customer journey stated: 'PERSONAL INFORMATION GUARANTEE... We do not cold call, spam or pass on your data for marketing'
claimsVsReality.reality: Allay sent 4.6 million unsolicited SMS marketing messages to consumers, directly contradicting this guarantee.

claimsVsReality.claim: Allay claimed it relied on the 'soft opt-in' exemption and therefore consent was not required.
claimsVsReality.reality: Allay failed to comply with the conditions for soft opt-in under Regulation 22(3)(c), which requires a simple means of refusing marketing at initial data collection. Allay only offered opt-out via email hidden in the privacy policy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Allay later claimed the SMS messages were 'service messages' continuing a prior customer relationship, not direct marketing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The messages were explicitly promotional, encouraging recipients to join a class action ('Join them today!') and promoting a third-party law firm. The ICO found no reasonable interpretation by which these could be service messages.

claimsVsReality.claim: All recipients were 'previous customers' who had proactively engaged with Allay in 2019.
claimsVsReality.reality: Contact details were obtained in 2019 for PPI claim services; many years later Allay sent unsolicited SMS promoting an unrelated group litigation order, with no evidence of fresh, explicit consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 22(2) of PECR prohibits transmission of unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Allay transmitted 4,046,947 direct marketing SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
violations: Allay transmitted 4,046,947 direct marketing SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 22(3)(c) of PECR requires that where soft opt-in applies, recipients must be given a simple means of refusing marketing use of contact details at the time details are initially collected and at each subsequent communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: Allay failed to provide a simple opt-out mechanism at initial data collection; customers had to email a generic address to opt out. Online journey stated 'We do not cold call, spam or pass on your data for marketing' yet contained no upfront opt-out checkbox.
violations: Allay failed to provide a simple opt-out mechanism at initial data collection; customers had to email a generic address to opt out. Online journey stated 'We do not cold call, spam or pass on your data for marketing' yet contained no upfront opt-out checkbox.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A(1) of the DPA requires that before serving a monetary penalty for a serious contravention of PECR, the Commissioner must be satisfied that the contravention was either deliberate or negligent, with knowledge/reasonable awareness of the risk and failure to take reasonable steps to prevent it.
regulatoryFindings.description: Allay knew or ought to have known of PECR obligations; it was previously investigated in 2020 for similar breaches. Allay failed to suspend marketing activity despite ICO investigation and continued sending 118,088 complaints' worth of messages from February 2024 to January 2026. Company changed its legal position midway (from 'soft opt-in' to 'service messages'), indicating awareness of potential non-compliance.
violations: Allay knew or ought to have known of PECR obligations; it was previously investigated in 2020 for similar breaches. Allay failed to suspend marketing activity despite ICO investigation and continued sending 118,088 complaints' worth of messages from February 2024 to January 2026. Company changed its legal position midway (from 'soft opt-in' to 'service messages'), indicating awareness of potential non-compliance.

outcome: The Information Commissioner's Office issued a Monetary Penalty Notice on 15 January 2026 requiring Allay Claims Limited to pay £120,000 (reduced to £96,000 if paid by 16 February 2026 under the early payment discount). The penalty is enforceable by County Court (England, Wales, Northern Ireland) or Sheriff Court (Scotland). Allay has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (General Regulatory Chamber) within 28 days of the notice. The notice compels compliance with PECR Regulation 22 prospectively; Allay must ensure valid consent or full soft opt-in compliance for all future direct marketing.
companyNow: Allay Claims Limited remains active as of the notice date (15 January 2026), registered at Studio 20, The Kiln, Newcastle Upon Tyne. However, the company faces significant reputational damage, ongoing regulatory scrutiny, and continued SMS complaints (118,088 additional complaints from Feb 2024 to Jan 2026) indicating persistent non-compliance.
dataType: contact details (phone numbers, email addresses), personal identifiers related to PPI tax refund claims
legalBasisViolated: Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, Regulation 22(2)
Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, Regulation 22(3)(c)

companyDescription: The Greek Fire Service Headquarters (Αρχηγείο Πυροσβεστικού Σώματος) is the central executive and administrative authority of the Greek Fire Service, responsible for operations, human resources, and policy across all regional fire stations nationwide.
companyLongDescription: The Greek Fire Service Headquarters (Αρχηγείο Πυροσβεστικού Σώματος) is the central executive and administrative authority of the Greek Fire Service, responsible for operations, human resources, and policy across all regional fire stations nationwide.
caseDescription: The Fire Service Headquarters unlawfully recorded and distributed sensitive health data of an employee, including her medical condition, prescribed medications, and treatment details, in public daily orders and electronic systems accessible to hundreds of staff. The data was recorded 'in error' in common rather than confidential registers, distributed to multiple recipients beyond the Health Service, and made accessible without proper access restrictions in the Fire Service application system.
violationSummary: Health data were exposed to unauthorized individuals and kept accessible in unclassified systems without proper safeguards or data minimization, making them discoverable by all staff members.
violations: Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Fire Service Headquarters recorded an employee's health diagnosis, medications, and treatment details in common daily orders accessible to all staff.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's sensitive health data was exposed to hundreds of staff members across multiple fire service locations without her consent or any legitimate operational need.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Fire Service stated data were recorded 'by mistake' (εκ παραδρομής) in July-August 2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even if recorded in error, the data remained visible in common registers, were reproduced in employee transfer documents, were sent to senior administration, and were accessible in unclassified electronic systems through at least February 2024 — long after discovery of the error in 2022.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Fire Service claimed it corrected the problem by designating the daily orders 'confidential' starting 01-06-2022 and later diagramming entries.
claimsVsReality.reality: By June 2022, an unknown number of staff had already seen the health information; the confidential redesignation came one year after the initial exposure; separate copies of the problematic entries persisted in other documents and electronic systems.

claimsVsReality.claim: Medical data must be recorded in daily orders per Presidential Decree 210/1992 articles 20, para. 4 (XIV-XV).
claimsVsReality.reality: The Decree required such data in CONFIDENTIAL orders for officers, not common ones. The Fire Service's own regulations mandated confidential classification; the Health Service circular (2022) explicitly prohibited sharing health data in non-confidential channels.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The Fire Service Headquarters recorded the employee's health data (diagnosis, medication, treatment details) in common daily orders rather than confidential ones, violating the requirement that such sensitive information be processed lawfully and in accordance with applicable regulations.
violations: The Fire Service Headquarters recorded the employee's health data (diagnosis, medication, treatment details) in common daily orders rather than confidential ones, violating the requirement that such sensitive information be processed lawfully and in accordance with applicable regulations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: The Fire Service recorded and distributed extensive medical details including specific medications and treatment regimens beyond what was necessary for personnel management purposes, and kept this data accessible in unclassified electronic systems.
violations: The Fire Service recorded and distributed extensive medical details including specific medications and treatment regimens beyond what was necessary for personnel management purposes, and kept this data accessible in unclassified electronic systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 9 permits processing of special category data (including health data) only under specific conditions and with appropriate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Health data were recorded in common registers and distributed to multiple recipients and systems without the specific protective measures required for special category data under Greek regulations and Fire Service internal rules.
violations: Health data were recorded in common registers and distributed to multiple recipients and systems without the specific protective measures required for special category data under Greek regulations and Fire Service internal rules.

outcome: The Authority found the Fire Service Headquarters liable as data controller for violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(c). An administrative fine of €10,000 was imposed. The Fire Service was required to implement proper data protection policies and procedures, ensure confidential classification of health data, restrict access appropriately, and provide guidance to all subordinate services on compliance with data protection laws. The Authority emphasized the systemic (structural) nature of the violation affecting all employees of the Fire Service, not merely this individual case.
companyNow: The Greek Fire Service Headquarters continues operations as the central command authority for the Fire Service. The decision and fine are enforceable as of 08-01-2026.
dataType: Health data (medical conditions, medication, sick leave records)

companyDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's federal law enforcement agency responsible for policing at the national level and provincial/territorial policing in most of Canada.
companyLongDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's federal law enforcement and national police service, established in 1873. It operates across Canada with detachments in every province and territory, investigating federal crimes, organized crime, terrorism, and providing policing services to jurisdictions that contract with it. The RCMP also provides specialized services including forensics, intelligence, and protection details.
caseDescription: The RCMP lost an unencrypted USB storage device containing sensitive personal information on 1,741 individuals, including witnesses, complainants, confidential informants, and employees. The device was found and its contents were copied and offered for sale to the public. The RCMP failed to encrypt the device, properly track it, or enforce policies requiring encryption and secure handling.
violationSummary: The RCMP failed to implement adequate security measures (encryption, password protection, asset tracking) for sensitive personal information stored on USB devices, resulting in unauthorized disclosure when the device was lost and misused.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The RCMP lost an unencrypted USB storage device containing sensitive personal information on 1,741 individuals including witnesses, informants, and employees, which was then found.
whyTheyWereWrong: Witnesses, informants, and police officers had their names, biographical data, criminal histories, photos, and videos exposed to criminal networks.

claimsVsReality.claim: The RCMP personnel attempted to find the lost device before reporting it.
claimsVsReality.reality: The device was lost and not reported for 21 days; it was only reported one day after a confidential informant informed the RCMP that copies were circulating in the criminal community and being offered for sale.

claimsVsReality.claim: The RCMP had adequate safeguards for USB storage devices containing sensitive personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The device was neither encrypted nor password protected; the RCMP had received multiple privacy breach recommendations since 2014 but had not implemented encryption requirements or device tracking procedures by the time of this 2022 breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: RCMP personnel understood their obligation to report security incidents involving loss of sensitive information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The initial security incident report omitted mention of the lost USB device entirely, mentioning only lost keys; DSS guidance was silent on required reporting timeframes despite stating incidents should be reported immediately.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8 – Personal information may only be disclosed with consent or under limited authorized exceptions
regulatoryFindings.description: Unauthorized disclosure of personal information of 1,741 individuals when unencrypted USB device was lost and contents copied by malicious actors
violations: Unauthorized disclosure of personal information of 1,741 individuals when unencrypted USB device was lost and contents copied by malicious actors
No consent obtained from individuals for disclosure
None of the Section 8(2) exceptions for disclosure without consent applied

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act – Institutions must take appropriate measures to safeguard personal information commensurate with sensitivity
regulatoryFindings.description: USB device was not encrypted or password protected despite containing highly sensitive information
violations: USB device was not encrypted or password protected despite containing highly sensitive information
No system in place to ensure USB devices were procured through approved process
No proper asset tracking or inventory system for USB devices
Devices were not encrypted prior to issuance to members
No system to detect unauthorized device connections
Inadequate security audits that failed to identify unauthorized USB devices
Sporadic or ineffective security awareness training and communications

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act – Institutions must ensure policies and procedures are followed and enforced
regulatoryFindings.description: RCMP Standard for USB device use (dated September 2021) was not followed at time of breach
violations: RCMP Standard for USB device use (dated September 2021) was not followed at time of breach
No enforcement mechanism to ensure detachments complied with encryption requirements
Limited security monitoring and compliance verification
Staff had not received privacy training in over a decade in some cases

regulatoryFindings.act: Timely reporting requirements for security breaches
regulatoryFindings.description: Loss of USB device not reported to Departmental Security Section for 21 days despite policy requiring reporting of security incidents
violations: Loss of USB device not reported to Departmental Security Section for 21 days despite policy requiring reporting of security incidents
Policy on timely reporting lacked specific timeframe requirements

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the complaint well-founded and unresolved. The OPC recommended that the RCMP: (1) implement measures to ensure only approved encrypted USB devices are used with an alert system for unauthorized devices (due within 1 year); (2) develop audit procedures to monitor return of devices after use (audit procedure due within 6 months, results within 1 year); and (3) revise security and privacy policies and awareness programs with ongoing training (schedule due within 6 months). The RCMP accepted the recommendations in principle but refused to commit to the proposed implementation timelines. As of December 2024, the RCMP is piloting interim solutions and exploring permanent alternatives to USB device use, but has not committed to specific deadlines. The complaint remains unresolved due to lack of committed timelines and continued reports of similar breaches at other RCMP detachments.
companyNow: The RCMP continues to operate as Canada's primary federal police service, though this incident highlighted systemic vulnerabilities in its data security practices for sensitive investigative information.
dataType: Names, biographical information, citizenship status, contact information, criminal history, dates and places of birth and death, employee identification, physical attributes, signatures, identification numbers, photos, videos
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act implicit requirement for sound security practices

companyDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is Canada's federal tax authority responsible for administering tax laws and delivering benefits programs including child tax credits.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is Canada's primary federal tax and revenue administration agency, operating under the Department of National Revenue. It administers income tax, goods and services tax (GST/HST), excise taxes, and delivers social benefits including the Canada Child Benefit and other family support programs. The CRA maintains extensive personal and family information on millions of Canadian taxpayers and their dependents through its integrated systems.
caseDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) inappropriately disclosed an adopted child's adoptive name and related personal information to the child's biological mother, in violation of the Privacy Act section 8. The disclosure occurred due to employee failure to follow internal procedures when processing the biological mother's application, resulting in the child's account being linked to both the adoptive and biological mother's accounts. The incident caused significant psychological and legal harm to the adoptive family.
violationSummary: The CRA disclosed personal information (the child's adoptive name and identity) without consent to an unauthorized third party (biological mother), enabling her to locate and contact the family contrary to the closed adoption arrangement. This constitutes unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Canada Revenue Agency failed to follow internal procedures when processing a biological mother's application, linking an adopted child's account to both the adoptive.
whyTheyWereWrong: A CRA employee verbally disclosed the child's adoptive name to the biological mother in 2018, enabling her to locate.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CRA's procedures adequately protect adopted children's personal information and privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CRA's Benefits Operation Manual procedures only addressed one adoption scenario (biological parent application first) and failed to cover the reverse scenario (adoptive parent application first), creating confusion that led to an employee not following procedures and inappropriately linking accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: CRA employees would have no reason to suspect the DIN contained information the biological mother was not entitled to know.
claimsVsReality.reality: The biological mother was able to obtain and use the child's adoptive name from a CRA call centre employee in 2018 to locate and make unwanted contact with the adoptive family, demonstrating the system failed to protect the child's identity despite the closed adoption.

claimsVsReality.claim: The closed adoption protects children and adoptive families from contact with biological parents.
claimsVsReality.reality: Due to the CRA's procedural failures and account linking, the biological mother learned the child's adoptive name and identity in 2018, enabling her to initiate contact with the family in December 2018, defeating the entire purpose of the closed adoption.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 8(1) — Personal information can only be disclosed with an individual's consent or in accordance with limited exceptions in subsection 8(2)
regulatoryFindings.description: CRA disclosed the child's full adoptive name and related personal information to the biological mother without the adoptive parents' consent
violations: CRA disclosed the child's full adoptive name and related personal information to the biological mother without the adoptive parents' consent
Disclosure occurred in 2018 when a CRA call centre employee verbally provided the child's adoptive name to the biological mother
No legal exception under section 8(2) applied to authorize this disclosure

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 3 — Definition and protection of personal information under the Act
regulatoryFindings.description: CRA failed to adequately safeguard the child's adoptive name, which is personal information under the Act
violations: CRA failed to adequately safeguard the child's adoptive name, which is personal information under the Act
CRA failed to protect the adoptive mother's personal information (her identity and whereabouts) which was linked to the child's information

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC) found the complaint well-founded. The CRA agreed to implement two of three recommendations: (1) reviewing and revising its procedures in the Benefits Operation Manual to better protect adopted children's personal information, and (2) providing comprehensive training to employees on updated procedures. However, the CRA declined to implement oversight measures to monitor compliance with new procedures for one year following implementation. The CRA took corrective measures in the specific case by manually deleting and unlinking the first DIN account from the biological mother's account and creating a new DIN account containing only information from her own application, with custody dispute indicators set on both accounts.
companyNow: The CRA continues to operate as Canada's primary revenue and benefits administration agency. Following this incident, it committed to reviewing and revising procedures for protecting adopted children's information and providing comprehensive employee training.
dataType: Child's adoptive name, adoptive parent's name, personal information of adopted child

companyDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency is Canada's federal tax administration and law enforcement authority responsible for administering federal tax laws and investigating tax-related offences.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is a federal Crown corporation that administers the Income Tax Act, the Excise Tax Act, and other federal tax laws. It collects taxes, pays benefits, and enforces tax compliance across Canada. The CRA also investigates tax fraud and administers the privacy complaint process under the Privacy Act for federal institutions.
caseDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency improperly withheld personal information from a complainant by relying on paragraph 22(1)(b) of the Privacy Act across dozens of pages without demonstrating a clear and direct connection between disclosure and actual harm. The CRA used general assertions of harm rather than case-by-case substantiation to justify the exemption. The complaint was found well-founded, and while the CRA agreed to release some information, it maintained its position on the remainder, leaving the complaint unresolved.
violationSummary: The CRA's improper denial of access to personal information by overrelying on exemption provisions without adequate substantiation of harm constitutes an exclusion violation, denying individuals their right to access their own information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The Canada Revenue Agency withheld personal information across dozens of pages by invoking paragraph 22(1)(b) of the Privacy Act without demonstrating a clear.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant was denied access to their own personal information and grievance records, leaving them unable to understand the full scope of how the CRA had processed their complaints.

claimsVsReality.claim: Paragraph 22(1)(b) applies broadly to withhold information related to ongoing investigations and grievances without case-by-case justification.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner found the exemption requires a clear and direct connection between disclosure and actual harm, with general assertions being insufficient.

claimsVsReality.claim: The mere existence of ongoing grievance proceedings justifies withholding all related personal information across dozens of pages.
claimsVsReality.reality: Much of the withheld information was transactional in nature and factual documentation; ongoing status alone does not meet the threshold for harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disclosure could give the complainant a strategic advantage before grievance boards, justifying blanket withholding.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner determined that potential strategic disadvantage to the institution does not meet the legal threshold for protecting law enforcement investigations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act paragraph 22(1)(b) — Information must not be withheld unless there is a clear and direct connection between disclosure and a risk of harm to the enforcement of any law of Canada or the conduct of lawful investigations
regulatoryFindings.description: CRA relied on paragraph 22(1)(b) to withhold information across dozens of pages without demonstrating specific, case-by-case harm
violations: CRA relied on paragraph 22(1)(b) to withhold information across dozens of pages without demonstrating specific, case-by-case harm
CRA used general assertions of harm rather than evidence of actual injurious effect
CRA failed to establish clear nexus between disclosure and risk of harm for each instance of withholding

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act — Institution must conduct reasonable searches to identify responsive records and apply exemptions only where justified
regulatoryFindings.description: CRA conducted reasonable searches but failed to substantiate its use of exemptions with sufficient evidence
violations: CRA conducted reasonable searches but failed to substantiate its use of exemptions with sufficient evidence

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded and recommended the CRA reassess its reliance on paragraph 22(1)(b) and disclose as much information as possible. The CRA agreed to release some information but maintained its withholding position on the remainder, leaving the complaint unresolved. The Commissioner issued guidance clarifying the threshold for harm, the burden of proof on institutions, and the requirement for case-by-case assessment rather than blanket application of exemptions.
companyNow: The CRA continues to operate as Canada's primary tax authority and is subject to privacy oversight by the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.
dataType: Personal information related to grievances, factual details, internal correspondence, transactional information

companyDescription: 23andMe is a multinational biotechnology company providing direct-to-consumer genetic testing, ancestry analysis, and health reporting services to millions of customers globally.
companyLongDescription: Founded in 2006, 23andMe offers DNA testing kits that provide customers with ancestry composition reports, genetic relative matching, and health predisposition reports. The company maintains extensive databases of genetic and health information collected from millions of customers worldwide. In March 2025, following the breach and financial losses, 23andMe filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy. The company was publicly traded and serves customers across North America, the UK, and other jurisdictions.
caseDescription: 23andMe suffered a credential stuffing attack from April to September 2023 affecting approximately 7 million customers globally. The company failed to implement adequate security safeguards, particularly mandatory multi-factor authentication, and inadequately detected the ongoing attack over five months. Notifications to regulators and affected individuals were incomplete, failing to disclose that sensitive health and raw DNA data had been accessed.
violationSummary: The primary violation concerns inadequate technical and organizational safeguards to protect highly sensitive genetic and health information. The company failed to implement mandatory MFA, had weak password requirements, insufficient monitoring and detection systems, and failed to conduct appropriate risk assessments for credential stuffing attacks—a well-known attack vector.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: 23andMe failed to implement mandatory multi-factor authentication and other security safeguards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of customers had their raw DNA data, health information, race and ethnicity data, and genetic relative information accessed.

claimsVsReality.claim: 23andMe decided not to implement mandatory MFA to avoid friction in user experience and maintain platform usability.
claimsVsReality.reality: The absence of mandatory MFA left over 75% of users exposed to credential-based attacks, directly enabling the breach that compromised 7 million customers' sensitive genetic and health data.

claimsVsReality.claim: 23andMe's password requirements met industry standards with an eight-character minimum and minimal complexity requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The eight-character minimum fell below the 2023 ICO guidance recommending at least 10 characters, and the minimal complexity requirements failed to protect against credential stuffing attacks.

claimsVsReality.claim: 23andMe had effective detection mechanisms in place to monitor for unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Detection systems failed to alert the company to clear signals of unauthorized access over five months, and three distinct anomalous events occurred that collectively should have triggered breach detection.

claimsVsReality.claim: 23andMe provided complete and timely breach notifications to regulators and affected individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: Notifications to regulators omitted that raw DNA data was accessed; notifications to individuals were delayed over one month after forensic analysis completed and failed to disclose that data was posted for sale online.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Security safeguards must be appropriate to the sensitivity of personal information and protect against unauthorized access, disclosure, use, copying, or modification
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to make multi-factor authentication mandatory (only 22% adoption)
violations: Failed to make multi-factor authentication mandatory (only 22% adoption)
Implemented 8-character minimum password requirement instead of industry standard 10+ characters
Did not perform robust checks against compromised password databases
Provided no additional identity verification before accessing raw DNA data
Detection systems failed to identify credential stuffing despite five months of attacks
No digital fingerprinting or device history available to customers
Inadequate investigation of three distinct anomalies (July platform crash, attempted profile transfers, August breach claims)
Delayed breach response: 4 days to disable sessions, 1 month to disable raw DNA download, 1+ month to implement mandatory MFA

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) – Personal data must be processed with appropriate technical and organizational measures ensuring integrity and confidentiality
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate safeguards against credential-based attacks despite known prevalence
violations: Inadequate safeguards against credential-based attacks despite known prevalence
Optional rather than mandatory MFA
Weak password policies (8-character minimum)
Insufficient compromised password screening
No additional protections for highly sensitive data
Detection mechanisms failed to identify ongoing attack
Inadequate logging and monitoring of suspicious activity
Failure to investigate anomalies that signaled unauthorized access

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 10.1 and Breach Regulations Sections 2-3 – Breach notifications must contain complete information about personal data involved, as soon as feasible
regulatoryFindings.description: October 2023 breach reports failed to disclose that raw DNA data, health reports, and ancestry information were accessible to threat actor
violations: October 2023 breach reports failed to disclose that raw DNA data, health reports, and ancestry information were accessible to threat actor
Incomplete disclosure of scope of compromised data in initial notifications
December 2023 supplementary report did not clarify raw DNA access despite knowing it was compromised
Notifications to OPC and ICO lacked complete information known to 23andMe at time of submission

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Articles 33(3)(a)/(c) and 34(1)/(2) – Breach notifications must describe breach nature, data categories affected, and include all relevant information to data subjects
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to include complete information about personal information involved in breach reports to ICO
violations: Failed to include complete information about personal information involved in breach reports to ICO
Failed to inform individuals that their personal information had been posted for sale online by threat actor
Initial notifications failed to disclose raw DNA data and health information compromises
Notifications to affected individuals delayed until January 2024 for directly accessed accounts (3+ months after breach discovery, 1+ month after forensic analysis completed)

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada concluded that 23andMe contravened PIPEDA Principle 4.7, Section 10.1, and Breach Regulations Sections 2-3. The UK Information Commissioner concluded that 23andMe breached Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1)(b), 32(1)(d), 33, and 34 of UK GDPR. Both Commissioners found the safeguards issues 'well-founded and resolved' following 23andMe's implementation of corrective measures by December 31, 2024, including: mandatory email-based two-factor authentication; 12-character minimum passwords with checks against 1 billion compromised credentials; additional verification for raw DNA data; 48-hour delay on DNA downloads; 253+ new detection alerts; trusted browser functionality with account event history; penetration testing of credential stuffing scenarios; and organizational security improvements. The Commissioners indicated they would not hesitate to take action if compliance concerns arise during the Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings or if another company acquires customer data.
companyNow: 23andMe filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on March 23, 2025, following the breach and mounting financial losses. A sale approval hearing was scheduled for June 17, 2025.
dataType: Genetic data, raw DNA, health information, ancestry composition, race/ethnicity, date of birth, location, email address, health reports, carrier status, pharmacogenetic data
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Breach of Safeguards Regulations Sections 2 and 3

companyDescription: Google is a multinational technology company subsidiary of Alphabet Inc., operating the world's largest search engine and various digital services.
companyLongDescription: Google LLC, a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc., operates the world's dominant search engine that processes billions of searches daily. The company organizes and indexes vast amounts of web content to make information universally accessible. Google's search platform is available across multiple country-specific websites and mobile applications globally. Beyond search, Google offers numerous digital services including Google News, Gmail, Maps, and other productivity tools.
caseDescription: Google's search engine displayed news articles linking to a complainant's name that revealed highly sensitive personal information including HIV status and a stayed criminal charge, causing significant harm through physical assault, employment discrimination, and social stigma. The OPC found Google violated PIPEDA's appropriate purposes principle (subsection 5(3)) by continuing to display these articles in response to searches for the complainant's name, as the significant harm to the individual's safety and dignity outweighed limited public interest, though Google did not comply with the de-listing recommendation.
violationSummary: Google disclosed extremely sensitive personal information about an individual (HIV status, sexual orientation, stayed criminal charge) through search results linked to the person's name. This constitutes improper disclosure of sensitive personal information that caused significant harm to the individual's dignity, safety, and reputation, despite the information being lawfully published elsewhere.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Google's search engine continued to display news articles linking to the complainant's name that revealed their HIV status and a stayed criminal charge in prominent search results.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant suffered physical assault, lost employment opportunities, and severe social stigma after sensitive personal information about their HIV status.

claimsVsReality.claim: Google's search results accurately reflect content and the company has no responsibility for the underlying information in linked articles.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the search results accurately reflected the article content, Google's continued prominence of highly sensitive personal information about the complainant's HIV status and stayed criminal charge caused documented physical assault, employment discrimination, and social stigma.

claimsVsReality.claim: Public interest in accessing articles through the complainant's name search is significant.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant is not a public figure; the articles were published years earlier, were never updated to reflect that charges were stayed, and public debate about HIV non-disclosure law does not require linking these articles to this individual's name.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 5(3) requires organizations to collect, use or disclose personal information only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: Google continued to display highly sensitive personal information (HIV status, sexual orientation, stayed criminal charge) in search results linked to the complainant's name despite the significant harm caused to the individual's safety and dignity outweighing the limited public interest in accessing these articles via search for the complainant's name
violations: Google continued to display highly sensitive personal information (HIV status, sexual orientation, stayed criminal charge) in search results linked to the complainant's name despite the significant harm caused to the individual's safety and dignity outweighing the limited public interest in accessing these articles via search for the complainant's name

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 requires personal information to be as accurate, complete, and up-to-date as necessary for purposes of use
regulatoryFindings.description: No violation found – OPC determined Google's accuracy obligations do not extend to underlying content of linked articles, only to search result snippets accurately reflecting article content
violations: No violation found – OPC determined Google's accuracy obligations do not extend to underlying content of linked articles, only to search result snippets accurately reflecting article content

outcome: The OPC found the complaint well-founded and unresolved. Google contravened subsection 5(3) of PIPEDA by continuing to display the articles in response to searches for the complainant's name. The OPC recommended that Google de-list the articles from search results for the complainant's name, which would prevent them from appearing when the complainant's name is searched while keeping the articles accessible through other search terms and on news organization websites. Google did not agree to implement the de-listing recommendation, stating that court guidance is needed on several important questions before de-listing news articles would be appropriate.
companyNow: Google remains the dominant global search engine and a core business of Alphabet Inc., one of the world's most valuable companies. The company continues to face privacy and data protection scrutiny internationally.
dataType: Sexual orientation, sexual activities, HIV status, criminal charge information, name
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 – accuracy (assessed but not violated)

companyDescription: TikTok is a global short-form video sharing and social media platform operated by TikTok Pte. Ltd., owned by Chinese parent company ByteDance. The platform allows users to create, share and view short videos with advanced recommendation and profiling algorithms.
companyLongDescription: TikTok is one of the world's most popular social media platforms, offering short-form video content to hundreds of millions of users globally. The platform operates through mobile apps and web services, collecting extensive user data including behavioral, demographic, biometric and interest information. TikTok uses sophisticated analytics, tracking technologies, facial and voice analytics to profile users for targeted advertising and content personalization. The platform is owned by ByteDance, a Chinese technology company, and processes user data across multiple jurisdictions.
caseDescription: TikTok collected, used, and disclosed vast amounts of personal information from Canadian users, including children despite a prohibition on users under 13 (14 in Quebec). The platform failed to implement adequate age assurance mechanisms, resulting in approximately 500,000 underage users being removed annually. TikTok did not obtain valid and meaningful consent from users for tracking, profiling, and targeted advertising, nor did it adequately explain its practices in accessible communications or in French.
violationSummary: TikTok conducted extensive surveillance of users through tracking and profiling for targeted advertising and content personalization. This surveillance was particularly problematic for children, who were explicitly prohibited from using the platform yet were subject to collection and use of sensitive personal information without appropriate age verification or consent mechanisms. The collection involved sophisticated analytics tools including computer vision and machine learning algorithms operating invisibly to users.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: TikTok collected vast amounts of personal information from Canadian users including approximately 500,000 underage users annually.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children and youth were profiled, tracked and served targeted advertisements without their understanding or meaningful consent, exposing them to manipulative advertising practices.

claimsVsReality.claim: TikTok prohibits users under 13 (14 in Quebec) from using the platform.
claimsVsReality.reality: TikTok's age assurance mechanism was largely ineffective; the company removed approximately 500,000 underage users annually, indicating widespread underage user penetration and data collection from children.

claimsVsReality.claim: TikTok has implemented adequate measures to keep children off the platform.
claimsVsReality.reality: TikTok relied only on a voluntary age gate requiring users to self-report birthdate; the company possessed more sophisticated age assurance technology (facial analytics) for its livestreaming function but failed to deploy it platform-wide.

claimsVsReality.claim: TikTok obtains valid and meaningful consent from users for tracking, profiling and targeted advertising.
claimsVsReality.reality: TikTok's Privacy Policy and consent processes did not clearly explain upfront what data would be collected and how it would be used for ad targeting; key information was buried, inaccessible, or unavailable in French, and communications were not age-appropriate for youth users.

claimsVsReality.claim: Advertisers cannot target users based on sensitive attributes like transgender status.
claimsVsReality.reality: During a demonstration of TikTok's advertising portal, investigators found that advertisers could potentially target users based on transgender status; TikTok claimed this was not supposed to be possible but could not explain why the functionality existed.

claimsVsReality.claim: TikTok adequately explains its use of biometric information to users.
claimsVsReality.reality: TikTok did not adequately disclose that facial and voice analytics would infer potentially sensitive information (age, gender) about users for ad targeting and content personalization purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 5(3) — Collection, use and disclosure of personal information must be for appropriate purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate, reasonable, and legitimate
regulatoryFindings.description: TikTok collected sensitive personal information from approximately 500,000 underage users annually without legitimate need or bona fide business interest
violations: TikTok collected sensitive personal information from approximately 500,000 underage users annually without legitimate need or bona fide business interest
TikTok used information from underage users for ad targeting and content personalization despite prohibiting their use of the platform
TikTok failed to implement reasonable age assurance mechanisms despite knowing hundreds of thousands of children access the platform yearly

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Clauses 4.3 and 4.3.2 — Organizations must obtain knowledge and consent of individuals, explaining purposes in a manner users can reasonably understand
regulatoryFindings.description: TikTok did not explain key information about data collection up-front during account sign-up
violations: TikTok did not explain key information about data collection up-front during account sign-up
Privacy Policy lacked sufficient detail on what personal information would be used for each purpose and how
Supplementary privacy resources were scattered across the website and not linked to Privacy Policy, making them difficult to find
Privacy Policy and key communications were not available in French, preventing meaningful consent from francophone users
TikTok did not adequately explain use of biometric information (facial analysis) and how it would be used for age/gender inference for ad targeting

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 6.1 — Valid consent requires individuals to reasonably understand the nature, purposes, and consequences of collection and use
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent could not be meaningful as practices fell outside reasonable expectations of users
violations: Consent could not be meaningful as practices fell outside reasonable expectations of users
Complex tracking and profiling practices were invisible to users and occurred in background via computer vision and machine learning
Users were not informed up-front about extent and nature of personal information collected and how it would be used

regulatoryFindings.act: Quebec's Act Respecting the Protection of Personal Information in the Private Sector Section 4.1 — Personal information concerning a minor under 14 may not be collected without parental consent except where clearly for benefit of minor
regulatoryFindings.description: TikTok collected information from Quebec users under 14 without parental consent
violations: TikTok collected information from Quebec users under 14 without parental consent
Collection was not for benefit of minors but for TikTok's commercial purposes (ad targeting, content personalization)

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPA BC and PIPA AB Sections 6-8, 11, 14, 16 — Collection, use, and disclosure must be for appropriate purposes and with proper consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection and use of personal information from underage users was not for appropriate purposes
violations: Collection and use of personal information from underage users was not for appropriate purposes
Consent obtained was not valid or meaningful due to inadequate transparency and explanation
Age assurance mechanisms were inadequate and inconsistently applied across provinces

outcome: Matter conditionally resolved. TikTok agreed to implement comprehensive remediation measures within 6 months of report issuance (September 23, 2025), including: (1) three new enhanced age assurance mechanisms demonstrably effective at keeping underage users off platform; (2) enhanced privacy policy explaining targeted advertising and content personalization practices with more accessible supplementary communications; (3) cessation of allowing advertisers to target under-18 users except via generic categories (language, approximate location); (4) new plain-language privacy summary for teens and educational video on key privacy practices; (5) enhanced privacy communications regarding biometric information collection and potential data processing in China; (6) implementation of 'Privacy Settings Check-up' mechanism centralizing important privacy settings for all Canadian users; (7) submission of privacy impact assessments, testing/research plans and results; (8) monthly updates to the Offices until all commitments fulfilled. The Offices retained supervisory authority to monitor implementation and address any non-compliance.
companyNow: TikTok remains one of the world's largest social media platforms with hundreds of millions of active users. Following this enforcement action, the company committed to implementing enhanced age assurance, improved transparency, restricted youth advertising targeting, and privacy-by-default settings across Canadian operations.
dataType: Profile information (name, age, gender, email, phone), user-generated content, biometric data (facial analysis), device information, geolocation, contacts, behavioral data, engagement data, purchase information, inferred demographics and interests, audio analytics

Quebec's Act Respecting the Protection of Personal Information in the Private Sector Section 4.1 – Collection from Minors
PIPA BC Sections 6, 7, 8, 11, 14 – Collection, Use, Disclosure, and Appropriate Purposes
PIPA AB Sections 7, 8, 11, 16 – Collection, Use, Disclosure, and Appropriate Purposes

companyDescription: Staples Canada ULC is a major Canadian retail chain with over 300 stores selling electronics and office supplies. The company operates the Openbox program, which refurbishes and resells returned laptops within 14 days of purchase.
companyLongDescription: Staples Canada ULC is a private Canadian retail company operating a nationwide network of over 300 stores across multiple provinces. The company sells electronics, office supplies, and other retail goods to consumers and businesses. Its Openbox program allows customers to return laptops within 14 days of purchase, after which designated staff refurbish the devices and make them available for resale. The program is designed to provide affordable refurbished electronics while allowing customers flexibility in their purchases.
caseDescription: Staples Canada failed to adequately wipe personal information from returned laptops before reselling them through its Openbox program. The company lacked clear, consistent procedures and adequate employee training for data removal, resulting in approximately 23% of sampled devices retaining residual personal data from previous users.
violationSummary: Staples failed to implement adequate security safeguards to protect personal information on returned devices. Procedures were unclear, contradictory, and not consistently applied; training was inadequate or absent; and technical analysis confirmed that full manufacturer-standard wipes were not being performed, leaving personal data accessible to employees and subsequent purchasers.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Staples Canada resold refurbished laptops through its Openbox program without adequately wiping personal information from devices.
whyTheyWereWrong: Previous customers' personal information—including names, email addresses, usernames, and fragments of emails—remained accessible on resold devices, exposing them to financial fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: Staples ensures that any data on tech items is erased upon return.
claimsVsReality.reality: Approximately 23% of sampled refurbished laptops retained residual personal information including names, email addresses, usernames, and email fragments from previous users.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees use manufacturer-recommended wipe and restore procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Employees were instructed to perform generic 'data wipe and restore' without details on manufacturer-specific procedures; training materials lacked technical guidance and some staff were self-taught without formal training.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tech services specialists perform data wipe and restore while the customer is present.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal procedures allowed wiping within a 72-hour window, and employees accepted returns without immediate wiping if customers did not want to wait or if a tech specialist was unavailable.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clear procedures and training equip staff to remove personal information from returned devices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal policies contained contradictory instructions, training materials were high-level without technical details, and some staff responsible for data wiping had never received formal training.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.7.1 requires businesses to have security safeguards that protect personal information against unauthorized access and disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Staples did not have clear, documented technical procedures for wiping personal information from returned laptops
violations: Staples did not have clear, documented technical procedures for wiping personal information from returned laptops
Internal policies contained contradictory instructions regarding when and how to wipe devices
Employees did not consistently follow manufacturer-recommended wipe and restore procedures
Approximately 23% of analyzed returned devices retained residual personal data including names, emails, usernames, and payment information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.7.3 requires methods of protection to include physical, organizational and technological measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: No adequate organizational measures: staff training was high-level, lacking technical details; some tech services specialists had never received formal training and were self-taught
violations: No adequate organizational measures: staff training was high-level, lacking technical details; some tech services specialists had never received formal training and were self-taught
No adequate technological measures: employees were not consistently applying manufacturer-specific data sanitization procedures; TechScan+ tool was used instead of full factory reset in some cases
Procedures did not require verification that full manufacturer-standard wipes had been completed

outcome: The OPC found the matter well-founded and conditionally resolved. Staples agreed to: (1) develop clear procedures and standards requiring employees to wipe devices consistent with manufacturer guidelines for factory restore and data sanitization; (2) improve training for employees responsible for wiping returned devices; (3) ensure all employees tasked with wiping devices complete training before doing so; and (4) arrange for independent third-party annual spot checks of returned devices in Openbox program stores across multiple provinces for 3 years, with demonstration of compliance required within 9 months of the report's issuance.
companyNow: Staples Canada continues to operate retail stores across Canada and has agreed to implement enhanced data-wiping procedures and independent third-party audits of its Openbox program following this enforcement action.
dataType: Names, email addresses, usernames, payment information, fragments of emails, facial images, file document titles
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.7.1 (security safeguards against unauthorized access and disclosure)
PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.7.3 (physical, organizational and technological measures)

companyDescription: Services Australia is the government agency delivering welfare and social security payments and services to Australian residents and citizens.
companyLongDescription: Services Australia (formerly Centrelink) is the primary government agency responsible for administering payments and services including unemployment benefits, disability support, aged care services, and family assistance. The agency manages sensitive personal information for millions of Australians and must comply with the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and Australian Privacy Principles. It is a critical government institution delivering essential social security and welfare support.
caseDescription: Services Australia intertwingled sensitive personal information of multiple individuals and unauthorisedly disclosed personal information to unrelated parties. The agency failed to take reasonable steps to ensure information was accurate and up-to-date, and failed to protect personal information from unauthorised disclosure, resulting in serious and repeated privacy interferences.
violationSummary: Unauthorised disclosure of personal information to unrelated individuals, combined with intertwinement of sensitive data across multiple individuals' records, constitutes improper information dissemination.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Services Australia intertwingled sensitive personal information of multiple individuals and unauthorisedly disclosed personal information to unrelated parties without proper safeguards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two individuals had their sensitive personal information mixed together and disclosed to unrelated parties, exposing private details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Services Australia maintained appropriate safeguards and separation of personal information between individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The agency intertwingled sensitive personal information belonging to different individuals, causing it to be mixed together.

claimsVsReality.claim: Services Australia took reasonable steps to protect personal information from unauthorised disclosure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information was unauthorisedly disclosed to unrelated third parties without proper controls or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Services Australia ensured personal information was accurate and up-to-date.
claimsVsReality.reality: The agency failed to take reasonable steps to maintain accuracy and currency of personal information in its systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) APP 6.1 – Australian Privacy Principles require personal information to be accurate, up-to-date and complete
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to take reasonable steps to ensure personal information was accurate and up-to-date

Allowed intertwinement of sensitive information with that of other individuals

violations: Failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from unauthorised disclosure

violations: Unauthorised disclosure of personal information to unrelated parties

outcome: Finding of breach of APP 6, APP 10, and APP 11. Remedies ordered include written apology and specified steps to be undertaken. Compensation for non-economic loss may be available. The agency is required to implement measures to prevent future privacy breaches.

companyDescription: Regional Australia Bank Limited is a regional financial institution operating in Australia, providing banking services to customers across the country.
companyLongDescription: Regional Australia Bank Limited is an Australian-based bank providing retail and commercial banking services to customers in regional and remote areas of Australia. violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Regional Australia Bank Limited failed to comply with Privacy Safeguard 1 under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and Consumer Data Right Rules in handling consumer data.
whyTheyWereWrong: The bank's failure to implement mandatory privacy safeguards exposed customers' personal financial information to inadequate protection.

violations: Regional Australia Bank failed to implement adequate privacy safeguards to protect consumer personal data as required under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth)

companyDescription: Kmart Australia Limited is a major Australian retailer operating discount department stores across the country. The company is part of the Kmart Group, which also operates other retail brands.

companyDescription: Fortrend Securities is a financial services company operating in Australia, providing securities brokerage and investment services.
companyLongDescription: Fortrend Securities Pty Ltd is an Australian financial services firm engaged in securities trading and investment activities.
