violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Fortrend Securities unlawfully disclosed an employee's personal information without justification, breaching Australian Privacy Principle 6.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee suffered emotional distress and reputational harm from the unauthorized disclosure of their personal information, which was unrelated to their employment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disclosure was justified as part of normal employment practices
claimsVsReality.reality: The disclosure was not directly related to the employment relationship and constituted an unjustified interference with privacy under APP 6

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 6 – An APP entity must not disclose personal information about an individual unless the entity reasonably believes that the disclosure is required or authorised by law, or reasonably believes that the disclosure is necessary to lessen or prevent a serious threat to life, health, safety or the environment, or in other permitted circumstances.
regulatoryFindings.description: Fortrend Securities disclosed personal information about an employee without lawful authority or justification
violations: Fortrend Securities disclosed personal information about an employee without lawful authority or justification
The disclosure was not directly related to the employment relationship and fell outside the employee records exemption
The company failed to comply with APP 6 requirements governing disclosure of personal information

outcome: The OAIC determined a breach of APP 6 and awarded compensation for non-economic loss and aggravated damages. The company was ordered to issue an apology and take specified steps to address the interference with privacy and prevent future breaches.
dataType: Employee records, personal information

companyDescription: Vinomofo is an Australian e-commerce platform specialising in online wine sales and delivery. The company operates a subscription-based wine club and marketplace model.
companyLongDescription: Vinomofo Pty Ltd is an Australian-based online wine retailer founded in 2011, offering wine subscriptions, individual bottle sales, and a marketplace for wine enthusiasts. The company collects and stores customer personal information including names, addresses, payment details, and transaction history. Vinomofo serves a substantial Australian customer base through its digital platform.
caseDescription: Vinomofo failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information held by the company, in breach of Australian Privacy Principle 11.1. The OAIC found that the company's security practices were inadequate to safeguard individual data. The company was ordered to cease the conduct and implement specified remedial steps.
violationSummary: Vinomofo failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal information, exposing it to potential misuse or breach, which falls under the Insecurity category of information processing harm.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Vinomofo failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal information held in its systems, falling short of reasonable data protection standards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' personal and financial data was exposed to unauthorised access and theft due to inadequate security practices, putting individuals at risk of identity fraud and financial harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vinomofo had implemented reasonable security measures to protect customer data
claimsVsReality.reality: The OAIC found the company's security practices were inadequate and failed to meet the reasonable steps standard required by APP 11.1

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 11.1 – Australian Privacy Principle 11.1 requires entities to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vinomofo failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information
violations: Vinomofo failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information
Inadequate security practices and safeguards

outcome: The OAIC found a breach of APP 11.1. Vinomofo must not repeat or continue the acts and practices found to be an interference with individuals' privacy and must implement specified steps to address the interference and prevent future breaches.
companyNow: Vinomofo continues to operate as an online wine retailer in Australia, now operating under enhanced privacy and data security compliance obligations following this determination.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified types)

companyDescription: Singapore Data Hub Pte Ltd is a SaaS provider specialising in point-of-sale (POS) and Customer Relationship Management (CRM) software solutions for small and medium enterprises.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Data Hub Pte Ltd provides cloud-based POS and CRM software solutions to SMEs, hosting and managing customer data on behalf of its clients. As a SaaS vendor, the company possessed and controlled high volumes of sensitive personal data including customer information and health records. The company operated web-accessible systems that were inadequately secured against common cybersecurity threats. Despite handling confidential business and health data for multiple enterprise clients, the company failed to implement industry-standard security practices.
caseDescription: Singapore Data Hub, a SaaS provider of point-of-sale and CRM software, suffered two separate data breaches in April and June 2024 affecting 698,112 individuals. Threat actors exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities, unpatched systems, and inadequate access controls to exfiltrate personal and health data. The company failed to implement basic security measures including network firewalls, vulnerability scanning, and proper credential protection.
violationSummary: The company failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and exfiltration of personal data under PDPA section 24(a). Specific failures included lack of access controls, no vulnerability scanning, use of outdated unsupported systems, absence of network firewalls, and unprotected hardcoded credentials.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Singapore Data Hub failed to implement basic security measures including network firewalls, vulnerability scanning.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 698,112 individuals had their personal data including names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, NRIC numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Singapore Data Hub's systems were secure and protected against unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's webservers were publicly accessible with multiple open ports, no network firewall protection, outdated unsupported operating systems and software, and hardcoded database credentials in source code files—allowing attackers to exploit SQL injection vulnerabilities and exfiltrate data on two separate occasions.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company conducted regular security testing and vulnerability scanning of its applications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation revealed the company had not conducted pre-launch security testing or periodic vulnerability scanning; it only performed internal acceptance testing focused on functionality, not cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

claimsVsReality.claim: Singapore Data Hub maintained up-to-date and supported software infrastructure.
claimsVsReality.reality: The affected webservers ran an operating system unsupported since June 2024 and used PHP scripting language unsupported since December 2018, with no robust processes in place for regular patching and upgrades.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24(a) – Protection Obligation requiring organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to implement reasonable access control measures: webservers were publicly accessible with exposed directory listings; no network firewall deployed initially; application source code and database configuration files containing hardcoded credentials were unprotected
violations: Failure to implement reasonable access control measures: webservers were publicly accessible with exposed directory listings; no network firewall deployed initially; application source code and database configuration files containing hardcoded credentials were unprotected

Failure to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews and vulnerability scanning: no pre-launch security testing or periodic vulnerability scans were performed despite monthly application changes; SQL injection vulnerabilities went undetected
Lack of robust patching and update processes: organisation continued using unsupported operating systems and outdated PHP scripting language without timely upgrades

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Singapore Data Hub breached section 24 of the PDPA and imposed a financial penalty of SGD $17,500 payable within 30 days. The organisation was directed to implement comprehensive security remediation within 90 days including: adequate perimeter security controls (network firewalls, VPN with location-specific access), rate limiting, network segmentation, segregation of production and training environments, endpoint detection and response, improved logging with central repository, documented periodic vulnerability assessment and penetration testing processes, strict input validation to prevent SQL injection, enhanced asset and patch management, encryption of credentials in configuration files, and reporting to the Commission upon completion.
companyNow: Singapore Data Hub Pte Ltd continues to operate following the PDPA enforcement action, having implemented remedial security controls including network firewalls, multi-factor authentication, and web application firewalls.
dataType: Name, address, personal email address, telephone number, date of birth, NRIC number, gender, health information (patient skin concerns, skin conditions, treatments, prescribed medications)

companyDescription: People Central Pte. Ltd. is a cloud-based HR management Software as a Service (SaaS) provider that offers online HR solutions to organisations across Singapore and the region.
companyLongDescription: People Central Pte. Ltd. operates as a cloud-based HR SaaS provider, delivering HR management solutions hosted on Amazon Web Services. The company processes sensitive employee personal data including NRIC numbers, salary information, bank accounts, and emergency contact details on behalf of its clients. As an SaaS provider, the company holds personal data entrusted to it by HR departments across multiple organisations. The company operates primarily in Singapore under the jurisdiction of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012.
caseDescription: People Central, a cloud-based HR SaaS provider, suffered a data breach on 29 April 2024 where threat actors exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities, weak access controls, and insufficient security testing to access and delete databases containing personal data of 95,000 employees and 24,765 emergency contacts/children. The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements including Web Application Firewall, two-factor authentication on remote access, and regular vulnerability scanning.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, specifically: absence of Web Application Firewall against SQL injection attacks, open RDP access without two-factor authentication, weak network access controls, and insufficient periodic vulnerability scanning (only every 2 years instead of quarterly), thus creating risk of unauthorised access and data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: People Central failed to implement reasonable security arrangements including Web Application Firewall, two-factor authentication on remote access.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees and emergency contacts had their sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers, salary information, bank account details, and children's information stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: We conducted vulnerability assessments and adhered to ISO procedures; there are no definitive standardised rules on frequency.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vulnerability scanning was only conducted every 2 years, when industry best practices (CIS Controls) require quarterly assessments for organisations holding sensitive HR data.

claimsVsReality.claim: We could not implement a WAF due to previous service disruption attempts.
claimsVsReality.reality: A WAF was necessary to defend against SQL injection attacks that actually compromised the system; technical difficulties do not excuse failure to implement critical security controls.

claimsVsReality.claim: Our financial difficulties should warrant a penalty waiver.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company remained profitable despite claiming financial hardship; financial constraints do not justify inadequate security for client personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – Organisations must protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews; vulnerability scanning only conducted every 2 years instead of quarterly
violations: Failed to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews; vulnerability scanning only conducted every 2 years instead of quarterly
Failed to implement Web Application Firewall to defend against SQL injection attacks
Failed to restrict RDP access; left open to internet without two-factor authentication requirement
Absence of network vulnerability assessments at time of incident
Failed to implement annual external and internal penetration testing as recommended by industry standards (CIS Critical Security Controls)

outcome: Organisation required to pay financial penalty of $17,500 SGD in 12 monthly instalments. Additionally directed to: (1) review web application for secure implementation per OWASP standards; (2) implement adequately configured Web Application Firewall; (3) complete implementation of regular annual external and internal penetration tests; (4) complete implementation of two-factor authentication for RDP access; (5) complete implementation of encryption for all personal data fields; (6) report to Commission upon completion of all remedial actions within 90 days. If payment not made by due dates, full outstanding amount becomes immediately due with interest at judgment debt rate.
companyNow: People Central continues to operate and has committed to implementing enhanced security controls including Web Application Firewall, two-factor authentication, encryption of all personal data fields, and quarterly vulnerability assessments.
dataType: Name, gender, employee pass type, NRIC number, date of employment, place and date of birth, nationality, salary, marital status, religion, bank account number, mobile number, email address, physical address, emergency contact names and numbers, children's names/aliases and dates of birth

companyDescription: Goldheart Jewelry is a Singapore-based retail jewelry company that operates both an online store and physical outlets throughout Singapore. It is a subsidiary of Aspial Corporation Limited.
companyLongDescription: Goldheart Jewelry Pte. Ltd. is a jewelry retailer in Singapore owned and controlled by Aspial Corporation Limited, operating through both an e-commerce website built on the Magento platform and multiple brick-and-mortar stores. The company stores customer data including names, contact details, addresses, and dates of birth on a MariaDB database hosted on its web server. Despite handling sensitive personal data, the company failed to implement adequate cybersecurity practices, relying heavily on a third-party vendor without proper oversight or contractual clarity regarding security responsibilities.
caseDescription: Goldheart Jewelry failed to implement adequate patch management processes and reasonable access controls, resulting in a data breach affecting 41,379 customers. A known vulnerability (CVE-2022-24086) remained unpatched for 11 months, allowing threat actors to exploit it and exfiltrate customer personal data. Plaintext credentials stored on the web server without encryption further facilitated unauthorized access.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically by not applying critical security patches in a timely manner and by failing to implement reasonable access controls for stored credentials. These failures created exploitable vulnerabilities that resulted in unauthorized access and disclosure of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Goldheart Jewelry failed to patch a critical Magento vulnerability (CVE-2022-24086) for 11 months.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unpatched vulnerability and exposed credentials enabled attackers to steal personal information from 41,379 customers including names, email addresses, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: Goldheart Jewelry had outsourced patch management entirely to its vendor and bore no responsibility for applying security patches.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Service Agreement and Patch Management Policy explicitly made the organization responsible for monitoring patches and requesting vendor application; the vendor acted only upon the organization's request.

claimsVsReality.claim: Goldheart Jewelry had no knowledge of plaintext credentials stored on the web server and should not be held responsible since the vendor left them there.
claimsVsReality.reality: Organizations cannot delegate responsibility for data protection to vendors; Goldheart Jewelry was ultimately accountable for ensuring reasonable access controls were in place and should have conducted regular security reviews.

claimsVsReality.claim: A single security scan using the Magento Security Scanner in December 2022 was sufficient to monitor for vulnerabilities.
claimsVsReality.reality: The scan proved inadequate in detecting the abnormalities within the server, and the organization failed to implement regular, comprehensive monitoring and testing procedures as required by data protection standards.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement adequate patch management processes: Known vulnerability CVE-2022-24086 was available on 13 February 2022 but was not patched until January 2023 (11 months delay)
violations: Failed to implement adequate patch management processes: Known vulnerability CVE-2022-24086 was available on 13 February 2022 but was not patched until January 2023 (11 months delay)
Failed to monitor patch releases and request vendor to apply patches as required by contractual Service Agreement
Failed to implement reasonable access controls: Plaintext credentials were stored in web server without encryption or password protection, allowing unauthorized access
Failed to properly oversee vendor responsibilities despite engaging vendor for maintenance services
Failed to conduct regular security audits and penetration testing to detect vulnerabilities

outcome: The Commission found the Organization in breach of Section 24 of the PDPA and imposed a financial penalty of $58,000 (reduced from preliminary determination of $64,000 following representations regarding plaintext credentials). The Organization was directed to: (1) engage a third-party cybersecurity vendor to conduct a targeted security audit to enhance access control within 60 days; (2) rectify any security gaps identified; and (3) furnish audit and rectification report to the Commission within 7 days of completion. The financial penalty must be paid within 30 days, with interest accruing at the rate specified in the Rules of Court for judgment debts on any outstanding amount.
companyNow: Following the 2023 data breach and subsequent investigation, Goldheart Jewelry has implemented comprehensive remedial security measures including multi-factor authentication, access controls, regular patching, and continuous monitoring systems.
dataType: Name, email address, date of birth, contact number, billing address, shipping address

companyDescription: Air Sino-Euro Associates Travel is a Singapore-based travel agency offering outbound travel services and tour bookings to customers worldwide.
companyLongDescription: Air Sino-Euro Associates Travel Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore travel agency that collects and stores customer personal data for tour group and air ticket bookings in a legacy booking system. The organization had limited internal data protection governance and outsourced IT security to third-party vendors. The company came into prominence following a significant data breach in December 2023 that exposed hundreds of thousands of customer records.
caseDescription: Air Sino-Euro Associates Travel, a Singapore travel agency, suffered a data breach in December 2023 when a threat actor gained unauthorized access to its legacy booking system and exfiltrated personal data of 336,759 individuals. The organization failed to implement adequate security measures and lacked internal data protection policies and a designated Data Protection Officer, constituting negligent breaches of accountability and protection obligations under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (outdated OS, no MFA, no password complexity requirements, no regular security reviews) and lacked internal data protection practices and accountability measures, creating systemic vulnerabilities that enabled unauthorized access and data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Air Sino-Euro Associates Travel failed to implement adequate security measures, lacked internal data protection policies, did not designate a Data Protection Officer.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's negligence enabled a threat actor to gain unauthorized access to sensitive personal data including names, NRIC numbers, passport images.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had implemented appropriate security measures including firewall protection and administrative access controls.
claimsVsReality.reality: The security was fundamentally inadequate: servers ran Windows Server 2012 (end-of-life October 2023), lacked multi-factor authentication, had no password complexity requirements, and received no regular security reviews from vendors.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had data protection policies in place to guide compliance with PDPA obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company only had an external-facing customer privacy policy but completely lacked internal data protection policies, processes, and employee training on data handling.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had appropriate governance structures for data protection compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not appoint a Data Protection Officer until April 2024, more than four months after the breach occurred, violating the basic accountability requirement under PDPA Section 11(3).

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had contractual oversight of its IT vendors' security responsibilities.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no written contracts with IT vendors specifying security requirements, patch management responsibilities, data protection obligations, or monitoring procedures, leaving critical security decisions entirely to external parties without organizational oversight.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 11(3) – Designation of individual responsible for PDPA compliance
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization did not appoint a Data Protection Officer until April 15, 2024, after the Incident occurred
violations: Organization did not appoint a Data Protection Officer until April 15, 2024, after the Incident occurred

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Development and implementation of data protection policies and practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization had only external-facing privacy policy but no internal data protection policies or practices
violations: Organization had only external-facing privacy policy but no internal data protection policies or practices
No internal processes for complaint handling and data handling
No documented communication of data protection policies to employees
External policy was effectively an empty promise without internal implementation

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation to implement reasonable security arrangements
regulatoryFindings.description: Server running outdated Windows Server 2012 with no further Microsoft support
violations: Server running outdated Windows Server 2012 with no further Microsoft support
No multi-factor authentication for administrative or user accounts
Insufficient password complexity requirements
No regular security reviews conducted prior to incident
No written contracts with IT vendors specifying data protection responsibilities
Lack of documented oversight and monitoring of vendor performance
Failure to ensure vendor compliance with security and data protection standards
No backup of audit and system logs when reformatting affected laptops

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD 47,000 (payable within 30 days) and directed the Organization to: (1) develop and implement data protection policies including password complexity requirements within 90 days; (2) review and update vendor contracts to include cybersecurity and data protection clauses covering regular security reviews, IT infrastructure maintenance, patch management and monitoring; (3) engage a CSA-licensed cybersecurity service provider to conduct vulnerability assessment, penetration testing and remediate vulnerabilities including implementing MFA for administrative and user accounts; and (4) provide supporting documentation to the Commission upon completion. Interest accrues on unpaid penalty at the rate specified in Rules of Court 2021.
companyNow: The company implemented remedial security measures post-breach including disabling RDP access, hardening firewall rules, upgrading operating systems, implementing multi-factor authentication, and finally appointing a Data Protection Officer in April 2024.
dataType: Names, addresses, NRIC numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers, full images of NRICs/passports/birth certificates, transaction information, masked credit card numbers

companyDescription: Marina Bay Sands is an integrated resort operator in Singapore offering hotel, casino, shopping, and museum facilities with loyalty membership programs for customers.
companyLongDescription: Marina Bay Sands Pte. Ltd. is one of Asia's largest integrated resort operators, featuring a luxury hotel, casino, shopping mall, and the ArtScience Museum. The company operates two membership programs: Sands Rewards Lifestyle (SRL) and ArtScience Friends (ASF), which collectively serve approximately 1.9 million members. The organization had implemented comprehensive security measures including ISO/IEC 27001 and PCI DSS certifications, security monitoring tools, and regular penetration testing before the October 2023 breach.
caseDescription: Marina Bay Sands experienced a data breach affecting approximately 665,495 Sands Rewards Lifestyle members when a threat actor exploited a misconfiguration error in the company's middleware platform migration. The breach resulted from a manual API replication process that inadvertently omitted a security token verification policy on the ArtScience Museum webpage, allowing unauthorized access to and exfiltration of customer personal data.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to mitigate the risk of human error during a critical manual API replication process in their middleware migration. The misconfiguration error created an acute security vulnerability that exposed personal data to unauthorized access and exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Marina Bay Sands failed to implement automated checks during a manual API migration, resulting in omission of a security token verification policy on the ArtScience Museum webpage.
whyTheyWereWrong: The misconfiguration exposed 665,495 customers' personal data including names, emails, phone numbers and residence information, which was exfiltrated.

claimsVsReality.claim: Marina Bay Sands had implemented robust security measures including comprehensive policies, security monitoring tools, regular penetration testing, and ISO/IEC 27001 and PCI DSS certifications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, a single manual configuration error during middleware migration omitted the token verification policy, allowing attackers to access 665,495 customer records by manipulating guessable numeric member IDs.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Token Verification Policy was a key security control that would only allow access to a user's own data within a 30-minute authenticated session window.
claimsVsReality.reality: The policy was not applied to the ArtScience Museum webpage due to the employee's omission of the external app ID from the inventory list, rendering this critical control ineffective for ASF webpage access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Members' access to sensitive data like transaction history and account information required SMS/email OTP verification with CAPTCHA, providing adequate protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: Attackers bypassed these controls by exploiting the missing token verification policy, gaining direct HTTP access to member IDs and extracting personal data without triggering any additional authentication or alerting systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data in their possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement robust process controls to mitigate human error risks during manual API replication in a complex, first-time middleware migration
violations: Failed to implement robust process controls to mitigate human error risks during manual API replication in a complex, first-time middleware migration
Relied entirely on a single employee to conduct manual API replication without meaningful secondary verification checks or independent validation
Did not implement adequate detection mechanisms post-deployment to identify omitted APIs or misconfigured security policies within the 6-month period before breach discovery
Failed to conduct comprehensive security testing to detect the API misconfiguration before it was exploited by threat actors

outcome: Marina Bay Sands admitted to negligently breaching the Protection Obligation under Section 24 of the PDPA through the Expedited Decision Procedure. The organization was ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD $450,000. The Commission recognized the company's prompt remedial actions including: disabling compromised accounts, enabling token verification on the ASF webpage, validating security policies across all webpages, notifying affected individuals, enhancing software configuration testing, implementing automated security monitoring for token reuse, setting up digital accounts with stronger passwords, and restricting 4-digit PIN usage to on-premises transactions only. No additional enforcement directions were necessary given the extensive remedial measures already implemented.
companyNow: Marina Bay Sands continues to operate as Singapore's premier integrated resort. Following the breach and regulatory decision, the company has implemented enhanced security protocols including automated token verification checks, improved configuration testing, and upgraded authentication methods for all digital member access.
dataType: Names, email addresses, phone numbers, countries of residence, membership information, account information, transaction history

company: The Management Corporation - Strata Title Plan No. 4599
companyDescription: The Management Corporation - Strata Title Plan No. 4599 is the management entity responsible for The Scotts Tower Condominium in Singapore, overseeing the administration and management of the building's common property and facilities.
companyLongDescription: The Management Corporation - Strata Title Plan No. 4599 (MCST) manages The Scotts Tower Condominium, a residential property in Singapore. As a strata management corporation, it is responsible for the maintenance, administration, and control of the condominium's common areas and facilities, including security systems and CCTV surveillance. The organisation engages external managing agents and security companies to carry out operational duties while remaining responsible for data protection compliance under Singapore law.
caseDescription: The Management Corporation failed to develop and implement proper data protection policies and procedures for handling access requests to CCTV footage, and failed to designate a data protection officer. When a resident requested access to CCTV footage of a traffic accident, the organisation improperly denied the request and the footage was automatically deleted before the 30-day preservation period required when refusing access requests.
violationSummary: The organisation's lack of policies, procedures, and designated data protection officer constituted systemic failures in data security governance. The failure to preserve CCTV footage following a refusal of an access request, and the inability of the security company to produce the footage due to missing administrator credentials, reflects inadequate security controls and data management practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The Management Corporation failed to develop and implement proper data protection policies and procedures for handling access requests to CCTV footage.
whyTheyWereWrong: A resident requesting access to CCTV footage of a traffic accident involving themselves was wrongfully denied access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation claimed it could refuse the access request based on section 21(3)(c) of the PDPA because the CCTV footage contained personal data of other individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CCTV footage was of a public road and any personal data captured would have been publicly available; the Organisation could have masked other individuals' data or taken other steps to comply with the access obligation rather than denying the request outright.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation asserted that section 47(1)(b)(viii) of the Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act 2004 applied and prevented access because the complainant was not a subsidiary proprietor or other specified category.
claimsVsReality.reality: Section 47 of the BMSMA only applies to specified categories; since the complainant did not fall into those categories, the request should have been handled under section 21 of the PDPA, which had no such limitation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation provided its managing agent Ohmyhome's Personal Data Protection Policy as its own policy when requested.
claimsVsReality.reality: The managing agent's policy was designed for that company's operational needs and did not address the Organisation's specific obligations, such as how to handle access requests for CCTV footage at the condominium.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 11(3) - Designation of Data Protection Officer
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to appoint a data protection officer at the time of the incident
violations: Organisation failed to appoint a data protection officer at the time of the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 - Accountability Obligation to Develop and Implement Policies
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation did not develop its own data protection policy tailored to its operations
violations: Organisation did not develop its own data protection policy tailored to its operations
Organisation relied on managing agent's policy instead of creating contextualised policies
No written instructions or standard operating procedures provided to managing agents or security company on handling access requests for personal data
Failure to identify and rectify that security company lacked administrator credentials to access CCTV footage

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 21 - Access Obligation
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation improperly denied access request relying on BMSMA section 47 instead of PDPA section 21
violations: Organisation improperly denied access request relying on BMSMA section 47 instead of PDPA section 21
Failed to consider masking or omitting other individuals' personal data before refusing access
Did not take reasonable steps to comply with access obligation

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner directed the organisation to: (1) develop and implement policies necessary to meet its obligations under section 12 of the PDPA within 60 days; (2) put in place procedures for management of CCTV footage upon receipt of access requests; (3) communicate these policies and procedures to relevant stakeholders including data intermediaries and contractors; and (4) furnish a written update to the Commission within 7 days of completion. No monetary penalty was imposed.
companyNow: The organisation has since appointed a Data Protection Officer (following the incident) and appointed Ohmyhome Property Management Pte Ltd as its managing agent from June 2024 onwards.
dataType: CCTV footage, visual/biometric data
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 11(3) - failure to designate a data protection officer
PDPA Section 12 - failure to develop and implement policies and practices for PDPA compliance
PDPA Section 21 - access obligation (improper handling of access request)
PDPA Section 22A - failure to preserve personal data following refusal (contextual)

companyDescription: The Institute of Mental Health is Singapore's tertiary psychiatric hospital providing mental healthcare services, outpatient treatment, and conducting medical research.
companyLongDescription: The Institute of Mental Health (IMH) is Singapore's national tertiary psychiatric hospital established to provide comprehensive mental health services including inpatient and outpatient care, psychological treatment, and medical research. As a public healthcare institution, IMH serves patients across Singapore's mental health system and conducts clinical research studies on psychiatric conditions affecting its patient population.
caseDescription: The Institute of Mental Health used a patient's name and health/age information to identify and approach him for research study recruitment without obtaining express consent. The Commission found the organisation had obtained implied consent through a notification displayed since 2014, but noted the organisation failed to provide clear opt-out mechanisms required for deemed consent by notification.
violationSummary: The organisation used personal data (name, age, health information) originally collected for medical treatment for a secondary purpose (research study recruitment) without obtaining express consent or properly implementing deemed consent procedures.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The Institute of Mental Health used a patient's name and health/age information to identify and approach him for research study recruitment without obtaining express consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The patient was approached and identified for a research study based on his medical condition and age group without his explicit agreement, exposing him to unwanted contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: The attending doctor only provided the names of suitable participants to the research officer and no other personal data such as medical information or diagnosis was shared.
claimsVsReality.reality: The research officer was able to identify and approach the patient based on his name, age, and medical profile (specific medical conditions), which required the doctor to have communicated information beyond just the patient's name.

claimsVsReality.claim: A notification displayed since 2014 provided adequate consent for using patient data for research study recruitment.
claimsVsReality.reality: While a notification was displayed, the organisation failed to provide clear opt-out mechanisms required under deemed consent by notification rules, making the consent framework legally deficient.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 13(a) – Consent Obligation
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation used complainant's personal data (name, age, health information) for study recruitment purpose without obtaining express consent
violations: Organisation used complainant's personal data (name, age, health information) for study recruitment purpose without obtaining express consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 15A – Deemed Consent by Notification Requirements
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to take reasonable steps to alert individuals of the means and time period by which they could notify the organisation of their refusal to consent to use of personal data for study recruitment
violations: Organisation failed to take reasonable steps to alert individuals of the means and time period by which they could notify the organisation of their refusal to consent to use of personal data for study recruitment
Organisation placed onus on individuals to navigate bureaucracy to find opt-out methods rather than providing clear, accessible notification of opt-out procedures

outcome: The Commission found the organisation in compliance with the Consent Obligation based on implied consent from the complainant's continued patronage and awareness of notifications since 2014. However, the Commission found the organisation could not rely on deemed consent by notification due to failure to provide clear opt-out mechanisms. The organisation has voluntarily implemented remedial measures requiring clinical staff to inform patients about research opportunities first, and research staff to obtain express consent before approaching patients using their medical information. The organisation must also revise its notification to clearly alert individuals of opt-out mechanisms and timeframes.

companyDescription: Ezynetic is a Singapore-incorporated Software-as-a-Service provider that delivers information technology solutions and services to licensed moneylenders.
companyLongDescription: Ezynetic Pte. caseDescription: Ezynetic, a SaaS provider serving moneylenders, suffered a ransomware attack in June 2024 that compromised personal data of 190,589 individuals. The breach resulted from inadequate access controls on a system administrator account with weak password security and failure to conduct periodic vulnerability assessments or penetration testing.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically through inadequate access controls on privileged accounts, weak password policies, and absence of periodic security reviews and vulnerability assessments.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Ezynetic failed to secure its system administrator account with weak passwords and did not conduct periodic vulnerability assessments or penetration testing.
whyTheyWereWrong: Moneylending customers' loan applicants and borrowers had their names, addresses, email, phone numbers, NRIC numbers, dates of birth, and financial information exfiltrated.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had expended significant financial commitment to investigate and fortify systems, suffered operational disruptions and financial losses, and maintained full transparency and cooperation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The financial and operational losses were consequences of the company's own failure to implement basic security practices (strong passwords, vulnerability assessments), which are mandatory obligations under the Protection Obligation, not mitigating factors that justify penalty reduction.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – Protection Obligation requiring organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal

violations: Failure to implement reasonable access controls – SA account password was weak (p@ssword1 or Password@1), susceptible to brute force attacks, and lacked adequate authorisation and authentication processes

outcome: The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of $17,500 within 30 days. companyNow: Following the June 2024 breach, Ezynetic rebuilt its entire network and migrated to a cloud environment, implemented enhanced security measures in consultation with Singapore's Cybersecurity Agency and Ministry of Law, and is required to obtain CSA Cyber Trustmark Certification.

The company monetizes its service through advertising partnerships handled by its affiliate Dish Media Sales L.L.C., which manages customer data for targeted advertising purposes.
caseDescription: Sling TV and its affiliate Dish Media Sales failed to provide California consumers with clear, conspicuous notices and easy opt-out mechanisms for the sale and sharing of personal information, and failed to implement special protections for children and minors on its streaming platform. The company sold and shared personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising without proper consumer consent mechanisms.

outcome: Sling TV and Dish Media Sales are permanently enjoined from violating the CCPA and UCL. The company must: (1) provide clear and conspicuous notices about personal information collection, sale, and sharing; (2) implement consumer-friendly opt-out mechanisms with minimal steps, including toggles for logged-in users and QR codes for in-app use where feasible; (3) create 'kids' profiles defaulting off sale/sharing and cross-context behavioral advertising; (4) default off sale/sharing on children's channels listed in Exhibit A; (5) delete personal information collected from known children and minors; (6) maintain a notice link titled 'Do Not Sell or Share My Personal Information' or 'Your Privacy Choices' on homepages and within apps; (7) avoid confusing language that could mislead consumers about opt-out choices; (8) implement compliance programs and provide annual reports for three years. The company must pay $530,000 ($265,000 within 30 days, $265,000 within one year).

caseDescription: Illuminate Education, a K-12 education technology vendor, failed to implement reasonable data security measures, resulting in a massive data breach affecting 49 California school districts and millions of students. Illuminate's security failures included inadequate access controls, lack of real-time monitoring and alerts, and unsecured backup systems.
violationSummary: Illuminate's failures to implement reasonable security procedures and practices—specifically inadequate account management, lack of monitoring for suspicious activity, and unsecured backup systems—resulted in unauthorized access and exfiltration of sensitive personal and medical information, directly falling under the Insecurity category of the Solove Privacy Taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence

companyDescription: Home Improvement Marketing Ltd is a direct marketing organisation registered at Companies House (Number 14756152) that engaged in automated telephone marketing campaigns for home improvement products and services.
companyLongDescription: Home Improvement Marketing Ltd is a direct marketing organisation registered at Companies House (Number 14756152) that engaged in automated telephone marketing campaigns for home improvement products and services.
caseDescription: Home Improvement Marketing Ltd made 2.45 million automated marketing calls to subscribers without prior consent between May and August 2023, resulting in 274 complaints. The company violated PECR regulations 19 and 24 by using an automated calling system for recorded direct marketing calls without obtaining freely given, specific, informed consent from recipients, and failed to provide required identification information.
violationSummary: HIML engaged in mass unsolicited automated calling to subscribers without their knowledge or consent, constituting systematic surveillance-like collection of subscriber engagement through unwanted communications.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between May and August 2023, Home Improvement Marketing Ltd instigated 2,449,380 automated recorded marketing calls to subscribers without obtaining prior consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: 2.45 million people received unsolicited automated calls they never agreed to, resulting in 274 complaints.

claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence of consent was obtained; HIML made no attempts to seek consent from any of the 2.45 million call recipients

violations: HIML failed to provide recipients of automated calls with required identification information (name and contact details)

violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance

claimsVsReality.reality: GSE instigated 9,587,050 automated marketing calls through overseas call centres 1 in 3 BPO and 1 in 4 BPO, paid them £70,230+ for services, and directors sent daily instructions on which postcodes to dial

companyDescription: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. is a Spanish financial microenterprise specializing in online loan provision. The company operates without published financial reporting.
companyLongDescription: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. is a Spanish financial microenterprise specializing in online loan provision. The company operates without published financial reporting.
caseDescription: KVIKU required customers to submit photographs holding their national ID card to process loan cancellations. This practice violated GDPR data minimization principles because less intrusive identification methods existed and complied with anti-money laundering requirements. The company processed personal data beyond what was strictly necessary.
violationSummary: The company collected excessive personal data (biometric + identity document combination) beyond what was strictly necessary for the stated purpose. This violated GDPR Article 5(1)(c) data minimization principle. The handling created security risks through unnecessary collection of sensitive biometric data when alternative, less intrusive methods existed.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: KVIKU required loan customers to submit photographs holding their national ID card in hand to process loan cancellations, collecting combined biometric.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' facial photographs combined with ID images exposed them to heightened identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: KVIKU claimed that photograph identification with DNI in hand was required to comply with anti-money laundering law (Law 10/2010 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism).
claimsVsReality.reality: Anti-money laundering law permits multiple identification methods (qualified electronic signatures, certified ID copies, first deposits from authorized accounts, or pre-approved secure procedures). Photograph identification is not mandated by law and was KVIKU's own choice, making it unjustifiable under data minimization principles.

claimsVsReality.claim: KVIKU's practice was justified by its obligation to identify customers for contract execution and legal compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customer identification obligations could be fulfilled through less invasive, equally effective methods already available in the financial sector—certified document copies, electronic signatures, or existing customer account verification systems. KVIKU's method created unnecessary biometric and identity fraud risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: KVIKU argued the data retention was necessary because the customer had not satisfied the loan obligation.
claimsVsReality.reality: This argument was not relevant to the investigation, which concerned the data collection method itself, not retention post-satisfaction. The infraction occurred at the point of requesting the photograph for cancellation processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU required photographs with DNI in hand for loan cancellations despite alternative identification methods satisfying anti-money laundering requirements being available and less intrusive.
violations: KVIKU required photographs with DNI in hand for loan cancellations despite alternative identification methods satisfying anti-money laundering requirements being available and less intrusive.
The company failed to verify whether the stated purpose (identity verification for loan cancellation) could be achieved using fewer personal data, less detailed data, or data aggregation methods.

Facial biometric data combined with identity document images created unnecessary risk of identity fraud and suplantation when certified ID copies, electronic signatures, or existing customer account verification systems were available.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 25 requires data protection by design and by default, meaning controllers must implement appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU did not assess proportionality of its identification procedure or consider less invasive alternatives before implementing the photograph requirement.
violations: KVIKU did not assess proportionality of its identification procedure or consider less invasive alternatives before implementing the photograph requirement.
The company did not design its cancellation process to minimize data collection while achieving compliance with anti-money laundering obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Law 10/2010 on Prevention of Money Laundering and Financing of Terrorism permits identification through: qualified electronic signatures, certified copies of identity documents from public notaries, first deposits from equivalent accounts, or other secure procedures pre-approved by relevant authorities.
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU established a photograph identification requirement not expressly authorized by anti-money laundering law.
violations: KVIKU established a photograph identification requirement not expressly authorized by anti-money laundering law.
The company invoked anti-money laundering compliance to justify an excessive data collection practice not actually required by sectoral law.

outcome: AEPD issued a final resolution confirming the infraction and imposing a €8,000 fine (reduced 20% from €10,000 for voluntary payment on 9 December 2025). KVIKU was ordered within 1 month from the effective date to implement measures ensuring customer identity verification for loan cancellations complies with GDPR Article 5(1)(c) through less invasive means. The company must notify AEPD of compliance measures adopted. Failure to comply may trigger additional enforcement action. Resolution is final and enforceable; administrative remedies exhausted.
companyNow: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. is a microenterprise (fewer than 10 employees) founded in 2022 with €3,000 capital stock, operating as an online lending platform. Financial performance data is unavailable.
dataType: Biometric data (facial photography), identity documents (DNI), financial data, personal identifiers
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 6(1)(b) – Lawful basis for contract performance
GDPR Article 25 – Data protection by design and by default

companyDescription: Greater Manchester Police is the territorial law enforcement agency responsible for policing Greater Manchester in Northwest England. As of March 2022, GMP employed 6,866 police officers, 3,524 police staff, and 560 police community support officers, covering 500 square miles and serving 2.8 million people.
companyLongDescription: Greater Manchester Police is the territorial law enforcement agency responsible for policing Greater Manchester in Northwest England. As of March 2022, GMP employed 6,866 police officers, 3,524 police staff, and 560 police community support officers, covering 500 square miles and serving 2.8 million people.
caseDescription: Greater Manchester Police systematically failed to respond to subject access requests (SARs) within legal timeframes under UK GDPR and DPA 2018. Between October 2022 and September 2024, GMP had compliance rates as low as 46%, with the oldest overdue request reaching 1,047 days. The backlog was caused by increased request volume (doubled from ~152 to ~300 per month in March 2020), COVID-19 response priorities, and insufficient staffing.
violationSummary: GMP systematically denied or delayed individuals' statutory right to access their personal data, preventing subjects from knowing what information police held or using that data, thereby excluding them from control over their own information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Greater Manchester Police failed to respond to hundreds of subject access requests within the legally required one-month deadline, with the oldest overdue request reaching 1,047 days.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens were systematically denied timely access to their personal data held by police for over two years.

claimsVsReality.claim: GMP's prioritization of front-line policing during COVID-19 was a temporary, justified measure consistent with other organisations.
claimsVsReality.reality: This decision, combined with increased SAR volume (doubled from March 2020) and insufficient staffing, created a backlog that persisted until mid-2024 — over 4 years after the initial surge.

claimsVsReality.claim: GMP acknowledged staffing difficulties and resource constraints prevented timely responses.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite resource challenges being known, GMP did not implement adequate staffing solutions until late 2023 (additional permanent staff) and early-mid 2024, leaving thousands of subjects without access for 18+ months beyond legal deadlines.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires the controller to provide information on action taken on data subject requests under Articles 15-22 without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, or within three months where complexity and number justify extension (with notice).
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP failed to respond to hundreds of SARs within the one-month deadline
violations: GMP failed to respond to hundreds of SARs within the one-month deadline
GMP did not consistently inform data subjects of extensions within one month
In October 2023, GMP had 1277 overdue SARs; oldest request from 2021 (1047 days overdue)

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15 UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data concerning them is being processed and, where applicable, access to that personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP systematically denied or delayed individuals' right to access their personal data
violations: GMP systematically denied or delayed individuals' right to access their personal data
Delay periods ranging from months to years prevented data subjects from exercising this fundamental right

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 45, Part 3 DPA 2018 entitles data subjects to obtain confirmation whether personal data is being processed and, where applicable, access to that data.
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP failed to provide timely confirmation or access to personal data held by the force
violations: GMP failed to provide timely confirmation or access to personal data held by the force

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 54, Part 3 DPA 2018 defines 'applicable time period' as one month from the relevant time, or up to three months where justified by complexity/volume, with a maximum of three months permitted.
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP repeatedly exceeded the three-month maximum period; oldest request reached 1047 days overdue
violations: GMP repeatedly exceeded the three-month maximum period; oldest request reached 1047 days overdue

outcome: ICO issued a reprimand to GMP under Article 58(2)(b) UK GDPR and Schedule 13(2)(c) DPA 2018. No monetary fine imposed. GMP was already implementing significant remedial measures: SAR recovery action plan, staff increases, appointment of dedicated complaints officer, internalization of Data Protection Officer role, process improvements, and strategic oversight enhancements. By September 2024, GMP achieved 97% compliance rate on new SARs and reduced the backlog from 1277 to 39 overdue requests. ICO recommends ensuring sufficient resources to maintain compliance and completing outstanding action plan items. Failure to maintain improvements may trigger further enforcement action.
companyNow: Greater Manchester Police continues to operate as England's territorial police force for the Greater Manchester metropolitan county. As of September 2024, GMP had improved SAR compliance to 97% and substantially cleared its historical backlog, though remains subject to ICO monitoring.
dataType: Personal data routinely captured in law enforcement activities; body-worn video, CCTV footage, identification data

company: ZOUGLA TZI-AR ANONYMI ETAIREIA MESON ILEKTRONIKON MAZIKIS EPIKOINONIAS
companyDescription: ZOUGLA TZI-AR is a Greek media company operating the news website zougla.gr, which publishes news, reportage of public interest, and citizen complaints. The company positions itself as an investigative news outlet.
companyLongDescription: ZOUGLA TZI-AR is a Greek media company operating the news website zougla.gr, which publishes news, reportage of public interest, and citizen complaints. The company positions itself as an investigative news outlet.
caseDescription: A news website published an article containing the full personal details and address of a public official and his family members in relation to a private property dispute. The article included identifying information that was not necessary for the public interest story. The company failed to cooperate with the data protection authority for over 8 months and republished the content after claiming to have removed it.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal data (name, address, professional details) of the complainant to the public without lawful basis and without necessity proportionate to the public interest being served. The disclosure was wider than needed to report the underlying news story.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Zougla.gr published an article identifying a public official by full name, home address, professional rank.
whyTheyWereWrong: The named official and his family suffered targeted exposure to public scrutiny and potential harassment over a private land dispute unrelated to his public duties.

claimsVsReality.claim: The article was based on a legitimate complaint from a citizen (Γ) seeking to expose alleged police misconduct and unlawful property disputes.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the underlying complaint may have had public interest merit, publishing the complainant's full name, address, and professional rank was not necessary to report that story. The news could have been published without identifying him.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company removed the article after receiving the authority's request (30-05-2023).
claimsVsReality.reality: The company republished the same article with identifying details three months later in August 2023, demonstrating that the initial removal was not final and the company did not genuinely remedy the violation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant was a 'public person' subject to press scrutiny by virtue of his public office.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the complainant held a public position, he was not a public figure in the sense of being a politician, celebrity, or someone who had voluntarily entered public life for scrutiny. His involvement in a private property dispute did not make him a legitimate target for full identification and public shaming.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires processing of personal data to be lawful, fair and transparent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company published full identifying details (name, address, professional rank) of the complainant without lawful basis under Art. 28 of Law 4624/2019, as the disclosure was not necessary and proportionate to the public interest in reporting the underlying property dispute story.
violations: Company published full identifying details (name, address, professional rank) of the complainant without lawful basis under Art. 28 of Law 4624/2019, as the disclosure was not necessary and proportionate to the public interest in reporting the underlying property dispute story.

regulatoryFindings.act: Law 4624/2019 Article 28 permits processing for freedom of expression only when the right to information outweighs data protection, the processing is limited to what is necessary, and it concerns matters of general public interest or public figures.
regulatoryFindings.description: The complainant was not a public figure requiring scrutiny; the property dispute was a private matter of lesser public concern; publishing his identifying details exceeded what was necessary—the news could have been reported without naming him; the company failed the necessity and proportionality test.
violations: The complainant was not a public figure requiring scrutiny; the property dispute was a private matter of lesser public concern; publishing his identifying details exceeded what was necessary—the news could have been reported without naming him; the company failed the necessity and proportionality test.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires processors and controllers to cooperate with supervisory authorities upon request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company ignored the authority's requests on 12-08-2022 and 02-12-2022; only responded after a third letter on 30-05-2023 and a phone call; failed to provide views as requested; later republished the article after claiming removal, demonstrating non-cooperation and inconsistency.
violations: Company ignored the authority's requests on 12-08-2022 and 02-12-2022; only responded after a third letter on 30-05-2023 and a phone call; failed to provide views as requested; later republished the article after claiming removal, demonstrating non-cooperation and inconsistency.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority found the company violated GDPR Article 5(1)(a) and Law 4624/2019 Article 28 by publishing unnecessary identifying details without proportionate justification. It also violated GDPR Article 31 by failing to cooperate with the authority. The company was ordered to: (1) pay €2,000 for the unlawful publication; (2) contact websites www.theworldnews.net and www.opennews.gr to inform them the article was unlawful and has been removed, requesting they do the same; and (3) pay €1,000 for failure to cooperate. The article has since been removed from zougla.gr as of 15-05-2024.
companyNow: ZOUGLA is an active Greek news website (zougla.gr) that continues to operate. Following this decision, it is now subject to a compliance order to notify third-party republishers and to remove similar unlawfully published personal data.
dataType: Name, address, professional title, rank, family relationships, audio recordings
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 31 – Cooperation with supervisory authority
Law 4624/2019 Art. 28 – Processing for freedom of expression (proportionality requirement)

companyDescription: Plataforma Cabanillas is a mid-sized Spanish logistics company specializing in storage, transport, and distribution of goods, as well as customs and international trade services. With annual revenue of €31.04 million (2023), it operates cargo handling facilities with potential access to secure airport zones subject to air safety regulations.
companyLongDescription: Plataforma Cabanillas is a mid-sized Spanish logistics company specializing in storage, transport, and distribution of goods, as well as customs and international trade services. With annual revenue of €31.04 million (2023), it operates cargo handling facilities with potential access to secure airport zones subject to air safety regulations.
caseDescription: Plataforma Cabanillas requested criminal history certificates and personal family information (civil status, number of children) from job candidates during the recruitment process, before any employment contract existed. The company collected these sensitive data without a valid legal basis and in violation of data minimization principles under GDPR Article 5(1)(c).
violationSummary: The company systematically collected sensitive personal data (criminal records, family status) from job candidates during interviews without adequate legal justification, exceeding what was necessary for the hiring process and treating all participants as data sources before any employment relationship existed.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Plataforma Cabanillas requested criminal background certificates and family information (marital status.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hundreds of job applicants were forced to disclose sensitive criminal history and intimate family details during screening.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed it was obligated by EU air safety regulations (Regulation 2015/1998) to verify criminal history 'during the selection process' to comply with aviation security requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The actual regulation refers to verification of 'selected persons'—those hired after selection is complete—not all interview candidates. The company was using an overbroad interpretation to justify pre-contractual collection of sensitive data from all participants.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated it was collecting Form 145 family data 'in good faith' to improve recruitment efficiency and that this data would not be used for candidate evaluation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Form 145 family information is required only for employees after hiring. Requesting it during interviews from non-employees violated data minimization principles and collected far more data than necessary for hiring assessment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company argued that no negligence occurred because it was simply trying to comply with applicable regulations and improve process speed.
claimsVsReality.reality: A company conducting systematic personal data processing (recruitment) must apply heightened diligence to comply with data protection law. Collecting sensitive criminal data from all interview candidates without a valid legal basis prior to any employment contract constituted negligent violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(c).

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimization').
regulatoryFindings.description: Company requested criminal history certificates from all interview candidates before any employment contract existed, exceeding necessity for hiring evaluation
violations: Company requested criminal history certificates from all interview candidates before any employment contract existed, exceeding necessity for hiring evaluation
Company requested family information (civil status, number of children) from candidates during interviews to populate Form 145, but this data is only required after employment begins

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 10 and LOPDGDD Article 10 restrict processing of criminal conviction data to circumstances authorized by EU or national law, with adequate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company relied on air safety regulations to justify requesting criminal certificates during selection phase, but those regulations refer to 'selected persons' (post-selection), not interview candidates
violations: Company relied on air safety regulations to justify requesting criminal certificates during selection phase, but those regulations refer to 'selected persons' (post-selection), not interview candidates
Company collected criminal data from all candidates, including those not selected, without proper legal authorization under GDPR Article 10

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed two administrative fines: €75,000 for requesting criminal history certificates during interviews before employment, and €25,000 for requesting Form 145 family data before employment contracts. The company was required to comply with updated selection procedures that defer collection of sensitive data until after final hiring decisions. No structural reforms or monitoring obligations were imposed, but the decision warns of further corrective measures if the company does not fully adopt the revised processes. The company has already updated its selection procedures to request criminal certificates and work-life documentation only after contracts are signed.
companyNow: Plataforma Cabanillas continues to operate as a logistics and customs services provider in Spain. Following the AEPD enforcement action, the company updated its recruitment procedures to request sensitive personal data only after employment contracts are finalized, effective January 2024.
dataType: Criminal history records, family status, number of children, identity documents
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 10 – Processing of criminal conviction data
LOPDGDD Art. 10 – Spanish implementation of criminal data processing restrictions

companyDescription: SERVACE, S.L. is a Spanish business services company founded in 1998, contracted to provide services to public agencies including work related to development/fomento (promotion/growth) initiatives.
companyLongDescription: SERVACE, S.L. is a Spanish business services company founded in 1998, contracted to provide services to public agencies including work related to development/fomento (promotion/growth) initiatives.
caseDescription: SERVACE, a contractor for a public agency, used an employee's personal email address for work communications without consent, and continued doing so even after being warned to stop. The company then displayed this personal email in visible copies to multiple colleagues and external parties. This violated GDPR requirements for lawful data processing and security.
violationSummary: The unauthorized use and visible disclosure of the personal email address to third parties (colleagues and government personnel) without the data subject's knowledge or consent constitutes a breach of confidentiality under GDPR Article 5(1)(f).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: SERVACE used an employee's personal email address for internal work communications without consent, ignored the employee's warning to stop.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's personal email address was processed and disclosed to numerous recipients without any legal authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: No implied evidence of claims; the company's conduct was simply non-compliant.
claimsVsReality.reality: SERVACE used personal email without any lawful basis and continued after being warned, then disclosed it to multiple parties without consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that personal data processing be lawful, based on at least one of six specified grounds (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: SERVACE processed the employee's personal email without obtaining consent and without any other lawful basis under Article 6(1).
violations: SERVACE processed the employee's personal email without obtaining consent and without any other lawful basis under Article 6(1).

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed with integrity and confidentiality, with appropriate technical and organizational measures to prevent unauthorized or unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: SERVACE disclosed the personal email address in visible copies to multiple work colleagues and government personnel without authorization, violating the confidentiality principle.
violations: SERVACE disclosed the personal email address in visible copies to multiple work colleagues and government personnel without authorization, violating the confidentiality principle.

outcome: SERVACE recognized responsibility and paid the reduced sanction of €840 (after 40% cumulative reduction for early recognition and payment). The company was ordered to adopt corrective measures within 3 months: establish lawful bases for all personal data processing, implement stricter email list controls, and ensure personal email addresses are not used without explicit consent. The procedure terminated upon payment and commitment to remediation.
companyNow: SERVACE, S.L. is a small Spanish contractor (€90,730 annual revenue in 2023) that continues operations. The company has committed to implementing data protection compliance measures as ordered by AEPD.
dataType: Email addresses (personal and work), names

companyDescription: ECO4U is a sole trader business operated by Darian Bishop engaged in direct marketing via unsolicited telephone calls. The company's business model involved high-volume outbound dialing for marketing purposes.
companyLongDescription: ECO4U is a sole trader business operated by Darian Bishop engaged in direct marketing via unsolicited telephone calls. The company's business model involved high-volume outbound dialing for marketing purposes.
caseDescription: Darian Bishop, trading as ECO4U, made 194,110 unsolicited direct marketing calls between January and October 2023 to telephone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), which prohibits such calls. The company failed to obtain valid consent from recipients before calling them and failed to provide required caller identification information during the calls.
violationSummary: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers. This represents systematic surveillance and targeting of individuals who explicitly opted out of marketing contact, without their knowledge or consent.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Made 194,110 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between January and October 2023.
whyTheyWereWrong: 194,110 individuals who had explicitly registered to block marketing calls received unwanted calls anyway, violating their opt-out choice.
