companyDescription: A Spanish residential property management company managing a community of property owners. Operated an online portal to distribute community documents and facilitate resident communications.
companyLongDescription: A Spanish residential property management company managing a community of property owners. Operated an online portal to distribute community documents and facilitate resident communications.
caseDescription: A property management company operating a residential community website failed to implement basic security protections required by GDPR. The website used unencrypted HTTP protocol instead of HTTPS, lacked SSL certificates, and distributed login credentials (shared username/password) to all residents via physical documents. This exposed residents' personal and financial data to interception.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement mandatory technical and organizational security measures (Article 32 GDPR) to protect personal data transmitted via their web portal. The lack of encryption and SSL certificate created direct risk of unauthorized access and interception.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A property management company distributed shared login credentials to all residents in physical notices, operated its website without HTTPS encryption or SSL certificates.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents' names, addresses, impayment records, bank account details, and other sensitive personal information were transmitted over unencrypted HTTP protocol.

claimsVsReality.claim: The community management company claimed it had outsourced data protection consulting services and was handling data appropriately
claimsVsReality.reality: The website lacked basic encryption and security controls for months despite the complaint, indicating no meaningful implementation of security measures

claimsVsReality.claim: Company asserted it stored no sensitive financial data beyond the community account itself
claimsVsReality.reality: Website contained residents' personal information, addresses, payment status, and references to bank account details accessible via unencrypted portal

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32 GDPR requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security adequate to the risk, including encryption of personal data and ability to ensure confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: Website used HTTP protocol without HTTPS or SSL encryption, exposing data transmission to interception attacks
violations: Website used HTTP protocol without HTTPS or SSL encryption, exposing data transmission to interception attacks
No SSL certificate installed despite processing personal and financial data
Shared username/password system prevented identification of individual access and breach detection
Failed to implement secure credential management and user authentication controls

outcome: Procedure terminated following voluntary payment and acknowledgment of responsibility. COMUNIDAD.1 paid €600.00 (representing 40% reduction for early payment and responsibility acknowledgment from base €1,000.00). Ordered to implement HTTPS protocol, install SSL certificates, and establish proper user/password management policies within 6 months of resolution becoming final. Failure to adopt corrective measures could trigger further administrative sanctions.
companyNow: Unknown. The entity remains a residential property management community subject to ongoing GDPR compliance obligations.
dataType: names, surnames, residential addresses, financial data (unpaid amounts), bank account details

companyDescription: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. is a Spanish company dedicated to the commercialization of electricity and energy services, operating as an energy advisor and service provider. The company engages in telemarketing and customer acquisition activities.
companyLongDescription: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. is a Spanish company dedicated to the commercialization of electricity and energy services, operating as an energy advisor and service provider. The company engages in telemarketing and customer acquisition activities.
caseDescription: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. unlawfully subcontracted personal data processing to third parties without explicit written authorization from the data controller (***EMPRESA.3). The company failed to maintain proper contractual safeguards and processor oversight, allowing unsolicited marketing calls and emails to be sent to complainants using data obtained without valid consent.
violationSummary: The company's failure to properly authorize and oversee subprocessors created systemic insecurity in personal data handling, allowing unauthorized processing and marketing activities without proper safeguards or consent mechanisms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. subcontracted personal data processing to third parties without obtaining prior written authorization from the data controller, violating Article 28 of the GDPR.
whyTheyWereWrong: A Spanish resident received unsolicited telemarketing calls and emails using his name, phone number, email address.

claimsVsReality.claim: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. claimed commitment to data protection compliance and stated it had implemented data processor agreements with safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: No written authorization existed for the subcontraction of ***EMPRESA.4; the subprocessor list (Annex IV) was blank; contractual safeguards were absent or unenforced; complainant received unsolicited calls and emails without valid consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted that ***EMPRESA.5 guaranteed having obtained the complainant's free and express consent for marketing communications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Complainant explicitly denied providing consent, was not registered in Robinson (anti-marketing list), and had never been a customer. The certificate of consent was unverified and could not override the complainant's denial.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(2) requires that a processor shall not engage another processor without prior specific or general written authorization from the controller. In the case of general written authorization, the processor must inform the controller of any intended changes concerning the addition or replacement of other processors, giving the controller the opportunity to object.
regulatoryFindings.description: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. subcontracted data processing services to ***EMPRESA.4 without documented written authorization from ***EMPRESA.3 (the data controller). The contract between the controller and processor contained an empty Annex IV listing subprocessors, with no authorization for subcontracting reflected therein.
violations: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. subcontracted data processing services to ***EMPRESA.4 without documented written authorization from ***EMPRESA.3 (the data controller). The contract between the controller and processor contained an empty Annex IV listing subprocessors, with no authorization for subcontracting reflected therein.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(4) requires that where a processor engages another processor, the same data protection obligations must be imposed via contract, and the initial processor remains fully responsible to the controller for subprocessor compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: The contract between ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. and ***EMPRESA.4 lacked enforceable data protection obligations for consent and proper data sourcing. The subcontracted entities (***EMPRESA.5) provided data with only a unilateral certificate of consent dated 30 July 2023, which the complainant contests; no independent verification or safeguards existed to ensure validity.
violations: The contract between ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. and ***EMPRESA.4 lacked enforceable data protection obligations for consent and proper data sourcing. The subcontracted entities (***EMPRESA.5) provided data with only a unilateral certificate of consent dated 30 July 2023, which the complainant contests; no independent verification or safeguards existed to ensure validity.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires lawful, fair, and transparent processing of personal data based on valid consent, legitimate interest, or other lawful basis.
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainant's personal data was processed for telemarketing without demonstrable consent and without transparency. The data was obtained from ***EMPRESA.5's database allegedly with consent, but complainant asserts no such consent was given and was not on Robinson list (anti-marketing registry).
violations: Complainant's personal data was processed for telemarketing without demonstrable consent and without transparency. The data was obtained from ***EMPRESA.5's database allegedly with consent, but complainant asserts no such consent was given and was not on Robinson list (anti-marketing registry).

outcome: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. recognized responsibility and paid the penalty voluntarily in full on 16 May 2025, applying both the 20% reduction for early recognition of responsibility and the 20% reduction for voluntary payment, resulting in a final penalty of €12,000. The company submitted to the two accumulated reductions permitted under Article 85 of the Spanish Administrative Procedure Act (LPACAP). The procedure was terminated following payment. The company stated it had ceased working with ***EMPRESA.4 and ***EMPRESA.5 after determining they were not safe data processors, demonstrating post-violation remediation. The resolution is final in administrative proceedings and fully enforceable.
companyNow: ALBOR ENERGÍA S.L. is an energy commercialization company founded in 2021 with 2023 revenues of €6,257,181. Following this enforcement action, the company ceased engagement with the problematic subprocessors and stated commitment to GDPR compliance.
dataType: Name, surname, email, telephone, IBAN bank account code, postal address
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 28(2) — Processor cannot subcontract without prior written authorization
GDPR Art. 28(3) — Processor must ensure same data protection obligations in subprocessor contracts
GDPR Art. 28(4) — Processor remains fully liable for subprocessor compliance
GDPR Art. 6 — Lack of valid lawful basis for processing
GDPR Art. 14 — Failure to provide transparency information to data subjects

companyDescription: SILVANERGIA 2022, S.L. is a Spanish company that engaged in telemarketing services for energy contract recruitment. Founded in 2022, the company attempted to act as a customer acquisition agent for Bassols Energía but never formalized a legal processing agreement.
companyLongDescription: SILVANERGIA 2022, S.L. is a Spanish company that engaged in telemarketing services for energy contract recruitment. Founded in 2022, the company attempted to act as a customer acquisition agent for Bassols Energía but never formalized a legal processing agreement.
caseDescription: SILVANERGIA conducted telemarketing campaigns to recruit customers for an energy company without a signed processing agreement or legal basis. The company obtained personal data from a third-party provider and made unsolicited calls using sensitive identifiers like DNI and partial bank account information, without lawful consent or contractual authority.
violationSummary: The company failed to establish lawful legitimacy (Article 6.1) for processing personal data. Personal data was acquired from a third party without evidence of lawful consent from data subjects, and processed without a Data Processing Agreement (DPA) despite acting as a processor.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SILVANERGIA made unsolicited telemarketing calls to consumers using personal data including names, national ID numbers, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' sensitive personal information including national IDs and financial details were processed.

claimsVsReality.claim: SILVANERGIA claimed it was acting as an authorized agent of Bassols Energía and that the call was to 'update tariffs' per new government regulations.
claimsVsReality.reality: SILVANERGIA had no signed Data Processing Agreement with Bassols Energía; preliminary discussions began in July 2023 but were never formalized. Bassols later terminated contact in August 2023 due to non-receipt of the signed contract and SILVANERGIA's poor financial condition. The company was not authorized to process customer data on Bassols' behalf.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed it obtained data from a legitimate source ('companies like...') and that the data provider guaranteed Robinson List filtering.
claimsVsReality.reality: SILVANERGIA provided only an invoice from a data provider dated 10 June 2023 (pre-call), with no documentation of lawful consent from data subjects or proof that the provider obtained the data legitimately. No evidence was submitted that the data transaction was compliant with GDPR or that the complainant had ever consented to sale/transfer of her data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data is lawful only if it complies with at least one of six legal bases: consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests (with a balance test for the last).
regulatoryFindings.description: SILVANERGIA processed the complainant's personal data (name, DNI, address, bank details) without establishing any lawful basis under Article 6(1). No consent was obtained from the data subject; no contractual relationship existed; no legal obligation applied; and no legitimate interest justified processing without consent.
violations: SILVANERGIA processed the complainant's personal data (name, DNI, address, bank details) without establishing any lawful basis under Article 6(1). No consent was obtained from the data subject; no contractual relationship existed; no legal obligation applied; and no legitimate interest justified processing without consent.

The company acquired data from a third-party provider without evidence that the provider had obtained it lawfully or with consent from data subjects, and failed to provide documentation of legitimacy of the data transaction.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28 requires that where processing is carried out on behalf of a controller, there must be a contract or other legally binding document binding the processor to the controller, establishing the subject, duration, nature, and purpose of the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: SILVANERGIA entered into preliminary discussions with Bassols Energía Comercial in July 2023 but never formalized a Data Processing Agreement (DPA). Despite this, the company began customer acquisition activities in July–August 2023 without a signed contract, meaning all processing lacked proper contractual legitimacy.
violations: SILVANERGIA entered into preliminary discussions with Bassols Energía Comercial in July 2023 but never formalized a Data Processing Agreement (DPA). Despite this, the company began customer acquisition activities in July–August 2023 without a signed contract, meaning all processing lacked proper contractual legitimacy.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: The complainant did not consent to or request contact. The company falsely presented itself as acting on behalf of Bassols Energía when it lacked contractual authority. The unsolicited call divulged sensitive data (DNI, partial bank details) under the false premise of a 'routine verification,' deceiving the consumer about the nature and purpose of the contact.
violations: The complainant did not consent to or request contact. The company falsely presented itself as acting on behalf of Bassols Energía when it lacked contractual authority. The unsolicited call divulged sensitive data (DNI, partial bank details) under the false premise of a 'routine verification,' deceiving the consumer about the nature and purpose of the contact.

outcome: SILVANERGIA recognized responsibility and paid the sanction voluntarily on 4 June 2025, obtaining a 40% cumulative reduction (20% for recognition of responsibility + 20% for voluntary payment), reducing the initial €5,000 fine to €3,000. The company is ordered to cease personal data processing in customer acquisition activities until it establishes lawful legitimacy under Article 6(1) GDPR. The company must notify the AEPD within one month of the final resolution of the measures adopted. The procedure is terminated; the resolution is final and enforceable; no further administrative remedies available.
companyNow: SILVANERGIA 2022, S.L. is a small Spanish energy/telemarketing company founded in 2022 with reported annual revenue of approximately €149,570 (2023). Current operational status unknown; company may be inactive or operating under compliance monitoring.
dataType: Full name, national ID number (DNI), home address, bank account numbers
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 28 – Data Processor Requirements (no DPA in place)

companyDescription: DIGI Spain Telecom, S.L. is a Spanish telecommunications provider offering mobile and internet services. Founded in 2006, it operates nationally and is part of a larger telecom group. The company processes substantial volumes of personal data in subscriber onboarding and service delivery.
companyLongDescription: DIGI Spain Telecom, S.L. is a Spanish telecommunications provider offering mobile and internet services. Founded in 2006, it operates nationally and is part of a larger telecom group. The company processes substantial volumes of personal data in subscriber onboarding and service delivery.
caseDescription: DIGI Spain processed personal data of a customer without valid consent or legal basis after a third party fraudulently requested a mobile line using her identity in October 2021. The company's inadequate identity verification procedures allowed the suplantation to occur. DIGI failed to implement sufficient technical and organizational measures to verify the true identity of the contract applicant before treating her data.
violationSummary: DIGI's inadequate identity verification procedures enabled unauthorized processing of personal data. The failure to implement robust, state-of-the-art technical safeguards to verify identity before processing constitutes a processing insecurity violation under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: DIGI accepted a mobile line registration using a customer's name, surname, and ID number without verifying that the person requesting the service was actually the legitimate owner of those.
whyTheyWereWrong: A fraudster used the customer's identity to activate a line, causing the customer to be registered as a debtor with unpaid charges.

claimsVsReality.claim: DIGI claimed the SMS-based signature verification via Logalty and the Correos Express delivery with ID check constituted sufficient identity verification procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The SMS verification only confirmed that the applicant possessed the phone number provided—not that they were the true owner of the DNI or person named in the data. The Correos Express delivery verification occurred after the fraudulent contract was already formalized and data processed.

claimsVsReality.claim: DIGI argued it could not be held responsible because a third party, not DIGI, committed the identity fraud.
claimsVsReality.reality: Spanish courts (Supreme Court 13/12/2021) and AEPD established that telecom operators owe a duty of diligent identity verification before processing; third-party fraud does not absolve the operator of its own failure to implement adequate safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: DIGI asserted that the date of birth field was only verified to confirm majority/capacity to contract, not for full identification purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: All identity-linked data (name, surname, DNI) require verification against the actual person to whom the contract attributes rights and obligations, especially in high-risk telecom contexts where fraud can cause significant financial and reputational harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: DIGI claimed it could not store or verify copies of DNI documents due to AEPD guidance on data minimization.
claimsVsReality.reality: AEPD has sanctioned only excessive DNI photocopying in specific low-risk delivery contexts; the principle of data protection by design (Art. 25) requires proportionate verification methods suited to the risk. For online contract processing, some documented verification is necessary to satisfy the accountability principle.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6.1 establishes that processing is lawful only if one of the listed conditions is met (consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interest).
regulatoryFindings.description: DIGI processed the complainant's name, surname, and DNI without any valid legal basis. No consent was given, the processing was not necessary for contract execution with the data subject (the contract was with an imposter), and no other basis existed. The processing was entirely unlawful.
violations: DIGI processed the complainant's name, surname, and DNI without any valid legal basis. No consent was given, the processing was not necessary for contract execution with the data subject (the contract was with an imposter), and no other basis existed. The processing was entirely unlawful.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5.2 requires the controller to demonstrate compliance with data protection principles (accountability/responsibility proactivity).
regulatoryFindings.description: DIGI failed to implement or demonstrate adequate technical and organizational measures to verify identity before processing. The SMS-PIN verification method only confirmed phone possession, not identity. DIGI could not prove it had deployed diligent controls appropriate to the risk, contrary to Articles 24-25.
violations: DIGI failed to implement or demonstrate adequate technical and organizational measures to verify identity before processing. The SMS-PIN verification method only confirmed phone possession, not identity. DIGI could not prove it had deployed diligent controls appropriate to the risk, contrary to Articles 24-25.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: DIGI's online contract process lacked effective identity verification. Measures were insufficient given the known risk of identity fraud in telecom subscription services and DIGI's national operational scale and technical capabilities.
violations: DIGI's online contract process lacked effective identity verification. Measures were insufficient given the known risk of identity fraud in telecom subscription services and DIGI's national operational scale and technical capabilities.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires security measures appropriate to the risk, including protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: The security measures (electronic signature via Logalty, SMS confirmation, and Correos Express delivery with visual ID check) proved inadequate to prevent fraudulent processing. The SMS-based authentication did not verify the identity of the person behind the provided data.
violations: The security measures (electronic signature via Logalty, SMS confirmation, and Correos Express delivery with visual ID check) proved inadequate to prevent fraudulent processing. The SMS-based authentication did not verify the identity of the person behind the provided data.

outcome: DIGI Spain Telecom was fined €150,000 for unlawful processing of personal data contrary to GDPR Article 6.1. The AEPD found DIGI liable despite third-party fraud, determining that DIGI owed a duty of diligent identity verification before processing and failed to meet the required standard of care for a large telecommunications operator. The complainant's data was unlawfully processed, leading to her registration as a debtor and inability to contract with DIGI. The company has previously been sanctioned for similar identity verification failures in SIM duplication cases (EXP202104009 and EXP202204881), both at €70,000 each. The fine reflects aggravating factors including prior infractions, the company's professional duty given its sector, and the severity of harm caused by loss of data control.
companyNow: DIGI Spain Telecom, S.L. (NIF B84919760) remains a major Spanish telecommunications operator. As of the 2023 financial year, the company reported annual revenue of €664,000,000. The entity continues to face regulatory scrutiny from AEPD for identity verification failures in both new contract activation and SIM card duplication processes.
dataType: Name, surname, national ID number (DNI)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 25 (Data protection by design and by default)

companyDescription: AFK Letters Co Ltd is a UK-based telemarketing company registered at 124 City Road, London (Companies House Registration Number 13473414). The company specializes in unsolicited direct marketing calls.
companyLongDescription: AFK Letters Co Ltd is a UK-based telemarketing company registered at 124 City Road, London (Companies House Registration Number 13473414). The company specializes in unsolicited direct marketing calls.
caseDescription: AFK Letters Co Ltd made 95,277 unsolicited direct marketing calls between January and September 2023 to numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), violating PECR Regulation 21. The company called TPS-registered subscribers without obtaining valid consent from individuals to override their registration. The ICO issued an enforcement notice requiring compliance within 30 days.
violationSummary: AFK systematically contacted individuals on a do-not-call registry without consent, representing ongoing surveillance-like collection of individuals' time and attention through uninvited contact.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: AFK Letters Co Ltd made 95,277 unsolicited direct marketing calls between January and September 2023 to phone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: 95,277 individuals who had taken steps to block unwanted marketing calls received them anyway, violating their explicit privacy choices.

claimsVsReality.claim: AFK could demonstrate that TPS-registered subscribers had consented to receive marketing calls from the company.
claimsVsReality.reality: AFK was unable to provide any evidence that individuals who were TPS-registered had indicated they did not object to receiving calls from AFK.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(1)(b) of PECR prohibits use of public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls where the number is listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: AFK made 95,277 calls to TPS-registered numbers without valid subscriber consent
violations: AFK made 95,277 calls to TPS-registered numbers without valid subscriber consent
AFK failed to obtain clear, positive notification from subscribers that they did not object to receiving calls
Notification requirement under Regulation 21(4) requires individuals to take deliberate action to override TPS registration; AFK could not demonstrate such consent

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(4) permits direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers only where the subscriber has notified the caller they do not object to such calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: AFK provided no evidence that called individuals gave valid consent under Regulation 21(4)
violations: AFK provided no evidence that called individuals gave valid consent under Regulation 21(4)
AFK could not demonstrate that consent was specific to AFK and not merely general marketing opt-ins

outcome: The ICO issued an enforcement notice requiring AFK to cease making unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers and to refrain from contacting subscribers who have previously objected. AFK must comply within 30 days of 27 March 2025. The notice specifies that future direct marketing calls must provide the caller's name and, upon request, address or free telephone contact number. AFK has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
dataType: Telephone numbers, subscriber contact information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, Regulation 21(1)(b)

companyDescription: South Yorkshire Police is the territorial police force responsible for law enforcement across South Yorkshire, formed in 1974 through merger of previous constabularies. It serves a population of 1.28 million across 1,554 square kilometres.
companyLongDescription: South Yorkshire Police is the territorial police force responsible for law enforcement across South Yorkshire, formed in 1974 through merger of previous constabularies. It serves a population of 1.28 million across 1,554 square kilometres.
caseDescription: South Yorkshire Police lost 96,174 pieces of body-worn video (BWV) footage containing sensitive personal data due to erroneous deletion on 26 July 2023. The force failed to implement adequate backup solutions, maintain oversight of third-party system access, or identify security risks in its data transfer processes. SYP could not demonstrate compliance with data protection obligations or recover the deleted evidence.
violationSummary: SYP failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to prevent accidental loss, destruction, or damage of personal data, particularly sensitive data processed for law enforcement purposes. Inadequate backup systems and lack of third-party oversight led to irreversible data loss.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: South Yorkshire Police permanently deleted 96,174 pieces of body-worn video footage from its storage system in July 2023.
whyTheyWereWrong: The loss of sensitive law enforcement evidence containing health data, biometric data, and criminal conviction information prevented prosecution of criminal cases.

claimsVsReality.claim: SYP had implemented a DPIA before introducing BWV use to ensure security risks were identified.
claimsVsReality.reality: The DPIA failed to identify specific security risks related to BWV data transfer, loss, or unavailability, leaving the force unprepared for data loss incidents.

claimsVsReality.claim: A contract was in place with the third-party supplier documenting each party's responsibilities.
claimsVsReality.reality: The contract lacked granular detail specifying how data processing should be carried out, and SYP provided unchecked role-specific access without oversight.

claimsVsReality.claim: BWV footage was stored securely across the Storage Grid and DAMS systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: 96,174 pieces of original footage were permanently deleted due to erroneous data transfer on 26 July 2023, with backup systems that had failed since 2019 unable to recover data uploaded after 21 July 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 34(3): The controller must be responsible for, and able to demonstrate, compliance with data protection principles.
regulatoryFindings.description: SYP failed to demonstrate compliance by deleting 96,174 pieces of BWV footage without proper backup systems in place
violations: SYP failed to demonstrate compliance by deleting 96,174 pieces of BWV footage without proper backup systems in place
Poor record-keeping and failure to maintain clear data labeling prevented SYP from proving the extent of data loss or compliance measures

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40 Part 3: Personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed with appropriate security using technical or organisational measures to prevent accidental loss, destruction, or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: SYP failed to implement adequate backup solutions despite identifying backup capacity failures in 2019
violations: SYP failed to implement adequate backup solutions despite identifying backup capacity failures in 2019
No specific security risk assessment was conducted for BWV data transfer and storage processes
SYP provided unchecked third-party access to critical systems without defined roles, responsibilities, or oversight

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to South Yorkshire Police under Schedule 13(2)(c) of the Data Protection Act 2018. SYP was required to comply with seven recommendations: continue supporting affected data subjects, continue shadowing third-party access, ensure adequate backup and restoration processes, define third-party roles and responsibilities, review and complete the Data Protection Impact Assessment with identified risks, conduct a security risk assessment for third-party access, and ensure clear record-marking. Future failure to rectify these infringements may be treated as an aggravating factor in further enforcement action.
companyNow: South Yorkshire Police remains the territorial police force responsible for policing in South Yorkshire, covering 1,554 square kilometres and a population of 1.28 million. The force has implemented remedial measures including impact assessments of lost footage prior to CPS referral, attempted data restoration, case-by-case notification of affected individuals, and enhanced third-party oversight.
dataType: Body Worn Video footage containing images, audio, health data, criminal convictions, biometric data
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 34(3) Part 3 – Compliance
Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40 Part 3 – Sixth Data Protection Principle (Security)

companyDescription: GOHIPOTECA is a Spanish mortgage intermediary that provides mortgage brokerage and consultation services, acting as a representative of clients in mortgage negotiations with financial institutions such as Banco Sabadell.
companyLongDescription: GOHIPOTECA is a Spanish mortgage intermediary that provides mortgage brokerage and consultation services, acting as a representative of clients in mortgage negotiations with financial institutions such as Banco Sabadell.
caseDescription: GOHIPOTECA, a mortgage intermediary, processed personal data of a spouse without any valid legal basis or consent. The spouse's DNI, employment records, and contact details were collected and transmitted to a bank for a mortgage application in her name, resulting in unauthorized charges to her account. The company relied on an invalid 'conjugal consent' theory rather than obtaining independent authorization.
violationSummary: Personal data provided for one purpose (spouse's mortgage study) was processed and used for a different purpose (unauthorized mortgage application in spouse's name) without lawful basis. This constitutes unlawful secondary use.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: GOHIPOTECA collected and transmitted a spouse's DNI, employment records, email, and phone number to Banco Sabadell for a mortgage application without her knowledge or consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The spouse was charged for services and included in a mortgage application she never authorized, exposing her to financial obligation.

claimsVsReality.claim: GOHIPOTECA claimed the spouse's data processing was lawful because both spouses were married under community property (ganancial) regime, and the spouse implicitly consented through her husband's knowledge of the application.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR requires independent, informed, explicit consent from the data subject. Spanish marital law concepts like 'conjugal consent' cannot override GDPR requirements. The spouse never authorized GOHIPOTECA, never signed any contract, and was charged without her knowledge or approval.

claimsVsReality.claim: GOHIPOTECA argued the spouse was a party to the contract because her husband's application mentioned marital status and intended co-borrower status for the mortgage.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only the husband signed the contract with GOHIPOTECA. The spouse never entered into any agreement with the company. The mortgage bank's later request for her participation does not retroactively create a valid contract basis for her data processing by the intermediary.

claimsVsReality.claim: GOHIPOTECA stated that because the €50.82 invoice was issued by Banco Sabadell (via GARSA gestoría), the company bore no responsibility for the unauthorized charge.
claimsVsReality.reality: GOHIPOTECA collected and transmitted the spouse's data to Banco Sabadell without authorization. The bank's subsequent charge to her account was a direct consequence of GOHIPOTECA's unlawful data processing and disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that personal data processing shall be lawful only if at least one of the following applies: (a) the data subject has given consent; (b) processing is necessary for contract execution where the data subject is a party; (c) processing is necessary for legal obligation compliance; (d) processing is necessary to protect vital interests; (e) processing is necessary for public task performance; or (f) processing is necessary for legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: GOHIPOTECA processed the spouse's personal data without her consent and without any valid contractual relationship with her. The company attempted to invoke a 'conjugal consent' or 'maritalis' doctrine, claiming spousal knowledge implied authorization. This is not recognized under GDPR, which requires independent, informed, freely-given, specific consent from the data subject.
violations: GOHIPOTECA processed the spouse's personal data without her consent and without any valid contractual relationship with her. The company attempted to invoke a 'conjugal consent' or 'maritalis' doctrine, claiming spousal knowledge implied authorization. This is not recognized under GDPR, which requires independent, informed, freely-given, specific consent from the data subject.

The contract existed only between GOHIPOTECA and the husband (A.A.A.). The spouse (C.C.C.) was never a party to any contract and did not authorize GOHIPOTECA to process her data. Article 6(1)(b) requires the data subject be a party to the contract; she was not.
No lawful basis under Article 6(1)(c)–(f) applied; the processing was not legally required, vital-interest protecting, or legitimate-interest driven.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1) requires personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently; article 5(2) requires the controller demonstrate compliance (accountability principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: GOHIPOTECA failed to demonstrate any valid legal basis for processing the spouse's data. The company provided no evidence of her independent consent, representation authorization, or other lawful ground. The 'conjugal consent' argument was legally invalid under GDPR.
violations: GOHIPOTECA failed to demonstrate any valid legal basis for processing the spouse's data. The company provided no evidence of her independent consent, representation authorization, or other lawful ground. The 'conjugal consent' argument was legally invalid under GDPR.
The spouse was not informed that her data would be collected, processed, or transmitted to a third party. No transparency documentation was provided to her prior to processing.

outcome: GOHIPOTECA recognized responsibility and paid a voluntary penalty of €1,200.00 on 20 August 2025, benefiting from two cumulative 20% reductions (40% total) for recognition of responsibility and prompt payment. The sanction was reduced from an initial €2,000.00 proposal. The procedure was terminated on confirmation of payment. No additional corrective measures were specified in the resolution, though compliance with GDPR was implicitly required. The decision is final in administrative proceedings; the company has renounced any administrative remedies.
companyNow: GOHIPOTECA remains operational as a mortgage intermediary in Spain. The settlement and early payment suggest the company has acknowledged the violation and accepted the financial consequence, though the document does not indicate structural reforms or ongoing monitoring.
dataType: Personal identity data, national ID documents, employment records, contact information, financial data

companyDescription: LÁSER METALPRINT 3D, S.L. is a Spanish manufacturing company established in 2018, engaged in metal 3D printing and related production processes. The company operates facilities in the Polígono Industrial Las Avenidas in Torrejón de la Calzada, Madrid, with reported annual revenue of €1,338,000.
companyLongDescription: LÁSER METALPRINT 3D, S.L. is a Spanish manufacturing company established in 2018, engaged in metal 3D printing and related production processes. The company operates facilities in the Polígono Industrial Las Avenidas in Torrejón de la Calzada, Madrid, with reported annual revenue of €1,338,000.
caseDescription: METALPRINT installed a video surveillance system at its facility without establishing a proper data processor contract with the security company handling the data. The company failed to formalize a written agreement meeting GDPR Article 28 requirements, creating uncertainty about data security obligations and leaving workers' personal data vulnerable.
violationSummary: The failure to establish a proper data processor agreement creates structural insecurity in personal data processing. Without contractual safeguards, there is no enforceable mechanism to ensure the processor applies required technical and organizational security measures or respects data subject rights.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: LÁSER METALPRINT 3D installed video surveillance cameras at its facility and engaged a security company to process the footage but failed to execute a formal written data processor contract as.
whyTheyWereWrong: All employees and customers visiting the facility had their video images captured and processed without legally binding safeguards specifying how their data would be protected.

claimsVsReality.claim: METALPRINT stated it operates cameras for legitimate process control and provided documentation titled 'Compromiso de confidencialidad empleados' (Employee Confidentiality Commitment) dated 15 March 2023, purporting to inform workers about video surveillance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The confidentiality document was based on a model used by a different affiliated company (***EMPRESA.1) and was never signed by METALPRINT's own workers. More critically, METALPRINT provided a security services contract signed by another company (***EMPRESA.1 and ***EMPRESA.2), not by METALPRINT itself with its actual data processor, revealing no valid binding data processor agreement existed for METALPRINT's surveillance system.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(3) requires that any processing of personal data by a processor on behalf of a controller must be governed by a written contract or other legal act binding the processor to the controller. The contract must establish the object, duration, nature and purpose of the processing, the type of personal data and categories of data subjects, and the obligations and rights of the controller.
regulatoryFindings.description: METALPRINT operates video surveillance cameras at its facility, determining the purposes and means of processing, thus acting as a data controller under GDPR Article 4(7). However, METALPRINT failed to execute any written processor agreement with the third-party security company (***EMPRESA.2) handling the video data despite the company treating it as the processor.
violations: METALPRINT operates video surveillance cameras at its facility, determining the purposes and means of processing, thus acting as a data controller under GDPR Article 4(7). However, METALPRINT failed to execute any written processor agreement with the third-party security company (***EMPRESA.2) handling the video data despite the company treating it as the processor.

The contract METALPRINT provided was not signed by METALPRINT itself but by a different company (***EMPRESA.1) with which it shares premises and management. This means no valid binding agreement exists between METALPRINT as controller and ***EMPRESA.2 as processor.

Without a formal processor contract, METALPRINT cannot ensure the processor complies with GDPR Article 32 security obligations, Article 28 confidentiality requirements, or provides the technical and organizational safeguards required to protect workers' and visitors' video data.

outcome: METALPRINT voluntarily recognized responsibility and paid €6,000 (a 40% reduction from the initial €10,000 penalty through early recognition and payment). The AEPD terminated the proceedings but ordered METALPRINT to formalize a proper Article 28 data processor contract within 30 days of the resolution becoming final and executable. METALPRINT must notify the AEPD of compliance. Failure to adopt corrective measures could result in additional administrative proceedings.
companyNow: METALPRINT remains active as a manufacturing company in Spain (Torrejón de la Calzada, Madrid). The company has been ordered to implement required corrective measures regarding data processor agreements.
dataType: Video surveillance footage, biometric/facial data

companyDescription: Green Spark Energy Ltd is a UK-based energy company registered at Belmont Business Park, Durham. The company was engaged in direct marketing activities prior to the ICO enforcement action.
companyLongDescription: Green Spark Energy Ltd is a UK-based energy company registered at Belmont Business Park, Durham. The company was engaged in direct marketing activities prior to the ICO enforcement action.
caseDescription: Green Spark Energy Ltd instigated 9.6 million automated recorded marketing calls to subscribers without their prior consent between May 2023 and May 2024, violating PECR regulations. The company provided no evidence of obtaining valid consent and failed to include required identification information in the calls. The ICO issued an Enforcement Notice requiring the company to cease these practices immediately.
violationSummary: GSE conducted mass surveillance through automated calling systems targeting subscribers without consent, fitting the surveillance/monitoring category of the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Green Spark Energy Ltd instigated transmission of 9,587,050 automated recorded direct marketing calls without obtaining subscriber consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 10 million people received unwanted automated marketing calls without their consent, generating 497 complaints, and had no way to identify or contact the caller to stop the harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: GSE could justify making automated marketing calls to subscribers
claimsVsReality.reality: GSE provided no evidence of subscriber consent and made no attempts to obtain it before making 9.6 million calls

claimsVsReality.claim: GSE could omit identification details from marketing calls
claimsVsReality.reality: PECR Regulation 24 explicitly requires provision of sender name and contact information on all direct marketing communications

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 19(1) prohibits transmission or instigation of communications comprising recorded matter for direct marketing purposes by means of an automated calling system except where the called line subscriber has previously notified the caller of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: GSE instigated transmission of 9,587,050 automated recorded direct marketing calls without evidence of prior subscriber consent
violations: GSE instigated transmission of 9,587,050 automated recorded direct marketing calls without evidence of prior subscriber consent
GSE made no attempts to seek consent from subscribers before initiating automated calls
GSE provided no evidence that subscribers had notified it of consent to receive such communications

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(1) and 24(2) require that where electronic communications services are used for direct marketing, the person using or instigating the service must provide the recipient with the sender's name and either their address or free-of-charge telephone contact number.
regulatoryFindings.description: GSE failed to provide required identification information to recipients of automated marketing calls
violations: GSE failed to provide required identification information to recipients of automated marketing calls
GSE did not include sender name and contact details in the recorded marketing communications

outcome: The ICO issued an Enforcement Notice on 28 August 2025 requiring GSE to cease making or instigating automated recorded direct marketing calls except where subscribers have previously provided specific, informed, and freely given consent. Within 30 days, GSE must implement procedures to obtain valid consent before initiating calls and provide required identification information (name and address or free-contact telephone number) with all direct marketing communications. The company must also implement monitoring and record-keeping to demonstrate compliance. A preliminary notice was issued 27 May 2025; GSE submitted representations on 10 June 2025 which the Commissioner considered but found insufficient to prevent the final Enforcement Notice.
companyNow: Green Spark Energy Ltd (Companies House Reg. 14652343) is based at Portland House, Belmont Business Park, Durham, DH1 1TW. Current status unknown; subject to ICO Enforcement Notice requiring immediate compliance with PECR regulations.
dataType: telephone numbers, subscriber contact information
legalBasisViolated: PECR Regulation 19(1) - Prohibition on automated calling systems for direct marketing without prior consent
PECR Regulation 24(1) and 24(2) - Requirement to provide identification in direct marketing communications
Data Protection Act 1998 Section 40 - Enforcement powers

companyDescription: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES, S.A. is a Spanish company established in 1951 that provides business services. The company had 2023 annual revenue classified as confidential in the document.
companyLongDescription: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES, S.A. is a Spanish company established in 1951 that provides business services. The company had 2023 annual revenue classified as confidential in the document.
caseDescription: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES sent workplace harassment investigation closure documents to all participants that identified both complainants and respondents by name, job title, and role. This exposed sensitive employment information about individuals in harassment investigations to the entire investigation group. The company failed to maintain confidentiality despite having internal protocols requiring it.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal data (names, job titles, investigatory status as complainant or respondent) that should have remained confidential, violating the principle that personal data must be treated with adequate confidentiality safeguards. This is a classic breach-of-confidentiality scenario under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES sent internal harassment investigation closure reports identifying 5 complainants and 10 respondents by full name.
whyTheyWereWrong: Five employees who filed harassment complaints had their identities and roles disclosed to all workplace colleagues without anonymity protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES stated in internal protocols that it protects confidentiality in harassment complaint proceedings.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company sent harassment investigation closure documents identifying all complainants and respondents by name and job title to 15 staff members, directly contradicting its purported confidentiality commitment and exposing sensitive investigatory information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company argued that all interested parties already knew the identities of complainants and respondents from the beginning.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the investigation committee and some staff may have had working knowledge, the company's deliberate distribution of formal closure documents identifying all parties by name and role constituted a breach of confidentiality obligations, regardless of informal awareness.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) GDPR requires that personal data be processed in a manner guaranteeing appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES sent harassment investigation closure documents containing names, job titles, and investigatory roles (complainant/respondent status) to all investigation participants, breaching the confidentiality of sensitive employment data without maintaining anonymity protections.
violations: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES sent harassment investigation closure documents containing names, job titles, and investigatory roles (complainant/respondent status) to all investigation participants, breaching the confidentiality of sensitive employment data without maintaining anonymity protections.

Despite internal protocols purporting to protect confidentiality in such proceedings, the company failed to implement adequate organisational measures to segregate disclosure only to relevant parties, instead sending identifying information about all complainants and respondents to 15 staff members.
The disclosure resulted in identifiable harm: one complainant suffered anxiety and medical leave upon learning her identity was known to accused colleagues.

outcome: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES recognised responsibility and paid €120,000 (reflecting 40% reduction for early payment and responsibility admission from an initial €200,000 proposed sanction). The company was ordered to adopt adequate measures within 3 months to guarantee confidentiality of personal data in harassment investigations. The procedure was terminated on 4 March 2025 following voluntary payment. No further administrative appeals are available.
companyNow: SERVICIOS ESPECIALES, S.A. remains operational. The company has implemented preventive training and seminars on data protection rights for investigation committee members and adopted an apology letter policy for affected individuals. Internal confidentiality protocols have been reaffirmed.
dataType: Employee identities, job titles, employment status (as complainants/respondents in harassment proceedings)

companyDescription: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. is a Spanish financial services company operating an online lending platform (www.kviku.es) offering personal loans to consumers. The company processes loan applications and personal credit data through its web platform.
companyLongDescription: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. is a Spanish financial services company operating an online lending platform (www.kviku.es) offering personal loans to consumers. The company processes loan applications and personal credit data through its web platform.
caseDescription: KVIKU processed personal data of a loan applicant without valid legal basis after the applicant explicitly denied submitting a loan request and claimed identity theft. The company failed to verify the applicant's identity before sending SMS codes, approval messages, and loan contract documents, and could not demonstrate valid consent despite claiming the data was freely provided.
violationSummary: KVIKU failed to implement adequate identity verification mechanisms before processing financial data and granting credit, creating a systemic security failure that enabled potential identity fraud without detection or prevention.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: KVIKU processed a complainant's personal data including national ID number, name, birth date, email and phone to generate a loan contract.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant received unsolicited SMS and emails approving a €20 loan in their name, then discovered a complete contract with their personal data filled in.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant submitted a loan application form on the KVIKU website on 26 October 2023 and provided explicit consent to the terms and conditions of the loan contract.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant explicitly denied submitting any application or registering with KVIKU on 26-27 October 2023, reported the situation as potential identity fraud, and requested immediate deletion of their data. An internal log claiming consent could not verify the applicant's identity or authenticate that the applicant personally submitted the form.

claimsVsReality.claim: All personal data collected were necessary, lawfully obtained with the applicant's consent for loan processing purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The applicant never consented. The company processed DNI, name, birthdate, email, and phone without verified consent, sent unsolicited SMS codes and loan approval messages, and continued to hold the data despite the applicant's explicit denial and deletion request.

claimsVsReality.claim: The loan was duly granted to the applicant based on internal evaluation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's own investigation revealed that after internal evaluation, the loan application was actually denied (not granted). The contract was drafted but never signed. The applicant received misleading communications suggesting approval when the loan had been refused.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1) requires that processing is lawful only if at least one of the listed conditions is met, including explicit consent (Art. 6(1)(a)) or necessity for contract performance (Art. 6(1)(b)).
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU processed the complainant's personal data without demonstrating valid, informed consent. The company claimed consent via a log dated 26 Oct 2023 stating 'The user has confirmed their consent and finalized loan number 1687507', but this internal log could not verify identity, authenticate the user, or establish that consent was freely given.
violations: KVIKU processed the complainant's personal data without demonstrating valid, informed consent. The company claimed consent via a log dated 26 Oct 2023 stating 'The user has confirmed their consent and finalized loan number 1687507', but this internal log could not verify identity, authenticate the user, or establish that consent was freely given.

The log did not prove the complainant submitted the form themselves. No technical identity verification, two-factor authentication, or document validation was provided. The applicant explicitly denied submitting any loan request on 26-27 Oct 2023.
No other lawful basis applied: the complainant did not request pre-contractual measures, no contract was executed (loan was denied), no legal obligation or vital interest justified processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(2) – Accountability principle requires the controller to demonstrate compliance with data processing principles.
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU failed to maintain sufficient records proving lawful basis and valid consent. The sole evidence provided was an internal log insufficient to prove the data subject's authenticated consent.
violations: KVIKU failed to maintain sufficient records proving lawful basis and valid consent. The sole evidence provided was an internal log insufficient to prove the data subject's authenticated consent.
The company did not implement proactive measures to verify applicant identity before processing financial data and sending SMS/emails approving credit.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 7 requires that the controller must be able to demonstrate that consent was given.
regulatoryFindings.description: KVIKU could not prove consent was freely given by the actual person. The applicant explicitly stated on 26-27 Oct 2023 that they had not registered with KVIKU and their data had been provided by another person, requesting deletion.
violations: KVIKU could not prove consent was freely given by the actual person. The applicant explicitly stated on 26-27 Oct 2023 that they had not registered with KVIKU and their data had been provided by another person, requesting deletion.

outcome: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. acknowledged responsibility and paid the reduced penalty of €2.400 (from an initial €4.000) on 8 August 2025 by using two cumulative 20% reductions for early recognition of responsibility and voluntary payment. The company must notify the AEPD within 3 months of implementing measures to ensure proper identity verification of credit product applicants and obtaining valid consent. The procedure terminated following the voluntary payment and acknowledgment of responsibility. No appeals or administrative remedies remain available.
companyNow: KVIKU SPAIN, S.L. (NIF B09804295) remains active. The company reported 2020 revenue of €3.000. Company status post-enforcement unknown, but it has designated a Data Protection Officer and claims to have implemented a protocol for clearer communication of loan application outcomes and updated consent procedures.
dataType: Name, surname, DNI/National ID, date of birth, email, phone number

companyDescription: SERVICIOS DE INTEGRACIÓN DE ANDALUCÍA is a Spanish limited company specializing in employment services and teleoperator recruitment, established in 2017 with €12,000 capital. Operates as a special employment center providing remote work arrangements.
companyLongDescription: SERVICIOS DE INTEGRACIÓN DE ANDALUCÍA is a Spanish limited company specializing in employment services and teleoperator recruitment, established in 2017 with €12,000 capital. Operates as a special employment center providing remote work arrangements.
caseDescription: SIA added an employee's personal mobile phone to a WhatsApp group without consent to send work communications outside business hours. The company failed to establish a lawful legal basis for processing the employee's phone number and sharing it with other workers. SIA paid €1,200 after acknowledging responsibility.
violationSummary: The company disclosed the employee's personal phone number to other workers through an internal WhatsApp group without valid consent or alternative legitimate legal basis, constituting unauthorized disclosure of personal contact data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: SIA added an employee's personal mobile phone to a WhatsApp work group for internal communications without obtaining consent, offering no corporate phone alternative.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee received excessive work notifications on their personal device outside work hours without agreeing to it, causing stress.

claimsVsReality.claim: SIA stated employees authorized the company to contact them via phone numbers provided in job portal profiles (Infojobs).
claimsVsReality.reality: Generic job portal terms do not constitute specific consent for including personal phone numbers in internal work WhatsApp groups shared with other employees. No contractual clause or explicit consent for WhatsApp group inclusion existed.

claimsVsReality.claim: SIA claimed WhatsApp use was voluntary and that email alternatives were offered with notification of reduced responsiveness.
claimsVsReality.reality: No written documentation was provided proving these alternatives were actually offered, and employment dynamics made refusal impractical. The alternative was not equivalent to immediate WhatsApp communication.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6.1 requires that processing of personal data shall be lawful only if at least one of the specified conditions is met, including consent (Article 6.1(a)), necessity for contract performance (Article 6.1(b)), legal obligation (Article 6.1(c)), protection of vital interests (Article 6.1(d)), public task (Article 6.1(e)), or legitimate interests (Article 6.1(f)).
regulatoryFindings.description: SIA processed the employee's personal phone number by including it in a WhatsApp group without establishing any valid lawful basis under Article 6.1. The company did not obtain explicit consent, did not demonstrate necessity for contract execution, and failed to conduct a legitimate interests assessment. The company's claim that consent was obtained through job portal authorization was deemed insufficient as it did not cover inclusion in personal WhatsApp work groups.
violations: SIA processed the employee's personal phone number by including it in a WhatsApp group without establishing any valid lawful basis under Article 6.1. The company did not obtain explicit consent, did not demonstrate necessity for contract execution, and failed to conduct a legitimate interests assessment. The company's claim that consent was obtained through job portal authorization was deemed insufficient as it did not cover inclusion in personal WhatsApp work groups.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 4.11 defines consent as any free, specific, informed and unambiguous manifestation of the data subject's wishes, including via clear affirmative action. Consent cannot be considered freely given when there exists an imbalance of power such as in employment relationships.
regulatoryFindings.description: SIA failed to obtain valid consent. Even if consent was required as a legal basis, the employment power dynamic prevented truly free consent. The employee could not refuse without suffering detriment to the employment relationship. No explicit written consent was provided for inclusion in the WhatsApp group.
violations: SIA failed to obtain valid consent. Even if consent was required as a legal basis, the employment power dynamic prevented truly free consent. The employee could not refuse without suffering detriment to the employment relationship. No explicit written consent was provided for inclusion in the WhatsApp group.

outcome: SIA acknowledged responsibility and paid a reduced fine of €1,200 (down from €2,000 after applying 20% reduction for responsibility admission and 20% for voluntary payment). The company must cease the unlawful processing, obtain proper consent or alternative legal basis for any future communications via personal phones, and implement documented consent procedures in employment contracts. The procedure was terminated on April 9, 2025. The company proposed internally to reflect WhatsApp consent explicitly in contracts and explore alternative communication tools.
companyNow: SERVICIOS DE INTEGRACIÓN DE ANDALUCÍA is a special employment center (centro especial de empleo) established in 2017 operating in Andalusia, Spain. Status following enforcement action unknown.
dataType: Phone numbers, employee contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 83.5(a) (Administrative fines for basic principles)

companyDescription: LEIVA BUS, S.L. is a Spanish transportation company that provides shuttle services, including a free shuttle service at Málaga Airport contracted through a larger transportation company. The company typically does not collect or directly manage passenger personal data due to the nature of free-service operations.
companyLongDescription: LEIVA BUS, S.L. is a Spanish transportation company that provides shuttle services, including a free shuttle service at Málaga Airport contracted through a larger transportation company. The company typically does not collect or directly manage passenger personal data due to the nature of free-service operations.
caseDescription: LEIVA BUS transmitted a damage assessment document to a claimant that contained personal data of a third party (another passenger affected by the same incident). The document included names, identification numbers coinciding with DNI, and bank account numbers of multiple injured parties. This constituted an unauthorized disclosure of third-party personal data in breach of the confidentiality and integrity principle.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to prevent unauthorized disclosure of third-party personal data in documents transmitted to claimants. Personal data (names, ID numbers, bank accounts) of a third party was revealed to someone with no legitimate need to access it, representing a direct breach of confidentiality obligations under Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: LEIVA BUS transmitted an insurance damage assessment form to a passenger that contained her personal data alongside another passenger's complete personal details including name.
whyTheyWereWrong: A third party's sensitive personal data including identity documents and banking information was exposed to someone unauthorized, creating risk of identity theft, financial fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: LEIVA BUS claimed it does not technically function as a data controller and lacks access to passenger data due to the free shuttle service model with no ticket sales.
claimsVsReality.reality: LEIVA BUS acted as a data controller by deciding to transmit insurance damage documents to claimants. In doing so, it exercised control over personal data processing and bore responsibility for the security and confidentiality of data within documents it transmitted.

claimsVsReality.claim: LEIVA BUS stated the insurance company (***EMPRESA.1) was responsible for the document format including the inappropriate inclusion of third-party data.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the insurance company prepared the document, LEIVA BUS had an independent obligation to implement safeguards before transmission and should have refused to distribute documents containing third-party personal data or requested revised, individualized documents.

claimsVsReality.claim: LEIVA BUS claimed it sent the document with a 'confidentiality warning' advising the claimant to delete third-party data.
claimsVsReality.reality: A confidentiality notice does not constitute adequate technical or organizational measures and does not prevent the unauthorized disclosure that has already occurred. The third-party data had already been exposed by transmission.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: LEIVA BUS failed to implement adequate technical or organizational measures to prevent disclosure of third-party personal data when transmitting damage assessment documents from the insurance company to claimants.
violations: LEIVA BUS failed to implement adequate technical or organizational measures to prevent disclosure of third-party personal data when transmitting damage assessment documents from the insurance company to claimants.
The company transmitted a document containing identification numbers (coinciding with DNI) and bank account numbers of multiple affected passengers without safeguards to segregate data by recipient.
No protocols existed to verify document contents before transmission or to prevent multi-recipient data on single documents.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5 establishes that infringements of basic principles for processing, including conditions for consent under Articles 5, 6, 7 and 9, shall be subject to administrative fines of up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: LEIVA BUS's failure to maintain data confidentiality and integrity constituted an infringement of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, a foundational processing principle.
violations: LEIVA BUS's failure to maintain data confidentiality and integrity constituted an infringement of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, a foundational processing principle.
The breach involved special sensitivity data (identification numbers and financial account details) capable of causing significant harm through identity theft or financial fraud.

outcome: LEIVA BUS recognized responsibility and voluntarily paid €1,800 (reduced from €3,000 through 20% early admission reduction + 20% voluntary payment reduction). The company adopted remedial measures including: (1) internal circular prohibiting delivery of documents containing third-party personal data to claimants; (2) communication to insurance partner requiring separated data presentation for each affected passenger. Procedure EXP202402874 terminated. Resolution became final and enforceable upon notification.
companyNow: LEIVA BUS, S.L. is a Spanish transportation company established in 1996 with reported 2023 revenue of €2,558,525. The company continues operations as a shuttle service provider, including contracted services at Málaga Airport.
dataType: Name, surname, identification number (DNI), bank account numbers (IBAN)

companyDescription: DELAFRUIT, S.L. is a food/agricultural company (indicated by the business name and reference to loading docks, production facilities) operating in Spain with employees and commercial facilities subject to labor law protections.
companyLongDescription: DELAFRUIT, S.L. is a food/agricultural company (indicated by the business name and reference to loading docks, production facilities) operating in Spain with employees and commercial facilities subject to labor law protections.
caseDescription: DELAFRUIT installed video surveillance cameras in employee rest areas (break room/dining areas) without proper signage, violating Article 5(1)(c) of the GDPR (data minimization). The company recorded employees in spaces designated for rest and leisure, which is explicitly prohibited under Spanish data protection law. After initial non-cooperation, DELAFRUIT acknowledged the infraction and paid a reduced penalty.
violationSummary: The company deployed video surveillance in areas explicitly designated by law as off-limits (rest rooms, dining areas). This is fundamentally a surveillance violation — capturing personal data in intimate spaces without consent or legal justification.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: DELAFRUIT installed video surveillance cameras in employee rest areas including the dining room and break room without proper informational signage.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees in break rooms and dining areas had no reasonable expectation of surveillance and received no clear warning.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed cameras were for employee labor control and this was disclosed in employment contracts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cameras in rest/break areas are categorically prohibited by law regardless of disclosure; no contract can override this absolute prohibition on surveillance in designated rest spaces.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company provided informational signage at camera locations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Signage was either absent or incomplete/incorrect, failing to properly inform employees of surveillance purposes and scope.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be 'adequate, pertinent and limited to what is necessary' (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: DELAFRUIT installed cameras in rest/break areas capturing employees during rest periods, exceeding what is necessary for legitimate business purposes.
violations: DELAFRUIT installed cameras in rest/break areas capturing employees during rest periods, exceeding what is necessary for legitimate business purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Art. 89(2) explicitly prohibits installation of sound recording or video surveillance systems in places intended for rest or leisure of workers (changing rooms, toilets, dining areas, etc.).
regulatoryFindings.description: DELAFRUIT placed cameras directly in the dining/break room (comedor), a designated rest area, in direct violation of this absolute prohibition.
violations: DELAFRUIT placed cameras directly in the dining/break room (comedor), a designated rest area, in direct violation of this absolute prohibition.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13 and GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) require transparency and communication of processing purposes to data subjects.
regulatoryFindings.description: Some cameras lacked proper informational signage or the signage present was incomplete/incorrect, preventing employees from understanding they were being monitored.
violations: Some cameras lacked proper informational signage or the signage present was incomplete/incorrect, preventing employees from understanding they were being monitored.

outcome: DELAFRUIT recognized responsibility and paid a voluntary penalty of €3,600 (after 40% reduction combining 20% for confession and 20% for voluntary payment). The company must remove or reposition cameras from rest areas and ensure proper signage on all surveillance equipment. The procedure terminated upon payment and acknowledgment of infraction. No further corrective measures beyond camera removal/repositioning were specified in the resolution.
companyNow: Following the enforcement action in 2025, DELAFRUIT is required to cease surveillance in employee rest areas and ensure compliance with GDPR data minimization principles. Current operational status is unknown.
dataType: Biometric/Video surveillance data of employees
legalBasisViolated: LOPDGDD Art. 89(2) – Prohibition on surveillance in rest/leisure areas

company: Disney Worldwide Services, Inc. and Disney Entertainment Operations LLC
companyDescription: The Walt Disney Company is a multinational media and entertainment conglomerate founded in 1923, operating major divisions including Disney Entertainment (streaming, traditional media), Disney Experiences (theme parks, resorts), and ESPN. Disney operates over 1,250 YouTube channels generating billions of views annually.
companyLongDescription: The Walt Disney Company is a multinational media and entertainment conglomerate founded in 1923, operating major divisions including Disney Entertainment (streaming, traditional media), Disney Experiences (theme parks, resorts), and ESPN. Disney operates over 1,250 YouTube channels generating billions of views annually.
caseDescription: Disney failed to properly mark child-directed videos as "Made for Kids" on YouTube, allowing personal information to be collected from children under 13 without parental notice or consent. Disney enabled targeted advertising on improperly-marked videos, violating COPPA requirements. YouTube redesignated over 300 videos as child-directed in 2020, but Disney did not revise its policy despite notice.
violationSummary: Disney's failure to mark videos allowed YouTube to collect persistent identifiers (tracking cookies, device IDs) from children via targeted advertising infrastructure. This constitutes surveillance of minors without notice or consent, a core privacy violation under COPPA.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
