claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant was alerted by SMS of the supply change and failed to act promptly, contributing to the error not being corrected.
claimsVsReality.reality: A consumer's delayed reaction does not excuse the controller's failure to verify data accuracy. GDPR places the compliance burden on the data controller, not on data subjects to detect and correct the company's errors.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires that personal data shall be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; all reasonable measures must be taken to erase or rectify inaccurate personal data without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: ENDESA ENERGIA associated the complainant's CUPS codes with a third party's contract in error, treating inaccurate data (wrong address without portal identifier) as valid without verification.
violations: ENDESA ENERGIA associated the complainant's CUPS codes with a third party's contract in error, treating inaccurate data (wrong address without portal identifier) as valid without verification.
Company failed to implement diligence checks to confirm the contractor's legitimate relationship to the supply point before processing a title transfer and commercializer change.
No verification of CUPS ownership, no demand for prior utility bills, no confirmation with the distribution company that the applicant was the actual titleholder.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 imposes on the controller the responsibility to comply with the principles in Article 5 and be capable of demonstrating such compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: ENDESA ENERGIA as the commercial entity (entering commercializer) was the sole point of contact during the supply change and bore responsibility for verifying the validity of the title transfer documentation.
violations: ENDESA ENERGIA as the commercial entity (entering commercializer) was the sole point of contact during the supply change and bore responsibility for verifying the validity of the title transfer documentation.
The company's delegate agent (Salesland S.L.) failed to apply the mandatory 'Change of Titleholder' procedure correctly, omitting the portal identifier without confirming it with the applicant.
Company did not require proof of rightful entitlement ('justo título') to proceed with the transfer, despite sector regulations and the CNE guidance requiring such verification.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72 classifies as 'very serious' infractions the treatment of personal data that violates the principles and guarantees in GDPR Article 5.
regulatoryFindings.description: Error resulted in real harm: temporary loss of essential utility services to the complainant for two days.
violations: Error resulted in real harm: temporary loss of essential utility services to the complainant for two days.
Complainant was forced to escalate to the Xunta de Galicia, which confirmed the unlawful suspension was attributable to ENDESA's errors.
The company's negligence affected both the contractor (who received incorrect CUPS) and the complainant (whose essential rights were interrupted).

outcome: ENDESA ENERGIA S.A.U. was ordered to pay €200,000 and comply within six months by implementing measures to ensure that any future supply point transfers with simultaneous title changes comply with GDPR Article 5(1)(d). The company must demonstrate that new contracting procedures for electricity and gas supply include adequate verification of the contractor's relationship to the supply point. Failure to comply may result in further enforcement action under GDPR Articles 83.5–83.6.
companyNow: ENDESA ENERGIA is a subsidiary of the ENDESA Group, Spain's largest energy company. As of 2022, the group reported revenues of €20.003 billion, operating across Spain and Portugal in electricity and gas supply.
dataType: Name, address, CUPS (utility supply point identifier), contact information

companyDescription: BANCO INVERSIS, S.A. is a Spanish credit institution founded in 2001 that offers technological and service outsourcing solutions to financial entities, insurance companies, and investment product distributors. The company acts as a custodian bank for investment portfolios and provides online banking services to individual and institutional clients.
companyLongDescription: BANCO INVERSIS, S.A. is a Spanish credit institution founded in 2001 that offers technological and service outsourcing solutions to financial entities, insurance companies, and investment product distributors. The company acts as a custodian bank for investment portfolios and provides online banking services to individual and institutional clients.
caseDescription: BANCO INVERSIS suffered a data breach affecting approximately 2 million individuals' personal data when an attacker used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to customer data via the bank's web service. The breach resulted from inadequate security measures, including a weak authentication exemption that failed to require multi-factor authentication for 90 days after initial login, allowing attackers to exploit a vulnerable parameter in the web service to access data beyond the user's authorized scope.
violationSummary: The breach resulted from inadequate technical and organizational security measures violating GDPR Article 5(1)(f), which requires integrity and confidentiality protections. The weak password policies, overly permissive authentication exemption, and vulnerable web service parameter represent systemic security failures that enabled unauthorized access to personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: BANCO INVERSIS failed to implement adequate security measures, allowing attackers to use compromised credentials with weak authentication requirements to access customer data through.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 2 million customers had their names, birth dates, national ID numbers, and addresses exposed to unauthorized third-party access.

claimsVsReality.claim: BANCO INVERSIS stated it had implemented appropriate security measures and regularly conducted penetration testing and continuous monitoring.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these security measures being in place, attackers exploited a vulnerable parameter in the web service and used compromised credentials to gain unauthorized access to customer data, accessing sensitive information for approximately 2 million individuals for at least 28 days before detection.

claimsVsReality.claim: The 90-day exemption from OTP requirement was necessary for PSD2 compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: While PSD2 permits a 90-day exemption, this created a significant security vulnerability that allowed attackers whose credentials were compromised outside BANCO INVERSIS's infrastructure to access systems without multi-factor authentication for extended periods.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized processing and accidental or unlawful loss, destruction, or damage through appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: BANCO INVERSIS failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data from unauthorized access. The weak password policy (minimum 6 characters), 90-day exemption from multi-factor authentication, and vulnerable web service parameter that allowed unauthorized data access collectively enabled the breach affecting approximately 2 million individuals.
violations: BANCO INVERSIS failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data from unauthorized access. The weak password policy (minimum 6 characters), 90-day exemption from multi-factor authentication, and vulnerable web service parameter that allowed unauthorized data access collectively enabled the breach affecting approximately 2 million individuals.

The security measures were inadequate for the high-risk nature of processing financial customer data. Despite having systems like IPS/IDS and SIEM in place since 2022, these failed to detect and prevent the exploitation of compromised user credentials through the vulnerable parameter.

outcome: BANCO INVERSIS recognized its responsibility and paid the fine voluntarily on 18 July 2025, receiving a 40% cumulative reduction (20% for recognition of responsibility + 20% for voluntary payment), reducing the fine from €10,000 to €6,000. The procedure was terminated on 18 July 2025. BANCO INVERSIS subsequently implemented stronger security measures including elimination of the 90-day OTP exemption, requiring multi-factor authentication for every login, and conducting additional penetration testing to strengthen the web service security.
companyNow: BANCO INVERSIS remains operational as a credit institution providing technology solutions and service externalization to financial entities. Post-breach, the company has enhanced security protocols, implemented mandatory multi-factor authentication on every login, and strengthened web service defenses through additional auditing and penetration testing.
dataType: Personally identifiable information (name, surname, date of birth, national ID number, sex, marital status, address), financial data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality of personal data

companyDescription: TRIVE CREDIT SPAIN, S.L. is a Spanish credit and lending services company founded in 2015. The company operates a lending platform and had approximately €96.8 million in annual revenue as of 2023.
companyLongDescription: TRIVE CREDIT SPAIN, S.L. is a Spanish credit and lending services company founded in 2015. The company operates a lending platform and had approximately €96.8 million in annual revenue as of 2023.
caseDescription: TRIVE CREDIT SPAIN failed to comply with a data protection authority order to respond to a data subject's access request. The company ignored the initial resolution and two subsequent enforcement notices over more than one year, violating the GDPR's enforcement mechanisms and the authority's corrective powers.
companyWorth: Unknown (based on available financial data: 2023 revenue €96.8 million, net profit €1.1 million)
violationSummary: The company unlawfully excluded an individual from accessing their own personal data by failing to comply with the regulatory order to provide or formally deny the access request. This constitutes exclusion of the individual from information held about them.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: TRIVE Credit Spain ignored multiple official AEPD orders requiring it to respond to a customer's data access request.
whyTheyWereWrong: One customer was unable to access or verify their personal data held by TRIVE for more than a year, preventing them from reviewing loan records.

claimsVsReality.claim: TRIVE claimed it had implemented data protection protocols, including 'Data Breach Procedure', 'Data Subjects' Rights Management Procedure', and engaged external audit support via a contracted firm.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these claimed procedures, TRIVE failed systematically to comply with its own 'Data Subjects' Rights Management Procedure' and the AEPD's explicit orders, ignoring two enforcement notices over 12+ months.

claimsVsReality.claim: TRIVE argued confusion between two overlapping proceedings (EXP202315972 and EXP202413243) caused an involuntary error in not responding.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company received clear written notifications with distinct case numbers, acuses of receipt, and explicit timeframes; confusion does not excuse failure to respond to direct regulatory orders across multiple separate notices.

claimsVsReality.claim: TRIVE claimed the claimant's conduct was abusive, involving 80 phone calls and multiple legal proceedings, and that the access request was excessive and tactical.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of the claimant's litigation strategy, TRIVE's legal obligation to respond to a valid access request and regulatory order was unconditional; the claimant's motives do not exempt the company from GDPR compliance duties.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing and a copy of personal data held by a controller.
regulatoryFindings.description: TRIVE failed to provide the claimant with certification responding to the access request or providing a motivated denial within the required 10-day period from the firm resolution.
violations: TRIVE failed to provide the claimant with certification responding to the access request or providing a motivated denial within the required 10-day period from the firm resolution.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58.2(c) empowers data protection authorities to order controllers to attend to data subject rights requests.
regulatoryFindings.description: TRIVE violated this corrective power by ignoring the AEPD's formal order to comply with the access request and failing to respond to two subsequent reiterative enforcement notices issued in August and October 2024.
violations: TRIVE violated this corrective power by ignoring the AEPD's formal order to comply with the access request and failing to respond to two subsequent reiterative enforcement notices issued in August and October 2024.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.6 establishes penalties for failure to comply with corrective orders issued under Article 58.2, up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: TRIVE's persistent non-compliance with the AEPD's binding order, evidenced by receipt of multiple notifications without response, constitutes a very serious infraction under Article 72.1(m) of LOPDGDD.
violations: TRIVE's persistent non-compliance with the AEPD's binding order, evidenced by receipt of multiple notifications without response, constitutes a very serious infraction under Article 72.1(m) of LOPDGDD.

outcome: TRIVE CREDIT SPAIN agreed to and executed voluntary payment of €180,000 (representing the €225,000 proposed fine reduced by 20% for voluntary payment) on 12 June 2025, conditional on waiver of administrative remedies. The company was ordered to notify the AEPD within 10 days of its final resolution that it has complied with the original access request. The procedure was terminated upon payment, consistent with Article 85 of LPACAP. The company remains subject to further enforcement if it fails to comply with the remedial measure.
companyNow: TRIVE CREDIT SPAIN, S.L. continues operations as a credit/lending company in Spain. The company reported 2023 revenue of €96.8 million and net profit of €1.1 million, representing a decline from 2022.
dataType: Personal financial data, loan agreements, personal identification information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 58.2(c) (Authority power to order compliance with data subject rights)
GDPR Art. 83.6 (Penalty for failure to comply with authority orders)

companyDescription: ARCONADA 1932, S.L. is a Spanish limited liability company (NIF B26555664) established in 2018. The document provides no detail on business sector or operations.
companyLongDescription: ARCONADA 1932, S.L. is a Spanish limited liability company (NIF B26555664) established in 2018. The document provides no detail on business sector or operations.
caseDescription: ARCONADA failed to respond to a data subject's access and deletion requests despite an AEPD administrative decision ordering compliance. The company received the initial order in October 2024 and two follow-up enforcement notices, but provided no response or remediation. This constitutes non-compliance with a regulatory authority decision.
violationSummary: ARCONADA's systematic failure to respond to data subject access and deletion requests, despite explicit regulatory orders, constitutes exclusion—denying individuals the ability to access and control their own personal data.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: ARCONADA failed to respond to a data subject's access and deletion rights requests and ignored three separate enforcement orders from Spain's data protection authority requiring compliance.
whyTheyWereWrong: One individual was systematically denied the ability to access or delete their personal data for over seven months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to access their personal data held by a controller.
regulatoryFindings.description: ARCONADA did not respond to the data subject's access request within the required timeframe or at all.
violations: ARCONADA did not respond to the data subject's access request within the required timeframe or at all.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 17 grants data subjects the right to erasure of their personal data under certain conditions.
regulatoryFindings.description: ARCONADA did not respond to the data subject's deletion request or provide reasoned denial.
violations: ARCONADA did not respond to the data subject's deletion request or provide reasoned denial.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58.2(c) empowers supervisory authorities to order controllers to respect data subject rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: ARCONADA ignored the AEPD's October 2024 order requiring compliance within 10 business days.
violations: ARCONADA ignored the AEPD's October 2024 order requiring compliance within 10 business days.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.6 makes non-compliance with supervisory authority decisions a sanctionable infraction.
regulatoryFindings.description: ARCONADA failed to comply with three successive AEPD enforcement notices (October 2024, January 2025, February 2025) and provided no evidence of compliance or denial.
violations: ARCONADA failed to comply with three successive AEPD enforcement notices (October 2024, January 2025, February 2025) and provided no evidence of compliance or denial.

outcome: ARCONADA recognized responsibility and paid the reduced fine of €900 (40% reduction from €1,500 base: 20% for voluntary payment + 20% for early responsibility recognition). The company is ordered to notify the AEPD within 10 days of implementing measures to comply with the original data subject rights order (EXP202407578). The resolution is final and non-appealable in the administrative system; judicial review is available at the National High Court.
companyNow: ARCONADA 1932, S.L. is a Spanish limited liability company founded in 2018 with business operations at the time of this case. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Personal data subject to access and deletion rights (specific categories not detailed)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 58.2(c) (Authority power to order data controller to respect rights)

company: Federación de Colombicultura de Castilla-La Mancha (FCCM)
companyDescription: Federación de Colombicultura de Castilla-La Mancha is a pigeon breeding and racing sports federation in Spain, responsible for organizing electoral processes and maintaining member registries for federation governance.
companyLongDescription: Federación de Colombicultura de Castilla-La Mancha is a pigeon breeding and racing sports federation in Spain, responsible for organizing electoral processes and maintaining member registries for federation governance.
caseDescription: FCCM published an electoral census containing sensitive personal data of federation members on its public website without access restrictions. The census included names, ID numbers, birth dates, and club affiliations accessible to anyone on the internet. The organization failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures to protect confidentiality, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of personal data.
violationSummary: The federation made personal data accessible to the general public without authorization or adequate safeguards, exposing identifiable individuals to potential misuse and harm.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: FCCM published an electoral census containing members' full names, national ID numbers, birth dates, federation license numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' sensitive personal data became accessible to anyone on the internet, exposing them to identity theft, unauthorized contact, and privacy violations without their consent or knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: The federation's Data Protection Officer stated in July 2024 that 'the publication of the electoral census on the entity's website was carried out in accordance with applicable regulations.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Spanish electoral regulations require census publication but with confidentiality protections and security measures under GDPR and Spanish data protection law; unrestricted public web access violated these requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: The electoral census had been 'properly' prepared following regulatory requirements for electoral processes.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the census content (names, DNI, etc.) was permissible under electoral regulations, publishing it without access controls, encryption, or authentication on a public website violated data protection confidentiality requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be treated in a manner that ensures adequate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: FCCM published electoral census data (names, DNI, birth dates, federation license numbers, club affiliations) on public website without access restrictions, authorization, or encryption.
violations: FCCM published electoral census data (names, DNI, birth dates, federation license numbers, club affiliations) on public website without access restrictions, authorization, or encryption.
No authentication mechanisms, access controls, or confidentiality measures were implemented to protect the personal data from public disclosure.
The organization failed to conduct risk analysis prior to publishing sensitive member data or to adopt privacy-by-design measures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5(a) classifies violations of basic processing principles including Article 5 as infringements subject to administrative fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: FCCM's failure to ensure data confidentiality and integrity constituted a violation of basic GDPR principles, qualifying as a 'very serious infraction' under GDPR Article 72 of the Spanish LOPDGDD with a 3-year prescription period.
violations: FCCM's failure to ensure data confidentiality and integrity constituted a violation of basic GDPR principles, qualifying as a 'very serious infraction' under GDPR Article 72 of the Spanish LOPDGDD with a 3-year prescription period.

outcome: FCCM recognized responsibility and made voluntary payment of €600 (reduced from €1,000 through two 20% reductions for early acknowledgment and payment). The organization was required to: (1) remove public access to the census on its website; (2) post census only on physical bulletin boards with restricted email access; (3) implement private website portal with authentication for federation members; (4) conduct staff training on data protection; and (5) reinforce information system usage policies. The procedure was terminated on March 31, 2025.
companyNow: FCCM is a sports federation established in 1999 with annual revenue of approximately €39,513. Following the enforcement action, the organization implemented corrective measures including a private portal for census access and staff training on data protection obligations.
dataType: Personal identifiers (name, surname, DNI/ID number), date of birth, license numbers, club affiliation

companyDescription: TECNOCRÁTICA CENTRO DE DATOS S.L. is a Spanish data center and IT services company established in 2011. The company operates as a small to medium enterprise with reported business volume of undisclosed amount in 2021.
companyLongDescription: TECNOCRÁTICA CENTRO DE DATOS S.L. is a Spanish data center and IT services company established in 2011. The company operates as a small to medium enterprise with reported business volume of undisclosed amount in 2021.
caseDescription: TECNOCRÁTICA CENTRO DE DATOS S.L. failed to respond to a lawful information request from the Spanish Data Protection Authority during an investigation. The company did not provide required information within the statutory deadline, obstructing the AEPD's investigative powers under GDPR Article 58.
violationSummary: The company's obstruction of investigative powers relates to insecurity in data protection governance, as failure to cooperate with regulators prevents oversight of personal data security measures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: TECNOCRÁTICA CENTRO DE DATOS S.L. failed to respond to a lawful information request from Spain's data protection authority within the required five business days.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's refusal to provide requested information obstructed the regulatory authority's ability to investigate potential unlawful processing of personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1) grants each supervisory authority powers to order data controllers and processors to provide any information necessary to perform its functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: TECNOCRÁTICA CENTRO DE DATOS S.L. did not furnish information required by AEPD's lawful request dated 7 June 2023 within the five business day deadline, obstructing the authority's investigative powers.
violations: TECNOCRÁTICA CENTRO DE DATOS S.L. did not furnish information required by AEPD's lawful request dated 7 June 2023 within the five business day deadline, obstructing the authority's investigative powers.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(5)(e) provides that failure to facilitate access in breach of Article 58(1) is a violation subject to administrative fines up to €20 million or 4% of annual global turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company's failure to respond to information request constituted a typified violation under GDPR Art. 83(5)(e), carrying maximum sanction of €20 million or 4% of turnover.
violations: Company's failure to respond to information request constituted a typified violation under GDPR Art. 83(5)(e), carrying maximum sanction of €20 million or 4% of turnover.

outcome: TECNOCRÁTICA CENTRO DE DATOS S.L. was found to have violated GDPR Art. 58(1) by failing to respond to AEPD's investigative information request. An administrative fine of €6,000 was proposed (17 Feb 2025). The company exercised voluntary payment on 3 March 2025, paying €4,800 (20% reduction) and accepting termination of the procedure without admission of liability. The reduction was conditioned on renouncement of any administrative appeal or action. The procedure was terminated under Art. 85 LPACAP, with the resolution final and enforceable from notification.
companyNow: TECNOCRÁTICA CENTRO DE DATOS S.L. (NIF B86333523) is a Spanish SME established in 2011. Current operational status unknown; company resolved the enforcement action through voluntary payment in March 2025.
dataType: Personal data (type not specified in document)

companyDescription: Club Baloncesto Telde is a basketball club located in Telde, Spain (NIF G35220821) that provides athletic services and training to youth and amateur players.
companyLongDescription: Club Baloncesto Telde is a basketball club located in Telde, Spain (NIF G35220821) that provides athletic services and training to youth and amateur players.
caseDescription: A basketball club published images of a minor on social media without valid consent from the child's father, who had explicitly denied permission. The club ignored the father's written refusal and continued to publish the photos online, violating GDPR's lawfulness requirements for data processing.
violationSummary: The club disclosed a minor's image on social media platforms without lawful basis. Although one parent consented, the father's explicit refusal should have prevented publication given joint custody, and GDPR Art. 8 requires reasonable efforts to verify parental authority in conflicts.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Club Baloncesto Telde published photographs of a minor on social media on 8 January 2024 despite the father's explicit written refusal of consent dated 12 September 2023.
whyTheyWereWrong: The minor's image was disseminated to the public without legal consent from an authorized parent, exposing the child to potential privacy violations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The club claimed it was unaware of any custody arrangement or separation of the child's parents and requested original documentation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The father submitted certified evidence (copies of DNI, child's DNI, and Libro de Familia) proving paternity and shared custody, yet the club had already published images despite the father's explicit written refusal dated 12 September 2023.

claimsVsReality.claim: The club claimed the reclamant's documents were manipulated and requested original images for metadata analysis.
claimsVsReality.reality: AEPD independently verified the social media publications on 8 March 2024, confirming the images were published on the club's social media accounts, validating the reclamant's allegations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data be lawful only if at least one specified condition is met, including explicit consent of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Club Baloncesto Telde processed the minor's image (a personal data element) by publishing it on social media without valid consent from the authorized parental representative (the father), who had explicitly marked 'NO' on the consent form dated 12 September 2023.
violations: Club Baloncesto Telde processed the minor's image (a personal data element) by publishing it on social media without valid consent from the authorized parental representative (the father), who had explicitly marked 'NO' on the consent form dated 12 September 2023.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 8(2) requires controllers to make reasonable efforts to verify consent for children's data, taking into account available technology.
regulatoryFindings.description: The club failed to verify the validity of contradictory consent forms (one parent 'YES', one parent 'NO') and did not adopt measures to resolve the conflict before publishing, particularly given joint custody arrangement.
violations: The club failed to verify the validity of contradictory consent forms (one parent 'YES', one parent 'NO') and did not adopt measures to resolve the conflict before publishing, particularly given joint custody arrangement.

outcome: Club Baloncesto Telde (NIF G35220821) was ordered to: (1) pay a fine of €1,000 for violation of GDPR Art. 6(1); (2) permanently remove all photographs of the minor from social media platforms within 10 days of the resolution becoming final and executable; (3) comply with all data protection obligations. The temporary suspension order issued during case initiation was elevated to a permanent processing restriction. Non-compliance may trigger additional enforcement proceedings.
companyNow: Club Baloncesto Telde is a sports organization based in Telde, Spain. Current operational status unknown from this document.
dataType: Biometric data (image/facial imagery), children's data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 8 – Processing of children's data

companyDescription: Telefónica Móviles España, S.A. is a major Spanish telecommunications operator providing mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services. It operates under the O2 brand in Spain and is a subsidiary of Telefónica, S.A., a global telecoms group.
companyLongDescription: Telefónica Móviles España, S.A. is a major Spanish telecommunications operator providing mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services. It operates under the O2 brand in Spain and is a subsidiary of Telefónica, S.A., a global telecoms group.
caseDescription: Telefónica issued a fraudulent E-SIM (electronic SIM card) duplicate to an unauthorized third party without verifying the requester's identity. The third party subsequently used the compromised phone line to commit fraud and theft, obtaining unauthorized access to the customer's phone service and sensitive account data. The company failed to follow its own security protocols and did not obtain proper consent or legitimacy basis for the data treatment.
violationSummary: The company's inadequate identity verification and failure to implement required security measures for a sensitive operation (SIM duplication) resulted in unauthorized data access and use by third parties, enabling fraud.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Telefónica issued an E-SIM duplicate to a third party without verifying the requester's identity, ignoring that the request came from an unregistered email address.
whyTheyWereWrong: A customer lost complete control of their mobile line, allowing a fraudster to intercept calls, access financial accounts, and commit identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica claimed its security procedures were adequate and that it followed the correct operational processes for E-SIM duplication.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation revealed Telefónica did not follow its own mandatory verification procedures: it failed to conduct the required security call when the request came from a different email address, and sent the E-SIM code to an unregistered email without proper identity confirmation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica stated the fraudster had 'correctly identified' with the customer's data and that the company could not prevent fraud by third parties who already possessed the customer's personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Telefónica's own systems showed the customer's email had been changed days before the fraudulent request, yet no additional verification was triggered. The company acknowledged its commercial agent did not follow the mandatory protocol requiring a verification call when the request source differed from the registered contact information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica claimed it had taken measures to correct the incident by refunding the SIM fee and restoring the customer's line.
claimsVsReality.reality: Remedial measures after the fact do not cure an unlawful processing of personal data without proper basis or consent. The infraction occurred because of negligent failure to apply existing security measures, not because the measures themselves were absent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that personal data processing is only lawful if at least one of the six specified bases applies: consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica processed the personal data of the customer (name, DNI, phone number, account details) to issue an E-SIM duplicate to an unauthorized third party without any valid legal basis—the customer neither consented nor authorized the request, and no contractual, legal, or legitimate interest basis applied to this specific unauthorized treatment.
violations: Telefónica processed the personal data of the customer (name, DNI, phone number, account details) to issue an E-SIM duplicate to an unauthorized third party without any valid legal basis—the customer neither consented nor authorized the request, and no contractual, legal, or legitimate interest basis applied to this specific unauthorized treatment.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure and demonstrate compliance with GDPR, especially concerning data security and proper identification procedures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica failed to implement and enforce its own internal procedures: it did not conduct mandatory verification calls when the request came from an email address different from the customer's registered email, and it processed the request without confirming the customer's actual consent.
violations: Telefónica failed to implement and enforce its own internal procedures: it did not conduct mandatory verification calls when the request came from an email address different from the customer's registered email, and it processed the request without confirming the customer's actual consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data against unauthorized processing, such as encryption, access controls, and identity verification.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica's identity verification process was inadequate: sending an E-SIM code to an unverified email address without additional security checks (e.g., OTP, verification call) exposed the customer's account to unauthorized access and fraudulent use.
violations: Telefónica's identity verification process was inadequate: sending an E-SIM code to an unverified email address without additional security checks (e.g., OTP, verification call) exposed the customer's account to unauthorized access and fraudulent use.

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed a fine of €200,000 on Telefónica Móviles España, S.A. for violating GDPR Article 6(1) by processing personal data without lawful basis. The company is required to comply with GDPR principles and enhance its security protocols for SIM duplication requests, including mandatory verification when requests originate from unregistered email addresses or phone numbers. Telefónica has already updated its procedures post-incident to include OTP (one-time password) verification as a second authentication factor. The resolution is final and enforceable; the company must pay the fine within the statutory payment period.
companyNow: Telefónica Móviles España, S.A. (Telefónica) remains one of Spain's largest telecommunications providers. The company has implemented enhanced security measures for SIM management following this enforcement action, including mandatory OTP verification for requests from different email addresses or phone numbers.
dataType: Personal identification data (name, DNI), phone number, account information, email address
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 24 – Responsibility of the Controller
GDPR Art. 25 – Data Protection by Design and by Default

company: IBERMUTUA, Mutua Colaboradora con la Seguridad Social Nº 274
companyDescription: IBERMUTUA is a Spanish mutual collaborator with the Social Security system that manages workplace accident, occupational disease, and other social security benefits. It operates Ibermutua Digital, a platform enabling associated companies and advisories to manage benefit claims and access employee benefit information.
companyLongDescription: IBERMUTUA is a Spanish mutual collaborator with the Social Security system that manages workplace accident, occupational disease, and other social security benefits. It operates Ibermutua Digital, a platform enabling associated companies and advisories to manage benefit claims and access employee benefit information.
caseDescription: IBERMUTUA's platform transmitted personal data of 3,395 employees to unintended recipients due to a programming error that concatenated Excel files across multiple weekly notifications. The breach exposed sensitive health and employment information including work leave dates, accident details, and salary bases to 354 unauthorized companies and advisories. The error stemmed from a commented code line that disabled the reset function for file attachments in automated emails.
violationSummary: The breach involved unauthorized disclosure of confidential personal data to entities not legitimized to receive it, directly compromising the confidentiality principle of GDPR Article 5(1)(f).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A programming error in IBERMUTUA's notification system caused weekly emails sent to 354 collaborating companies to include Excel files with concatenated personal data of 3,395 employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: 3,395 workers' sensitive health and employment data—including medical leave reasons, accident classifications, salary bases.

claimsVsReality.claim: IBERMUTUA claimed it had implemented appropriate risk analyses and security measures prior to the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: The risk analyses did not identify high risk in the treatments affected, and no controls prevented a single commented code line from causing mass data disclosure to 354 unauthorized entities.

claimsVsReality.claim: IBERMUTUA stated an external audit in data protection commenced in July 2024.
claimsVsReality.reality: No completion date or results of the audit were provided, and the breach occurred before audit findings could influence system design.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in a manner guaranteeing appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: IBERMUTUA failed to implement adequate technical controls (such as file concatenation prevention, recipient verification, or pre-send testing) in a system handling 250,000 monthly emails with sensitive health and employment data for 3,395 affected individuals.
violations: IBERMUTUA failed to implement adequate technical controls (such as file concatenation prevention, recipient verification, or pre-send testing) in a system handling 250,000 monthly emails with sensitive health and employment data for 3,395 affected individuals.
The error resulted from a single commented code line that disabled the reset function for email attachments, indicating insufficient code review, testing, and change management procedures.
No mechanism existed to detect or prevent misconfiguration in the sender process before sending to 354 unintended recipients.

outcome: IBERMUTUA recognized responsibility and paid €600,000 (original fine of €1,000,000 with 40% reduction for early payment and responsibility admission). The company must implement technical and organizational measures within 3 months to prevent similar breaches, including: limiting file attachment numbers, verifying attachment IDs match intended recipients, implementing pre-send sample testing, and implementing AWS-based secure document delivery system with logging and access controls. The resolution is final and executable; IBERMUTUA has renounced administrative appeal rights.
companyNow: IBERMUTUA continues as a mutual collaborator with Spanish Social Security. The company is implementing enhanced security architecture including AWS Lambda, S3, and CloudWatch for secure document delivery as mandated by the enforcement resolution.
dataType: Health data (work leave details, accidents), Personal identifiers (name, NIF, Social Security number), Employment data, Financial data (benefit calculations, salary bases)

companyDescription: SUNERIS, S.A. is a Spanish hotel operator (NIF A17109091) that provides lodging and related hospitality services. It qualifies as a small enterprise under Spanish business classification.
companyLongDescription: SUNERIS, S.A. is a Spanish hotel operator (NIF A17109091) that provides lodging and related hospitality services. It qualifies as a small enterprise under Spanish business classification.
caseDescription: SUNERIS, a Spanish hotel operator, scanned and retained complete copies of guests' national identity documents (DNI), including facial images and other sensitive data, without legal justification. Spanish data protection law required only specific data fields for security reporting, not full document scans. The hotel's practice violated GDPR's data minimization principle by collecting excessive personal data beyond what was necessary.
violationSummary: The company collected and stored excessive personal data beyond legal requirements, creating unnecessary security risks. Full DNI images containing facial biometrics and other sensitive identifiers created heightened exposure risk compared to collecting only mandated name/number/nationality fields.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: SUNERIS scanned guests' complete national ID documents including facial photographs and transmitted full images to security authorities.
whyTheyWereWrong: Complete DNI scans exposed guests to identity fraud risk by collecting unnecessary facial images, document expiration dates.

claimsVsReality.claim: SUNERIS claimed state security authorities legally required full DNI document scans and transmission to secure guest check-in.
claimsVsReality.reality: Spanish Real Decreto 933/2021 requires only specific data fields (name, ID number, nationality, etc.) for security reporting. Full document scanning and retention were not legally mandated; visual verification of displayed ID or form-based data collection satisfied legal obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Guests signed consent forms authorizing data processing and understanding data would be shared only for legal compliance purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consent forms do not override GDPR's data minimization requirement. Processing must be limited to necessary data regardless of consent. Collecting complete biometric images of faces and document metadata was not necessary for security registration purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires personal data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimization').
regulatoryFindings.description: SUNERIS scanned complete DNI documents containing facial images, expiration dates, and parental names—data not required by Spanish hospitality law (RD 933/2021 Annex I), creating unnecessary data processing and security exposure.
violations: SUNERIS scanned complete DNI documents containing facial images, expiration dates, and parental names—data not required by Spanish hospitality law (RD 933/2021 Annex I), creating unnecessary data processing and security exposure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Real Decreto 933/2021 Article 4.3 requires hotel operators to verify accuracy of guest data by matching forms to identity documents exhibited or facilitated, but does not mandate copying, scanning, or storing full document images.
regulatoryFindings.description: SUNERIS justified DNI scanning as legally mandated but in fact could satisfy verification obligations through visual inspection or form-based collection without capturing or retaining complete document scans.
violations: SUNERIS justified DNI scanning as legally mandated but in fact could satisfy verification obligations through visual inspection or form-based collection without capturing or retaining complete document scans.

outcome: SUNERIS recognized responsibility and paid €5,400 (original proposed penalty €9,000 reduced by 40% for voluntary payment and responsibility admission). The company was ordered within 3 months to: (1) modify its guest registration system to cease soliciting DNI copies or scans as a check-in requirement; (2) prove deletion of all previously scanned identity documents. The procedure is concluded. No further administrative appeal available; administrative remedies exhausted.
companyNow: SUNERIS is a small Spanish hospitality enterprise with reported 2023 revenue of €3.836 million. Current operational and compliance status unknown beyond settlement of this enforcement action.
dataType: Identity documents (DNI/passport), facial images, name, nationality, date of birth, residence address
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 4(1) and (2) – Definition of personal data and processing
Real Decreto 933/2021 Art. 4.3 – Guest registration obligations (Spain)

companyDescription: COLEGIO VIRGEN DE EUROPA, S.L. is a private educational institution founded in 1982 offering primary and secondary education services. The school operates in Madrid, Spain, and maintains facilities for student enrollment including extracurricular activities.
companyLongDescription: COLEGIO VIRGEN DE EUROPA, S.L. is a private educational institution founded in 1982 offering primary and secondary education services. The school operates in Madrid, Spain, and maintains facilities for student enrollment including extracurricular activities.
caseDescription: An educational institution failed to secure audiovisual recordings of minors, resulting in a data breach where unauthorized third parties accessed sensitive images found in a backpack on a roadside. The school lacked adequate technical and organizational security measures, failed to obtain valid consent, and provided insufficient transparency information to parents regarding image capture and storage.
violationSummary: The school failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures (Article 5(1)(f), 32 GDPR) to protect audiovisual data of minors. An unsecured recording device was lost and accessed by an unauthorized third party, constituting a data breach and breach of confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The school recorded minors without obtaining or maintaining proper parental consent documentation.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hundreds of minors' images, including some showing children in bathing attire, were accessed by unauthorized third parties when a recording device was lost on a roadside.

claimsVsReality.claim: School claimed it 'maintains control of recordings and data contained in devices' with 'appropriate limitations on extraction of devices' authorized to a designated manager, with required logging of entries and exits.
claimsVsReality.reality: An authorization document from 2018 permitted unlimited device removal without purpose limitation, time restriction, content specification, security measures, or functional access logging system. A recording device was lost and accessed by an unauthorized third party.

claimsVsReality.claim: School provided detailed information about data protection compliance in enrollment forms and stated parental consent was obtained and renewed annually.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consent forms were incomplete, lacking retention periods, withdrawal procedures, recipient information, and complaint mechanisms. School failed to provide renewal forms for 8 consecutive academic years (2014–2015 through 2022–2023), destroying documentation chain for claimed annual renewal practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: School implemented security measures including staff training (conducted in 2022, after breach discovery), written protocols, and password-protected server access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Training occurred after Guardia Civil investigation commenced and after the initial data breach on 29 June 2022. No evidence of these measures existing at time of breach. No documented system for monitoring device exits, no encryption protocols for portable devices, and no incident response procedures pre-existed.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated with integrity and confidentiality, protected against unauthorized or unlawful processing, loss, destruction, or accidental damage through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: School authorized unlimited device removal without access logs, purpose restrictions, or security controls, allowing unsecured recordings to be extravasated and accessed by unauthorized third party who found device in roadside backpack.
violations: School authorized unlimited device removal without access logs, purpose restrictions, or security controls, allowing unsecured recordings to be extravasated and accessed by unauthorized third party who found device in roadside backpack.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing is lawful only if at least one legal basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests) applies. Consent must be freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous.
regulatoryFindings.description: School failed to provide complete enrollment forms documenting parental consent for all academic years 2014–2023, claiming article 6(1)(e) legitimacy without demonstrating actual legal basis; simultaneously asserted consent as primary basis without documenting it for most years of processing.
violations: School failed to provide complete enrollment forms documenting parental consent for all academic years 2014–2023, claiming article 6(1)(e) legitimacy without demonstrating actual legal basis; simultaneously asserted consent as primary basis without documenting it for most years of processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are obtained from the data subject, the controller must provide specified information including identity, purposes, legal basis, storage duration criteria, recipients, and rights to access, deletion, and complaint.
regulatoryFindings.description: School's consent forms and privacy notices omitted mandatory information: no specified retention periods, no mention of withdrawal right, no recipient details, no complaint mechanism, and no reference to recording of minors in swimwear or educational contexts, preventing informed parental decision-making.
violations: School's consent forms and privacy notices omitted mandatory information: no specified retention periods, no mention of withdrawal right, no recipient details, no complaint mechanism, and no reference to recording of minors in swimwear or educational contexts, preventing informed parental decision-making.

outcome: School recognized responsibility and paid €24,000 in reduced penalty (40% reduction for voluntary payment and admission). Required to: (1) accredly implement effective technical and organizational measures under GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) to prevent unauthorized access by third parties; (2) cease recording minors without valid legal basis under GDPR Art. 6; (3) provide complete, mandatory information per GDPR Art. 13 to parents. Compliance must be demonstrated within 3 months of resolution becoming final. School must notify AEPD of implementation.
companyNow: COLEGIO VIRGEN DE EUROPA, S.L. remains operational. The school is a private educational institution constituted in 1982 with approximately €11.2 million in annual revenue (2023). Ownership and operational status unchanged following GDPR enforcement action.
dataType: Images and video recordings of minors, personal data of students and staff
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be Provided
GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of Data Breach

companyDescription: Bharat Singh Chand is an individual who engaged in large-scale unsolicited direct marketing campaigns via SMS, targeting millions of individuals with marketing messages about financial services.
companyLongDescription: Bharat Singh Chand is an individual who engaged in large-scale unsolicited direct marketing campaigns via SMS, targeting millions of individuals with marketing messages about financial services.
caseDescription: Bharat Singh Chand transmitted 966,449 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages between December 2023 and July 2024 without obtaining valid consent from recipients. He sourced contact data from third parties without verifying consent and concealed his identity using hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards. The campaign violated PECR regulations protecting individuals from unwanted electronic marketing and caused over 19,000 complaints, exposing financially vulnerable individuals to harmful debt reduction and energy grant scams.
violationSummary: Unsolicited marketing messages were sent to a large population without proper consent, exposing individuals to deceptive financial schemes and causing documented harm via spam complaints.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Between December 2023 and July 2024, Bharat Singh Chand transmitted 966,449 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to individuals using third-party data without obtaining valid consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Recipients received unwanted spam messages about debt reduction schemes and energy grants without their permission, causing inconvenience, annoyance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Contact data sourced from third parties implied valid consent existed
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence of valid consent was found; 19,138 spam complaints and search warrant evidence proved recipients had not consented

claimsVsReality.claim: Using unregistered pre-pay SIM cards protected legitimate business operations
claimsVsReality.reality: Identity concealment violated PECR and prevented recipients from identifying the sender or requesting opt-out

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission or insigation of unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Mr Chand transmitted 966,449 direct marketing SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients
violations: Mr Chand transmitted 966,449 direct marketing SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients
He sourced contact data from third parties without verifying that consent had been properly obtained
Evidence from 7726 spam reporting service and search warrant showed no valid consent was acquired

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 23(a) prohibits sending direct marketing communications where the identity of the person on whose behalf the communication is sent has been disguised or concealed.
regulatoryFindings.description: Mr Chand used hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal his identity
violations: Mr Chand used hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal his identity
Recipients could not identify the sender or instigator of the messages

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 23(b) prohibits sending direct marketing communications where a valid address to which the recipient may request cessation has not been provided.
regulatoryFindings.description: No valid opt-out mechanism or address was provided to recipients of the marketing messages
violations: No valid opt-out mechanism or address was provided to recipients of the marketing messages

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring Mr Chand within 30 days to cease all unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail unless recipients have previously provided explicit, clear, and specific consent. He must refrain from concealing identity, must provide valid cessation addresses, and must ensure compliance with all PECR requirements. The Notice is enforceable through the Data Protection Act 1998 Section 40, and Mr Chand has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (General Regulatory Chamber) within 28 days.
companyNow: Bharat Singh Chand is an individual subject to an enforcement action requiring cessation of all unsolicited direct marketing activity and compliance with PECR regulations.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, SMS contact details
legalBasisViolated: PECR Regulation 22(2) – Unsolicited electronic direct marketing without prior consent
PECR Regulation 23(a) – Concealing identity of sender
PECR Regulation 23(b) – Failure to provide valid address for cessation requests
Data Protection Act 1998 Section 40 – Enforcement authority

companyDescription: Lead Pronto Ltd is a lead generation company that generates and sells leads of potential customers in the energy and home improvements sector. The company operates primarily through digital advertising channels and collects customer data via web forms.
companyLongDescription: Lead Pronto Ltd is a lead generation company that generates and sells leads of potential customers in the energy and home improvements sector. The company operates primarily through digital advertising channels and collects customer data via web forms.
caseDescription: Lead Pronto Ltd sent 76,605 direct marketing SMS messages without valid consent between October 2023 and February 2024. The company collected contact details through web forms but failed to obtain proper informed consent and did not provide clear opt-out mechanisms as required by PECR. The ICO found consent was not freely given, specific, informed, or unambiguous.
violationSummary: The company collected personal data for one purpose (eligibility checking) but used it for direct marketing without proper consent, a classic secondary use violation under privacy law.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Lead Pronto Ltd sent 76,605 unsolicited SMS marketing messages to mobile users between October 2023 and February 2024 without obtaining their valid prior consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: 76,605 individuals received direct marketing SMS messages they did not genuinely agree to receive, as the company bundled consent into privacy policies without providing clear opt-out mechanisms.

claimsVsReality.claim: LP claimed it provided consent evidence for marketing and that data was not 'mixed up' between different enquiries (e.g., boiler vs. solar panel enquiries).
claimsVsReality.reality: The evidence demonstrated that consent was obtained through bundled privacy policies without clear distinction for SMS marketing, and 76,605 messages were sent without valid prior consent as defined by UK GDPR.

claimsVsReality.claim: LP stated that 'all we are trying to do is remind people who have opted into our websites before, that they still could qualify for a free boiler grant' and that people may have forgotten their enquiry.
claimsVsReality.reality: People never explicitly opted into SMS marketing. The privacy policy in effect during the violation period lacked any information on how to opt-out, and the form's statement about agreeing to the privacy policy by completing it did not constitute valid, freely given consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: LP claimed it provided an opt-out option and that SMS marketing had been 'amended to now include an opt-out.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The privacy policy in place throughout the contravention period (October 2023–February 2024) contained no opt-out information. A valid opt-out was only added after 29 January 2024, after the Commissioner's investigation began.

claimsVsReality.claim: LP stated that it provided training to staff on PECR consent requirements, rules regarding consent for electronic marketing, and consequences of non-compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite this training, LP's consent mechanisms failed to meet legal standards—consent was not freely given, specific, informed, or unambiguous. The company sent 76,605 messages in violation of these trained requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited communications for direct marketing by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: LP sent 76,605 SMS marketing messages without prior consent from recipients
violations: LP sent 76,605 SMS marketing messages without prior consent from recipients
Consent was bundled into privacy policy and not clearly distinguishable from other matters
No unambiguous affirmative action indicated consent to receive SMS marketing

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(3) permits soft opt-in only where contact details were obtained during sale/negotiation, marketing is for similar products/services only, and a simple means of refusal is provided at data collection and each subsequent communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: LP did not provide a simple means of refusing marketing at the time personal data was initially collected
violations: LP did not provide a simple means of refusing marketing at the time personal data was initially collected
LP did not provide valid opt-out options in the body of SMS messages sent
Consent could not be freely given as completing the form required agreeing to the privacy policy to access quotation functionality

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 4(11) requires consent to be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous, indicated by a clear affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent was not freely given—people could not request quotation without accepting privacy policy terms
violations: Consent was not freely given—people could not request quotation without accepting privacy policy terms
Consent was not specific—privacy policy did not clearly distinguish marketing from other data uses
Consent was not informed—privacy policy lacked details on how to contact company to withdraw consent or list of data recipients
Consent was not unambiguous—statement 'by completing this form you agree to privacy policy' did not clearly indicate SMS marketing consent

outcome: The ICO issued a Monetary Penalty Notice of £30,000 (reduced from £30,000 to £24,000 if paid by 8 December 2025). LP was required to comply with PECR requirements for future direct marketing, ensure valid consent mechanisms, and provide clear opt-out procedures. LP updated its data protection policies and SMS campaign procedures in response. The company has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal within 28 days.
companyNow: Lead Pronto Ltd remains an active lead generation company operating in the energy and home improvements sector. The company has implemented updated data protection policies and consent procedures to comply with PECR following the ICO enforcement action.
dataType: Phone numbers, email addresses, contact details
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 4(11) – valid consent definition

company: CURENERGÍA COMERCIALIZADOR DE ÚLTIMO RECURSO S.A.U.
companyDescription: CURENERGÍA COMERCIALIZADOR DE ÚLTIMO RECURSO S.A.U. is a regulated electricity commercializer in Spain established in 2008. As the last-resort supplier for the Spanish electricity market, it operates under regulatory frameworks governing the separation of activities between distribution, regulated supply, and free-market commercialization within the Grupo Iberdrola.
companyLongDescription: CURENERGÍA COMERCIALIZADOR DE ÚLTIMO RECURSO S.A.U. is a regulated electricity commercializer in Spain established in 2008. As the last-resort supplier for the Spanish electricity market, it operates under regulatory frameworks governing the separation of activities between distribution, regulated supply, and free-market commercialization within the Grupo Iberdrola.
caseDescription: CURENERGÍA collected personal data from a customer for contracting regulated electricity supply but through a contact center operator error, transferred that customer's data to IBERDROLA (a competing affiliate) without authorization. The customer received an unsolicited contract offer from IBERDROLA instead of CURENERGÍA, in violation of the purpose limitation principle. CURENERGÍA acknowledged the violation and paid the reduced penalty.
violationSummary: CURENERGÍA disclosed personal data to IBERDROLA without the customer's consent, breaching the purpose limitation principle under GDPR Article 5(1)(b). The data was collected for a specific purpose (contracting with CURENERGÍA) and processed for an incompatible purpose (offering services from a different entity).
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: CURENERGÍA's call center operator collected a customer's personal data for a regulated electricity contract, then mistakenly sent it to IBERDROLA, a separate group company.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's personal information was shared with a company they never contacted and did not authorize.

claimsVsReality.claim: CURENERGÍA stated that 'each of the two commercializers maintains its own treatments, without any confusion or permeability between them, such that each commercializer uniquely treats the information of its own customers.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The operator error demonstrated a failure in the internal controls and separation procedures. Customer data collected for CURENERGÍA was transferred to IBERDROLA's systems, resulting in an unsolicited commercial offer from the competing affiliate entity.

claimsVsReality.claim: CURENERGÍA claimed the error was 'isolated and punctual' and that the Grupo Iberdrola had adopted 'precise measures to guarantee compliance with activity separation obligations.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite claimed separation protocols and a guide for operators, the contact center processing for both entities failed to prevent cross-disclosure. The shared processor did not adequately segregate data handling or enforce access restrictions to prevent the commercial agent's mistake.

claimsVsReality.claim: Both CURENERGÍA and IBERDROLA asserted that the customer's data were already in IBERDROLA's possession from a prior contract, so no new data breach occurred.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the customer had been an existing IBERDROLA client, the unauthorized disclosure of data for an incompatible purpose—under the original CURENERGÍA contact—still constituted a violation of purpose limitation, regardless of whether IBERDROLA already held similar data from a separate relationship.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(b) – Personal data shall be 'collected for determined, explicit and legitimate purposes, and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.'
regulatoryFindings.description: CURENERGÍA collected the customer's personal data for the purpose of formalizing an electricity supply contract with CURENERGÍA. The operator's error caused those data to be transferred to IBERDROLA, a separate commercializer, for an incompatible purpose—offering a different contract from a competing entity.
violations: CURENERGÍA collected the customer's personal data for the purpose of formalizing an electricity supply contract with CURENERGÍA. The operator's error caused those data to be transferred to IBERDROLA, a separate commercializer, for an incompatible purpose—offering a different contract from a competing entity.
The customer had no reasonable expectation that data provided to CURENERGÍA would be shared with IBERDROLA or used to contact them on behalf of that company.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 4(7) & 4(8) – A controller determines the purposes and means of processing; a processor acts on behalf of a controller. Both entities are distinct and maintain separate customer bases and treatment operations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Although CURENERGÍA and IBERDROLA operate as independent commercializers within the same group, CURENERGÍA failed to maintain adequate safeguards to prevent unauthorized disclosure of customer data to IBERDROLA, despite both entities sharing a common contact center processor.
violations: Although CURENERGÍA and IBERDROLA operate as independent commercializers within the same group, CURENERGÍA failed to maintain adequate safeguards to prevent unauthorized disclosure of customer data to IBERDROLA, despite both entities sharing a common contact center processor.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(5)(a) – Infringements of the principles under Article 5 constitute violations subject to administrative fines of up to €20,000,000 or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: The infringement was classified as grave given the breach of fundamental purpose limitation principles, even though the number of affected individuals was low (1 person) and the offered contract was never activated.
violations: The infringement was classified as grave given the breach of fundamental purpose limitation principles, even though the number of affected individuals was low (1 person) and the offered contract was never activated.

outcome: CURENERGÍA acknowledged responsibility and made voluntary payment of €6,000.00 (representing a 40% reduction from the initial €10,000 penalty: 20% for early recognition of responsibility plus 20% for voluntary payment). The company has been ordered to implement corrective measures within 6 months to prevent unauthorized treatment of personal data for incompatible purposes, particularly preventing customer data collected for CURENERGÍA contracts from being disclosed to IBERDROLA. The procedure was terminated as of the notification date with full binding effect in administrative proceedings.
companyNow: CURENERGÍA remains operational as a regulated electricity commercializer in Spain's last-resort supply market (mercado regulado). The company is part of the larger Grupo Iberdrola corporate structure and continues to serve customers under regulatory oversight.
dataType: Name, surname, national identification number (DNI/NIF), date of birth, supply address, CUPS (electricity supply point identifier), home address, email address

companyDescription: CUBILLO GALLEGO, S.L. is a Spanish company incorporated in 2021. The company operates a website at cubillogallego.com but has not disclosed financial information to public registries.
companyLongDescription: CUBILLO GALLEGO, S.L. is a Spanish company incorporated in 2021. The company operates a website at cubillogallego.com but has not disclosed financial information to public registries.
caseDescription: CUBILLO GALLEGO, S.L. failed to comply with a prior AEPD enforcement order requiring implementation of privacy policy information on its website and contracts with data subjects. After repeated notices and warnings over 7 months, the company made no effort to demonstrate compliance, leading to a sanction for breach of the enforcement order.
violationSummary: Company excluded data subjects from access to required privacy information by failing to incorporate mandated disclosures into contracts and website, preventing informed consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: CUBILLO GALLEGO, S.L. failed to comply with a data protection authority's order to incorporate mandatory privacy policy information and GDPR Article 13 disclosures into its website.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers entering contracts with CUBILLO GALLEGO had no access to required privacy notices explaining how their personal data would be used, stored, or protected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company would comply with AEPD enforcement orders within specified timeframes
claimsVsReality.reality: Over 7 months (May 23, 2024 to December 9, 2024), company ignored four administrative reminders and provided no evidence of compliance whatsoever.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company would respond to official administrative communications
claimsVsReality.reality: First and fourth electronic notifications were rejected; second and third postal notifications were returned as 'desconocido' (unknown recipient); company never submitted written response despite having multiple contact addresses on file.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58.2(d) empowers each data protection authority to order the controller or processor to bring processing operations into compliance with the Regulation within a specified timeframe.
regulatoryFindings.description: CUBILLO GALLEGO failed to comply with a May 22, 2024 enforcement order requiring incorporation of privacy policy information and Article 13 disclosures into website and contracts within one month.
violations: CUBILLO GALLEGO failed to comply with a May 22, 2024 enforcement order requiring incorporation of privacy policy information and Article 13 disclosures into website and contracts within one month.
Company did not respond to four subsequent administrative reminders issued between September and December 2024 requesting evidence of compliance.
No written submission or evidence demonstrating adoption of corrective measures was ever submitted to AEPD.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.6 prescribes administrative fines up to €20 million or 4% of global annual turnover (whichever is higher) for failure to comply with corrective measures ordered by the authority under Article 58.2.
regulatoryFindings.description: CUBILLO GALLEGO's non-compliance with the prior enforcement order constitutes an infringement under Article 83.6, classified as a 'very grave' violation under LOPDGDD Article 72.1(m).
violations: CUBILLO GALLEGO's non-compliance with the prior enforcement order constitutes an infringement under Article 83.6, classified as a 'very grave' violation under LOPDGDD Article 72.1(m).

The violation is characterized by persistent disregard for administrative authority—multiple notifications were rejected or returned undelivered, and the company made no effort to engage with the process.

outcome: On March 6, 2025, the AEPD initiated a sanctioning procedure against CUBILLO GALLEGO, S.L. for violation of GDPR Article 58.2(d) through failure to comply with a prior enforcement order. The company was proposed an administrative fine of €900.00. On May 7, 2025, the company recognized responsibility and made voluntary payment of €540.00 (representing two cumulative 20% reductions: one for early responsibility recognition and one for voluntary payment, totaling 40% reduction). The procedure was terminated on the basis of this payment and responsibility recognition. As a condition of the reduced fine, the company must within one month notify the AEPD of adoption of the measures ordered in the original enforcement action (incorporation of privacy policy information into website and contracts). The resolution became final and executory upon notification. Failure to comply with the new corrective order could result in a new sanctioning procedure.
companyNow: CUBILLO GALLEGO, S.L. is a Spanish commercial entity constituted in 2021. Current financial status is unknown as the company reported no financial statements in available records (AXESOR database).
dataType: Personal data subject to GDPR privacy policy requirements; unclear specific categories

companyDescription: GRUPO BONATEL SL, founded in 2000, provides business support services (administration, HR, finance, accounting, IT consulting) and exclusive distribution of Vodafone telecommunications services. The company acted as data processor and IT support provider for multiple affiliated entities.
companyLongDescription: GRUPO BONATEL SL, founded in 2000, provides business support services (administration, HR, finance, accounting, IT consulting) and exclusive distribution of Vodafone telecommunications services. The company acted as data processor and IT support provider for multiple affiliated entities.
caseDescription: GRUPO BONATEL suffered a ransomware attack in September 2023 that exposed employee personal data across five related companies due to critical security failures. The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures required by GDPR Article 5(1)(f), including no multi-factor authentication, outdated systems, and no login attempt limits.
