companyLongDescription: The Department of National Defence is a federal government institution responsible for Canada's military operations, defence strategy, and the administration of benefits and services for Canadian Armed Forces members and veterans. As a public sector organization, it is subject to the Canadian Privacy Act and must comply with information access requests for personal information. The DND maintains extensive personnel records, service files, medical records, and estate information for current and former military members.
caseDescription: The Department of National Defence (DND) refused to disclose personal information of a deceased Canadian Armed Forces member to the deceased's executor, claiming the request did not meet regulatory criteria and withholding information under section 26 of the Privacy Act. The DND did not conduct any search for the requested records and made a blanket refusal. The investigation found that the executor was authorized under the Privacy Regulations to make the request for estate administration purposes, and that DND failed to conduct an adequate search and improperly applied privacy exemptions without confirming the existence of records.
violationSummary: DND improperly withheld personal information of the deceased that the executor was entitled to access under the Privacy Act and Regulations for the legitimate purpose of administering the deceased's estate. The breach involved failure to disclose information and applying privacy exemptions without proper legal basis or adequate search procedures.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Department of National Defence refused to disclose personal information of a deceased Canadian Armed Forces member to the executor.
whyTheyWereWrong: The executor was legally authorized to access the deceased's records for estate administration purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: The request did not meet the criteria outlined in paragraph 10(b) of the Privacy Regulations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The executor was properly authorized under the Privacy Regulations and had sufficiently articulated the connection between the requested records and estate administration purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: The information must be withheld entirely under section 26 of the Privacy Act because it relates to other individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: DND failed to conduct any search for the requested records before making the blanket refusal, making it impossible to properly apply the exemption or determine what information could legitimately be released.

claimsVsReality.claim: Email accounts and other records had been deleted or were not under DND control.
claimsVsReality.reality: While some records may have been deleted, DND did not conduct a reasonable search to confirm whether records actually existed or had been destroyed, instead deferring the complainant to other avenues without formally processing the access request.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 12(1) and Regulations paragraph 10(b)
regulatoryFindings.description: DND failed to recognize that the executor was authorized to request personal information of the deceased under paragraph 10(b) of the Regulations for the purpose of administering the estate
violations: DND failed to recognize that the executor was authorized to request personal information of the deceased under paragraph 10(b) of the Regulations for the purpose of administering the estate
DND did not conduct a reasonable search to confirm whether it held responsive records before making a blanket refusal
DND improperly deferred the complainant to an informal process without formally processing the access request

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 26 (exemption for personal information of other individuals)
regulatoryFindings.description: DND withheld information in its entirety based solely on the text of the request without reviewing actual records
violations: DND withheld information in its entirety based solely on the text of the request without reviewing actual records
DND claimed section 26 exemption without conducting a search to determine what personal information of others (if any) was actually contained in the records
DND failed to consider that the executor, standing in the shoes of the deceased, was entitled to access the deceased's own personal information

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded and conditionally resolved. DND agreed to conduct reasonable searches for responsive records across nine separate file requests (P-2024-00319, P-2024-00323, P-2024-00326, P-2024-00327, P-2024-00328, P-2024-00337, P-2024-00449) and process any responsive records in accordance with the Privacy Act. DND will provide a new response to the complainant for each item. The resolution is conditional on DND's compliance with these undertakings.
companyNow: The Department of National Defence continues to operate as Canada's primary military administration and defence agency, responsible for managing personnel records and benefits for active and former Armed Forces members.
dataType: Personal information of deceased individual including military personnel records, medical records, mental health records, employment records, performance evaluations, financial/benefits information, email correspondence, next of kin forms, wills and testamentary documents

companyDescription: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is the Canadian federal department responsible for immigration, refugee, and citizenship services.
companyLongDescription: IRCC is a federal agency of the Government of Canada that administers immigration, refugee protection, and citizenship programs. It processes passport applications, visa requests, permanent residence applications, and citizenship matters. The department operates under the Privacy Act and manages personal information of millions of individuals seeking to immigrate to or travel within Canada.
caseDescription: A parent requested access to his minor child's passport application from IRCC under the Privacy Act, supported by a court order granting him access to children's information from third parties. IRCC denied the request, requiring the child's consent instead. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the denial reasonable, as the request did not meet the requirement of being made 'on behalf of' the child, and the child had decision-making capacity to provide or withhold consent.
violationSummary: The complainant alleged improper denial of access to personal information. However, the OPC found IRCC's denial was justified under the Privacy Act and Regulations, as the access request did not meet the statutory requirements for accessing a minor's information on their behalf. The issue centers on exclusion from access rather than a privacy violation by IRCC.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: IRCC denied a parent's access request for his minor child's passport application, requiring the child's consent instead of accepting the parent's court order authorizing access to the child's.
whyTheyWereWrong: No real-world harm occurred; IRCC's decision was found reasonable and privacy-protective, as the request was not made on behalf of the child's interests.

claimsVsReality.claim: The parent claimed the court order granted him automatic access to his child's information from all third parties, including IRCC.
claimsVsReality.reality: Court orders granting access to third parties do not automatically override the Privacy Act's requirements; IRCC's requirements for access on the child's behalf still applied.

claimsVsReality.claim: The parent asserted he should obtain the passport application information to prove he did not consent to a 'fraudulent' application.
claimsVsReality.reality: The request was for the parent's own interests in investigating his former spouse's actions, not made on behalf of the child's interests or best interests as required by the Regulations.

claimsVsReality.claim: IRCC suggested that releasing information without consent would contravene the Privacy Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: The child had decision-making capacity given their age and maturity, and Canadian law recognizes minors' ability to make autonomous decisions about their own information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Regulations Paragraph 10(a) – permits exercise of access rights on behalf of a minor if: (1) the request relates to a minor or incompetent person, (2) the requester has legal authorization to administer their affairs, and (3) the request is made on the minor's behalf
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainant did not meet the third requirement – the request was for his own interests (investigating a 'fraudulent passport application') rather than on behalf of the child's benefit, goals, or best interests
violations: Complainant did not meet the third requirement – the request was for his own interests (investigating a 'fraudulent passport application') rather than on behalf of the child's benefit, goals, or best interests

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8 – protects personal information from unauthorized disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: IRCC properly invoked Section 8 to require consent from the minor child before releasing their personal information, given the child's decision-making capacity
violations: IRCC properly invoked Section 8 to require consent from the minor child before releasing their personal information, given the child's decision-making capacity

outcome: The complaint was found not well-founded. IRCC's decision to deny access to the child's personal information without the child's consent was reasonable and privacy-protective. The OPC concluded that the request did not meet the statutory requirements for parental access under Privacy Regulations Paragraph 10(a), as it was not made on the child's behalf. The OPC affirmed that IRCC properly required the child's consent, recognizing the child's evolving decision-making capacity and right to be heard in matters affecting them.
companyNow: IRCC continues to operate as a federal department responsible for Canada's immigration and citizenship services, processing applications and managing personal data of applicants and citizens.
dataType: Passport application information, personal information of a minor

companyDescription: Aylo (formerly MindGeek) is a global technology company based in Montreal that operates multiple pornographic websites including Pornhub, Youporn, and RedTube, generating revenue through user-uploaded content and advertising.
companyLongDescription: MindGeek, rebranded as Aylo in 2024, is a major online adult entertainment platform operator with approximately 1,800 employees globally and over 1,000 in Canada. The company owns and operates some of the world's most visited websites, with Pornhub alone receiving 4.5+ billion visits in April 2020 and hosting 6.83 million video uploads in 2019. The company's business model relies on user-uploaded intimate content that is monetized through subscriptions and advertising, with content easily downloadable and cross-posted across multiple platforms.
caseDescription: MindGeek (rebranded as Aylo) collected, used, and disclosed intimate images and associated personal information without obtaining valid consent directly from individuals depicted in the content. The company relied exclusively on uploaders to attest to consent, despite evidence that approximately 70% of uploads lacked proper consent documentation. The company also failed to provide an accessible, simple, and effective process for individuals to have non-consensual content removed from its extensive network of adult entertainment websites.
violationSummary: MindGeek systematically collected highly sensitive intimate images and personally identifiable information without meaningful consent from the individuals depicted. The company's surveillance-like collection practices, combined with public dissemination without individual knowledge or permission, constitute systematic information collection violations. The company monitored and collected data at massive scale (6.83 million video uploads in 2019 alone) with inadequate consent mechanisms.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Aylo (MindGeek) collected and distributed intimate images and personal information without obtaining direct consent from individuals depicted in the content.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 70% of non-consensual uploads went undetected, allowing intimate images to be spread globally; affected individuals experienced social stigmatization, psychological damage.

claimsVsReality.claim: Collecting uploader identity and making it available to law enforcement would discourage non-consensual uploads.
claimsVsReality.reality: MindGeek provided no evidence of ever referring uploaders to law enforcement; banned accounts could be recreated instantly with new usernames and emails until October 2022.

claimsVsReality.claim: Account bans would deter uploaders from posting non-consensual content.
claimsVsReality.reality: Banned users simply created new accounts with different credentials, circumventing the ban mechanism entirely.

claimsVsReality.claim: Moderators and AI tools checking 500+ videos daily would identify non-consensual content effectively.
claimsVsReality.reality: Approximately 70% of audited uploads lacked the consent documentation uploaders had promised, and absence of visible non-consent signs does not establish actual consent to mass distribution.

claimsVsReality.claim: Changes implemented in 2020 remedied the consent violation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Pornhub's own non-consensual content reports documented continued uploads without proper consent even after 2020 changes.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.3 requires knowledge and consent for collection, use and disclosure of personal information except where inappropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: MindGeek failed to obtain express consent directly from individuals depicted in intimate content
violations: MindGeek failed to obtain express consent directly from individuals depicted in intimate content
Company relied exclusively on uploaders to attest consent without reasonable verification measures
In 2015, technological requirements for upload were minimal (only username and email required)
No systematic verification that uploaders actually obtained consent from depicted individuals
Approximately 70% of verified uploaders who did not appear in content failed to provide required consent documentation within two weeks
For content where uploader appears, no systematic collection of consent documentation for other depicted individuals

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.3.6 requires organizations to seek express consent when information is likely to be considered sensitive
regulatoryFindings.description: Intimate images and videos are highly sensitive personal information requiring express consent
violations: Intimate images and videos are highly sensitive personal information requiring express consent
Company collected additional sensitive identifiers (full names, mother's maiden names, university, sorority information) alongside intimate images
Sexual content depicting individuals in sexual situations is inherently sensitive and difficult/impossible to change
Individuals experienced severe harms including reputational damage, psychological injury, loss of employment opportunities, and anxiety from non-consensual disclosure

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 6.1 requires meaningful consent whereby individual understands nature, purpose and consequences of collection, use or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: MindGeek did not ensure individuals understood their intimate images would be publicly distributed on adult entertainment websites
violations: MindGeek did not ensure individuals understood their intimate images would be publicly distributed on adult entertainment websites
Company made 'reasonable efforts' standard inapplicable by failing to advise individuals of purposes
Uploaders motivated by image-based abuse could intentionally misrepresent consent
Moderation reviews (500+ videos per day per moderator) cannot establish meaningful consent
Absence of signs of non-consensual sexual activity does not establish consent to public distribution

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.10.2 requires organizations to put accessible and simple procedures in place to receive complaints and ensure compliance mechanisms are easily accessible and simple to use
regulatoryFindings.description: In 2015, takedown process was not explained in Pornhub Terms of Service or privacy policy
violations: In 2015, takedown process was not explained in Pornhub Terms of Service or privacy policy
Process required individuals to provide specific URL, title, username or exact upload date to locate content
Individuals who never consented were unaware of all instances of their content across multiple MindGeek websites
Process required separate requests for each URL, even for duplicate or similar content across different MindGeek platforms
No mechanism existed for individuals to request removal of all their personal information across all MindGeek websites
Process was emotionally taxing and required hiring expensive professional takedown services
Content was often re-uploaded after takedown, requiring repeated requests

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.1 requires organizations to be responsible for personal information under their control
regulatoryFindings.description: MindGeek outsourced critical privacy responsibilities to uploaders with misaligned interests
violations: MindGeek outsourced critical privacy responsibilities to uploaders with misaligned interests
Company relied on human moderators reviewing 500+ videos daily to assess consent
Downloaded content could be edited and re-uploaded by any viewer, creating re-upload cycles
Account banning by username/email was easily circumvented by creating new accounts
Company's Monthly Non-Consensual Content reports show 85% of removals resulted from individual complaints rather than company detection
Only 3% of non-consensual content was caught by internal moderation (97% went live first)
Videos removed for non-consensual distribution had been viewed approximately 35,000 times (pre-2021) and 11,000 times (2021-2022)
MindGeek commercially benefited from larger content volume/library despite knowing practices enabled image-based abuse

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the complaint to be well-founded on all three issues: (1) failure to obtain valid consent for collection, use and disclosure of intimate personal information; (2) failure to provide an accessible, simple, and effective content takedown process; and (3) failure to be accountable for personal information under its control. The OPC recommended that MindGeek/Aylo: (i) immediately cease collection, use and disclosure of user-generated intimate images and associated personal information until PIPEDA contraventions are addressed; (ii) delete all content for which compliant consent has not been obtained; (iii) establish a comprehensive privacy management program within 9 months; and (iv) agree to oversight by a qualified independent third-party monitor appointed by and serving the Privacy Commissioner for an extended period. MindGeek expressly disagreed with the findings and refused to accept responsibility or implement corrective measures at the time of the report's release in February 2024.
companyNow: The company rebranded to Aylo in 2024 following this privacy enforcement action. It continues to operate its adult content platforms with stated commitments to improved content moderation practices.
dataType: Intimate images and videos, sexual content, biometric data (facial recognition), personally identifiable information (name, mother's maiden name, university, sorority information), government-issued identification documents
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.3.6 (Express Consent for Sensitive Information)

companyDescription: Brinks Home (Monitronics International, Inc.) is an alarm monitoring and home security company operating across North America with approximately 800,000 customers.
companyLongDescription: Brinks Home is a subsidiary of Monitronics International, Inc., operating as a major alarm monitoring and home security services provider across Canada and the United States. The company works with authorized dealers who sell and install alarm systems, and operates an online customer portal for account management. At the time of the incident, Brinks served approximately 800,000 customers across North America, including over 10,000 in Canada.
caseDescription: Brinks Home failed to implement adequate safeguards, resulting in unauthorized access to personal information of 3,340 customers through its online portal due to employee error during account setup. The company did not escalate the initial breach report for 10 weeks, and only 20 customers could have accessed the exposed data. While the breach was well-founded, no mandatory breach notification was required as the incident did not pose a real risk of significant harm.
violationSummary: Brinks failed to implement adequate technical and organizational safeguards to protect personal information from unauthorized access, including lack of activity logging, inadequate employee protocols for breach escalation, and employee error in account setup resulting in unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Brinks Home failed to implement adequate safeguards in its online portal, allowing 3,340 customers' personal information to be accessible to 102 other customers for several months due.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive information including home addresses, emergency contacts, and alarm system locations were exposed to other customers for over 10 weeks after initial notification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Brinks could not determine which customers accessed others' data due to lack of system logs
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no technical capability to detect unauthorized access even though it occurred, representing a critical failure in security monitoring infrastructure

claimsVsReality.claim: The incident did not pose real risk of significant harm because only 20 customers could have accessed the data
claimsVsReality.reality: Home addresses, emergency contact information, and alarm system locations of 3,340 customers were exposed for months, providing burglars with intelligence about which homes had security systems and when residents might be absent

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach was quickly resolved after the complainant's second notification
claimsVsReality.reality: The problem persisted for over 10 weeks after initial customer report due to failure to escalate the incident through proper channels

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 requires organizations to protect personal information against loss or theft, as well as unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use, or modification
regulatoryFindings.description: Employee error during account setup resulted in 102 customer accounts being configured as dealer accounts, granting unauthorized access to 3,340 customers' personal information
violations: Employee error during account setup resulted in 102 customer accounts being configured as dealer accounts, granting unauthorized access to 3,340 customers' personal information
Lack of activity logging on customer portal prevented identification of which accounts were accessed
Customer service representative failed to escalate breach report to supervisor, security team, or incident response team upon initial notification
Breach remained unresolved for approximately 10 weeks after initial report

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 10.1 requires breach notification to affected individuals and the Privacy Commissioner where a breach poses a real risk of significant harm
regulatoryFindings.description: No notification requirement triggered as the OPC determined the breach did not pose a real risk of significant harm despite affecting 3,340 customers
violations: No notification requirement triggered as the OPC determined the breach did not pose a real risk of significant harm despite affecting 3,340 customers

outcome: The OPC found the safeguards aspect of the complaint well-founded and resolved. Brinks implemented corrective measures including: resetting account permissions, updating customer portal registration process to prevent dealer account misconfigurations, establishing regular monitoring of newly created accounts, reinforcing CSR protocols and training, revising employee instruction materials, and ultimately selling all individual customer accounts in Canada. No monetary penalty was imposed. The breach notification aspect was found not well-founded as the OPC determined no real risk of significant harm existed given the sensitivity of data and low probability of misuse by the 20 customers who could have accessed the information.
companyNow: Brinks Home sold all of its individual customer accounts in Canada following this incident, and Canadian customers no longer have access to the Brinks Home online portal.
dataType: Customer contact information, emergency contact information, alarm system details, address
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1 (Protection against unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use, or modification)

companyDescription: Court Data Australia is an Australian legal information services company that collects and publishes court-related data and personal information derived from legal proceedings.
companyLongDescription: Court Data Australia, operating under the name JFA (Aust) Pty Ltd, is a legal data services provider that collects personal information from Australian court records and other legal sources. The company maintains databases of individual information linked to legal proceedings, litigation, and court matters. It operates in the legal research and information services sector in Australia.
caseDescription: Court Data Australia unlawfully collected and disclosed personal information without proper fairness, lawfulness, or notification procedures. The company failed to take reasonable steps to notify individuals of collection and disclosure, and did not ensure accuracy of personal information. The OAIC determined breaches of multiple Australian Privacy Principles and ordered cessation of unlawful collection and destruction of improperly collected records.
violationSummary: The primary violation involves unlawful collection of personal information without fair and lawful means, and disclosure without proper notification — core surveillance and collection issues under the Privacy Act.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Court Data Australia collected and disclosed personal information without proper consent, fairness, or lawfulness procedures, and failed to notify individuals of collection.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals had no knowledge their personal information was being collected and shared, exposing them to potential misuse, identity risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: Court Data Australia could collect and disclose personal information from court records without individual notification or consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OAIC determined the company failed to take reasonable steps to notify individuals of collection and disclosure, breaching APP 5 fairness requirements and APP 10 notification obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had lawful authority to collect and publicly disclose all personal information derived from court proceedings.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OAIC found the collection and disclosure was unlawful under APP 3.5 and did not meet lawfulness requirements, requiring cessation and destruction of improperly collected records.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 3.5 – Collection of personal information must be fair and lawful
regulatoryFindings.description: Unlawful collection of personal information
violations: Unlawful collection of personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 5 – Reasonable steps to notify of collection and disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to take reasonable steps to notify individuals of collection and disclosure
violations: Failed to take reasonable steps to notify individuals of collection and disclosure

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 10 – Accuracy of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Did not ensure reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information
violations: Did not ensure reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 13 – Privacy governance and handling
regulatoryFindings.description: Breached privacy management requirements
violations: Breached privacy management requirements

outcome: The OAIC determined that Court Data Australia breached APP 3.5, APP 5, APP 10, and APP 13. The company was ordered to: cease unlawful collection of personal information, remove unlawfully collected personal information, and destroy records containing the unlawfully collected data.

companyDescription: HMI Institute of Health Science is a healthcare training provider in Singapore offering professional development and educational programs.
companyLongDescription: HMI Institute of Health Science Pte. Ltd. is a healthcare training provider based in Singapore that offers educational and career development programs. The organisation previously operated a Students' Career Portal from 2017 to 2019 through which students submitted personal data for career services. The institute provides training and qualification programs in the healthcare sector to students across Singapore.
caseDescription: HMI Institute of Health Science inadvertently exposed an Excel file containing personal data of 761 individuals on the internet for an extended period. The file remained accessible via search engines after the organisation decommissioned its Students' Career Portal in 2019 due to inadequate vendor oversight and failure to verify data deletion. The organisation breached the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24 by not implementing reasonable security arrangements and adequate vendor management policies.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data. The breach resulted from inadequate oversight of vendor decommissioning activities, lack of access controls on web directories, and failure to verify deletion of personal data, allowing the file to be indexed and publicly accessible via search engines.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: HMI Institute failed to verify that an Excel file containing personal data of 761 individuals was deleted when decommissioning its Students' Career Portal in 2019.
whyTheyWereWrong: 761 individuals had their sensitive personal data including names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, NRIC numbers, dates of birth, nationality, race.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation checked and confirmed the Portal was no longer accessible at its original URL address during decommissioning in 2019.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Excel file containing 761 individuals' personal data remained in the web directory with no access controls, was indexed by search engines, and remained publicly accessible for years until discovered in May 2024.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation relied on the vendor to properly decommission the Portal and lacked technical expertise to oversee the process.
claimsVsReality.reality: Reasonable vendor oversight did not require technical expertise—the organisation could have simply verified with the vendor that personal data was deleted and no longer accessible, but had no policies or processes in place to do so.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – organisations must protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to exercise reasonable vendor oversight when decommissioning the Portal
violations: Failed to exercise reasonable vendor oversight when decommissioning the Portal
Did not verify with vendor that personal data had been properly deleted after Portal decommissioning
Did not implement policies and processes to adequately supervise vendor work
Left Excel file in web directory with no access controls to prevent search engine indexing
Failed to implement data asset inventory and vendor management policies

outcome: The organisation was required to pay a financial penalty of $10,000 SGD within 30 days. Additionally, the organisation was directed to: (1) create and maintain a personal data asset inventory; (2) establish a documented vendor management policy and processes; (3) conduct vulnerability assessment and penetration testing of IT systems; and (4) submit a written remediation report within 60 days. The organisation had already taken prompt remedial actions including removing the Excel file, liaising with search engines to delist the file, implementing an IT solutions commissioning/decommissioning checklist, and establishing website monitoring protocols.
companyNow: The organisation continues to operate as a healthcare training provider in Singapore. Following the data breach incident in 2024, it has implemented enhanced security protocols and vendor management procedures.

companyDescription: The Consumers' Association of Singapore (CASE) is a non-profit, non-governmental organization dedicated to promoting consumer interests and fair trade practices through dispute resolution and consumer advocacy.
companyLongDescription: Founded to serve Singapore's consumer protection needs, CASE handles consumer-to-business disputes and helps consumers negotiate amicable settlements with businesses. The organization manages sensitive personal data from consumer complaints, including names, contact details, and detailed complaint information. As a trusted consumer advocacy body, CASE holds a position of public responsibility in protecting the personal data of vulnerable consumers seeking its assistance.
caseDescription: Consumers' Association of Singapore suffered two separate data breaches exposing personal data of thousands of consumers. Incident 1 involved unauthorized access to email accounts leading to phishing attacks affecting 4,945 recipients and harvesting of 22,542 email addresses. Incident 2 involved data exfiltration during a vendor data migration affecting approximately 12,218 individuals whose complaint details were used in targeted phishing attacks.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, including inadequate password policies, lack of staff training, insufficient vendor management, absence of ICT policies, and vulnerable computer systems with unpatched security gaps.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The Consumers' Association of Singapore failed to implement adequate cybersecurity measures, resulting in two separate data breaches that exposed personal data of over 34,000 individuals.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers received phishing emails impersonating CASE, with some victims losing up to SGD 149,000 to fraudulent transactions.

claimsVsReality.claim: CASE had adequate password policies and security measures in place to protect consumer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: CASE's password policy was manifestly insufficient; credentials were not enforced, systems ran outdated operating systems with unpatched vulnerabilities, and no ICT policies existed at the time of the breaches.

claimsVsReality.claim: CASE's phishing emails were generic and posed minimal risk to consumers.
claimsVsReality.reality: In Incident 2, phishing emails reproduced exact details from victims' original complaints, enabling highly targeted fraud that resulted in confirmed losses of SGD 900, SGD 68,000, and SGD 149,000 from at least three victims.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data migration vendor process was secure and properly controlled.
claimsVsReality.reality: During the vendor migration between Exabytes and TES in December 2019-January 2020, approximately 12,218 individuals' complete complaint records were exfiltrated without CASE implementing data protection clauses or security protocols with vendors.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation requires organizations to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to enforce adequate password policy - passwords not changed for 4 years and password complexity requirements not system-enforced
violations: Failed to enforce adequate password policy - passwords not changed for 4 years and password complexity requirements not system-enforced
Failed to stipulate clear security responsibilities in vendor contracts during data migration
Failed to conduct adequate staff training on cybersecurity and phishing risks (last training in 2017, 5 years prior)
Failed to implement basic ICT policies covering security patches, software updates, and system monitoring

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12(a) - Accountability Obligation requires organizations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations
regulatoryFindings.description: Absence of ICT policies prior to the incidents
violations: Absence of ICT policies prior to the incidents
No documented IT infrastructure management plan
Insufficient email security measures to detect suspicious login attempts
Lack of logging and monitoring practices to detect unauthorized access
No internal controls to monitor system security
No security reviews conducted in 3 years preceding Incident 1
Over 30 of 45 computers contained critical and high-risk vulnerabilities

outcome: The organization is required to pay a financial penalty of SGD $20,000 within 30 days. The organization must review and update policies including ICT and password policies, rectify all security gaps identified by the forensic expert including applying security patches, enabling security settings, and ensuring proper system configuration. The organization must update the Commission within 1 week of completion. The organization has implemented comprehensive remedial actions including multi-factor authentication, enhanced password requirements, staff training programs, vendor management improvements, patch management software, and planned cybersecurity certifications.
companyNow: CASE continues to operate as Singapore's primary consumer advocacy organization. Following the 2024 enforcement action, the organization has implemented comprehensive cybersecurity improvements including multi-factor authentication, enhanced vendor management protocols, and is pursuing cyber security certifications.
dataType: Names, email addresses, contact numbers, consumer complaint details

companyDescription: Keppel Telecommunications & Transportation Ltd is a Singapore-based logistics and data centre services provider operating across Asia Pacific and Europe. The company provided shared IT infrastructure and managed data assets for its subsidiaries and related entities.
companyLongDescription: Keppel Telecommunications & Transportation Ltd was a Singapore-listed company that provided logistics and data centre services across the Asia Pacific and Europe regions. The company held personal data of its employees, ex-employees, directors, shareholders, and business contacts on shared IT servers. In July 2022, the company divested its logistics subsidiary (then Keppel Logistics Pte Ltd, later renamed Geodis Logistics Singapore Pte Ltd) to Geodis International SAS. The company maintained data centre and logistics operations and was responsible for protecting personal data stored on its IT infrastructure.
caseDescription: Keppel Telecommunications & Transportation failed to delete personal data from a shared server after migrating to cloud storage in May 2020 and again before divesting the server to a third party in July 2022. The server was subsequently compromised in September 2022, putting approximately 22,659 individuals' personal data at risk of unauthorized access and exfiltration, with up to 7,184 individuals' data potentially exfiltrated by a ransomware group.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements for data deletion and disposal, leaving sensitive personal data on a server for over 2 years post-migration without proper safeguards, supervision, or clear instructions to staff. This systemic failure in data protection processes exposed the data to unauthorized access and exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Improper Data Disposal

whyTheyWereWrong: The undeleted personal data of approximately 22,659 individuals remained exposed on the server for over two years.

claimsVsReality.reality: The company again failed to delete personal data from the affected server before transferring it to the new owner, repeating the same oversight from 2020.

claimsVsReality.reality: Staff were not given clear instructions to delete data after migration, and the migration was left unsupervised, resulting in personal data remaining on the server.

claimsVsReality.reality: The company's data asset inventory did not include the personal data on the affected server, so it remained unaware of the data's presence despite periodic reviews.

claimsVsReality.reality: A threat actor gained unauthorized access through a compromised vendor account in September 2022 and exfiltrated data that should have been deleted years earlier.

outcome: The Organization was found to have negligently breached the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24. A financial penalty of SGD $120,000 was imposed, payable within 30 days.
