companyDescription: Academy of Medicine Singapore is a professional institution providing postgraduate medical education and specialist training to healthcare professionals in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: The Academy of Medicine Singapore is a professional body dedicated to advancing medical education and specialist training in Singapore. It serves current and former medical professionals, event participants, and examination candidates. The organisation maintains sensitive personal data including financial information as part of its administrative operations for membership and training programmes.
caseDescription: Academy of Medicine Singapore suffered a ransomware attack on 13 July 2023 that resulted in exfiltration of personal data of 6,574 individuals, including full credit card information of 1,083 individuals posted on the dark web. The organisation breached the PDPA Protection Obligation by failing to implement adequate security measures including outdated firewall firmware not patched since July 2021, servers with end-of-life operating systems, inadequate access controls for sensitive financial data stored in plain text, and lack of documented patch management processes.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data. Specific failures included unpatched firewall vulnerabilities, servers with end-of-life operating systems, plain text storage of credit card data with CVVs, disabled endpoint detection tools, and absence of robust patch management processes.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Academy of Medicine Singapore failed to patch its firewall since July 2021, operated servers with end-of-life operating systems, stored credit card numbers in plain text.
whyTheyWereWrong: The organisation's security failures exposed 1,083 individuals' full credit card information including CVV codes to criminals on the dark web.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had implemented appropriate security measures to protect personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Firewall firmware had not been patched since July 2021, two servers ran end-of-life operating systems unsupported since 2015-2020, credit card data was stored in plain text without encryption or password protection, and EDR applications either could not run on the operating systems or had outdated signatures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had robust processes for software and firmware updates.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented patch management policies or procedures existed at the time of the breach, and the new IT vendor onboarded in April 2023 was only focused on troubleshooting recent system downtimes rather than implementing systematic security maintenance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Financial data held by the organisation was adequately protected.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bank account details and full credit card numbers with CVV codes were stored in clear text on servers without password protection, encryption, or real-time security monitoring, and approximately 12.7GB of data including financial information was leaked on the dark web.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – organisations must protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Firewall FortiOS not patched since July 2021, creating critical vulnerability (CVE-2023-27997) exploitable at pre-authentication
violations: Firewall FortiOS not patched since July 2021, creating critical vulnerability (CVE-2023-27997) exploitable at pre-authentication
Servers operating with end-of-life operating systems from July 2015 and January 2020, unsupported and unpatched
Credit card numbers with CVV security codes stored in plain text without password protection or encryption
Endpoint Detection and Response manager compromised and disabled, failing to detect and prevent malicious tool execution
Absence of documented robust processes for regular patching and updates of important software and firmware
Lack of adequate access controls for sensitive financial data despite heightened risk of identity theft and financial loss
Failure to include data protection requirements in IT vendor contracts regarding system security management and security reviews

outcome: The organisation is required to pay a financial penalty of $9,000 SGD within 30 days. The organisation must report on completion of remedial actions including: assessing perimeter firewall restrictions, conducting security architecture review and network segregation, implementing endpoint and server hardening, identifying and encrypting sensitive personal data, deleting stored CVV numbers and implementing policy against CVV storage, conducting annual security reviews, and submitting written completion report within 60 days.
companyNow: The Academy of Medicine Singapore continues operating and has implemented significant security improvements following the 2023 breach, including automated patch management, two-factor authentication, network segregation, and third-party credit monitoring services for affected individuals.
dataType: Name, address, email, telephone, NRIC number, passport number, photograph, date of birth, financial information (bank account details, credit card numbers with CVV)

companyDescription: Top Mobile Gallery is a mobile phone retailer in Singapore operated as a sole proprietorship by Tok Leng Leng. The business sells pre-paid SIM cards and related mobile services.
companyLongDescription: Top Mobile Gallery (BR) is a small retail mobile phone shop located in a foreign worker dormitory at 2 Seletar North Link, Singapore. Operated since 2014 as a sole proprietorship by Tok Leng Leng, the business sells M1 pre-paid SIM cards and provides mobile phone services to customers. The retailer used M1's terminal device and mobile application to register customers for pre-paid SIM cards, requiring scanning of identity documents and processing of personal data.
caseDescription: Top Mobile Gallery, a mobile phone retailer, failed to implement adequate security controls over personal data when registering M1 pre-paid SIM cards, allowing employees to fraudulently register illicit SIM cards under the names of foreign workers without their knowledge or consent. These illicit SIM cards were subsequently used to send unsolicited messages to phone numbers registered on the Do Not Call register. The organisation had no inventory controls, shared login credentials among staff, provided equal access to registration systems, and failed to supervise employee use of customer personal data.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, specifically: no inventory controls, shared login credentials, lack of access controls, no employee accountability mechanisms, and insufficient supervision. This enabled unauthorised use and access to customers' personal data by rogue employees.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Top Mobile Gallery failed to implement security controls over personal data when registering M1 pre-paid SIM cards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Foreign workers had their identities stolen and used to register SIM cards that sent unsolicited spam messages to people on the Do Not Call register, causing inconvenience.

claimsVsReality.claim: Top Mobile Gallery maintained adequate security over customer personal data used for SIM card registration.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no inventory controls, shared login credentials among all employees, allowed employees to use personal mobile devices to access the registration system, and failed to supervise how staff accessed customer data, enabling fraudulent SIM card registrations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The owner was unaware of employee misconduct in registering illicit SIM cards.
claimsVsReality.reality: The owner had been the registered proprietor since 2014 and should have been aware of the practice; her lackadaisical attitude and infrequent CCTV review demonstrated negligence rather than ignorance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer data was secure and protected from misuse.
claimsVsReality.reality: 44 illicit SIM cards were registered under 33 foreign workers' identities without their knowledge, and these cards were used to send 435 unsolicited messages to people on the Do Not Call register.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – Protection Obligation: Organisations must protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to maintain inventory of M1 pre-paid SIM cards
violations: Failed to maintain inventory of M1 pre-paid SIM cards
Failed to maintain processes requiring employees to account for each SIM card sold and to whom it was registered
Shared login credentials to M1 registration application among all employees
Failed to implement access control restrictions
Allowed employees to use personal mobile devices to access registration system
Failed to supervise employee use and access to customer personal data
Did not regularly review CCTV footage despite its installation
Complete failure to adopt any security arrangements to protect customer personal data from misuse

outcome: The Commission found the organisation in breach of Section 24(a) of the PDPA and imposed a financial penalty of $7,000 SGD (approximately $5,190 USD) payable within 30 days. The organisation must implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, use, disclosure, and misuse of personal data. The decision requires compliance with PDPA protection obligations going forward.
companyNow: The company continues to operate under corrective measures following the PDPA enforcement action and financial penalty.
dataType: Name, sex, FIN/work permit number, date of birth, nationality, employer name

companyDescription: CH Offshore Ltd. is an owner-operator and ship manager of offshore support vessels serving the offshore marine oil and gas sector in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: CH Offshore Ltd. operates as a significant player in the maritime and offshore energy sector, managing a fleet of offshore support vessels that serve the oil and gas industry. The company employs hundreds of seafarers and maintains operations in Singapore and internationally. As a maritime services provider, CH Offshore handles sensitive employee and operational data including crew records, medical certifications, and financial information critical to maritime commerce.
caseDescription: CH Offshore suffered a ransomware attack (Alpha/Blackcat) on 28 March 2023 that encrypted files and exfiltrated personal data of 5,906 employees, ex-employees, and stakeholders. The attack exploited multiple security lapses including unpatched firewall firmware (since December 2021), lack of multi-factor authentication, weak network segmentation, and insufficient vendor oversight. The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements required under the PDPA Protection Obligation.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to maintain reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically: unpatched firewall firmware exposed to remote code execution attacks for over 15 months; absence of multi-factor authentication for VPN access; weak network segmentation allowing lateral movement; and insufficient periodic security reviews and vendor oversight.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: CH Offshore failed to patch its firewall firmware since December 2021, lacked multi-factor authentication for VPN access, had weak network segmentation.
whyTheyWereWrong: The security lapses allowed attackers to access and steal sensitive personal data including health records, financial information, passport numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation had supervised its IT vendor to ensure that maintenance services for its IT system were performed, with an audit conducted in December 2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: The firewall firmware was never patched after December 2021 deployment, remaining unpatched for over 15 months before the March 2023 attack; no meaningful vendor oversight occurred and the next audit cycle had not commenced when the breach happened.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation should not be penalised for failing to procure Managed Security Services because this was not an express requirement under the PDPA.
claimsVsReality.reality: The PDPA requires reasonable security arrangements; the lack of any managed detection and response services meant the organisation had no capability to detect the suspicious VPN connections and data exfiltration occurring on their network in real-time.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees were given local administrator rights so they could work and receive IT support remotely.
claimsVsReality.reality: This practice allowed the threat actor to disable endpoint security software before deploying ransomware, directly facilitating the attack that encrypted files and compromised 5,906 individuals' personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – Protection Obligation: Organisations must protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Firewall firmware not patched since December 2021, exposing organisation to multiple Remote Code Execution attacks
violations: Firewall firmware not patched since December 2021, exposing organisation to multiple Remote Code Execution attacks
No multi-factor authentication implemented for remote access VPN logins with high-level system access
High-risk IT infrastructure with weak network segmentation and access controls; all servers, clients and devices connected on single network segment
RDP protocols enabled on all servers without tightened firewall rules
Password policy feature not enabled in firewall for affected user accounts
Employees given local administrator rights on laptops enabling unrestricted application installation
Absence of regular vulnerability scanning for critical hosts
Endpoint security software (Symantec SEP) compromised and ineffective; SEP Manager disabled early
Absence of Managed Security Services/Managed Detection and Response
Insufficient periodic security reviews and robust patch management processes
Inadequate vendor oversight – last IT vendor audit in December 2021 with no review cycle established for next audit before incident occurred

outcome: The organisation is required to pay a financial penalty of SGD $18,000 within 30 days. The organisation must: (1) furnish a schedule for completion of all remedial actions within 30 days including hardening perimeter firewall with 2FA for VPN, implementing periodic vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, enhancing identity and access management with MFA for privileged accounts, installing Endpoint Detection and Response on all systems, implementing Managed Detection and Response, ensuring all systems are patched with latest updates, implementing network segmentation and access controls, improving logging capabilities with centralised log server, and obtaining Cyber Essential certification; and (2) report to the Commission upon completion of all remedial actions. The organisation's prompt response, cooperation with the Commission, voluntary acceptance of responsibility, and this being a first instance of non-compliance were considered mitigating factors.
companyNow: CH Offshore continues operations following remediation of its cybersecurity infrastructure and implementation of enhanced security measures required by the PDPA enforcement action.
dataType: Name, address, date of birth, email, NRIC number, foreign ID number, telephone number, passport number, photograph, thumbprints, health information (medical records, laboratory test reports, vaccinations), financial information (bank account numbers, pay slips), educational certificates, seaman's book details

companyDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based ferry operator providing passenger services between Singapore and Batam, Indonesia.
companyLongDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry Pte. Ltd. operates ferry services connecting Singapore and Batam, Indonesia, handling thousands of ticket bookings through its website. The company relies on external IT vendors for system maintenance and support due to the absence of an in-house IT department. Despite managing significant volumes of customer personal data including passport details, the organisation historically lacked foundational data protection practices and policies.
caseDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect customer personal data, resulting in unauthorised access and exfiltration of data for 108,488 individuals. The breach occurred due to poor vendor management, lack of ICT security policies, and failure to disable root account credentials after contractor termination.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (section 24 PDPA Protection Obligation) by: (1) not managing IT vendors through written policies and contracts; (2) lacking ICT security policies covering account/access control, passwords, and asset management; and (3) failing to implement security solutions like firewalls and web application scanning on its web server.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Horizon Fast Ferry failed to disable root account credentials after terminating a website contractor, lacked written vendor management policies, had no ICT security policy.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 108,000 customers had their passport numbers, dates of birth, and contact details stolen when attackers used the abandoned root credentials to breach the server.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT Supervisor verified that the root account credentials were no longer accessible after Contractor I claimed they were disabled in 2019.
claimsVsReality.reality: The IT Supervisor failed a login attempt and incorrectly assumed the account was inactive; the credentials remained valid and active until changed in March 2023 after the breach was discovered.

claimsVsReality.claim: Contractor II would conduct regular web application scanning on the website as part of their maintenance services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Web application scanning was never specified in the contract with Contractor II, and no such scanning was performed; after contract termination in November 2022, no IT vendor was engaged to perform security monitoring.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had reasonable security arrangements in place to protect customer personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no ICT security policy, no written vendor management procedures, no security solutions on its web server, and no formal contracts defining vendor responsibilities for data protection.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement written policies and procedures for vendor management
violations: Failed to implement written policies and procedures for vendor management
Failed to establish clear contractual obligations with IT support vendor regarding competencies and security responsibilities
Failed to implement ICT policy covering critical aspects of IT security such as account/access control, password management, and IT risk management
Failed to implement security solutions on web server such as firewalls and web application scanning
Failed to properly disable or verify disabling of root account credentials when contractor was terminated
Relied informally on single IT supervisor without documented scope of responsibilities or technical competencies

outcome: The organisation was found in breach of section 24 PDPA. Directed to pay a financial penalty of S$28,000 within 30 days. The organisation must also provide written confirmation by 31 March 2024 that it has implemented remedial measures including: (1) PDPA training for managers and vendors; (2) written service agreement with IT support vendor specifying designated staff with relevant IT knowledge; (3) enhanced internal data protection guidelines; and (4) vendor guidelines for data handling, password management, and security measures.
companyNow: Horizon Fast Ferry continues to operate as a ferry service provider between Singapore and Batam. Following the 2024 enforcement action, the company implemented cyber incident response measures, developed a new website with penetration testing, and committed to enhanced data protection governance.
dataType: Passport number, name, date of birth, passport issue and expiry date, nationality, email address, telephone number

companyDescription: Cortina Watch Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based luxury retailer specializing in the import, export, and retail of timepieces, branded pens, and high-end accessories.
companyLongDescription: Cortina Watch Pte. Ltd. operates as a retail business focused on luxury goods, particularly timepieces and branded accessories. The company maintains both retail operations and wholesale import/export activities in Singapore. In June 2023, the organization notified the Personal Data Protection Commission of a significant data breach affecting customer personal information.
caseDescription: Cortina Watch suffered a ransomware attack (Lockbit 3.0) between April-June 2023 due to compromised VPN credentials and weak access controls, resulting in exfiltration of personal data of 3,953 individuals. The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements as required by PDPA section 24, specifically lacking multi-factor authentication, robust password policies, and proper VPN account management. Despite the breach, the organisation received no financial penalty due to prompt remedial actions and cooperation, but was directed to conduct a third-party cyber security audit.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, specifically: lack of multi-factor authentication (MFA) on VPN accounts and privileged access, weak password complexity policies (only 8 characters minimum vs. recommended 12+ alphanumeric with special characters), poor access control through unmanaged 'test' VPN accounts, and absence of encryption on stored data. These deficiencies directly enabled the ransomware attack.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Cortina Watch failed to implement multi-factor authentication, enforce strong password policies, and properly manage test VPN accounts.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's weak security controls enabled attackers to access and steal sensitive personal information including names, contact details, addresses, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had adequate security arrangements in place to protect personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked multi-factor authentication, enforced only weak 8-character passwords without complexity requirements, failed to manage test VPN accounts, and used default usernames like 'Administrator' and 'Guest', enabling a brute force attack that compromised the VPN account on 27 May 2023.

claimsVsReality.claim: Test VPN accounts were properly maintained and secured like production systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization admitted to lack of 'house-keeping' on test VPN user accounts; attackers successfully accessed and compromised a test VPN account used to access live environments, which then became a pivot point for lateral movement across servers.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal, or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) on VPN accounts with remote access to sensitive personal data, despite PDPC guidance that MFA is a baseline requirement for privileged accounts
violations: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) on VPN accounts with remote access to sensitive personal data, despite PDPC guidance that MFA is a baseline requirement for privileged accounts
Failed to enforce a robust password policy (only 8 character minimum); did not require alphanumeric complexity with special characters as baseline practice
Failed to manage 'test' VPN user accounts properly, leaving them active and uncontrolled despite being used only for testing purposes
Used default account names (Administrator, Guest) making systems vulnerable to brute force attacks
Did not implement encryption on files and folders containing personal data
Failed to implement account lockout mechanisms or limits on failed login attempts to prevent brute force attacks
Failed to conduct security assessments to determine what reasonable access control measures were necessary given the volume and sensitivity of personal data held

outcome: The Commission declined to impose a financial penalty in light of the organisation's prompt remedial actions, cooperation during investigation, and the impact context. Instead, the organisation was directed to: (1) engage a third-party cyber security vendor to conduct a targeted security audit to enhance access control to personal data within its network, and (2) complete the audit and submit a comprehensive report to PDPC within 67 days total (60 days for completion plus 7 days to submit report). Remedial measures already implemented by the organisation included: decommissioning legacy servers, deploying endpoint detection response tools, implementing centralised log management, introducing certificate-based authentication with 2FA for VPN access, hardening new network environments, implementing file/folder encryption, and establishing proper backup procedures.
companyNow: Following the 2023 breach, Cortina Watch implemented comprehensive security remediation measures including multi-factor authentication, encryption, updated server infrastructure, and managed backup services.
dataType: Full name, contact number, address, email, date of birth, NRIC/passport number, bank account number

companyDescription: Payroll2U Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based payroll service provider offering payroll outsourcing services and SaaS solutions to businesses.
companyLongDescription: Payroll2U Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based payroll and human resources service provider that offers both traditional payroll outsourcing services and cloud-based Software as a Service (SaaS) solutions. The company handles sensitive employee personal data including salary information, bank account details, and identification numbers on behalf of its clients. As a payroll service provider, the organisation is entrusted with highly sensitive financial and personal information of thousands of employees across multiple client organisations.
caseDescription: Payroll2U, a payroll service provider, suffered a ransomware attack on 29 December 2022 that resulted in the exfiltration of personal data of 5,640 employees. The breach was caused by inadequate access controls, including failure to implement multi-factor authentication, improper administrative privileges, and lack of network segmentation. The organisation admitted to breaching the Protection Obligation under the Personal Data Protection Act 2012.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable access control measures required under section 24 of the PDPA. Specific failures included absence of MFA for administrator and sensitive data accounts, excessive local administrator rights, unsecured storage of sensitive personal data on shared drives, and inadequate detection of unauthorised software installation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Payroll2U failed to implement multi-factor authentication, allowed excessive administrator privileges.
whyTheyWereWrong: The security failures exposed 5,640 employees' sensitive personal data including bank account numbers, salary information, NRIC numbers, and addresses to theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Payroll2U had adequate cybersecurity controls in place
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation lacked multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts, gave excessive local administrator rights to employees, stored sensitive data on unsecured shared drives, and had no network segmentation

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had effective security monitoring
claimsVsReality.reality: The threat actor remained undetected within the network for 18 days (29 December 2022 to 16 January 2023) before the organisation received extortion emails

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation could protect employee data with baseline password protection
claimsVsReality.reality: Storing bank account numbers, salary information, NRIC numbers and addresses required additional access controls beyond password protection, which the organisation failed to implement

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal and other risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication for administrator and non-administrative accounts with access to personal data
violations: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication for administrator and non-administrative accounts with access to personal data
Granted excessive local administrator rights enabling unauthorised software installation without detection
Stored sensitive personal data (bank account numbers, salary information, NRIC numbers) on unsecured internal shared drives with inadequate access controls
Failed to implement network segmentation to restrict access based on user roles and need-to-know basis
Lacked tools to detect and remove unauthorised software downloads on company devices
Inadequate incident response and management controls allowing unauthorised access to remain undetected for 18 days

outcome: The organisation admitted to breaching the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA and was ordered to pay a financial penalty of $4,000 SGD within 30 days. The organisation implemented comprehensive remedial actions including: deployment of multi-factor authentication, forced password changes, endpoint protection on all workstations, enhanced firewall and web-filtering controls, network access logging and monthly reviews, regular service account validation, and host-checking for VPN access.
companyNow: Following the 2022 breach, Payroll2U implemented comprehensive remedial measures including multi-factor authentication, network segmentation, enhanced endpoint protection, and improved incident response capabilities.
dataType: Full name, bank account number, salary information, NRIC number, address, date of birth, email address

companyDescription: Blackbaud is a publicly traded cloud-based software-as-a-service company providing solutions for nonprofits, foundations, educational institutions, healthcare organizations, and other entities to manage operations and resources.
companyLongDescription: Blackbaud, founded in 1981, is a major SaaS provider serving over 45,000 customers across more than 100 countries with solutions for resource management, operations delivery, program management, and impact measurement. The company maintains sensitive personal information for its customers' constituents, including names, Social Security numbers, bank account information, and medical data. Despite claims of following industry-standard security practices, the company suffered a significant 2020 data breach affecting over 13,000 customers. Blackbaud is headquartered in Charleston, South Carolina and is a Delaware corporation.
caseDescription: Blackbaud, a cloud-based software company, suffered a 2020 data breach affecting over 13,000 customers including California residents. The company failed to implement reasonable security measures such as multi-factor authentication, network segmentation, and encryption, allowing a threat actor to access and exfiltrate sensitive personal data. Blackbaud further violated consumer protection laws by making false and misleading statements about its security practices both before and after the breach, initially denying that Social Security numbers and bank account information were compromised when it knew or should have known they were.
violationSummary: Blackbaud failed to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to protect personal information from unauthorized access, including inadequate password controls, lack of multi-factor authentication, poor network segmentation, unencrypted data storage, excessive data retention, and insufficient threat detection mechanisms. This insecurity enabled the data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Blackbaud failed to implement reasonable security measures including multi-factor authentication, network segmentation, encryption.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive personal information including Social Security numbers, bank account details, and medical records were stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud's security, privacy, and risk-management teams work every day to ensure the safety of customers' data by adhering to industry standard practices, conducting ongoing risk assessments, aggressively testing security, and continually assessing infrastructure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Blackbaud failed to implement multi-factor authentication, proper password controls, network segmentation, encryption for sensitive fields, adequate data retention policies, and threat detection systems, allowing a threat actor to access systems undetected for four months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud protects its databases with various physical, technical and procedural measures and restricts access to information by unauthorized persons.
claimsVsReality.reality: A threat actor gained entry using a compromised customer login without multi-factor authentication, escalated to administrator access due to lack of network segmentation, and moved across multiple environments to access unencrypted personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The threat actor did not access bank account information or Social Security numbers.
claimsVsReality.reality: By early August 2020, Blackbaud knew that bank account information and Social Security numbers had been exfiltrated, but continued making this false statement until late September 2020.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud follows industry-standard best practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Blackbaud lacked reasonable security procedures and practices to protect personal information from unauthorized access or disclosure, as evidenced by the successful breach and multiple critical security gaps.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.81.5(b) requires businesses to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of personal information and to protect it from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement password controls such as mandatory rotation and prohibition of default/weak passwords
violations: Failed to implement password controls such as mandatory rotation and prohibition of default/weak passwords
Failed to mandate multi-factor authentication as a security layer
Failed to implement appropriate network segmentation
Allowed personal information to be stored in unencrypted fields
Failed to implement adequate inventory processes to detect unencrypted personal information
Retained customer data longer than necessary without implementing data minimization principles
Failed to implement appropriate threat and intrusion detection processes

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17500 prohibits untrue or misleading statements made with intent to induce use of products or services when the maker knew or should have known the statements were untrue or misleading
regulatoryFindings.description: Falsely represented that security, privacy, and risk-management teams adhered to industry standard practices
violations: Falsely represented that security, privacy, and risk-management teams adhered to industry standard practices
Falsely stated in initial breach notification that threat actor did not access bank account information or Social Security numbers when such access had occurred
Continued making false representations about data not being compromised for over two months after learning the truth
Falsely claimed to follow industry-standard best practices despite lacking reasonable security measures

outcome: This is a complaint filing seeking injunctive relief, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation of Business and Professions Code §§ 17200 and 17500, recovery of investigation costs, and such other relief as the court determines just and proper. The complaint does not yet represent a final resolution but rather the initiation of litigation by the California Attorney General against Blackbaud.
companyNow: Blackbaud remains a major SaaS provider but faces ongoing scrutiny regarding data security practices and has faced multiple regulatory actions related to the 2020 breach and subsequent statements about the incident.
dataType: Social Security numbers, bank account information, medical information, names
legalBasisViolated: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 (Unfair Competition Law)
California Business and Professions Code § 17500 (False Advertising Law)
California Civil Code § 1798.81.5(b) (reasonable security procedures requirement)

companyDescription: Tilting Point Media is a mobile gaming publisher and developer known for creating and publishing games featuring popular licensed characters. The company operates games directed at children, including titles featuring SpongeBob SquarePants.
companyLongDescription: Tilting Point Media LLC is a Delaware-based mobile gaming company that develops and publishes games for iOS and Android platforms. The company is known for publishing games featuring licensed intellectual property characters popular with younger audiences, including SpongeBob SquarePants. Tilting Point Media integrates third-party software development kits (SDKs) into its games to monetize user data. The company faced enforcement action for systematically violating children's privacy laws by collecting and selling personal information from underage players without adequate parental consent.
caseDescription: Tilting Point Media violated COPPA and CCPA by collecting personal information from children under 13 and teens aged 13-15 without proper parental consent, failing to provide adequate notice, and selling/sharing children's data through software development kits (SDKs) in games featuring SpongeBob SquarePants and other apps directed to children.
violationSummary: The company engaged in systematic collection of personal information from children through passive tracking, SDKs, and behavioral monitoring in apps directed to or accessible by children, without adequate parental consent or notice mechanisms.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Tilting Point Media collected personal information from children under 13 and teens aged 13-15 in games without proper parental consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children's personal data was monetized and shared with advertisers and data brokers without parents' knowledge or permission, exposing minors to targeted tracking.

claimsVsReality.claim: Games directed to children can collect and monetize personal data through SDKs without specific parental consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: COPPA and CCPA prohibit collecting or selling children's data without verifiable parental consent and clear notice of data sharing practices.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tilting Point Media obtained adequate parental consent for data collection and sales in its children's games.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to provide direct notice to parents about data collection practices and did not obtain verifiable parental consent before sharing children's data with third parties.

claimsVsReality.claim: Generic privacy policies adequately disclosed SDK data sharing practices to parents of child players.
claimsVsReality.reality: Tilting Point Media's privacy policies failed to clearly identify the categories of SDKs, the specific personal information shared through them, or the third parties receiving children's data.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA requires direct notice to parents, clear and conspicuous privacy policy links, and verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children
violations: Failed to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children
Failed to provide direct notice to parents of collection, use, and disclosure practices
Failed to post clear and conspicuous privacy policy links on apps and websites directed to children
Collected more personal information than necessary from children to participate in activities

regulatoryFindings.act: CCPA prohibits sale or sharing of personal information of consumers under 16 without proper authorization and notice
regulatoryFindings.description: Sold and shared personal information of children under 13 and teens aged 13-15 through SDKs without proper consent
violations: Sold and shared personal information of children under 13 and teens aged 13-15 through SDKs without proper consent
Failed to provide just-in-time notice explaining data collection, purposes, and sales/sharing
Failed to obtain affirmative opt-in authorization from parents for children under 13

companyLongDescription: RivX Automation Corp., based in Doral, Florida, was the primary vehicle for a coordinated fraud scheme operated by Antonio Rivodo (Founder/CEO) and Noah Wooten (Vice President). The enterprise used multiple interrelated LLC and corporate entities to market and sell fake trucking automation business opportunities to consumers nationwide. Defendants falsely promised that consumers investing $75,000-$85,000+ would receive trucks, logistics management, load booking services, and $5,000-$7,000 monthly passive income, with full investment recovery within 12-24 months. In reality, consumers received neither trucks nor promised earnings, losing their entire investments while operators extracted millions in profits and used non-disparagement clauses to silence complaints.
caseDescription: RivX engaged in a multi-year scheme to defraud consumers by falsely promising $5,000-$7,000 monthly passive income through trucking business opportunities in exchange for $75,000-$85,000+ investments. Consumers rarely received promised trucks or income and lost their entire investments. Defendants made millions in profits while failing to disclose required information and using non-disparagement clauses to silence complaints.

caseDescription: L.A.D.H Limited, a financial services company, sent 31,329 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages between March and April 2022 promoting debt advice services without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients. The company relied on verbal assurances from a third-party data supplier rather than written confirmation that recipients had opted in, and most messages lacked opt-out mechanisms. The company failed to cooperate with the ICO's investigation.
violationSummary: Company conducted direct marketing surveillance by sending unsolicited messages to individuals who had not consented, and failed to establish proper consent mechanisms or respect individuals' right to refuse.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between March and April 2022, L.A.D.H Limited transmitted 31,329 unsolicited SMS marketing messages promoting debt consolidation services to mobile subscribers without obtaining valid prior.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 106 individuals complained about receiving unwanted debt marketing texts; recipients had never agreed to receive these messages.

claimsVsReality.reality: LADH remained active on Companies House and was sending marketing SMS at scale (49,938 messages) between March and April 2022

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A DPA 1998 authorises monetary penalties for serious contraventions of PECR where the contravention was deliberate or where the organisation knew or ought to have known of the risk but failed to take reasonable steps.
regulatoryFindings.description: Contravention was serious: 31,329 messages delivered, 106 complaints, high weekly volumes in short period
violations: Contravention was serious: 31,329 messages delivered, 106 complaints, high weekly volumes in short period

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £50,000 (reducible to £40,000 with early payment by 12 February 2024). LADH was required to pay by 13 February 2024. The penalty was issued under Section 55A of the Data Protection Act 1998 for serious contraventions of PECR Regulations 22 and 23. LADH has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The company is subject to monitoring and compliance expectations under PECR.
companyNow: L.A.D.H Limited remains registered at Companies House (Company Number 12065159) with its registered office at Oak House Beal Lane, Shaw, Oldham. caseDescription: BBVA bank branch employee forged customer signatures on data protection documents without consent, falsely marking consent boxes for marketing and profiling. The bank acknowledged the isolated procedural breach and agreed to preventive measures. BBVA paid a reduced penalty of €120,000 after recognizing responsibility.
violationSummary: The failure to obtain genuine, informed consent through proper signature procedures represents a breakdown in data controller security and procedural integrity, exposing personal data to unauthorized processing.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A BBVA bank employee forged customer signatures on data protection documents and pre-marked consent boxes for commercial data use and profiling without customer knowledge or authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' personal data was unlawfully processed for marketing and profiling without their genuine consent, exposing them to unwanted commercial communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employee said falsifying customer signatures to expedite loan mortgage documentation 'is something we usually do normally' (routine practice).
claimsVsReality.reality: BBVA's own investigation concluded this was an isolated, unauthorized violation of established document signature procedures by a single branch employee.

claimsVsReality.claim: BBVA stated it 'always acted with maximum diligence and respect for data protection regulations' in its relationship with the complainant.
claimsVsReality.reality: BBVA did not enforce its own signature procedures; the employee violated documented protocols and customers' signatures were forged without knowledge or authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) establishes that processing of personal data is lawful only if at least one specified condition (including explicit informed consent) is met.
regulatoryFindings.description: BBVA processed personal data of the complainant and spouse without valid consent basis because signatures on consent documents were forged by branch staff, rendering purported consent invalid.
violations: BBVA processed personal data of the complainant and spouse without valid consent basis because signatures on consent documents were forged by branch staff, rendering purported consent invalid.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires processing to be lawful, fair, and transparent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Processing was neither transparent nor fair; customers did not authorize their signatures and were unaware their personal data was being processed for commercial and profiling purposes.
violations: Processing was neither transparent nor fair; customers did not authorize their signatures and were unaware their personal data was being processed for commercial and profiling purposes.

outcome: BBVA acknowledged responsibility and paid €120,000 (40% reduction from initial €200,000 for prompt payment and admission). The bank implemented corrective measures including staff retraining videos distributed to 12,617 commercial banking employees and 2,602 central service staff, annual quality audits of tablet signatures (750 reviews/month), office visits to ~1,000 branches annually, and internal audit procedures. Procedure investigated by Internal Audit; findings elevated to Discipline Committee. Mandatory awareness notices issued in March 2024 and planned for May 2024. The enforcement action terminated on 17 December 2024.
companyNow: BBVA remains one of Spain's largest banking groups. Founded in 1900 and headquartered in Spain, it continues to operate as a major financial institution serving retail and commercial customers.

companyLongDescription: Southend on Sea City Council is a local government authority responsible for providing public services to residents of Southend-on-Sea in Essex, England. The Council handles significant volumes of personal data in its employment, benefits, and service delivery functions.
caseDescription: Southend on Sea City Council disclosed a spreadsheet containing hidden personal data of over 2,000 employees, former employees, and associated individuals in response to a Freedom of Information request. The hidden data included special category data and sensitive employment information. The breach resulted from lack of staff training on Excel security tools, specifically the 'Inspect Document' function.
violationSummary: Personal and special category data was exposed to the public via the WDTK website due to failure to detect hidden data in Excel files before release, creating increased accessibility of sensitive information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Southend on Sea City Council released an Excel spreadsheet containing hidden personal data in response to a Freedom of Information request.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 2,000 council employees, former employees, and associated individuals had their special category data including health information, ethnicity, contact details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Council conducted a two-person review of the spreadsheet before releasing it to WDTK, suggesting adequate checking procedures were in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite two staff members reviewing the document, the hidden personal data was not detected, indicating the review process lacked technical knowledge of Excel security tools and was therefore inadequate.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Council had 'generally satisfactory' data protection training for staff.
claimsVsReality.reality: While general data protection training was adequate, specialist training on the tools actually used (Excel) was severely lacking, preventing staff from identifying or preventing hidden data exposure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage using appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: The Council failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data by releasing Excel spreadsheets containing hidden personal data without using available 'Inspect Document' tools
violations: The Council failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data by releasing Excel spreadsheets containing hidden personal data without using available 'Inspect Document' tools
Staff were not trained or made aware of Excel security functions despite the Council processing substantial amounts of personal data
Two-person manual review process was insufficient and did not identify hidden data, demonstrating lack of proper technical safeguards

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to Southend on Sea City Council under Article 58(2)(b) of UK GDPR. The Council was directed to implement remedial measures including: updated FOI policy to avoid Excel spreadsheet disclosure where possible; mandatory use of 'Inspect Document' function when Excel documents must be shared; comprehensive staff training on Excel tools; and ongoing monitoring. The Council cooperated fully, contacted all affected data subjects, and implemented its Data Security Incident Management Procedure. No evidence was found of the data being republished or misused.
companyNow: Southend on Sea City Council continues to operate as a local government authority in Essex, England. Following this enforcement action, the Council has implemented enhanced data protection procedures and staff training protocols.

caseDescription: DELPASO failed to respond to a data subject's access request for nearly one year, only complying after intervention by the Spanish Data Protection Authority. The company initially refused to disclose personal data held about the complainant and did not properly address the legally-mandated four certified access requests sent to multiple company email addresses.
violationSummary: DELPASO denied the data subject's right to access their personal data and failed to provide a timely response to legally-mandated access requests under GDPR Article 15, effectively excluding them from knowledge of their own personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection

whatTheyDid: DELPASO Car Hire failed to respond to a customer's certified request for access to their personal data for nearly one year.
whyTheyWereWrong: A customer was denied knowledge of what personal information the company held about them for 11 months, leaving them unable to verify accuracy of their name, address, phone, email, ID.

claimsVsReality.claim: DELPASO claimed the access request was sent to email address ***EMAIL.2, which corresponds to a wholesaler intermediary, not to DELPASO itself, and that it only learned of the request via the AEPD requerimiento.

claimsVsReality.claim: DELPASO stated in its initial response that the information was confidential for internal use only and could not be disclosed to the customer.

DELPASO refused to disclose information about what personal data it held, initially claiming it was confidential for internal use only
Only after AEPD intervention on 24 March 2023 did DELPASO provide a response, nearly 11 months after the initial request

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72(1)(k) classifies as a very serious infraction any impediment, obstruction, or repeated failure to attend to the exercise of data subject rights under GDPR Articles 15-22, prescribing within three years.
regulatoryFindings.description: DELPASO's failure to respond to the access request for 11 months constituted an obstruction of the data subject's statutory right
violations: DELPASO's failure to respond to the access request for 11 months constituted an obstruction of the data subject's statutory right
The company ignored certified communications to multiple official email addresses listed in its own privacy policy

outcome: DELPASO paid €1,200 (the proposed €2,000 fine reduced by 20% for voluntary payment plus 20% for recognition of responsibility) on 24 April 2024, within the hearing period. Payment terminated the procedure. The company acknowledged its infraction and waived any right to administrative appeal. The resolution confirms the company must comply with GDPR Article 15 in all future access requests.
companyNow: DELPASO Car Hire is a Spanish car rental company with operations across multiple EU countries. The company is listed as an active subsidiary in Spain but no current financial data is publicly available.
dataType: Name, address, telephone, email, national ID number, driving license, birth country, birth date, rental history
legalBasisViolated: LOPDGDD Article 72(1)(k) (obstruction of data subject rights)

companyDescription: WerepairUK Ltd offers repair services for household white goods and service/maintenance plans for home appliances. The company was incorporated on 2 July 2019 and is registered in Tonbridge, UK.
companyLongDescription: WerepairUK Ltd offers repair services for household white goods and service/maintenance plans for home appliances. The company was incorporated on 2 July 2019 and is registered in Tonbridge, UK.
caseDescription: WerepairUK Ltd made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between September 2022 and May 2023, violating UK privacy regulations. The company failed to obtain valid consent from recipients and did not cooperate with the ICO investigation. The Commissioner found the contravention was deliberate due to lack of cooperation and false claims about consent.
violationSummary: WRUK systematically called individuals who had explicitly opted out of unsolicited marketing, violating their fundamental privacy right to refuse unwanted communications. The high volume and deliberate targeting of TPS-registered numbers constitutes systematic surveillance-like collection of consumer attention.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: WerepairUK made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls between September 2022 and May 2023 to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers who had explicitly registered with TPS to stop unwanted marketing calls were repeatedly contacted anyway.

claimsVsReality.claim: Both complainants supplied their contact details via door-to-door canvassers working for WRUK and consented to direct marketing calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: One complainant stated they had lived at their address 30 years, could not recall any unsolicited tradesman visit, and explicitly stated 'I believe this company is lying.' No documentary evidence of canvassing, consent forms, or opt-in records was ever provided by WRUK.

claimsVsReality.claim: WRUK did not recognise the telephone numbers listed in the complaint (CLI 02034758929 and related numbers).
claimsVsReality.reality: Telecoms provider confirmed on 13 February 2023 that CLI 02034758929 and the range 02034758920-02034758925 were allocated to WRUK, and call detail records proved WRUK made 49,833 calls from these numbers.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits use of public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers listed on the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: WRUK made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered on the TPS for more than 28 days, without obtaining valid prior notification that recipients did not object to receiving such calls.
violations: WRUK made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered on the TPS for more than 28 days, without obtaining valid prior notification that recipients did not object to receiving such calls.
Company failed to obtain clear, positive consent from individuals overriding their TPS registration, as required by Regulation 21(4).

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A permits monetary penalties for serious contraventions where the breach is either deliberate or the organisation knew/ought to have known of the risk but failed to take reasonable steps.
regulatoryFindings.description: Contravention was deliberate: WRUK made false and misleading statements to the ICO about consent source, claimed door-to-door canvassing without evidence, and failed to cooperate substantively with the investigation.
violations: Contravention was deliberate: WRUK made false and misleading statements to the ICO about consent source, claimed door-to-door canvassing without evidence, and failed to cooperate substantively with the investigation.

Alternatively, contravention was negligent: WRUK knew/ought to have known of the risk (ICO guidance and registration were available), and failed to take reasonable steps such as cleansing contact lists against TPS register or verifying third-party consent claims.

outcome: WerepairUK Ltd was issued a Monetary Penalty Notice of £80,000 (reducible to £64,000 with early payment by 18 October 2024). The company must pay by 19 October 2024. The penalty is payable to the Consolidated Fund (UK Government account). There is a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. Enforcement action will be taken if payment is not received after all appeal periods expire.
companyNow: WerepairUK Ltd (Companies House 12080599) remains registered. Director Connor Budden is also listed director of Home Care Protect Ltd, Southern Plumbing Drainage & Water UK Limited, and Southern Drainage Assist Limited, suggesting potential pattern of multi-company operations in similar sectors.
dataType: Telephone numbers, names, personal contact details

companyDescription: Charnwood Borough Council is a local government authority serving the Borough of Charnwood in Leicestershire, England. It provides statutory services including housing, social services, and local planning to members of the public, many of whom are vulnerable individuals.
companyLongDescription: Charnwood Borough Council is a local government authority serving the Borough of Charnwood in Leicestershire, England. It provides statutory services including housing, social services, and local planning to members of the public, many of whom are vulnerable individuals.
caseDescription: Charnwood Borough Council disclosed a domestic abuse survivor's new address to her ex-partner through a procedural failure. The Council failed to implement a clear written process for address changes, did not flag the case as involving a vulnerable person requiring heightened vigilance, and did not ensure staff received recent data protection training. This violated the data security and integrity principles of UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f).
violationSummary: The Council disclosed sensitive personal data (address) of a vulnerable individual to an unauthorized third party (ex-partner) due to procedural failure and lack of appropriate security measures, fitting the Disclosure category.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Charnwood Borough Council failed to properly update a domestic abuse survivor's address in its system.
whyTheyWereWrong: A domestic abuse survivor's confidential new address was exposed to her abuser, causing significant distress.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data subject's new address had been successfully updated on the system.
claimsVsReality.reality: The address was only added to case notes; the address field was never updated, and the data subject was not informed she would need to update her online application herself.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Council was not aware that the data subject required heightened data protection due to domestic abuse allegations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data subject had explicitly informed the Council of domestic abuse allegations made against her ex-partner during the call to report her address change.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires personal data to be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: Charnwood failed to implement a clear written process for address changes that staff must follow
violations: Charnwood failed to implement a clear written process for address changes that staff must follow
No alert system flagged the case to indicate heightened vigilance required for vulnerable service users
Staff involved in the incident had not received data protection training in the 12 months prior
The address was added to case notes instead of the proper address field, bypassing system safeguards
The new address was disclosed to an unauthorized third party via correspondence sent to a shared old address

outcome: Charnwood Borough Council was issued a formal reprimand. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps already undertaken and those planned in the Council's Action Plan. The Commissioner recommended three compliance actions: (1) full implementation of all stated remedial measures as soon as possible, including a letter creation feature with automatic address population, an alert system for vulnerable service users, and revised letter templates; (2) provision of regular refresher data protection training for all staff; and (3) robust guidance and training for all staff dealing with vulnerable service users. No monetary penalty was issued.
companyNow: Charnwood Borough Council continues to operate as a local authority in Leicestershire. The Council is implementing recommendations to strengthen data protection safeguards and staff training.
dataType: Address, household information, vulnerable person indicators

companyDescription: Pinnacle Life Limited is a financial services/insurance company registered in England (Wigan, Lancashire) involved in direct marketing of life and financial products by telephone.
companyLongDescription: Pinnacle Life Limited is a financial services/insurance company registered in England (Wigan, Lancashire) involved in direct marketing of life and financial products by telephone.
caseDescription: Pinnacle Life Limited made at least 47,998 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) without their explicit consent between May 2021 and May 2022. The company violated PECR Regulation 21 by calling TPS-registered numbers and failed to provide required caller identification information. The ICO issued an enforcement notice requiring compliance within 30 days.
violationSummary: The company systematically surveilled and called individuals who had taken affirmative action to opt out of marketing calls by registering with TPS, representing surveillance-like collection activity despite their explicit refusal.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between May 2021 and May 2022, Pinnacle Life Limited made at least 47,998 unsolicited direct marketing calls to phone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of individuals who had registered their numbers to opt out of marketing calls received unwanted calls anyway, exposing them to harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pinnacle could make unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers if subscribers had consented
claimsVsReality.reality: Pinnacle provided zero evidence of valid consent from the complainants; consent must be clear, positive, specific to that company, and must explicitly address willingness to receive telephone marketing

claimsVsReality.claim: Standard opt-in to marketing communications satisfies PECR consent requirements
claimsVsReality.reality: Individuals must take clear and positive action specific to that company; generic opt-ins to receive marketing from 'partners' or 'similar organisations' do not override TPS registration

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits use or instigation of unsolicited calls for direct marketing to numbers listed in the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: Pinnacle instigated minimum 47,998 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers between May 2021–May 2022
violations: Pinnacle instigated minimum 47,998 unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers between May 2021–May 2022
Calls were made without evidence that subscribers had notified Pinnacle of willingness to receive such calls
No clear, positive action by individuals to override TPS registration was demonstrated by Pinnacle

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(2) requires that direct marketing calls provide the name of the caller and address or free telephone number on request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Pinnacle failed to provide required caller identification particulars to call recipients
violations: Pinnacle failed to provide required caller identification particulars to call recipients

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) permits calls to TPS-registered numbers only where the subscriber has notified the caller they do not object, via clear and positive action specific to that company.
regulatoryFindings.description: Pinnacle provided no evidence of valid consent from complainants
violations: Pinnacle provided no evidence of valid consent from complainants
Notifications must be specific to Pinnacle; generic opt-ins to 'similar organisations' or 'partners' are insufficient

outcome: The ICO issued an enforcement notice on 15 February 2024 requiring Pinnacle Life Limited to cease making unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers and to individuals who previously requested no calls within 30 days. Pinnacle must also ensure all future direct marketing calls include caller identification. The company has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The Commissioner determined no monetary damage was likely in this instance but required compliance to protect future recipients.
companyNow: Unknown. Pinnacle Life Limited (Companies House Reg. 11896017) continues to operate but is now subject to this enforcement notice and monitoring by the ICO.
dataType: telephone numbers, personal contact information
legalBasisViolated: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) – Unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
PECR Regulation 24(2) – Failure to provide caller identification
Data Protection Act 1998 Section 40(1)(a) – Enforcement provisions

company: UNIQLO EUROPE, LTD, SUCURSAL EN ESPAÑA
companyDescription: UNIQLO is a Japanese multinational fast-fashion retailer and subsidiary of Fast Retailing Group, operating thousands of stores worldwide with significant employee bases in multiple countries.
companyLongDescription: UNIQLO is a Japanese multinational fast-fashion retailer and subsidiary of Fast Retailing Group, operating thousands of stores worldwide with significant employee bases in multiple countries.
caseDescription: UNIQLO sent an HR employee's entire payroll file containing 447 employees' personal and financial data to an unauthorized recipient via unencrypted email due to human error. The company failed to implement adequate security measures and did not report the breach to authorities until notified of a complaint months later.
violationSummary: The breach involved unauthorized access to and transmission of confidential personal and financial data of 447 employees through negligent use of unsecured email, resulting in loss of confidentiality and integrity of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: An HR employee sent an unencrypted PDF containing payroll information for 447 workers—including names, national IDs, Social Security numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 447 employees faced direct exposure to identity theft, account fraud, and phishing attacks because their financial.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had internal information security protocols and policies in place (ISO portal, incident reporting procedures, data protection handbook).
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite documented policies, the HR employee did not follow internal procedures, was not trained adequately on practical application of protocols, and did not report the incident to management or security teams.

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach was caused solely by human error of one employee who violated internal processes.
claimsVsReality.reality: While human error was the immediate cause, the company's organizational failures in implementing adequate technical controls (unencrypted email, no file-level access restrictions), lack of effective monitoring, and inadequate employee training allowed the breach to go undetected for 8 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: No evidence of data exfiltration or unauthorized use was detected.
claimsVsReality.reality: Although threat intelligence monitoring found no evidence of published data, the exposure occurred via unencrypted transmission and the recipient (a former employee) could have retained or misused the data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in such a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: UNIQLO failed to ensure confidentiality and integrity of employee personal data by sending sensitive payroll information (447 workers' names, national IDs, Social Security numbers, bank accounts, salaries) via unencrypted email to an unauthorized recipient.
violations: UNIQLO failed to ensure confidentiality and integrity of employee personal data by sending sensitive payroll information (447 workers' names, national IDs, Social Security numbers, bank accounts, salaries) via unencrypted email to an unauthorized recipient.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires that the controller and processor apply appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including inter alia encryption, capacity to ensure confidentiality and integrity, and regular verification of measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: UNIQLO did not implement appropriate technical measures (encryption, access controls) or organizational procedures (verification processes, incident reporting protocols) for payroll data management, allowing an HR employee to accidentally send unencrypted files containing sensitive data of all employees.
violations: UNIQLO did not implement appropriate technical measures (encryption, access controls) or organizational procedures (verification processes, incident reporting protocols) for payroll data management, allowing an HR employee to accidentally send unencrypted files containing sensitive data of all employees.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33 requires the controller to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and in any case not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it.
regulatoryFindings.description: UNIQLO did not discover or report the breach that occurred on 8 August 2022 until receiving notification from the Data Protection Authority in April 2023, a delay of approximately 8 months due to failure of the HR employee to report the incident.
violations: UNIQLO did not discover or report the breach that occurred on 8 August 2022 until receiving notification from the Data Protection Authority in April 2023, a delay of approximately 8 months due to failure of the HR employee to report the incident.

outcome: UNIQLO paid €270,000 (representing a 40% reduction from the proposed €450,000 penalty: 20% for voluntary payment + 20% for early acknowledgment of responsibility). The company was ordered to adopt appropriate technical and organizational measures to guarantee security of employee personal data within 3 months. The company committed to enhanced security training, revised payroll transmission procedures (individualized rather than batch), and implementation of threat intelligence monitoring to detect data exfiltration.
companyNow: UNIQLO is a major Japanese fast-fashion retailer (Fast Retailing Group) with global operations. The company has reportedly implemented enhanced data security practices and employee training following this enforcement action.
dataType: Employee personal data including name, DNI/NIE, Social Security number, bank account number, salary information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of a Personal Data Breach

company: Central Young Men's Christian Association (Central YMCA)
companyDescription: Central YMCA is an education and wellbeing charity that provides community programmes, including the Positive Health Programme, an exercise scheme for people living with HIV run as part of YMCA Club.
companyLongDescription: Central YMCA is an education and wellbeing charity that provides community programmes, including the Positive Health Programme, an exercise scheme for people living with HIV run as part of YMCA Club.
caseDescription: On 6 October 2022, a coordinator at Central YMCA sent a nutrition talk invitation to 270 recipients using the CC function instead of BCC, exposing 264 unique email addresses to all recipients. 166 data subjects were affected, and recipients could reasonably infer that the disclosed individuals were living with HIV, making this special category health data. The organisation lacked written security policies, adequate training, and technical safeguards despite having access to secure email marketing tools.
violationSummary: Unintended disclosure of personal data (email addresses) and inferred health data to unauthorised recipients due to inadequate security controls and staff error.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A programme coordinator sent an email to 270 recipients using CC instead of BCC, exposing 264 email addresses to all recipients, including a recall email the next day.
whyTheyWereWrong: 166 individuals' email addresses were disclosed, revealing they were participants in an HIV exercise programme, exposing their health status and sensitive personal information to strangers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Central YMCA had policies in place to protect email communications and data security.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only a verbal policy to use BCC existed; no written information security policies or procedures were documented. Mandatory data protection training was not being monitored or enforced.

claimsVsReality.claim: Central YMCA did not have the means to implement secure email communication tools.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Communications and Marketing team within the same organisation already used BrotherMailer, a secure email marketing tool that could send individual emails to each recipient. The organisation had the financial and organisational capacity but failed to deploy it in the Programme team.
