regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Central YMCA failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data by relying only on a verbal policy to use BCC in emails, which proved insufficient when a coordinator used CC instead.
violations: Central YMCA failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data by relying only on a verbal policy to use BCC in emails, which proved insufficient when a coordinator used CC instead.

The organisation did not implement technical measures (such as BrotherMailer email marketing tool already available elsewhere in the organisation) that could have prevented disclosure of 166 individuals' email addresses and inferred health data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) and (2) of the UK GDPR require that the controller and processor implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs, nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Central YMCA lacked sufficient written information security policies and procedures to prevent the breach; only a verbal BCC policy existed.
violations: Central YMCA lacked sufficient written information security policies and procedures to prevent the breach; only a verbal BCC policy existed.

The organisation failed to provide role-specific data protection training of sufficient quality to staff handling special category data; the coordinator had not completed mandatory training prior to the breach.

Central YMCA had financial and organisational means to implement BrotherMailer (secure email tool used by its Communications and Marketing team) in the Programme team but failed to do so, despite processing sensitive health data.

outcome: Central YMCA accepted the Notice of Intent and the Commissioner's findings without representation. The ICO issued a reprimand and a monetary penalty of £7,500 (reduced from a considered £300,000 under ICO policy). Central YMCA implemented remedial measures including: notification to all 166 affected individuals; reporting to the ICO; conducting an organisational audit of external communications; issuing a new External Communications Procedure; and updating its data protection training programme. Incident was escalated to the Data Protection Officer and learnings were shared across the organisation.
companyNow: Central YMCA continues to operate as an education and wellbeing charity providing community programmes. Following the incident, it has strengthened its data protection governance, written email security procedures, and mandatory training requirements.
dataType: Email addresses, health data (HIV status inferred from context)
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 32(1) – Technical and organisational measures
UK GDPR Article 32(2) – Risk assessment for security

company: Birmingham Children's Trust Community Interest Company
companyDescription: Birmingham Children's Trust Community Interest Company (BCTCIC) is an independent organisation owned by Birmingham City Council that provides child protection and family support services in the Birmingham area. Its Child Protection & Review (CP&R) department, staffed primarily by trained social workers, manages child protection planning and intervention for at-risk families.
companyLongDescription: Birmingham Children's Trust Community Interest Company (BCTCIC) is an independent organisation owned by Birmingham City Council that provides child protection and family support services in the Birmingham area. Its Child Protection & Review (CP&R) department, staffed primarily by trained social workers, manages child protection planning and intervention for at-risk families.
caseDescription: BCTCIC's Child Protection & Review department inappropriately disclosed sensitive criminal allegations and identifying information about a child (Child X) in a Child Protection Plan sent to an unintended family. The breach occurred because the social worker copied content from a police strategy meeting into the document without proper security controls or independent review. The organization lacked adequate technical and organizational measures, granular data protection policies, and independent verification procedures to prevent unauthorized disclosure of highly sensitive information.
violationSummary: The organization breached the confidentiality of sensitive criminal data and children's personal data by disclosing it to an unauthorized third party (unintended family) due to inadequate security measures and lack of independent oversight mechanisms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A social worker retroactively accessed police strategy meeting minutes and copied criminal allegations about a child into a Child Protection Plan sent to an unrelated family without independent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Serious criminal allegations and identifying information about a minor were disclosed to neighboring family A, exposing child X to risks of vigilantism, physical harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: BCTCIC's Social Work England professional standards and general data protection training provided adequate data protection expertise for safe processing of sensitive children's and criminal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Social Work England standards are not designed specifically for data protection compliance and cannot substitute for granular, role-specific operational procedures, redaction protocols, and independent review mechanisms required to prevent unauthorized disclosure of sensitive information.

claimsVsReality.claim: BCTCIC's Initial Child Protection Process Map and Quality Assurance Checklist provided sufficient practical guidance to prevent inappropriate disclosure of data in Child Protection Plans.
claimsVsReality.reality: These documents designated responsibility for screening but provided no practical guidance on what data is inappropriate for release, how to redact it, or how to verify compliance—resulting in serious criminal allegations against a minor being disclosed to an unintended family.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: BCTCIC failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect sensitive criminal data and children's personal data, resulting in unauthorised disclosure to an unintended family
violations: BCTCIC failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect sensitive criminal data and children's personal data, resulting in unauthorised disclosure to an unintended family

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: BCTCIC lacked secondary/independent review procedures, corporate redaction policies, and practical guidance on identifying and screening inappropriate data for disclosure, allowing criminal allegations against a child to be included in document sent to wrong family
violations: BCTCIC lacked secondary/independent review procedures, corporate redaction policies, and practical guidance on identifying and screening inappropriate data for disclosure, allowing criminal allegations against a child to be included in document sent to wrong family

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 32(2) requires that in assessing the appropriate level of security, account shall be taken of the risks presented by processing, including risks from accidental or unlawful disclosure of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: BCTCIC failed to conduct adequate risk assessment of its Child Protection Plan disclosure process; social worker was permitted to copy-paste content from police strategy meeting without verification, increasing risk of inadvertent disclosure of sensitive criminal data
violations: BCTCIC failed to conduct adequate risk assessment of its Child Protection Plan disclosure process; social worker was permitted to copy-paste content from police strategy meeting without verification, increasing risk of inadvertent disclosure of sensitive criminal data

outcome: ICO issued a formal reprimand to BCTCIC under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR for infringements of Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1)(b), and 32(2). BCTCIC has undertaken remedial measures including: immediate recovery of the breached CP plan from the unintended recipient; notification to affected families; revised CP plan template with optional 'confidential' sections and dual-output capability (with/without confidential information); system updates requiring staff to confirm whether information needs withholding; and comprehensive review of all related case files. The ICO issued non-binding recommendations for BCTCIC to implement granular Standard Operating Procedures, corporate redaction policies, independent document review processes, and role-specific data protection training. Compliance monitoring and feedback expected within six months.
companyNow: Birmingham Children's Trust Community Interest Company continues to operate as an independent data controller owned by Birmingham City Council, delivering child protection services in the Birmingham area. The organisation has implemented significant governance and system reforms following the ICO enforcement action.
dataType: Children's personal data, criminal offence data, identifying information
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Art. 32(1)(b) – Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability and Resilience
UK GDPR Art. 32(2) – Assessment of Processing Risks

companyDescription: Blackbaud, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing data services and financial, fundraising, and administrative software services to more than 45,000 companies, nonprofits, foundations, educational institutions, healthcare organizations, and individual consumers in the U.S. and abroad. The company generated approximately $1.1 billion in annual revenues as of 2022.
companyLongDescription: Blackbaud, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing data services and financial, fundraising, and administrative software services to more than 45,000 companies, nonprofits, foundations, educational institutions, healthcare organizations, and individual consumers in the U.S. and abroad. The company generated approximately $1.1 billion in annual revenues as of 2022.
caseDescription: Blackbaud failed to implement reasonable information security practices, allowing attackers to access customer databases containing personal information of millions of consumers for over three months undetected. The company then misrepresented the scope of the breach in initial customer notifications and failed to implement proper data retention policies. Blackbaud ultimately agreed to a comprehensive consent order requiring substantial security improvements, data deletion, third-party assessments, and ongoing compliance monitoring for 20 years.
violationSummary: The core violation was Blackbaud's failure to implement reasonable safeguards (encryption, access controls, monitoring, patch management, network segmentation) to protect sensitive personal information in its custody, resulting in unauthorized access and data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Blackbaud failed to implement basic security controls including weak password policies, lack of multi-factor authentication, unencrypted sensitive fields, unpatched legacy systems.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of consumers' highly sensitive personal data including Social Security numbers, bank account information, medical records, and religious beliefs were stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud stated in its July 2020 breach notification: 'The cybercriminal did not access credit card information, bank account information, or social security numbers.'
claimsVsReality.reality: By July 31, 2020, Blackbaud's own investigation confirmed the attacker had exfiltrated consumers' bank account numbers and social security numbers, which the company did not disclose to customers until October 2020.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud stated in its July 2020 notification: 'No action is required on your end because no personal information about your constituents was accessed.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Millions of consumers' highly sensitive personal information including SSNs, financial data, medical records, religious beliefs, and employment information had been exfiltrated by the attacker.

claimsVsReality.claim: Blackbaud's Privacy Policy (December 17, 2019) stated: 'We maintain appropriate physical, electronic and procedural safeguards to protect your personal information...Inside Blackbaud, data is stored in password-controlled servers with limited access.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Blackbaud failed to implement appropriate password controls, did not require multi-factor authentication, allowed sensitive data to be stored in unencrypted fields, did not encrypt backup files, lacked proper monitoring and logging, and failed to implement network segmentation—enabling an attacker to freely move across systems for over three months undetected.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Blackbaud failed to take reasonable steps to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive consumer data maintained on its network by employing weak passwords, not requiring multi-factor authentication, failing to encrypt sensitive fields and backup files, not monitoring for data exfiltration, and failing to implement network segmentation.
violations: Blackbaud failed to take reasonable steps to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive consumer data maintained on its network by employing weak passwords, not requiring multi-factor authentication, failing to encrypt sensitive fields and backup files, not monitoring for data exfiltration, and failing to implement network segmentation.

Blackbaud failed to implement and enforce reasonable data retention practices, retaining consumer data for years longer than necessary, including data of former customers, customers who switched products, and even potential customers.

Blackbaud misrepresented the scope and severity of the breach in its July 2020 customer notification, falsely stating that credit card information, bank account information, and social security numbers were not accessed when the company knew by July 31, 2020 that these data types had been exfiltrated.

Blackbaud made explicit representations in its Privacy Policy (December 17, 2019) about maintaining appropriate safeguards to protect personal information when in fact it did not maintain reasonable information security practices.

outcome: Blackbaud agreed to a 20-year consent order requiring: (1) prohibition on misrepresentations about data protection practices; (2) deletion of unnecessary customer backup files within 90 days; (3) implementation of publicly documented data retention schedules with defined deletion timeframes; (4) establishment and maintenance of a comprehensive information security program within 90 days with specific requirements including strong passwords, multi-factor authentication for employees and customers, encryption of sensitive fields, continuous monitoring and logging, intrusion detection, file integrity monitoring, data loss prevention, properly configured firewalls, network segmentation, regular risk assessments, vulnerability scanning, and penetration testing; (5) annual risk assessments and security testing; (6) service provider oversight; (7) third-party security assessments (initial assessment within 180 days, then biennial assessments for 20 years); (8) annual CISO certifications to the FTC; (9) Covered Incident reporting within 10 days of notification to government entities; (10) Order acknowledgement and delivery to relevant personnel; (11) annual compliance reporting and updates on changes; and (12) recordkeeping for compliance demonstration. Delayed Update Customers have extended implementation timelines but must receive multi-factor authentication updates. The order is effective May 17, 2024 and terminates 20 years from issuance or from the most recent federal complaint alleging violations, whichever is later.
companyNow: Blackbaud remains operational as a Delaware corporation with principal place of business in Charleston, South Carolina. The company is subject to ongoing FTC monitoring and third-party security assessments through at least 2044.
dataType: Full names, age, date of birth, social security numbers, home addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, financial information (bank account, credit card, debit card, estimated wealth), medical information (patient/medical record identifiers, physician names, health insurance, visit dates, treatment reasons), gender, religious beliefs, marital status, spouse names, employment information (salary), educational information, account credentials
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair and Deceptive Acts or Practices
FTC Act Section 5(n) – Unfair Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Caja Rural de Asturias, S.C.C. is a cooperative credit bank in Spain providing retail and commercial banking services, including online banking (electronic banking services) to thousands of customers. It had annual gross margin of €118.7 million in 2022.
companyLongDescription: Caja Rural de Asturias, S.C.C. is a cooperative credit bank in Spain providing retail and commercial banking services, including online banking (electronic banking services) to thousands of customers. It had annual gross margin of €118.7 million in 2022.
caseDescription: Caja Rural de Asturias failed to implement adequate security measures to protect customer data, resulting in a cyberattack that exposed personal and financial information of clients. The bank did not encrypt sensitive data, monitor access controls, or implement multi-factor authentication despite handling thousands of customers' banking data. The responsible party was found to have violated the confidentiality principle of GDPR.
violationSummary: The bank failed to apply appropriate technical and organizational measures under GDPR Article 32 to guarantee confidentiality and integrity of personal data, resulting in a security breach (Article 5.1.f) where data was accessed without authorization.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures for its online banking system, allowing attackers to access customer data between November and December 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nine customers had their financial records including account numbers, balances, and personal data exposed to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had implemented adequate security measures and was certified in information security standards.
claimsVsReality.reality: Caja Rural lacked essential security controls (encryption, access controls, multi-factor authentication) for its online banking platform, and security certifications did not prevent the breach from occurring or being detected.

claimsVsReality.claim: The cyberattack could not have been prevented by additional security measures because attackers had legitimate credentials.
claimsVsReality.reality: The AEPD and the processor (RSI) both confirmed that additional security measures could have prevented the breach; the incident report explicitly stated the breach could have been avoided with implementation of further security controls.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank was not responsible because the breach occurred in systems managed by the processor (RSI).
claimsVsReality.reality: As the data controller, Caja Rural remained responsible for ensuring adequate security measures were implemented and maintained by its processor, regardless of who operated the systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be treated with integrity and confidentiality, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Caja Rural failed to implement encryption, access controls, or multi-factor authentication, allowing cybercriminals to access 9 customers' financial data (account numbers, balances) and personal information without authorization.
violations: Caja Rural failed to implement encryption, access controls, or multi-factor authentication, allowing cybercriminals to access 9 customers' financial data (account numbers, balances) and personal information without authorization.
The bank did not maintain adequate confidentiality of data, as evidenced by the successful breach that occurred on 10 November 2022 and was detected 7 December 2022.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security commensurate with risk, including capability to guarantee confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems, and capacity to restore availability and access to data rapidly in case of incident.
regulatoryFindings.description: Caja Rural failed to conduct adequate risk assessments and implement proportionate security measures despite handling large-scale treatment of customers' banking data accessed via internet-facing applications.
violations: Caja Rural failed to conduct adequate risk assessments and implement proportionate security measures despite handling large-scale treatment of customers' banking data accessed via internet-facing applications.
The bank did not implement or maintain essential security controls that were identified as missing or deficient in audit reports prior to the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33 requires the controller to notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and in any case within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach, unless unlikely to result in risk to rights and freedoms.
regulatoryFindings.description: Caja Rural provided evidence of proper instruction to its processor to notify the AEPD in its name, and the breach was notified; therefore the infraction was archived as the data subject met the notification requirement.
violations: Caja Rural provided evidence of proper instruction to its processor to notify the AEPD in its name, and the breach was notified; therefore the infraction was archived as the data subject met the notification requirement.

outcome: The AEPD issued a final resolution on 15 January 2025 confirming a violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The original penalty was €15,000. Caja Rural de Asturias paid €12,000 voluntarily on 21 December 2024, invoking a 20% reduction under Article 85 of the Administrative Procedure Act (LPACAP). This payment terminated the procedure and the entity waived any right to administrative appeal. The infraction under GDPR Article 32.1 was archived (no independent violation found). The infraction under GDPR Article 33 was also archived after evidence showed proper notification instructions were given to the processor.
companyNow: Caja Rural de Asturias is a Spanish cooperative credit bank. As of the document date, it remains operational and is part of the larger Caja Rural group. It is required to implement corrective measures to ensure GDPR compliance going forward.
dataType: Personal data, contact data, financial data (account numbers, balances), identifiers

companyDescription: ASOCIACIÓN ESCUELA NACIONAL DE EQUITACIÓN is a Spanish equestrian education association founded in 2021, involved in equestrian training and instruction.
companyLongDescription: ASOCIACIÓN ESCUELA NACIONAL DE EQUITACIÓN is a Spanish equestrian education association founded in 2021, involved in equestrian training and instruction.
caseDescription: AENE failed to comply with a data protection authority order requiring complete deletion of a complainant's personal data within one month. Despite two notifications and a formal follow-up requirement, the organization never responded or provided evidence of compliance, leading to a sanction for violating Article 58.2 of the GDPR.
violationSummary: AENE failed to execute a mandated data deletion order, thereby failing to protect personal data through proper handling and timely erasure as required under GDPR Article 58.2(d).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: AENE received a court order to delete a person's personal data within one month but completely ignored the requirement.
whyTheyWereWrong: The person's personal data remained stored and unprotected in AENE's systems despite a binding legal order, leaving their information vulnerable to continued misuse.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 58.2(d) of the GDPR grants authorities power to order data controllers to adjust processing operations to comply with the Regulation within a specified timeframe.
regulatoryFindings.description: AENE received an explicit order to delete personal data within one month but never confirmed compliance or responded to follow-up requests.
violations: AENE received an explicit order to delete personal data within one month but never confirmed compliance or responded to follow-up requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 83.6 of the GDPR establishes penalties for non-compliance with authority decisions under Article 58.2, with administrative fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is greater.
regulatoryFindings.description: AENE violated the enforcement order and was sanctioned for failure to implement the mandatory data deletion.
violations: AENE violated the enforcement order and was sanctioned for failure to implement the mandatory data deletion.

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed an administrative fine of €750 on AENE for failing to comply with a prior enforcement order requiring deletion of personal data. The authority ordered AENE to comply with the original deletion order within one month from the date this resolution becomes final and executable. Non-compliance with this new order may trigger additional administrative proceedings. The organization must demonstrate compliance through written notification to the AEPD.
companyNow: AENE is a small equestrian education association with approximately €81,661 in annual revenue (2023). Current compliance status unknown.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types)

companyDescription: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES, S.L. is a Spanish company that manages tourist apartments and listings on online reservation platforms. The company provides short-term rental accommodations and handles guest check-in processes.
companyLongDescription: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES, S.L. is a Spanish company that manages tourist apartments and listings on online reservation platforms. The company provides short-term rental accommodations and handles guest check-in processes.
caseDescription: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES required guests to provide selfies holding their national ID documents as part of online check-in, claiming this was necessary for identity verification and legal compliance. The Spanish data protection authority found the company collected excessive personal data—including biometric facial images and full document copies—that exceeded what Spanish and EU law actually required, violating the data minimisation principle.
violationSummary: The company engaged in excessive collection of biometric facial data and full identity document images beyond what was legally required, creating unnecessary surveillance and privacy intrusion.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES required guests to submit selfies holding their DNI and full copies of identity documents during online check-in, denying room access unless guests complied.
whyTheyWereWrong: Guests were coerced into surrendering biometric facial data and complete identity document images unnecessary for hotel registration, creating risk of identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Collection of guest selfies with DNI is required by law to comply with Madrid Community regulations and Real Decreto 933/2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: RD 933/2021 and LO 4/2015 require only specific identity data (name, ID number, type, nationality, birth date) to be collected and verified. Facial images and full document copies are not mandated; alternative verification methods (digital certificates, payment verification, security codes) are legally sufficient.

claimsVsReality.claim: The selfie requirement is necessary for 'security' and to prevent booking fraud with stolen documentation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The stated purpose does not justify the means. Facial biometrics create greater privacy and identity-theft risks than the fraud they purportedly prevent. Less intrusive alternatives adequately address fraud concerns.

claimsVsReality.claim: Guest data is 'protected' and ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES has 'no access' because verification is done by a third-party service provider.
claimsVsReality.reality: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES is the data controller and responsible party under GDPR. Outsourcing to a processor does not eliminate its obligation to ensure data minimisation and does not protect guest data from the company's own collection practices.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimisation principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES collected and required submission of guest facial biometrics (selfies) and complete identity document images, which are not mandated by Spanish hospitality registration law (RD 933/2021 and LO 4/2015)
violations: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES collected and required submission of guest facial biometrics (selfies) and complete identity document images, which are not mandated by Spanish hospitality registration law (RD 933/2021 and LO 4/2015)

The company collected only specific data fields (name, ID number, nationality, birth date) are legally required; facial images and document images are excessive and create unnecessary identity-theft risk

Guest was coerced into providing the data—check-in was denied unless selfies with documents were sent—even though less invasive alternatives (digital certificates, payment method verification, security codes) exist

regulatoryFindings.act: Real Decreto 933/2021 Article 4.3 requires hospitality providers to verify accuracy of guest data by matching them against identity documents, but does not mandate collection of document copies or facial biometrics.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES misinterpreted the verification requirement as justifying collection of full document images and facial selfies
violations: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES misinterpreted the verification requirement as justifying collection of full document images and facial selfies
The company denied access until guests submitted selfies and DNI copies, despite having already received the legally required data (name, ID number, document type)

outcome: AEPD imposed a €5,000 administrative fine for violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(c). The company was ordered to: (1) modify its registration system to stop requiring identity document copies or guest selfies as a condition of check-in, and (2) certify deletion of all stored guest photographs and document images within 3 months of the resolution becoming final and enforceable. Failure to comply with the corrective order may result in further administrative sanctions.
companyNow: ACTIVOS INTELIGENTES, S.L. (NIF B05374657) is a Spanish hospitality management company founded in 2021 with annual turnover of approximately €1.13 million as of 2022. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Biometric data (facial photographs), identification documents (DNI/passport images), personal identification information, contact details

companyDescription: Dover Harbour Board is a non-departmental public body that owns and operates the Port of Dover, a major UK port facility. It funds and operates the Port of Dover Police, a constabulary force providing security and general policing services at the port.
companyLongDescription: Dover Harbour Board is a non-departmental public body that owns and operates the Port of Dover, a major UK port facility. It funds and operates the Port of Dover Police, a constabulary force providing security and general policing services at the port.
caseDescription: Dover Harbour Board, through its Port of Dover Police officers, created and operated an unencrypted social media distribution group (WhatsApp, later Telegram) to share law enforcement intelligence about vehicle crime. The group had 241 members across multiple police forces and international agencies. The organization failed to implement adequate security measures, conduct risk assessments, provide data protection training specific to law enforcement, or maintain records management safeguards for the personal data being shared.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to secure personal data being processed for law enforcement purposes, resulting in exposure of sensitive intelligence data via inadequately encrypted commercial platforms without proper oversight or member governance.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Dover Harbour Board's Port of Dover Police created and operated a WhatsApp/Telegram distribution group with 241 officers sharing personal data including photographs.
whyTheyWereWrong: 241 law enforcement officers shared suspects' personal data and photographs on messaging apps with default encryption disabled.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dover Harbour Board stated that no personal data has been processed during members' use of the Group.
claimsVsReality.reality: The ICO found that personal data and special category data were being processed, including photographs and intelligence relating to individuals suspected of vehicle crime, shared across 241 group members without consent or notification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Group members suggested Telegram was a more secure network than WhatsApp.
claimsVsReality.reality: Telegram's default user settings do not have adequate encryption automatically activated; most messages are cloud chats stored on Telegram's servers accessible to Telegram itself; servers hosted in Netherlands with possibility of data sharing to Dubai or other parent company locations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Supervisory officers were unaware of data protection risks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple senior officers supervising Officer A were aware of the group's creation, promotion, and use over a sustained period, yet none identified that use of the group was likely to contravene data protection legislation, evidencing corporate-level inadequate awareness of compliance responsibilities.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 35(1) of the Data Protection Act 2018 requires that the processing of personal data for any of the law enforcement purposes must be lawful and fair.
regulatoryFindings.description: Dover Harbour Board failed to afford adequate or appropriate consideration to compliance with data protection legislation; affected individuals were not informed their data was being processed via social media or uploaded to such platforms, denying them transparency and awareness of their rights.
violations: Dover Harbour Board failed to afford adequate or appropriate consideration to compliance with data protection legislation; affected individuals were not informed their data was being processed via social media or uploaded to such platforms, denying them transparency and awareness of their rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 40 of the Data Protection Act 2018 requires that personal data processed for any of the law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telegram's default settings lack adequate encryption; most messages are cloud chats stored on Telegram's servers accessible to Telegram; servers hosted in Netherlands with possible data sharing to Dubai or parent company locations; no risk assessment conducted; no written constitution, terms of reference, or membership governance; no training provided to administrators; officers accessed via personal devices without enterprise security; no oversight of posts or member removal procedures; inadequate organisational safeguards for managing the 241-member group sharing sensitive intelligence data.
violations: Telegram's default settings lack adequate encryption; most messages are cloud chats stored on Telegram's servers accessible to Telegram; servers hosted in Netherlands with possible data sharing to Dubai or parent company locations; no risk assessment conducted; no written constitution, terms of reference, or membership governance; no training provided to administrators; officers accessed via personal devices without enterprise security; no oversight of posts or member removal procedures; inadequate organisational safeguards for managing the 241-member group sharing sensitive intelligence data.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal Reprimand to Dover Harbour Board. Although the ICO considered imposing an administrative penalty of £500,000, it declined to do so under its revised June 2022 approach to public sector enforcement. Dover Harbour Board must implement remedial steps: cease all group activity (completed 17 February 2021), provide enhanced data protection training to all Port of Dover Police officers including College of Policing online training on DPA 2018 law enforcement requirements, issue guidance on information types appropriate for social media sharing, instruct officers on deletion of WhatsApp/Telegram data, and conduct investigation into other social media group usage. The ICO issued four recommendations: review policies and procedures; conduct training content review to ensure relevance to law enforcement purposes; issue instruction and guidance on officially approved apps requiring staff confirmation of understanding; and investigate other social media group usage. Future non-compliance with these recommendations may constitute an aggravating factor in any subsequent enforcement action.
companyNow: Dover Harbour Board continues to operate as the port authority managing the Port of Dover. It funds and oversees the Port of Dover Police, a non-Home Office constabulary providing general policing services at the port.
dataType: Personal data and special category data relating to vehicle crime investigations; photographs and intelligence data

companyDescription: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL, S.C.C. is a Spanish cooperative credit entity (Sociedad Cooperativa de Crédito) that provides banking services to customers, including electronic banking through its Ruralvía platform. The company is part of the broader Caja Rural banking group.
companyLongDescription: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL, S.C.C. is a Spanish cooperative credit entity (Sociedad Cooperativa de Crédito) that provides banking services to customers, including electronic banking through its Ruralvía platform. The company is part of the broader Caja Rural banking group.
caseDescription: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL suffered a data breach in November 2022 affecting thousands of customers' personal, contact, and financial data through its legacy banking application (Ruralvía Clásica). The breach resulted from inadequate security measures and failure to implement proper access controls despite known vulnerabilities. The company was found to have violated GDPR Article 5(1)(f) by failing to maintain confidentiality and integrity of customer data.
violationSummary: The company failed to apply appropriate technical and organisational measures to guarantee confidentiality and integrity of personal data, as required by Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. The breach exposed sensitive financial data through inadequate access controls and lack of multi-factor authentication.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL failed to implement adequate security measures for its electronic banking platform, allowing attackers to access thousands of customers' personal, contact.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of the bank's customers lost control over their personal and financial data, exposing them to identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed that adequate security measures were in place and cited security certifications held by its processor (RSI).
claimsVsReality.reality: The Ruralvía Clásica application lacked multi-factor authentication and other controls adequate to protect against credential-based attacks. Security certifications in information security are distinct from GDPR compliance certifications and do not guarantee protection of fundamental rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company and processor asserted that attackers required legitimate credentials to access data, suggesting the breach was inevitable.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was responsible for implementing security measures appropriate to the risk level. Inadequate controls allowing credential-based attacks to succeed represent a failure of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR, regardless of attack method.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed to have conducted audits and held security certifications, demonstrating compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite audits and certifications in information security standards, the company failed to implement adequate measures to guarantee confidentiality and integrity of personal data, particularly multi-factor authentication for a financial application accessible via the internet.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that guarantees appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures for the Ruralvía Clásica application, allowing attackers to access customer data through credential-based attacks between November and December 2022.
violations: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures for the Ruralvía Clásica application, allowing attackers to access customer data through credential-based attacks between November and December 2022.
The company did not implement multi-factor authentication or other controls adequate to the risk level despite handling thousands of customers' financial data accessible via the internet.
Security audits performed before the breach identified vulnerabilities that were not remediated before the attack occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including capacity to ensure confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's legacy banking system lacked adequate access controls and multi-factor authentication despite handling sensitive financial data at scale.
violations: The company's legacy banking system lacked adequate access controls and multi-factor authentication despite handling sensitive financial data at scale.
Although the company contracted with a processor (RSI) to implement security measures, it failed in its supervisory obligation to ensure those measures were appropriate and effective.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33 requires controllers to notify supervisory authorities of data breaches without undue delay and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of the breach.
regulatoryFindings.description: This charge was archived during proceedings; the company demonstrated it had instructed its processor to notify the AEPD and that notification occurred within required timeframes.
violations: This charge was archived during proceedings; the company demonstrated it had instructed its processor to notify the AEPD and that notification occurred within required timeframes.

outcome: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL S.C.C. was ordered to pay €90,000 in fines for violating GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The company availed itself of a 20% voluntary payment reduction, resulting in a final penalty of €72,000, paid on 20 December 2024. The fine was imposed as the company failed to maintain adequate security measures protecting customer data. Charges under Articles 32 and 33 were archived. The case was terminated following the company's voluntary payment and waiver of administrative appeals.
companyNow: CAJA RURAL CENTRAL S.C.C. is a Spanish cooperative credit entity and part of the Caja Rural banking group. Following the enforcement action, the company is required to implement enhanced security measures and ongoing compliance monitoring.
dataType: Personal data, contact information, financial data including bank account details and transaction history
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of Data Breach

companyDescription: Kent Police is the local law enforcement agency responsible for policing Kent, England. It operates under the supervision of the Kent Police and Crime Commissioner and is subject to UK data protection and law enforcement regulations.
companyLongDescription: Kent Police is the local law enforcement agency responsible for policing Kent, England. It operates under the supervision of the Kent Police and Crime Commissioner and is subject to UK data protection and law enforcement regulations.
caseDescription: A Kent Police officer photographed an individual's identity document on a personal mobile phone and uploaded it to Telegram, a messaging app used by multiple police forces and international law enforcement for vehicle crime investigation. The officer did not inform the data subject of further processing, purpose, or how their data would be used. Kent Police failed to adequately inform staff of data protection responsibilities and lacked sufficient policies governing personal device use for official duties.
violationSummary: Personal data was disclosed to unauthorised recipients (international law enforcement on social media) without data subject knowledge or consent, and stored insecurely on third-party servers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A Kent Police officer photographed an individual's identity document using a personal mobile phone and uploaded it to Telegram, a social media application shared by 25 Kent officers.
whyTheyWereWrong: An unknown number of individuals' identity documents were exposed on an unencrypted social media platform with international access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telegram use was not officially sanctioned by Kent Police and the app was blocked on official devices
claimsVsReality.reality: 25 officers had downloaded the app onto personal devices and were active members of the distribution group; two officers held admin rights; the group had been in sustained use for years without management detection

claimsVsReality.claim: Only five officers had previously used Telegram to share personal data
claimsVsReality.reality: At least 25 officers were group members with capability to share; full extent of data sharing prior to investigation discovery could not be determined

claimsVsReality.claim: Officers needed to make operational decisions and personal devices were permitted for limited scenarios (recording incidents, photography, sensitive calls)
claimsVsReality.reality: Officers used personal devices to upload identity documents to international social media without operational justification or authorisation

claimsVsReality.claim: Data protection policies and training were in place
claimsVsReality.reality: Policies existed but failed to adequately communicate that personal device use for official data processing was prohibited; sustained group use undetected indicates training was ineffective

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40: Personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed with appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kent Police failed to ensure personal data (identity documents) was processed with appropriate security measures
violations: Kent Police failed to ensure personal data (identity documents) was processed with appropriate security measures
Data was uploaded to Telegram, a social media application, without adequate encryption or access controls
Data was stored on Telegram servers hosted internationally, creating uncontrolled access risks
Personal devices were used to process law enforcement data without adequate technical or organisational safeguards
No policy existed to prevent or restrict use of personal devices for official data processing
Supervisory oversight failed to detect sustained misuse of unsanctioned apps by 25 officers over significant period

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to the Chief Constable of Kent Police under DPA 2018 Schedule 13(2)(c) and UK GDPR Article 58(2)(b) for infringement of Section 40. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps taken: incident reported to ICO and originating organisation; officers instructed to cease use; disciplinary action imposed on identified officers. The ICO issued four recommendations: (1) regularly review ICT Acceptable Use Policy with clear guidance on personal device use; (2) enhance procedure for policy distribution with documented compliance monitoring; (3) expand data protection training to include acceptable personal device use and real incident examples; (4) provide force-wide guidance on social media app compliance. Kent Police invited to update ICO on implementation progress. No monetary penalty imposed but failure to rectify infringements may be treated as aggravating factor in future enforcement action.
companyNow: Kent Police remains the primary law enforcement agency for Kent, England. Following this incident, the force has implemented corrective measures and is subject to ICO monitoring regarding data protection compliance.
dataType: Identity documents, personal identification data
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40 (sixth data protection principle – security)
UK GDPR Article 58(2)(b) (authority to issue reprimand)

companyDescription: Avanza Bank AB is a Swedish digital bank and online investment broker offering trading, savings, and banking services. The company operates primarily through digital channels and web/mobile applications.
companyLongDescription: Avanza Bank AB is a Swedish digital bank and online investment broker offering trading, savings, and banking services. The company operates primarily through digital channels and web/mobile applications.
caseDescription: Avanza Bank AB unintentionally activated two advanced tracking functions (AAM and AH) within Meta's pixel tracking tool between November 2019 and June 2021, causing approximately 500,000–1,000,000 customer personal records to be transmitted to Meta without authorization. The data included highly sensitive information such as personal identity numbers, account details, loan amounts, and securities holdings. The bank failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures to prevent this unauthorized disclosure, and was unaware of the ongoing data transfers for over 18 months until notified externally.
violationSummary: The bank's failure to implement adequate technical and organizational safeguards resulted in unauthorized disclosure of confidential banking information to Meta, a third party. Statutory banking secrecy obligations were breached, and personal data were exposed through inadequate security.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Avanza Bank deployed Meta-pixel tracking on its website and app without adequate security controls, allowing two automated data-transfer functions to activate without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 500,000 and 1 million customers had their personal identity numbers, account numbers, loan amounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank claimed it had formalized routines and documented procedures to ensure proper data protection before implementing new features.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these documented procedures, the bank failed to follow them when implementing Meta-pixel functions, resulting in unauthorized activation of two tracking functions without the knowledge of the data controller.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank stated the two functions (AAM and AH) were activated accidentally and that it was not possible to verify how or by whom they were activated.
claimsVsReality.reality: The failure to verify activation occurred because the bank did not document the implementation of these features in accordance with its own stated protocols, leaving no audit trail.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank asserted that the data transmitted posed no risk because Meta did not use the information for its own purposes and eventually deleted the data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data remained exposed and accessible to Meta for over 18 months; the unauthorized transmission itself constituted a breach of banking secrecy and GDPR security obligations regardless of Meta's eventual deletion.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Avanza Bank transmitted approximately 500,000–1,000,000 customer records containing identity numbers, account details, loan amounts, and other highly sensitive financial information to Meta without authorization over 18 months.
violations: Avanza Bank transmitted approximately 500,000–1,000,000 customer records containing identity numbers, account details, loan amounts, and other highly sensitive financial information to Meta without authorization over 18 months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires data controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank failed to follow its own formalized data protection protocols when Meta-pixel functions were activated, lacked systematic monitoring to detect unauthorized data transfers, and had no controls to identify unintended configuration changes to third-party scripts.
violations: Bank failed to follow its own formalized data protection protocols when Meta-pixel functions were activated, lacked systematic monitoring to detect unauthorized data transfers, and had no controls to identify unintended configuration changes to third-party scripts.

regulatoryFindings.act: Swedish Banking Act § 1 kap. 10 prohibits unauthorized disclosure of information concerning a customer's dealings with a credit institution.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank disclosed detailed customer financial information (account numbers, loan amounts, credit limits, securities holdings) to Meta through inadequate security controls on tracking tools.
violations: Bank disclosed detailed customer financial information (account numbers, loan amounts, credit limits, securities holdings) to Meta through inadequate security controls on tracking tools.

outcome: Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten (Swedish Data Protection Authority) determined that Avanza Bank AB violated GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) by failing to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures. The bank was ordered to pay an administrative fine of 15,000,000 SEK. The decision found the breach serious enough to constitute violation of both the integrity principle and the security requirement. Meta confirmed deletion of transferred data. Avanza implemented additional governance documents, enhanced third-party script management processes, and established monitoring for data exfiltration. The decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: Avanza Bank AB continues to operate as a Swedish digital bank and online broker. Following the regulatory decision, the company has strengthened its data protection and information security governance frameworks.
dataType: Financial data, account numbers, loan amounts, credit limits, securities holdings, personal identity numbers, contact information, employment details
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality principle
Swedish Complementary GDPR Act § 3 kap. 10 (Personal identity numbers)

companyDescription: Quick Tax Claims Limited is a tax claims service provider registered in Manchester, UK (Companies House Reg. No. 14377745). The company operated a direct marketing campaign via SMS using purchased lead lists without obtaining valid consumer consent.
companyLongDescription: Quick Tax Claims Limited is a tax claims service provider registered in Manchester, UK (Companies House Reg. No. 14377745). The company operated a direct marketing campaign via SMS using purchased lead lists without obtaining valid consumer consent.
caseDescription: Quick Tax Claims Limited transmitted 4.98 million unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages between February and May 2023 without valid recipient consent, violating PECR Regulations 22 and 23. The company failed to obtain freely-given, specific, and informed consent, and did not provide valid opt-out mechanisms. The ICO issued an enforcement notice requiring immediate compliance with PECR within 30 days.
violationSummary: QTC conducted direct marketing surveillance via SMS without consent, collecting and using phone numbers for unsolicited commercial contact, which is a form of privacy-intrusive information collection.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Quick Tax Claims Limited transmitted 4,983,499 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers between February.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 5 million subscribers received intrusive marketing texts they never clearly consented to.

claimsVsReality.claim: Leads arranged as 'single use' means subscribers will not receive multiple messages from QTC
claimsVsReality.reality: 7726 spam complaints data documented 50 instances where subscribers received multiple messages from QTC with no opt-out option

claimsVsReality.claim: Consent obtained from data suppliers was valid and informed
claimsVsReality.reality: Consent was conditioned on service access (not freely-given), obtained from vague lists of dozens of companies (not specific), and users could not have seen QTC named in privacy policies at time of consent (not informed)

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: QTC transmitted 4,983,499 unsolicited SMS messages without valid prior consent from recipients
violations: QTC transmitted 4,983,499 unsolicited SMS messages without valid prior consent from recipients
Consent obtained was not freely-given (made conditional on service access), specific (vague lists of dozens of companies), or informed (privacy policy language unclear)

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 23(b) requires a valid address where recipients may request cessation of direct marketing communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: 93% of SMS messages lacked a valid opt-out mechanism
violations: 93% of SMS messages lacked a valid opt-out mechanism
50 instances documented where subscribers received multiple messages from QTC with no opt-out option provided, despite company claim that leads were 'single use'

outcome: The ICO issued a binding Enforcement Notice dated 26 September 2024 requiring Quick Tax Claims Limited to cease all unsolicited direct marketing via electronic mail within 30 days, except where valid freely-given and specific consent exists. The notice mandates compliance with PECR Regulations 22 and 23, including providing valid opt-out mechanisms. QTC has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. No monetary penalty was issued; compliance is mandatory.
dataType: Phone numbers (SMS recipients)
legalBasisViolated: PECR Regulation 22(2) – unsolicited direct marketing communications
PECR Regulation 23(b) – failure to provide valid opt-out mechanism

companyDescription: Penny Appeal is a UK-registered charity supporting vulnerable populations in crisis situations. The organisation collects donations and maintains donor databases for fundraising and direct marketing purposes.
companyLongDescription: Penny Appeal is a UK-registered charity supporting vulnerable populations in crisis situations. The organisation collects donations and maintains donor databases for fundraising and direct marketing purposes.
caseDescription: Penny Appeal transmitted 461,650 unsolicited direct marketing emails to individual subscribers without obtaining valid prior consent, contrary to PECR Regulation 22. The organisation could not evidence that recipients had freely, specifically, and informedly consented to receive marketing messages. Messages were sent to donors who had explicitly opted out of marketing communications.
violationSummary: Unsolicited electronic direct marketing communications without prior explicit consent constitute surveillance-based marketing targeting of individuals without their knowledge or agreement.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between April 22 and May 1, 2022, Penny Appeal transmitted and instigated transmission of approximately 461,650 unsolicited direct marketing emails to 52,179 customers without valid consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of subscribers received marketing emails they had never consented to, including donors who had explicitly opted out, causing unwanted invasions of their email accounts and privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Penny Appeal could rely on existing customer relationships to send marketing emails without separate consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: PECR Regulation 22(2) requires explicit prior notification of consent for unsolicited direct marketing; soft opt-in exemption (Reg 22(3)) does not apply to non-commercial charity fundraising, and Penny Appeal held no valid consent evidence.

claimsVsReality.claim: Marketing emails sent to opted-in customers were legitimately targeted.
claimsVsReality.reality: Messages were sent to 52,179 customers including donors who had explicitly opted out of marketing from Penny Appeal; no valid consent was obtained or evidenced.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission or instigation of unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail to individual subscribers unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent for such communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: Penny Appeal transmitted 461,650 unsolicited marketing emails without prior explicit consent from recipients.
violations: Penny Appeal transmitted 461,650 unsolicited marketing emails without prior explicit consent from recipients.
No evidence of freely given, specific, informed consent as required by UK GDPR Article 4(11).
Messages sent to donors who had explicitly opted out of marketing from Penny Appeal.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(3) permits direct marketing only where contact details were obtained in course of sale/negotiation, marketing concerns similar products/services only, and recipient given simple means to refuse at collection and with each subsequent communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: Penny Appeal could not demonstrate compliance with soft opt-in exemption conditions.
violations: Penny Appeal could not demonstrate compliance with soft opt-in exemption conditions.
No evidence that opt-out mechanism was provided to recipients at initial collection or with each communication.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 40(1)(a) empowers the Commissioner to serve enforcement notices if satisfied a person has contravened requirements of the Regulations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Commissioner satisfied Penny Appeal contravened PECR through systematic transmission of 461,650 non-consensual marketing emails.
violations: Commissioner satisfied Penny Appeal contravened PECR through systematic transmission of 461,650 non-consensual marketing emails.

outcome: ICO issued an Enforcement Notice (dated 18 April 2024, varied pursuant to DPA 1998 Section 41(1)) requiring Penny Appeal to cease transmission and instigation of unsolicited direct marketing emails within 30 days, except where: (1) circumstances under PECR Regulation 22(3) or other legal exemption apply, or (2) recipient has previously notified Penny Appeal of ongoing consent. No monetary penalty imposed. Commissioner determined damage unlikely despite contravention severity. Right of appeal to First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) available.
companyNow: Penny Appeal continues to operate as a UK-registered charity (Companies House No. 06578382). The Enforcement Notice requires immediate cessation of non-consensual direct marketing or compliance with PECR exemptions.
dataType: Email addresses, phone numbers

companyDescription: West Midlands Police is a statutory police force serving the West Midlands region of England. It processes personal data for law enforcement purposes including criminal investigations, victim protection, and safeguarding.
companyLongDescription: West Midlands Police is a statutory police force serving the West Midlands region of England. It processes personal data for law enforcement purposes including criminal investigations, victim protection, and safeguarding.
caseDescription: West Midlands Police incorrectly linked and merged the personal data records of two individuals with the same name and date of birth on multiple occasions from January 2020 onwards. This resulted in inaccurate data being processed, leading to officers attending the wrong addresses and disclosing sensitive information. The force failed to maintain adequate records of incidents, implement proper technical safeguards, and provide sufficient employee training.
violationSummary: The core failure involves inadequate technical and organisational measures to prevent inaccurate data merging, resulting in security breaches (disclosure to wrong recipient) and inability to maintain data accuracy, falling squarely under information processing insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: West Midlands Police incorrectly merged and linked personal data records of two individuals with identical names.
whyTheyWereWrong: One individual received a letter disclosing another person's victim assault information, and officers conducted home visits.

claimsVsReality.claim: WMP had systems and processes in place to accurately manage and distinguish between records of individuals with similar identifiers
claimsVsReality.reality: Records of two identically-named individuals were repeatedly and incorrectly merged without clear technical or organisational safeguards to prevent or quickly identify such errors

claimsVsReality.claim: Adding system notes and manually unlinking records would prevent future incidents
claimsVsReality.reality: These remedial actions proved ineffective; records continued to be incorrectly linked and merged despite multiple instances of manual intervention

claimsVsReality.claim: WMP could track and manage security incidents and inaccurate data processing
claimsVsReality.reality: Inadequate record-keeping meant WMP could not determine the true number of times records were incorrectly linked, when incidents occurred, which employees were involved, or the full extent of inappropriate disclosures

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 34(3): The controller in relation to personal data is responsible for, and must be able to demonstrate, compliance with the data protection principles.
regulatoryFindings.description: WMP failed to demonstrate adequate records and systems to ensure accuracy and security of personal data relating to the two individuals
violations: WMP failed to demonstrate adequate records and systems to ensure accuracy and security of personal data relating to the two individuals
Inadequate record-keeping and incident management prevented WMP from monitoring and rectifying non-compliance

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 38(1): Personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be accurate, kept up to date, and inaccurate data must be erased or rectified without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Information relating to one individual was incorrectly linked to the other's record on numerous occasions throughout 2020-2022
violations: Information relating to one individual was incorrectly linked to the other's record on numerous occasions throughout 2020-2022
WMP unable to demonstrate inaccurate data was rectified without delay; some records remain incorrectly merged
True number and duration of inaccuracies unknown due to inadequate record-keeping

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 38(3): A clear distinction must be made between personal data relating to different categories of data subject (suspects, convicted persons, victims, witnesses).
regulatoryFindings.description: One individual known as a crime victim while the other was both a suspect and victim; incorrect linking prevented clear distinction between these categories
violations: One individual known as a crime victim while the other was both a suspect and victim; incorrect linking prevented clear distinction between these categories

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 40: Personal data processed for law enforcement must be processed with appropriate security using technical and organisational measures to prevent unauthorised processing, loss, or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Letter disclosing victim assault information sent to wrong individual on 12 July 2022
violations: Letter disclosing victim assault information sent to wrong individual on 12 July 2022
Multiple incidents involving actual or potential inappropriate disclosure; WMP unable to determine full extent due to inadequate records
Failed to demonstrate personal data kept secure across incidents affecting both individuals

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Section 57(1): Controllers must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures designed to implement data protection principles effectively.
regulatoryFindings.description: Testing and risk assessment of new systems failed to prevent inaccurate merging of records
violations: Testing and risk assessment of new systems failed to prevent inaccurate merging of records
Manual editing tool needed to separate merged records not developed in timely manner, delaying rectification
Employees not provided clear policies and procedures for system use; mandatory training completion only 30-35% of workforce
Inadequate records prevented identifying affected employees for refresher training following incidents

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to West Midlands Police for violations of DPA 2018 sections 34(3), 38(1), 38(3), 40, and 57(1). No monetary penalty was imposed. WMP was required to implement remedial steps including: maintaining adequate processing records and governance measures; distinguishing and preventing future merging of the two individuals' records by completing technical changes to unmerge records on relevant systems; sharing security incident learnings organisation-wide; ensuring all employees complete mandatory data protection training and system-specific training; and implementing an action plan to improve refresher training completion rates. WMP submitted representations on 16 January 2024 confirming progress on these recommendations. A further progress update was requested within six months of the reprimand date.
companyNow: West Midlands Police remains a large regional police force serving the West Midlands region. The force is implementing governance and technical improvements to address data protection compliance gaps identified in the reprimand.
dataType: Criminal records, victim data, suspect data, witness information, personal identifiers, address information

companyDescription: InMarket Media is a digital marketing platform and data aggregator that collects consumer location data through a proprietary SDK embedded in mobile apps, purchases additional consumer data from third parties, and uses this combined data to create targeted advertising audiences for brands and advertising agencies.
companyLongDescription: InMarket Media is a digital marketing platform and data aggregator that collects consumer location data through a proprietary SDK embedded in mobile apps, purchases additional consumer data from third parties, and uses this combined data to create targeted advertising audiences for brands and advertising agencies.
caseDescription: InMarket Media collected precise location data from approximately 100 million unique devices annually through its SDK and apps without adequately disclosing it would be used for targeted advertising and audience profiling. The company failed to obtain informed consent in its own apps (CheckPoints and ListEase) and failed to verify that third-party apps incorporating its SDK obtained proper consumer consent. Additionally, InMarket retained sensitive location data for up to five years—far longer than necessary for its stated purposes.
violationSummary: InMarket conducted systematic, ongoing surveillance of consumer location at high frequency (from idle to every few seconds), tracking sensitive movements over time and across multiple apps without transparent disclosure or meaningful consent. This constitutes mass surveillance under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Collected precise location data from approximately 100 million devices annually through software embedded in over 300 third-party apps and two proprietary apps (CheckPoints.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers using CheckPoints and ListEase were told their location data would only be used for earning rewards or shopping reminders.

claimsVsReality.claim: CheckPoints app: 'Allow CheckPoints to access your location? This allows us to award you extra points for walking into stores.' (iOS) and 'CheckPoints finds nearby earning opportunities by using your device's location' (Android).
claimsVsReality.reality: InMarket used location data not just for earning points, but to build detailed consumer profiles tracking where users live, work, worship, receive medical care, and attend protests. This data was combined with purchased demographic information and used for targeted advertising across third-party platforms. Data was retained for up to 5 years.

claimsVsReality.claim: ListEase app: 'Allow ListEase to use your location? Uses location so you don't forget items on your list when you are at the store.' (iOS) and 'Allow Location Permissions to unlock reminders. Get a reminder when you're in the store so you never forget to grab the items you need!' (Android).
claimsVsReality.reality: Location data was collected multiple times per hour (regardless of store proximity) and shared with InMarket for creation of advertising audiences based on consumer movement patterns, income level, family structure, religion, and predicted behavior. Data was retained for 5 years and made available on real-time bidding platforms.

claimsVsReality.claim: Third-party app example: 'Your location is used to provide you with rewards and discounts when you visit retail partners.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Location data was collected continuously multiple times per day and shared with InMarket, which combined it with other data sources, created detailed consumer profiles, and used it to target advertising without user knowledge that a third party (InMarket) was amassing and monetizing their movement data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits 'unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.'
regulatoryFindings.description: InMarket represented that CheckPoints and ListEase would use location only for awarding points and list reminders, but actually used it for targeted advertising and consumer profiling without disclosure.
violations: InMarket represented that CheckPoints and ListEase would use location only for awarding points and list reminders, but actually used it for targeted advertising and consumer profiling without disclosure.
InMarket failed to disclose to CheckPoints and ListEase users that location data would be used for advertising, supplemented with purchased data, shared with third parties, and retained for 5 years.
InMarket failed to verify that third-party apps incorporating its SDK obtained informed consumer consent for its use of location data for advertising.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(n) of the FTC Act defines unfairness as acts causing substantial injury to consumers that consumers cannot reasonably avoid and that are not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: InMarket's collection of location data without disclosure caused substantial loss of privacy about day-to-day movements of millions of consumers and increased risk of disclosure of sensitive information (home, workplace, places of worship, medical facilities, protests).
violations: InMarket's collection of location data without disclosure caused substantial loss of privacy about day-to-day movements of millions of consumers and increased risk of disclosure of sensitive information (home, workplace, places of worship, medical facilities, protests).
