InMarket's retention of location data for 5 years exposed consumers to unnecessary risk of data breach, misuse, and re-identification without consumer awareness or ability to avoid.
Consumers could not reasonably avoid the injury because they were not aware of the scope of InMarket's data collection, use, and retention practices due to misleading consent screens.

outcome: FTC issued a Complaint (April 29, 2024) alleging four counts: (1) Unfair Collection and Use of Consumer Location Data from InMarket's own apps; (2) Unfair Collection and Use of Consumer Location Data from third-party apps; (3) Unfair Retention of Consumer Location Data; (4) Deceptive Failure to Disclose use of location data. The complaint is pending adjudication. No settlement or final order has been issued as of the complaint date. InMarket must respond to the allegations and the case will proceed through FTC administrative proceedings.
companyNow: InMarket Media, LLC remains in operation as a digital marketing platform and data aggregator. The company is facing FTC enforcement proceedings alleging violations of consumer privacy protection standards. Current operations and any changes to practices are unknown pending resolution of the case.
dataType: Location data, device identifiers, purchasing history, demographic and socioeconomic information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair and deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(n) – unfairness standard (substantial injury not reasonably avoidable)

company: ROCA & ASOCIADOS ABOGADOS Y ECONOMISTAS, S.L.P.
companyDescription: ROCA & ASOCIADOS ABOGADOS Y ECONOMISTAS, S.L.P. is a Spanish law firm (despacho de abogados) classified as a microenterprise, founded in 2017. The firm provides legal and economic consulting services.
companyLongDescription: ROCA & ASOCIADOS ABOGADOS Y ECONOMISTAS, S.L.P. is a Spanish law firm (despacho de abogados) classified as a microenterprise, founded in 2017. The firm provides legal and economic consulting services.
caseDescription: A law firm published employee photographs, names, and professional information on its website without obtaining valid, informed, and explicit consent from the employees. The company claimed consent was given through informal email communications, but failed to provide proper data protection information and evidence of affirmative consent as required by GDPR Article 6(1).
violationSummary: The company exposed employees' personal data (photographs, names, professional details) publicly on the internet without proper consent, making the data accessible to the general public and increasing privacy risks.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Published employee photographs with names and professional details on the company website without obtaining valid prior consent from the employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees had their images, names, and professional information exposed publicly without their informed agreement, creating privacy harm and loss of control over their personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated that the employee gave consent by posing for the photograph and providing curriculum data, and was informed through emails about photo availability.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR requires free, specific, informed, and unequivocal consent obtained through affirmative action before processing begins. Informal email stating 'new employees who want them' is not affirmative consent; company provided no Article 13 mandatory information; consent must be documented and demonstrable.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company argued that the employee had published the same data on LinkedIn, implying prior consent or public disclosure justifying republication.
claimsVsReality.reality: Publication by the data subject on a personal social media account does not constitute consent to corporate publication. Each processing activity requires separate, valid consent under GDPR. The employee's LinkedIn publication does not waive their right to control corporate use of their image.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data shall only be lawful if at least one of the specified conditions is met, including explicit consent of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: ROCA & ASOCIADOS published employee photographs and personal data without valid consent meeting GDPR requirements.
violations: ROCA & ASOCIADOS published employee photographs and personal data without valid consent meeting GDPR requirements.
Consent was not free, specific, informed, and unequivocal; company relied on informal email and presumed consent rather than affirmative action.
Company failed to provide information required by Article 13 GDPR before obtaining consent.
No evidence of proper consent documentation or mechanism to demonstrate valid consent had been obtained.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 4(11) defines valid consent as a free, specific, informed, and unequivocal manifestation of will by which the data subject accepts processing through a clear affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: Email communication mentioning 'new employees who want them' was not an affirmative declaration of consent.
violations: Email communication mentioning 'new employees who want them' was not an affirmative declaration of consent.
Silence, pre-marked checkboxes, and inaction do not constitute valid consent; company did not obtain clear affirmative action.
Fact that complainant had previously posted photos on LinkedIn did not constitute consent to employer's publication.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are obtained from the data subject, the controller shall provide specific information including identity of controller, purposes of processing, right to withdraw consent, and other mandatory details.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company provided no formal information sheet or privacy notice to employees before taking and publishing their photographs.
violations: Company provided no formal information sheet or privacy notice to employees before taking and publishing their photographs.
Employees were not informed of the purposes of processing, the legal basis, their rights, or other Article 13 requirements.
Informal emails did not constitute adequate provision of mandatory transparency information.

outcome: AEPD (Spanish Data Protection Authority) imposed a €5,000 administrative fine on ROCA & ASOCIADOS for violation of GDPR Article 6(1). Additionally, the company was ordered to adopt compliance measures within 3 months to ensure that personal data are not published on its website without complying with Article 6(1) GDPR requirements. The company must demonstrate implementation of these measures to the AEPD. The resolution is final after one month from notification if no appeal is filed. The company has the right to request a suspension of the resolution if it intends to file an administrative appeal before the National Court.
companyNow: Unknown. ROCA & ASOCIADOS is a Spanish legal services firm established in 2017 with approximately €[undisclosed] in annual business volume as of 2022. Current operational status not documented.
dataType: Photographs, names, first surnames, professional information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 4(11) – Definition of valid consent
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided to data subjects

company: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust
companyDescription: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust is one of the largest acute hospital trusts in England, providing acute and specialist healthcare services across Lincolnshire and neighbouring counties through four hospital sites (Lincoln, Boston, Grantham, and Louth). It employs approximately 9,136 staff with an annual income of £740 million.
companyLongDescription: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust is one of the largest acute hospital trusts in England, providing acute and specialist healthcare services across Lincolnshire and neighbouring counties through four hospital sites (Lincoln, Boston, Grantham, and Louth). It employs approximately 9,136 staff with an annual income of £740 million.
caseDescription: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust failed to respond to 32% of Subject Access Requests within the statutory one-month timeframe during March 2021 to March 2022. The Trust's deficient case management systems, lack of adequate resources, and poor oversight meant data subjects could not timely access their personal health information. The ICO issued a reprimand under UK GDPR Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3).
violationSummary: The Trust systematically excluded data subjects from accessing their personal health information by failing to meet statutory response deadlines, preventing individuals from exercising their data access rights.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Between March 2021 and March 2022, the Trust failed to respond to 32% of Subject Access Requests within the required one-month statutory timeframe.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients requesting their own medical records experienced significant delays accessing their health data, with some waiting months beyond the legal deadline.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Trust claimed it had responded to approximately 68% of SARs within the one-month statutory timeframe during the relevant period.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Trust had actually failed to respond to 32% of SARs within statutory deadlines. The Trust later acknowledged serious data quality issues and could not guarantee the accuracy of its quantitative reporting due to system failures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Trust stated it had processes and procedures in place for managing SARs effectively.
claimsVsReality.reality: The case management system lacked basic compliance-tracking functionality, the Trust was still operating primarily with paper records, and there was no adequate oversight or resource allocation for SAR processing for several years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Trust indicated its data provided to the ICO was reliable.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Trust acknowledged data quality issues, later advised that quantitative data was inaccurate because it included deceased individuals' records (outside GDPR scope), and admitted it could not guarantee data accuracy throughout the investigation.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide information on action taken in response to data subject rights requests without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two months where necessary, with notice to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to respond to 32% of SARs within the one-month statutory timeframe
violations: Trust failed to respond to 32% of SARs within the one-month statutory timeframe
Trust could not confirm how many SARs received the extended three-month timeframe or how many were answered within it
Trust's case management system lacked functionality to record or track compliance data

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide data subjects with confirmation of whether personal data concerning them is being processed and, where applicable, access to the personal data and specified information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to provide timely confirmation and access to personal health data to data subjects
violations: Trust failed to provide timely confirmation and access to personal health data to data subjects
32% of data subjects were unable to exercise their right of access within the required timeframe

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing to data subjects.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to provide copies of personal health data within statutory deadlines due to system deficiencies and resource constraints
violations: Trust failed to provide copies of personal health data within statutory deadlines due to system deficiencies and resource constraints
Inadequate paper-based record systems and lack of oversight prevented timely fulfilment of data access requests

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand on 13 December 2024. The Trust acknowledged the infringements and did not submit representations. As remedial steps, the Trust has implemented an Information Asset Management Strategy (IAMS), procured a bespoke SAR management system and Records of Processing Activities (ROPA) solution (concluded March 2024), updated its Access to Records Policy, provided staff training, and recruited additional temporary staff. The Trust is planning to digitise patient records by March 2025 in line with NHS England's digital health plan. The Commissioner notes the backlog is improving but continues monitoring. Future failure to rectify these infringements could result in escalated enforcement action including substantial fines.
companyNow: United Lincolnshire Teaching Hospitals NHS Trust continues to operate as a major acute hospital trust in England, serving approximately 769,474 people annually across four hospital sites. It is implementing significant systemic improvements to SAR handling and digitising health records.
dataType: Health data, Personal medical records

companyDescription: WerepairUK Ltd is a repair services company registered in the UK. The company conducted direct marketing operations via unsolicited telephone calls.
companyLongDescription: WerepairUK Ltd is a repair services company registered in the UK. The company conducted direct marketing operations via unsolicited telephone calls.
caseDescription: WerepairUK Ltd made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between September 2022 and May 2023, violating PECR Regulation 21. The company failed to obtain valid consent from TPS-registered subscribers before calling them for marketing purposes. Despite being notified of the Commissioner's concerns, the company continued its unlawful calling activity.
violationSummary: The company systematically contacted individuals who had explicitly registered to avoid such contact, constituting surveillance-type collection through unsolicited direct marketing calls.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to telephone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service between September 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: 42,688 individuals who had explicitly registered to block marketing calls experienced unwanted sales calls, violating their stated privacy preferences.

claimsVsReality.claim: Implied by compliance: WerepairUK obtained valid consent from subscribers to receive marketing calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: WerepairUK failed to demonstrate any valid notifications from the 42,688 called individuals overriding their TPS registration.

claimsVsReality.claim: Implied: The company respected TPS opt-out preferences.
claimsVsReality.reality: WerepairUK made 42,688 calls to TPS-registered numbers without valid exceptions under Regulation 21(4).

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(1)(b) of PECR prohibits using public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls where the called number is listed in the TPS register kept under Regulation 26.
regulatoryFindings.description: WerepairUK made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with TPS for at least 28 days prior without valid subscriber notification under Regulation 21(4).
violations: WerepairUK made 42,688 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with TPS for at least 28 days prior without valid subscriber notification under Regulation 21(4).
The company failed to obtain clear and positive action from individuals to override their TPS registration.
Notification (if any) did not clearly indicate willingness to receive marketing calls specifically from WerepairUK.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 21(4) permits calls to TPS-registered numbers only where the subscriber has notified the caller they do not object to such calls, requiring clear and positive action.
regulatoryFindings.description: WerepairUK demonstrated no valid notifications from subscribers overriding their TPS registration.
violations: WerepairUK demonstrated no valid notifications from subscribers overriding their TPS registration.
The company could not demonstrate that signing up to use products/services constituted clear consent to receive marketing calls.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring WerepairUK Ltd to cease making unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered subscribers and subscribers who have previously notified the company not to call within 30 days. The company must also ensure direct marketing communications recipients receive the caller's name and contact details on request. The company has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: WerepairUK Ltd remains a registered company (Companies House Registration 12080599) based in Tonbridge, UK. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Telephone numbers
legalBasisViolated: Privacy and Electronic Communications (EC Directive) Regulations 2003, Regulation 21(1)(b)

company: Comunidad de Propietarios Conjunto Hotel Apartamentos Don B.B.B.
companyDescription: A residential property owners' collective managing a hotel apartment complex in Spain. The association is responsible for common areas and facilities including security systems for the building.
companyLongDescription: A residential property owners' collective managing a hotel apartment complex in Spain. The association is responsible for common areas and facilities including security systems for the building.
caseDescription: A property owners' association installed video surveillance cameras that were improperly oriented toward public space without adequate signage or access controls. The system exceeded permissible limits by capturing images of public areas, which is exclusively the competence of state security forces under Spanish law, and failed to provide proper transparency to individuals whose data was being collected.
violationSummary: The primary violation involved unauthorized video surveillance oriented toward public space beyond the property's legitimate interest, combined with lack of transparency to data subjects and inadequate access controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed video surveillance cameras oriented toward public streets without prior authorization, inadequate warning signs, and allowed unauthorized personnel access to the system.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents and passersby captured on video had no meaningful notice of surveillance and no way to exercise their data rights, exposing them to undisclosed monitoring in public areas.

claimsVsReality.claim: The property association claimed the cameras do not record or permit viewing of the community swimming pool.
claimsVsReality.reality: While pool monitoring may have been excluded, the cameras still recorded public space and areas beyond the property's legitimate scope, violating data minimization principles.

claimsVsReality.claim: The association provided documents showing approval by general assembly of owners and establishment of a protocol for system operation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite procedural approval by owners, the physical installation exceeded legal limits by capturing public space, which no private entity may do regardless of internal authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be adequate, pertinent and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: The property association installed cameras capturing public space beyond the building's curtilage, exceeding permissible scope for a private entity.
violations: The property association installed cameras capturing public space beyond the building's curtilage, exceeding permissible scope for a private entity.
The system was not limited to necessity for security of the property and its residents.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are collected from an individual, the controller must provide specified information including the identity of the controller, purposes of processing, legal basis, and rights of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Surveillance signage was inadequate and not properly identifying the responsible party or providing required information.
violations: Surveillance signage was inadequate and not properly identifying the responsible party or providing required information.
Data subjects passing through or near the property had no clear notice of the surveillance system.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 22(4) establishes that the information duty is satisfied through placement of an informative device in a sufficiently visible location identifying the existence of processing, controller identity, and rights available.
regulatoryFindings.description: The property association failed to install adequate signage complying with visibility and completeness standards.
violations: The property association failed to install adequate signage complying with visibility and completeness standards.

outcome: The property owners' association paid €600 (original proposed fine of €1,000 reduced by 40% through voluntary payment and responsibility recognition). The association was ordered to reorient and/or remove cameras improperly pointed toward public space and to install compliant warning signage within 30 days. The procedure was terminated upon payment with acknowledgment of responsibility. The association must notify AEPD within one month of implementing corrective measures once the resolution becomes final and enforceable.
companyNow: The property owners' association (Comunidad de Propietarios) was ordered to bring its video surveillance system into compliance with GDPR and Spanish data protection law by reorienting cameras away from public space and installing proper transparency signage.
dataType: Images/footage from video surveillance cameras
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
LOPDGDD Art. 22(4) – Information requirements for video surveillance

companyDescription: Glasgow City Council is the local government authority for Glasgow City Area in Scotland, responsible for providing services to approximately 622,820 residents and managing 27,064 employees across multiple departments including social work, housing, and administration.
companyLongDescription: Glasgow City Council is the local government authority for Glasgow City Area in Scotland, responsible for providing services to approximately 622,820 residents and managing 27,064 employees across multiple departments including social work, housing, and administration.
caseDescription: Glasgow City Council failed to respond to Subject Access Requests (SARs) within statutory timeframes, with only 45% of SARs answered within one month during April 2023–March 2024. As of July 2024, the council had a backlog of 427 cases and failed to provide data subjects with progress updates or inform them of extension requests as required by UK GDPR Article 12(3). These failures prevented thousands of data subjects from exercising their right to access their personal data within statutory deadlines.
violationSummary: GCC systematically denied data subjects timely access to their personal data by failing to respond to Subject Access Requests within statutory timeframes and refusing to provide meaningful communication about delays, effectively excluding them from exercising their legal rights.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Glasgow City Council failed to respond to 55% of Subject Access Requests within the one-month statutory deadline, maintaining a backlog of 427 cases as of July 2024.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 622,820 residents and employees were systematically denied timely access to their personal data, with many never informed of request extensions or case progress.

claimsVsReality.claim: GCC acknowledged the backlog was due to increased demand from the Scottish Government's Redress Scheme with staffing challenges and no additional funding.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite cited constraints, GCC failed to meet statutory obligations for 55% of SARs and did not proactively communicate with data subjects, as required by law regardless of workload.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to provide information on action taken on requests under Articles 15–22 to data subjects without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, with possibility of two-month extension if necessary with notice to data subject of reasons.
regulatoryFindings.description: GCC responded to only 45% of SARs within the one-month statutory deadline during April 2023–March 2024
violations: GCC responded to only 45% of SARs within the one-month statutory deadline during April 2023–March 2024
GCC failed to inform data subjects of extension requests or reasons for delays
GCC provided only an initial acknowledgment email and did not regularly update data subjects on case progression

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(1) establishes the right to obtain from a controller confirmation as to whether personal data concerning the data subject are being processed, and where that is the case, access to the personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: GCC failed to respond to over 50% of SARs within the statutory timeframe of one month (or three months for complex SARs)
violations: GCC failed to respond to over 50% of SARs within the statutory timeframe of one month (or three months for complex SARs)
GCC failed to demonstrate provision of timely confirmation of processing or access to personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(3) requires the controller to provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: GCC failed to provide copies of personal data due to significant delays in SAR responses persisting over 12 months
violations: GCC failed to provide copies of personal data due to significant delays in SAR responses persisting over 12 months
427 cases remained in backlog as of July 12, 2024

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to Glasgow City Council for infringements of UK GDPR Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3). Additionally, an Assessment Notice was issued to provide ongoing assurance of compliance. GCC committed to implementing a new system to support timely SAR completion and engaged transparently with the ICO. The reprimand serves as a warning that future non-compliance may be treated as an aggravating factor in escalated enforcement action under Article 83(2)(i) of the UK GDPR.
companyNow: Glasgow City Council remains the local government authority serving 622,820 residents and 27,064 employees in Glasgow, Scotland. The council is actively implementing remedial measures and pursuing procurement of new SAR management systems to improve compliance.
dataType: Social care records, employment records, personal identifiers

company: ORANGE BANK S.A. SUCURSAL EN ESPAÑA
companyDescription: Orange Bank S.A. is a French digital banking subsidiary of Orange S.A. (the telecommunications group). It operates a Spanish branch providing financial services and consumer lending, including device financing for telecom customers.
companyLongDescription: Orange Bank S.A. is a French digital banking subsidiary of Orange S.A. (the telecommunications group). It operates a Spanish branch providing financial services and consumer lending, including device financing for telecom customers.
caseDescription: Orange Bank's data security systems failed to protect customer financial information, resulting in unauthorized access to personal data through a ransomware attack on its service provider Marktel. The bank failed to implement adequate encryption measures (specifically unencrypted IBAN numbers) and did not maintain confidentiality safeguards required by GDPR. Orange Bank was found responsible as a data controller despite the attack originating from a third-party processor.
violationSummary: Orange Bank failed to apply adequate technical and organizational measures to guarantee data confidentiality and security, resulting in unauthorized access to personal data. This is a core information processing failure involving inadequate security controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Orange Bank failed to encrypt customer financial data and IBAN numbers stored on its service provider's systems, leaving sensitive information accessible to attackers in a ransomware breach.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of Orange Bank customers lost complete control over their financial data when cybercriminals gained unauthorized access to unencrypted IBANs.

claimsVsReality.claim: Orange Bank claimed it had implemented adequate security measures and selected a high-level service provider (Marktel) with appropriate contractual security obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Orange Bank allowed customer IBAN numbers to be stored unencrypted in Marktel's systems for one year, and failed to implement the encryption protections required by its own contracts until November 2022, leaving data vulnerable to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Orange Bank argued that the ransomware attack was an act of a third party (Marktel) beyond the bank's control, and that it should not be held responsible for criminal hacking.
claimsVsReality.reality: As the responsible controller, Orange Bank remained obligated to ensure adequate security measures; third-party criminal activity does not excuse the bank's failure to encrypt sensitive financial data as required by GDPR Article 5(1)(f).

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be treated in a manner that ensures adequate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Orange Bank failed to implement encryption of IBAN numbers stored in Marktel's systems for approximately one year, leaving financial account identifiers exposed without confidentiality protection.
violations: Orange Bank failed to implement encryption of IBAN numbers stored in Marktel's systems for approximately one year, leaving financial account identifiers exposed without confidentiality protection.
Orange Bank did not ensure that data held by its processor Marktel was subject to adequate technical safeguards, allowing unauthorized access during a ransomware attack.
The bank's failure to encrypt or pseudonymize financial data resulted in complete loss of customer control and disposition over their personal financial information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection against accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Orange Bank did not require adequate encryption standards from Marktel for sensitive financial data, despite known risks of cyberattacks.
violations: Orange Bank did not require adequate encryption standards from Marktel for sensitive financial data, despite known risks of cyberattacks.
The bank failed to implement necessary safeguards such as data encryption, pseudonymization, or anonimization that would have prevented unauthorized access to customer financial records.
Orange Bank did not conduct sufficient risk assessment to identify that IBAN data required encryption, only implementing obfuscation measures halfway through the contract period.

outcome: Orange Bank was sanctioned with a €200,000 administrative fine for violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The bank is ordered to implement necessary technical and organizational measures to guarantee confidentiality of customer data within six months and report on adopted measures to the AEPD. The resolution is final and enforceable; Orange Bank must pay the fine and demonstrate remediation through encryption and proper security protocols.
companyNow: Orange Bank S.A. Sucursal en España continues to operate as a financial services subsidiary of Orange S.A. in Spain. The company must comply with enhanced data security requirements and ongoing AEPD monitoring following this enforcement action.
dataType: Financial data, personal identifiers, IBAN numbers, names, contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality Principle

company: Marriott International, Inc. and Starwood Hotels & Resorts Worldwide, LLC
companyDescription: Marriott International is a multinational hospitality company that manages and franchises hotels and related lodging facilities under 30 brands with over 7,000 properties worldwide. Starwood Hotels & Resorts Worldwide, LLC is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Marriott acquired for $12.2 billion in September 2016.
companyLongDescription: Marriott International is a multinational hospitality company that manages and franchises hotels and related lodging facilities under 30 brands with over 7,000 properties worldwide. Starwood Hotels & Resorts Worldwide, LLC is a wholly-owned subsidiary of Marriott acquired for $12.2 billion in September 2016.
caseDescription: Marriott and Starwood failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect consumer personal information across their hotel networks. Three separate data breaches between 2014 and 2020 compromised the information of hundreds of millions of consumers, including payment cards, passport numbers, and loyalty account data. The companies made deceptive claims about their security safeguards while maintaining inadequate password controls, outdated software, weak firewalls, and poor network segmentation.
violationSummary: The breaches resulted in unauthorized disclosure of highly sensitive personal information (payment cards, passports, loyalty data) that were entrusted to Marriott and Starwood in confidence. The scale and nature constitute a material breach of confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Marriott and Starwood failed to implement reasonable security measures including inadequate password controls, unpatched outdated software, weak firewalls, poor network segmentation.
whyTheyWereWrong: 339 million consumer records were exposed across three breaches between 2014 and 2020, including 5.25 million unencrypted passport numbers, payment card data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Starwood's privacy policy stated: 'we safeguard your information using appropriate administrative, procedural and technical safeguards, including password controls, firewalls and encryption'
claimsVsReality.reality: Starwood and Marriott failed to implement appropriate password controls (employees used default/blank/weak passwords), maintained outdated unpatched software vulnerable to attacks, had inadequate firewalls, and lacked proper network segmentation for four years during the Second Breach

claimsVsReality.claim: Marriott's privacy policy stated: 'We seek to use reasonable organizational, technical and administrative measures to protect Personal Data'
claimsVsReality.reality: Marriott failed to detect a four-year breach of Starwood's network despite having responsibility for information security post-acquisition, and lacked adequate monitoring and logging to identify intruder activity for years

claimsVsReality.claim: Both companies represented they were 'constantly reviewing and enhancing' security practices
claimsVsReality.reality: Both companies failed to remediate identical security vulnerabilities that caused the First Breach before the Second Breach occurred using the same attack vectors, indicating no meaningful security review occurred

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Marriott and Starwood represented that they used appropriate safeguards to protect personal information through privacy policy statements claiming continuous review, technical/procedural safeguards, password controls, firewalls, and encryption, while in fact maintaining inadequate password controls, outdated unpatched software, inadequate firewalls and network segmentation, poor access controls, lack of multifactor authentication, and inadequate monitoring and logging.
violations: Marriott and Starwood represented that they used appropriate safeguards to protect personal information through privacy policy statements claiming continuous review, technical/procedural safeguards, password controls, firewalls, and encryption, while in fact maintaining inadequate password controls, outdated unpatched software, inadequate firewalls and network segmentation, poor access controls, lack of multifactor authentication, and inadequate monitoring and logging.

Marriott and Starwood failed to employ reasonable security measures, causing substantial injury to 339 million consumers whose personal information was compromised in three separate breaches, and this injury was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on 20 December 2024 alleging both deceptive security statements (Count I) and unfair information security practices (Count II) under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint seeks compliance orders requiring Marriott and Starwood to implement reasonable security practices, establish an information security program, conduct regular assessments, provide consumer notification, and submit to ongoing monitoring and compliance verification. No monetary penalty is specified in this complaint document, which initiates the formal enforcement action.
companyNow: Marriott International remains the world's largest hotel company, operating over 1.1 million rooms across 30+ brands in 131 countries. Following the breaches, it has faced significant reputational damage and regulatory scrutiny.
dataType: Payment card numbers, passport numbers, names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, gender, addresses, loyalty account information, travel information, usernames
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Failure to provide reasonable security measures

company: Caja Rural de Nueva Carteya, Sociedad Cooperativa Andaluza de Crédito
companyDescription: Caja Rural de Nueva Carteya is a Spanish cooperative agricultural credit bank providing banking services to customers, primarily in rural areas. The entity operates an electronic banking platform (Ruralvía) used by thousands of customers for online financial transactions.
companyLongDescription: Caja Rural de Nueva Carteya is a Spanish cooperative agricultural credit bank providing banking services to customers, primarily in rural areas. The entity operates an electronic banking platform (Ruralvía) used by thousands of customers for online financial transactions.
caseDescription: A Spanish cooperative bank failed to implement adequate security measures to protect customer data from a cyber breach affecting its electronic banking system. Attackers gained unauthorized access to customer credentials and personal information between November and December 2022. The bank was responsible for ensuring data security despite outsourcing IT services to a processor.
violationSummary: The bank failed to implement measures ensuring confidentiality, integrity and availability of customer data systems, leading to unauthorized access and loss of control over personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Caja Rural failed to implement adequate security measures for its online banking system Ruralvía Clásica.
whyTheyWereWrong: Attackers exploited these security gaps to gain unauthorized access to thousands of customer banking records, exposing personal financial data and enabling potential identity theft and fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: The processor RSI had implemented adequate security measures and held relevant certifications demonstrating compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Certifications were for information security, not GDPR data protection. Known vulnerabilities in the authentication system remained unpatched, and attackers successfully compromised customer data despite claimed security standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Security audits and third-party evaluations demonstrated effective protection of customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite multiple audits, the SSO vulnerability and other weaknesses were not detected or remediated before the November–December 2022 breach, showing audits did not ensure actual operational security.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank bore no responsibility because RSI, as processor, was contractually obligated to ensure security.
claimsVsReality.reality: As data controller, the bank retained ultimate responsibility for security and compliance, including oversight and verification of the processor's controls, which it failed to exercise adequately.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: The bank failed to guarantee adequate confidentiality and integrity of customer data. Attackers accessed customer credentials and personal information due to unpatched vulnerabilities in the electronic banking system and inadequate technical safeguards.
violations: The bank failed to guarantee adequate confidentiality and integrity of customer data. Attackers accessed customer credentials and personal information due to unpatched vulnerabilities in the electronic banking system and inadequate technical safeguards.
No adequate measures existed to prevent unauthorized access through known security gaps in the SSO authentication system, exposing the treated data to breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires that the controller and processor implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security adequate to the risk, including pseudonymization, encryption, ability to restore availability, and regular verification of measure effectiveness.
regulatoryFindings.description: Measures listed in the processor contract were limited to information security standards rather than GDPR-specific data protection requirements. Certificates referenced were for information security, not data protection compliance.
violations: Measures listed in the processor contract were limited to information security standards rather than GDPR-specific data protection requirements. Certificates referenced were for information security, not data protection compliance.

Despite audits and third-party assessments, vulnerabilities exploited in the breach remained unaddressed, and the entity did not implement additional protective measures recommended in security evaluations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24 requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures and be capable of demonstrating compliance with data protection principles, including through proactive responsibility and oversight of processors.
regulatoryFindings.description: The bank failed to adequately supervise the processor's security implementation and verify effectiveness of technical controls before and after the breach occurred.
violations: The bank failed to adequately supervise the processor's security implementation and verify effectiveness of technical controls before and after the breach occurred.
The entity did not take sufficient measures to ensure compliance with security obligations despite contractual requirements imposing such responsibility on the data controller.

outcome: The bank was found to have violated GDPR Article 5(1)(f) concerning the security principle. An initial penalty of €10,000 was proposed. The bank made voluntary payment of €8,000 (with a 20% reduction for prompt payment) on 18 December 2024, resulting in termination of the procedure. The payment constitutes acceptance of the infraction and waiver of administrative remedies. The bank must implement enhanced security measures and strengthen compliance with GDPR data protection obligations.
companyNow: Caja Rural de Nueva Carteya remains operational as a Spanish cooperative bank. The entity has committed to improved security protocols following the enforcement action.
dataType: Customer financial and banking data, credentials, personal identifiers
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Security principle (integrity and confidentiality)

company: Grocery Delivery E-Services UK Limited T/A HelloFresh
companyDescription: HelloFresh is a German-founded online meal delivery service that delivers ingredients and recipes to customers on a subscription basis. The company operates across multiple countries including the UK and provides meal-kit services for customers to prepare at home.
companyLongDescription: HelloFresh is a German-founded online meal delivery service that delivers ingredients and recipes to customers on a subscription basis. The company operates across multiple countries including the UK and provides meal-kit services for customers to prepare at home.
caseDescription: HelloFresh transmitted approximately 80.9 million unsolicited direct marketing messages (emails and SMS) to subscribers without valid consent between August 2021 and February 2022. The company's consent statement was unclear, bundled multiple purposes together, failed to disclose SMS as a channel, and did not inform users they could receive marketing for up to 24 months after cancelling subscriptions. The contravention was serious and resulted from negligence.
violationSummary: HelloFresh collected and used contact details (phone numbers and emails) for direct marketing without properly interrogating/obtaining informed consent. The consent mechanism failed to communicate the specific channels, purposes, and duration of marketing.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: HelloFresh sent 80.9 million direct marketing emails and SMS messages between August 2021 and February 2022 without obtaining valid consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of subscribers received unwanted marketing messages on channels they never agreed to, including SMS texts at unsociable hours.

claimsVsReality.claim: HelloFresh claimed it had consent to contact all individuals who complained to the 7726 spam reporting service.
claimsVsReality.reality: HelloFresh did not have valid, specific, informed consent; the consent statement failed to disclose SMS as a channel and did not inform customers of the 24-month post-cancellation marketing period.

claimsVsReality.claim: HelloFresh stated it checked telephone numbers against communication settings before sending SMS messages.
claimsVsReality.reality: Communication preference settings did not allow users to set marketing preferences by channel (email, SMS, phone); the consent statement was not specific to channels, making any opt-in ineffective for SMS marketing.

claimsVsReality.claim: HelloFresh explained it had consent from 'reactivation customers' to receive SMS marketing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The consent mechanism was flawed and did not communicate that marketing would continue for up to 24 months after subscription cancellation, contrary to reasonable customer expectations.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) requires that unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail to individual subscribers may only be sent if the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: HelloFresh sent 80,893,013 direct marketing messages without demonstrating valid prior consent from recipients.
violations: HelloFresh sent 80,893,013 direct marketing messages without demonstrating valid prior consent from recipients.
The consent statement did not mention SMS as a channel for marketing, violating the requirement for specific consent.

The consent statement combined age confirmation, free samples, and email marketing into a single bundled checkbox, failing to allow separate consent and making it unclear what users were consenting to.
HelloFresh did not inform customers they could receive marketing for up to 24 months after cancelling subscriptions, making consent uninformed.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 4(11) defines valid consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of wishes by statement or clear affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: HelloFresh's consent statement was not specific as to marketing channels (SMS not mentioned) or duration (24 months post-cancellation not disclosed).
violations: HelloFresh's consent statement was not specific as to marketing channels (SMS not mentioned) or duration (24 months post-cancellation not disclosed).
The consent was not informed because customers lacked awareness of post-cancellation marketing duration and SMS channel usage.
Consent was not freely given without separate consent options for different purposes and channels.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 1998 Section 55A(3) permits a monetary penalty if the person knew or ought to have known of a risk of contravention but failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it.
regulatoryFindings.description: HelloFresh failed to exercise proper due care regarding unsolicited marketing requirements, showing misunderstanding of PECR and UK GDPR interplay.
violations: HelloFresh failed to exercise proper due care regarding unsolicited marketing requirements, showing misunderstanding of PECR and UK GDPR interplay.
HelloFresh did not implement channel-specific consent mechanisms (phone, text, email) despite this being standard practice.
HelloFresh did not provide clear transparency notices explaining the 24-month reactivation marketing period.
HelloFresh did not document internal policies, procedures, and training demonstrating organizational understanding of PECR requirements.

outcome: HelloFresh was issued a monetary penalty of £140,000 (reducible to £112,000 with early payment by 12 February 2024). The penalty was payable by 13 February 2024 via BACS or cheque to the ICO. The funds are paid into the Consolidated Fund (UK Government general account). HelloFresh has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The Commissioner found the contravention serious due to the scale (80.9 million messages) and negligent (failure to take reasonable steps despite available guidance). HelloFresh is required to cease the non-compliant practices and improve consent management.
companyNow: HelloFresh is a publicly traded online meal-kit delivery company (NASDAQ: HF) that has continued operations. Following this investigation, the company has taken steps to improve its marketing practices and customer journey.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, email addresses
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 4(11) – consent definition (freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous)
UK GDPR Recital 32 – separate consent for multiple purposes
UK GDPR Recital 43 – consent not freely given without separate consent options

company: THE RED KIWI, S.L. (trading as CLÍNICA DORSIA)
companyDescription: THE RED KIWI, S.L. is a Spanish aesthetic clinic company founded in 2003, operating under the commercial name CLÍNICA DORSIA. It provides cosmetic and aesthetic medical services.
companyLongDescription: THE RED KIWI, S.L. is a Spanish aesthetic clinic company founded in 2003, operating under the commercial name CLÍNICA DORSIA. It provides cosmetic and aesthetic medical services.
caseDescription: An aesthetic clinic created a WhatsApp group with approximately 90 clients' phone numbers visible to all group members for promotional purposes, without consent. When clients protested, the clinic abandoned the group without deleting it. The exposed phone numbers included health-related data revealing client relationships with the clinic.
violationSummary: The clinic exposed personal data (phone numbers) and indirectly revealed sensitive health information (client status at an aesthetic clinic) to unauthorized third parties (other clients) through improper use of a group messaging platform without adequate security measures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Clínica Dorsia created a WhatsApp group called 'Medicina Estética 2' and added approximately 90 clients' phone numbers without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 90 clients' mobile phone numbers and health-related data were exposed to strangers without authorization, allowing other group members to contact them.

claimsVsReality.claim: The clinic claimed it was promoting a service offering.
claimsVsReality.reality: The promotion method exposed approximately 90 clients' personal phone numbers and revealed their implicit involvement with aesthetic services without authorization or protective measures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The clinic stated it had 'eliminated' the group after being informed it was illegal.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal messages revealed the clinic's staff were uncertain whether the group had been deleted and asked a client for proof of the chat content, demonstrating the clinic never properly secured or deleted the data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in a manner guaranteeing adequate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: THE RED KIWI created a WhatsApp group with clients' phone numbers visible to all members without implementing any technical or organizational safeguards to maintain confidentiality.
violations: THE RED KIWI created a WhatsApp group with clients' phone numbers visible to all members without implementing any technical or organizational safeguards to maintain confidentiality.
The clinic failed to conduct a risk assessment of the messaging platform's features before including sensitive data, demonstrating gross negligence.
When clients protested, the clinic abandoned the group without deleting it, leaving approximately 90 individuals' data exposed in an active group chat.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 9 prohibits processing of special categories of personal data (including health data) except in specific circumstances, such as with explicit consent of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Information that a person is or has been a client of an aesthetic clinic constitutes health data under GDPR Article 9.
violations: Information that a person is or has been a client of an aesthetic clinic constitutes health data under GDPR Article 9.
THE RED KIWI disclosed this information indirectly by exposing phone numbers in a group specifically named for aesthetic services, without obtaining explicit consent from clients.
No lawful basis under GDPR Article 9(2) was established for this processing and disclosure.

outcome: THE RED KIWI, S.L. was fined €30,000 for violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The authority ordered the company to: (1) delete the WhatsApp group within one month of the resolution becoming enforceable; (2) implement communication systems within three months that prevent visibility of group member lists except to administrators. The company is required to demonstrate compliance within specified timeframes. Non-compliance with these orders may result in additional administrative sanctions and a new enforcement proceeding.
companyNow: THE RED KIWI, S.L. operates CLÍNICA DORSIA aesthetic clinics in Spain. The company is a medium-sized enterprise (€19.8M revenue in 2021) and subsidiary of WOW AESTHETICS, S.L.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, health data (client status at aesthetic clinic)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 9 – Processing of Special Categories of Data (health data)

company: University Hospital of Southampton NHS Foundation Trust
companyDescription: University Hospital of Southampton NHS Foundation Trust is a large NHS provider operating five hospitals and one birth centre across Southampton and Southern England. It processes significant volumes of personal data including health records and employee information for millions of service users and employees.
companyLongDescription: University Hospital of Southampton NHS Foundation Trust is a large NHS provider operating five hospitals and one birth centre across Southampton and Southern England. It processes significant volumes of personal data including health records and employee information for millions of service users and employees.
caseDescription: University Hospital of Southampton NHS Foundation Trust failed to respond to 41% of Subject Access Requests within the statutory one-month deadline under UK GDPR Articles 15 and 12. The organisation maintained a backlog of 621 cases as of January 2024 and did not inform data subjects of request progress. Until January 2021, SARs were processed alphabetically rather than chronologically, significantly delaying responses.
violationSummary: UHS systematically denied data subjects timely access to their personal data and excluded them from knowledge of processing delays by failing to respond within statutory timeframes and withholding progress information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: University Hospital of Southampton NHS Foundation Trust failed to respond to 41% of Subject Access Requests within the statutory one-month deadline, maintained a backlog of 621 cases.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients and employees seeking access to their medical records and personal data were systematically denied timely access.

claimsVsReality.claim: UHS handled SARs with adequate and appropriate procedures in line with current data protection legislation.
claimsVsReality.reality: UHS processes and procedures for SARs were inadequate and non-compliant. Until January 2021, SARs were processed alphabetically, causing multi-month delays. The Access to Records policy was based on the 1998 Data Protection Act, not current UK GDPR.

claimsVsReality.claim: UHS responded to SARs within statutory timeframes.
claimsVsReality.reality: UHS responded to only 59% of SARs within the one-month deadline during August 2022–July 2023, failing to meet statutory obligations for 41% of requests.

claimsVsReality.claim: UHS properly managed request extensions by only applying them to complex cases with appropriate notification.
claimsVsReality.reality: UHS automatically applied extensions to all requests regardless of complexity, without informing data subjects or providing reasons for delays.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to provide information on action taken on data subject rights requests without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, or within three months for complex requests, with extension notification and reasons for delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: UHS failed to inform data subjects of any extension to requests, instead automatically applying extensions to all requests without justification or notification, leaving requestors without knowledge of delays.
violations: UHS failed to inform data subjects of any extension to requests, instead automatically applying extensions to all requests without justification or notification, leaving requestors without knowledge of delays.
UHS provided only an acknowledgement email and no further progress updates, leading to direct complaints to both UHS and the ICO.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data is being processed and, if so, access to that personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: UHS failed to provide confirmation and access to 41% of Subject Access Requests within the one-month statutory timeframe, denying data subjects their legal right to timely access.
violations: UHS failed to provide confirmation and access to 41% of Subject Access Requests within the one-month statutory timeframe, denying data subjects their legal right to timely access.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(3) requires controllers to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: UHS failed to deliver copies of personal data within statutory deadlines to 41% of requestors, many of whom waited months or longer due to alphabetical processing order and inadequate procedures.
violations: UHS failed to deliver copies of personal data within statutory deadlines to 41% of requestors, many of whom waited months or longer due to alphabetical processing order and inadequate procedures.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand to UHS. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps taken by UHS from October 2023 onwards, including implementation of progress notification letters/emails (as of 7 November 2023) and plans for a new records management system. The ICO recommended that UHS: (1) resolve the backlog; (2) ensure SARs are answered within statutory deadlines; (3) ensure adequate staff training with refresher courses; (4) review and update all data protection policies; (5) implement SAR process improvements; and (6) continue monitoring SAR compliance. UHS was invited to provide a progress update by 25 September 2024. The reprimand notes that failure to rectify infringements may be treated as an aggravating factor in future enforcement action under Article 83(2)(i) of the UK GDPR.
companyNow: University Hospital of Southampton NHS Foundation Trust continues to operate as one of the UK's largest university hospitals, serving 1.9 million people in Southampton and South Hampshire as primary providers and 3.7 million as specialist service providers. Remediation efforts from October 2023 onwards are ongoing.
dataType: Personal identifiers, health data, employee records

companyDescription: Chelmer Valley High School is a UK academy school located in Broomfield, Chelmsford, Essex, providing secondary education to approximately 1,200 students aged 11-18.
companyLongDescription: Chelmer Valley High School is a UK academy school located in Broomfield, Chelmsford, Essex, providing secondary education to approximately 1,200 students aged 11-18.
caseDescription: Chelmer Valley High School deployed facial recognition technology for cashless catering in March 2023 without completing a mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) required by UK GDPR. The school relied on assumed opt-out consent (invalid under GDPR) for eight months, depriving students of their ability to exercise rights. The school only submitted a completed DPIA in January 2024 after the regulator contacted them.
violationSummary: The failure to conduct a DPIA meant no risk assessment was performed before processing high-risk biometric data of children, leaving students unable to exercise rights and the school unable to implement proper consent mechanisms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Introduced facial recognition technology for cashless catering in March 2023 without completing a mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 1,200 students, including minors unable to exercise independent consent, had their facial biometric data processed without prior risk assessment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The school's Data Protection Officer (IGS) submitted a completed DPIA considering the facial recognition processing to be high risk.
claimsVsReality.reality: The DPIA was only completed in November 2023 and submitted in January 2024—10 months after the facial recognition system went live in March 2023. No DPIA was completed prior to deployment as legally required.

claimsVsReality.claim: The school obtained consent for facial recognition processing via opt-out mechanism.
claimsVsReality.reality: Opt-out consent does not satisfy UK GDPR Article 4(11)'s requirement for 'affirmative action.' Valid consent requires affirmative opt-in, and students (the majority competent to consent) were deprived of this choice by parental opt-out arrangements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 35(1) of the UK GDPR requires controllers to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) prior to processing operations likely to result in high risk to rights and freedoms of natural persons.
regulatoryFindings.description: Chelmer Valley High School failed to conduct a DPIA before deploying facial recognition technology in March 2023, despite it being biometric data processing involving children (vulnerable subjects) using new technological solutions—both triggering DPIA requirements under the ICO's published list.
violations: Chelmer Valley High School failed to conduct a DPIA before deploying facial recognition technology in March 2023, despite it being biometric data processing involving children (vulnerable subjects) using new technological solutions—both triggering DPIA requirements under the ICO's published list.
The school only submitted a DPIA in January 2024, ten months after processing began and after ICO contact.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 4(11) of the UK GDPR defines consent as any freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous affirmative action signifying agreement to processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: From March to November 2023, the school relied on assumed opt-out consent (consent by default unless parents opted children out), which does not constitute valid affirmative action required by Article 4(11).
violations: From March to November 2023, the school relied on assumed opt-out consent (consent by default unless parents opted children out), which does not constitute valid affirmative action required by Article 4(11).
The opt-out model deprived students—the majority of whom were competent to provide their own consent—of the ability to exercise their data protection rights.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to Chelmer Valley High School under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR for failing to conduct a mandatory DPIA before deploying facial recognition technology. The school has taken remedial steps including completing a DPIA in November 2023 and obtaining explicit opt-in consent from students. The Commissioner welcomed these steps but warned that any future failure to rectify the infringements (or follow voluntary recommendations) may be treated as an aggravating factor in future enforcement actions. The Commissioner issued five voluntary recommendations covering DPIA completion before high-risk processing, necessity and proportionality review, consultation of ICO guidance, improved privacy information for students, and closer DPO engagement.
companyNow: Chelmer Valley High School remains an operational academy school in Essex. The school has implemented remedial measures including completing the required DPIA and refreshing consent mechanisms to obtain explicit opt-in consent from students for facial recognition processing.
dataType: Biometric data (facial recognition and fingerprint)

companyDescription: Breathe Services Ltd is a debt advice provider offering debt management services. The company was found to conduct unsolicited direct marketing campaigns primarily targeting financially vulnerable individuals regarding life insurance and later-life planning products.
companyLongDescription: Breathe Services Ltd is a debt advice provider offering debt management services. The company was found to conduct unsolicited direct marketing campaigns primarily targeting financially vulnerable individuals regarding life insurance and later-life planning products.
caseDescription: Breathe Services Ltd made over 4.3 million unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS), deliberately violating their privacy preferences. The company used number spoofing to conceal its identity and failed to provide required caller identification information. It also deliberately obstructed the ICO investigation by ceasing cooperation.
violationSummary: The company systematically targeted vulnerable individuals by making unsolicited calls to numbers explicitly registered to opt out of marketing calls, constituting systematic surveillance and harassment of privacy preferences.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Breathe Services Ltd made 4,376,037 unsolicited direct marketing calls to phone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service, which explicitly blocks unwanted marketing calls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Vulnerable individuals received repeated harassment—some called 5–12 times monthly—causing anxiety, stress.

claimsVsReality.claim: BSL claimed it had not made any unsolicited telephone calls between January 2022 and January 2023.
claimsVsReality.reality: Call records and complaints proved BSL made over 4.3 million calls to TPS-registered numbers during this period using a spoofed account.

claimsVsReality.claim: BSL stated it did not make calls to the numbers listed in complaints and had not received notification of complaints.
claimsVsReality.reality: The same calling account generated 58 TPS complaints and 193 ICO online reporting tool complaints, with evidence linking them to BSL's operations.

claimsVsReality.claim: BSL claimed leads were sourced from third parties but the origin was unknown.
claimsVsReality.reality: Evidence showed BSL directly contracted with lead generators, contracted a third party to provide leads generated from calls made on BSL's account, and used those leads themselves.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits making unsolicited calls for direct marketing to subscribers whose numbers are registered with the Telephone Preference Service register, unless the subscriber has specifically notified the caller they do not object to such calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: BSL made 4,376,037 calls to TPS-registered numbers without evidence of subscriber consent.
violations: BSL made 4,376,037 calls to TPS-registered numbers without evidence of subscriber consent.
BSL deliberately concealed its identity using spoofed calling numbers.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24 requires that communications for direct marketing purposes include the name of the person and either their address or a free-call contact number.
regulatoryFindings.description: BSL failed to provide required caller identification to any recipients of the calls.
violations: BSL failed to provide required caller identification to any recipients of the calls.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 1998 Section 55A allows the Commissioner to issue a monetary penalty where there is a serious contravention and the contravention was deliberate or negligent (knowing risk of contravention but failing to take reasonable steps to prevent it).
regulatoryFindings.description: BSL deliberately contravened Regulations 21 and 24 by concealing its identity and ceasing cooperation with the ICO investigation.
violations: BSL deliberately contravened Regulations 21 and 24 by concealing its identity and ceasing cooperation with the ICO investigation.
BSL knew or ought to have known of TPS and PECR obligations (due diligence document included explicit references) but failed to screen data against TPS register before calling.

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £170,000 (reduced to £136,000 if paid early by 6 January 2025). BSL must cease unsolicited marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers, implement TPS screening before calling, and provide evidence of subscriber consent. The company was required to comply within the notice period, with payment enforced via County Court or High Court if unpaid. Right of appeal exists to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: Breathe Services Ltd remains registered with the ICO as a debt advice provider (ZA835390), though it has demonstrated non-compliance with data protection law and resistance to regulatory investigation. Current operational status and financial viability are unclear.
dataType: Telephone numbers, personal contact information
legalBasisViolated: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) – unsolicited calls to TPS-registered numbers
PECR Regulation 24 – failure to provide caller identification
DPA 1998 Section 55A – serious contravention with deliberate conduct

companyDescription: Skean Homes Ltd is a property development and real estate company registered in the United Kingdom with offices in Bournemouth, Dorset. The company appears to specialize in residential property marketing.
companyLongDescription: Skean Homes Ltd is a property development and real estate company registered in the United Kingdom with offices in Bournemouth, Dorset. The company appears to specialize in residential property marketing.
caseDescription: Skean Homes Ltd made 614,342 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between March and May 2022, violating PECR regulations 21 and 24. The company failed to obtain valid consent from TPS registrants before calling them and did not provide required caller identification information. This resulted in 31 complaints to the TPS and Information Commissioner.
violationSummary: Skean used telecommunications services to conduct systematic, unsolicited direct marketing surveillance and contact of individuals who had explicitly registered to opt out of such calls, representing mass surveillance without consent.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Skean Homes Ltd made 614,342 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between March and May 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 614,000 individuals who had explicitly registered to opt out of marketing calls received unwanted calls anyway, generating 31 complaints.

claimsVsReality.claim: Skean implicitly claimed to have obtained valid consent from individuals to make direct marketing calls
claimsVsReality.reality: Skean provided no evidence of any notifications or consents whatsoever, and generic opt-ins to marketing communications do not constitute valid consent under PECR Regulation 21(4).

claimsVsReality.claim: Skean marketed itself as able to contact TPS registrants
claimsVsReality.reality: TPS registration represents an explicit opt-out from unsolicited marketing calls; only valid individual notifications to a specific company can override this protection, which Skean had not obtained.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits any person from using or instigating the use of a public electronic communications service for unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes to numbers listed on the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: Skean made 614,342 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were listed on the TPS register, with no evidence the numbers had been listed less than 28 days prior to the calls.
violations: Skean made 614,342 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers whose numbers were listed on the TPS register, with no evidence the numbers had been listed less than 28 days prior to the calls.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) allows calls to TPS-listed numbers only where the subscriber has notified the caller in writing that they do not object to such calls, requiring clear and positive action by the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: Skean provided no evidence of any valid notifications or consents from subscribers. The company failed to demonstrate how any generic opt-in terms could constitute clear, positive notification to override TPS registration for that specific company.
violations: Skean provided no evidence of any valid notifications or consents from subscribers. The company failed to demonstrate how any generic opt-in terms could constitute clear, positive notification to override TPS registration for that specific company.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(1) and 24(2) require that direct marketing communications include the name of the person making the call and either their address or a free-of-charge telephone number.
regulatoryFindings.description: Skean failed to provide required caller identification information (name and contact details) with the direct marketing calls.
violations: Skean failed to provide required caller identification information (name and contact details) with the direct marketing calls.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring Skean Homes Ltd to comply within 30 days of the notice dated 11 January 2024. Skean must cease unsolicited direct marketing calls to TPS-registered numbers unless valid consent from that specific company has been obtained, and must provide required caller identification information. The company has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. No monetary penalty was imposed.
companyNow: Unknown current status. Skean Homes Ltd is a UK property developer registered at Companies House (Registration Number 13011912). The company is now subject to mandatory compliance with PECR requirements and monitoring by the Information Commissioner.
dataType: Telephone numbers, direct marketing contact data

companyDescription: GRUAS IGNACI, S.L. is a Spanish vehicle recovery and towing service company (B57144412) that operates wrecker/impound facilities where customers retrieve their vehicles.
companyLongDescription: GRUAS IGNACI, S.L. is a Spanish vehicle recovery and towing service company (B57144412) that operates wrecker/impound facilities where customers retrieve their vehicles.
caseDescription: GRUAS IGNACI photographed a customer's national ID (DNI) using a personal smartphone without consent or informing them, then stored the image. The company lacked adequate security measures, failed to provide required privacy information, and had no warning signs for its video surveillance system.
violationSummary: Primary violation is failure to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures (GDPR Art. 32) when processing sensitive identity document data. Secondary violations include data minimization failure (Art. 5.1.c) by capturing full ID photo when simpler verification methods existed, and failure to provide required privacy transparency (Art. 13).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Photographed a customer's DNI (national ID) with a personal smartphone without consent or lawful basis, stored the image insecurely.
