whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's identity document was photographed and stored with no security safeguards, exposing sensitive personal data to unauthorized access, loss.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated it needed to photograph the customer's ID to 'demonstrate that [customer] collects [the vehicle] as authorized.'
claimsVsReality.reality: A customer's mere presentation and visual verification of an ID, or notation of key identifying information, would have been sufficient to establish authorization without capturing and storing a permanent image of the entire document.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed it was properly handling customer data by documenting vehicle collection.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to inform customers of any data processing, did not provide privacy notices required by law, and stored sensitive identity document images using an uncontrolled personal smartphone with no security measures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed (data minimization principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: GRUAS IGNACI photographed the full front of a customer's national ID document when merely displaying and noting key details would have been sufficient to verify the customer as the authorized vehicle recipient.
violations: GRUAS IGNACI photographed the full front of a customer's national ID document when merely displaying and noting key details would have been sufficient to verify the customer as the authorized vehicle recipient.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires that data controllers implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including preventing unauthorized access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: GRUAS IGNACI used an employee's personal mobile phone to capture and store a photograph of the customer's ID, without implementing any security controls, encryption, or secure data handling procedures.
violations: GRUAS IGNACI used an employee's personal mobile phone to capture and store a photograph of the customer's ID, without implementing any security controls, encryption, or secure data handling procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data are obtained from a data subject, the controller shall provide specific information including the controller's identity, purposes of processing, retention periods, and the individual's rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: GRUAS IGNACI provided no privacy notice to the customer at the time of collecting their ID and capturing its photograph, preventing the customer from understanding what data was being processed, why, or how to exercise their access/deletion rights.
violations: GRUAS IGNACI provided no privacy notice to the customer at the time of collecting their ID and capturing its photograph, preventing the customer from understanding what data was being processed, why, or how to exercise their access/deletion rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 (in conjunction with LOPDGDD Article 22) requires that video surveillance systems display informative signs indicating the existence of surveillance, controller identity, and data subject rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: GRUAS IGNACI's premises contained video surveillance cameras but lacked the required warning signs informing customers they were being recorded and under what authority.
violations: GRUAS IGNACI's premises contained video surveillance cameras but lacked the required warning signs informing customers they were being recorded and under what authority.

outcome: GRUAS IGNACI recognized responsibility and paid €6,600 (€11,000 reduced by 40% for early settlement and admission). The company must within 2 months: (1) implement measures to prevent capturing customer ID images; (2) adopt appropriate technical/organizational security controls per GDPR Art. 32; (3) provide customers with GDPR Art. 13 privacy information; (4) install video surveillance warning signs. Failure to comply with corrective measures may result in further enforcement action. The procedure is terminated and the resolution is final and enforceable in administrative law.
companyNow: Unknown. As a small-to-medium vehicle recovery service operator in Spain, current operational status is not disclosed in the resolution.
dataType: Identity documents (DNI), name, address, vehicle registration, photographs of identity documents
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject

companyDescription: Dorset Police is the territorial police force responsible for policing Dorset in South West England. Since April 2017, it has operated as part of an alliance with Devon and Cornwall Police to improve operational efficiency and resilience across administrative and operational functions.
companyLongDescription: Dorset Police is the territorial police force responsible for policing Dorset in South West England. Since April 2017, it has operated as part of an alliance with Devon and Cornwall Police to improve operational efficiency and resilience across administrative and operational functions.
caseDescription: Dorset Police failed to respond to subject access requests within statutory timeframes for over four years, with 243 overdue requests in September 2022 (33% older than seven months). By November 2023, 140 requests remained pending with 85% exceeding the one-month deadline. The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand under UK GDPR Article 12(3) and DPA 2018 Section 54.
violationSummary: The failure to process and respond to subject access requests within mandatory timeframes represents systemic inadequacy in handling personal data requests, falling under information processing deficiencies.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Dorset Police continuously failed to respond to subject access requests within the one-month statutory deadline for over four years, with 243 overdue requests in September 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens exercising their legal right to access personal data held by police were denied timely responses for months or years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The alliance was formed to improve delivery, resilience, flexibility, and efficiency in data protection and other business areas.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite the alliance structure, Dorset Police accumulated a persistent backlog of subject access requests, with some requests remaining unresponded for over one year.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) of the UK GDPR requires controllers to provide information on action taken on data subject requests (Articles 15–22) without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months where necessary based on complexity.
regulatoryFindings.description: Dorset Police maintained a backlog of 243 overdue subject access requests as of September 2022, with 81 requests (33%) older than seven months and 52 requests (24%) older than one year.
violations: Dorset Police maintained a backlog of 243 overdue subject access requests as of September 2022, with 81 requests (33%) older than seven months and 52 requests (24%) older than one year.
As of November 2023, 140 requests remained pending with 120 (85%) exceeding the one-month statutory deadline and 13 (9%) exceeding four months.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018 Section 54 defines the applicable time period for responding to data subject requests as one month, or such longer period as specified in regulations (maximum three months).
regulatoryFindings.description: Dorset Police systematically failed to meet the one-month deadline for processing subject access requests, with a continuous backlog spanning over four years since 2018.
violations: Dorset Police systematically failed to meet the one-month deadline for processing subject access requests, with a continuous backlog spanning over four years since 2018.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to Dorset Police. The Commissioner acknowledged mitigating factors including staffing increases (8 FTE data protection advisors from July 2023) and implementation of overtime funding. Dorset Police was recommended to: (1) maintain adequate staff resources for processing subject access requests; (2) continue implementing their action plan to ensure compliance with statutory deadlines. Dorset Police declined to make representations.
companyNow: Dorset Police continues operating as the police force for Dorset, South West England, part of the Devon and Cornwall Police & Dorset Police Alliance formed in April 2017. As of 2024, staffing improvements implemented in 2023 are ongoing to address the backlog.
dataType: Personal data subject to subject access requests (unspecified types)
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018 Part 3, Chapter 3, Section 54

companyDescription: CAJA RURAL GRANADA is a Spanish cooperative credit union (founded 2003) part of the Grupo Caja Rural network. It provides banking services, including electronic banking (Ruralvía platform), to customers primarily in Spain with approximately €137M in annual revenue (2022).
companyLongDescription: CAJA RURAL GRANADA is a Spanish cooperative credit union (founded 2003) part of the Grupo Caja Rural network. It provides banking services, including electronic banking (Ruralvía platform), to customers primarily in Spain with approximately €137M in annual revenue (2022).
caseDescription: CAJA RURAL GRANADA suffered a data breach in November 2022 affecting thousands of customer records through vulnerabilities in its electronic banking system (Ruralvía Clásica). The bank failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures to prevent unauthorized access to customer personal and financial data. Although the breach was detected in December 2022 and reported, the AEPD found the bank responsible for insufficient confidentiality protections under GDPR Article 5.1(f).
violationSummary: The bank failed to implement and maintain adequate security measures to protect personal data from unauthorized access, resulting in a breach affecting customer confidentiality and financial information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: CAJA RURAL GRANADA operated the Ruralvía Clásica electronic banking platform with inadequate security measures, allowing a cyberattacker to access thousands of customers' names.
whyTheyWereWrong: The bank's negligent security practices exposed thousands of customers to identity theft, financial fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: RSI and CAJA RURAL GRANADA claimed to have implemented the highest standards of security, including multiple security audits and certifications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite certifications and audits, critical vulnerabilities existed in the Ruralvía Clásica system that were not remediated; the breach occurred because of exploitable weaknesses in authentication and access controls.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank and processor claimed adequate security measures were in place through contractual requirements and third-party audits.
claimsVsReality.reality: RSI's own incident reports confirmed that additional security measures could have prevented the breach and that deficiencies in implemented security measures contributed to the attack.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank treated information security certifications as evidence of data protection compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Information security certifications (ISO standards) do not equate to GDPR compliance; the distinction between information security and data protection is material, and certifications alone do not guarantee adequate safeguards for personal data rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner that guarantees appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: CAJA RURAL GRANADA failed to guarantee confidentiality and integrity of customer data; thousands of customers' personal, contact, and financial data were accessed without authorization due to unpatched vulnerabilities in the Ruralvía Clásica banking application.
violations: CAJA RURAL GRANADA failed to guarantee confidentiality and integrity of customer data; thousands of customers' personal, contact, and financial data were accessed without authorization due to unpatched vulnerabilities in the Ruralvía Clásica banking application.
The bank did not implement appropriate technical and organizational measures proportionate to the risk, despite handling large-scale sensitive financial data accessible via internet-facing systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 requires the data controller to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure compliance with data protection principles, and to be able to demonstrate compliance (accountability).
regulatoryFindings.description: CAJA RURAL GRANADA failed to implement adequate security controls and oversight of its processor RSI; known vulnerabilities existed and were not remediated in a timely manner.
violations: CAJA RURAL GRANADA failed to implement adequate security controls and oversight of its processor RSI; known vulnerabilities existed and were not remediated in a timely manner.
The bank did not exercise sufficient supervisory control over its data processor to ensure compliance with security obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to apply appropriate technical and organizational security measures to guarantee a level of security adequate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Security audits identified critical vulnerabilities prior to the breach, but these were not resolved before the breach occurred.
violations: Security audits identified critical vulnerabilities prior to the breach, but these were not resolved before the breach occurred.

While RSI held security certifications, these were in general information security (ISO standards) rather than data protection; the bank did not ensure concrete protective measures were implemented and maintained.

outcome: CAJA RURAL GRANADA was sanctioned €15,000 for violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The bank exercised voluntary payment on 21 December 2024, reducing the final penalty to €12,000 (20% reduction under LPACAP Article 85). Investigations into violations of Articles 32 and 33 were archived. The bank is required to implement enhanced security measures and comply with ongoing data protection obligations. The AEPD clarified that responsability for the breach rests with the bank as controller, despite engaging a processor (RSI), because the bank determined the essential means of treatment and retained ultimate accountability.
companyNow: CAJA RURAL GRANADA remains operational as a Spanish agricultural cooperative credit union. The bank is part of the broader Grupo Caja Rural network and continues to provide banking services. Post-breach, the entity is subject to heightened regulatory scrutiny and ongoing compliance monitoring.
dataType: Personal data, contact information, financial data including banking credentials
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 24 – Responsibility of Data Controller
GDPR Art. 25 – Data Protection by Design and Default

companyDescription: Caja Rural de Aragón is a cooperative credit institution (Sociedad Cooperativa de Crédito) regulated under Spanish law and providing retail and commercial banking services to customers in Spain through online and branch channels.
companyLongDescription: Caja Rural de Aragón is a cooperative credit institution (Sociedad Cooperativa de Crédito) regulated under Spanish law and providing retail and commercial banking services to customers in Spain through online and branch channels.
caseDescription: Caja Rural de Aragón failed to implement adequate security measures to protect customer data, resulting in unauthorized access to personal information through vulnerabilities in its e-banking system. The bank was responsible as the data controller despite contracting security implementation to a third party (RSI). A cyberattack in November 2022 exposed customer credentials and personal data stored in the Ruralvía Clásica online banking platform.
violationSummary: The bank's failure to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures (Article 32) directly enabled unauthorized access to personal data, representing a fundamental breach of data security obligations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Caja Rural de Aragón failed to implement adequate security measures to protect customer banking data.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of bank customers' personal and financial data was exposed to unauthorized access by hackers, enabling potential identity theft and fraud without their knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: RSI (the processor) had implemented high security standards and carried multiple certifications in information security
claimsVsReality.reality: The certifications were not in data protection but in general information security; they did not prevent the breach and vulnerabilities existed in the authentication system despite audits

claimsVsReality.claim: Caja Rural had entered a contract with RSI clearly defining security obligations and measures in Annex B
claimsVsReality.reality: The measures listed were generic information security policies rather than specific technical controls; they proved inadequate and the known vulnerabilities were not addressed before the breach

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank exercised due diligence in supervising RSI
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank failed to implement adequate supervision and did not ensure compliance with Article 32 requirements; the SSO vulnerability had been identified in prior audits but not remediated

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be treated with integrity and confidentiality through appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Caja Rural failed to guarantee adequate confidentiality and integrity of customer data, allowing unauthorized access via inadequate security measures in the Ruralvía online banking system
violations: Caja Rural failed to guarantee adequate confidentiality and integrity of customer data, allowing unauthorized access via inadequate security measures in the Ruralvía online banking system

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires the controller and processor to apply technical and organizational measures appropriate to the risk, considering state of the art, implementation costs, nature/scope/context/purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Caja Rural did not implement sufficient security controls despite being the data controller responsible for determining means and purposes; vulnerabilities in SSO authentication were known and unpatched before the breach
violations: Caja Rural did not implement sufficient security controls despite being the data controller responsible for determining means and purposes; vulnerabilities in SSO authentication were known and unpatched before the breach

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33 requires notification of a personal data breach to the competent authority without undue delay, and in any case within 72 hours of becoming aware of it.
regulatoryFindings.description: Caja Rural failed to timely notify authorities; the responsible party (RSI) notified on 12 December 2022 but the breach was detected on 7 December 2022, though the archive proposes dismissal of this charge
violations: Caja Rural failed to timely notify authorities; the responsible party (RSI) notified on 12 December 2022 but the breach was detected on 7 December 2022, though the archive proposes dismissal of this charge

outcome: AEPD imposed a €15,000 fine for violations of GDPR Article 5(1)(f) (integrity and confidentiality principle). The company made voluntary payment of €12,000 (with 20% reduction for prompt payment) on 20 December 2024, which concluded the proceedings. The bank must implement enhanced security measures, conduct regular audits, and ensure proper responsibility allocation between itself as controller and RSI as processor. The AEPD found the bank remained liable despite contractual terms with RSI, emphasizing the controller's duty under Article 5(2) to demonstrate proactive accountability.
companyNow: Caja Rural de Aragón continues operations as a Spanish cooperative bank. The enforcement outcome and remediation requirements have been implemented as conditions of the settlement.
dataType: Financial data, customer identification information, online banking credentials
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality principle

companyDescription: Individual lawyer in Greece (identity redacted) who was retained as counsel by the complainant in one or more legal matters and held the complainant's case files and personal data.
companyLongDescription: Individual lawyer in Greece (identity redacted) who was retained as counsel by the complainant in one or more legal matters and held the complainant's case files and personal data.
caseDescription: A lawyer failed to respond to a client's repeated requests to access personal data contained in files held by the lawyer for nearly 5 years (from November 2019 onwards). The lawyer ignored the access requests and refused to cooperate with Greece's Data Protection Authority during its investigation, violating GDPR Article 15 (right of access) and Article 31 (obligation to cooperate with supervisory authorities).
violationSummary: The lawyer's refusal to provide access to personal data is a classic exclusion violation — the data subject was denied lawful access to information about them held by a data controller, and the controller obstructed regulatory oversight.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A lawyer refused to provide a client access to personal data and case files after the client repeatedly requested them via SMS, email, and formal notices between 2019 and 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: The client's persistent inability to access their own personal data caused prolonged uncertainty and powerlessness; they could not verify information, correct inaccuracies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Lawyer claimed the access request was indefinitely delayed (filed late in December 2022 vs. initial refusal in November 2019), rendering it stale and subject to a claim of 'abusive exercise of the right of access' under GDPR Article 12(5).
claimsVsReality.reality: The client exercised the right of access within the law (immediately upon termination of representation) and reiterated it multiple times from 2019–2021; no legal basis supports withholding access for 3+ years; the DPA found the request timely and the claim of abuse baseless.

claimsVsReality.claim: Lawyer claimed the client already had access to the documents from other sources (e.g., court files, electronic registry 'DIAVGEIA') and could obtain copies as a party to litigation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Availability of documents from alternative sources does not relieve the lawyer's legal obligation to respond to an access request under Article 15. Each controller's copy and records are a distinct archive; the existence of external sources does not eliminate the controller's duty to cooperate.

claimsVsReality.claim: Lawyer claimed not to retain physical copies of older case files, only digital versions, and stated the client could obtain them via the criminal docket or from public registries.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even if a controller does not maintain an archive, the law requires the controller to respond (if necessary, negatively) and to explain why data is not held. Silence and refusal to communicate are not lawful alternatives under GDPR Article 12(4).

claimsVsReality.claim: Lawyer argued the client's request and subsequent complaint to the DPA were 'frivolous' and constituted abuse of the supervisory process, citing the principle of non-reversal of burden of proof.
claimsVsReality.reality: The DPA was obligated to investigate the complaint; the lawyer bore the burden of justifying the refusal; silence and evasion during the investigation itself violated Article 31 and proved the lawyer had no legitimate legal basis for withholding access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 establishes the right of a data subject to obtain from a controller confirmation of whether personal data concerning them is being processed, and if so, the right to access a copy of such data and related information about the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lawyer withheld client's personal data for nearly 5 years despite repeated access requests (SMS 27-11-2019, email 27-04-2020, formal notices 30-09-2020 and 22-06-2021), violating Article 15(1) GDPR.
violations: Lawyer withheld client's personal data for nearly 5 years despite repeated access requests (SMS 27-11-2019, email 27-04-2020, formal notices 30-09-2020 and 22-06-2021), violating Article 15(1) GDPR.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3)–(4) requires the controller to provide the requested information without undue delay and at the latest within one month of receipt, or inform the data subject of reasons for non-action and their rights to lodge a complaint or pursue judicial remedies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lawyer never provided the requested personal data, provided no reasoned response explaining refusal, and offered no legal basis or justification within the required timescale, violating Article 12(3)–(4) GDPR.
violations: Lawyer never provided the requested personal data, provided no reasoned response explaining refusal, and offered no legal basis or justification within the required timescale, violating Article 12(3)–(4) GDPR.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires controllers to cooperate with supervisory authorities upon request in the exercise of the Authority's functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lawyer failed to answer the DPA's detailed requests for clarification (14-03-2023 letter), submitted only a cryptic response without addressing specific questions (11-04-2023), and did not respond to a follow-up reminder with explicit reference to Article 31 obligations (19-07-2023), obstructing the DPA's investigation into the alleged violation.
violations: Lawyer failed to answer the DPA's detailed requests for clarification (14-03-2023 letter), submitted only a cryptic response without addressing specific questions (11-04-2023), and did not respond to a follow-up reminder with explicit reference to Article 31 obligations (19-07-2023), obstructing the DPA's investigation into the alleged violation.

outcome: The DPA found the lawyer violated GDPR Articles 15, 12(3)–(4), and 31. The Authority imposed two administrative fines totaling €1,400 (€700 for failure to provide access; €700 for failure to cooperate). The lawyer must now comply with the client's access requests and cooperate fully with future DPA investigations. The decision is final unless appealed to Greek administrative courts.
companyNow: Unknown. The decision does not identify the lawyer by name (referred to as a lawyer in region 'X') or indicate the current status of the lawyer's practice.
dataType: Personal data of clients and case files

company: ΜΕΤΡΟ Ανώνυμη Εμπορική και Βιομηχανική Εταιρεία Ειδών Διατροφής και Οικιακής Χρήσης (METRO AEBE)
companyDescription: METRO AEBE is a leading cash-and-carry wholesaler and grocery retailer operating physical stores and an e-commerce platform (eshop.mymarket.gr) across Greece and Europe, serving approximately 400,000 e-shop customers.
companyLongDescription: METRO AEBE is a leading cash-and-carry wholesaler and grocery retailer operating physical stores and an e-commerce platform (eshop.mymarket.gr) across Greece and Europe, serving approximately 400,000 e-shop customers.
caseDescription: A pregnant customer's personal mobile phone number was misused by a former METRO delivery employee after order fulfillment. METRO failed to investigate the breach, did not report it to the DPA, and improperly denied the customer's rights of access and deletion by claiming the customer was not the data subject.
violationSummary: Former employee retained and misused customer personal data (phone number) without authorization after employment ended. Breach occurred due to inadequate security measures, failure to properly return/destroy data upon employee departure, and lack of breach investigation/notification.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: METRO retained customer personal data beyond lawful purpose, failed to investigate a data breach, did not report it to authorities, and denied the customer's access and deletion rights.
whyTheyWereWrong: A pregnant woman's phone number was shared without permission by a former employee, causing severe emotional distress that required emergency hospitalization during her pregnancy.

claimsVsReality.claim: The former employee was responsible for the breach and METRO had no involvement; he retained the number on his own initiative.
claimsVsReality.reality: The former employee obtained the phone number from METRO's delivery records and retained it after METRO failed to implement procedures for data return/destruction upon termination. METRO provided the employee access to customer data as part of normal duties.

claimsVsReality.claim: This was not a breach of personal data because the employee already had the phone number from the order delivery record and METRO did not provide it after employment ended.
claimsVsReality.reality: An unauthorized disclosure and misuse of personal data occurred; the employee used the data months after employment ended and after METRO had terminated him, violating confidentiality obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The customer cannot exercise data subject rights because the account was registered in her husband's name and he is the sole data subject.
claimsVsReality.reality: The account was created and used by the customer (username 'B', customer's email) though delivery instructions referenced her husband's name on the doorbell. She was the actual data subject and account holder.

claimsVsReality.claim: METRO has comprehensive security and organizational measures (employee confidentiality statements, data breach policy) to protect personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: These measures existed on paper but were not implemented in practice; METRO relied on oral assurance from departing employee rather than documented return/destruction of data, and failed to investigate the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: METRO unlawfully disclosed customer phone number to employee and failed to prevent unauthorized use after employment termination.
violations: METRO unlawfully disclosed customer phone number to employee and failed to prevent unauthorized use after employment termination.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security and confidentiality of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: METRO failed to implement adequate controls to prevent retention of customer data by departing employees; reliance on verbal assurance was insufficient.
violations: METRO failed to implement adequate controls to prevent retention of customer data by departing employees; reliance on verbal assurance was insufficient.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33 requires controllers to notify the supervisory authority of personal data breaches within 72 hours unless unlikely to cause harm.
regulatoryFindings.description: METRO received notice of unauthorized phone number usage but failed to assess it as a breach or notify the DPA, instead dismissing it as not constituting a breach.
violations: METRO received notice of unauthorized phone number usage but failed to assess it as a breach or notify the DPA, instead dismissing it as not constituting a breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation and access to their personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: METRO refused to provide access to the customer's data, falsely claiming she was not the data subject because the account bore her husband's name on delivery address.
violations: METRO refused to provide access to the customer's data, falsely claiming she was not the data subject because the account bore her husband's name on delivery address.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 17 grants data subjects the right to erasure of their personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: METRO only honored deletion request after DPA inquiry (months later), having initially refused on grounds customer was not the data subject.
violations: METRO only honored deletion request after DPA inquiry (months later), having initially refused on grounds customer was not the data subject.

outcome: METRO AEBE was issued three separate administrative fines totaling €50,000: €35,000 for failures under GDPR Articles 24, 32, and 33 (breach investigation, notification, and security measures); €10,000 for violation of the right of access (Art. 15); and €5,000 for violation of the right to erasure (Art. 17). The company is required to comply with GDPR obligations, implement enhanced security procedures for employee data handling upon termination, and properly document and respond to data subject requests in accordance with its established policies.
companyNow: METRO AEBE remains operational as a major cash-and-carry wholesaler in Greece and Europe with significant retail operations. The company has over 400,000 registered customers in its e-shop.
dataType: Mobile phone number, name, address, order history

companyDescription: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA is a Spanish cooperative credit union providing banking services, including online electronic banking platforms to thousands of customers. The institution is governed by cooperative law and regulated as a credit entity under Spanish banking regulations.
companyLongDescription: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA is a Spanish cooperative credit union providing banking services, including online electronic banking platforms to thousands of customers. The institution is governed by cooperative law and regulated as a credit entity under Spanish banking regulations.
caseDescription: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA, a Spanish cooperative bank, suffered a data breach in November 2022 affecting customer personal and financial data via its electronic banking platform. The breach occurred due to inadequate security measures and insufficient technical and organizational safeguards protecting against unauthorized access. The bank was held responsible as the data controller for failing to ensure confidentiality and integrity of personal data under GDPR Article 5(1)(f).
violationSummary: The bank failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures (Article 32) resulting in a data breach causing loss of confidentiality (Article 5(1)(f)). This is classified as insecurity due to inadequate safeguards against unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Caja Rural de Onda failed to implement adequate security measures for its electronic banking system, allowing hackers to exploit SSO vulnerabilities.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 7,326 customers had their personal, financial, and contact information exposed to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: RSI (data processor) maintained adequate security measures and compliance with GDPR Article 32 requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Critical vulnerabilities in the SSO system allowed attackers to access customer data; security measures were insufficient despite third-party audits and certifications.

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach could not have been prevented with additional security measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: RSI's own forensic analysis confirmed that additional security measures could have prevented the breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA properly supervised its data processor's compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank failed to conduct adequate ongoing oversight and verification of security measures, despite obligations under Article 5(2) regarding proactive accountability.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA failed to ensure adequate security of personal data, allowing attackers to access customer data through vulnerabilities in the SSO (Single Sign-On) authentication system.
violations: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA failed to ensure adequate security of personal data, allowing attackers to access customer data through vulnerabilities in the SSO (Single Sign-On) authentication system.
The bank did not implement sufficient mitigating security measures to prevent unauthorized access despite known risks in the electronic banking platform.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires that the controller and processor shall apply appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA contracted RSI as data processor but failed to supervise and verify that appropriate security measures were actually implemented and effective.
violations: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA contracted RSI as data processor but failed to supervise and verify that appropriate security measures were actually implemented and effective.
Security measures listed in the data processing agreement were insufficient and not properly applied to prevent the breach.

outcome: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA was sanctioned with an initial fine of €15,000 for violating GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The company paid €12,000 voluntarily (applying a 20% reduction for early payment) and waived administrative appeal rights. The infraction regarding Article 32 was archived. The company is required to implement enhanced security measures and undergo monitoring compliance.
companyNow: CAJA RURAL DE ONDA continues operations as a Spanish cooperative credit institution. Following the enforcement action, the bank is subject to ongoing AEPD monitoring and must demonstrate compliance with strengthened data security protocols.
dataType: Personal data, financial data, contact information

companyDescription: DoorDash, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in San Francisco, California, operating a website and mobile application that enables consumers to order food delivery from restaurants. It is one of the largest third-party food delivery platforms in North America.
companyLongDescription: DoorDash, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in San Francisco, California, operating a website and mobile application that enables consumers to order food delivery from restaurants. It is one of the largest third-party food delivery platforms in North America.
caseDescription: DoorDash sold personal information of California customers to marketing cooperatives without notice or opt-out rights, violating both the CCPA and CalOPPA. The company failed to disclose in its privacy policy that customer data was being shared with third-party marketing co-ops, and did not provide the required 'Do Not Sell My Personal Information' link or opt-out mechanisms.
violationSummary: DoorDash disclosed customer personal information to third parties (marketing co-ops) without notice or consent, and failed to provide transparency regarding these disclosures in its privacy policy.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: DoorDash sold California customers' names, addresses, and transaction histories to marketing cooperatives in exchange for advertising access without notifying consumers or offering them.
whyTheyWereWrong: A customer who deliberately used an alias to protect her privacy received mailed advertisements at her home address from unrelated companies.

claimsVsReality.claim: DoorDash's privacy policy indicated that DoorDash could use customer data to contact customers with advertisements.
claimsVsReality.reality: DoorDash actually shared customer personal information with unrelated marketing co-ops that used the data to send unsolicited advertisements from third-party businesses, without any privacy policy disclosure of this practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: The customer who used an alias believed her identity was protected based on DoorDash's privacy policy disclosures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite using an alias and reviewing the privacy policy, her actual home address was exposed and sold to marketing co-ops, which resulted in unsolicited mailed advertisements to her real address using the alias.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Consumer Privacy Act § 1798.135(a) requires businesses that sell personal information to provide notice of the sale and a clear, conspicuous 'Do Not Sell My Personal Information' link, plus two or more methods for consumers to opt-out of such sales.
regulatoryFindings.description: DoorDash sold customer personal information to marketing co-ops but failed to disclose this in its privacy policy
violations: DoorDash sold customer personal information to marketing co-ops but failed to disclose this in its privacy policy
DoorDash did not post a 'Do Not Sell My Personal Information' link on its website or mobile app
DoorDash did not provide consumers an opportunity to opt-out of the sale of their personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: California Online Privacy Protection Act § 22575(b)(1) requires operators of commercial websites that collect personally identifiable information to disclose in their privacy policy the categories of third parties with whom they share such information.
regulatoryFindings.description: DoorDash's privacy policy failed to disclose that customer personally identifiable information was shared with marketing co-ops
violations: DoorDash's privacy policy failed to disclose that customer personally identifiable information was shared with marketing co-ops
DoorDash's privacy policy did not explain that unrelated businesses could contact customers with advertisements using DoorDash-collected data
DoorDash participated in two marketing co-ops between 2018 and 2020 but made no corresponding privacy policy disclosures

outcome: On February 21, 2024, the California Attorney General filed a civil complaint seeking injunctive relief, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation or $7,500 per intentional violation, and all necessary orders to prevent future violations. DoorDash is required to cease the unauthorized sale of consumer personal information and implement compliant privacy practices. The complaint alleges uncured violations of the CCPA despite a September 2020 notice of noncompliance and the 30-day cure period then available. DoorDash later stopped the sales and instructed deletion of California customer data, but did not cure by restoring consumers to their pre-violation position since data had already been sold downstream multiple times.
companyNow: DoorDash continues to operate as a major food delivery platform in the United States and internationally. Following this enforcement action, the company has implemented enhanced privacy practices and compliance measures to address CCPA and CalOPPA requirements.
dataType: Name, address, transaction history

companyDescription: City of Edinburgh Council is the local government authority serving the City of Edinburgh area in Scotland. With over 17,000 employees, it delivers public services including social care, education, housing, and benefits administration across the Council area.
companyLongDescription: City of Edinburgh Council is the local government authority serving the City of Edinburgh area in Scotland. With over 17,000 employees, it delivers public services including social care, education, housing, and benefits administration across the Council area.
caseDescription: City of Edinburgh Council systematically failed to respond to Subject Access Requests (SARs) within the statutory one-month timeframe required by UK GDPR, with backlogs extending years. In 2022, 31% of 665 SARs (206 cases) missed deadlines; in 2023, 40% of 698 SARs (279 cases) were overdue. As of December 2024, 116 of 213 open cases remained overdue, with eight cases between 18–24 months old.
violationSummary: The Council systematically failed to provide data subjects with access to personal data held about them, denying individuals the ability to exercise their right of access within the statutory period, thereby excluding them from knowledge of their own records.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: City of Edinburgh Council failed to respond to Subject Access Requests within the one-month legal deadline, with 31% of requests delayed in 2022.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens seeking their own personal records were denied timely access for years, leaving some individuals waiting nearly two years to obtain documents needed for legal claims related to child.

claimsVsReality.claim: Council has committed to recruiting further staff to support SAR work and absorb increased demand.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite staff commitments, 116 of 213 open cases remained overdue as of December 2024, with eight cases 18–24 months old, indicating staffing measures have not yet resolved systemic delays.

claimsVsReality.claim: Delays are attributable to increased complexity and volume of SARs related to Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry.
claimsVsReality.reality: While complexity and volume are acknowledged mitigating factors, the fundamental failure is the Council's chronic inability to meet statutory one-month deadlines across all years (2022–2024), indicating systemic resource insufficiency.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires the controller to provide information on action taken on Subject Access Requests without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months where necessary for complexity; the controller must inform the data subject of any extension and reasons within one month.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council responded to only 69% of 2022 SARs and 60% of 2023 SARs within the one-month statutory deadline.
violations: Council responded to only 69% of 2022 SARs and 60% of 2023 SARs within the one-month statutory deadline.
Oldest backlog case dated March 2021, demonstrating multi-year delays in excess of statutory timeframes.
116 of 213 open cases (December 2024) remained overdue, with eight cases 18–24 months old.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether personal data concerning them are being processed, and access to the personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council's failure to respond within statutory timeframes prevented data subjects from exercising the fundamental right to access personal data held about them.
violations: Council's failure to respond within statutory timeframes prevented data subjects from exercising the fundamental right to access personal data held about them.
Individuals seeking records related to Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry faced years-long delays accessing documents critical to redress claims.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires the controller to provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council failed to provide copies of personal data within required timeframes due to systemic SAR backlog and inadequate resource allocation.
violations: Council failed to provide copies of personal data within required timeframes due to systemic SAR backlog and inadequate resource allocation.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to City of Edinburgh Council under Article 58(2)(b) UK GDPR. The decision was non-monetary but carried the warning that failure to rectify infringements could trigger future enforcement action as an aggravating factor. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps already undertaken, including the Council's commitment to recruit additional staff to support SAR processing. Three voluntary recommendations were issued: (1) ensure subject access team has required staff and resources to meet statutory timeframes; (2) keep data subjects informed on request status, especially if delayed; (3) continue engagement with ICO's Assurance team during voluntary audit of data protection compliance. The Commissioner indicated that future non-compliance could result in escalated enforcement under Article 83(2)(i) GDPR.
companyNow: City of Edinburgh Council continues to operate as the local government authority for Edinburgh, covering a population of over 540,000. As of December 2024, the Council reported ongoing SAR compliance issues with 116 overdue cases of 213 open, indicating the problem persists despite remedial commitments.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Requests (SARs); includes records related to Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry and financial redress schemes

companyDescription: ESL Consultancy Services Ltd is a UK-based consultancy that engaged in direct marketing campaigns. The company instigated unsolicited email marketing and sourced contact data from third parties without proper consent verification.
companyLongDescription: ESL Consultancy Services Ltd is a UK-based consultancy that engaged in direct marketing campaigns. The company instigated unsolicited email marketing and sourced contact data from third parties without proper consent verification.
caseDescription: ESL Consultancy Services Ltd sent unsolicited direct marketing emails to 37,961+ recipients without valid consent, using unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal sender identity. The company knowingly used data sourced from old logs where consent had not been properly obtained, and doctored compliance forms to hide this fact. The marketing messages related to loans and posed financial harm to vulnerable individuals.
violationSummary: ESL sent unsolicited communications to individuals without consent, which constitutes surveillance-style collection and dissemination of contact data for direct marketing purposes in violation of PECR.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between September 2022 and December 2023, ESL Consultancy Services Ltd instigated transmission of 37,961 unsolicited direct marketing emails to individual subscribers without valid consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 37,000 financially vulnerable individuals received unlawful loan marketing emails without consent, exposing them to predatory lending offers.

claimsVsReality.claim: ESL's data provider Mr Bentley indicated he was compliant in marketing practices
claimsVsReality.reality: ESL doctored FCA forms completed by Mr Bentley, removing his statement that he was acting in a non-compliant manner by sending marketing messages without consent

claimsVsReality.claim: Data sourced from Mr Bentley was compliant and properly consented
claimsVsReality.reality: The data was sourced from old logs created or obtained by Mr Bentley; ESL showed no effort to verify valid consent had been obtained, and engaged with Bentley despite no evidence of consent for direct marketing

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 22(2) of PECR: A person shall neither transmit nor instigate unsolicited direct marketing emails unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: ESL instigated transmission of 37,961 unsolicited direct marketing emails without obtaining prior valid consent from recipients
violations: ESL instigated transmission of 37,961 unsolicited direct marketing emails without obtaining prior valid consent from recipients
ESL used data sourced from old logs created by Mr Bentley where consent had not been properly obtained for direct marketing purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 23(a) of PECR: A person shall not transmit or instigate direct marketing emails where the identity of the sender has been disguised or concealed.
regulatoryFindings.description: ESL used unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal the true identity of the sender
violations: ESL used unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal the true identity of the sender

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 4(11): Consent must be freely given, specific, informed and unambiguous.
regulatoryFindings.description: ESL did not obtain freely given consent—data was sourced from old logs with no evidence of consideration for consent
violations: ESL did not obtain freely given consent—data was sourced from old logs with no evidence of consideration for consent
Consent was not specific—individuals were not informed of ESL as the actual sender or the exact nature of loan marketing
Consent was not informed—ESL doctored FCA forms to remove evidence of non-compliance and hid the true source of contact
ESL showed no effort to verify valid consent had been acquired from primary data provider Mr Bentley

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice under Section 40 of the Data Protection Act 1998, requiring ESL to cease all unsolicited direct marketing email transmissions within 30 days unless prior valid, explicit consent is obtained. ESL must ensure sender identity is clearly disclosed, provide valid unsubscribe mechanisms, and comply with all PECR Regulation 22 and 23 requirements. The notice is enforceable and ESL has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
companyNow: Unknown current operational status. ESL Consultancy Services Ltd (Companies House Reg. 11483654) was subject to enforcement action in December 2024.
dataType: Email addresses, contact details

companyDescription: PILLOW HOTELS, S.L. (NIF B66964255) operates a boutique hotel called 'Irala, by Pillow' in Bilbao, Spain. The company is part of a group structure with parent entity MD MANAGEMENT, S.L. and was represented in proceedings by RAPINFORMES ON LINE, S.L.
companyLongDescription: PILLOW HOTELS, S.L. (NIF B66964255) operates a boutique hotel called 'Irala, by Pillow' in Bilbao, Spain. The company is part of a group structure with parent entity MD MANAGEMENT, S.L. and was represented in proceedings by RAPINFORMES ON LINE, S.L.
caseDescription: PILLOW HOTELS suffered two security breaches via phishing attacks that compromised customer personal data. The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures, allowed unauthorized access to customer accounts on the Booking.com platform, and did not notify the data protection authority of either breach.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure data security (GDPR Art. 32), resulting in unauthorized disclosure of personal data. The insecurity was a direct cause of the data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Pillow Hotels failed to implement adequate security measures, resulting in unauthorized access to customer personal data through phishing attacks in February 2023 and August 2023.
whyTheyWereWrong: At least 24 customers had their names, phone numbers, emails, and booking details exposed to fraudsters who impersonated the hotel via WhatsApp to steal payment information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated it had policies for data protection and security in place prior to the breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: Risk analysis did not address phishing threats; no multi-factor authentication or access logging was implemented; employee training was minimal and conducted late (December 2022, after initial compromise); and security measures listed as 'previous' had proven ineffective, as evidenced by two breaches.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed that breach notification was not necessary because the risk to rights and freedoms was unlikely.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customer data was actively exploited in real-time phishing and fraud attempts; customers received fraudulent WhatsApp messages impersonating hotel staff, soliciting banking details; the hotel itself acknowledged awareness of 'similar cases,' confirming systemic vulnerability.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company asserted that changing email passwords and Booking.com credentials resolved the first breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: A second, similar breach occurred in August 2023 (months after the first), indicating that underlying security vulnerabilities and processes were not remediated; attackers repeatedly changed the Booking.com password, suggesting persistent unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated in a manner guaranteeing appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction, or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: PILLOW HOTELS failed to guarantee confidentiality and integrity of customer personal data; unauthorized third parties accessed booking information including names, contact details, and reservation dates via compromised email and Booking.com accounts.
violations: PILLOW HOTELS failed to guarantee confidentiality and integrity of customer personal data; unauthorized third parties accessed booking information including names, contact details, and reservation dates via compromised email and Booking.com accounts.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including encryption, access logging, and regular security reviews.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company did not implement multi-factor authentication, had no unauthorized access controls or logging for the corporate email system, failed to identify phishing as a risk in its risk analysis, provided minimal employee cybersecurity training, and had no timely breach response protocol—all while handling substantial volumes of customer personal data.
violations: Company did not implement multi-factor authentication, had no unauthorized access controls or logging for the corporate email system, failed to identify phishing as a risk in its risk analysis, provided minimal employee cybersecurity training, and had no timely breach response protocol—all while handling substantial volumes of customer personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33 requires the controller to notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where possible, no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach.
regulatoryFindings.description: PILLOW HOTELS did not notify the AEPD of either the January–February 2023 or August 2023 breach. The company incorrectly determined that notification was unnecessary, claiming the breaches posed no risk to rights and freedoms, despite evidence that customer data was actively being misused in phishing and fraud attempts.
violations: PILLOW HOTELS did not notify the AEPD of either the January–February 2023 or August 2023 breach. The company incorrectly determined that notification was unnecessary, claiming the breaches posed no risk to rights and freedoms, despite evidence that customer data was actively being misused in phishing and fraud attempts.

outcome: PILLOW HOTELS paid €4,200 (reduced from €7,000 via two 20% reductions for early recognition of responsibility and voluntary payment). The company was ordered to implement technical and organizational security measures within 6 months to ensure compliance with Articles 5(1)(f), 32, and 33 of the GDPR. Measures must include adequate encryption, access controls, logging of unauthorized access attempts, timely breach detection and notification procedures, and enhanced employee training on phishing and data protection. The company must demonstrate compliance to the AEPD within six months. Failure to comply may trigger further enforcement action.
companyNow: PILLOW HOTELS, S.L. is a small Spanish hotel operator (2022 revenue ~€844,500; 13 employees). Status and remediation efforts post-penalty are not detailed in the resolution.
dataType: Name, surname, telephone number, email address, reservation dates, room type, payment information, companion names, guest preferences, booking history, misconduct warnings, guest reviews
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality principle
GDPR Art. 33 – Notification of a personal data breach to the authority

companyDescription: GALENICUM HEALTH is a Spanish healthcare entity providing laboratory and security-related services from a facility in Spain.
companyLongDescription: GALENICUM HEALTH is a Spanish healthcare entity providing laboratory and security-related services from a facility in Spain.
caseDescription: GALENICUM HEALTH installed videovigilance cameras that captured public roads and sidewalks beyond the scope of their private facility, violating the data minimization principle. The company's surveillance system recorded pedestrians and vehicles on public streets without proper justification or masking of excessive footage. The AEPD found the cameras captured more data than necessary and ordered remediation within one month.
violationSummary: The company engaged in excessive surveillance beyond the scope of their private premises, capturing identifiable footage of pedestrians and vehicles in public spaces without justification or technical safeguards to minimize data collection.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed videovigilance cameras (EXT-C9, EXT-C16, EXT-C17) at their facility that captured video footage of public sidewalks, streets.
whyTheyWereWrong: The cameras recorded the images of pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicle occupants lawfully using public roads.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed cameras EXT-C9, EXT-C16, and EXT-C17 only captured private spaces on Galenicum property separated from public roads by architectural barriers (fences, hedges, parking barriers).
claimsVsReality.reality: The photographic evidence submitted by the company itself showed complete visibility of sidewalks, parked vehicles on public streets, and emergency exit areas clearly visible to the public, proving public space capture regardless of claimed barriers.

claimsVsReality.claim: GALENICUM asserted the videovigilance system recorded only private areas of access and was 'totally separated from public roads.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The AEPD determined from submitted images that at least one photograph showed the entire sidewalk with parked vehicles, demonstrating undisputed capture of public pedestrian and vehicle traffic beyond the company's control.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimization').
regulatoryFindings.description: GALENICUM installed cameras capturing video footage of public roads and sidewalks beyond the scope of their facility, recording identifiable images of unknown individuals without justification and without technical masking to minimize the excessive capture.
violations: GALENICUM installed cameras capturing video footage of public roads and sidewalks beyond the scope of their facility, recording identifiable images of unknown individuals without justification and without technical masking to minimize the excessive capture.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(2)(d) empowers data protection authorities to order the controller to bring processing into compliance with the Regulation.
regulatoryFindings.description: The AEPD ordered GALENICUM to remove, reorient, or mask cameras EXT-C9, EXT-C16, and EXT-C17 to prevent capture of public roads within one month, with failure to comply constituting a further administrative infraction.
violations: The AEPD ordered GALENICUM to remove, reorient, or mask cameras EXT-C9, EXT-C16, and EXT-C17 to prevent capture of public roads within one month, with failure to comply constituting a further administrative infraction.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 22 permits videovigilance only for legitimate security purposes and only of spaces under the controller's authority, not public areas or third-party property.
regulatoryFindings.description: GALENICUM's surveillance system captured areas beyond its premises including public sidewalks and streets where security justification did not apply.
violations: GALENICUM's surveillance system captured areas beyond its premises including public sidewalks and streets where security justification did not apply.

outcome: The AEPD imposed a €500 administrative fine on GALENICUM HEALTH for violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(c). The company was ordered, within one month of the resolution becoming final and enforceable, to remove, reorient, or apply masking/shadowing to cameras EXT-C9, EXT-C16, and EXT-C17 to ensure no public roads are captured. The resolution is binding and enforceable once the optional one-month appeal period expires. Non-compliance may trigger additional enforcement proceedings.
dataType: Biometric data (video surveillance footage of individuals)

companyDescription: The Municipality of Athens (Δήμος Αθηναίων) is a major local government authority responsible for public administration, services, and data processing for the Athens metropolitan area and its residents.
companyLongDescription: The Municipality of Athens (Δήμος Αθηναίων) is a major local government authority responsible for public administration, services, and data processing for the Athens metropolitan area and its residents.
caseDescription: The Greek Data Protection Authority found that the Municipality of Athens failed to cooperate with a regulatory investigation into data protection officer (DPO) appointment and position requirements. The authority had sent a questionnaire three times between May–June 2023, but the municipality did not respond despite multiple reminders and extended deadlines, ultimately only submitting answers after being summoned to a hearing.
violationSummary: The violation concerns failure to cooperate with data protection oversight authority, which undermines the supervisory regime that protects all personal data processing. This falls under 'Insecurity' as insufficient accountability and oversight enables broader data protection risks.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Athens Municipality failed to submit a data protection questionnaire within the set deadline, ignored multiple reminders and telephone follow-ups.
whyTheyWereWrong: The municipality's failure to cooperate delayed the data protection authority's investigation into whether the Data Protection Officer was properly appointed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The municipality claimed that the delayed response was due to technical problems with the website where the questionnaire was hosted, preventing submission despite multiple attempts.
claimsVsReality.reality: The link to the survey was fully functional and intentionally deactivated by the authority only after the initial submission deadline had passed. The municipality did not submit responses within any of the extended deadlines, and only provided answers after being summoned to a formal hearing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires the data controller and processor to cooperate on request with the supervisory authority for the exercise of the authority's duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Athens Municipality failed to provide the questionnaire responses requested by the authority within the set deadline of 19 May 2023
violations: Athens Municipality failed to provide the questionnaire responses requested by the authority within the set deadline of 19 May 2023
Did not respond to second request dated 26 May 2023 with extended deadline of 31 May 2023
Attempted to complete questionnaire between 12–20 June 2023 without success after authority reactivated link, then again failed to submit when link was reactivated with deadline 21 June 2023
Only submitted answers on 18 December 2023 after being summoned to a hearing, demonstrating non-cooperation throughout the investigation period

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1)(a) grants supervisory authorities power to order data controllers and processors to provide all information required for performance of the authority's duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Municipality refused or failed to supply requested information about DPO appointment and position despite three formal requests and multiple deadline extensions
violations: Municipality refused or failed to supply requested information about DPO appointment and position despite three formal requests and multiple deadline extensions

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 4624/2019 Article 13(η) empowers the authority to conduct on its own initiative or upon complaint investigations and inspections for compliance with law and other regulations concerning personal data protection.
regulatoryFindings.description: Municipality hindered the authority's coordinated investigation into DPO definition and position in the public sector by failing to respond to the questionnaire
violations: Municipality hindered the authority's coordinated investigation into DPO definition and position in the public sector by failing to respond to the questionnaire

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority found Athens Municipality in violation of GDPR Article 31 (cooperation obligation) and imposed a monetary penalty of €5,000. The decision emphasises the municipality's failure to timely cooperate despite multiple reminders and extended deadlines. The authority stressed that public sector entities have a legal duty to cooperate with data protection oversight, and the municipality's delay and non-response hindered the authority's ability to verify compliance with mandatory DPO appointment requirements under GDPR Articles 37–39 and Greek Law 4624/2019 Articles 6–8. The penalty was calibrated as effective, proportionate, and deterrent, taking into account the municipality's negligence, absence of intent, lack of material harm to data subjects, and fact that no prior similar violation had been recorded.
companyNow: The Municipality of Athens continues to operate as a public administration entity in Greece. The decision requires compliance with cooperation obligations and data protection rules going forward.
dataType: Personal data subject to data protection processing
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 37–39 (DPO appointment and position requirements)
GDPR Art. 58(1)(a) (supervisory authority power to request information)
Greek Law 4624/2019 Art. 6–8 (DPO requirements for public sector)
Greek Law 4624/2019 Art. 13(η) (authority power to conduct investigations)
Greek Law 4624/2019 Art. 15(1) (authority power to conduct investigations)

companyDescription: L.A.D. H Limited is a UK-registered company (Companies House Registration Number 12065159) based in Shaw, Oldham, that engaged in direct marketing campaigns via SMS.
companyLongDescription: L.A.D. H Limited is a UK-registered company (Companies House Registration Number 12065159) based in Shaw, Oldham, that engaged in direct marketing campaigns via SMS.
caseDescription: L.A.D. H Limited transmitted 31,329 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages between March and April 2022 without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients, in violation of UK PECR. The messages related to debt management and contained insufficient opt-out mechanisms. The company also failed to disclose its identity clearly in the messages, breaching additional PECR requirements.
violationSummary: The company exposed subscribers' contact details to unsolicited direct marketing without consent, and failed to provide adequate identification or opt-out mechanisms, increasing accessibility of the data to unwanted communications.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Between 14 March 2022 and 30 April 2022, L.A.D. H Limited transmitted 31,329 direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers without obtaining their prior consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: 31,329 financially vulnerable individuals received unsolicited debt management marketing SMS messages that exposed them to further financial harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: LADH could lawfully send direct marketing SMS messages
claimsVsReality.reality: LADH had no valid consent documentation for any of the 31,329 recipients and could not demonstrate recipients had agreed to receive the messages

claimsVsReality.claim: Recipients could identify the sender and opt out of messages
claimsVsReality.reality: Messages contained only a phone number; most lacked any opt-out mechanism; the company's identity was effectively concealed from recipients

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 22(2) of PECR prohibits transmission of unsolicited communications for direct marketing by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: LADH transmitted 31,329 direct marketing SMS messages without demonstrating valid prior consent from recipients
violations: LADH transmitted 31,329 direct marketing SMS messages without demonstrating valid prior consent from recipients
No evidence was provided that recipients had notified LADH of their consent to receive such messages

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 23(a) of PECR prohibits direct marketing communications where the identity of the person on whose behalf the communication is sent has been disguised or concealed.
regulatoryFindings.description: Messages contained only a telephone number as identifying information; the company's identity was not clearly disclosed
violations: Messages contained only a telephone number as identifying information; the company's identity was not clearly disclosed
Recipients could not identify LADH as the sender without third-party intervention

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 23(b) of PECR requires a valid address for recipients to request that communications cease.
regulatoryFindings.description: Most SMS messages did not contain an opportunity for individuals to opt out or request cessation of communications
violations: Most SMS messages did not contain an opportunity for individuals to opt out or request cessation of communications

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 4(11) of UK GDPR defines consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication by the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: LADH failed to provide evidence of freely given, specific, informed consent from any recipient
violations: LADH failed to provide evidence of freely given, specific, informed consent from any recipient
No consent mechanism was documented or traceable to the 31,329 message recipients

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice on 11 January 2024 requiring LADH to cease all unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail unless clear and specific prior consent is obtained. Within 30 days, LADH must comply with PECR Regulations 22 and 23, including: refraining from transmitting unsolicited marketing without explicit recipient notification; ensuring sender identity is not disguised or concealed; providing valid addresses where recipients can request cessation of communications; and ensuring compliance with Electronic Commerce Regulations. LADH has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days.
dataType: Phone numbers, personal contact information

company: ΕΛΛΗΝΙΚΑ ΤΑΧΥΔΡΟΜΕΙΑ ΑΝΩΝΥΜΗ ΕΤΑΙΡΕΙΑ (Greek Postal Service - ELTA)
companyDescription: ELTA (Hellenic Post) is Greece's national postal service, providing mail delivery, parcel services, and financial services across the country. As a critical infrastructure provider, it handles personal data of millions of employees, customers, and citizens.
companyLongDescription: ELTA (Hellenic Post) is Greece's national postal service, providing mail delivery, parcel services, and financial services across the country. As a critical infrastructure provider, it handles personal data of millions of employees, customers, and citizens.
caseDescription: ELTA suffered a ransomware attack in March 2022 that encrypted systems and exposed 4-5 million individuals' personal data, which was subsequently published on the dark web. The company failed to implement adequate technical security measures, lacked proper access controls, and did not deploy effective monitoring systems despite known vulnerabilities. The Greek Data Protection Authority found multiple violations of security and integrity obligations under GDPR Articles 5 and 32.
companyWorth: €500M-€1B (estimated based on state-owned postal utility status and 2022 turnover of €299.5M)
violationSummary: The company's systemic failure to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures under GDPR Art. 32 resulted in unauthorised access, data encryption by attackers, and subsequent data breach affecting millions of individuals.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: ELTA failed to implement adequate technical security measures, lacked access controls limiting data access to authorised personnel only.
whyTheyWereWrong: 4-5 million individuals' personal data including financial records, employee information, witness statements, and sensitive correspondence was accessed without authorisation.

claimsVsReality.claim: ELTA claimed it had a comprehensive security policy approved in 2018 and privacy-by-design protections approved in 2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: These policies were not properly implemented; critical security measures were non-functional, access controls were inadequate, and monitoring systems failed to detect the intrusion for hours.

claimsVsReality.claim: ELTA stated that security measures were limited only by economic constraints during a period of financial difficulty.
claimsVsReality.reality: The DPA found fundamental gaps in security architecture that went beyond budget limitations—including missing multi-factor authentication, inadequate network segmentation, and disabled security alerts.

claimsVsReality.claim: ELTA claimed rapid response and recovery, with most systems restored from backups within hours.
claimsVsReality.reality: While recovery was initiated quickly, some encrypted systems could not be recovered, and attackers successfully exfiltrated and published data on the dark web before the company detected the intrusion.
