regulatoryFindings.description: Canada Post argued the marketing program was not an administrative purpose, but the Office found that including individuals in mailing lists is a decision-making process that directly affects those individuals by targeting them for marketing
violations: Canada Post argued the marketing program was not an administrative purpose, but the Office found that including individuals in mailing lists is a decision-making process that directly affects those individuals by targeting them for marketing

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded and not resolved. Canada Post was recommended to cease using and disclosing personal information from its operational data for mail marketing activities without obtaining authorization from individuals. The Office recommended Canada Post implement a properly structured mail-out process to inform residents of the collection and provide an easily accessible opt-out mechanism. Canada Post disagreed with the finding and refused to implement the recommendation, instead proposing only to enhance transparency on its website and at retail outlets, which the Office determined did not constitute obtaining valid authorization.
companyNow: Canada Post remains Canada's primary postal service operator, though it has faced declining mail volumes and financial pressures. The company continues to operate its Smartmail Marketing Program despite the privacy ruling.
dataType: Name, address, suite/unit number, online shopping habits (inferred from package origins), location data
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act section 5(1) – requirement to collect personal information directly from individuals and obtain authorization for indirect collection
Privacy Act section 5(2) – requirement to inform individuals of the purpose for collection

companyDescription: Transport Canada is the federal department responsible for transportation policy, regulation, and administration in Canada, including managing federal incentive programs for zero-emission vehicles.
companyLongDescription: Transport Canada is a federal government department within the Canadian government tasked with developing and implementing transportation policy. It administers various programs to support national transportation objectives, including the Incentives for Zero-Emission Vehicles Program (iZEV), launched in May 2019 to encourage adoption of electric and hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles and reduce transportation-related greenhouse gas emissions. The department is subject to the Privacy Act, which requires transparency in how personal information is collected and used.
caseDescription: Transport Canada failed to submit a required Personal Information Bank (PIB) description to the Treasury Board Secretariat for 19 months after launching the federal Incentives for Zero-Emission Vehicles Program (iZEV), and the description was not publicly published for nearly 4 years. This violated the Privacy Act's transparency requirement that government institutions must publicly disclose how they collect and use personal information before launching programs. The individual complainant was directed to an outdated, unrelated PIB description, leaving him unable to understand how his personal information was being handled.
violationSummary: The failure to timely publish required PIB descriptions exposed individuals to uncertainty about how their personal information was collected, used, and stored, limiting their ability to understand and assess privacy risks associated with the program.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Transport Canada launched the iZEV program in May 2019 and collected personal information from participants but did not submit a required Personal Information Bank description to Treasury Board.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens applying for the zero-emission vehicle incentive could not find accurate information about how Transport Canada collected, stored.

claimsVsReality.claim: Transport Canada directed applicants to consult a Personal Information Bank describing the iZEV program
claimsVsReality.reality: The PIB referenced on the consent form actually described an outdated, unrelated ecoAUTO Rebate Program with no relevant details about iZEV data practices

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information collected by Transport Canada for iZEV was included in a publicly available Personal Information Bank as required by the Privacy Act
claimsVsReality.reality: No PIB description for iZEV was submitted for 19 months after launch, and it remained unapproved and unpublished for nearly 4 years total

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 10 – Government institutions must ensure all personal information under their control used for administrative purposes be included in a Personal Information Bank
regulatoryFindings.description: Transport Canada did not submit an updated PIB description to Treasury Board Secretariat until 19 months after the iZEV program launched
violations: Transport Canada did not submit an updated PIB description to Treasury Board Secretariat until 19 months after the iZEV program launched
The PIB referenced on the iZEV Program Consumer Consent Form described an outdated, unrelated program (ecoAUTO Rebate Program)

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 11 and Subsection 71(4) – Treasury Board is responsible for approving new or substantially modified PIBs and ensuring annual publication of an index of PIBs
regulatoryFindings.description: Treasury Board Secretariat failed to approve Transport Canada's PIB submission within a reasonable timeframe, with no approval granted for 25 months after the investigation began
violations: Treasury Board Secretariat failed to approve Transport Canada's PIB submission within a reasonable timeframe, with no approval granted for 25 months after the investigation began
PIB description for the iZEV program was not published for nearly 4 years after program launch

regulatoryFindings.act: TBS Directive on Privacy Impact Assessment – Institutions must obtain TBS approval for new or substantially modified PIBs before implementing programs and must publicly report their PIBs
regulatoryFindings.description: Transport Canada implemented the iZEV program without first obtaining TBS approval for the associated PIB
violations: Transport Canada implemented the iZEV program without first obtaining TBS approval for the associated PIB
Transport Canada failed to identify, describe, and publicly report the PIB for the iZEV program on a timely basis

outcome: Transport Canada subsequently confirmed it has published a PIB description for the iZEV program on its website. The Privacy Commissioner recommended that Transport Canada and Treasury Board Secretariat collaborate to finalize, approve, and publish the PIB description, and recommended that TBS develop service standards for PIB approval and consider delegating portions of its PIB responsibilities to government institutions. TBS implemented business improvements including a triage process for PIB requests, active communication with institutions, automation tools, and internal standards for review. TBS confirmed that by March 31, 2023, it had reviewed all PIBs submitted more than 12 months prior and committed to processing new PIB registration requests on an ongoing basis.
companyNow: Transport Canada continues to administer the iZEV program and other transportation initiatives. Following the investigation, it has published the required Personal Information Bank description for the program.
dataType: Vehicle purchase information, personal identification, consent form data
legalBasisViolated: TBS Directive on Privacy Impact Assessment

company: Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada
companyDescription: The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (IRB) is a quasi-judicial administrative tribunal responsible for making final decisions on refugee protection claims, immigration appeals, and admissibility issues in Canada.
companyLongDescription: The IRB is an independent administrative body established under the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. It conducts hearings and makes binding decisions on refugee protection claims, immigration appeals, and matters of inadmissibility. The IRB employs hundreds of staff across multiple locations in Canada and handles thousands of cases annually. As a federal government agency, it is subject to the Privacy Act and Treasury Board Secretariat standards.
caseDescription: The Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada disclosed a confidential fitness-to-work report containing detailed medical and intimate personal information to an employee's management team without documented consent. The report was prepared by an independent medical examiner and included sensitive health information beyond what was necessary for workplace accommodation purposes. The IRB failed to comply with Treasury Board Secretariat standards requiring that confidential medical information be disclosed to employers only with written consent and only when necessary for appropriate accommodation measures.
violationSummary: The IRB disclosed sensitive medical and intimate personal information to third parties (management team) without the individual's consent and without a valid legal basis. The disclosure was not a 'consistent use' under the Privacy Act because the information fell outside what was reasonably necessary for the original purpose (fitness-to-work assessment), and a mandatory TBS standard explicitly prohibited such disclosure without written consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The IRB disclosed a complete 10-page fitness-to-work report containing intimate medical details to an employee's management team without documented consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's detailed medical and intimate personal information was shared with multiple managers without consent, exposing private health details to people who did not need them.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant signed a consent form authorizing disclosure of medical information to their manager.
claimsVsReality.reality: IRB could not produce any consent form for disclosure to management; the only consent on record was for disclosure to the medical examiner, not to employers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disclosure of the full report to managers was a consistent use with the original purpose of the fitness-to-work evaluation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Treasury Board Standard in effect required that only fitness-relevant information be disclosed to employers, and intimate medical details could only be shared with written consent—which was never obtained.

claimsVsReality.claim: HR professionals cannot be expected to review what doctors include in medical reports.
claimsVsReality.reality: The applicable standard explicitly required HR to limit disclosures and respect medical confidentiality; HR has a responsibility to apply judgment about what managers genuinely need to know for accommodation purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act, Section 8(1) – Personal information may be disclosed only with consent of the individual or under specific exceptions
regulatoryFindings.description: IRB disclosed confidential medical information without documented consent; IRB claimed consent was obtained but failed to produce evidence of a valid consent form authorizing disclosure to management team
violations: IRB disclosed confidential medical information without documented consent; IRB claimed consent was obtained but failed to produce evidence of a valid consent form authorizing disclosure to management team

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act, Section 8(2)(a) – Information may be disclosed without consent only for a use consistent with the original purpose of collection
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosure of intimate personal and sensitive medical details to managers was not a use reasonably expected by the individual and was inconsistent with TBS standards requiring written consent for such disclosures
violations: Disclosure of intimate personal and sensitive medical details to managers was not a use reasonably expected by the individual and was inconsistent with TBS standards requiring written consent for such disclosures
Information disclosed exceeded what was necessary to enable managers to take appropriate accommodation measures

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Secretariat Occupational Health Evaluation Standard, Section 8.1 – Assessing health professional discloses only information enabling appropriate measures; confidential medical information not provided unless required for accommodation and provided with written consent
regulatoryFindings.description: IME and IRB failed to limit disclosed information to what was necessary for workplace accommodation
violations: IME and IRB failed to limit disclosed information to what was necessary for workplace accommodation
No written consent obtained from complainant authorizing disclosure of medical information to the employer/management team
Detailed intimate medical information included in disclosure that could not reasonably be said to enable employer to take appropriate measures

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the complaint well-founded and unresolved. The IRB was directed to: (1) delete medical and sensitive information from its systems within six months; (2) provide comprehensive training to staff on medical confidentiality and handling of fitness-to-work information; and (3) issue a meaningful apology to the complainant. The IRB's responses were inadequate: it declined to delete records citing legal concerns, did not expressly commit to recommended training, and offered only a limited apology for 'misunderstanding' rather than acknowledging wrongdoing. The Privacy Commissioner urged the IRB to reconsider and take meaningful action to fulfill the recommendations within six months.
companyNow: The IRB continues to operate as Canada's primary decision-making body for refugee and immigration appeals. Since this 2023 complaint, it has implemented new disability management tools and processes to prevent similar medical information disclosures.
dataType: Medical information, health data, intimate personal information, fitness to work evaluation details
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act, Section 8(1) – disclosure without consent
Privacy Act, Section 8(2)(a) – disclosure inconsistent with purpose of collection
Treasury Board Secretariat Occupational Health Evaluation Standard, Section 8.1 – requirement for written consent to disclose confidential medical information

companyDescription: Correctional Service Canada (CSC) is the federal agency responsible for managing federal prisons and supervising offenders in Canada.
companyLongDescription: Correctional Service Canada is a federal government department that operates within the Canadian justice system, managing federal correctional institutions and administering sentences for offenders convicted under federal law. The agency employs thousands of staff across multiple institutions nationwide. CSC operates under the mandate of the Department of Justice and is accountable to Parliament through the Minister of Justice.
caseDescription: Correctional Service Canada's assistant warden collected nine screenshots from a spouse's public Facebook profile without authorization to investigate the employee's use of 699 leave during COVID-19. The collection included personal information with no bearing on the leave claim, violating Section 4 of the Privacy Act. The collected information was subsequently shared with three senior managers.
violationSummary: The institution collected personal information from a public social media source without proper authorization and beyond the scope necessary for its stated purpose. This constitutes surveillance of an individual's online activity without justification, as much of the collected material had no connection to the operating program or activity being investigated.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: An assistant warden collected nine screenshots from a spouse's public Facebook profile without authorization to investigate the employee's use of COVID-19 leave.
whyTheyWereWrong: The spouse's personal information was collected and disclosed without consent, exposing intimate details of their life that had no connection to the leave investigation.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC stated the personal information was collected to respond to a claim that the employee may be in contravention of 699-leave policy regarding COVID-19.
claimsVsReality.reality: The nine screenshots collected contained numerous photos, comment threads, and personal information about the spouse that had no bearing on assessing the employee's leave entitlement or COVID-19 isolation compliance.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC argued that because the information came from a public Facebook profile, the collection was permissible under the Privacy Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Act's exclusion for publicly available information applies only to use and disclosure, not to collection; all collection must still relate directly to an operating program or activity.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 requires that personal information collected by government institutions must relate directly to an operating program or activity of the institution
regulatoryFindings.description: CSC collected nine screenshots from the complainant's Facebook profile, including photos, comments, and information unrelated to assessing the employee's 699-leave eligibility
violations: CSC collected nine screenshots from the complainant's Facebook profile, including photos, comments, and information unrelated to assessing the employee's 699-leave eligibility
Collection occurred without explicit authorization and extended beyond what was necessary to investigate the alleged leave policy violation

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Subsection 69(2) exclusion applies only to use and disclosure of publicly available information, not collection
regulatoryFindings.description: CSC argued the information was from a public Facebook page, but the public availability does not exempt the collection requirement under Section 4
violations: CSC argued the information was from a public Facebook page, but the public availability does not exempt the collection requirement under Section 4

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Sections 7-8 restrict use and disclosure of collected personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: The improperly collected screenshots were subsequently disclosed to three senior managers in the employee's management chain
violations: The improperly collected screenshots were subsequently disclosed to three senior managers in the employee's management chain

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada determined that CSC contravened the collection provisions of the Privacy Act by collecting personal information not related directly to an operating program or activity. CSC acknowledged the violation, confirmed deletion of all screenshot copies, and committed to developing and disseminating guidance to managers on proper procedures for collecting information in labour relations contexts, including identifying appropriate authorization channels and limiting collection to information directly relevant to the investigation.
companyNow: Correctional Service Canada continues to operate as a federal government agency responsible for federal corrections. Following this investigation, CSC committed to improving privacy practices through manager guidance and better internal complaint handling processes.
dataType: Social media profile information, photographs, comments, personal communications
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Sections 7-8 (use and disclosure provisions)

companyDescription: The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat (TBS) is the central administrative agency of the Government of Canada responsible for implementing Treasury Board decisions and managing federal government operations, including personnel and compensation programs.
companyLongDescription: The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat is the administrative centre of the Government of Canada, established to support the Treasury Board in its governance functions. TBS manages federal government operations, including compensation programs for employees affected by the Phoenix pay system failures. The department is responsible for developing and enforcing privacy policies and procedures across federal institutions, making privacy compliance a core operational duty.
caseDescription: The Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat mistakenly disclosed the email addresses and identities of 400+ federal employees who filed claims under the Severe Phoenix Impacts program by using the carbon copy ('cc') field instead of blind carbon copy ('bcc') when sending notification emails. The breach revealed to all recipients that each individual had suffered severe personal or financial hardship and filed a compensation claim, causing complainants humiliation, embarrassment, and stress.
violationSummary: The unauthorized disclosure of personal information (email addresses, names, and claim filing status) to unintended recipients constitutes exposure under the Solove taxonomy. The sensitive contextual nature of the information—relating to individuals claiming severe hardship—amplifies the harm despite the type of data being relatively basic contact information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Treasury Board of Canada Secretariat sent notification emails to 400+ federal employees using the carbon copy field instead of blind carbon copy, exposing their email addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposed employees had not disclosed their hardships or compensation claims to anyone outside the claims process, and the breach caused them humiliation, embarrassment, stress.

claimsVsReality.claim: TBS assessed the breach as non-material because it did not involve sensitive personal information like SINs or banking details, and the email addresses were only shared among individuals in similar circumstances.
claimsVsReality.reality: The breach was material because it revealed to all recipients that each person had suffered severe personal or financial hardship and filed a compensation claim—information many had intentionally kept private—causing documented humiliation, stress, and mental anguish.

claimsVsReality.claim: The sharing of information among a group of individuals who filed similar claims was unlikely to result in severe impacts such as reputational loss or lasting harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple complainants reported humiliation, embarrassment, violation, stress, and one was contacted by media following the breach, demonstrating the real and documented harm to reputation and well-being.

claimsVsReality.claim: The generic nature of the message content meant the breach could not cause serious injury or harm to affected individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The categorization of the distribution list as 'Severe Phoenix Impacts' combined with exposure of who else was on the list created a breach of sensitive personal information that revealed private hardships individuals had not disclosed outside the claims process.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Personal information can only be disclosed with individual consent or in accordance with permitted disclosure categories under Section 8(2)
regulatoryFindings.description: TBS disclosed email addresses and names of 400+ individuals without their consent
violations: TBS disclosed email addresses and names of 400+ individuals without their consent
The disclosure was not authorized under any permitted disclosure category
TBS categorized the breach as an inadvertent administrative error but this does not exempt it from legal obligations

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Definition of personal information includes information about identifiable individuals related to financial transactions and personal opinions
regulatoryFindings.description: Email addresses revealing identities combined with claim filing status and indication of severe hardship constitutes personal information
violations: Email addresses revealing identities combined with claim filing status and indication of severe hardship constitutes personal information
Context of the information (Severe Phoenix Impacts claimants) made the disclosure particularly sensitive

regulatoryFindings.act: TBS Directive on Privacy Practices and Guidelines for Privacy Breaches – Institutions must assess breaches as 'material' when involving sensitive information and reasonably expected to cause serious injury or harm
regulatoryFindings.description: TBS failed to assess the breach as material despite clear indicators of sensitivity and harm
violations: TBS failed to assess the breach as material despite clear indicators of sensitivity and harm
TBS applied an overly narrow interpretation of 'serious injury or harm', focusing only on identity theft or material loss rather than embarrassment and well-being impacts
TBS did not conduct a holistic, context-informed harm assessment

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the complaints well-founded and conditionally resolved in part. TBS contravened Section 8 of the Privacy Act. The OPC rejected TBS's assertion that the breach was non-material, emphasizing that proper materiality assessment must be holistic and context-informed. TBS agreed to implement recommendations to: (1) share the final report with staff and raise awareness about breach prevention; and (2) engage with the Canadian Digital Service to explore more secure communication methods. TBS remains resistant to acknowledging the materiality of this specific breach and has not fully committed to strengthening its harm assessment frameworks. The OPC expects TBS to provide updates within four months on implementation of accepted recommendations and encourages continued refinement of policy instruments to better assess privacy breach harms and materiality across government.
companyNow: TBS continues to operate as a central government agency responsible for federal administration and policy governance. Following this incident, the organization committed to enhancing privacy training and exploring more secure communication methods for sensitive stakeholder notifications.
dataType: Email addresses, names, claim filing status, indication of severe financial/personal hardship
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) – Section 3 (definition of personal information)

companyDescription: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is the Canadian federal department responsible for immigration, refugees, citizenship, and travel documents.
companyLongDescription: IRCC is a federal department of the Government of Canada that administers immigration and citizenship programs. It processes visa applications, manages refugee claims, issues passports and travel documents, and oversees citizenship matters. The department operates multiple offices across Canada and internationally through diplomatic missions.
caseDescription: IRCC failed to conduct a reasonable search for records in response to an access request under the Privacy Act. The department initially reduced the scope of the request without the complainant's approval and did not search all appropriate offices for records relating to visa cancellation and reissuance. After investigation, IRCC expanded its search to include all appropriate offices of primary interest, ultimately resolving the complaint.
violationSummary: IRCC violated the complainant's right to access personal information by restricting the scope of the search without authorization and failing to search all offices that may have held responsive records, thereby excluding relevant information from disclosure.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: IRCC reduced the scope of an access request without the complainant's approval and failed to search all appropriate offices for records relating to visa cancellation and reissuance.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant and her children were denied timely access to information about their own visa cases.

claimsVsReality.claim: IRCC conducted a complete search of all relevant offices for the complainant's access request.
claimsVsReality.reality: IRCC initially tasked only three offices and reduced the request scope without approval, failing to search all offices that held relevant records about visa cancellation and reissuance.

claimsVsReality.claim: The two offices of primary interest identified held all responsive records.
claimsVsReality.reality: The investigation identified additional offices of primary interest that may have held responsive records, which were not initially consulted.

regulatoryFindings.description: IRCC reduced the scope of the request without the complainant's approval

IRCC did not originally conduct a specific search for all records relating to visa cancellation and reissuance
IRCC tasked only two offices of primary interest initially, when other offices may have held responsive records
IRCC failed to search all appropriate offices before providing its response

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. IRCC agreed to expand the breadth of its search and tasked all appropriate offices of primary interest. After conducting expanded searches across multiple offices and consulting with missions, IRCC met its obligations under the Privacy Act. The complaint is now resolved, though no additional information was ultimately located beyond what was already released.
companyNow: IRCC continues to operate as Canada's primary immigration and citizenship authority, processing applications and maintaining case records through its Global Case Management System (GCMS) and multiple offices.

companyDescription: Home Depot is a major North American home improvement retailer operating thousands of stores across the United States and Canada, providing tools, materials, and supplies for home repair and renovation projects.
companyLongDescription: Home Depot is one of the largest home improvement retailers in North America, founded in 1978 and headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia. The company operates a vast network of retail stores and an e-commerce platform serving millions of customers annually who seek tools, building materials, and home improvement supplies. Home Depot generates annual revenues in the tens of billions and serves as a major employer and cornerstone retailer in communities across North America.
caseDescription: Home Depot disclosed customer personal information including hashed email addresses and offline purchase details to Meta without valid consent through Meta's Offline Conversions tool. Customers requesting e-receipts in-store were not informed that their data would be shared with Meta for advertising effectiveness measurement and Meta's own targeted advertising purposes. The Privacy Commissioner found Home Depot failed to obtain express opt-in consent and discontinued the practice in October 2022.
violationSummary: Home Depot disclosed personal information to Meta without obtaining valid consent. The disclosure went beyond the reasonable expectations of customers, who believed they were only providing email for e-receipt purposes, and Meta used the information for purposes unrelated to Home Depot's business, constituting improper disclosure.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Home Depot shared hashed email addresses and offline purchase details of customers requesting e-receipts with Meta's Offline Conversions tool without obtaining express consent from those.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers unknowingly had their shopping behavior tracked and linked to their Facebook profiles, allowing Meta to measure ad effectiveness.

claimsVsReality.claim: Home Depot claimed it obtained implied consent through its privacy statement and Meta's privacy policy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customers requesting e-receipts were not informed about data sharing with Meta and would not reasonably expect their purchase data to be sent to Meta for advertising targeting and analytics.

claimsVsReality.claim: Home Depot stated Meta acts as a mere service provider processing information on Home Depot's behalf.
claimsVsReality.reality: Meta used the customer data for its own independent business purposes including targeted advertising, ad optimization, and creating lookalike audiences—far beyond what customers would expect.

claimsVsReality.claim: Home Depot argued consent fatigue justified not providing just-in-time notification at point of e-receipt request.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customers had no awareness whatsoever of the data sharing practice and could not make an informed choice about participation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires knowledge and consent for collection, use and disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Depot disclosed customer email addresses and purchase details to Meta without obtaining valid consent
violations: Home Depot disclosed customer email addresses and purchase details to Meta without obtaining valid consent
Home Depot relied on implied consent through privacy policies that were not accessible at point of sale and did not adequately explain the practice

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.4 requires appropriate form of consent based on sensitivity of information and reasonable expectations
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Depot failed to obtain express opt-in consent despite disclosure going beyond customer reasonable expectations
violations: Home Depot failed to obtain express opt-in consent despite disclosure going beyond customer reasonable expectations
Customers could not reasonably expect their in-store purchase data would be shared with Meta for advertising measurement and Meta's own targeted advertising purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 requires reasonable effort to advise individuals of purposes in understandable language
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Depot's Privacy Statement used vague language such as 'improve products and services' and 'may share information for business purposes' without clearly disclosing Meta sharing
violations: Home Depot's Privacy Statement used vague language such as 'improve products and services' and 'may share information for business purposes' without clearly disclosing Meta sharing
Customers requesting e-receipts were given no notification of Meta sharing and no reason to consult privacy policies
Information about the practice was not presented at point of collection in accessible form

outcome: Home Depot discontinued use of Meta's Offline Conversions Tool in October 2022. The company committed to implementing the Privacy Commissioner's recommendations, which include: ceasing disclosure of personal information to Meta without valid consent; implementing express prior opt-in consent if the practice resumes; providing key information at point of sale regarding what data will be shared with Meta and how it will be used; and updating privacy communications with detailed explanations of the practice and withdrawal procedures.
companyNow: Home Depot remains the leading home improvement retailer in North America as of 2024, with continued store expansion and digital transformation initiatives.
dataType: email address (hashed), purchase history, transaction details, spending patterns
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (knowledge and consent for collection, use and disclosure)
PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 (reasonable effort to advise of purposes)
PIPEDA Principle 4.3.4 (appropriate form of consent based on sensitivity)

companyDescription: Agronomy Company of Canada Ltd. is a subsidiary of Sollio Groupe Coopératif that provides agricultural products, services, and IT infrastructure to the Agromat Group of joint-venture companies across Ontario and Eastern Canada.
companyLongDescription: Agronomy is a wholly owned subsidiary of Sollio Groupe Coopératif, a major Canadian agricultural cooperative. The company operates as both a service provider and affiliate within the Agromat Group, a collection of joint-venture agricultural companies offering seeds, fertilizers, crop production products, advisory services, and nutrient management across Ontario and Eastern Canada. Agronomy manages IT infrastructure and credit services for multiple Agromat member companies through approximately 22 retail locations and distribution sites. The company processes sensitive customer financial and personal information as part of its credit and information technology service offerings.
caseDescription: Agronomy's systems were breached in April 2020 by threat actors using stolen administrator credentials, resulting in unauthorized access to personal information of 845 individuals over two months before detection via ransomware deployment. The company lacked critical security safeguards including multifactor authentication, network segregation, data encryption, and detection tools, as well as comprehensive privacy policies and a designated accountability officer. While consent for credit services was properly obtained, the company failed to implement security controls appropriate to the sensitivity of financial and identity data stored.
violationSummary: Agronomy's security infrastructure was fundamentally inadequate to protect highly sensitive personal information. Multiple critical gaps in technical safeguards (no MFA, no encryption, no network segregation, no detection tools) and organizational safeguards (no incident response protocol, poor data storage practices, inadequate documentation) created conditions enabling a two-month undetected breach affecting 845 individuals' most sensitive data including SINs and financial information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Agronomy's systems were breached in April 2020 via stolen administrator credentials, exposing personal information of 845 individuals including SINs, dates of birth.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's lack of basic security controls—no multifactor authentication, no network segregation, no data encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agronomy asserted it was a data processor providing services to Agromat members and should only be subject to PIPEDA as a processor.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OPC determined that Agronomy collected, used and disclosed personal information directly through its provision of credit and IT services, making it a controller subject to full PIPEDA obligations regardless of processor claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant alleged they had not consented to collection and use of their personal information for credit services.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant had signed a prominently titled credit application form that clearly explained their information would be used for credit purposes and subsequently received and utilized $100,000 in credit, constituting valid consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agronomy's IT infrastructure provided secure and segregated systems for its affiliate partners.
claimsVsReality.reality: Agronomy's systems were deliberately amalgamated without network segregation, allowing a threat actor with admin credentials to move freely across systems belonging to multiple Agromat member companies and access all customer data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 requires security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of personal information to protect against loss, theft, unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use, or modification
regulatoryFindings.description: Lack of multifactor authentication on administrator accounts, enabling threat actor access with stolen credentials
violations: Lack of multifactor authentication on administrator accounts, enabling threat actor access with stolen credentials
Lack of network segregation allowing lateral movement across multiple Agromat systems
Lack of encryption on databases and sensitive data stored in shared folders
Lack of detection and response tools (SIEM, EDR/XDR) enabling two-month undetected presence
Lack of web application firewall and server hardening measures
Lack of patch management policy resulting in ad-hoc, incomplete software updates
Inadequate information management and data storage practices with sensitive data in miscellaneous shared folders

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1 and 4.1.4 require organizations to be accountable for personal information, designate individuals accountable for compliance, implement procedures to protect information, train staff, and develop documentation of policies
regulatoryFindings.description: Lack of comprehensive privacy policy (only website-specific policy existed)
violations: Lack of comprehensive privacy policy (only website-specific policy existed)
General lack of privacy policies, practices, and associated training
Failure to designate an individual accountable for PIPEDA compliance
Lack of incident response protocols for cyberattacks
Inadequate security-related documentation and records
Unable to confirm whether IT training had been provided to staff

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 and 4.3.6 require knowledge and consent of individuals for collection, use, or disclosure of personal information, with express consent required for sensitive information clearly explained

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the safeguards and accountability aspects of the complaint to be well-founded and conditionally resolved. Agronomy committed to and implemented significant security improvements including multifactor authentication, network segregation, encryption via Data Loss Prevention service, EDR/antivirus products, automated patch management, incident management protocols for zero-day attacks, comprehensive privacy policy, Privacy Officer designation, and ongoing cybersecurity training. The consent aspect was found not well-founded as the credit application form clearly disclosed the purpose and the complainant received and used the extended credit. The company must maintain these improvements and the OPC will monitor compliance.
companyNow: Following the 2023 PIPEDA findings, Agronomy committed to implementing a comprehensive incident management plan, zero-day attack protocols, privacy policies, and appointing a designated privacy officer to ensure PIPEDA compliance.
dataType: Social insurance number, date of birth, driver's license number, name, address, phone number, bank account number, credit card information, passport information, salary/pension information, email address, electronic signature
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1 (Protection against loss, theft, unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use, modification)
PIPEDA Principle 4.7.3 (Physical, organizational, and technological safeguards)

violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Datateks failed to conduct a reasonable and expeditious assessment of a suspected eligible data breach within 30 days.
whyTheyWereWrong: The delayed breach assessment and notification prevented the Commissioner and affected individuals from being informed promptly about the data exposure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 26WH(2) - Reasonable and expeditious assessment of eligible data breach within 30 days
regulatoryFindings.description: Datateks failed to conduct a reasonable and expeditious assessment of the suspected eligible data breach within 30 days as required by law
violations: Datateks failed to conduct a reasonable and expeditious assessment of the suspected eligible data breach within 30 days as required by law

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 26WK(2) - Provision of breach statement to Commissioner as soon as practicable
regulatoryFindings.description: Datateks failed to provide a copy of the statement about the eligible data breach to the Commissioner as soon as practicable
violations: Datateks failed to provide a copy of the statement about the eligible data breach to the Commissioner as soon as practicable

outcome: Datateks was ordered not to repeat or continue the conduct. The company must prepare an incident response plan addressing the breaches and provide a copy to the Commissioner within 3 months of the determination dated 24 October 2023.
companyNow: Datateks remains subject to the Compliance Order issued by the OAIC requiring the company to prepare and submit an incident response plan within 3 months.
dataType: Personal data subject to eligible data breach notification requirements

companyDescription: Serco is a multinational public services company providing infrastructure, facilities management, and detention services globally. In Australia, Serco operates immigration detention facilities and other government contracts.
companyLongDescription: Serco Group Pty Limited is a major facilities and public services contractor operating across government services, defence, transport, and justice sectors in multiple countries. In Australia, Serco operates several immigration detention centres and provides other government services under contract. The company manages sensitive personal data as part of its detention and facility management operations.
caseDescription: Serco failed to ensure personal information was complete, accurate, up-to-date and relevant, and failed to provide written notice with mechanisms for complaining about refusal to correct information. The organisation interfered with the complainant's privacy through its handling of personal data and correction requests.
violationSummary: Serco failed to take reasonable steps to maintain data quality (completeness, accuracy, currency, relevance) and failed to provide proper notice mechanisms for data correction disputes, which constitutes insecurity in information processing under privacy taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Serco failed to maintain complete, accurate, and up-to-date personal information and refused to provide written notice with complaint mechanisms when the complainant requested correction.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's personal data remained inaccurate and outdated in Serco's systems, and Serco obstructed their ability to challenge.

claimsVsReality.claim: Serco maintained accurate and up-to-date personal information in compliance with privacy obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Serco's records contained inaccurate and outdated personal information about the complainant that were not kept current.

claimsVsReality.claim: Serco provided proper mechanisms for complainants to formally object to refusals to correct their personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Serco failed to provide written notice or any formal complaint mechanism when refusing to correct the complainant's information.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 10.1 – Australian Privacy Principles – Data Quality and Accuracy: APP entities must take reasonable steps to ensure personal information is complete, accurate, up-to-date and relevant
regulatoryFindings.description: Serco failed to take reasonable steps to ensure personal information held was complete, accurate, up-to-date and relevant
violations: Serco failed to take reasonable steps to ensure personal information held was complete, accurate, up-to-date and relevant

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 13.3 – Australian Privacy Principles – Correction of Personal Information: APP entities must give written notice of mechanisms available to complain about a refusal to correct information
regulatoryFindings.description: Serco failed to provide written notice with mechanisms available to complain about refusal to correct personal information
violations: Serco failed to provide written notice with mechanisms available to complain about refusal to correct personal information

outcome: Serco ordered to acknowledge interference with complainant's privacy in a written apology and commit to not repeating or continuing the conduct. Serco ordered to pay compensation of $1,500 AUD to the complainant as reasonable redress for loss or damage.
companyNow: Serco remains a major government contractor globally, though it has faced ongoing scrutiny over its management of Australian immigration detention facilities and privacy practices.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified types)

companyDescription: Burwood Westfield Medical Centre is a healthcare provider in Australia operating a medical practice in the Burwood/Westfield area.
companyLongDescription: Burwood Westfield Medical Centre is a general medical practice in Australia providing healthcare services to patients in the Burwood and Westfield regions. The centre is registered to maintain and access My Health Records under Australian legislation. The centre's failure to implement proper privacy policies and safeguards resulted in regulatory enforcement action by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner.
caseDescription: Burwood Westfield Medical Centre breached the My Health Records Act 2012 and Privacy Act 1988 by failing to maintain appropriate safeguards for healthcare recipients' privacy. The centre did not have a written policy that reasonably addressed required matters under the My Health Record Rules, and interfered with the privacy of patients.
violationSummary: The centre failed to implement adequate written policies and procedures to protect health records as required by the My Health Record Rules 2016, resulting in insecurity of personal health information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Burwood Westfield Medical Centre failed to maintain a written policy addressing required safeguards under the My Health Record Rules.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients' sensitive health information was at risk of unauthorised access or misuse because the centre lacked documented privacy safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: The centre was maintaining adequate privacy safeguards for patient health records.
claimsVsReality.reality: The centre had no written policy addressing required privacy matters under the My Health Record Rules and failed to protect patients' healthcare information appropriately.

regulatoryFindings.act: My Health Records Act 2012 (Cth) s 73(1)(a) — Healthcare providers must not interfere with the privacy of healthcare recipients
regulatoryFindings.description: Burwood Westfield Medical Centre interfered with patients' privacy by failing to maintain adequate safeguards
violations: Burwood Westfield Medical Centre interfered with patients' privacy by failing to maintain adequate safeguards

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 13 — Must not repeat or continue an act or practice that breaches privacy
regulatoryFindings.description: Centre did not have a written policy reasonably addressing required matters under My Health Record Rule 2016 s 42(4)
violations: Centre did not have a written policy reasonably addressing required matters under My Health Record Rule 2016 s 42(4)

regulatoryFindings.act: My Health Record Rule 2016, rules 41 and 42 — Providers must comply with security and eligibility requirements
regulatoryFindings.description: Centre failed to maintain compliance with rules 41 and 42 regarding privacy protections for health records
violations: Centre failed to maintain compliance with rules 41 and 42 regarding privacy protections for health records

outcome: The OAIC determined a breach and required Burwood Westfield Medical Centre to not repeat the conduct and to take specified steps to address the interference with privacy. The centre must implement appropriate written policies and procedures to comply with the My Health Records Act and Privacy Act requirements.
dataType: Health records, personal health information
legalBasisViolated: My Health Record Rule 2016, rules 41 and 42

companyDescription: Cardiac Dynamics is an Australian healthcare organisation that provides cardiac care services and participates in the My Health Records system.
companyLongDescription: Cardiac Dynamics is a healthcare provider in Australia registered to access and manage My Health Records for patients. The organisation was found to have breached privacy obligations under both the My Health Records Act 2012 (Cth) and the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) by failing to implement and maintain appropriate written privacy policies. This case involved OAIC enforcement action regarding compliance with the My Health Record Rules 2016.
caseDescription: Cardiac Dynamics breached the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and My Health Records Act 2012 (Cth) by interfering with the privacy of healthcare recipients. The organisation failed to maintain a written policy that reasonably addressed matters required under the My Health Record Rules 2016, specifically rule 42(4).
violationSummary: The breach relates to failure to implement adequate written policies and procedures to protect health data security and privacy, resulting in interference with privacy rights of healthcare recipients.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Cardiac Dynamics failed to maintain a written privacy policy addressing requirements under My Health Record Rule 42(4).
whyTheyWereWrong: Healthcare recipients' sensitive medical information was at risk because the organisation lacked documented privacy safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cardiac Dynamics had adequate privacy safeguards in place for My Health Records access.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation lacked a written policy reasonably addressing matters required by My Health Record Rule 42(4), leaving healthcare recipients' privacy unprotected.

regulatoryFindings.act: My Health Records Act 2012 (Cth) s 73(1)(a)
regulatoryFindings.description: Interference with privacy of healthcare recipients through inadequate policy implementation
violations: Interference with privacy of healthcare recipients through inadequate policy implementation

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 13
regulatoryFindings.description: Breach of privacy obligation to not engage in conduct that is an interference with privacy
violations: Breach of privacy obligation to not engage in conduct that is an interference with privacy

regulatoryFindings.act: My Health Record Rule 2016 rule 42(4)
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to maintain a written policy that reasonably addressed required matters
violations: Failure to maintain a written policy that reasonably addressed required matters

outcome: Cardiac Dynamics must not repeat the conduct and must take specified steps to address the interference with privacy of healthcare recipients. The organisation is required to implement compliant written policies under My Health Record Rules.
companyNow: Cardiac Dynamics remains operational in Australia but is now subject to a Compliance Order requiring remediation of privacy policy deficiencies and ongoing adherence to privacy obligations.
dataType: Health data, My Health Records

companyDescription: PPLingo (operating as LingoAce) is an online language learning platform offering virtual Chinese and English classes to students aged 4-15 globally, based in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: PPLingo Pte Ltd operates LingoAce, a digital education platform providing synchronous online language classes in Chinese and English to students worldwide, primarily targeting children aged 4-15 years old. The platform serves a diverse user base including students, parents, teachers, and support staff across multiple countries. The company maintains an operations support system (OPS System) to manage teacher assignments, student records, class scheduling, and financial transactions for class credits and payments.
caseDescription: PPLingo, an online language learning platform, suffered a data breach affecting 557,144 users (students, parents, teachers, and staff) due to inadequate password security on an administrator account. The threat actor obtained the weak password "lingoace123" via brute force attacks and accessed sensitive personal data including financial information and records of approximately 303,238 minors. The organisation also failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer as required by the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data by using an inadequate password policy (weak password without expiry, no complexity requirements), failing to implement two-factor authentication for administrative accounts, and not appointing a Data Protection Officer. These security failures directly enabled unauthorised access to a high volume of sensitive personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: PPLingo failed to implement adequate password security for an administrator account controlling access to its learning platform.
whyTheyWereWrong: The weak password "lingoace123" was easily cracked via brute force attack, exposing personal data of 557,144 users including 303,238 minors' financial information.

claimsVsReality.claim: PPLingo had implemented certain security measures for the LingoAce platform, including network access control measures and firewall protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: Security was fundamentally inadequate—the administrator account lacked any password expiry policy, complexity requirements, or multi-factor authentication, with the same weak password in use for over 2 years.

claimsVsReality.claim: PPLingo organized two rounds of internal security awareness training for its IT development team in April 2022, one month before the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite conducting security training, the company failed to enforce basic password hygiene practices, leaving a simple guessable password (incorporating the company name and sequential numbers) unprotected against brute force attacks.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, or disposal of personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement adequate password policy for privileged administrative accounts (only 8-character minimum, no expiry, no complexity requirements)
violations: Failed to implement adequate password policy for privileged administrative accounts (only 8-character minimum, no expiry, no complexity requirements)
Used a weak password containing the organisation's name and common number sequence ("lingoace123") that remained unchanged for over 2 years
Did not implement two-factor or multi-factor authentication for administrative accounts accessing systems with sensitive and high-volume personal data
Failed to implement enhanced security practices such as account lockout after failed login attempts or CAPTCHAs to prevent brute force attacks

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 11(3) – Accountability Obligation: All organisations must designate an individual to be responsible for compliance with the PDPA
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer from incorporation in 2016 until after the breach notification on 18 May 2022 (more than 5 years)
violations: Failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer from incorporation in 2016 until after the breach notification on 18 May 2022 (more than 5 years)

outcome: PPLingo was ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD 74,000 within 30 days. The organisation had already taken remedial actions including engaging forensic experts, resetting all administrator passwords, implementing two-factor authentication, appointing a Data Protection Officer, notifying affected users, implementing enhanced password requirements, conducting security training, and enhancing monitoring and audit procedures. The Commission determined no further directions were necessary given the remedial measures already undertaken.
companyNow: Following the 2023 enforcement action, PPLingo implemented comprehensive remedial measures including appointment of a Data Protection Officer, two-factor authentication across all systems, enhanced password policies, third-party security audits, and expanded staff training programs.
dataType: Name, date of birth, gender, photos, mobile phone numbers, email addresses, financial information (bank account numbers, salary), identity card numbers, educational records, learning data

companyDescription: Whiz Communications is a Singapore telecommunications service provider offering broadband internet access, digital IP telephony, and calling plans.
companyLongDescription: Whiz Communications Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based telecommunications provider that delivers broadband internet access, local and long-distance digital IP telephony services, and prepaid and postpaid calling plans to customers across Singapore. The company maintains a customer management system that stores sensitive personal identification documents and supporting documentation for its subscribers. As a telecommunications service provider, the company is subject to stringent data protection obligations under Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: Whiz Communications, a Singapore telecommunications provider, suffered a data breach in March-April 2023 where threat actors exploited a design flaw in the company's customer management system to extract identification documents and supporting documents of 24,323 individuals using Python scripts. The company failed to implement adequate security controls, including insufficient password complexity requirements, inadequate vendor security specifications, and lack of multi-factor authentication and access controls.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically by: (1) accepting Python script requests in the CMS design without proper controls; (2) failing to specify security requirements to the IT vendor; (3) implementing weak password policies (9 characters vs. recommended 12+); and (4) lacking multi-factor authentication and geographic access restrictions.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Whiz Communications failed to implement adequate security controls in its customer management system, allowing threat actors to exploit a design flaw.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of customers had their identity documents, passports, work permits, and tenancy agreements stolen, exposing them to identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: The customer management system was secure and protected customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CMS had a fundamental design flaw that accepted Python script requests, allowing attackers to extract 24,323 customers' identity documents over 5 days in March-April 2023.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had adequate password security measures in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: Admin account passwords required only 9 characters with one uppercase letter, falling far short of PDPC's recommended 12+ alphanumeric characters with mixed case and special characters.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had proper access controls for its customer management system.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CMS lacked multi-factor authentication, had no IP address restrictions, and no web application firewall, allowing overseas threat actors to access and extract data unimpeded.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vendor security specifications were properly defined and enforced.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company provided no security requirements to the external vendor who developed the CMS in 2016, and had no contractual obligation requiring the vendor to protect personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal of personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide security requirements to IT vendor for CMS development, particularly regarding Python script handling
violations: Failed to provide security requirements to IT vendor for CMS development, particularly regarding Python script handling
Did not stipulate clear job specifications or data protection requirements in vendor contract
Implemented weak password complexity policy (9 characters vs. recommended 12+ with mixed case, numbers, special characters)
Failed to enforce adequate password policies for admin accounts
Lacked reasonable access controls including multi-factor authentication, geographic IP restrictions, and web application firewall
System design accepted any Python script requests without blocking or managing them, creating exploitable vulnerability

outcome: The Organisation was required to pay a financial penalty of SGD 9,000 within 30 days. The decision noted mitigating factors including the Organisation's cooperation during investigation, voluntary admission of breach under Expedited Decision Procedure, and prompt remedial actions taken post-incident (blocking Python requests, restricting overseas IPs, implementing two-factor authentication, conducting penetration testing).
dataType: Identification documents (NRIC, passport, student pass, dependent pass), tenancy agreements, work permit approval letters

companyDescription: Lee Chee Meng is a registered real estate salesperson operating as an independent agent for ERA Realty Network in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Lee Chee Meng is an individual real estate salesperson registered under the Estate Agents Act 2010 and appointed by ERA Realty Network Pte Ltd to engage in estate agency work and promote real estate transaction services. Operating as an independent agent on commission, he purchased large personal data sets from third parties for telemarketing purposes over approximately 10 years. His business model involved acquiring contact lists and sending targeted marketing communications to individuals in specific geographic areas to promote property transactions.
caseDescription: A real estate salesperson purchased approximately 420,000 personal data records from an unknown third-party seller without verifying consent or notification. He then used this data to send unsolicited telemarketing emails and SMS messages to individuals without their knowledge or permission. The Commission found he failed to perform required due diligence to ensure the individuals had consented to the collection and use of their data.
violationSummary: The respondent conducted systematic collection and use of personal data for telemarketing purposes without obtaining or verifying consent from individuals. This constitutes unauthorized surveillance-like collection of individuals' contact information for targeted marketing.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Lee Chee Meng purchased approximately 420,000 personal data records from an unknown third-party seller and used them to send unsolicited telemarketing emails.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals received unwanted marketing communications about property sales to their private contact details without having agreed to receive such messages.

claimsVsReality.claim: Lee Chee Meng included an unsubscribe function in marketing emails and checked contact numbers against the Do Not Call Registry before sending SMS.
claimsVsReality.reality: These compliance measures did not cure the fundamental breach: he never verified that the 420,000 individuals had consented to receive marketing messages in the first place, and the data may have originated from a data breach (RedMart Limited).

claimsVsReality.claim: The data came from a third-party seller named 'Ali' contacted through social media, implying a legitimate commercial transaction.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lee Chee Meng performed no due diligence on the seller's identity, legitimacy, or how the data was originally obtained, and could not verify the data's lawful provenance or the individuals' consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Lee Chee Meng only used 25% of the purchased data that contained residential information, suggesting limited harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even the 105,000 individuals who received marketing messages (25% of 420,000) had never consented to receive unsolicited telemarketing communications about property sales.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 13 – Consent Obligation requires obtaining consent before collecting, using or disclosing personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Purchased personal data from third-party seller without ascertaining that individuals had consented to the collection, sale, or use
violations: Purchased personal data from third-party seller without ascertaining that individuals had consented to the collection, sale, or use
Failed to perform due diligence to verify consent was obtained by the seller
Did not contact individuals directly to obtain consent
Sent unsolicited telemarketing communications without consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 20 – Notification Obligation requires informing individuals of purposes before collecting, using or disclosing their data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to inform individuals of the purposes for which their data was being collected, used and disclosed
violations: Failed to inform individuals of the purposes for which their data was being collected, used and disclosed
Did not perform due diligence to ensure individuals were notified by the seller
Did not contact individuals directly to provide notification

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 4(1)(a) and (b) – Exemption for personal/domestic capacity and employment does not apply
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent was operating as an 'organisation' under PDPA definition, not in personal/domestic capacity
violations: Respondent was operating as an 'organisation' under PDPA definition, not in personal/domestic capacity
Actions were done for profit in furtherance of business as real estate salesperson
Respondent was independent agent, not employee, so employment exemption did not apply

outcome: The Commission imposed a reduced financial penalty of S$16,800 (reduced from S$28,000 due to exceptional financial hardship), and issued compliance directions requiring: (1) immediate cessation of use of all purchased data; (2) retention cessation within 7 days; and (3) notification to Commission within 7 days of completion. The respondent must also comply with PDPA consent and notification obligations in future.
companyNow: Lee Chee Meng continues to operate as a real estate salesperson, but the case findings and financial penalty now form part of his regulatory record under Singapore's PDPA enforcement.
dataType: Name, email address, contact number, residential/office address, partial credit card number (last 4 digits)
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Sections 4(1)(a) and 4(1)(b) (scope of application to individuals acting in business capacity)

companyDescription: Carousell is a Southeast Asian online marketplace platform for buying and selling new and second-hand goods and services, with operations across Singapore, Malaysia, Taiwan, the Philippines, and Indonesia.
companyLongDescription: Carousell Pte. Ltd. operates a digital marketplace platform available as both website and mobile application, enabling peer-to-peer transactions for various goods and services. The platform has expanded to include property listings alongside traditional e-commerce offerings. It serves millions of users across five major Southeast Asian markets and is one of the region's largest community commerce platforms.
caseDescription: Carousell, an online marketplace platform, suffered two separate data breaches in 2022 affecting millions of users. The first incident involved unintended disclosure of contact information (emails and phone numbers) of 44,477 users due to coding bugs in the chat function. The second incident resulted in unauthorized access and exfiltration of personal data of approximately 2.6 million users through an unfiltered API that was exploited by a threat actor.
violationSummary: Carousell failed to implement adequate pre-launch testing and code review procedures, and failed to maintain proper documentation of software specifications. These security failures allowed data protection risks and defects to go undetected before deployment, resulting in unauthorized disclosure and access to personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Carousell suffered two data breaches in 2022: one exposed 44,477 users' emails and phone numbers through chat function bugs.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Carousell users had their email addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth exposed to threat actors.

claimsVsReality.claim: The July 2022 chat function update was properly scoped to only affect Registered Users in Philippines property listings.
claimsVsReality.reality: Due to human error, the update caused email and phone numbers to be appended for all Guest and Registered Users across all listing categories and all markets.

claimsVsReality.claim: The API with follow/follower functionality would only expose publicly available user data (username, name, profile image).
claimsVsReality.reality: The API exposed non-public personal data including email addresses, phone numbers, and dates of birth due to an omitted security filter.

claimsVsReality.claim: Carousell conducted adequate pre-launch testing before deploying new features to production.
claimsVsReality.reality: Carousell failed to test code changes against unintended user categories and did not mandate comprehensive code reviews for security issues prior to the 2nd Incident.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation: Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data in their possession or under their control
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct reasonably scoped pre-launch testing before deploying changes to the chat function on 13 July 2022 and 18 August 2022, resulting in unintended disclosure of personal data of 44,477 users
violations: Failed to conduct reasonably scoped pre-launch testing before deploying changes to the chat function on 13 July 2022 and 18 August 2022, resulting in unintended disclosure of personal data of 44,477 users

Failed to conduct comprehensive code reviews and testing during system migration, allowing an unfiltered API to be deployed that enabled unauthorized access to personal data of approximately 2.6 million users
Failed to adequately document software functional and technical specifications, which contributed to errors in implementing code changes and deploying security-critical APIs

outcome: Carousell was ordered to pay a monetary penalty of SGD $58,000. The company was also directed to review its software testing procedures and documentation processes within 90 days, rectify any identified gaps, and furnish a report to the Commission detailing the reviews and remediation actions taken. Carousell implemented multiple remedial measures including automated unit tests, enhanced SLA policies with faster breach resolution times, security audits of APIs, rate limiting, penetration testing, and improved code review requirements for features involving personal data.
companyNow: Carousell continues to operate as a major Southeast Asian marketplace platform. Following the 2023 enforcement action, the company has implemented enhanced security measures including automated testing, API security audits, and improved incident response protocols.
dataType: Email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, user names, profile information

companyDescription: Mobile Chat is a mobile phone retailer operated by Koh Wei Ming from a shop in Geylang, Singapore, selling mobile phones, prepaid SIM cards, and accessories since 2015.
companyLongDescription: Mobile Chat was a small mobile phone retail business in Singapore operated as a sole proprietorship by Koh Wei Ming. The organization sold and serviced mobile phones, prepaid SIM cards, and mobile phone accessories from a Geylang shop location starting in 2015. As a retailer of M1 SIM cards, the business was provided with an M1 Terminal Device for legitimate SIM card registration purposes. The business has since ceased operations following the enforcement action.
caseDescription: Koh Wei Ming, trading as Mobile Chat, a mobile phone retailer, unlawfully used customers' personal data without consent to register additional prepaid SIM cards that customers did not purchase. The SIM cards were then sold to unauthorized third parties, and subsequently used to send unsolicited marketing messages to numbers registered on the Do Not Call Register. Over 4 years, KWM registered approximately 95 illicit SIM cards using the personal data of 73 confirmed customers (affecting approximately 1,000 individuals estimated).
violationSummary: KWM collected personal data ostensibly for registering SIM cards customers intended to purchase, but then used that same data for an entirely different, undisclosed purpose: registering illicit SIM cards for unauthorized sale to third parties for profit. This is a clear case of secondary use without consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Koh Wei Ming, trading as Mobile Chat, unlawfully used customers' personal data without consent to register additional prepaid SIM cards that customers did not purchase.
whyTheyWereWrong: The illicit SIM cards were used to send unsolicited marketing messages to phone numbers registered on the Do Not Call Register, violating the privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Koh Wei Ming was legitimately registering SIM cards for customers who requested them.
claimsVsReality.reality: He deliberately scanned customer identity documents twice without consent (Method 1) or activated incomplete transactions without authorization (Method 2) to register illicit SIM cards he sold for profit (~$35,000 over 4 years).

claimsVsReality.claim: The SIM cards were being used for legitimate purposes by authorized purchasers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The illicit SIM cards were sold to unauthorized third parties and subsequently used to send unsolicited marketing messages to 1,391 Do Not Call Register subscribers between February 2020 and September 2021.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers consented to all uses of their personal data in the registration process.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customers only consented to registration of the specific SIM cards they intended to purchase; they had no knowledge of or consent for the registration of additional duplicate cards or for KWM's retention and sale of their personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 13 – Consent Obligation: Organisations prohibited from collecting, using or disclosing personal data without individual's consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Method 1 (Duplicate Scanning): Customers consented only to registration of requested SIM cards; KWM scanned identity documents twice to register additional unauthorized SIM cards without consent
violations: Method 1 (Duplicate Scanning): Customers consented only to registration of requested SIM cards; KWM scanned identity documents twice to register additional unauthorized SIM cards without consent
Method 2 (Incomplete Transactions): Customers withdrew consent by declining to proceed; KWM activated and sold the SIM cards anyway despite lack of consent
