regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 18 – Purpose Limitation Obligation: Personal data may only be used for purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate, and individual must be informed of such purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: KWM used customers' personal data for registering illicit SIM cards for unauthorized sale and personal profit, which was not a purpose customers consented to or would reasonably anticipate
violations: KWM used customers' personal data for registering illicit SIM cards for unauthorized sale and personal profit, which was not a purpose customers consented to or would reasonably anticipate
The purpose was clearly unreasonable under any circumstances, involving misuse for financial gain

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD 48,000 payable within 30 days. Interest accrues at the rate specified in the Rules of Court for judgment debts on any outstanding amount. No further directions required as the Organisation has ceased the unauthorised sale of preregistered SIM cards. KWM was separately sentenced to 16 months' imprisonment for unauthorized use of computer material under the Computer Misuse Act.
companyNow: Mobile Chat has ceased the unauthorised sale of preregistered SIM cards following the enforcement action. The sole proprietor was sentenced to 16 months' imprisonment in September 2023 for unauthorized computer misuse.
dataType: Name, address, NRIC/FIN/passport numbers

companyDescription: Tipros is a sole proprietorship based in Singapore engaged in the wholesale and repair of electrical appliances, particularly refrigerators and other domestic equipment.
companyLongDescription: Tipros operates as a small electrical appliance repair business in Singapore, offering services including refrigerator repair and maintenance. The business maintains a presence on Google reviews under the name 'Tipros.sg' (formerly '24hr fridge refrigerator #1 Quick repair service Trusted in Singapore'). As a sole proprietorship operated by Er Lee Cheng @ Angela Er Wei Leng, the company markets itself as providing round-the-clock service to customers in Singapore.
caseDescription: Tipros, an electrical appliance repair business, unreasonably disclosed a complainant's personal data (residential address and mobile number) when responding to a negative review on its Google reviews page. The Commission found 13 other similar instances of personal data disclosure in responses to customer reviews. The organisation was directed to remove these disclosures and review all similar responses within 30 days.
violationSummary: The organisation disclosed personal data (residential address and mobile number) publicly on Google reviews without reasonable justification or proportionality. The disclosure was not necessary to respond to the complaint and exceeded what was appropriate in the circumstances.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Tipros disclosed customers' residential addresses and mobile numbers in public Google review responses without reasonable justification, doing so in at least 14 instances.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers had no reason to expect their home addresses and phone numbers would be publicly posted online when leaving reviews, exposing them to unsolicited contact, harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation advertised itself as providing round-the-clock service availability.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation's technician was not available over the weekend when the complainant needed weekend service, contradicting the 24-hour service claim.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disclosing customer addresses and phone numbers in public review responses was necessary to respond to complaints.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Commission found that the disclosure was unreasonable and disproportionate; the customer's grievance about poor service quality required no address or phone number to be addressed.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 18(a) – Organisations must collect, use or disclose personal data for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed complainant's residential address and mobile number in response to a review about poor service quality, which was disproportionate and unnecessary
violations: Disclosed complainant's residential address and mobile number in response to a review about poor service quality, which was disproportionate and unnecessary
Disclosed personal data of 13 other customers in similar fashion without reasonable justification or proportionality

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 18(b) – Organisations must inform individuals of the purposes for which personal data will be used or disclosed prior to collection, use or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to appropriately inform individuals that their personal data would be disclosed in public responses to reviews
violations: Failed to appropriately inform individuals that their personal data would be disclosed in public responses to reviews

outcome: The Commission directed Tipros to: (1) Remove the disclosure of the complainant's residential address and mobile number from its Google reviews response; and (2) Review the 13 other responses containing personal data disclosures and remove any that are not reasonable or proportionate. The organisation was given 30 days to comply. The organisation's refusal to respond to investigative notices and failure to remedy the breaches were considered aggravating factors.
companyNow: Following the 2023 PDPC decision, Tipros was required to review and remove customer personal data disclosures from its Google reviews page within 30 days. The company's current operational status is unclear.
dataType: residential address, mobile number

companyDescription: Tokyo Century Leasing (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. is a leasing and hire-purchase finance company that operates an online platform for customers to submit lease and hire-purchase applications. It is part of the Tokyo Century Corporation group based in Japan.
companyLongDescription: Tokyo Century Leasing (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. is a subsidiary of Tokyo Century Corporation, a major Japanese equipment leasing and finance company. The Singapore entity operates in the vehicle leasing and hire-purchase business, providing financing services to customers through both online and traditional channels. It handles sensitive financial and personal data from tens of thousands of customers and guarantors seeking leasing and hire-purchase agreements. The company is part of a larger multinational group with operations across Asia.
caseDescription: Tokyo Century Leasing failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data of 141,412 individuals after a ransomware attack encrypted data on 7 servers and 6 employee computers. The organisation had not patched a known vulnerability in its firewall device for nearly 3 years despite the patch being available, failed to monitor for software patches, and had not implemented multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts. No evidence indicated the encrypted data was exfiltrated.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data by: (1) not conducting regular monitoring for software patches; (2) not implementing processes to manage software patches and upgrades; and (3) not implementing multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts. These failures allowed malicious actors to exploit a known vulnerability to access systems containing highly sensitive personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Tokyo Century Leasing failed to patch a known firewall vulnerability for nearly 3 years, lacked software patch monitoring processes.
whyTheyWereWrong: The organisation's security failures allowed attackers to exploit a publicly known firewall vulnerability to access administrator credentials.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT vendor was responsible for monitoring and patching software vulnerabilities.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the IT vendor had patching responsibility, the contract contained no requirement for the vendor to conduct regular monitoring; patching only occurred upon the organisation's request, which never came because the organisation itself failed to monitor for patches.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had adequate security arrangements for the personal data of 141,412 individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation left a critical firewall vulnerability unpatched for nearly 3 years despite the patch being publicly available since May 2019, had no processes to track software patches, and lacked multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts, which allowed attackers to compromise admin credentials and encrypt all data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal, or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct regular monitoring for software patches on the FortiGate firewall device, leaving a known vulnerability (CVE-2018-13379) unpatched for nearly 3 years despite the patch being available since May 2019
violations: Failed to conduct regular monitoring for software patches on the FortiGate firewall device, leaving a known vulnerability (CVE-2018-13379) unpatched for nearly 3 years despite the patch being available since May 2019

Failed to implement processes to manage software patches and upgrades; patching was done on an ad-hoc basis only upon the organisation's request without any formal monitoring or contractual obligation with IT vendor

Failed to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for administrator accounts despite having access to confidential and sensitive personal data, contrary to the Commission's baseline requirement established in Lovebonito Singapore Pte. Ltd.

outcome: The Commission imposed a financial penalty of $82,000 SGD to be paid within 30 days. The Commission recognised the organisation's cooperative attitude, prompt remedial actions (including patching the vulnerability, implementing MFA for VPN access, changing administrator passwords, and conducting forensic monitoring), and voluntary acceptance of responsibility through the expedited breach procedure. No further directions were issued as the organisation had already implemented appropriate remedial measures.
companyNow: Tokyo Century Leasing continues to operate in Singapore following the incident and enforcement action, having implemented remedial security measures including multi-factor authentication, vulnerability patching, and improved patch management processes.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, date of birth, address, contact number, income statement, email address, employer information, bank account, passport numbers, employment pass numbers, resume information, medical check-up information

companyDescription: Ascentis Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based software development company specialising in Customer Relationship Management (CRM) and e-commerce platform solutions.
companyLongDescription: Ascentis develops, provides, and integrates software solutions for CRM systems and e-commerce platforms. The company was engaged by Starbucks Singapore in 2014 to develop and maintain a CRM system supporting the Starbucks Rewards loyalty program, and later contracted in 2020 to develop a separate e-commerce platform. The company outsourced development work to a Vietnamese software firm, Kyanon Digital, while maintaining overall control and responsibility for security and account management.
caseDescription: Ascentis, a software development company, failed to implement reasonable security arrangements for personal data of 332,774 Starbucks Rewards Program members stored on an e-commerce platform. A malicious actor exploited an undisabled administrator account (with a weak password that had been shared via Google Sheet) to exfiltrate customer data, which was subsequently offered for sale on the dark web.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically: failing to disable an employee's admin account after departure, using weak and guessable passwords, sharing credentials via shared Google Sheet, and not implementing multi-factor authentication for administrative accounts with access to large volumes of sensitive personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Ascentis failed to disable a former contractor's administrator account after he left the project, allowed the account password to be shared via Google Sheet.
whyTheyWereWrong: Starbucks Rewards members' names, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, and physical addresses were stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Peter's Admin Account credentials were securely managed and passwords were hashed, so the Organisation was unaware of the weak password.
claimsVsReality.reality: The password 'Kyanon@123456' was easily guessable (containing company name + sequential digits), was shared on an unencrypted Google Sheet accessible to anyone with link access, and the account was never disabled after Peter left employment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation maintained control and management of the Platform and had responsibility for account management.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Organisation failed to implement basic account management practices such as disabling accounts when users left the project, creating new accounts for replacement personnel, or requiring multi-factor authentication on administrative accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Master Services Agreement with Kyanon imposed adequate data protection obligations requiring 'secure authentication and authorisation processes'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The contract lacked specific mandates for critical account management practices, allowing vulnerable processes like credential sharing and disabled accounts to continue unchecked.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 (Protection Obligation) – An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to disable Peter's admin account after he left employment with Kyanon despite retaining responsibility for platform management
violations: Failed to disable Peter's admin account after he left employment with Kyanon despite retaining responsibility for platform management
Permitted use of weak, easily guessable password 'Kyanon@123456' that incorporated company name and sequential digits
Shared administrator credentials via a shared Google Sheet, creating heightened risk of unauthorised access
Failed to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) for administrative accounts with access to large volumes of personal data
Did not assign rights to admin accounts based on principle of least privilege – exported data rights granted unnecessarily
Did not include specific account management requirements in contracts with third-party vendor Kyanon

outcome: The Organisation was required to pay a financial penalty of SGD 10,000 within 30 days. The Commission determined no further directions were necessary as the Organisation had already taken comprehensive remedial measures including: activating emergency response and investigation teams, disabling all platform access and resetting accounts, blocking the malicious actor's IP address, requiring all vendors to perform antivirus scans, and implementing multi-factor authentication for all accounts. Starbucks SG accepted a voluntary undertaking to implement enhanced security arrangements and no further enforcement action was taken against them.
dataType: Names, email addresses, dates of birth, membership details, physical addresses, telephone numbers

companyDescription: Century Evergreen is a manpower contracting services company based in Singapore that connects jobseekers with employment opportunities.
companyLongDescription: Century Evergreen Private Limited is a Singapore-based manpower contracting services company that requires jobseekers to submit identification documents for identity verification and suitability assessment. The company operated a website launched in November 2015 where jobseekers uploaded sensitive personal documents. Despite engaging an IT vendor to develop and maintain the website, the company failed to establish adequate security protocols or contractual safeguards, resulting in a major data exposure incident.
caseDescription: Century Evergreen, a manpower contracting services company, failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect identification documents submitted by jobseekers. An Insecure Direct Object References (IDOR) vulnerability on their website, which existed since launch in 2015, allowed public access to 96,889 images of identification documents belonging to 23,940 individuals. The company failed to include security requirements in its contract with the IT vendor and conducted no security testing prior to or after website launch.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession and control. The IDOR vulnerability exposed sensitive identification document images to unauthorised access for seven years, demonstrating gross negligence in data protection practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Century Evergreen failed to implement reasonable security arrangements and did not include security requirements in its contract with its IT vendor.
whyTheyWereWrong: The vulnerability allowed 23,940 jobseekers' sensitive identification documents, including National Registration Identity Cards with personal numbers, to be publicly downloaded.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had adequate security measures in place for jobseeker identification documents.
claimsVsReality.reality: An IDOR vulnerability existed from website launch in 2015 that allowed public access to identification document images throughout the company's operation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT vendor was responsible for security of personal data on the website.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company remained solely responsible for protecting personal data even though it engaged an IT vendor; the vendor's contract contained no security requirements whatsoever.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company conducted appropriate security testing before and after website launch.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company only performed functionality testing at launch and conducted no security tests before or after launch, with no security arrangements in place with the vendor.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24(a) – Protection Obligation
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access to personal data
violations: Failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access to personal data
Failed to include security requirements in contract with IT vendor
Conducted no security testing prior to website launch or thereafter
Allowed IDOR vulnerability to persist from website launch (9 November 2015) until disclosure (December 2022)
Did not impose security requirements on IT vendor despite retaining responsibility for data protection

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the Organisation in breach of Section 24(a) of the PDPA and directed payment of a financial penalty of S$9,000 within 30 days. The Organisation had already undertaken remedial actions including fixing the IDOR vulnerability, implementing vulnerability scans, migrating to an encrypted remote backup server, deploying additional security software, securing security services, and negotiating a new security management contract with its vendor.
companyNow: As of 2023, Century Evergreen remains operational but has implemented significant security remediation measures including vulnerability fixes, server configuration improvements, encryption protocols, and enhanced security services following the PDPA enforcement action.
dataType: identification document images, national registration identity card numbers

companyDescription: Autobahn Rent A Car Pte. Ltd. operates Shariot, a car-sharing service in Singapore. The company provides vehicle rental and mobility services to consumers through a mobile application platform.
companyLongDescription: Autobahn Rent A Car Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based transportation and car-sharing operator that runs the Shariot mobile application platform. The service allows customers to rent vehicles through a digital platform. The company collects and stores sensitive personal data including customer names, contact information, national identification numbers, and location data. Following the 2022 data breach, the company implemented enhanced security measures including multi-factor authentication and improved access control procedures.
caseDescription: Autobahn Rent A Car failed to revoke administrator account credentials of a departed employee, allowing a threat actor to access the company's backend admin portal and exfiltrate personal data of 53,000 Shariot users. The company also failed to implement multi-factor authentication on administrative accounts with access to sensitive user databases. The breach exposed names, email addresses, phone numbers, NRIC numbers, and location data.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and disclosure of personal data. Specifically, it failed to revoke dormant administrator credentials and did not implement multi-factor authentication on privileged accounts accessing sensitive databases containing significant volumes of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Autobahn Rent A Car failed to revoke administrator account credentials of a departed employee and did not implement multi-factor authentication on administrative accounts.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unrevoked credentials enabled a threat actor to steal sensitive personal information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, NRIC numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Administrator accounts were secure and only accessible to active employees.
claimsVsReality.reality: An ex-employee's administrator credentials remained active for 4 months after departure in May 2022, enabling unauthorized access when compromised in September 2022.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had reasonable security arrangements in place to protect sensitive personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked multi-factor authentication on administrative accounts, allowing a single compromised password to grant full access to the database containing 53,000 customer records with NRIC numbers and location data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Shariot backend admin portal was adequately protected against unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: A threat actor was able to log in using a compromised former employee's credentials and successfully export the entire customer database using the CSV export function without any additional authentication barriers.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 — An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to revoke administrator login credentials of ex-employee after employment ended in May 2022, leaving dormant account active
violations: Failed to revoke administrator login credentials of ex-employee after employment ended in May 2022, leaving dormant account active
Failed to implement multi-factor authentication (MFA) or two-factor authentication (2FA) on administrator accounts with access to large user databases
Failed to ensure reasonable access control measures to backend admin web portal
These failures enabled unauthorized access and exfiltration of 53,000 personal data records

outcome: The organization was required to pay a financial penalty of SGD $3,000 within 30 days. In addition, the organization must: (a) implement processes for timely revocation of system and application access upon employee departure; (b) strengthen access controls on administrator accounts accessing personal data databases; (c) conduct a security review of technical and administrative arrangements within 60 days; (d) rectify identified security gaps; and (e) inform the Commission within one week of completing these directions. The organization was cooperative during investigations, voluntarily admitted to the breach under the Expedited Decision Procedure, and took prompt remedial actions including conducting internal audits, enhancing software code to mask NRIC numbers, and providing cyber hygiene training.
companyNow: Autobahn Rent A Car continues to operate Shariot in Singapore. The company has implemented the remedial security measures directed by the PDPC including multi-factor authentication, credential revocation procedures, and regular security reviews.
dataType: Names, email addresses, mobile phone numbers, NRIC numbers, general location data

companyDescription: E-Commerce Enablers is a Singapore-based e-commerce platform that offers cashback rewards, coupons, and voucher codes for purchases through affiliated merchants.
companyLongDescription: E-Commerce Enablers operated an online platform providing cashback incentives, coupons, voucher codes, and price comparison features to users making purchases through its network of affiliated merchants. The platform hosted sensitive customer data including personal information and financial details on Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud infrastructure. The company employed a 12-person Site Reliability Engineering team responsible for maintaining infrastructure and managing cloud security.
caseDescription: E-Commerce Enablers failed to implement sufficiently robust processes for managing AWS access keys, resulting in a key being inadvertently committed to GitHub and remaining usable for 15 months. A malicious actor used this key to access the company's AWS environment and exfiltrate personal data of approximately 1.46 million users in September 2020. The company also failed to conduct periodic security reviews that could have detected the compromised key.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement adequate security arrangements and robust key management processes, combined with lack of periodic security reviews, enabled unauthorized access to and exfiltration of personal data. This directly violates the duty to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: E-Commerce Enablers failed to implement robust processes for managing AWS access keys, allowing a key with full administrative privileges to remain active.
whyTheyWereWrong: A malicious actor exploited the exposed AWS key to access the company's servers and steal personal data—including email addresses, names, phone numbers, bank account numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The compromise of the AWS Key arose from human error, not systemic security issues, because the SRE team member was senior and had dutifully rotated other keys.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation relied entirely on employee compliance without independent verification or supervisory checks on critical security tasks, and failed to conduct periodic security reviews that would have detected the active compromised key during the 15-month exposure period.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation's security practices were sound and the incident was a one-off case.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation took 15 days to respond to the exposure of a full administrative privilege AWS key, and lacked robust incident management processes to ensure reasonable remediation speed.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal, or similar risks to personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement sufficiently robust processes for AWS key management – relied solely on employee seniority and performance without independent verification or testing of key rotation/deletion
violations: Failed to implement sufficiently robust processes for AWS key management – relied solely on employee seniority and performance without independent verification or testing of key rotation/deletion
Failed to conduct periodic security reviews on AWS keys to detect whether keys had been properly rotated or deleted
Took 15 days to respond to the exposure of the AWS Key, indicating inadequate incident management processes

outcome: The Commissioner required E-Commerce Enablers to pay a financial penalty of SGD $74,400 within 30 days. No further directions were imposed as the organization had already implemented comprehensive remedial measures including: full deletion and rotation of AWS keys, forced password resets for all customers, enhanced monitoring of logs, separation of development and production accounts, implementation of VPN and IP whitelisting, database encryption, and creation of a platform for employee security suggestions and breach reporting.
companyNow: Following the 2020 data breach and 2023 enforcement action, the company's current operational status is not publicly documented. The company implemented enhanced security measures including separated development and production environments, VPN access controls, and database encryption.
dataType: Email address, name, mobile number, physical address, gender, NRIC numbers, date of birth, bank account numbers, partial credit card information
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation (reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Fullerton Healthcare Group is an enterprise healthcare service provider in Singapore that delivers healthcare services to individuals and corporate clients.
companyLongDescription: Fullerton Healthcare Group Pte Limited is a Singapore-based healthcare service provider offering comprehensive healthcare services to both individual patients and corporate clients. The company engages third-party service providers, including data intermediaries, to support its operations. In 2018, FHG engaged Agape CP Holdings to provide call centre and appointment booking services, which resulted in a significant data breach affecting over 156,000 customers.
caseDescription: Fullerton Healthcare Group engaged Agape as a data intermediary to provide call centre services, but failed to exercise reasonable oversight of how Agape stored and accessed customer data. Agape created an internet-facing file server without proper password protection and failed to include it in periodic security reviews, resulting in unauthorised access and exfiltration of 156,900 customers' personal data offered for sale on the dark web. Additionally, FHG inadvertently disclosed sensitive financial and health information to Agape that was not necessary for service provision.
violationSummary: Both organisations failed to implement and maintain reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data. Agape's failures included inadequate password management, failure to conduct periodic security reviews covering all systems, and leaving an internet-facing file server unprotected. FHG's failures included inadequate vendor oversight and unnecessary disclosure of sensitive data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Fullerton Healthcare Group failed to exercise reasonable oversight of data intermediary Agape, which stored 156,900 customers' personal data on an internet-facing server without password.
whyTheyWereWrong: Healthcare customers' sensitive data including NRIC numbers, financial information, and diagnosis codes were exposed on the dark web for sale.

claimsVsReality.claim: FHG stated it did not provide Agape permission to upload Customer Data to the Online Drive and that the local copy was only for emergencies.
claimsVsReality.reality: Agape uploaded all Customer Data to an internet-facing server and maintained it there for 20+ months with disabled password protection, regardless of original intent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agape conducted periodic security reviews to ensure data protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: Agape's security reviews failed to cover the internet-facing Online Drive—a critical system—for over three years, leaving 156,900 records unprotected.

claimsVsReality.claim: FHG conducted high-level IT due diligence and required Agape to comply with PDPA security obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: FHG failed to monitor how Agape actually stored and controlled access to sensitive customer data throughout the engagement, discovering the breach only after data appeared on the dark web.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or control
regulatoryFindings.description: Agape failed to conduct periodic security reviews that covered the internet-facing Online Drive, a legacy system used specifically for FHG
violations: Agape failed to conduct periodic security reviews that covered the internet-facing Online Drive, a legacy system used specifically for FHG
Agape's password for the Online Drive was inadvertently disabled for approximately 20 months, leaving it as an open directory listing with no password protection
Agape implemented inadequate password management by allowing multiple Agents to share a common password with no expiry date
FHG failed to exercise reasonable oversight of Agape's data processing activities by not monitoring how Agape stored and granted access to customer data
FHG inadvertently disclosed sensitive financial and health information to Agape that was not necessary for service provision, amplifying the impact of the breach

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 4(2) requires data intermediaries to comply with the Protection Obligation
regulatoryFindings.description: Agape breached the Protection Obligation through inadequate security reviews and password management
violations: Agape breached the Protection Obligation through inadequate security reviews and password management

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 4(3) requires data controllers to bear the same obligations as if processing data themselves when engaging a data intermediary
regulatoryFindings.description: FHG failed to exercise supervisory role and reasonable oversight of Agape despite being the data controller responsible for ensuring vendor compliance
violations: FHG failed to exercise supervisory role and reasonable oversight of Agape despite being the data controller responsible for ensuring vendor compliance

outcome: FHG is required to pay a financial penalty of S$58,000 and Agape S$10,000 within 30 days. Both organisations must implement comprehensive remedial measures within 60 days including: FHG must review vendor processes and contractual obligations, ensure only necessary personal data is disclosed to vendors with proper access controls, and notify the Commission of completion. Agape must expand the scope of periodic security reviews to cover all systems, resolve data protection requirements with FHG in writing, and provide regular oversight documentation. Both organisations have voluntarily implemented additional security measures including multi-factor authentication, enhanced data protection policies, vulnerability assessments, and staff training.
companyNow: Following the 2023 PDPC enforcement action and S$68,000 penalty, Fullerton Healthcare Group implemented enhanced data protection measures including restricted access controls, data minimisation efforts, and improved vendor oversight protocols.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, FIN, date of birth, gender, email address, telephone number, bank account numbers, bank codes, health information (ICD codes, surgical procedure codes), health benefit utilisation details
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 4(3) (Data controller responsibility for data intermediaries)

companyDescription: The Law Society of Singapore is a statutory body established under the Legal Profession Act 1966 that represents advocates and solicitors in Singapore. Every lawyer called to the Singapore bar is a statutory member of the organisation.
companyLongDescription: The Law Society of Singapore is a professional regulatory body for the legal profession, established by statute in 1966. It serves as the representative body for all advocates and solicitors in Singapore who hold practising certificates. The organisation maintains records and databases of its members to carry out its statutory functions, including professional oversight and regulation of the legal profession. As a professional body, it manages significant volumes of sensitive personal data of practitioners.
caseDescription: The Law Society of Singapore suffered a ransomware attack in January 2021 that encrypted servers containing personal data of 16,009 current and former members. Investigations found the organization negligently breached its data protection obligations by using a weak, easily guessable administrator password, failing to change it within required intervals, and not conducting security reviews for three years prior to the incident.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements as required by PDPA Section 24. Specific failures included: use of a weak password ('Welcome2020lawsoc') vulnerable to dictionary attacks despite meeting complexity rules, failure to enforce password rotation policy (password used for over 90 days instead of mandatory 3-month changes), and absence of periodic security reviews for three years. These failures were characterized as negligent breaches of the Protection Obligation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The Law Society of Singapore used a weak, easily guessable administrator password, failed to change it within required intervals.
whyTheyWereWrong: 16,009 current and former lawyers had their sensitive personal data including names, addresses, dates of birth, and national ID numbers encrypted.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation had implemented strong security controls including password complexity requirements and antivirus software.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite having password complexity policies, the organisation used the weak password 'Welcome2020lawsoc' for its administrator account, failed to change it every 3 months as required, and had not conducted security reviews in 3 years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The vendor was responsible for patching the VPN System vulnerability.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the vendor had contractual responsibility, the organisation failed to exercise adequate oversight and did not query the vendor about the publicly disclosed vulnerability that had been published online in November 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requiring reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Use of easily guessable administrator password 'Welcome2020lawsoc' incorporating organization name, vulnerable to dictionary and brute force attacks
violations: Use of easily guessable administrator password 'Welcome2020lawsoc' incorporating organization name, vulnerable to dictionary and brute force attacks
Failure to enforce mandatory password rotation policy – compromised admin account password was used for more than 90 days instead of required 3-month changes
Failure to conduct periodic security reviews in the three years prior to the incident, preventing detection of security control gaps

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the Law Society negligently breached the Protection Obligation but did not impose a financial penalty, considering that the breaches were not the most proximate cause of the incident (the VPN vulnerability was the primary cause), the data affected was not highly sensitive, unauthorized access was detected and contained promptly with no evidence of exfiltration or misuse, and the organization took prompt remedial actions. Instead, compliance directions were issued requiring the organization to: (a) engage qualified security service providers to conduct a thorough security audit of technical and administrative arrangements for privileged account management; (b) furnish an audit scope within 14 days; (c) provide the full audit report within 60 days; (d) rectify security gaps and update data protection policies; and (e) inform the Commission of completion within one week.
companyNow: The Law Society of Singapore continues to operate as the statutory regulator of the legal profession in Singapore. Following the incident, it strengthened its cybersecurity posture by hiring an in-house cybersecurity professional and implementing multi-factor authentication and IP whitelisting controls.
dataType: Name, residential address, date of birth, NRIC number

companyDescription: Kingsforce Management Services is a Singapore-based recruitment and jobseeker management company that operates online platforms to connect job candidates with employment opportunities.
companyLongDescription: Kingsforce Management Services is a Singapore-registered recruitment services provider that maintained a jobseeker database used to match candidates with employment opportunities. The company operated a website-based platform to manage jobseeker profiles and facilitate job placements. The organisation engaged external IT vendors for website maintenance and security. Following the 2021 breach, the company cooperated fully with regulators and undertook remediation efforts including immediate website suspension and engagement of new development resources.
caseDescription: Kingsforce Management Services failed to adequately protect a jobseeker database containing approximately 54,900 records, which was breached and sold on RaidForums in December 2021. The breach resulted from outdated website coding with critical vulnerabilities and the organisation's failure to conduct regular security reviews or provide clear data protection specifications to IT vendors. The Commission found a breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24(a) of the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data. Specifically, it used outdated technology with critical vulnerabilities, failed to conduct periodic security reviews and vulnerability scans, and did not provide adequate data protection specifications to IT vendors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Kingsforce Management Services failed to protect a jobseeker database containing 54,900 records, which was breached.
whyTheyWereWrong: Jobseekers' personal information including names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, and salary expectations were exposed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Website was adequately secured through engagement of IT maintenance vendors.
claimsVsReality.reality: Maintenance was ad-hoc, limited to troubleshooting bugs and glitches, with no meaningful security reviews conducted and critical vulnerabilities left unpatched for years.

claimsVsReality.claim: IT vendors understood and were protecting personal data on the database.
claimsVsReality.reality: No clear data protection specifications or contractual terms regarding personal data security were provided to vendors, leaving them unaware of their security obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website was regularly monitored for security threats.
claimsVsReality.reality: No periodic security reviews, vulnerability scans, or assessments were conducted post-deployment despite this being an established standard practice.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24(a) requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement reasonable security arrangements – used outdated website coding with critical vulnerabilities
violations: Failed to implement reasonable security arrangements – used outdated website coding with critical vulnerabilities
Failed to conduct regular periodic security reviews and vulnerability scans post-deployment
Failed to provide clear data protection specifications and requirements to IT vendors
Maintenance was ad-hoc and limited to troubleshooting functional issues rather than proactive security management
Did not exercise reasonable oversight over vendor performance regarding data protection requirements

outcome: The Commission found a breach of section 24(a) of the PDPA. Given the organisation's cooperation, voluntary admission, prompt remediation (immediate website suspension and engagement of new developer), and consideration that the compromised data was no longer accessible after RaidForums shutdown, the Commission issued a Compliance Order directing the organisation to: (1) submit a plan within 21 days to ensure regular patching, updates and upgrades for all software and firmware; (2) specify whether implementation will use external services or internal resources and provide detailed vendor job specifications; and (3) outline implementation steps with deadlines for completion within 60 days.
companyNow: Kingsforce Management Services continues to operate under compliance orders issued by Singapore's PDPA commission, with mandatory security improvements and regular patching requirements for all systems handling personal data.
dataType: Name, address, email address, telephone number, date of birth, job qualifications, salary information

companyDescription: Fortytwo Pte. Ltd. is an online furniture store operating in Singapore that processes customer personal data including email addresses, passwords, shipping/billing addresses, dates of birth, and credit card information.
companyLongDescription: Fortytwo Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce retailer specializing in online furniture sales. The company operates an e-commerce website built on the Magento open-source platform and collects personal data from customers including contact information, addresses, dates of birth, and payment card details. In December 2021, the company suffered a significant data breach due to inadequate cybersecurity practices and failure to maintain its software infrastructure.
caseDescription: Fortytwo, an online furniture store, suffered a malicious code injection attack on its website that exposed the email addresses and passwords of 6,241 individuals and credit card details of 98 individuals. The breach occurred because the company failed to apply critical security patches to its outdated Magento 1.9.x software and did not upgrade to a supported version despite ample notice from Adobe that support would end.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by not applying critical security patches and not upgrading to a supported software version, directly enabling malicious code injection and unauthorized access to personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Fortytwo failed to apply critical security patches to its Magento 1.9.x software and did not upgrade to a supported version despite Adobe's ample notice that support would end on 30 June 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unpatched software allowed attackers to inject malicious code that captured email addresses, passwords.

claimsVsReality.claim: The impact of the incident might be more limited as some users' names may be incomplete, fictitious or pseudonymous.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of data accuracy, Fortytwo collected and bore responsibility for protecting all 6,339 customers' personal data including verified email addresses and passwords.

claimsVsReality.claim: COVID-19 pandemic disrupted our planned upgrade from early 2020.
claimsVsReality.reality: Adobe had announced the end of Magento 1 support in November 2015 (extended to June 2020), giving Fortytwo ample notice from 2015 onwards to plan and execute upgrades before the pandemic began in early 2020.

claimsVsReality.claim: The four security patches we considered were routine updates.
claimsVsReality.reality: Adobe released these patches specifically to address high-severity risk issues and critical bugs including malicious code injection attacks—precisely the vulnerability that was exploited in the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to apply four critical security patches released by Adobe on 28 Nov 2017, 25 June 2019, 8 October 2019, and 28 April 2020
violations: Failed to apply four critical security patches released by Adobe on 28 Nov 2017, 25 June 2019, 8 October 2019, and 28 April 2020
Failed to upgrade from unsupported Magento version 1.9.x to supported version 2.0 after Adobe ended support on 30 June 2020
Failure to patch increased the risk of malicious code injection capable of capturing users' personal data
Inadequate security measures allowed threat actors to successfully exploit known vulnerabilities

outcome: The Organisation was found in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24(a). The Deputy Commissioner directed the Organisation to pay a financial penalty of S$8,000 within 30 days. The Organisation was also directed to: (1) complete the upgrading of its website to a supported software version, including vulnerability assessment and penetration testing, within 6 months; and (2) inform the Commission within 14 days of completion of the upgrade.
companyNow: Following the breach, Fortytwo undertook remedial actions including notifying affected customers and implementing technical security improvements. The company was directed to complete an upgrade to a supported Magento version within 6 months and was fined S$8,000.
dataType: Email addresses, passwords, names, credit card numbers, expiry dates, CVV/CVN numbers, shipping addresses, billing addresses, date of birth

companyDescription: OrangeTee & Tie is a Singapore-based real estate enterprise founded in 2000 that provides property transaction and agent services across Singapore.
companyLongDescription: OrangeTee & Tie is a Singapore real estate company that has operated since 2000, providing residential and commercial property services including sales, rentals, and agent representation. The company manages a significant customer base and employs hundreds of staff and thousands of licensed agents across Singapore. In August 2021, the company suffered a major data breach affecting its IT infrastructure when threat actors exploited security vulnerabilities in internet-facing web servers.
caseDescription: OrangeTee & Tie, a Singapore real estate company, suffered a data breach in August 2021 when threat actors exploited vulnerabilities in internet-facing web servers to access 11 databases containing personal data of 256,583 employees, customers, and agents. The company failed to conduct periodic security reviews, used unencrypted production data in less-secure development environments, and did not update outdated Microsoft SQL Server software, enabling SQL injection attacks that exfiltrated sensitive personal data.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data from unauthorized access, specifically: (1) using live production data in development environments without robust security assessments; (2) failing to conduct periodic security reviews that would have identified vulnerabilities from outdated software; and (3) not installing critical security patches for almost 4 years. These failures created unreasonable security risks that directly enabled the data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: OrangeTee & Tie stored unencrypted production data in internet-facing development servers and failed to conduct periodic security reviews.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees, customers, and real estate agents had their full national identity numbers, bank account numbers, and transaction details stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation's IT team relied on Microsoft's auto-scan function to manage security updates.
claimsVsReality.reality: Microsoft had ceased support for SQL Server 2012 in October 2018, and the Service Pack 3 running at the time of the breach was outdated; Service Pack 4 was never installed, leaving critical vulnerabilities unpatched for years.

claimsVsReality.claim: Using live production data in development environments was necessary for accurate testing computations and effective business process flow testing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The development servers were internet-facing and less secure than production environments, creating an unnecessary security risk; the Commission determined anonymised or synthetic data should have been used instead, or robust security assessments should have been conducted to protect the live data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The threat actor's claims of stealing 'hundreds of databases' were accurately reported.
claimsVsReality.reality: Forensic investigation confirmed the threat actor exfiltrated personal data from exactly eleven databases across both production and development servers, not hundreds as claimed in ransom demands.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organisation must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal, or similar risks to personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Used live production personal data in development environment without sufficiently robust security assessment processes
violations: Used live production personal data in development environment without sufficiently robust security assessment processes
Failed to conduct reasonable periodic security reviews of internet-facing servers connected to production databases
Relied solely on Microsoft auto-scan alerts for critical software patching instead of implementing robust patch management; failed to install Service Pack 4 available for almost 4 years

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD $37,000 payable within 30 days. The company was not issued further directions as it had already implemented comprehensive remedial measures including: isolating affected servers, updating security patches, testing for vulnerabilities, deploying enterprise-grade anti-malware, conducting security hardening, implementing web application firewall, separating public-facing website from internal portals, and liaising with forensic experts on recovery and IT security improvements.
companyNow: OrangeTee & Tie continues operations in Singapore's real estate sector following remediation of its IT security infrastructure after the 2021 incident. The company implemented enterprise-grade security measures, web application firewalls, and improved security protocols to prevent recurrence.
dataType: Name, national identity numbers (NRIC/FIN/passport), bank account numbers, property transaction amounts
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation (reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Tai Shin Fatt is an insurance director who managed a team of 25 insurance agents at a large insurance company in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Tai Shin Fatt held a director position at a major insurance company and oversaw 25 insurance agents. In 2021, he engaged call automation vendors and telephone number providers to improve marketing efficiency. He authorized the use of dictionary attack software to generate telephone numbers for automated marketing calls, resulting in a significant breach of Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: An insurance director used automated software with randomly generated telephone numbers (dictionary attack) to make 22,268 automated marketing calls in June 2021, including 433 calls to the SCDF emergency line. The Individual breached the PDPA Section 48B prohibition by using a dictionary attack to generate recipient telephone numbers without proper safeguards. The Individual cooperated with investigators and voluntarily ceased the calls upon discovering the breach.
violationSummary: The use of dictionary attack methodology to indiscriminately generate and target telephone numbers for automated unsolicited marketing calls constitutes surveillance-type information collection through automated means designed to reach a large volume of recipients without proper safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: An insurance director used automated software with randomly generated telephone numbers to make 22,268 automated marketing calls in June 2021, including 433 calls to the SCDF emergency line.
whyTheyWereWrong: The dictionary attack method exposed thousands of people to unsolicited robocalls and critically disrupted Singapore's emergency services by flooding the SCDF emergency line with 433 marketing.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Call Automation Vendor and Checker systems were designed to work together to avoid calling numbers on the Do Not Call Registry.
claimsVsReality.reality: The SCDF emergency line was not registered in the DNCR, so 433 calls reached the emergency line despite the intended safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Individual made efforts to comply with Do Not Call obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The dictionary attack method used to generate 18,809 telephone numbers with randomly created permutations deliberately bypassed normal acquisition of valid recipient numbers.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 48B(1) prohibits sending applicable messages to telephone numbers generated through dictionary attack or address-harvesting software
regulatoryFindings.description: Individual authorized generation of 18,809 telephone numbers using automated means in Microsoft Excel by combining common starting digits with randomly generated final 4 digits
violations: Individual authorized generation of 18,809 telephone numbers using automated means in Microsoft Excel by combining common starting digits with randomly generated final 4 digits
Individual caused 22,268 automated marketing calls to be made to these dictionary-attack-generated numbers
Calls were made from Singapore with Singapore link, meeting all elements of Section 48B Prohibition

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 48A(1) defines dictionary attack as obtaining telephone numbers using automated means that generates possible telephone numbers by combining numbers into numerous permutations
regulatoryFindings.description: The methodology used (common first 4 digits + random last 4 digits via Microsoft Excel) created 18,809 permutations matching the dictionary attack definition
violations: The methodology used (common first 4 digits + random last 4 digits via Microsoft Excel) created 18,809 permutations matching the dictionary attack definition

outcome: The Commission administered a warning to the Individual for breach of PDPA Section 48B(1). No further directions were imposed given the Individual's cooperation, lack of prior violations, efforts to comply with Do Not Call Registry obligations, and voluntary cessation of calls upon discovery of the breach.
dataType: Telephone numbers
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 48B(1) - prohibition on sending applicable messages to telephone numbers generated by dictionary attack
PDPA Section 48A(1) - definition of applicable telephone numbers and dictionary attack

companyDescription: Sembcorp Marine is a Singapore-based marine and offshore engineering company providing shipbuilding, ship repair, and offshore platform services. The company is a subsidiary of Sembcorp Industries.
companyLongDescription: Sembcorp Marine Ltd is a leading Asia-Pacific marine and offshore engineering group headquartered in Singapore. It specialises in shipbuilding, ship repair, and conversion services, as well as offshore rig and platform engineering. The company serves major clients in the oil and gas, marine transportation, and offshore energy sectors. Sembcorp Marine is a significant contributor to Singapore's maritime industry and operates multiple shipyards in Singapore and Indonesia.
caseDescription: Sembcorp Marine suffered a data breach in June 2022 when threat actors exploited Log4J zero-day vulnerabilities to gain unauthorised access to a server and exfiltrate personal data of 25,925 individuals. The organisation was infiltrated as early as January 2022 but took prompt action to patch vulnerabilities after learning of the Log4J flaw in December 2021. The Personal Data Protection Commission found the organisation had implemented reasonable security measures and made no enforcement action.
violationSummary: While a breach occurred, the organisation's reasonable security arrangements and prompt response to the Log4J vulnerability meant no violation of the Protection Obligation was found. The breach itself resulted from exploitation of a zero-day vulnerability that was difficult to anticipate.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Sembcorp Marine's server was compromised through Log4J zero-day vulnerabilities exploited by threat actors, leading to the exfiltration of personal data including names, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: The breach exposed sensitive personal information of thousands of individuals including financial details, national identification numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation implemented reasonable security measures and good cybersecurity practices including vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and cyber security monitoring.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, attackers exploited Log4J vulnerabilities present in their systems as early as January 2022, and the organisation only learned of the Log4J flaw in December 2021, leaving them vulnerable for weeks before patches could be applied.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation took prompt action to patch vulnerabilities after learning of the Log4J flaw in December 2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: Although the organisation began identifying Log4J instances on 14 December 2021 and applied patches when available, threat actors had already infiltrated the system on 4 January 2022, before many patches were released, and data was exfiltrated in June 2022.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA s. 24 – Protection of personal data: An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal data of 25,925 individuals was exfiltrated through exploitation of Log4J zero-day vulnerabilities
violations: Personal data of 25,925 individuals was exfiltrated through exploitation of Log4J zero-day vulnerabilities
Threat actor gained unauthorised access to a server and conducted reconnaissance and lateral movements before exfiltrating data

outcome: No enforcement action was taken. The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection determined that the Organisation had met its Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA by making reasonable security arrangements. The Organisation had adopted good ICT practices including cybersecurity testing, regular vulnerability assessments, penetration testing, and cyber security monitoring. The Organisation was recognised for its prompt response to the Log4J vulnerability, beginning identification of affected systems on 14 December 2021 and immediately applying security patches.
companyNow: Sembcorp Marine continues to operate as a major Southeast Asian marine and offshore engineering provider, though facing challenges in the energy transition. The company has been adapting its business to renewable energy and decarbonisation initiatives.
dataType: Name, address, email, NRIC number, telephone, passport number, photograph, date of birth, bank account details, salary, medical screening results

companyDescription: RedMart is a Singapore-based e-commerce company operating warehouses for storage and distribution of goods and produce sold through its platform.
companyLongDescription: RedMart Limited is an e-commerce retailer in Singapore that operates warehouse facilities for storing and distributing goods and produce. The company maintained two warehouses at CWT Distripark used to store inventory for its retail operations. RedMart serves as a marketplace connecting suppliers and consumers, with regular visits from delivery personnel and suppliers accessing its warehouse facilities.
caseDescription: RedMart collected photographs of supplier delivery personnel's physical identification documents (NRICs) at its warehouses without proper notice or legal basis. The company initially failed to inform visitors of the collection purpose and did not obtain valid consent. RedMart subsequently demonstrated compliance by conducting a legitimate interests assessment and implementing robust access controls to protect the collected data.
violationSummary: While the primary violation involved failure to provide notice and lack of valid legal basis for collection (breaching PDPA sections 13, 14(1)(a), 18(b), and 20), the core insecurity issue relates to RedMart's inadequate protection of highly sensitive identification data containing full NRIC numbers. The lack of notification and access controls prior to remediation constituted insecurity in handling personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: RedMart collected photographs of supplier delivery personnel's NRICs and identification documents at its warehouses without providing notice of the collection purpose or obtaining valid consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Delivery personnel were forced to provide photographs of their identification documents as a condition of warehouse access without being informed why their data was being collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Collection of ID Photographs was in the national interest to deter food security incidents.
claimsVsReality.reality: RedMart's food security concerns were limited to its own warehouses and did not rise to the level of national defence or national security contemplated by PDPA national interest exceptions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Collection was necessary to facilitate investigations into food security incidents.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Investigations Exception only applies to ongoing investigations, not to hypothetical future investigations that RedMart was attempting to prevent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Visitors provided deemed consent by voluntarily providing their IDs.
claimsVsReality.reality: Visitors had no choice in the matter—photographing IDs was a mandatory condition of warehouse access, and visitors were not informed that photographic images would be taken and stored.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 13 – Collection of personal data must be on a lawful basis (consent, legitimate interests exception, national interest exception, or investigations exception)
regulatoryFindings.description: RedMart collected ID photographs without obtaining valid consent from visitors
violations: RedMart collected ID photographs without obtaining valid consent from visitors
RedMart did not establish a proper lawful basis for collection prior to 8 July 2022

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 14(1)(a) and Section 18(b) read with Section 20 – Organisation must notify individuals of the purpose for collection of personal data before or when collecting
regulatoryFindings.description: Prior to the incident, RedMart failed to place notices at warehouse security checkpoints informing visitors of the purpose for collection of ID photographs
violations: Prior to the incident, RedMart failed to place notices at warehouse security checkpoints informing visitors of the purpose for collection of ID photographs
Visitors were not provided with reasonable access to information about the collection

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA First Schedule Part 3 Paragraph 1 – Legitimate Interests Exception allows collection without consent if organisation's interests outweigh adverse effects to individuals, with proper assessment and disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Prior to 8 July 2022, RedMart did not conduct or document a legitimate interests assessment before collecting ID photographs
violations: Prior to 8 July 2022, RedMart did not conduct or document a legitimate interests assessment before collecting ID photographs
RedMart did not identify and implement measures to mitigate adverse effects to visitors

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA First Schedule Part 2 Paragraph 2 – National Interest Exception applies only to national defence or national security concerns
regulatoryFindings.description: RedMart incorrectly claimed national interest exception based on food security concerns limited to its own warehouses, which do not constitute national defence or security
violations: RedMart incorrectly claimed national interest exception based on food security concerns limited to its own warehouses, which do not constitute national defence or security

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA First Schedule Part 3 Paragraph 3 – Investigations Exception requires collection be for purpose of ongoing investigation, not hypothetical future investigation
regulatoryFindings.description: RedMart incorrectly relied on investigations exception for purposes of deterring and investigating potential future food security incidents, not an ongoing investigation
violations: RedMart incorrectly relied on investigations exception for purposes of deterring and investigating potential future food security incidents, not an ongoing investigation

outcome: The Commission found RedMart in breach of the PDPA for collection of ID photographs prior to 8 July 2022. However, the Commission accepted RedMart's subsequent reliance on the Legitimate Interests Exception after the company conducted a comprehensive assessment (LIE Assessment) dated 22 July 2022. RedMart demonstrated compliance by: (1) limiting ID photograph collection to only visitors accessing high-risk food storage areas; (2) implementing restricted access controls to tablets and backend servers; (3) restricting data access to on-site DevOps team members on internal networks; (4) implementing immediate uploading to backend servers (not local storage); (5) setting maximum retention period of one year; and (6) providing visitor notification of the legitimate interests exception via posted notices. The Commission accepted the legitimacy of RedMart's interests in deterring food security incidents and recognized that the implemented security measures significantly reduced risks of unauthorized access, use, or disclosure.
companyNow: RedMart continues to operate as an e-commerce platform in Singapore, now operating with enhanced data protection compliance measures following the 2023 PDPA enforcement decision.
dataType: National identification numbers (NRIC), identification documents, photographic images of identity documents
legalBasisViolated: PDPA First Schedule Part 2 Paragraph 2 (National Interest Exception)
PDPA First Schedule Part 3 Paragraph 3 (Investigations Exception)

companyDescription: Join the Triboo Limited is a UK-registered company that operated online platforms including job recruitment websites. The company collected email addresses and contact details from job applicants and used them to send direct marketing emails on behalf of third-party 'business partners' and 'clients'.
companyLongDescription: Join the Triboo Limited is a UK-registered company that operated online platforms including job recruitment websites. The company collected email addresses and contact details from job applicants and used them to send direct marketing emails on behalf of third-party 'business partners' and 'clients'.
caseDescription: Join the Triboo Limited transmitted 107 million unsolicited direct marketing emails without valid consent between August 2019 and August 2020. The consent obtained was vague and non-specific, failing to clearly identify the sender or describe the types of marketing. The ICO found the company violated PECR Regulation 22 by sending unsolicited marketing emails without freely given, specific, and informed consent.
violationSummary: The company engaged in mass unsolicited direct marketing communication without valid prior consent from recipients, exploiting ambiguous consent mechanisms to target millions of individuals.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between August 2019 and August 2020, Join the Triboo Limited transmitted 107 million direct marketing emails to individual subscribers without obtaining valid consent compliant with PECR.
whyTheyWereWrong: 107 million subscribers received unsolicited marketing emails based on vague consent statements like 'I agree with marketing activity' that did not clearly identify which organizations would.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consent statements stated 'I agree with marketing activity' or referenced receipt of emails from 'selected companies'
claimsVsReality.reality: These statements were too vague to constitute valid consent; recipients could not identify which organisations would contact them or what types of marketing they would receive

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy policy referenced 'similar organisations', 'business partners', and 'clients' across 'any business sector'
claimsVsReality.reality: This was too generic and broad to inform individuals about specific senders, rendering consent non-specific and non-informed

claimsVsReality.claim: Consent was obtained from job website applicants
claimsVsReality.reality: Data was not collected during a sale or negotiation with JTT, so the 'soft opt-in' exemption under PECR Regulation 22(3) did not apply

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited communications for direct marketing by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of consent to such communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: JTT transmitted 107 million direct marketing emails without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
violations: JTT transmitted 107 million direct marketing emails without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
Consent statements were vague and generic, failing to specify the sender or types of marketing, violating the 'specific' and 'informed' requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 4(11) defines consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of agreement via affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent statements such as 'I agree with marketing activity' lack specificity regarding sender identity and marketing types.
violations: Consent statements such as 'I agree with marketing activity' lack specificity regarding sender identity and marketing types.
Consent was pre-packaged across multiple channels without separate granular consent options, violating the 'freely given' principle.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Recital 32 requires that when processing has multiple purposes, consent should be given for all of them.
regulatoryFindings.description: Single vague consent statements were used to authorize marketing on behalf of multiple 'business partners', 'clients', and organisations across 'any business sector' without separate consent for each purpose.
violations: Single vague consent statements were used to authorize marketing on behalf of multiple 'business partners', 'clients', and organisations across 'any business sector' without separate consent for each purpose.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Recital 42 requires that for consent to be informed, the data subject should be aware of the identity of the controller.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent statements referred to marketing by 'similar organisations', 'selected companies', and generic categories without identifying which specific entities would send marketing.
violations: Consent statements referred to marketing by 'similar organisations', 'selected companies', and generic categories without identifying which specific entities would send marketing.

outcome: The ICO issued an Enforcement Notice under section 40 of the Data Protection Act 1998 requiring JTT to cease unsolicited direct marketing via electronic mail unless recipients have previously notified JTT of clear and specific consent. JTT must comply within 30 days. The company has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days of the notice date (12 April 2023).
companyNow: Unknown. Join the Triboo Limited remains registered at Companies House (Registration No. 07152223) but current operational status is not disclosed in the document.
dataType: Email addresses, contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Recital 32 – multiple purposes require separate consent
GDPR Recital 42 – consent must be informed
GDPR Recital 43 – consent presumed not freely given without separate consent options

companyDescription: Nomad was a cryptocurrency cross-chain bridging platform founded circa 2021 that allowed users to transfer digital assets between different blockchain networks. The company raised $22 million in seed funding and positioned itself as a 'security-first' solution for interoperability.
companyLongDescription: Nomad was a cryptocurrency cross-chain bridging platform founded circa 2021 that allowed users to transfer digital assets between different blockchain networks. The company raised $22 million in seed funding and positioned itself as a 'security-first' solution for interoperability.
caseDescription: Nomad operated a cross-chain cryptocurrency bridge while making prominent security claims, but implemented inadequate software security practices including insufficient code testing, no circuit breakers, and no incident response plan. In August 2022, hackers exploited a vulnerability in their smart contracts and drained approximately $186 million in user assets; over $100 million in user losses resulted.
violationSummary: Nomad failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures for a financial services platform handling user assets worth hundreds of millions. The company's inadequate security practices directly led to a massive breach of user funds despite explicit security representations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
