outcome: F12 Management Ltd was issued an Enforcement Notice under Data Protection Act 1998 section 40 requiring compliance within 30 days. The notice requires F12 to: (1) cease making unsolicited calls to TPS-registered subscribers without valid consent; (2) cease calls to subscribers who previously objected; and (3) provide required caller identification (name and contact details) on all future direct marketing calls. F12 has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal within 28 days.
dataType: Telephone numbers, personal phone line registrations

companyDescription: Lin DaoWen Kenny is a self-employed financial advisor in Singapore who uses telemarketing to generate leads for financial advisory services.
companyLongDescription: Lin DaoWen Kenny is a self-employed financial advisor in Singapore who uses telemarketing to generate leads for financial advisory services.
caseDescription: A financial advisor generated 1,000 random telephone numbers using an Excel formula to generate leads and engaged a telemarketer to make unsolicited marketing calls. Of those numbers, 384 were registered on Singapore's Do Not Call Registry. The advisor failed to screen the numbers against the DNC Registry before making calls and could not demonstrate consent from recipients.
violationSummary: The individual used an automated tool to generate telephone numbers and systematically contacted individuals who had explicitly registered to avoid unsolicited telemarketing, constituting surveillance and unsolicited contact collection.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Generated 1,000 random Singapore telephone numbers using Excel's randbetween formula and engaged a telemarketer to make unsolicited marketing calls promoting financial advisory services.
whyTheyWereWrong: 384 of the recipients had explicitly registered their phone numbers on the No Voice Call Register to avoid telemarketing calls.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Individual claimed to have inadvertently overlooked screening the numbers on the Phone List on this occasion.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Individual admitted he failed to check if the telephone numbers were registered with the Do Not Call Registry before providing the Phone List to the telemarketer, and he was unable to provide evidence of obtaining consent from any of the 384 DNC-registered numbers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 43(1) of the PDPA requires that a person must not send a specified message to a Singapore telephone number unless the person has valid confirmation at the time of sending that the number is not listed in the relevant Do Not Call register.
regulatoryFindings.description: The Individual failed to check if the 384 telephone numbers were registered with the Do Not Call Registry before providing the phone list to the telemarketer and engaging marketing calls.
violations: The Individual failed to check if the 384 telephone numbers were registered with the Do Not Call Registry before providing the phone list to the telemarketer and engaging marketing calls.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 48B(1) of the PDPA prohibits a person from sending, causing to be sent, or authorising the sending of an applicable message generated through dictionary attacks or address-harvesting techniques.
regulatoryFindings.description: The Individual generated the 384 Singapore telephone numbers through an Excel spreadsheet formula (randbetween) designed to systematically generate numbers across a numerical spectrum, which constitutes a form of automated number generation similar to dictionary attacks.
violations: The Individual generated the 384 Singapore telephone numbers through an Excel spreadsheet formula (randbetween) designed to systematically generate numbers across a numerical spectrum, which constitutes a form of automated number generation similar to dictionary attacks.

outcome: The Individual negligently contravened sections 43(1) and 48B(1) of the PDPA. The Assistant Commissioner issued a warning to the Individual. In mitigation, the Individual had a previous compliance record of screening telephone numbers, immediately ceased the telemarketing calls upon discovery, and promptly purchased additional screening credits to ensure future compliance with DNC Provisions.
dataType: Telephone numbers

company: Hälso- och sjukvårdsnämnden i Region Dalarna
companyDescription: Region Dalarna (Dalarna Region Council) is a public healthcare authority responsible for providing healthcare services to residents of Dalarna County in central Sweden. It operates multiple clinics including pediatric, psychiatric, and specialized treatment centers.
companyLongDescription: Region Dalarna (Dalarna Region Council) is a public healthcare authority responsible for providing healthcare services to residents of Dalarna County in central Sweden. It operates multiple clinics including pediatric, psychiatric, and specialized treatment centers.
caseDescription: Region Dalarna's healthcare board sent medical appointment letters in window envelopes where sensitive health information—patient names, addresses, and specific clinic names—were fully visible to anyone handling the mail. The board failed to implement adequate technical and organizational safeguards for this sensitive data despite identifying the risk, violating GDPR Article 32 security requirements.
violationSummary: The board failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures (Article 32) proportionate to the high risk of processing sensitive health data, resulting in unauthorized exposure to third parties during physical mail distribution.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: From May 2021 to July 2022, Hälso- och sjukvårdsnämnden sent approximately 2,500 annual healthcare appointment letters in window envelopes that displayed patients' names, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Sensitive health information revealing that children and adolescents were patients at specialized psychiatric.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Dalarna claimed it had implemented safeguards by purchasing a 'masking service' that hides sender clinic information on envelopes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The masking service only worked for documents ≤5 A4 pages; larger appointment letters (the majority) continued using standard dual-window envelopes fully exposing clinic names and patient data for 14 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Dalarna stated sender clinic names should not appear on envelopes and that it had contracted for this protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: The actual service did not provide envelope masking for all appointment letter sizes, leaving sensitive health information visible to mail handlers and household members.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32.1 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a security level appropriate to the risk, considering the nature, scope, context, and purposes of processing, and the varying likelihood and severity of risks to individuals' rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Dalarna sent appointment letters in window envelopes where patient names, addresses, and specific healthcare clinic names (revealing health conditions) were fully visible to mail handlers and potential recipients of misdelivered mail.
violations: Region Dalarna sent appointment letters in window envelopes where patient names, addresses, and specific healthcare clinic names (revealing health conditions) were fully visible to mail handlers and potential recipients of misdelivered mail.
The board's 'masking service' was inadequate—it only applied to documents ≤5 A4 pages; larger letters continued using standard dual-window envelopes exposing sensitive data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5.2 (accountability principle) requires controllers to demonstrate compliance with principles in Article 5.1 and implement appropriate safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Dalarna failed to verify that its service provider's contractual solution actually protected all outgoing letters before deploying it at scale over 14 months.
violations: Region Dalarna failed to verify that its service provider's contractual solution actually protected all outgoing letters before deploying it at scale over 14 months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Articles 4.15 and 9 classify health data as sensitive personal data requiring heightened protection and prohibit processing except under specified lawful bases.
regulatoryFindings.description: Appointment letters to pediatric psychiatric and sleep disorder clinics for children aged 0–17 reveal sensitive health information that became exposed through inadequate envelope design.
violations: Appointment letters to pediatric psychiatric and sleep disorder clinics for children aged 0–17 reveal sensitive health information that became exposed through inadequate envelope design.

outcome: Region Dalarna was ordered to pay 200,000 SEK administrative penalty. The board must ensure all future appointment letters are sent in envelopes that completely conceal sender clinic information and patient health data from external view. By July 6, 2022, the board modified templates for three problem clinics to use dual-window envelopes with Region Dalarna's generic postadress (not clinic name) visible. IMY found no evidence the board conducted adequate risk assessment or verified service provider compliance before 14-month deployment.
companyNow: Region Dalarna is a Swedish regional health authority that continues operating healthcare services in Dalarna County. It has implemented envelope masking measures for appointment letters following this enforcement action.
dataType: health data, patient names, addresses, clinical department information
legalBasisViolated: Swedish Data Protection Act (2018:218) s.6 cap. 2

companyDescription: Epic Games, Inc. is an American video game and software company founded in 1991, best known for developing and publishing Fortnite, a free-to-play battle royale game with over 400 million registered users. The company also operates the Epic Games Store, a digital distribution platform for PC games.
companyLongDescription: Epic Games, Inc. is an American video game and software company founded in 1991, best known for developing and publishing Fortnite, a free-to-play battle royale game with over 400 million registered users. The company also operates the Epic Games Store, a digital distribution platform for PC games.
caseDescription: Epic Games charged millions of consumers and children for in-game purchases without express informed consent, using deceptive design patterns ('dark patterns') to obscure purchase mechanics. The company also denied consumers access to paid-for content when they disputed unauthorized charges with their credit card providers, effectively penalizing them for exercising their right to dispute fraudulent billing.
violationSummary: Epic's failure to obtain express informed consent before charging, combined with deliberate use of dark patterns to obscure consent mechanisms and obstruct refunds, constitutes a processing failure that left account holder payment data and purchasing decisions vulnerable to manipulation and unauthorized use.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Epic Games charged millions of consumers without express informed consent by saving payment cards by default.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents discovered their children had incurred hundreds to thousands of dollars in unauthorized in-game purchases; consumers lost permanent access to all paid-for content on banned accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: Fortnite is 'free' and consumers would see warnings about in-game purchases if they downloaded and played
claimsVsReality.reality: While the base game is free, in-game purchases required no parental consent or authorization, payment cards were saved by default without user awareness, and consumers were charged without express consent

claimsVsReality.claim: Users can easily undo or cancel unwanted charges through refund mechanisms
claimsVsReality.reality: The 'Undo' button was intentionally obscured, renamed to 'Cancel Purchase,' moved off-screen, made smaller, and hidden in Settings; consumers were limited to three lifetime refunds and faced barriers to accessing the refund path

claimsVsReality.claim: Account bans for chargebacks are necessary fraud prevention
claimsVsReality.reality: Epic permanently denied access to all paid-for content (sometimes worth hundreds or thousands of dollars) merely for disputing unauthorized charges, effectively punishing consumers for exercising legal chargeback rights

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees recommended safeguards to prevent accidental purchases and unauthorized kid charges
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite internal emails and recommendations (2018–2019) to add purchase confirmation, require CVV re-entry, and give users opt-out options, Epic delayed these changes for years until after FTC investigation began

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Epic charged account holders without obtaining express informed consent, in violation of Section 5(n) unfairness standard
violations: Epic charged account holders without obtaining express informed consent, in violation of Section 5(n) unfairness standard
Epic used dark patterns to obscure refund mechanisms and make cancellation difficult, deceiving consumers about their ability to reverse charges
Epic denied consumers access to paid-for content upon chargeback disputes, punishing legitimate fraud disputes

outcome: Epic Games agreed to a consent order requiring: (1) $245 million civil penalty; (2) mandatory express informed consent prior to all charges, including clear disclosure of billing terms; (3) prohibition on denying account access for chargebacks; (4) simple consent revocation mechanisms at least as easy as purchase mechanisms; (5) elimination of dark patterns in user interface; (6) comprehensive compliance reporting and monitoring for 10–20 years; (7) consumer redress fund. Epic must also provide customer information to enable FTC-administered refunds to affected account holders.
companyNow: Epic Games continues to operate as a major video game developer and publisher. The company operates the Epic Games Store and Fortnite remains one of the most popular free-to-play games globally, with over 400 million registered users. The company is privately held and valued in the billions.
dataType: Payment card information, account credentials, transaction history
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: A Hungarian debt collection company that acquires and manages loan claims, including those transferred by banks. The company engages in contact, settlement negotiation, and enforcement proceedings involving borrowers and guarantors.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian debt collection company that acquires and manages loan claims, including those transferred by banks. The company engages in contact, settlement negotiation, and enforcement proceedings involving borrowers and guarantors.
caseDescription: A Hungarian debt collection company illegally processed phone numbers of borrowers without lawful basis from 2018 onwards. The company treated contract performance as justification for call handling, but GDPR requires separate justified processing. The authority found the company violated transparency and legality principles by processing telephone data for debt collection without proper interest balancing.
violationSummary: The company processed sensitive contact data (phone numbers) without adequate legal basis or consent, failing accountability and transparency requirements under GDPR Art. 5(2) and 6(1).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Kérelmezett 2 retained and processed phone numbers of two loan guarantors for debt collection calls.
whyTheyWereWrong: The two guarantors received repeated collection calls and SMS messages to phone numbers they did not consent to share, causing harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Phone numbers are necessary for rapid, effective contact with borrowers to facilitate settlement agreements and avoid costly legal action.
claimsVsReality.reality: Postal addresses suffice for written contact, which the company also maintained. Borrowers had the legal right to choose written-only communication. No evidence that calls prevented litigation or materially improved collection outcomes more than mail.

claimsVsReality.claim: Phone number processing is required by Magyar Nemzeti Bank (MNB) supervisory recommendations for proactive loan restructuring.
claimsVsReality.reality: MNB Recommendation 2/2019 explicitly states it contains no data-protection requirements and does not authorize personal data processing. It calls for 'proactive' remediation but does not mandate telephony.

claimsVsReality.claim: Contract performance (GDPR Art. 6(1)(b)) justified phone-number processing from 2016 (engedményezés) through March 2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: Once a claim is assigned, the debt collector becomes the creditor; performance of the assignee's contract with the debtor does not encompass aggressive call-based collection. Art. 6(1)(b) does not extend to post-contractual dunning operations or calls to guarantors.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) requires data controllers to be accountable and demonstrate compliance with data protection principles (lawfulness, fairness, transparency).
regulatoryFindings.description: Kérelmezett 2 processed phone numbers without demonstrating lawful basis; cited contract-performance (Art. 6(1)(b)) until April 2021, then switched to legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f)) without interim disclosure.
violations: Kérelmezett 2 processed phone numbers without demonstrating lawful basis; cited contract-performance (Art. 6(1)(b)) until April 2021, then switched to legitimate interest (Art. 6(1)(f)) without interim disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) permits processing only where one of six grounds applies; legitimate interest requires prior interest-balancing test weighing data subject rights against controller interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Phone number processing lacked adequate interest balancing; company submitted general interest-balancing templates, not specific to phone numbers. Did not address data subjects' choice to receive only written contact. No evidence that business interest in rapid/direct calls outweighs borrowers' privacy and freedom from unwanted calls.
violations: Phone number processing lacked adequate interest balancing; company submitted general interest-balancing templates, not specific to phone numbers. Did not address data subjects' choice to receive only written contact. No evidence that business interest in rapid/direct calls outweighs borrowers' privacy and freedom from unwanted calls.

outcome: The National Data Protection Authority (NAIH) ordered Kérelmezett 2 to delete all phone number data from operational debt-collection records within 15 days of decision finality, permitting retention only on accounting documents under statutory (Art. 6(1)(c)) grounds. A restriction order suspended collection-focused phone processing pending compliance. A 1,000,000 HUF fine was imposed for the violations, with the company required to pay within 15 days or face enforcement execution. The decision is subject to judicial review at the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
companyNow: Unknown. The company is likely a debt collection or credit management firm operating in Hungary, subject now to the authority's compliance monitoring and public enforcement action.
dataType: Name, birth date, mother's name, ID number, mobile phone, landline phone, address, citizenship, bank account number

companyDescription: Chegg, Inc. is a Santa Clara-based education technology company that provides direct-to-student services including textbook rentals, online tutoring, writing assistance, math problem solving, and scholarship search services targeting high school and college students.
companyLongDescription: Chegg, Inc. is a Santa Clara-based education technology company that provides direct-to-student services including textbook rentals, online tutoring, writing assistance, math problem solving, and scholarship search services targeting high school and college students.
caseDescription: Chegg collected sensitive personal data from millions of students and employees but failed to implement basic security controls for nearly a decade. The company stored data in plain text, shared AWS root credentials with contractors, used deprecated password hashing, and lacked employee security training, resulting in at least four major breaches exposing approximately 40 million users' information and 700 employees' W-2 data.
violationSummary: Chegg's failure to implement reasonable and appropriate technical and organizational security measures—including encryption at rest, access controls, multi-factor authentication, and monitoring—directly resulted in unauthorized access to and exfiltration of highly sensitive personal information in multiple breaches.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Chegg failed to implement reasonable access controls, encryption, multi-factor authentication, or security monitoring for sensitive personal data stored in AWS S3 buckets from 2017 through 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 40 million users had their religious beliefs, sexual orientation, disabilities, financial details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Chegg takes commercially reasonable security measures to protect personal information submitted to us, both during transmission and once we receive it (March 2017–January 2020).
claimsVsReality.reality: Chegg stored personal information in plain text without encryption, shared unrestricted AWS root credentials with all employees and contractors, used deprecated MD5 password hashing until April 2018, lacked access controls based on job function, did not require multi-factor authentication, failed to rotate access keys, did not monitor systems for unauthorized exfiltration, and did not provide employee security training—enabling at least four major breaches exposing 40 million users' and 700 employees' data.

claimsVsReality.claim: We take steps to ensure that your information is treated securely and in accordance with this Privacy Policy (January 2020–present).
claimsVsReality.reality: Even after the April 2018 breach of 40 million users, Chegg continued to store consumer personal information in plain text in AWS S3 buckets and maintained other critical security failures, as evidenced by subsequent breaches in April 2019 and April 2020 affecting executive email and payroll systems respectively.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Chegg engaged in unfair data security practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers in the form of fraud, identity theft, monetary loss, and emotional distress—injuries not reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves.
violations: Chegg engaged in unfair data security practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers in the form of fraud, identity theft, monetary loss, and emotional distress—injuries not reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves.

Chegg made false or misleading representations in its privacy policy (March 2017–January 2020: 'Chegg takes commercially reasonable security measures'; January 2020–present: 'We take steps to ensure that your information is treated securely'), when in fact it did not implement reasonable measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access.

outcome: The FTC issued a Complaint against Chegg on January 25, 2023, alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act under two counts: unfair data security practices and data security misrepresentations. The complaint alleges that Chegg's lax security practices from 2017 onward—including failure to implement access controls, encryption, multi-factor authentication, security monitoring, and employee training—enabled multiple data breaches exposing ~40 million users' and 700 employees' sensitive personal information. No settlement or final order has been issued as of the complaint date; this represents the initiation of enforcement proceedings.
companyNow: Chegg remains an active publicly traded company (CHGG on NYSE) in the education technology sector, offering textbook rentals and online learning services to students. Following the FTC complaint in January 2023, the company faces potential compliance orders and ongoing regulatory scrutiny.
dataType: Names, email addresses, passwords, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, religious denomination, heritage, sexual orientation, disabilities, parents' income range, financial information, medical information, employee W-2 information, tutoring session videos with images and voices
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce
FTC Act Section 5 – Implied duty to maintain reasonable data security

companyDescription: A German bank providing credit card and financial services through automated digital application processes. The bank uses algorithmic decision-making systems for credit applications.
companyLongDescription: A German bank providing credit card and financial services through automated digital application processes. The bank uses algorithmic decision-making systems for credit applications.
caseDescription: A bank automatically rejected a customer's credit card application without providing transparent or understandable reasons. When the customer requested details, the bank refused to explain the specific factors, criteria, or data that led to the rejection, violating GDPR transparency requirements for automated decision-making.
violationSummary: The bank's automated decision-making process directly interfered with the customer's right to obtain credit, and the bank's refusal to provide transparent reasoning prevented the individual from understanding or challenging the decision that affected their ability to access financial services.
violations: Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: A bank rejected a customer's credit card application using an automated algorithm and refused to explain which specific data points and decision criteria led to the rejection.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer, who had a good credit score and stable high income, could not understand why he was denied or challenge the decision.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank's algorithm fairly and objectively evaluates creditworthiness based on defined criteria
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank refused to disclose which criteria, data, or logic actually determined the customer's rejection, indicating the decision was not properly explained or justified.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank provides customers information about automated decisions upon request
claimsVsReality.reality: When questioned, the bank provided only generic, case-unrelated information and explicitly refused to explain the specific reasons for the individual's rejection.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 22(3) requires that data subjects receive information about the existence of automated decision-making and have a right to obtain explanation of the decision.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank refused to provide meaningful explanation of which data, criteria, and factors led to the automated rejection decision in this specific case.
violations: Bank refused to provide meaningful explanation of which data, criteria, and factors led to the automated rejection decision in this specific case.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed transparently and in a manner intelligible to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank provided only generic, case-unrelated statements about its scoring procedure instead of transparent, specific information about the individual's decision.
violations: Bank provided only generic, case-unrelated statements about its scoring procedure instead of transparent, specific information about the individual's decision.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1)(h) grants data subjects the right to obtain information about the existence of automated decision-making and meaningful information about the logic involved.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank refused to inform customer of the specific logic, data basis, and decision factors that applied to their rejected application.
violations: Bank refused to inform customer of the specific logic, data basis, and decision factors that applied to their rejected application.

outcome: The Berlin Data Protection Authority (BlnBDI) issued a €300,000 fine. The bank acknowledged the violation, accepted the decision, has already implemented process changes, and committed to further improvements. The company cooperated fully with the investigation.
companyNow: The bank has cooperated with the regulator, acknowledged violations, and implemented process improvements to provide transparent explanations for automated credit decisions. Further enhancements are planned.
dataType: Financial data, Income, Employment, Personal identification, Credit scoring data

company: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust
companyDescription: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust is a large NHS healthcare provider serving the Bristol and Weston areas of England, operating multiple hospitals and providing comprehensive healthcare services.
companyLongDescription: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust is a large NHS healthcare provider serving the Bristol and Weston areas of England, operating multiple hospitals and providing comprehensive healthcare services.
caseDescription: The Trust terminated an Electronic Document Viewing System without ensuring patient records were safely migrated. A failed download resulted in 1,159 patient records becoming inaccessible from January 2020 to October 2021, with 115 pages permanently deleted. One patient's care planning was negatively impacted.
violationSummary: The Trust failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data during system decommissioning, resulting in accidental loss and destruction of patient records.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS terminated an Electronic Document Viewing System license without verifying the patient records download was complete.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,159 patients' medical records became inaccessible or permanently deleted, with 115 pages irretrievably lost, disrupting one patient's care planning.

claimsVsReality.claim: Patient records were safely downloaded prior to system licence expiry.
claimsVsReality.reality: The download was incomplete, 1,159 patient records became inaccessible, and 115 pages were permanently lost, but the failure was not investigated before licence expiry.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to ensure appropriate security during system decommissioning, resulting in inaccessibility of records for 1,155 data subjects from 19 January 2020 until 12 October 2021 and permanent deletion of partial records for 4 patients.
violations: Trust failed to ensure appropriate security during system decommissioning, resulting in inaccessibility of records for 1,155 data subjects from 19 January 2020 until 12 October 2021 and permanent deletion of partial records for 4 patients.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 24(1) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure processing complies with the Regulation, which shall be reviewed and updated.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust did not implement adequate oversight procedures or risk assessments before allowing the system licence to expire, and failed to investigate download anomalies.
violations: Trust did not implement adequate oversight procedures or risk assessments before allowing the system licence to expire, and failed to investigate download anomalies.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 24(2) requires implementation of appropriate data protection policies where proportionate to processing activities.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust had no decommissioning policy in place at the time of the breach, resulting in lack of proper procedural safeguards.
violations: Trust had no decommissioning policy in place at the time of the breach, resulting in lack of proper procedural safeguards.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand under Article 58 of the UK GDPR. The Trust was required to provide a progress update by 14 April 2023 regarding implementation of eight recommended remedial measures, including drafting and circulating a decommissioning policy, conducting risk assessments prior to system decommissioning, and ensuring data extraction completeness. The Trust has already implemented measures 7 and 8 (staff circulation of policies and regular risk assessment of case management systems). The matter is now closed.
companyNow: University Hospitals Bristol and Weston NHS Foundation Trust remains an active NHS healthcare provider in England. Following this enforcement action, the Trust has implemented new information asset management and decommissioning policies.
dataType: Patient medical records, health data
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 24(1) – Data Protection by Design
UK GDPR Article 24(2) – Data Protection Policies

companyDescription: Gloucester City Council is a local government authority responsible for providing public services to residents in Gloucester, England, including housing, benefits, social care, and other administrative functions.
companyLongDescription: Gloucester City Council is a local government authority responsible for providing public services to residents in Gloucester, England, including housing, benefits, social care, and other administrative functions.
caseDescription: Gloucester City Council suffered a ransomware attack that exposed personal data of residents. The council lacked adequate security logging, monitoring systems, and incident response procedures. Post-incident, the council failed to restore data access timely, identify affected individuals, and notify data subjects.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures (logging, monitoring, resilience, and testing) required to secure personal data processing under Article 32 of UK GDPR.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Gloucester City Council failed to implement centralized logging systems, protect logs from tampering, establish timely data recovery procedures.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents' personal data was exposed to compromise because the council could not detect the attack early, could not recover systems for weeks, deleted logs prevented investigation.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(b) of UK GDPR requires organisations to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Gloucester City Council did not have a centralised logging system or SIEM in place, significantly restricting ability to monitor and respond to security incidents and detect anomalous activities.
violations: Gloucester City Council did not have a centralised logging system or SIEM in place, significantly restricting ability to monitor and respond to security incidents and detect anomalous activities.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(c) of UK GDPR requires organisations to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to restore availability and access to personal data in a timely manner in the event of a physical or technical incident.
regulatoryFindings.description: Gloucester City Council did not restore access to personal data or systems in a timely manner following the ransomware attack. Backups existed but were not utilised in favour of a full system rebuild. Recovery process took significantly longer than necessary.
violations: Gloucester City Council did not restore access to personal data or systems in a timely manner following the ransomware attack. Backups existed but were not utilised in favour of a full system rebuild. Recovery process took significantly longer than necessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(d) of UK GDPR requires organisations to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures including a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Gloucester City Council did not have adequate incident response procedures, data classification documents, or regular security testing in place. Ad-hoc incident response and data analysis processes were used that proved insufficient for large-scale incidents.
violations: Gloucester City Council did not have adequate incident response procedures, data classification documents, or regular security testing in place. Ad-hoc incident response and data analysis processes were used that proved insufficient for large-scale incidents.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to Gloucester City Council under Article 58(2)(b) of UK GDPR. The Commissioner recommended three remedial actions: (1) ensure regular testing of technical and organisational measures with documented evaluation processes; (2) perform full review of backup and disaster recovery measures, including testing processes; (3) review records of processing and asset registers to enable rapid identification of impacted data in future incidents. The Commissioner welcomed post-incident remedial steps, particularly implementation of a SIEM and security hardening measures outlined in correspondence dated 14 March 2023. The matter is considered closed.
companyNow: Gloucester City Council continues to operate as a local government authority in England. Following the incident and ICO enforcement action, the council has implemented a SIEM system and undertaken security hardening measures.
dataType: Housing, benefits, personal identification, financial records, health data (inferred from council services)

companyDescription: F12 Management Ltd was a telemarketing company incorporated in February 2021, registered as 'Combined office administrative service activities' at Companies House. The sole director was Anna Allen. The company made unsolicited marketing calls primarily about white goods warranties and maintenance products, often targeting vulnerable individuals.
companyLongDescription: F12 Management Ltd was a telemarketing company incorporated in February 2021, registered as 'Combined office administrative service activities' at Companies House. The sole director was Anna Allen. The company made unsolicited marketing calls primarily about white goods warranties and maintenance products, often targeting vulnerable individuals.
caseDescription: F12 Management Ltd made over 1.3 million unsolicited direct marketing calls to individuals registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between August and December 2021. The calls were about white goods warranties and maintenance products, many made to vulnerable individuals. F12 failed to comply with PECR regulations requiring screening against the TPS register and providing caller identification.
violationSummary: F12 systematically made unsolicited calls to individuals who had registered with the TPS specifically to prevent such contact, constituting surveillance-like behaviour of telephony preferences and deliberate circumvention of consumer privacy protections.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: F12 Management Ltd made 1,346,019 unsolicited direct marketing calls between August and December 2021 to telephone numbers registered on the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 1.3 million people who had explicitly registered with TPS to stop unwanted marketing calls received abusive calls anyway, including vulnerable individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: F12 (through director Anna Allen) claimed they were in the process of dissolution and could not provide information requested by the ICO.
claimsVsReality.reality: F12 continued making over 500,000 calls to TPS-registered numbers after the dissolution claim, demonstrating the company was still operating. The strike-off application appeared to be an attempt to evade regulatory action.

claimsVsReality.claim: F12 claimed the company was not operational and records were not held.
claimsVsReality.reality: Call detail records showed F12 made 1,708,306 connected calls between 5 August and 20 December 2021, of which 1,346,019 (78.7%) were to TPS-registered numbers, proving active operations.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits making unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes to numbers listed on the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: F12 made 1,346,019 calls to TPS-registered numbers without valid opt-in consent between 5 August and 20 December 2021.
violations: F12 made 1,346,019 calls to TPS-registered numbers without valid opt-in consent between 5 August and 20 December 2021.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 24(2) requires that direct marketing calls must include the caller's name and either address or free callback number.
regulatoryFindings.description: F12 failed to clearly identify itself; callers used different company names, preventing recipients from identifying the caller and requesting suppression.
violations: F12 failed to clearly identify itself; callers used different company names, preventing recipients from identifying the caller and requesting suppression.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A(1) permits monetary penalties for serious contraventions of PECR where the contravention was deliberate or negligent.
regulatoryFindings.description: F12 deliberately or negligently contravened PECR; adopted tactics to avoid detection; failed to respond to TPS complaints or investigation requests; applied for voluntary strike-off to evade regulatory action.
violations: F12 deliberately or negligently contravened PECR; adopted tactics to avoid detection; failed to respond to TPS complaints or investigation requests; applied for voluntary strike-off to evade regulatory action.

outcome: F12 Management Ltd was issued a monetary penalty of £200,000 (reduced to £160,000 with early payment discount by 31 August 2023), payable by 1 September 2023. The penalty was issued under Section 55A of the Data Protection Act 1998 as applied to PECR cases. F12 has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The Commissioner found the contravention serious due to the volume of calls, breach of TPS protections, abusive nature of some calls, targeting of vulnerable individuals, and F12's evasion tactics including the strike-off application.
companyNow: F12 Management Ltd was in the process of voluntary dissolution/strike-off at the time of the investigation. The company deactivated its calling service in December 2021 due to non-payment and appears to be defunct.
dataType: Phone numbers, personal contact information

company: Mediahuis Ireland Limited / Mediahuis UK Limited
companyDescription: Mediahuis Ireland Limited, Mediahuis UK Limited, and related subsidiaries are European media publishers operating print and digital news publications across Ireland and the United Kingdom, including the Irish Independent, Sunday Independent, Belfast Telegraph, and regional titles.
companyLongDescription: Mediahuis Ireland Limited, Mediahuis UK Limited, and related subsidiaries are European media publishers operating print and digital news publications across Ireland and the United Kingdom, including the Irish Independent, Sunday Independent, Belfast Telegraph, and regional titles.
caseDescription: Mediahuis published contributor terms and conditions that impose unilateral restrictions on contributor rights, requiring perpetual licensing of content and imposing strict invoice deadlines with forfeiture of payment rights. The terms assert copyright ownership of commissioned photographs and contain broad indemnification clauses that shift tax and employment compliance liability to independent contractors.
violationSummary: The company unilaterally granted itself perpetual rights to reuse, syndicate, translate, and license contributor content indefinitely after an initial 12-month exclusivity period, with no additional compensation or ongoing consent mechanism.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Mediahuis Ireland Limited published Contributor Terms and Conditions requiring freelance writers.
whyTheyWereWrong: These terms exposed freelance contributors to permanent loss of control over their intellectual property.

claimsVsReality.claim: Contributors grant rights 'in consideration of the rights in the Contribution granted by you in accordance with these terms and conditions' and receive a stated Contribution Fee as full compensation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Contributors grant perpetual, worldwide, sub-licensable rights for all future formats and purposes, while the publisher reserves the right to exploit content indefinitely post-publication without additional compensation or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Contributors are engaged as 'independent contractors' responsible for their own tax and employment obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The publisher imposes indemnification obligations on contributors for tax claims, effectively treating them as quasi-employees while denying employee benefits and protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Contribution Fee constitutes 'full payment for the rights granted hereunder' with 'no further claim for compensation' under EU law.
claimsVsReality.reality: EU Directive 2019/790 Article 16 grants inalienable author's rights to fair compensation for broadcast/online exploitation; this waiver may be unenforceable.

regulatoryFindings.act: EU Directive (EU) 2019/790 Article 16 requires that authors retain the right to claim fair compensation when publishers use their works, and prohibits complete waiver of this right.
regulatoryFindings.description: Mediahuis required contributors to agree that 'the Contribution Fee is full payment for the rights granted hereunder and that no further claim for compensation shall be made by you under Article 16 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 or otherwise' (Clause 6.3), effectively stripping authors of statutory fair compensation rights.
violations: Mediahuis required contributors to agree that 'the Contribution Fee is full payment for the rights granted hereunder and that no further claim for compensation shall be made by you under Article 16 of Directive (EU) 2019/790 or otherwise' (Clause 6.3), effectively stripping authors of statutory fair compensation rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: Unfair Contract Terms legislation prohibits terms that create a significant imbalance in parties' rights and obligations, particularly in adhesion contracts with independent contractors in weaker bargaining positions.
regulatoryFindings.description: The T&Cs impose unilateral termination of payment rights for missed invoice deadlines (Clause 5), permanent copyright assignment for commissioned work (Clause 8.B), and perpetual exploitation rights with no ongoing compensation or consent mechanism.
violations: The T&Cs impose unilateral termination of payment rights for missed invoice deadlines (Clause 5), permanent copyright assignment for commissioned work (Clause 8.B), and perpetual exploitation rights with no ongoing compensation or consent mechanism.

regulatoryFindings.act: Employment and tax law prohibits employers/principals from unilaterally shifting income tax, PRSI, and social insurance liability to independent contractors without proper legal structure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Clause 6 requires contributors to 'indemnify and hold harmless the Group companies against any claims or demands' for tax and employment-related liabilities, improperly placing tax compliance burden on freelancers rather than the publisher.
violations: Clause 6 requires contributors to 'indemnify and hold harmless the Group companies against any claims or demands' for tax and employment-related liabilities, improperly placing tax compliance burden on freelancers rather than the publisher.

outcome: No enforcement action documented. Document is a published terms and conditions agreement effective 1 June 2023. The terms remain in force but may be subject to challenge under EU copyright law, unfair contract terms doctrine, and employment law principles.
companyNow: Mediahuis is a major pan-European media company with operations in Ireland, UK, and other markets, publishing major titles including the Irish Independent and Belfast Telegraph. Current operations continue under these T&Cs.
dataType: Contributor personal data, VAT numbers, tax information, payment details
legalBasisViolated: EU Directive 2019/790 Article 16 (Author's right to fair compensation)
GDPR Article 6 (Lawfulness of processing - unfair contract terms)
Copyright law - perpetual license without ongoing compensation

companyDescription: UK Direct Business Solutions Limited is a business energy consultancy that acts as an intermediary between energy suppliers and businesses. The company was incorporated on 4 September 2017 and is a subsidiary of UK Direct Business Solutions (Group) Limited.
companyLongDescription: UK Direct Business Solutions Limited is a business energy consultancy that acts as an intermediary between energy suppliers and businesses. The company was incorporated on 4 September 2017 and is a subsidiary of UK Direct Business Solutions (Group) Limited.
caseDescription: UKDBS made 410,369 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) between March 2020 and October 2021, contrary to PECR Regulation 21. Despite receiving 17 letters from TPS about complaints and being aware of TPS registration requirements, the company failed to implement adequate screening procedures. The ICO found the contravention was serious and negligent, resulting in 96 complaints from affected businesses.
violationSummary: UKDBS engaged in systematic, unsolicited collection of contact through direct marketing calls to individuals who had explicitly registered their desire not to receive such communications via TPS/CTPS.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between March 2020 and October 2021, UKDBS made 410,369 unsolicited direct marketing calls to phone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: 410,369 businesses received persistent, unwanted calls despite opting into the TPS do-not-call register, disrupting their operations during a pandemic.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed data from certain suppliers was 'TPS and CTPS checked at source before being provided'
claimsVsReality.reality: No invoices or documentation provided by suppliers referred to TPS/CTPS screening; only one email dated 19 January 2022 confirmed TPS checking, provided well after investigation began

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated they 'purchased call data' from legitimate data providers and had filtering mechanisms in place
claimsVsReality.reality: Staff were obtaining numbers from Google and other public domain sources without any screening; manual screening by compliance team was inconsistent and unclear after team restructure

claimsVsReality.claim: UKDBS representatives told complainants that 'TPS rules did not apply as details were in public domain'
claimsVsReality.reality: PECR Regulation 21 applies regardless of data source; TPS/CTPS registration overrides any public domain exemption under UK law

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed to operate 'an internal blacklist, run regular training with sales staff' with 'compliance with PECR discussed'
claimsVsReality.reality: No direct written references to PECR or TPS in training materials; procedures were ineffective as evidenced by 410,369 calls to TPS/CTPS numbers and 96 complaints

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits use of public electronic communications services for unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers listed in the TPS register without prior subscriber notification of willingness to receive such calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: UKDBS made 410,369 calls to TPS-registered numbers without valid prior opt-in notifications
violations: UKDBS made 410,369 calls to TPS-registered numbers without valid prior opt-in notifications
Calls made to CTPS-registered numbers (56,102) without subscriber consent
Calls made to TPS-registered numbers (354,267) without subscriber consent
Company did not obtain clear, positive notification from subscribers overriding TPS registration

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A allows the Commissioner to issue monetary penalties where there is a serious contravention of PECR and the person either deliberately contravened the regulation or knew/ought to have known of the risk and failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it.
regulatoryFindings.description: Serious contravention evidenced by 410,369 calls over 20-month period to registered numbers
violations: Serious contravention evidenced by 410,369 calls over 20-month period to registered numbers
Negligent failure: UKDBS was registered with ICO since June 2019 and should have known PECR requirements
Failed to take reasonable steps despite receiving 17 TPS notifications about complaints
No evidence of due diligence checks on data suppliers or contracts verifying TPS screening
Manual screening was unclear and not consistently applied; no automated safeguards in place

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(4) allows calls to TPS-registered numbers only if subscriber has notified the company they do not object to receiving such calls from that company specifically.
regulatoryFindings.description: UKDBS provided no evidence that any of the 410,369 called subscribers gave valid prior notification
violations: UKDBS provided no evidence that any of the 410,369 called subscribers gave valid prior notification
Company could not confirm data source for complained-about calls in their CRM system
Staff were using Google searches and public domain sources without screening

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £100,000 (reduced to £80,000 for early payment by 8 June 2023). Payment deadline is 9 June 2023 via BACS or cheque. UKDBS is required to implement automated TPS/CTPS screening in their CRM and conduct mandatory staff training on PECR compliance. The company acknowledged it would remove manual screening elements and automate the process. UKDBS has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days. The Commissioner will not enforce the penalty until all appeals are resolved and the payment deadline has passed.
companyNow: UK Direct Business Solutions Limited remains a registered company (Companies House 10943501) as of the notice date. The company committed to implementing automated TPS/CTPS screening and mandatory staff training programs to address compliance failures identified during investigation.
dataType: Business telephone numbers, contact information

companyDescription: Intellexa A.E. is a Greek software development company engaged in designing, developing and maintaining applications, networks, systems and technological solutions. The company has demonstrated involvement in developing surveillance software targeting mobile devices.
companyLongDescription: Intellexa A.E. is a Greek software development company engaged in designing, developing and maintaining applications, networks, systems and technological solutions. The company has demonstrated involvement in developing surveillance software targeting mobile devices.
caseDescription: Intellexa A.E., a software company developing surveillance spyware (Predator), failed to cooperate with Greek data protection authority during an investigation into the deployment of surveillance software on mobile devices. The company unjustifiably delayed providing requested information for over 40 days and selectively withheld critical financial and contractual documents despite being in their possession.
violationSummary: The company's failure to cooperate with supervisory authority prevented proper assessment of security and lawfulness of surveillance processing; failure also relates to processing of sensitive data without proper oversight.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Intellexa A.E. failed to cooperate with the Data Protection Authority by refusing to provide requested documents for over 40 days despite repeated requests.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's obstruction prevented regulators from investigating how its Predator spyware was deployed to secretly surveil Greek citizens' mobile phones without consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated it was in process of finalizing answers and would submit responses in beginning of following week (October 21, 2022 letter)
claimsVsReality.reality: Company did not submit responses until four weeks later on November 18, 2022, only after receiving formal hearing notice

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed information requested was already available and would be provided to DPA immediately from National Transparency Authority materials
claimsVsReality.reality: Company never provided the referenced materials; materials provided to other authority covered only limited timeframe and limited to public sector relationships

claimsVsReality.claim: Company represented it was cooperating with DPA and other Greek authorities and providing detailed information
claimsVsReality.reality: Company deliberately withheld invoices, financial records and contracts it admittedly possessed; cooperation only manifested after formal enforcement action

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 31 requires that data controllers and processors cooperate with supervisory authorities upon request for the exercise of the authority's duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Intellexa A.E. failed to provide information and documentation requested by DPA for over 40 days despite multiple reminders and authority requests
violations: Intellexa A.E. failed to provide information and documentation requested by DPA for over 40 days despite multiple reminders and authority requests
Company withheld invoices, receipts, financial statements, and contractual information known to be in its possession without justification
Company selectively referenced materials provided to a different authority (National Transparency Authority) instead of complying with DPA's independent investigation

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1) authorizes supervisory authorities to order controllers and processors to provide information required for exercising authority duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Intellexa A.E. failed to respond to formal information requests under Article 58 within reasonable timeframe
violations: Intellexa A.E. failed to respond to formal information requests under Article 58 within reasonable timeframe
Company only provided responses after receiving formal hearing notice, demonstrating deliberate non-compliance

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(4) establishes administrative penalties up to €10,000,000 or 2% of global annual turnover for violations of cooperation obligations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Unjustified delay and refusal to cooperate with supervisory authority investigating deployment of surveillance software on Greek citizens' mobile devices
violations: Unjustified delay and refusal to cooperate with supervisory authority investigating deployment of surveillance software on Greek citizens' mobile devices

outcome: DPA Decision 2/2023 (January 13, 2023) imposed €50,000 administrative fine on Intellexa A.E. for violating GDPR Article 31 cooperation obligations. Additionally, DPA issued binding order requiring immediate disclosure of: (1) all invoices and receipts from company inception to present; (2) all customer and supplier statements; (3) all materials submitted to National Transparency Authority; (4) all contracts relating to software development, customization or deployment with any entity including Intellexa BVI and Intellexa Ireland. Company must comply with disclosure order immediately. Investigation into surveillance spyware operations remains ongoing.
companyNow: Intellexa A.E. remains subject to ongoing DPA investigation into surveillance spyware operations. Company headquarters established in Chalandri, Athens. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Mobile device location data, communications metadata, keystroke data, biometric data, communications content
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 83(4) (Administrative fines for failure to cooperate)

companyDescription: GRS (Roadstone) Limited is an independent supplier of material to the construction industry operating across 41 sites in the UK with at least 800 employees. The company is predominantly a Business-to-Business operation but holds personal data on current and former employees.
companyLongDescription: GRS (Roadstone) Limited is an independent supplier of material to the construction industry operating across 41 sites in the UK with at least 800 employees. The company is predominantly a Business-to-Business operation but holds personal data on current and former employees.
caseDescription: GRS (Roadstone) Limited suffered a ransomware attack on 11 March 2022 that exposed personal data of 2,022 individuals due to inadequate security measures. The company failed to implement multi-factor authentication on a Remote Desktop Service and did not conduct regular vulnerability scanning, allowing a threat actor to exploit a known vulnerability and exfiltrate sensitive personal data including financial and medical information.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures (Article 32), specifically: absence of multi-factor authentication on internet-facing systems and lack of regular vulnerability testing. These failures created conditions for a successful ransomware attack and mass data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication on internet-facing Remote Desktop Service for over four years after acquiring S.
whyTheyWereWrong: A threat actor exploited a single compromised credential to infiltrate the network and steal personal data for 2,022 employees including National Insurance numbers, bank details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company had adequate security measures in place for data protection
claimsVsReality.reality: No multi-factor authentication on internet-facing Remote Desktop Service; no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing conducted; no formal Incident Response Plan existed

claimsVsReality.claim: Data Breach Policy referenced an appointed Data Protection Officer for breach handling
claimsVsReality.reality: GRS (Roadstone) Limited did not actually have an appointed Data Protection Officer at the time of the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) of the UK GDPR requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs of implementation, nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
regulatoryFindings.description: GRS (Roadstone) Limited failed to ensure the ongoing confidentiality of systems as required by Article 32(1)(b). Specifically, the company deployed a Remote Desktop Service without multi-factor authentication despite ICO guidance explicitly stating that single-factor authentication should not be used on internet-facing services that can lead to access to personal data. This vulnerability was left unpatched for over 4 years after the acquisition of the subsidiary that operated the service.
violations: GRS (Roadstone) Limited failed to ensure the ongoing confidentiality of systems as required by Article 32(1)(b). Specifically, the company deployed a Remote Desktop Service without multi-factor authentication despite ICO guidance explicitly stating that single-factor authentication should not be used on internet-facing services that can lead to access to personal data. This vulnerability was left unpatched for over 4 years after the acquisition of the subsidiary that operated the service.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(d) requires organisations to implement a process for regular testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: GRS (Roadstone) Limited conducted no formalised testing on their IT infrastructure prior to the incident, including no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing. The organisation operates across 41 sites in the UK, and given the size and scale, regular assessment was clearly necessary. A threat actor was able to exploit a documented Common Vulnerabilities and Exposure (CVE) published over 2 years before the incident. Had periodic vulnerability assessments been conducted, this threat would have been identified and mitigated.
violations: GRS (Roadstone) Limited conducted no formalised testing on their IT infrastructure prior to the incident, including no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing. The organisation operates across 41 sites in the UK, and given the size and scale, regular assessment was clearly necessary. A threat actor was able to exploit a documented Common Vulnerabilities and Exposure (CVE) published over 2 years before the incident. Had periodic vulnerability assessments been conducted, this threat would have been identified and mitigated.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand to GRS (Roadstone) Limited under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. While no monetary fine was imposed, the company was found in infringement of Articles 32(1), 32(1)(b), and 32(1)(d). GRS (Roadstone) Limited has since taken remedial actions including: deployment of vulnerability management tools, centralised logging, increased employee security awareness training, and significant expansion of multi-factor authentication across applications. The ICO recommended further actions: implementation, testing and periodic review of a formal Incident Response Plan; and clarification of breach handling procedures with clear documentation regarding who is responsible for managing data breaches (correcting references to a non-existent Data Protection Officer). The company also provided credit monitoring services and paid for replacement driving licences and passports for affected individuals.
companyNow: GRS (Roadstone) Limited continues to operate as an independent supplier of materials to the construction industry with at least 800 employees across 41 UK sites. Following the incident and ICO enforcement action, the company has implemented enhanced security infrastructure and practices.
dataType: Names, addresses, National Insurance numbers, passports, driving licences, birth/marriage certificates, bank details, dates of birth, HR records, medical information

companyDescription: Bank of Ireland Group plc is a major financial services organisation providing retail and commercial banking services across Ireland and internationally via online platforms including Banking365, a digital banking service offering account access, fund transfers, payments, and bill payment functionality to hundreds of thousands of customers.
companyLongDescription: Bank of Ireland Group plc is a major financial services organisation providing retail and commercial banking services across Ireland and internationally via online platforms including Banking365, a digital banking service offering account access, fund transfers, payments, and bill payment functionality to hundreds of thousands of customers.
caseDescription: Bank of Ireland failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures on its Banking365 platform, resulting in ten personal data breaches between January and May 2020. Six breaches were caused by staff failing to follow procedures correctly; four resulted from a flaw in the Customer Information System's account merging algorithm. Unauthorised persons gained access to customer accounts and viewed sensitive financial data.
violationSummary: Bank failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures required by Articles 5(1)(f) and 32 GDPR to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data processed via Banking365.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Bank of Ireland failed to implement adequate security measures on its Banking365 platform, allowing staff to manually grant account access without proper validation controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Ten customers had their sensitive financial transaction data and account details unauthorisedly accessed and disclosed to third parties, exposing them to risks of fraud and identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank stated 'there has never been an instance of fraud or identity theft arising from these types of events' and 'risk of fraud and/or identity theft is a potential harm'.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ten customers' accounts were compromised and unauthorised third parties gained access to sensitive financial transaction details, creating genuine fraud and identity theft risk regardless of whether realised harm occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank claimed it had adequate data protection policies and procedures in place and quality assurance frameworks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Procedures existed but were not followed; quality assurance testing (10% sampling of account merges) was insufficient; training did not adequately address risks; and internal audit identified the CIS flaw in 2019 but remediation took 21 months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank failed to implement robust validation procedures and quality assurance controls to prevent staff errors when manually populating user access fields on Banking365 platform.
violations: Bank failed to implement robust validation procedures and quality assurance controls to prevent staff errors when manually populating user access fields on Banking365 platform.
Bank did not implement adequate testing measures for account merging operations in Customer Information System, allowing a known 2019 coding flaw to persist unremediable for 21 months.
Training materials did not adequately emphasise importance of data protection procedures or detail risks of account merging and potential for unauthorised disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including pseudonymisation, encryption, ability to ensure confidentiality and integrity, ability to restore availability in timely manner, and processes for regularly testing and evaluating effectiveness of measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Monthly call monitoring sampled only one call per agent per month, insufficient oversight for high-risk manual data entry on widely-used platform.
violations: Monthly call monitoring sampled only one call per agent per month, insufficient oversight for high-risk manual data entry on widely-used platform.
Quality assurance procedures did not include additional controls to minimise human error in account access provisioning despite documented risks.
Security measures including proprietary fraud detection and SIEM system failed to identify over-merged accounts until late remediation in 2021, revealing inadequate ongoing effectiveness evaluation.

outcome: Bank of Ireland ordered to: (1) upgrade validation controls and implement quality assurance controls for data input within 90 days; (2) implement staff training on data protection and account merging risks within 90 days; (3) implement appropriate testing measures for coding errors within 90 days; (4) implement process ensuring coding errors affecting customer account access are remediated without delay within 90 days. Additionally, Bank received formal reprimand recognising serious nature of infringements. Bank required to submit compliance report within one month of notification. Administrative fine of €750,000 imposed.
companyNow: Bank of Ireland Group plc remains operational as one of Ireland's major financial institutions. The bank has since implemented enhanced data protection governance and account management systems in response to this enforcement decision.
dataType: financial data, account balances, transaction details, credit card information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) — Integrity and Confidentiality Principle

companyDescription: Argentum Data Solutions Limited is a UK-based telecommunications and SMS messaging services provider that offers bulk SMS transmission infrastructure to businesses for marketing campaigns.
companyLongDescription: Argentum Data Solutions Limited is a UK-based telecommunications and SMS messaging services provider that offers bulk SMS transmission infrastructure to businesses for marketing campaigns.
caseDescription: Argentum Data Solutions sent 2.33 million unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers between January 2021 and January 2022, the vast majority (2.3 million) through third parties using the company's lines. The company failed to obtain valid prior consent from recipients and did not identify the sender in any messages, violating PECR Regulations 22 and 23.
violationSummary: ADS collected and used subscriber contact information for direct marketing surveillance without obtaining freely given, specific, and informed consent as required by PECR Regulation 22. The company enabled mass unsolicited contact to individuals who had not explicitly agreed to receive such communications.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between January 2021 and January 2022, Argentum Data Solutions sent 24,309 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 2.3 million individuals received unwanted marketing messages they had never consented to, were unable to identify the sender.

claimsVsReality.claim: ADS claimed that 'legitimate interest' was the lawful basis for sending direct marketing SMS messages.
claimsVsReality.reality: PECR Regulation 22 explicitly requires prior consent from recipients for unsolicited direct marketing communications; legitimate interest is not a permissible alternative basis under PECR.

claimsVsReality.claim: ADS operates a compliant SMS platform for direct marketing.
claimsVsReality.reality: Of 2.33 million messages transmitted, 99% lacked valid recipient consent and violated PECR; sender identity was concealed in all messages, violating Regulation 23.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited direct marketing electronic communications unless the recipient has previously notified the sender that they consent to such communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: ADS sent 24,309 direct marketing SMS messages directly without valid prior consent from recipients
violations: ADS sent 24,309 direct marketing SMS messages directly without valid prior consent from recipients
ADS allowed third parties to send 2,306,114 direct marketing SMS messages via company lines without valid recipient consent
No evidence of valid consent was provided; ADS claimed 'legitimate interest' which is not a lawful basis under PECR Regulation 22

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 23(b) requires that direct marketing communications identify the person on whose behalf the communication is sent and provide a valid address where recipients can request cessation of communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: None of the SMS messages sent or transmitted by ADS identified the sender of the communication
violations: None of the SMS messages sent or transmitted by ADS identified the sender of the communication
Recipients were unable to determine who initiated the marketing message and therefore could not exercise their right to refuse

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 4(11) defines consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes by statement or clear affirmative action.
regulatoryFindings.description: ADS failed to demonstrate freely given consent (no evidence consent was not conditional on service receipt)
violations: ADS failed to demonstrate freely given consent (no evidence consent was not conditional on service receipt)
No evidence of specific consent to direct marketing from ADS or third parties
Consent could not have been informed as recipients did not know the identity of senders

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice requiring ADS to cease sending unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages without valid prior consent within 30 days. ADS is required to: (1) obtain clear and specific consent from recipients before sending or allowing others to send direct marketing communications; (2) identify the sender in all direct marketing emails; (3) provide valid addresses for unsubscribe requests; and (4) ensure communications comply with Electronic Commerce Regulations 2002. The case involves ongoing monitoring compliance. Right of appeal exists to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights).
companyNow: Argentum Data Solutions Limited remains registered at Companies House (Registration Number 08935427) as of the enforcement notice date. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Phone numbers (SMS recipients), subscriber contact information

company: Piraeus Leasing (Πειραιώς Leasing) / Piraeus Financial Leasing MAE (formerly CPB Leasing)
