The company deliberately failed to screen calls against the TPS register and did not respond to the ICO's investigation. The violation resulted in a £70,000 monetary penalty.
violationSummary: The company systematically made unsolicited calls to individuals who had explicitly registered their preference not to receive direct marketing calls, constituting a surveillance-like intrusion into consumer privacy through persistent unwanted contact.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: SGS Home Protect Limited made 24,241 unsolicited direct marketing calls between January and June 2021 to phone numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service.
whyTheyWereWrong: Vulnerable consumers, including an elderly 90-year-old man who had been scammed 35 times previously.

claimsVsReality.claim: SGS's marketing calls were legitimate unsolicited direct marketing communications
claimsVsReality.reality: 81% of calls were made to consumers who had explicitly registered with TPS to block such calls, indicating systematic non-compliance with legal requirements

claimsVsReality.claim: SGS had systems and procedures in place for PECR compliance
claimsVsReality.reality: SGS made 24,241 calls to TPS-registered numbers with no evidence of TPS screening procedures or compliance controls

claimsVsReality.claim: The calls targeted willing consumers
claimsVsReality.reality: One documented call targeted an elderly, vulnerable 90-year-old with serious memory loss who had been scammed 35 times previously; he was nearly defrauded again by the call

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1)(b) prohibits use or instigation of unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes where the called line number is listed on the TPS register.
regulatoryFindings.description: SGS made 24,241 calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with TPS for 28+ days without obtaining their prior written consent that they do not object to receiving such calls
violations: SGS made 24,241 calls to subscribers whose numbers were registered with TPS for 28+ days without obtaining their prior written consent that they do not object to receiving such calls
SGS failed to screen telephone numbers against the TPS register before making calls
SGS did not respond to ICO investigation requests, providing no evidence of subscriber consent

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 1998 Section 55A(1) permits monetary penalties where there is a serious contravention of PECR requirements and either the contravention was deliberate or the person knew or ought to have known of the risk but failed to take reasonable steps.
regulatoryFindings.description: SGS deliberately contravened PECR by making systematic calls to TPS-registered numbers without screening
violations: SGS deliberately contravened PECR by making systematic calls to TPS-registered numbers without screening
As a direct marketing business, SGS ought to have known of TPS requirements and published ICO guidance
SGS failed to take reasonable steps (TPS screening) to prevent the contravention despite knowledge of legal obligations

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £70,000 (reduced to £56,000 if paid by 31 August 2023). SGS was ordered to cease unlawful calling practices and implement TPS screening procedures. SGS has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal within 28 days. The penalty is recoverable by court order if not paid by 1 September 2023.
companyNow: SGS Home Protect Limited (formerly Finesta Limited) remains registered as a company but the enforcement action indicates serious compliance failures. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Telephone numbers, contact information

companyDescription: Daniel George Bentley operated as a sole trader direct marketer under the name Daniel George, registered with the ICO from December 2021 to November 2022. He engaged in SMS marketing campaigns targeting subscribers for the purposes of promoting financial products and services.
companyLongDescription: Daniel George Bentley operated as a sole trader direct marketer under the name Daniel George, registered with the ICO from December 2021 to November 2022. He engaged in SMS marketing campaigns targeting subscribers for the purposes of promoting financial products and services.
caseDescription: Daniel George Bentley sent over 2.26 million unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers without valid consent between May and October 2022. He admitted obtaining data indiscriminately through third parties and attempted to conceal his identity using hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards. The enforcement notice requires him to cease such activity and obtain clear, specific consent before any future marketing communications.
violationSummary: Bentley engaged in mass surveillance-scale collection and transmission of direct marketing communications to individual subscribers without consent, exploiting electronic communications channels to target large populations indiscriminately.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Between May and October 2022, sent 2,261,352 unsolicited direct marketing SMS messages to subscribers using data obtained indiscriminately from third parties.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 2 million individuals received unwanted marketing messages without their knowledge or consent, including financially vulnerable people targeted with loans.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bentley implied he was operating a legitimate direct marketing business with proper data acquisition.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bentley admitted he could not obtain sufficient legally-compliant data and resorted to sending SMS messages 'indiscriminately' using data obtained indirectly through third parties without valid consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The messages came from an identifiable sender with proper contact information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bentley used hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards and non-identifying websites to conceal his identity and prevent recipients from identifying the actual sender or requesting cessation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 22(2) prohibits transmission of unsolicited communications for direct marketing by electronic mail unless the recipient has previously notified the sender of their consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bentley transmitted 2,261,352 SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
violations: Bentley transmitted 2,261,352 SMS messages without obtaining valid prior consent from recipients.
He admitted obtaining data indiscriminately through third parties, which does not constitute the clear and specific consent required for electronic marketing.
Indirect consent obtained through third-party data sources is insufficient under PECR for SMS/electronic marketing.

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 23 prohibits direct marketing communications where the sender's identity is disguised or concealed, or where a valid address to refuse further communications is not provided.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bentley used hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal his identity as the sender.
violations: Bentley used hundreds of unregistered pre-pay SIM cards to conceal his identity as the sender.
He used websites that did not correctly identify the sender or instigator of the messages.
Recipients had no valid means of identifying who was sending the messages or where to request cessation.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 4(11) defines valid consent as freely given, specific, informed, and unambiguous indication of the data subject's wishes signifying agreement to processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent obtained indirectly through third parties was not freely given by the actual recipients.
violations: Consent obtained indirectly through third parties was not freely given by the actual recipients.
Consent was not specific—recipients had not agreed to receive marketing from Bentley specifically.
Consent was not informed—recipients did not understand they were consenting to SMS marketing from an unidentified sender.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued an Enforcement Notice under Data Protection Act 1998 s.40, requiring Daniel George Bentley to cease all unsolicited direct marketing communications by electronic mail within 30 days unless he obtains clear and specific prior consent from recipients. The notice further requires him to cease all direct marketing communications where his identity is disguised, no valid opt-out address is provided, or communications would violate the Electronic Commerce Regulations 2002. The recipient has the right to appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days of the notice date (5 December 2023).
dataType: Phone numbers (SMS contact details)

companyDescription: Greater Manchester Police (GMP) is the police service responsible for law enforcement across Greater Manchester, England. It operates multiple police stations including Pendleton Police Station and maintains custody suites, forensic services, and professional standards departments.
companyLongDescription: Greater Manchester Police (GMP) is the police service responsible for law enforcement across Greater Manchester, England. It operates multiple police stations including Pendleton Police Station and maintains custody suites, forensic services, and professional standards departments.
caseDescription: GMP failed to provide a detained individual's CCTV footage within the one-month subject access request deadline and lost two hours of footage due to inadequate quality checks and security measures when retaining data beyond the standard 90-day period. The force lacked documented procedures, clear responsibility assignments, and a required Data Protection Impact Assessment for CCTV processing.
violationSummary: GMP failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures to protect against accidental loss of CCTV data, resulting in the loss of two hours of footage. Additionally, the failure to provide complete data in response to a SAR within the statutory timeframe constitutes a separate breach of the right of access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Greater Manchester Police retained CCTV footage of a detainee held for 48 hours without implementing quality checks to verify data integrity.
whyTheyWereWrong: A detainee was unable to obtain their own personal data (CCTV recording from custody) within the legally required timeframe.

claimsVsReality.claim: GMP staff at Professional Standards Department believed data retention procedures were being followed and quality checks were conducted before the data subject's SAR.
claimsVsReality.reality: No quality checks were actually performed. Two hours of CCTV footage was lost because neither PPS nor PSD checked data integrity, each assuming the other had done so. The loss went undetected until May 2022, over a year after retention was authorized in April 2021.

claimsVsReality.claim: GMP had a data protection regime in place providing staff training during induction.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite the training regime, GMP's Custody Inspector did not receive data protection training because GMP failed to deploy appropriate administrative monitoring to ensure all staff actually received it.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 s.45(3)(a) and (b) requires that where a data subject requests access to their personal data, it must be provided in writing without undue delay and in any event before the end of the applicable time period (one month).
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP failed to provide the data subject with their complete CCTV footage within one month of the SAR request. After exemptions expired, GMP could not release all applicable data as two hours of footage had been lost due to inadequate retention procedures.
violations: GMP failed to provide the data subject with their complete CCTV footage within one month of the SAR request. After exemptions expired, GMP could not release all applicable data as two hours of footage had been lost due to inadequate retention procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Sixth Data Protection Principle requires that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, protecting against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: GMP failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to protect CCTV data from accidental loss. The CCTV system could only download footage in half-hour/one-hour segments without chronological ordering or backup error alerts. No quality checks were performed when data was retained beyond 90 days. The 2017 SOP was never updated or reviewed. No DPIA was conducted. Staff confusion about responsibility meant two hours of footage was lost undetected until May 2022.
violations: GMP failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to protect CCTV data from accidental loss. The CCTV system could only download footage in half-hour/one-hour segments without chronological ordering or backup error alerts. No quality checks were performed when data was retained beyond 90 days. The 2017 SOP was never updated or reviewed. No DPIA was conducted. Staff confusion about responsibility meant two hours of footage was lost undetected until May 2022.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to GMP under Schedule 13(2)(c) of DPA 2018. No monetary fine was imposed, taking into account mitigating factors (form 708G authorisation requirement in place, sealed evidence bag storage) and remedial steps undertaken by GMP. GMP has undertaken significant remediation including: system upgrade in 2023 with restricted access controls; centralized SAR administration within Information Access team; improved auditing with comprehensive officer access logs and timestamps; complete rewrite of SOP with annual review requirement; improved data protection training monitoring. The Commissioner issued non-binding recommendations for further compliance improvements including mandatory DPIA completion, enhanced staff training, and breach reporting procedures.
companyNow: Greater Manchester Police continues to operate as a major police force serving Greater Manchester, England. Following the reprimand, GMP has invested significantly in system upgrades and procedural improvements to ensure data protection compliance.
dataType: CCTV footage, biometric data (video recording of individual in custody)
legalBasisViolated: DPA 2018 s.45(3)(a) – provide information without undue delay
DPA 2018 s.45(3)(b) – provide information within one month
DPA 2018 Sixth Data Protection Principle – appropriate security of personal data

companyDescription: Telefónica Móviles España, S.A.U. is a major Spanish mobile telecommunications operator providing wireless services to millions of customers. As a large-scale processor of personal data, it manages customer identities, contact information, billing records, and service requests.
companyLongDescription: Telefónica Móviles España, S.A.U. is a major Spanish mobile telecommunications operator providing wireless services to millions of customers. As a large-scale processor of personal data, it manages customer identities, contact information, billing records, and service requests.
caseDescription: Telefónica issued a duplicate SIM card to an identity thief without verifying the requester's identity, enabling unauthorized access to the customer's phone, banking data, and personal accounts. The company failed to apply adequate identity verification procedures during SIM card replacement, breaching GDPR Article 6 (lawfulness of processing) by processing personal data without a valid legal basis.
violationSummary: Telefónica's failure to verify identity before issuing the SIM duplicate exposed the customer's personal data and enabled a third party to gain unauthorized access to sensitive information including banking credentials.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Issued a duplicate SIM card to an unauthorized third party without verifying the person's identity or obtaining the legitimate account holder's consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The fraudster used the duplicate SIM to intercept the victim's banking access, steal passwords and financial data, and execute unauthorized transfers that drained the victim's bank account.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica stated it has consolidated and adequate customer identity verification procedures that provide sufficient guarantees to identify SIM duplicate requesters.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to apply those procedures in this case, issuing a duplicate SIM to an identity thief without verifying the requester's identity, demonstrating that the procedures either did not exist or were not properly implemented.

claimsVsReality.claim: Telefónica claimed the fraud was perpetrated by an external attacker ('hacker') and that the company lacked responsibility.
claimsVsReality.reality: Telefónica bears responsibility for failing to implement adequate identity verification controls; the third party's ability to obtain the SIM depended entirely on Telefónica's negligent issuance process.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) provides that processing is lawful only if at least one lawful basis applies: consent, contract execution, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica processed the customer's personal data (phone number, SIM identifiers) for SIM card issuance without consent and without verifying the requester's identity, lacking any valid lawful basis.
violations: Telefónica processed the customer's personal data (phone number, SIM identifiers) for SIM card issuance without consent and without verifying the requester's identity, lacking any valid lawful basis.
The company failed to verify the identity of the person requesting the duplicate SIM, enabling an unauthorized third party to process the customer's personal data without any legal justification.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Telefónica failed to implement adequate security measures during SIM card issuance, specifically the identity verification procedures required to prevent unauthorized access.
violations: Telefónica failed to implement adequate security measures during SIM card issuance, specifically the identity verification procedures required to prevent unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires data controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company did not demonstrate that proper identity verification procedures were followed before issuing the duplicate SIM, indicating inadequate organizational measures.
violations: The company did not demonstrate that proper identity verification procedures were followed before issuing the duplicate SIM, indicating inadequate organizational measures.

outcome: Telefónica was fined €70,000 for violating GDPR Article 6(1) by processing personal data without lawful basis. The company failed to verify the identity of the person requesting a duplicate SIM card, enabling identity fraud. The agency found that Telefónica, as a professional data handler with extensive customer data processing obligations, was negligent in applying inadequate due diligence. The company previously blocked the fraudulent line and refunded the customer's SIM card fee. Telefónica indicated it would implement enhanced identity verification procedures, OTP authentication, and digital onboarding with biometric verification for sensitive operations. The resolution is final and enforceable.
companyNow: Telefónica Móviles España remains one of Spain's largest mobile operators. The company stated it is implementing enhanced security measures including OTP-based authentication and digital identity verification for sensitive operations.
dataType: Personal identifiers (phone number, SIM card identifiers), banking data, email addresses, passwords

companyDescription: London Borough of Lewisham is a local government authority in London responsible for delivering public services including housing, adult social care, highways, and other municipal functions. As a public authority, it is subject to FOIA obligations to provide information transparency to citizens.
companyLongDescription: London Borough of Lewisham is a local government authority in London responsible for delivering public services including housing, adult social care, highways, and other municipal functions. As a public authority, it is subject to FOIA obligations to provide information transparency to citizens.
caseDescription: London Borough of Lewisham systematically failed to respond to Freedom of Information requests within statutory 20 working day timeframes, leaving 338 requests overdue as of enforcement date, with 221 outstanding for over 12 months. The oldest request dated back to December 2020. The Council prioritised new requests over clearing its substantial backlog, breaching FOIA sections 1(1) and 10(1).
violationSummary: The failure to respond to FOI requests constitutes a breach of the public's right to access government-held information and accountability, though not 'confidentiality' in the traditional sense. Better categorized as an administrative/procedural failure under FOIA, but within Solove framework this maps closest to breach of duty to disclose.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Failed to respond to 338 overdue Freedom of Information requests within the required 20 working days, with 221 requests outstanding over 12 months old and the oldest dating to December 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens seeking critical information about Adult Social Care and Housing were left without responses for years.

claimsVsReality.claim: Council reported 73% compliance rate for responding to FOI requests within 20 working days (April-September 2022)
claimsVsReality.reality: Even at 73%, this meant 27% of requests were already overdue; corrected data (April-December 2022) revealed 338 total overdue requests, not the originally stated 100, with 221 over 12 months old

claimsVsReality.claim: Council's strategy was to focus resources on new requests to prevent backlog growth
claimsVsReality.reality: This strategy abandoned existing requestors for years; oldest request from December 2020 remained unanswered, effectively adding to backlog rather than clearing it

claimsVsReality.claim: Council put new management structure in place and agreed to recruit additional staff
claimsVsReality.reality: These measures came only after Commissioner's escalated inquiry (October-January 2022-2023) and were insufficient to address existing backlog within statutory timescales

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 1(1) FOIA requires public authorities to inform requestors in writing whether they hold information requested and, if so, communicate it to them.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council failed to provide written confirmation or communication for 338 overdue requests
violations: Council failed to provide written confirmation or communication for 338 overdue requests
Council did not comply with duty to respond to information requestors

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 10(1) FOIA requires public authorities to comply with section 1(1) promptly and in any event not later than the twentieth working day following receipt of a request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council responded to only 73% of requests within 20 working days (April-December 2022)
violations: Council responded to only 73% of requests within 20 working days (April-December 2022)
221 requests were outstanding for over 12 months
Oldest unanswered request submitted 3 December 2020, unresponded for over 2 years

outcome: Information Commissioner issued Enforcement Notice under FOIA Section 52 requiring Council to: (1) within 6 months, respond to all overdue requests (either provide information per section 1(1)(b) or issue valid refusal notice per section 17 FOIA), and (2) within 35 calendar days, devise and publish an action plan formalising measures to comply with statutory duties and clear backlog. Failure to comply may result in Commissioner certification to High Court for contempt of court proceedings. Council has right of appeal to First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 calendar days.
companyNow: London Borough of Lewisham is an operational London local authority. As of the enforcement date (March 2023), the Council acknowledged the problem and had implemented a new FOI management structure (December 2022) and agreed to recruit additional FOI team staff, indicating ongoing remediation efforts.
dataType: Government service requests; information potentially includes Adult Social Care, Housing, Highways data
legalBasisViolated: FOIA 2000 Section 1(1)(a) – duty to confirm holding of information
FOIA 2000 Section 1(1)(b) – duty to communicate information
FOIA 2000 Section 10(1) – duty to respond within 20 working days

companyDescription: Ice Telecommunications Ltd is a business-to-business telecommunications solutions provider incorporated in 2014 (originally as Talkfair Converged Solutions Ltd). The company operates a direct marketing calling operation targeting businesses to promote telecom services. It has three active directors: James Taylor (Managing Director), Stuart William Bonell, and Jamie Steven Ward.
companyLongDescription: Ice Telecommunications Ltd is a business-to-business telecommunications solutions provider incorporated in 2014 (originally as Talkfair Converged Solutions Ltd). The company operates a direct marketing calling operation targeting businesses to promote telecom services. It has three active directors: James Taylor (Managing Director), Stuart William Bonell, and Jamie Steven Ward.
caseDescription: Ice Telecommunications Ltd made 72,682 unsolicited direct marketing calls to subscribers registered with the Telephone Preference Service (TPS) and Corporate Telephone Preference Service (CTPS) between September 2021 and January 2022, violating PECR regulation 21. Despite receiving 23 complaints to TPS and 7 to the ICO, plus 19 warning letters from TPS, the company continued making contravening calls for months after the investigation began. The company failed to implement adequate due diligence on data providers and did not properly screen contact lists against TPS/CTPS registers.
violationSummary: The company systematically conducted unsolicited direct marketing calls (surveillance activity) to individuals who had explicitly registered their preference not to receive such calls, violating their explicit opt-out and privacy preference.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Ice Telecommunications made 72,682 unsolicited marketing calls to numbers registered with the Telephone Preference Service between September 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: 72,682 individuals who had explicitly registered to block marketing calls were repeatedly contacted anyway, including some who asked multiple times to be removed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ice Comms claimed they obtained marketing lists from [data broker] which were screened against TPS and CTPS
claimsVsReality.reality: While lists may have been screened by the broker, Ice Comms could not produce a contract or evidence of due diligence; some staff members independently sourced unscreened data from public websites like Yell.com, Thomson Local, and Google

claimsVsReality.claim: Ice Comms stated staff were 'fully trained with the knowledge that calling individuals and businesses registered with the TPS and CTPS was prohibited'
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite claimed training, a minority of staff breached policy by obtaining and using unscreened prospect data; the company had no written PECR policy and received 19 TPS warning letters and 30+ complaints that were not adequately acted upon

claimsVsReality.claim: Ice Comms claimed they 'take their responsibilities under PECR and data protection legislation seriously' and had implemented an 'internal suppression list'
claimsVsReality.reality: The company continued making 72,682 contravening calls over a 4.5-month period despite complaints, failed to respond to TPS warnings, and did not implement TPS screening service until January 2022—only after ICO investigation began

regulatoryFindings.act: PECR Regulation 21(1) requires that a person shall not use or instigate the use of a public electronic communications service for unsolicited calls for direct marketing purposes where the called line is that of a subscriber registered with TPS/CTPS.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ice Comms made 72,682 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with TPS/CTPS for more than 28 days prior to the calls
violations: Ice Comms made 72,682 unsolicited direct marketing calls to numbers registered with TPS/CTPS for more than 28 days prior to the calls
The company did not obtain explicit prior notification from subscribers that they did not object to receiving such calls as required by Regulation 21(4)
Company obtained marketing lists from data brokers without rigorous due diligence; some staff sourced unscreened data from public websites in violation of policy

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 55A DPA 1998 permits the ICO to issue monetary penalties where there is a serious contravention of PECR that was either deliberate or involved negligence (knowing or ought to know risk but failing to take reasonable steps).
regulatoryFindings.description: The contravention was serious—involving multiple breaches, 30 complaints during the violation period, and calls made to 72,682 subscribers
violations: The contravention was serious—involving multiple breaches, 30 complaints during the violation period, and calls made to 72,682 subscribers
Ice Comms knew or ought to have known of the risk: registered with ICO since 2015, received 19 letters from TPS, received direct complaints, and operates in direct marketing sector

Ice Comms failed to take reasonable steps: no written PECR policy, no verification of data broker screening, no proper investigation of TPS complaints, inadequate staff training and controls, delayed implementation of TPS screening service until January 2022

outcome: The ICO issued a monetary penalty of £80,000 (reducible to £64,000 with early payment by 8 June 2023). Ice Comms must comply with PECR going forward and has implemented screening procedures with a TPS service provider (effective 7 January 2022). The company must pay by 9 June 2023. Ice Comms has a right of appeal to the First-tier Tribunal (Information Rights) within 28 days, though exercising this right forfeits the early payment discount. Enforcement action will not be taken unless payment is not made after appeal periods expire.
companyNow: Ice Telecommunications Ltd remains operational. Following the investigation, the company implemented TPS screening procedures (effective 7 January 2022) and stated measures had been taken to prevent recurrence, though further complaints were received post-investigation period, suggesting continued compliance challenges.
dataType: Telephone numbers, business contact information

companyDescription: Alpha Bank is a major Greek financial services provider offering retail and corporate banking, investment services, and financial products. It is one of the four largest banks in Greece.
companyLongDescription: Alpha Bank is a major Greek financial services provider offering retail and corporate banking, investment services, and financial products. It is one of the four largest banks in Greece.
caseDescription: Alpha Bank failed to timely respond to a data subject's access request for CCTV footage and subsequently destroyed the requested data before fulfilling the request. The bank delayed its response by 13 days beyond the legal one-month deadline and then cited data retention policy expiration to refuse access, despite the data still being within the retention period when the request was made.
violationSummary: The bank's failure to preserve personal data after receiving an access request, and subsequent destruction of that data before fulfilling the request, constitutes a breach of data processing integrity and security obligations under GDPR Article 5(1)(f) and denial of access rights under Article 15.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Alpha Bank received a data subject access request for CCTV footage within its 45-day retention window, failed to respond within the required 30 days.
whyTheyWereWrong: The bank's delay and destruction of the requested footage prevented the requester from obtaining evidence of a fraudulent transaction affecting his business.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank claimed it responded to the request and satisfied its substantive scope by providing a written confirmation of the visit date and time, along with web banking access logs.
claimsVsReality.reality: A written confirmation is not a statutory equivalent to providing a copy of the requested personal data (CCTV footage). The data subject has a specific right to obtain the data itself, not just a summary or confirmation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank stated that high workload caused the delay and justified the late response by citing operational pressure.
claimsVsReality.reality: As a large financial institution processing vast amounts of personal data, the bank has an obligation to maintain adequate procedures and mechanisms to handle data subject requests within the legal timeframe regardless of workload.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank's retention policy permitting 45-day retention excused the later destruction of the data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Once an access request is submitted, the retention policy's automatic deletion schedule must be suspended to preserve the data until the request is fulfilled, even if the standard retention period expires in the interim.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) establishes that personal data must be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Alpha Bank destroyed CCTV footage after receiving an access request but before providing the data to the requester, rendering fulfillment impossible and violating the principle of lawfulness.
violations: Alpha Bank destroyed CCTV footage after receiving an access request but before providing the data to the requester, rendering fulfillment impossible and violating the principle of lawfulness.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) and (3) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing and receive a copy of personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Alpha Bank refused to provide the requested CCTV footage copy despite the data being within its 45-day retention policy when the request was submitted, denying the fundamental right of access.
violations: Alpha Bank refused to provide the requested CCTV footage copy despite the data being within its 45-day retention policy when the request was submitted, denying the fundamental right of access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to provide information on actions taken in response to rights requests without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt, with possible two-month extension if justified.
regulatoryFindings.description: Alpha Bank responded 13 days late (43 days instead of 30) and failed to notify the requester of the extension or reasons for delay, as required by the regulation.
violations: Alpha Bank responded 13 days late (43 days instead of 30) and failed to notify the requester of the extension or reasons for delay, as required by the regulation.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (Αρχή Προστασίας Δεδομένων Προσωπικού Χαρακτήρα) imposed a €10,000 administrative fine on Alpha Bank for violating Articles 5(1)(a), 6, 12(3), and 15(1)–(3) of the GDPR. The Authority found that the bank unlawfully destroyed CCTV data after receiving an access request and failed to timely respond or preserve the requested information. The decision emphasizes that once an access request is received while data is within the retention period, the controller must immediately take steps to prevent scheduled deletion and preserve the data until the request is fulfilled. This decision sets binding precedent that data destruction following a rights request constitutes a fundamental breach of processing lawfulness.
companyNow: Alpha Bank remains one of Greece's largest financial institutions and continues to operate under enhanced regulatory scrutiny following this and prior GDPR enforcement decisions (2014, 2018).
dataType: CCTV video footage, web banking access logs, financial transaction records
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Legal basis for processing
GDPR Art. 12(3) – Timely response to requests
GDPR Art. 15(3) – Provision of copy of data

companyDescription: Norfolk County Council is a local government authority in England responsible for providing public services including education, social care, highways, and other functions across Norfolk. As a public sector body, it is subject to UK GDPR compliance obligations for personal data processing.
companyLongDescription: Norfolk County Council is a local government authority in England responsible for providing public services including education, social care, highways, and other functions across Norfolk. As a public sector body, it is subject to UK GDPR compliance obligations for personal data processing.
caseDescription: Norfolk County Council failed to respond to 251 out of 511 Subject Access Requests (SARs) within the statutory one-month deadline (or three-month extension) during April 2021 to April 2022. The Council violated Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3) of the UK GDPR by failing to provide timely confirmation of data processing and access to personal data. While COVID-19 pandemic restrictions and subsequent remedial staffing measures were considered mitigating factors, the Commissioner issued a reprimand and required compliance improvements.
violationSummary: The Council systematically excluded data subjects from timely access to information about their data processing by failing to meet statutory deadlines, denying individuals prompt exercise of their rights.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Norfolk County Council failed to respond to 251 out of 511 Subject Access Requests within the statutory one-month deadline between April 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: 251 individuals experienced significant delays in exercising their fundamental right to access their personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Council had appropriate capacity to process Subject Access Requests in a timely manner
claimsVsReality.reality: The Council responded to only 260 out of 511 SARs (51%) within statutory deadlines, indicating capacity issues

claimsVsReality.claim: COVID-19 pandemic access restrictions were the primary cause of delay
claimsVsReality.reality: While COVID-19 contributed to backlog, the Council's failure to meet deadlines for nearly half of requests suggests systemic resource management issues beyond pandemic-related factors

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide information on action taken on data subject rights requests (Articles 15–22) without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two further months only where necessary, with notification of extension within one month.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council responded to only 260 of 511 SARs within the statutory one-month (or extended three-month) deadline
violations: Council responded to only 260 of 511 SARs within the statutory one-month (or extended three-month) deadline

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation from the controller whether personal data concerning them are being processed and, where applicable, access to the personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council failed to provide timely confirmation of data processing and access to personal data for 251 data subjects
violations: Council failed to provide timely confirmation of data processing and access to personal data for 251 data subjects

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires the controller to provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council's failure to respond to requests within statutory deadlines prevented data subjects from obtaining copies of their data
violations: Council's failure to respond to requests within statutory deadlines prevented data subjects from obtaining copies of their data

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to Norfolk County Council for infringements of Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3) of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner acknowledged mitigating factors including COVID-19 pandemic impacts on building access and manual record retrieval, and welcomed the Council's remedial measures including increased staffing dedicated to SAR processing and backlog closure. The Commissioner required the Council to provide details of actions taken to address three recommendations by 6 November 2023: (1) ensure SARs are responded to within statutory deadlines, (2) maintain adequate staff resources for SAR processing and continue monitoring, and (3) continue implementing effective measures to address the backlog.
companyNow: Norfolk County Council continues to operate as a local government authority in Norfolk, England. The Council has implemented remedial measures including increased staffing and a dedicated SAR response team to address identified compliance gaps.
dataType: Personal data (general); may include sensitive categories based on council functions

companyDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is a Canadian federal law enforcement agency responsible for border security, customs enforcement, and immigration control at all Canadian ports of entry.
companyLongDescription: The CBSA is a federal agency under the Canada Border Services Act that manages border security, customs operations, and immigration enforcement across Canada. It operates land, air, and marine border crossings and employs approximately 15,000 officers and staff. The agency collects and processes sensitive traveller data including licence plate information for security and intelligence purposes. The CBSA also contracts with third-party technology vendors to support its operations, including licence plate recognition system providers.
caseDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) contractor suffered a ransomware attack that compromised approximately 1.4 million licence plate image files collected at Canadian border crossings. Malicious actors accessed and copied files, with approximately 11,000 confirmed posted on the Dark Web. The CBSA's contract with the contractor lacked adequate security safeguards and privacy protection clauses for personal information.
violationSummary: The CBSA failed to implement adequate security measures and contractual safeguards to protect personal information (licence plate images with metadata) held by a third-party contractor. The breach resulted from inadequate security standards, lack of data retention limits, and absence of cybersecurity requirements in the contract.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The CBSA contracted with a third-party vendor to process licence plate images at border crossings, but failed to include adequate security safeguards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Travellers crossing Canadian borders had their licence plate images, metadata including crossing times and locations, and vehicle details exposed to malicious actors.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only 9,000 licence plate images were compromised in the breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: The actual number was 1,385,198 licence plate image files on the contractor's systems were accessed and compromised; approximately 11,000 were confirmed posted on the Dark Web.

claimsVsReality.claim: Licence plate information does not constitute personal information as defined under the Privacy Act because it only identifies the vehicle, not the driver or passengers.
claimsVsReality.reality: In context, licence plate images combined with metadata (crossing time, location, lane number, province/state, and vehicle make/model) constitute personal information capable of identifying individuals and their border crossing patterns.

claimsVsReality.claim: The contract with the third-party contractor had appropriate security measures in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The contract lacked clauses with respect to security safeguards and protection of personal information; the breach occurred through an unpatched decommissioned server.

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach posed no security vulnerabilities to CBSA systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information of 1.4 million travellers was compromised and partially released on the Dark Web, exposing border crossing patterns and vehicle information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Personal information is information about an identifiable individual recorded in any form
regulatoryFindings.description: CBSA initially failed to recognize licence plate image files with metadata (jurisdiction, characters, date, time, border crossing location) as personal information
violations: CBSA initially failed to recognize licence plate image files with metadata (jurisdiction, characters, date, time, border crossing location) as personal information
Licence plate images revealed vehicle ownership and travel patterns (time, date, location of border crossing), allowing identification of registered owners

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Personal information can only be disclosed with individual consent or under permitted disclosure categories
regulatoryFindings.description: Approximately 1.4 million licence plate images were inappropriately accessed by malicious actors
violations: Approximately 1.4 million licence plate images were inappropriately accessed by malicious actors
Approximately 11,000 images were confirmed disclosed on the Dark Web without consent or authorized disclosure purpose

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act general obligation – Institutions must ensure adequate safeguards for personal information under their control, including when held by contractors
regulatoryFindings.description: Contract lacked specific clauses regarding protection of personal information and cybersecurity standards
violations: Contract lacked specific clauses regarding protection of personal information and cybersecurity standards
No compliance visits were conducted to verify security measures
Contract did not specify adequate data retention periods (CBSA's standard is six years plus current year; contractor retained images for contract duration, resulting in 11-year-old data on systems)
Images were transmitted over open internet without dedicated VPN tunnel
Contractor used freeware FTP software instead of enterprise-level solutions

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the complaint well-founded and resolved. The CBSA accepted all recommendations to: (1) fully review and amend its contract with the contractor to clearly identify licence plate images as personal information and include appropriate safeguards for storage, use, access, and destruction; (2) seek guarantees that data retained beyond three months is destroyed; (3) conduct audits ensuring CBSA assets are managed per contract terms; and (4) implement a dedicated VPN tunnel and enterprise-level secure file transfer protocols. The CBSA committed to implementing these recommendations in its upcoming Request for Proposal and future contracts. The contract was amended in February 2020 to include cybersecurity compliance requirements and a three-month data retention limit.
companyNow: The CBSA remains Canada's primary border security and customs enforcement agency. Following this incident, the agency strengthened its contractual privacy requirements and data security practices with vendors.
dataType: Licence plate images, vehicle metadata (jurisdiction, plate characters, date, time, border crossing location, lane number)
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 3 (definition of personal information)
Privacy Act general obligation to protect personal information from unauthorized disclosure

companyDescription: The Department of National Defence (DND) is Canada's federal military and defence agency, responsible for national defence operations and military personnel management.
companyLongDescription: The Department of National Defence is a major Canadian federal government institution that operates Canada's military and manages defence policy, operations, and personnel. As a government employer, DND is subject to the Privacy Act and must protect personal information of employees and complainants in workplace investigations. DND operates across multiple locations and manages thousands of military and civilian personnel, making workplace safety and confidentiality critical to its operations.
caseDescription: The Department of National Defence disclosed the identity of a workplace violence complainant to a second investigator conducting a separate administrative investigation into the complainant's conduct, despite the complainant's consent form limiting disclosure to parties directly involved in investigating and resolving the original complaint. DND violated the Privacy Act by using the complainant's personal information for a purpose inconsistent with the original collection purpose, failing the 'reasonable expectation' test for consistent use.
violationSummary: DND disclosed personal information (complainant identity and investigation report) to parties and for purposes beyond what the individual reasonably expected based on the written consent form and regulatory framework. The disclosure to a second investigator for disciplinary proceedings against the complainant was not a sufficiently direct connection to the original purpose of investigating the complainant's own violence complaint.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: DND disclosed a workplace violence complainant's identity and investigation report to a second investigator conducting a separate administrative investigation into the complainant's own conduct,.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant reasonably expected their identity would remain confidential for resolving their own complaint, but DND used it against them in a separate disciplinary investigation.

claimsVsReality.claim: DND claimed the disclosure to the administrative investigator was a 'consistent use' permissible under the Privacy Act because it was necessary to address allegations raised against the complainant during the WPV investigation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The disclosure was not a consistent use because a reasonable person would not expect information collected to investigate their own complaint would later be used as evidence in disciplinary proceedings against them.

claimsVsReality.claim: DND argued that the consent form did not expressly preclude sharing the complainant's identity with other parties for purposes outside the original WPV investigation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The consent form gave the complainant a clear impression of broad confidentiality protection, limited only to specific parties listed for the purpose of investigating and resolving their own complaint, not other unrelated investigations.

claimsVsReality.claim: DND claimed that using the complainant's information to assess the need for disciplinary action was consistent with the original purpose of collecting the information for workplace violence investigation.
claimsVsReality.reality: A complainant in a workplace violence process would not reasonably expect their own disclosure to be used as evidence against them in a separate administrative investigation into their conduct.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act, Section 8(2)(a) — permits disclosure without consent where for the purpose information was obtained or for a use consistent with that purpose
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed workplace violence complaint report and complainant identity to investigator conducting separate administrative investigation into complainant's conduct
violations: Disclosed workplace violence complaint report and complainant identity to investigator conducting separate administrative investigation into complainant's conduct
This use was not sufficiently directly connected to original purpose (investigating complainant's violence complaint) such that individual would reasonably expect it
Violated reasonable expectation standard established in jurisprudence and Treasury Board guidance

regulatoryFindings.act: COHSR Part XX, Section 20.9(3) and 20.9(5)(b) — require employer consent for identity disclosure to specific parties for WPV investigation
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent form limited disclosure to specified parties (competent person, health and safety committees, respondent, witnesses) for purpose of investigating and resolving the complaint
violations: Consent form limited disclosure to specified parties (competent person, health and safety committees, respondent, witnesses) for purpose of investigating and resolving the complaint
Disclosed to labour relations and administrative investigator, neither of whom were listed on consent form
Disclosure to administrative investigator exceeded scope of consent granted

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Directive on Privacy Practices, Section 6.2.9 — individuals must be notified at time of collection of any uses or disclosures consistent with original purpose
regulatoryFindings.description: DND provided only the consent form as written material explaining handling of personal information in WPV process
violations: DND provided only the consent form as written material explaining handling of personal information in WPV process
Did not notify complainant of potential uses such as disciplinary proceedings or labour relations review
Inconsistency between notice provided and actual uses

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded and conditionally resolved. DND committed to implement corrective actions within nine months: (1) ensure disclosures as 'consistent uses' do not fall outside participants' reasonable expectations based on DND-provided information; (2) review and modify all products and tools used in WPV processes to implement these protections consistently; (3) submit revised products and tools to the OPC for review before finalization. DND also committed to comply with Treasury Board Directive requirements to notify participants of potential uses and disclosures, and to update Personal Information Bank statements to include any new consistent uses arising from the revised Workplace Harassment and Violence Prevention Regulations (effective January 1, 2021).
companyNow: DND continues to operate as Canada's primary defence institution. Following this case, DND committed to implementing corrective actions to better align confidentiality communications with actual disclosure practices in workplace investigations.
dataType: Identity, workplace violence complaint details, investigation report, allegations of misconduct
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act, Section 8(2)(a) (disclosure for purpose obtained or consistent use)
Canada Occupational Health and Safety Regulations (COHSR), Part XX, Section 20.9(3) and 20.9(5)(b) (consent requirements for identity disclosure)
Treasury Board Directive on Privacy Practices, Section 6.2.9 (notification of consistent uses)
Privacy Act, Section 11(1)(a)(iv) (Personal Information Bank statements of consistent uses)

companyDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is a federal law enforcement and border management agency responsible for border security, immigration, and customs enforcement in Canada.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency is a federal institution operating under the Department of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness. It enforces Canada's immigration and customs laws, manages border security, and processes travellers and goods at ports of entry. As a government agency, CBSA is subject to the Canadian Privacy Act and Access to Information Act, which govern how it collects, uses, and discloses personal information.
caseDescription: Canada Border Services Agency disclosed sensitive labour relations and workplace investigation materials to the Information Commissioner in support of a request to decline responding to an individual's access to information requests. The disclosure included a Review Report concerning workplace harassment and violence that was originally collected for an entirely different purpose, violating the Privacy Act's requirements for 'consistent use' disclosure.
violationSummary: CBSA disclosed personal information originally collected for workplace conflict management to the Information Commissioner for an unrelated purpose (declining to act on access requests). The disclosure lacked sufficient connection to the original purpose of collection, and an individual would not reasonably expect their sensitive labour relations information to be used in this manner.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: CBSA disclosed a Review Report containing sensitive workplace harassment and violence investigation materials to the Information Commissioner without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: A former CBSA employee's personal information about harassment and workplace violence was disclosed to justify declining their access requests.

claimsVsReality.claim: CBSA claimed the disclosure of the Review Report was a 'consistent use' because information was originally collected in the context of workplace conflict and the disclosure related to determining how to handle the complainant's request for personal information about that conflict.
claimsVsReality.reality: The original purpose of collecting the Review Report was addressing workplace violence and harassment, which is substantially distinct from the purpose of seeking Information Commissioner approval to decline access requests under the Access to Information Act. The complainant could not reasonably have expected workplace investigation materials to be disclosed to support arguments about whether to respond to their access requests.

claimsVsReality.claim: CBSA argued that disclosure was necessary and only 'as much personal information as necessary' was provided to give the Information Commissioner sufficient information to make an informed decision.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under the Privacy Act, the test for permissible disclosure is not whether an institution believes disclosure was necessary, but whether disclosure for that purpose is sufficiently directly related to the original purpose of collection such that an individual would reasonably expect it. CBSA's necessity argument did not override the fundamental privacy protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: CBSA contended that the ATIP Office had obtained the information for the purpose of responding to the complainant's access request, making the disclosure to the Information Commissioner consistent with that subsequent purpose.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Act makes clear that it is the original purpose for which information was obtained or compiled by the institution that matters for determining consistent use, not the purpose for which any individual unit within the institution subsequently collected or handled the information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(2)(a) requires that disclosure without consent be for the purpose for which the information was obtained or for a use consistent with that purpose, with a sufficiently direct connection such that an individual would reasonably expect it
regulatoryFindings.description: CBSA disclosed a Review Report concerning workplace harassment and violence to the Information Commissioner, which was originally collected for addressing workplace conflict—a substantially distinct purpose from deciding whether to decline an access request under section 6.1 of the ATIA
violations: CBSA disclosed a Review Report concerning workplace harassment and violence to the Information Commissioner, which was originally collected for addressing workplace conflict—a substantially distinct purpose from deciding whether to decline an access request under section 6.1 of the ATIA

CBSA failed to limit disclosure to only information collected in the course of administering access requests, instead including sensitive labour relations material unrelated to the access request process

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the disclosure of the Review Report to be in contravention of Section 8 of the Privacy Act. The Commissioner recommended that CBSA develop guidance within nine months to establish a clear process for assessing the merit of proposed consistent use disclosures to other government institutions. CBSA disagreed with the finding and refused to implement the recommendation. The matter remains unresolved, and the OPC called on CBSA to reconsider and demonstrate implementation of the recommendation within 9 months.
companyNow: CBSA remains the primary border and immigration enforcement agency for Canada, continuing its mandate under federal authority.
dataType: Labour relations material, workplace investigation reports, personal information related to harassment and workplace violence, access request details

companyDescription: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is a Canadian government department responsible for immigration, refugee, and citizenship matters. It administers Canada's immigration programs and processes asylum and sponsorship applications.
companyLongDescription: IRCC is a federal government department within the Government of Canada tasked with managing immigration, refugee resettlement, and citizenship programs. It processes applications, administers special immigration measures during crises, and provides support services to individuals seeking to immigrate to or obtain citizenship in Canada. During the Afghanistan crisis of 2021, IRCC established dedicated support mailboxes and special facilitative measures to assist Afghan nationals and individuals with ties to Afghanistan seeking emergency assistance and refuge.
caseDescription: IRCC sent four mass emails to 636 individuals seeking Afghan emergency assistance with recipient email addresses in the 'TO' field instead of 'BCC', inadvertently disclosing all recipients' identities to each other. The breach revealed that individuals—some potentially still in Afghanistan—had contacted the government seeking refuge from Taliban persecution, creating serious safety risks. The disclosure violated section 8 of the Privacy Act due to lack of consent and permissible purpose.
violationSummary: The company exposed personal information (email addresses, photographs, and sensitive context about refugee status) to a large, unintended audience through mass email misconfiguration. This is a classic exposure scenario where sensitive data became accessible to unknown third parties without authorization or consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: IRCC sent four mass emails to 636 individuals seeking Afghan emergency assistance with recipient email addresses in the 'TO' field instead of 'BCC'.
whyTheyWereWrong: The disclosure exposed individuals potentially still in Afghanistan who feared Taliban persecution to public identification, creating serious threats to their safety.

claimsVsReality.claim: IRCC had procedures in place to protect sensitive personal information when communicating with vulnerable individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: IRCC had no oversight, monitoring procedures, or robust administrative controls to prevent accidental disclosure of inherently sensitive information during mass email communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: A simple employee error using the 'TO' field instead of 'BCC' would not result in a serious breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: The error exposed 636 individuals—some potentially in Taliban-controlled territory—to identification and created tangible risks of persecution, harm, and death.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1): Personal information can only be disclosed with consent or under specified permissible purposes in subsection 8(2)
regulatoryFindings.description: IRCC disclosed 636 individuals' email addresses, thumbnail photos, and sensitive refugee status information to unintended recipients without consent
violations: IRCC disclosed 636 individuals' email addresses, thumbnail photos, and sensitive refugee status information to unintended recipients without consent
The disclosure had no permissible purpose under section 8(2) as it was purely accidental
Information was disclosed to large unknown group, increasing risk of misuse

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act implied obligation: Institutions must take reasonable measures appropriate to information sensitivity to prevent unauthorized disclosures
regulatoryFindings.description: IRCC had insufficient procedural controls and no oversight when sending mass emails containing highly sensitive information
violations: IRCC had insufficient procedural controls and no oversight when sending mass emails containing highly sensitive information
Job Aid procedures lacked verification steps, compliance monitoring, or recipient limits
No internal detection mechanism; breach only discovered when external recipients reported it
Employees lacked adequate training on risks of mass email disclosure to sensitive populations

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.1.2 and Treasury Board Guidelines for Privacy Breaches Section 4: Institutions must establish breach management plans and notify affected individuals as soon as possible
regulatoryFindings.description: While IRCC's mitigation response was adequate (4-day notification), the breach itself demonstrated inadequate preventive measures
violations: While IRCC's mitigation response was adequate (4-day notification), the breach itself demonstrated inadequate preventive measures

outcome: IRCC acknowledged the contravention of section 8 of the Privacy Act and the complaint was found well-founded and conditionally resolved. IRCC implemented corrective measures including: revised mass email procedures with manager verification ('two pairs of eyes rule'), limitation to 25 recipients per email, new secure webform for Afghanistan inquiries, mandatory privacy training for relevant staff, software solutions to prevent misdirected emails, Privacy Policy Suite development, updated Privacy Breach Guidelines distinguishing sensitive information categories, and new employee training tools. IRCC committed to providing an update on technological measures by March 3, 2023, and subsequently confirmed full implementation of all recommendations. The matter was closed based on satisfaction with IRCC's corrective actions.
companyNow: IRCC continues to operate as a federal government department managing Canada's immigration and refugee programs, with an expanded focus on crisis response and enhanced privacy protection measures following the 2021 Afghanistan email breach incident.
dataType: Email addresses, thumbnail photographs, immigration status information, location data (Afghanistan), personal inquiry details
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 8(1) - Disclosure without consent or permissible purpose
Privacy Act Section 8(2) - No applicable exemption for accidental disclosures
Treasury Board Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.1.2 - Obligation to establish privacy breach management plan
Treasury Board Guidelines for Privacy Breaches Section 4 - Requirement to notify affected individuals

companyDescription: Biron Health Group is a Canadian healthcare company that conducts COVID-19 testing services at Montreal Trudeau Airport and other locations.
companyLongDescription: Biron Health Group is a Canadian healthcare organization operating testing and diagnostic services. During the COVID-19 pandemic, the company was contracted by the Montreal Trudeau Airport to conduct mandatory testing for international travellers entering Canada. The company collected personal information including email addresses as part of its testing operations, which it subsequently used for marketing purposes.
caseDescription: Biron Health Group collected email addresses from travellers undergoing mandatory COVID-19 testing at Montreal airport and subsequently used those addresses to send unsolicited promotional emails without consent. The company initially claimed implicit consent based on an assumed business relationship, but the OPC found this unreasonable given travellers had no choice in selecting Biron as the service provider.
violationSummary: Biron collected personal information (email and health data) for the specific purpose of conducting COVID-19 tests and communicating test results, but then used that information for a secondary purpose (marketing promotions) without proper consent. This is a classic secondary use violation where sensitive health information was repurposed for commercial gain.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Biron Health Group collected email addresses from international travellers undergoing mandatory COVID-19 testing at Montreal airport.
whyTheyWereWrong: Travellers had no choice in selecting Biron as their testing provider and provided email addresses solely to receive test results.

claimsVsReality.claim: Biron claimed it had established an implicit business relationship with travellers that justified sending them promotional emails.
claimsVsReality.reality: Travellers had no choice in selecting Biron (it was the only provider at the airport), provided information solely for COVID-19 testing and results delivery, and would not reasonably expect marketing for unrelated services.

claimsVsReality.claim: Biron assumed travellers consented to receive promotional emails about its services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Individuals required to undergo mandatory COVID-19 testing at the border do not expect their health information to be used for promotional purposes by the testing provider.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2.3 – Organizations must limit use, disclosure and retention of personal information to the purposes for which it was collected
regulatoryFindings.description: Biron collected email addresses and health data solely for COVID-19 testing and result delivery but subsequently used the email addresses for promotional marketing without consent
violations: Biron collected email addresses and health data solely for COVID-19 testing and result delivery but subsequently used the email addresses for promotional marketing without consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Organizations must obtain consent before using personal information for purposes unrelated to the original collection
regulatoryFindings.description: Biron assumed 'implicit consent' for marketing based on an alleged business relationship, but travellers had no choice in selecting Biron and would not reasonably expect their data to be used for secondary promotional purposes
violations: Biron assumed 'implicit consent' for marketing based on an alleged business relationship, but travellers had no choice in selecting Biron and would not reasonably expect their data to be used for secondary promotional purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 1.2 – Organizations must be accountable for personal information in their possession and must implement safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Biron failed to consider the sensitive nature of health information and the coercive context (mandatory government-mandated testing) before using the data for marketing
violations: Biron failed to consider the sensitive nature of health information and the coercive context (mandatory government-mandated testing) before using the data for marketing

outcome: Biron ceased sending promotional emails to non-client travellers arriving in Canada and deleted the email addresses of affected travellers from its marketing database. The complaint was settled during the course of the investigation with the complainant satisfied by Biron's corrective actions.
companyNow: Biron Health Group continues to operate healthcare testing services in Canada, having ceased the problematic promotional email practice.
dataType: Email address, health data (COVID-19 test results)
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA – Principle 2.3 (Use, disclosure and retention of personal information must be limited to the purposes for which it was collected, unless consent is obtained)
PIPEDA – Principle 4.3 (Before using personal information for a new purpose, organizations must obtain consent unless the new purpose is obviously related)

companyDescription: Tim Hortons is a Canadian multinational fast casual restaurant chain and coffee company, owned by Restaurant Brands International, operating thousands of locations across Canada and internationally.
companyLongDescription: Tim Hortons is Canada's largest quick-service restaurant chain, founded in 1964 and now a subsidiary of Restaurant Brands International (RBI), which also owns Burger King and Popeyes. The company operates over 5,000 locations globally, primarily in Canada, and is known for its coffee, donuts, and breakfast offerings. In 2022, it faced significant privacy enforcement action regarding location tracking through its mobile application.
caseDescription: Tim Hortons collected granular GPS location data through its mobile app from May 2019 to August 2020, tracking users' locations every few minutes even when the app was closed. The company stated it would use this data for targeted advertising but never actually did so. Users were misled through permission requests and FAQs that falsely stated location collection occurred only when the app was open, and were not informed of the continuous, pervasive nature of the tracking.
violationSummary: Tim Hortons engaged in large-scale, continuous surveillance of users' precise physical locations without legitimate business purpose, collecting location data as frequently as every few minutes from devices carrying the app, regardless of whether the app was in active use. This systematic monitoring of users' movements constitutes surveillance under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Tim Hortons collected granular GPS location data from its mobile app users every few minutes between May 2019.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 1.6 million users had their precise movements tracked continuously without meaningful consent, exposing their home locations, workplaces, travel patterns.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tim Hortons stated it would only collect location information when the app was open
claimsVsReality.reality: The app collected location data continuously every few minutes even when closed, with one user tracked 2,700+ times in less than 5 months

claimsVsReality.claim: Location data would be used for targeted advertising to promote coffee and products
claimsVsReality.reality: Tim Hortons never actually used the collected data for targeted advertising; it used data only in aggregated form for limited analytics after shifting priorities

claimsVsReality.claim: Users granted permission for location collection based on permission requests and FAQs
claimsVsReality.reality: Permission requests and FAQs contained materially misleading statements that did not accurately reflect the continuous, extensive nature of tracking

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 5(3) / PIPA sections on appropriate purpose
regulatoryFindings.description: Tim Hortons collected vast amounts of granular location data for stated purpose of targeted advertising but never used the data for that purpose
violations: Tim Hortons collected vast amounts of granular location data for stated purpose of targeted advertising but never used the data for that purpose
Collection was not proportional to stated business needs; the overwhelming majority of data collected when app was closed
No legitimate need to collect sensitive location information that was never used for its identified purpose

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 and section 6.1 / PIPA consent requirements
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to inform iOS users that location collection would occur when app was closed
violations: Failed to inform iOS users that location collection would occur when app was closed
Made false and misleading statements in Android permission requests and FAQs stating location collection occurred 'only when app was open'
Failed to communicate consequences of consent – that location would be collected every few minutes, every day, everywhere users traveled
Consent obtained via false or misleading information, rendering any consent invalid

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.3 / PIPA sections on third-party processor accountability
regulatoryFindings.description: Contractual clause 4.3 with Radar was vague and permissive, allowing processor could use data for its own purposes or disclose de-identified data in connection with its business
violations: Contractual clause 4.3 with Radar was vague and permissive, allowing processor could use data for its own purposes or disclose de-identified data in connection with its business
Lacked clear definitions and unambiguous limitations on use and disclosure
Failed to provide adequate contractual protections proportional to sensitivity and volume of location data

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA and PIPA requirements for privacy management and accountability
regulatoryFindings.description: No documentary evidence of privacy impact assessments prior to app launch or when collection practices changed
violations: No documentary evidence of privacy impact assessments prior to app launch or when collection practices changed
Permission requests materially different across mobile platforms and inconsistent with actual app operation
Continued collecting vast amounts of sensitive data for 13+ months after deciding not to use it for stated purpose, without privacy reassessment
