outcome: Tim Hortons agreed to: (1) permanently cease collection of granular location data for targeted advertising (completed August 2020); (2) delete all collected Radar Location Data and derived data within one month after lifting litigation holds, and direct third-party service providers to do the same; (3) establish and maintain a privacy management program for the Tim Hortons app and future apps, including privacy impact assessments and ensuring consistency between privacy communications and actual practices; (4) provide written confirmation of deletions and quarterly written updates on privacy program implementation for 12 months. The OPC and provincial authorities will monitor compliance over the 12-month period following the final report.
companyNow: Tim Hortons continues to operate as a major coffee and quick-service restaurant chain under RBI ownership, but has implemented enhanced privacy controls and privacy management programs following the 2022 enforcement action.
dataType: GPS location data, precise longitude and latitude coordinates, inferred home address, inferred workplace address, travel patterns, competitor visit tracking, timestamps
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 and section 6.1 – consent requirements
Quebec Act Respecting the Protection of Personal Information sections 5, 8, 10, 12, 13, 14

companyDescription: Rogers Communications Inc. is one of Canada's largest federally regulated telecommunications companies providing internet, television, telephone, and wireless services to millions of Canadians.
companyLongDescription: Rogers Communications Inc. is a major Canadian telecommunications provider headquartered in Toronto. The company offers wireless, internet, television, and telephone services across Canada. In 2018, Rogers launched Voice ID, a biometric authentication program designed to improve account security and reduce fraud. The program used passive voice recognition technology that collected voiceprints in the background of customer service calls without active customer participation.
caseDescription: Rogers enrolled customers in its Voice ID biometric authentication program without obtaining valid express consent. The company collected voiceprints through a passive 'tuning' process during calls based only on an automated message, and failed to provide clear opt-out mechanisms. Rogers also retained voiceprints of customers who opted out without any legitimate purpose.
violationSummary: The passive voiceprinting system collected biometric data without individuals' knowledge or clear consent, operating in the background of calls. This constitutes surveillance-based collection of sensitive biometric information under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Rogers enrolled customers in its Voice ID biometric voiceprint program by passively collecting voice data during calls without obtaining express consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two million Canadians had their unique biometric voiceprints secretly captured and stored without knowing it was happening, leaving them vulnerable to account takeover.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers provided express consent before voiceprints were collected and enrolled
claimsVsReality.reality: Rogers performed 'tuning' (biometric collection) without first obtaining valid consent, and CSRs frequently enrolled customers without consent or by clicking through enrollment options by mistake

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers had a clear and accessible way to opt out of the Voice ID program
claimsVsReality.reality: The opt-out process was only mentioned in a FAQ document buried on Rogers' website, and CSRs did not proactively inform customers of the opt-out option

claimsVsReality.claim: Retained voiceprints of customers who opted out were kept for legitimate security purposes
claimsVsReality.reality: Rogers retained voiceprints after opt-out but later admitted they were never actually used for any purpose—the company simply stored them in its database

claimsVsReality.claim: CSR training and monitoring ensured valid consent was consistently obtained
claimsVsReality.reality: Rogers lacked robust monitoring mechanisms, relied only on ad-hoc call reviews by supervisors, and training materials were general and high-level without critical details

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Knowledge and consent required for collection, use or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to obtain express consent before conducting 'tuning' (voiceprint collection)
violations: Failed to obtain express consent before conducting 'tuning' (voiceprint collection)
Relied on single-line automated message regarding 'recordings' for 'identification purposes' rather than meaningful explanation of biometric collection
Enrolled customers in the program without their consent on multiple occasions, as evidenced by the complainant's experience

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 6.1 – Valid consent requires individuals understand purpose, nature and consequences
regulatoryFindings.description: Automated message did not explain that 'identification' meant biometric voiceprint creation
violations: Automated message did not explain that 'identification' meant biometric voiceprint creation
Training materials lacked detail and contained erroneous information about the tuning process
CSRs failed to consistently obtain or document express consent due to inadequate protocols and monitoring

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.8 – Individuals may withdraw consent at any time and withdrawal mechanisms must be clearly explained
regulatoryFindings.description: Opt-out process only mentioned in FAQ document on website, not clearly communicated at time of consent
violations: Opt-out process only mentioned in FAQ document on website, not clearly communicated at time of consent
Voiceprint deletion process was separate and not clearly explained; customers directed to privacy office rather than informed of easy deletion option
CSRs told customers voiceprints would be retained for 'security purposes' without explaining separate deletion option

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5.3 – Personal information no longer required to fulfill identified purpose must be destroyed, erased or made anonymous
regulatoryFindings.description: Retained voiceprints of opt-out customers 'for security purposes' but never actually used them for any purpose
violations: Retained voiceprints of opt-out customers 'for security purposes' but never actually used them for any purpose
Failed to delete voiceprints upon opt-out, keeping them indefinitely in the database without legitimate business need

outcome: Rogers agreed to implement comprehensive remedial measures by 30 September 2022, including: (1) obtaining express consent through the IVR system before any voiceprint tuning or enrolment; (2) clearly informing customers of opt-out and deletion rights in privacy communications and during enrollment; (3) deleting voiceprints of all individuals who previously opted out; (4) implementing robust monitoring, training and compliance tracking mechanisms for CSRs; (5) reconfirming consent from all previously enrolled customers as they call in; and (6) providing detailed implementation plans and documentary evidence of compliance to the OPC.
companyNow: Rogers remains one of Canada's largest telecom providers and continues operating its services across the country, though the Voice ID program was significantly modified following this enforcement action.
dataType: Biometric data (voiceprints), voice recordings

companyDescription: MGM Resorts International is a U.S.-based hospitality company that owns and operates hotels and casinos across the United States and serves a substantial Canadian customer base.
companyLongDescription: MGM Resorts International is one of the world's largest casino and hotel operators, headquartered in Las Vegas, Nevada. The company operates multiple resort properties and casino brands across the United States and internationally. MGM maintains significant interactions with Canadian customers through online reservations, marketing activities, and partnerships with major Canadian organizations such as Air Canada Vacations and the Canadian Automobile Association. The company collects and stores extensive guest data including names, contact information, dates of birth, and in some cases government-issued identification numbers.
caseDescription: MGM suffered a large-scale data breach in summer 2019 affecting approximately 10.6 million guests, including 1,934,090 Canadians. MGM failed to promptly assess whether the breach posed a real risk of significant harm to affected Canadians and did not report the breach to the Privacy Commissioner or notify affected individuals until June 2020, nearly 11 months after discovery. The delay occurred because MGM did not commence analysis of the data concerning Canadian residents until February 2020, after the OPC contacted them about media reports.
violationSummary: MGM's breach of security safeguards resulted in unauthorized access to and exfiltration of sensitive personal information, which was subsequently offered for sale on a dark web hacking forum. The breach constitutes a breach of confidentiality of the personal information in MGM's possession.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: MGM discovered a data breach affecting 10.6 million guests in July 2019 but delayed assessing risk to Canadian residents until February 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 2 million Canadians, including 5,635 whose government IDs were compromised, remained unaware they were exposed to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data set had little value due to its poor condition and was not readily useable without knowledge of MGM's source systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: OPC technical analysis demonstrated the data could be organized by malicious actors without significant effort; the OPC's own analysts successfully reconstructed and identified the personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: MGM promptly assessed whether the breach posed a real risk of significant harm to affected Canadians.
claimsVsReality.reality: MGM did not commence analysis of Canadian resident data until February 2020, more than 7 months after discovering the July 2019 breach and 8 months after beginning U.S. guest notifications.

claimsVsReality.claim: The purchased data set was secured and no longer posed risk after MGM bought it back from the attacker in July 2019.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data set reappeared for sale on the dark web in February 2020, demonstrating that MGM's efforts to contain it failed and the information remained in circulation among malicious actors.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 10.1 requires organizations to report breaches of security safeguards to the Privacy Commissioner and notify affected individuals as soon as feasible if the breach poses a real risk of significant harm (RROSH)
regulatoryFindings.description: MGM failed to promptly assess whether the breach posed a RROSH to affected Canadians
violations: MGM failed to promptly assess whether the breach posed a RROSH to affected Canadians
MGM did not report the breach to the Privacy Commissioner until 3 June 2020, nearly 11 months after becoming aware of the breach in July 2019
MGM did not notify affected Canadian residents as soon as feasible; notification commenced 3 June 2020 and was completed 17 July 2020
MGM did not commence analysis of the data with respect to Canadian residents until 28 February 2020, despite beginning U.S. guest notifications on 5 September 2019

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Subsection 10.1(8) requires organizations to assess RROSH by considering the sensitivity of personal information involved and the probability of misuse
regulatoryFindings.description: MGM incorrectly assessed that there was no RROSH, claiming the data was in poor condition and non-sensitive, when government-issued identifiers (5,635 individuals) and combined personal information clearly met the sensitivity threshold
violations: MGM incorrectly assessed that there was no RROSH, claiming the data was in poor condition and non-sensitive, when government-issued identifiers (5,635 individuals) and combined personal information clearly met the sensitivity threshold

MGM failed to properly assess the probability of misuse despite evidence of malicious intent (hacking, data exfiltration, attempted sale on dark web), exposure to unknown malicious actors, large volume of data breached, and technical accessibility of the data

outcome: MGM was found to have contravened Section 10.1 of PIPEDA by failing to report the breach as soon as feasible and failing to promptly assess whether the breach posed a real risk of significant harm to affected Canadians. The matter is conditionally resolved. MGM committed to amend its privacy breach response framework by 30 June 2022 to ensure that: (1) it will promptly conduct appropriate RROSH assessments consistent with OPC guidance when learning of breaches involving Canadian residents; (2) if a breach gives rise to RROSH, it will report to the Privacy Commissioner as soon as feasible; and (3) it will notify affected individuals as soon as feasible. MGM also committed to provide a report with documentary evidence by 30 June 2022 demonstrating compliance with these commitments. The OPC will monitor compliance.
companyNow: MGM Resorts continues to operate as a major hospitality and gaming corporation. Following this investigation, the company agreed to enhance its privacy breach response procedures to ensure prompt risk assessment and timely notification of Canadian residents affected by future breaches.
dataType: Names, contact details, dates of birth, government-issued identification numbers (driver's licenses, passports, military ID cards, health card numbers, Nexus numbers), email addresses, phone numbers, residence addresses

companyDescription: Marriott International is a global hospitality company operating hotel and resort properties worldwide through various brands including the Ritz-Carlton and Starwood Hotels.
companyLongDescription: Marriott International is one of the world's largest hospitality chains, operating thousands of hotel properties across multiple luxury and mid-range brands. In September 2016, Marriott acquired Starwood Hotels and Resorts, integrating its guest database and loyalty programs. The company manages guest personal information including passport numbers, contact details, and payment card data through centralized reservation and loyalty systems serving millions of customers globally.
caseDescription: Marriott suffered a data breach affecting approximately 339 million guest records worldwide (12.8 million with Canadian residents) spanning from 2014 to 2018 involving the Starwood Hotels database acquired in 2016. The breach exposed personal information including names, addresses, passport numbers, and encrypted payment card details due to inadequate security safeguards, incomplete access controls, insufficient logging and monitoring, and lack of encryption consistency. The Privacy Commissioner of Canada found Marriott violated PIPEDA principles regarding security safeguards, accountability for acquired systems, and excessive information retention.
violationSummary: Marriott failed to implement appropriate security safeguards commensurate with the sensitivity and volume of personal information held, including inadequate access controls, anti-virus software, logging and monitoring measures, and inconsistent encryption of sensitive data. The company also failed to perform adequate ongoing assessment of security measures and retained personal information longer than necessary.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Marriott failed to detect unauthorized access to the Starwood Hotels database it acquired in 2016 for over four years.
whyTheyWereWrong: Canadians had their passport numbers, payment card information, and personal details exposed to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Marriott had adequate security safeguards in place to protect guest personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Starwood database lacked comprehensive logging and monitoring, did not adequately apply multi-factor authentication, had inconsistent encryption of sensitive data, and retained information far longer than necessary, allowing unauthorized access from 2014 to 2018 to go undetected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Marriott exercised appropriate due diligence when acquiring Starwood's systems in 2016.
claimsVsReality.reality: Marriott failed to identify pre-existing security deficiencies in the Starwood network introduced before the acquisition, including malware and credential harvesting tools already present, and did not detect the breach until September 2018 when a managed service provider alert was triggered.

claimsVsReality.claim: Marriott's mitigation measures adequately protected affected individuals from identity theft and fraud.
claimsVsReality.reality: Canadians' passport numbers (approximately 86,000 records), encrypted payment card details (approximately 483,000 records), and other sensitive personal information remained at ongoing risk despite Marriott's notification and remediation efforts.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Organizations must protect personal information by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate access controls – multi-factor authentication not fully deployed on administrative accounts
violations: Inadequate access controls – multi-factor authentication not fully deployed on administrative accounts
Insufficient anti-virus software – did not detect remote access trojans installed by attacker

Inadequate logging and monitoring – Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) not applied to Starwood network until March 2018; Guardium alerts not configured to detect attacker activities over four-year period
Insufficient encryption – passport numbers stored in both encrypted and unencrypted formats; approximately 260 unencrypted payment card numbers found in non-designated fields
Inadequate privileged account monitoring – logs did not monitor or audit administrator accounts

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4 – Organizations must implement policies and practices to give effect to PIPEDA principles, including procedures to protect personal information, with particular emphasis on due diligence when acquiring new systems
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate post-acquisition assessment – while Marriott conducted some due diligence on Starwood systems after September 2016 acquisition, it failed to identify that multi-factor authentication was not fully deployed on administrative accounts until breach discovery in September 2018
violations: Inadequate post-acquisition assessment – while Marriott conducted some due diligence on Starwood systems after September 2016 acquisition, it failed to identify that multi-factor authentication was not fully deployed on administrative accounts until breach discovery in September 2018

Insufficient ongoing assessment and revision – Marriott relied on third-party compliance certifications but did not perform continuous review of logging and monitoring measures to detect deficiencies; did not discover the breach until September 2018 despite attacker access beginning in July 2014

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5 – Personal information shall be retained only as long as necessary for fulfillment of collection purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Excessive retention period – Marriott retained Canadian guest information for 10 years from record creation date based on Alberta tax and limitation act requirements; however, retained data from as far back as 2002 (16 years old at breach discovery), exceeding stated retention purposes
violations: Excessive retention period – Marriott retained Canadian guest information for 10 years from record creation date based on Alberta tax and limitation act requirements; however, retained data from as far back as 2002 (16 years old at breach discovery), exceeding stated retention purposes

Failure to consider retention necessity – did not adequately assess whether retention period was appropriate for all categories of personal information or consider increased risk from retaining aged data

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada found Marriott's complaints well-founded and conditionally resolved based on Marriott's agreement to remedial actions. Marriott decommissioned the breached Starwood database in December 2018 and migrated operations to Marriott systems. The Commissioner required Marriott to: (1) engage an independent external assessor within nine months to evaluate enhancements to access controls, anti-virus software, logging and monitoring, and information storage practices; (2) detail and explain acceptance or rejection of assessor recommendations with implementation schedule; (3) review organizational and governance measures to ensure ongoing assessment of privacy framework, information security program, information security controls, incident response capabilities, and due diligence for acquired assets; and (4) submit assessment report to the OPC within nine months. Marriott also offered affected individuals one year of free web monitoring through WebWatcher, established a dedicated call center, implemented a passport verification and reimbursement claims process, and notified payment card networks of affected card numbers.
companyNow: Marriott continues to operate as a leading global hospitality company with properties in over 130 countries. Following this breach and enforcement action, the company has implemented enhanced security measures and external assessments of its information security program.
dataType: Guest profiles, contact details, reservation information, Starwood Preferred Guest account information, passport numbers, payment card details, date of birth, gender, email addresses, phone numbers, mailing addresses
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.5 (Limiting use, disclosure and retention)

companyDescription: Trimac Transportation Services Inc. is one of the largest bulk delivery service companies in North America, providing short and long-haul transportation services across the continent.
companyLongDescription: Trimac Transportation Services Inc. is a major North American bulk delivery company offering wide-ranging transportation services for both short and long-haul operations. The company deployed a dash camera system across its fleet to improve road safety and asset protection. However, the system's continuous audio recording functionality—active even when drivers were off-duty in their sleeper cabs—captured sensitive personal conversations without adequate privacy safeguards or appropriate technological access controls.
caseDescription: Trimac installed dash cameras with continuous audio and video recording in truck cabins without properly informing drivers that the data could be used for disciplinary purposes. The audio recording functionality was active even when drivers were off-duty, capturing private conversations in their sleeper cabs. The company failed to limit access to recorded clips and did not implement technological safeguards, allowing approximately 150 employees unnecessary access to sensitive driver information.
violationSummary: Trimac conducted continuous surveillance of drivers through audio and video recording, including during off-duty periods when drivers had a reasonable expectation of privacy in their sleeper cabins. The systematic monitoring of conversations and activities constitutes surveillance under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Trimac installed dash cameras with continuous audio recording in truck cabins that remained active during off-duty hours, capturing private conversations in sleeper cabs.
whyTheyWereWrong: Drivers had their private conversations recorded while sleeping or resting in their truck cabins.

claimsVsReality.claim: The dash camera system was necessary to protect company assets and ensure safe operation of trucks, with recordings limited to only 1% of driver time.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system recorded audio continuously whenever the truck was powered on—including during off-duty periods when drivers slept in their cabins—capturing private conversations unrelated to road safety or asset protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Access to recorded clips was restricted only to employees who needed them for coaching and disciplinary purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Approximately 150 employees across branches and regions could access all clips via the portal's 'View All' tab for 90 days, with only a verbal instruction (not technological controls) preventing unauthorized viewing of sensitive recordings.

claimsVsReality.claim: The audio recording functionality was needed to detect collisions and coach drivers on unsafe behaviour.
claimsVsReality.reality: Audio recording during off-duty hours when drivers were sleeping provided no coaching value and minimal utility for collision detection, as other system signals could serve that purpose.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 5(3) - An organization may collect, use or disclose personal information only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection of audio recordings from drivers during off-duty hours when they had reasonable expectation of privacy in sleeper cabins
violations: Collection of audio recordings from drivers during off-duty hours when they had reasonable expectation of privacy in sleeper cabins
Continual audio recording system active whenever truck was on, regardless of driver duty status
Lack of less privacy-intrusive alternatives despite availability of Sleep Mode/Privacy mode functionality
Disproportionate impact on driver privacy relative to benefits gained

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (Schedule 1) - Knowledge and consent of individual required for collection, use, or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Initial failure to obtain informed consent for collection of personal information via dash camera system
violations: Initial failure to obtain informed consent for collection of personal information via dash camera system
System deployed without proper authorization mechanism for audio collection

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 7.3 - Organization must inform individual that personal information will or may be collected, used or disclosed for employment management purposes to rely on consent exception
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to initially inform drivers that data from cameras could be used for disciplinary purposes
violations: Failure to initially inform drivers that data from cameras could be used for disciplinary purposes
Failure to inform drivers that data could be used for terminating employment relationships
Two-year delay between system implementation and provision of clear written guidance on disciplinary uses
Initial communications focused only on system functionalities and driver protection, not on disciplinary purposes

outcome: Trimac's complaint was found well-founded on both issues but conditionally and separately resolved. On the appropriateness of purposes (Issue 1), Trimac was required to: (1) limit audio functionality to active only when drivers are on-duty and/or driving - Trimac deployed a 'Sleep Mode/Privacy mode' function as of March 11, 2022 that shuts off the microphone five minutes after ignition off, after 15 minutes of idling, or immediately when parking brake is detected; (2) technologically limit access to recorded clips to only 'need to know' employees - Trimac removed the 'View All' tab from the portal and restricted access to only two individuals (Vice President of Safety and Director of Safety), then conducted an audit reducing access from 151 to a limited group; and (3) develop and implement internal standard procedures for access controls and monitoring frequency, with submission to the Office by July 31, 2022. On consent (Issue 2), Trimac was found non-compliant for not initially informing drivers of disciplinary uses, but the complaint was resolved after Trimac provided clear written guidance to employees regarding potential disciplinary and employment termination purposes of the system.
companyNow: Following the PIPEDA investigation, Trimac agreed to implement corrective measures including limiting audio recording to on-duty and driving periods only, and implementing technological safeguards to restrict portal access to employees with a legitimate need-to-know basis.
dataType: Audio recordings, video recordings, driver conversations, location data, vehicle telemetry, biometric signals (G-Force)
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA subsection 5(3) - collection of personal information only for appropriate purposes in the circumstances
PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (Schedule 1) - knowledge and consent of individual required for collection, use, or disclosure
PIPEDA subsection 7.3 - failure to inform individual of disciplinary purposes for collection

companyDescription: ABG (Body Corporate Services Pty Ltd) is an Australian strata management company that handles residential property administration and maintenance for apartment buildings and unit complexes.
companyLongDescription: ABG operates as a strata management service provider in Australia, managing common property administration, levy collection, and resident services for body corporates. The company is responsible for protecting sensitive personal information of residents including contact details, financial records, and property ownership information. As a strata manager, ABG has fiduciary duties to residents and must comply with privacy legislation in handling this data.
caseDescription: ABG, a strata management company, improperly disclosed personal information of residents and failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy, protect against unauthorised disclosure, and correct personal information. The Australian Information Commissioner found breaches of multiple Australian Privacy Principles (APP 6, 10, 11, and 13) relating to the handling of personal information.
violationSummary: The primary violation involved improper disclosure of personal information, which falls under Information Dissemination – Disclosure. Secondary issues of insecurity (failure to protect against unauthorised disclosure) and exclusion (failure to correct information) also present.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ABG improperly disclosed personal information of residents and failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy, protect against unauthorised disclosure, and correct personal information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents' personal information was exposed to unauthorised parties through improper disclosure practices, leaving them vulnerable to identity misuse, harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: ABG took reasonable steps to protect personal information and prevent unauthorised disclosure.
claimsVsReality.reality: ABG improperly disclosed residents' personal information without authorisation and failed to implement adequate safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: ABG maintained accurate personal information about residents.
claimsVsReality.reality: ABG failed to take reasonable steps to ensure the accuracy of personal information it held about residents.

claimsVsReality.claim: ABG promptly corrected inaccurate personal information when identified.
claimsVsReality.reality: ABG failed to take reasonable steps to correct personal information held about residents.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 6 – Personal information must be protected by reasonable steps against misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information against unauthorised disclosure
violations: Failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information against unauthorised disclosure

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 10 – An APP entity must take reasonable steps to ensure personal information is accurate, up to date and complete
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information
violations: Failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 11 – An APP entity must take reasonable steps to ensure personal information is accurate, up to date, complete, relevant and not misleading, and correct inaccurate personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to take reasonable steps to correct personal information
violations: Failed to take reasonable steps to correct personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 13 – An APP entity must not disclose personal information about an individual to a third party unless the individual would reasonably expect such disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Improper disclosure of personal information without reasonable expectation of disclosure
violations: Improper disclosure of personal information without reasonable expectation of disclosure

outcome: The OAIC determination found ABG in breach of APP 6, APP 10, and APP 13. The respondent is required to acknowledge the interference with privacy, must not repeat or continue the conduct, provide an apology, and take specified actions as directed by the Commissioner.
dataType: Personal information of residents/owners in strata scheme

companyDescription: Serco Group is a multinational provider of public services and government contracts, operating across defence, justice, transport, and healthcare sectors globally.
companyLongDescription: Serco Group PLC is a British multinational company that provides public services and government outsourcing solutions across multiple sectors including defence, justice, transport, immigration, and healthcare. The company operates in numerous countries and manages critical government contracts. Serco employs tens of thousands of people and processes sensitive personal information as part of its service delivery to government agencies and the public.
caseDescription: Serco Group disclosed personal information of an individual to a third party without authorization or valid exception under Australian Privacy Principle 6. The disclosure violated the individual's privacy rights by using or disclosing their personal information outside the primary or related secondary purposes for which it was collected.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal information to a third party without lawful basis, falling squarely within Solove's Disclosure category—unauthorized sharing of information with external parties.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Serco Group disclosed an individual's personal information to a third party without authorization or valid exception under Australian Privacy Principle 6.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individual's private information was shared beyond the purposes for which it was collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Serco had authority to disclose the individual's personal information to the third party
claimsVsReality.reality: No authorization or valid exception under APP 6.2 existed for the disclosure; it fell outside primary or related secondary purposes for collection

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 6 – Australian Privacy Principles – Personal information must not be used or disclosed for a secondary purpose unless an exception applies or the individual has consented
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosure of personal information to a third party without valid exception under APP 6.2
violations: Disclosure of personal information to a third party without valid exception under APP 6.2
Use or disclosure outside primary or related secondary purposes

outcome: Breach of APP 6 found. Serco Group must acknowledge the interference with privacy, cease the conduct, and not repeat or continue such breaches. Compensation for non-economic loss awarded to the individual.
companyNow: Serco Group continues to operate as a major government services contractor, managing facilities, transportation systems, and public administration services across multiple countries.
dataType: Personal information (type not specified in document excerpt)

companyDescription: Relationships Australia is a major Australian community organisation providing relationship counselling, family support, and mediation services across multiple states.
companyLongDescription: Relationships Australia is a not-for-profit organisation that delivers relationship and family counselling, dispute resolution, and community education services throughout Australia. The organisation operates multiple state-based services, including Relationships Australia (South Australia), and serves thousands of individuals and families seeking support for relationship issues, separation, and family conflict. As a regulated service provider holding sensitive personal information about clients, it must comply with the Australian Privacy Principles.
caseDescription: Relationships Australia breached APP 12 by unreasonably refusing access to personal information requested by the complainant. The organisation failed to demonstrate that the exceptions under APP 12.3 applied or that providing access in the requested manner was impracticable. The OAIC determined the organisation must acknowledge the privacy interference and implement corrective measures.
violationSummary: The respondent denied the complainant access to their personal information without lawful justification, preventing the individual from exercising their right to access their own data — a core exclusion violation under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Relationships Australia unreasonably refused to provide a complainant with access to their personal information held by the organisation.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant was denied access to their own personal records without lawful justification, preventing them from understanding the organisation's interactions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Providing access to the complainant's personal information in the manner requested was impracticable or would breach exceptions under APP 12.3.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OAIC found no valid basis for the refusal and determined the organisation failed to demonstrate that the legal exceptions applied or that providing access was genuinely impracticable.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disclosure would reveal the organisation's confidential negotiation strategy and intentions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OAIC determined this argument did not justify refusing access to the complainant's own personal information under APP 12.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 12 - An entity must take reasonable steps to give an individual access to personal information held about them, unless an exception applies
regulatoryFindings.description: Unreasonably refused access to personal information without adequate justification
violations: Unreasonably refused access to personal information without adequate justification
Failed to apply a trauma-informed approach to access requests
Did not adequately demonstrate that exceptions under APP 12.3 applied

outcome: The OAIC determined a breach of APP 12. Relationships Australia must acknowledge the interference with privacy and ensure the conduct is not repeated or continued. The respondent is required to take specified action and engage an independent reviewer to assess current APP 12 privacy compliance procedures, policies and processes.
companyNow: Relationships Australia continues to operate as a major provider of relationship counselling and family support services across Australia, with renewed focus on privacy compliance and client access rights following this determination.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified type, likely counselling/relationship records)
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) - Australian Privacy Principle 12 (Access to personal information)

companyDescription: Spring Hill Specialist Day Hospital is a private specialist day hospital facility operating in Queensland, Australia, providing surgical and medical procedures on an outpatient basis.
companyLongDescription: Spring Hill Specialist Day Hospital, trading as The Trustee for QFD Day Theatres Unit Trust, is a Queensland-based private day hospital offering specialist surgical and medical procedures to private patients. The facility operates under Australian Privacy Principles and is subject to oversight by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC). The hospital provides outpatient surgical services in the Brisbane metropolitan area.
caseDescription: Spring Hill Specialist Day Hospital breached APP 12 by refusing to provide access to personal information without taking reasonable steps to offer alternative access methods. The organisation failed to properly consider whether the requested information could be disclosed without unreasonably affecting the privacy of other individuals.
violationSummary: The breach involves wrongful denial of access to personal information held by the organisation. APP 12 requires organisations to provide individuals with access to their personal information, and the hospital's refusal to do so (without offering reasonable alternatives) constitutes exclusion from information processing.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Spring Hill Specialist Day Hospital refused to provide a patient access to their personal health information without offering reasonable alternative access methods or properly assessing whether.
whyTheyWereWrong: The patient was denied timely access to their own medical records without the hospital exploring whether redaction or other reasonable steps could enable disclosure.

claimsVsReality.claim: The hospital could refuse access to personal health information when disclosure might affect third parties' privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: APP 12.5 requires organisations to take reasonable steps to provide access through alternative means (such as redaction) rather than simply refusing the request outright.

claimsVsReality.claim: No alternative access methods were available for the requested medical records.
claimsVsReality.reality: The hospital failed to properly assess whether redacting third-party information or other reasonable alternatives could enable the patient to access their own health information.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 12 – Access to personal information. Organisations must take reasonable steps to give individuals access to personal information held by the organisation, and must provide access unless an exception applies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Refused to provide access to personal information without considering or offering reasonable alternative methods of access under APP 12.5
violations: Refused to provide access to personal information without considering or offering reasonable alternative methods of access under APP 12.5
Failed to properly assess whether disclosure would have an unreasonable impact on the privacy of other individuals

outcome: The OAIC found a breach of APP 12. Spring Hill Specialist Day Hospital was required to acknowledge the interference with privacy and take specified steps to remedy the breach, including reconsidering the access request and implementing proper procedures for assessing access refusals.
companyNow: The hospital continues to operate in Queensland; this 2022 determination required it to implement compliance measures regarding patient access to medical records.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified types)
legalBasisViolated: APP 12.5 – Reasonable steps to provide alternative access

companyDescription: Redimed is an Australian healthcare organization that conducts pre-employment medical assessments and occupational health services.
companyLongDescription: Redimed Pty Ltd is an Australian healthcare provider specializing in pre-employment medical examinations, occupational health services, and medical assessments. The company collects sensitive personal health information from individuals undergoing employment medical screening. Redimed failed to maintain transparent practices around how it collected and managed this personal health data, and actively prevented individuals from accessing their own medical records.
caseDescription: Redimed failed to provide access to personal information contained in a pre-employment medical report in response to an individual's access request. The organisation did not take reasonable steps to notify the individual of the collection of personal information and failed to implement appropriate practices, procedures and systems relating to its functions and activities.
violationSummary: The company improperly denied access to personal information (medical records) that should have been disclosed under the Privacy Act, constituting exclusion from one's own information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Redimed refused to provide access to personal information in a pre-employment medical report when requested by an individual.
whyTheyWereWrong: An individual was denied access to their own medical records, preventing them from knowing what health information the employer held about them.

claimsVsReality.claim: Redimed could withhold the pre-employment medical report from the individual
claimsVsReality.reality: Under the Australian Privacy Principles, individuals have a right to access their personal information, including medical records, unless a specific exemption applies

claimsVsReality.claim: Redimed was not required to notify the individual about collecting their health information
claimsVsReality.reality: Redimed was obligated to take reasonable steps to ensure the individual was aware their personal health information was being collected

claimsVsReality.claim: Redimed's existing systems adequately protected personal information and complied with privacy requirements
claimsVsReality.reality: Redimed's practices, procedures and systems were inadequate and failed to comply with APP requirements for handling personal health data

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 1 – Personal Information held by Australian Privacy Principles entities must be collected and managed in accordance with the Australian Privacy Principles
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to collect and manage personal information in accordance with the principles
violations: Failure to collect and manage personal information in accordance with the principles

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 5 – Entities must take reasonable steps to notify individuals when collecting personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to take reasonable steps to notify the individual of collection of personal information
violations: Failure to take reasonable steps to notify the individual of collection of personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 12 – An individual has a right of access to personal information held by an entity
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to give access to personal information contained in pre-employment medical report
violations: Failure to give access to personal information contained in pre-employment medical report
Improper reliance on exemptions to deny access to medical records under APP 12.3

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 12.9 – Entities must implement practices, procedures and systems to ensure compliance with the Privacy Act
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to implement adequate practices, procedures and systems relating to the entity's functions and activities
violations: Failure to implement adequate practices, procedures and systems relating to the entity's functions and activities

outcome: Finding of breach of APP 1, APP 5, and APP 12.9 of the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). The OAIC determined that Redimed must not repeat or continue the conduct in breach.
dataType: Health data, medical records, pre-employment medical information

companyDescription: Eatigo is an online restaurant reservation platform that offers users discounts and incentives to book dining experiences through its digital platform.
companyLongDescription: Eatigo International Pte. Ltd. operates an online restaurant reservation platform that connects users with dining establishments and provides incentive-based offers such as discounts. The company collects and processes user personal data to facilitate restaurant reservations and deliver promotional benefits. Eatigo migrated from a legacy data infrastructure to a new platform in 2018 but failed to properly track or secure the old database containing historical user records.
caseDescription: Eatigo failed to maintain a comprehensive personal data asset inventory, resulting in a legacy database containing 2.76 million user records being left internet-accessible and outside the organisation's data protection architecture. The database was breached and personal data was offered for sale on an online forum. The company failed to implement reasonable security measures including data exfiltration monitoring, security audits, and proper access controls.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security steps and arrangements to protect personal data under section 24 of the PDPA. Specific lapses included failure to maintain a personal data asset inventory, lack of security monitoring for data exfiltration, absence of periodic security audits, inadequate password rotation policies, and poor access controls on an internet-accessible database.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Eatigo failed to maintain a comprehensive personal data asset inventory, leaving a legacy database containing 2.76 million user records internet-accessible.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unmonitored database was breached and personal data including names, emails, phone numbers, passwords, and Facebook tokens were exfiltrated.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation migrated to a new platform and no longer needed the legacy database.
claimsVsReality.reality: The legacy database was retained to support data migration but was then lost from institutional memory and left internet-accessible for approximately two years before being breached.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had security measures in place including password requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The legacy database had no password rotation implemented despite organisation policies requiring 13-character alphanumeric passwords, and the database was accessible directly from the internet without VPN protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation could track unauthorised access to its databases.
claimsVsReality.reality: No access logs, personal data asset inventory, or data exfiltration monitoring systems existed, making it impossible to determine when or how the threat actor gained access.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must take reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data in their possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to maintain a personal data asset inventory, resulting in the Affected Database being omitted from security arrangements and periodic reviews
violations: Failed to maintain a personal data asset inventory, resulting in the Affected Database being omitted from security arrangements and periodic reviews
Did not implement data exfiltration monitoring systems to detect large volumes of data being copied from the Affected Database
Failed to conduct periodic security audits or vulnerability assessments that would have discovered the forgotten legacy database
Did not implement proper password rotation rules for the Affected Database despite having RDS infrastructure that should have enforced 13-character minimum alphanumeric passwords
Left the Affected Database internet-accessible without VPN protection for approximately 2 years (October 2018 to late 2020)
Failed to maintain access logs or monitor unauthorised access to the database
Did not conduct proper handover documentation or knowledge transfer when staff turnover occurred, resulting in complete loss of institutional memory regarding the database

outcome: The Commission determined that Eatigo breached section 24 of the PDPA through failure to implement reasonable security arrangements. The organisation was ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD 62,400 (approximately USD 46,080) payable in 12 monthly instalments. The penalty was reduced from the preliminary decision amount due to the organisation's demonstrated financial distress caused by the COVID-19 pandemic, though the Commission rejected arguments for a mere warning given the egregiousness of the breach affecting 2.76 million individuals. No further directions were issued as the organisation had already implemented comprehensive remedial actions including deletion of the affected database, VPN protection for all remaining databases, password policy improvements, staff retraining, enhanced logging and monitoring systems, penetration testing, and security infrastructure upgrades.
dataType: Name, email, telephone number, gender, passwords (MD5 Hash), Facebook ID and tokens

companyDescription: CPR Vision Management is a Singapore-based CRM system vendor that processes and stores customer data for e-commerce retailers including luxury brands L'Oreal and L'Occitane.
companyLongDescription: CPR Vision Management Pte Ltd is a customer relationship management (CRM) system vendor operating in Singapore as a data intermediary. The company processes and manages personal data on behalf of major e-commerce retailers, including high-volume customer information for brands like L'Oreal and L'Occitane. As a data processor handling sensitive customer information at scale, the company was expected to maintain stringent security and data governance standards.
caseDescription: CPR Vision Management, a CRM system vendor, suffered a ransomware attack on its office network in October 2021 that encrypted personal data of approximately 118,719 customers of L'Oreal and L'Occitane. The organisation failed to deploy adequate endpoint security to the affected network and failed to delete legacy personal data that should have been retained according to data retention obligations under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by not deploying its available endpoint security solution to the affected office network for over 18 months, despite operating as a high-risk CRM vendor processing sensitive customer data. This directly enabled the ransomware attack.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: CPR Vision Management failed to deploy endpoint security to its office network and retained legacy customer data of 118,719 L'Oreal.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's security gaps and failure to delete obsolete data exposed over 118,000 customers' names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, NRIC numbers, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: CPR Vision Management had appropriate endpoint security protecting all office networks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Endpoint security solution was not deployed to the affected office network despite being available, leaving the network vulnerable for over 18 months from April 2020 to October 2021.

claimsVsReality.claim: CPR Vision Management maintained proper data retention practices and only stored data with active business purpose.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company retained legacy customer data that should have been deleted per L'Oreal's March 2021 deletion instruction and had no ongoing business or legal purpose, yet the data remained on NAS devices and was encrypted in the ransomware attack.

claimsVsReality.claim: CPR Vision Management issued a Certificate of Destruction confirming data deletion on 6 May 2021.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data was not actually deleted and remained on the affected NAS device at the time of the October 2021 ransomware attack, rendering the May 2021 certificate false.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to deploy endpoint security solution to the affected office network despite having the solution available
violations: Failed to deploy endpoint security solution to the affected office network despite having the solution available
Lack of data asset inventory management allowing critical infrastructure to remain unprotected for 18+ months
Inadequate security arrangements on the domain controller server and network attached storage devices

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 25 – Retention Limitation Obligation: An organisation must cease to retain documents containing personal data as soon as it is reasonable to assume that the purpose for which the data was collected is no longer being served and retention is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Retained legacy personal data on NAS devices beyond business and legal necessity
violations: Retained legacy personal data on NAS devices beyond business and legal necessity
Failed to delete personal data despite L'Oreal's explicit written instruction dated 26 March 2021
Duplicated personal data to non-production environments without obtaining prior written consent from data principals

outcome: The Commission directed CPR Vision Management to: (1) conduct a thorough security audit of its technical and administrative arrangements for personal data protection; (2) rectify any security gaps identified; (3) conduct a comprehensive review of all databases to ensure compliance with the Retention Limitation Obligation; (4) review and update personal data policies within 60 days of receiving the security audit report; and (5) inform the Commission within 1 week of completing these steps. No financial penalty was imposed in lieu of these compliance actions, given the organisation's upfront admission of liability and absence of evidence of data exfiltration or modification.
dataType: Name, address, email, mobile number, NRIC number, date of birth, age, gender, race, nationality, loyalty points, transaction history

companyDescription: Supernova Pte Ltd is an online retailer based in Singapore that used Shopify's e-commerce platform to sell products to customers.
companyLongDescription: Supernova Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based online retailer that began using Shopify's e-commerce platform in 2018 to conduct retail operations. The company collected and processed customer personal data through the platform for billing, payment processing, and shipping purposes. Supernova relied on Shopify and its Singapore subsidiary Shopify Commerce Singapore Pte Ltd to handle payment processing and other services, which involved transferring customer data internationally.
caseDescription: Supernova Pte Ltd and Shopify Commerce Singapore Pte Ltd failed to comply with Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act's transfer limitation obligations when transferring customer personal data outside Singapore to Shopify Inc in Canada. Two Philippines-based contractors illegally accessed and exfiltrated the personal data of 23,928 individuals between June and September 2020. Both organisations lacked legally binding contractual clauses ensuring comparable data protection standards when transferring personal data internationally.
violationSummary: The violation falls under Insecurity because both organisations failed to implement adequate contractual safeguards and due diligence processes to ensure overseas data transfers maintained comparable protection standards. This security deficit enabled unauthorized access by third-party contractors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Supernova and Shopify Commerce Singapore transferred customer personal data to Canada without legally binding contractual clauses ensuring comparable data protection standards under Singapore's.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two Philippines-based contractors illegally accessed and exfiltrated personal data of 23,928 individuals including names, email addresses, billing/shipping addresses, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Supernova conducted a due diligence assessment of Shopify's data protection approach in 2018 before entering into the Shopify Plus Agreement.
claimsVsReality.reality: The 2018 due diligence exercise was inadequate and failed to ensure binding contractual clauses requiring personal data transferred to Shopify to be protected to a standard comparable to Singapore's PDPA.

claimsVsReality.claim: Shopify's Data Processing Addendum provided adequate data protection standards for cross-border transfers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Shopify Data Processing Addendum made references only to EU and California data protection legislation but did not cover Singapore's PDPA, leaving customer data unprotected under comparable standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: The personal data was secure when transferred to Shopify's systems in Canada.
claimsVsReality.reality: Two Philippines-based contractors with access to Shopify's systems illegally accessed and exfiltrated the personal data of 23,928 individuals between June and September 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 26(1) and PDPR 2014 Regulation 9(1)(b) - Transfer Limitation Obligation
regulatoryFindings.description: Supernova failed to put in place contractual clauses ensuring personal data transferred to Shopify in Canada received comparable protection to PDPA standards
violations: Supernova failed to put in place contractual clauses ensuring personal data transferred to Shopify in Canada received comparable protection to PDPA standards
Supernova's 2018 due diligence assessment was inadequate and did not ensure binding contractual obligations
Shopify SG failed to establish legally binding obligations for intra-group data transfers from Shopify SG to Shopify for Platform Processing, with no references to PDPA protection requirements

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 4(3) - Data Intermediary Obligations
regulatoryFindings.description: Supernova remained responsible for Transfer Limitation Obligation compliance despite assignment to Shopify SG without notice, as the data flow remained unchanged
violations: Supernova remained responsible for Transfer Limitation Obligation compliance despite assignment to Shopify SG without notice, as the data flow remained unchanged

outcome: Supernova Pte Ltd directed to establish within 6 months a process ensuring compliance with the Transfer Limitation Obligation for future overseas data processing engagements. Shopify Commerce Singapore Pte Ltd directed to establish within 60 days a similar compliance process. The Commission recommended Supernova consider using ASEAN Model Contractual Clauses for future cross-border transfers. No financial penalty was imposed, with the Commission noting both organisations' high level of cooperation during investigations.
dataType: full names, email addresses, billing addresses, shipping addresses, phone numbers, bank identification numbers, IP addresses, payment card details (last 4 digits), purchase histories
legalBasisViolated: PDPR 2014 Regulation 9(1)(b) - Requirement for legally enforceable obligations on data recipients
PDPR 2014 Regulation 10(1)(b) and 10(1)(c) - Contractual or binding corporate rules requirements
PDPA Section 4(3) - Obligations regarding data intermediaries

companyDescription: Thomson Medical is a private healthcare provider in Singapore offering a range of medical services and facilities. The company operates multiple clinics and medical centers across Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Thomson Medical is one of Singapore's leading private healthcare providers, offering comprehensive medical services including general practice, specialist consultations, and health screening services. The company operates multiple clinics and medical centers across Singapore and serves thousands of patients annually. During the COVID-19 pandemic, Thomson Medical implemented a Health Declaration Portal to collect visitor health information for pandemic containment purposes. The company is known for its network of medical facilities and commitment to healthcare delivery in Singapore.
caseDescription: Thomson Medical's Health Declaration Portal stored visitor personal data in a publicly accessible CSV file from April to September 2020 due to a developer's failure to remove legacy code and change default server configurations. The exposed data of 44,679 visitors included names, contact details, identification numbers, and COVID-19 health declaration responses. Although no evidence suggested the data was actually accessed by unauthorized third parties, the Commission found the organization breached its Protection Obligation by failing to implement adequate pre-launch security testing and oversight mechanisms.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data. Specifically, data was stored in an unsecured, publicly accessible CSV file due to inadequate pre-launch security testing, lack of oversight of developer implementation, and failure to change default server configurations. This constitutes a failure to implement reasonable safeguards against unauthorized access and disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Thomson Medical's Health Declaration Portal stored 44,679 visitors' personal data including names, contact details, identification numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Visitors' sensitive personal data including identification numbers, contact details, and health declaration information was exposed to potential unauthorized access for five months.

claimsVsReality.claim: The developer followed proper procedures and instructions to store data only in the secured database.
claimsVsReality.reality: The developer failed to remove legacy code that stored data in a publicly accessible CSV file and failed to change default web server configurations that allowed public access to the file.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Health Declaration Portal had adequate security testing before launch.
claimsVsReality.reality: While acceptance and technical testing were conducted, no security testing was performed to verify access controls were in place.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had adequate oversight and supervision of IT personnel.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization relied solely on a single in-house developer with no verification or oversight from other staff members to confirm security protocols were implemented.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – Protection Obligation: Organizations must protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to ensure compliance with internal policies requiring data storage in secured database; relied solely on individual developer with no oversight or verification
violations: Failed to ensure compliance with internal policies requiring data storage in secured database; relied solely on individual developer with no oversight or verification
Conducted inadequate pre-launch testing – no security testing was performed to verify access controls before portal went live
Failed to maintain proper server configuration – default web server settings were not changed, leaving CSV file publicly accessible
Failed to implement process controls – developer omitted required code removal and configuration changes despite instructions

outcome: The Commission imposed compliance directions in lieu of a monetary penalty. The organization must within 60 days: (1) implement reasonable pre-launch security testing procedures for new online services; (2) develop and implement a data retention policy; (3) conduct Clear/Surface Web and renewed Dark Web scans to confirm no data exfiltration; and (4) submit written updates to the Commission detailing actions taken. The Commission noted mitigating factors including the developer's swift rectification upon discovery, limited actual unauthorized access (only 4 accesses from 3 local IPs), no evidence of data exfiltration, and prompt remedial action including password resets and vulnerability scanning.
companyNow: Thomson Medical continues to operate as a major private healthcare provider in Singapore with multiple clinics and medical facilities.
dataType: Health declaration information, visitor names, contact numbers, NRIC/FIN/passport numbers, clinic/room information, health questionnaire responses, date and time of visit, temperature readings

companyDescription: RedMart was an online grocery delivery platform in Singapore that was acquired by Lazada Group in 2016. The company operated a customer-facing e-commerce platform selling groceries and fresh produce.
companyLongDescription: RedMart Limited was a Singapore-based online grocery and fresh produce retailer that provided home delivery services to consumers. Founded as an independent e-commerce platform, the company was acquired by Lazada Group in 2016 and subsequently integrated into Lazada's broader e-commerce ecosystem. While RedMart's public-facing website and mobile application were shut down on 15 March 2019 following the acquisition, backend systems continued operating to support order fulfillment, inventory management, and seller operations until the September 2020 data breach.
caseDescription: RedMart, an online grocery platform acquired by Lazada in 2016, suffered a data breach in September 2020 affecting 898,791 individuals. A threat actor gained unauthorized access to a GitHub user account, obtained sensitive API keys (Chef and Hubot keys), and used them to access the company's AWS and cloud environments, ultimately exfiltrating the customer and seller database. The breach resulted from multiple security failures including insufficient access controls, hardcoded API keys in source code, lack of database authentication, and no encryption of the affected database.
violationSummary: RedMart failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data in its possession, contrary to section 24 of the PDPA. The breach occurred due to inadequate access controls on GitHub accounts, storage of sensitive API keys in plain text and hardcoded in source code, lack of periodic access reviews, absence of database-level authentication, and failure to encrypt the MongoDB database containing 898,791 customer and seller records. These fundamental security lapses created multiple pathways for unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: RedMart failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect API keys and databases, storing sensitive Chef and Hubot keys in GitHub repositories with weak access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: A threat actor exploited these vulnerabilities to steal personal data of nearly 900,000 customers and sellers, including names, addresses, email, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: RedMart had implemented reasonable security arrangements appropriate to the sensitivity of customer and seller data
claimsVsReality.reality: RedMart stored sensitive API keys (Chef and Hubot) in GitHub repositories with weak password-only access controls (8-16 character passwords) for user accounts, allowing a compromised employee account to expose high-privilege access keys

claimsVsReality.claim: RedMart's MongoDB database containing customer and seller personal data was adequately protected
claimsVsReality.reality: The Affected Database in the RedMart Cloud had no encryption and no password authentication requirements, allowing an attacker who gained AWS access via the stolen Chef key to freely exfiltrate 898,791 customer and seller records

claimsVsReality.claim: RedMart's layered network architecture provided effective defense-in-depth security
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite having multiple network layers, each level contained critical security gaps that could be exploited sequentially: weak GitHub access controls led to stolen API keys, which led to AWS access, which led to discovery of additional keys, which led to rogue instance creation and lateral movement to the unprotected MongoDB database

claimsVsReality.claim: Sensitive data like API keys were treated with appropriate security commensurate with their importance
claimsVsReality.reality: The Chef key providing high-privilege access to the entire AWS environment and the Hubot key for further lateral movement were stored in GitHub repositories accessible with the same basic password requirements as less sensitive development code

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of PDPA - Protection Obligation: Organizations must take reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and disclosure of personal data in their possession or control
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement sufficient access controls on GitHub user accounts; sensitive data like the Chef key was accessible to many developers with standard user account credentials rather than requiring elevated privileges
violations: Failed to implement sufficient access controls on GitHub user accounts; sensitive data like the Chef key was accessible to many developers with standard user account credentials rather than requiring elevated privileges

Did not implement reasonable restrictions on access to highly privileged API keys (Chef and Hubot keys); no periodic management reviews were conducted to determine whether continued access was necessary

Stored sensitive API keys in plain text without encryption or password protection: Chef key was hardcoded in source code within GitHub repositories and accessible to large groups of developers; Hubot key was stored in plain text in AWS S3 bucket

Failed to implement separate authentication requirements for the Affected Database; only relied on RedMart Cloud environment access controls rather than adding database-level authentication and encryption
Did not implement encryption for the MongoDB database containing personal data of 898,791 individuals
Failed to remove unnecessary GitHub accounts and developer access keys or restrict access to the principle of least privilege
Did not store API keys in secure separate locations such as AWS Secrets Manager or key vaults as recommended by industry best practices

outcome: The Commission determined that RedMart breached Section 24 of the PDPA by failing to implement reasonable security measures to protect the personal data in the Affected Database. RedMart is required to pay a financial penalty of SGD $72,000 within 30 days. The Commission noted that no further directions were necessary as RedMart had already implemented comprehensive remedial measures post-incident, including: implementing database authentication, enabling two-factor authentication for all GitHub accounts, conducting vulnerability scans, implementing network traffic logging, establishing identity and access management rules to restrict geographical access to API keys, removing access for inactive accounts, implementing network Access Control lists and endpoint detection/response systems, enabling VPC logs for security monitoring, and requiring all employees to complete privacy training. The Organization's voluntary acceptance of liability and swift remedial actions were considered mitigating factors in determining the penalty amount.
companyNow: RedMart no longer operates as an independent platform. Following its 2016 acquisition by Lazada Group, it was integrated into Lazada's systems and its public-facing operations were ceased in March 2019.
dataType: Customer names, email addresses, contact numbers, residential addresses, partial credit card details (first 6 and last 4 digits, expiry date, billing information), hashed passwords, call recording URL links, seller business account information

companyDescription: Farrer Park Hospital is a private tertiary healthcare institute in Singapore providing a range of medical services to patients. It is part of the Farrer Park medical group.
companyLongDescription: Farrer Park Hospital is a private tertiary healthcare institute in Singapore that offers comprehensive healthcare services including specialist consultations, diagnostic imaging, and medical procedures. The organization processes large volumes of sensitive patient personal data including medical information, contact details, and identification numbers through its marketing and administrative departments. As a healthcare provider, it handles highly confidential patient information requiring robust security protections under Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: Farrer Park Hospital failed to implement reasonable security arrangements for email accounts handling sensitive patient medical data. Between March 2018 and October 2019, 9,271 emails containing personal data of 3,539 individuals (including 1,923 with medical information) were automatically forwarded to an unauthorized third party due to compromised email accounts.
violationSummary: The hospital failed to implement adequate security measures (particularly multi-factor authentication and controls on email auto-forwarding) to protect highly sensitive medical data processed through web-accessible email accounts. The breach resulted from inadequate access controls and failure to assess risks from default software settings.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Farrer Park Hospital failed to implement multi-factor authentication on email accounts handling sensitive patient medical data until June 2019, 15 months after a data breach began.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between March 2018 and October 2019, 3,539 patients' personal data was exposed to an unauthorized third party, including 1,923 patients' detailed medical conditions, histories.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organization had implemented comprehensive IT security measures including endpoint protection, behavior analytics, firewalls, and intrusion prevention systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, email accounts handling sensitive patient data lacked multi-factor authentication for 15 months after the breach began, allowing unauthorized forwarding of emails for 19 months undetected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Security solutions did not detect anomalies and unusual activities in email traffic before 24 October 2019.
claimsVsReality.reality: 9,271 emails were automatically forwarded to an unauthorized third party over 19 months without detection by any of the organization's security monitoring tools.
