claimsVsReality.claim: The Organization had implemented various policies regulating data protection including Data Protection Handbook, Access Control Standards, and Acceptable Use Policy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Policies existed but were insufficient for high-risk medical data; the organization failed to implement authentication methods proportionate to the sensitivity of patient medical information being processed.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal, or similar risks to personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement stronger access controls (MFA/multi-factor authentication) for web-mail accounts processing sensitive medical data
violations: Failed to implement stronger access controls (MFA/multi-factor authentication) for web-mail accounts processing sensitive medical data
Failed to implement enhanced security policies and controls for medical information handling (e.g., secure portal, regular purging from email, password-protected attachments)
Failed to assess and mitigate risks from Office 365 default Email Auto-Forwarding setting despite conducting business impact assessments
Failed to implement reasonable security arrangements proportionate to the sensitivity and volume of medical data being processed

outcome: Farrer Park Hospital was required to pay a financial penalty of SGD $58,000 within 30 days. The Commission accepted the hospital's voluntary acceptance of liability and remedial measures already undertaken (including disabling auto-forwarding, increased training, enhanced technical measures, and planned network/endpoint security upgrades by 2022). No further compliance directions were issued as adequate remediation had already occurred.
companyNow: Farrer Park Hospital continues to operate as a private healthcare provider in Singapore. Following the 2022 enforcement action, it implemented enhanced cybersecurity measures including network and endpoint security upgrades.
dataType: Name, gender, nationality, date of birth, NRIC number, passport details, contact number, photograph, medical condition, medical history, medical results/reports

companyDescription: QCP Capital is a cryptocurrency and digital asset trading firm based in Singapore. The company provides trading and investment services in the digital asset space.
companyLongDescription: QCP Capital is a Singapore-based cryptocurrency and digital asset trading and research firm. Founded in 2013, the company serves institutional and professional traders with cryptocurrency trading services, market research, and investment products. QCP Capital operates as a regulated entity under Singapore's financial frameworks and maintains a focus on digital asset trading infrastructure.
caseDescription: QCP Capital suffered an unauthorised access incident where threat actors compromised employee accounts and exfiltrated personal data of 675 individuals including identity documents, contact information, and trading records. The company was found to have implemented reasonable security measures and responded promptly with remediation, resulting in no enforcement action.
violationSummary: The breach resulted from unauthorised access to employee accounts leading to exfiltration of personal data. While the organisation had reasonable security arrangements in place, the incident itself represents a security failure, though the organisation was found compliant with its legal obligations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: QCP Capital's employee accounts were compromised by threat actors, leading to unauthorised access and exfiltration of personal data including identity documents, contact information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals had their sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers, passport scans, account balances.

claimsVsReality.claim: QCP Capital implemented reasonable security measures to protect customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite reasonable security arrangements, two employee accounts were compromised due to credential-based attack, allowing threat actors to exfiltrate sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers, passport scans, and trading records of 675 customers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had internal monitoring systems in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: While monitoring systems detected and flagged anomalous transactions, they did not prevent the initial unauthorised access or data exfiltration from occurring.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks, and loss of storage media.
regulatoryFindings.description: Threat actors gained unauthorised access to employee accounts and exfiltrated personal data of 675 individuals
violations: Threat actors gained unauthorised access to employee accounts and exfiltrated personal data of 675 individuals
However, investigations found the Organisation had provided and made reasonable security arrangements and maintained internal monitoring systems

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection determined that QCP Capital was in compliance with its Protection Obligation under Section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation had implemented reasonable security measures, maintained internal monitoring systems that detected and mitigated the incident, and took prompt and extensive remedial action including notification of affected individuals, layering access controls, and introducing mandatory hardware key access authentication. No enforcement action was taken.
companyNow: QCP Capital continues to operate as a digital asset trading firm in Singapore, maintaining its position in the cryptocurrency trading sector.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, date of birth, address, passport scan, passport number, photograph, email address, phone number, Telegram and WeChat ID, whitelisted address, trading records, account balances

companyDescription: Cognita Asia Holdings is an education provider operating three schools in Singapore. The company manages student enrollment and employee payroll systems containing sensitive personal and financial data.
companyLongDescription: Cognita Asia Holdings Pte Ltd is an education organisation that operates multiple schools in Singapore, serving students and employing staff across three school facilities. The company collects and processes sensitive personal data including student identification documents and employee financial information such as salaries and bank account details. As an educational institution, the organisation is responsible for safeguarding this data in accordance with Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: Cognita Asia Holdings suffered a ransomware attack in June 2021 that encrypted personal data of 1,260 individuals including students' identification documents and employees' salary and bank account information. The organisation failed to implement adequate security controls, including multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts and proper password policy enforcement, and did not provide adequate staff training on data protection.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data by not deploying multi-factor authentication for VPN access to administrator accounts, not enforcing minimum password requirements (8 vs 10 characters), not enforcing default password change policies, and failing to provide adequate data protection training to staff. These failures directly enabled the ransomware attack.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Cognita Asia Holdings failed to implement adequate security controls including multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts, enforce its own password policies.
whyTheyWereWrong: Students' identification documents and employees' salary and bank account details were exposed to threat actors, creating risks of identity theft, financial fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cognita's VPN authentication was sufficiently secure with username and password credentials.
claimsVsReality.reality: The weak single-factor authentication allowed threat actors to access administrator accounts using compromised credentials, enabling broad network access and ransomware deployment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cognita had a password policy requiring 10 characters minimum and mandatory default password changes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation enforced only 8-character passwords in practice and did not enforce default password change requirements, making accounts vulnerable to compromise.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cognita adequately trained staff on data protection security practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation failed to conduct mandatory personal data protection training for staff, leaving employees unprepared to identify or respond to security threats.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation: Organisations must protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication for VPN administrator account access despite holding sensitive data (ID documents, salary, bank details)
violations: Failed to implement multi-factor authentication for VPN administrator account access despite holding sensitive data (ID documents, salary, bank details)
Failed to enforce minimum password requirements (8 characters enforced vs 10 character policy)
Failed to enforce default password change requirement after first usage
Failed to provide adequate personal data protection training to staff

outcome: The organisation is required to pay a financial penalty of S$26,000 within 30 days. The Commission acknowledged the organisation's prompt notification of the incident, implementation of threat monitoring, and remedial actions including engagement of cybersecurity experts, enforcement of multi-factor authentication, enhanced password requirements, increased security reviews and training, and provision of 12 months personal identity monitoring services to affected staff and parents. No further directions were issued under section 48I of the PDPA due to the remedial measures undertaken.
companyNow: Cognita Asia Holdings continues to operate in Singapore following the 2021 incident. The company has implemented remedial security measures including multi-factor authentication, enhanced password requirements, and expanded cybersecurity training for staff.
dataType: Identification documents (passport/ID pages), salary information, bank account details

companyDescription: MyRepublic Limited is a Singapore-based telecommunications operator licensed to provide fixed and mobile telecommunications services. The company collects customer identity verification documents as required by its Facilities-Based Operations licence.
companyLongDescription: MyRepublic Limited is a Singapore-incorporated telecommunications operator holding a Facilities-Based Operations licence under the Telecommunications Act 1999. The company provides mobile and fixed-line services to customers in Singapore and collects and stores Know-Your-Customer (KYC) documents including identity cards and work passes as part of its regulatory compliance requirements. At the time of the 2021 incident, MyRepublic maintained customer personal data in Amazon Web Services cloud storage for its mobile order portal.
caseDescription: MyRepublic, a telecommunications operator, failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect customer personal data stored in a publicly accessible Amazon Web Services bucket. An external threat actor obtained an access key embedded in the company's source code and portal, exfiltrated personal data from 79,388 customers including sensitive identity documents and biometric information, and threatened to publish the data unless a ransom was paid.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement sufficiently robust security measures to protect an access key that allowed unauthorized access to sensitive personal data, and failed to implement reasonable security controls for its AWS environment by leaving the bucket publicly accessible and embedding credentials in source code.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: MyRepublic stored an AWS access key in publicly accessible source code and portal configuration.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposed access credentials enabled a criminal to steal and threaten to publish sensitive identity documents, NRIC numbers, thumbprints.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Access Key was protected through Amazon Identity and Access Management features and could only access the specific Bucket, not other systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Access Key was embedded in plaintext in source code and publicly exposed through the php-info URL, allowing any external actor to discover and use it to access and exfiltrate all customer data from the Bucket.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cloud infrastructure security is the responsibility of the AWS vendor.
claimsVsReality.reality: MyRepublic retained ultimate responsibility for reasonable security arrangements protecting customer data under its control, regardless of which vendor hosted it, and failed to implement basic controls like not making buckets publicly accessible.

claimsVsReality.claim: The storage of sensitive KYC documents in the cloud was secure through access restrictions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Bucket was configured as publicly accessible, and 79,388 customers' NRIC numbers, photographs, thumbprints, and address documents were exfiltrated and held for ransom due to the exposed access key.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement sufficiently robust processes to manage the AWS access key, including storing it in source code available to all developers, displaying it through a PHP Info function publicly accessible via URL, and embedding it in application log files without redaction
violations: Failed to implement sufficiently robust processes to manage the AWS access key, including storing it in source code available to all developers, displaying it through a PHP Info function publicly accessible via URL, and embedding it in application log files without redaction
Failed to implement reasonable security controls for the AWS environment by allowing the bucket containing 79,388 customers' sensitive personal data to be publicly accessible
Failed to layer security defences or implement IP-based access restrictions to limit access to authorized applications or users only
Failed to adequately protect high-volume, sensitive personal data (NRIC numbers, biometric data, photographs, thumbprints) commensurate with the increased risk of identity theft

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of $60,000 SGD to be paid within 30 days. The organisation was found in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24. No further directions were deemed necessary as MyRepublic had already implemented comprehensive remedial measures including revoking the compromised access key, removing environment configuration files exposing credentials, restricting bucket access to specific IP addresses, enabling version control, rotating all access keys, consolidating AWS accounts with central monitoring, notifying affected customers with credit monitoring services, and commissioning a security improvement program.
companyNow: MyRepublic continues to operate as a telecommunications provider in Singapore. Following the 2022 enforcement action and the cyber incident, the company implemented comprehensive security remediation measures and security improvement programmes.
dataType: National identity documents (NRIC), biometric data (thumbprints, photographs), work pass information, residential address, date of birth, gender, race, mobile phone numbers

companyDescription: Quoine Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based cryptocurrency exchange operating under the 'Liquid' brand that provides global digital asset trading services. It is a subsidiary of Japan-incorporated Liquid Group Inc.
companyLongDescription: Quoine Pte Ltd operates a global cryptocurrency exchange platform under the Liquid brand, serving customers worldwide with digital asset trading and financial services. As a financial technology company handling sensitive customer data including identity documents, financial information, and transaction records, Quoine maintained significant cryptocurrency exchange operations with a large international customer base. The company is a subsidiary of Liquid Group Inc., a Japanese parent company, and was based in Singapore at the time of the incident.
caseDescription: Quoine, a global cryptocurrency exchange, suffered a data breach affecting 652,564 customers after an external actor gained control of its domain hosting account through social engineering attacks on the domain registrar's employees. The attacker used this access to redirect the organization's email traffic, reset credentials for a privileged DevOps automation account lacking two-factor authentication, and exfiltrate sensitive customer data including identity documents, financial information, and bank account details. The breach resulted from Quoine's failure to conduct properly-scoped security reviews of automation accounts and implement reasonable ICT controls such as two-factor authentication on privileged access accounts.
violationSummary: The violation falls under Information Processing – Insecurity because the organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically by: (1) failing to review and assess the security implications and risks of the DevOps Account which lacked two-factor authentication despite having privileged access to sensitive data; (2) failing to implement reasonable ICT controls such as two-factor authentication and restricted password change functions for a high-privilege automation account; and (3) conducting improperly-scoped periodic security reviews that excluded automation accounts from vulnerability assessments.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Quoine failed to implement two-factor authentication on a privileged DevOps automation account with access to customer databases.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 652,000 customers had their identity documents, financial records, bank account details, and transaction history exposed to an external actor.

claimsVsReality.claim: Quoine had implemented periodic security reviews of its IT infrastructure and access controls.
claimsVsReality.reality: The periodic security reviews were improperly scoped and only examined accounts used interactively by humans, failing to identify the unprotected DevOps automation account with privileged database access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The DevOps Account was created with appropriate security due diligence and risk assessment.
claimsVsReality.reality: The account was created without sufficient due diligence regarding security risk profiles and lacked two-factor authentication despite having privileged access to databases containing sensitive customer data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Quoine had reasonable security arrangements in place to protect customer personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Critical security gaps existed, including lack of 2FA on privileged accounts and failure to assess the security implications of automation accounts with database access, which directly enabled the exfiltration of 652,564 customer records.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to review and assess the security implications and risks of the DevOps Account, which was created without sufficient due diligence and lacked two-factor authentication despite having privileged access to the Cloud Platform containing API keys and customer databases
violations: Failed to review and assess the security implications and risks of the DevOps Account, which was created without sufficient due diligence and lacked two-factor authentication despite having privileged access to the Cloud Platform containing API keys and customer databases
Conducted improperly-scoped periodic security reviews that focused only on accounts used interactively by humans and incorrectly excluded automation bot accounts from vulnerability assessment

Failed to implement reasonable ICT controls for the DevOps Account, including two-factor authentication for password resets and restrictions on password change functions, despite these controls being implemented for other privileged accounts
Failed to maintain proper documentation and security assessment procedures for legacy IT systems, allowing critical security vulnerabilities to persist through staff turnover
Did not design and organize security arrangements to fit the sensitive nature of the personal data held (financial data, identity documents, KYC information) and the possible harm from a breach

outcome: The Commissioner found Quoine in breach of PDPA Section 24 (Protection Obligation) for failing to implement reasonable security arrangements, specifically: (1) failure to review and assess the DevOps Account's security implications and risks, and (2) failure to implement reasonable ICT controls including two-factor authentication for the DevOps Account. The organization was ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD 67,000 within 30 days. The Commissioner noted mitigating factors including Quoine's prompt remedial actions (notification of affected individuals, migration to more robust domain service provider with enterprise-level support and 2FA, migration of the entire exchange to a different cloud platform with improved service account controls, strengthened DevOps Account security with IP whitelist restrictions, and ongoing evaluation of additional cloud security tools). No further directions were imposed given the remedial measures already undertaken.
companyNow: Quoine continues to operate as a cryptocurrency exchange under the Liquid brand, though the incident and enforcement action led to significant remediation efforts including migration to more robust infrastructure providers and enhanced security controls.
dataType: Name, address, email, phone number, identity document images (NRIC, passport), KYC documents, financial information, transaction history, bank account details, cryptocurrency transaction records

companyDescription: Budgetcars is a Singapore-based logistics company that delivers parcels on behalf of retailers and provides customers with tracking functionality.
companyLongDescription: Budgetcars Pte. Ltd. is a logistics and parcel delivery company operating in Singapore. The company provides delivery services for retailers and operates a tracking function that allows customers and retailers to monitor parcel delivery status and confirm recipient identity. The company handles parcels from multiple retailers and maintains personal data of delivery recipients including names, addresses, contact numbers, and signature photographs.
caseDescription: Budgetcars, a logistics company, failed to implement adequate access controls on its delivery tracking function, allowing unauthorised access to customer personal data by manipulating tracking IDs. The vulnerability exposed the personal data of 44,357 individuals for an extended period, and the company also failed to archive completed delivery records within reasonable timeframes.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access to personal data. The use of sequential and non-sequential numerical tracking IDs without proper access controls created an insecure direct object reference vulnerability, a well-known security risk that had been previously identified in similar cases.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Budgetcars failed to implement access controls on its delivery tracking function, allowing unauthorized access to 44,357 individuals' personal data by manipulating tracking IDs.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' names, addresses, phone numbers, and signature photographs were exposed to unauthorized access for an extended period because the company did not use basic security measures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The tracking function was secure and protected customer data appropriately.
claimsVsReality.reality: The tracking function had no meaningful access controls; users could view any customer's data by simply changing numbers in the tracking ID URL.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data was retained only for active deliveries.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no archival process and retained completed delivery data indefinitely on the tracking page, expanding the pool of exposed personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement reasonable access controls on the Tracking Function Page by adopting Tracking IDs without factoring in the well-known risk of insecure direct object reference
violations: Failed to implement reasonable access controls on the Tracking Function Page by adopting Tracking IDs without factoring in the well-known risk of insecure direct object reference
Allowed unauthorised access to personal data by permitting manipulation of numerical Tracking IDs to access other individuals' data
Failed to archive or remove personal data from the Tracking Function Page within a reasonable period after delivery completion, increasing the volume of data at risk

outcome: The Commission did not impose a financial penalty, recognising the organisation's upfront voluntary admission of liability and prompt remedial action. The organisation was directed to: (1) establish appropriate contractual provisions defining data protection obligations between data controller and intermediary; (2) engage a qualified security service provider to conduct a thorough security audit of its website's technical and administrative security arrangements; (3) provide the full audit report to the Commission within 60 days; (4) rectify identified security gaps and update personal data protection policies within 60 days of receiving the audit report; and (5) inform the Commission within 1 week of completion of rectification and implementation.
companyNow: Following the 2022 enforcement action, Budgetcars implemented security improvements including Tracking ID expiry after 14 days, prevention of sequential Tracking ID uploads, and engagement of external IT security providers.
dataType: Name, address, contact number, photographs of signatures

companyDescription: Toll Holdings Limited is an integrated logistics services provider headquartered in Australia with multiple Singapore-registered subsidiary entities operating in forwarding, offshore petroleum services, and regional logistics.
companyLongDescription: Toll Holdings Limited is a multinational logistics and transportation company that provides integrated services including freight forwarding, offshore petroleum logistics, and regional supply chain management. The company operates through various subsidiary entities across multiple jurisdictions, including Toll Logistics (Asia) Limited, Toll Global Forwarding Singapore, and others. As a large-scale logistics operator, Toll processes significant volumes of employee and operational data across its distributed IT infrastructure. The company is part of a broader international group managing IT systems and services on a centralized basis.
caseDescription: Toll Holdings and its Singapore entities failed to implement legally enforceable data protection obligations when transferring employee personal data to servers outside Singapore via an HR platform, violating the Personal Data Protection Act's Transfer Limitation Obligation. Although a ransomware attack affected the company's IT systems in Australia and Singapore, the entities had implemented reasonable security arrangements and were not found to have breached their Protection Obligation. The entities received a warning and were required to ensure future data transfers comply with comparable protection standards.
violationSummary: The primary violation relates to improper transfer of personal data outside Singapore without legally enforceable obligations ensuring comparable protection standards, which constitutes a breach of confidentiality obligations under Singapore's PDPA Transfer Limitation Obligation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Toll Holdings and its Singapore entities transferred 1,748 employee records including names, addresses, ages.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees' personal data including salary information and sensitive identifiers were transferred outside Singapore without contractual guarantees of comparable protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data was transferred to the HR Platform for legitimate HR functions with vendor protections in place
claimsVsReality.reality: No legally enforceable data protection obligations existed between the Organisations and the HR Vendor; the CSAs did not contain data protection provisions, and the vendor contract did not bind Toll Holdings entities

claimsVsReality.claim: The Group implemented reasonable security arrangements sufficient to protect employee data
claimsVsReality.reality: While security measures were present, the transfer of sensitive data (including salary information and identification numbers) to external servers without contractual protections created a compliance gap, even though the specific ransomware attack did not ultimately exfiltrate the transferred employee records

claimsVsReality.claim: Toll Holdings' IT support services under the CSAs implied data protection responsibility was centralized
claimsVsReality.reality: The CSAs failed to specify data protection obligations; the Organisations retained primary Protection Obligation responsibility despite centralizing IT support, creating ambiguity about accountability

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 26 and PDPR 2014 Regulation 9(1)(b) / PDPR 2021 Regulation 10(1) – Transfer Limitation Obligation requires organisations to take appropriate steps to ensure recipients of transferred personal data outside Singapore are bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide protection standards at least comparable to the PDPA
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisations transferred personal data of 1,748 current and former employees to HR Platform hosted in European Economic Area without ensuring legally enforceable obligations were in place between the Organisations and the HR Vendor
violations: Organisations transferred personal data of 1,748 current and former employees to HR Platform hosted in European Economic Area without ensuring legally enforceable obligations were in place between the Organisations and the HR Vendor
Organisations were not party to the contract between Toll Holdings and the HR Vendor that contained data protection obligations
Corporate Services Agreements centralising HR functions with Toll Holdings did not contain any provisions relating to protection of personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: No violation found; Organisations had implemented industry-standard security solutions including endpoint protection, logging and monitoring, firewalls, intrusion prevention, vulnerability scanning, and engaged a Managed Security Service Provider
violations: No violation found; Organisations had implemented industry-standard security solutions including endpoint protection, logging and monitoring, firewalls, intrusion prevention, vulnerability scanning, and engaged a Managed Security Service Provider

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to the Organisations in respect of their breach of the Transfer Limitation Obligation. No monetary penalty was imposed. The Deputy Commissioner considered mitigating factors including the Organisations' cooperation with the investigation, that access to transferred personal data was limited to entities within the same corporate group, that there was no evidence of loss or damage, and that the Group had already implemented intra-group contractual arrangements (Singapore Data Export Agreement) to govern future transfers of personal data. The Organisations were required to ensure that all future transfers of personal data outside Singapore comply with the Protection Obligation requirements by obtaining legally enforceable commitments from recipients.
companyNow: Toll Holdings continues to operate as a major logistics provider. Following the 2020 ransomware incident and subsequent PDPA enforcement action, the company has implemented enhanced data protection measures and intra-group data transfer agreements.
dataType: Employee personal data including name, address, age, salary, driver's licence number, emergency contact details, national ID, fingerprint, medical details, passport details

companyDescription: Lovebonito is a Singapore-based e-commerce platform specializing in the retail of clothing and accessories.
companyLongDescription: Lovebonito Singapore Pte. Ltd. operates an online fashion retail platform selling clothing and accessories to customers. The company uses third-party solutions including Magento Cloud CMS to manage its website and Adyen for payment processing. In December 2019, the company suffered a significant data breach that exposed personal and payment data of thousands of customers due to inadequate security measures.
caseDescription: Lovebonito's e-commerce platform suffered a data breach affecting 5,561 customers when a malicious actor compromised an administrator account in Magento CMS and injected unauthorized JavaScript code to intercept credit card data. The company failed to implement adequate password policies, two-factor authentication, network security controls, and system hardening measures, resulting in exposure of both payment and personal data.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession and control, specifically: inadequate password policies allowing easily-guessable credentials, failure to implement two-factor authentication despite availability, weak network security, insufficient system logging and monitoring, lack of access controls, and failure to patch/maintain systems. These security failures directly led to unauthorized access and data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Lovebonito failed to implement adequate password policies, two-factor authentication, and network security controls, allowing a malicious actor to compromise an administrator account.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' payment card details and personal information were intercepted and stolen due to weak security, exposing them to financial fraud, identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Lovebonito employed industry-standard e-commerce platforms (Magento Cloud and Adyen) and relied on their security features.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement its own security controls around these platforms, using weak default password policies and lacking basic protections like two-factor authentication, network monitoring, and access controls.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had reasonable security arrangements protecting customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: An administrator account using the easily-guessable password 'ilovebonito88' was compromised, allowing attackers to inject malicious code and steal credit card data and personal information from 5,561 customers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization's IT systems had appropriate protections against unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: The systems lacked remote access monitoring, network filtering, security patching, session management, and proper access control logging, leaving them vulnerable to compromise.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement a robust password policy for Magento CMS administrator accounts; default settings did not mandate periodic password changes and permitted easily-guessable passwords (e.g., 'ilovebonito88' incorporating company name)
violations: Failed to implement a robust password policy for Magento CMS administrator accounts; default settings did not mandate periodic password changes and permitted easily-guessable passwords (e.g., 'ilovebonito88' incorporating company name)
Failed to enable two-factor authentication for administrative accounts despite it being available as an out-of-the-box feature in Magento CMS version 2.3.2

Failed to implement adequate host, network, remote access, and webpage security: no/limited system logging, no/limited system hardening, unpatched/unmaintained systems, lack of network monitoring, lack of ingress/egress filtering, inadequate remote access connection attempt logging, improper access controls
Failed to recognize foreseeable risk that unauthorized access to Magento CMS could enable malicious modification of checkout page to intercept credit card data
Despite credit card data being collected directly by Adyen via iframe, organization failed to secure the website against unauthorized changes that could intercept and exfiltrate such data

outcome: The organization was found in breach of the Protection Obligation under Section 24 of the PDPA. A financial penalty of SGD 24,000 (reduced from preliminary SGD 29,000) was imposed, payable within 30 days. The Commissioner found that while the organization's representation regarding 2FA implementation merit some consideration (given the sophisticated API-based attack vector), the breach was sustained based on more fundamental failures including inadequate password policies and systemic IT security weaknesses. No further directions were issued given the comprehensive remedial actions already undertaken by the organization (password resets, 2FA implementation, two-factor authentication, session management, access permission reviews, VPN deployment, endpoint protection, script monitoring for JavaScript injections, API whitelisting, alert monitoring, penetration testing, Magento CMS upgrade, and CAPTCHA implementation). The decision established 2FA/MFA as a baseline requirement for administrative accounts to systems holding sensitive or large volumes of personal data going forward.
companyNow: Lovebonito continues to operate as a fashion e-commerce retailer in Southeast Asia, having implemented comprehensive security upgrades following the 2019 breach.
dataType: Personal names, email addresses, phone numbers, shipping/billing addresses, date of birth, payment type, partial credit card data (last 4 digits, expiry date, CVV), PayPal account email
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 (Singapore), Section 24 (Protection Obligation)

companyDescription: PINC Interactive Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce company that operated the fashion website www.pincstyle.com. The company was founded in 2018 and provided online shopping services to users.
companyLongDescription: PINC Interactive Pte. Ltd. was a Singapore-incorporated e-commerce platform operator running www.pincstyle.com, a fashion retail website. Founded in 2018, the company was a relatively young startup that experienced significant operational losses. The organization engaged in typical e-commerce operations including user account management, order processing, and customer data collection.
caseDescription: PINC Interactive failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its staging database. Developers stored copies of a database containing 3,916 real users' data on personal devices without security controls, and the staging API lacked authentication despite being accessible over the internet. The database was compromised in October 2019, exposing names, usernames, email addresses, contact numbers, and password hashes.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements under PDPA Section 24, allowing personal data to be stored on unsecured personal devices and exposed via an unauthenticated API. This constitutes a failure to protect against unauthorised access and exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: PINC Interactive allowed developers to store copies of a database containing 3,916 real users' personal data on unprotected personal devices.
whyTheyWereWrong: Real users' names, usernames, email addresses, contact numbers, and password hashes were exposed when developers' compromised devices.

claimsVsReality.claim: Developers were instructed to use strong passwords and had antivirus software installed on their personal devices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no oversight of actual security implementations, could not provide product names, versions, or update frequencies of purported antivirus software, and left security decisions entirely to individual employees.

claimsVsReality.claim: The staging API without authentication was acceptable because it mirrored the production environment and contained mostly synthetic data (248,897 dummy records).
claimsVsReality.reality: The staging database contained personal data of 3,916 real users mixed with synthetic data, and an unauthenticated API accessible over the internet exposed those real users' records for at least 5 months without any access controls.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had data protection policies and practices in place for technical staff.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had only informal onboarding briefings about system rules and code standards—no actual data protection policies or practices existed for any employees, demonstrating fundamental misunderstanding of data protection obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organisations to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal of personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Allowed employees to store copies of staging database containing real users' personal data on personal devices without implementing security requirements
violations: Allowed employees to store copies of staging database containing real users' personal data on personal devices without implementing security requirements
Failed to enforce security measures on personal devices, merely instructing employees not to use weak passwords
Failed to implement authentication for staging API despite it being accessible over the internet and containing personal data of real users
Mixed real personal data with synthetic data in staging environment without appropriate security controls

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12(a) – Accountability Obligation requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to develop and implement data protection policies or practices for any employees, particularly those with access to user data
violations: Failed to develop and implement data protection policies or practices for any employees, particularly those with access to user data
Provided only system briefings and code standards during onboarding, which do not constitute data protection policies
Failed to provide guidance to employees on how to comply with PDPA in carrying out work functions

outcome: The Commission imposed a financial penalty of $12,500 (reduced from an initially intended higher amount due to the organisation's financial hardship). The organisation was directed to: (1) develop and implement internal data protection policies and practices compliant with PDPA within 60 days; (2) ensure no local copies of databases are stored on personal computers of any employees within 60 days; (3) notify the Commission within 1 week of completion. The organisation was also required to pay the penalty within 30 days, with interest accruing under the Rules of Court for any unpaid balance.
companyNow: The company's current status is unclear. As of the 2022 decision, PINC Interactive was operating at a financial loss and required to implement significant data protection remediation measures under PDPA enforcement.
dataType: name, username, email address, contact number, password hash

companyDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. (formerly Vodafone Group España) is a leading telecommunications provider in Spain offering mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services to millions of customers.
companyLongDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. (formerly Vodafone Group España) is a leading telecommunications provider in Spain offering mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services to millions of customers.
caseDescription: Vodafone España failed to verify the identity of a person who obtained a duplicate SIM card for a customer's line without authorization. This enabled SIM swapping fraud, allowing unauthorized access to the customer's mobile line and attempted account takeover. The company's inadequate identity verification procedures violated GDPR Article 6 requirements for lawful processing.
violationSummary: Vodafone failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures (Art. 32) to prevent unauthorized access to customer data via SIM duplication. The insecure process allowed a third party to obtain control of personal data (mobile line) without consent, violating the lawfulness principle.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Vodafone staff issued a duplicate SIM card to an unauthorized third party without verifying the person's identity or obtaining the customer's consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: An attacker gained control of the customer's phone line, attempted to port it to another carrier.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone stated that 'all SIM changes realized by Vodafone surpass the security policy established for these effects' and that the company had implemented policies requiring ID verification for in-store SIM changes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite security policies on paper, Vodafone staff facilitated a SIM duplication to an unauthorized person without verifying their identity against the account holder's ID, demonstrating the policies were not effectively enforced.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone claimed the physical distributor would be penalized for failure to obtain and retain identity documentation, shifting responsibility downstream.
claimsVsReality.reality: The responsibility for ensuring lawful processing rests with Vodafone as the controller; inadequate training, monitoring, or enforcement of partner compliance does not eliminate Vodafone's legal liability for the unlawful processing that occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data be lawful only if it meets at least one of the specified conditions: consent, contract necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone processed the customer's personal data (mobile line credentials, identity details) through SIM duplication without the customer's consent and without any lawful basis, enabling unauthorized third-party access.
violations: Vodafone processed the customer's personal data (mobile line credentials, identity details) through SIM duplication without the customer's consent and without any lawful basis, enabling unauthorized third-party access.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone failed to implement adequate identity verification controls for SIM duplication requests, allowing an unauthorized person to obtain a duplicate SIM without authentication, enabling fraud.
violations: Vodafone failed to implement adequate identity verification controls for SIM duplication requests, allowing an unauthorized person to obtain a duplicate SIM without authentication, enabling fraud.

outcome: Vodafone made voluntary payment of €56,000 on 21 October 2022, equivalent to one 20% reduction from the proposed €70,000 penalty. The company waived administrative appeals. The procedure was terminated under Article 85 of Law 39/2015. Vodafone committed to additional security measures including mandatory ID photocopying for in-store SIM changes (since May 2019) and €300 penalties for non-compliant distributors.
companyNow: Vodafone España remains a major Spanish telecom operator, part of Vodafone Group plc. The company has since implemented enhanced SIM security protocols and fraud detection measures.
dataType: Mobile phone number, SIM card access, personal identity data

companyDescription: Direct Clothing Co. (UK) Limited is a retail clothing company operating an e-commerce website from which it collects customer payment card information.
companyLongDescription: Direct Clothing Co. (UK) Limited is a retail clothing company operating an e-commerce website from which it collects customer payment card information.
caseDescription: Direct Clothing Co. failed to implement adequate security measures to protect customer payment card data on its website. A malicious actor exploited a WordPress vulnerability to inject code that harvested payment card details from customers. The company had not applied security patches since February 2019, conducted no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing, and lacked a contractual security arrangement with its third-party IT provider.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures required by GDPR Article 32, directly enabling unauthorized access to payment card data through known exploitable vulnerabilities.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Direct Clothing Co. failed to apply security patches or updates since at least February 2019, conducted no vulnerability scanning or penetration tests.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customer payment card details were stolen when attackers exploited unpatched WordPress vulnerabilities on the company's website, exposing customers to fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: A third-party IT provider was responsible for the security and maintenance of the affected website.
claimsVsReality.reality: No contractual security agreement was actually in place with any third-party provider at the time of the incident.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Direct Clothing Co. failed to apply security patches or updates since at least February 2019, contrary to NCSC guidance recommending regular vulnerability scanning.
violations: Direct Clothing Co. failed to apply security patches or updates since at least February 2019, contrary to NCSC guidance recommending regular vulnerability scanning.
The company conducted no vulnerability scanning or penetration testing despite NCSC guidance recommending regular scanning.
The company lacked a contractual security agreement with its third-party IT provider, resulting in no regular patching, testing, or monitoring.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires implementing measures to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Direct Clothing Co. failed to maintain system integrity and availability by allowing WordPress vulnerabilities to remain unpatched, enabling malicious code injection that compromised customer payment data.
violations: Direct Clothing Co. failed to maintain system integrity and availability by allowing WordPress vulnerabilities to remain unpatched, enabling malicious code injection that compromised customer payment data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(d) requires a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Direct Clothing Co. did not conduct any vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, or regular security assessments of its website systems.
violations: Direct Clothing Co. did not conduct any vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, or regular security assessments of its website systems.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand to Direct Clothing Co. (UK) Limited under Article 58(2)(b) of the GDPR. The company was advised to implement the security guidance provided and warned that if further incidents or complaints are reported, further formal regulatory action may be considered. The matter is now closed, but the ICO reserves the right to revisit if new information emerges.
dataType: Payment card details, financial data

companyDescription: South Wales Police is the territorial police force responsible for policing South Wales, serving a large civilian population across multiple local authority areas. The force is a public sector law enforcement organisation accountable to the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner.
companyLongDescription: South Wales Police is the territorial police force responsible for policing South Wales, serving a large civilian population across multiple local authority areas. The force is a public sector law enforcement organisation accountable to the Office of the Police and Crime Commissioner.
caseDescription: South Wales Police disclosed the identities of two vulnerable women who had applied for information under domestic violence and child sexual offender disclosure schemes. Officers carelessly revealed their identities during conversations with offenders and while performing safeguarding duties, causing significant distress. The ICO found the force failed to provide adequate data protection training and had no proper guidance on handling such sensitive disclosures.
violationSummary: The core violation was breach of confidentiality under data protection law. Sensitive personal data (identities of domestic violence and child protection applicants) was disclosed without authorization to third parties (offenders), breaching the duty of confidentiality and appropriate security measures required under law enforcement data processing.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Police officers disclosed the identities of two women to individuals they had sought protection information about through domestic violence and child sex offender disclosure schemes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two vulnerable women seeking safety assessments had their identities exposed to the very people they feared, causing documented emotional distress.

claimsVsReality.claim: Officers were appropriately trained and aware of their obligations under DVDS and CSODS schemes when dealing with offenders and applicants
claimsVsReality.reality: First officer had received no DVDS training and minimal Sexual Offences Liaison training, with no data protection training since July 2018. Second officer had no CSODS training since 2015 and no data protection training since December 2018.

claimsVsReality.claim: South Wales Police had implemented improvements in data protection practices following ICO audit recommendations in September 2019
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite ICO audit identifying lack of formal training programme and warning of increased breach risk, South Wales Police failed to implement adequate training before both incidents occurred in February and April 2020.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clear procedures existed to ensure confidentiality of applicant identities under domestic violence and child protection disclosure schemes
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented processes or guidance existed for officers regarding what could and could not be communicated, particularly where MAPPA and DVDS overlapped, resulting in confused officers making disclosures.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 40, Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 requires that data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: South Wales Police failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data by disclosing applicant identities to offenders without authorization
violations: South Wales Police failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data by disclosing applicant identities to offenders without authorization
Officers and staff failed to act in a manner expected to preserve identity of data subjects
Police failed to provide full and appropriate training to officers and staff on handling sensitive disclosures under DVDS and CSODS schemes
No documented processes or guidance existed for officers regarding confidentiality obligations when MAPPA and DVDS overlapped
Officers had not received relevant data protection training (2018 and 2015 respectively) or scheme-specific training (DVDS, CSODS)
Prior ICO audit in September 2019 identified lack of formal training programme but South Wales Police failed to remediate before these incidents occurred

outcome: ICO issued a formal reprimand to South Wales Police under Schedule 13(2) of the DPA 2018 for infringement of Section 40, Part 3. The force is required to: (1) fully implement all recommendations from the Independent Office for Police Conduct (IOPC) report; (2) establish clear lines of communication and guidance on disclosure responsibilities across all officers and staff; (3) conduct a comprehensive review of data protection reporting procedures to ensure incidents are reported within 72 hours; (4) implement comprehensive data protection and scheme-specific training for all relevant officers. The ICO noted it will revisit the matter and consider further formal regulatory action if additional incidents or complaints are reported. The matter is closed but subject to ongoing monitoring.
companyNow: South Wales Police continues operations as the regional police force for South Wales. The force has begun implementing recommendations from the IOPC and ICO investigations but remains under ICO monitoring.
dataType: Identity information, personal information of domestic violence and child protection applicants

companyDescription: Sjukhusstyrelsen i Region Uppsala is a Swedish regional public authority that oversees hospital administration for Akademiska sjukhuset (Academic Hospital), providing specialized healthcare services including international patient care.
companyLongDescription: Sjukhusstyrelsen i Region Uppsala is a Swedish regional public authority that oversees hospital administration for Akademiska sjukhuset (Academic Hospital), providing specialized healthcare services including international patient care.
caseDescription: Sjukhusstyrelsen sent sensitive patient health data via unencrypted email over the internet to patients and referrers in third countries, and stored this data in Outlook. The organization failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures to protect health data, despite knowing of the risks through its own guidelines.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to protect sensitive personal data (health information) from unauthorized access or disclosure, exposing it to interception during transmission and unauthorized access in storage.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Sent approximately 500–1,000 unencrypted email messages monthly containing patient health records to recipients in third countries.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 300 patients annually had sensitive health data exposed via unencrypted internet transmission where unauthorized parties could intercept it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sjukhusstyrelsen used Microsoft's standard TLS encryption settings for email transmission to protect data in transit.
claimsVsReality.reality: The encryption used (opportunistic TLS 1.2) fell back to unencrypted transmission when recipient servers lacked TLS support, and the organization did not verify or control how many sensitive patient emails were actually sent unencrypted over the internet.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Uppsala's guidelines permitted sensitive patient data transmission via email.
claimsVsReality.reality: Region Uppsala's own email handling guidelines explicitly stated that sensitive personal data must not be communicated via email, yet Sjukhusstyrelsen continued the practice systematically for over one year.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sjukhusstyrelsen transmitted unencrypted patient health data over open internet, exposing it to unauthorized access and interception by third parties.
violations: Sjukhusstyrelsen transmitted unencrypted patient health data over open internet, exposing it to unauthorized access and interception by third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing, and the risks to individuals' rights and freedoms.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization used opportunistic TLS encryption that fell back to unencrypted transmission when recipient email servers did not support TLS; stored sensitive patient health data in Outlook, an internet-exposed email system inherently unsuitable for long-term storage of sensitive data; did not verify how many emails were sent unencrypted despite knowing about the vulnerability.
violations: The organization used opportunistic TLS encryption that fell back to unencrypted transmission when recipient email servers did not support TLS; stored sensitive patient health data in Outlook, an internet-exposed email system inherently unsuitable for long-term storage of sensitive data; did not verify how many emails were sent unencrypted despite knowing about the vulnerability.

outcome: Sjukhusstyrelsen must pay 1,600,000 SEK administrative penalty for violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32. The decision found that the organization systematically transmitted and stored sensitive health data without adequate protection for over 12 months despite awareness of security risks through its own regional guidelines. The organization implemented a file encryption solution in September 2019 after the incident was reported. The decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: Sjukhusstyrelsen i Region Uppsala continues operations as a regional hospital administration board in Sweden. The organization has implemented file encryption measures following the May 2019 incident and is undergoing systematic improvement efforts.
dataType: Health data, patient names, contact information, identification numbers

companyDescription: North Yorkshire Police is a law enforcement agency responsible for policing North Yorkshire in England. The force handles criminal prosecutions, including driving offences, through the Single Justice Procedure.
companyLongDescription: North Yorkshire Police is a law enforcement agency responsible for policing North Yorkshire in England. The force handles criminal prosecutions, including driving offences, through the Single Justice Procedure.
caseDescription: North Yorkshire Police generated a duplicate Single Justice Procedure (SJP) for a driving offence on 3 July 2018, resulting in a data subject being convicted twice of the same offence. The individual received a second fine and driving disqualification. Although the disqualification was later removed, the police failed to notify their compliance team of the breach until 31 August 2021 (nearly 3 years later), delaying ICO notification until 8 September 2021—well beyond the 72-hour reporting requirement.
violationSummary: Lack of adequate safeguards and processes to ensure accuracy of sensitive criminal justice data, combined with failure to detect and prevent duplicate processing of law enforcement data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: North Yorkshire Police generated a duplicate Single Justice Procedure record for a driving offense on 3 July 2018 without documented processes to check for existing records before creating new.
whyTheyWereWrong: A person was wrongly convicted twice for the same offense, paid duplicate fines and prosecution costs, suffered a driving disqualification due to 'totting up' on false records.

claimsVsReality.claim: The disqualification had minimal impact on the data subject as they had already decided not to renew their driving licence.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data subject suffered significant financial loss from paying two fines and prosecution costs, and the stress from the breach exacerbated an existing eye condition with negative effects on eyesight.

claimsVsReality.claim: NYP had suitable data protection processes in place for generating SJPs.
claimsVsReality.reality: There was no documented process in place requiring staff to check for duplicates before generating a new SJP, and no specific DPA 2018 training had been provided to staff prior to the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Part 3, Chapter 2, Section 38(1) requires that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be accurate and kept up to date, and every reasonable step must be taken to ensure inaccurate data is erased or rectified without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: NYP generated a duplicate SJP without documented process to check for existing records, resulting in inaccurate duplicate conviction data
violations: NYP generated a duplicate SJP without documented process to check for existing records, resulting in inaccurate duplicate conviction data
No specific data protection training was provided to staff on the importance of accurate recording of personal data prior to the breach

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA 2018 Part 3, Chapter 4, Section 67(1) requires controllers to notify the Commissioner of a personal data breach without undue delay and where feasible not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it.
regulatoryFindings.description: NYP became aware of the breach on 4 October 2018 but multiple staff failed to notify the Compliance Team
violations: NYP became aware of the breach on 4 October 2018 but multiple staff failed to notify the Compliance Team
Compliance Team only learned of the breach on 31 August 2021 (nearly 3 years later) upon notification of a civil claim
ICO was not notified until 8 September 2021, approximately 3 years after the breach occurred

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand to North Yorkshire Police under Schedule 13(2) of the DPA 2018. NYP has implemented remedial measures including: a documented SJP process with additional steps to avoid duplicate processing, a mandatory Managing Information e-learning package for all staff, and governance improvements. The Commissioner recommended NYP review data breach reporting policies, implement contingency planning for data protection issues, and ensure regular data protection training for all employees. The matter is now closed, but further incidents may trigger additional formal regulatory action.
companyNow: North Yorkshire Police continues to operate as the police force for the North Yorkshire area in England. Following this investigation, the organisation has implemented documented processes and enhanced training to prevent similar incidents.
dataType: Criminal offence data, driving offence records, conviction data, personal identifiers

companyDescription: Grindr LLC operates a location-based social networking and dating application primarily used by LGBTQ+ individuals worldwide, with a significant user base in the United Kingdom.
companyLongDescription: Grindr LLC operates a location-based social networking and dating application primarily used by LGBTQ+ individuals worldwide, with a significant user base in the United Kingdom.
caseDescription: Grindr failed to provide transparent and clear privacy information to UK users regarding how their personal and special category data was being processed and shared with advertising partners. The company's privacy policy contained contradictions and omissions about data sharing practices, legal bases for processing, and the distinction between different categories of personal data. The ICO found systematic failures in transparency compliance under UK GDPR Article 5(1)(a).
violationSummary: Grindr disclosed personal and special category data to third-party advertisers without providing clear, transparent information to users about the scope, legal basis, and recipients of such disclosures, violating the transparency principle.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Grindr's Privacy Policy contradicted its actual data-sharing practices by claiming it only shared user data with advertisers based on consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of UK users, including vulnerable LGBTQ+ individuals, were unable to understand how their intimate personal and special category data was being collected, processed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grindr stated that user personal data is only shared with advertising partners on the basis of consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Grindr's Privacy and Cookie Policy table explicitly referenced 'legitimate interest' as a legal basis for sharing data with third-party ad partners in rows 5 and 9.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grindr stated that it does not share users' profile information for advertising purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Profile information was listed in multiple rows (5, 9, 21, 22) of the 'EEA and U.K Legal Basis For Processing' table as being shared for advertising.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grindr stated that IP address and advertising ID do not constitute personal data and therefore should not be reflected in privacy information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The ICO determined that IP address and advertising ID may constitute personal data in certain circumstances (e.g., when combined with other data) and must be disclosed transparently.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grindr stated that it does not 'process' special category data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Grindr processes special category data through voluntary user input and storage on its platform, regardless of whether it shares such data with third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(a) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Grindr failed to provide effective and transparent privacy information to UK data subjects regarding the processing of their personal data, including contradictions between stated and actual data sharing practices, unclear disclosure of profile information processing, and insufficient clarity on special category data handling and third-party recipients.
violations: Grindr failed to provide effective and transparent privacy information to UK data subjects regarding the processing of their personal data, including contradictions between stated and actual data sharing practices, unclear disclosure of profile information processing, and insufficient clarity on special category data handling and third-party recipients.

outcome: The ICO issued Grindr with a formal reprimand under Article 58 of the UK GDPR. The company was required to amend its Privacy and Cookie Policy and 'EEA and U.K Legal Basis For Processing' table to eliminate contradictions and clarify actual data sharing practices. Grindr must provide users with clearer information about: the distinction between personal and special category data; data flow restrictions with advertising partners; the full list of third-party recipients; information collected via third-party sign-up processes; and SDK integration security measures. The company was instructed to ensure special category data remains subject to appropriate safeguards and to submit a progress update to the ICO by 26 January 2023. The ICO indicated that further breaches could result in formal regulatory action.
companyNow: Grindr LLC remains operational as a dating application for LGBTQ+ users globally. Following the ICO investigation, the company has faced continued scrutiny over data privacy practices and has made updates to its privacy policies.
dataType: Sexual orientation, profile information, location data, IP address, advertising ID, personal data, special category data
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, transparency

company: Secretary of State for the Home Department (Home Office)
companyDescription: The Home Office is the UK government department responsible for immigration, crime, policing, counterterrorism, and related policy. It processes sensitive personal data from millions of individuals seeking asylum, visas, and other immigration services.
companyLongDescription: The Home Office is the UK government department responsible for immigration, crime, policing, counterterrorism, and related policy. It processes sensitive personal data from millions of individuals seeking asylum, visas, and other immigration services.
caseDescription: The Home Office failed to respond to Subject Access Requests within statutory timescales under UK GDPR. Only 45.73% of SARs received between April 2020 and December 2021 were answered within the required one-month deadline, leaving 20,862 requests unanswered. The ICO issued a reprimand and required compliance improvements and progress reporting.
violationSummary: The Home Office excluded data subjects from their statutory right to access personal data by failing to respond within required timescales, preventing individuals from exercising their rights under Article 15 of UK GDPR.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The Home Office failed to respond to 54.27% of Subject Access Requests within the required one-month statutory deadline, leaving 20,862 requests unanswered between April 2020 and December 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: 20,862 individuals were denied timely access to their personal data held by the Home Office, preventing them from understanding what information the government held about them.

claimsVsReality.claim: Home Office had implemented a Subject Access Request Unit (SARU) Improvement Plan to address SAR compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Home Office failed to improve its SAR compliance during the investigation period; SARU continued to have a backlog of cases and did not meet statutory timescales for the vast majority of requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires a controller to provide information on action taken on a request under Articles 15–22 to the data subject without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt (or within two months for complex requests), with notice of any extension.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office did not provide responses within the statutory one-month deadline for 54.27% of requests (20,862 cases) during the review period.
violations: Home Office did not provide responses within the statutory one-month deadline for 54.27% of requests (20,862 cases) during the review period.
Failed to inform data subjects of extensions or reasons for delay as required.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data is being processed and, if so, access to that personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office denied thousands of individuals their right to access their own personal data by failing to respond within statutory timescales.
violations: Home Office denied thousands of individuals their right to access their own personal data by failing to respond within statutory timescales.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires a controller to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office failed to provide copies of personal data to requesters within required timeframes, breaching the right to receive data in accessible form.
violations: Home Office failed to provide copies of personal data to requesters within required timeframes, breaching the right to receive data in accessible form.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand under Article 58 UK GDPR. The Home Office was required to: (1) take steps to ensure Subject Access Requests are responded to within statutory deadlines in line with Articles 12(3), 15(1), and 15(3); (2) ensure adequate staff resources are in place to process and respond to SARs. The Home Office was required to provide progress updates to the ICO three months from 21 September 2022 (by 21 December 2022) and again at six months (by 21 March 2023). The ICO indicated it may pursue further formal regulatory action if additional information comes to light or further incidents occur. The matter is now considered closed.
companyNow: The Home Office remains the UK government department responsible for immigration, justice, and policing policy. As a government ministry, it continues to process Subject Access Requests but faces ongoing compliance scrutiny.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Requests (SAR) — nature not specified in findings
