regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 – Security of Processing: Controllers and processors must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk, including ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: No security controls were in place to manage risks of using private correspondence channels; platforms lacked authentication requirements, remote access controls, or encryption adequate for government data.
violations: No security controls were in place to manage risks of using private correspondence channels; platforms lacked authentication requirements, remote access controls, or encryption adequate for government data.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand to DHSC under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The decision was based on findings that private communication channels were in regular use, most messages contained personal data, and no appropriate controls existed to manage processing risks. No monetary penalty was imposed. The ICO recommended eight remedial actions: (1) review security and access controls on platforms (Google Mail, Hotmail, WhatsApp); (2) assess platform terms and privacy notices; (3) require users to adhere to NCSC security guidance including two-factor authentication; (4) review secure bring-your-own-device options; (5) limit situations where private accounts can be used; (6) establish deletion protocols for information once added to official record; (7) ensure personal device use adheres to data minimization; (8) extend DHSC email policies to all @dhsc.gov.uk account holders including Ministers and Non-Executive Directors. DHSC was required to provide progress updates by 14 October 2022 and 6 January 2023, with responses copied to the DHSC Select Committee for public transparency. The investigation was closed after these findings.
companyNow: The Department of Health and Social Care continues to operate as a UK government department. Following this investigation, it has been required to implement enhanced data protection controls and align policies across all staff levels regarding use of private communication channels.
dataType: Names, contact details, professional work information, medical data, political party membership
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 25 – Data Protection by Design and Default

caseDescription: A Deputy Minister/political figure sent unsolicited SMS and email messages to a citizen for political campaign purposes without prior consent. The messages included greetings and campaign promotion based on personal contact details obtained during the citizen's formal complaint to the ministry. The Authority found the data processing violated electronic communications protection laws and GDPR requirements for political communications.
violationSummary: The company reused personal data collected in a professional/governmental context (work-related complaint) for an unrelated secondary purpose (political campaign communications) without lawful basis, notice, or consent.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A political figure sent unsolicited SMS and email messages promoting his electoral candidacy to a citizen whose contact information was collected during an official government complaint.
whyTheyWereWrong: The citizen received unwanted political campaign messages on his personal phone and email over multiple years without being informed his data would be used this way.

claimsVsReality.claim: The contact details were provided to a 'political office' of the Deputy Minister and political communications are lawful political activity.
claimsVsReality.reality: The contact details were provided in the context of a formal work-related labor complaint to the ministry as a whole, not to any political entity; the complainant did not know a separate political office existed and had no notice that work-related contact would be used for campaign purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Compliant removal of the number from mailing lists within two weeks shows cooperation and minimal harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: The removal occurred only after the formal complaint was filed with the Authority and only after explicit objection; the respondent had sent multiple unwanted messages over 18+ months without any opt-out option or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 3471/2006 Art. 11: Electronic communications for direct marketing via SMS, email, or other electronic means without human intervention require prior explicit consent from the subscriber, with limited exceptions for existing customers.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent sent multiple SMS and email messages for political campaign purposes without demonstrating prior consent of the recipient
violations: Respondent sent multiple SMS and email messages for political campaign purposes without demonstrating prior consent of the recipient
No evidence of lawful basis for reusing contact details collected in work-related context for political communications

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12: The controller must provide information regarding processing of personal data without undue delay and in any case within one month of request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent failed to respond to the data subject's requests for deletion and termination of unwanted communications
violations: Respondent failed to respond to the data subject's requests for deletion and termination of unwanted communications
No timely notification or acknowledgment of the subject's objections to the processing

regulatoryFindings.act: Authority Guideline 1/2010 on Political Communications: Political communications via electronic means without human intervention require prior consent unless contact details were obtained through prior similar contact and data subject was informed with opportunity to object.
regulatoryFindings.description: Initial contact was work-related (labor union complaint), not political in nature; reuse for political purposes constitutes different secondary use
violations: Initial contact was work-related (labor union complaint), not political in nature; reuse for political purposes constitutes different secondary use
No evidence that complainant was informed contact details would be used for political communications
No easy mechanism provided to object at time of collection or in each message

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority found the respondent liable for violations of Art. 11 of Greek Law 3471/2006 and Art. 12 of GDPR. The Authority imposed an administrative monetary penalty of €2,000, finding that the political figure failed to obtain required consent for reusing work-related contact information for campaign communications. The respondent was required to cease processing and comply with data subject rights. The respondent did eventually remove the complainant from distribution lists within two weeks of the formal objection, satisfying the substantive remedy in practice.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, email addresses

companyDescription: Factor Energía is an electrical energy commercializer operating in Spain, particularly in Catalonia, that markets power supply services to residential and commercial customers.
companyLongDescription: Factor Energía is an electrical energy commercializer operating in Spain, particularly in Catalonia, that markets power supply services to residential and commercial customers.
caseDescription: Factor Energía sent unsolicited direct marketing postal communications to non-customers containing their personal data (name, surname, address) without a valid legal basis. The company claimed data came from public sources but could not specify the exact source, and failed to obtain prior consent or demonstrate legitimate interest that outweighed individuals' rights. The treatment lacked proportionality as non-personalized marketing could have been achieved without processing personal identifiers.
violationSummary: Company processed personal data (names, addresses) obtained from unspecified public sources for a purpose (unsolicited direct marketing) that individuals had no reason to expect, constituting impermissible secondary use without proper legal basis.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Factor Energía sent 42,670 unsolicited postal advertisements to non-customers in Catalonia using their names, addresses, and consumption data without legal authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: Non-customers received targeted marketing communications revealing the company possessed their personal identifying information without consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data were obtained from public sources in accordance with data protection law and used only for legitimate marketing purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company could not identify or specify which public sources were actually used; data sources remain unverified. Processing lacked a valid legal basis under GDPR Article 6(1).

claimsVsReality.claim: Postal communications are less invasive than phone or email marketing and pose minimal impact on recipients.
claimsVsReality.reality: Receipt of personalized postal communications with name, surname, and address from an unknown company creates legitimate concern about data security and control, and the channel's reduced invasiveness does not overcome the lack of legal basis or prior relationship.

claimsVsReality.claim: Individuals should reasonably expect to receive unsolicited marketing from companies in the energy sector.
claimsVsReality.reality: Individuals have no reasonable expectation of receiving personalized marketing communications from a company with which they have no prior contact or relationship, particularly when the source of their data is unknown to them.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data is lawful only if it meets at least one of six conditions: consent, contract necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests (where those interests do not override individuals' rights and freedoms).
regulatoryFindings.description: Factor Energía processed names, surnames, and postal addresses of non-customers without consent, contractual necessity, or legal obligation.
violations: Factor Energía processed names, surnames, and postal addresses of non-customers without consent, contractual necessity, or legal obligation.

The company failed the legitimate interest balancing test because: (1) the interest was non-urgent customer acquisition; (2) individuals had no reasonable expectation of being contacted; (3) no prior customer relationship existed; (4) less invasive alternatives existed (anonymous mailings); (5) power imbalance between consumer and commercial entity; and (6) individuals received communications raising uncertainty about data source and control.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires processing to be lawful, fair, and transparent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Processing was not transparent: company could not identify the actual source of personal data despite claiming public sources.
violations: Processing was not transparent: company could not identify the actual source of personal data despite claiming public sources.
Processing was not fair: individuals had no reasonable expectation their data would be obtained and used for unsolicited marketing by a company with which they had no relationship.

outcome: Factor Energía paid a voluntary penalty of €24,000 (reduced from €40,000 by applying two 20% reductions: one for early recognition of responsibility and one for voluntary payment). This payment terminated the administrative procedure and constituted admission of responsibility. The company is required to adjust its data processing practices to comply with GDPR.
dataType: Name, surname, postal address, technical supply point data (CUPS), consumption habits (estimated)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) – Legitimate interest (failed balancing test)

companyDescription: Optionis Group Limited is a payroll and HR services company based in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, UK, operating from Kd Tower, Cotterells.
companyLongDescription: Optionis Group Limited is a payroll and HR services company based in Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, UK, operating from Kd Tower, Cotterells.
caseDescription: Optionis Group Limited failed to implement appropriate security measures to protect personal data, resulting in unauthorized access to employee financial records. The company lacked multi-factor authentication, had no clear Bring Your Own Device policy, and maintained inadequate account lockout controls. The breach exposed sensitive personal data and took 11 months to notify affected individuals.
violationSummary: The core failure was inadequate technical and organisational security measures, resulting in a data breach affecting personal data integrity and confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Optionis Group Limited failed to implement multi-factor authentication, lacked a clear Bring Your Own Device policy, had inadequate account lockout procedures.
whyTheyWereWrong: An unauthorized attacker gained access to employee payroll systems and personal financial data because basic security controls were absent, exposing employees' sensitive information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's work-from-home arrangements were necessary due to Covid-19 pandemic response
claimsVsReality.reality: Work-from-home arrangements had been in place for approximately 2 years before the incident, so Covid-19 was not accepted as a sufficient mitigation for inadequate security measures

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: Optionis did not implement multi-factor authentication for user accounts
violations: Optionis did not implement multi-factor authentication for user accounts
Optionis had no clear Bring Your Own Device (BYOD) policy
Optionis maintained an inadequate account lockout policy
Optionis lacked appropriate organisational measures to ensure confidentiality and integrity of systems

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) of the UK GDPR requires that the controller and processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Optionis failed to implement security measures aligned with NCSC guidance on account lockout and multi-factor authentication
violations: Optionis failed to implement security measures aligned with NCSC guidance on account lockout and multi-factor authentication
Optionis did not deploy appropriate security measures despite extensive guidance being available
Security measures were inadequate relative to the risk of unauthorised access to personal financial data

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand to Optionis Group Limited under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner considered remedial steps taken by the company, including: commissioning third-party cyber security investigation, implementing comprehensive security policies, deploying 24/7 Managed Detection and Response (EDR) covering all corporate devices, enabling multi-factor authentication on user accounts, enforcing conditional access on user accounts, and correcting all underpayments to individuals by 6 February 2022. No monetary penalty was imposed.
dataType: Financial data, personal employee information

companyDescription: Individual child psychologist providing psychological therapy and assessment services to minors in Greece. Maintained patient records in structured files including session notes, diagnoses, and treatment protocols.
companyLongDescription: Individual child psychologist providing psychological therapy and assessment services to minors in Greece. Maintained patient records in structured files including session notes, diagnoses, and treatment protocols.
caseDescription: A child psychologist failed to properly respond to a parent's access request for their child's therapy records and medical information within required timeframes. The psychologist provided incomplete information late and subsequently ignored multiple orders from the Greek Data Protection Authority to fulfill the access request in full.
violationSummary: The psychologist failed to establish and maintain proper data access procedures, failing to respond to lawful access requests and subsequently failing to comply with regulatory enforcement orders, demonstrating inadequate data processing security and governance.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Child psychologist B failed to provide a parent with complete access to therapy records within legal timeframes, delivering scientific findings.
whyTheyWereWrong: A custodial parent was denied timely access to their child's medical and psychological information, preventing them from understanding their child's condition.

claimsVsReality.claim: Psychologist (via counsel) claimed to have called the parent multiple times to inform him about the requested information in satisfaction of the access right.
claimsVsReality.reality: The parent's attorney categorically denied this claim during the hearing; psychologist provided no evidence (such as call logs or witness testimony) to support the assertion.

claimsVsReality.claim: Psychologist implied the information had already been provided to the parent through court proceedings in the ongoing custody dispute.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Authority found no evidence that the requested scientific findings and diagnostic information were actually submitted to courts, and provision to courts does not satisfy the GDPR obligation to respond to direct data subject requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires the data controller to demonstrate accountability and implement measures ensuring lawful, fair processing compliant with GDPR principles.
regulatoryFindings.description: Psychologist failed to establish procedures to respond to access requests within the one-month timeframe mandated by Art. 12(3)
violations: Psychologist failed to establish procedures to respond to access requests within the one-month timeframe mandated by Art. 12(3)
Provided incomplete information and scientific conclusions only after Authority intervention

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12(3) requires data controllers to provide information and take action on requests (Arts. 15-22) without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt.
regulatoryFindings.description: Initial access request submitted May 5, 2020; incomplete response provided July 23, 2020 (79 days late)
violations: Initial access request submitted May 5, 2020; incomplete response provided July 23, 2020 (79 days late)
Did not provide scientific findings or diagnostic information until forced by Authority

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data concerning them is being processed and to access such data including purposes, categories, recipients, and retention periods.
regulatoryFindings.description: Psychologist refused to disclose therapeutic diagnosis, clinical findings, and scientific conclusions regarding child's condition and treatment necessity
violations: Psychologist refused to disclose therapeutic diagnosis, clinical findings, and scientific conclusions regarding child's condition and treatment necessity
Failed to explain rationale for ongoing intensive therapy despite parent's direct request

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 31 requires data controllers and processors to cooperate with supervisory authorities upon request when the authority exercises its duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ignored three separate Authority requests (July 2020, October 2020, June 2021) for clarifications and information about access request compliance
violations: Ignored three separate Authority requests (July 2020, October 2020, June 2021) for clarifications and information about access request compliance
Failed to respond to mandatory cooperation orders even after explicit notice of this independent obligation

outcome: The Authority found the psychologist violated GDPR Articles 12(3), 15, and 31. The psychologist issued a reprimand for late and incomplete provision of access information and ordered immediate fulfillment of the outstanding portions of the parent's request (scientific conclusions and information regarding the child's condition and treatment rationale). The Authority also found the psychologist violated Article 31 by failing to cooperate with the Authority's enforcement inquiries and imposed an administrative fine of €3,000. The psychologist is now under monitoring to ensure compliance with data access and cooperation obligations.
companyNow: Unknown current status of this private healthcare practitioner.
dataType: health data, psychotherapy records, medical information on a minor
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 12(3) - timely response to data subject requests
GDPR Art. 31 - cooperation with supervisory authority

companyDescription: Lillestrøm kommune is a Norwegian municipal government (local authority) providing public services including education, administration, and social services to residents of Lillestrøm in Akershus county.
companyLongDescription: Lillestrøm kommune is a Norwegian municipal government (local authority) providing public services including education, administration, and social services to residents of Lillestrøm in Akershus county.
caseDescription: Lillestrøm municipality accidentally published a document containing 10 attachments with protected personal data about students—including names, birth dates, parents' addresses, behavioral assessments, diagnoses, and special education records—on its public website for two days. The breach affected sensitive information about minors that was legally confidential under Norwegian law. No security review procedures or post-publication monitoring were in place to catch the error before a journalist discovered and reported it.
violationSummary: Sensitive personal data about minors was exposed to the public internet and accessed by unauthorized third parties due to inadequate technical and organizational security measures, failure to establish post-publication monitoring procedures, and lack of proper access controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Lillestrøm kommune published a government document with 10 attachments containing highly sensitive student data on its public website without proper access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: A journalist from local media accessed and potentially downloaded confidential student records including names, birthdates, parent addresses, behavioral assessments.

claimsVsReality.claim: Lillestrøm kommune had established multiple quality control procedures for documents published on its website and in the public journal.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the municipality had some routine procedures in place, they were insufficient. No post-publication monitoring procedures existed to catch errors after documents were published. The breach went undetected by the municipality and was only discovered by an external journalist, indicating fundamental gaps in the control framework.

claimsVsReality.claim: The municipality's quality controls (including two manual reviews by the document center) would catch errors in marking documents as confidential.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite two manual quality checks, the error was not detected internally. The 10 attachments containing student data remained marked as public and accessible on the internet for two days until discovered externally, demonstrating the inadequacy of the existing manual control procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection of confidentiality.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lillestrøm kommune failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures for documents published on its public website. No post-publication monitoring or review procedures existed to detect and prevent exposure of confidential data. The breach went undetected by the municipality and was only discovered by an external journalist, indicating deficient security protocols.
violations: Lillestrøm kommune failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures for documents published on its public website. No post-publication monitoring or review procedures existed to detect and prevent exposure of confidential data. The breach went undetected by the municipality and was only discovered by an external journalist, indicating deficient security protocols.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires a lawful basis for any processing of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lillestrøm kommune published personal data online that was prohibited from internet publication under Norwegian law (confidential data, special categories of data concerning minors). No lawful processing basis existed for making this data publicly accessible, and none of the alternative lawful basis criteria could be satisfied.
violations: Lillestrøm kommune published personal data online that was prohibited from internet publication under Norwegian law (confidential data, special categories of data concerning minors). No lawful processing basis existed for making this data publicly accessible, and none of the alternative lawful basis criteria could be satisfied.

regulatoryFindings.act: Norwegian Public Access Regulation § 7(2) prohibits publication on the internet of personal data subject to confidentiality requirements, birth numbers, and special categories of data per GDPR Articles 9 and 10.
regulatoryFindings.description: The municipality published student data including names, birthdates, parent addresses, behavioral assessments, and medical diagnoses (protected special categories) to the internet in violation of the explicit prohibition in the regulation, making confidential information accessible to journalists and the public.
violations: The municipality published student data including names, birthdates, parent addresses, behavioral assessments, and medical diagnoses (protected special categories) to the internet in violation of the explicit prohibition in the regulation, making confidential information accessible to journalists and the public.

outcome: Datatilsynet (Norwegian Data Protection Authority) imposed a fine of 300,000 NOK on Lillestrøm kommune for violations of data security and lawful basis requirements under GDPR and Norwegian law. The authority acknowledged the municipality's swift response in removing the documents and notifying affected individuals, but emphasized the seriousness of exposing confidential student data. The decision requires the municipality to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures, including post-publication monitoring procedures for documents containing sensitive personal data. The decision is subject to appeal to the Data Protection Board (Personvernnemnda) within three weeks. The authority noted the case has principled importance as a signal to all public sector organizations handling citizens' personal data about their obligations to maintain appropriate security levels.
companyNow: Lillestrøm kommune is a municipality in Akershus county, Norway. Following this enforcement action, the municipality has implemented corrective measures to prevent similar breaches, including enhanced security procedures and post-publication monitoring protocols for documents containing sensitive personal data.
dataType: Student names, birth dates, parent contact information, school behavioral assessments, test results, special education needs, diagnoses (dyslexia, ADHD), sensitive personal data about minors
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) – Lack of adequate technical and organizational measures to ensure confidentiality
GDPR Article 6 – Lack of lawful basis for processing
Norwegian Public Access Act (Offentleglova) § 10 and Public Access Regulation (Offentlegforskrifta) § 7 – prohibition on publishing confidential data online
Norwegian Administrative Code (Forvaltningsloven) § 13(1) – confidentiality of sensitive personal data

companyDescription: The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is the UK's central government department responsible for implementing defence policy, managing the Armed Forces, and overseeing defence operations. It processes large volumes of personnel data for military and civilian employees.
companyLongDescription: The Ministry of Defence (MoD) is the UK's central government department responsible for implementing defence policy, managing the Armed Forces, and overseeing defence operations. It processes large volumes of personnel data for military and civilian employees.
caseDescription: The UK's Ministry of Defence failed to process Subject Access Requests (SARs) within statutory timescales, leaving approximately 9,000 requests unresolved by April 2022. The Army Personnel Centre (APC), a key business unit, processed only 26% of its allocated 22,562 SARs within one month, compared to 75-100% compliance across other MoD units. Despite two recovery plans submitted in 2020 and 2022, the MoD did not address underlying resource shortages until July 2022.
violationSummary: The MoD systematically denied data subjects timely access to their personal data by failing to process SARs within statutory deadlines, excluding them from knowledge of what personal data was held about them.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The Ministry of Defence failed to respond to over 9,000 Subject Access Requests within the statutory one-month deadline.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of individuals requesting access to their personal data experienced delays of many months, with some waiting well over a year.

claimsVsReality.claim: The MoD submitted a Covid-19 recovery plan in July 2020 stating it would clear the SAR backlog by 2022.
claimsVsReality.reality: By March 2022, the backlog had grown to 6,600 requests, and by April 2022 it had reached 9,000 requests, demonstrating the plan failed to achieve its targets.

claimsVsReality.claim: The March 2022 revised recovery plan identified resourcing issues and the need for additional resources.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite identifying the problem in the revised plan, the MoD did not secure funding for additional resources until 1 July 2022, over three months later, with contractors not starting until September 2022.

claimsVsReality.claim: Other MoD business units achieved 75-100% SAR compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Army Personnel Centre achieved only 26% compliance on the same SARs during the same period, revealing a critical failure in one key unit rather than organization-wide dysfunction.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 12(3) requires that the controller provide information on action taken on a request to the data subject without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request.
regulatoryFindings.description: The MoD failed to respond to Subject Access Requests within one month, with the Army Personnel Centre processing only 26% of requests on time between April 2021 and May 2022.
violations: The MoD failed to respond to Subject Access Requests within one month, with the Army Personnel Centre processing only 26% of requests on time between April 2021 and May 2022.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(1) establishes the data subject's right to obtain from the controller confirmation of whether personal data concerning them is being processed and, where applicable, access to that personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The MoD's nine-month and longer delays in responding to SARs prevented data subjects from exercising their statutory right of access, leaving them without confirmation of what data was held about them.
violations: The MoD's nine-month and longer delays in responding to SARs prevented data subjects from exercising their statutory right of access, leaving them without confirmation of what data was held about them.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 15(3) requires the controller to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing in response to a data subject request.
regulatoryFindings.description: The MoD's 9,000-request backlog meant that data subjects could not obtain copies of their personal data within the required timeframe, directly breaching their right to a copy.
violations: The MoD's 9,000-request backlog meant that data subjects could not obtain copies of their personal data within the required timeframe, directly breaching their right to a copy.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand to the Ministry of Defence under Article 58 of the UK GDPR on 27 July 2022. The MoD was ordered to ensure all future SARs are responded to within one month (or two months for complex requests) and to maintain adequate staff resources. The MoD secured funding for 40 external contractors effective September 2022. The ICO requires monthly progress reports on the Army Personnel Centre's SAR backlog from August 2022 through March 2023, with recovery expected by March 2023. The ICO reserved the right to take further formal regulatory action if additional incidents or complaints emerge. The case is now closed.
companyNow: The Ministry of Defence is the UK's principal defence and security organization, operating under the Department for Defence. As of 2022, it continues to process defence, military operations, and personnel matters for the Armed Forces and civilian staff.
dataType: Personnel records, identity information, employment data

companyDescription: Cadena SER is Spain's largest radio broadcaster and a major Spanish media outlet providing news, sports, and entertainment programming to millions of listeners across Spain and Latin America.
companyLongDescription: Cadena SER is Spain's largest radio broadcaster and a major Spanish media outlet providing news, sports, and entertainment programming to millions of listeners across Spain and Latin America.
caseDescription: SER published an unedited audio recording of a rape victim's testimony during a high-profile trial on its website and podcast, making her voice – a personal data element – clearly identifiable. The company failed to apply the data minimization principle despite having the ability to distort the voice, and did so only after receiving an enforcement order from AEPD.
companyWorth: Unknown (Prisa Media is private; parent company valuation approximately €500M–€1B)
violationSummary: The company's publication of the victim's unmodified voice made her identifiable to the general public, violating the principle of data minimization and exposing her to serious harm despite having no journalistic need for the unedited audio.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: SER published an audio recording of a multiple rape victim's unmodified voice and testimony on its website and podcast to illustrate coverage of a high-profile trial.
whyTheyWereWrong: The undistorted voice made the victim identifiable to people in her community who did not know she was a victim, exposing her to recognition, stigmatization.

claimsVsReality.claim: SER claimed it made use of the constitutional right to freedom of information and treated the story in the public interest with full protection of the victim's rights.
claimsVsReality.reality: SER published the victim's unmodified voice, making her identifiable to a potentially unlimited audience; published unedited audio for ~30 days without conducting a risk assessment; only distorted the voice after AEPD's mandatory enforcement order.

claimsVsReality.claim: SER argued that the audio remained accessible for only a brief period and that minimal readers would have played the audio fragment.
claimsVsReality.reality: The video was published the day of the trial judgment and remained online for over one month; internet content has unlimited temporal persistence via search engines, archives, and social media; even if few individuals accessed it, data protection applies to all persons without exception.

claimsVsReality.claim: SER contended that identifying the victim through voice was unlikely because only those in her 'intimate family circle' who already knew her situation could recognize her voice.
claimsVsReality.reality: A case with high media coverage and contextual information (location, details of the crime) meant that acquaintances, colleagues, and extended family members could recognize her voice and connect it to her victim status, causing serious psychological harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: SER stated that the Court's communication office did not warn about data protection, implying the media had no independent obligation to protect the victim's data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Communication Protocol explicitly states that media bear responsibility for data protection of individuals in judicial content; absence of a court warning does not diminish the media's controller obligations under GDPR.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which it is processed ('data minimization').
regulatoryFindings.description: SER published the victim's unmodified voice without demonstrating necessity; the informational purpose (reporting trial proceedings) could have been achieved via voice distortion, transcription, or journalism describing the testimony without the audio.
violations: SER published the victim's unmodified voice without demonstrating necessity; the informational purpose (reporting trial proceedings) could have been achieved via voice distortion, transcription, or journalism describing the testimony without the audio.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) places responsibility ('accountability') on the controller to demonstrate compliance through risk assessments, technical measures (privacy by design), and proportional balancing of conflicting rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: SER conducted no pre-publication risk assessment despite the sensitive nature (sexual violence victim), high-profile status of case, and foreseeable harm; failed to implement standard voice-distortion techniques routinely used by media.
violations: SER conducted no pre-publication risk assessment despite the sensitive nature (sexual violence victim), high-profile status of case, and foreseeable harm; failed to implement standard voice-distortion techniques routinely used by media.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 85 permits reconciliation of freedom of information with data protection obligations, but neither right is absolute and must be balanced case-by-case; victims of violent sexual crimes warrant special protection.
regulatoryFindings.description: SER asserted absolute right to publish unedited audio under journalism privilege but failed to balance this against the victim's heightened vulnerability and the lack of necessity for undistorted voice.
violations: SER asserted absolute right to publish unedited audio under journalism privilege but failed to balance this against the victim's heightened vulnerability and the lack of necessity for undistorted voice.

outcome: AEPD imposed a €50,000 fine on SER for violating GDPR Article 5(1)(c). Confirmed provisional measures requiring SER to: (1) remove or distort the victim's voice from all web locations; (2) prevent re-uploading of unedited copies; (3) preserve original for evidence in ongoing police/judicial investigations. SER immediately distorted the voice upon receiving the enforcement order, demonstrating technical feasibility and lack of genuine necessity for the original.
companyNow: Cadena SER remains Spain's largest radio network, owned by Prisa Media. No indication of structural changes or additional sanctions have been imposed beyond the fine and compliance order.
dataType: Voice (audio), identity, sensitive data related to sexual violence victim
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 83.5(a) – Sanctions for violation of basic principles

companyDescription: ALI MARKET is a small food retail store operating in Spain with video surveillance systems for security purposes.
companyLongDescription: ALI MARKET is a small food retail store operating in Spain with video surveillance systems for security purposes.
caseDescription: ALI MARKET, a food retail store in Spain, operated video surveillance cameras without displaying required information notices, failed to provide customers with mandatory privacy disclosures about data processing, and did not maintain a processing activities register. A Civil Guard inspection on 13 June 2022 identified these violations; the company paid a reduced penalty of €360 on 15 October 2022 after recognizing responsibility.
violationSummary: ALI MARKET conducted systematic video surveillance of retail customers without adequate transparency measures, notice, or access to mandatory privacy information—the quintessential privacy harm of unchecked surveillance without informed consent or awareness.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: ALI MARKET installed video surveillance cameras in its food store without displaying required informational signage, failed to maintain a register of data processing activities.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' facial images and physical appearances were captured and processed without clear notice or transparency, leaving them unaware their biometric data was being recorded.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13 requires that when personal data are collected from the data subject, the controller must provide specified information in a transparent and comprehensible manner, including identity of controller, purposes of processing, and rights of the data subject (Arts. 15–22).
regulatoryFindings.description: ALI MARKET failed to display required informational signage identifying the video surveillance zone in a sufficiently visible location
violations: ALI MARKET failed to display required informational signage identifying the video surveillance zone in a sufficiently visible location
Provided no accessible printed information sheets detailing mandatory processing information or directing customers where to obtain such information

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 30 requires the controller to maintain a record of processing activities under its responsibility containing specified information about the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: ALI MARKET did not maintain or produce a Records of Processing Activities register for its video surveillance system
violations: ALI MARKET did not maintain or produce a Records of Processing Activities register for its video surveillance system

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Art. 22 permits video surveillance for security purposes but requires a 'layered information' approach: first layer (at access points) identifying existence of surveillance, controller identity, and rights; second layer (accessible location) providing full Art. 13 GDPR information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Store lacked first-layer informational signage at video-surveilled zone access points
violations: Store lacked first-layer informational signage at video-surveilled zone access points
No second-layer information available to affected customers in any accessible location

outcome: ALI MARKET paid €360 (representing base penalties of €400 and €200 for Arts. 13 and 30 violations respectively, reduced by 40% for early voluntary payment and responsibility recognition). The company was ordered to adopt corrective measures within one month, including: (1) placing visible informational signage in all video-surveilled areas identifying the processing, controller, and data subject rights; (2) maintaining accessible privacy information sheets per GDPR Art. 13–14; and (3) creating and maintaining a Records of Processing Activities register. Failure to comply could trigger further administrative penalties under GDPR Arts. 83.5–83.6.
dataType: Biometric data (images/video surveillance)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13 (Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject)

companyDescription: Clyde Valley Housing Association is a Scottish registered charity established in 1996 that owns and manages approximately 4,700 properties and provides housing services to 3,000 homeowners across Lanarkshire and East Dunbartonshire.
companyLongDescription: Clyde Valley Housing Association is a Scottish registered charity established in 1996 that owns and manages approximately 4,700 properties and provides housing services to 3,000 homeowners across Lanarkshire and East Dunbartonshire.
caseDescription: Clyde Valley Housing Association released a customer portal on 14 July 2022 with a critical configuration error that allowed residents with anti-social behaviour cases to access confidential information about other residents. The defect went undiscovered in testing and remained exposed for five days until properly escalated and remediated. Despite the data being viewable for five days, only 11 residents actually accessed it.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement appropriate technical measures to protect personal data from unauthorised processing, resulting in accidental exposure of sensitive resident information through a misconfigured system.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Clyde Valley Housing Association released a customer portal on 14 July 2022 with a configuration error that allowed residents with anti-social behaviour cases to access all other residents'.
whyTheyWereWrong: 139 residents' sensitive anti-social behaviour data was exposed to other residents for five days, with 62 facing high risk of privacy invasion, financial loss from identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Testing plan was adequate and identified all issues with the portal
claimsVsReality.reality: Testing plan did not identify data security issues and focused only on functionality, completely ignoring data protection risks

claimsVsReality.claim: Portal was ready for launch on 14 July 2022
claimsVsReality.reality: Portal had critical configuration error that exposed sensitive resident data from day one, remaining undiscovered until 19 July 2022

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) UK GDPR requires that personal data is processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: Clyde Valley Housing Association failed to carry out adequate testing prior to portal launch, resulting in a configuration error that exposed sensitive anti-social behaviour data to unauthorised access by other residents.
violations: Clyde Valley Housing Association failed to carry out adequate testing prior to portal launch, resulting in a configuration error that exposed sensitive anti-social behaviour data to unauthorised access by other residents.
Testing plan did not identify data security issues and focused only on functionality without considering data protection or breach risks.
No post-launch testing was conducted to verify correct functionality after portal went live.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to Clyde Valley Housing Association under Article 58(2)(b) UK GDPR. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps taken including: (1) root cause analysis with the portal development company; (2) updated staff data protection training; (3) identification and instruction of the 11 users who accessed the anti-social behaviour portal not to share or use the data. The Commissioner recommended: (1) complete root cause analysis and rigorous testing focused on data protection prior to future portal rollout; (2) review of data protection training content for relevance and adequacy. Future non-compliance with these recommendations may be treated as an aggravating factor in enforcement decisions.
companyNow: Clyde Valley Housing Association continues to operate as a registered charity providing social housing to approximately 4,700 properties across Lanarkshire and East Dunbartonshire areas of Scotland serving around 3,000 homeowners.
dataType: Anti-social behaviour case information, personal identifiers, resident contact and property data

companyDescription: The Crown Prosecution Service is the principal prosecuting authority for England and Wales, responsible for conducting criminal prosecutions. It was established in 1986 and is a non-departmental public body accountable to the Attorney General.
companyLongDescription: The Crown Prosecution Service is the principal prosecuting authority for England and Wales, responsible for conducting criminal prosecutions. It was established in 1986 and is a non-departmental public body accountable to the Attorney General.
caseDescription: The CPS lost three separate case files and removable media containing sensitive personal data relating to sexual assault and rape victims over a 13-month period. The data was lost due to inadequate end-to-end logging processes for tracking the movement and handling of case files and removable media within and between CPS offices. While no actual detriment occurred to affected data subjects, the sensitive nature of the data (victim interview recordings and case details) posed significant risk of distress.
violationSummary: CPS failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect against accidental loss, destruction, or damage of personal data, specifically by not maintaining adequate end-to-end logging and tracking systems for sensitive case files and removable media.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: The Crown Prosecution Service failed to implement and enforce end-to-end logging processes to track the movement of case files.
whyTheyWereWrong: Sexual assault and rape victims' sensitive personal data—including unencrypted video and audio interview recordings.

claimsVsReality.claim: Some procedures were in place for records management and logging movements of files and removable media
claimsVsReality.reality: Such procedures were not adequately documented at the time of incidents and did not provide sufficiently clear guidance on logging and transfer, resulting in three separate data losses over 13 months

claimsVsReality.claim: CPS believed a lost case file was returned and incorrectly destroyed
claimsVsReality.reality: There was no record of the file's return to CPS premises, making its actual location and status unknown

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018 Section 40 states that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: CPS did not have a suitable end-to-end logging process to record movements of case files and removable media containing personal and special category data to, from and within CPS offices
violations: CPS did not have a suitable end-to-end logging process to record movements of case files and removable media containing personal and special category data to, from and within CPS offices
This failure contributed to the loss of sensitive victim interview recordings and case files with potential to cause substantial distress to affected data subjects
Procedures that existed at the time were not adequately documented and policies did not provide sufficiently clear guidance on logging and transfer of data

outcome: The Information Commissioner's Office issued CPS with a reprimand under Schedule 13(2) of the Data Protection Act 2018. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps already taken (searches for lost materials, risk assessments, data subject notifications) but recommended CPS: (1) implement appropriate end-to-end logging processes for all file and media movements including destruction records; (2) raise staff awareness through documented guidance; (3) monitor and review logs at regular intervals. The ICO noted it may revisit the matter with further formal action if additional incidents or complaints emerge. The matter is now closed.
companyNow: The Crown Prosecution Service continues to operate as the primary prosecuting authority for England and Wales. The organisation has implemented recommended logging and records management improvements.
dataType: Sensitive personal data including victim interview recordings (audio/video), case files relating to sexual assault and rape allegations
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018 Section 40 (sixth data protection principle)

companyDescription: Allied Health Professionals (AHP) is a healthcare provider organisation that processes patient health data. The incident involved unauthorized data exposure through system misconfigurations by its IT service provider.
companyLongDescription: Allied Health Professionals (AHP) is a healthcare provider organisation that processes patient health data. The incident involved unauthorized data exposure through system misconfigurations by its IT service provider.
caseDescription: AHP's IT provider Infotex made unexpected, undocumented system changes that exposed patient data to unauthorized healthcare providers without consent. The incident affected 2,573 patients and was not caught during testing due to inadequate change management processes and insufficient data processor contracts. The ICO issued a reprimand for failure to ensure lawful processing under Article 6(1)(a) of the UK GDPR.
violationSummary: Patient health data was made accessible to third parties (healthcare providers) beyond the scope of patient consent due to organizational failures in access control and change management processes.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Allied Health Professionals failed to implement adequate change management processes and processor contracts.
whyTheyWereWrong: 2,573 patients' sensitive health information became accessible to healthcare providers without their consent, directly violating patients' privacy expectations.

claimsVsReality.claim: AHP's systems had routine testing procedures to catch errors and unintended changes
claimsVsReality.reality: Unexpected system changes made by Infotex were not documented or agreed, and therefore were not identified during testing, indicating routine testing was insufficient without proper change management

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 6(1)(a) UK GDPR requires that processing shall be lawful only if and to the extent that the data subject has given consent to the processing of his or her personal data for one or more specific purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: AHP did not have suitable policies or contracts in place to ensure patients could give or withhold consent to data sharing
violations: AHP did not have suitable policies or contracts in place to ensure patients could give or withhold consent to data sharing
Inadequate change management contracts with Infotex allowed undocumented system changes to go undetected
Patient health data was made accessible to healthcare providers without patient consent

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 28 UK GDPR requires a data controller to ensure that any natural person acting under the authority of the controller who has access to personal data does not process them except on instructions from the controller, and ensure data processor obligations are contractually documented.
regulatoryFindings.description: AHP did not have a sufficient contract in place with data processor Infotex outlining necessary data protection clauses and requirements
violations: AHP did not have a sufficient contract in place with data processor Infotex outlining necessary data protection clauses and requirements

outcome: ICO issued a formal reprimand under Article 58 UK GDPR. AHP must: (1) continue checking all data processor contracts for legal compliance; (2) ensure future change management documents are clear and specific; (3) maintain staff awareness and implementation of remedial measures. All 2,573 affected data subjects were informed. AHP introduced a processing contract with Infotex and reviewed contracts to prevent recurrence. The matter is closed but subject to reopening if further incidents emerge.
dataType: Health data, patient records

companyDescription: A Hungarian telecommunications company operating customer service with telephone support. The company processes customer data including voice recordings during service calls.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian telecommunications company operating customer service with telephone support. The company processes customer data including voice recordings during service calls.
caseDescription: A telecommunications company failed to provide prior notice to customers before recording their telephone calls with customer service. The company did not inform customers at the start of calls that conversations were being recorded, violating GDPR transparency requirements. The authority found systemic failures in the company's general notification practices and issued a substantial fine.
violationSummary: The company systematically recorded customer communications without adequate prior transparency, preventing subjects from knowing they were being monitored or understanding the scope and purpose of the surveillance.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: The telecommunications company recorded customer service calls without providing clear prior notification at the beginning of calls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers had no meaningful opportunity to consent or refuse recording before disclosing sensitive personal information like account details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers were informed of call recording in accordance with legal requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customers received no clear, prior notification or delayed/vague notification mid-call, depriving them of knowledge before consenting to recording.

claimsVsReality.claim: Call recording was mandatory under consumer protection law.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumer protection law only mandates recording for complaint handling, not for general network information calls, making the claimed legal basis false for most calls.

claimsVsReality.claim: Recordings were retained for 5 years as permitted by law.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company later changed the retention period and legal basis, admitting the 5-year period was not justified; the new script (from March 10, 2022) ties retention to civil law statute of limitations or 1 year post-contract.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12(1): Data controller must provide information to the data subject in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form, clearly and plainly worded.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company provided no notification at all on the September 17 call, and delayed notification until mid-conversation on September 30 with vague language ('this rögzített vonalon') that did not clearly state the call was being recorded.
violations: The company provided no notification at all on the September 17 call, and delayed notification until mid-conversation on September 30 with vague language ('this rögzített vonalon') that did not clearly state the call was being recorded.
Notification was not provided at the start of the call as required, preventing customers from making informed decisions before conversation began.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(1) and (2): At the time of obtaining personal data, the controller must provide the data subject with information including the controller's identity, the purpose of processing, the legal basis, retention period, and the subject's rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company failed to disclose any of the required information (identity, purpose, legal basis, retention period, rights) on September 17.
violations: The company failed to disclose any of the required information (identity, purpose, legal basis, retention period, rights) on September 17.

On September 30, notification was provided mid-call without explaining the legal basis (initially claimed consumer protection law, later changed to legitimate interest), data retention (initially 5 years, later changed), or subject rights.

The general script applied to all customers from June 2021 to March 2022 cited a false legal basis (consumer protection statute) for mandatory recording when no complaint was involved, and kept recordings for 5 years without justification.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 4(1): 'Personal data' is any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person.
regulatoryFindings.description: Voice recordings of customers constitute personal data, requiring full GDPR compliance including prior notification and lawful basis before processing.
violations: Voice recordings of customers constitute personal data, requiring full GDPR compliance including prior notification and lawful basis before processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: Hungarian Consumer Protection Law (Fgytv.) § 17/B(3): Call recordings are mandatory only for handling complaints, not for general customer service calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company recorded all customer calls with uniform scripts citing consumer protection law as the basis, but most calls involved network information, not complaints, making the legal basis false.
violations: The company recorded all customer calls with uniform scripts citing consumer protection law as the basis, but most calls involved network information, not complaints, making the legal basis false.

outcome: The authority found the company violated GDPR Arts. 12(1), 13(1), and 13(2) by failing to provide adequate prior notification of call recording. The company was ordered to pay 5,000,000 HUF (approximately €16.8M) in administrative fines within 30 days. The authority also noted that the company's general data processing notice used from June 2021 to March 2022 was inadequate. The company acknowledged the violations and modified its practices effective March 10, 2022, moving notification to the start of calls and changing the legal basis from consumer protection law to legitimate interest with corrected retention periods. The applicant also received 10,000 HUF compensation for the authority's delay in processing. The decision is subject to judicial review before the Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: Unknown. The company made internal changes to its call recording notification practices in March 2022, but current status is not disclosed in the decision.
dataType: Voice recordings, personal identifiers (phone numbers, subscriber information)

companyDescription: Drizly operated an e-commerce platform enabling local retailers to sell alcohol online to consumers of legal drinking age across 1,600+ urban and suburban markets in over 33 US states. The company served as North America's largest online alcohol marketplace, partnering with 4,000+ retailers and processing thousands of orders monthly before being acquired by Uber in 2021.
companyLongDescription: Drizly operated an e-commerce platform enabling local retailers to sell alcohol online to consumers of legal drinking age across 1,600+ urban and suburban markets in over 33 US states. The company served as North America's largest online alcohol marketplace, partnering with 4,000+ retailers and processing thousands of orders monthly before being acquired by Uber in 2021.
caseDescription: Drizly failed to implement reasonable information security practices, allowing a malicious actor to access and exfiltrate personal data of 2.5 million consumers via compromised GitHub credentials in July 2020. The company stored AWS credentials insecurely in GitHub repositories and failed to require multifactor authentication or unique passwords for employee accounts. Drizly only discovered the breach through media reports, not its own security monitoring.
companyWorth: Unknown (subsidiary of Uber; Uber market cap ~$95B as of 2024)
violationSummary: Drizly's failures to implement reasonable information security practices directly enabled the breach and exposure of consumer personal information, constituting a core insecurity violation under Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Drizly failed to implement reasonable security practices, storing AWS credentials in GitHub repositories, not requiring multifactor authentication for employee access.
whyTheyWereWrong: A malicious actor compromised 2.5 million consumers' personal data including names, addresses, payment information.

claimsVsReality.claim: All information is 'securely stored within our database' and 'we use standard, industry-wide, commercially reasonable security practices such as 128-bit encryption, firewalls and SSL'
claimsVsReality.reality: Credentials were stored unencrypted in GitHub repositories, no multifactor authentication was required, employee access was never revoked, no vulnerability scanning or monitoring systems existed, and passwords were hashed using broken MD5 algorithm.

claimsVsReality.claim: We use 'standard security practices such as encryption and firewalls'
claimsVsReality.reality: No formal security program, no intrusion detection, no data loss prevention monitoring, no regular security audits or penetration testing, and no incident response capabilities (only learned of breach from media reports).

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to employ reasonable security measures to protect consumer personal information, causing substantial injury not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
violations: Failed to employ reasonable security measures to protect consumer personal information, causing substantial injury not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

Made explicit representations in Privacy Policy claiming use of 'standard, industry-wide, commercially reasonable security practices' and '128-bit encryption, firewalls and SSL,' which were false or misleading given the company's actual security failures.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging both unfair information security practices (Count I) and deceptive security statements (Count II). As a complaint document, this represents the initiation of enforcement proceedings. The complaint establishes that Respondents' failures to implement reasonable security measures violated Section 5(a), and that their Privacy Policy representations were misleading. Typical outcomes for such FTC actions include consent orders requiring implementation of comprehensive information security programs, independent security audits, board-level security oversight, and ongoing monitoring and reporting obligations.
companyNow: Drizly, LLC became a wholly-owned subsidiary of Uber Technologies, Inc. on October 13, 2021, prior to the breach discovery. As of 2024, Drizly's operational status is unclear, as Uber discontinued the Drizly service in 2024 as part of organizational restructuring.
dataType: Names, email addresses, postal addresses, phone numbers, device identifiers, order histories, partial payment information, geolocation, consumer demographics (income, marital status, gender, ethnicity, children, home value), passwords
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Practices
Implied promise in Privacy Policy regarding 'standard, industry-wide, commercially reasonable security practices'

companyDescription: London Borough of Croydon is a local authority in Greater London, England, providing public services including education, social care, planning, and leisure services to approximately 390,000 residents.
companyLongDescription: London Borough of Croydon is a local authority in Greater London, England, providing public services including education, social care, planning, and leisure services to approximately 390,000 residents.
caseDescription: The London Borough of Croydon failed to respond to Subject Access Requests (SARs) within statutory timescales required under UK GDPR. Only 49.85% of SARs received between April 2020 and April 2021 were answered on time, leaving 155 requests unanswered. The council had not improved compliance during the investigation and maintained a moderate backlog of SAR cases.
violationSummary: The council excluded data subjects from accessing their personal data within the legal timeframe, violating their fundamental right of access under GDPR Article 15.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: London Borough of Croydon failed to respond to 155 of 310 Subject Access Requests within the one-month statutory deadline between April 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens seeking their own personal data faced prolonged delays of months beyond legal limits, preventing them from accessing records needed for employment disputes, medical decisions.

claimsVsReality.claim: The council implemented a Subject Access Request improvement plan to address SAR processing delays.
claimsVsReality.reality: The improvement plan lacked detail on ownership, contingencies, and timeframes and had not achieved full implementation by the time of the ICO investigation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The council was processing Subject Access Requests in compliance with UK GDPR requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only 49.85% of SARs were answered within the one-month statutory deadline; 155 of 310 requests failed to meet legal timescales.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) requires that 'the data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether or not personal data concerning him or her are being processed, and, where that is the case, access to the personal data'.
regulatoryFindings.description: London Borough of Croydon failed to provide timely confirmation and access to personal data for 155 SARs.
violations: London Borough of Croydon failed to provide timely confirmation and access to personal data for 155 SARs.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(3) requires that 'The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.'
regulatoryFindings.description: The council did not provide copies of personal data within statutory timeframes for 50.15% of requests received.
violations: The council did not provide copies of personal data within statutory timeframes for 50.15% of requests received.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires controllers to 'provide information on action taken on a request from the data subject without undue delay and at the latest within one month of receipt of the request.'
regulatoryFindings.description: Only 49.85% of SARs were responded to within one month; the remaining 155 requests exceeded the statutory deadline.
violations: Only 49.85% of SARs were responded to within one month; the remaining 155 requests exceeded the statutory deadline.

outcome: The ICO issued London Borough of Croydon a formal reprimand under Article 58 of UK GDPR. The council is required to: (1) ensure all Subject Access Requests are responded to within statutory deadlines; (2) complete a policy and procedure review for SARs; (3) ensure adequate staff resourcing; (4) improve SAR recording and monitoring; (5) develop a detailed improvement plan addressing the SAR backlog. The council must provide updates to the ICO after 3 months (26 October 2022) and 6 months (26 January 2023). The ICO warned that further non-compliance or incidents could result in additional formal regulatory action. The matter is now closed pending receipt of progress updates.
companyNow: London Borough of Croydon continues to operate as a local government authority in England, responsible for providing public services to residents in Croydon.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Requests (type not specified in document)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 15(1) – Right to confirmation and access to personal data
GDPR Article 15(3) – Obligation to provide copy of personal data
GDPR Article 12(3) – Obligation to respond to requests without undue delay and at latest within one month

companyDescription: Regionstyrelsen i Region Uppsala is the governing body of Region Uppsala, a regional healthcare authority in Sweden responsible for administering hospitals, clinics, and healthcare services across the Uppsala region.
companyLongDescription: Regionstyrelsen i Region Uppsala is the governing body of Region Uppsala, a regional healthcare authority in Sweden responsible for administering hospitals, clinics, and healthcare services across the Uppsala region.
caseDescription: Region Uppsala transmitted sensitive patient health data and personal identification numbers via unencrypted email over nearly four years. Although the email transport was encrypted (TLS 1.2), the actual patient information in Excel files was sent in plaintext, exposing 100,000 to 500,000 individuals to potential unauthorized access. The practice violated the organization's own internal guidelines prohibiting sensitive data transmission via email.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures (encryption at rest) to protect sensitive health data against unauthorized access and disclosure, despite knowing the risks and having internal guidelines prohibiting email transmission of such data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Region Uppsala transmitted unencrypted patient health records, diagnosis codes, and personal ID numbers via email approximately 25 times monthly (automated).
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 100,000 and 500,000 patients' sensitive health data and identification numbers were accessible in plaintext to email recipients despite transport encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Uppsala's internal guidelines stated that sensitive personal data must not be communicated via email.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite this explicit policy, the organization transmitted approximately 25–250 emails per month containing unencrypted sensitive patient health data and identification numbers via email for nearly four years.

claimsVsReality.claim: Email transport was encrypted using TLS 1.2 protocol, providing secure transmission.
claimsVsReality.reality: Although transport encryption prevented interception during transmission, the data within Excel files was not encrypted and remained readable in plaintext once received, exposing it to unauthorized access by recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32.1 requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Uppsala transmitted sensitive health data and personal identification numbers via email in unencrypted Excel files, accessible in plaintext to all recipients despite encrypted transport.
violations: Region Uppsala transmitted sensitive health data and personal identification numbers via email in unencrypted Excel files, accessible in plaintext to all recipients despite encrypted transport.
No technical measures (e.g., file-level encryption) were implemented to prevent unauthorized reading or modification of patient data by recipients.
The treatment was systematic and prolonged over multiple years despite the organization's own internal guidelines explicitly prohibiting transmission of sensitive personal data via email.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24.1 requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure and demonstrate compliance with the regulation, taking into account the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing and the risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Uppsala identified risks inherent in transmitting sensitive health data via email but failed to implement adequate security measures to mitigate those risks.
violations: Region Uppsala identified risks inherent in transmitting sensitive health data via email but failed to implement adequate security measures to mitigate those risks.
Internal guidelines existed prohibiting email transmission of sensitive data, but the organization did not enforce them through technical controls such as encryption.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Patient data containing health information and personal identification numbers was maintained in cleartext within email files, exposing it to unauthorized reading by both authorized and unauthorized personnel.
violations: Patient data containing health information and personal identification numbers was maintained in cleartext within email files, exposing it to unauthorized reading by both authorized and unauthorized personnel.

outcome: Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten (IMY, Swedish Data Protection Authority) determined that Region Uppsala violated GDPR Article 32.1 by transmitting unencrypted sensitive patient data. IMY imposed an administrative fine of 300,000 SEK (approximately €32,000) as the primary enforcement action. The decision noted mitigating factors (transport-layer encryption via TLS 1.2, internal-only transmission, and cessation upon incident discovery) but emphasized aggravating factors (systematic multi-year violation, large volume of data, high-risk health information, breach of internal policy). Region Uppsala stopped the practices upon incident notification on 7 May 2019 and initiated work to implement email encryption solutions. The decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: Region Uppsala is a regional health authority in Sweden responsible for healthcare delivery and administration in the Uppsala region. It continues to operate as a public regional healthcare organization under Swedish governance.
dataType: Health data, patient records, personal identification numbers, diagnosis codes, contact dates
