outcome: Eurobank ordered to pay €20,000 fine. Authority found violation of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 13. Bank began issuing new cards without this feature from July 2019 (debit) and October 2019 (credit). By decision date, over 2/3 of Eurobank cards no longer stored transaction history. Bank must cease the non-compliant processing and ensure transparency in future card products.
companyNow: Eurobank is a major Greek bank and part of the Eurobank Ergasias group. The bank has implemented compliance measures to cease storing transaction history on new cards issued after mid-2019.
dataType: Financial transaction data (transaction amounts and dates)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, transparency principle
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject

companyDescription: RAMONA FILMS, S.L. (formerly KALANDRAKAS FILMS, SL) operates an adult content website at putalocura.com serving Spanish-speaking audiences.
companyLongDescription: RAMONA FILMS, S.L. (formerly KALANDRAKAS FILMS, SL) operates an adult content website at putalocura.com serving Spanish-speaking audiences.
caseDescription: RAMONA FILMS operated an adult content website that failed to comply with GDPR privacy notice requirements and collected analytics cookies without proper user consent. The company's privacy policy referenced a 1999 law that had been repealed in 2018, and its cookie implementation allowed non-essential tracking before consent was obtained.
violationSummary: Company deployed tracking cookies and collected personal data through forms without obtaining clear prior consent or providing mandatory GDPR transparency information, characteristic of surveillance-based data collection.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: RAMONA FILMS operated an adult content website that collected visitor names and emails through a contact form while installing Google Analytics tracking cookies before obtaining user consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Website visitors had no access to compliant privacy policies explaining data collection practices.

claimsVsReality.claim: Website displayed warning 'Abandon this web if you are under age: Adult content' and legal notices stating content is for adults only (minimum 18 years).
claimsVsReality.reality: No effective age verification or consent mechanisms were implemented; website had contact form collecting personal data from any visitor without verification, and analytics tracked all users including minors.

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy policy complied with data protection law.
claimsVsReality.reality: Policy referenced Ley Orgánica 15/1999 (repealed May 25, 2018) and did not address GDPR requirements effective since May 25, 2018.

claimsVsReality.claim: Banner indicated cookies were used and provided options to accept.
claimsVsReality.reality: Non-technical cookies were installed before any user action; no mechanism existed to reject all cookies or manage granularly; inactivity/scrolling was treated as consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13 requires controllers to provide specified transparency information to data subjects at the moment personal data is obtained.
regulatoryFindings.description: RAMONA FILMS' privacy policy was based on repealed LOPD (1999) and did not comply with GDPR Art. 13 requirements for information about identity of controller, purposes, retention periods, or data subject rights.
violations: RAMONA FILMS' privacy policy was based on repealed LOPD (1999) and did not comply with GDPR Art. 13 requirements for information about identity of controller, purposes, retention periods, or data subject rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: LSSI Art. 22.2 requires clear and complete information about storage devices and data processing purposes, with prior user consent before installing cookies on terminals.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google Analytics cookies (_ga, _gid, _gat) were installed without user consent before any action taken. Banner lacked identification of cookie purposes, distinction between first/third-party cookies, and granular consent/rejection options.
violations: Google Analytics cookies (_ga, _gid, _gat) were installed without user consent before any action taken. Banner lacked identification of cookie purposes, distinction between first/third-party cookies, and granular consent/rejection options.

outcome: Procedure initiated January 3, 2022 with initial proposed sanction of €10,000 (€5,000 per violation). Company paid €8,000 on February 22, 2022, utilizing one available 20% voluntary payment reduction. Payment triggered automatic termination of proceedings pursuant to LPACAP Art. 85(2). Company must bring privacy policy and cookie implementation into GDPR compliance.
dataType: name, email address, analytics tracking data (cookies), browsing data

companyDescription: HDIKA A.E. is a Greek public company responsible for managing and distributing diagnostic self-testing kits and operating the https://self-testing.gov.gr platform during the COVID-19 pandemic. It served as the primary data controller for recording test results across multiple occupational categories.
companyLongDescription: HDIKA A.E. is a Greek public company responsible for managing and distributing diagnostic self-testing kits and operating the https://self-testing.gov.gr platform during the COVID-19 pandemic. It served as the primary data controller for recording test results across multiple occupational categories.
caseDescription: Greece's Data Protection Authority found that HDIKA A.E. and multiple government ministries violated GDPR requirements when processing personal data from mandatory COVID-19 self-tests during 2021. The violations included inadequate transparency in informing data subjects, retaining diagnostic test results beyond permitted periods, and failing to conduct required impact assessments before processing commenced. Administrative penalties were imposed on HDIKA A.E., the Ministry of Interior, Ministry of Labor, and the Naval Veterans' Fund.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement adequate technical and organizational measures (Art. 25 GDPR) to ensure data deletion after the retention period, combined with inadequate data minimization practices and lack of transparency, constitutes processing insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: HDIKA A.E. operated the self-testing.gov.gr platform for COVID-19 test result reporting and retained citizens' personal health data for longer than legally permitted.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens submitting COVID-19 test results had their sensitive health data retained indefinitely without proper technical safeguards, exposing them to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: HDIKA stated that test data were retained only for the prescribed statutory period and that any retention beyond that period was a 'technical error' detected and immediately rectified.
claimsVsReality.reality: HDIKA retained COVID-19 test results on its platform for an indefinite period longer than the 7-day statutory retention period (extended to 30 days), and its own impact assessment indicated the technical problem was systemic, not merely an isolated incident. The company lacked adequate automated controls to enforce deletion.

claimsVsReality.claim: HDIKA provided 'transparent' notice to data subjects through the self-testing.gov.gr platform.
claimsVsReality.reality: The transparency notice omitted critical information required by GDPR Article 13, specifically failing to identify the government authorities (Ministry of Education or Interior) who would be recipients of test results and enforcers of testing requirements in case of non-compliance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data protection impact assessments were conducted to identify and mitigate processing risks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Impact assessments were conducted only after processing commenced (in June 2021, months after processing began in April 2021) and failed to assess or propose measures for the risk of non-compliance with storage limitation principles.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires data processing to be lawful, fair, and transparent with respect to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: HDIKA A.E. failed to provide transparent information to data subjects about recipients (the Ministry of Education or Interior) responsible for enforcing testing requirements, contrary to Article 13(1)(e).
violations: HDIKA A.E. failed to provide transparent information to data subjects about recipients (the Ministry of Education or Interior) responsible for enforcing testing requirements, contrary to Article 13(1)(e).
Ministry of Labor provided misleading information about processing purposes in the initial notice, later corrected in August 2021.
Ministry of Interior and NAT provided incomplete or vague information about data retention periods, failing to specify the concrete timeframe.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(e) requires personal data be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects only for as long as necessary for the purposes for which they are processed.
regulatoryFindings.description: HDIKA A.E. retained COVID-19 test results on the platform for an indefinite period longer than the 7-day retention period specified in Law 4792/2021 Article 27(6)(d), later extended to 30 days.
violations: HDIKA A.E. retained COVID-19 test results on the platform for an indefinite period longer than the 7-day retention period specified in Law 4792/2021 Article 27(6)(d), later extended to 30 days.

HDIKA's impact assessment acknowledged the need for automatic deletion after 7 days but failed to implement adequate technical controls, attributing the breach to a 'technical error' without providing remedial details.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 25(1) requires controllers to implement effective technical and organizational measures at the time of determining processing means and during processing itself.
regulatoryFindings.description: HDIKA A.E. did not implement adequate technical measures to ensure automatic deletion of diagnostic test results after the statutory retention period, despite its own impact assessment highlighting this requirement.
violations: HDIKA A.E. did not implement adequate technical measures to ensure automatic deletion of diagnostic test results after the statutory retention period, despite its own impact assessment highlighting this requirement.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 35(1) requires controllers to conduct a data protection impact assessment prior to processing if the processing is likely to result in high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons.
regulatoryFindings.description: HDIKA A.E. and Ministry of Labor conducted impact assessments only after processing had commenced, contrary to the requirement to assess before processing begins.
violations: HDIKA A.E. and Ministry of Labor conducted impact assessments only after processing had commenced, contrary to the requirement to assess before processing begins.

Ministry of Interior and NAT did not conduct impact assessments at all prior to processing, despite high-risk factors (systematic evaluation, automated processing, large-scale processing of health data).
Impact assessments submitted by HDIKA and the Ministry of Labor did not assess risks related to failure to comply with storage limitation principles and did not address compensation measures.

outcome: The Hellenic Data Protection Authority issued an administrative penalty of €5,000 against HDIKA A.E. for violations of Article 5(1)(e) (storage limitation) due to inadequate technical safeguards for data deletion. The Authority issued warnings (reprimands) to HDIKA, Ministry of Labor, Ministry of Interior, and Naval Veterans' Fund for violations of Article 13 (transparency). HDIKA and Ministry of Labor received warnings for failing to conduct timely data protection impact assessments under Article 35. The Authority ordered the Naval Veterans' Fund to remove the COVID-19 testing application it had developed and delete any remaining sailor data. All entities were required to take corrective measures to ensure compliance with GDPR requirements.
companyNow: HDIKA A.E. (Hellenic Data Interchange Company) remains an active government entity responsible for data management functions. The company was required to implement corrective technical and procedural measures to ensure compliance with GDPR storage limitation and transparency requirements.
dataType: Health data, COVID-19 test results, personal identification data, biometric-adjacent diagnostic information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 13 – Right to be informed
GDPR Article 25 – Data protection by design and by default
GDPR Article 35 – Data protection impact assessment

company: Φροντιστήριο (Tutoring Center - name anonymized as Γ)
companyDescription: A tutoring center (φροντιστήριο) in Greece that offered both in-person and remote online classes via the Zoom platform. The center employed multiple teachers and served students including minors.
companyLongDescription: A tutoring center (φροντιστήριο) in Greece that offered both in-person and remote online classes via the Zoom platform. The center employed multiple teachers and served students including minors.
caseDescription: An employer (tutoring center owner) continuously monitored an employee's live online teaching sessions via video surveillance without a clear legal basis, despite the employee's repeated and explicit written objections. The employer failed to provide proper transparency information and violated the employee's right to object under GDPR Articles 5, 13, and 21.
violationSummary: The employer engaged in continuous systematic surveillance of an employee's teaching sessions via video and audio capture without lawful basis, transparency, or respect for the employee's right to object.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A tutoring center owner continuously monitored an employee's online teaching sessions via Zoom, recording video.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee explicitly objected multiple times in writing to the monitoring, yet the employer continued the surveillance anyway, exposing the teacher's image, voice.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employer claimed the continuous surveillance was necessary to monitor technical problems during online classes and to ensure quality of teaching.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee demonstrated that the employer could receive notifications of technical issues via phone, SMS, or Viber messages without the need for continuous real-time video/audio monitoring of the teacher.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employer claimed she did not actually monitor what the employee said (the content), only observed her visually via the computer screen.
claimsVsReality.reality: The surveillance included both video and audio capture for the entire duration of each lesson, giving the employer full access to both image and sound data of the employee.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employer claimed the employee provided implicit or later explicit consent to the surveillance via written messages.
claimsVsReality.reality: All written communications from the employee expressed opposition and objection to the monitoring; no consent was ever given, and the employee explicitly invoked her right to object under GDPR Article 21.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employer claimed the legal basis was the execution of the employment contract.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employment contract and related data processing documentation made no mention of continuous video/audio surveillance of teaching sessions, so this legal basis could not be validly applied to this specific processing activity.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer processed employee's image and audio data without establishing a clear, transparent legal basis and without respecting the employee's explicit written objections to the monitoring.
violations: Employer processed employee's image and audio data without establishing a clear, transparent legal basis and without respecting the employee's explicit written objections to the monitoring.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) imposes a duty of accountability on the controller to demonstrate compliance with the principles.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer failed to maintain clear documentation of the legal basis for the surveillance and could not prove compliance with transparency obligations.
violations: Employer failed to maintain clear documentation of the legal basis for the surveillance and could not prove compliance with transparency obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires that processing be based on at least one lawful basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer invoked multiple contradictory legal bases (contract execution, legitimate interests, implied consent) without clearly establishing any single valid basis for continuous surveillance.
violations: Employer invoked multiple contradictory legal bases (contract execution, legitimate interests, implied consent) without clearly establishing any single valid basis for continuous surveillance.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires controllers to provide data subjects with specified information at the time personal data is obtained.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer never provided the required transparency information to the employee, including the specific purposes, legal basis, or data handling details for the surveillance.
violations: Employer never provided the required transparency information to the employee, including the specific purposes, legal basis, or data handling details for the surveillance.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 21 grants data subjects the right to object to processing based on legitimate interests, and the controller must cease processing unless it can demonstrate compelling legitimate reasons.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employee explicitly objected multiple times in writing; employer ignored these objections and continued monitoring without justification, violating the employee's right to object.
violations: Employee explicitly objected multiple times in writing; employer ignored these objections and continued monitoring without justification, violating the employee's right to object.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (DPA) found the employer in violation of GDPR Articles 5, 6, 13, and 21. The employer was ordered to cease the unlawful processing and impose an administrative fine of €2,000. The DPA emphasised that in employment relationships, consent is rarely a valid legal basis due to the power imbalance between employer and employee, and that the employer's failure to establish a clear legal basis and respect the employee's objection constituted serious violations of foundational GDPR principles.
companyNow: Unknown — the tutoring center operator's current status is not disclosed in the decision.
dataType: Image and audio data, video surveillance of employee during online classes
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) - Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
GDPR Art. 6 - Lack of lawful basis
GDPR Art. 13 - Failure to provide required information
GDPR Art. 21 - Right to object not respected

companyDescription: CASA 7 PERSONAL SHOPPER, S.L. is a Spanish company providing real estate and personal shopping services, managing property sales and customer inquiries.
companyLongDescription: CASA 7 PERSONAL SHOPPER, S.L. is a Spanish company providing real estate and personal shopping services, managing property sales and customer inquiries.
caseDescription: CASA 7 sent a mass email to multiple recipients without using BCC (blind carbon copy), exposing all recipients' email addresses to each other. This violated the confidentiality principle under GDPR Article 5(1)(f) and the security requirement under Article 32. The company failed to implement basic technical safeguards to protect email recipient privacy.
violationSummary: The unauthorized disclosure of recipients' email addresses to other recipients constitutes a breach of confidential personal data handling, as individuals could not control who learned their contact information and inferred interests.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: CASA 7 PERSONAL SHOPPER sent a property sale inquiry email to multiple recipients on June 2, 2021, displaying all recipient email addresses visibly instead of using BCC.
whyTheyWereWrong: Multiple individuals received email addresses and inferred personal interests of unknown strangers without their knowledge or consent, creating privacy risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company would respond to customer inquiries about properties with relevant information.
claimsVsReality.reality: When responding, the company disclosed all recipients' email addresses to each other, breaching their privacy and exposing their identity and inferred interests without consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated with integrity and confidentiality, with appropriate technical or organisational measures to ensure security against unauthorised or unlawful processing, loss, destruction or accidental damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: CASA 7 failed to ensure confidentiality by sending an email without using BCC functionality, allowing all recipients to view each other's email addresses and infer personal interests.
violations: CASA 7 failed to ensure confidentiality by sending an email without using BCC functionality, allowing all recipients to view each other's email addresses and infer personal interests.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires that the controller and processor implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security adequate to the risk, including measures to guarantee confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: CASA 7 did not implement the basic technical measure (BCC) necessary to ensure adequate security and confidentiality when sending emails containing personal data to multiple recipients.
violations: CASA 7 did not implement the basic technical measure (BCC) necessary to ensure adequate security and confidentiality when sending emails containing personal data to multiple recipients.

outcome: AEPD (Spanish Data Protection Authority) imposed a total fine of €3,500 (€2,000 for Article 5(1)(f) violation; €1,500 for Article 32 violation). The company was ordered to comply with data protection principles. The sanctions are enforceable once the resolution becomes final. The company may appeal within one month to the AEPD Director or file an administrative contentious action within two months.
companyNow: Unknown. CASA 7 PERSONAL SHOPPER, S.L. (CIF: B87396172) was difficult to contact during enforcement, with notifications returned as 'absent from delivery' and electronic notifications rejected, suggesting possible operational inactivity or relocation.
dataType: Email addresses, personal identity information

company: Telecommunications service provider (name redacted in document)
companyDescription: Hungarian telecommunications provider offering prepaid card mobile services. The company operates a public directory service (online directory/tudakozó) where subscribers' data may be listed. The company processes subscriber data under framework contracts and renewal procedures.
companyLongDescription: Hungarian telecommunications provider offering prepaid card mobile services. The company operates a public directory service (online directory/tudakozó) where subscribers' data may be listed. The company processes subscriber data under framework contracts and renewal procedures.
caseDescription: A telecommunications provider published a subscriber's personal data (name, address, phone number) in a public directory without valid consent. When the subscriber requested deletion, the company failed to comply for over 3 months, misclassifying the data subject's requests as complaints rather than rights requests, and citing technical and administrative errors.
violationSummary: Personal data (name, address, phone) was made publicly accessible without valid consent and remained exposed for nearly 3 years. Company failed to facilitate deletion and improperly categorised rights requests as complaints, preventing proper legal handling.
violations: Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Published a subscriber's name, address, and phone number in a public online directory without documented consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The subscriber's personal contact information remained publicly searchable and accessible to anyone for nearly three years without a valid legal basis.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated that subscribers consent to data publication by agreeing to terms at contract renewal (June 2018).
claimsVsReality.reality: Company provided only a system screenshot showing a checkbox marked in their records; no recording, transcript, or documentary evidence proved the subscriber actually gave consent. The original 2015 contract explicitly stated the subscriber did not consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it processes deletion requests within 30 days as standard.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company took 3 months (May–July 2021) to delete one subscriber's data, citing technical errors. Deletion only occurred after the subscriber made a second phone call and filed a complaint with the data protection authority.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated it treats subscriber service requests appropriately according to applicable law.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company mishandled deletion requests by routing them as formal complaints (status: closed, no further action) rather than rights requests, preventing proper legal processing and delay of compliance.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) requires data controllers to demonstrate compliance with data protection principles (accountability).
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to prove the subscriber had given valid consent for data publication; only system records showed a checkbox marked, not proof that the subscriber actually consented.
violations: Company failed to prove the subscriber had given valid consent for data publication; only system records showed a checkbox marked, not proof that the subscriber actually consented.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires lawful basis for processing personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company published subscriber's data without documented legal basis; claimed consent but could not prove the subscriber had actually consented.
violations: Company published subscriber's data without documented legal basis; claimed consent but could not prove the subscriber had actually consented.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 17(1)(b) grants the right to erasure when consent is withdrawn and no other lawful basis applies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to delete subscriber's data within 30 days of request made in May 2021; deletion occurred only in July 2021 after the data protection authority intervened, more than 2 months late.
violations: Company failed to delete subscriber's data within 30 days of request made in May 2021; deletion occurred only in July 2021 after the data protection authority intervened, more than 2 months late.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(2) requires controllers to facilitate the exercise of data subject rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company misclassified deletion requests as complaints, routing them through complaint procedures instead of rights request procedures, preventing timely processing.
violations: Company misclassified deletion requests as complaints, routing them through complaint procedures instead of rights request procedures, preventing timely processing.

outcome: The authority found the company violated GDPR Articles 5(2), 6(1), 12(2), and 17(1)(b). The company was ordered to pay 5,000,000 HUF and directed to delete the subscriber's data (completed 2 July 2021, before the decision). The company offered nominal 5,000 HUF compensation to the complainant. The decision is enforceable and may be appealed to the Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: Unknown. The company continues to operate as a telecommunications provider in Hungary but remains unnamed in the public decision.
dataType: Name, home address, telephone number

companyDescription: C.P. COMUNIDAD B.B.B. is a property/community management entity responsible for managing a residential community of property owners in Andalusia, Spain.
companyLongDescription: C.P. COMUNIDAD B.B.B. is a property/community management entity responsible for managing a residential community of property owners in Andalusia, Spain.
caseDescription: A property management company added a cleaning worker to a WhatsApp group without consent to monitor her work activity and order her to send images of completed tasks. The company failed to respond to the worker's access rights request, violating her right to data portability and lawful processing grounds.
violationSummary: Company conducted ongoing work activity monitoring via WhatsApp without consent or legal basis, capturing personal data (phone, photos) through surveillance mechanism. Secondary violation includes refusal to honor access rights.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Community property management included a cleaning worker in a WhatsApp group without consent to monitor her daily work activities and required her to send photographs of completed tasks.
whyTheyWereWrong: The worker's phone number and images were processed without any legal permission, exposing her personal data to surveillance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed employee had obligation to send work photos to WhatsApp group.
claimsVsReality.reality: No lawful basis existed for this data processing; employee had right to refuse and filed complaint instead.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company could monitor employee work activity via WhatsApp without consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR Article 6 requires lawful basis; surveillance without consent or contractual necessity is unlawful.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires processing of personal data to be lawful only if at least one condition applies: consent, contract execution, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company processed phone number and photos without employee consent and without any lawful basis under Article 6(1). No contract, legal obligation, or legitimate interest justified the surveillance.
violations: Company processed phone number and photos without employee consent and without any lawful basis under Article 6(1). No contract, legal obligation, or legitimate interest justified the surveillance.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain from the controller confirmation of whether personal data is being processed and to receive a copy of such data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employee exercised right of access on 04/11/2021; company failed to respond within the required one-month period or provide any information about data processing.
violations: Employee exercised right of access on 04/11/2021; company failed to respond within the required one-month period or provide any information about data processing.

outcome: Company C.P. COMUNIDAD B.B.B. was fined €1,500 for violation of Article 6(1) GDPR (lack of lawful basis) and €500 for violation of Article 15 GDPR (failure to honor access request). Company was required within one month to adopt measures to effectively respond to future data subject rights requests and to establish lawful processing bases for any personal data handling.
companyNow: Unknown – limited public information available on this property management company.
dataType: Phone number, photographs of work activities, personal location data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(1) – Lack of lawful basis for processing
GDPR Art. 15 – Right of access not honored

companyDescription: NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) is a UK public health service organisation responsible for providing blood, organs, tissues, and associated services to hospitals and patients. It operates critical life-saving matching and allocation systems for organ transplants.
companyLongDescription: NHS Blood and Transplant (NHSBT) is a UK public health service organisation responsible for providing blood, organs, tissues, and associated services to hospitals and patients. It operates critical life-saving matching and allocation systems for organ transplants.
caseDescription: NHSBT inadvertently integrated untested development code into its live liver matching system, excluding prospective transplant patients from the matching run between 11-18 September 2019. The integration error resulted from inadequate version control, peer review, and staff training on code testing procedures. Five patients were directly affected, with three experiencing delays in receiving liver transplants.
violationSummary: NHSBT failed to implement sufficient technical and organisational security measures to protect the integrity, availability and resilience of transplant matching systems processing vulnerable patient data, resulting in patient exclusion and harm.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: NHSBT inadvertently merged untested development code for a future liver allocation scheme into its live transplant matching system.
whyTheyWereWrong: Five vulnerable transplant patients awaiting life-saving organ offers were excluded from matching during the breach period; three patients experienced significant delays in receiving liver.

claimsVsReality.claim: NHSBT systems were adequately tested and controlled before code deployment
claimsVsReality.reality: Untested development code for a future liver scheme was integrated directly into the live environment, causing five patients to be excluded from the Liver Matching Run

claimsVsReality.claim: Staff understood and implemented proper regression testing before launching new organ matching schemes
claimsVsReality.reality: Relevant staff had inadequate knowledge and understanding of the scope of regression testing required, contributing to the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: NHSBT lacked appropriate branch or version control preventing developers from unknowingly introducing untested code into the live environment
violations: NHSBT lacked appropriate branch or version control preventing developers from unknowingly introducing untested code into the live environment
NHSBT lacked appropriate peer review of developers' work to reduce likelihood of inadvertent coding errors
NHSBT staff had inadequate knowledge and understanding of regression testing required prior to launching new organ matching schemes
NHSBT provided insufficient training to staff on code testing, branch control, and peer review procedures

outcome: The ICO issued NHSBT a reprimand under Article 58 of the GDPR instead of an administrative fine. NHSBT must complete all remedial measures in its Root Cause Analysis action plan (including fitness review of system MPD1226), provide appropriate training to internal staff and external contractors on established branch control and testing procedures, and ensure mandatory data protection training for supplier-provided contractors. NHSBT must provide progress update by 9 November 2022. The ICO reserved the right to revisit and pursue formal enforcement if further related incidents occur. Case closed.
companyNow: NHS Blood and Transplant remains an active NHS agency responsible for managing organ donation and transplantation services across England. Following this enforcement action, the organisation has implemented enhanced code deployment controls and testing procedures.
dataType: Health data, organ transplant patient records, patient identification and matching data

company: Office of the Secretary of State for the Home Department (UK Home Office)
companyDescription: The UK Home Office is the government department responsible for immigration, law enforcement, counter-terrorism, and domestic security policy in the United Kingdom. It is a major government agency reporting to the Home Secretary.
companyLongDescription: The UK Home Office is the government department responsible for immigration, law enforcement, counter-terrorism, and domestic security policy in the United Kingdom. It is a major government agency reporting to the Home Secretary.
caseDescription: The UK Home Office lost an envelope containing four classified documents with personal data on a visa applicant and two police officers at a London venue on 5 September 2021. The documents were found unsecured by venue staff and handed to police. The Home Office failed to report the breach to the ICO for over 6 months (until 4 April 2022) and lacked adequate security measures and document tracking procedures.
violationSummary: The Home Office failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures (Article 5(1)(f)) to protect personal data, resulting in unauthorised disclosure of sensitive documents containing special category data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Home Office staff lost four classified 'Official-Sensitive' documents containing personal data at a London venue on 5 September 2021, where they were accessed by unauthorised individuals.
whyTheyWereWrong: A foreign visa applicant and two police officers had their sensitive personal data including extremism.

claimsVsReality.claim: Documents were classified 'Official-Sensitive' and contained specific handling instructions requiring secure storage and protection against unauthorised processing
claimsVsReality.reality: Handling instructions were not followed; documents were left unsecured in a public venue and accessed by unauthorised individuals

claimsVsReality.claim: Home Office had procedures in place to manage sensitive documents
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented sign-out process existed for removal of 'Official-Sensitive' documents from premises prior to this incident

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office failed to ensure appropriate level of security, resulting in inappropriate disclosure of personal data relating to three data subjects when classified documents were left unsecured at a London venue and accessed by unauthorised individuals.
violations: Home Office failed to ensure appropriate level of security, resulting in inappropriate disclosure of personal data relating to three data subjects when classified documents were left unsecured at a London venue and accessed by unauthorised individuals.
No documented sign-out process existed for removal of 'Official-Sensitive' documents from premises despite handling instructions requiring secure safekeeping.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 33(1) requires that in the case of a personal data breach, the controller shall without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it, notify the breach to the Commissioner, unless unlikely to result in risk to rights and freedoms.
regulatoryFindings.description: Home Office staff became aware of breach on 6 September 2021 but did not report to ICO until 4 April 2022 – a delay of over 6 months, far exceeding the 72-hour statutory requirement despite knowing classified documents with personal data and special category data were involved.
violations: Home Office staff became aware of breach on 6 September 2021 but did not report to ICO until 4 April 2022 – a delay of over 6 months, far exceeding the 72-hour statutory requirement despite knowing classified documents with personal data and special category data were involved.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand to the Secretary of State for the Home Department under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The ICO welcomed remedial steps already taken (implementing unique reference numbers for documents) but required further compliance actions: review of handling instructions for 'Official-Sensitive' information; implementation of sign-out process for sensitive documents; review of policies for guidance on physical records removal; demonstration of accountability through staff monitoring and auditing; and strict adherence to 72-hour breach reporting. The ICO stated it may revisit the matter if further incidents occur.
companyNow: The UK Home Office continues to operate as the principal domestic security and law enforcement department of the UK Government. It has implemented the recommended compliance improvements.
dataType: Personal data including special category data (extremism analysis, counter-terrorism intelligence); data on visa applicants and police staff
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Security/Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 33(1) – Breach notification requirements

companyDescription: The Electoral Commission is the independent statutory body that oversees elections and regulates political finance in the United Kingdom. It works to promote public confidence in the democratic process and ensure its integrity.
companyLongDescription: The Electoral Commission is the independent statutory body that oversees elections and regulates political finance in the United Kingdom. It works to promote public confidence in the democratic process and ensure its integrity.
caseDescription: The Electoral Commission's Microsoft Exchange Server was breached via the ProxyShell vulnerability chain, exposing approximately 40 million individuals' names and home addresses from the Electoral Register. The breach occurred because the organisation failed to implement timely security patches and lacked appropriate password management policies. The ICO issued a reprimand for violations of UK GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(b).
violationSummary: The failure to patch known vulnerabilities and maintain basic password security resulted in the exposure of sensitive Electoral Register data containing 40 million individuals' personal information to unauthorized threat actors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The Electoral Commission failed to patch known ProxyShell vulnerabilities on its Microsoft Exchange Server for months after fixes were released in April-May 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: Unknown threat actors exploited these security failures to gain unauthorized access to systems holding the names.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Electoral Commission considered the incident isolated and remedial action with old servers was limited due to planned Cloud migration.
claimsVsReality.reality: Three separate clusters of threat actor activity were identified with multiple re-compromise events over 12+ months (August 2021–August 2022), and the NCSC recommended a wider investigation by CIR-accredited company, which was not immediately undertaken.

claimsVsReality.claim: Electoral Commission had appropriate password security measures in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: 178 active accounts used default passwords vulnerable to guessing, with no dedicated password management policy, only a general 'do not reveal' instruction.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) UK GDPR requires personal data to be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Electoral Commission did not have an appropriate patching regime in place, leaving on-premise Exchange Server vulnerable to ProxyShell exploits (CVE-2021-31207, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-34473) that were patched in April and May 2021 but remained unpatched when exploited in August 2021.
violations: Electoral Commission did not have an appropriate patching regime in place, leaving on-premise Exchange Server vulnerable to ProxyShell exploits (CVE-2021-31207, CVE-2021-34523, CVE-2021-34473) that were patched in April and May 2021 but remained unpatched when exploited in August 2021.
Eight additional vulnerabilities were identified on servers that could have been exploited while present on systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(b) UK GDPR requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including the ability to ensure ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Electoral Commission lacked appropriate password management policies. One compromised account still used the password allocated at account creation.
violations: Electoral Commission lacked appropriate password management policies. One compromised account still used the password allocated at account creation.
Audit revealed 178 active accounts with passwords identical or similar to defaults provided by Service Desk upon account creation or reset, making them highly susceptible to password guessing.
No dedicated password management policy existed; Acceptable Use policy contained only 'do not reveal or write down passwords' guidance.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand to The Electoral Commission for violations of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1)(b) of the UK GDPR. No monetary fine was imposed. The Electoral Commission accepted the Notice of Intent and the Commissioner's findings. Since the incident, the organisation has implemented remedial measures including: Technology Modernisation Plan, Managed Infrastructure Support Service, server and firewall monitoring, Threat and Vulnerability management solution, password policy controls in Active Directory, and Multi-factor authentication (MFA) for all users.
companyNow: The Electoral Commission continues to operate as the independent regulator of elections and political finance in the UK. The organisation has substantially modernised its IT infrastructure and security controls following this incident.
dataType: Names, home addresses (Electoral Register)

company: Scottish Government and NHS National Services Scotland (NHS NSS)
companyDescription: Scottish Government and NHS National Services Scotland are public sector bodies responsible for health policy and vaccination services in Scotland. They developed the NHS Scotland Covid Status App to provide digital proof of COVID-19 vaccination status.
companyLongDescription: Scottish Government and NHS National Services Scotland are public sector bodies responsible for health policy and vaccination services in Scotland. They developed the NHS Scotland Covid Status App to provide digital proof of COVID-19 vaccination status.
caseDescription: The NHS Scotland Covid Status App contained misleading consent statements and a complex, inaccessible privacy notice that failed to clearly inform users about data processing. Users were told they could consent to processing when data was actually being processed under a public task lawful basis. The app was launched with these compliance failures despite ICO warnings and a late-submitted Data Protection Impact Assessment revealing concerning third-party data retention practices for facial recognition training.
violationSummary: Sensitive health and biometric data of hundreds of thousands was exposed to misunderstanding and misuse due to deceptive transparency practices and inadequate information provision.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Scottish Government and NHS NSS launched the COVID Status App with a misleading consent statement asking users to consent to data processing when consent was not actually required; failed.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 554,504 and 615,639 users were deceived about their control over sensitive health data, and the inaccessible privacy notice led to public misunderstandings about data sharing with major.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users needed to consent to data processing in order to use the app
claimsVsReality.reality: Processing was based on public task lawful basis; consent was neither required nor collected, making the consent statement misleading

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy notice clearly informed users about how their health and biometric data would be processed
claimsVsReality.reality: Privacy notice was complex, inaccessible, difficult to navigate, and not linked from the app at launch; users could not easily understand their data processing rights

claimsVsReality.claim: Third-party identity verification provider would not retain facial images beyond verification purposes
claimsVsReality.reality: Provider intended to retain images for 5 days to train proprietary facial recognition algorithms; this was suspended only after ICO intervention

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: App contained misleading consent statement until 4 October 2021, giving 554,504–615,639 users false impression of control over their data when processing was based on public task, not consent
violations: App contained misleading consent statement until 4 October 2021, giving 554,504–615,639 users false impression of control over their data when processing was based on public task, not consent

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 12 requires information be provided in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form using clear and plain language.
regulatoryFindings.description: Privacy notice was not easily accessible from the app at launch and required ICO intervention to locate online; when reviewed, notice was complex, unnecessarily long, difficult to navigate, covering multiple services, making it impossible for users to clearly understand their rights and how data was being processed
violations: Privacy notice was not easily accessible from the app at launch and required ICO intervention to locate online; when reviewed, notice was complex, unnecessarily long, difficult to navigate, covering multiple services, making it impossible for users to clearly understand their rights and how data was being processed

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 13 sets out mandatory information that must be provided to individuals when data is collected.
regulatoryFindings.description: While all required information was eventually provided, it was buried in a confusing privacy notice covering multiple unrelated services, defeating the purpose of transparency and informed consent
violations: While all required information was eventually provided, it was buried in a confusing privacy notice covering multiple unrelated services, defeating the purpose of transparency and informed consent

outcome: ICO issued a reprimand (not a monetary penalty) in accordance with Article 58(2)(b) of UK GDPR. Scottish Government and NHS NSS were required to redraft the privacy notice to present Article 13 information in concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form using clear plain language within 30 days (by 28 March 2022). ICO warned that failure to comply would result in an Enforcement Notice. The ICO acknowledged remedial steps (preventing third parties from using data to train algorithms) and considered public health context, but found that delaying launch would have been appropriate given alternative methods existed for obtaining vaccine status.
companyNow: The Scottish Government and NHS NSS continue to operate the NHS Scotland Covid Status App and related health services. As public sector entities, they remain subject to ICO oversight and data protection compliance requirements.
dataType: Health data, vaccination status, biometric data (facial images), identity verification data
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
UK GDPR Article 12 – Transparent information in concise, intelligible form
UK GDPR Article 13 – Information to be provided where personal data collected

companyDescription: INSEKT FOOD S.L. (NIF B01594860) is a Spanish food company operating in the insect-based food sector. The company was subject to investigation for unlawful disclosure of customer personal data via WhatsApp.
companyLongDescription: INSEKT FOOD S.L. (NIF B01594860) is a Spanish food company operating in the insect-based food sector. The company was subject to investigation for unlawful disclosure of customer personal data via WhatsApp.
caseDescription: INSEKT FOOD S.L. shared a customer's personal data (name, address, postal code, locality, and province) across multiple WhatsApp group chats without consent. The company distributed this information to group members in three separate chats with 27–257 members each. No lawful basis for the processing existed.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal data (address and location identifiers) to multiple third parties via WhatsApp groups without consent or lawful basis, causing unauthorized dissemination of private information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: INSEKT FOOD S.L.'s owners shared a complainant's personal data—including name, surname, street address, postal code, locality.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unauthorized sharing exposed one person's full address and identity to hundreds of strangers across multiple messaging groups, creating real risk of harassment, stalking.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of the specified conditions is met, including explicit consent (Article 6(1)(a)).
regulatoryFindings.description: INSEKT FOOD S.L. processed and disseminated the complainant's personal data (name, address, postal code, locality, province) via WhatsApp group chats without obtaining the individual's consent or establishing any other lawful basis under Article 6.
violations: INSEKT FOOD S.L. processed and disseminated the complainant's personal data (name, address, postal code, locality, province) via WhatsApp group chats without obtaining the individual's consent or establishing any other lawful basis under Article 6.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5(a) provides that infringements of fundamental data processing principles (Articles 5–9) shall be subject to administrative fines of up to €20,000,000 or 4% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher.
regulatoryFindings.description: The unlawful disclosure constitutes a very serious infringement under LOPDGDD Article 72.1(b), which categorizes treatment of personal data without a lawful basis as highly grave and subject to a 3-year prescription period.
violations: The unlawful disclosure constitutes a very serious infringement under LOPDGDD Article 72.1(b), which categorizes treatment of personal data without a lawful basis as highly grave and subject to a 3-year prescription period.

outcome: The Director of the Spanish Data Protection Agency (AEPD) issued a final resolution finding INSEKT FOOD S.L. liable for violating GDPR Article 6. The company was ordered to pay a €4,000 fine. The decision became enforceable after the 10-day period for lodging objections expired without response. The company is required to make payment within the prescribed timeframe or face enforcement collection proceedings. The complainant may appeal via administrative remedy or direct challenge to the National Court.
companyNow: Unknown – No public information available regarding the current operational status of INSEKT FOOD S.L. following the enforcement action.
dataType: Name, surname, physical address, postal code, locality, province
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(1)(a) – Lack of valid consent
GDPR Art. 6 – General principle that processing must have a lawful basis

companyDescription: Parkside Community Primary School is a primary education institution in the United Kingdom serving children from early years through secondary transition, with a focus on safeguarding, pastoral support, and wellbeing.
companyLongDescription: Parkside Community Primary School is a primary education institution in the United Kingdom serving children from early years through secondary transition, with a focus on safeguarding, pastoral support, and wellbeing.
caseDescription: Parkside Community Primary School inappropriately disclosed sensitive personal data and special category data of four individuals, including three children, in a classroom environment via electronic whiteboard screen-sharing. The school lacked adequate policies, procedures, and guidance for secure email handling and system-specific protocols. Two employees failed to report the breach internally, compounding the violation.
violationSummary: The school's failure to implement adequate security measures resulted in sensitive personal data (including special category data relating to children) being exposed to unintended recipients in a classroom setting, exemplifying information exposure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Parkside Community Primary School inappropriately disclosed sensitive special category data, including information about safeguarding.
whyTheyWereWrong: Three children and one adult were exposed to sensitive personal information about vulnerable individuals in a shared classroom setting, causing potential distress.

claimsVsReality.claim: Parkside had overarching data protection policies in place (July 2020 Data Protection and Security Policy).
claimsVsReality.reality: These policies lacked critical detail on secure email handling, when to access sensitive data, and safeguarding system protocols, failing to provide practical guidance for classroom environments.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees were instructed to report breaches to the Headmaster without delay per the Data Breach Response Plan.
claimsVsReality.reality: Both employees involved in the incident failed to report the breach internally, suggesting the policies were either unknown or inadequately reinforced.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Parkside failed to implement adequate technical or organisational measures to ensure security and confidentiality when sharing personal data internally by email.
violations: Parkside failed to implement adequate technical or organisational measures to ensure security and confidentiality when sharing personal data internally by email.
No security classification or labelling system existed to indicate emails contained sensitive or special category data.
No written guidance was in place for when employees should access emails containing sensitive data during the school day.
Lack of policy governing the use of the case management system processing sensitive safeguarding and pastoral data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 24(1) of the UK GDPR requires that the controller shall be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate compliance with, the principles relating to the processing of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Parkside's data protection policies contained shortcomings and did not outline procedures for secure internal sharing of personal data by email.
violations: Parkside's data protection policies contained shortcomings and did not outline procedures for secure internal sharing of personal data by email.
Policies did not specify when it was appropriate to open emails containing personal data in a classroom environment.
No adequate governance or oversight mechanisms were in place for the management and monitoring of sensitive data systems.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32 of the UK GDPR requires that the controller and processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lack of written guidance for employees on using security and confidentiality classifications on emails containing sensitive or special category data.
violations: Lack of written guidance for employees on using security and confidentiality classifications on emails containing sensitive or special category data.
No written procedures or guidance for safe operation of electronic whiteboards when screen-sharing from employee devices.
Inadequate access controls and data handling procedures for the case management system used for sensitive safeguarding data.
No restrictions on when sensitive data could be accessed or displayed during the school day in classroom environments.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to Parkside Community Primary School. The school was required to implement comprehensive remedial measures including: reviewing and updating data protection policies with detailed breach reporting procedures; issuing staff guidance on secure email handling and classification of sensitive data; restricting access to sensitive case management system records; implementing scheduled access windows for sensitive alerts outside classroom times; providing UK GDPR refresher training to all staff and governors; and taking steps to test and embed new processes. The Commissioner recommended continued monitoring, refresher training on electronic whiteboard operation, evaluation of case management system guidance adequacy, emphasis on breach reporting consequences, and regular policy reviews with staff awareness campaigns.
companyNow: Parkside Community Primary School remains operational. As of the decision, the school has implemented comprehensive data protection improvements and governance reviews overseen by a designated governor responsible for UK GDPR compliance.
dataType: Special category data, safeguarding data, pastoral information, children's sensitive personal data
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 24(1) – Responsibility of the Controller
UK GDPR Article 32 – Security of Processing

companyDescription: Bolton at Home Ltd is a housing provider based in Bolton, England, that manages accommodation and housing services. It operates a subsidiary company, Starts With You (SWY), which provides support services including energy advice.
companyLongDescription: Bolton at Home Ltd is a housing provider based in Bolton, England, that manages accommodation and housing services. It operates a subsidiary company, Starts With You (SWY), which provides support services including energy advice.
caseDescription: Bolton at Home disclosed a domestic abuse victim's new address and relocation plans to her abusive husband by leaving a voicemail on his phone number, which was incorrectly copied from a shared record to her new accommodation application. The disclosure resulted in the husband visiting the property. Reporting to the ICO was delayed beyond the 72-hour requirement due to failures in internal breach notification procedures.
violationSummary: The organisation disclosed sensitive personal data (address and relocation intent) related to domestic abuse to an unauthorized third party (the abuser) due to inaccurate record creation and lack of safeguarding protocols.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Bolton at Home copied a domestic abuse victim's husband's phone number into her new accommodation record without verification, then shared it with a subsidiary that called him.
whyTheyWereWrong: The victim's abusive husband learned of her escape plan and new address, visited the property to find her.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bolton at Home had systems and processes in place to handle sensitive domestic abuse cases appropriately.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation had no formal record creation policy, only a draft (not embedded) warning code policy, and no safeguarding markers were applied to the new accommodation record or shared data, resulting in disclosure of the victim's location to her abuser.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bolton at Home had internal breach reporting mechanisms that complied with GDPR notification requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Staff treated the complaint as a routine service matter rather than a data breach, delaying notification by nine days beyond the 72-hour requirement, and the Information Governance Team was never alerted.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires data controllers to ensure that personal data remains accurate and up to date in line with the purposes for which it is being processed.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bolton at Home created a new record by copying data from a shared record without verification, including the husband's telephone number in error, with no formal policy or procedure in place to prevent inaccurate record creation.
violations: Bolton at Home created a new record by copying data from a shared record without verification, including the husband's telephone number in error, with no formal policy or procedure in place to prevent inaccurate record creation.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires data controllers to process personal data securely by means of appropriate technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: No safeguarding markers were applied to the new record or data shared with Starts With You regarding domestic abuse or that the husband should not be contacted. The informal warning code policy was only in draft form and not formally embedded.
violations: No safeguarding markers were applied to the new record or data shared with Starts With You regarding domestic abuse or that the husband should not be contacted. The informal warning code policy was only in draft form and not formally embedded.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 33(1) requires data controllers to notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bolton at Home took nine days to notify the ICO (16 March to 25 March 2021). Internal reporting mechanisms failed because the staff member who received the complaint treated it as a service matter, and discussion followed about whether it constituted a data breach at all, delaying notification.
violations: Bolton at Home took nine days to notify the ICO (16 March to 25 March 2021). Internal reporting mechanisms failed because the staff member who received the complaint treated it as a service matter, and discussion followed about whether it constituted a data breach at all, delaying notification.

outcome: ICO issued a reprimand under Article 58 of the UK GDPR. Bolton at Home was required to: (1) implement a formal record creation policy and process; (2) formalise the draft warning code policy; (3) embed these policies within data protection practices; (4) review and improve internal breach reporting policies to ensure future Article 33 compliance; (5) provide adequate staff training. Progress update due by 7 December 2022. The ICO warned that if further information or incidents emerge, further formal regulatory action may be considered. The data subject and her son were accommodated in the property with extra security measures and a domestic abuse marker placed on it. The husband's phone number was removed from the record.
companyNow: Bolton at Home Ltd operates as a housing provider in Bolton. The organisation has undertaken remedial measures including implementing safeguarding systems and planning integrated housing management systems.
dataType: Name, address, telephone number, domestic violence status
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Art. 33(1) – Notification to supervisory authority

company: Tochtergesellschaft eines Berliner E-Commerce-Konzerns (subsidiary of Berlin e-commerce conglomerate)
companyDescription: A subsidiary of a Berlin-based e-commerce conglomerate with three-digit millions in annual revenue, operating customer service and order fulfillment operations within a larger corporate group.
companyLongDescription: A subsidiary of a Berlin-based e-commerce conglomerate with three-digit millions in annual revenue, operating customer service and order fulfillment operations within a larger corporate group.
caseDescription: A data protection officer appointed by an e-commerce company subsidiary held a conflict of interest by simultaneously serving as CEO of two service companies that processed personal data on behalf of the main company. The officer was required to oversee compliance with data protection law at entities he himself managed, creating a self-monitoring situation that violates GDPR Article 38(6). Despite a 2021 warning, the violation persisted, resulting in a €525,000 fine.
violationSummary: The conflict of interest compromised the DPO's independent oversight function, undermining internal controls and safeguards that protect personal data during processing by service companies within the corporate group.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Appointed a data protection officer who simultaneously served as CEO of two service subsidiaries that processed personal data on contract for the parent company.
whyTheyWereWrong: The officer could not independently oversee data protection compliance while simultaneously directing the operations he was supposed to monitor, undermining safeguards for customer.

claimsVsReality.claim: A data protection officer was appointed to independently oversee data protection compliance across the organization.
claimsVsReality.reality: The appointed DPO was simultaneously managing the very service companies whose data processing activities he was supposed to oversee, making independent oversight impossible.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 38(6) requires that a data protection officer must not be subject to instructions or conflicts of interest from other duties, and must be able to perform their role independently.
regulatoryFindings.description: The DPO was simultaneously CEO of two service companies processing personal data under contract for the main company, creating an irresolvable conflict of interest where he could not independently oversee operations he directly controlled.
violations: The DPO was simultaneously CEO of two service companies processing personal data under contract for the main company, creating an irresolvable conflict of interest where he could not independently oversee operations he directly controlled.

outcome: The Berliner Beauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit (BlnBDI) issued a warning in 2021. Upon reinspection in 2022, the violation persisted despite the warning. A fine of €525,000 was imposed. The fine is not yet legally binding (still subject to appeal). The company cooperated extensively with the authority and resolved the violation during the penalty proceedings by removing the DPO from the conflicted position.
dataType: Customer data, order data, general personal data processed through customer service and order fulfillment
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 38(6) - Requirement that data protection officer be free from conflicts of interest

companyDescription: Alpha Bank A.E. is a major Greek commercial and investment bank, one of the four largest banking groups in Greece, founded in 1926. It provides retail, corporate, and investment banking services throughout Greece and internationally.
companyLongDescription: Alpha Bank A.E. is a major Greek commercial and investment bank, one of the four largest banking groups in Greece, founded in 1926. It provides retail, corporate, and investment banking services throughout Greece and internationally.
caseDescription: Alpha Bank stored transaction history (amount and date of last ten transactions) on credit/debit card chips without informing cardholders. The Greek Data Protection Authority found the bank violated GDPR transparency requirements by failing to inform customers about this data processing, even though the data was stored by the card manufacturer as an optional feature.
violationSummary: The bank failed to implement data protection by design and transparency, storing financial transaction data without user knowledge or consent, creating potential for unauthorized access if cards were lost or stolen.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Alpha Bank issued Mastercard credit/debit cards with chip-stored transaction history (amounts and dates of last 10 transactions) without informing cardholders of this data processing.
whyTheyWereWrong: Cardholders could not make informed decisions about their financial data because Alpha Bank secretly stored.

claimsVsReality.claim: The transaction data (amount and date) stored on the chip are not personal data and therefore do not require GDPR protections or notification.
claimsVsReality.reality: The transaction data can be linked to the cardholder via the cardholder's name printed on the card face and the card number, making them personal data under GDPR. The data revealed consumer spending patterns and could be read wirelessly without card loss.

claimsVsReality.claim: The stored data poses no practical risk because customers already know their own transaction history and thieves would not bother reading the chip.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data was accessible via widely available smartphone NFC readers without requiring card theft, and family members or close associates could easily access it. Unauthorized readers could profile the cardholder's spending habits.

claimsVsReality.claim: Informing customers would create unjustified panic and damage trust in card payment systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: Transparent, well-drafted notices do not inherently cause panic. The Authority determined that proper risk-based notification is required by law regardless of perceived market impact.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Alpha Bank processed transaction data on cardholders' chips without transparent notification to those cardholders, violating the transparency principle.
violations: Alpha Bank processed transaction data on cardholders' chips without transparent notification to those cardholders, violating the transparency principle.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13 requires controllers to provide specified information to data subjects when collecting personal data directly from them, including the purposes and legal basis for processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Alpha Bank failed to inform cardholders about the storage of their transaction history on the chip, despite the data being collected directly from them via card usage.
violations: Alpha Bank failed to inform cardholders about the storage of their transaction history on the chip, despite the data being collected directly from them via card usage.

outcome: Alpha Bank was ordered to pay an administrative monetary fine of €20,000. The Authority required the bank to inform affected cardholders about the data processing and provide them with the ability to opt out. The bank committed to gradually phasing out affected Mastercard cards (stopping orders in April 2018, stock depleted by July 2019) and issued replacement cards without this feature. Monitoring by the Authority was implied.
companyNow: Alpha Bank continues operations as a major Greek lender. The fine and compliance order represent a small enforcement action relative to the bank's substantial asset base and market presence.
dataType: Financial transaction data (transaction amounts and dates)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject

companyDescription: Virgin Media Limited is a UK telecommunications company providing broadband, television, and mobile services to residential and business customers. It is a major provider of fixed-line and mobile services in the United Kingdom.
companyLongDescription: Virgin Media Limited is a UK telecommunications company providing broadband, television, and mobile services to residential and business customers. It is a major provider of fixed-line and mobile services in the United Kingdom.
caseDescription: Virgin Media failed to respond to Subject Access Requests (SARs) within statutory one-month timeframes during July 2021–April 2022. The company did not respond to 14% of SARs during the first half of this period and received 493 complaints about SAR delays, representing 51% of all Virgin Media complaints to the ICO in 2021. The ICO issued a reprimand and recommended Virgin Media improve staffing and compliance procedures.
violationSummary: The company's failure to respond to data access requests within statutory timeframes constitutes systemic mishandling of personal data processing obligations and inadequate operational safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Virgin Media failed to respond to 14% of Subject Access Requests (1,316 requests) within the statutory one-month deadline during July–December 2021, and received 493 complaints about SAR delays.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers were denied timely access to their own personal data, preventing them from understanding what information Virgin Media held about them and how it was being used for an extended period.

claimsVsReality.claim: Virgin Media processes Subject Access Requests in compliance with UK GDPR requirements
claimsVsReality.reality: Virgin Media failed to respond to 14% of SARs within one month and received 493 complaints about delays, with 95% relating to response delays

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Art. 12(3): The controller shall provide information on action taken on a request under Articles 15–22 to the data subject without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt of the request (extendable by two months where necessary).
