regulatoryFindings.description: Virgin Media did not respond to 14% of SARs within one calendar month during July–December 2021
violations: Virgin Media did not respond to 14% of SARs within one calendar month during July–December 2021
Virgin Media systematically failed to meet the one-month statutory deadline across the investigation period (July 2021–April 2022)

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Art. 15(1): The data subject shall have the right to obtain from the controller confirmation as to whether personal data concerning them are being processed, and where that is the case, access to the personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Virgin Media failed to confirm whether personal data was being processed or provide access within statutory timeframes, effectively denying data subjects timely exercise of their rights
violations: Virgin Media failed to confirm whether personal data was being processed or provide access within statutory timeframes, effectively denying data subjects timely exercise of their rights

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Art. 15(3): The controller shall provide a copy of the personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Virgin Media did not provide copies of personal data within required timeframes, preventing subjects from obtaining information about their processed data
violations: Virgin Media did not provide copies of personal data within required timeframes, preventing subjects from obtaining information about their processed data

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand to Virgin Media under Article 58 of the UK GDPR. Virgin Media was directed to: (1) take further steps to ensure SARs are responded to within statutory deadlines; (2) ensure adequate staff resources are in place to process and respond to SARs. Virgin Media must provide updates on SAR compliance and improvement plan progress to the ICO after three months (20 December 2022) and six months (20 March 2023) from the letter date. The ICO warned that further information, incidents, or complaints could lead to revisiting the matter and considering additional formal regulatory action. The matter is closed pending compliance verification.
companyNow: Virgin Media is a major UK telecom provider offering broadband, TV, and mobile services. The company continues operations as a subsidiary of Liberty Global.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types subject to access requests)

companyDescription: Kent Police is a territorial police force responsible for policing Kent County and Medway in South East England. As a public law enforcement agency, it is accountable to statutory data protection requirements and the public.
companyLongDescription: Kent Police is a territorial police force responsible for policing Kent County and Medway in South East England. As a public law enforcement agency, it is accountable to statutory data protection requirements and the public.
caseDescription: Kent Police failed to respond to Subject Access Requests (SARs) within statutory timescales. During April 2020 to April 2021, only 60% of SARs were answered within one month, declining further to 22% by June 2022. The ICO found systematic delays in processing requests for personal data access, driven by inadequate staffing and procedural failures.
violationSummary: Kent Police systematically excluded data subjects from exercising their right of access by failing to respond within statutory timeframes, preventing individuals from knowing what personal data was held and processed about them.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Kent Police failed to respond to 40% of Subject Access Requests within the one-month statutory deadline from April 2020 to April 2021.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of individuals were denied timely access to their own personal data held by police, preventing them from exercising fundamental rights to know what information law enforcement held.

claimsVsReality.claim: Kent Police's policies and procedures were designed to process SARs in compliance with GDPR requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: In practice, only 60% of SARs were processed within statutory deadlines during the investigation period, declining to 22% by mid-2022, indicating systemic failure in implementation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Adequate resourcing was in place to handle SARs.
claimsVsReality.reality: The ICO found insufficient staff resources dedicated to SAR processing, with heavy reliance on the Digital Forensics Unit creating bottlenecks.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 12(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide information on action taken on data subject requests without undue delay and in any event within one month of receipt, extendable by two months for complex requests with notification.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kent Police failed to meet the one-month deadline for 40% of SARs in the investigation period and only 22% of SARs by June 2022, without adequate notification of extensions.
violations: Kent Police failed to meet the one-month deadline for 40% of SARs in the investigation period and only 22% of SARs by June 2022, without adequate notification of extensions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(1) UK GDPR grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of whether personal data is being processed and to access such personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kent Police denied data subjects timely access to their personal data by systematically failing to respond to access requests within statutory timeframes.
violations: Kent Police denied data subjects timely access to their personal data by systematically failing to respond to access requests within statutory timeframes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 15(3) UK GDPR requires controllers to provide a copy of personal data undergoing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kent Police failed to provide copies of personal data within the statutory deadline for the majority of requests.
violations: Kent Police failed to provide copies of personal data within the statutory deadline for the majority of requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 45, Part 3, DPA 2018 entitles data subjects to obtain from the controller access to personal data without undue delay and in any event before the end of the applicable time period.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kent Police breached this statutory right by failing to respond to requests within the prescribed timeframe.
violations: Kent Police breached this statutory right by failing to respond to requests within the prescribed timeframe.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand under Article 58 of the UK GDPR for infringements of Article 12(3), Article 15(1), Article 15(3), and Section 45 DPA 2018. Kent Police was ordered to: (1) ensure SARs are responded to within statutory deadlines; (2) secure adequate staff resources; (3) review reliance on Digital Forensics Unit for redactions; (4) provide data subjects with information about making SARs including verbal requests; (5) produce a detailed improvement plan. Kent Police must provide progress updates to the ICO after three months (23 December 2022) and six months (23 March 2023). The matter is closed pending receipt of compliance updates.
companyNow: Kent Police continues to operate as the primary police force for Kent County in England. As of 2022, the organization remains under ongoing monitoring by the ICO to verify compliance with data protection obligations regarding Subject Access Request timelines.
dataType: personal data subject to Subject Access Requests (including identifiable information held in police records)

companyDescription: The Welsh Language Commissioner is a public sector regulatory body in Wales responsible for promoting and facilitating use of the Welsh language. It holds personal data in its administrative and regulatory functions.
companyLongDescription: The Welsh Language Commissioner is a public sector regulatory body in Wales responsible for promoting and facilitating use of the Welsh language. It holds personal data in its administrative and regulatory functions.
caseDescription: The Welsh Language Commissioner suffered a ransomware attack via phishing email that encrypted all systems and backups. The ICO found the organisation failed to implement industry-standard backup and patch management practices, violating GDPR security requirements. The organisation was issued a reprimand and must implement remedial measures.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures (backups, patch management, system hardening) to protect personal data against unauthorised destruction and loss, as required by GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The Welsh Language Commissioner failed to maintain offline, logically-separated backups; operated end-of-life infrastructure without security updates for 12 months; ran outdated vulnerable.
whyTheyWereWrong: Makop ransomware encrypted all WLC systems and backups, permanently destroying all organizational data because backups were accessible from the main network.

claimsVsReality.claim: Initial forensic investigator reported logging/auditing was switched off on almost all machines.
claimsVsReality.reality: WLC stated logging/auditing was in place on all desktop computers and servers at time of attack; attacker disabled it on infected equipment post-compromise.

claimsVsReality.claim: Threat actor claimed all corporate data was exfiltrated.
claimsVsReality.reality: Police dark web search found no evidence of published data; insufficient evidence to confirm accuracy of exfiltration claims.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised disclosure, unlawful destruction, loss, or alteration.
regulatoryFindings.description: WLC failed to implement multiple, logically-separated offline backups as recommended by NCSC guidance, allowing ransomware to encrypt all backups simultaneously.
violations: WLC failed to implement multiple, logically-separated offline backups as recommended by NCSC guidance, allowing ransomware to encrypt all backups simultaneously.
WLC operated systems without security updates for 12 months and used outdated vulnerable software, enabling initial compromise via phishing.
WLC had no written patching policy to ensure systems remained secure and up-to-date.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection against ransomware and data loss.
regulatoryFindings.description: Backup solution lacked logical separation and offline-only status, failing NCSC and industry standards for ransomware resilience.
violations: Backup solution lacked logical separation and offline-only status, failing NCSC and industry standards for ransomware resilience.
End-of-life infrastructure and outdated software created critical security posture vulnerabilities exploitable by threat actors.
Absence of documented patch management procedures prevented systematic application of security updates.

outcome: The ICO issued a formal reprimand on 18 January 2022. The WLC must implement remedial measures including: suitable backup solution in line with industry guidance; automated software updates; Multi-Factor Authentication for all users; review and hardening of logging/monitoring systems. The ICO welcomed completed migrations to cloud infrastructure and deployment of MFA. Investigation closed with notice that further incidents or information may trigger additional formal regulatory action.
companyNow: The Welsh Language Commissioner has implemented cloud migration, automated patching, and MFA systems. As a public body, it continues regulatory operations with enhanced security posture.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types, held by public regulatory body)

companyDescription: Arbeidstilsynet is Norway's government labour inspection authority responsible for enforcing workplace safety and employment law. Founded in 1915, it conducts workplace inspections and investigations.
companyLongDescription: Arbeidstilsynet is Norway's government labour inspection authority responsible for enforcing workplace safety and employment law. Founded in 1915, it conducts workplace inspections and investigations.
caseDescription: Arbeidstilsynet (Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority) conducted an unlawful credit check on a sole proprietor without legal basis. An inspector deliberately obtained credit rating information from Bisnode/Proff Forvalt to investigate potential misconduct by a related company, but the sole proprietor was not under supervision. The authority lacked formal procedures and legal justification for the credit assessment, violating GDPR's lawfulness principle.
violationSummary: Authority conducted systematic surveillance of personal financial data (credit rating) without legal authorization, statutory basis, or internal safeguards. This falls squarely within GDPR's prohibition on unlawful processing and violates the legality principle.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Arbeidstilsynet's inspector obtained a credit rating of a sole proprietor through Proff Forvalt on April 1, 2020, without legal authority, internal procedures, or prior notice to the individual.
whyTheyWereWrong: The sole proprietor's sensitive financial data including credit score, payment history, and debt levels was accessed without legal basis.

claimsVsReality.claim: Inspector claimed credit check was necessary to investigate a company under supervision and check its business network.
claimsVsReality.reality: The sole proprietor was never under supervision; credit information was obtained from third party (Bisnode) without consent or legal basis, and no rettslig grunnlag existed under Norwegian law

claimsVsReality.claim: Arbeidstilsynet personnel told the proprietor 'No one at Arbeidstilsynet can perform credit assessments or has access to programs to do so.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Arbeidstilsynet had access to Proff Forvalt credit tool and an inspector had deliberately used it to obtain the proprietor's credit rating on 1 April 2020

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Arbeidstilsynet obtained credit rating without lawful basis; no legal justification existed to process the proprietor's personal data
violations: Arbeidstilsynet obtained credit rating without lawful basis; no legal justification existed to process the proprietor's personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1)(e) permits processing only where necessary to perform a task in the public interest or exercise official authority, and Article 6(3) requires supplementary legal basis in national law.
regulatoryFindings.description: Norwegian Labour Law §18-5 does not authorize credit checks of third parties not under supervision; no national legal basis supported the credit assessment
violations: Norwegian Labour Law §18-5 does not authorize credit checks of third parties not under supervision; no national legal basis supported the credit assessment

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, including written procedures and internal controls.
regulatoryFindings.description: Arbeidstilsynet had no written procedures, internal guidelines, or access controls for credit assessments; no routine documented when/how credit tool could be used
violations: Arbeidstilsynet had no written procedures, internal guidelines, or access controls for credit assessments; no routine documented when/how credit tool could be used

outcome: Datatilsynet issued a final administrative decision on 16 May 2022 imposing a penalty of 150,000 NOK. Arbeidstilsynet accepted the penalty and issued on 2 December 2021. The authority updated procedures to prohibit credit assessments in supervision cases, completing a mapping of personal data processing by December 2020. A separate reprimand decision was issued (doc. 20/02875-11). The proprietor retained right to appeal to Personvernnemnda (Privacy Board) within three weeks.
companyNow: Arbeidstilsynet is the official Norwegian Labour Inspection Authority and continues to operate as a government agency. It has since implemented updated routines explicitly prohibiting credit assessments in inspection cases.
dataType: Credit ratings, financial data, payment history, debt information, creditworthiness scores
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(1)(e) and Art. 6(3) - Lack of supplementary legal basis in national law
GDPR Art. 24 - Failure to implement controller safeguards and internal procedures

companyDescription: Jackson Quinn is a legal practice in Retford, Nottinghamshire specializing in family law matters, including adoption proceedings and representation of vulnerable parties such as children in family court proceedings.
companyLongDescription: Jackson Quinn is a legal practice in Retford, Nottinghamshire specializing in family law matters, including adoption proceedings and representation of vulnerable parties such as children in family court proceedings.
caseDescription: Jackson Quinn, a legal representative, disclosed confidential adoption bundle documents containing sensitive personal data about two children, their mother, and extended family to the birth father in error. The documents included current photographs, family addresses, and school information, and remained in the possession of a high-risk individual (imprisoned for rape convictions) for seven weeks. The disclosure occurred due to inadequate document handling procedures, lack of proper redaction practices, and outdated data protection policies.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of confidential personal data to an unwanted third party (birth father) due to lack of proper safeguards, document handling procedures, and redaction practices. High-risk recipient posed direct threat to data subjects.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Jackson Quinn included sensitive adoption reports containing children's personal data, family addresses, school information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two children and their mother, a rape survivor, had intimate personal information disclosed to a high-risk individual imprisoned for rape offenses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Jackson Quinn claimed the third-party family members in the Annex A reports were all known to all parties involved in the adoption case.
claimsVsReality.reality: The reports contained sensitive information about extended family members, current photographs, and family addresses that should have been redacted or withheld given the high-risk recipient (imprisoned violent offender).

claimsVsReality.claim: Jackson Quinn claimed the data protection policy was annually reviewed and current.
claimsVsReality.reality: The policy provided to the ICO was dated 2019 with no version control, contained an incorrect link to the ICO website (linking to non-existent 'ISO'), and no evidence existed that staff had read or understood it.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed with integrity and confidentiality, with appropriate security against unauthorised processing, unlawful processing, and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Jackson Quinn failed to implement suitable policies for creation of adoption bundles, leaving no guidelines for staff to follow and resulting in disclosure of sensitive data to wrong recipient.
violations: Jackson Quinn failed to implement suitable policies for creation of adoption bundles, leaving no guidelines for staff to follow and resulting in disclosure of sensitive data to wrong recipient.
Jackson Quinn did not redact documents to proper standard; redacted information remained legible through marker-pen strikethrough when viewed on computer screen.

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Art. 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security level appropriate to risk, considering state of the art, implementation costs, and nature/scope/context/purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Jackson Quinn lacked adequate policies and procedures for handling sensitive family court documents, particularly adoption cases involving vulnerable children.
violations: Jackson Quinn lacked adequate policies and procedures for handling sensitive family court documents, particularly adoption cases involving vulnerable children.
Jackson Quinn failed to implement proper redaction software despite having means and resources to do so, relying instead on marker-pen redactions that were inadequate.

outcome: The ICO issued Jackson Quinn a reprimand under Article 58 of the UK GDPR on 19 August 2022. The Commissioner recommended three remedial steps: (1) update data protection policy to version-controlled format with corrected external links and staff confirmation of understanding; (2) implement written bundle creation policy covering domestic abuse, adoption, and children's cases, circulated to staff; (3) review redaction policy and implement appropriate redaction software, including review of previously redacted documents. Jackson Quinn was required to provide updates by 19 November 2022. The ICO stated that if further incidents or complaints emerge, the matter would be revisited and formal regulatory action may be considered. The matter is now closed.
companyNow: Jackson Quinn appears to be a small legal practice based in Retford, Nottinghamshire. Following the ICO investigation, the firm implemented remedial policies for protecting confidential data, particularly in domestic abuse, adoption, and children's cases.
dataType: Children's personal data, family addresses, school information, photographs, mother and extended family information
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Art. 32 – Security of Processing

companyDescription: Egnatia Odos A.E. is a Greek public-private partnership company responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Egnatia Motorway, a major highway corridor in northern Greece connecting Igoumenitsa to Kipi (Turkish border). It operates toll collection systems across multiple stations.
companyLongDescription: Egnatia Odos A.E. is a Greek public-private partnership company responsible for the operation and maintenance of the Egnatia Motorway, a major highway corridor in northern Greece connecting Igoumenitsa to Kipi (Turkish border). It operates toll collection systems across multiple stations.
caseDescription: Egnatia Odos failed to respond timely to a data subject's access request under GDPR Article 15 and initially denied access to personal data, claiming only law enforcement could receive it. The company eventually provided limited information after the DPA's intervention, but violated the mandatory response deadline and transparency obligations.
violationSummary: The company improperly excluded the data subject from accessing his own personal data by invoking a third-party protection exception that did not apply and misrepresenting legal requirements.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Egnatia Odos initially denied a motorist's request for access to personal data about a toll violation charge.
whyTheyWereWrong: The motorist was unable to challenge the toll violation fine or verify the legality of the charges against him because Egnatia Odos unlawfully withheld evidence of the alleged violation for over.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data can only be provided to third parties with a prosecutorial order and DPA permission.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data subject (the motorist charged with the violation) was not a third party but the person to whom the data related, and was entitled to access under GDPR Article 15 without such prerequisites.

claimsVsReality.claim: The passage was recorded in a video system at toll station X.
claimsVsReality.reality: After investigation, the company could produce no video evidence, only a handwritten entry in the incident log, undermining the reliability of its initial claim and suggesting technical failures in data management.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company was cooperating in a friendly manner and had started compliance procedures with GDPR from the outset.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company initially denied access, misrepresented the legal framework, and only began providing information after repeated intervention by the DPA, delaying the data subject's ability to challenge the allegation for years.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires the controller to provide information and take action on a data subject's request without undue delay and within one month of receipt, extendable by two months for complex requests with proper notice.
regulatoryFindings.description: Egnatia Odos initially refused to provide access, citing a need for prosecutorial order and DPA permission, which were not legal prerequisites under Article 15.
violations: Egnatia Odos initially refused to provide access, citing a need for prosecutorial order and DPA permission, which were not legal prerequisites under Article 15.
The company failed to respond within the one-month deadline, only providing partial data after the DPA's intervention months later.
The initial response was misleading, suggesting the data subject was a third party when he was in fact the subject of the data and the party charged with the violation.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects an unconditional right to confirmation of processing and a copy of personal data concerning them, subject only to exceptions under Article 15(4) for protecting third-party rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company incorrectly applied third-party protection reasoning to deny access to data that were fundamentally about the data subject himself (vehicle registration linked to a toll violation allegation against him).
violations: The company incorrectly applied third-party protection reasoning to deny access to data that were fundamentally about the data subject himself (vehicle registration linked to a toll violation allegation against him).
Video recordings of the passage, though containing potential third-party data, should have been assessed for redaction and disclosure under Article 15(4), not wholesale denial.
The company had received prior written guidance from the DPA in 2017 on this exact obligation but did not adapt its practices.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 4(1) and Article 4(10) define 'data subject' as the person to whom personal data relates, distinct from a 'third party.' A person charged with a violation and seeking evidence about the allegation is a data subject with respect to that data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Egnatia Odos treated the complainant as a third party seeking access to toll system records, when he was the actual subject of the toll violation allegation and thus the data subject with respect to his own passage and charge.
violations: Egnatia Odos treated the complainant as a third party seeking access to toll system records, when he was the actual subject of the toll violation allegation and thus the data subject with respect to his own passage and charge.

outcome: The Greek DPA (Αρχή Προστασίας Δεδομένων Προσωπικού Χαρακτήρα) imposed a fine of €1,000 for violation of GDPR Article 12(3) due to delayed and initially refused response to the data access request. The decision found that Egnatia Odos had received prior guidance from the DPA (in 2017) on its obligations to honor subject access requests for video evidence, yet the company persisted in denying access based on a misinterpretation of law enforcement exceptions. After the DPA's intervention, the company eventually provided a one-page excerpt from its incident log but no video footage, claiming a technical malfunction prevented recording on the day in question. The DPA emphasized that the company's negligence in satisfying the right of access, combined with knowledge of its obligations, warranted an administrative penalty, even though the company ultimately complied.
companyNow: Egnatia Odos A.E. continues to operate as Greece's toll highway operator. The company has reportedly commenced compliance procedures with GDPR following the enforcement action.
dataType: Vehicle registration data, license plate information, personal identification data, video surveillance recordings
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 4(1) – definition of data subject vs. third party

companyDescription: Wakefield Council is a local government authority in West Yorkshire, England, responsible for public services including children's social care and legal proceedings.
companyLongDescription: Wakefield Council is a local government authority in West Yorkshire, England, responsible for public services including children's social care and legal proceedings.
caseDescription: Wakefield Council disclosed a mother's home address and her two children's details in court protection documents sent to the father, despite the mother's documented fear of domestic violence. The breach occurred due to failure to redact confidential information and lack of documented procedures for handling sensitive court documents.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of personal data (home address) to third party (father) not authorized to receive it, resulting in breach of confidentiality and integrity of sensitive personal information in child protection context.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Wakefield Council sent a Child Protection Medical Report containing the home address of a domestic violence victim.
whyTheyWereWrong: The mother, who feared the father due to ongoing domestic violence and a previous break-in, was forced to move herself.

claimsVsReality.claim: Court documents were prepared and sent as standard legal proceeding bundles to parents
claimsVsReality.reality: Documents contained unredacted sensitive home address of abuse victim and children despite available 'hide' function and clear need to protect from perpetrator

claimsVsReality.claim: Social Worker identified documents were ready for filing
claimsVsReality.reality: Social Worker failed to identify that mother's confidential address was included in the Child Protection Medical Report

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Wakefield Council failed to ensure appropriate security by allowing unredacted home address of mother (fleeing domestic violence) to be disclosed to father in court documents without identification and redaction controls
violations: Wakefield Council failed to ensure appropriate security by allowing unredacted home address of mother (fleeing domestic violence) to be disclosed to father in court documents without identification and redaction controls

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 24(1) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure processing complies with regulation, reviewed and updated where necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Council had no documented policies, procedures or guidance for Social Workers on redacting confidential addresses from court documents or using available 'hide' function on Children's Services system prior to breach
violations: Council had no documented policies, procedures or guidance for Social Workers on redacting confidential addresses from court documents or using available 'hide' function on Children's Services system prior to breach

outcome: ICO issued formal reprimand under Article 58 of UK GDPR. Council required to implement remedial measures including updated Data Protection training, reviewed policies/procedures for redacting confidential information, accountability monitoring through assurance testing/auditing, and organisational sharing of breach lessons learned. Follow-up ICO audit planned for November 2022. Matter closed pending any future incidents.
companyNow: Wakefield Council continues to operate as local government authority. As of May 2022, Council implemented guidance on redaction procedures and mandatory review questions for Team Managers to verify sensitive information redaction.
dataType: Home address, child protection medical information, family circumstances

companyDescription: A small retail fuel station (gas station/petrol station) operator in Greece engaged in the provision of fuel and related services. The operator installed video surveillance equipment to protect the premises and its assets.
companyLongDescription: A small retail fuel station (gas station/petrol station) operator in Greece engaged in the provision of fuel and related services. The operator installed video surveillance equipment to protect the premises and its assets.
caseDescription: A gas station operator recorded surveillance footage capturing a minor picking up a lost item and subsequently shared this recording with police and disclosed it to the alleged victim without proper legal basis or notice. The operator failed to respond to the minor's parent's access request and did not inform the data subject that their personal data had been further processed and transmitted to authorities.
violationSummary: The operator disclosed the personal data (video imagery of a minor) to third parties (police and alleged victim) without adequate legal basis or consent, and failed to provide transparency about this disclosure to the data subject.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A gas station operator installed a surveillance system that recorded a minor, shared the footage with police and an alleged victim without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The minor's image was displayed to a third party and transmitted to authorities without parental consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator claimed she did not have the technical knowledge to edit and transmit only the portion of footage showing the minor.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lack of technical capability does not excuse non-compliance with GDPR rights. The operator should either have not transmitted the footage at all without consent, or obtained the data subject's permission and only then transmitted necessary portions.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator claimed she was unaware that the complainant's son was accused of a crime and that no one had informed her of the allegations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ignorance of criminal proceedings against an individual does not eliminate the requirement to seek consent before disclosing that individual's image or to respond to data access requests from the data subject.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator transmitted video imagery of a minor to police and disclosed it to the alleged victim without prior consent or transparent notification to the data subject.
violations: The operator transmitted video imagery of a minor to police and disclosed it to the alleged victim without prior consent or transparent notification to the data subject.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12 requires the controller to take action on a data subject's access request and, if not acting, to inform the data subject without undue delay (maximum one month) of the reasons and the right to lodge a complaint.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator failed to respond to the parent's repeated access requests via phone, personal visits, and through their attorney, and did not provide any explanation for the refusal or notification of the right to complain.
violations: The operator failed to respond to the parent's repeated access requests via phone, personal visits, and through their attorney, and did not provide any explanation for the refusal or notification of the right to complain.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 14(4) requires that when a controller intends to further process personal data for a purpose other than the original collection, the controller must provide information about the new purpose prior to processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator did not inform the data subject that the surveillance footage would be processed further and transmitted to police or shown to third parties.
violations: The operator did not inform the data subject that the surveillance footage would be processed further and transmitted to police or shown to third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: Guideline 1/2011 Article 9 permits transmission of surveillance data to third parties only upon prior consent of the data subject, or in specified legal circumstances such as legitimate requests from law enforcement, provided the transmission is necessary and proportionate.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator transmitted the minor's image without first establishing whether a legal basis existed and without confirming the proportionality of disclosing a minor's image to resolve a property dispute.
violations: The operator transmitted the minor's image without first establishing whether a legal basis existed and without confirming the proportionality of disclosing a minor's image to resolve a property dispute.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority imposed an effective, proportionate and deterrent administrative monetary penalty of €3,000 on the gas station operator for failing to respond to the data subject's access request, failing to provide notice of the refusal with reasons, failing to inform the data subject about further processing and transmission of their personal data to law enforcement and third parties, and failing to establish proper legal basis and transparency for the disclosure of surveillance footage containing a minor's image.
companyNow: Unknown — the entity is a sole proprietorship (gas station) in Greece; current operational status not specified in the decision.
dataType: Video surveillance imagery of a minor
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 12 - Right of access and duty to respond
GDPR Article 14(4) - Obligation to provide information when processing for different purpose
Guideline 1/2011 Article 9 - Transmission of surveillance data to third parties
GDPR Article 6 - Legal basis for processing

companyDescription: HM Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS) is an executive agency of the UK Ministry of Justice responsible for operating the courts and tribunal system in England and Wales.
companyLongDescription: HM Courts & Tribunals Service (HMCTS) is an executive agency of the UK Ministry of Justice responsible for operating the courts and tribunal system in England and Wales.
caseDescription: HMCTS staff used a bulk amendment tool (ATM) to adjourn court cases during COVID-19 lockdowns, causing guilty/not guilty plea records to be incorrectly recorded and automatically cascaded to the Police National Computer. The organisation failed to provide adequate staff guidance, conduct risk assessments, or implement additional safeguards for remote processing, and missed opportunities to identify and stop the ongoing breach.
companyWorth: Part of UK Ministry of Justice (UK government agency)
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement appropriate security measures (technical and organisational) to protect personal data processed for law enforcement purposes, particularly when processing shifted to remote work during the pandemic.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: HMCTS used a bulk amendment tool to adjourn court cases during COVID without proper staff instructions or safeguards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of people had their criminal court records wrongly recorded and transmitted to law enforcement databases, exposing them to reputational harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bulk amendment tool (ATM) was introduced in February 2019 with guidance stating it could not be used for adjournments.
claimsVsReality.reality: Staff were not adequately re-trained or reminded of this restriction when the COVID-19 emergency required mass adjournments in April-May 2020, and the original guidance was buried and not re-issued.

claimsVsReality.claim: HMCTS issued a staff bulletin on 25 June 2020 informing staff of 'a number of incidents' and errors.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bulletin did not issue a clear directive to cease using the problematic function; it merely repeated old guidance saying 'If you do not want to copy the plea over to other cases, please do not use the ATM functionality,' leaving the flawed tool enabled and allowing the breach to continue.

claimsVsReality.claim: The incident was an unforeseeable emergency response to COVID-19 closures.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the pandemic was unpredictable, the organisation's failure to implement risk assessments, additional safeguards, proper guidance, or adequate training compounded an avoidable breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40: Personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: HMCTS did not provide adequate instruction or re-issue critical safety warnings when bulk adjournment functionality was introduced during COVID-19, despite the tool being marked as unsuitable for adjournments in earlier guidance issued over one year prior.
violations: HMCTS did not provide adequate instruction or re-issue critical safety warnings when bulk adjournment functionality was introduced during COVID-19, despite the tool being marked as unsuitable for adjournments in earlier guidance issued over one year prior.
No central directive was issued to staff on how to properly adjourn cases; staff had discretion but lacked clear guidance on risks and proper procedures.
The IT helpdesk failed to recognise reports of errors as indicating a wider data breach, and simply re-issued existing guidance rather than escalating the issue.
No additional safeguards were implemented to ensure security of personal information being processed remotely during the pandemic, despite functionality existing for adequate checks.
Data protection training was inadequate and lacked specific detail on law enforcement processing, risk assessments, DPIAs, and special category data considerations.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand under Schedule 13(2) of the DPA 2018. The organisation was required to take remedial steps including: correcting all affected records; disabling the problematic functionality; implementing a review of guidance available to staff; conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments; establishing a central repository for current guidance and procedures; requiring staff to confirm acceptance of new/updated policies; and reviewing and enhancing data protection training. The matter is now closed pending any further information or incidents.
companyNow: HMCTS remains an executive agency of the UK Ministry of Justice. The enforcement decision and recommendations have been implemented to improve data protection compliance and safeguards.
dataType: Court case data, guilty/not guilty plea records, verdict information
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40 (sixth data protection principle – security of personal data)
Data Protection Act 2018, Schedule 13(2) (power to issue reprimand)

companyDescription: The Department for Education (DfE) is a UK government department established in 1964 responsible for policy and oversight of education services in England, including administration of the Learning Records Service (LRS) database.
companyLongDescription: The Department for Education (DfE) is a UK government department established in 1964 responsible for policy and oversight of education services in England, including administration of the Learning Records Service (LRS) database.
caseDescription: The DfE permitted unauthorized third-party access to the Learning Records Service (LRS) database containing 28 million records, including children's data, for age verification without appropriate controls, oversight, or transparency. Personal data was processed insecurely and for unintended purposes without data subject awareness.
violationSummary: The DfE disclosed personal data stored on the LRS database to third parties who then processed it without appropriate authorization or the knowledge of data subjects. This represents unauthorized disclosure and subsequent secondary use of sensitive educational data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Department for Education permitted third-party access to the Learning Records Service database containing 28 million personal records.
whyTheyWereWrong: 28 million individuals, including children aged 14 and over, had their educational records shared with external organizations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Third-party organizations accessing the LRS database were processing data for educational service provision purposes as authorized.
claimsVsReality.reality: Third parties processed data for age verification—a purpose not initially intended and not authorized by data subjects, performed without appropriate controls or oversight.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data on the LRS database was being processed securely with appropriate safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: No regular checks were conducted on user activities; the database lacked adequate technical and organizational measures to prevent unauthorized access or misuse.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data subjects were aware of and had consented to third-party processing of their educational records.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data subjects were unaware of the processing and could not object or withdraw consent, as no transparency information was provided.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: DfE shared LRS database records with third parties and permitted further processing without appropriate lawful basis.
violations: DfE shared LRS database records with third parties and permitted further processing without appropriate lawful basis.
Data subjects were unaware of the processing and could not exercise their rights to object or withdraw consent.
Processing occurred for age verification purposes not disclosed to or authorized by data subjects.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: DfE failed to have adequate measures in place to prevent unauthorised access to the LRS database.
violations: DfE failed to have adequate measures in place to prevent unauthorised access to the LRS database.
No regular checks were carried out on user activities, leaving the database vulnerable to misuse.
Insufficient oversight of third-party processing exposed 28 million records to unauthorized secondary use.

outcome: The ICO issued a reprimand (rather than a monetary fine due to revised approach to public sector enforcement). The DfE was required to implement five compliance measures: (1) improve transparency around LRS processing so data subjects can exercise rights; (2) regularly review internal security procedures to prevent recurrence; (3) communicate process changes to all staff; (4) conduct thorough Data Protection Impact Assessments for high-risk processing; (5) continue data protection training. The DfE had already permanently removed the third-party's access to the database and implemented enhanced registration controls including verification steps, accreditation checks, and routine monitoring for excessive use. Updates were to be provided to the ICO's Assurance Department. The matter is now closed, but the ICO reserved the right to revisit if further incidents are reported.
companyNow: The Department for Education continues to operate as the UK government agency responsible for education policy and services. Following this enforcement action, it has implemented enhanced data protection measures and continues ongoing engagement with the ICO's Assurance Department.
dataType: Educational records, personal data, special category data, children's data (aged 14+)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
GDPR Art. 35 – Data Protection Impact Assessment

companyDescription: Statistics Canada is the federal agency responsible for collecting, analyzing, and publishing statistical data about Canada's population, economy, and society.
companyLongDescription: Statistics Canada is Canada's national statistical office, a Crown corporation mandated to collect and disseminate reliable statistical information to support evidence-based decision-making in government, business, and academia. The agency conducts surveys, manages administrative data collections, and maintains statistical databases on demographics, economics, health, labour, and social conditions. In 2018-2019, it proposed two administrative data projects involving collection of financial and credit information from private sector institutions.
caseDescription: Statistics Canada proposed two administrative data collection projects: the Financial Transactions Project (collecting line-by-line transaction data from financial institutions) and the Credit Agency Data Project (collecting credit files from credit bureaus) to be linked with other government databases. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found no legal contraventions but identified significant privacy concerns regarding necessity and proportionality, requiring the organization to better demonstrate that data collection goals were sufficiently specific, that proposed means were effective, and that privacy impacts were proportional to public objectives.
violationSummary: The projects involved systematic collection of detailed personal financial and credit information at scale (potentially millions of Canadians), linked with other government databases to create comprehensive profiles. This constitutes surveillance in the form of systematic monitoring and aggregation of financial behavior and creditworthiness without adequate justification of necessity and proportionality.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Statistics Canada proposed to collect detailed financial transaction records and credit file data from financial institutions.
whyTheyWereWrong: Canadians faced unauthorized surveillance of their financial activities and credit histories without clear justification.

claimsVsReality.claim: The projects were designed with necessity and proportionality in mind.
claimsVsReality.reality: StatCan failed to demonstrate that all personal information sought was necessary, that projects were proportionate to privacy invasion, or that less invasive alternatives were unavailable.

claimsVsReality.claim: Public goals for the projects were clearly defined and sufficiently specific.
claimsVsReality.reality: StatCan focused on collection methods without describing public goals with sufficient precision and specificity to meaningfully assess against privacy impacts.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Financial Transactions Project was within StatCan's legal authority.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner raised serious concerns that the project as originally designed would have exceeded StatCan's legal authority to collect personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Adequate transparency was provided regarding data collection.
claimsVsReality.reality: StatCan failed to be adequately transparent with respect to collection of personal information via the projects, contributing to public outcry and numerous complaints.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – Necessity Principle
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to demonstrate that all personal information sought to be collected was necessary for stated objectives
violations: Failed to demonstrate that all personal information sought to be collected was necessary for stated objectives
Did not limit collection to 'need to have' rather than 'nice to have' information
Public goals were described too vaguely to assess necessity

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – Proportionality Principle
regulatoryFindings.description: Did not adequately demonstrate that privacy impacts were proportional to public goals
violations: Did not adequately demonstrate that privacy impacts were proportional to public goals
Failed to analyze privacy impacts in context, including sensitivity, breadth, depth, and reasonable expectations
Did not acknowledge the highly intrusive nature of collecting line-by-line financial transactions revealing lifestyle, consumer choices, and private interests
Lacked sufficient analysis of potential harms to individuals

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – Transparency Obligation
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to be adequately transparent with respect to collection of personal information via the projects
violations: Failed to be adequately transparent with respect to collection of personal information via the projects
Did not describe public goals with sufficient specificity and precision

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – Security Safeguards
regulatoryFindings.description: Insufficient measures to mitigate against internal threat vulnerabilities
violations: Insufficient measures to mitigate against internal threat vulnerabilities
Inadequate monitoring for internal unauthorized access and use

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner did not issue a formal penalty or prohibition. Instead, it issued four recommendations: (1) Statistics Canada must describe public goals with specificity and precision allowing meaningful assessment against privacy impacts; (2) effectiveness must be demonstrated once feasibility testing is complete; (3) privacy impacts must be analyzed in context considering risk of harm to individuals and broad-based harms; (4) revised plans must be resubmitted for OPC review before final implementation. Statistics Canada committed to redesigning both projects according to an iterative approach with feasibility phases and reduced data collection scope. The organization also implemented privacy-enhancing measures including establishment of a data ethics secretariat, creation of an external Advisory Council on Ethics and Modernization of Microdata Access, development of a data sensitivity scale, and creation of a public Trust Centre on privacy and data protection.
companyNow: Statistics Canada continues to operate as Canada's national statistical agency, now with enhanced privacy governance structures including a data ethics secretariat and external ethics advisory council established following this investigation.
dataType: Financial transaction data, credit information, account balances, demographic data, socio-economic data
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) – General principles of necessity and proportionality

companyDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's federal law enforcement agency responsible for maintaining the National Repository of Criminal Records and conducting Vulnerable Sector checks.
companyLongDescription: The RCMP serves as Canada's national police force and steward of the Canadian Police Information Centre (CPIC) system. It provides criminal record checks and Vulnerable Sector verification services to employers and volunteer organizations across the country. The agency operates through regional divisions and detachments, conducting background checks that search national repositories and local police records management systems.
caseDescription: The RCMP used non-conviction information and mental health incident records in Vulnerable Sector (VS) checks without obtaining proper informed consent from applicants. Complaints 1 and 3 found that consent forms were ambiguous and did not clearly disclose that non-criminal police interactions would be reported as adverse information, contravening section 7 of the Privacy Act. The RCMP's broad policy of reporting mental health incidents and unsubstantiated charges was found to be disproportionate and insufficiently protective of individual privacy.
violationSummary: The RCMP disclosed non-conviction information (mental health apprehensions, unfounded complaints, stayed charges) originally collected for law enforcement purposes to third parties (employers/volunteer organizations) without proper informed consent and without safeguards provided by the criminal justice system. This represents an improper change in use of personal information and disclosure of sensitive data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The RCMP included non-conviction information and mental health incident records in Vulnerable Sector checks without obtaining clear informed consent from applicants.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals were barred from employment and volunteer opportunities based on unsubstantiated charges and mental health contacts, causing them to lose career prospects and face stigmatization.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vulnerable Sector checks are designed to identify dangerous offenders and protect vulnerable Canadians from criminal risks.
claimsVsReality.reality: The RCMP was reporting unfounded complaints, stayed charges, and mental health apprehensions without criminal convictions, creating false impressions of criminality and barring innocent individuals from employment and volunteering.

claimsVsReality.claim: Applicants consented to the use of non-conviction information by signing the VS check request forms.
claimsVsReality.reality: The consent forms were ambiguous and suggested adverse information was limited to criminal convictions, failing to clearly disclose that unsubstantiated charges and mental health incidents would be reported.

claimsVsReality.claim: Mental health incidents and non-criminal police contacts are appropriately relevant to VS checks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Individuals with no criminal charges or convictions—including those taken to hospital for mental health crises—were stigmatized and prevented from pursuing careers, with mental health status conflated with dangerousness.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 7 - Personal information under the control of a government institution shall not, without the consent of the individual, be used except for the purpose for which obtained or a consistent purpose
regulatoryFindings.description: RCMP used non-conviction information from Complainants 1 and 3 without obtaining informed consent - consent forms were ambiguous and did not clearly disclose that non-criminal police interactions would be reported as adverse information
violations: RCMP used non-conviction information from Complainants 1 and 3 without obtaining informed consent - consent forms were ambiguous and did not clearly disclose that non-criminal police interactions would be reported as adverse information
RCMP failed to inform applicants of their right to request independent review of decisions to include non-conviction information
Consent forms did not clearly set out which types of non-conviction information would or would not be included in VS checks

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 6 and Privacy Regulations section 4(1) - Personal information used for administrative purposes must be retained for at least two years following last use unless individual consents to disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Complaint 2 allegation regarding retention of stayed charge information for 70 years was found not to contravene the Act, as neither the Act nor Regulations stipulate maximum retention periods
violations: Complaint 2 allegation regarding retention of stayed charge information for 70 years was found not to contravene the Act, as neither the Act nor Regulations stipulate maximum retention periods

outcome: The RCMP agreed to revise its vulnerable sector check consent forms within 6 months to clearly specify the types of non-conviction information that will be used and reported, and to inform applicants of their right to request independent review. The RCMP further committed to implementing a new policy that non-conviction information will only be disclosed when it meets criteria for 'exceptional disclosure' similar to Alberta's procedures, and that mental health-related occurrences will not be disclosed unless they meet exceptional disclosure criteria. Complaints 1 and 3 are well-founded and conditionally resolved; Complaint 2 is not well-founded.
companyNow: The RCMP continues to operate as Canada's primary federal law enforcement and national police service, now with enhanced privacy protocols following this investigation.
dataType: Personal information including non-conviction information, mental health records, police interactions, criminal charges, mental health apprehensions
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act section 7 (use of personal information without consent)
Privacy Act section 6 (retention of personal information)

companyDescription: Public Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC) is the federal agency responsible for pay administration and procurement services for Canadian public servants across all Government of Canada institutions.
companyLongDescription: PSPC provides pay services, benefits administration, and overpayment tracking for federal employees through its Phoenix Pay System. The agency operates the Pay Administration Branch which generates personnel overpayment reports sent to client institutions for payment recovery coordination. PSPC processes payroll for tens of thousands of public servants across multiple government departments and agencies.
caseDescription: Public Services and Procurement Canada improperly disclosed pay-related personal information about 69,087 public servants to the wrong Government of Canada institutions due to a data entry error in its personnel overpayment reporting system. The breach occurred when the Pay Administration Branch failed to delete data from a previous pay period report before splitting it by institution, resulting in employee information being sent to departments other than their employers. Although the breach was unintentional, it exposed sensitive employment and financial data to unauthorized recipients across multiple government agencies.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal information (names, addresses, financial information, employment status) to recipients who had no authorized need to access it. This constitutes an unauthorized disclosure of personal information that did not comply with any permitted disclosure category under the Privacy Act, fitting squarely within the Disclosure category of the Solove Privacy Taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Public Services and Procurement Canada failed to delete data from a previous pay period before splitting personnel overpayment reports by institution.
whyTheyWereWrong: Public servants received breach notifications showing their names, home addresses, and financial arrears information had been disclosed to unrelated departments.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSPC concluded that only psychological impact and no financial or physical harm could occur from the breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information including home addresses, names, financial arrears balances, and employee status was exposed to unauthorized recipients across multiple departments, creating real risk of identity fraud and financial harm through combined information sources.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSPC had been producing personnel overpayment reports safely since 2018 using the same manual spreadsheet extraction method.
claimsVsReality.reality: The 2018-2020 period lacked documented quality control processes or checks and balances, allowing the February 2020 data deletion failure to occur undetected until recipients reported receiving wrong employee information.

claimsVsReality.claim: All affected individuals received consistent breach notification information about compromised data elements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Departments modified PSPC's standardized notification letter before distribution, resulting in some employees not being informed that arrears balance, agreement status, and deduction amounts had also been compromised.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Personal information can only be disclosed with an individual's consent or in accordance with permitted disclosure categories under Section 8(2)
regulatoryFindings.description: PSPC disclosed personal information (name, PRI, arrears balance, home address, employment status, financial deduction data) to 164 individuals in 61 institutions without consent and not in accordance with any permitted disclosure category
violations: PSPC disclosed personal information (name, PRI, arrears balance, home address, employment status, financial deduction data) to 164 individuals in 61 institutions without consent and not in accordance with any permitted disclosure category
The recipients (across 9 institutions) did not have a need-to-know about employees in other government departments
The disclosure was unauthorized and contravened Section 8 of the Privacy Act

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Definition of personal information includes employment history, financial transactions, identifying numbers, and personal information recorded in any form
regulatoryFindings.description: The disclosed data elements (name, PRI, arrears balance, home address, employment status, minimum deduction amount, agreement status) constitute personal information under this definition
violations: The disclosed data elements (name, PRI, arrears balance, home address, employment status, minimum deduction amount, agreement status) constitute personal information under this definition
These elements were improperly disclosed to unauthorized recipients

regulatoryFindings.act: Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.1.2 – Heads of institutions must establish plans for addressing privacy breaches and notify affected individuals as soon as possible
regulatoryFindings.description: While PSPC notified individuals within 9-17 days (meeting the 13-day standard), the breach notification letter contained inaccuracies and incomplete information about compromised data elements
violations: While PSPC notified individuals within 9-17 days (meeting the 13-day standard), the breach notification letter contained inaccuracies and incomplete information about compromised data elements
Departments modified the notification letter before distributing it, resulting in inconsistent information provided to affected individuals
The notification letter incorrectly described the positions of unintended recipients and omitted some compromised data elements from the list

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the complaints well-founded but also resolved. PSPC implemented comprehensive corrective measures to prevent recurrence: (1) established a documented process and quality assurance checklist for producing personnel overpayment reports with verification steps and multi-level oversight; (2) implemented the Privacy Breach Protocol requiring immediate action upon discovery of breaches; (3) expeditiously secured compromised records, had recipients delete flawed reports within 18 days, and searched the government network for residual copies; (4) removed home addresses from future reports based on departmental survey feedback; (5) is exploring automated solutions and centralized repository access to eliminate the need for email distribution of sensitive overpayment reports. No monetary penalty was imposed, but the Office emphasized the importance of complete breach notification and proper quality controls in document handling.
companyNow: PSPC continues to operate as the federal public service pay and procurement administration agency, having implemented corrective measures and quality control procedures following the 2020 breach.
dataType: Employment information, pay-related data, home address, arrears balance, financial information, employee status
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – unauthorized disclosure of personal information
Privacy Act Section 3 – definition of personal information
Interim Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.2.5

companyDescription: Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) is the federal department responsible for managing Canada's Passport Program in collaboration with Employment and Social Development Canada, Global Affairs Canada, and Canada Post Corporation.
companyLongDescription: IRCC is a Canadian federal government institution under the Department of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship. It administers the Canadian Passport Program, which issues travel documents to Canadian citizens through a multi-institutional delivery network. The Passport Program involves application processing, printing, validation, and delivery across domestic offices, consular missions abroad, and mail services. IRCC holds full functional authority and accountability for program management, policy, and compliance with privacy legislation.
caseDescription: A Privacy Commissioner investigation examined passport protection practices across four federal institutions (IRCC, ESDC, GAC, and Canada Post) and found that between 2016-2019, 1,148 passports were lost, stolen, or misdirected while under government control. While the overall proportion of breaches was low (0.005%-0.010% of passports issued), the investigation identified significant gaps in breach detection, delayed notification to affected individuals (averaging 4-5 months), and inconsistent risk assessment regarding materiality of breaches.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of passports occurred through loss, theft, and misdirection during processing and mail delivery, violating Section 8(1) of the Privacy Act which prohibits disclosure of personal information without consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Four federal institutions (IRCC, ESDC, GAC, Canada Post) lost, stole, or misdirected 1,148 passports between 2016–2019.
whyTheyWereWrong: Delayed notifications averaging 4–5 months left individuals exposed to identity theft and fraudulent international travel for extended periods.

claimsVsReality.claim: The four institutions had reasonable measures in place to prevent unauthorized disclosures of passports.
claimsVsReality.reality: While prevention controls were adequate, 1,148 passports were lost, stolen, or misdirected between 2016–2019, exposing individuals to identity theft and fraudulent travel for months before notification.

claimsVsReality.claim: The overall volume of passports lost or stolen is not high as a proportion of passports issued (0.005%–0.010%).
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of the low percentage, each breach exposed an individual to 4–5 months of undetected risk of illicit travel and identity theft, with inconsistent remediation and no standardized notification timelines.

claimsVsReality.claim: Institutions had adequate measures to detect and remediate breaches when they occur.
claimsVsReality.reality: Breach detection was delayed, notifications to victims averaged 4–5 months, and risk assessments were inconsistent across institutions, resulting in some individuals receiving no credit monitoring or protective assistance.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) - Prohibition on unauthorized disclosure of personal information under control of government institutions without consent
regulatoryFindings.description: 1,148 passports lost, stolen, or misdirected while under control of federal institutions between 2016-2019
violations: 1,148 passports lost, stolen, or misdirected while under control of federal institutions between 2016-2019
64 passports misdirected to wrong recipients
29 passports stolen
1,055 passports lost in transit or misplaced
Only 146 of 1,148 incidents (12%) properly reported to Office of Privacy Commissioner as material breaches

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Secretariat Guidelines for Privacy Breaches - Requirements for risk assessment, timely notification, and remediation measures
regulatoryFindings.description: Inconsistent assessment of 'materiality' of breaches across institutions - GAC changed position to not consider lost passports alone as material when lost abroad
violations: Inconsistent assessment of 'materiality' of breaches across institutions - GAC changed position to not consider lost passports alone as material when lost abroad
ESDC historically did not consider lost or stolen passports alone as material breaches until January 2019
Delayed notification to affected individuals - average 4+ months after incident for ESDC, and 5+ months to inform TBS/OPC
In approximately 50% of cases reviewed, individuals had not been notified of breach despite months passing
No offers of concrete assistance (e.g., credit monitoring) to affected individuals in IRCC notification letters; inconsistent advice in ESDC and GAC letters

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Secretariat Policy on Government Security - Requirements for assessment, investigation, and documentation of security incidents
regulatoryFindings.description: ESDC unable to corroborate claims of discussing prevention measures with Canada Post despite stating so in notification letters
violations: ESDC unable to corroborate claims of discussing prevention measures with Canada Post despite stating so in notification letters
No evidence of systematic collection of information to reduce specific risks of recurrence in transit incidents
Unclear dissemination of post-event analysis findings from IRCC to relevant stakeholders
Lack of robust incident assessment processes to identify suspicious patterns or trends indicative of malicious activity

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner issued recommendations to IRCC and partner institutions to: (1) establish consistent written guidance on assessing materiality of passport breaches by November 30, 2021; (2) implement reasonable service standards for timely notification to affected parties by March 31, 2022; (3) ensure consistent risk mitigation advice and offer concrete assistance such as credit monitoring by September 30, 2022; (4) implement client notification mechanism for mail delivery by September 30, 2022; and (5) enhance incident assessment and investigation processes by March 31, 2022. All institutions agreed to implement these recommendations.
companyNow: IRCC remains the primary federal institution responsible for passport issuance and immigration services in Canada. Following this investigation, the department committed to implementing the Privacy Commissioner's recommendations to improve breach detection, timely notification, and risk remediation practices.
dataType: Passport information (passport number, full name, date of birth, place of birth)
legalBasisViolated: Treasury Board Secretariat Policy on Government Security
Treasury Board Secretariat Guidelines for Privacy Breaches
Treasury Board Secretariat Interim Directive on Privacy Practices

companyDescription: Clearview AI is a US-based facial recognition technology company that developed a tool enabling users to upload face images and match them against a database of billions of scraped facial images to identify individuals.
companyLongDescription: Clearview AI developed and operated a facial recognition software and database solution marketed primarily to law enforcement agencies. The company's core business model involved automatically scraping facial images from publicly accessible websites—including social media platforms like Facebook, YouTube, Instagram, Twitter, and Venmo—without consent, storing them indefinitely, converting them into biometric identifiers (512-point facial vectors), and then selling search access to law enforcement and other organizations. The company claimed the images were 'publicly available' and therefore exempt from privacy consent requirements.
caseDescription: Clearview AI developed and operated a facial recognition tool that indiscriminately scraped over 3 billion images of faces from publicly accessible websites including social media platforms without consent. The company created biometric identifiers and sold access to law enforcement and other organizations, enabling mass identification and surveillance of individuals. Clearview did not obtain requisite consent, falsely claimed images were 'publicly available' and exempt from privacy laws, and collected sensitive biometric data for purposes a reasonable person would not consider appropriate.
violationSummary: Clearview's mass indiscriminate scraping of facial images and creation of biometric vectors from over 3 billion images constitutes systematic surveillance of individuals by a private commercial entity without consent or knowledge. The collection is unrelated to individuals' expectations when posting images, enabling continuous identification and tracking capabilities.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Clearview AI scraped over 3 billion facial images from public websites including social media without consent, created biometric identifiers from them.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals whose images were collected had no reasonable expectation their photos would be used for identification purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Images collected are 'publicly available' and exempt from privacy consent requirements under PIPEDA, PIPA BC, and PIPA AB.
claimsVsReality.reality: Information scraped from public websites and repurposed for unrelated uses does not qualify for the 'publicly available' exemption when used for identification purposes unrelated to the original posting context.

claimsVsReality.claim: The facial recognition tool is intended solely for legitimate law enforcement investigative purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company provided free-trial access to private sector entities and other organizations, enabling uses beyond law enforcement and without meaningful restrictions.

claimsVsReality.claim: There is an absence of harms to individuals from Clearview's activities.
claimsVsReality.reality: The mass scraping and processing of facial images without consent creates broad-based privacy harms, risks of false or misapplied matches causing reputational damage, and subjects the vast majority of people—who are never involved in crimes—to mass surveillance by a private commercial entity.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clearview would be willing to take steps on a 'best efforts' basis to limit collection and distribution of images identifiable as Canadian.
