claimsVsReality.reality: Clearview did not commit to following the regulatory recommendations to cease operations in Canada, delete collected images, or comply with biometric consent requirements; instead it offered only vague best-effort compliance.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 6.1 and Principle 4.3: Organizations must obtain consent before collecting, using or disclosing personal information, unless an exception applies. Consent must be express when information is sensitive, use is outside reasonable expectations, or creates meaningful risk of significant harm.
regulatoryFindings.description: Clearview collected over 3 billion facial images without obtaining any consent from individuals
violations: Clearview collected over 3 billion facial images without obtaining any consent from individuals
Clearview falsely relied on 'publicly available' exception, which does not apply to information collected from social media or professional websites for unrelated purposes
Clearview created biometric identifiers (vectors) from images, constituting distinct collection and use of sensitive personal information without consent
Quebec's LCCJTI explicitly requires express consent for biometric data; Clearview made no attempt to seek consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Subsection 5(3), PIPA AB Sections 11/16/19, PIPA BC Sections 11/14/17, Quebec Private Sector Act Section 4: Organizations must only collect, use and disclose personal information for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances.
regulatoryFindings.description: Mass indiscriminate scraping of millions of images from Canada, including children, for commercial facial recognition database
violations: Mass indiscriminate scraping of millions of images from Canada, including children, for commercial facial recognition database
Purposes (law enforcement identification service) unrelated to individuals' reasons for posting images on social media
Purposes often to detriment of individuals (investigation, potential prosecution, reputational harm)
Creation of surveillance infrastructure enabling identification of individuals, vast majority of whom have never been involved in crimes
Collection conducted in manner contravening privacy laws (automated scraping without authorization)

regulatoryFindings.act: LCCJTI Sections 44-45: When building a biometric system in Quebec, companies must obtain express consent before using biometric information to verify or confirm identity, and must disclose the creation of biometric databases to the Commission.
regulatoryFindings.description: Clearview created biometric facial recognition database without obtaining express consent of individuals
violations: Clearview created biometric facial recognition database without obtaining express consent of individuals
Clearview failed to disclose the existence and creation of its biometric database to the Commission d'accès à l'information du Québec

outcome: The four Canadian privacy commissioners found the matter well-founded and issued recommendations that Clearview: (1) cease offering facial recognition services to clients in Canada; (2) cease collection, use and disclosure of images and biometric facial arrays from individuals in Canada; and (3) delete all images and biometric facial arrays collected from Canadians in its possession. Clearview disagreed with the findings and refused to commit to the recommendations, instead offering to remain outside the Canadian market for two years on a voluntary best-efforts basis. The commissioners rejected suspension of the investigation and published the report in the public interest. The commissioners reserved the right to pursue other enforcement actions under their respective Acts to bring Clearview into compliance with Canadian privacy law.
companyNow: After the joint Canadian investigation in 2020–2021, Clearview AI withdrew from the Canadian market but continued operating internationally. The company faces ongoing legal challenges and regulatory scrutiny in multiple jurisdictions globally.
dataType: Biometric data (facial recognition vectors), digital images of faces, metadata (names, source links, descriptions), location data from social media, personal information of minors
legalBasisViolated: Quebec Private Sector Act Section 4 (appropriate purpose)
Quebec Private Sector Act Sections 6, 12-14 (consent requirement)
LCCJTI Section 44 (express consent for biometric verification)
LCCJTI Section 45 (disclosure of biometric database creation)

companyDescription: CoreFour is a Canadian educational technology company that develops Edsby, a Kindergarten to Grade 12 learning management and analytics system used by school districts across Canada and internationally.
companyLongDescription: CoreFour provides Edsby, a cloud-based learning management platform designed for K-12 schools to manage student information, grades, attendance, and facilitate parent-teacher communication. The company serves as a service provider to school boards and districts across Canada and other countries, handling sensitive personal information on hundreds of thousands of students. Despite its role managing critical student data, CoreFour lacked formal privacy management procedures and a robust information security framework during the period under investigation.
caseDescription: CoreFour's Edsby learning management system for K-12 schools had multiple security vulnerabilities including weak password requirements for parental accounts and inadequate protection of student profile picture thumbnails accessible via sequential file numbering. The company lacked a comprehensive information security framework and formal privacy management procedures despite handling hundreds of thousands of sensitive records on children across Canada and internationally.
violationSummary: CoreFour failed to implement security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity and volume of personal information collected, specifically weak password controls, sequential file naming that allowed unauthorized access to student images, lack of malware scanning on imported content, and absence of an overarching information security framework compliant with PIPEDA Principles 4.7 and 4.1.4.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: CoreFour's Edsby learning management system had weak password requirements for parental accounts, inadequate protection of student profile pictures via sequential file numbering.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children's sensitive personal information including grades, health details, and profile pictures were exposed to unauthorized access through easily guessable passwords.

claimsVsReality.claim: CoreFour followed security best practices and had adequate information security measures in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked a robust overarching information security framework and had multiple undetected vulnerabilities including weak password requirements and sequential file numbering exposing student images.

claimsVsReality.claim: CoreFour had appropriate safeguards proportionate to the volume and sensitivity of personal information it collected.
claimsVsReality.reality: CoreFour collected personal information on hundreds of thousands of children including sensitive data like grades and health information but lacked heightened security safeguards commensurate with this volume and sensitivity.

claimsVsReality.claim: The respondent had adequate privacy management frameworks and accountability procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: CoreFour lacked appropriate written internal policies, complaint-handling procedures, data retention protocols, and adequate privacy training for employees despite being required by PIPEDA.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Security Safeguards: Organizations must protect personal information by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Implemented weak password requirements for parental accounts (minimum as short as one character) for approximately 150,000 accounts, allowing unauthorized access
violations: Implemented weak password requirements for parental accounts (minimum as short as one character) for approximately 150,000 accounts, allowing unauthorized access
Used sequential file numbering for student profile picture thumbnails, allowing unauthorized iteration and access to approximately 120,000 images of children
Failed to scan for malware when importing content from third-party applications like Google Workspace and Microsoft Office 365
Lacked web application firewall and granular file-level access controls to protect sensitive student images

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4 – Accountability: Organizations must implement policies and practices to give effect to privacy principles, including procedures to protect personal information, handle complaints, train staff, and develop information to explain policies
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to develop and implement a formal, documented information security management framework despite handling hundreds of thousands of sensitive records
violations: Failed to develop and implement a formal, documented information security management framework despite handling hundreds of thousands of sensitive records
Relied on informal, undocumented 'best practices' rather than written policies aligned with recognized industry standards
Lacked single designated person responsible for information security and governance structure
Failed to provide formal privacy training to employees, consultants, contractors and student users
Lacked documented data retention and destruction policies and procedures
Privacy policy was unclear and potentially confusing regarding what constitutes personal information collected and how data is shared with third parties
Privacy policy contained language that appeared to disclaim responsibility for security breaches

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Sections 10.1-10.3 – Mandatory Breach Reporting (effective November 1, 2018): Organizations must report breaches creating real risk of significant harm and maintain breach registers
regulatoryFindings.description: Finding: Not violated. Breach reporting was voluntary at time of password vulnerability discovery (November 2017); mandatory reporting commenced after student image vulnerability disclosed (January 2019)
violations: Finding: Not violated. Breach reporting was voluntary at time of password vulnerability discovery (November 2017); mandatory reporting commenced after student image vulnerability disclosed (January 2019)

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada found that CoreFour's safeguards and accountability obligations were breached but conditionally resolved. The company was required to: (1) complete and implement a comprehensive information security management framework within 6 months including written policies, back-up IT security resources, segregation of security responsibilities, and malware scanning; (2) develop a privacy management framework including documented complaint-handling procedures, data retention/destruction policies, and mandatory privacy training for all personnel; (3) revise its Privacy Policy to clarify what constitutes personal information and remove language disclaiming responsibility for security breaches; (4) provide an independent third-party audit report (ISO 27001 certification audit) documenting compliance with recommendations. CoreFour accepted all recommendations and committed to ISO 27001 certification by June 2021. The Office indicated it would monitor implementation. The breach reporting matter was found to be not well-founded due to the timing of mandatory reporting obligations and the complainant's own role in accessing the images without creating real risk of significant harm.
companyNow: CoreFour committed to implementing recommendations from the investigation, including ISO 27001 certification and enhanced security measures. The company was cooperative throughout the regulatory process and has addressed identified vulnerabilities.
dataType: Student names, dates of birth, student ID numbers, student pictures, parent contact information, home addresses, school attendance records, absence details, medical information (allergies), school assignments, test results, report cards, grades
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.1.4 (accountability and privacy management framework)
PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.7.1 (protection against unauthorized access)
PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.7.2 (appropriate safeguards for sensitivity)
PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.7.3 (technological, organizational and physical measures)

companyDescription: Bank of Montreal is one of Canada's largest federally regulated financial institutions providing banking, investment, and online financial services to millions of customers across North America.
companyLongDescription: Founded in 1817, Bank of Montreal (BMO) is Canada's oldest bank and a major financial services provider offering retail banking, wealth management, and investment services. The bank operates one of Canada's primary online banking platforms, serving millions of customers who depend on it for secure access to their financial accounts. BMO is a publicly traded company and a critical infrastructure provider in Canada's financial system.
caseDescription: Bank of Montreal's online banking application contained a critical session corruption vulnerability between June 2017 and January 2018 that allowed attackers to bypass authentication and access the personal information of 113,154 customers. The bank failed to detect the vulnerability during secure development testing, did not implement adequate bot management and monitoring tools to detect the large-scale attack, and did not assess the full scope of personal data exfiltration for six months until receiving a ransom demand.
violationSummary: BMO failed to implement security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of financial and identity data it controlled. Deficiencies included inadequate secure software development testing, gaps in vulnerability management protocols, lack of bot detection and monitoring capabilities, and insufficient real-time alerting systems—all contributing to the compromise of over 113,000 customer accounts.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Bank of Montreal's online banking application contained a session corruption vulnerability from June 2017 to January 2018 that allowed attackers to bypass authentication.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive financial data including social insurance numbers, account numbers, and card details were stolen and publicly posted online, exposing them to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: BMO had adequate safeguards commensurate with the sensitivity of customer financial data.
claimsVsReality.reality: BMO's online banking application had critical session corruption vulnerabilities, inadequate secure software development testing, no bot management tools, and weak intrusion detection that allowed large-scale undetected theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The December 2017 attack was a brute-force credential attack affecting approximately 6,076 accounts.
claimsVsReality.reality: The attack exploited a session corruption vulnerability allowing attackers to access 113,154 customer accounts by cycling through card numbers, with personal information exfiltrated from unencrypted session cache files.

claimsVsReality.claim: BMO responded promptly to the breach when discovered in December 2017.
claimsVsReality.reality: BMO did not assess the full scope of personal information compromise for six months until receiving a ransom demand in May 2018, leaving customers' sensitive data at risk without notification during this period.

claimsVsReality.claim: BMO had implemented appropriate vulnerability management protocols.
claimsVsReality.reality: BMO failed to identify the session corruption vulnerability during secure development testing and left it unpatched for approximately seven months after implementation in June 2017.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Personal information must be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement adequate safeguards commensurate with the sensitivity of financial account numbers, SINs, and identity data
violations: Failed to implement adequate safeguards commensurate with the sensitivity of financial account numbers, SINs, and identity data
Deployed a public-facing banking application with a critical vulnerability in production without adequate pre-launch security testing
Did not conduct penetration testing as part of application release process
Failed to detect vulnerability for at least 7 months despite maintaining a vulnerability assessment program
Lacked bot management solution despite ubiquity of bot-facilitated attacks
Lacked proper SIEM configuration with basic detection rules for suspicious activity patterns
Did not implement automated alerts to notify security personnel of detected threats
Failed to assess risk to customer personal information after December 2017 breach was discovered, waiting until May 2018

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.3 – Security methods should include physical, organizational, and technological measures such as passwords and encryption
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to properly configure encryption and access controls—personal information stored in unencrypted cache files accessible via application pages
violations: Failed to properly configure encryption and access controls—personal information stored in unencrypted cache files accessible via application pages
Inadequate testing and validation protocols in secure application development lifecycle
Insufficient monitoring and oversight of system access patterns and session activity
Lack of proper organizational procedures for detecting and responding to botting attacks

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada determined the complaint well-founded. BMO was required to implement remedial measures and demonstrated substantial improvements including: deployment of bot management and fraud prevention tools; replacement of penetration testing providers with enhanced testing protocols including red team exercises; implementation of new vulnerability scanning and robust testing before production deployment; significant expansion of security monitoring use cases with centralized analysis; creation of a Financial Crimes Unit consolidating cybersecurity and fraud functions; development of new procedures for botting attacks and incident management; and enhancement of authentication mechanisms. The OPC assessed that BMO's post-breach improvements adequately addressed the identified deficiencies and resolved the matter.
companyNow: Bank of Montreal remains one of Canada's largest financial institutions and continues to operate its online banking services with enhanced security measures implemented following this breach.
dataType: Financial account numbers, social insurance numbers, names, occupations, dates of birth, addresses, credit/debit card numbers, security questions and answers, account passwords, account balances, transaction history

companyDescription: Fido is a wireless telecommunications subsidiary of Rogers Communications Inc., one of Canada's largest telecommunications and media companies. Fido provides wireless services to Canadian consumers.
companyLongDescription: Fido Solutions Inc. is a subsidiary of Rogers Communications Inc., a major Canadian telecommunications conglomerate. Fido operates as a wireless service provider offering mobile phone plans and services to Canadian customers. The company is known for its consumer-focused wireless offerings in Canada's competitive telecommunications market. As part of the Rogers family, Fido benefits from the parent company's infrastructure and resources.
caseDescription: Fido customer service representatives repeatedly bypassed authentication protocols, allowing fraudsters to access and modify a customer's account over several days in January 2019. The fraudsters obtained the customer's personal information including name, date of birth, postal code, account number, and email address. Additionally, Fido failed to provide access to call recordings in a generally understandable format, initially refusing to provide transcripts and restricting the customer's ability to pause, rewind, or replay poor-quality recordings.
violationSummary: Fido failed to implement and enforce adequate security safeguards to protect personal information from unauthorized access. Customer service representatives systematically bypassed established authentication protocols, allowing fraudsters repeated access to accounts despite multiple authentication methods being in place. This constitutes a failure to protect against unauthorized access and disclosure of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Fido customer service representatives repeatedly bypassed authentication protocols, allowing fraudsters to access.
whyTheyWereWrong: A customer's personal information including name, date of birth, postal code, account number, and email address were exposed to fraudsters who repeatedly gained unauthorized account access due.

claimsVsReality.claim: Fido had adequate authentication protocols in place to protect customer accounts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple customer service representatives bypassed the same authentication protocols across five separate fraudulent calls, demonstrating the protocols were not being followed despite being documented.

claimsVsReality.claim: Fido was protecting the fraudsters' privacy by refusing to provide call transcripts to the affected customer.
claimsVsReality.reality: The information Fido redacted from recordings was not the fraudsters' personal information but rather was unnecessary restriction that prevented the customer from accessing his own personal information in a usable format.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees were properly trained and incentivized to follow authentication procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple CSRs systematically failed to authenticate callers, often providing authentication answers to fraudsters or bypassing multi-factor authentication entirely, suggesting inadequate training or competing incentives favoring sales over security.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 requires that personal information shall be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customer service representatives repeatedly failed to follow established authentication protocols
violations: Customer service representatives repeatedly failed to follow established authentication protocols
CSRs bypassed authentication requirements in all five fraudulent calls reviewed
CSRs disclosed authentication information (name, account number, date of birth, address) that fraudsters then used in subsequent calls
Failed to place fraud alert on account in timely manner despite learning of fraudulent activity on the third call
Systemic failure to enforce and monitor compliance with authentication protocols despite their existence

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 requires that upon request, an individual shall be given access to their personal information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Initial refusal to provide transcripts of calls containing personal information
violations: Initial refusal to provide transcripts of calls containing personal information
Provided access to call recordings in poor sound quality format
Imposed unreasonable listening restrictions (no ability to pause, rewind, or replay recordings)

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9.4 requires that access be provided in a form that is generally understandable.
regulatoryFindings.description: Poor quality audio recordings made on locked laptop in open retail location
violations: Poor quality audio recordings made on locked laptop in open retail location
Inability to pause, rewind, or replay recordings rendered format not generally understandable
Customer unable to adequately review personal information despite restrictions

outcome: Fido committed to implementing comprehensive safeguard enhancements by November 30, 2021, including: consolidating authentication protocols, providing regular refresher training to staff on authentication requirements and consequences of non-compliance, implementing proactive feedback systems to monitor and remediate staff non-compliance with authentication protocols, and extending these measures across all Rogers call centres. Regarding the access request issue, Fido provided the complainant with transcripts of the calls on March 22, 2021, resolving that aspect of the complaint. The Office found the safeguards issue to be conditionally resolved pending implementation of recommendations, and the access issue to be fully resolved.
companyNow: Fido continues to operate as a Rogers subsidiary providing wireless services in Canada. Following this enforcement action, the company implemented enhanced authentication protocols and staff training to prevent similar security breaches.
dataType: Name, date of birth, postal code, account number, email address

companyDescription: Yahoo is a web services company providing email, news, search, and other online services globally. It has operated as a major internet portal since its founding in 1994.
companyLongDescription: Yahoo is a web services and media company that provides email (Yahoo Mail), news, search, finance, and other digital services to millions of users worldwide. Founded in 1994, Yahoo has been a prominent internet company through multiple ownership changes, including acquisition by Verizon and later Zimmerman Asset Management. Yahoo Mail is one of the world's largest email services, serving hundreds of millions of users globally across various regional subsidiaries and partners.
caseDescription: Yahoo Canada's Rogers Yahoo Mail service defaulted users to staying signed in on shared or public computers, exposing highly sensitive email content to unauthorized third-party access. The company failed to implement adequate security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of email data and did not obtain meaningful consent for disclosure of personal information to subsequent users of shared devices.
violationSummary: Yahoo failed to implement security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of personal information (emails containing health, financial, and intimate data) and did not protect against unauthorized access, disclosure, and use by third parties on shared devices. The inadequate technical and procedural safeguards directly enabled information insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Yahoo Canada set its Rogers Yahoo Mail service to keep users signed in by default on shared or public computers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users accessing shared devices had their highly sensitive emails—containing health, financial, intimate.

claimsVsReality.claim: The 'Stay signed in' setting is clearly and prominently displayed during sign-in.
claimsVsReality.reality: The setting appears only on the first login page in small light grey and blue font below a large bright blue 'Next' button, making it inconspicuous and easy to overlook.

claimsVsReality.claim: Each reasonable person understands the setting is 'on' by default and has control over it.
claimsVsReality.reality: Many users, including the complainant, did not notice the pre-checked setting, meaning their accounts remained signed in without their knowledge or authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: The 'Stay signed in' default setting is consistent with industry standards.
claimsVsReality.reality: Testing of other major email providers showed one offered opt-in 'stay signed in' while another required active logout with no opt-in/opt-out option, indicating no such industry standard exists.

claimsVsReality.claim: A public access computer detection algorithm deselects the setting on shared devices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Testing on multiple public access computers showed the algorithm failed to deselect the setting even once, and Yahoo acknowledged it did not always work as intended.

claimsVsReality.claim: The universal header logout option is easily accessible to protect users.
claimsVsReality.reality: The logout option only appears after users click on their name to reveal further options, making it non-obvious and insufficient protection against unintentional exposure.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Personal information shall be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information and shall protect against theft, unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use, or modification.
regulatoryFindings.description: Default 'Stay signed in' setting was not clearly or prominently displayed to users during login
violations: Default 'Stay signed in' setting was not clearly or prominently displayed to users during login
Algorithm to detect public access computers and deselect the setting failed in testing
Universal logout option was not apparent without clicking on user's name
14-day session expiration does not prevent immediate unauthorized access on shared devices
Password reset option was cumbersome and only available after user realized they remained logged in
Security information about shared computers was not clearly linked during sign-in process
Safeguards were not appropriate to the extreme sensitivity of email content containing health, financial, and intimate information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 and 4.3.6 – Organizations must obtain knowledge and consent for collection, use, and disclosure of personal information. Express consent is required when information is sensitive or collection/use is outside reasonable expectations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Yahoo disclosed users' emails to third parties (subsequent users of shared devices) without obtaining valid consent
violations: Yahoo disclosed users' emails to third parties (subsequent users of shared devices) without obtaining valid consent
Consent obtained was not express opt-in but rather implicit opt-out via pre-checked box
Users would not reasonably expect their accounts to default to 'stay signed in' allowing others to access all email content
Language 'stay signed in' did not communicate that any person accessing the device would gain access to all potentially sensitive information in emails

Consent was not meaningful as users were not informed of key elements: what information would be disclosed, to whom, and what harms could result (reputational damage, identity theft, exposure of sexual orientation or health conditions)

outcome: Yahoo committed to implement the following remedial measures within one month of report issuance: (1) change the 'stay signed in' setting from opt-out to opt-in; (2) add a prominent pop-up warning 'Don't use this option on a shared computer because your account will be available to others' when users hover over the setting; (3) move the setting from the first login page (username entry) to the second page (password entry). Rogers, which had taken over authentication for Rogers Yahoo Mail users, committed to: (1) not offer a 'stay signed in' option or implement it on opt-in basis if added in future; (2) by April 2022, amend the Rogers Email Member Center to allow users to view session history and change password to force logout of all sessions. The Office will monitor implementation of these measures.
companyNow: Yahoo operates as a portfolio of digital properties and services under Zimmerman Asset Management ownership (as of 2021), continuing to provide email and media services to a global user base.
dataType: Email content, health information, financial information, intimate content, private opinions, sexual orientation
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.6 (Express consent for sensitive information)

companyDescription: CashHere was a short-term payday lender operating in Ontario, Canada that offered rapid personal loans without credit checks through an online application platform.
companyLongDescription: CashHere was a short-term payday lender based in Ontario, Canada that provided rapid personal loans without credit checks. The company operated through an online application system where borrowers could apply for loans via its website. During the loan application process, CashHere requested highly sensitive personal financial information from applicants, including full online banking login credentials, to assess applications and verify applicant income and identity.
caseDescription: CashHere, a payday lender, collected online banking credentials (usernames, passwords, security questions) from loan applicants to verify identity and income. The Privacy Commissioner found this practice violated PIPEDA because less privacy-invasive alternatives existed (such as redacted bank statements and employer verification), and the privacy harms of granting full account access were disproportionate to the lender's commercial benefits.
violationSummary: CashHere conducted broad surveillance of applicants' financial accounts by collecting full banking login credentials, enabling access to complete financial history and transaction capabilities far beyond what was necessary for loan assessment. This represents systematic monitoring of sensitive financial information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: CashHere collected online banking passwords, usernames, and security question answers from payday loan applicants to verify identity and income during the loan application process.
whyTheyWereWrong: Applicants who provided their banking credentials exposed themselves to fraud, theft of funds.

claimsVsReality.claim: CashHere stated it was following industry practice in requiring online banking credentials.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner found this practice violated PIPEDA and was inappropriate; the company was collecting highly sensitive information with disproportionate privacy harms.

claimsVsReality.claim: CashHere claimed it would not use applicants' banking credentials to make transactions.
claimsVsReality.reality: CashHere made no written commitment to this effect to applicants, leaving them exposed to liability even if unauthorized transactions occurred due to employee misuse or security breaches.

claimsVsReality.claim: CashHere represented that direct online access to banking information was necessary for efficient loan processing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner questioned these efficiency claims, noting that applicants could easily screenshot or download and send bank statements electronically, making the direct access unnecessary.

claimsVsReality.claim: CashHere needed full access to applicants' complete banking history to assess creditworthiness.
claimsVsReality.reality: Redacted bank statements showing only recent income information, combined with employer verification and pay stubs, would achieve the same lending assessment goals without exposing applicants' entire financial history.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA section 5(3) — Organizations may collect, use or disclose personal information only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: CashHere collected highly sensitive banking login credentials without appropriate justification
violations: CashHere collected highly sensitive banking login credentials without appropriate justification
Collection was not proportionate to legitimate business needs
Less privacy-invasive alternatives (redacted bank statements, employer verification) were available at comparable cost and benefit

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.4 (Schedule 1) — Organizations must collect personal information by fair and lawful means and only collect information necessary for identified purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection of full banking credentials exceeded what was necessary to verify identity and income
violations: Collection of full banking credentials exceeded what was necessary to verify identity and income
Applicants were exposed to unnecessary risks of fraud and unauthorized transactions

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded and not resolved. CashHere ceased responding to the OPC and its website was listed for sale. A related entity, MoneyHome, subsequently appeared to operate under similar practices. The Commissioner published findings recommending that CashHere and other payday lenders cease collecting banking login credentials. MoneyHome was added to Ontario's Consumer Beware List. Neither organization has responded to the OPC's follow-up communications.
companyNow: CashHere ceased operations during the Privacy Commissioner investigation. The company's website was listed for sale, and it stopped responding to regulatory correspondence. A successor entity operating as MoneyHome appeared to continue similar practices from the same address.
dataType: Banking login credentials, passwords, security questions and answers, Social Insurance Number, Ontario Health Card, driver's license, date of birth, bank account details, financial transaction history

companyDescription: A Canadian computer services company that sold laptops and provided managed IT help desk services to individual customers and small businesses, with remote access software pre-installed on devices.
companyLongDescription: The respondent operated as a computer retailer and IT service provider in Canada, selling laptops through its own channels and third-party retail websites. It bundled a 'Personal Help Desk' service with certain laptop purchases, which relied on pre-installed remote access software to provide technical support. The service was offered as part of special promotional packages including anti-virus and office suite software. During the investigation, the company ceased offering these help desk services to individual customers.
caseDescription: A computer services company pre-installed remote access software on customer laptops and accessed them during help desk calls without obtaining meaningful express consent. The company failed to demonstrate documented consent procedures and lacked adequate safeguards to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive personal information stored on customers' computers.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate security safeguards commensurate with the sensitivity of personal information at risk. Static customer ID numbers, undocumented oral consent protocols, and lack of real-time user intervention mechanisms created vulnerability to unauthorized access by employees.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The company pre-installed remote access software on customer laptops and accessed them during help desk calls without obtaining documented express consent or implementing adequate safeguards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers unknowingly had their laptops accessed without clear permission, exposing sensitive personal information like passwords, financial details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Technicians always notify and involve customers in the remote access process and obtain their consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company relied on undocumented oral consent protocols and could not demonstrate that valid consent was actually obtained before accessing customer computers, as evidenced by the complainant's surprise when access began without warning.

claimsVsReality.claim: The remote access software is secure because access is limited to trained technicians, requires two-factor authentication, and is logged.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement adequate safeguards such as real-time user consent confirmation or the ability for users to unilaterally end sessions, and used static customer ID numbers that could be reused for unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The software prevents technicians from copying or extracting customer personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the software had technical limitations, technicians could still capture sensitive information through alternative means such as using cameras, cellphones, or pen and paper, and the company provided no evidence of controls preventing such behavior.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires knowledge and consent of the individual for collection, use or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent failed to obtain meaningful express consent prior to remotely accessing customers' laptops
violations: Respondent failed to obtain meaningful express consent prior to remotely accessing customers' laptops
Respondent relied on undocumented oral consent protocols without evidence or recording
Website, privacy policy, and customer documentation did not explain remote access procedures or that customer ID operated as access key
Technician accessed complainant's computer and moved mouse cursor without warning or prior express consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7, 4.7.1, and 4.7.3 require security safeguards appropriate to sensitivity of personal information and protection against unauthorized access
regulatoryFindings.description: Static customer ID numbers insufficient as security measure, particularly with master list accessible to technicians
violations: Static customer ID numbers insufficient as security measure, particularly with master list accessible to technicians
Reliance on undocumented oral consent rather than real-time user intervention mechanisms
No requirement for users to click consent box or enter code to confirm awareness of third-party access
Users unable to unilaterally end remote access sessions in real-time
Technicians could theoretically access computers when users not present, with no visual indication
No technological controls preventing technicians from accessing information via alternative means (phone photos, pen and paper)

outcome: The respondent ceased offering personal help desk services and terminated use of remote access software on customer computers. The company restructured into two separate entities, with the renamed respondent no longer providing managed IT services to individuals. The matter was found well-founded and resolved through cessation of the problematic practices. If the respondent provides such services again in future, it must implement mechanisms requiring real-time user intervention (e.g., clicking consent box, entering code) and allowing users to unilaterally end remote access sessions.
companyNow: The company ceased its Personal Help Desk service to individual customers and discontinued use of the remote access software during the investigation. Current operational status is unknown.
dataType: Passwords, financial account information, medical information, private documents, photos, user credentials, office productivity files

companyDescription: Oculus Transport Ltd. is an interprovincial trucking company operating in Alberta and British Columbia, primarily serving remote areas including forest service roads.
companyLongDescription: Oculus Transport Ltd. is a Canadian trucking company that operates interstate routes across Alberta and British Columbia, primarily in remote regions such as forest service roads. The company operates commercial truck fleets and employs drivers for logistics and transportation services. In 2017, the company introduced surveillance technology in truck cabs ostensibly to support incident investigation, liability determination, and regulatory compliance.
caseDescription: Oculus Transport, an interprovincial trucking company, installed audio surveillance devices in truck cabs that recorded driver conversations 24/7, including during off-duty hours. The company collected potentially sensitive personal information disproportionate to its legitimate business needs (incident investigation, regulatory compliance). The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the audio surveillance more intrusive than necessary and not appropriate in the circumstances.
violationSummary: The company conducted continuous, 24-hour audio surveillance of drivers, including sensitive conversations during off-duty periods when drivers were sleeping or with family. This constitutes systematic surveillance exceeding what was necessary for legitimate business purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Oculus Transport installed audio surveillance devices in truck cabs that continuously recorded driver conversations 24/7, including during off-duty hours and while drivers slept.
whyTheyWereWrong: Drivers had their private conversations with family, friends, and doctors recorded without knowing it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Audio surveillance was necessary to investigate incidents, determine liability, and ensure compliance with radio-controlled road regulations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner found that audio recording was unnecessary 24/7—it could have been limited to on-duty hours or even just to two-way radio communications, making continuous recording disproportionate.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company explored alternatives and could not find a less privacy-invasive method to achieve its objectives.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner questioned why Oculus could not limit recordings to two-way radio communications only, indicating viable alternatives existed that the company dismissed without adequate justification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Audio recordings were adequately safeguarded with physical locks and limited access to authorized personnel in specified circumstances.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even with safeguards, the system retained up to 72 hours of continuous audio including drivers' private conversations while off-duty and sleeping, creating disproportionate privacy invasion.

claimsVsReality.claim: Drivers were informed about the audio surveillance in the cabs.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant stated he initially believed the device was only a dashboard camera and did not know it recorded audio until conducting his own research.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 5(3) – An organization may only collect, use or disclose personal information for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: Oculus collected audio recordings of all conversations in truck cabs 24/7, including when drivers were off-duty and sleeping
violations: Oculus collected audio recordings of all conversations in truck cabs 24/7, including when drivers were off-duty and sleeping
Audio surveillance was more intrusive than necessary — company could have limited recording to on-duty hours or only two-way radio communications
Collection of up to 72 hours of audio recordings was disproportionate to stated purposes (incident investigation, regulatory compliance)
Sensitive personal information was collected (private conversations with relatives, friends, doctors) without limitation to what was necessary

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded and resolved after Oculus Transport voluntarily discontinued audio surveillance and transitioned to forward-facing video cameras without audio recording. The Privacy Commissioner expects that should the company implement in-cab audio surveillance in future, it must limit collection to only that which is necessary for achieving its stated purposes, considering proportionality and less privacy-invasive alternatives.
companyNow: As of the 2021 PIPEDA decision, Oculus Transport has discontinued audio surveillance and transitioned to forward-facing video cameras that do not record sound.
dataType: Audio recordings, location data, conversations
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Section 5(3) – Collection, use or disclosure for appropriate purposes

companyDescription: A Canadian charitable organization that operates a donor list trading program to share contact information with other not-for-profits to expand fundraising reach.
companyLongDescription: The respondent is a Canadian charity that implemented a donor list trading program as a cost-effective fundraising strategy. The program involved sharing donor names, mailing addresses, and donation status with other participating charitable organizations for one-time mail solicitations. The charity argued this was a standard industry practice among not-for-profit organizations, but failed to obtain proper express consent from donors before sharing their personal information.
caseDescription: A Canadian charity used opt-out consent for a donor list trading program that shared donor contact information with other charitable organizations. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner determined that express opt-in consent was required because such information sharing falls outside donors' reasonable expectations, and the information provided to donors was insufficient to support meaningful consent.
violationSummary: The charity disclosed personal information (names, addresses, donation fact) to third parties without obtaining meaningful consent. The disclosure of donor information to third-party charities for solicitation purposes constitutes unauthorized information dissemination without adequate consent mechanisms.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The charity used an opt-out consent mechanism on mail-in donation forms to enroll donors in a program that shared their names, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Donors received solicitation mail from other charities using their personal information without realizing they had consented.

claimsVsReality.claim: Donor list trading is a widely accepted, long-standing practice among not-for-profit organizations that donors should reasonably expect.
claimsVsReality.reality: Donors did not reasonably expect their information to be shared with other charities; the complainant was surprised to receive solicitation mail from an unaffiliated organization using his address obtained through the program.

claimsVsReality.claim: An opt-out checkoff box on donation forms provides adequate consent for the information sharing program.
claimsVsReality.reality: An opt-out mechanism is insufficient when the practice falls outside donors' reasonable expectations; express opt-in consent is required, and the small unchecked box was easily overlooked by recurring donors.

claimsVsReality.claim: The donation form and insert provided sufficient information to support meaningful consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Key information was missing from the initial donation form, including specifics about what information would be shared with whom and how donors could withdraw consent; the insert was not consistently provided to all donors, including recurring ones.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 4.3 – Knowledge and consent required for collection, use, or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Charity obtained only opt-out consent via checkoff box instead of express opt-in consent for donor list trading program
violations: Charity obtained only opt-out consent via checkoff box instead of express opt-in consent for donor list trading program
Opt-out mechanism was inappropriate given that disclosure fell outside reasonable expectations of donors

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 4.3.2 – Organizations must make reasonable effort to advise individuals of purposes in manner they can reasonably understand
regulatoryFindings.description: Donation form did not clearly state that donor names, addresses, and donation fact would be disclosed to third parties
violations: Donation form did not clearly state that donor names, addresses, and donation fact would be disclosed to third parties
Insert was not consistently provided to recurring donors
Privacy policy contained insufficient detail about the program

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 4.3.5 – Reasonable expectations of individual are relevant to consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Donors would not reasonably expect their information to be shared with other charities for solicitation purposes
violations: Donors would not reasonably expect their information to be shared with other charities for solicitation purposes
Disclosure was for secondary purpose (enabling third-party solicitation) rather than primary purpose (processing donation)

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 6.1 – Consent is only valid if individual understands nature, purpose and consequences of collection, use or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Information provided on donation form did not explain what information would be disclosed, to whom, or for what purpose
violations: Information provided on donation form did not explain what information would be disclosed, to whom, or for what purpose
Lack of clear explanation of how to withdraw consent

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner determined the complaint was well-founded and conditionally resolved. The Respondent committed to implement all recommendations: (1) obtain express opt-in consent for the donor list trading program; (2) provide key information up front on donation forms explaining what personal information will be disclosed, to whom, and for what purpose; (3) include the insert with each donation form and provide withdrawal instructions; and (4) update the privacy policy with more detailed program explanation. The Respondent agreed to submit a detailed implementation plan by April 30, 2021, quarterly progress reports through January 2022, and a final compliance report by April 30, 2022. Subsequent to the findings, the Respondent ceased participation in the donor list trading program entirely.
dataType: donor names, mailing addresses, donation history
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Section 4.3.2 (Reasonable effort to advise purposes)
PIPEDA Section 4.3.4 (Form of consent based on circumstances and sensitivity)

companyDescription: Sydney Catholic Schools Ltd is an educational organisation operating Catholic schools across the Sydney metropolitan area in Australia.
companyLongDescription: Sydney Catholic Schools Ltd is a Catholic education provider managing multiple primary and secondary schools throughout Sydney, Australia. The organisation is responsible for the personal information of thousands of students, families, and staff members. As an educational institution, it collects and maintains sensitive personal data including student records, health information, and family contact details.
caseDescription: Sydney Catholic Schools Ltd breached the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) under Australian Privacy Principle 12. The organisation failed to take reasonable steps to implement practices and procedures to ensure compliance with the Privacy Act and to protect personal information from misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification, or disclosure.
violationSummary: The breach involved failure to implement adequate security measures and practices to protect personal information held by the school, falling under APP 12 which requires entities to take reasonable steps to protect personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Sydney Catholic Schools Ltd failed to implement adequate security practices and procedures to protect personal information from unauthorised access, misuse, loss, modification, and disclosure.
whyTheyWereWrong: Students and families had their personal information exposed to unauthorised access and potential misuse because the school failed to maintain reasonable security safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sydney Catholic Schools had implemented adequate security practices and procedures for personal information protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation failed to take reasonable steps to implement such practices and procedures, exposing personal information to unauthorised access, misuse, loss, modification, and disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Australian Privacy Principle 12 requires entities to take reasonable steps to implement practices, procedures and systems relating to the entity's functions and activities that ensure the entity complies with the Privacy Principles and to protect personal information from misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sydney Catholic Schools Ltd failed to take reasonable steps to implement adequate practices and procedures to protect personal information
violations: Sydney Catholic Schools Ltd failed to take reasonable steps to implement adequate practices and procedures to protect personal information

outcome: Finding of breach of Australian Privacy Principle 12. The organisation was required to implement compliance measures to ensure future adherence to privacy obligations and protection of personal information.
companyNow: The organisation continues to operate Catholic schools in Sydney and is subject to compliance obligations under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).
dataType: Personal information related to school records and student data

caseDescription: A complaint was filed against a school regarding alleged privacy violations under the Australian Privacy Act. The OAIC investigated the complaint but found no breach of the relevant Australian Privacy Principles (APP 1, 10, 11, and 12).

whatTheyDid: The school was alleged to have violated privacy principles under the Australian Privacy Act 1988 regarding the handling of personal information.
whyTheyWereWrong: No breach was found; the investigation concluded the school complied with the Australian Privacy Principles (APP 1, 10, 11, and 12).

violations: No violations found; complaint dismissed

companyDescription: MedHealth Pty Ltd (trading as mlcoa) is an Australian healthcare provider handling personal health information.
companyLongDescription: MedHealth Pty Ltd operates as a healthcare service provider in Australia under the trading name mlcoa. The organization was found to have systematically breached multiple Australian Privacy Principles in its handling of such sensitive data.

violationSummary: The breach relates to MedHealth's failure to adequately manage and protect personal information in accordance with Australian Privacy Principles, indicating systemic issues with information processing and security practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: MedHealth failed to comply with Australian Privacy Principles (APP 6-11) in collecting, using, disclosing, and managing personal health information of patients.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients' sensitive health records were mishandled without proper safeguards, exposing their medical histories and personal details to unauthorized access or disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.description: Breach of Australian Privacy Principles governing collection, use, disclosure, data quality, data security, and access to personal information
violations: Breach of Australian Privacy Principles governing collection, use, disclosure, data quality, data security, and access to personal information

company: Australian Centre for International Agricultural Research

violations: ACIAR used or disclosed personal information in breach of APP 6 requirements

violations: ACIAR failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information as required by APP 11

companyDescription: Clearview AI is a facial recognition company that builds searchable databases of facial images scraped from public internet sources for identification purposes.
companyLongDescription: Clearview AI developed a facial recognition search engine by scraping billions of images from public websites and social media platforms without user consent. The company marketed its database to law enforcement agencies, government bodies, and private clients for facial identification and investigative purposes. The company operates with minimal transparency about its data collection practices and the scope of its facial recognition capabilities.
caseDescription: Clearview AI collected and used biometric data (facial images) from individuals without consent or lawful authority, breaching Australian Privacy Principles. The company scraped facial images from public sources and created a searchable database without proper notification or compliance with privacy obligations.
violationSummary: Clearview AI engaged in systematic surveillance-type data collection by harvesting biometric data (facial images) from individuals without their knowledge or consent, then aggregating this data into a searchable facial recognition database.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Clearview AI scraped and collected facial images from public online sources without consent and built a searchable biometric database accessible to law enforcement and other clients.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals' facial images were harvested and indexed without their knowledge or agreement, enabling mass surveillance and identification of people without their consent or awareness.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clearview AI's images are sourced only from publicly available information and therefore lawfully collected.
claimsVsReality.reality: Public availability does not provide lawful authority to collect and repurpose biometric data without consent or notification under privacy law, and individuals had no knowledge their facial images were being indexed in a searchable database.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company complied with applicable privacy laws in jurisdictions where it operated.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OAIC determined Clearview AI breached multiple Australian Privacy Principles by failing to notify individuals, obtain consent, handle personal information responsibly, and provide access to collected data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) APP 1.2 - Personal Information Handling Principles
regulatoryFindings.description: Clearview AI collected personal information (facial images) without lawful authority or consent
violations: Clearview AI collected personal information (facial images) without lawful authority or consent

regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to notify individuals that their facial images were collected and stored
violations: Failed to notify individuals that their facial images were collected and stored

violations: Did not provide individuals with access to their personal information held in the facial recognition database

companyDescription: The Australian Federal Police (AFP) is Australia's federal law enforcement agency, responsible for investigating criminal matters and protecting national security.
companyLongDescription: The Australian Federal Police is the primary federal law enforcement and security agency of Australia, established under the Australian Federal Police Act 1979. caseDescription: The Australian Federal Police breached the Australian Privacy Principles, specifically APP 1.2, in their handling of personal information. The OAIC Commissioner initiated an investigation and found a breach of privacy obligations.
violationSummary: The breach of APP 1.2 indicates failure to comply with the Australian Privacy Principle regarding the collection, use, or disclosure of personal information in accordance with the Privacy Act 1988(Cth).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The Australian Federal Police failed to manage personal information in accordance with Australian Privacy Principles, specifically breaching APP 1.2 requirements for open.
whyTheyWereWrong: Officers and members of the public whose personal information was handled by AFP without proper transparency.

violations: Australian Federal Police failed to comply with APP 1.2 in their handling of personal information

companyDescription: 7-Eleven is a global convenience store chain operating thousands of franchised locations across multiple countries. In Australia, it operates a significant retail footprint selling food, beverages, and household items.

violations: Complainant alleged Telstra failed to take reasonable steps to notify about fact and circumstances of collection and purposes of personal information

regulatoryFindings.description: Complainant alleged Telstra failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information when account was opened with stolen identity documents
violations: Complainant alleged Telstra failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information when account was opened with stolen identity documents

outcome: Complaint dismissed. The OAIC found no breach of APP 5 or APP 10. Telstra was not found to have violated the requirement to notify individuals or ensure accuracy of personal information in the credit reporting context, despite the fraudulent account opening.
companyNow: Telstra remains Australia's leading telecommunications company with extensive networks and services. It continues operating as a publicly listed entity on the ASX with significant market presence in Australia.
dataType: Identity information, credit reporting data, personal account information

companyDescription: The Australian Commissioner of Taxation is the chief executive of the Australian Taxation Office (ATO), responsible for administering federal tax laws and collecting taxes on behalf of the Australian government.
companyLongDescription: The Commissioner of Taxation heads the Australian Taxation Office, the statutory authority responsible for administering Australia's tax system. The office collects income tax, goods and services tax, and other federal taxes. As a government agency, it holds extensive personal and financial information on millions of Australian taxpayers. The Commissioner's role includes managing tax compliance, conducting investigations, and pursuing debt collection.
caseDescription: The Commissioner of Taxation disclosed personal information to a mercantile agent for debt collection purposes. The complaint alleged privacy interference through unauthorised access to case management systems and secondary use of information beyond its original collection purpose. The OAIC investigated whether the disclosure and access arrangements violated Australian Privacy Principles.
violationSummary: The primary concern involved disclosure of personal information held in case management systems to external debt collection agents, raising questions about whether such secondary use and dissemination was authorised and proportionate under the Privacy Act.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Commissioner of Taxation disclosed personal information of individuals to a mercantile agent for debt collection purposes and granted the agent access to case management systems.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals had their personal financial and tax information accessed and disclosed to third-party debt collectors without clear understanding of how broadly their data would be used beyond.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Commissioner appropriately managed personal information disclosed to mercantile agents under 'need to know' principles and contractual protections.
claimsVsReality.reality: The investigation found that individuals' reasonable expectations about secondary use of their tax information for debt collection purposes were not adequately addressed, raising questions about the transparency of such disclosures.

claimsVsReality.claim: Access to case management systems was sufficiently restricted and monitored.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complaint raised concerns that the level of system access granted to debt collection agents may have exceeded what was necessary for their specific debt collection role.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 6 - Use or Disclosure: Personal information must only be used or disclosed for the primary purpose or a directly related secondary purpose unless consent is obtained or an exception applies
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosure of complaints information to mercantile agent for debt collection activities
violations: Disclosure of complaints information to mercantile agent for debt collection activities

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 10 - Quality of Personal Information: An entity must take reasonable steps to ensure that personal information it collects is accurate, up to date, complete, relevant and not misleading
regulatoryFindings.description: Consideration of access controls and need-to-know principle in case management system
violations: Consideration of access controls and need-to-know principle in case management system

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 11 - Security of Personal Information: An entity must take reasonable steps to protect personal information it holds from misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Level of access granted to case management system by external debt collection agents
violations: Level of access granted to case management system by external debt collection agents

outcome: The OAIC determined that no breach occurred. The Commissioner of Taxation's referral of files to the mercantile agent for debt collection was found to be a directly related secondary purpose under APP 6. The contractual and legal non-disclosure obligations, application of 'need to know' principle, and reasonable steps taken to secure information were deemed sufficient to comply with APP 10 and APP 11. The determination considered the volume of cases and extent of activities in reaching this conclusion.
companyNow: The ATO continues to operate as Australia's primary tax authority, managing tax administration for millions of individuals and businesses. It has expanded its role to include compliance activities and data exchange with other agencies.
dataType: Complaints information, debt collection records, case management system data

companyDescription: Wurli-Wurlinjang Health Service is an Australian healthcare provider offering primary and community health services.
companyLongDescription: Wurli-Wurlinjang Health Service is a healthcare organisation based in Australia providing primary care, community health services, and medical support to its patient population. The service operates within the Australian healthcare system and is subject to the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and Australian Privacy Principles regarding the handling of sensitive personal health information.
caseDescription: The OAIC investigated whether Wurli-Wurlinjang Health Service improperly collected and disclosed sensitive health information about an individual. The investigation examined whether the health service took reasonable steps to protect health information from unauthorised disclosure under the Australian Privacy Principles. The determination found no breach of the relevant privacy legislation.
violationSummary: The case involved alleged disclosure of health information and examination of whether reasonable safeguards were implemented to prevent unauthorised disclosure, which falls under information dissemination violations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Wurli-Wurlinjang Health Service collected and disclosed sensitive health information about an individual.
whyTheyWereWrong: The health service failed to take reasonable steps to protect the individual's sensitive health information from unauthorised disclosure, exposing their private medical details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The health service had taken reasonable steps to protect health information from unauthorised disclosure.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OAIC investigation examined whether reasonable steps were taken under APP 6-11, and the case involved alleged disclosure of sensitive health information without proper safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 3.3 & APP 3.4 - Sensitive information collection
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection of sensitive health information required individual consent and reasonable necessity for entity functions; no other exceptions applied
violations: Collection of sensitive health information required individual consent and reasonable necessity for entity functions; no other exceptions applied

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 6-11 - Information handling and disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Alleged failure to take reasonable steps to protect sensitive health information from unauthorised disclosure
violations: Alleged failure to take reasonable steps to protect sensitive health information from unauthorised disclosure

outcome: The OAIC determination found no breach of the Australian Privacy Principles. The health service was found to have taken reasonable steps to protect health information from unauthorised disclosure. No penalty or compliance orders were imposed.
dataType: Health data, sensitive personal information

companyDescription: Services Australia is the Australian government agency responsible for delivering social security payments and services to eligible individuals.
companyLongDescription: Services Australia administers payments and services for unemployed, disabled, aged, and other eligible Australians on behalf of the Department of Social Services. The agency manages sensitive personal information including residential addresses, income, and family circumstances for millions of Australians. It operates under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and must comply with the Australian Privacy Principles when handling personal information.
caseDescription: Services Australia disclosed a complainant's residential address to their former partner without adequate verification of the separation or reasonable steps to protect against unauthorised disclosure. The agency linked the complainant's records with those of the former partner despite being notified of the separation, creating a serious privacy and safety risk given the domestic violence history.
violationSummary: The agency breached confidentiality by disclosing sensitive residential information to an unauthorised third party (former partner) without proper safeguards, particularly concerning given the domestic violence context.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Services Australia disclosed a complainant's residential address to their former partner without adequately verifying the separation or taking reasonable steps to protect against unauthorised.
whyTheyWereWrong: A woman with a history of domestic violence had her home address revealed to her former partner, putting her at serious physical risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: The separation had not been adequately verified by the complainant, justifying the continued linkage of records.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant had explicitly notified Services Australia of the separation, and the agency failed to take reasonable steps to verify this notification or to unlink the records despite the notification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Standard record-linkage procedures were sufficient to protect the complainant's information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant's address was disclosed to the former partner without any verification of the separation or protective measures, exposing her to serious harm given the domestic violence history.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 6 – Use or disclosure of personal information must be for primary purpose or related secondary purpose; individuals must be reasonably notified
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed residential address to former partner without reasonable expectation of such disclosure
violations: Disclosed residential address to former partner without reasonable expectation of such disclosure
Failed to treat separation notification as sufficient change in circumstances

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 10 – Take reasonable steps to ensure personal information is accurate, up to date, complete, relevant and not misleading
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to update records to reflect separation despite complainant notification
violations: Failed to update records to reflect separation despite complainant notification
Continued to link records with former partner despite knowledge of separation

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 11 – Take reasonable steps to protect personal information against misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate safeguards against disclosure of sensitive address information
violations: Inadequate safeguards against disclosure of sensitive address information
Failed to implement protections specific to domestic violence risk

outcome: Determination that Services Australia breached APPs 6, 10 and 11. The agency was ordered to provide an apology to the complainant, award compensation for economic and non-economic loss, conduct an audit of relevant practices, and implement measures to prevent similar breaches. Ongoing monitoring of compliance required.
companyNow: Services Australia continues to operate as the primary government agency for delivering welfare and social security services to eligible Australians. The agency has implemented compliance improvements following various privacy enforcement actions.
dataType: Residential address, personal identity information, domestic violence history
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) - APP 10 (Quality of personal information)
Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) - APP 11 (Security of personal information)

companyDescription: Services Australia is the Australian federal government agency responsible for delivering social security payments, welfare services, and related administrative functions to eligible Australians.
companyLongDescription: Services Australia is the primary delivery agency for the Australian Department of Social Services, managing payments such as pensions, unemployment benefits, family assistance, and disability support. The agency processes personal and financial information for millions of Australians and has responsibility for accurate record-keeping and appropriate disclosure of sensitive data. Founded as a unified agency combining Centrelink and other service delivery functions, it operates under the Privacy Act 1988 and must comply with the Australian Privacy Principles.
caseDescription: Services Australia disclosed personal information to an external debt collection agency without proper authority and failed to notify the individual when debts were overturned. The agency breached Australian Privacy Principles by disclosing information to a third party and failing to take reasonable steps to correct records and notify affected parties of changes to debt status.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of personal information (financial and contact details) to an external debt collection agency, combined with failure to communicate material changes (debt overturn) to the individual and relevant entities.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Services Australia disclosed personal information to an external debt collection agency without proper authority and failed to notify the individual when debts were overturned.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individual's debt status changed but Services Australia did not correct their records or inform them, leaving them incorrectly listed as a debtor to a third party.
