claimsVsReality.claim: Services Australia had authority to disclose personal information to the external debt collection agency.
claimsVsReality.reality: The disclosure lacked proper legal authority under the Privacy Act and Australian Privacy Principles.

claimsVsReality.claim: Once debts were overturned, the matter was resolved.
claimsVsReality.reality: Services Australia failed to notify the individual or correct their records, leaving them exposed as a debtor to a third party.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 6 – Personal information must not be used or disclosed except for primary purpose or related secondary purpose
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosure of personal information to external debt collection agency without lawful authority or proper justification
violations: Disclosure of personal information to external debt collection agency without lawful authority or proper justification

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 13 – Entity must take reasonable steps to notify other APP entities and individuals if personal information held is inaccurate, out of date, incomplete, irrelevant or misleading
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to notify the individual when debts were overturned
violations: Failure to notify the individual when debts were overturned
Failure to take reasonable steps to update records and inform relevant entities of the change in debt status

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 10 – Entity must take reasonable steps to ensure personal information is accurate, up to date, complete, relevant and not misleading
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to accurately record preference for online communication (no breach found on this specific point)
violations: Failure to accurately record preference for online communication (no breach found on this specific point)

outcome: The OAIC determined that Services Australia breached APP 6 by disclosing personal information to a debt collection agency and breached APP 13 by failing to notify the individual of overturned debts. Compensation for non-economic loss was awarded. The entity is required to implement compliance measures and monitoring.
companyNow: Services Australia continues to operate as the primary welfare and social security delivery agency in Australia, managing payments and services for millions of beneficiaries.
dataType: Financial data, debt records, contact information, communication preferences

companyDescription: Uber is a global ride-sharing and mobility platform that connects drivers with passengers through a mobile app. The company operates in over 70 countries and is one of the world's largest transportation network companies.
companyLongDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a multinational mobility and logistics company founded in 2009 that revolutionized urban transportation through its ride-sharing platform. The company operates in multiple countries and jurisdictions, collecting vast amounts of personal data from drivers, passengers, and users. Uber also offers food delivery (Uber Eats), freight services, and other mobility solutions. The company's Australian operations fall under both Uber Technologies, Inc. and Uber B.V., which were subject to this privacy enforcement action.
caseDescription: The OAIC found that Uber Technologies, Inc. and Uber B.V. breached the Australian Privacy Principles by failing to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from unauthorised third-party access and by not adequately notifying individuals of data collection. The investigation determined that Uber did not implement sufficient practices, procedures, and systems to ensure compliance with privacy obligations.
violationSummary: Uber failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from unauthorised access by third parties, a core insecurity violation under the Solove taxonomy involving inadequate safeguards and breach of confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Uber failed to implement sufficient security practices and systems to protect user personal information from unauthorized third-party access.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Uber users in Australia had their personal information exposed to unauthorized access because Uber's security systems were inadequate, putting their names, locations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber implemented reasonable steps to protect personal information from unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Uber's security practices and systems were insufficient, allowing unauthorized third-party access to user personal information including names, locations, and payment details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber adequately notified individuals about collection of their personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Uber failed to take reasonable steps to notify Australian users about the collection of their personal data as required by the Australian Privacy Principles.

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber had compliant policies, procedures, and systems in place to ensure compliance with Australian Privacy Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: Uber lacked sufficient practices, procedures, and systems to ensure compliance with privacy obligations, requiring a compliance order for policy remediation and independent review.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 11.1 & 11.2 – Security of Personal Information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from unauthorised access by third parties
violations: Failed to take reasonable steps to protect personal information from unauthorised access by third parties
Did not implement adequate practices, procedures and systems to ensure APP compliance

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 5 – Notification of Collection
regulatoryFindings.description: Did not take reasonable steps to notify individuals of the collection of personal information
violations: Did not take reasonable steps to notify individuals of the collection of personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 1.2 – Open and Transparent Management of Personal Information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to manage personal information in an open and transparent manner
violations: Failed to manage personal information in an open and transparent manner

outcome: The OAIC determination required Uber to take reasonable steps to notify individuals of personal information collection, prepare compliant privacy policies and programs, and undergo independent review of those policies and programs to ensure compliance with the Australian Privacy Principles.
companyNow: Uber remains one of the world's largest mobility and logistics platforms, operating globally with significant market presence. The company has since implemented enhanced privacy and data protection measures following regulatory enforcement actions.
dataType: Personal information accessed by third parties (specific types not detailed in summary)

companyDescription: Comcare is Australia's national workers' compensation scheme and insurer, providing compensation and rehabilitation services to Australian Government employees and eligible workers.
companyLongDescription: Comcare is a statutory authority and self-insuring agency established under the Safety, Rehabilitation and Compensation Act 1988 (Cth). It administers workers' compensation for Australian Government employees and certain eligible workers, managing claims, providing rehabilitation services, and handling dispute resolution through tribunal proceedings. As a government body, it is subject to the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and Australian Privacy Principles.
caseDescription: Comcare failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information in an Independent Medical Expert report used for tribunal proceedings, resulting in inaccuracies. Comcare also failed to respond to a correction request within the statutory timeframe required by the Privacy Act. The determination found a breach of APP 13.5 but dismissed the complaint otherwise.
violationSummary: The violation relates to failure to ensure accuracy of personal information and inadequate data handling processes (failure to respond to correction requests within statutory timeframes), which falls under the insecurity category of information processing vulnerabilities.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Comcare failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information in an Independent Medical Expert report used for tribunal proceedings.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant was exposed to inaccurate medical information in tribunal proceedings that could have affected legal decisions about their workers' compensation claim.

claimsVsReality.claim: Comcare took reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information in the Independent Medical Expert report.
claimsVsReality.reality: The report contained inaccuracies in personal information that Comcare failed to verify or correct before using in tribunal proceedings.

claimsVsReality.claim: Comcare responded to the correction request within statutory timeframes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Comcare failed to respond to the correction request within the timeframe required by the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth).

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 13.5 requires entities to take reasonable steps to ensure personal information is accurate, up-to-date, and complete
regulatoryFindings.description: Comcare failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of information in an Independent Medical Expert report
violations: Comcare failed to take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of information in an Independent Medical Expert report
Comcare failed to respond to a correction request within the statutory timeframe

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 10-13 establish principles for collection, use, disclosure, data quality, and data safety
regulatoryFindings.description: Breach of APP 13.5 regarding accuracy obligations
violations: Breach of APP 13.5 regarding accuracy obligations

outcome: The complaint was largely dismissed. The determination found a breach of APP 13.5 due to Comcare's failure to ensure accuracy and respond to correction requests within the statutory timeframe. The OAIC acknowledged interference with privacy but determined it inappropriate to take any further action beyond the finding.
companyNow: Comcare continues to operate as Australia's national workers' compensation scheme for Australian Government employees, maintaining its role in administering compensation and rehabilitation services.
dataType: Medical records, health information, tribunal proceedings documentation

companyDescription: Terra Systems Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based communication solutions and call centre services provider. The company was contracted by Singapore's Immigration and Checkpoints Authority in June 2020 to operate a call centre verifying the whereabouts of persons serving Stay-Home Notices during the COVID-19 pandemic.
companyLongDescription: Terra Systems Pte. Ltd. provides communication solutions and call centre services to businesses in Singapore and the region. In June 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, the company was awarded a government contract to operate a call centre for the Immigration and Checkpoints Authority, verifying compliance with Stay-Home Notice requirements. The company created a customer relationship management portal to manage the personal data of persons under SHN, but implemented inadequate access controls. The organisation operates within Singapore's regulatory framework under the Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: Terra Systems operated a customer relationship management portal for a government call centre verifying persons under Stay-Home Notices during the COVID-19 pandemic. The portal was breached by a disgruntled ex-employee on two occasions (14 and 21 July 2020) who accessed and modified sensitive personal data due to poor access controls including shared common passwords and generic user IDs. The organization failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect the data, violating Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable IT access controls and security arrangements to protect personal data from unauthorized access and modification. Specifically, they used generic user IDs and a daily common password shared across multiple users, defeating segregation of access and enabling unauthorized access to sensitive Stay-Home Notice data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Terra Systems operated a COVID-19 call centre portal with shared passwords and generic user IDs, allowing a disgruntled ex-employee to access.
whyTheyWereWrong: Persons under Stay-Home Notices faced potential discrimination or social stigma if their isolation status became publicly known during the early COVID-19 pandemic when public health concerns.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only 4 individuals' personal data was actually accessed and modified, representing a very low number of affected persons.
claimsVsReality.reality: While only 4 distinct cases showed evidence of modification, the perpetrator could have accessed the sensitive personal data of all 125 persons assigned to his former team due to the generic user IDs and shared common password.

claimsVsReality.claim: The SHN Data was not sensitive information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The SHN Data was sensitive at the material time in July 2020 during the early COVID-19 pandemic when uncertainty about the virus's virulence was high and public concern was acute; being subject to an SHN denoted risk of virus exposure and could cause discrimination or social stigma.

claimsVsReality.claim: There was no exfiltration or public exposure of the SHN Data, and no members of the public complained or held the organisation to ransom.
claimsVsReality.reality: The fact that exfiltration did not occur does not mitigate the organisation's failure to implement reasonable security measures; the vulnerability existed and was exploited, creating serious risk to 125 individuals' sensitive data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The circumstances were similar to or less egregious than precedent cases where only warnings were issued.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation's culpability was significantly higher than precedent cases because it employed very poor access control measures easily circumvented by an unsophisticated actor, with a common password shared by over 50 users via unsecure platforms and no audit trail.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requiring organizations to protect personal data by taking reasonable security steps to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement reasonable IT access controls by using generic user IDs (e.g., 'D03') that were known or guessable to all agents
violations: Failed to implement reasonable IT access controls by using generic user IDs (e.g., 'D03') that were known or guessable to all agents
Failed to implement unique passwords for agents; instead used a daily common password shared across over 50 users via insecure platform (Zoom, WhatsApp) with no audit trail
Failed to implement adequate policies to mitigate risks from common password use, such as prohibiting password sharing or requiring verification of requestor employment status
Failed to implement two-factor authentication or web server logging initially to track unauthorized access
The poor access controls allowed ex-employee to access and modify SHN Data of at least 4 individuals and exposed 125 individuals to risk of unauthorized access

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD $12,000 payable within 30 days. The organization was required to cease use of common passwords and implement unique user IDs and passwords for all agents, adopt two-factor authentication for portal access, and enable web server logging for audit trails. No additional directions were necessary given remedial actions already undertaken.
companyNow: Terra Systems continues to operate as a communication solutions provider in Singapore, though the specific status of the company following the 2021 enforcement action is not documented in the case materials.
dataType: Name, NRIC (last 4 digits), gender, contact number, address, COVID-19 test appointment dates, Stay-Home Notice status

companyDescription: Crawfort is a Singapore-based fintech lending company providing loan services and digital financial products.
companyLongDescription: Crawfort Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based financial services company specializing in lending and loan origination through digital platforms. The company enables customers to apply for loans remotely and manage their financial products online. During the COVID-19 pandemic in 2020, Crawfort rapidly shifted to remote operations to maintain business continuity while adhering to lockdown restrictions.
caseDescription: Crawfort failed to conduct a risk assessment before a data migration exercise and left an S3 server port open for one week, resulting in the unauthorized disclosure of personal data for 5,421 customers on the dark web. The organization's AWS environment was misconfigured, allowing a threat actor to access publicly accessible S3 buckets containing sensitive financial and identity information.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access to personal data. Specific failures included: omitting risk assessment before data migration, leaving an S3 server port open to the internet, and misconfiguring S3 bucket permissions to be publicly accessible. These failures resulted in actual unauthorized access and disclosure of sensitive personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Crawfort failed to conduct a risk assessment before a data migration exercise and left an S3 server port open for one week, exposing 5,421 customers' sensitive financial.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' most sensitive personal and financial information—national ID images, loan details, income statements—was publicly accessible on the dark web for a week.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data migration was conducted under emergency COVID-19 circumstances with very short notice due to Circuit Breaker lockdown.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of circumstances, failing to conduct any risk assessment before opening public access to a bucket containing 5,421 customers' NRIC images, loan contracts, and income documents was a fundamental security failure.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization took prompt remedial measures after discovery of the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: Remedial measures occurred only after the data had already been sold on the dark web and customers' most sensitive information was compromised—prevention through basic security practices would have been far more effective.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal and loss of storage media.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct a reasonable risk assessment before carrying out the data migration exercise
violations: Failed to conduct a reasonable risk assessment before carrying out the data migration exercise
Opened S3 server port connected directly to S3 buckets containing personal data without adequate access controls
S3 bucket containing affected personal data was publicly accessible due to misconfiguration
Lack of adequate access control measures during the one-week migration period
These security failures resulted in actual unauthorized access and disclosure of 5,421 customers' personal data on the dark web

outcome: The Commission accepted the Organization's request for expedited breach decision procedure. In lieu of a financial penalty, considering the Organization's voluntary admission of liability and prompt remedial actions, the Commission directed the Organization to: (1) engage a qualified security service provider to conduct a thorough security audit of its AWS S3 environment; (2) provide the full security audit report within 60 days; (3) rectify any identified security gaps and update personal data protection policies within 60 days of receiving the audit report; and (4) inform the Commission within 1 week of completion of rectification.
dataType: NRIC images, loan contracts, income documents (payslips, CPF statements, tax assessments), email addresses, contact numbers
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 24 (Protection of Personal Data – reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Audio House Marketing is a retail company in Singapore that sells audio equipment and related products through an online e-commerce platform.
companyLongDescription: Audio House Marketing Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based retailer specializing in audio equipment and accessories. The company operates an online sales platform through which it collects customer contact information for order fulfillment and communication purposes. The company's website was developed by a third-party vendor and launched in April 2017, serving as the primary channel for customer transactions and data collection.
caseDescription: Audio House Marketing suffered a ransomware attack exploiting SQL injection vulnerabilities in PHP files on its website, exposing approximately 98,000 customers' contact information. The company failed to conduct adequate vulnerability scanning, security assessments, and periodic security reviews despite these being well-known security practices. Additionally, the company failed to impose data protection requirements on its IT vendors and sub-contractors.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and protect personal data, specifically through inadequate vulnerability detection, lack of periodic security reviews, and failure to contractually mandate data protection standards with IT vendors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Audio House Marketing failed to conduct vulnerability scanning, security assessments, and periodic security reviews of its website.
whyTheyWereWrong: The undetected SQL injection vulnerabilities allowed attackers to access and expose the names, addresses, email addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Audio House Marketing conducted pre-launch testing to ensure website security before going live in April 2017.
claimsVsReality.reality: Pre-launch testing only covered functionality (shopping cart, payment features) and failed to identify SQL injection vulnerabilities that existed in the PHP files at launch.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had adequate vendor management and contractual protections in place with its IT service providers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no direct contract with the website developer, failed to impose data protection requirements on vendors or sub-contractors, and did not stipulate clear security maintenance specifications.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company maintained reasonable ongoing security practices through periodic reviews and updates.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company conducted no vulnerability scanning, security assessments, or periodic security reviews between April 2017 and June 2021, leaving SQL injection vulnerabilities undetected for over four years.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24(a) – An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct vulnerability scanning and security assessments during pre-launch testing
violations: Failed to conduct vulnerability scanning and security assessments during pre-launch testing
Failed to conduct periodic security reviews that would have detected SQL injection vulnerabilities
Failed to stipulate data protection requirements in contracts with IT vendors and sub-contractors
Failed to conduct reasonable oversight over IT vendors responsible for website development and maintenance
Allowed SQL injection vulnerabilities to persist since April 2017 without detection

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found Audio House Marketing in breach of Section 24(a) of the PDPA and directed the company to pay a financial penalty of S$10,000 within 30 days. No further directions under Section 48I were necessary given the organization's cooperation, voluntary admission, prompt remediation actions (including disabling the website, reformatting the webserver, adding SQL injection protections, and implementing vulnerability assessment and penetration testing), and successful restoration of all affected personal data without loss.
dataType: Names, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers (contact information)

companyDescription: Vhive Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based e-commerce company that operates an online storefront selling various products to customers.
companyLongDescription: Vhive Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based e-commerce platform that operates an online retail business. The company engaged an IT vendor to host and maintain its e-commerce server and IT systems. Following the 2021 ransomware incident, the company transitioned to conducting online sales solely through third-party platforms and rebuilt its IT infrastructure with enhanced security measures.
caseDescription: Vhive suffered a ransomware attack affecting approximately 186,281 customers due to outdated IT infrastructure with multiple vulnerabilities, including an unpatched firewall and outdated webserver. The organisation failed to establish a written contract with its IT vendor specifying security and data protection requirements, and did not implement its own security maintenance policies or conduct security reviews. The breach resulted in unauthorised access to customer personal data through remotely executed code.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, as required by PDPA section 24(a). This manifested through outdated infrastructure, unpatched systems, lack of written vendor contracts specifying security requirements, absence of security maintenance policies, and failure to conduct scheduled security reviews.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Vhive failed to establish a written contract with its IT vendor specifying security requirements, did not implement security maintenance policies.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' names, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, hashed passwords and customer IDs were exposed to unauthorised access due to the company's failure to maintain secure systems.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vhive had engaged an IT vendor to properly host, manage and maintain its e-commerce server and IT systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: No written contract existed between Vhive and its IT vendor at the time of the incident, leaving security requirements and responsibilities undefined and unspecified.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vhive's IT infrastructure was adequately protected and maintained.
claimsVsReality.reality: The infrastructure was outdated with multiple vulnerabilities including an unpatched firewall and outdated webserver that allowed remote code execution and backdoor access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vhive had security oversight processes in place to detect vulnerabilities.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vhive had no security maintenance policy and conducted no scheduled security reviews, which could have detected the security inadequacies before the attack.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24(a) requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation maintained outdated e-commerce server running outdated webserver service
violations: Organisation maintained outdated e-commerce server running outdated webserver service
Firewall was unpatched, allowing threat actor to remotely execute unauthorised code
No written contract with IT vendor specifying security maintenance and data protection requirements
Organisation had no security maintenance policy
No scheduled security reviews conducted to detect vulnerabilities
Failure to ensure proper scope, roles and responsibilities with data intermediary

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 4(2) requires organisations engaging data intermediaries to do so pursuant to a contract evidenced or made in writing
regulatoryFindings.description: No written contract existed between Organisation and IT vendor at time of incident despite purported engagement
violations: No written contract existed between Organisation and IT vendor at time of incident despite purported engagement

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 12(a) requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices including contractual documentation relating to data intermediary relationships
regulatoryFindings.description: Lack of contractual documentation delineating scope of data intermediary relationship
violations: Lack of contractual documentation delineating scope of data intermediary relationship
Failure to implement written security maintenance requirements

outcome: The organisation is found in breach of section 24(a) of the PDPA and ordered to pay a financial penalty of SGD $22,000 within 30 days. The Commission acknowledged the organisation's cooperation, voluntary admission of breach, and prompt remediation actions. Following the incident, the organisation decommissioned the vulnerable e-commerce server, rebuilt its IT infrastructure with new firewalls and updated systems, engaged a new IT vendor with written data protection provisions, and reviewed and updated internal data protection policies. No further directions under section 48I were deemed necessary given the remedial measures undertaken.
companyNow: Following the 2021 incident, Vhive restructured its operations to rely on third-party e-commerce platforms for sales rather than maintaining its own servers, and implemented comprehensive IT security upgrades.
dataType: Names, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, hashed passwords, customer IDs
legalBasisViolated: PDPA section 24(a) – Protection Obligation (reasonable security arrangements)
PDPA section 4(2) – Data intermediary contracts must be in writing
PDPA section 12(a) – Development and implementation of policies and practices

companyDescription: Aviva Financial Advisers Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based financial advisory firm specialising in insurance products and investment advice.
companyLongDescription: Aviva Financial Advisers Pte Ltd is a Singapore-registered financial services company that provides insurance and investment advisory services to clients. The firm employs independent financial advisers who represent the company and provide personalised financial planning services. The company maintains policies and security measures for personal data protection in accordance with Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: Three individuals (Dennis, Melissa, and Winarto) involved with Aviva Financial Advisers engaged in the unauthorised sale of approximately 1,000 client personal data records, including names, addresses, and contact numbers. Dennis sold the list to Melissa and Winarto for $1,000 each without obtaining client consent or notification. The buyers failed to conduct adequate due diligence to verify consent before purchasing the data.
violationSummary: The individuals disclosed and traded client personal data without consent or notification, violating core data protection obligations. This represents unauthorised secondary disclosure of personal information collected for insurance purposes, now being transferred to other financial advisers without individual knowledge or permission.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Dennis sold a list of approximately 1,000 client personal data records including names, addresses, and contact numbers to Melissa.
whyTheyWereWrong: Clients' personal data was sold without their knowledge or permission, exposing them to risks of identity theft, nuisance calls.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dennis claimed he had obtained necessary consent and duly notified clients regarding disclosure of their personal data to other insurance financial advisers.
claimsVsReality.reality: None of the 1,000 clients verified that Dennis had contacted them to seek consent or notified them of the disclosure of their personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Melissa and Winarto relied on Dennis' verbal assurances that he had informed the clients about the change in their insurance financial adviser.
claimsVsReality.reality: No written notifications or evidence of client consent existed; Melissa and Winarto failed to conduct proper due diligence before purchasing the client list.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dennis stated he was leaving the insurance industry and looking for a reliable agent to take over his clientele.
claimsVsReality.reality: Dennis sold the client list for $1,000 to each buyer (Melissa and Winarto) for profit without any legitimate transfer of advisory relationship.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 13 & 20 – Consent and Notification Obligations
regulatoryFindings.description: Dennis disclosed approximately 1,000 clients' personal data to Melissa and Winarto without obtaining prior consent from the clients or providing notification of the disclosure
violations: Dennis disclosed approximately 1,000 clients' personal data to Melissa and Winarto without obtaining prior consent from the clients or providing notification of the disclosure
Melissa and Winarto purchased and collected the client list without conducting reasonable due diligence to verify that proper consent and notification had been obtained from the individuals involved

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation
regulatoryFindings.description: Dennis failed to protect client personal data by selling it without authorisation or safeguards ensuring proper consent
violations: Dennis failed to protect client personal data by selling it without authorisation or safeguards ensuring proper consent

outcome: The Commission issued warnings to Dennis, Melissa, and Winarto in respect of their breaches of the Consent and Notification Obligations under the PDPA. No financial penalties were imposed. Dennis received a warning considering his poor health, unemployment since 2018, minimal savings, and financial dependence on his aged father, which the Commission found would cause undue hardship if a monetary penalty were imposed. Melissa and Winarto received warnings as they did not profit from the sale and did not use the personal data without consent, and they cooperated with the investigation. Aviva Financial Advisers Pte Ltd was found to have no breach of the PDPA as Dennis was an independent contractor, not an employee, and the company had reasonable security measures and contractual protections in place.
dataType: Names, mailing addresses, contact numbers, insurance policy information

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunication Limited (SingTel) is a major telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and IT services across Asia-Pacific.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunication Limited (SingTel) is one of Asia's leading telecommunications companies, providing mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and IT services to millions of customers across Singapore and the Asia-Pacific region. The company operates as a publicly listed entity on the Singapore Exchange and serves residential, business, and enterprise customers with comprehensive telecommunications and digital solutions.
caseDescription: Singapore Telecommunication Limited suffered a data breach affecting 163,370 individuals when threat actors exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities in a third-party File Transfer Appliance to gain unauthorized access to personal data. The Commission found that the organization had implemented reasonable security measures and could not have detected or prevented the breach as the vulnerabilities were in the third-party vendor's proprietary system.
violationSummary: While a breach occurred resulting in unauthorized access and exfiltration of personal data, the Commission determined the organization itself did not violate the Protection Obligation as it had implemented reasonable security arrangements and the vulnerability was in a third-party system beyond its control.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Singapore Telecommunication Limited suffered a data breach affecting 163,370 individuals when threat actors exploited two zero-day vulnerabilities in a third-party File Transfer Appliance.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company was not found to be wrong; regulators determined the organization had implemented reasonable security measures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization may have failed to protect personal data against unauthorized access through inadequate security measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization had implemented reasonable security measures including regular patching (within 5 days of updates) and maintained appropriate protective arrangements; the vulnerabilities were zero-day exploits in third-party proprietary code that no organization could have detected.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization bore responsibility for security vulnerabilities in third-party systems it used.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only the third-party vendor (Accellion) had access to the proprietary source code and control over the File Transfer Appliance; the organization had no visibility into or control over the zero-day vulnerabilities and could not have discovered or prevented their exploitation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Breach occurred through exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities in third-party File Transfer Appliance resulting in exfiltration of personal data of 163,370 individuals
violations: Breach occurred through exploitation of zero-day vulnerabilities in third-party File Transfer Appliance resulting in exfiltration of personal data of 163,370 individuals

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection determined that Singapore Telecommunication Limited had met its Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA by implementing reasonable security arrangements, including timely patching and updates. The Commission found the organization could not have detected or prevented the breach as the zero-day vulnerabilities were in the third-party vendor's proprietary system beyond the organization's control. No enforcement action was taken. The organization took extensive remedial measures including shutting down the affected system, reviewing file sharing protocols, and offering identity monitoring services to affected individuals.
companyNow: SingTel remains a major regional telecommunications provider, though it has faced increased competition in mobile and fixed-line markets while expanding digital and cloud service offerings.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, FIN, UIN, nationality, date of birth, address, email address, mobile number, photograph, staff/company pass/ID, bank account number, credit card information, billing information, vehicle number

companyDescription: Southaven Boutique is a brick-and-mortar retailer of clothes and accessories operating in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Southaven Boutique is a physical retail store specialising in clothing and accessories in Singapore. The company operates Point-of-Sale systems to process customer transactions and collect personal data including names, addresses, contact information and dates of birth. The retailer relies on third-party POS vendors for system supply and support.
caseDescription: Southaven Boutique, a clothing retailer, suffered a ransomware attack on its Point-Of-Sale system on 4 February 2021, affecting 4,709 customers' personal data. The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures, including outdated operating systems, anti-virus software, and no scheduled software updates or security reviews. The organisation also failed to establish data protection requirements with its POS vendor, creating unclear responsibility for system maintenance and patching.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements as required by PDPA section 24, specifically failing to conduct software updates, maintain security patches, and perform periodic security reviews. This insecurity directly enabled the ransomware attack and encryption of customer personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Southaven Boutique failed to implement adequate security measures for its Point-of-Sale system, including using outdated operating systems.
whyTheyWereWrong: The inadequate security left 4,709 customers' personal data including names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had engaged appropriate third-party support for POS system maintenance and security.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation failed to establish any data protection requirements or responsibilities with its POS vendor and did not actually engage the vendor for necessary maintenance support, leaving the system unpatched and vulnerable.

claimsVsReality.claim: The POS system was adequately maintained with current software and security patches.
claimsVsReality.reality: The operating system and anti-virus software were outdated, no software updates or security reviews were scheduled or conducted, and patches were only applied after the ransomware attack occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – An organisation shall protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement adequate administrative and technical security arrangements
violations: Failed to implement adequate administrative and technical security arrangements
Failed to conduct or schedule software updates, maintenance, and security reviews before the incident
Operating system and anti-virus software were outdated at time of attack
Failed to establish data protection requirements and responsibilities with POS vendor
Created unclear responsibility allocation for system maintenance and patching with third-party vendor

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of S$5,000 (reduced from initial S$5,000 following reconsideration application to S$2,000, then the editorial note indicates the final amount remains S$5,000 in this decision). The organisation was required to pay the penalty within 30 days. The Commission acknowledged the organisation's remediation efforts and investment in a more secure IT system but determined the organisation bore full responsibility for implementing adequate security measures. No further directions under section 48I of the PDPA were issued.
dataType: Names, addresses, email addresses, contact numbers, date of birth
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 24 – Protection of personal data (reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Trinity Christian Centre is a church organisation operating in Singapore that maintains a database of members' personal information.
companyLongDescription: Trinity Christian Centre Limited operates Trinity Christian Church in Singapore and maintains databases containing personal information of its congregation members, including names, identification numbers, addresses, contact details, photographs, dates of birth, education levels, and medical conditions. The organisation provides counselling and mission services to its members. At the time of the incident, the centre held data on 72,285 individuals.
caseDescription: Trinity Christian Centre's database servers containing personal data of 72,285 individuals were infected with ransomware on 17 February 2021 due to an exposed remote desktop protocol port and inadequate access controls. The organisation failed to implement separate access controls for database protection and did not stipulate data protection requirements in its contract with an IT vendor who had administrator account access.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data as required by PDPA section 24, specifically by not implementing separate access controls to protect backend database servers and failing to include data protection contractual terms with IT vendors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Trinity Christian Centre failed to implement separate access controls for its database servers and did not require data protection measures in its IT vendor contract.
whyTheyWereWrong: Church members, including 8,300 minors, had sensitive personal data including medical conditions.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had adequate security measures to protect member data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation maintained an open, publicly exposed remote desktop protocol port and lacked separate access controls for database protection, allowing ransomware infection of servers containing 72,285 individuals' records.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT vendor relationship was adequately governed by contractual terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: The vendor contract contained only a general confidentiality clause and no specific requirements for protecting personal data, despite the vendor having administrator account access to systems processing sensitive church member information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24 – An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement separate access controls (separate logins) to protect databases containing personal data despite the high number and sensitivity of datasets
violations: Failed to implement separate access controls (separate logins) to protect databases containing personal data despite the high number and sensitivity of datasets
Failed to stipulate data protection requirements in contract with IT vendor despite knowing the vendor would process personal data, only including a general confidentiality clause

outcome: The Organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of $20,000 (SGD) within 30 days. Following the incident, the Organisation implemented comprehensive remediation measures including: notifying affected church members on 8 April 2021, changing all user and administrator passwords, closing all unused and open remote access ports, restricting domain administrator logon privileges, conducting a security review, and implementing real-time threat monitoring, detection, and response measures.
companyNow: Following the 2021 ransomware incident, Trinity Christian Centre implemented enhanced security measures including real-time threat monitoring and restricted access controls.
dataType: Name, identification number, residential address, contact number, email address, photograph, date of birth, age, marital status, education level, medical condition descriptions

companyDescription: GeniusU is a Singapore-based technology company that provides online learning or educational technology services to users across multiple regions.
companyLongDescription: GeniusU Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-incorporated technology company operating a digital platform serving approximately 1.26 million users globally. The company stores sensitive user personal data including names, email addresses, location information, and sign-in records. Following a security incident in January 2021, the company was found to have failed to implement industry-standard security practices for protecting user data in both production and non-production environments.
caseDescription: GeniusU failed to implement adequate security measures, resulting in unauthorized access to a staging database containing personal data of 1.26 million users. A developer's compromised GitHub credentials allowed a threat actor to access stored database login credentials in the codebase and exfiltrate personal data. The company also improperly stored actual personal data in a non-production testing environment known to have weaker security.
violationSummary: The organization failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access to personal data, in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA section 24. Specific failures included storing database credentials in the codebase and storing actual personal data in less-secure testing environments.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: GeniusU stored database login credentials in its GitHub codebase and kept actual personal data in a non-production testing environment with weaker security controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: When a developer's GitHub account was compromised, the threat actor accessed the hardcoded credentials and exfiltrated names, emails, locations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Developer used weak password or account was independently compromised
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of the compromise method, GeniusU had no compensating controls — credentials were hardcoded in the codebase, allowing immediate database access once GitHub was breached

claimsVsReality.claim: Testing environment is a safe place to store real user data
claimsVsReality.reality: Testing environments are known to have weaker security controls and should never contain production personal data; the company's own practices proved this when the staging database was accessed

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24 – An organisation shall protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Stored database login credentials in plaintext within the GitHub codebase, allowing threat actor to access the database once GitHub was compromised
violations: Stored database login credentials in plaintext within the GitHub codebase, allowing threat actor to access the database once GitHub was compromised
Stored actual personal data in non-production testing environment with weaker security controls than production systems
Failed to implement adequate access controls and credential management practices

outcome: GeniusU was found in breach of PDPA section 24 and issued a financial penalty of $35,000 SGD, payable within 30 days. The Commission did not issue further directions under section 48I, given the organization's prompt remedial actions including credential rotation, removal of hard-coded credentials from codebase, purging of personal data from non-production servers, implementation of multi-factor authentication, adoption of standardized cyber security policies, and notification of affected users and relevant authorities.
dataType: First and last name, email address, location, IP address

companyDescription: Yoshi Mobile was a mobile SIM card retailer operating in Singapore, operating as a sole proprietorship under Neo Yong Xiang. The business was an exclusive retailer of M1 prepaid SIM cards.
companyLongDescription: Yoshi Mobile, located on Geylang Road in Singapore, was a retail shop selling prepaid M1 SIM cards. Operated since 2013 by sole proprietor Neo Yong Xiang, it was provided with an M1 Terminal Device to conduct legitimate SIM card registrations for customers. The business exploited this legitimate function by misusing customer personal data to register additional SIM cards without customer knowledge or consent, which were then sold to anonymous buyers at approximately SGD 50 per card.
caseDescription: Neo Yong Xiang, operating as Yoshi Mobile, a mobile SIM card retailer, unlawfully used personal data from at least 78 customers to register additional prepaid SIM cards without consent, which were then sold to anonymous buyers for profit over approximately 3 years. These illicit SIM cards were subsequently used to send unsolicited spam and scam messages to telephone numbers registered with Singapore's Do Not Call register.
violationSummary: The company collected personal data (names, addresses, NRIC/work permit numbers) with consent for the limited purpose of registering requested SIM cards, but then used that same data for an entirely different purpose—registering additional illicit SIM cards for resale—without obtaining fresh consent or notification of this secondary use.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Neo Yong Xiang, operating as Yoshi Mobile, used personal data from at least 78 customers without consent to register additional prepaid SIM cards that were then sold to anonymous buyers.
whyTheyWereWrong: The illicit SIM cards sold by Yoshi Mobile were used by unknown perpetrators to send unsolicited spam.

claimsVsReality.claim: Yoshi Mobile was a legitimate SIM card retailer operating with M1's trust and authorization.
claimsVsReality.reality: The proprietor systematically abused the authorized SIM card registration process to fraudulently register additional cards using customer data without consent, then sold them to generate unauthorized income of approximately SGD 15,000 over 3 years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach was a minor misuse of customer data limited to SIM card registration.
claimsVsReality.reality: The illicit SIM cards were subsequently used by unknown perpetrators to send thousands of unsolicited spam and scam messages to phone numbers on Singapore's Do Not Call register, affecting innocent parties with no connection to the original customers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The proprietor merely registered SIM cards without further involvement.
claimsVsReality.reality: Neo Yong Xiang deliberately planned and premeditated the scheme over 3 years, using two distinct methods to evade detection, and directly profited by selling the fraudulently registered cards to anonymous buyers.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 13 – Consent Obligation: Organisations must not collect, use or disclose personal data unless the individual has given consent after being notified of the purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Used customer personal data to register additional illicit SIM cards without consent (Method 1)
violations: Used customer personal data to register additional illicit SIM cards without consent (Method 1)
Activated and registered SIM cards after customers withdrew consent by declining to complete purchase (Method 2)
Did not notify customers that their data would be used for registering SIM cards beyond those requested

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 18 – Purpose Limitation Obligation: Organisations may collect, use or disclose personal data only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate, regardless of whether consent was obtained
regulatoryFindings.description: Used personal data for the fraudulent purpose of registering illicit SIM cards for resale, which was not a reasonable purpose
violations: Used personal data for the fraudulent purpose of registering illicit SIM cards for resale, which was not a reasonable purpose
The purpose (NYX's financial gain through unauthorized SIM card sales) was not one individuals could reasonably have anticipated or approved

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD 21,000 payable in 18 monthly instalments, reduced from an initial preliminary decision of SGD 35,000 to account for NYX's demonstrated financial hardship. The penalty was imposed despite mitigating factors (early admission of liability) based on aggravating factors including premeditation, breach of trust, facilitation of downstream DNC violations, and financial gain from the misuse. M1 telecommunications barred NYX from offering the sale of its prepaid SIM cards, eliminating the need for further compliance directions.
companyNow: Yoshi Mobile's operational status following the 2021 enforcement action is not specified in the decision document.
dataType: Name, address, NRIC number, work permit number

companyDescription: ACL Construction (S) Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based construction company that provides pre-fabricated structures, structural steel products, and construction services.
companyLongDescription: ACL Construction is a Singapore-incorporated construction services provider specialising in pre-fabricated structures and structural steel products. The company works with corporate clients on construction projects and maintains business contact information and technical documentation. In June 2021, the company experienced a ransomware attack in which encrypted files were offered for sale on the darkweb, triggering a PDPA investigation.
caseDescription: ACL Construction experienced a ransomware attack in which files were encrypted and offered for sale on the darkweb. While the breached files contained primarily business contact information (which falls outside PDPA scope), investigations revealed the organisation had failed to designate a Data Protection Officer and had no data protection policies in place, violating accountability requirements under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate safeguards and accountability measures (no DPO designation, no data protection policies) required to protect personal data it processes, as evidenced by the ransomware incident and lack of compliance infrastructure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: ACL Construction failed to designate a Data Protection Officer and had no data protection policies in place, leaving the organisation unable to ensure PDPA compliance.
whyTheyWereWrong: Without a designated Data Protection Officer and no policies in place, ACL Construction could not identify or protect personal data of employees.

claimsVsReality.claim: ACL Construction's breached files contained only business contact information outside PDPA scope.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the encrypted files contained primarily business contact information, ACL Construction still processed personal data of employees and others, requiring PDPA compliance regardless of the incident.

claimsVsReality.claim: ACL Construction had adequate data protection governance in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation had failed to designate a Data Protection Officer and had no data protection policies, violating core PDPA accountability requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 11(3) – An organisation must designate one or more individuals to be responsible for ensuring that the organisation complies with the PDPA
regulatoryFindings.description: ACL Construction failed to designate a Data Protection Officer prior to the incident
violations: ACL Construction failed to designate a Data Protection Officer prior to the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12(a) – An Organisation must develop and implement policies and practices that are necessary for the organisation to meet the obligations under the PDPA
regulatoryFindings.description: ACL Construction had no data protection policies in place
violations: ACL Construction had no data protection policies in place

outcome: The Commission, noting the organisation's low level of awareness and prompt remedial actions post-incident (including appointment of a DPO), directed ACL Construction to: (a) develop and implement policies and practices to comply with PDPA provisions; and (b) establish a compulsory employee training programme on PDPA compliance when handling personal data. No financial penalty was imposed.
dataType: Business contact information (names, business contact numbers, business emails); employee personal data

companyDescription: North London Collegiate School (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. is an educational institution operating in Singapore that offers school admission programs to prospective students.
companyLongDescription: North London Collegiate School (Singapore) Pte. Ltd. is the Singapore branch of the London-based independent school, providing primary and secondary education. The school operated a website through which prospective students could submit admission application documents. The organization relied on a related group company for IT services and website management but failed to establish clear data protection requirements for the handling of sensitive student data collected through the admission process.
caseDescription: North London Collegiate School failed to adequately secure a website directory containing student admission application documents, allowing search engines to index and expose sensitive personal data including passports, identity cards, and academic records. The organisation relied solely on a non-mandatory robots.txt file and failed to implement proper access controls, leaving documents of prospective students accessible via internet search results from December 2019 to July 2021.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access to personal data. It relied on a non-mandatory robots.txt file instead of implementing proper folder permissions and access controls, and failed to ensure contractual data protection requirements with the third-party IT service provider managing the website.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: North London Collegiate School failed to secure a website directory containing student admission documents.
whyTheyWereWrong: Prospective students' passports, identity cards, birth certificates, and academic records were exposed via search engine results for nearly two years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The school had adequately secured student admission documents by deploying a robots.txt file on its website.
claimsVsReality.reality: The robots.txt file is non-mandatory and lacks enforcement mechanisms; documents remained accessible via search engines from December 2019 to July 2021, exposing 1,742 individuals' passport data and other sensitive information.

claimsVsReality.claim: A sister company was responsible for implementing security arrangements for personal data on the website.
claimsVsReality.reality: No written agreements or contractual stipulations placed data protection responsibilities on the related company; the school remained responsible for implementing proper access controls regardless of outsourcing arrangements.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation must protect personal data in its possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, and disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement proper folder/directory permissions and access controls to prevent web crawler indexing
violations: Failed to implement proper folder/directory permissions and access controls to prevent web crawler indexing
Relied solely on non-mandatory robots.txt file without enforcement mechanism
Failed to establish clear written contractual data protection requirements with third-party IT service provider
Did not ensure adequate security arrangements for personal data stored in website directory from December 2019 to July 2021

outcome: The organisation was found in breach of section 24 of the PDPA. The Deputy Commissioner required the organisation to pay a financial penalty of $10,000 within 30 days. The organisation has ceased collecting documents via its website, implemented a specialised school admission software, and established appropriate binding corporate rules governing data protection and cybersecurity within its corporate group.
companyNow: The school has since migrated to specialized school admission software and implemented binding corporate rules for data protection governance across its group entities.
dataType: Identity documents (passports, NRIC, birth certificates), photographs, immunization records, academic reports, name, address, date of birth

companyDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club is a private members' country club in Singapore offering hospitality and recreational services.
companyLongDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club is a Singapore-based country club providing hospitality and recreational facilities to its members. The club manages member data and personal information as part of its operations. In February 2021, the organisation experienced a significant data breach when an employee's email account was compromised, exposing personal data of both club members and the general public.
caseDescription: An employee's email account at Tanah Merah Country Club was compromised via password spraying attacks, allowing a threat actor to access personal data of 467 individuals and send 600 phishing emails. The breach occurred because the employee used a weak, unchanged password and the organisation failed to maintain a written password policy or provide adequate staff training on data protection obligations.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically by not maintaining a written password policy, failing to enforce password changes, allowing weak passwords to remain in use, and not providing structured training to employees on data protection and password security practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Tanah Merah Country Club failed to maintain a written password policy and provide adequate staff training, allowing an employee's email account to be compromised via password spraying.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's unchanged weak password for 5 years made the account vulnerable to attack, and 467 people's email addresses, names.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation had informed employees via IT newsletters in August 2018 and September 2019 about password requirements and implemented a system-enforced domain password policy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these notifications, the Organisation failed to create a written password policy document until 23 February 2021—after the breach occurred—and the employee's password remained unchanged for nearly 5 years (2016-2021).

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation cited 'TMCC_Password_123' as an example of a good password in its IT newsletters.
claimsVsReality.reality: This password example was weak because it incorporated the organisation's name/abbreviation (TMCC), making it easily guessable despite meeting complexity requirements in form.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation provided training to staff on data protection obligations and password management.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only ad-hoc and informal training was provided; no structured or organised training programme existed, leaving employees unaware of the need for regular password changes and strong password practices.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to document a written password policy despite informing employees of password requirements via email newsletters
violations: Failed to document a written password policy despite informing employees of password requirements via email newsletters
Permitted an employee to use the same weak password ('TMCC@1234') for nearly 5 years without change
Failed to enforce password change requirements and system-enforced domain password policy for all employees
Failed to provide structured and organised training to staff on PDPA compliance and proper handling of personal data
Did not ensure password complexity best practices were communicated effectively, including avoidance of organisation-related terms

outcome: The organisation was found in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24. The Deputy Commissioner required the organisation to pay a financial penalty of $4,000 SGD within 30 days. The organisation cooperated with investigations, admitted to the breach under the Expedited Breach Decision Procedure, and implemented comprehensive remedial measures including documenting a written password policy, implementing forensic recommendations for cybersecurity improvements, conducting user awareness training, and conducting personal data protection training for staff. No further directions were issued given the remedial actions taken.
companyNow: The club continues operations in Singapore. Following the 2021 breach, it implemented enhanced cybersecurity measures, documented password policies, and provided staff training on data protection.
dataType: Email addresses, names, NRIC numbers

companyDescription: Belden is a global manufacturer of networking, connectivity, and cable products with subsidiaries and operations across multiple continents. Belden Singapore is part of the larger Belden Group, which is headquartered in St. Louis, Missouri.
companyLongDescription: Belden Inc. is a multinational corporation specializing in the design, manufacture, and distribution of networking and connectivity solutions, including cables, connectors, and related products. The company operates through numerous subsidiary entities across the Americas, Europe, Middle East, Africa, and Asia Pacific regions. Belden Singapore, a subsidiary of the parent company, conducts HR operations through its US parent, requiring regular cross-border transfers of employee personal data. The group centralizes key corporate functions at the parent company level.
caseDescription: Belden Singapore failed to comply with Singapore's Transfer Limitation Obligation under the PDPA by not executing a legally binding Deed of Accession to the Global Data Transfer Agreement before transferring employee personal data to its US parent company. A data breach at Belden Inc.'s servers resulted in exfiltration of personal data of 189 individuals (126 from Belden Singapore, 63 from Grass Valley Singapore). Although Belden Singapore's substantive security measures were adequate, the lack of formal legal documentation meant no enforceable mechanism existed to ensure transferred data received comparable protection under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The violation falls under Information Processing – Insecurity because Belden Singapore failed to ensure adequate security safeguards through formal legal mechanisms when transferring personal data overseas. The absence of a binding contract meant no legal means existed to enforce security obligations on the overseas recipient, exposing the data to the breach that occurred.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Belden Singapore transferred employee personal data to its US parent company without executing a legally binding Deed of Accession to the Global Data Transfer Agreement.
whyTheyWereWrong: The lack of proper data transfer safeguards left 189 individuals' sensitive personal information—including names, addresses, identification numbers, salary information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Belden Singapore had adequate contractual provisions in the GDTA to protect transferred personal data to a standard comparable with the PDPA.
claimsVsReality.reality: Although the GDTA contained appropriate contractual language requiring comparable protection standards, Belden Singapore failed to execute a legally binding Deed of Accession, meaning the agreement was not formally binding on the parties at the time of the breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: Belden Inc. implemented appropriate security safeguards for the servers storing transferred personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite having substantively adequate security measures in place, unauthorized threat actors gained access to Belden Group servers between September and November 2020 and successfully exfiltrated sensitive personal data of 189 individuals, including salary information and tax details.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 26(1) and PDPR Regulation 9(1)(b) require organisations transferring personal data outside Singapore to ensure the recipient is bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide comparable protection
regulatoryFindings.description: Belden Singapore transferred personal data to Belden Inc. (USA) without executing a legally binding Deed of Accession to the Global Data Transfer Agreement
violations: Belden Singapore transferred personal data to Belden Inc. (USA) without executing a legally binding Deed of Accession to the Global Data Transfer Agreement
Although the GDTA required Belden Inc. to comply with PDPA standards, Belden Singapore was not a party to the contract and could not legally enforce those obligations
Lack of enforceable legal mechanism meant Belden Singapore had no way to ascertain and ensure transferred data received comparable protection

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPR Regulation 10(1)(b) and 10(2) require contracts governing overseas transfers to specify the countries and territories to which data may be transferred and require recipients to provide comparable protection
regulatoryFindings.description: Belden Singapore relied on the GDTA but was not a signatory, making the contract's protective provisions unenforceable against Belden Singapore itself
violations: Belden Singapore relied on the GDTA but was not a signatory, making the contract's protective provisions unenforceable against Belden Singapore itself

outcome: Belden Singapore was issued a warning for breach of the Transfer Limitation Obligation. No monetary penalty or additional directions were imposed because: (1) the breach was technical and a lapse in legal formalities rather than substantive, (2) Belden group's operational policies, practices and technical measures were in fact sufficient to ensure comparable protection at the time, and (3) Belden Singapore remedied the oversight by executing a Deed of Accession on 18 June 2021. GVSPL was found to have complied with the Transfer Limitation Obligation as it had properly executed a Data Sharing Agreement with Belden Inc.
companyNow: Belden Inc. continues to operate as a major player in the industrial connectivity and networking sector. The company has implemented extensive security remediation measures following the 2020 breach incident.
dataType: Employee personal data including name, address, email, phone, date of birth, identification number, marital status, photographs, salary information, tax information
legalBasisViolated: PDPR Regulation 9(1)(b) – Requirement for legally enforceable obligations
PDPR Regulation 10(1)(b) and 10(2) – Contractual requirements for overseas transfers

companyDescription: Commeasure Pte Ltd operates RedDoorz, a hotel booking platform serving Southeast Asian customers across Indonesia, Singapore, Philippines, Vietnam, and Thailand.
companyLongDescription: Commeasure Pte Ltd, incorporated in Singapore in 2014, is a hospitality technology company that operates RedDoorz (www.reddoorz.com), a hotel booking platform serving the Southeast Asian region. The company maintains Singapore-based sales, finance, and administrative functions while delegating IT management to its Indian subsidiary, Commeasure Solutions India Pvt Ltd. RedDoorz facilitates hotel bookings for customers across Indonesia, Singapore, Philippines, Vietnam, and Thailand.
caseDescription: Commeasure, a hotel booking platform operator, suffered a data breach affecting 5,892,843 customer records after embedding an AWS access key in a publicly available Android application. The Organisation failed to include the outdated app and credentials in its security reviews, leaving the vulnerability undetected for 2 years and 9 months until the breach was discovered in September 2020.
violationSummary: The Organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements under PDPA section 24 by embedding production database credentials in publicly available code and failing to include legacy systems in security reviews, resulting in unauthorised access and exfiltration of customer data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Commeasure embedded an AWS access key with production database credentials in a publicly available Android app on Google Play Store.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 6 million hotel customers had their names, contact numbers, email addresses, dates of birth, password hashes.

claimsVsReality.claim: The affected Android app was a 'defunct' application no longer in use and did not require security review.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app remained publicly available for download on Google Play Store until the breach was discovered, and contained valid production credentials providing unrestricted access to the live customer database.

claimsVsReality.claim: The AWS access key was marked as a 'test' key and therefore posed minimal risk.
claimsVsReality.reality: The key provided full access to the production database containing 5.9 million customer records; the 'test' label was an error by developers and did not reflect the key's actual permissions or scope.

claimsVsReality.claim: Conducting periodic security reviews and penetration testing provided adequate protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: The security reviews conducted from September-December 2019 were insufficient because the organisation negligently excluded the vulnerable app from their scope, leaving the exposed credentials undetected for 2 years and 9 months until external attackers found and exploited them.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, or disposal of personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Embedded AWS access key (production database credentials) directly in Android application publicly available on Google Play Store
violations: Embedded AWS access key (production database credentials) directly in Android application publicly available on Google Play Store
Failed to implement sufficient processes to manage infrastructure access key inventory
Negligently excluded legacy/defunct APK and its credentials from security reviews and periodic audits
Did not deploy protective measures (Proguard) on affected APK despite using them on current apps
Security reviews conducted from September 2019 to December 2019 were not sufficiently rigorous and did not capture all systems in production

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD 74,000 (approximately USD 54,500) payable within 30 days.
