The Organisation is required to implement comprehensive remedial actions including: credential policy amendments prohibiting embedded access codes, infrastructure upgrade to private isolated database environment with IP whitelisting, separation of production and staging credentials, two-factor authentication implementation, web application firewalls, MySQL query alerts, and engagement of cybersecurity firm for ongoing vulnerability assessment and penetration testing of all applications.
companyNow: Following the 2020 data breach and subsequent PDPC enforcement action, Commeasure implemented significant security infrastructure improvements including credential policy amendments, private database isolation, two-factor authentication, and appointed external cybersecurity firms for ongoing vulnerability assessment.
dataType: Customer name, contact number, email address, date of birth, hashed password, booking information

companyDescription: The National Kidney Foundation is a prominent non-profit health organisation in Singapore that provides subsidised kidney dialysis treatment and other renal health services.
companyLongDescription: The National Kidney Foundation is one of Singapore's leading non-profit health organisations, providing critical healthcare services including subsidised dialysis treatment to patients with kidney disease. As a major healthcare provider, the organisation handles sensitive medical and financial data for thousands of patients, employees, and third parties. The foundation operates clinical operations, budget management, and healthcare standards oversight across its operations.
caseDescription: The National Kidney Foundation's employee email account was compromised via phishing attack on 17 May 2020, resulting in exfiltration of personal data of approximately 500 individuals including patients, employees, and third parties. The organisation failed to implement adequate access controls, specifically two-factor authentication, for webmail accounts containing sensitive health and financial data. Although the organisation had various security measures in place, the Commission found these insufficient given the sensitive nature of the personal data routinely handled.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data from unauthorised access, specifically by not implementing two-factor authentication and risk-based access controls for webmail accounts handling sensitive health and financial data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The National Kidney Foundation failed to implement two-factor authentication for employee webmail accounts containing sensitive health.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 500 patients, employees, and third parties had their sensitive medical conditions, financial arrears, bank account numbers, health screening reports.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had implemented various security measures including email filtering, phishing simulations, and employee training to protect against data breaches.
claimsVsReality.reality: These measures were insufficient to prevent a basic phishing attack; an employee's credentials were stolen and used to download 23,145 emails containing sensitive health and financial data of 500 individuals because two-factor authentication was not deployed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had adequate access controls with password policies and account lockout mechanisms in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: Password-only authentication proved inadequate for webmail accounts containing highly sensitive medical conditions, financial arrears, and health screening reports; the stolen password alone was sufficient for the hacker to gain full access and exfiltrate all data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation was managing a reasonable level of cybersecurity given its size and operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite being a major healthcare provider routinely handling sensitive patient medical and financial data, the organisation had not conducted a risk assessment to identify which employee roles required stronger authentication, leaving critical accounts unprotected.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation must take reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data in its possession or control
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct risk assessment to identify employees handling sensitive personal data and strengthen access controls accordingly
violations: Failed to conduct risk assessment to identify employees handling sensitive personal data and strengthen access controls accordingly
Did not implement two-factor authentication for webmail accounts containing sensitive health and financial data
Relied on basic password policy and account lockout mechanisms inadequate for web-accessible email accounts
Did not adopt risk-based approach proportionate to the sensitivity of data (medical conditions, financial arrears, health screening reports)

outcome: The organisation was administered a warning in respect of its breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. No additional directions were imposed given the remedial actions already undertaken by the organisation, which included implementation of two-factor authentication on 22 May 2020, appointment of a third-party service provider for daily scans, and notification of affected individuals with identity theft service subscriptions.
companyNow: The National Kidney Foundation continues to operate as a prominent Singapore healthcare provider. Following the 2020 breach, it implemented two-factor authentication and strengthened its cybersecurity posture.
dataType: Health data, financial data, bank account numbers, age, date of birth, medical conditions, dialysis readings, family status, psycho-social information, curriculum vitae, education certificates, foreign identification numbers, headshot photos, household income band, marriage certificates, emergency contact numbers

companyDescription: ChampionTutor is an education technology company providing online tutoring services based in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: ChampionTutor Inc. (Private Limited) is an online education platform that provides tutoring services to students in Singapore. The company operates a website-based platform where students register and access educational services. In 2021, the company suffered a significant data breach affecting thousands of students due to inadequate security practices and delayed vulnerability remediation.
caseDescription: ChampionTutor's database containing personal data of 4,625 students was compromised and sold on the dark web due to an unpatched SQL injection vulnerability. The organisation was aware of the vulnerability since December 2020 but failed to take active steps to fix it, leaving it unresolved until the breach occurred. The organisation admitted to breaching the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data from unauthorised access, specifically by failing to remediate a known SQL injection vulnerability despite having identified it during a penetration test.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ChampionTutor discovered a SQL injection vulnerability in December 2020 but failed to fix it, allowing the database containing personal data of 4,625 students to be compromised.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unpatched vulnerability exposed students' names, email addresses, contact numbers and addresses to criminals on the dark web, putting 4,625 individuals at risk of identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation's developer would fix the SQL injection vulnerability identified in December 2020.
claimsVsReality.reality: The developer based in India did not act on the request and left the vulnerability unresolved for months, eventually leading to the breach and data compromise.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had adequate security measures in place to protect student data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation failed to take active steps to remediate a known SQL injection vulnerability despite being aware of it for over two months before the breach occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or other loss
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation identified a SQL injection vulnerability in December 2020 but failed to take active remedial steps to fix it
violations: Organisation identified a SQL injection vulnerability in December 2020 but failed to take active remedial steps to fix it
Organisation did not escalate or follow up when the developer did not respond to fix the vulnerability
The vulnerability remained unpatched for months until the data breach occurred

outcome: ChampionTutor was directed to pay a financial penalty of $10,000 SGD in 12 instalments. No directions were issued under section 48I of the PDPA. The organisation's prompt remedial actions (engaging new developers, parameterising SQL statements, and revamping website source codes) and upfront voluntary admission of liability were taken into consideration in determining the penalty.
companyNow: ChampionTutor continues to operate but has undertaken significant security remediation, including engaging new developers, implementing parameterised SQL statements, and revamping website source code to prevent future vulnerabilities.
dataType: Name, email address, contact number, address

companyDescription: Bossini is a Hong Kong-listed fashion retail and brand franchising company operating across multiple regions including Singapore, with a subsidiary J & R Bossini Fashion Pte Ltd.
companyLongDescription: Bossini International Holdings Limited is a Hong Kong Stock Exchange-listed fashion retail group engaged in garment retail and brand franchising operations across multiple countries. The company operates through subsidiary entities, including J & R Bossini Fashion Pte Ltd in Singapore, and maintains a global IT infrastructure centrally managed from Hong Kong. The group operates customer loyalty programmes and maintains extensive personal data on customers and employees across its subsidiaries.
caseDescription: Bossini's Singapore subsidiary was compromised in a ransomware attack on 27 May 2020 that encrypted the personal data of approximately 154,213 customers and 120 employees. The company failed to implement legally binding agreements governing cross-border data transfers to Hong Kong and lacked clear group-level policies defining data protection responsibilities, leaving it unable to ensure adequate security protections.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data from unauthorised access and encryption. The breach resulted from failure to patch a known VPN vulnerability for nine months and lack of clear accountability for security responsibilities within the corporate group.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Bossini failed to establish legally binding agreements for cross-border data transfers to Hong Kong.
whyTheyWereWrong: A ransomware attack encrypted personal data of 154,213 customers and 120 employees, with at least 14,082 customer records exfiltrated to the dark web, exposing names, ID numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Group had implemented adequate group-level security arrangements for all IT systems across subsidiaries.
claimsVsReality.reality: A critical VPN vulnerability identified in September 2019 was not patched for nine months, allowing attackers to breach the network and encrypt all customer and employee data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data transfers to Hong Kong were protected by appropriate safeguards comparable to Singapore's PDPA standards.
claimsVsReality.reality: No legally binding agreements, contracts, or binding corporate rules governed the cross-border data transfer, leaving 154,213 customer records unprotected under enforceable standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clear data protection responsibilities existed across the corporate group.
claimsVsReality.reality: No group-level policies or intra-group agreements defined whether Bossini Holdings or the subsidiary was responsible for software patching and security testing, creating critical accountability gaps.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation: Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement clear group-level policies defining responsibility for software patching and security testing
violations: Failed to implement clear group-level policies defining responsibility for software patching and security testing
Failed to ensure timely deployment of a critical VPN security patch released in September 2019; patch was not deployed until June 2020, nine months later
Lack of documented binding agreements specifying data protection responsibilities between subsidiary and parent company, creating uncertainty about accountability

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 26 / PDPR Regulation 9(1)(b) - Transfer Limitation Obligation: Organisations transferring personal data outside Singapore must ensure the recipient is bound by legally enforceable obligations to provide comparable protection
regulatoryFindings.description: Transferred Customer Data from Singapore to Hong Kong without any intra-group contracts, binding corporate rules, or legally binding instruments
violations: Transferred Customer Data from Singapore to Hong Kong without any intra-group contracts, binding corporate rules, or legally binding instruments
Took no steps to ascertain whether transferred data would receive comparable protection standards

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 - Accountability Obligation: Organisations must develop and implement policies and practices to meet PDPA obligations
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement group-level policies, intra-group agreements, or binding corporate rules governing data protection across the multinational group
violations: Failed to implement group-level policies, intra-group agreements, or binding corporate rules governing data protection across the multinational group
Absence of documented framework clarifying roles and responsibilities for data protection between parent and subsidiary

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner directed the Organisation to: (1) within 30 days, put in place intra-group agreements, contracts, or binding corporate rules for compliance with PDPA Sections 24 and 26; and (2) inform the Commission of completion within 7 days of implementation. No monetary penalty was imposed. The Commission noted that the parent company Bossini Holdings took extensive remedial actions post-incident, including appointing a cybersecurity vendor, notifying affected parties, patching the vulnerability, implementing multi-factor authentication, and engaging third-party security monitoring. The Hong Kong privacy regulator (PCPD) also did not proceed with further investigations after reviewing the circumstances and remedial measures.
companyNow: Bossini continues to operate as a listed fashion retailer on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange, though the company has faced significant challenges in recent years in the competitive retail sector.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, phone number, email address, residential address, date of birth, gender, marital status, salary details, bank account details, medical claims records

companyDescription: Stylez Pte Ltd operated iCompare.sg, a quotation and service comparison portal for renovation and interior design clients in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Stylez Pte Ltd was a Singapore-based company that operated iCompare.sg, a web portal allowing renovation and interior design clients to request and compare quotations from service providers. The company created and managed databases of client inquiries spanning from 2009 to 2016. In July 2016, Stylez created a separate testing database to develop new portal features, but failed to implement proper security measures or data retention protocols.
caseDescription: Stylez operated iCompare.sg, a quotation and service comparison portal. The company created a testing database containing client data from 2009-2016 that was stored in a publicly accessible directory without access controls, allowing it to be crawled by search engines and eventually exfiltrated to the Dark Web, exposing nearly 10,000 individuals' personal data. The company failed to implement reasonable security measures, proper data retention practices, and failed to match its external data protection commitments with actual internal policies.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements under PDPA Section 24, including lack of access controls on publicly accessible directories, inadequate privileged access management, unencrypted data storage for extended periods, and absence of authentication measures. This constitutes a fundamental failure in data security practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Stylez created a testing database containing 9,983 individuals' personal data from 2009-2016 and stored it in a publicly accessible directory without access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 10,000 people had their names, email addresses, and phone numbers exposed on the Dark Web, with data stored unencrypted for over two years in an insecure testing environment that Stylez.

claimsVsReality.claim: We have developed guidelines and implemented procedures to govern the destruction of personal data that are no longer required to fulfil the identified purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Stylez had developed no such internal guidelines or procedures; the external policy was an empty promise unsupported by actual practices.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Testing Database exposure was due to failure to activate an anti-indexing function.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even with anti-indexing activated, the publicly accessible directory could still be crawled by search engines and directly accessed without authentication—anti-indexing is not access control.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Testing Database was retained for business analysis purposes and could not have used production databases due to contamination risks.
claimsVsReality.reality: The business analysis described did not require personally identifiable data; the data could have been aggregated or anonymised, and relying on 10-year-old data for customer studies was not commercially necessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Testing Database stored in publicly accessible directory without access controls
violations: Testing Database stored in publicly accessible directory without access controls
Database directly accessible from the Internet and crawled by search engines
Failure to implement proper authentication measures such as password protection or access whitelisting
Privileged access to Server not adequately secured - no limit on unsuccessful login attempts making account vulnerable to brute-force attacks
Administrator password stored in clear-text in email account without two-factor authentication
Production data held unencrypted in development environment for over 2.5 years

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12(a) - Accountability Obligation requires organisations to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations
regulatoryFindings.description: External data protection policy made promises about data destruction procedures that were never implemented internally
violations: External data protection policy made promises about data destruction procedures that were never implemented internally
No corresponding internal data protection policies developed to give effect to externally communicated standards
Reliance only on undocumented verbal reminders to staff about data protection importance
Gap between external commitments and internal practices

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 25 - Retention Limitation Obligation requires organisations to cease retaining data if the purpose of collection no longer exists and no business or legal reason exists for retention
regulatoryFindings.description: Testing Database retained for over 2.5 years after testing purpose was completed
violations: Testing Database retained for over 2.5 years after testing purpose was completed
Claimed business analysis purposes did not justify retention of identifiable personal data
Data could have been aggregated or anonymised for claimed business purposes but was retained in identifiable form
Retention of historical data from 2009 was not commercially justified for customer behaviour studies

outcome: The Commissioner directed Stylez to pay a financial penalty of $37,500 SGD in 12 monthly instalments. Additionally, the organisation was directed to develop and implement comprehensive internal data protection policies and practices compliant with the PDPA within 60 days, with notification to the Commission required within 1 week of completion. The remedial actions already taken by the organisation (deletion of testing database, malware scan, system updates, security tools installation, and victim notification) were acknowledged as mitigating factors.
companyNow: Stylez remains operational in Singapore but under increased regulatory oversight following the 2021 PDPA enforcement decision. The company was required to implement comprehensive internal data protection policies and practices.
dataType: Name, email address, phone number

companyDescription: Carousell is a Southeast Asian mobile marketplace and classifieds platform enabling peer-to-peer buying and selling of goods.
companyLongDescription: Carousell is a leading mobile-first marketplace platform in Southeast Asia, particularly strong in Singapore, Malaysia, and Indonesia. The platform allows users to buy and sell items through a mobile app and web interface, functioning as a digital classifieds service. Founded in 2012, Carousell has grown to become one of the region's most popular e-commerce platforms with millions of users.
caseDescription: Carousell experienced unauthorized account access through credential stuffing attacks in April and June 2021, where threat actors used compromised credentials from other platforms to hijack user accounts and make unauthorized purchases. The Personal Data Protection Commission found that Carousell had implemented reasonable security measures at the time of the incident and took prompt remedial action, therefore did not breach its Protection Obligation under the PDPA.
violationSummary: While the organization experienced a security incident involving unauthorized access to user accounts, the regulator determined that the organization had implemented objectively reasonable security standards and did not fail in its obligation to protect personal data. The incident resulted from compromised credentials from external sources rather than a failure of Carousell's own security measures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Carousell's systems experienced unauthorized account access in April and June 2021 when threat actors used credentials compromised on other platforms to hijack user accounts.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users lost control of their accounts, had unauthorized purchase attempts made, and their personal account data was accessed and modified by criminals without their knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Carousell had reasonable security measures in place to protect user data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite reasonable measures like OTP requirements and fraud detection, the company's security was vulnerable to credential stuffing attacks originating from third-party platform breaches.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only isolated cases of account takeover occurred due to users reusing passwords across platforms.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple coordinated attacks successfully compromised user accounts across two separate incident periods (April and June 2021), exposing users' personal data and financial information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must protect personal data under their control against unauthorized access
regulatoryFindings.description: Unauthorized access to user accounts through credential stuffing attacks
violations: Unauthorized access to user accounts through credential stuffing attacks
Threat actors able to perform actions as authorized users and access account data

outcome: The Personal Data Protection Commission concluded that Carousell did not breach its Protection Obligation under the PDPA. The organization had implemented reasonable security arrangements including user alerts for account changes, account takeover detection, transaction fraud scoring, one-time passwords, regular policy reviews, staff training, and annual penetration testing. Following the incident, Carousell took prompt remedial action including suspending compromised accounts, forcing password resets, disabling payment features for affected users, blocking suspicious IP addresses, implementing mandatory two-factor authentication for device changes, and enhancing user education against phishing.
companyNow: Carousell continues to operate as a major e-commerce platform in Southeast Asia, serving millions of buyers and sellers across multiple markets.
dataType: Login credentials, passwords, email addresses, phone numbers, account settings, transaction data, device information
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 – Protection Obligation

companyDescription: Newcastle Research and Innovation Institute is an academic research organisation with a Singapore subsidiary (NUInternational Singapore) that collaborates internationally with parent entities in the UK and related companies in Malaysia.
companyLongDescription: Newcastle Research and Innovation Institute operates in Singapore with connections to a UK parent company and Malaysian subsidiary, focusing on research and innovation activities. The organisation manages personal data of staff members, undergraduate and postgraduate students across multiple jurisdictions. It failed to implement proper data protection mechanisms when transferring personal information internationally, which exposed it to security incidents. The organisation appears to be part of a larger academic or research group spanning multiple countries.
caseDescription: Newcastle Research and Innovation Institute and NUInternational Singapore transferred personal data of 1,083 Singapore-based individuals to the UK and 194 to Malaysia without establishing legally enforceable agreements or comparable data protection standards as required by the PDPA. A ransomware attack on 30 August 2020 resulted in the exfiltration of names and user account IDs from databases in both jurisdictions.
violationSummary: The organisations failed to ensure comparable protection standards when transferring personal data outside Singapore, and subsequently the data was compromised in a ransomware attack due to inadequate safeguards.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Newcastle Research and Innovation Institute and NUInternational Singapore transferred personal data of 1,083 Singapore residents to the UK.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data of employees, undergraduates and postgraduate students including names and account IDs were exfiltrated in a ransomware attack on poorly protected systems because the organisations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had met the Transfer Limitation Obligation by virtue of UK laws applying to receiving organisations within their group.
claimsVsReality.reality: No proper analysis was conducted before the transfer to verify comparable data protection standards, and no legally enforceable agreements were in place, rendering the claim unsupported.

claimsVsReality.claim: 44 employees had consented to transfer of their personal data in their employment contracts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even where consent was claimed, the organisation failed to provide the required written summary of comparative data protection standards, making the consent procedurally invalid under PDPA regulations.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 26(1) requires organisations to transfer personal data outside Singapore only in accordance with prescribed requirements to ensure comparable protection standards
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisations transferred 1,083 records to UK and 194 records to Malaysia without intra-group agreements, binding corporate rules, or other legally binding instruments
violations: Organisations transferred 1,083 records to UK and 194 records to Malaysia without intra-group agreements, binding corporate rules, or other legally binding instruments
No written summary of comparable protection standards was provided to 44 employees whose consent was claimed
No proper analysis was conducted to determine whether receiving jurisdictions provided comparable protection before transfer

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Regulations 2014 Regulation 9(4) and 2021 Regulation 10(3) require written summary of comparable protection standards when relying on consent for data transfer
regulatoryFindings.description: Summary in writing was not provided to 44 Singapore employees for whom consent was allegedly obtained
violations: Summary in writing was not provided to 44 Singapore employees for whom consent was allegedly obtained

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the Organisations in breach of the Transfer Limitation Obligation under section 26 of the PDPA. The Organisations are directed to: (a) establish intra-group agreements or binding corporate rules for compliance with section 26 within 30 days; (b) review and amend consent and notification processes for compliance with section 26 and Regulation 10(3) of the 2021 Regulations; and (c) inform the Commission of completion within 7 days of implementation.
companyNow: The organisation remains operational but subject to compliance orders issued by Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission requiring implementation of intra-group agreements and binding corporate rules for international data transfers.
dataType: Names, user account identifications, staff and student records
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Regulations 2021 Regulation 10 and 11

companyDescription: Specialized Asia Pacific is a software development company that created and operated the Cadence application development tool.
companyLongDescription: Specialized Asia Pacific Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based software development organisation that developed, operated and maintained the Cadence application. The company provides application development tools and services. In January 2021, the company discovered a critical privacy misconfiguration in its Cadence tool that exposed user personal data due to a default 'visible' privacy setting that had not been reconfigured.
caseDescription: Specialized Asia Pacific failed to properly configure privacy settings in its Cadence application development tool, leaving the default setting as 'visible' instead of 'hidden'. This allowed the personal data of 2,445 users to be intercepted and accessed by third parties using publicly available security testing software. The organisation did not comply with its obligations to understand and properly configure the privacy policies and security features of online tools it employed.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures by not reconfiguring the default privacy settings of the online development tool, resulting in unauthorised access risk to personal data stored in the application.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Specialized Asia Pacific failed to reconfigure the default privacy setting in its Cadence application development tool from 'visible' to 'hidden'.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unprotected default privacy setting allowed members of the public to intercept and access users' personal data including names, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation's developers believed the online development tool's privacy setting was secure and would protect user data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The tool had a default 'visible' setting that made all data accessible to anyone with publicly available security testing software, regardless of the developers' assumptions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Adopting the default privacy policies of the online tool was sufficient to meet the Protection Obligation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Organisations must actively understand and reconfigure privacy settings to protect user data; relying on unreviewed default settings does not discharge this obligation.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 — Protection Obligation requires organisations to understand the privacy policies and security features of all online tools or software they employ and to set or reconfigure privacy policies and security features to protect personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to reconfigure the default 'visible' privacy setting of the online development tool
violations: Organisation failed to reconfigure the default 'visible' privacy setting of the online development tool
Organisation did not properly understand or implement the privacy policies of the tool it employed
Organisation adopted the same default privacy policies without modification to protect user data

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a Warning to the Organisation. The Organisation was required to remediate by turning off all external access to the Application, changing the privacy setting from 'visible' to 'hidden', engaging a third-party IT security firm to test and address security and privacy issues, and commencing discussions with IT application designers and employees to adopt 'privacy-by-design' in future applications development.
dataType: names, addresses, dates of birth, telephone numbers, email addresses, gender
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24 (Protection Obligation)

companyDescription: Sendtech Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based technology company that provides backend server and data management services.
companyLongDescription: Sendtech Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore technology company that developed server infrastructure and backend services. The company provides data management and storage solutions, including AWS-based systems for managing customer and contractor information. As of 2021, Sendtech was a relatively small technology service provider operating in Singapore.
caseDescription: Sendtech suffered an unauthorized access breach to its Amazon Web Services account via a compromised access key that had not been rotated since 2015. The attacker gained admin privileges and accessed personal data of 64,196 customers and 3,401 contractors and their employees, though no data exfiltration occurred. The organization failed to implement proper credential management practices and access key rotation procedures.
violationSummary: The organization breached its obligation to protect personal data by failing to implement adequate security measures, specifically the failure to rotate access keys created in 2015 and inadequate credential management policies. This constitutes a failure of the protection obligation under section 24 of the PDPA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Sendtech failed to rotate an AWS access key created in 2015, which became compromised and allowed an attacker to gain admin privileges.
whyTheyWereWrong: The compromised access key exposed customers' home addresses, contact numbers, email addresses, and partial card details, as well as contractors' identity documents.

claimsVsReality.claim: The AWS access key was secure and properly managed.
claimsVsReality.reality: The access key had not been rotated or changed since 2015, remained in use for six years, and was eventually compromised, likely through former or current employees or insecure home network access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Access credentials were managed with appropriate controls for staff movement.
claimsVsReality.reality: There were no detailed steps to manage credentials access of outgoing staff, and credentials were not rotated or changed whenever staff left or transitioned roles.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data was adequately protected from unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: A single compromised access key allowed an attacker to gain full admin privileges and query all buckets containing the personal data of over 67,000 individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organizations to protect personal data against unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to rotate AWS access key created in 2015
violations: Failed to rotate AWS access key created in 2015
Lacked specific AWS policies for credential rotation
Lacked detailed steps to manage credentials access for outgoing staff
Did not implement credential rotation upon staff movement
Inadequate security setup allowing compromised access key to grant admin privileges

outcome: The organization was directed to pay a financial penalty of $9,000 SGD in 12 monthly instalments of $750 from September 2021 to August 2022. No further directions were issued under section 48I of the PDPA due to the remedial actions undertaken by the organization, which included rotating all access keys, changing server passwords, enhancing audit trails, verifying GitHub repository settings, engaging cybersecurity consultants for assessment, and developing new cybersecurity policies with credentials management measures.
companyNow: Sendtech continues to operate in Singapore. Following the 2021 breach, the company implemented comprehensive credential management policies and engaged cybersecurity consultants to strengthen its security infrastructure.
dataType: Email address, contact number, home address, last four digits of debit/credit card, profile photo, NRIC, work permit

companyDescription: SAP Asia Pte. Ltd. is a subsidiary of German enterprise software giant SAP that provides IT solutions and HR/payroll systems to organizations across Asia.
companyLongDescription: SAP Asia Pte. Ltd. is part of SAP SE, a global leader in enterprise resource planning (ERP) and business software solutions. The company provides HR and payroll system implementations and support to organizations throughout Asia. SAP Asia engaged an external vendor to develop an automated payslip distribution feature for its HR system but failed to adequately specify requirements or test the functionality before deploying it to handle real employee data.
caseDescription: SAP Asia failed to properly specify and test a new HR system feature designed to automate payslip distribution to former employees. The organisation's ambiguous requirements led the vendor to develop a program capable only of single payslip issuance, but when the organisation attempted to send 43 payslips simultaneously on 31 March 2020, the flawed design caused 29 former employees to receive each other's payslips containing sensitive financial and identity information.
violationSummary: The inadequate programme design and testing resulted in unauthorised disclosure and exposure of former employees' personal data (payslips containing salary, bank details, NRIC numbers) to unintended recipients. This constitutes exposure of personal data due to a system vulnerability arising from poor requirements management and insufficient pre-launch testing.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: SAP Asia failed to clearly specify that a new payslip distribution program should handle multiple former employees simultaneously.
whyTheyWereWrong: When SAP Asia executed the flawed program on 31 March 2020 to send payslips to 43 former employees, 29 of them received each other's sensitive financial.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Program was ready for production use and capable of distributing multiple payslips simultaneously to multiple former employees in a single execution.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Program was designed only for single payslip issuance and was never tested for multi-payslip scenarios, causing 29 of 43 former employees to receive other employees' sensitive payslip data when executed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Requirements were clearly communicated to the vendor regarding the need for multiple payslip distribution functionality.
claimsVsReality.reality: Communications were brief and ambiguous, consistently referring only to 'a selected employee' (singular) rather than multiple employees, leading the vendor to misunderstand the actual business requirement.

claimsVsReality.claim: User acceptance testing adequately validated the Program before deployment.
claimsVsReality.reality: Pre-launch testing did not include any multiple payslip issuance scenarios and thus failed to detect the design flaw before the program was used with real employee data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, disclosure, copying, modification, and similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to adequately specify business requirements to the external vendor – the requirement for multiple payslip issuance in one execution was not clearly communicated, resulting in the vendor designing the programme to handle only single payslip issuance
violations: Failed to adequately specify business requirements to the external vendor – the requirement for multiple payslip issuance in one execution was not clearly communicated, resulting in the vendor designing the programme to handle only single payslip issuance

Failed to conduct adequate user acceptance testing (UAT) – only tested single payslip issuance scenarios despite intending to use the programme to send payslips to multiple former employees simultaneously
The combination of poor requirements communication and inadequate testing meant the data protection risks of the flawed design were not identified before deployment

outcome: SAP Asia was found to have breached PDPA Section 24 (Protection Obligation) due to failure to properly specify requirements and conduct adequate user acceptance testing for the new payslip issuance programme. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 13,500 within 30 days. No further directions were deemed necessary as the organisation had already taken remedial measures including disabling the flawed programme, reverting to manual payslip generation, notifying all affected former employees, obtaining deletion confirmations, and agreeing on continuous process improvements with the vendor.
companyNow: SAP SE remains one of the world's largest enterprise software companies, serving millions of businesses globally. The company continues to be a major provider of HR and payroll solutions, though data security and user acceptance testing practices remain critical compliance areas.
dataType: Employment records, payroll data, financial information (bank account numbers, salary details, year-to-date earnings), NRIC/FIN numbers

companyDescription: HMI Institute of Health Sciences Pte. Ltd. is a private healthcare training provider in Singapore that offers professional training courses to individuals and manages personal data of participants and employees.
companyLongDescription: HMI Institute of Health Sciences Pte. Ltd. is a dedicated private provider of healthcare training services in Singapore. The organisation collects and maintains personal data from training participants for course registration and enrollment administration, as well as from employees for employment management purposes. The organisation operated a file server established in 2014 that stored this personal data in Microsoft Word and Excel files, many of which were password-protected.
caseDescription: HMI Institute of Health Sciences suffered a ransomware attack on its file server on 4 December 2019, affecting personal data of approximately 110,080 participants and 253 employees. The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures, including keeping an open Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) port for over four years without proper protective controls, failing to enforce strong password policies, and not establishing clear data protection requirements with its IT vendor. While no data exfiltration occurred and the organisation took prompt remedial actions, the breach exposed sensitive personal and financial information to unauthorized access and modification.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to take reasonable security steps to protect personal data as required by PDPA Section 24. Specific security failures included: leaving an RDP port open for 4+ years without alternative protective measures, implementing weak password policies (passwords with organizational acronym, insufficient complexity), sharing administrator credentials among multiple users without 2FA, and failing to establish clear data protection requirements with the IT vendor. These combined failures created a systematic insecurity in the handling and protection of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: HMI Institute of Health Sciences kept a Remote Desktop Protocol port open for over four years without proper protective controls, failed to enforce strong password policies.
whyTheyWereWrong: The organisation's security failures exposed the personal data of 110,080 training participants and 253 employees to attackers, including names, NRIC numbers, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Keeping the RDP Port permanently closed was not practicable because half a day of downtime would be required whenever the RDP Port needed to be opened or closed.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation failed to implement alternative security measures such as using non-standard ports, IP whitelisting, RDP gateways, or log reviews—any of which would have been proportionate to the risk posed by leaving the port open for over four years to store sensitive personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had adopted and directed staff to follow a password policy consistent with the Commission's recommendations.
claimsVsReality.reality: None of the passwords used for the administrator account or files containing affected personal data actually met the recommended complexity rules, and passwords incorporated the organisation's name acronym, making them easy to guess and vulnerable to brute force attacks.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT vendor was responsible for maintaining the server and its security.
claimsVsReality.reality: The vendor was not a data intermediary and did not process personal data on behalf of the organisation; the organisation owned the server and retained full responsibility for protecting the personal data stored on it.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation: An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to adequately regulate remote access to the server by keeping the RDP Port open for more than four years (2014-2019) without sufficient protective measures such as IP whitelisting, use of non-standard ports, RDP gateways, or automated monitoring of unusual activity
violations: Failed to adequately regulate remote access to the server by keeping the RDP Port open for more than four years (2014-2019) without sufficient protective measures such as IP whitelisting, use of non-standard ports, RDP gateways, or automated monitoring of unusual activity

Failed to implement proper password management policies in practice despite having a Password Policy in place; administrator account passwords incorporated the organisation's acronym (easily guessable), lacked required complexity, and were shared among multiple individuals without 2FA or anti-hammering features

Failed to take reasonable or sufficient steps to stipulate clear data protection requirements with the IT vendor, despite the vendor handling personal data and making decisions affecting the security of the server; no contract specified business requirements for data protection in the server

outcome: The Commissioner found the organisation in breach of Section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation is directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 35,000 within 30 days. No additional directions were deemed necessary given the organisation's prompt remedial actions, which included decommissioning the affected server, notifying affected individuals and authorities, implementing password management policies, disconnecting remote access, adopting internet separation measures, deploying endpoint enhancements and gateway security measures, engaging external IT security consultants for ISO 27001 certification, conducting cybersecurity training and awareness workshops, performing email phishing tests, and establishing monthly IT bulletins to staff.
companyNow: Following the 2019 ransomware incident and subsequent regulatory enforcement, HMI Institute of Health Sciences implemented comprehensive security improvements including internal password management policies, internet separation measures, endpoint protections, and obtained ISO 27001 certification.
dataType: NRIC number, name, date of birth, address, nationality, race, gender, email address, contact number, course details, employer details, employment history, financial information (salary/payment), CPF information, bank account numbers, vehicle licence plate

companyDescription: HSBC Bank (Singapore) Limited is a full-service banking subsidiary of HSBC Holdings plc, offering retail and commercial banking services including credit card facilities to individuals and businesses in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: HSBC Bank (Singapore) Limited is the Singapore operations of HSBC Holdings plc, one of the world's largest banking and financial services organizations. The bank provides a comprehensive range of personal banking products including credit cards, deposits, loans, and investment services to retail customers. HSBC uses proprietary algorithms and big data analytics to assess creditworthiness and determine customer eligibility for financial products. The bank is regulated by the Monetary Authority of Singapore and operates under Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: An applicant for a credit card at HSBC requested access to the bank's internal evaluation report on his application. HSBC provided the report but redacted certain fields containing algorithmically-generated opinion data used to assess his credit worthiness. The applicant challenged this redaction, arguing he was entitled to access all personal data held about him.
violationSummary: The case concerns HSBC's claimed right to exclude certain personal data (opinion data) from a data subject access request. While not ultimately found to be a violation, the core issue involves the organization's assertion of an exception to limit access to personal data held about the individual.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: HSBC redacted algorithmically-generated opinion data from a credit card applicant's internal evaluation report, withholding fields that assessed his creditworthiness and suitability for the card.
whyTheyWereWrong: The applicant could not understand why his credit card application was rejected or verify the accuracy of data used to make a decision that directly affected him.

claimsVsReality.claim: HSBC claimed the redacted data consisted of opinion data kept solely for an evaluative purpose and therefore was exempt from disclosure under the PDPA.
claimsVsReality.reality: The court agreed HSBC was legally entitled to withhold the evaluative opinions, but the applicant was left unable to verify the accuracy of algorithmic assessments that determined his creditworthiness and directly affected his access to financial services.

claimsVsReality.claim: HSBC provided two publications explaining how it ethically uses big data and AI in credit decisioning to mitigate transparency concerns.
claimsVsReality.reality: Generic policy documents could not substitute for access to the specific algorithmic opinions and scoring that determined the applicant's individual eligibility, preventing him from understanding or challenging the decision made about him.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 21(1) – Right of access to personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: HSBC withheld portions of the evaluation report containing opinion data, claiming exemption under the Evaluative Purpose Exception
violations: HSBC withheld portions of the evaluation report containing opinion data, claiming exemption under the Evaluative Purpose Exception

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Fifth Schedule, paragraph 1(a) – Evaluative Purpose Exception
regulatoryFindings.description: HSBC successfully invoked the exception for opinion data kept solely for evaluative purposes (credit card suitability assessment)
violations: HSBC successfully invoked the exception for opinion data kept solely for evaluative purposes (credit card suitability assessment)

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner confirmed HSBC's refusal to disclose the redacted data, finding that the Evaluative Purpose Exception lawfully applied to opinion data generated through HSBC's proprietary algorithm for assessing credit card eligibility. The Commissioner noted that HSBC had acted reasonably by providing separate publications (Credit Decisioning Policy Statement and Principles for Ethical Use of Big Data and AI) to explain how it uses data and technology in credit assessments. Other grounds cited by HSBC (confidential commercial information, investigation, burden/expense, frivolous request, MAS Notice 626) were not fully considered as unnecessary, though the Commissioner rejected some of these arguments on their merits.
companyNow: HSBC continues to operate as a major global banking institution with significant presence in Asia-Pacific, including Singapore. The bank has expanded its focus on digital banking and AI-driven decision-making while navigating evolving privacy regulations.
dataType: Credit application data, financial information, algorithmic analysis/opinions, employment information, income, education level, age
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 21(2) – Exceptions to Access Obligation
PDPA Fifth Schedule, paragraph 1(a) – Evaluative Purpose Exception

companyDescription: Greatearth Corporation Pte. Ltd. is a construction company operating as a main contractor for housing projects in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Greatearth Corporation Pte. Ltd. is a construction company based in Singapore that serves as a main contractor for residential housing projects. The company operates worksites and is responsible for managing workplace safety and security at its construction sites. In 2021, the company was subject to investigation by Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission for unauthorized disclosure of personal data.
caseDescription: Greatearth Corporation's workplace safety officer received a list of banned crane operators from an informal WhatsApp group and instructed staff to display it on the external façade of a construction worksite. The list, containing full names, NRIC numbers, contact numbers, and photos of 8 individuals, remained publicly visible for approximately 2 months without the individuals' consent. The disclosure was unauthorized and violated the Personal Data Protection Act.
violationSummary: The company exposed personal data (names, ID numbers, contact details, photographs) of 8 individuals to the public by posting the banned operators list on the external facade of the worksite where it was visible to all passersby, creating widespread accessibility to sensitive information without consent.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Greatearth Corporation's workplace safety officer instructed staff to display a list of banned crane operators containing full names, NRIC numbers, contact numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Eight crane operators had their sensitive personal data publicly exposed to all passersby without consent, compromising their privacy, safety, and professional reputation in their industry.

claimsVsReality.claim: GCPL's WSHO instructed the safety coordinator to place the Banned Operators List in the guard room for internal security screening purposes only.
claimsVsReality.reality: The safety coordinator misunderstood and instead posted the list on the external façade of the worksite, making it visible to all passersby for 2 months before removal.

claimsVsReality.claim: GCPL's WSHO had noticed the Poster on the external façade in late September 2019 and intended to remove it promptly.
claimsVsReality.reality: GCPL only removed the Poster after being notified of complaints by the Personal Data Protection Commission on 26 September 2019, meaning it had been publicly displayed for approximately 2 months.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 13 – Consent Obligation: Organisations are prohibited from collecting, using or disclosing personal data unless the individual gives consent or collection/use/disclosure is authorised under the PDPA or other written law.
regulatoryFindings.description: Greatearth Corporation disclosed the personal data of 8 complainants (full names, NRIC numbers, contact numbers, and photographs) by posting the Banned Operators List on the external façade of the Clementi Worksite without obtaining their consent.
violations: Greatearth Corporation disclosed the personal data of 8 complainants (full names, NRIC numbers, contact numbers, and photographs) by posting the Banned Operators List on the external façade of the Clementi Worksite without obtaining their consent.
The disclosure was not authorised under the PDPA or any other written law.
The complainants had not voluntarily provided their personal data to Greatearth Corporation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 53(1) – Employer Responsibility: Any act done or conduct engaged in by an employee in the course of employment is treated as done or engaged in by the employer, regardless of knowledge or approval.
regulatoryFindings.description: Greatearth Corporation's workplace safety officer and safety coordinator were acting in the course of their employment when they used and disclosed the complainants' personal data by instructing that the list be posted and posting it on the external façade.
violations: Greatearth Corporation's workplace safety officer and safety coordinator were acting in the course of their employment when they used and disclosed the complainants' personal data by instructing that the list be posted and posting it on the external façade.

outcome: Greatearth Corporation was issued a Warning under section 48I of the PDPA. No monetary penalty was imposed. The Deputy Commissioner found mitigating factors including: the safety coordinator's misunderstanding of instructions as a new employee, the WSHO's actions motivated by workplace safety concerns, limited disclosure scope (only to those entering the worksite on foot), and Greatearth Corporation's prompt remedial action in removing the poster after notification of the complaints. Greatearth Corporation was required to cease the unauthorized disclosure and has already removed the poster from the external façade.
dataType: Full name, NRIC number, contact number, photograph/photo ID
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 53(1) (Employer responsibility for employee actions in course of employment)

companyDescription: Iapps Pte Ltd is a financial technology company specialising in mobile application development and marketing. It was engaged by Sport Singapore to develop and operate the ActiveSG mobile application, a national sports facility booking and membership system.
companyLongDescription: Iapps Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based fintech company focused on mobile application development and marketing services. The company was contracted by Sport Singapore to develop, deploy and operate the Super Sports Club Membership Management System (SSCMMS) and the ActiveSG App, which allowed members to book sports facilities, register for fitness classes, and purchase entry passes. Iapps maintained the production servers and provided ongoing technical operations for the platform serving Singapore's national sports movement.
caseDescription: Iapps, a financial technology company operating the ActiveSG mobile application for Sport Singapore, failed to implement adequate security controls for code deployment. Due to human error, a security fix was deployed to the production environment instead of the test environment, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of personal data (names and NRIC numbers) of 108 individuals to 84 other users. For 6 individuals, additional sensitive data including addresses, contact details, and demographic information was also exposed.
violationSummary: The incident resulted in the exposure of personal data (names, NRIC numbers, and additional sensitive information) to unauthorized individuals due to inadequate technical and procedural security controls. The data was accessible and visible to unintended users logging into their accounts.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Iapps deployed a security code fix to the production environment instead of the test environment due to human error, exposing names and NRIC numbers of 108 individuals to 84 other users.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users of the ActiveSG app could view other people's personal data including names, ID numbers, and for 6 individuals, home addresses and contact details, creating identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Iapps stated it had second-level checks for code deployment as described in its Standard Operating Procedure.
claimsVsReality.reality: The SOP only described multi-level checks at the User Acceptance Testing stage, but contained no references to deployment checks in the enterprise or production environments, and no evidence of second-level checks existed after UAT.

claimsVsReality.claim: The incident was caused by human error in a rush and would not have been prevented by a second-level check.
claimsVsReality.reality: A second-level approval process or automated code deployment software would have prevented the engineer from deploying code to the wrong environment, regardless of time pressure.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organisations must protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Deployment process lacked second-level approvals or supervisory checks after User Acceptance Testing (UAT)
violations: Deployment process lacked second-level approvals or supervisory checks after User Acceptance Testing (UAT)
No oversight or supervision of code deployment after UAT stage
Code intended for test environment was deployed directly to production environment due to absence of automated controls or secondary checks
Weak internal work process controls failed to identify and mitigate high-risk deployment activities
Reliance solely on employee diligence without practical safeguarding steps

outcome: Iapps was ordered to pay a financial penalty of S$9,000 (reduced from the initially proposed S$11,000 in consideration of timely remedial actions). The Commission accepted that remedial measures taken by Iapps were sufficient and timely (issue fixed within 2 hours), including separation of test and production environments, implementation of 2-factor authentication for production access, monitoring of affected users, and implementation of dynamic QR codes for member IDs. No further directions were issued.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers (national identity card numbers), email addresses, mobile telephone numbers, home telephone numbers, home addresses, gender, date of birth, race, employment status, sports interests

company: Kuuhubb Inc., Kuu Hubb Oy, Recolor Oy
companyDescription: Kuuhubb Inc. is a Canadian company with Finnish subsidiaries (Kuu Hubb Oy and Recolor Oy) that developed and marketed the Recolor coloring book mobile application, which was popular with 1–5 million active monthly users in the United States during 2017–2019.
companyLongDescription: Kuuhubb Inc. is a Canadian company with Finnish subsidiaries (Kuu Hubb Oy and Recolor Oy) that developed and marketed the Recolor coloring book mobile application, which was popular with 1–5 million active monthly users in the United States during 2017–2019.
caseDescription: Defendants operated the Recolor coloring app with a 'Kids' category explicitly targeted at children under 13, yet collected personal information including names, emails, photos, and comments without parental consent. The app contained hidden social media features allowing children to publicly post content, interact with strangers, and be tracked for behavioral advertising without any notice to parents.
violationSummary: Defendants allowed persistent identifiers (device IDs) to be collected and shared with behavioral advertising networks (AdMob, AppLovin, Facebook Audience Network, etc.) without parental consent or notice. The Kids category was explicitly designed to attract children, creating a surveillance mechanism targeting minors.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Operated the Recolor coloring app with a 'Kids' category targeting children under 13, collected their names, emails, photos, and comments through social media features.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children under 13 unknowingly posted personal photos, selfies, and comments publicly accessible on the internet, with their data shared to advertisers for targeting.

claimsVsReality.claim: Recolor is a coloring book app for adults.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app contained a Kids category with content explicitly designed to appeal to children (simplified outlines, cartoon animals, licensed characters like My Little Pony), which attracted significant numbers of actual children to the app.

claimsVsReality.claim: The app is a passive coloring activity with no social features.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app incorporated extensive social media features including account creation, public profile pages, ability to post user-generated content (photos, selfies, comments), follow other users, and comment on their work — all without parental knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: User information is secure and not shared with third parties.
claimsVsReality.reality: Children's personal information (names, emails, photos, device IDs, behavioral data) was shared with six advertising networks for behavioral targeting without parental notice or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The app is safe for families and all ages.
claimsVsReality.reality: Between August 2017 and June 2019, Defendants received over 120 reports from parents and users that children were using the app as social media; dozens described children posting selfies, graphic images, using graphic language, engaging in bullying, and interacting with adults.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants engaged in deceptive practices by marketing Recolor as a coloring book for adults while operating a Kids category explicitly targeted at children; parents were unaware the app contained social media features enabling public sharing of children's personal information.
violations: Defendants engaged in deceptive practices by marketing Recolor as a coloring book for adults while operating a Kids category explicitly targeted at children; parents were unaware the app contained social media features enabling public sharing of children's personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Section 1303(c) and the COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.2 define 'operator' and require operators of websites/services directed to children under 13 to comply with specific requirements.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants were operators of a service directed to children (the Kids category contained cartoon animals, My Little Pony characters, and simplified drawings appealing to minors) but failed to treat the service as subject to COPPA.
violations: Defendants were operators of a service directed to children (the Kids category contained cartoon animals, My Little Pony characters, and simplified drawings appealing to minors) but failed to treat the service as subject to COPPA.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b)–(d) requires operators to provide clear, understandable notice of information practices to parents and to post privacy policies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants failed to provide any parental notice of their collection of children's personal information, including names, emails, photos, comments, and device identifiers; no privacy policy was presented to parents prior to collection.
violations: Defendants failed to provide any parental notice of their collection of children's personal information, including names, emails, photos, comments, and device identifiers; no privacy policy was presented to parents prior to collection.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5 requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants collected personal information from children with no parental consent mechanism whatsoever; parents were unaware children were creating accounts and posting content.
violations: Defendants collected personal information from children with no parental consent mechanism whatsoever; parents were unaware children were creating accounts and posting content.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(c)(7) prohibits collection of persistent identifiers for behavioral advertising absent notice and verifiable parental consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants allowed six third-party advertising networks (AdMob, AppLovin, Facebook Audience Network, HyprMX, Vungle, Unity Ads) to collect device identifiers for behavioral/targeted advertising to users of the app, including children, without any notice or parental consent.
violations: Defendants allowed six third-party advertising networks (AdMob, AppLovin, Facebook Audience Network, HyprMX, Vungle, Unity Ads) to collect device identifiers for behavioral/targeted advertising to users of the app, including children, without any notice or parental consent.

outcome: The FTC filed a civil complaint seeking monetary penalties of up to $43,792 per violation (adjusted for inflation as of January 13, 2021), a permanent injunction against future COPPA violations, and other equitable relief including rescission or reformation of contracts and refunds. The complaint alleges separate violations for each collection, use, or disclosure of a child's personal information, potentially resulting in massive statutory damages. Defendants are required to cease all violations and comply with COPPA requirements going forward.
dataType: Name, email address, profile photos, user-generated content (comments, selfies), persistent device identifiers, location/behavioral tracking
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) — unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) 15 U.S.C. § 6502(c)
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.2 — definition of personal information and operators
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b)–(d) — privacy notice requirements
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5 — verifiable parental consent requirement
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(c)(7) — prohibition on behavioral advertising without consent

companyDescription: Individual political candidate running for national office in July 2019 Greek elections who engaged in direct telephone-based political campaigning.
companyLongDescription: Individual political candidate running for national office in July 2019 Greek elections who engaged in direct telephone-based political campaigning.
caseDescription: A political candidate made unsolicited political telephone calls to voters without proper consent verification or compliance with the Greek electronic communications law's opt-out registry requirements. The candidate failed to check the national do-not-call list before calling and did not provide adequate information about data subject rights.
violationSummary: The candidate engaged in systematic collection of personal contact data and direct targeting of individuals via telephone without lawful basis under opt-out framework, constituting surveillance of electoral preferences.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A political candidate made unsolicited telephone calls to voters' mobile phones for campaign purposes without obtaining or checking telecommunications providers' opt-out registries to exclude.
whyTheyWereWrong: Recipients received unwanted political calls without their prior consent, and the candidate failed to verify she had permission to contact them, exposing voters to harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The candidate maintained an accurate electoral contact list that was verified and updated months before the campaign.
claimsVsReality.reality: The candidate did not obtain or check the mandatory opt-out registries from telecom providers, failed to verify current consent status, and could not document which specific sources provided the phone numbers or when consent was obtained.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant's data were in lists provided by the political party.
claimsVsReality.reality: When the complainant contacted the party, they were told they were not a party member and their name did not appear on party-distributed lists, contradicting the candidate's claim.

claimsVsReality.claim: The candidate provided proper notice and options for the complainant to opt out.
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence was provided that the candidate informed the recipient about their right to access data, to decline future contact, or other data subject rights during the calls.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15 requires controllers to facilitate the exercise of data subject rights and provide information about the action taken without undue delay, and in any case within one month of receipt of the request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Candidate failed to properly satisfy the complainant's right of access request by not providing an adequate response regarding whether the caller's data were in their electoral lists.
violations: Candidate failed to properly satisfy the complainant's right of access request by not providing an adequate response regarding whether the caller's data were in their electoral lists.

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 3471/2006 Art. 11(2) prohibits unsolicited promotional calls with human intervention unless the subscriber has declared to the service provider that they do not wish to receive such calls, and requires operators to maintain a free do-not-call registry available to all interested parties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Candidate made political telephone calls without obtaining and checking current opt-out registries from telecom providers before calling, failed to exclude phone numbers registered in do-not-call lists within the required 30-day window.
violations: Candidate made political telephone calls without obtaining and checking current opt-out registries from telecom providers before calling, failed to exclude phone numbers registered in do-not-call lists within the required 30-day window.

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 3471/2006 Art. 13 requires callers to inform recipients about their rights and the identity of the caller during marketing communications.
regulatoryFindings.description: Candidate did not inform the recipient about the right to access their personal data during the political telephone calls.
violations: Candidate did not inform the recipient about the right to access their personal data during the political telephone calls.

outcome: The Hellenic Authority for the Protection of Personal Data (DPA) found violations of GDPR Art. 15 (right of access), Greek Law 3471/2006 Art. 11(2) (unsolicited calls/do-not-call compliance), and Art. 13 (information provision). The candidate was ordered to cease unlawful processing and impose an administrative fine of €2,000. The decision is final and the candidate must comply with data protection requirements in future political communications.
companyNow: The political candidate was subject to enforcement action by the Greek DPA and is bound by compliance obligations in future political communications.
dataType: Contact information (mobile phone numbers)

companyDescription: Irish Credit Bureau DAC is a credit reference agency that maintains a database of credit performance data from approximately 280 financial institutions, processing data on approximately 2.8 million individuals. The ICB provides credit reports and credit scores to assist lenders in making credit decisions.
companyLongDescription: Irish Credit Bureau DAC is a credit reference agency that maintains a database of credit performance data from approximately 280 financial institutions, processing data on approximately 2.8 million individuals. The ICB provides credit reports and credit scores to assist lenders in making credit decisions.
caseDescription: Irish Credit Bureau failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure accuracy of personal data in its credit database. A code change on 28 June 2018 unintentionally removed a filter protecting closed loan accounts from updates, resulting in 15,120 inaccurate records being processed and 1,062 disclosed to lenders and data subjects. The ICB also failed to maintain documented records of testing for code changes and lacked a formal approval procedure for system modifications.
