violationSummary: The ICB's failure to implement appropriate technical safeguards (filter protection, comprehensive change management, documented testing procedures) directly resulted in inaccurate data being processed and disclosed, causing loss of data subject control and potential economic harm in credit decisions.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: On 28 June 2018, Irish Credit Bureau implemented a code change that unintentionally removed a filter protecting closed loan accounts from updates.
whyTheyWereWrong: The inaccurate records were disclosed to lenders and 118 data subjects, causing one mortgage applicant's credit card closure date to be incorrectly shown as February 2018 instead of February.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ICB submitted that its change management process complied with ISO27001 standard and included appropriate safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: The process lacked any provision for testing proposed coding changes or a formal approval procedure, both recommended by ISO guidance and essential for protecting sensitive financial data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ICB stated it carried out testing of the code change per ISO requirements by technical staff.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented record of testing was maintained; the actual testing failed to identify that the change would remove the filter protecting closed accounts, indicating inadequate test coverage.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ICB claimed the inaccuracies caused minimal impact on data subjects, limited to changed closure dates.
claimsVsReality.reality: Inaccurate closure dates were disclosed to lenders considering credit applications, influencing lending decisions (evidenced by complaint C-18-10-11 where a mortgage applicant was questioned due to the inaccuracy); data subjects lost control over financial data for up to 9 weeks.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 25(1) GDPR requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures designed to implement data protection principles, including accuracy, both at the determination of processing means and during processing itself.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to maintain a technical filter preventing payment profile updates to closed accounts; filter was unintentionally removed 28 June 2018 and not restored until 30 August 2018
violations: Failed to maintain a technical filter preventing payment profile updates to closed accounts; filter was unintentionally removed 28 June 2018 and not restored until 30 August 2018
Failed to implement a comprehensive documented change management process with testing requirements and formal approval procedures for code changes

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(2) and 24(1) GDPR require controllers to demonstrate compliance with data protection principles and processing requirements through appropriate technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to maintain documented records of testing undertaken for the 28 June 2018 code change, preventing demonstration of compliance with Article 25(1) testing obligations
violations: Failed to maintain documented records of testing undertaken for the 28 June 2018 code change, preventing demonstration of compliance with Article 25(1) testing obligations
Submitted blank DPIA template and change control form with no analysis of risks or testing measures

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 26(1) GDPR requires joint controllers to determine their respective responsibilities for compliance by means of an arrangement.
regulatoryFindings.description: No infringement found; ICB determined all means of processing alone; ICB members are not joint controllers
violations: No infringement found; ICB determined all means of processing alone; ICB members are not joint controllers

outcome: Irish Credit Bureau DAC is subject to: (1) a reprimand for infringements of Articles 25(1), 5(2), and 24(1) GDPR; (2) an administrative fine of €90,000 for the Article 25(1) infringement; (3) no requirement for an order to implement formal approval procedures, as the ICB has since implemented comprehensive change management policies (dated 17 February 2021) including formal approval requirements and testing documentation. The ICB must continue to maintain compliance through ongoing assessment of technical and organisational measures. No order under Article 58(2)(d) was necessary given remediation undertaken.
companyNow: Irish Credit Bureau DAC operates as a credit reference agency in Ireland with approximately 280 financial institution members. Following this decision, the ICB has implemented comprehensive remediation measures including new change management, testing, and DPIA policies (as of February 2021).
dataType: Credit performance data, financial history, personal identifiers (name, address, date of birth, occupation, gender)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 25(1) – Data protection by design

companyDescription: TIGERS MARKET, S.L. (CIF B67245209) is a Spanish telemarketing services company that conducted unsolicited commercial calls for electricity provider switching campaigns.
companyLongDescription: TIGERS MARKET, S.L. (CIF B67245209) is a Spanish telemarketing services company that conducted unsolicited commercial calls for electricity provider switching campaigns.
caseDescription: TIGERS MARKET conducted unsolicited commercial telemarketing calls to a consumer registered on Spain's Robinson List (opt-out registry), requesting they switch electricity providers. The company made multiple calls despite the complainant's explicit preference not to receive such communications. TIGERS operated the calling lines and violated the recipient's right to object to direct marketing.
violationSummary: The company conducted targeted telemarketing surveillance of a consumer who had explicitly opted out via the Robinson List. This constitutes surveillance without consent despite clear prior objection.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: TIGERS MARKET made unsolicited commercial telemarketing calls on November 5-6, 2020 to a mobile line registered on Spain's Robinson List opt-out registry to promote electricity provider.
whyTheyWereWrong: The recipient had explicitly registered to block direct marketing calls; TIGERS ignored this opt-out preference.

claimsVsReality.claim: TIGERS claimed in its response to the AEPD that it had no knowledge of the phone line holders and had not processed any personal data of the complainant.
claimsVsReality.reality: NEOTEL (the telecom operator) confirmed TIGERS held the calling line numbers and was conducting telemarketing activities; TIGERS was the confirmed data controller for the personal processing involved in the calls.

regulatoryFindings.act: Spanish LGT Art. 48.1(b) requires users to have the right to object to unwanted direct marketing calls and to be informed of this right.
regulatoryFindings.description: TIGERS made multiple commercial telemarketing calls to a number registered on the Robinson List without consent or proper opt-out compliance.
violations: TIGERS made multiple commercial telemarketing calls to a number registered on the Robinson List without consent or proper opt-out compliance.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 21 grants data subjects the right to object to processing of personal data for direct marketing purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: TIGERS processed the complainant's telephone number for direct marketing despite their registration on the Robinson List opt-out registry.
violations: TIGERS processed the complainant's telephone number for direct marketing despite their registration on the Robinson List opt-out registry.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Art. 23.4 implements protections against unwanted direct marketing in accordance with privacy and consumer rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: TIGERS failed to honour the opt-out preference recorded in the Robinson List before conducting telemarketing calls.
violations: TIGERS failed to honour the opt-out preference recorded in the Robinson List before conducting telemarketing calls.

outcome: AEPD (Spanish Data Protection Authority) imposed a €4,000 monetary penalty on TIGERS MARKET, S.L. (CIF B67245209) classified as a 'leve' (minor) infraction. The respondent did not submit allegations and the penalty became enforceable. The sanction must be paid within the voluntary payment period specified in Spanish administrative procedure rules, with failure to pay resulting in executive recovery proceedings. The resolution is final in administrative channels but subject to judicial review before Spain's National Court.
companyNow: Unknown. TIGERS MARKET, S.L. was identified as a telemarketing services company operating in Spain. Current operational status is not disclosed in the decision.
dataType: telephone numbers, contact information

companyDescription: Municipal transportation company operating bus services in Rhodes, Greece. Public sector enterprise responsible for public transit with employees including drivers and ticket collectors.
companyLongDescription: Municipal transportation company operating bus services in Rhodes, Greece. Public sector enterprise responsible for public transit with employees including drivers and ticket collectors.
caseDescription: A former bus driver/collector was denied access to video surveillance footage needed for his legal defense in a criminal case and received a reference certificate containing unnecessary personal data about his dismissal due to criminal conduct. The company failed to respond to his data access request and violated proportionality principles.
violationSummary: Company disclosed sensitive information about employee's criminal conduct in reference certificates without necessity and failed to provide access to data subject needed for legal defense, constituting improper disclosure and denial of data subject rights.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: RODA issued employment reference certificates stating the former employee was dismissed for criminal conduct.
whyTheyWereWrong: The former employee needed the video evidence to defend himself in criminal proceedings and pursue a civil compensation claim, but RODA destroyed the footage automatically after 7 days.

claimsVsReality.claim: Video surveillance footage was erased after 7 days per retention policy; employee was informed orally
claimsVsReality.reality: Employee testified he was never informed of the 7-day deletion policy; company changed its account during proceedings, first claiming footage existed then claiming it was automatically deleted

claimsVsReality.claim: Reference certificate was lawful, truthful and complete
claimsVsReality.reality: Certificate unnecessarily disclosed dismissal reason (criminal conduct) beyond what Civil Code Art. 678 permits; employee later received three different versions with conflicting information

claimsVsReality.claim: All employees were informed of video surveillance processing
claimsVsReality.reality: Employee was not properly informed; company failed to provide written notice of the surveillance policy until forced to do so mid-investigation

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires personal data to be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes of processing (data minimisation principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: Company issued reference certificates stating employee was dismissed due to criminal conduct when only type and duration of employment needed to be certified
violations: Company issued reference certificates stating employee was dismissed due to criminal conduct when only type and duration of employment needed to be certified

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12(3) requires controller to provide information on action taken on a rights request without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company never responded in writing to employee's July 2019 request for video surveillance footage, silently refusing the request
violations: Company never responded in writing to employee's July 2019 request for video surveillance footage, silently refusing the request

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15 grants data subject the right to obtain confirmation whether personal data is being processed and access to that data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company denied employee access to video footage recorded by bus surveillance system that would document events on the date of alleged incident
violations: Company denied employee access to video footage recorded by bus surveillance system that would document events on the date of alleged incident

outcome: Authority imposed total administrative fine of €8,000 (€5,000 for Articles 12(3) and 15 violations; €3,000 for Article 5(1)(c) violation). Company ordered to comply with data access requests and data minimisation requirements in future. Employee entitled to compensation for denial of data needed for legal defense.
companyNow: Unknown current operational status; municipal transportation company subject to Greek data protection authority oversight and required to implement compliant data handling procedures.
dataType: Employment records, video surveillance footage, personal identification data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 12(3) – duty to inform on action taken on request
Greek Civil Code Art. 678 – employment reference certificate rules

companyDescription: BRABANK ASA (formerly Easybank ASA) is a Norwegian bank providing consumer lending, refinancing, and financial services. The company operates an online banking platform serving thousands of customers.
companyLongDescription: BRABANK ASA (formerly Easybank ASA) is a Norwegian bank providing consumer lending, refinancing, and financial services. The company operates an online banking platform serving thousands of customers.
caseDescription: BRABANK launched 'Min Side', a customer portal showing loan details, but failed to conduct adequate risk assessments and security testing. Due to session verification flaws, customers could view other customers' financial information and contact details. The bank deployed insufficient technical and organizational safeguards before launch.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational security measures required under GDPR Article 32, and failed to conduct required risk assessments under Articles 24 and 32, resulting in a breach of data confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Launched the 'Min Side' loan portal on September 3, 2019 without conducting adequate risk assessments or security testing.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 91 and 500 customers were exposed to unauthorized access of sensitive financial information such as loan details, account balances.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank assessed the risk to customer rights and freedoms as 'low' because information presented was not sensitive and customers could not make changes in the system.
claimsVsReality.reality: Financial data, particularly information about consumer loans, is highly sensitive and private to individuals. Datatilsynet's research showed 89% of respondents view financial information as deserving special protection. Customers could access other customers' contact information and loan details, causing real harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank conducted testing from May to August 2019 in its test environment, then verified the solution in an internal environment pointing to the production database.
claimsVsReality.reality: Testing was inadequate and undocumented. Critical session handling vulnerabilities were not identified until live deployment. The defect appeared within 10 minutes of launch, indicating testing failed to simulate realistic user behavior and session management scenarios.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal identification numbers (personnummer) were not accessible to other customers, and customers could not see whose financial information they viewed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Other sensitive identifiers were exposed: customers accessed contact details (names, addresses, phone numbers, email) and could link loan information to individuals through follow-up clicks.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24(1) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure and demonstrate that processing is performed in compliance with the Regulation.
regulatoryFindings.description: BRABANK failed to conduct documented risk assessments required by Article 24 before launching 'Min Side'
violations: BRABANK failed to conduct documented risk assessments required by Article 24 before launching 'Min Side'
The bank did not implement adequate technical measures to prevent unauthorized access to customer financial data
No evidence of proper evaluation of appropriate safeguards relative to the nature and scope of the treatment

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to achieve a level of security appropriate to the risk, including testing, risk assessment, and security controls.
regulatoryFindings.description: BRABANK failed to conduct proper risk assessment despite handling sensitive financial data for 500+ customers
violations: BRABANK failed to conduct proper risk assessment despite handling sensitive financial data for 500+ customers
Testing was inadequate; defects appeared immediately upon launch, indicating insufficient test coverage
Session handling vulnerabilities were not identified or remediated prior to production deployment
No documented evidence of technical security measures commensurate with the risks to confidentiality and integrity

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customer financial information was left accessible to unauthorized users due to session verification failures
violations: Customer financial information was left accessible to unauthorized users due to session verification failures
The bank's flawed session management allowed customers to view loan details, balances, and contact information of other customers

outcome: Datatilsynet (Norwegian Data Protection Authority) issued a binding administrative fine of NOK 400,000 on 28 May 2021. The bank was required to pay the penalty within 4 weeks if not appealed. BRABANK accepted the fine without objection on 19 May 2021. The bank implemented remedial measures including replacing the data connector, additional system verification, and relaunched 'Min Side' after 14 days of error-free testing. After 6 months of operation, no new incidents were reported.
companyNow: BRABANK ASA operates as a Norwegian financial services company offering consumer loans and refinancing products. The company rebranded from Easybank ASA and continues operations following the enforcement action.
dataType: Financial data, customer loan information, contact details, personal identifiers

company: University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust (UHDB)
companyDescription: University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust is a major public healthcare provider formed in July 2018 from the merger of Derby Teaching Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and Burton Hospitals NHS Foundation Trusts. It operates five hospitals across Burton, Derby, Tamworth, and Lichfield, processing approximately 1.7 million patient referrals annually.
companyLongDescription: University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust is a major public healthcare provider formed in July 2018 from the merger of Derby Teaching Hospital NHS Foundation Trust and Burton Hospitals NHS Foundation Trusts. It operates five hospitals across Burton, Derby, Tamworth, and Lichfield, processing approximately 1.7 million patient referrals annually.
caseDescription: UHDB failed to implement adequate security measures for patient referral data processed through the NHS e-RS system. After 180 days, referrals dropped off the worklist, and after 550 days, patient data was permanently lost. The hospital used email and manual processes to manage referrals instead of implementing formal procedures, affecting 4,768 patients, some of whom experienced treatment delays exceeding two years.
violationSummary: UHDB failed to maintain appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security, integrity, and confidentiality of special category health data, resulting in accidental loss and delays in patient referrals.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: UHDB failed to implement formal processes or adequate security measures for patient health data, instead relying on email instructions.
whyTheyWereWrong: 4,768 patients experienced lost or significantly delayed medical referrals due to inadequate data protection controls; 569 patients' health records disappeared entirely from the system.

claimsVsReality.claim: UHDB explained the infringement had occurred due to staff failing to follow manual steps in a Standing Operating Procedure (SOP), implying the process was clear and documented.
claimsVsReality.reality: Prior to the SOP being created, the process involved staff receiving emailed instructions about referral drop-offs, which was not an effective way of managing reinstatement. No formal process existed when the failures occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: This was considered to be a routine task requiring no specific training.
claimsVsReality.reality: Processing special category health data requires extra security measures beyond routine treatment; failure to implement formal processes or adequate security controls caused 4,768 patients' data to be lost or delayed.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures ('integrity and confidentiality').
regulatoryFindings.description: UHDB failed to implement a formal process or apply suitable security when processing special category health data on e-RS
violations: UHDB failed to implement a formal process or apply suitable security when processing special category health data on e-RS
Use of email and manual staff reinstatement of referrals did not provide effective system or adequate protection to prevent loss of personal data
No data protection impact assessment (DPIA) was ever carried out for the handling of referral drop-offs, despite processing of special category data requiring extra measures
Failed to have formal oversight in place to ensure referrals were being effectively managed and reinstated onto the worklist

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to UHDB under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. UHDB has remediated by: (1) conducting full internal investigation and external review; (2) contacting all 4,768 affected patients and actioning appointments where possible; (3) creating a new documented Standing Operating Procedure (SOP); and (4) implementing robotic process automation (RPA) to eliminate manual handling and human error. The Commissioner recommends UHDB: (1) continue supporting affected patients; (2) assess and monitor new processes over time; and (3) share learning organisation-wide to prevent recurrence.
companyNow: UHDB continues to operate as an NHS Foundation Trust providing hospital services across five locations in the East Midlands. It has implemented automated systems and enhanced data protection procedures following this enforcement action.
dataType: Health data, patient referrals, special category data
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality

companyDescription: AVILON CENTER 2016, S.L. is a Spanish company providing television shopping and telemarketing services. It was registered as a service provider with ADIGITAL, granting it access to the Robinson List opt-out database.
companyLongDescription: AVILON CENTER 2016, S.L. is a Spanish company providing television shopping and telemarketing services. It was registered as a service provider with ADIGITAL, granting it access to the Robinson List opt-out database.
caseDescription: AVILON CENTER 2016 made unsolicited commercial marketing calls to a telephone number registered in Spain's Robinson List (opt-out registry). Due to a temporary software error, the company's system failed to check the Robinson List before placing the call. The company was found liable for inadequate technical safeguards despite claiming the call occurred during a 30-minute system outage.
violationSummary: The company processed phone numbers for marketing despite the individual's prior opt-out election, and lacked adequate safeguards to respect that exclusion even during system failures.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: AVILON CENTER 2016 made commercial marketing calls to a consumer's mobile phone registered in the Robinson opt-out list due to a 30-minute software malfunction that prevented verification.
whyTheyWereWrong: The recipient had explicitly opted out of commercial calls by registering with the Robinson list in September 2018, but received an unsolicited marketing call in August 2019.

claimsVsReality.claim: The call occurred due to a brief, unavoidable 30-minute software error that temporarily blocked the Robinson List table, resolved quickly.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement adequate risk controls or fallback procedures to prevent marketing calls during system outages; the call should never have been placed if proper safeguards existed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company updates Robinson List data monthly and maintains proper procedures to respect opt-outs.
claimsVsReality.reality: Monthly updates are insufficient when a system failure causes the live blocking mechanism to fail; proper procedures must include failsafes to halt calling during database access failures.

regulatoryFindings.act: LGT Art. 48.1(b) requires that users have the right to object to receiving unwanted commercial calls and be informed of this right.
regulatoryFindings.description: AVILON called a number registered in the Robinson opt-out list, violating the recipient's right of objection exercised on 24 September 2018.
violations: AVILON called a number registered in the Robinson opt-out list, violating the recipient's right of objection exercised on 24 September 2018.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 21 grants individuals the right to object to processing of personal data for direct marketing purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: AVILON processed the recipient's phone number for marketing despite prior registration in Robinson List, indicating earlier objection.
violations: AVILON processed the recipient's phone number for marketing despite prior registration in Robinson List, indicating earlier objection.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Art. 23.4 implements protections against direct marketing violations in Spanish law.
regulatoryFindings.description: AVILON failed to maintain adequate controls to respect the individual's manifest objection recorded in the Robinson List.
violations: AVILON failed to maintain adequate controls to respect the individual's manifest objection recorded in the Robinson List.

outcome: AVILON paid €12,000 (reduced from €20,000 initial sanction by 40% through early payment and responsibility recognition). Payment occurred 17 February 2021, within the ten-day response period. The company waived all administrative appeals and acknowledged responsibility. The procedimiento terminated with finality under LPACAP Art. 85.
companyNow: Unknown. AVILON CENTER 2016, S.L. is a Spanish teletemarketing or sales services provider registered with ADIGITAL as of the document date.
dataType: Telephone numbers, personal contact information

company: Budapest Főváros Kormányhivatala XI. kerületi Hivatala (Budapest Metropolitan Government Office, District XI)
companyDescription: Budapest Főváros Kormányhivatala XI. kerületi Hivatala (Budapest Metropolitan Government Office, District XI) is a public health administration entity responsible for public health services, disease surveillance, and pandemic response within Budapest's 11th district. During the COVID-19 pandemic, it managed rapid COVID-19 testing and results reporting.
companyLongDescription: Budapest Főváros Kormányhivatala XI. kerületi Hivatala (Budapest Metropolitan Government Office, District XI) is a public health administration entity responsible for public health services, disease surveillance, and pandemic response within Budapest's 11th district. During the COVID-19 pandemic, it managed rapid COVID-19 testing and results reporting.
caseDescription: A government health authority transmitted detailed COVID-19 test data for 1,153 patients via unencrypted email in a single Excel spreadsheet to district physicians without filtering by district, exposing sensitive health information to unauthorized access. The organization failed to report the incident as required and did not notify affected individuals of the breach.
violationSummary: The unencrypted transmission of sensitive health data to recipients without need-to-know access, combined with failure to implement basic security controls and subsequent unauthorized disclosure, constitutes a breach of confidentiality under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Sent an unencrypted Excel spreadsheet containing 1,153 patients' detailed health data, addresses, phone numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,153 patients' highly sensitive health data including diagnoses, symptoms, and precise home addresses became accessible to unintended recipients, enabling potential identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization stated that transmission to healthcare professionals (physicians) mitigated risk because they are bound by medical confidentiality, so no risk existed.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data was forwarded to unauthorized third parties (public citizens, and ultimately the data protection authority) and physicians cannot control how data shared with them is subsequently handled, so the risk was not eliminated or sufficiently mitigated.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization claimed that the urgent pandemic situation justified bypassing proper data segregation and security measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR obligations for appropriate security measures and risk assessment apply regardless of emergency circumstances. Simple password protection and district-level filtering would have been feasible without delaying care delivery.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization claimed that no harm occurred because none of the intended recipients reported misuse.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data was subsequently leaked to unauthorized parties (the public); the absence of reported complaints does not eliminate the inherent risk of unencrypted transmission of 1,153 patients' detailed diagnoses and addresses.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires data controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk, considering the state of the art, implementation costs, processing nature, scope, circumstances, purposes, and risks to individuals.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization transmitted 1,153 patients' detailed health data via unencrypted email in Excel format without district-level segmentation, filtering, or access controls, exposing data to all recipients regardless of their patient relationships.
violations: Organization transmitted 1,153 patients' detailed health data via unencrypted email in Excel format without district-level segmentation, filtering, or access controls, exposing data to all recipients regardless of their patient relationships.
No encryption, password protection, or hashed access methods were applied to health data despite the high-risk nature of COVID-19 medical information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33(1) requires data controllers to report data breaches to the supervisory authority without undue delay and no later than 72 hours after becoming aware, unless the breach is unlikely to pose risk to natural persons' rights and freedoms.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization failed to report the high-risk incident to the authority, determining incorrectly that no risk existed because data was sent to healthcare providers, despite knowing data had been forwarded to unauthorized third parties.
violations: Organization failed to report the high-risk incident to the authority, determining incorrectly that no risk existed because data was sent to healthcare providers, despite knowing data had been forwarded to unauthorized third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 34(1) requires data controllers to notify affected individuals without undue delay if a breach likely poses high risk to their rights and freedoms.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization did not notify 1,153 affected patients of the breach of their health data, despite the high-risk nature of exposure (detailed diagnoses, symptoms, addresses, contact information).
violations: Organization did not notify 1,153 affected patients of the breach of their health data, despite the high-risk nature of exposure (detailed diagnoses, symptoms, addresses, contact information).

outcome: The Nemzeti Adatvédelmi és Információszabadság Hatóság (Hungarian Data Protection Authority) found the organization liable for three violations of GDPR Articles 32, 33, and 34. The organization was ordered to: (1) notify all affected individuals within 15 days of the final decision regarding the incident, affected data scope, and remediation measures; (2) pay a 10,000,000 HUF administrative fine within 30 days; (3) have the final decision with the organization's identifying information published. The decision is subject to administrative court review within 30 days. No criminal referral was made.
companyNow: Budapest District XI Government Office continues to operate as a public health administration authority. The decision has been published with identifying details as required by Hungarian law, and the organization must implement improved data security and breach notification procedures.
dataType: Health data, personal identifiers, contact information, COVID-19 test results, symptoms, medical diagnoses, occupation, residence address, telephone numbers, birth date

companyDescription: Ascension Data & Analytics is an analytics company providing data services and technology solutions to mortgage-related businesses, including document management, valuation models, and due diligence reviews. It operates as a subsidiary within the Ascension corporate family.
companyLongDescription: Ascension Data & Analytics is an analytics company providing data services and technology solutions to mortgage-related businesses, including document management, valuation models, and due diligence reviews. It operates as a subsidiary within the Ascension corporate family.
caseDescription: Ascension Data & Analytics failed to protect the sensitive personal and financial information of 60,593 consumers when it contracted with an unvetted third-party vendor, OpticsML, to process mortgage documents. OpticsML misconfigured cloud servers, leaving the data publicly accessible for one year (January 2018–January 2019) without password protection. Approximately 52 unauthorized IP addresses from Russia, China, and elsewhere accessed the exposed data.
violationSummary: The core violation was inadequate oversight of service providers and failure to implement appropriate safeguards and risk assessment. The misconfigured cloud storage and exposed data constitute insecurity of personal information in storage and transmission.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Ascension contracted with OpticsML to process mortgage documents containing sensitive data on 60,593 consumers including Social Security numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: OpticsML misconfigured cloud servers, leaving 60,593 consumers' names, Social Security numbers, birth dates, account numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ascension maintained a Third Party Vendor Risk Management policy requiring evaluation of vendor security measures and contractual safeguard requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ascension never actually implemented or followed the policy in practice—it did not evaluate OpticsML's security, did not require security questionnaires, and did not include specific safeguard requirements in vendor contracts.

claimsVsReality.claim: Service provider contracts included provisions protecting nonpublic personal information under the GLB Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: Contract language was vague, failed to specify actual security safeguards, and did not clarify vendor responsibility for GLB Safeguards Rule compliance or expected security measures.

regulatoryFindings.act: The GLB Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive information security program with administrative, technical, and physical safeguards appropriate to the institution's size, complexity, activities, and data sensitivity.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ascension failed to take reasonable steps to select and retain service providers capable of maintaining appropriate safeguards, and did not require service providers by contract to implement such safeguards.
violations: Ascension failed to take reasonable steps to select and retain service providers capable of maintaining appropriate safeguards, and did not require service providers by contract to implement such safeguards.
Ascension did not evaluate OpticsML's security capabilities or conduct due diligence before providing sensitive consumer data, despite maintaining a Third Party Vendor Risk Management policy.
Service provider contracts failed to specify security requirements or make clear that vendors were responsible for GLB Safeguards Rule compliance.
Ascension failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information security and failed to assess the sufficiency of existing safeguards to control those risks.
Ascension did not conduct adequate risk assessments of service providers prior to September 2017, and limited assessments in 2017–2018 excluded OpticsML and other major vendors.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on December 22, 2021, alleging violation of the GLB Safeguards Rule. The document does not specify a final settlement amount or order, but indicates enforcement proceedings initiated. Typical FTC remedies for such violations include mandatory implementation of comprehensive information security programs, third-party security assessments, breach notification protocols, and ongoing monitoring and reporting requirements.
companyNow: Unknown. Ascension Data & Analytics remains a subsidiary of Ascension Health, a major healthcare organization. No public information indicates the resolution of this FTC enforcement action or whether penalties were assessed.
dataType: Financial data, names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, loan information, credit and debit account numbers, drivers' license numbers, credit files
legalBasisViolated: GLB Safeguards Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 314, §§ 314.3 and 314.4

companyDescription: Hälso- och sjukvårdsnämnden Region Stockholm is a Swedish public health authority that operates healthcare services for Stockholm County, including the 1177 telephone medical advice line. It acts as the principal healthcare provider for approximately 2.4 million residents.
companyLongDescription: Hälso- och sjukvårdsnämnden Region Stockholm is a Swedish public health authority that operates healthcare services for Stockholm County, including the 1177 telephone medical advice line. It acts as the principal healthcare provider for approximately 2.4 million residents.
caseDescription: Region Stockholm's Health and Medical Care Board failed to inform callers to the 1177 medical advice hotline that their sensitive health data and identifiers were being collected, pseudonymized, and analyzed for quality purposes. The region collected call information including symptoms, referral outcomes, and personal identifiers from approximately 2.4 million Stockholm residents without providing required transparency notices.
violationSummary: The violation involves failure to disclose to data subjects how their sensitive health information was being systematically collected and processed. This prevented individuals from exercising control over their personal data and increased vulnerability to potential misuse.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Region Stockholm failed to inform callers to the 1177 healthcare helpline that their telephone numbers, municipality IDs, and sensitive health information were collected.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 2.4 million healthcare callers in Stockholm were unable to exercise their privacy rights or understand how their sensitive health data was being used because the region provided no.

claimsVsReality.claim: The region and its web information (1177.se) stated: 'It is your healthcare provider who is responsible for ensuring that personal data are handled correctly and lawfully.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Region Stockholm itself was the data controller responsible for informing callers about data processing, but it provided no notice to the 2.4 million individuals whose sensitive health data were collected and analyzed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The region asserted that it lacked obligation to inform callers because the processing instructions were delegated to MedHelp AB and Inera AB.
claimsVsReality.reality: As the controller under GDPR Article 4(7), Region Stockholm remained responsible for ensuring transparency and had to provide mandatory disclosure notices regardless of processor involvement.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Stockholm failed to provide any transparency to 1177 callers about data collection, purposes, controller identity, or their rights, making the processing non-transparent and unfair.
violations: Region Stockholm failed to provide any transparency to 1177 callers about data collection, purposes, controller identity, or their rights, making the processing non-transparent and unfair.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires the controller to provide specified information to data subjects when collecting their personal data directly.
regulatoryFindings.description: No information was provided to callers about the region's identity, the purposes of processing, legal basis, or their right to access their health data.
violations: No information was provided to callers about the region's identity, the purposes of processing, legal basis, or their right to access their health data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 14 requires the controller to provide specified information when personal data are obtained from sources other than the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Stockholm collected call information and health details from MedHelp AB without informing affected individuals about this secondary collection, the controller's identity, purposes, or their rights.
violations: Region Stockholm collected call information and health details from MedHelp AB without informing affected individuals about this secondary collection, the controller's identity, purposes, or their rights.

outcome: The Swedish Privacy Authority (IMY) issued a compliance order requiring Region Stockholm to inform all 1177 callers about the data collection within two months of the decision becoming final. The region must provide notice regarding collection of telephone numbers and municipality IDs to route calls to MedHelp AB, and about the separate collection of call information for quality and follow-up purposes. Additionally, a 500,000 SEK administrative fine was imposed. The decision is subject to appeal to the Stockholm Administrative Court.
companyNow: Region Stockholm is a public healthcare authority in Sweden. It remains responsible for health and medical care services in Stockholm County and continues to operate the 1177 medical advice service.
dataType: Health data, personal identity numbers, telephone numbers, contact reasons, referral information, call metadata
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
GDPR Art. 14 – Information to be provided where personal data have not been obtained from the data subject

companyDescription: Regionstyrelsen Region Sörmland is the regional government authority responsible for healthcare and regional services in Södermanland County, Sweden. It coordinates the 1177 healthcare advice telephone line for residents.
companyLongDescription: Regionstyrelsen Region Sörmland is the regional government authority responsible for healthcare and regional services in Södermanland County, Sweden. It coordinates the 1177 healthcare advice telephone line for residents.
caseDescription: Region Sörmland collected phone numbers and municipality IDs from callers to the 1177 healthcare advice line to route calls to healthcare provider MedHelp AB, but failed to inform callers about this data collection. The Swedish Data Protection Authority (IMY) found the region violated transparency and lawfulness principles by not providing mandatory information about the processing.
violationSummary: The region systematically collected caller identifying information (phone numbers, municipality IDs) without transparent disclosure to the data subjects, a core surveillance violation under privacy taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Region Sörmland collected phone numbers and municipality IDs from approximately 300,000 callers to the 1177 healthcare hotline to route calls to MedHelp AB without informing callers about.
whyTheyWereWrong: Callers received no notice that their phone numbers and location data were being collected, preventing them from understanding how their data was used or being able to exercise their legal.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Sörmland stated that information about 1177 on its website made clear that 'your healthcare provider is responsible for handling personal data correctly.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The website statement was vague and did not provide the comprehensive mandatory information required by GDPR Article 13, including the region's identity as controller, specific processing purposes, legal basis, data subject rights, or contact details for exercising those rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Sörmland claimed the collection of phone numbers and municipality IDs was necessary and proportionate for routing calls to MedHelp AB.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the collection purpose was lawful, the complete absence of transparency and information to callers about this processing violated fundamental GDPR requirements, regardless of the legitimacy of the underlying processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Sörmland processed phone numbers and municipality IDs without transparency—callers were not informed about collection, purposes, or their rights regarding this data processing.
violations: Region Sörmland processed phone numbers and municipality IDs without transparency—callers were not informed about collection, purposes, or their rights regarding this data processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13 requires the controller to provide comprehensive information to data subjects when personal data are collected directly from them, including controller identity, processing purposes, legal basis, and data subject rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Sörmland failed to provide any Article 13 information to callers. The region did not disclose: its identity as controller, contact details, processing purpose, legal basis, rights to access/rectification, or data protection officer contact information.
violations: Region Sörmland failed to provide any Article 13 information to callers. The region did not disclose: its identity as controller, contact details, processing purpose, legal basis, rights to access/rectification, or data protection officer contact information.

outcome: IMY imposed an administrative fine of 250,000 SEK on Region Sörmland for violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 13. The region was required to comply with transparency and information disclosure obligations. The region had begun transitioning to in-house healthcare advisory operations by January 2020, reducing ongoing exposure. IMY noted the region's willingness to clarify information on the 1177.se website but determined this did not retroactively cure the violations that occurred during the period of non-compliance (until 31 December 2019).
companyNow: Region Sörmland is an elected regional government body in Sweden responsible for healthcare delivery in Södermanland County. As of January 2020, it operates its 1177 healthcare advice service entirely in-house rather than through external contractors.
dataType: Telephone numbers, municipality IDs, healthcare/health data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject

companyDescription: Exclusive importer of automotive brand in Hungary, operating a network of authorized dealerships and service centers. Conducted systematic customer satisfaction surveys across dealership network without proper data protection compliance.
companyLongDescription: Exclusive importer of automotive brand in Hungary, operating a network of authorized dealerships and service centers. Conducted systematic customer satisfaction surveys across dealership network without proper data protection compliance.
caseDescription: An automotive importer conducted customer satisfaction surveys without proper individual notification or valid legal basis. Customers received unsolicited survey emails without clear identification of the data controller, source of contact information, or purpose. The importer collected and processed unnecessary personal data including vehicle identification numbers, addresses, and phone numbers for statistical surveys where only email contact was required.
violationSummary: The importer systematically collected personal data from large numbers of vehicle owners without their knowledge or meaningful consent, using an intermediary (data processor) to obscure its role. This constitutes surveillance of customer satisfaction across its entire dealer network without transparent notice.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: An automotive importer processed customer email addresses, home addresses, phone numbers, and vehicle identification data to send unsolicited satisfaction survey emails through a third-party.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers who serviced their vehicles at authorized dealers had no reasonable expectation that the importer would contact them directly.

claimsVsReality.claim: Importer stated it had justified 'legitimate interest' in quality control monitoring of authorized dealers and brand partners.
claimsVsReality.reality: Authority determined importer failed to demonstrate that its business interest outweighed data subjects' privacy rights, especially given that statistical analysis could be achieved with anonymized or minimally-identified data without collecting addresses, phone numbers, and vehicle identifiers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Importer argued that providing data controller notification via printed work orders (which dealership failed to deliver to customers) and reception area notices constituted adequate individual notification.
claimsVsReality.reality: Authority found recipients had no reasonable way to connect dealership visit to later importer contact, did not receive paper notices (due to dealership staff error), and could not identify importer from survey emails themselves, rendering notification ineffective.

claimsVsReality.claim: Importer claimed prior absence of complaints and customer concerns demonstrated lawful processing.
claimsVsReality.reality: Authority noted lack of complaints resulted from lack of transparency—customers did not know who actually contacted them or what company to complain to—so absence of complaints reflected notification failure, not legitimate processing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Importer stated all collected data types (name, address, phone, vehicle identifiers) were necessary for customer satisfaction measurement and complaint handling.
claimsVsReality.reality: Authority found address, phone, and vehicle chassis numbers were not necessary for statistical trend analysis (which was the stated primary purpose), and complaint handling could be achieved through voluntary self-identification in survey responses rather than blanket collection.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Importer processed customer data without clear identification in communications or proper notification, obscuring its role through third-party processor references that did not identify the actual data controller.
violations: Importer processed customer data without clear identification in communications or proper notification, obscuring its role through third-party processor references that did not identify the actual data controller.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires personal data be adequate, relevant, and limited to what is necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Importer collected vehicle chassis numbers, registration data, addresses, and phone numbers for statistical surveys where only email contact was needed, and for identifying complaint origins where only service date and location identification would suffice.
violations: Importer collected vehicle chassis numbers, registration data, addresses, and phone numbers for statistical surveys where only email contact was needed, and for identifying complaint origins where only service date and location identification would suffice.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires a valid lawful basis for processing; Article 6(1)(f) permits processing for legitimate interests only if the data subject's rights do not override those interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Importer claimed legitimate interest in quality monitoring but failed to demonstrate that its interest in market research outweighed recipients' fundamental right to privacy when proper notice and minimized data use could achieve the same goal.
violations: Importer claimed legitimate interest in quality monitoring but failed to demonstrate that its interest in market research outweighed recipients' fundamental right to privacy when proper notice and minimized data use could achieve the same goal.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Articles 12-13 require clear, transparent, concise information about processing to be provided to data subjects before or when collecting data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Recipients received survey emails with no explanation of who was collecting data (importer not identified), why they were contacted, how contact information was obtained, or what data would be processed; notification was embedded in work orders not provided to customers.
violations: Recipients received survey emails with no explanation of who was collecting data (importer not identified), why they were contacted, how contact information was obtained, or what data would be processed; notification was embedded in work orders not provided to customers.

outcome: Importer ordered to: (1) pay 5,000,000 HUF administrative fine; (2) bring all customer satisfaction survey processing into compliance with GDPR within 30 days, with written proof of compliance required; (3) modify data collection to minimize unnecessary personal data collection; (4) provide clear, individual notification to all data subjects about the importer's identity, processing purpose, and legal basis before survey contact. Fine justified by: systematic, multi-year practice affecting tens of thousands of vehicle owners; importer's market dominance as sole distributor; lack of transparent identification in customer communications; and failure to implement data minimization despite scale of operation. Decision affirmed by authority with no monetary reduction despite importer's COVID-19 hardship claims, as legal violations and public interest in privacy protection required penalty.
companyNow: Unknown current status. As automotive importer with exclusive distribution rights for a major vehicle brand in Hungary, company likely continues operations under new compliance requirements.
dataType: Email address, home address, phone number, vehicle technical identifiers (chassis number, registration), service details
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(1) – No valid legal basis
GDPR Art. 12(1) – Information to be provided

company: Everalbum, Inc. (also d/b/a Ever and Paravision)
companyDescription: Everalbum, Inc. provided Ever, a cloud-based photo storage and organization application available on iOS, Android, web, and desktop platforms. The company developed facial recognition technology to automatically group and organize user photos by face. It also offered enterprise facial recognition services through its Paravision brand.
companyLongDescription: Everalbum, Inc. provided Ever, a cloud-based photo storage and organization application available on iOS, Android, web, and desktop platforms. The company developed facial recognition technology to automatically group and organize user photos by face. It also offered enterprise facial recognition services through its Paravision brand.
caseDescription: Everalbum enabled facial recognition on users' photos by default without affirmative consent, then misrepresented users' control over the feature. The company also extracted millions of facial images from user photos to train its own facial recognition technology without proper authorization. Additionally, Everalbum falsely claimed it would delete photos upon account deactivation but retained them indefinitely.
violationSummary: The unauthorized application of facial recognition technology to user photos constitutes systematic surveillance of biometric data without affirmative consent. Additionally, the extraction and use of facial images for training proprietary technology represents secondary use without authorization.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Everalbum enabled facial recognition by default for millions of users without consent, extracted facial images from user photos to train its proprietary face recognition technology.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 12 million users uploaded intimate family photos to cloud storage believing they controlled facial recognition.

claimsVsReality.claim: Face recognition will only be used if users enable or turn it on (stated in Help article and privacy documentation).
claimsVsReality.reality: For approximately 75% of users (those outside Texas, Illinois, Washington, and EU), face recognition was enabled by default from February 2017 to April 2019, with no option to disable it.

claimsVsReality.claim: When face recognition is turned on, you are letting us know that it's ok for us to use the face embeddings of people in your photos (Help article, July 2018).
claimsVsReality.reality: Most users could not 'turn on' face recognition because it was already on by default and uncontrollable; the statement implied affirmative user consent where none existed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Photos and videos will be permanently deleted upon account deactivation (account deactivation messages and customer support).
claimsVsReality.reality: Until October 2019, Everalbum retained all photos and videos from deactivated accounts indefinitely and only began deleting them if accounts had been deactivated for more than three months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facial images extracted from user photos were used only for the Friends feature.
claimsVsReality.reality: Between September 2017 and August 2019, Everalbum extracted millions of facial images from user photos and combined them with public datasets to create four new datasets for developing proprietary facial recognition technology, some of which was sold to enterprise customers via Paravision.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent represented that face recognition would only be used if users enabled or turned it on, but in fact enabled it by default for approximately 75% of users until April 2019 without providing a means to disable it.
violations: Respondent represented that face recognition would only be used if users enabled or turned it on, but in fact enabled it by default for approximately 75% of users until April 2019 without providing a means to disable it.

Respondent represented in its Help article that 'when face recognition is turned on, you are letting us know that it's ok for us to use the face embeddings,' but users outside Texas, Illinois, Washington, and EU could not take any affirmative action to enable or disable the feature.

Respondent represented through account deactivation messages and customer support responses that photos and videos would be permanently deleted upon account deactivation, but retained them indefinitely until October 2019.

outcome: FTC issued a Complaint alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document does not specify the final resolution, but the complaint alleges that Everalbum engaged in deceptive practices regarding (1) user control over facial recognition and (2) deletion of photos upon account deactivation. Respondent was required to cease these practices and comply with specified remedies.
companyNow: Everalbum rebranded its enterprise facial recognition division as Paravision and continued operating. The company implemented corrective measures including opt-in consent for facial recognition and delayed deletion of deactivated account photos. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Biometric data (facial images, face embeddings), photos, videos, location data, IP addresses
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Innovasjon Norge is a Norwegian public enterprise that provides financing, grants, and business development services to support innovation and entrepreneurship. The agency operates under state ownership and serves as a key instrument of Norwegian industrial and innovation policy.
companyLongDescription: Innovasjon Norge is a Norwegian public enterprise that provides financing, grants, and business development services to support innovation and entrepreneurship. The agency operates under state ownership and serves as a key instrument of Norwegian industrial and innovation policy.
caseDescription: Innovasjon Norge, a Norwegian government agency, failed to implement adequate safeguards for credit report handling and allowed multiple unauthorized credit inquiries on behalf of customers. The agency mishandled credit worthiness checks without proper legal basis and failed to establish required internal controls, exposing customers' sensitive financial data and credit histories to unnecessary risk.
violationSummary: The agency failed to implement adequate technical and organisational safeguards for personal data processing, particularly credit information. The lack of internal controls and authorization procedures for credit inquiries constitutes a security failure under GDPR Article 32.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Innovasjon Norge performed at least four credit inquiries on customer accounts without proper authorization between January and April 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive credit and financial data were accessed without documented consent or legal basis, exposing them to unauthorized scrutiny of their creditworthiness.

claimsVsReality.claim: Innovasjon Norge claimed it had proper legal grounds to conduct multiple credit inquiries on customers' accounts.
claimsVsReality.reality: The agency failed to document any lawful basis for the credit checks and could not show customer authorization or valid contractual or statutory justification for the inquiries.

claimsVsReality.claim: The agency stated it followed proper procedures for credit information handling.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal controls for credit inquiries were entirely absent; there were no documented authorization requirements, no audit trails, and no verification of legitimate business purpose prior to credit checks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Innovasjon Norge indicated it had implemented adequate safeguards for personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The agency lacked mandatory technical and organisational measures, including access restrictions, logging systems, and supervisory controls required under GDPR Article 32.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires all processing of personal data to have a lawful basis such as explicit consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge processed credit information without establishing a valid lawful basis. The agency could not document that customers had authorized credit inquiries or that processing fell under an explicit legal exemption.
violations: Innovasjon Norge processed credit information without establishing a valid lawful basis. The agency could not document that customers had authorized credit inquiries or that processing fell under an explicit legal exemption.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including internal controls and access restrictions.
regulatoryFindings.description: The agency failed to implement mandatory internal control procedures for credit inquiries. There were no documented authorization requirements, no verification of legitimate business purpose, and no audit trails for multiple credit checks made in early 2020.
violations: The agency failed to implement mandatory internal control procedures for credit inquiries. There were no documented authorization requirements, no verification of legitimate business purpose, and no audit trails for multiple credit checks made in early 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33(1) requires controllers to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay and in any case not later than 72 hours after becoming aware of it.
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge failed to timely notify Datatilsynet of the credit inquiry breaches. Notification delays occurred for the first three credit inquiries made in January–February 2020, which were not reported until May 2020.
violations: Innovasjon Norge failed to timely notify Datatilsynet of the credit inquiry breaches. Notification delays occurred for the first three credit inquiries made in January–February 2020, which were not reported until May 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: Norwegian Personal Data Protection Act Article 6 nr. 1 and Article 4 nr. 12 require lawful basis and justified purpose for handling credit information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Credit inquiries were made without documented lawful basis under Norwegian law. The agency failed to establish that customers had consented to or authorized these inquiries, violating requirements for handling sensitive credit data.
violations: Credit inquiries were made without documented lawful basis under Norwegian law. The agency failed to establish that customers had consented to or authorized these inquiries, violating requirements for handling sensitive credit data.

outcome: Datatilsynet issued a fine of NOK 1,000,000 and issued a compliance order requiring Innovasjon Norge to: (1) immediately cease unauthorized credit inquiries; (2) implement written internal control procedures governing all credit handling; (3) establish clear authorization protocols and audit trails; (4) conduct mandatory data protection training for staff; (5) undergo regular monitoring by Datatilsynet. The agency was required to document implementation within specified timeframes. The decision was enforceable and no appeal was recorded.
companyNow: Innovasjon Norge is a Norwegian government agency under the Ministry of Trade, Fisheries and Food Policy. The agency continues to operate with mandated enhanced data protection oversight following the 2021 enforcement action.
dataType: Credit information, personal identification data, financial records
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(1) – lawful basis for processing
Norwegian Personal Data Protection Act Art. 4 nr. 12, Art. 6 nr. 1

companyDescription: VODAFONE ESPAÑA, S.A.U. is a major Spanish telecommunications operator providing mobile, broadband, and fixed-line services. It is a subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc, one of the world's largest mobile network operators.
companyLongDescription: VODAFONE ESPAÑA, S.A.U. is a major Spanish telecommunications operator providing mobile, broadband, and fixed-line services. It is a subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc, one of the world's largest mobile network operators.
caseDescription: VODAFONE ESPAÑA failed to respond to investigative information requests from the Spanish data protection authority (AEPD), obstructing the authority's investigation into a data handling complaint. The company received a formal information request in February 2021 and provided no response within the required timeframe, violating Article 58(1) of the GDPR.
companyWorth: €46B (Vodafone Group plc market cap as of 2021)
violationSummary: The violation is classified as insecurity because the company's obstruction of investigation prevented authorities from assessing the security and lawfulness of its personal data processing. Non-cooperation with regulators creates risk that undiscovered data handling violations continue unaddressed.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Vodafone España received a formal information request from Spain's data protection authority on 8 February 2021 but failed to provide any response within the required 10 business days or at any.
whyTheyWereWrong: Vodafone's non-cooperation prevented authorities from investigating potential data handling violations affecting its millions of customers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Compliance with data protection obligations, including cooperation with regulatory authorities.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company failed to respond to mandatory investigative information request within required timeframe, demonstrating systemic failure in procedures for regulatory cooperation.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(1) grants supervisory authorities the power to order data controllers and processors to provide any information required for performance of their supervisory functions.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone España failed to comply with AEPD's formal information request (O00007128s2100006950) issued 4 February 2021, despite receipt on 8 February 2021 and a 10 business day response deadline.
violations: Vodafone España failed to comply with AEPD's formal information request (O00007128s2100006950) issued 4 February 2021, despite receipt on 8 February 2021 and a 10 business day response deadline.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(5)(e) defines as a very serious infraction the failure to facilitate access in breach of Article 58(1), punishable by fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of global annual turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: Non-response to regulatory information request constitutes obstruction of supervisory authority's investigation powers, falling under Article 83(5)(e).
violations: Non-response to regulatory information request constitutes obstruction of supervisory authority's investigation powers, falling under Article 83(5)(e).

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72.1 classifies as very serious: (ñ) failure to provide access to personal data, information, premises, equipment and data processing means required by supervisory authority; (o) resistance or obstruction of supervisory authority's inspection function.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone España's failure to respond to information request constitutes obstruction under Article 72.1(o) of LOPDGDD.
violations: Vodafone España's failure to respond to information request constitutes obstruction under Article 72.1(o) of LOPDGDD.

outcome: AEPD initiated sanctioning procedure PS/00155/2021 on 16 April 2021. Initial proposed sanction was €5,000. Vodafone España paid €3,000 on 17 May 2021, utilizing two 20% reductions: (1) recognition of responsibility within the allegations deadline, and (2) voluntary payment before resolution. Payment within the allegations deadline period triggered immediate termination of procedure under LPACAP Article 85. Company waived all administrative appeals and remedies.
companyNow: VODAFONE ESPAÑA, S.A.U. remains an active telecommunications provider in Spain, a subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc. The 2021 penalty was a minor enforcement action compared to its overall operations.
dataType: Telecommunications customer data, call records, subscription information

company: ΚΑΠΑ ΛΑΜΔΑ ΩΜΕΓΑ ΔΙΑΦΗΜΙΣΤΙΚΗ ΕΜΠΟΡΙΚΗ ΜΟΝΟΠΡΟΣΩΠΗ ΕΤΑΙΡΕΙΑ ΠΕΡΙΟΡΙΣΜΕΝΗΣ ΕΥΘΥΝΗΣ (ΚΛΩ)
companyDescription: ΚΛΩ is a Greek limited liability advertising and telemarketing company specializing in telephone sales (telesales) of cosmetic and personal care products. The company maintains customer records for 5 years for tax compliance and has historically conducted direct marketing campaigns via unsolicited calls.
companyLongDescription: ΚΛΩ is a Greek limited liability advertising and telemarketing company specializing in telephone sales (telesales) of cosmetic and personal care products. The company maintains customer records for 5 years for tax compliance and has historically conducted direct marketing campaigns via unsolicited calls.
caseDescription: ΚΛΩ, a telemarketing firm, made unsolicited promotional calls to individuals based on personal data collected during previous purchases, without valid legal basis or explicit consent. The company continued calls despite customer objections and failed to respect opt-out requests under Greek electronic communications law. Three complainants filed multiple complaints over extended periods regarding repeated unwanted marketing calls.
violationSummary: Company repurposed personal data (phone numbers) collected for transaction completion into marketing use without explicit consent or transparency, and then processed that data for a fundamentally different purpose (promotional calls) than originally stated.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Made repeated unsolicited telemarketing calls promoting cosmetic products to customers over 12+ months using phone numbers from prior purchases.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers received dozens of unwanted sales calls targeting their personal phone numbers without clear consent, leaving them harassed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed all customers were existing clients who gave 'verbal consent' during initial purchase transactions to remain on file for future marketing calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documentary evidence of any consent, written or oral, was ever produced. In at least one case (Complainant C), the complainant denied ever making a purchase from the company; his father had made a single purchase years earlier. In others, objections were explicitly stated but calls continued.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated that calls were made for 'customer satisfaction surveys' to assess whether customers were satisfied with prior purchases.
claimsVsReality.reality: Complainants consistently reported that calls were explicitly for product promotion and sales, not satisfaction surveys. Calls often occurred long after purchases and to individuals who had not made purchases themselves.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated customers were informed of their right to request deletion and that no one contacted the company to withdraw consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Complainants testified that they repeatedly objected verbally during calls, and company records showed continued outreach. No written policy regarding objection procedures was ever provided to customers, and company failed to respect verbal objections in real time.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it engaged a GDPR compliance consultant in August 2019 and was implementing compliance measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Nearly two years after the claimed engagement (through at least September 2020), no compliance documentation was produced, and violations continued. The contract was referenced but no evidence of actual implementation was ever submitted.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires processing to be lawful only if at least one specified condition is met, including explicit prior consent or legitimate interests balancing.
regulatoryFindings.description: ΚΛΩ claimed 'verbal consent' from phone calls without documentary evidence; no written record or demonstrable proof of consent existed
violations: ΚΛΩ claimed 'verbal consent' from phone calls without documentary evidence; no written record or demonstrable proof of consent existed
Company reused customer phone numbers obtained for purchase transactions as basis for marketing calls without separate informed consent
No transparency provided to customers that their data would be used for ongoing promotional purposes distinct from the original transaction

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 21(2) gives data subjects the absolute right to object to processing for direct marketing at any time, and the controller must cease processing immediately.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customers verbally objected during calls; company continued placing calls despite stated objections
violations: Customers verbally objected during calls; company continued placing calls despite stated objections
In one case (Complainant A), objections persisted for over one year; company made 11 separate calls across 13+ months despite repeated refusals
