Company provided no written procedure for customers to formally exercise objection rights and did not facilitate the right under Article 12(2)

regulatoryFindings.act: Law 3471/2006 Article 11(2) prohibits unsolicited calls with human intervention for commercial promotion unless the called party previously consented or is registered in the opt-out registry.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company made calls to phone numbers registered in the national Do Not Call registry prior to the calls
violations: Company made calls to phone numbers registered in the national Do Not Call registry prior to the calls
No evidence that customers were informed of their right to register objections or how to exercise it
Company failed to obtain updated opt-out lists from telecommunications providers before initiating campaigns

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (APDPD) found ΚΛΩ in violation of GDPR Articles 6, 12(2), and 21, and Law 3471/2006. The Authority determined that the company lacked valid legal basis for processing customer phone numbers for marketing, failed to facilitate customer objection rights, and continued harassment despite stated refusals. The company was ordered to pay an administrative fine of €20,000 and must cease all unlawful processing. ΚΛΩ represented that it has deleted the phone numbers of complainants and discontinued contact; however, the Authority emphasized that this remedial action occurred only after regulatory intervention, not voluntarily. The Authority also noted that while ΚΛΩ claimed engagement of a GDPR compliance consultant in mid-2019, no documentary evidence of implementation was provided and violations continued into 2021.
dataType: Telephone numbers, customer contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 6(1) – Lawfulness of processing (lack of valid legal basis)
GDPR Article 12(2) – Facilitating exercise of data subject rights
Law 3471/2006 Article 11(1)-(2) – Restrictions on unsolicited electronic communications

companyDescription: Asker Kommune is a municipality in Akershus, Norway, providing local government services including education, social services, and public administration to approximately 31,000 residents.
companyLongDescription: Asker Kommune is a municipality in Akershus, Norway, providing local government services including education, social services, and public administration to approximately 31,000 residents.
caseDescription: Asker municipality published 127 complete national identification numbers and names of individuals on its public website via document title listings from 2004–2020, exposing confidential information about children receiving special education, disability support, and housing assistance. The municipality failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures and lacked proper procedures to detect and prevent such breaches, which was only discovered when a private citizen reported it.
violationSummary: Confidential personal data was made publicly accessible on the internet without legal basis or security safeguards. The data exposure was continuous over 16 years and only discovered by a third party, not through internal monitoring.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Asker Kommune published 127 citizens' complete national ID numbers and confidential document titles involving children, special education.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 120 residents, including children, had their full national ID numbers and sensitive personal information about disability services.

claimsVsReality.claim: Asker Kommune stated it had robust procedures with daily manual proofreading of postlists by two employees.
claimsVsReality.reality: These procedures failed entirely; the breach persisted for 16 years undetected and was only discovered when a citizen reported it.

claimsVsReality.claim: The municipality asserted that confidential information was adequately protected on its systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive data about children's special education, disability status, and housing support was publicly accessible on the internet without any access controls or logging.

claimsVsReality.claim: The municipality indicated a commitment to data protection (per follow-up letter of 22 May 2020).
claimsVsReality.reality: The municipality lacked even basic audit procedures (sampling) for legacy data and had not detected the 16-year-old breach itself.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Asker Kommune failed to establish adequate security measures to prevent confidential information from being publicly accessible on its website for 16 years.
violations: Asker Kommune failed to establish adequate security measures to prevent confidential information from being publicly accessible on its website for 16 years.
No monitoring or audit procedures were in place to detect the ongoing exposure; a private citizen, not the municipality, discovered the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires a lawful basis for processing personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The publication of 127 citizens' national ID numbers and confidential information on the municipality's website had no lawful basis. No individual consented; no legal authority permitted such publication.
violations: The publication of 127 citizens' national ID numbers and confidential information on the municipality's website had no lawful basis. No individual consented; no legal authority permitted such publication.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed securely with integrity and confidentiality.
regulatoryFindings.description: Confidential data about vulnerable individuals (children, those with special needs, recipients of housing support) was exposed publicly without protection, violating the confidentiality principle.
violations: Confidential data about vulnerable individuals (children, those with special needs, recipients of housing support) was exposed publicly without protection, violating the confidentiality principle.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 requires controllers to implement accountability measures and adequate procedures to ensure compliance with GDPR.
regulatoryFindings.description: Asker Kommune had no procedures for sampling or auditing old postlists. Daily proofreading by two staff was inadequate and failed to prevent the 16-year breach.
violations: Asker Kommune had no procedures for sampling or auditing old postlists. Daily proofreading by two staff was inadequate and failed to prevent the 16-year breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: Offentlegforskrifta § 7 (Norwegian Public Disclosure Regulation) prohibits publishing national ID numbers and confidential personal information online.
regulatoryFindings.description: The municipality violated the specific Norwegian prohibition by exposing complete national ID numbers and confidential administrative records on the public internet.
violations: The municipality violated the specific Norwegian prohibition by exposing complete national ID numbers and confidential administrative records on the public internet.

outcome: Datatilsynet (Norwegian DPA) imposed a fine of NOK 1,000,000 (approximately USD 104,000) on Asker Kommune, payable to the state treasury. The municipality is required to: (1) immediately cease publication of protected personal data; (2) implement adequate technical and organisational security controls to prevent future breaches; (3) establish mandatory sampling and audit procedures for legacy postlists; (4) contact affected individuals. The decision is subject to appeal to Datatilsynet within three weeks, with further appeal to Personvernemnda (Privacy Board). The municipality acknowledged the breach, took down offending documents, and stated willingness to implement remedial measures.
companyNow: Asker Kommune remains a local government authority in Akershus county, Norway. Following the 2021 decision, the municipality has implemented enhanced data protection procedures and digital governance standards, though specific post-decision improvements are not detailed in this document.
dataType: Personal identification numbers (national ID/fødselsnummer), names, confidential administrative documents (special educational needs, housing benefits), family status information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Lack of valid processing basis
GDPR Art. 32 – Inadequate technical and organisational measures
Offentleglova § 10 and Offentlegforskrifta § 7 – Prohibition on publishing national ID numbers and confidential information online

companyDescription: Storstockholms Lokaltrafik (SL) is the publicly owned operator of public transportation (subway, commuter rail, bus, tram) across Stockholm region and surrounding areas, serving millions of daily commuters.
companyLongDescription: Storstockholms Lokaltrafik (SL) is the publicly owned operator of public transportation (subway, commuter rail, bus, tram) across Stockholm region and surrounding areas, serving millions of daily commuters.
caseDescription: SL deployed body-worn cameras on ticket inspectors to record passengers with both video and audio without adequate legal basis, transparency, or consent. The continuous pre-recording function (1 minute buffer) captured all transit users indiscriminately, including children, even when no violation or incident occurred. SL failed to provide meaningful information to the public before deployment.
companyWorth: Unknown (public authority/state-owned enterprise; not traded on stock exchange)
violationSummary: Systematic, continuous surveillance of identifiable persons in a public place they depend on (transit) with audio capture, a particularly sensitive form of monitoring. The pre-recording technique meant all-comers were monitored even before any wrongdoing occurred.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: SL equipped ticket inspectors with body cameras that continuously recorded video and audio with a one-minute buffer across Stockholm's entire transit network.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of transit-dependent commuters, including children, were secretly audio and video recorded in environments they could not avoid, with no legal basis.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pre-recording for 1 minute is necessary to capture events that arise suddenly during ticket control or hotfoul/violent situations, ensuring inspectors can preserve evidence.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vast majority of 1-minute buffers capture innocent passengers unrelated to any incident; IMY found 15 seconds maximally necessary and that this still captured excessive irrelevant persons.

claimsVsReality.claim: Audio recording is essential to understand what was said during disputes and threats, improving evidence quality.
claimsVsReality.reality: Audio was continuously captured in public transit spaces where passengers have no reasonable expectation of being recorded; IMY deemed audio particularly sensitive and inadequately disclosed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Badge on inspector uniforms constitutes adequate notice of video recording under Article 12.7 (standardized symbols).
claimsVsReality.reality: Badge did not clearly convey audio capture (marked as especially sensitive); it did not inform all passengers before they entered the surveillance zone; only those already approached by inspector would see it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Fare-evasion prevention and inspector safety are compelling interests justifying continuous surveillance of millions of transit-dependent users.
claimsVsReality.reality: ~30,000 fare violations annually from millions of trips; SL's own data showed ticket inspectors report fewer serious assaults post-camera, but balancing test showed commuters' privacy interest in exercising right to travel outweighed SL's administrative convenience.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: SL processed video and audio of millions of transit users without legal basis; pre-recording occurred before information was given to passengers
violations: SL processed video and audio of millions of transit users without legal basis; pre-recording occurred before information was given to passengers
Continuous 1-minute buffer capture of all persons in camera range violated transparency principle—passengers had no meaningful notice before being filmed

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires personal data be adequate, relevant, and not excessive in relation to the purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Pre-recording for 60 seconds captured vast numbers of uninvolved passengers, far exceeding what was necessary to identify fare evaders or document incidents
violations: Pre-recording for 60 seconds captured vast numbers of uninvolved passengers, far exceeding what was necessary to identify fare evaders or document incidents
All-day continuous recording with 1-minute buffer collected excessive data from innocent commuters unrelated to any violation

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) allows processing based on legitimate interest only if the data subject's fundamental rights and freedoms do not override the controller's interest, assessed through a balancing test.
regulatoryFindings.description: SL's interest in identifying fare evaders (≈30,000 annually from millions of trips) did not outweigh the massive intrusion on privacy of entire transit-dependent population including children
violations: SL's interest in identifying fare evaders (≈30,000 annually from millions of trips) did not outweigh the massive intrusion on privacy of entire transit-dependent population including children
Active recording during fare disputes and audio capture of intimate moments (confessions, anxiety, distress) in confined public spaces created severe privacy invasion disproportionate to SL's aims

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires data controller provide specified information to data subjects when personal data are obtained from them.
regulatoryFindings.description: Only passengers receiving a ticket fine received brief written notice; millions of other recorded passengers received zero information
violations: Only passengers receiving a ticket fine received brief written notice; millions of other recorded passengers received zero information
Badge on inspector uniforms inadequate—it did not inform that audio was being recorded (marked as particularly sensitive in Swedish law)
No clear notice before entering surveillance zone; passengers could not make informed choice to avoid transit system

outcome: IMY imposed a total administrative penalty of 16,000,000 SEK (€1.7M) divided as: 4M SEK for unlawful pre-recording and audio capture for assault prevention (overly excessive under Article 6.1(f) and 5.1(c)); 8M SEK for identity verification recordings (not necessary when ID shown, and audio capture unjustified); 4M SEK for failure to provide transparency information. IMY required SL to cease using pre-recording exceeding 15 seconds and to provide clear notice (signage) before surveillance zones. SL must modify badge and disseminate comprehensive information to all passengers. Decision is subject to appeal to Stockholm Administrative Court within 3 weeks.
companyNow: SL (Storstockholms Lokaltrafik) continues as the primary public transport operator for Stockholm region, owned by Region Stockholm. Following the decision, SL has begun implementing mandatory compliance measures including badge modifications and signage.
dataType: Video/image data, audio recordings, biometric identifiers (facial recognition), personal identifiers
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) – Legitimate Interest Test (failed balancing)
GDPR Article 13 – Information to Data Subject (failure to provide)

companyDescription: Support King, LLC (formerly SpyFone.com) is a Puerto Rico-based company that develops and sells mobile device monitoring software. The company marketed its products as tools for parental and employee monitoring but actively enabled stalking and domestic abuse through surreptitious surveillance capabilities.
companyLongDescription: Support King, LLC (formerly SpyFone.com) is a Puerto Rico-based company that develops and sells mobile device monitoring software. The company marketed its products as tools for parental and employee monitoring but actively enabled stalking and domestic abuse through surreptitious surveillance capabilities.
caseDescription: Support King sold surreptitious mobile device monitoring software (SpyFone) marketed for parental and employee monitoring, but actively enabled stalking and domestic abuse. The company failed to implement reasonable data security, resulting in a 2018 breach exposing approximately 2,200 consumers' sensitive data, and falsely claimed to have partnered with security firms and law enforcement to investigate.
violationSummary: SpyFone enabled systematic, surreptitious surveillance of device users without their knowledge or consent. The software was deliberately designed to hide from the monitored person, making it an intrusion into private communications and location data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: Support King sold SpyFone monitoring apps that secretly captured SMS messages, GPS locations, emails, photos.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 2,200 consumers' sensitive data including photos and GPS locations were exposed in an August 2018 breach, and stalkers.

claimsVsReality.claim: SpyFone cares about the integrity and security of your personal information. We will take all reasonable precautions to safeguard customer information, including encrypted personal information storage.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information including photos, text messages, web histories, and GPS locations were stored unencrypted on accessible servers. In August 2018, an unauthorized third party accessed the server, exposing data from approximately 2,200 consumers.

claimsVsReality.claim: SpyFone products are designed for monitoring children and employees.
claimsVsReality.reality: The products enabled surreptitious monitoring specifically designed to hide from the device user, with instructions to disable security warnings and hide the application. Stalkers and domestic abusers used SpyFone to monitor victims without consent, causing physical, emotional, financial, and social harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondents partnered with leading data security firms to assist in the investigation of the data breach and coordinated with law enforcement authorities.
claimsVsReality.reality: Respondents did not partner with any data security firms and did not work with or coordinate with law enforcement on any aspect of the unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents sold monitoring products enabling surreptitious surveillance without reasonable safeguards to prevent use for stalking and domestic abuse.
violations: Respondents sold monitoring products enabling surreptitious surveillance without reasonable safeguards to prevent use for stalking and domestic abuse.

Respondents represented they would take all reasonable precautions to safeguard customer information and encrypt personal data, but failed to encrypt data, restrict API access, or implement basic security controls.
Respondents represented they partnered with leading data security firms and coordinated with law enforcement following the August 2018 breach, but did neither.

outcome: On December 20, 2021, the FTC issued a complaint against Support King, LLC and Scott Zuckerman alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act based on unfair and deceptive practices. The complaint asserts that the company sold surreptitious monitoring software without adequate safeguards against misuse for stalking and abuse, failed to implement reasonable data security resulting in a breach, and made false representations about data encryption and breach response. The document does not indicate a settlement or final order, but represents the FTC's formal charges initiating enforcement proceedings.
companyNow: Support King, LLC operating as SpyFone.com remained active as of the complaint date (December 2021). No information is provided regarding current operational status, settlement, or closure following the complaint.
dataType: SMS messages, call history, GPS location, web history, contacts, photos, calendar, files, emails, video chats, social media activity, financial information, biometric data (microphone recordings)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: The Executive Office is the Northern Ireland government department. The Interim Advocate's Office was a temporary body established in August 2019 to support survivors of Historical Institutional Abuse pending establishment of a statutory commissioner.
companyLongDescription: The Executive Office is the Northern Ireland government department. The Interim Advocate's Office was a temporary body established in August 2019 to support survivors of Historical Institutional Abuse pending establishment of a statutory commissioner.
caseDescription: The Executive Office (via the Interim Advocate's Office) sent a newsletter email to 251 subscribers on 22 May 2020 with recipient email addresses visible to all recipients instead of using blind carbon copy. This exposed 209 email addresses, 110 of which contained individuals' full names, to unintended disclosure. The organisation lacked appropriate security measures, documented processes, staff training, and data protection policies to prevent the breach.
violationSummary: The incident involved unintended exposure of personal data (email addresses and names) to a wider audience than intended, making it a classic disclosure/exposure violation rather than a breach of confidentiality with intent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The Interim Advocate's Office sent a newsletter email to 251 subscribers with all recipient email addresses visible to every recipient by placing them in the 'To' field instead of using blind.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposure of 209 email addresses to all recipients breached the privacy of survivors of institutional childhood abuse, with 110 addresses containing full names.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IAO described itself at the time of reporting as an arm's length organisation, independent of the Executive Office
claimsVsReality.reality: Following legal advice on 11 December 2020, the Executive Office clarified that the IAO was a constituent part of the Executive Office with no separate legal basis, making the Executive Office the actual data controller

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires personal data to be processed with appropriate security including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures (integrity and confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to ensure appropriate security resulting in inappropriate disclosure of 209 email addresses to all newsletter recipients
violations: Failed to ensure appropriate security resulting in inappropriate disclosure of 209 email addresses to all newsletter recipients

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24(1) and (2) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure processing complies with the Regulation, with measures reviewed and updated where necessary, and data protection policies implemented where proportionate.
regulatoryFindings.description: No technical solution for group email sending (such as mail merge), no documented process for sending newsletters, no staff training on secure email procedures, inadequate data protection policies (only guidance in telephone induction pack)
violations: No technical solution for group email sending (such as mail merge), no documented process for sending newsletters, no staff training on secure email procedures, inadequate data protection policies (only guidance in telephone induction pack)

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1) and (2) requires the controller to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk, considering state of the art, costs, nature and scope of processing, and risks of destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure or access.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement security measures appropriate to the high-risk context of Historical Institutional Abuse data requiring maximum confidentiality, demonstrating insufficient consideration of data security and risks to data subject rights
violations: Failed to implement security measures appropriate to the high-risk context of Historical Institutional Abuse data requiring maximum confidentiality, demonstrating insufficient consideration of data security and risks to data subject rights

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to the Executive Office under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The organisation took immediate remedial steps including: notifying all affected individuals, providing emotional support, creating Newsletter Desk Instructions (8 July 2020), placing data protection responsibility under Executive Office's Data Protection Officer (1 July 2020), developing comprehensive data protection and information management policies, reviewing and updating the Data Protection Impact Assessment (July 2020), and sharing lessons learned across the Northern Ireland Civil Service (20 July 2020).
companyNow: The Interim Advocate's Office ceased to exist on 11 December 2020 when the Commissioner for Survivors of Institutional Childhood Abuse (COSICA) was established. The Executive Office remains the responsible data controller.
dataType: Email addresses, personal identifiers (names, initials)

companyDescription: Zoom Video Communications is a Delaware corporation founded in 2011 that provides cloud-based videoconferencing and collaboration services. As of early 2020, Zoom experienced explosive growth due to COVID-19 pandemic-driven demand for remote communication tools.
companyLongDescription: Zoom Video Communications is a Delaware corporation founded in 2011 that provides cloud-based videoconferencing and collaboration services. As of early 2020, Zoom experienced explosive growth due to COVID-19 pandemic-driven demand for remote communication tools.
caseDescription: Zoom made false and misleading claims about end-to-end encryption for video meetings when it actually lacked this capability. The company also used AES 128-bit encryption instead of the advertised 256-bit encryption, and stored meeting recordings unencrypted for up to 60 days. Additionally, Zoom secretly deployed software to bypass Safari browser security safeguards without user consent.
violationSummary: Zoom's failure to implement adequate security measures (weak encryption, unencrypted storage, secret surveillance bypass) directly enabled potential compromise of sensitive communications and personal data. The deception about encryption strength and end-to-end encryption compounded the insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Zoom falsely claimed to offer end-to-end encryption and 256-bit AES encryption for video meetings while actually using weaker 128-bit encryption.
whyTheyWereWrong: 3.8 million Mac users had a hidden web server secretly installed that bypassed Safari's security protections, exposing them to remote webcam surveillance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Zoom offers end-to-end encryption for all Zoom Meetings
claimsVsReality.reality: Zoom servers, including some in China, maintain cryptographic keys that allow Zoom to decrypt meeting content. Only Connector product (on-premises) supported true end-to-end encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: Meetings use AES 256-bit encryption
claimsVsReality.reality: Zoom actually used AES 128-bit encryption in ECB mode, which provides significantly less protection than 256-bit encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cloud Recordings are stored encrypted immediately after meetings end
claimsVsReality.reality: Recorded meetings remained unencrypted on Zoom servers for up to 60 days before being transferred to encrypted cloud storage.

claimsVsReality.claim: July 2018 Mac App update would fix minor bugs
claimsVsReality.reality: Update secretly deployed ZoomOpener web server that bypassed Safari browser protections, persisted after app deletion, and exposed users to RCE and DoS attacks.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Deceptively represented that Zoom Meetings used end-to-end encryption when Zoom servers maintained cryptographic keys allowing Zoom to access meeting content
violations: Deceptively represented that Zoom Meetings used end-to-end encryption when Zoom servers maintained cryptographic keys allowing Zoom to access meeting content
Deceptively claimed AES 256-bit encryption when actually using weaker AES 128-bit encryption in ECB mode
Falsely stated Cloud Recordings were stored encrypted immediately after meetings when recordings remained unencrypted on Zoom servers for up to 60 days
Secretly deployed ZoomOpener web server without adequate notice or consent to circumvent Apple Safari browser's privacy and security safeguard
Failed to disclose that ZoomOpener installation would bypass Safari protections, expose users to RCE and DoS attacks, and persist after app deletion

outcome: FTC issued a complaint alleging five counts of unfair and deceptive practices. The complaint alleges violations of FTC Act Section 5(a) and seeks compliance orders requiring Zoom to implement comprehensive information security improvements, submit to regular third-party security assessments, maintain an incident response plan, implement secure software development practices, and obtain express informed consent before deploying web servers or similar technologies.
companyNow: Zoom continues to operate as a major videoconferencing platform. The company has since updated its security practices and transparency disclosures in response to regulatory and public scrutiny.
dataType: video and audio communications, chat messages, screen sharing recordings, personal identifiers, location data, device and network technical information, health information, financial information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: SkyMed International, Inc. is a Nevada corporation headquartered in Scottsdale, Arizona that advertised and sold emergency travel medical evacuation insurance and membership plans nationwide, covering up to 18 emergency services (hospital-to-hospital transport, repatriation, medical escort, etc.) for travelers sustaining serious illness or injury.
companyLongDescription: SkyMed International, Inc. is a Nevada corporation headquartered in Scottsdale, Arizona that advertised and sold emergency travel medical evacuation insurance and membership plans nationwide, covering up to 18 emergency services (hospital-to-hospital transport, repatriation, medical escort, etc.) for travelers sustaining serious illness or injury.
caseDescription: SkyMed International collected extensive personal and health information from consumers purchasing emergency travel insurance but failed to implement reasonable security measures. The company displayed a deceptive HIPAA compliance seal despite lacking any third-party certification, and misrepresented the results of its investigation after 130,000 consumer records were exposed in an unsecured public cloud database for at least five months.
violationSummary: The primary violation involves failure to implement reasonable security measures (data stored in plain text, no access controls, no monitoring) leading to exposure of sensitive health information in a public cloud database. Secondary violations include Information Dissemination – Exposure (actual breach of 130,000 records) and deceptive practices regarding HIPAA compliance and incident response.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: SkyMed International collected thousands of consumers' sensitive health information including medications.
whyTheyWereWrong: An unsecured cloud database exposed approximately 130,000 consumers' complete health records linked to names, addresses, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Display of 'HIPAA Compliance' seal signified that government agency or third party had reviewed and approved SkyMed's information practices as meeting HIPAA requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: No government agency or third party ever reviewed SkyMed's information practices for HIPAA compliance. The seal was self-created and displayed without any certification or audit.

claimsVsReality.claim: In May 2, 2019 breach notification, SkyMed stated: 'There was no medical or payment-related information visible and no indication that the information has been misused.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The exposed cloud database contained health information fields including 'hospitalized,' 'hos_explanation,' 'prescription,' 'prescription_list,' and 'medical' linked to consumer names, DOBs, addresses, and other identifying data. SkyMed never examined the actual database contents to verify what was exposed.

claimsVsReality.claim: SkyMed's investigation determined that the exposure was limited to 'only a portion of our information' restricted to 'names, street and email addresses, phone and membership ID numbers.'
claimsVsReality.reality: SkyMed's investigation never examined what was actually stored in the database. Upon confirming the database existed and was public, SkyMed immediately deleted it without verifying the types or scope of data exposed, without identifying affected consumers, and without investigating other potential unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SkyMed displayed a 'HIPAA Compliance' seal on every website page from 2014–April 2019, falsely implying government or third-party review and certification of compliance, when no such review or certification had occurred.
violations: SkyMed displayed a 'HIPAA Compliance' seal on every website page from 2014–April 2019, falsely implying government or third-party review and certification of compliance, when no such review or certification had occurred.

SkyMed represented in its May 2, 2019 breach notification email that its investigation determined health information was neither stored on the exposed cloud database nor accessed by unauthorized parties, when the investigation never examined the database contents and could not verify these claims.

SkyMed failed to implement reasonable security measures (no written policies, no encryption, no access controls, no monitoring, no risk assessments, data stored in plain text), directly causing exposure of 130,000 records in a publicly accessible database for over 5 months, causing substantial and unavoidable injury to consumers.

outcome: FTC issued a complaint on January 26, 2021 alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act based on deceptive practices (HIPAA seal misrepresentation and misleading incident response communication) and unfair practices (failure to implement reasonable security). The complaint sought a compliance order requiring implementation of comprehensive information security standards, employee training, data inventory management, risk assessments, and periodic third-party security audits, along with monitoring and reporting provisions.
companyNow: Unknown – current operational status not disclosed in complaint document.
dataType: Health data, medical conditions, prescription medications, hospitalizations, personal identifiers (name, DOB, address, email, phone, passport number), payment card information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair and deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Regionstyrelsen Region Värmland is a Swedish regional public authority responsible for healthcare delivery and organisation in the Värmland region, with approximately 282,885 residents. It operates the 1177 healthcare advisory telephone line as a public health service.
companyLongDescription: Regionstyrelsen Region Värmland is a Swedish regional public authority responsible for healthcare delivery and organisation in the Värmland region, with approximately 282,885 residents. It operates the 1177 healthcare advisory telephone line as a public health service.
caseDescription: Region Värmland failed to inform patients calling the 1177 healthcare advisory line that their telephone numbers and municipality identifiers were being collected and transferred to a third-party healthcare provider (MedHelp AB). The region violated transparency requirements under GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 13 by not providing mandatory privacy disclosures to approximately 283,000 residents.
violationSummary: Failure to provide mandatory transparency disclosures (Article 13) at the point of collection left individuals unaware their health-related data was being processed, exposing them to loss of control and inability to exercise rights.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Collected telephone numbers and municipality IDs from approximately 283,000 callers to the 1177 healthcare advisory service without providing any information about data collection.
whyTheyWereWrong: Callers to 1177 were denied transparency about their personal data being collected and forwarded to a private contractor.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Värmland's website (1177.se) stated: 'It is your healthcare provider that is responsible for personal data being handled correctly and lawfully.'
claimsVsReality.reality: This generic statement did not satisfy GDPR Article 13 requirements. Callers were never told that Region Värmland (not just 'the healthcare provider') was the controller, nor were they informed about data collection of phone numbers/IDs, the specific purpose (routing to MedHelp), the legal basis, or their data rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: Region Värmland claimed it had a lawful basis under GDPR Article 6(1)(e) (public task) to collect and transfer phone numbers and municipality IDs.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the legal basis may have been valid, the complete absence of transparency disclosures violated the overarching fairness and transparency requirement in Article 5(1)(a) and the mandatory information provision in Article 13, regardless of legal basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Värmland processed telephone numbers and municipality IDs without disclosing to callers that data collection was occurring, violating the transparency principle.
violations: Region Värmland processed telephone numbers and municipality IDs without disclosing to callers that data collection was occurring, violating the transparency principle.
Absence of required Article 13 disclosures severely curtailed callers' ability to understand and exercise their data protection rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires the controller to provide comprehensive information when collecting personal data directly from the data subject, including controller identity, processing purposes, legal basis, and rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Region Värmland provided no information about being the data controller, the purposes of data collection/transfer, the legal basis for processing, or callers' rights to access/rectification.
violations: Region Värmland provided no information about being the data controller, the purposes of data collection/transfer, the legal basis for processing, or callers' rights to access/rectification.

Information on the 1177.se website did not satisfy Article 13 requirements; it only stated vaguely that 'your healthcare provider is responsible' without identifying the region as controller or explaining the 1177-specific data handling.

outcome: Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten (IMY, Sweden's Data Protection Authority) issued a decision on 7 June 2021 requiring Region Värmland to pay an administrative fine of 250,000 SEK. The authority found violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 13. Region Värmland has been implicitly ordered to implement proper transparency measures (Article 12) and ensure future callers receive mandatory disclosures at the point of collection. The region discontinued the MedHelp AB contract on 1 November 2019 and now operates 1177 services in-house. The decision is subject to appeal to the Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks of notification.
companyNow: Region Värmland continues to operate the 1177 healthcare advisory service in-house as of November 2019, having terminated the MedHelp AB outsourcing contract. The region is responsible for healthcare delivery across the Värmland area of Sweden.
dataType: Telephone numbers, commune identifiers, health/medical information (inferred from 1177 medical advisory calls)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency principle
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where personal data are collected from the data subject
GDPR Art. 12(1) – Clear and transparent communication to data subjects

companyDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. is a leading telecommunications provider in Spain, offering mobile, broadband, and fixed-line services. It operates as part of the Vodafone Group, a multinational telecom conglomerate.
companyLongDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. is a leading telecommunications provider in Spain, offering mobile, broadband, and fixed-line services. It operates as part of the Vodafone Group, a multinational telecom conglomerate.
caseDescription: Vodafone España improperly enrolled a customer in services without authorization and associated telephone lines with the customer's name but another person's data. The company failed to verify customer identity during account creation and did not respond to the data protection authority's information request, demonstrating lack of diligence in personal data handling.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement adequate verification procedures and safeguards allowed unauthorized processing of personal data belonging to both the customer and third parties. This represents a systematic failure in technical and organizational measures to secure data handling.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Vodafone associated a customer's telephone lines with another person's personal data and activated paid professional services without authorization or consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: A customer's identity was fraudulently linked to third-party data in Vodafone's systems, creating financial liability and exposing both the customer.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone's systems accurately maintained customer account information and service enrollments.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vodafone's systems contained telephone lines associated with the customer but showing third-party data, with unauthorized service enrollments and no proper identity verification controls.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone properly managed customer consent and contractual authorizations for services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vodafone enrolled the customer in Vodafone Professional services without authorization and failed to verify the customer's identity or obtain proper consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone cooperated with the data protection authority's investigation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vodafone did not respond to AEPD's information request issued March 17, 2021, despite confirmed delivery on March 18, 2021.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires personal data processing to be lawful on one of six grounds: consent, contract performance, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone processed the customer's personal data to create services (Vodafone Professional) without obtaining consent or having a valid contractual basis; the customer never authorized these services.
violations: Vodafone processed the customer's personal data to create services (Vodafone Professional) without obtaining consent or having a valid contractual basis; the customer never authorized these services.
Vodafone processed third-party data (another person's details) associated with the customer's telephone lines without any lawful basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security of personal data, including protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone failed to implement adequate identity verification procedures during account creation, allowing unauthorized service enrollments and data association with third parties.
violations: Vodafone failed to implement adequate identity verification procedures during account creation, allowing unauthorized service enrollments and data association with third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72(1)(a) classifies as very grave the processing of personal data without meeting any lawfulness condition in GDPR Article 6.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone's processing of customer and third-party data lacked any lawful basis, constituting a very grave infraction under Spanish data protection law.
violations: Vodafone's processing of customer and third-party data lacked any lawful basis, constituting a very grave infraction under Spanish data protection law.

outcome: Vodafone España paid €64,000 (a 20% reduction from the proposed €80,000 fine) on October 14, 2021, under Article 85 of the LPACAP voluntary payment provision. The payment terminates the procedure and constitutes a waiver of administrative remedies. The company did not formally admit responsibility but accepted the penalty as a reduced settlement. The procedure PS/00249/2021 was formally closed on October 4, 2021.
companyNow: Vodafone España remains a major telecom provider in Spain, operating as a subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc. Following this enforcement action, the company's compliance posture regarding customer identity verification and data lawfulness has been under regulatory scrutiny.
dataType: Personal identification data, telephone numbers, third-party data, service account information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 32 — Security of Processing (implied by lack of verification controls)
LOPDGDD Art. 72(1)(a) — Very Grave Infraction (processing without lawful basis)

companyDescription: PURPLE SEA ΜΟΝΟΠΡΟΣΩΠΗ ΙΚΕ is a small maritime or shipping-related company based in Piraeus, Greece, operating from a fourth-floor office in a multi-tenant building that houses only commercial tenants. The company employed a small number of staff.
companyLongDescription: PURPLE SEA ΜΟΝΟΠΡΟΣΩΠΗ ΙΚΕ is a small maritime or shipping-related company based in Piraeus, Greece, operating from a fourth-floor office in a multi-tenant building that houses only commercial tenants. The company employed a small number of staff.
caseDescription: PURPLE SEA installed and operated video surveillance cameras in office spaces including desks, conference rooms, and break rooms without proper legal basis, employee notification, or transparency. The company failed to establish legitimate security purposes or demonstrate accountability for the processing, violating core GDPR principles on lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, and accountability.
violationSummary: The company engaged in systematic collection of biometric data (facial images) from employees via video surveillance in workspace areas without establishing lawful basis, obtaining proper consent, or maintaining transparency, fitting the definition of surveillance in Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: PURPLE SEA installed and operated surveillance cameras in office workspaces including employee desks, conference rooms, and kitchen areas that continuously captured.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees were exposed to unlawful workplace surveillance with inadequate notice; the company falsely claimed cameras were disabled since 2008 while keeping them installed, powered.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cameras were installed in spring/summer 2008 only for security reasons when company members occasionally stayed overnight, and were deactivated before hiring employees.
claimsVsReality.reality: As of the 2021 decision, cameras were still physically installed, connected to live monitoring systems, and capable of transmitting images to display screens and recorders. Deactivation was only through software settings that could be easily reversed. Company never removed the hardware or informed employees of alleged 'deactivation'.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cameras cannot capture photographs and obtain only 'black screen' images due to system settings.
claimsVsReality.reality: System operator could take real-time 'printscreen' screenshots of live video feeds and reverse the 'blackening' setting at any time via recorder menu, as evidenced by photos submitted to the Authority. Image capture was technically feasible with a single configuration change.

claimsVsReality.claim: No monitoring screens exist and no employees have been recorded by the surveillance system.
claimsVsReality.reality: System operator (E) monitored all cameras from his personal computer screen, which served as a live monitoring display. The presence of installed, connected cameras in office spaces with live transmission to a monitored screen constitutes automatic processing and recording of personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Updated privacy notices inform employees of the CCTV system and their rights.
claimsVsReality.reality: Initial notices were generic and omitted required details (controller identity, specific purpose, data retention, employee rights). Updated notices were posted only after the investigation began, and did not remedy the years of unlawful processing that preceded them.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires processing to be lawful, fair, and transparent. Art. 5(2) requires the controller to demonstrate compliance (accountability principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: Company installed cameras without lawful basis assessment and failed to document internal compliance or communicate processing purposes to employees
violations: Company installed cameras without lawful basis assessment and failed to document internal compliance or communicate processing purposes to employees
Cameras remained installed since ~2008 and connected to live monitoring systems despite claims of being 'disabled', creating continuous collection and transmission of biometric data
Company provided only generic signage stating 'space is video recorded' without disclosing controller identity, lawful basis, data retention, or employee rights

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) (Purpose Limitation) requires that personal data be collected for specified, explicit, and legitimate purposes and not processed further in ways incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company cited vague 'security of persons and assets' but had not formally specified this as a purpose prior to installation
violations: Company cited vague 'security of persons and assets' but had not formally specified this as a purpose prior to installation
Cameras were installed in office spaces and break rooms where security monitoring of specific goods or equipment was not credible
Company reserved right to reactivate cameras if office use changed, treating them as general surveillance tools rather than addressing a documented security risk

regulatoryFindings.act: DPA Guideline 1/2011 Art. 7 prohibits surveillance in typical office spaces except in limited circumstances (entry/exit points, not general office areas or break rooms).
regulatoryFindings.description: Five cameras were positioned in office desks, conference rooms, and kitchen areas — all prohibited under the Guideline
violations: Five cameras were positioned in office desks, conference rooms, and kitchen areas — all prohibited under the Guideline
Company failed to conduct necessity assessment or proportionality analysis for each camera location
No evidence that less intrusive security measures were considered or exhausted

regulatoryFindings.act: Law 4624/2019 Art. 27(7) prohibits use of video surveillance data to evaluate employee productivity and requires employees be informed in writing of installation and operation.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to provide written notice to employees of the CCTV system's installation or operation
violations: Company failed to provide written notice to employees of the CCTV system's installation or operation
Despite claims cameras were disabled, company maintained the infrastructure and signage, creating ongoing expectation of surveillance

outcome: The DPA ordered PURPLE SEA to: (1) immediately remove all five cameras from office spaces (desks, conference rooms, kitchen) within one month and destroy all collected footage; (2) provide written notice to the DPA of compliance; and (3) pay an administrative fine of €15,000 for violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(b), and 5(2), and national law. The Authority found the company acted with negligence rather than intent but imposed sanctions as a deterrent and to enforce accountability. No criminal referral was made. Monitoring obligations may be imposed to ensure future compliance.
companyNow: Unknown current operational status. The company is subject to an active compliance order requiring camera removal and ongoing monitoring by the Greek DPA.
dataType: Biometric data (facial images from video surveillance)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, and transparency
GDPR Art. 6 – Lawful basis for processing
Law 4624/2019 Art. 27(7) – Greek national data protection law
DPA Guideline 1/2011 – Use of CCTV systems (Articles 7, 19)

companyDescription: Moss Municipality is a Norwegian local government authority formed on 1 January 2020 through the merger of the former municipalities of Moss and Rygge. It provides municipal services including healthcare, education and social services to residents in Akershus county.
companyLongDescription: Moss Municipality is a Norwegian local government authority formed on 1 January 2020 through the merger of the former municipalities of Moss and Rygge. It provides municipal services including healthcare, education and social services to residents in Akershus county.
caseDescription: Moss Municipality failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures when converting patient health data from a legacy system (HSPro) to CGM Journal following a municipal merger on 1 January 2020. The conversion resulted in multiple serious errors affecting approximately 2,000 individuals, including incorrect vaccine registrations, erroneous maternal health data, and unauthorised access to patient information by healthcare staff without legitimate need.
violationSummary: The failure to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures to maintain confidentiality, integrity and availability of health data during a large-scale system conversion directly constitutes insecurity under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Moss kommune converted 28,000 patient records from one health system to another without conducting risk assessments, data protection impact assessments, or adequate testing.
whyTheyWereWrong: 2,000 people's health records were corrupted: pregnant women were falsely classified as substance abusers, vaccine records were missing or incorrect.

claimsVsReality.claim: The municipality stated it had established a test environment with superuser testing and spot-checking of corrections before deployment to production.
claimsVsReality.reality: Testing was insufficient and inadequately documented; CGM confirmed inadequate testing was performed, and many errors went undetected until after production deployment, requiring corrective action from 7 February to 4 March 2020.

claimsVsReality.claim: The municipality initially assessed that the breach posed no high risk to data subjects' rights and freedoms.
claimsVsReality.reality: The breach directly compromised confidentiality (unauthorised access), integrity (corrupted records), and availability (incorrect data). 2,000 individuals' health records were affected, including false substance abuse classifications and missing critical medical information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(b) requires the controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Moss Municipality failed to implement adequate security measures during data conversion, resulting in patient data being made available to healthcare staff at a facility (Bredsand Rygge) without legitimate clinical need.
violations: Moss Municipality failed to implement adequate security measures during data conversion, resulting in patient data being made available to healthcare staff at a facility (Bredsand Rygge) without legitimate clinical need.
The conversion process introduced critical errors in vaccine registrations and maternal health data, compromising data integrity and accuracy for 2,000 individuals.
No testing regime with documented test scenarios was established prior to the conversion of sensitive health data, violating the requirement for regular testing and evaluation of security measures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1)(d) requires a process for regular testing, analysing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: The municipality conducted insufficient pre-conversion testing despite handling large volumes of sensitive health data. CGM (the processor) confirmed that adequate testing was not performed.
violations: The municipality conducted insufficient pre-conversion testing despite handling large volumes of sensitive health data. CGM (the processor) confirmed that adequate testing was not performed.
No formal test report documenting test scenarios and results was created to guide post-conversion verification or to establish a baseline for detecting errors.
Risk assessment and data protection impact assessment were not conducted prior to the migration, leaving the municipality unaware of potential failure modes.

outcome: Datatilsynet (Norwegian Data Protection Authority) imposed an administrative fine of 500,000 NOK on Moss Municipality for violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1)(b), and 32(1)(d). The fine was issued on 4 June 2021 and originally set higher but reduced following the municipality's response of 21 January 2021. The municipality was required to address the violations and implement corrective measures. The municipality has a three-week appeal period from receipt of the decision, with appeal submitted to Datatilsynet and potentially escalated to the Personal Data Protection Board (Personvernnemnda) if Datatilsynet upholds its decision. Compliance deadline is four weeks after the appeal period expires if no appeal is filed.
companyNow: Moss Municipality continues to operate as a Norwegian local government authority. Following the merger with Rygge in January 2020, it serves approximately 32,000 residents in the Akershus region. The municipality has implemented remedial measures to prevent similar breaches.
dataType: Health data, patient records, vaccination records, pregnancy monitoring data, substance abuse information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 32(1)(b) – ensuring confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems
GDPR Art. 32(1)(d) – regular testing, analysis and evaluation of security measures

companyDescription: Aquateknikk AS is a Norwegian water technology and industrial equipment company based in Varhaug. The company conducts routine credit checks on potential customers and suppliers as part of normal business due diligence.
companyLongDescription: Aquateknikk AS is a Norwegian water technology and industrial equipment company based in Varhaug. The company conducts routine credit checks on potential customers and suppliers as part of normal business due diligence.
caseDescription: Aquateknikk AS obtained credit information about a competing business owner without any legal basis under GDPR Article 6. The company credit-checked a private individual with whom it had no relationship, violating the lawfulness principle. Datatilsynet (Norwegian Data Protection Authority) imposed a fine and required remedial internal controls.
violationSummary: The company systematically obtained financial/credit data about an individual without their knowledge or consent, using credit information systems to monitor a competitor's financial status without legal justification.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Aquateknikk AS obtained detailed credit information about a private individual competitor without legal basis, consent, or any business relationship with that person.
whyTheyWereWrong: The competitor had no relationship with Aquateknikk and had no reasonable expectation that his private financial data—including credit scores, payment history.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed the credit check of the individual was a legitimate business due diligence check of a potential supplier company where the individual was owner, CEO and managing director.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Bisnode system logs showed Aquateknikk first credit-checked the company, then credit-checked the individual 5 minutes later with no contractual relationship. The individual was a competitor with no legitimate business reason to be checked separately.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it 'aborted' the search when it realised the error and deleted the credit information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bisnode logs proved the full credit profile was retrieved and processed. The company's assertion of aborting the search was not credible based on system records.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it had no prior violations and took the matter seriously by developing new procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bisnode logs showed the company regularly (frequently) credit-checked private individuals during 2018-2020, indicating systemic practice without lawful basis, not a one-off mistake.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires all personal data processing to be lawful, fair and transparent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aquateknikk obtained credit information without any lawful basis under Article 6(1). The individual had no customer, supplier or contractual relationship with the company and no reasonable expectation his financial data would be retrieved.
violations: Aquateknikk obtained credit information without any lawful basis under Article 6(1). The individual had no customer, supplier or contractual relationship with the company and no reasonable expectation his financial data would be retrieved.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) permits processing based on legitimate interest only where the interest is lawful, clearly defined, real, substantive, and after balancing outweighs data subject privacy interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: No legitimate interest existed. The individual competed with Aquateknikk and was a stranger to the company. Privacy interest in financial data is especially high for unrelated individuals. Any claimed competitive intelligence interest did not outweigh privacy protection.
violations: No legitimate interest existed. The individual competed with Aquateknikk and was a stranger to the company. Privacy interest in financial data is especially high for unrelated individuals. Any claimed competitive intelligence interest did not outweigh privacy protection.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24 requires organisations to establish adequate internal controls and policies to ensure lawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aquateknikk had no written procedures, training, or governance for credit information retrieval. Employees could freely credit-check anyone without documented legal basis review.
violations: Aquateknikk had no written procedures, training, or governance for credit information retrieval. Employees could freely credit-check anyone without documented legal basis review.

outcome: Datatilsynet imposed two remedies: (1) Monetary penalty of 100,000 NOK (approximately USD 11,000) for unlawful credit information retrieval; (2) Compliance order requiring Aquateknikk to develop and implement documented internal controls describing when and why credit information may be obtained, with examples of lawful use cases and procedures for legal basis verification. The company was ordered to complete remediation within 4 weeks of final decision or complaint expiry. The decision is subject to appeal to Personvernemnda (Norwegian Data Protection Board).
companyNow: Aquateknikk AS remains operational. The company acknowledged the breach, apologised, and committed to implementing corrective internal controls. Economic impact from COVID-19 pandemic was considered in penalty mitigation.
dataType: Financial data, credit rating, payment history, debt information

company: Dixons South East Europe Α.Ε.Β.Ε. - ΚΩΤΣΟΒΟΛΟΣ (Kotsovolos) and Εθνική Τράπεζα της Ελλάδος (National Bank of Greece)
companyDescription: Kotsovolos is a Greek electronics and consumer goods retailer founded in the early 20th century, now operating as part of the Dixons group. The National Bank of Greece is the country's oldest and largest commercial bank, established in 1842.
companyLongDescription: Kotsovolos is a Greek electronics and consumer goods retailer founded in the early 20th century, now operating as part of the Dixons group. The National Bank of Greece is the country's oldest and largest commercial bank, established in 1842.
caseDescription: A retail electronics company (Kotsovolos) and the National Bank of Greece failed to properly respond to a customer's data access requests under GDPR Article 15. The customer sought confirmation of a payment maturity request his bank card issuer had received, but both entities either refused or ignored his lawful requests without proper justification or response.
companyWorth: Kotsovolos parent company (Currys/Dixons Carphone) ~£500M; National Bank of Greece ~€1.2B market cap
violationSummary: Both entities failed to provide the data subject with access to information concerning the processing of his personal data, denying him transparency and control over his financial records as required by GDPR Article 15.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Kotsovolos refused to disclose internal correspondence with the bank regarding card payment maturation, claiming it was 'internal communication,'.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer was unable to verify whether his payment maturation request was actually submitted to the bank.

claimsVsReality.claim: Kotsovolos: 'The communication with the bank is internal communication and cannot be shared.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The correspondence contained the customer's personal financial data and directly concerned his transaction, making it subject to his GDPR access rights regardless of whether it was labeled 'internal.'

claimsVsReality.claim: Kotsovolos: 'We provided all necessary information and the customer knew the submission date from our communications.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer never received clear confirmation of the actual date the maturation request was sent, the specific bank recipient, or proof of delivery—information necessary for him to exercise further rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: National Bank: 'The customer's inquiry concerned consumer complaint procedures, not a GDPR data access request.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer explicitly requested confirmation of whether the bank had received a maturation request and sought information about data processing, constituting a lawful GDPR Article 15 request regardless of framing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of whether personal data concerning them is being processed, and to receive a copy of that data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kotsovolos refused to provide the customer with a copy of its correspondence with the bank regarding the maturation request, falsely claiming it was 'internal communication' not subject to disclosure.
violations: Kotsovolos refused to provide the customer with a copy of its correspondence with the bank regarding the maturation request, falsely claiming it was 'internal communication' not subject to disclosure.
The National Bank of Greece completely failed to acknowledge or respond to the customer's written data access request submitted on 6 July 2020, violating the obligation to respond within one month.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) establishes the accountability principle, requiring controllers to demonstrate compliance with data protection rules at all times.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kotsovolos did not have a documented policy or procedure for handling data access requests via social media (Facebook Messenger), resulting in an incomplete and inadequate response.
violations: Kotsovolos did not have a documented policy or procedure for handling data access requests via social media (Facebook Messenger), resulting in an incomplete and inadequate response.
Kotsovolos failed to provide adequate staff training to recognize and properly handle GDPR subject rights requests submitted through non-traditional channels.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12 requires controllers to take appropriate measures to facilitate the exercise of data subject rights without undue delay and at no cost.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kotsovolos delayed responding for months and only provided the requested document after the DPA's hearing, not in response to the original request.
violations: Kotsovolos delayed responding for months and only provided the requested document after the DPA's hearing, not in response to the original request.
The National Bank provided no response whatsoever, failing to either grant or properly deny the access request with adequate reasoning.

outcome: The Greek Data Protection Authority (DPA) found both Kotsovolos and the National Bank of Greece violated GDPR Article 15 (right of access) in conjunction with Articles 5(2), 12(1)–(3). The DPA imposed administrative fines of €20,000 on each entity. Kotsovolos was ordered to ensure future compliance by updating its internal data access policies to include alternative submission channels (including social media) and retraining staff. The National Bank was required to establish proper procedures for acknowledging and responding to all data access requests. Both entities must submit proof of compliance measures to the DPA.
companyNow: Kotsovolos operates as a subsidiary of Dixons Carphone (later Currys) and continues as a major electronics retailer in Greece. The National Bank of Greece remains one of Greece's largest financial institutions.
dataType: Financial transaction data, credit card transaction records, customer purchase history and payment information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 12(1)–(3) – Facilitating exercise of rights

company: ΚΑΡΙΕΡΑ ΜΟΝΟΠΡΟΣΩΠΗ ΑΝΩΝΥΜΗ ΕΤΑΙΡΕΙΑ ΤΕΧΝΟΓΝΩΣΙΑΣ ΕΠΙΜΕΛΕΙΑΣ, ΕΜΠΟΡΙΚΗΣ ΠΡΟΩΘΗΣΗΣ ΚΑΙ ΕΚΜΕΤΑΛΛΕΥΣΗΣ ΕΙΔΙΚΩΝ ΕΚΔΟΣΕΩΝ (KARIERA A.E.)
companyDescription: KARIERA A.E. is a Greek-based online job portal and recruitment platform offering job listings, job seeker profiles, and employer services. The company operates the website kariera.gr and processes personal data of job candidates and recruiters.
companyLongDescription: KARIERA A.E. is a Greek-based online job portal and recruitment platform offering job listings, job seeker profiles, and employer services. The company operates the website kariera.gr and processes personal data of job candidates and recruiters.
caseDescription: KARIERA, a Greek job portal, failed to delete user personal data when explicitly requested despite multiple deletion requests. A technical error created duplicate email records; the company did not detect the error or promptly fix it, causing 79 users' data to remain in marketing systems for six months. The company only corrected the issue after the data protection authority intervened.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures (Art. 25) to ensure personal data deletion requests were properly processed and verified across all systems. The technical vulnerability (duplicate database entries) exposed users to continued unwanted marketing despite clear deletion requests.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: KARIERA continued sending marketing emails to a user who explicitly requested deletion four times.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users who exercised their right to be forgotten were instead harassed with continued marketing communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed it had established procedures to manage deletion requests, including a ticketing system and confirmation mechanisms.
claimsVsReality.reality: The procedures did not work in practice: deletion requests were processed in the master database but failed to propagate to the email marketing database due to a technical error that went undetected for six months.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company attributed the continued emails to a one-time technical error in database synchronization.
claimsVsReality.reality: The error persisted for six months (not one-time) and affected at least 79 data subjects. The company's lack of verification procedures and failure to detect complaints about unsubscribe failures (5 recorded complaints) revealed systemic deficiencies in data deletion processes.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company represented that it responds 'immediately' to user objections and deletion requests.
claimsVsReality.reality: Response took months despite multiple requests; the complainant sent deletion requests on multiple dates (with specific ticketing submission on one date, confirmation received weeks later), and continued receiving marketing emails afterwards for an unknown additional period.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 17(1) requires controllers to erase personal data without undue delay when the data subject requests deletion, particularly when the data subject objects to processing for direct marketing.
regulatoryFindings.description: KARIERA failed to delete the complainant's email address from marketing databases despite four explicit deletion requests over several months.
violations: KARIERA failed to delete the complainant's email address from marketing databases despite four explicit deletion requests over several months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 21(2) grants data subjects an unconditional right to object to processing of their personal data for direct marketing purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: KARIERA continued sending marketing emails to the user after he objected, because the company did not properly honour the objection due to technical failures.
violations: KARIERA continued sending marketing emails to the user after he objected, because the company did not properly honour the objection due to technical failures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 25(1) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure that personal data processing meets the regulation's requirements and protects data subjects' rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: KARIERA did not maintain proper procedures to verify that deletion requests were executed across all databases. A duplicate database entry error went undetected for six months, affecting 79 users. The company only identified the problem and 5 unresponded complaints after the authority's investigation.
violations: KARIERA did not maintain proper procedures to verify that deletion requests were executed across all databases. A duplicate database entry error went undetected for six months, affecting 79 users. The company only identified the problem and 5 unresponded complaints after the authority's investigation.

outcome: Greek Data Protection Authority (DPA) imposed a €5,000 administrative fine on KARIERA. The authority found violations of Articles 17, 21, and 25 of the GDPR. KARIERA acknowledged the technical issue and represented that after the intervention it: (1) identified and corrected the duplicate entry error, (2) deleted all affected users' data retroactively, (3) committed to simplifying internal deletion procedures to reduce response time significantly, and (4) continues developing new systems to improve data management efficiency. The company is now subject to compliance monitoring.
companyNow: KARIERA A.E. continues to operate as a Greek job portal. As of 2019 (latest available data in the decision), the company had annual revenue of €4,202,734.53 and post-tax profits of €879,150.88. No information on current status is provided.
dataType: Email addresses, user contact details, preferences, professional profiles
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 21(2) – Right to object to direct marketing
GDPR Article 25(1) – Data protection by design and by default

companyDescription: St. Olavs Hospital HF is a public university hospital in Trondheim, Norway, operating under the Helse Midt-Norge regional health authority. It provides tertiary and specialist care across multiple disciplines including cardiology, psychiatry, and addiction medicine.
companyLongDescription: St. Olavs Hospital HF is a public university hospital in Trondheim, Norway, operating under the Helse Midt-Norge regional health authority. It provides tertiary and specialist care across multiple disciplines including cardiology, psychiatry, and addiction medicine.
