caseDescription: St. Olavs Hospital failed to implement adequate access controls and logging on servers storing sensitive patient health data, leaving ~21,000 cardiac reports and psychiatric/addiction treatment records accessible to all authenticated users across the regional health authority for 2–9 years. No logs existed to detect whether staff had improperly accessed the data. The hospital was ordered to pay 750,000 NOK for violations of security and internal control requirements.
violationSummary: The hospital failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures (access controls, logging, monitoring) required to protect health data against unauthorized access and to maintain accountability. This is a classic 'insecurity' violation under the Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: St. Olavs Hospital HF failed to implement adequate access controls and logging on file servers storing approximately 21,000 patient health reports.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 21,000 patients' highly sensitive health information including psychiatric treatment details, cardiac procedures.

claimsVsReality.claim: St. Olavs Hospital had access control procedures in place for data handling.
claimsVsReality.reality: Procedures existed on paper but were not followed in practice. All authenticated users in the region could access restricted patient data, and in at least one case, passwords were stored in plaintext.

claimsVsReality.claim: Test servers and temporary storage folders were secured during system upgrades.
claimsVsReality.reality: Test servers retained ~21,000 cardiac patient reports in folders intended to be 'temporary'; they were never deleted over a 9-year period and remained accessible to any regional user who knew how to search for them.

claimsVsReality.claim: The hospital could detect and investigate unauthorized access to patient data.
claimsVsReality.reality: No logging was implemented for two of the three incident types, making it impossible to determine whether staff had accessed sensitive patient information.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to achieve a security level appropriate to the risk, including confidentiality, integrity, availability, and robustness; and Art. 32(1)(d) requires regular testing and assessment of security measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: St. Olavs Hospital failed to restrict access to shared folders containing patient data; no access controls were properly applied despite procedures existing on paper.
violations: St. Olavs Hospital failed to restrict access to shared folders containing patient data; no access controls were properly applied despite procedures existing on paper.
No logging was implemented or monitored on two of three file areas, making it impossible to detect unauthorized access or data exfiltration.
Access control rules were breached during system upgrades; test servers and temporary folders were not deleted; database passwords were stored in plaintext.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24 imposes on the data controller the responsibility for and ability to demonstrate compliance with data protection principles and requirements.
regulatoryFindings.description: St. Olavs Hospital lacked a complete processing protocol (Art. 30) at the time of the incidents, preventing management from having oversight of all personal data handling.
violations: St. Olavs Hospital lacked a complete processing protocol (Art. 30) at the time of the incidents, preventing management from having oversight of all personal data handling.
The hospital lacked tailored access control rules for data stored outside the main patient journal (for quality assurance), even though all three incidents involved such off-journal storage.

regulatoryFindings.act: Patient Journal Act § 22 requires technical and organisational measures appropriate to risk, including access controls, logging, and subsequent monitoring.
regulatoryFindings.description: Access control routines were not followed; authentication was applied, but actual permission-level segregation was absent.
violations: Access control routines were not followed; authentication was applied, but actual permission-level segregation was absent.
Logging was absent or incomplete, preventing audit trails necessary to fulfill the 'subsequent control' requirement.

regulatoryFindings.act: Patient Journal Act § 23 requires the controller to implement measures to ensure and demonstrate that processing complies with GDPR, the Data Protection Act, and this law, and to document these measures and make them available to staff and supervisors.
regulatoryFindings.description: St. Olavs Hospital's documented procedures did not cover quality-assurance data storage outside the journal, creating a gap in the control framework that enabled the incidents.
violations: St. Olavs Hospital's documented procedures did not cover quality-assurance data storage outside the journal, creating a gap in the control framework that enabled the incidents.

outcome: Datatilsynet found St. Olavs Hospital HF liable for breaches of GDPR Articles 5(1)(f), 24, and 32, and Patient Journal Act §§ 22 and 23. The hospital was ordered to pay 750,000 NOK (approximately €100,500 or $110,000 USD) by 20 September 2021. In response, the hospital implemented immediate remedial actions: (1) deleted compromised files and reviewed all systems with shared folders; (2) restricted access to delet folders to only staff with a legitimate need; (3) implemented new password routines, login attempt limits, and monitoring/log analysis systems; (4) developed a formal processing protocol per GDPR Art. 30 using the Norwegian health sector 'Normen' template; (5) restricted server access via Remote Desktop to administrators with documented operational need. The decision is subject to appeal within three weeks; if upheld, the matter may be referred to the Privacy Appeals Board (Personvernnemnda).
companyNow: St. Olavs Hospital HF remains a major teaching hospital affiliated with the Norwegian University of Science and Technology (NTNU) and serves as a regional tertiary care centre in Trøndelag. Following the 2021 enforcement action, the hospital has continued to strengthen its information security and data governance practices.
dataType: Health data, patient records, medical procedures, cardiac imaging, psychiatric treatment records, pulse oximetry measurements
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 24 – Data controller's responsibility for compliance

companyDescription: Voice Integrate Nordic AB is a Swedish software development company that provides call handling and recording solutions for contact centres, including the development of the 'Biz' call recording platform used by MedHelp's 1177 healthcare advice line.
companyLongDescription: Voice Integrate Nordic AB is a Swedish software development company that provides call handling and recording solutions for contact centres, including the development of the 'Biz' call recording platform used by MedHelp's 1177 healthcare advice line.
caseDescription: Voice Integrate Nordic AB, a software development company, stored 2.7 million recorded telephone calls from Sweden's 1177 healthcare advice line on a network-connected storage server without encryption or access controls. A security misconfiguration exposed the server to the internet, making stored recordings of sensitive health consultations accessible to anyone with internet access for an unknown duration until discovered by a journalist on 18 February 2019.
violationSummary: The core harm is unauthorised exposure of personal data (health records) to the public via an internet-facing server without security controls. This fits 'Exposure' in the Solove taxonomy — unintended but massive public disclosure of sensitive information due to inadequate technical safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Voice Integrate Nordic AB stored 650,000 to 900,000 recorded healthcare consultation calls on a network-accessible server that became publicly exposed to the internet due to a misconfigured.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients calling 1177 for health advice had their sensitive medical information, names, and personal details exposed without protection to anyone on the internet for an unknown period.

claimsVsReality.claim: Voice stated that inspelningar (call recordings) skulle ha lagrats hos Voice ('call recordings should not have been stored at Voice').
claimsVsReality.reality: In reality, MedHelp transferred 2.7 million call files to Voice's NAS server starting in 2013 after MedHelp's own servers crashed; by February 2019, 650,000–900,000 calls were stored there and exposed online.

claimsVsReality.claim: Voice claimed it was not a data processor (personuppgiftsbiträde) under GDPR.
claimsVsReality.reality: Voice's formal Data Processor Agreement with MedHelp (signed May 2018), combined with Voice's documented role in recording, storing, and managing healthcare call files, established it as a clear data processor under GDPR Art. 4(8).

claimsVsReality.claim: Voice stated the server was 'passiv' (passive) and was not intended to store customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Voice's internal documentation and activity logs confirm it had assigned a public IP address and public domain to the storage server, and MedHelp had been actively uploading files to it for six years.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1) requires data processors and data controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including encryption, maintaining confidentiality and integrity, and resilience of processing systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: Voice stored 650,000–900,000 recorded healthcare calls on a network-connected NAS server without encryption, access controls, or login credentials.
violations: Voice stored 650,000–900,000 recorded healthcare calls on a network-connected NAS server without encryption, access controls, or login credentials.
A misconfiguration of Apache web server software exposed the storage server directly to the internet, making all files accessible to anyone with internet access.
Voice failed to segregate or firewall the storage server from public-facing networks, leaving sensitive health data unprotected for months.
No evidence of regular security testing, vulnerability assessments, or monitoring procedures existed to detect or prevent the exposure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(2) requires that when determining appropriate security measures, particular regard be given to risks of unauthorised destruction, loss, alteration, or unauthorised disclosure of or access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Voice did not conduct a risk assessment considering the sensitive nature of health data or the risk of internet-facing storage exposure.
violations: Voice did not conduct a risk assessment considering the sensitive nature of health data or the risk of internet-facing storage exposure.
No compensating controls (e.g. encryption, IP whitelisting, network segmentation) were implemented despite the server being reachable from the public internet.

outcome: On 7 June 2021, Sweden's data protection authority (Integritetsskyddsmyndigheten, IMY) issued a final decision finding Voice Integrate Nordic AB liable as a data processor for failure to secure personal data in breach of GDPR Art. 32(1). IMY imposed an administrative penalty of 650,000 SEK (approximately €62,272 USD). Voice was ordered to pay the fine. IMY concluded that Voice acted responsibly once it discovered the breach on 18 February 2019 by shutting down the server and implementing firewall rules to block internet access; however, this did not mitigate the seriousness of the prior months-long exposure. The authority rejected Voice's argument that it was not a data processor, finding that Voice's contracts with MedHelp (the data controller) and its role in recording, storing and managing call files clearly established processor status. The decision is final unless appealed to the Stockholm Administrative Court within three weeks.
companyNow: Voice Integrate Nordic AB appears to remain in operation as a private software development company based in Kista, Stockholm. The company specializes in call centre telephony solutions and recording systems. No public records indicate closure or significant corporate restructuring following the 2021 enforcement action.
dataType: Health data, personal identifiers (name, address, contact information), audio recordings of healthcare consultations, sensitive personal data per GDPR Art. 9
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 32(1) – Duty of data processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security of personal data
GDPR Art. 32(2) – Obligation to assess and mitigate risks of unauthorised disclosure or access to personal data
GDPR Art. 4(8) – Definition of data processor and attendant security responsibilities

companyDescription: West Mercia Police is a territorial police force in England serving approximately 1.3 million residents across four counties. Between March 2012 and March 2020, it shared IT infrastructure and functions with Warwickshire Police under a Strategic Alliance to achieve operational efficiencies.
companyLongDescription: West Mercia Police is a territorial police force in England serving approximately 1.3 million residents across four counties. Between March 2012 and March 2020, it shared IT infrastructure and functions with Warwickshire Police under a Strategic Alliance to achieve operational efficiencies.
caseDescription: West Mercia Police and Warwickshire Police, acting as joint data controllers, erroneously decommissioned a server on 21 June 2021 containing Warwickshire Police application data spanning November 2001 to early 2014. The deletion was irreversible. The decommissioning resulted from inadequate security procedures, outdated documentation, and failure to cross-check systems before removal, violating obligations to maintain appropriate security of law enforcement data.
violationSummary: The case exemplifies 'Information Processing – Insecurity' under the Solove taxonomy because the organisation failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures, resulting in accidental destruction of sensitive law enforcement personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: West Mercia Police decommissioned a server on 21 June 2021 containing 13 years of Warwickshire Police law enforcement data without adequate verification.
whyTheyWereWrong: Unsanitised law enforcement records including officer names and identities, criminal allegations, previous convictions.

claimsVsReality.claim: The server was marked by the KCOM project as ready for decommissioning and had been unused since March 2016.
claimsVsReality.reality: The server was actively in use with outstanding user tickets; documentation was not updated since the original 2016 move and was out of date. An active IT ticket raised by a user would have flagged the system for retention but was missed due to the cut-down decommissioning process.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ITSS decommissioning process provided adequate security safeguards for sensitive law enforcement data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The process lacked mandatory attendance, record-keeping, cross-system verification, and failed to enforce mandatory IT ticket review, resulting in the permanent destruction of 13 years of unsanitised criminal records affecting 55,195 individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 40 of the Data Protection Act 2018 requires that personal data processed for law enforcement purposes must be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security using appropriate technical or organisational measures, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: West Mercia Police failed to ensure appropriate security of Warwickshire Police law enforcement data, resulting in permanent destruction of 13 years of records containing unsanitised logs with source details, officer information, criminal allegations, and risk assessments affecting 55,195 individuals.
violations: West Mercia Police failed to ensure appropriate security of Warwickshire Police law enforcement data, resulting in permanent destruction of 13 years of records containing unsanitised logs with source details, officer information, criminal allegations, and risk assessments affecting 55,195 individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 66(1) of the Data Protection Act 2018 requires each controller and processor to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risks arising from processing personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: The ITSS decommissioning process was inadequate: documentation incorrectly marked the server unused since March 2016 without update verification; no cross-checking between applications and server details occurred; a cut-down decommissioning process pre-approved final removal without reviewing all outstanding IT tickets; POTLS attendance was non-mandatory and unrecorded, allowing a critical user ticket flagging the system for retention to be missed.
violations: The ITSS decommissioning process was inadequate: documentation incorrectly marked the server unused since March 2016 without update verification; no cross-checking between applications and server details occurred; a cut-down decommissioning process pre-approved final removal without reviewing all outstanding IT tickets; POTLS attendance was non-mandatory and unrecorded, allowing a critical user ticket flagging the system for retention to be missed.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to West Mercia Police for violations of sections 40 and 66(1) of the Data Protection Act 2018. The Commissioner acknowledged remedial steps taken, including an internal investigation and replacement of the POTLS process with the Change Advisory Board (CAB) under the subsequent Hosted Services Agreement (October 2021 to March 2022). Both forces subsequently gained independent IT infrastructures and IT services. No monetary fine was issued.
companyNow: West Mercia Police continues as a territorial police force covering Shropshire, Herefordshire, Worcestershire, and Warwickshire. As of March 2022, the force operates with independent IT infrastructure following the conclusion of shared services arrangements with Warwickshire Police.
dataType: Criminal records, source information, officer details, risk assessments, allegations, convictions, cautions, personal relationships and associations
legalBasisViolated: Data Protection Act 2018, Section 40 (sixth data protection principle – appropriate security of law enforcement data)
Data Protection Act 2018, Section 66(1) (controllers and processors must implement appropriate technical and organisational measures)

companyDescription: VfB Stuttgart 1893 AG is a German professional football club based in Stuttgart, Baden-Württemberg. The club operates youth football academies and maintains extensive member databases.
companyLongDescription: VfB Stuttgart 1893 AG is a German professional football club based in Stuttgart, Baden-Württemberg. The club operates youth football academies and maintains extensive member databases.
caseDescription: VfB Stuttgart AG failed to maintain adequate accountability and documentation of its data processing activities as required by GDPR Article 5(2). The club's data protection governance was deficient, lacking proper records and procedures to demonstrate compliance with data protection obligations. The enforcement action resulted in a €300,000 fine and required the organization to implement significant organizational and technical improvements.
violationSummary: The violation concerned inadequate organizational and technical measures to ensure accountability in data processing, which falls under the information processing category of insecurity—failure to implement safeguards for personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: VfB Stuttgart 1893 AG failed to maintain proper records and accountability documentation for data processing activities as required under GDPR Article 5(2).
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' personal data was processed without documented procedures or accountability measures, exposing their information to processing without demonstrable safeguards or transparency regarding.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) requires that the controller be responsible for, and be able to demonstrate, compliance with the principles of lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimization, accuracy, integrity and confidentiality, and accountability.
regulatoryFindings.description: VfB Stuttgart AG failed to maintain adequate records and documentation demonstrating compliance with data protection obligations
violations: VfB Stuttgart AG failed to maintain adequate records and documentation demonstrating compliance with data protection obligations
The organization lacked proper accountability procedures and governance structures for data processing activities

outcome: Der Landesbeauftragte für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit Stefan Brink closed the proceedings and issued a fine of €300,000 for negligent violation of the accountability obligation under GDPR Article 5(2). In addition to the monetary penalty, VfB Stuttgart AG agreed to implement significant organizational and technical improvements to its data protection management, including enhanced training and documentation procedures. The club also committed to promoting data protection awareness among young people through the 'Datenschutz geht zur Schule' project and specialized training for youth football teams (U10-U21). The investigation concluded with this settlement.
companyNow: VfB Stuttgart 1893 AG is a professional German sports club. Following the enforcement action, the organization has implemented structural data protection improvements and participates in public data protection education initiatives.
dataType: Member personal data

companyDescription: One Way Private Company is a call center operator providing outbound telemarketing and promotional services for Greek utility and commercial clients, including ZENITH gas company.
companyLongDescription: One Way Private Company is a call center operator providing outbound telemarketing and promotional services for Greek utility and commercial clients, including ZENITH gas company.
caseDescription: One Way Private Company, operating as a call center processor for ZENITH gas company, made illegal promotional telephone calls to subscribers who had registered their numbers on the national do-not-call registry (Article 11 register). Due to a systemic error and employee negligence, the company failed to automatically exclude registered numbers from calling lists, resulting in over 1.5 million unlawful calls during November 2020–February 2021.
violationSummary: The company conducted systematic unsolicited promotional calls to individuals who had explicitly opted out, constituting surveillance and unwanted collection of attention/engagement without consent.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: One Way Private Company made promotional telephone calls to approximately 1.5 million phone numbers registered on Greece's national do-not-call registry between November 2020.
whyTheyWereWrong: Subscribers who registered on the do-not-call registry made clear they did not want promotional calls, yet received unsolicited calls anyway, causing harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: One Way claimed it maintained proper processes compliant with Law 3471/2006 and GDPR, with appropriate safeguards and organizational measures in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company operated a partially manual exclusion process dependent on employee action; a single employee's failure to activate the automated filter resulted in 1.5+ million unlawful calls over three months.

claimsVsReality.claim: One Way characterized the violations as 'purely systemic error' with no intent or negligence on its part.
claimsVsReality.reality: An employee's documented negligence in failing to enable the exclusion mechanism, combined with the absence of supervisory controls to prevent or detect the omission, demonstrates organizational failure in security procedures.

claimsVsReality.claim: ZENITH claimed it had provided strict instructions, conducted audits, and delegated compliance responsibility to the processor.
claimsVsReality.reality: ZENITH's audit on 13 February 2020 was insufficient; the company did not identify the systemic gap in automated exclusion and did not provide specific corrective guidance after receiving complaints, relying on general oversight.

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 3471/2006 Article 11(2): Unsolicited calls for direct marketing are prohibited unless the subscriber has explicitly opted in, or permitted via opt-out if the subscriber has not declared objection to receipt of such calls.
regulatoryFindings.description: One Way made calls to subscribers registered on the Article 11 opt-out register, violating the prohibition on calls to those who had explicitly declared non-consent.
violations: One Way made calls to subscribers registered on the Article 11 opt-out register, violating the prohibition on calls to those who had explicitly declared non-consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 28(3)(c): A processor must only process personal data on written instructions of the controller and must apply appropriate technical and organizational measures per Article 32.
regulatoryFindings.description: One Way failed to implement the automated exclusion mechanism required by its processing contract with ZENITH, resulting in systematic calls to blacklisted numbers despite contractual obligations.
violations: One Way failed to implement the automated exclusion mechanism required by its processing contract with ZENITH, resulting in systematic calls to blacklisted numbers despite contractual obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1), (2), (4): Processors must apply appropriate technical and organizational security measures; both controller and processor are responsible for ensuring staff process data only on instruction.
regulatoryFindings.description: One Way's exclusion process was manual and not fully automated; employee negligence prevented activation of the exclusion mechanism, and no supervisory controls were in place to catch the omission.
violations: One Way's exclusion process was manual and not fully automated; employee negligence prevented activation of the exclusion mechanism, and no supervisory controls were in place to catch the omission.

outcome: The Authority (APDPPC) imposed a fine of €30,000 on One Way Private Company for violations of GDPR Articles 28 and 32 in connection with the insecure processing of telephone numbers and failure to implement required safeguards. ZENITH received a reprimand (Επίπληξη) under GDPR Article 28(3) for inadequate oversight of the processor's security measures. One Way was ordered to implement automated exclusion procedures and to place all complainants on its do-not-call register. No further calls have occurred to the registered numbers following remediation.
companyNow: One Way Private Company remains in operation as a call center service provider. The company implemented automated exclusion procedures post-enforcement to prevent recurrence of similar violations.
dataType: Telephone numbers, personal phone numbers

companyDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. is a Spanish subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc, one of the world's largest telecommunications companies. It provides mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services to millions of customers in Spain.
companyLongDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. is a Spanish subsidiary of Vodafone Group plc, one of the world's largest telecommunications companies. It provides mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services to millions of customers in Spain.
caseDescription: Vodafone Spain processed personal data (name, DNI, address) of a customer without lawful basis when two prepaid phone lines were contracted in his name by a third party through an unauthorized distributor. The company failed to maintain adequate documentation to prove valid consent or legitimate basis for the processing and could not properly verify the customer's identity at point of sale.
violationSummary: Vodafone's failure to maintain adequate identity verification procedures and documentation created conditions enabling identity usurpation. Processing occurred without demonstrated lawful basis under Article 6.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Vodafone contracted two prepaid phone lines in a customer's name through a distributor without obtaining valid consent or verifying the customer's identity or authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: A third party was able to fraudulently impersonate the customer and activate phone services in his name, exposing him to identity theft, unauthorized billing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone asserted the distributor (Disashop) bore responsibility for the contract terms and customer verification.
claimsVsReality.reality: As the controller responsible for lawful processing, Vodafone remained liable regardless of distributor involvement. No contractual delegation exempts a controller from Article 6 obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone stated lines were 'dadas de alta' (activated) on specified dates with customer data on file.
claimsVsReality.reality: No signed contracts, consent documents, or identity verification records existed in Vodafone's systems. Documentation available was unsigned and did not prove customer authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that personal data processing is lawful only if it meets at least one specified condition: (a) the data subject has given consent for processing; or (b) processing is necessary for contract execution or precontractual measures at the data subject's request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone processed the complainant's personal data (name, surname, DNI) in relation to two prepaid phone line contracts without documented consent from the data subject and without valid contractual basis.
violations: Vodafone processed the complainant's personal data (name, surname, DNI) in relation to two prepaid phone line contracts without documented consent from the data subject and without valid contractual basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) establishes the accountability principle: the controller is responsible for compliance with paragraph 1 and must be capable of demonstrating it.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone lacked documentation evidencing lawful basis for processing. No signed contracts, consent forms, or identity verification records were retained. Controller could not prove compliance with lawfulness requirements despite having processed the data.
violations: Vodafone lacked documentation evidencing lawful basis for processing. No signed contracts, consent forms, or identity verification records were retained. Controller could not prove compliance with lawfulness requirements despite having processed the data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(5)(a) provides that violations of basic processing principles (Articles 5, 6, 7, 9) shall be sanctioned with administrative fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover (whichever is higher).
regulatoryFindings.description: Infraction of Article 6(1) regarding lawfulness of processing classified as very serious violation under Spanish LOPDGDD Article 72.1(b), subject to administrative sanctions.
violations: Infraction of Article 6(1) regarding lawfulness of processing classified as very serious violation under Spanish LOPDGDD Article 72.1(b), subject to administrative sanctions.

outcome: On 15 November 2021, AEPD initiated a sanction procedure proposing a €70,000 fine. Vodafone paid €56,000 on 23 December 2021, exercising the 20% voluntary payment reduction under LPACAP Article 85(2). The payment carried waiver of all administrative remedies. On the date of the termination resolution, the procedure was closed. No structural remedies or ongoing monitoring were imposed beyond implicit compliance requirements.
companyNow: Vodafone Spain remains a major telecommunications provider in Spain, operating as part of Vodafone Group plc. The company continues mobile and broadband services across the Spanish market.
dataType: Name, surname, national ID number (DNI), postal address

caseDescription: A political candidate made unsolicited marketing telephone calls to voters during the 2019 Greek national election campaign without checking opt-out registers or obtaining prior consent. The candidate failed to properly handle a data subject's access request. The calls violated Greece's electronic communications privacy law and GDPR data subject rights provisions.
violationSummary: The candidate disclosed/contacted individuals' personal phone numbers for political marketing without proper consent or opt-out verification, and failed to facilitate data subject rights (access request).
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A political candidate made unsolicited promotional phone calls to voters' personal mobile phones without checking telecom provider opt-out registers or obtaining prior consent before the July.
whyTheyWereWrong: Voters received unwanted calls promoting the candidate without their permission, and the candidate failed to exclude phone numbers from mandatory opt-out registries.

claimsVsReality.claim: The phone numbers were maintained in a large electoral list compiled over many years, and the complainant may have registered voluntarily or through a relative/friend.
claimsVsReality.reality: No evidence was provided that the complainant had affirmatively consented. The candidate did not check opt-out registers required by law before calling.

claimsVsReality.claim: The contact details were in the candidate's electoral list and had been verified and updated by her office before the campaign.
claimsVsReality.reality: Verification does not constitute consent, and the candidate made no attempt to exclude numbers on the mandatory opt-out register.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 requires a data controller to facilitate and respond to data subject access requests within one month, providing information about processing without unwarranted delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: The political candidate did not properly satisfy the complainant's right of access request, failing to provide clear information about whether phone calls had been made to her number or confirm whether she had refused communication.
violations: The political candidate did not properly satisfy the complainant's right of access request, failing to provide clear information about whether phone calls had been made to her number or confirm whether she had refused communication.

regulatoryFindings.act: Law 3471/2006 Article 11(2) prohibits unsolicited direct marketing calls with human intervention unless the subscriber has declared they do not wish to receive such calls, requiring maintenance of opt-out registries by telecom providers.
regulatoryFindings.description: The candidate made political marketing calls without demonstrating she had obtained opt-out registers from telecom providers to exclude subscribers who had opted out, and without providing evidence she called only numbers with affirmative consent.
violations: The candidate made political marketing calls without demonstrating she had obtained opt-out registers from telecom providers to exclude subscribers who had opted out, and without providing evidence she called only numbers with affirmative consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) and guidance on political communication require that processing for legitimate interests be necessary and proportionate, with proper safeguards including respect for opt-out preferences.
regulatoryFindings.description: The candidate failed to implement required procedures to exclude opted-out phone numbers before placing marketing calls, and did not inform calees about their rights (access right).
violations: The candidate failed to implement required procedures to exclude opted-out phone numbers before placing marketing calls, and did not inform calees about their rights (access right).

outcome: The Data Protection Authority of Greece (DPA) imposed a fine of €2,000 on the political candidate for violations of GDPR Article 15 (failure to properly satisfy the data subject's right of access) and Law 3471/2006 Article 11 (making unsolicited marketing calls without checking opt-out registers or obtaining prior consent). The fine was determined to be effective, proportionate, and deterrent. The decision requires the candidate to comply with opt-out verification procedures and properly handle future access requests. The candidate must implement procedures to ensure phone numbers are checked against telecom provider opt-out registries before any marketing calls are made.
dataType: Contact information, phone numbers, personal contact details

companyDescription: Direktionen för Räddningstjänsten Östra Skaraborg is a Swedish municipal fire and emergency services authority (kommunalförbund) operating across eight fire stations in the Östra Skaraborg region (Skövde, Mariestad, Hjo, Tibro, Karlsborg, Hova, Gullspång, and Töreboda). It is responsible for rescue operations, disaster prevention, and emergency response within its jurisdiction.
companyLongDescription: Direktionen för Räddningstjänsten Östra Skaraborg is a Swedish municipal fire and emergency services authority (kommunalförbund) operating across eight fire stations in the Östra Skaraborg region (Skövde, Mariestad, Hjo, Tibro, Karlsborg, Hova, Gullspång, and Töreboda). It is responsible for rescue operations, disaster prevention, and emergency response within its jurisdiction.
caseDescription: A Swedish fire department conducted continuous 24/7 video surveillance of eight fire stations' equipment halls, including the area where staff changed into emergency gear. The surveillance captured employees in intimate situations—in undergarments or partially clothed—without adequate privacy safeguards or masking of the sensitive changing area. The organization lacked clear policies governing who could access the footage and when, violating GDPR principles of fairness, data minimization, and security.
violationSummary: The organization engaged in continuous, systematic video surveillance of employees in privacy-sensitive settings (changing areas) without appropriate technical or organizational safeguards, directly implicating surveillance-based privacy violations under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Operated continuous 24/7 camera surveillance across eight fire stations' equipment halls, including areas where employees changed into emergency gear.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees in dependent working relationships were systematically recorded in undergarments and underclothing during mandatory uniform changes.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization stated that continuous 24/7 surveillance was necessary to achieve its operational objectives (leadership capability, presence verification, vehicle selection, staff welfare checks, physical security).
claimsVsReality.reality: The fire department acknowledged that surveillance was only operationally necessary during active emergency alarms, not 24/7, yet maintained continuous monitoring. Additionally, one station (Tibro) did not automatically monitor the changing area due to misconfiguration, yet that station's operations were reported as 'less efficient'—undermining the necessity claim.

claimsVsReality.claim: No employees ever appeared naked or in only undergarments; staff could choose to wear undergarments under emergency gear without any functional loss.
claimsVsReality.reality: The changing room was filmed without masking or screening. Employees described arriving in the middle of the night during emergency calls in robes with no or minimal clothing underneath, and the fire department's own policies prohibited being naked in facilities except designated changing rooms—indicating the surveillance created pressure to expose intimate areas during rapid changes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Appropriate access controls and limited viewer populations mitigated privacy risks.
claimsVsReality.reality: 29 individuals across the organization (6 shift commanders, 16 supervisors/chiefs, 7 maintenance technicians) had potential access to real-time footage, but zero formal policies, guidelines, or instructions existed specifying who could view footage, when, or for what purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully and fairly, with appropriate balance between the controller's legitimate interests and the privacy rights of data subjects.
regulatoryFindings.description: Fire department captured employees in intimate situations (undergarments, underclothing) during emergency gear changes without masking or screening the changing area, rendering the surveillance unfair and disproportionate despite operational necessity for real-time coordination during emergency calls.
violations: Fire department captured employees in intimate situations (undergarments, underclothing) during emergency gear changes without masking or screening the changing area, rendering the surveillance unfair and disproportionate despite operational necessity for real-time coordination during emergency calls.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) mandates that personal data be adequate, relevant, and not excessive in relation to the purposes for which they are processed.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization operated 24/7 continuous surveillance despite acknowledging that monitoring was needed only during active emergency alarms, and failed to mask or segregate the employee changing area, thereby collecting far more personal data than necessary.
violations: Organization operated 24/7 continuous surveillance despite acknowledging that monitoring was needed only during active emergency alarms, and failed to mask or segregate the employee changing area, thereby collecting far more personal data than necessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires that organizations implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure security proportionate to the risks of processing, including protection against unauthorized access.
regulatoryFindings.description: 29 individuals had potential access to real-time footage in the operations center, but no formal policies, guidelines, or instructions existed governing who could view footage, when, or under what circumstances, creating risk of unauthorized viewing of intimate imagery.
violations: 29 individuals had potential access to real-time footage in the operations center, but no formal policies, guidelines, or instructions existed governing who could view footage, when, or under what circumstances, creating risk of unauthorized viewing of intimate imagery.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(4) requires that organizations ensure individuals processing personal data do so only on instruction from the data controller.
regulatoryFindings.description: Without written guidelines, the fire department could not demonstrate or ensure that staff viewing real-time surveillance footage—particularly sensitive footage of employees changing—were doing so only as authorized and necessary for emergency coordination.
violations: Without written guidelines, the fire department could not demonstrate or ensure that staff viewing real-time surveillance footage—particularly sensitive footage of employees changing—were doing so only as authorized and necessary for emergency coordination.

outcome: The Swedish Data Protection Authority (IMY) determined the fire department violated GDPR articles 5(1)(a), 5(1)(c), 32(1), and 32(4). IMY issued a compliance order requiring the organization to cease the surveillance and implement privacy-protective measures if resuming monitoring. The department paid a 350,000 SEK administrative fine (€37,625 USD equivalent). The camera surveillance was discontinued on 6 May 2021, before the decision was issued. No remediation beyond payment and cessation has been publicly documented.
companyNow: Direktionen för Räddningstjänsten Östra Skaraborg (Eastern Skaraborg Fire Service Authority) continues to operate as a public emergency service in Sweden. As of the decision, the organization has discontinued the surveillance system entirely and must reassess any future monitoring against GDPR requirements.
dataType: Biometric (facial recognition in video), video footage, location data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness and fairness principle
GDPR Art. 32(1) – Appropriate technical and organizational security measures
GDPR Art. 32(4) – Instructions for personal data processing

companyDescription: Vivint Smart Home, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Provo, Utah, providing smart home security devices, automation equipment, and related monitoring services. The company operates a large door-to-door seasonal sales force and offers financing through both internal retail installment contracts (RICs) and third-party bank partnerships (Vivint Flex Pay).
companyLongDescription: Vivint Smart Home, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Provo, Utah, providing smart home security devices, automation equipment, and related monitoring services. The company operates a large door-to-door seasonal sales force and offers financing through both internal retail installment contracts (RICs) and third-party bank partnerships (Vivint Flex Pay).
caseDescription: Vivint Smart Home used deceptive schemes called 'white paging' and impermissible co-signers to bypass credit checks and qualify unqualified customers for financing. Sales representatives obtained third-party credit reports without permission and used them fraudulently to approve loans. When customers defaulted, innocent third parties were pursued by debt collectors for debts they never incurred.
violationSummary: Consumer credit reports obtained and used without permission; innocent third parties' personal information disclosed to debt collectors without consent, causing direct financial and reputational harm.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Vivint sales representatives systematically obtained third-party credit reports without permission using 'white paging' (pulling credit scores of similarly-named strangers).
whyTheyWereWrong: Innocent individuals whose credit information was misused were pursued by debt collectors for Vivint accounts they never opened or knew about, damaging their credit scores.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vivint's software system limited running credit inquiries to only two consumers per address.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sales representatives circumvented this control by modifying the sale location address slightly (adding 'BLDG 1' or 'Apartment A' after the street address), allowing unlimited inquiries on a single address until a consumer 'passed' credit.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vivint took meaningful action after discovering 'white paging' in 2016; hundreds of sales representatives were terminated in early 2017.
claimsVsReality.reality: Vivint later rehired many terminated representatives and allowed those from high-revenue sales teams to work at the company's sister company for a year before returning. Controls were easily circumvented and practices continued through 2020.

claimsVsReality.claim: Internal controls and employee monitoring prevented identity theft.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple Vivint employees warned managers since at least 2017 that sales representatives continued to evade prevention measures. Company was aware of back-end analysis revealing white-paging and impermissible co-signer issues but allowed practices to continue.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vivint permitted sales representatives to systematically obtain consumer credit reports for unrelated third parties without permission and use them to fraudulently qualify unqualified customers for financing, deceiving both the credit system and the customers themselves.
violations: Vivint permitted sales representatives to systematically obtain consumer credit reports for unrelated third parties without permission and use them to fraudulently qualify unqualified customers for financing, deceiving both the credit system and the customers themselves.

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 604(f) restricts use of consumer reports to permissible purposes and requires truthful certification of purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vivint obtained credit reports for third parties with no permissible purpose; the reports were obtained solely to circumvent software credit-check limitations, which is not an authorized purpose under FCRA Section 604(a).
violations: Vivint obtained credit reports for third parties with no permissible purpose; the reports were obtained solely to circumvent software credit-check limitations, which is not an authorized purpose under FCRA Section 604(a).

regulatoryFindings.act: Red Flags Rule 16 C.F.R. § 681.1(d) requires financial institutions and creditors to develop and implement a written Identity Theft Prevention Program designed to detect, prevent, and mitigate identity theft.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vivint failed to develop a written Identity Theft Prevention Program until January 2020, despite awareness of 'white paging' since at least 2016. The Company allowed the practice to continue despite internal warnings and retaliation against whistleblowing employees.
violations: Vivint failed to develop a written Identity Theft Prevention Program until January 2020, despite awareness of 'white paging' since at least 2016. The Company allowed the practice to continue despite internal warnings and retaliation against whistleblowing employees.

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 615(e) requires creditors to have policies and procedures to detect and respond to red flags indicating identity theft.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vivint did not identify or respond appropriately to obvious red flags: multiple credit inquiries for same address, accounts opened with third-party names and addresses, and known patterns of fraud among sales teams. Terminated offending reps were rehired.
violations: Vivint did not identify or respond appropriately to obvious red flags: multiple credit inquiries for same address, accounts opened with third-party names and addresses, and known patterns of fraud among sales teams. Terminated offending reps were rehired.

outcome: Complaint for civil penalties, permanent injunction, and other relief filed April 29, 2021 in U.S. District Court for District of Utah. Plaintiff (United States) seeks: (A) judgment for each violation; (B) permanent injunction preventing future violations; (C) rescission, reformation, restitution, refund of monies, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains; (D) monetary civil penalties up to $4,111 per knowing FCRA violation constituting pattern or practice; (E) costs of action and such other relief as court deems just and proper. Document filed indicates complaint stage; final judgment and penalty amount not yet determined.
companyNow: Vivint remains operational as of 2021 as a home security and smart home technology provider serving over 1.5 million customers in the United States and Canada. Following the FTC complaint, the company was required to implement compliance measures.
dataType: consumer credit reports, personal financial information, names, addresses
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) — unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604(f) — permissible purpose requirement
Red Flags Rule 16 C.F.R. § 681.1(d) — identity theft prevention program requirement
FCRA Section 615(e) — duties regarding detection, prevention, and mitigation of identity theft

company: PREMIUMMEDIA ΠΑΡΑΓΩΓΗ ΟΠΤΙΚΟ-ΑΚΟΥΣΤΙΚΩΝ ΕΡΓΩΝ ΙΔΙΩΤΙΚΗ ΚΕΦΑΛΑΙΟΥΧΙΚΗ ΕΤΑΙΡΙΑ (PREMIUMMEDIA ΙΚΕ)
companyDescription: PremiumMedia is a Greek media production company that operates the monopoli.gr website, which hosts theatrical contests and sends newsletters to participants.
companyLongDescription: PremiumMedia is a Greek media production company that operates the monopoli.gr website, which hosts theatrical contests and sends newsletters to participants.
caseDescription: PremiumMedia sent unwanted marketing emails and failed to honour unsubscribe requests. When a user repeatedly attempted to opt out from newsletters, a technical malfunction in the unsubscribe function prevented compliance. The company did not manually remove the user despite receiving his complaints, violating his right to object to direct marketing.
violationSummary: The company continued processing personal data (email address) for direct marketing despite the data subject's explicit objection, constituting unauthorised dissemination of unwanted communications.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Sent repeated unsolicited marketing emails to a subscriber who attempted multiple times to unsubscribe through a malfunctioning unsubscribe function that the company failed to repair immediately.
whyTheyWereWrong: The subscriber was trapped receiving unwanted promotional emails for over one month despite exercising his right to opt-out, causing him to file a complaint.

claimsVsReality.claim: The unsubscribe function malfunctioned unintentionally during a system upgrade and was fixed as soon as detected.
claimsVsReality.reality: The unsubscribe function was disabled on 15 December 2019 but remained non-functional until 18 January 2020—33 days—despite the user reporting it on 10 January. Even after the technical fix, the company did not manually remove the user until 31 January.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only the complainant was affected by the unsubscribe malfunction.
claimsVsReality.reality: 592 other users also attempted to unsubscribe during the 15 December 2019–18 January 2020 period and were unable to do so, indicating a systemic failure affecting hundreds.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company immediately resolved the technical problem upon learning of it.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the technical fix was applied on 18 January 2020, the complainant's manual removal did not occur until 31 January 2020, despite multiple complaints and explicit objections.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 21(3) requires that when a data subject objects to direct marketing processing, their personal data shall no longer be processed for those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: PremiumMedia continued sending marketing emails to the complainant after he explicitly objected, and failed to honour his unsubscribe request despite his repeated attempts over multiple months.
violations: PremiumMedia continued sending marketing emails to the complainant after he explicitly objected, and failed to honour his unsubscribe request despite his repeated attempts over multiple months.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 25(1) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure compliance with data protection principles, including effective processing interruption mechanisms.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's unsubscribe mechanism was disabled during a system update on 15 December 2019 and remained broken until 18 January 2020. No monitoring procedures were in place to detect the failure, and the company did not manually process the objection after learning of it.
violations: The company's unsubscribe mechanism was disabled during a system update on 15 December 2019 and remained broken until 18 January 2020. No monitoring procedures were in place to detect the failure, and the company did not manually process the objection after learning of it.

regulatoryFindings.act: Greek Law 3471/2006 Article 11 requires prior explicit consent for unsolicited electronic communications, and mandates that easy opt-out mechanisms be provided in every message.
regulatoryFindings.description: The unsubscribe function was non-functional during the relevant period, and when the user contacted the company to report the problem, the company failed to manually remove him, resulting in 592 other users also experiencing unsubscribe failures during that window.
violations: The unsubscribe function was non-functional during the relevant period, and when the user contacted the company to report the problem, the company failed to manually remove him, resulting in 592 other users also experiencing unsubscribe failures during that window.

outcome: PremiumMedia was found to have violated the data subject's right to object under GDPR Article 21(3) and failed to implement adequate organisational measures under Article 25(1). The company was ordered to pay an administrative fine of €5,000 and must ensure compliance with data protection requirements. The company subsequently implemented dual unsubscribe options (in header and footer of newsletters), automatic confirmation of unsubscribe success, and weekly monitoring of the unsubscribe function to prevent future failures.
companyNow: The company cooperated with the investigation and implemented remedial measures including enhanced unsubscribe mechanisms and weekly technical audits. Current status unknown.
dataType: Email address, personal data submitted for contests

companyDescription: The Department of National Defence (DND) is Canada's federal military department responsible for the Canadian Armed Forces, operating the military justice system including summary trials.
companyLongDescription: The Department of National Defence is a Canadian federal government institution that oversees the Canadian Armed Forces and administers military justice through a two-tiered tribunal structure. It operates summary trials and court martial proceedings to adjudicate violations of the Code of Service Discipline by military members. The DND is subject to the Privacy Act and must balance constitutional open court principles with privacy protections for individuals.
caseDescription: A former military member alleged that he was wrongfully compelled to publicly disclose personal medical information during an open military summary trial. The Privacy Commissioner found the complaint not well-founded, determining that the disclosure was consistent with the Privacy Act because it occurred during a public court proceeding pursuant to the National Defence Act and the open courts principle.
violationSummary: While the complainant alleged unauthorized disclosure of sensitive medical information, the Privacy Commissioner determined this fell within permitted disclosures under Privacy Act sections 8(2)(a) and 8(2)(b) for information disclosed in authorized tribunal proceedings that are public by constitutional principle. The core issue involved disclosure of personal information, though ultimately no violation was found.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Department of National Defence compelled a former military member to publicly disclose personal medical information during an open summary trial to defend himself against an AWOL charge.
whyTheyWereWrong: The former soldier was forced to reveal private medical details in a public courtroom without being informed of confidentiality options or offered private hearing alternatives.

claimsVsReality.claim: DND claimed that the Privacy Act cannot override the constitutional open courts principle and that disclosure was lawful under sections 8(2)(a) and 8(2)(b) of the Privacy Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the Privacy Commissioner upheld DND's legal position, the former soldier suffered real harm: his private medical condition was disclosed publicly without his advance knowledge of consequences or offer of confidentiality protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: DND stated that individuals are entitled to request confidentiality from the presiding officer and that the complainant failed to do so.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant was not proactively informed of his right to request confidentiality or the implications of public disclosure before being forced to testify about his medical condition.

claimsVsReality.claim: DND asserted that summary trials are public by default under the open courts principle with only limited exceptions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant was ordered to disclose sensitive medical information in open court without being advised of alternatives, privacy safeguards, or the permanent public nature of court testimony.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Personal information under control of government institution can only be disclosed with individual's consent or pursuant to authorized exceptions
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainant alleged wrongful public disclosure of medical information without consent during summary trial
violations: Complainant alleged wrongful public disclosure of medical information without consent during summary trial

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Sections 8(2)(a) and 8(2)(b) – Government institution may disclose information for authorized purposes or pursuant to Act of Parliament
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosure occurred in authorized tribunal proceeding under National Defence Act and was consistent with open courts principle
violations: Disclosure occurred in authorized tribunal proceeding under National Defence Act and was consistent with open courts principle

regulatoryFindings.act: National Defence Act Section 163 – Presiding officer authorized to receive evidence relevant to determining if accused committed offences
regulatoryFindings.description: Medical information provided as evidence in authorized legal proceeding
violations: Medical information provided as evidence in authorized legal proceeding

regulatoryFindings.act: Queen's Regulations and Orders Section 108.28 – Summary trials shall be public with limited exceptions; discretion to exclude public in certain circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainant did not request confidentiality; presiding officer did not exclude public or clear court
violations: Complainant did not request confidentiality; presiding officer did not exclude public or clear court

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found the complaint not well-founded and concluded there was no contravention of the Privacy Act. The disclosure of medical information during the public summary trial was consistent with sections 8(2)(a) and 8(2)(b) of the Privacy Act because it was authorized testimony provided in a quasi-judicial proceeding pursuant to the National Defence Act and the constitutionally protected open courts principle. Once disclosed in open court, the information became publicly available under section 69(2), removing Privacy Act restrictions. However, the Commissioner recommended that the Department of National Defence implement measures to ensure participants in summary trials are advised in advance that disclosed information is publicly available and of any processes to protect personal information from disclosure.
companyNow: The DND continues to operate the Canadian military justice system, conducting summary trials as the primary forum for service discipline matters.
dataType: Medical/health information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Consent requirement for disclosure
Privacy Act Section 8(2)(a) – Disclosure for authorized purposes
Privacy Act Section 8(2)(b) – Disclosure pursuant to Act of Parliament
Privacy Act Section 69(2) – Publicly available information exemption
National Defence Act Section 163 – Summary trial authority
Queen's Regulations and Orders Section 108.28 – Public summary trials

companyDescription: Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) is a federal government department responsible for employment insurance, Canada Pension Plan, and related social programs.
companyLongDescription: ESDC is a Canadian federal department that administers employment and social development programs including Employment Insurance, the Canada Pension Plan, and labour standards. Operating under the Privacy Act, the department manages personal information from millions of Canadians and must comply with strict privacy requirements. ESDC maintains office facilities across Canada, including the Guy Favreau Complex in Montreal, equipped with security surveillance systems.
caseDescription: Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) used video surveillance footage obtained for security purposes to monitor an employee's departure times during a fact-finding exercise, without the employee's consent and in violation of the Privacy Act. The department failed to inform employees about the location of cameras and collection purposes, and used the personal information for purposes inconsistent with the original collection rationale.
violationSummary: The surveillance footage was originally collected for security purposes but was repurposed to verify an employee's work hours and departure times during an administrative verification, which constitutes a secondary use beyond the original collection purpose without consent or exemption.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: ESDC accessed security video surveillance footage to monitor an employee's departure times during a fact-finding exercise without consent or proper authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee was unaware cameras existed or their purposes, and faced potential disciplinary action based on video evidence obtained through surveillance intended only for building security,.

claimsVsReality.claim: Video surveillance access was essential with no other reliable means to verify allegations of early departures.
claimsVsReality.reality: Less privacy-invasive alternatives existed, such as questioning the employee, consulting other managers, or requesting the employee to attest to his attendance records.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Passport Canada Surveillance Policy authorized the Departmental Security Officer to approve video surveillance use for administrative purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Passport Canada policy applies only to Passport Canada offices and requires signage in both official languages informing employees of surveillance—neither of which existed at the employee's workplace.

claimsVsReality.claim: The use was comparable to the Murdoch case involving CBSA enforcement of time fraud through video surveillance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Unlike Murdoch, ESDC conducted no formal security investigation, wrote no investigation report, and the employee was not a law enforcement officer subject to a security misconduct investigation under applicable codes of conduct.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees were informed about video surveillance collection and its purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: No signage existed at camera locations, no communication informed employees of surveillance purposes, and ESDC lacked a department-wide surveillance policy covering all buildings and offices.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 – Collection of personal information must relate directly to an operating program or activity of the federal institution
regulatoryFindings.description: Initial collection of video surveillance was compliant with Section 4 as it was for security purposes
violations: Initial collection of video surveillance was compliant with Section 4 as it was for security purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 5 – Institutions must inform individuals from whom personal information is collected about the purpose of collection
regulatoryFindings.description: ESDC failed to post signage indicating camera locations or collection purposes
violations: ESDC failed to post signage indicating camera locations or collection purposes
No communication provided to employees about surveillance camera purposes
Department lacked a department-wide policy on video surveillance use (relied only on Passport Canada-specific policy)

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 7(a) – Personal information cannot be used without consent except for the purpose obtained or a consistent use
regulatoryFindings.description: Video recordings collected for security purposes were used to verify employee departure times during administrative verification under collective agreement
violations: Video recordings collected for security purposes were used to verify employee departure times during administrative verification under collective agreement
Use was not consistent with original security purpose and no consent was obtained
No exemption under Section 8(2) applied
Less privacy-invasive alternatives existed (questioning employee, seeking attestation, consulting managers)

outcome: ESDC acknowledged that the use of video surveillance was not consistent with the security purpose for which it was collected. The complaint was found well-founded. ESDC agreed to: (1) adopt a department-wide policy within six months clearly identifying the purpose for video surveillance and ensuring compliance with policy provisions; (2) within six months, advise individuals who might be captured by surveillance cameras about the collection of personal information and include required notice elements; (3) limit use of video surveillance and employ less intrusive measures for verifying misconduct allegations. ESDC confirmed acceptance of these recommendations and committed to implementation with close monitoring by the Privacy Commissioner's office.
companyNow: ESDC continues to operate as a major federal department delivering employment and social benefits to Canadians. The department has implemented surveillance policies to address the Privacy Commissioner's findings.
dataType: Video surveillance footage, images, location data, employee whereabouts and behaviour
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 5 (duty to inform individuals)
Privacy Act Section 8(2) (exemptions for secondary use)

companyDescription: The Canadian Border Service Agency (CBSA) is Canada's federal law enforcement and border management agency, responsible for enforcing immigration, customs, and security regulations at Canada's borders and ports of entry.
companyLongDescription: The Canadian Border Service Agency (CBSA) is a federal agency within Canada's Department of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness, established to administer and enforce the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act and customs legislation. The agency operates at all Canadian borders and ports of entry, making decisions on immigration status, detention, deportation, and bond conditions for individuals entering or residing in Canada. The CBSA has significant powers to collect, use, and disclose personal information in the course of its immigration enforcement and border security operations.
caseDescription: The Canadian Border Service Agency disclosed a complainant's personal medical information by carbon copying his bondsperson on a letter containing health status details provided during CBSA detention. Although the medical information had been included in publicly available Federal Court documents by the complainant himself, the CBSA did not exercise restraint in its disclosure and could have notified the bondsperson separately without including the sensitive health data.
violationSummary: The CBSA disclosed personal medical information to a third party (bondsperson) without explicit consent. While the information was technically publicly available through court records, the disclosure itself constituted an unnecessary dissemination of sensitive health data that could have been avoided through alternative notification methods.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The CBSA carbon copied a complainant's bondsperson on a letter containing the complainant's personal medical information regarding health changes during detention.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's private health status was unnecessarily exposed to a third party when CBSA could have notified the bondsperson separately.

claimsVsReality.claim: CBSA claimed the disclosure was authorized under its operational bulletin (ENF 8) requiring notification of bondspersons about condition modifications.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner found the bulletin would not authorize disclosure of medical information under the Privacy Act, and that separate notification without medical details would have satisfied operational requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: CBSA argued the information was publicly available because it appeared in Federal Court documents, therefore Privacy Act restrictions did not apply.
claimsVsReality.reality: While technically correct that publicly available information is exempt from section 8 restrictions, the Commissioner noted CBSA should have exercised restraint and privacy sensitivity regardless of public availability, and would have breached the Act but for the complainant's own disclosure in court.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act s. 8(1) – Personal information can only be disclosed with consent or under permitted categories in s. 8(2)
regulatoryFindings.description: CBSA disclosed complainant's medical information without explicit consent
violations: CBSA disclosed complainant's medical information without explicit consent
Disclosure was not authorized under CBSA's operational bulletin ENF 8, as notice could have been provided separately

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act s. 69(2) – Restrictions on disclosure do not apply to publicly available information
regulatoryFindings.description: Information was publicly available in Federal Court records, therefore s. 8 did not apply
violations: Information was publicly available in Federal Court records, therefore s. 8 did not apply

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act – General obligation to protect privacy of the public
regulatoryFindings.description: CBSA failed to exercise restraint in use and disclosure despite public availability of information
violations: CBSA failed to exercise restraint in use and disclosure despite public availability of information

outcome: Complaint found not well-founded because the disclosed medical information was publicly available in Federal Court documents; therefore, subsection 69(2) of the Privacy Act exempted the disclosure from the restrictions in section 8. However, the investigator cautioned that but for the complainant's own inclusion of the information in court records, the CBSA would have breached its obligations. The investigator reminded CBSA of its obligation to protect privacy and encouraged exercise of restraint in disclosing personal information, even when publicly available.
companyNow: The CBSA continues to operate as Canada's primary border services and immigration enforcement agency. The case highlights ongoing tensions between operational efficiency and privacy obligations in government administration.
dataType: Medical/health information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act s. 8(1) – Disclosure without consent
Privacy Act s. 8(2) – Disclosure not authorized under permitted categories
Privacy Act s. 3 – Definition of personal information (medical history)

companyDescription: CATSA is a Canadian Crown corporation established in 2002 to provide airport security screening services, including passenger and baggage screening at Canadian airports.
companyLongDescription: The Canadian Air Transport Security Authority (CATSA) is a federal Crown corporation created in response to the September 11, 2001 terrorist attacks. It operates under the Canadian Air Transport Security Authority Act and is responsible for screening passengers, baggage, and personnel at Canadian airports to detect prohibited items and threats to aviation security. CATSA is fully funded by parliamentary appropriations and accountable to Parliament through the Minister of Transport. The organization implements security protocols aligned with Transport Canada's Prohibited Items List and aviation security regulations.
caseDescription: CATSA disclosed personal information of air travellers carrying legal medical cannabis to police without legal authority, violating the Privacy Act. CATSA exceeded its aviation security mandate by collecting and disclosing passenger information for general law enforcement purposes when cannabis—not listed as a prohibited item—was discovered during screening.
violationSummary: CATSA disclosed personal information (name, boarding pass details, medical documentation) to police for general law enforcement purposes without statutory authority. This disclosure was beyond CATSA's mandate as a screening authority and violated Section 8 of the Privacy Act, which restricts disclosure of personal information without consent except in limited circumstances.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: CATSA disclosed personal information of air travellers carrying legal medical cannabis to police without legal authority, exceeding its aviation security mandate.
whyTheyWereWrong: Travellers with lawful medical cannabis faced police involvement and public exposure of their medical information because CATSA overstepped its security role to enforce general drug laws,.

claimsVsReality.claim: CATSA must notify police of cannabis discoveries to determine legality because Screening Officers lack authority to verify medical documentation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cannabis was not listed on Transport Canada's Prohibited Items List as a threat to aviation security; CATSA had no aviation security mandate to police drug legality, which is a law enforcement function.

claimsVsReality.claim: CATSA's notification of police is consistent with its screening mandate and Transport Canada direction.
claimsVsReality.reality: CATSA's collection and disclosure of passenger personal information for general law enforcement purposes violated sections 4 and 8 of the Privacy Act and exceeded its lawful authority.

claimsVsReality.claim: Screening Officers need to notify police because they cannot determine the validity of medical cannabis documentation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The proper response was to allow legal medical cannabis through screening unchanged, not to collect personal information and alert police to investigate passenger legality.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 — Personal information collection must relate directly to an operating program or activity of the government institution
