regulatoryFindings.description: CATSA collected personal information (name, boarding pass, photo ID, prescription details) from travellers carrying cannabis under the premise this related to aviation security, but cannabis is not a prohibited item and poses no aviation security threat
violations: CATSA collected personal information (name, boarding pass, photo ID, prescription details) from travellers carrying cannabis under the premise this related to aviation security, but cannabis is not a prohibited item and poses no aviation security threat
The collection was actually for general law enforcement purposes, which is outside CATSA's mandate as a screening authority

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8 — Personal information under control of government institution cannot be disclosed without consent except in limited circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: CATSA disclosed personal information of travellers with cannabis to police without statutory authority
violations: CATSA disclosed personal information of travellers with cannabis to police without statutory authority
The disclosure was not for a purpose consistent with original collection (aviation security screening) nor authorized by any Act of Parliament
CATSA lacked legal authority to determine legality of cannabis possession and make referrals to law enforcement for general law enforcement investigative purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 6 — Retention and disposal of personal information must follow prescribed schedules
regulatoryFindings.description: Two instances where CATSA retained personal information relating to cannabis possession in database incident summaries (found not to be contraventions as destroying records was appropriate given no administrative purpose)
violations: Two instances where CATSA retained personal information relating to cannabis possession in database incident summaries (found not to be contraventions as destroying records was appropriate given no administrative purpose)

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found CATSA's practices with respect to collection and disclosure of personal information relating to cannabis possession to be contraventions of Sections 4 and 8 of the Privacy Act. CATSA agreed to cease collecting and disclosing personal information of travellers found to be in possession of cannabis and to update its Standard Operating Procedures accordingly by November 30, 2020. CATSA committed to destroying all retained records containing personal information relating to cannabis possession. CATSA was directed to instruct screening officers not to disclose information to law enforcement regarding cannabis discoveries unless the quantity is 'clearly illegal' (over 150g) without need for further investigation, or where screening officers suspect a threat to aviation security.
companyNow: CATSA continues to operate as Canada's aviation security screening authority. Following this investigation, CATSA agreed to amend its policies to cease disclosing passenger personal information to police for cannabis possession matters outside its security mandate.
dataType: Name, boarding pass information, photo identification, prescription documentation, medical records
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 4 (collection of personal information must relate directly to operating program or activity)
Privacy Act Section 8 (disclosure of personal information restricted without consent)
Privacy Act Section 6 (retention and disposal of personal information)

companyDescription: TD Canada Trust is the personal banking division of Toronto-Dominion Bank, one of Canada's largest financial institutions, offering deposit accounts, credit cards, and fraud claim services to Canadian consumers.
companyLongDescription: TD Canada Trust is a subsidiary of Toronto-Dominion Bank (TD), a major Canadian multinational financial services company. It provides retail banking services including chequing and savings accounts, credit cards, mortgages, and fraud claims processing. TD is one of the Big Five banks in Canada with millions of customers. The bank operates across North America and manages significant volumes of customer personal and financial information.
caseDescription: A former employee of TD Canada Trust complained that the bank outsourced fraud claims processing to a third-party service provider in India without customer consent or opt-out options. The Privacy Commissioner of Canada found that TD was not required to obtain additional consent because the service provider used the information for the same purpose it was originally collected, that TD was sufficiently transparent about the transfer, and that TD ensured comparable data protection through robust contracts and monitoring.
violationSummary: The complainant alleged inadequate safeguards and accountability for personal information transferred across borders to a third-party processor in a foreign jurisdiction where different legal protections apply. However, the investigation found no actual violation—TD had implemented comprehensive security and contractual measures meeting PIPEDA's comparable protection standard.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: TD Canada Trust outsourced fraud claims processing to a third-party service provider in India, where employees accessed.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers faced exposure of sensitive financial and personal data to foreign jurisdiction processing without explicit knowledge or opt-out options.

claimsVsReality.claim: TD claimed it does not transfer customer personal information to the service provider in India, but rather provides only limited remote access via a secure portal.
claimsVsReality.reality: TD employees of the service provider in India accessed and processed customer personal information to perform fraud claims tasks, constituting a transfer of personal information under PIPEDA.

claimsVsReality.claim: TD claimed it was sufficiently transparent about outsourcing fraud claims processing to customers.
claimsVsReality.reality: While TD included disclosure language in account opening agreements and privacy documents, the specific practice of outsourcing to India was not explicitly highlighted at the time information was collected, and customers had no option to opt out.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Consent for collection, use, or disclosure of personal information
PIPEDA Principle 4.8 – Openness regarding personal information management practices
PIPEDA Principle 4.1.3 – Accountability for personal information transferred to third parties; organizations must use contractual or other means to provide comparable level of protection

outcome: The complaint was found to be not well-founded on all three grounds. The Privacy Commissioner determined that: (1) TD was not required to obtain separate consent for the transfer because the service provider used information for the same purpose for which it was originally collected; (2) TD was sufficiently open about the outsourcing practice through account opening agreements, privacy codes, and website resources; and (3) TD had ensured a comparable level of protection through comprehensive contractual requirements, employee background verification, work environment controls, cybersecurity measures, and ongoing independent audits and monitoring.
companyNow: TD Canada Trust remains a major retail banking provider in Canada as part of Toronto-Dominion Bank, continuing to serve millions of customers with deposit and credit products.
dataType: Financial transaction history, fraud claim details, cardholder information

companyDescription: RateMDs is a health professional ratings and review website that allows patients to anonymously post ratings and reviews of doctors, dentists, and other healthcare providers across Canada and the United States.
companyLongDescription: RateMDs operates an online platform where patients can create profiles for health professionals and post anonymous reviews and ratings to help other patients make informed healthcare decisions. The company allows users to rate professionals on criteria such as staff quality, punctuality, helpfulness, and knowledge. Health professionals can claim their profiles for free and add additional information, but the company's paid subscription model included a problematic feature allowing professionals to hide negative reviews from their profiles.
caseDescription: RateMDs, a health professional ratings website, was found to have engaged in an inappropriate 'pay-for-takedown' practice by charging subscribers a fee to hide negative reviews from their profiles. While consent to publish reviews was not found to be violated due to public interest considerations, RateMDs' practice of monetizing the removal of personal information it made public contravened PIPEDA's appropriate purposes principle. RateMDs agreed to cease this practice and improve transparency regarding review correction processes.
violationSummary: RateMDs appropriated and monetized personal information (reviews) by charging for their removal/hiding, representing a 'pay-for-takedown' scheme that treats personal information as a commodity for profit extraction rather than respecting individuals' informational interests.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: RateMDs charged health professionals a subscription fee that included the ability to hide negative reviews from their publicly visible profiles.
whyTheyWereWrong: Health professionals were forced to pay to remove personal information that RateMDs had made public, monetizing the takedown of reviews.

claimsVsReality.claim: RateMDs claimed its subscription service was a legitimate business feature offering enhanced services to health professionals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The subscription's inclusion of review-hiding functionality constituted an inappropriate 'pay-for-takedown' practice that monetized removal of personal information RateMDs had made public.

claimsVsReality.claim: RateMDs stated it had a process in place for health professionals to challenge inaccurate information posted about them.
claimsVsReality.reality: RateMDs did not adequately communicate or explain to health professionals how they could challenge accuracy or completeness of information, violating the Openness Principle.

claimsVsReality.claim: RateMDs represented that reviews serve the public interest by informing patients' healthcare decisions.
claimsVsReality.reality: While reviews do serve a public interest, this does not justify charging health professionals to remove personal information about themselves from public view.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA s. 5(3) - Appropriate Purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: RateMDs charged subscribers to hide up to 3 negative reviews from their profiles through the 'Ratings Manager' service, creating a 'pay-for-takedown' scheme identified as a no-go zone under OPC guidance
violations: RateMDs charged subscribers to hide up to 3 negative reviews from their profiles through the 'Ratings Manager' service, creating a 'pay-for-takedown' scheme identified as a no-go zone under OPC guidance
Hidden reviews reappeared if subscribers did not maintain monthly payments, making the practice a continuous revenue stream from suppression of personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.8 - Openness
regulatoryFindings.description: RateMDs did not clearly communicate to health professionals their ability to request correction or amendment of inaccurate, incomplete or out-of-date information
violations: RateMDs did not clearly communicate to health professionals their ability to request correction or amendment of inaccurate, incomplete or out-of-date information
Website explanation of practices was unclear regarding review removal and correction policies

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 & 4.9.5 - Accuracy and Correction
regulatoryFindings.description: While not specifically found in violation, RateMDs' process for challenging accuracy was hampered by anonymous review posting, making it difficult for health professionals to demonstrate inaccuracy without knowing reviewer identity
violations: While not specifically found in violation, RateMDs' process for challenging accuracy was hampered by anonymous review posting, making it difficult for health professionals to demonstrate inaccuracy without knowing reviewer identity

outcome: RateMDs agreed to cease the 'Ratings Manager' hide reviews feature and replaced it with 'Ratings Concierge' service that eliminates the ability to hide reviews. Annual subscribers received a sunset period of up to one year to transition; monthly subscribers were required to transition immediately. RateMDs updated its Terms of Use and FAQs to clearly explain that personal information will be removed or amended where demonstrated to be inaccurate or out-of-date, and that health professionals can claim their profile to correct or update business information and post responses to reviews.
companyNow: RateMDs ceased its 'pay-for-takedown' subscription feature following the 2020 PIPEDA enforcement action and agreed to improve transparency regarding how health professionals can challenge inaccurate information on their profiles.
dataType: Professional reputation information, health professional reviews and ratings, business contact information (name, address, phone), IP addresses, user agent data

companyDescription: Dell is a multinational technology company best known for manufacturing and selling computer hardware products including laptops, monitors, and printers to consumers and businesses worldwide.
companyLongDescription: Dell Technologies is one of the world's largest computer hardware manufacturers, offering personal computers, workstations, servers, storage systems, and related support services. The company was founded in 1984 and operates globally through various business segments including consumer electronics, enterprise solutions, and IT infrastructure. Dell provides warranty and technical support services to millions of customers worldwide through both internal and outsourced service providers.
caseDescription: Dell's service provider employees in India stole and sold customer personal information in June and November 2017, affecting approximately 7,883 Canadian customers. The stolen data was used in targeted tech support scams that deceived customers into providing remote computer access and payment. Dell failed to adequately investigate early customer complaints about the breach or implement sufficient security controls for access management and monitoring.
violationSummary: Dell failed to implement adequate security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of customer personal information, despite operating in a known high-risk environment for targeted tech support scams. Specific gaps included insufficient access controls, inadequate logging and monitoring of employee access, delayed USB restriction policies, and lack of breach investigation procedures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Dell's service provider employees in India stole and sold customer personal information in June and November 2017, affecting approximately 7,883 Canadian customers whose names.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers were targeted by tech support scammers using their stolen Dell information to convince victims they were legitimate Dell representatives.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dell claimed the complainant 'should have known that the call was a scam' and that the call originated from untargeted random tech scam activity or other sources.
claimsVsReality.reality: The scammer possessed accurate Dell-specific information including the customer's service tag, express service code, warranty details, and last service date that only Dell and the customer should know—information later confirmed to have come from Dell's breached systems in November 2017.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dell assured customers that 'Dell's systems were secure' when the complainant's father reported the fraudulent calls and requested urgent warning.
claimsVsReality.reality: Two of Dell's service provider employees had already breached customer data in June 2017 and November 2017, with the November breach affecting 7,883 Canadian customers whose information was actively being used in targeted scams.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dell maintained it could not link the scam call to a Dell information breach because the service tag number provided by the complainant was 'incorrect'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant's service tag information was actually correct and matched records Dell later confirmed were included in the November 2017 exfiltrated customer list.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.3 – Organization remains responsible for personal information transferred to service providers and must ensure comparable level of protection
regulatoryFindings.description: Dell transferred customer personal information to service provider without adequate contractual safeguards and oversight mechanisms
violations: Dell transferred customer personal information to service provider without adequate contractual safeguards and oversight mechanisms
Dell failed to ensure the service provider implemented security measures appropriate to the sensitivity of the information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Organizations must protect personal information by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information, considering nature of information, foreseeable risks, and potential harm
regulatoryFindings.description: Access controls: Excessive number of employees could create and access detailed customer reports; 75% reduction in report-builders was possible post-breach, indicating controls were not appropriately restrictive
violations: Access controls: Excessive number of employees could create and access detailed customer reports; 75% reduction in report-builders was possible post-breach, indicating controls were not appropriately restrictive

Monitoring and Logging: No evidence of logging/monitoring to detect anomalous employee requests for customer information; Data Leakage Protection System was easily circumvented by sending smaller file attachments
Technical Measures: USB drives were not restricted until after breaches occurred, despite known risk environment for insider theft
Breach Investigation: June 2017 breach was not thoroughly investigated; scope and affected data remain unknown, allowing vulnerabilities to persist

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.10.4 – Organizations shall investigate all complaints and take appropriate measures if justified
regulatoryFindings.description: Dell inadequately investigated Complainant A's complaint regarding targeted fraud call with Dell customer information, providing generic tech support scam information instead of investigating the breach allegation
violations: Dell inadequately investigated Complainant A's complaint regarding targeted fraud call with Dell customer information, providing generic tech support scam information instead of investigating the breach allegation
Dell dismissed or minimized customer complaints despite receiving over 1,000 scam reports since 2015 and 26 specific reports (June-October 2017) mentioning Dell customer information
Dell failed to adequately investigate June 2017 breach circumstances, determining only that physical means were used without establishing scope or implementing preventive measures

outcome: Matter found well-founded and resolved. Dell agreed to implement all recommendations including: (1) thorough investigation procedures for breach allegations and privacy complaints; (2) adequate staff training on Act obligations and privacy incident response; (3) formal breach investigation procedures; (4) logging and monitoring systems to detect anomalous data requests. Dell implemented enhancements including improved monitoring/logging, strengthened access controls with two-factor authentication, information masking, USB restrictions, email domain controls, enhanced Breach Incident Response Plan, expanded Security Investigations team, and new enterprise-wide insider risk program. Transitioned to two new service providers with enhanced safeguards. All front-line staff to receive training on identifying and reporting privacy/security incidents.
companyNow: Dell Technologies remains a major player in the global technology hardware market, operating as a publicly traded company and continuing to provide computing solutions and support services worldwide.
dataType: Customer names, contact details (phone numbers, email addresses), product information (service tags, model names, warranty details), service request numbers, service history
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.3 (responsibility for information transferred to third parties)
PIPEDA Principle 4.7 (security safeguards appropriate to sensitivity)
PIPEDA Principle 4.7.2 (safeguards based on amount, distribution, format and storage method)
PIPEDA Principle 4.7.3 (use of physical, organizational and technological measures)

companyDescription: Cadillac Fairview Corporation Limited is one of North America's largest owners, operators, and developers of office, retail, and mixed-use properties, including shopping malls across Canada.
companyLongDescription: Cadillac Fairview is a major real estate company operating numerous shopping malls and commercial properties throughout Canada. In 2018-2020, the company deployed Anonymous Video Analytics (AVA) technology in wayfinding directories to monitor foot traffic and demographic patterns. The company is a significant property management and real estate development firm with extensive mall operations across multiple provinces.
caseDescription: Cadillac Fairview deployed Anonymous Video Analytics (AVA) technology in mall wayfinding directories that captured facial images and converted them into biometric numerical representations without obtaining valid consent. The company collected approximately 5 million facial biometric records and retained them on a decommissioned server for no apparent purpose. Additionally, the company's privacy disclosures were inadequate, buried in lengthy privacy policies, and not readily accessible to mall visitors.
violationSummary: The AVA technology involved covert facial detection and biometric collection from individuals in public spaces (mall directories) without meaningful notice or express consent. This constitutes surveillance through deployment of hidden cameras and facial analytics technology.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Cadillac Fairview deployed facial recognition technology in mall directories that captured.
whyTheyWereWrong: Visitors to Cadillac Fairview malls had their sensitive facial biometric information collected without their knowledge or meaningful consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Biometric numerical representations were not retained beyond processing.
claimsVsReality.reality: Approximately 5 million facial biometric numerical representations were actually stored on a decommissioned server indefinitely with no stated purpose.

claimsVsReality.claim: Valid consent was obtained through the privacy policy for AVA technology use.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consent was inadequate—the privacy policy was buried in a 5,000-word document that would not be easily accessible to individuals using mall directories, and guest services staff were unaware of the policy when asked.

claimsVsReality.claim: AVA technology was not collecting personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The technology captured facial images and converted them into biometric numerical representations, which constitutes sensitive personal information capable of identifying individuals based on unique facial features.

claimsVsReality.claim: The biometric information was used only for assessing age range and gender for foot traffic monitoring.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company retained 5 million biometric records on a decommissioned server for no apparent purpose, suggesting data was collected far beyond stated operational needs.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires knowledge and consent of individuals for collection, use, or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Cadillac Fairview collected and used personal information including biometric facial data without obtaining valid consent
violations: Cadillac Fairview collected and used personal information including biometric facial data without obtaining valid consent
Company failed to obtain express opt-in consent for collection of sensitive biometric information
Consent was purportedly obtained through a 5,000-word privacy policy buried in the document, not readily accessible at point of collection

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 6.1 requires that consent be reasonable to expect an individual would understand the nature, purpose and consequences of collection, use or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Privacy policy language was overly broad and not sufficiently specific about AVA technology, facial recognition, and biometric data collection
violations: Privacy policy language was overly broad and not sufficiently specific about AVA technology, facial recognition, and biometric data collection
Individuals using mall directories would not reasonably expect their facial images to be captured and converted to biometric representations
Signage at mall entrances only referenced 'safety and security' purposes, not analytics or demographic profiling

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5.3 requires destruction or depersonalization of personal information when no longer needed for identified purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Cadillac Fairview retained approximately 5 million numerical facial representations on a decommissioned server with no apparent purpose or justification
violations: Cadillac Fairview retained approximately 5 million numerical facial representations on a decommissioned server with no apparent purpose or justification
Server was not properly deleted; it remained readily re-activatable with all personal information accessible
Mappedin could not articulate any legitimate purpose for retaining the biometric data beyond the brief processing period

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPA AB Section 7(1) and PIPA BC Section 6 require consent for collection, use or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection of facial images and biometric representations occurred without valid consent
violations: Collection of facial images and biometric representations occurred without valid consent
Testing and calibration phase resulted in collection of 16 hours of video recordings with audio in some cases, without consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPA AB Section 13(1) and PIPA BC Section 10(1) require notice of collection purposes before or at time of collection
regulatoryFindings.description: No notice was provided to individuals at point of interaction with wayfinding directories
violations: No notice was provided to individuals at point of interaction with wayfinding directories
Privacy policy reference was not readily accessible to directory users
Guest services staff were unable to properly assist customers requesting privacy policy information

outcome: Cadillac Fairview has committed to the following remedial actions: (1) deletion of all numerical facial representations and associated biometric data collected via AVA technology; (2) deletion of calibration video and audio recordings not required for legal purposes; (3) commitment that retained information will not be used for purposes outside legal compliance; (4) implementation of privacy training for guest services staff; (5) correction of privacy policy language regarding geolocation practices; (6) removal of consent requests for location-based offers not actually being used. The company ceased use of AVA technology in July 2018 and has no current plans to resume it. The company refused to commit to obtaining express opt-in consent should it resume AVA technology in the future, despite investigative recommendations. For the geolocation technology issue (Issue 2), Cadillac Fairview was found to not be collecting personal information in the Anonymous Shopper Journey context, and clarified that it does not associate granular geolocation data with logged-in Wi-Fi accounts. The matter is considered well-founded and resolved with respect to AVA technology violations; the geolocation matter is considered not well-founded.
companyNow: Cadillac Fairview continues to operate shopping malls and commercial properties in Canada. Following the 2020 enforcement action, the company ceased use of AVA technology and implemented privacy training for staff.
dataType: Biometric data (facial recognition, numerical face representations), location data (geolocation, MAC addresses), demographic information (age, gender), personal information (name, email address), audio recordings
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.5.3 (retention and destruction of personal information)
PIPA AB Section 35 (retention and destruction requirement)
PIPA BC Section 35 (retention and destruction requirement)

companyDescription: Desjardins is a major Canadian financial cooperative federation providing banking, credit, and insurance services primarily in Quebec and other Canadian provinces.
companyLongDescription: Fédération des caisses Desjardins du Québec is one of Canada's largest financial cooperatives, operating as a network of credit unions and financial institutions. It serves millions of members and clients across Canada and internationally, offering retail banking, credit facilities, insurance products, and wealth management services. The organization operates dual data systems for credit and banking information, serving both members (shareholders in affiliated credit unions) and non-member clients.
caseDescription: Desjardins suffered a major data breach between 2017 and 2019 affecting 9.7 million individuals, perpetrated by a malicious employee who exfiltrated personal information over 26 months. The investigation found that Desjardins failed to implement adequate security safeguards, maintain proper data retention procedures, and establish effective oversight and monitoring mechanisms despite having policies in place. The company's organizational culture of trust was not accompanied by sufficient verification and control measures to detect insider threats.
violationSummary: Desjardins' security safeguards were inadequate throughout the data lifecycle. The company failed to implement technological, organizational, and physical measures to protect highly sensitive personal information. Specific failures included inadequate access controls, lack of data segregation, insufficient employee training, absence of active monitoring, and failure to enforce existing policies and procedures. These gaps collectively created conditions enabling a malicious insider to exfiltrate 9.7 million individuals' personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Desjardins failed to implement adequate security safeguards, allowing a malicious employee to exfiltrate personal information of 9.7 million individuals over 26 months by copying data.
whyTheyWereWrong: The stolen data included social insurance numbers, dates of birth, and addresses that were sold to private lenders, exposing millions of people to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Desjardins had policies and security safeguards in place to protect personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite policies existing on paper, the company failed to implement organizational controls preventing employees from copying confidential data to shared drives accessible to the entire marketing department, enabling a single employee to steal from these repositories for 26 months undetected.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's culture of trust and employee oversight was sufficient to prevent insider threats.
claimsVsReality.reality: A malicious employee exploited weak access controls and lack of monitoring to systematically copy and exfiltrate personal information to USB keys monthly over two years without detection, later selling the data to private lenders.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information was retained only as long as necessary and then destroyed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Desjardins retained sensitive personal information beyond required periods and failed to destroy aged data, leaving obsolete records in accessible systems where they were eventually compromised and sold.

claimsVsReality.claim: Access to confidential information in data warehouses was properly restricted and controlled.
claimsVsReality.reality: While database access was theoretically segmented, marketing employees with limited authorization could download confidential files to shared drives, where the malicious employee accessed data he was explicitly denied direct access to in the banking warehouse.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Safeguards Principle 4.7 – Personal information must be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information throughout its entire life cycle, including protection against loss, theft, unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use or modification through physical, organizational, and technological measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Desjardins failed to implement adequate access controls and data segregation, allowing authorized marketing employees to copy confidential personal information from secure data warehouses to shared directories accessible to all marketing staff
violations: Desjardins failed to implement adequate access controls and data segregation, allowing authorized marketing employees to copy confidential personal information from secure data warehouses to shared directories accessible to all marketing staff

The company did not prevent the transfer of personal information from data warehouses to shared drives, then to employee computers, and finally to USB keys without any technological controls or masking
Desjardins had not fully deployed Data Loss Prevention (DLP) solutions during the breach period, only partially implementing them, and lacked User Entity Behavior Analytics (UEBA) monitoring
The organization relied on passive log analysis rather than active, real-time monitoring systems to detect suspicious data exfiltration activities
Desjardins did not prevent the use of personal removable storage devices despite having a directive prohibiting such storage of personal information
The company failed to implement procedures to mask or tokenize sensitive data being transferred outside production environments, contrary to its own security standards

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Accountability Principle 4.1.4(a) – Organizations must implement procedures to protect personal information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Desjardins had developed numerous policies and directives for information protection but failed to adequately implement them
violations: Desjardins had developed numerous policies and directives for information protection but failed to adequately implement them
Security standards for confidential data protection, acceptable use of technology, and data backup were not consistently enforced across the organization
No procedures were in place to verify and ensure employee compliance with data protection policies
Monthly automated and manual transfers of personal information from data warehouses to shared directories occurred despite policies prohibiting this practice

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Accountability Principle 4.1.4(c) – Organizations must train staff and communicate to staff information about the organization's policies and practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Despite providing 23 hours of onboarding training including 3.75 hours on personal information protection, Desjardins provided no indicators demonstrating that employees understood the content
violations: Despite providing 23 hours of onboarding training including 3.75 hours on personal information protection, Desjardins provided no indicators demonstrating that employees understood the content
Authorized marketing employees copied confidential information to shared directories accessible to all marketing staff, suggesting insufficient awareness of confidentiality requirements
Training and awareness programs were not sufficient for the sensitivity of personal information handled and the complexity of protection requirements
Critical gaps existed in employee training and awareness at the time of the breach, particularly regarding insider threat prevention

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5 – Organizations must not retain personal information longer than necessary to fulfill the purposes for which it was collected, and must develop guidelines and implement procedures for destruction of personal information no longer required.
regulatoryFindings.description: Desjardins had no finalized personal information retention schedule at the time of the breach, despite having a directive and policy requiring one
violations: Desjardins had no finalized personal information retention schedule at the time of the breach, despite having a directive and policy requiring one
No procedures were in place to destroy personal information at the end of its lifecycle
The company retained 3.9 million inactive files, some inactive for decades, without justification
Desjardins could not determine retention periods for compromised inactive accounts even seven months after the incident

outcome: The OPC found all complaints against Desjardins to be well-founded and conditionally resolved. Desjardins was required to: (1) provide six-monthly progress reports on security improvements addressing safeguards, access controls, monitoring, and training; (2) finalize and submit a retention schedule and destruction process within six months; (3) delete or anonymize personal information exceeding retention periods within six months of schedule finalization; (4) demonstrate monitoring of data access requests below the new analysis environment threshold within six months; (5) demonstrate protection of personal information throughout its lifecycle within six months; and (6) retain an independent external auditing firm to assess and certify its information security and privacy program within two years, with detailed audit findings covering safeguards, governance, resources, data platforms, risk assessment, training, retention practices, and residual risks. Desjardins accepted all recommendations and proposed an 18-month plan for retention schedule finalization and data destruction in three stages, to be completed by June 2022. The OPC will monitor Desjardins' implementation progress.
companyNow: Desjardins remains one of Canada's largest financial cooperatives and continues operations. Following the 2020 investigation, the company implemented comprehensive security reforms and compliance measures as ordered by Canadian privacy regulators.
dataType: Names, dates of birth, social insurance numbers, residential addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses, transaction histories, financial information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Safeguards Principle 4.7 (Protection of Personal Information)
PIPEDA Safeguards Principle 4.7.1 (Protection against loss, theft, unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use or modification)

PIPEDA Principle 4.5 (Limiting Use, Disclosure and Retention)

companyDescription: Services Australia is the Australian government agency responsible for delivering social security payments and services to eligible Australians.
companyLongDescription: Services Australia (formerly Department of Human Services) is a federal government agency that administers welfare payments, aged care, and other social services. It processes personal information for millions of Australians receiving various government benefits and services. The agency is a key touchpoint for Australian citizens interacting with the social safety net.
caseDescription: Services Australia disclosed personal information about the complainant to tribunal proceedings without proper authorization under the Privacy Act. The unauthorized network entry occurred through compromised credentials obtained via phishing. However, the organization had implemented industry-standard encryption and reasonable security measures consistent with PDPC recommendations, and no evidence of data exfiltration or decryption was found.
violationSummary: The case examines whether the organization's security measures met the Protection Obligation standard. While a breach occurred, the organization had implemented reasonable security measures including encryption, backups, endpoint security, and system monitoring, which mitigated the harm.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Giordano Originals suffered a ransomware attack on 12 July 2020 through compromised phishing credentials that affected systems storing personal data of 790,000 members and 184 employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: The attack exposed sensitive employee data including names, NRICs, addresses, salaries and educational information, and member contact details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had implemented reasonable and adequate security measures to protect personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite industry-standard protections, attackers gained unauthorized network access through phishing-compromised credentials, affecting 790,000+ customer and employee records.

claimsVsReality.claim: Encryption and backups protected the data from harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: While encryption prevented decryption and backups enabled recovery, the breach still exposed sensitive unencrypted personal information during the attack period.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organizations to protect personal data against unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Unauthorized network entry and ransomware infection occurred on 12 July 2020 affecting systems with personal data
violations: Unauthorized network entry and ransomware infection occurred on 12 July 2020 affecting systems with personal data
Breach was determined to have occurred through compromised credentials via phishing attack

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection determined that the Organization had met its Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA despite the incident. The organization's implementation of industry-standard encryption, regular backups, endpoint security solutions, real-time monitoring, vulnerability scanning, and prompt remedial actions (including enhanced phishing training and additional monitoring) demonstrated reasonable and appropriate security measures. No directions or further enforcement action were issued.
companyNow: Giordano Originals continues to operate as a retail fashion business in Singapore, having strengthened its cybersecurity practices following the 2020 incident.
dataType: Names, contact numbers, dates of birth, NRIC, addresses, gender, age, email addresses, educational information, salary information

companyDescription: Seriously Keto Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce company operating an online platform for keto diet products and membership services.
companyLongDescription: Seriously Keto Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce retailer specialising in ketogenic diet products and services. The company operates an e-commerce and membership website to serve customers interested in keto lifestyle products. As a digital retail business, it collects and stores customer personal data including names, addresses, email addresses, and phone numbers to fulfil orders and manage memberships.
caseDescription: Seriously Keto suffered a ransomware infection in June 2020 that exposed personal data of approximately 3,073 individuals. The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements, including encrypting login credentials and conducting periodic security reviews. An unprotected file containing unencrypted credentials in the network infrastructure provided a channel for unauthorised access.
violationSummary: The organisation negligently failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data in its possession, resulting in a data breach through an unprotected file containing unencrypted credentials that could be located through infrastructure scanning.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Seriously Keto failed to encrypt login credentials and conduct security reviews, leaving an unprotected file in its network that exposed the personal data of 3,073 customers to ransomware.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' names, addresses, email addresses and phone numbers were exposed to unauthorised access, putting them at risk of identity theft, targeted fraud, and unwanted contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: We relied on our vendor to implement necessary security arrangements for the personal data in the e-commerce platform they developed.
claimsVsReality.reality: No clear contractual stipulations or business requirements were established making the vendor responsible for security; the organisation remained primarily responsible for protecting customer data in its possession and ultimately failed to do so.

claimsVsReality.claim: We had adequate security measures in place to protect customer personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: An unprotected file containing unencrypted login credentials existed in the network infrastructure and was discoverable by automated scanning, providing direct unauthorised access to servers containing 3,073 customers' personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation: Organisations must implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or under their control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct periodic security reviews prior to the incident
violations: Failed to conduct periodic security reviews prior to the incident
Stored unencrypted login credentials in an unprotected file within network infrastructure
Failed to implement encryption for sensitive credentials
Did not clearly define security responsibilities and outsourcing arrangements with the vendor
Neglected to give due attention to personal data protection prior to the incident

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found that Seriously Keto negligently contravened the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation was required to pay a financial penalty of $8,000 SGD within 30 days. Following the incident, the organisation took comprehensive remedial measures including a full security audit, setup of a new website with robust security infrastructure, mandatory password changes for all users, activation of a firewall, engagement of a cybersecurity vendor, and commitment to engage consultants to improve data protection policies and outsource data protection functions. No other directions were deemed necessary given the prompt remedial action taken.
companyNow: Following the 2020 incident, Seriously Keto implemented comprehensive security upgrades including a new website with robust internal security infrastructure, mandatory password changes, firewalls, and engagement of cybersecurity vendors and data protection consultants.
dataType: Names, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) is a major telecommunications provider in Singapore offering mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services to millions of customers.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited, commonly known as Singtel, is one of Asia's leading telecommunications companies and the primary fixed-line and mobile operator in Singapore. Founded in 1979 as a government entity and later privatized, Singtel provides comprehensive telecommunications services including mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and digital services to both consumer and enterprise customers across Singapore and the region. The company operates extensive network infrastructure and serves millions of subscribers.
caseDescription: A threat actor gained unauthorized access to 17 subscriber accounts at Singapore Telecommunications through social engineering attacks targeting staff, enabling fraudulent SIM card issuance and service manipulation. The company's investigation found no data exfiltration occurred and that reasonable security measures had been in place; the threat actor accessed accounts via compromised staff credentials rather than system vulnerabilities. The organization responded promptly with account suspension and password resets, and the Deputy Commissioner determined no enforcement action was warranted as the Protection Obligation had been met.
violationSummary: The unauthorized access to subscriber accounts by threat actors through compromised staff credentials constitutes an intrusion into the subscribers' accounts and systems, fitting the Solove category of Invasion–Intrusion.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: Threat actors gained unauthorized access to 17 subscriber accounts through social engineering attacks targeting staff, enabling fraudulent SIM card issuance and service manipulation.
whyTheyWereWrong: Subscribers lost access to their own accounts and were unable to receive calls or use their mobile services after threat actors fraudulently requested SIM replacements and service changes.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had reasonable security measures in place including password requirements aligned to industry best practices, continuous system enhancements, and comprehensive staff training.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, threat actors were able to successfully social engineer staff and compromise their credentials to gain unauthorized access to subscriber accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: No data exfiltration occurred and system integrity was not compromised.
claimsVsReality.reality: While data may not have been exfiltrated, threat actors were able to access and manipulate subscriber accounts to request fraudulent SIM cards and service changes, directly impacting account access for 17 individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 27 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must take reasonable precautions to protect personal data against unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Threat actors gained access to 17 subscriber accounts through social engineering attacks targeting staff
violations: Threat actors gained access to 17 subscriber accounts through social engineering attacks targeting staff

outcome: No enforcement action was taken. The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found that Singapore Telecommunications had met its Protection Obligation despite the incident. The organization had implemented reasonable security measures including password requirements aligned to industry best practices, continuous system enhancements, mandatory staff training on PDPA requirements, and reasonable security measures for staff work environments. The organization took prompt remedial action by suspending compromised accounts, resetting passwords, and implementing confidential preventive measures.
companyNow: Singtel remains a major telecommunications operator in Singapore and the Asia-Pacific region, continuing to provide essential connectivity services to millions of customers.
dataType: Account credentials, subscriber account information, telecommunications service records

companyDescription: ST Logistics Pte Ltd is a logistics services provider operating in Singapore's government, defence, and commercial sectors with approximately 800 employees worldwide.
companyLongDescription: ST Logistics Pte Ltd provides logistical and supply chain services primarily to Singapore's Ministry of Defence (MINDEF) and Singapore Armed Forces (SAF), as well as commercial sector clients. The company has approximately 800 employees worldwide and reported annual revenue of approximately S$350 million. The company operates as a critical logistics provider to Singapore's defence infrastructure.
caseDescription: ST Logistics failed to conduct periodic security reviews of its IT systems, resulting in undetected security gaps that allowed an Emotet malware infection via phishing emails. Six user laptops were infected, and unencrypted personal data of 2,400 MINDEF and SAF personnel was stored on four of these laptops without proper endpoint protection or security software updates.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement and maintain reasonable security arrangements as required by PDPA Section 24. Specific failures included: (1) anti-virus software not updated due to improper configuration, and (2) failure to ensure complete rollout of advanced endpoint protection (Traps Software) across all user laptops. These preventable gaps directly enabled the malware infection and unauthorised access to personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: ST Logistics failed to conduct periodic security reviews of its IT systems, leaving security software unpatched and endpoint protection software uninstalled on employee laptops.
whyTheyWereWrong: 2,400 military and defence personnel had their names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, and national ID numbers exposed to potential compromise when Emotet malware infected unprotected laptops.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had security software and endpoint protection in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: Six user laptops were infected because anti-virus software was not properly configured to receive updates and advanced endpoint protection (Traps Software) was not installed on four of the infected laptops.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data of defence personnel was adequately protected through existing IT controls.
claimsVsReality.reality: Unencrypted files containing names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, and NRIC numbers of 2,400 MINDEF and SAF personnel were stored on infected laptops with undetected security gaps.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation conducted adequate security reviews of its IT systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation failed to conduct periodic security reviews that would have detected the failure of anti-virus software configuration and the incomplete rollout of advanced endpoint protection software.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct periodic security reviews to detect vulnerabilities in IT systems
violations: Failed to conduct periodic security reviews to detect vulnerabilities in IT systems
Antivirus software not properly configured to receive updates on laptops of Infected Users
Endpoint protection software (Traps) not installed on all user laptops due to rollout gap
Failure to detect and remediate these security gaps prior to the phishing incident

outcome: ST Logistics found in breach of PDPA Section 24. Ordered to pay S$8,000 financial penalty within 30 days. Organisation had already implemented comprehensive remediation measures including: PDPA awareness training, enhanced firewall protection, mandatory endpoint protection software installation across all devices, phishing email blocking rules, Sender Policy Framework verification, email warning banners, periodic phishing simulation exercises, and independent security assessment.
companyNow: ST Logistics continues to operate as a logistics services provider in Singapore, having implemented comprehensive security remediation measures following the 2019 Emotet incident.
dataType: Names, mailing addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, NRIC numbers (national identification)

companyDescription: Larsen & Toubro Infotech (LTI) is a global IT services and consulting company and subsidiary of Indian multinational Larsen & Toubro Limited. The Singapore branch handled recruitment and HR operations.
companyLongDescription: Larsen & Toubro Infotech is a major Indian IT services firm specializing in digital transformation, enterprise solutions, and consulting. As part of the Larsen & Toubro group, one of India's largest conglomerates, LTI operates globally with offices in multiple countries. The Singapore branch processed recruitment and HR functions, handling substantial volumes of job applicant personal data. LTI provides services to Fortune 500 companies across finance, healthcare, manufacturing, and other sectors.
caseDescription: LTI negligently disclosed personal data of 13 past job applicants to 74 other job applicants through employee emails between 2016 and 2020. Violations included sending sample forms containing another applicant's data and sending a recruitment reminder email with all recipients' names visible in the 'To' field. The company failed to provide adequate instructions to employees handling recruitment on how to properly manage personal data.
violationSummary: LTI breached confidentiality by disclosing sensitive personal data of job applicants to unauthorized third parties (other applicants) through inadequate employee handling of recruitment emails and forms. This represents a failure to maintain confidentiality of personal information entrusted to the organization.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: LTI employees sent personal data of 13 past job applicants to 74 other applicants through recruitment emails between 2016.
whyTheyWereWrong: Job applicants had their names, signatures, national ID numbers, dates of birth, addresses, contact numbers, medical status, employment history, salary information.

claimsVsReality.claim: LTI had a general Corporate Privacy Policy and Employee Privacy Notice covering all employees and adequate employee guidance.
claimsVsReality.reality: LTI's privacy documents provided notice only; recruitment employees had no targeted policies or standard operating procedures despite handling highly sensitive personal data, and 10 different employees committed the same breaches over 4 years.

claimsVsReality.claim: LTI's Data Privacy Awareness training was sufficient for all employee roles.
claimsVsReality.reality: General privacy training did not adequately prepare recruitment staff to handle personal data, as evidenced by widespread unauthorized disclosures across multiple employees over an extended period.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation – Organizations must take reasonable precautions to protect personal data and provide adequate instructions to employees
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide targeted policies or standard operating procedures for employees handling recruitment matters despite handling sensitive personal data
violations: Failed to provide targeted policies or standard operating procedures for employees handling recruitment matters despite handling sensitive personal data
Relied only on generic 'Data Privacy Awareness' training materials without role-specific guidance
10 employees engaged in similar unauthorized disclosures over 4 years, indicating systemic inadequacy of instructions

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 13 – Consent Obligation – Organizations must obtain consent before disclosing personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed names and email addresses of 54 job applicants in a single email with all recipients visible in the 'To' field without consent
violations: Disclosed names and email addresses of 54 job applicants in a single email with all recipients visible in the 'To' field without consent
Disclosed personal data of past applicants (including ID numbers, DOB, address, medical status, salary, criminal records) to other applicants through sample forms without consent

outcome: LTI was ordered to pay a financial penalty of $7,000 SGD within 30 days. LTI proactively notified all 87 affected job applicants of the wrongful disclosures, implemented new procedures for email communications to external applicants, and conducted refresher training for employees involved. No further enforcement actions were required given LTI's cooperation, voluntary review of historical breaches, and prompt remedial measures.
companyNow: LTI merged with Mindtree in 2021 and is now known as LTIMindtree, a leading global IT services and digital solutions provider. The combined entity serves clients globally across multiple industries.
dataType: Name, email address, national identification/passport numbers, date of birth, address, contact number, medical health status, employment history, salary information, criminal records

companyDescription: Webcada Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based technology company that operates database services and manages customer data. The company was subject to a major ransomware attack in August 2020 due to inadequate security controls.
companyLongDescription: Webcada Pte Ltd is a Singapore-registered technology services provider that manages customer databases containing personal information. In August 2020, the company suffered a significant ransomware attack that exploited misconfigured server management interfaces, leading to the compromise of over 522,000 individuals' personal data. The incident revealed systemic gaps in the company's data protection practices, including the absence of written data protection policies and inadequate vulnerability scanning procedures.
caseDescription: Webcada suffered a ransomware attack on three database servers in August 2020 that compromised the personal data of over 522,000 individuals. The attack exploited misconfigured IPMI access settings that were exposed to the public internet and were not included in the company's vulnerability scanning procedures. The company lacked a written data protection policy and failed to implement adequate security controls required under Singapore's PDPA.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal data, specifically: (1) misconfigured IPMI access exposed to public internet, (2) omission of IPMI from monthly vulnerability scans, and (3) absence of written data protection policy. These failures constitute breaches of the Protection Obligation under section 24 and Accountability Obligation under section 12 of the PDPA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Webcada failed to secure its database servers, leaving IPMI access misconfigured and exposed to the public internet, which allowed attackers to upload ransomware.
whyTheyWereWrong: The misconfigured IPMI settings exposed names, phone numbers, dates of birth, addresses and order histories of over 522,000 people to unauthorized access, creating identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Webcada maintained adequate security controls and vulnerability management procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had misconfigured IPMI settings exposed to the public internet and failed to include IPMI in its monthly vulnerability scans, allowing ransomware to be uploaded to servers without detection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Webcada had documented data protection policies in place to ensure compliance with PDPA obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not have a written data protection policy prior to the August 2020 incident, failing to meet the Accountability Obligation requirement under section 12 of the PDPA.

claimsVsReality.claim: Webcada implemented adequate Protection Obligations to safeguard personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to configure IPMI access settings correctly, unnecessarily enabling access from the public internet and omitting IPMI from vulnerability scanning procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Accountability Obligation: Organisations must document data protection policies and practices in writing
regulatoryFindings.description: Webcada did not have a written data protection policy prior to the incident
violations: Webcada did not have a written data protection policy prior to the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must implement appropriate security measures to protect personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: IPMI access was incorrectly configured and enabled from the public internet without necessity
violations: IPMI access was incorrectly configured and enabled from the public internet without necessity
IPMI was omitted from monthly vulnerability scans, preventing detection of exploitable vulnerabilities
Lack of adequate security controls allowed ransomware upload via unmonitored IPMI interface

outcome: Webcada was ordered to pay a financial penalty of $25,000 SGD within 30 days. No directions were issued under section 48I of the PDPA in view of the organisation's prompt remedial actions, which included: permanently disabling IPMI, removing public IP addresses, restricting remote management access to trusted IPs only, installing endpoint protection software with threat hunting capabilities, and developing a written data protection policy compliant with PDPA provisions.
companyNow: Webcada implemented comprehensive remedial measures following the 2020 breach, including disabling IPMI access, restricting remote management to trusted IP addresses, deploying endpoint protection software, and establishing written data protection policies to comply with PDPA requirements.
dataType: Names, phone numbers, dates of birth, addresses, order histories

companyDescription: Tripartite Alliance Limited is a Singapore-based organization that promotes fair employment practices and provides mediation and advice services for employment-related disputes.
companyLongDescription: Tripartite Alliance Limited operates in Singapore with a focus on advancing progressive employment practices and resolving workplace conflicts. The organization handles employment-related enquiries, feedback, and complaints from both individuals and companies through its customer relationship management systems. It serves as a neutral party in employment disputes and advocacy for workplace fairness.
caseDescription: Tripartite Alliance's customer relationship management system was infected with ransomware on 17 February 2020, affecting approximately 20,000 individuals' and companies' data. The organization failed to adequately monitor its software vendor's performance to ensure proper information security standards were met, in breach of section 24 of the PDPA Protection Obligation.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement adequate security measures and oversight of its third-party vendor, resulting in a ransomware attack that compromised personal data. The database was unencrypted and security monitoring was inadequate despite contracted security services.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Tripartite Alliance failed to adequately monitor its software vendor's performance to ensure proper information security standards were met.
whyTheyWereWrong: The ransomware infection exposed approximately 20,000 individuals' and companies' sensitive employment dispute data, including names, identification numbers, contact details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had expanded IT services from the vendor to include security monitoring services for the CRM system since June 2019, including blocking of cyber-attacks based on alerts.
claimsVsReality.reality: There was inadequate process in place to ensure the vendor proactively monitored alerts and took timely action to block malicious activities; hacking attempts occurred between 7-14 February 2020 without being stopped despite the monitoring services supposedly being in place.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization exercised adequate oversight of its vendor's delivery of contracted data protection services.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization had not monitored the vendor's performance to ensure it met required information security standards, failing to provide proper instructions or reasonable oversight of the outsourced security provider.

claimsVsReality.claim: The database was adequately protected against unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: The database in the CRM system was not protected by encryption at the time of the incident, making it vulnerable to exposure if the attacker had exfiltrated the data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organisations to put in place reasonable security measures and to ensure outsourced data processors meet required information security standards through proper instructions and reasonable oversight
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to monitor vendor's performance to ensure required information security standards were met
violations: Failed to monitor vendor's performance to ensure required information security standards were met
Did not have adequate processes in place to ensure vendor proactively monitored security alerts
Failed to exercise reasonable oversight of vendor's delivery of contracted security monitoring services
Database containing personal data was not encrypted, leaving it vulnerable to exposure

outcome: The Organisation is directed to pay a financial penalty of $29,000 SGD within 30 days. No other directions were issued in view of the Organization's prompt admission of breach and remedial actions, including close monitoring of vendor IT services on a weekly basis, organization-wide review of third-party IT service provider management, implementation of cybersecurity audits and vulnerability assessments, and migration to a new CRM system.
companyNow: Following the 2020 incident, Tripartite Alliance implemented weekly vendor monitoring, expanded cybersecurity audit requirements for third-party providers, and migrated to a new CRM system while terminating the vulnerable legacy system.
dataType: Name, identification number, contact number, email address, age, race, marital status, salary and compensation information

companyDescription: St. Joseph's Institution International is an educational institution in Singapore providing schooling services to students from primary through secondary levels.
companyLongDescription: St. Joseph's Institution International is a Singapore-based independent school offering comprehensive education to students. The institution serves families across the island and maintains records containing sensitive personal data of students and parents. As an educational provider, the school is responsible for safeguarding student information and implementing appropriate data protection measures to comply with Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: St. Joseph's Institution International deployed a Google Chrome security extension that unknowingly shared uploaded files with VirusTotal's premium members for research purposes. Personal data of 3,155 parents and students, including names, email addresses, dates of birth, class information, and grades, were exposed through this mechanism. The organisation lacked sufficient processes to assess security risks before deploying software.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate safeguards and risk assessment processes before deploying software, resulting in unauthorised disclosure of personal data to third parties. This constitutes a failure to maintain security and protect personal data from unauthorised access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: St. Joseph's Institution International deployed a Google Chrome security extension without reviewing its privacy policy, unknowingly exposing personal data of 3,155 parents.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents and students' names, email addresses, dates of birth, class information, and grades were shared with third parties without consent or knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Chrome extension was deployed for additional security scanning with no other function.
claimsVsReality.reality: The extension also automatically forwarded scanned files to VirusTotal's premium members for security analysis and research, as disclosed in VirusTotal's privacy policy that the school staff did not review.

claimsVsReality.claim: The school had adequate processes for assessing security risks before deploying software.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization lacked sufficiently robust processes to assess such risks, resulting in staff overlooking the privacy policy disclosure about file sharing with third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 – Protection Obligation requiring organisations to protect personal data in their possession through reasonable security measures
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to implement sufficiently robust processes for assessing risks prior to deploying downloaded software including Chrome Extensions
violations: Failure to implement sufficiently robust processes for assessing risks prior to deploying downloaded software including Chrome Extensions
Lack of functional understanding of deployed software's capabilities and data handling practices
Inadequate risk assessment procedures before deployment of third-party tools

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection issued a Warning to the organisation. While a breach of the Protection Obligation was found, the warning (rather than a monetary penalty) was issued in consideration of the limited risk of disclosure (limited to premium members for research purposes only), the organisation's prompt mitigation efforts (immediate contact with VirusTotal to remove the file and notification of affected individuals), and the organisation's commitment to improve its processes.
companyNow: St. Joseph's Institution International continues to operate as an independent school in Singapore, having strengthened its software deployment and data protection processes following this 2020 incident.
dataType: Names, email addresses, date of birth, class information, grades
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24 (Protection Obligation)

companyDescription: Flying Cape Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based data intermediary that hosts, manages, and operates websites for clients. The company manages personal data on behalf of organizations that lack in-house technical infrastructure.
companyLongDescription: Flying Cape Pte Ltd is a Singapore-incorporated data intermediary and web hosting provider. The company acts as a data processor for organizations, hosting and managing their websites and associated databases containing personal data. Flying Cape manages infrastructure including database management, file storage, and IT security policies. The company's role involves responsibility for implementing robust data protection measures to safeguard personal data entrusted to it by its clients.
caseDescription: Flying Cape, a data intermediary managing the ACCA Singapore website, failed to protect personal data of 191 users. An employee extracted data into an unencrypted Excel file and stored it in a publicly accessible online storage bucket, leading to unauthorized exfiltration. Flying Cape did not supervise employee compliance with its internal data protection policies.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data. Specifically, the data was not encrypted, was not password-protected, and was stored in an unsecured location due to lack of employee supervision and verification mechanisms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Flying Cape extracted personal data of 191 users into an unencrypted Excel file and stored it in a publicly accessible online storage bucket.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unencrypted data file stored in a publicly accessible location was exfiltrated by an unauthorized party, exposing the names, email addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Flying Cape had internal data protection policies requiring encryption and password protection of sensitive data files.
claimsVsReality.reality: An employee extracted personal data into an unencrypted Excel file and stored it in a publicly accessible bucket, directly violating these policies, with no supervisory mechanisms in place to detect or prevent such violations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Flying Cape had secure storage infrastructure in place for sensitive data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee incorrectly stored the data in a publicly accessible online storage bucket instead of the secured storage bucket, indicating either inadequate system controls or lack of employee training and oversight.

claimsVsReality.claim: Flying Cape maintained adequate oversight of employee compliance with data protection policies.
claimsVsReality.reality: The investigation found no arrangements to supervise or verify employee compliance with internal policies or detect non-compliance, allowing the data breach to occur undetected.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must take reasonable steps to protect personal data in their possession or under their control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Flying Cape extracted personal data into an unencrypted Excel file without password protection
violations: Flying Cape extracted personal data into an unencrypted Excel file without password protection
Flying Cape stored the file in a publicly accessible online storage bucket instead of a secured storage bucket
Flying Cape failed to supervise or verify employee compliance with its internal data protection policies
Flying Cape did not detect the employee's non-compliance with IT security requirements

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Flying Cape in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24. However, due to the low number of affected individuals, low sensitivity of the exfiltrated data, Flying Cape's immediate remedial actions, and voluntary notification to the Commission, a Warning was issued instead of a monetary penalty or compliance directions.
dataType: Names, email addresses, contact numbers

companyDescription: Chapel of Christ the Redeemer is a religious organisation in Singapore that maintains records of its members.
companyLongDescription: Chapel of Christ the Redeemer is a faith-based organisation in Singapore that maintains membership records. At the time of this incident, the organisation lacked formal data protection policies, practices, and technical controls required to safeguard member information. The organisation discovered in 2020 that it had inadvertently exposed sensitive member data online.
caseDescription: Chapel of Christ the Redeemer accidentally uploaded a file containing personal data of 815 members to a publicly accessible sub-directory on its website on 24 November 2019. The file remained accessible and indexed by search engines until discovered on 8 September 2020.
