The organisation lacked data protection policies, access controls, and file upload checks required under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to implement adequate security measures and access controls resulted in unintended exposure of personal data to the public through search engine indexing. This falls under 'Exposure' as it made sensitive personal information accessible to the general public.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: A staff member accidentally uploaded a file containing personal data of 815 members to a publicly accessible website sub-directory on 24 November 2019.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' sensitive personal information including names, national ID numbers, addresses, dates of birth, marital status, email and phone numbers were exposed online.

claimsVsReality.claim: The sub-directory was intended to be accessible to the public with no access controls.
claimsVsReality.reality: The file contained highly sensitive member data (NRICs, addresses, dates of birth, phone numbers) that should never have been made public, regardless of the sub-directory's intended purpose.

claimsVsReality.claim: Access to the exposed file was minimal.
claimsVsReality.reality: While documented accesses were few, the file was indexed by Google search and remained discoverable online for nearly 10 months, exposing all 815 members' data to potential discovery and misuse by unknown parties.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had no data protection policies at the time of the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: The PDPA requires all organisations to develop and implement data protection policies; Chapel of Christ the Redeemer's complete absence of such policies left member data entirely unprotected.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Obligation to develop and implement data protection policies and practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation had not developed any internal policies and practices to ensure PDPA compliance
violations: Organisation had not developed any internal policies and practices to ensure PDPA compliance
No system of checks for uploading files on the organisation's website

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Obligation to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements
regulatoryFindings.description: No access controls to the sub-directory despite containing sensitive member data
violations: No access controls to the sub-directory despite containing sensitive member data
File was indexed by search engines and accessible to the public
Personal data of 815 members exposed online for approximately 10 months

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner did not impose a financial penalty due to the organisation's voluntary notification, full cooperation, minimal actual access to the data, and absence of evidence of misuse. However, the organisation was directed to develop and implement internal data protection policies and practices compliant with the PDPA within 90 days and inform the Commission within 1 week of implementation.
companyNow: Following the 2020 incident, the organisation has implemented password protections, weekly file checks, automated file deletion policies, and is undergoing PDPA compliance training.
dataType: Name, NRIC (National Registration Identity Card), address, date of birth, marital status, email address, mobile and residential phone numbers
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 12 (obligation to develop and implement data protection policies and practices)
PDPA Section 24 (obligation to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements)

companyDescription: Jigyasa is a human resources and management consultancy business that generates 360-degree feedback reports for client employees. The organization was operated by a sole proprietor with one part-time employee.
companyLongDescription: Jigyasa is a small human resources and management consultancy that specializes in generating 360-degree feedback assessments for employees of client organizations. These reports document performance evaluations and peer feedback including character qualities, ratings, and verbatim comments. The company operated as a sole proprietorship with minimal staff, relying on a web application to collect survey data and generate assessment reports for storage and retrieval.
caseDescription: Jigyasa, a human resource consultancy, failed to protect 671 employee assessment reports (360 Feedback Reports) on its website, which became publicly accessible during a website redesign in February 2017. The reports remained exposed online for over 7 years and contained sensitive performance evaluations, ratings, and verbatim feedback that could affect individuals' employment prospects. The organization lacked basic security controls, failed to conduct vulnerability scans, and demonstrated insufficient awareness of its data protection obligations.
violationSummary: The organization's failure to implement reasonable security arrangements during website redesign resulted in sensitive personal data being inadvertently exposed to the public without access controls. The Reports containing performance assessments and evaluative feedback were accessible via internet search, creating risk of unauthorized disclosure to the world at large.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Jigyasa failed to protect 671 employee assessment reports containing performance ratings and feedback on its website.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees whose sensitive performance evaluations, ratings, and verbatim feedback were publicly discoverable online suffered potential damage to their employment prospects.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Reports were dynamically generated by the Web Application and presented for viewing, without storing a copy on the Website.
claimsVsReality.reality: Reports were being saved as PDF files on the Organization's server and remained stored there for years after the Web Application was discontinued in 2010.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data should have been automatically removed from the server when the Web Application was discontinued in 2010.
claimsVsReality.reality: No deletion or archival procedures were implemented; reports remained on the server and became publicly accessible during the website redesign in 2017, seven years later.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization was unaware of the incident and did not have knowledge of security arrangements for its Website.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization demonstrated fundamental lack of care through failure to conduct vulnerability scans, lack of documented security instructions to developers, and no personal data inventory management.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to maintain knowledge of where personal data was stored and how it was created
violations: Failed to maintain knowledge of where personal data was stored and how it was created
Did not provide clear security instructions to third-party developer during website redesign
Failed to conduct vulnerability scans or security testing before or after website went live
Did not implement access controls (password protection) during website redesign despite previous implementation
Allowed personal data to remain on server for 7+ years without removal after Web Application was discontinued in 2010

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 11(3) – Appointment of Data Protection Officer
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to appoint a designated Data Protection Officer
violations: Failed to appoint a designated Data Protection Officer
Organization was unaware of PDPA obligations beyond Do-Not-Call provisions

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Data Protection Policies
regulatoryFindings.description: Did not develop or implement documented Data Protection Policies
violations: Did not develop or implement documented Data Protection Policies
Relied only on unwritten policies communicated verbally to staff
Lack of written policy prevented effective internal training and staff reference material

outcome: The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of SGD 90,000 (payable within 30 days), and directed the organization to: (1) appoint a Data Protection Officer within 30 days; and (2) develop and implement documented Data Protection Policies and communicate them to staff within 30 days. The financial penalty was reduced from an initially higher amount in consideration of the organization's financial circumstances and prompt remedial actions taken after notification, though this reduction was characterized as exceptional and not setting precedent.
dataType: Employee assessment reports, 360 feedback scores, work performance appraisals, employer names and addresses
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 24 (Protection Obligation – reasonable security arrangements)
PDPA Section 11(3) (Designation of Data Protection Officer)
PDPA Section 12 (Development and implementation of Data Protection Policies)

companyDescription: Singapore Technologies Engineering Limited is a Singapore-incorporated multinational defence and engineering company with subsidiaries across Asia, Europe, USA, and the Middle East. The company operates in aerospace, defence, and engineering sectors.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Technologies Engineering Limited is a major Singapore-based conglomerate with a global network of subsidiaries spanning Asia, Europe, USA, and the Middle East. The company specializes in aerospace engineering, defence systems, and related engineering services. It operates through various subsidiary entities including VT San Antonio Aerospace Inc. in the USA. The organization processes employee data internationally for regulatory filings, employment management, and security clearance purposes.
caseDescription: A ransomware attack on a subsidiary's US-based IT network resulted in unauthorised access to personal data of 287 Singapore-based individuals, with 49 individuals' data likely exfiltrated. The parent company had transferred this personal data internationally to subsidiaries in the USA for employment, regulatory, and security clearance purposes. The investigation focused on whether the data transfer complied with Singapore's PDPA transfer limitation obligations.
violationSummary: While the organisation complied with transfer requirements, the violation relates to the security incident itself—a cybersecurity breach resulting in unauthorised access to personal data due to inadequate security measures in the recipient organisation's systems.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Singapore Technologies Engineering transferred personal data of 287 Singapore-based individuals to US subsidiaries for employment, regulatory.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's data transfer resulted in 49 individuals' personal information including NRIC numbers, passport details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had implemented binding corporate rules that ensured comparable data protection standards across all subsidiaries.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite having binding corporate rules in place, a US subsidiary's IT network was successfully breached by threat actors who deployed ransomware and exfiltrated personal data of 49 individuals, demonstrating that the rules did not prevent actual security failures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The receiving company (VT SAA) had implemented appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorised access and protect transferred personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: VT SAA's US-based IT network was compromised by a ransomware attack, resulting in unauthorised access to and likely exfiltration of sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers, passport details, and US social security numbers of affected individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 26(1) – Transfer Limitation Obligation requiring organisations to transfer personal data outside Singapore only in accordance with prescribed requirements ensuring comparable protection
regulatoryFindings.description: The Organisation's personal data transfer processes did not prevent a subsequent ransomware attack on recipient systems, though the Organisation itself complied with binding corporate rules requirements at the time of transfer
violations: The Organisation's personal data transfer processes did not prevent a subsequent ransomware attack on recipient systems, though the Organisation itself complied with binding corporate rules requirements at the time of transfer

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPR Regulation 9(1)(b) – Requirement that organisations ensure recipients are bound by legally enforceable obligations providing comparable protection
regulatoryFindings.description: Despite binding corporate rules being in place requiring reasonable security arrangements, the recipient organisation (VT SAA) experienced a cybersecurity incident resulting in unauthorised access to transferred personal data
violations: Despite binding corporate rules being in place requiring reasonable security arrangements, the recipient organisation (VT SAA) experienced a cybersecurity incident resulting in unauthorised access to transferred personal data

outcome: The Commission found that Singapore Technologies Engineering had complied with the Transfer Limitation Obligation under the PDPA at the time of transfer, as it had established binding corporate rules meeting all regulatory requirements. The subsidiaries based in the USA were not subject to PDPA obligations as they did not carry out collection, use, or disclosure activities in Singapore. The Commission deferred to ongoing US federal law enforcement investigations. The Organisation implemented remedial cybersecurity measures including enhanced endpoint security controls, additional network monitoring, security hardening, and a 24/7 Security Operations Centre, and accelerated its IT harmonisation plan across all entities.
companyNow: Singapore Technologies Engineering remains a major player in Singapore's defence and engineering sector. The company has enhanced its cybersecurity infrastructure following the 2020 incident.
dataType: Name, address, email, telephone, NRIC number, passport details, photograph, date of birth, citizenship, country of residence, place of birth, USA Social Security number, visa information, government/military service details, CV information, foreign identification numbers, government-issued ID, information about minors, employee status
legalBasisViolated: PDPR Regulation 9(1)(b) – Transfer to countries outside Singapore
PDPR Regulation 10(1)(c) – Legally enforceable obligations of recipients
PDPR Regulation 10(3) – Binding corporate rules requirements

companyDescription: The Future of Cooking Pte. Ltd. operates an e-commerce website (thermomix.com.sg) retailing kitchen appliances and accessories in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: The Future of Cooking Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based e-commerce retailer specializing in kitchen appliances and accessories, operating through their online storefront at thermomix.com.sg. The company engaged third-party vendors for website redesign and data migration services. At the time of the data breach in 2020, the company's database contained personal data of approximately 3,500 customers.
caseDescription: The Future of Cooking's e-commerce website exposed a text file containing personal data of 178 customers through a publicly accessible URL for over three months. A WordPress plugin bug generated and uploaded the temporary file to a publicly accessible directory. The company failed to implement data protection requirements in its vendor contract and did not conduct pre-launch security testing.
violationSummary: TFC failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically by not requiring data protection measures from its service provider and failing to conduct pre-launch vulnerability assessments that would have detected the publicly accessible temporary file.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The Future of Cooking failed to implement data protection measures in its vendor contract and did not conduct pre-launch security testing.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive personal information including names, email addresses, billing and shipping addresses, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Hachi Web Solutions should be held responsible for the data breach as the web design vendor.
claimsVsReality.reality: The breach was caused by a WordPress plugin bug during website redesign, not by Hachi's data intermediary role in backup and migration—Hachi was not found in breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: The temporary file was generated by the plugin and would not be discoverable without knowing about the bug.
claimsVsReality.reality: Pre-launch security testing such as vulnerability assessments would have detected the publicly accessible temporary file regardless of awareness of the specific plugin bug.

claimsVsReality.claim: The vendor contract and security requirements were adequately specified to Hachi.
claimsVsReality.reality: TFC failed to specify any data protection requirements or security measures to be implemented in the Website within its contract or project documentation with Hachi.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Data controllers must put in place reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data collected
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to specify data protection requirements in contract with service provider (Hachi)
violations: Failed to specify data protection requirements in contract with service provider (Hachi)
Failed to conduct pre-launch security testing such as vulnerability assessments
Did not detect publicly accessible temporary file containing customer personal data

outcome: TFC was found in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24 and directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $9,000 within 30 days. The company had already taken remedial actions including removing the plugin, disabling public access to the directory, engaging a vendor for penetration testing, and enhancing website security. No further directions were required given the remedial measures undertaken.
dataType: Name, email address, billing address, shipping address, telephone number, customer notes, order information, payment status, payment mode, transaction ID, product ID

companyDescription: BLS International Services Singapore is a visa and consular services provider operating on behalf of the High Commission of India in Singapore. The company processes government-to-citizen applications and bookings.
companyLongDescription: BLS International Services Singapore provides visa appointment booking and consular services for the High Commission of India in Singapore. The company developed an online booking system to streamline appointment scheduling for visa applicants. In June 2020, a newly implemented booking system contained a critical security vulnerability in its URL encryption mechanism. The organization admitted the breach and took immediate corrective action upon discovery.
caseDescription: BLS International Services Singapore failed to properly encrypt URLs in its visa appointment booking system, allowing attackers to manipulate URLs to access other individuals' personal data. A coding error went undetected because the organisation did not conduct adequate testing before deploying the system. The vulnerability exposed the personal data of 3,357 individuals over approximately one month.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures (proper URL encryption) and failed to conduct sufficient testing to detect security flaws before deployment, resulting in exposure of personal data through URL manipulation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: BLS International Services Singapore deployed a visa appointment booking system with improperly encrypted URLs that could be manipulated to access other users' personal data.
whyTheyWereWrong: The undetected coding error exposed the personal data of 3,357 individuals including passport numbers, contact information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation intended for URLs in the booking system to be encrypted to prevent manipulation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The encryption was not implemented properly due to a coding error that went undetected because testing was not extensive enough.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation conducted testing on the new booking system before deployment.
claimsVsReality.reality: The testing was insufficient to detect the critical coding error in the URL encryption mechanism.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must take reasonable security measures to protect personal data in their possession or under their control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement proper URL encryption despite intending to do so; coding error was not detected
violations: Failed to implement proper URL encryption despite intending to do so; coding error was not detected
Conducted inadequate testing of the new booking system before deployment, which would have identified the encryption failure
Left personal data of 3,357 individuals at risk of exposure through URL manipulation for approximately one month

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the organisation in breach of Section 24 of the PDPA and directed payment of a $5,000 financial penalty within 30 days. The organisation had already taken remedial actions by modifying the booking system to send confirmations via email instead of providing manipulable URLs, eliminating the security gap. No further directions were required.
companyNow: The company continues to operate visa and consular services for the High Commission of India in Singapore, now with enhanced security testing procedures implemented post-breach.
dataType: Name, passport number, contact number, email address, service request type, booking date/time, appointment date/time

companyDescription: Water + Plants Lab Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based technology company that processes personal data of employees and potentially customers.
companyLongDescription: Water + Plants Lab Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-registered organisation in the technology sector. The company was affected by a ransomware incident in March 2020 that highlighted significant security deficiencies in its data protection practices. Despite maintaining some baseline security measures like anti-virus protection and regular backups, the organisation failed to implement critical security maintenance procedures required to protect personal data.
caseDescription: Water + Plants Lab suffered a ransomware infection in March 2020 that encrypted personal data of 28 employees. The organisation had failed to conduct server patching and security scanning for 12 months prior to the incident, which allowed the vulnerability to be exploited. While minimal data loss occurred due to backups and no exfiltration was detected, the organisation was found in breach of its obligation to protect personal data under the Personal Data Protection Act 2012.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures (patching and security scanning) to protect personal data from unauthorised access and encryption, resulting in a ransomware attack that compromised employee data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Water + Plants Lab failed to conduct server patching and security scanning for 12 months before a ransomware infection in March 2020 encrypted personal data of 28 employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: The lack of security patching left vulnerabilities that attackers exploited to encrypt employee personal data including names, identification numbers, addresses, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: Water + Plants Lab had adequate security measures in place to protect personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation had not performed any server patching or security scanning in 12 months, leaving critical vulnerabilities unaddressed that enabled the ransomware attack.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation maintained sufficient cybersecurity practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Security scanning and timely patching are essential maintenance activities that Water + Plants Lab completely neglected, contrary to data protection obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA 2012 Section 24 – Obligation to protect personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct server patching for 12 months preceding the incident
violations: Failed to conduct server patching for 12 months preceding the incident
Failed to perform regular security scanning of the server
Did not maintain sufficient security measures to prevent exploitation of vulnerabilities

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to the Organisation. Post-incident, the Organisation installed a firewall with enhanced capabilities including deeper content inspection to identify malware, and conducted staff training on personal data protection and security threat identification.
companyNow: Following the enforcement action, Water + Plants Lab implemented enhanced security measures including a firewall with advanced malware detection and conducted staff training on data protection and security threat identification.
dataType: Name, NRIC/FIN/Work Permit number, address, date of birth, mobile number, photograph

companyDescription: R.I.S.E Aerospace is a Singapore-based aerospace company. The organization processes employee personal data as part of normal HR and operational functions.
companyLongDescription: R.I.S.E Aerospace Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-registered aerospace company that maintains employee records including identification documents, contact information, and financial details. The company operates network storage infrastructure for data management and HR functions. As of 2020, the organization had at least 21 employees whose data was subject to the incident.
caseDescription: R.I.S.E Aerospace suffered a ransomware attack on 23 August 2020 that encrypted personal data of 21 employees. The organisation failed to implement adequate technical security measures, including security scans, firmware updates, and documented IT security policies. The company had vulnerabilities that enabled the hacker to inject ransomware into the server.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures to protect personal data, allowing a ransomware attack to encrypt sensitive employee information. This directly violates the requirement to secure personal data against unauthorised access and loss.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: R.I.S.E Aerospace failed to implement adequate technical security measures, including security scans, firmware updates.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's security negligence resulted in the personal data of 21 employees—including names, addresses, NRIC numbers, passport details.

claimsVsReality.claim: R.I.S.E Aerospace maintained a secure IT infrastructure with up-to-date systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had not performed firmware updates despite manufacturer prompts and lacked documented IT security policies, creating exploitable vulnerabilities.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had no way to prevent unauthorized access to stored personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Standard security practices such as security scans, patching, and documented policies could have prevented the ransomware injection that encrypted employee data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must implement and maintain appropriate technical and organisational security measures to protect personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to carry out security scans on the network storage server
violations: Failed to carry out security scans on the network storage server
Failed to perform firmware updates despite manufacturer prompts
Did not implement any documented IT security policies including password policy and patching/updating procedures
System vulnerabilities allowed ransomware injection and encryption of personal data

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection issued a Warning to the Organisation for breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24. The organisation had already taken remedial actions including discontinuing the vulnerable network storage server, adopting cloud storage, implementing data encryption, and storing sensitive data on offline devices. No additional directions were issued given the low number of affected individuals, absence of evidence of data misuse, retention of backup copies, and the organisation's voluntary notification of the incident.
companyNow: Following the 2020 incident, R.I.S.E Aerospace discontinued its network storage server in favor of cloud storage and implemented encryption for sensitive data stored on offline devices.
dataType: Name, address, contact number, NRIC number, Work Permit details, passport details, bank account numbers, child's date of birth

companyDescription: Everlast Projects Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based construction and architectural metalworks company specializing in the supply and installation of metal works, glass, and aluminium products. The company operated as a group with related entities Everlast Industries and ELG Specialist, sharing centralized payroll processing.
companyLongDescription: Everlast Projects Pte Ltd and its related entities (Everlast Industries (S) Pte Ltd and ELG Specialist Pte Ltd) are Singapore-based companies in the architectural metalworks and construction materials sector. The three organizations operated as an integrated group under common ownership and management, sharing premises and centralizing their payroll processing functions through Everlast Projects' HR department. The group collectively employed over 380 staff members across the three entities. In August 2019, their centralized server storing employee personal data was infected with ransomware, triggering a regulatory investigation by Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission.
caseDescription: Everlast Projects and related entities failed to protect employee personal data when their server was encrypted by ransomware in August 2019, affecting 384 employees across three companies. The organizations lacked written data protection policies, adequate security arrangements, and proper oversight mechanisms for centralized payroll processing. No evidence of data exfiltration was found, and the companies voluntarily disclosed the incident to regulators.
violationSummary: The organizations failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and modification of personal data, specifically: no firewall installation, no periodic security reviews, no written IT security policies, and inadequate oversight of data intermediaries processing employee data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Everlast Projects and related entities failed to protect 384 employees' personal data when ransomware encrypted their server in August 2019, lacking written data protection policies.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees' sensitive data including names, ID numbers, bank account details and salary information became unreadable.

claimsVsReality.claim: Everlast relied on verbal instructions to manage data protection across the group.
claimsVsReality.reality: Verbal instructions alone are ineffective; employees had no written reference materials, creating risk of inconsistent implementation and leaving the organizations unable to demonstrate compliance to regulators.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organizations operated from common premises with shared management and ownership.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite physical proximity and shared resources, there were no written data protection agreements, intra-group policies, or oversight mechanisms between the three entities, leaving employee data vulnerable when processed centrally.

claimsVsReality.claim: The server had both onsite physical backup and cloud backup for redundancy.
claimsVsReality.reality: The physical backup was also encrypted by the same ransomware and rendered unusable, eliminating the intended redundancy protection.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Accountability Obligation requires organizations to develop and implement written policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations and communicate them to staff
regulatoryFindings.description: All three organizations (EPPL, EIPL, ESPL) failed to establish any written data protection policies
violations: All three organizations (EPPL, EIPL, ESPL) failed to establish any written data protection policies
Organizations relied only on verbal instructions to employees regarding data protection
No binding group-level written policies, intra-group agreements, or binding corporate rules were implemented despite operating as a unified corporate group with centralized payroll processing

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organizations to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, or similar risks to personal data in their possession or control
regulatoryFindings.description: EPPL failed to install a firewall for the server, leaving it vulnerable to web-based security threats
violations: EPPL failed to install a firewall for the server, leaving it vulnerable to web-based security threats
EPPL did not conduct periodic security reviews or vulnerability scans of its IT systems despite handling sensitive financial and employment data
EPPL provided no written IT security policies (password policy, patching and updating policies, etc.) and conceded ignorance of requirements for protecting electronic personal data

EIPL and ESPL failed to implement any written contract, agreement, or operational processes to supervise or control EPPL's protection of their employees' personal data despite EPPL acting as their data intermediary
Ransomware successfully encrypted all files on the server and physical backup, rendering employee personal data unreadable and unusable

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found all three organizations in breach of PDPA Sections 12 and 24. No financial penalty was imposed due to voluntary notification of the incident, lack of evidence of data exfiltration or misuse, and the financial hardship such a penalty would cause. Instead, the organizations were directed to: (1) develop and implement intra-group agreements or binding corporate rules setting common standards for personal data processing within 90 days; (2) review and ensure internal policies align with these new standards within 90 days; and (3) inform the Commission of completion within one week of the directions.
dataType: Employee personal data including name, NRIC/FIN number, date of birth, bank account details, salary information

companyDescription: Hello Travel is a travel website (www.havehalalwilltravel.com) that operated in Singapore and allowed users to create accounts to access travel services.
companyLongDescription: Hello Travel Pte. Ltd. was a Singapore-based travel company operating a website that enabled users to create accounts and access travel-related services and information. The company attracted approximately 71,002 registered users between February 2015 and July 2018. However, the organisation failed to maintain adequate cybersecurity practices, leaving user data vulnerable to exploitation.
caseDescription: Hello Travel's database containing personal data of approximately 71,002 users was posted publicly on an internet forum after a possible hack in 2018. The organisation failed to implement basic security measures, including regular system patching, security assessments, and proper data protection policies. The company admitted to breaching section 24 of the PDPA (Protection Obligation) and subsequently implemented remedial measures including data encryption and notification to affected individuals.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to put in place basic procedural and technical security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, including lack of regular system patching, security assessments, and ICT change management protocols. This resulted in a data breach through exploitation of vulnerabilities in an unpatched WordPress plugin.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Hello Travel failed to implement basic security measures including regular system patching and security assessments.
whyTheyWereWrong: 71,002 users had their names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth and nationalities exposed online without their knowledge, creating risk of identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: Hello Travel maintained appropriate security measures to protect user data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not have basic procedural and technical security arrangements, including no regular system patching or security assessment protocols.

claimsVsReality.claim: User data was protected from unauthorized access and exfiltration.
claimsVsReality.reality: A database containing personal data of 71,002 users was publicly posted on an internet forum, likely after exploitation of vulnerabilities in an unpatched WordPress plugin.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 (Protection Obligation) — Organisations must take reasonable steps to protect personal data from unauthorised access, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement regular system patching protocols
violations: Failed to implement regular system patching protocols
Did not conduct security assessments or testing when making changes to ICT systems
Lacked basic procedural and technical security arrangements
Allowed vulnerable open-source WordPress plugin to remain unpatched, enabling unauthorised access and data exfiltration

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Hello Travel in breach of section 24 of the PDPA (Protection Obligation). The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of $8,000 SGD payable in 10 monthly instalments from January 2021 to October 2021. The Deputy Commissioner considered mitigating factors including the organisation's cooperation, voluntary admission of liability, prompt remedial actions (encryption of personal data, removal of compromised database, notification to affected individuals), and lack of evidence of data misuse. No further directions were issued in view of the remedial actions taken.
companyNow: Unknown current operational status following the 2020 enforcement action and COVID-19 pandemic impact on the travel industry.
dataType: name, email address, date of birth, nationality, phone number

companyDescription: Secur Solutions Group Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based IT services company engaged by the Health Sciences Authority to develop and maintain IT systems, including queue management systems for blood donor operations.
companyLongDescription: Secur Solutions Group is a small to medium-sized enterprise operating in Singapore's competitive IT services industry. Since 2013, the company has been contracted by the Health Sciences Authority (HSA) to develop, maintain, and enhance various IT systems and infrastructure. The company was tasked with building and maintaining a queue management system (QMS) for blood donors, which required access to production databases containing sensitive donor information for testing and development purposes.
caseDescription: Secur Solutions Group stored a database of approximately 800,000 blood donors' personal data on an internet-accessible testing server without adequate security measures. Between 236,023 and 328,546 records were exfiltrated by an unauthorized party. The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements as required by the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organization failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access to personal data, storing sensitive blood donor information on an unsecured, internet-facing server without firewalls, patches, or access controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Secur Solutions Group stored approximately 800,000 blood donors' personal data including names, identification numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 236,023 and 328,546 blood donors' sensitive personal information was exfiltrated by unauthorized parties, exposing their identities, government ID numbers, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Testing and Development Server was not intended to store personal data and was therefore appropriately configured for its intended use.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company actually received copies of production databases containing 800,000 real blood donors' personal information from HSA beginning in July 2018, making the unsecured server inappropriate for this sensitive data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company did not anticipate receiving actual copies of production databases from HSA.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's own past experience with HSA projects involved directly retrieving personal data from production environments, and HSA even provided the company with direct server access from July to August 2018 to retrieve database updates, making it reasonably foreseeable that actual personal data would be involved.

claimsVsReality.claim: Appropriate security measures were in place for the intended purpose of the server.
claimsVsReality.reality: The server had no active patching or updates, no perimeter firewall, no firewalls, and no security protocols to restrict internet access—making it fundamentally insecure for any confidential information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organisation must protect personal data in its possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Stored personal data on testing and development server accessible from the internet without security infrastructure
violations: Stored personal data on testing and development server accessible from the internet without security infrastructure
Failed to implement firewalls, perimeter firewall setup, or security protocols to restrict access
Server system was not actively patched or updated
Between 236,023 to 328,546 records were exfiltrated due to lack of reasonable security measures
Gaps in data governance and processes with respect to receipt of test data from clients

outcome: Commissioner found the organisation in breach of Section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 120,000 within 30 days. The Commissioner noted that remedial actions already taken (disconnection of server, disabling remote access, appointing external vendors for forensic analysis, employee training, security infrastructure review and enhancement) were sufficient to address risks and no further directions were imposed. The organisation rejected a request for instalment payments due to lack of supporting financial documentation.
companyNow: Following the 2020 enforcement action, Secur Solutions Group implemented significant remedial measures including appointing additional Data Protection Officers, enhancing cybersecurity infrastructure, and establishing defense-in-depth security protocols.
dataType: Name, NRIC, gender, phone number, blood donation history, blood type, height, weight

companyDescription: Worksmartly is a finance and payroll processing vendor based in Singapore that provides data handling services to corporate clients.
companyLongDescription: Worksmartly Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based financial services company specializing in finance and payroll processing for corporate clients. The company was engaged by pharmaceutical multinational Roche to handle employee payroll and financial data processing. Despite terminating its contract with Roche at the end of 2018, Worksmartly retained sensitive employee data in its systems, leading to a significant data protection breach in 2020.
caseDescription: Worksmartly, a finance and payroll processing vendor, failed to delete personal data of 308 Roche employees and dependents after the service contract ended. An employee accidentally changed the GitHub repository from private to public, exposing the data for five days before discovery. The company lacked proper security controls and file management procedures to prevent this incident.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate safeguards to protect personal data, including lack of checks on GitHub security settings and failure to delete files no longer needed. This breaches the Protection Obligation under PDPA section 24, which requires organisations to put in place security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Worksmartly failed to delete employee and dependent personal data from a GitHub repository after the service contract with Roche ended.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees' and dependents' sensitive personal information including national ID numbers, salaries, bank account details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The file would only be accessible to other members of the Organisation when the GitHub setting was changed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Changing the GitHub repository from private to public made the file containing 308 individuals' personal data publicly accessible to anyone on the internet for five days.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation had adequate file management procedures to ensure deletion of personal data after service contracts ended.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Organisation lacked proper housekeeping procedures and inadvertently retained sensitive employee data in a different folder, which was never deleted despite the contract termination in December 2018.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation had proper security controls to prevent unauthorised disclosure of personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Organisation had no checks to manage correct GitHub security settings and relied solely on employees to manually set correct access levels, resulting in a critical exposure.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must take steps to protect personal data in their possession against unauthorised access, use, modification, disclosure or other misuse.
regulatoryFindings.description: Worksmartly lacked checks to manage correct security settings on its GitHub account and relied solely on employee compliance
violations: Worksmartly lacked checks to manage correct security settings on its GitHub account and relied solely on employee compliance
No controls were in place to prevent accidental exposure of sensitive data through misconfigured repository settings

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 25 – Retention Obligation: Organisations must not retain personal data longer than necessary for the purposes for which it was collected.
regulatoryFindings.description: Worksmartly retained the File containing personal data after the service contract ended on 31 December 2018
violations: Worksmartly retained the File containing personal data after the service contract ended on 31 December 2018
The File was stored in a different folder and was inadvertently omitted from deletion procedures, leading to unnecessary retention for over 14 months

outcome: Worksmartly was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 5,000 within 30 days. The Deputy Commissioner noted the organisation's full admission of breaches, cooperation with the Commission's investigation, and prompt remedial actions taken (immediately securing the GitHub account, deleting the exposed file, resetting passwords, conducting file housekeeping, and implementing new security protocols). No additional directions were issued given the comprehensive remedial measures implemented.
companyNow: Following the 2020 PDPA enforcement action, Worksmartly implemented enhanced security controls and GitHub access management procedures. The company's current status is not publicly documented.
dataType: Name, national identification numbers (NRIC/FIN/Passport), address, date of birth, race, citizenship, employee ID, email address, job title, employment commencement date, salary, bank account details, contact number

companyDescription: Times Software Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based information technology services vendor that develops and hosts payroll software applications for corporate clients.
companyLongDescription: Times Software Pte Ltd is an IT services company based in Singapore that specializes in developing and maintaining payroll software solutions for enterprise clients. The company has been operating since at least 1999, providing services to major organizations including law firms, multinational technology companies, and professional services firms. Times Software operates as a data intermediary, processing and storing sensitive employee data on behalf of its clients.
caseDescription: Times Software failed to implement adequate security measures for personal employee data stored on its servers. Following a hard disk failure in December 2017, Times reset server settings to default, disabling password protection, which exposed 616 employees' data to web crawlers and Google indexing from December 2017 to February 2018. The company also failed to delete data after project completion and used live customer data for testing purposes.
violationSummary: Times failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data. Specific failures included: inadequate authentication function after server restoration, poor password management policies, failure to encrypt sensitive financial data, use of live customer data for testing, and failure to delete data after project completion. The company's SOPs were insufficient and lacked adequate monitoring mechanisms to prevent employee errors.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Times Software failed to enable password protection after restoring a hard disk backup in December 2017, exposing 616 employees' personal data to web crawlers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 616 employees had sensitive personal data including names, identification numbers, addresses, salaries, bank account information, and tax details exposed online.

claimsVsReality.claim: Times had adequate security measures and SOPs in place to protect employee data
claimsVsReality.reality: Times failed to implement password protection after server restoration and did not verify that security protocols were actually enforced, leaving 616 employees' sensitive data publicly accessible for two months

claimsVsReality.claim: Times properly managed the lifecycle of personal data provided for development purposes
claimsVsReality.reality: Times retained live customer data well after project completion without deletion, using it for testing purposes despite not having authorization to do so

claimsVsReality.claim: Times' existing SOPs were sufficient to prevent data breaches
claimsVsReality.reality: Times' employee failed to enable authentication after server restoration, and the supervisor failed to verify compliance; no proactive detection mechanisms existed to catch such failures

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation. Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to enable authentication/password protection function after server restoration despite SOP requirements
violations: Failed to enable authentication/password protection function after server restoration despite SOP requirements
Supervisor failed to verify that authentication function was enabled
Poor password management practices – reused same passwords before and after server restoration
Sensitive financial data (bank account numbers, salaries) not encrypted when stored
Used live customer data for testing purposes rather than anonymised or synthetic data
No adequate monitoring procedures to detect non-compliance with SOPs

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 25 – Retention Limitation Obligation. Organisations must cease retaining personal data or remove means of association once the purpose for collection is no longer served and retention is no longer necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to delete Red Hat and LIU employee data after the data migration and new functionality development was completed in December 2015
violations: Failed to delete Red Hat and LIU employee data after the data migration and new functionality development was completed in December 2015
Employee responsible for development did not follow SOP requiring deletion upon project sign-off
No checks conducted to ensure SOP was followed

outcome: Times Software was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $20,000 within 30 days. The company implemented extensive remedial actions including: disabled password protection on internet-facing servers, developed new data handling policies and SOPs with weekly, monthly and bi-monthly audit requirements, and implemented encryption for servers published online. Dentons and TMF were issued warnings in lieu of financial penalties due to various mitigating factors. Red Hat and LIU were found not to have breached their obligations.
companyNow: Times Software continues to operate as an IT services vendor in Singapore, though the company faced reputational and financial consequences following the 2017 data breach and subsequent regulatory penalties.
dataType: Employee data including name, NRIC, residential address, contact numbers, work designation, duration of employment, base salary, date of birth, marital status, nationality, race, bank account information, income tax account number

companyDescription: Majestic Debt Recovery Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based debt collection agency that collects debts on behalf of clients. The company operated without any data protection policies or awareness of privacy regulations prior to this enforcement action.
companyLongDescription: Majestic Debt Recovery Pte Ltd is a Singapore-incorporated debt collection company that recovers outstanding debts on behalf of its clients. Prior to the 2020 enforcement action, the company had no knowledge of the Personal Data Protection Act (PDPA), no data protection policies or practices, and no designated data protection officer. The company's business model involved sending representatives to debtors' premises to collect debts, during which it began recording video footage of interactions.
caseDescription: A debt collection company recorded video footage of exchanges with debtors and their employees at a company's premises, then posted the recordings on its public Facebook page to shame the debtor despite explicit objections. The company lacked any data protection policies, practices, or a designated data protection officer, and violated PDPA requirements for consent and organizational accountability.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal data (video recordings containing identifiable images and audio of individuals) to the public via Facebook without valid consent, contrary to PDPA section 13. The disclosure was made intentionally to shame the debtor, and the complainant expressly objected at the time.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Majestic Debt Recovery recorded video footage of exchanges with debtors and their employees at a company's premises.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals captured in the videos were publicly identified and shamed on social media without their consent, exposing them to humiliation and reputational harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation had obtained consent from the Complainant on previous occasions to record Representatives' visits.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Organisation could not provide any evidence of prior consent and could not produce the claimed 'video proof' of consent, and the Complainant expressly objected at the material time.

claimsVsReality.claim: Recording and posting debtor interactions on social media was an acceptable debt collection practice.
claimsVsReality.reality: The practice violated PDPA consent requirements, caused public humiliation and reputational harm to identified individuals, and served no legitimate business purpose related to responsible debt collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation was unaware of its obligations under the PDPA.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lack of knowledge did not excuse non-compliance; the company was required to have data protection policies, a designated officer, and valid consent mechanisms regardless of prior PDPA awareness.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 13 – Prohibition on collecting, using or disclosing personal data without consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Recorded video footage of individuals (debtor company personnel and the complainant) without valid consent
violations: Recorded video footage of individuals (debtor company personnel and the complainant) without valid consent
Posted recordings on public Facebook page despite explicit objections from the complainant
No legal basis under PDPA or written law authorized the collection, use, and disclosure

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 11(3) – Requirement to designate one or more individuals responsible for data protection compliance
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to appoint a data protection officer prior to the incident
violations: Failed to appoint a data protection officer prior to the incident

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 12 – Requirement to develop and implement necessary data protection policies and practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Had no knowledge of PDPA requirements
violations: Had no knowledge of PDPA requirements
Admitted to having no data protection policies or practices in place
No guidelines for employees regarding use of recording devices

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 14(3) – Vitiates consent obtained through unfair, deceptive or misleading practices
regulatoryFindings.description: If consent were to be obtained ex ante (e.g., as a condition of obtaining a loan), the purpose of shaming the debtor may exceed what is reasonable and would constitute unfair practice
violations: If consent were to be obtained ex ante (e.g., as a condition of obtaining a loan), the purpose of shaming the debtor may exceed what is reasonable and would constitute unfair practice

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner directed the organisation to: (1) pay a financial penalty of SGD $7,500 within 30 days; (2) develop and implement data protection policies and practices necessary for PDPA compliance; and (3) implement a compulsory training program for all employees on PDPA compliance. The organisation had already removed all recordings from its Facebook page and designated a data protection officer.
companyNow: Following the PDPA enforcement action, Majestic Debt Recovery appointed a data protection officer, removed all unauthorized videos from social media, and implemented mandatory employee training on PDPA compliance and data protection policies.
dataType: Video recordings, images, audio, personal identifiers
legalBasisViolated: PDPA section 13 (consent requirement for collection, use, disclosure)
PDPA section 11(3) (designation of data protection officer)
PDPA section 12 (development and implementation of data protection policies)
PDPA section 14(3) (vitiation of consent through unfair/deceptive practices)

companyDescription: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre is a Buddhist religious and community organisation based in Singapore that serves members and non-members through spiritual and community programmes.
companyLongDescription: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre is a non-profit Buddhist religious organisation in Singapore that maintains records of members and non-members for community engagement and donation purposes. The organisation operates a data management system to store personal information of its constituents. As a religious institution, it collects and maintains sensitive personal data including identification numbers, contact information, and donation records.
caseDescription: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre suffered a ransomware attack on 31 March 2020 that encrypted personal data of approximately 8,500 individuals (members and non-members). The organisation failed to implement adequate procedural and technical security measures, including lack of security software and protective protocols. The Centre admitted breach of section 24 of the PDPA's Protection Obligation and voluntarily cooperated with the investigation.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate technical and procedural security arrangements to protect personal data under its control, allowing ransomware to encrypt sensitive information. This constitutes a failure of the Protection Obligation under PDPA section 24.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Vimalakirti Buddhist Centre failed to implement adequate security software and protective protocols.
whyTheyWereWrong: The organisation's neglect of security measures resulted in the encryption and inaccessibility of sensitive personal information including names, addresses, contact numbers, NRIC numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had adequate data protection measures in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation lacked security software and protective protocols, making its system vulnerable to ransomware attacks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data was adequately secured.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal data of 8,500 individuals including NRIC numbers and addresses was encrypted and rendered inaccessible by ransomware.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data in their possession or control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement procedural and technical security arrangements
violations: Failed to implement procedural and technical security arrangements
Lacked security software and protective protocols
Did not have firewall or adequate network filtering in place
Allowed ransomware to access and encrypt personal data containing sensitive information (NRIC numbers, dates of birth, contact details, donation records)

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the organisation in breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA section 24. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of $5,000 within 30 days. Following the incident, the organisation implemented remedial measures including setting up a new server with backup, installing a firewall, cleaning and reinstalling connected computers, and committing to engage consultants to produce a data protection manual and train staff in cyber hygiene and incident response. No other directions were issued given the organisation's admission, cooperation, and prompt remedial action.
companyNow: The organisation has implemented remedial cybersecurity measures including a new server with backups, firewall installation, and committed to staff training in cyber hygiene and incident response.
dataType: Name, address, contact number, NRIC number, date of birth, donation details

companyDescription: Security Masters Pte Ltd is a security services company based in Singapore that manages building access and visitor management systems.
companyLongDescription: Security Masters Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based security services organization that provides facility and visitor management services for commercial buildings. The company employs security personnel responsible for managing visitor access control, including the collection and handling of visitor personal data such as phone numbers and identification information. Prior to the 2020 incident, the organization lacked formal procedures for protecting this sensitive personal data.
caseDescription: A security employee at Security Masters used the mobile phone numbers of eight building visitors without authorization to contact them about returning visitor passes and sending greetings. The organization lacked standard operating procedures or guidelines for the retrieval and use of visitor personal data, allowing unauthorized access to occur.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security measures and standard operating procedures to protect personal data in its possession, specifically mobile phone numbers, allowing a security employee to access and use visitor data without authorization.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A security employee at Security Masters used the mobile phone numbers of eight building visitors without authorization to contact them about returning visitor passes.
whyTheyWereWrong: The eight visitors had their personal mobile numbers accessed and used without their consent, exposing them to unsolicited contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: Security Masters maintained appropriate safeguards for visitor personal data collected during building access procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization had no standard operating procedures or guidelines for the retrieval and use of visitor personal data, allowing a security employee to access and misuse eight visitors' mobile numbers without authorization or oversight.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only authorized personnel would contact visitors using their personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: A security employee independently decided to contact eight visitors using their personal mobile numbers for non-work purposes (sending Chinese New Year greetings), demonstrating inadequate access controls and authorization requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA 2012 Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organizations to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data against unauthorized access
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to establish standard operating procedures or guidelines for retrieval and use of visitor personal data
violations: Failed to establish standard operating procedures or guidelines for retrieval and use of visitor personal data
Lack of access controls allowed security employee to use mobile phone numbers of eight visitors without authorization
No documented procedures governing the circumstances under which personal data could be accessed or used

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner directed the Organization to: (a) within 60 days revise its training curriculum to ensure security personnel understand the rationale for personal data protection, the importance of consent and authorization, and appropriate use and disclosure of personal data on social media for work purposes; and (b) inform the Commission within 1 week of implementation. The Organization implemented remedial measures including restricting access to personal data to senior personnel and requiring security personnel to sign undertakings not to contact visitors in their personal capacity.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, National Registration Identification Card numbers, photographs, closed-circuit television footage
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24 (Protection Obligation)

companyDescription: Courts is a well-known consumer electronics and furniture retailer operating multiple physical stores across Singapore with an online membership program called "homeclub by COURTS".
companyLongDescription: Courts (Singapore) Pte Ltd is a major electronics and furniture retailer with physical store presence in Singapore. The company operates an online membership program called "homeclub by COURTS" that provides exclusive member benefits including access to events and discounts. The organization uses the Magento e-commerce platform and Salesforce for customer communications. Courts has been operating in the Singapore retail market for decades as a recognized consumer electronics and furniture brand.
caseDescription: Courts failed to implement adequate security arrangements when sending a marketing email with a login link to 76,844 members. The email link contained a session identifier embedded in the URL, which allowed users to access other members' accounts without authentication if they clicked the link within 60 minutes of another member's login. This was the first time Courts used such a link and testing was inadequate, with only a single employee sending a test email to himself.
violationSummary: Courts failed to make reasonable security arrangements under PDPA section 24 by: (1) conducting inadequate pre-launch testing that did not mimic real-world concurrent usage scenarios; (2) failing to assess whether default system settings were appropriate for the new use case; and (3) not understanding the security implications of embedding session identifiers in email URLs.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Courts sent a marketing email with a login link containing an embedded session identifier to 76,844 members.
whyTheyWereWrong: 128 members' personal data including names, addresses, birthdates, email addresses, phone numbers, passwords and purchase history were exposed to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The default system settings were appropriate for sending the new eDM link to the login page
claimsVsReality.reality: The default settings embedded a session identifier in the URL which allowed any member clicking the link within 60 minutes of another member's login to access that member's account without authentication

claimsVsReality.claim: A single employee's self-test of the eDM link was adequate testing before sending to 76,844 members
claimsVsReality.reality: The self-test only verified the link worked for one person and did not identify the critical flaw that would occur under real-world conditions with multiple concurrent or sequential member logins

claimsVsReality.claim: The second-level content and layout check on eDMs would catch technical security issues
claimsVsReality.reality: The existing review process was not effective at identifying the technical issue of the embedded session identifier in the URL

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct adequate testing before implementation – only a single employee sent a limited test email to himself, which did not mimic real-world concurrent login scenarios
violations: Failed to conduct adequate testing before implementation – only a single employee sent a limited test email to himself, which did not mimic real-world concurrent login scenarios
Failed to assess the appropriateness of default system settings (SID embedded in URL, 60-minute cookie refresh) for a use case requiring user authentication
Did not fully understand the differences between creating email links with and without session identifiers embedded in the URL
Email containing the New eDM Link with embedded session identifier was sent to 76,844 members on 31 August 2019, resulting in unauthorised access risk for 128 members who clicked the link

outcome: Courts was found in breach of PDPA section 24. The Commissioner imposed a financial penalty of S$9,000 (reduced from the originally intended amount due to COVID-19 pandemic impact on the business). Courts must pay this penalty within 30 days. The Commissioner noted this is Courts' second breach of the Protection Obligation. Courts implemented remedial actions including: fixing the system setting on 1 September 2019, implementing password verification for account changes (effective 6 January 2020), establishing a standard operating procedure for eDM link insertion with concurrent user testing, engaging an external security vendor, and notifying the 128 affected members.
companyNow: Courts continues to operate as a retail electronics and furniture company in Singapore, though it faced significant business challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic when all 14 stores were temporarily closed during circuit breaker measures in 2020.
dataType: Name, email address, mobile number, date of birth, residential address, password, transactional/purchase history

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited is a multinational telecommunications conglomerate headquartered in Singapore providing mobile, broadband, and TV services to customers through mobile applications and other platforms.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) is a leading Asia-Pacific telecommunications company providing integrated communications services including mobile, broadband, TV, and ICT solutions. The company operates the MySingtel mobile application which allows customers to manage their services, track usage, and pay bills. Singtel serves millions of customers across Singapore and the region, with significant market presence in telecom infrastructure and services.
caseDescription: A software vendor's code update to Singapore Telecommunications' MySingtel mobile application inadvertently removed a security condition that decoupled recycled phone numbers from their previous users, allowing 384 customers to view other users' previously assigned service numbers and related usage information. The vendor failed to report the removal of this critical code in the technical change request, and the organisation's pre-launch testing did not detect the undisclosed change.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access to personal data. The removal of the decoupling condition in the API allowed active service numbers to retrieve both current and recycled numbers, exposing customer data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A vendor's code update removed a security condition that decoupled recycled phone numbers from previous users.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers gained unauthorised access to other people's phone numbers, installation addresses, usage details, service subscriptions, price plans.

claimsVsReality.claim: The vendor included the removal of the critical security condition in the Technical Change Request submitted to the organisation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The vendor omitted to report the removal of the Condition in the TCR, meaning the organisation was unaware of this critical change and could not test for its impact.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation should have detected the undisclosed code change through standard pre-launch testing procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation's testing was reasonably scoped to only cover changes reported in the TCR, making it impossible to detect an unreported change without additional reason to suspect the vendor's work.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – organisations must protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Removal of critical security condition in API code that decoupled recycled phone numbers from previous users
violations: Removal of critical security condition in API code that decoupled recycled phone numbers from previous users
Failure to implement sufficiently scoped pre-launch testing to detect undisclosed code changes

outcome: The Commission found that the organisation had NOT contravened Section 24 of the PDPA. The security arrangements were deemed reasonable in the circumstances. The organisation had: implemented contractual data protection clauses with the vendor, conducted audits of the vendor's IT controls, provided mandatory annual PDPA briefings, and conducted appropriate pre-launch testing given that the critical code removal was not disclosed in the technical change request. The incident was found to be a one-off occurrence difficult to foresee. The organisation promptly mitigated the incident by blocking access to the Mobile App, implementing a fix, and reversing erroneous transactions. Going forward, the organisation will implement additional regression test scenarios and enhanced Mobile App functionality to prevent historical services from being displayed.
companyNow: Singapore Telecommunications remains a major telecommunications provider in Asia-Pacific, continuing to operate its MySingtel mobile platform and broadband services with enhanced security measures following this incident.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, service numbers, installation addresses, usage details (talk time, SMS, mobile data), value-added services, price plans, billing cycles

companyDescription: The Singapore Medical Association is a professional organization representing doctors and medical practitioners in Singapore. It provides advocacy, support services, and professional development for its members.
companyLongDescription: The Singapore Medical Association (SMA) is the primary professional body for medical doctors in Singapore, established to promote medical excellence and ethics in healthcare practice. The organization provides advocacy, continuing medical education, and support services to its members. As a professional association, SMA maintains member databases containing sensitive personal and professional information. The organization plays a key role in medical governance and regulation alongside official health authorities.
caseDescription: The Singapore Medical Association failed to implement adequate IT security controls, resulting in an unauthorized user gaining access to a Microsoft Office 365 email account via brute force attack and forwarding 137 emails containing personal data of 68 individuals to an external address between January 28-30, 2020. The organization had not conducted periodic security reviews, failed to implement password rotation policies (with one account unchanged since 2013), lacked anti-brute force measures, and had not enhanced encryption for sensitive financial data.
violationSummary: The organization failed to adopt reasonable security measures to protect personal data against unauthorized access, specifically: absence of periodic password changes, lack of anti-brute force protections, no encryption of sensitive financial data, and failure to conduct periodic security reviews. This falls squarely within the Insecurity category under the Solove taxonomy, which covers inadequate security safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Singapore Medical Association failed to implement adequate IT security controls, allowing an unauthorized user to access a Microsoft Office 365 email account via brute force attack.
whyTheyWereWrong: The organization's lack of password rotation policies, absence of anti-brute force measures, and failure to conduct security reviews exposed sensitive personal information including national ID.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had password-protected email accounts securing member data.
