claimsVsReality.reality: At least one email account password had not been changed since November 2013 — a 6+ year period — making it vulnerable to brute force attacks despite the nominal protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization's IT systems were adequately protected against common attack vectors.
claimsVsReality.reality: The systems lacked anti-brute force measures such as login attempt limits or account lockouts, allowing attackers to conduct unlimited automated login attempts until finding the correct password.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization maintained reasonable security oversight of its IT environment.
claimsVsReality.reality: No periodic security reviews were conducted, meaning critical vulnerabilities including missing password rotation, absent brute force protections, and unencrypted sensitive financial data went undetected for extended periods.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, section 24 – Organizations must adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data in their possession or under their control against risk of unauthorized access
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct periodic security reviews of IT systems
violations: Failed to conduct periodic security reviews of IT systems
Did not implement periodic password changes (affected account password unchanged since November 2013)
Lacked anti-brute force measures such as login attempt limits or account lockouts
Failed to enhance security measures such as email encryption for sensitive financial data (bank account details, SWIFT codes)
Did not detect or prevent unauthorized access via brute force attack due to inadequate security arrangements

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection issued a warning to the Singapore Medical Association for breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012. No formal directions were required as the organization had already taken remedial actions to address the security gaps identified, including implementing enhanced security measures and protocols.
companyNow: The Singapore Medical Association continues to operate as Singapore's leading medical professional body, serving thousands of healthcare practitioners across the nation.
dataType: National identification numbers, dates of birth, insurance coverage information, educational information, financial information (bank account details, SWIFT codes)
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, section 24 (Protection Obligation)

companyDescription: Grab is a Southeast Asian ride-hailing and digital services company offering transportation, food delivery, and payment solutions through its mobile application.
companyLongDescription: Grab is a Singapore-based technology company that operates a multi-service mobile platform providing ride-hailing (GrabCar), carpooling (GrabHitch), food delivery, and digital payment solutions across Southeast Asia. The company processes large volumes of personal data daily from millions of drivers, passengers, and merchants. Grab has been subject to multiple data protection enforcement actions by Singapore's PDPA regulator, indicating recurring deficiencies in its security and testing practices.
caseDescription: Grab deployed a software update to its GrabHitch carpooling service that inadvertently removed a critical variable from an API endpoint, causing the app's caching mechanism to serve the same profile data to all drivers for 10-second intervals. This exposed profile data of 21,541 drivers and passengers to unauthorized access risk. The company failed to conduct adequate pre-deployment testing or assess how the changes would interact with existing system features.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data by deploying a system change without understanding its interaction with existing features (caching mechanism) and without conducting properly scoped testing to simulate real-world multi-user scenarios before deployment.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Grab deployed a software update to GrabHitch that removed a critical variable from an API endpoint.
whyTheyWereWrong: The failure to test how the update would interact with the caching mechanism exposed the profile pictures, names, vehicle details, wallet balances.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Update was designed to fix a security vulnerability by removing the userID variable from the API endpoint.
claimsVsReality.reality: The removal of userID broke the caching mechanism's ability to differentiate between drivers, serving all cached profile data indiscriminately to every user for 10-second intervals.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organization conducted adequate testing before deployment.
claimsVsReality.reality: Grab admitted it did not conduct tests simulating multiple concurrent or consecutive users, and performed no specific testing of how the caching mechanism would interact with the update.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only 5,651 drivers' data was exposed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation revealed that 21,541 GrabHitch drivers' and passengers' personal data was exposed to unauthorized access risk, including profile pictures, names, vehicle details, wallet balances, and booking information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organizations must protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement sufficiently robust processes to manage changes to IT systems that process personal data
violations: Failed to implement sufficiently robust processes to manage changes to IT systems that process personal data
Deployed an update to the Grab App without understanding how changes would interact with existing features, specifically the URL-based caching mechanism
Failed to conduct properly scoped pre-deployment testing including simulation of multiple concurrent or consecutive users accessing the app
Failed to conduct testing to verify how the caching mechanism would function with the deployed update
This was the second similar incident for the organization, demonstrating a pattern of inadequate change management

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Grab in breach of PDPA Section 24 and directed the organization to: (1) pay a financial penalty of S$10,000 within 30 days; and (2) implement a data protection by design policy for its mobile applications within 120 days. The organization had already taken remedial actions including rolling back the update within 40 minutes, notifying affected drivers, increasing cash-out minimums, deploying a fixed version, reviewing testing procedures, updating governance procedures, and conducting an architecture review of legacy applications.
companyNow: Grab continues to operate as one of Southeast Asia's largest ride-hailing and digital services platforms, serving millions of users across multiple countries.
dataType: Profile pictures, passenger names, vehicle plate numbers, wallet balance/payment history, booking details (addresses, pickup/drop-off times), driver details (total rides, vehicle model and make)

companyDescription: Civil Service Club is a social club in Singapore for Public Service officers and associate members offering sports facilities, function rooms, and recreational activities.
companyLongDescription: Civil Service Club is a membership-based social club in Singapore established to serve public sector employees. The club offers diverse benefits including booking of sports facilities, function rooms, chalets, and discounted rates for club events and recreational activities. The organisation operates a Club Management System and Membership Portal to manage member services and virtual membership cards. It serves both public service officers and associate members from social service organisations and the general public.
caseDescription: Civil Service Club failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect members' personal data, including NRIC/FIN numbers and profile photographs, stored on its Membership Portal. When an IT vendor performed troubleshooting, the vendor inadvertently left a web directory containing approximately 1,770 members' personal data publicly accessible for an extended period. The Organisation did not review its IT vendor contract or system design specifications to include data protection requirements after the PDPA came into force.
violationSummary: The Organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data. The breach stemmed from inadequate contractual protections with the vendor and lack of system design specifications incorporating data protection measures, resulting in publicly accessible personal data for an extended period.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Civil Service Club failed to implement reasonable security arrangements for its Membership Portal, allowing an IT vendor to inadvertently leave a web directory containing 1,770 members' NRIC/FIN.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' sensitive identity documents (NRIC/FIN numbers) and photographs were exposed to public access for an extended period, putting 1,770 individuals at risk of identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Vendor disabled public access to the Directory on the third troubleshooting occasion on 24 June 2019.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Vendor's engineer omitted to disable public access and erroneously reported that he had done so, leaving 1,770 members' data publicly accessible until 2 July 2019.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organisation was unaware that Members Data had been stored temporarily in the Directory and that troubleshooting involved enabling public access.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Organisation's lack of awareness reflected its failure to review the IT vendor contract or system design specifications for data protection requirements—a responsibility that fell squarely on the Organisation as data controller.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to review and update IT vendor contract to include data protection requirements after PDPA came into force on 2 July 2014
violations: Failed to review and update IT vendor contract to include data protection requirements after PDPA came into force on 2 July 2014
Failed to include personal data protection requirements in system specifications and software design documentation for the CMS and Membership Portal
Failed to ensure the Vendor was subject to sufficient obligations regarding protection of Members Data during development and troubleshooting activities
Failed to maintain a personal data asset inventory that would have identified the storage of Members Data in the Directory
Omitted to implement data protection measures for approximately five years (2 July 2014 to 2 July 2019) despite knowing the Vendor was working on systems containing personal data

outcome: The Commissioner directed the Organisation to pay a financial penalty of S$20,000 within 30 days. The Organisation had already implemented remedial measures including: disabling access to the Directory, enhancing housekeeping processes to delete profile photographs immediately after display, and discontinuing the use of NRIC/FIN numbers as membership numbers and file names. No additional directions were imposed given the remediation measures already undertaken.
companyNow: Civil Service Club continues to operate with enhanced data protection measures, including immediate deletion of profile photographs after display and discontinuation of using NRIC/FIN numbers as file names.
dataType: National identity numbers (NRIC/FIN), profile photographs

companyDescription: Singapore Red Cross Society is a charity organisation that operates a website enabling members of the public to make appointments for blood donations.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Red Cross Society is a humanitarian charity operating in Singapore that provides blood donation services to the community. The organisation maintains a website that collects and stores personal data from blood donors, including names, contact numbers, email addresses, and blood types, to facilitate appointment scheduling. The society depends on public donations to fund its operations and programmes benefiting disadvantaged and vulnerable members of the community.
caseDescription: Singapore Red Cross Society failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal data in its blood donor appointment database, resulting in unauthorised access and exfiltration of data for approximately 4,297 individuals. The organisation also failed to properly retain and manage personal data, with approximately 900 individuals' records unnecessarily retained due to improper purging instructions and lack of verification checks.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data, including inadequate vendor supervision, weak password management, and lack of regular security reviews. This constitutes a breach of the Protection Obligation under Section 24 of the PDPA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Singapore Red Cross Society failed to implement adequate security measures for its blood donor appointment database.
whyTheyWereWrong: Blood donors' personal data including names, contact numbers, email addresses, and blood types were exposed to unauthorised access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The attackers were skilled hackers who exploited a weak administrator password that was created during the development stage and never used by organisation staff.
claimsVsReality.reality: The weak password ('12345') was set during development due to lack of supervision over the vendor and absence of password management policies; the database administration tool remained connected to the website after development was completed, allowing unauthorised access.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had various IT security measures in place before the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation failed to conduct regular security reviews, did not detect the presence of the phpMyAdmin tool on the live website, and did not implement proper password management policies or verification checks for data purging.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had provided correct instructions for purging personal data of 900 individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation provided wrong purging instructions to its vendor, instructing removal of only some data elements instead of entire records, and failed to verify that the purging exercise was properly completed.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement adequate security measures in the blood donor database
violations: Failed to implement adequate security measures in the blood donor database
Lack of supervision over vendor's work during website development
No password management policy requiring strong passwords; weak password '12345' set for database administration tool
Did not conduct regular security reviews or vulnerability assessments
Failed to identify and remove database administration tool left connected to website after development

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 25 – Retention Limitation Obligation: organisations must cease retaining documents containing personal data or remove means of association as soon as retention is no longer necessary
regulatoryFindings.description: Unnecessary retention of personal data for approximately 900 individuals
violations: Unnecessary retention of personal data for approximately 900 individuals
Provided incorrect purging instructions to vendor (partial data removal instead of complete record deletion)
Failed to conduct verification checks to ensure purging exercise was properly executed

outcome: The Commissioner directed Singapore Red Cross Society to pay a financial penalty of $5,000 within 30 days. The reduced penalty was imposed in light of the organisation's upfront voluntary admission of liability under the Expedited Breach Decision procedure and comprehensive remedial actions taken after the incident, including removal of the database from the website, implementation of layered and restricted access controls, password training, vulnerability assessment and penetration testing regimes, and strengthened vendor oversight procedures. No additional directions were imposed given the remedial measures undertaken.
companyNow: Singapore Red Cross Society continues to operate its blood donation services with significantly strengthened security measures including layered access controls, network isolation of sensitive systems, regular vulnerability assessments and penetration testing.
dataType: names, contact numbers, email addresses, blood types

companyDescription: MDIS Corporation is a Singapore-based not-for-profit professional institute providing lifelong learning and professional development courses.
companyLongDescription: MDIS Corporation Pte Ltd is a not-for-profit organisation in Singapore that offers training and professional development courses to individuals seeking lifelong learning opportunities. The organisation operates a website with online course registration functionality to manage participant enrollment and issue completion certificates. It serves course participants seeking to develop professional skills and claim SkillsFuture credits. The organisation contracts external vendors for website development and maintenance.
caseDescription: MDIS Corporation failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data collected through its course registration form. A vulnerability in the website's content management system allowed a Google search to expose a spreadsheet containing personal data of 304 course participants for approximately 6 months. The organisation lacked written contracts with vendors, failed to communicate data protection requirements, and did not conduct adequate security testing before launch.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to take reasonable steps to prevent unauthorised access and disclosure of personal data by failing to secure the administrative backend, conduct adequate security testing, and ensure proper technical implementation of access controls. This directly caused a data security incident where personal data became accessible through search engines.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: MDIS Corporation failed to implement reasonable security measures for a course registration website, leaving a spreadsheet with 304 people's personal data including NRIC numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Course participants' sensitive personal data including identity card numbers, contact information.

claimsVsReality.claim: MDIS stated it verbally communicated data protection requirements to the Vendor and Developer.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Vendor asserted no such communication occurred, and MDIS could not produce any written documentation to corroborate its assertion, so the Commissioner found the organisation failed to communicate data protection requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: MDIS believed that password protection on the administrative panel was 'secure enough' and did not require security testing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The password protection was inadequate; the administrative backend was accessible via Google search crawling, allowing the spreadsheet containing 304 people's NRIC numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, employment details, and billing addresses to be publicly exposed for 6 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: MDIS was not responsible for security because it relied on its Vendor to identify risks and implement security measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: As the data controller and website owner, MDIS bore full responsibility for protecting personal data and could not delegate its statutory obligations under the PDPA, regardless of vendor engagement.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Organisations must protect personal data in their possession or under their control by taking reasonable steps to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to communicate data protection requirements to vendors in writing or provide clear specifications for securing personal data
violations: Failed to communicate data protection requirements to vendors in writing or provide clear specifications for securing personal data
Failed to conduct security testing prior to website launch to verify that password protection and login credentials functioned properly
Failed to exercise reasonable oversight of security arrangements despite being the data controller
Allowed personal data to remain exposed to unauthorised access risk for approximately 6 months due to undetected CMS administrative backend vulnerability
Did not include data protection and security as a key design consideration at the development stage of the website

outcome: The Commissioner found MDIS Corporation in breach of PDPA Section 24 and directed the organisation to pay a financial penalty of S$10,000 within 30 days. The Commissioner acknowledged the organisation's prompt remedial actions including blocking the CMS administrative backend, inserting robot.txt file to prevent search engine crawling, deploying security patches to remove the vulnerable codes, and planning to deploy a new backend system. No further directions were imposed given the remediation measures already implemented.
companyNow: MDIS Corporation continues to operate as a professional learning institute in Singapore. Following the 2020 enforcement action, the organisation deployed a new backend system and implemented security patches to remediate the vulnerabilities that led to the data exposure.
dataType: NRIC number, name, email address, mobile phone number, citizenship, company name, designation, contact details, billing address, course information

company: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 3400
companyDescription: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 3400 is a strata management entity in Singapore responsible for managing a residential property development and administering subsidiary proprietor records.
companyLongDescription: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 3400 is a strata management corporation operating under Singapore's Building Maintenance and Strata Management Act. The organization manages a residential strata-titled property and maintains administrative records for its council members and subsidiary proprietors. In April 2012, it purchased a Network Attached Storage device for internal file sharing among administrative staff. The organization stores personal data including council member identification, contact information, property ownership details, and financial records related to share values and arrears.
caseDescription: A management corporation failed to implement adequate security measures for a Network Attached Storage device that was inadvertently connected to the Internet, exposing personal data of 562 individuals without authentication controls. The organisation had not conducted any security reviews of its IT systems and was unaware the directory was publicly accessible. Upon notification by the Commission, the organisation promptly disconnected the device.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, specifically by not conducting code reviews, pre-launch testing, or periodic security reviews of IT systems. The NAS was exposed to the Internet without access controls, login credentials, or directory access restrictions, representing a fundamental security vulnerability.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The management corporation failed to implement security measures for a Network Attached Storage device containing personal data.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposed personal data of 562 individuals—including names, contact numbers, email addresses, NRIC numbers, property details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The NAS was intended for internal file sharing over a local network only.
claimsVsReality.reality: The NAS directory was inadvertently connected to the Internet and publicly accessible via IP address without authentication, exposing data to any member of the public.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had adequate IT security practices in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization admitted it had conducted no security reviews of its IT systems and was unaware the directory was publicly accessible, demonstrating complete absence of security oversight.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only non-sensitive contact information was exposed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Exposed data included NRIC numbers, passport numbers, property ownership details, resident identities, financial statements, share values, payment arrears, and car plate numbers—highly sensitive personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organisations to protect personal data by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct code reviews and pre-launch testing before deploying IT systems
violations: Failed to conduct code reviews and pre-launch testing before deploying IT systems
Failed to conduct periodic security reviews of IT systems including the NAS and Directory
Failed to implement access controls or authentication mechanisms for Internet-accessible storage
Failed to maintain a personal data asset register to track data in possession or control
Failed to implement network segmentation or policies restricting Internet access to internal systems
Allowed NAS to be connected to Internet without login credentials or directory access restrictions

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to the organisation for breach of section 24 of the PDPA. No directions were required given the organisation's prompt remedial action in disconnecting the NAS from the Internet immediately upon notification. The decision emphasised the importance of periodic security reviews, code reviews, pre-launch testing, vulnerability scanning, and maintenance of personal data asset registers as best practices for IT security compliance.
dataType: Name, NRIC/Passport Number, Contact number, Email address, Block and Unit number, Property ownership details, Resident identity, Statement of accounts, Car plate numbers, Share values/arrears

companyDescription: Central Depository (Pte) Limited provides integrated clearing, settlement and depository facilities for the Singapore securities market, managing accounts for investors and processing dividend payments.
companyLongDescription: Central Depository (Pte) Limited is a critical financial infrastructure entity in Singapore that operates clearing, settlement and depository services for the securities market. The company manages Central Depository (CDP) accounts for investors and is responsible for automating key financial processes including dividend cheque distribution to account holders. As a financial institution handling sensitive personal and financial data, it is subject to strict data protection obligations under Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: Central Depository failed to implement adequate security measures and insufficient testing when migrating from its Post Trade System to a new system, resulting in a software error that caused dividend cheques containing sensitive personal data to be mailed to 211 outdated account holder addresses. The Organisation's testing scope did not include change of address scenarios despite this being a known risk, violating security obligations under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The Organisation failed to take reasonable security steps to protect sensitive personal data (NRIC numbers, financial information) by conducting inadequate pre-migration testing that omitted critical change-of-address scenarios. This insecurity in system implementation directly resulted in unauthorised disclosure of personal data to third parties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Central Depository failed to include change-of-address scenarios in testing before migrating to a new post-trade system.
whyTheyWereWrong: The security failure exposed 211 individuals' names, national ID numbers, account numbers, securities held.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had expended its best efforts in testing and both the Notification Letter Test and Dividend Cheque Module Test did not return any errors.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Dividend Cheque Module test scope was too narrow and deliberately excluded change-of-address scenarios—a known risk that was actually tested for other modules—meaning the testing was insufficient by design.

claimsVsReality.claim: There was no risk of actual financial loss because dividend cheques were made out to named individuals and disclosure occurred only to a single recipient.
claimsVsReality.reality: Risk of fraud existed as unauthorised recipients could have fraudulently altered cheque names; affected individuals were also deprived of fund access during the period between incident and replacement cheque issuance.

claimsVsReality.claim: The specific 'Private & Confidential' envelopes minimised unauthorised access to the disclosed data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The fact that dividend cheque mailers were sent to unauthorised individuals meant the envelope protections were irrelevant and sensitive data including NRIC numbers and financial details were actually exposed to strangers.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct proper and adequate testing of the new NPTS system before migration
violations: Failed to conduct proper and adequate testing of the new NPTS system before migration
Testing scope for Dividend Cheque Module was too narrow and did not include change of address scenarios despite this being a known scenario
Failed to test in an environment simulating real world usage with sufficient test cases
Failed to implement stronger security measures commensurate with the sensitivity of the disclosed data (NRIC numbers and financial data)

outcome: The Commissioner directed the Organisation to pay a financial penalty of $32,000 within 30 days. The Organisation had already implemented remedial measures including: introducing a defensive measure/fix to consistently extract updated addresses (deployed 20 April 2019), reviewing all modules involving address retrieval to confirm the error was specific to the Dividend Cheque Module, re-issuing replacement cheques and explanation letters to affected individuals, and committing to refresher training to ensure timely reporting of issues. No further directions were imposed given the remediation measures already undertaken.
companyNow: Central Depository continues to operate as Singapore's central securities depository and is now part of the Singapore Exchange group following a merger. The company remains the primary infrastructure provider for settlement and custody services in Singapore's capital markets.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, CDP account number, security holdings, dividend amount

company: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 4375
companyDescription: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 4375 (Alexandra Central Mall) is a property management entity responsible for a shopping mall in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: MCST 4375 operates Alexandra Central Mall in Singapore and is responsible for maintaining security, property management, and compliance with data protection laws. The corporation engaged external contractors—Smart Property Management (Singapore) Pte Ltd as managing agent and A Best Security Management Pte Ltd for security services—to handle day-to-day operations including CCTV system management. As a management corporation, it has legal obligations to protect personal data captured by its security systems.
caseDescription: CCTV footage of a woman injured by a falling glass door at Alexandra Central Mall was disclosed without authorization to multiple parties and subsequently posted on YouTube, exposing personal data publicly. The Management Corporation failed to implement data protection policies and establish adequate security procedures for handling CCTV footage, while the security contractor also failed to provide proper training and clear procedures for CCTV data disclosure.
violationSummary: Personal data (CCTV footage containing the injured woman's image) was disclosed to unauthorized parties without proper consent or authorization procedures, violating confidentiality obligations and ultimately being exposed publicly on the internet.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Management Corporation failed to implement data protection policies and establish adequate security procedures for CCTV footage.
whyTheyWereWrong: An injured woman's identity and medical condition were exposed publicly online without consent, causing her personal data to be accessible to the entire internet.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCST 4375 had security arrangements in place by restricting physical access to the Fire Control Centre where CCTV could be viewed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Physical access controls were insufficient; staff had no written procedures governing disclosure of CCTV footage, allowing unauthorized copying and distribution via personal devices and messaging apps.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCST 4375 expected its managing agent SPMS to develop and implement necessary data protection policies on the corporation's behalf.
claimsVsReality.reality: MCST 4375 had not included any data protection requirements or clauses in its contract with SPMS and gave no instructions to SPMS regarding PDPA compliance, placing full responsibility on MCST 4375.

claimsVsReality.claim: ABSM had a Personal Data Protection Policy prohibiting third-party disclosure without consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Although ABSM had a policy, its Standard Operating Procedures contained no specific guidance on CCTV footage handling, and staff were not adequately trained on these internal rules, leading to unauthorized disclosure by a security employee.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Organisations must develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 4375 failed to develop or implement any data protection policies
violations: MCST 4375 failed to develop or implement any data protection policies
MCST 4375 did not provide written instructions to service providers regarding access to personal data or CCTV footage management

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organisations must ensure reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or control
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 4375 failed to establish written procedures for CCTV footage access and disclosure requests
violations: MCST 4375 failed to establish written procedures for CCTV footage access and disclosure requests
MCST 4375 did not provide clear instructions to data intermediaries (ABSM and SPMS) regarding personal data handling
ABSM failed to include CCTV footage handling procedures in its Standard Operating Procedures
ABSM failed to provide adequate training to staff on CCTV data protection procedures
ABSM employee (SE) disclosed CCTV footage to unauthorized third party (Cleaning Supervisor) without required approval

outcome: Deputy Commissioner directed MCST 4375 to: (1) develop and implement data protection policies within 60 days; (2) establish reasonable security arrangements including access control policies within 60 days; (3) conduct staff training on PDPA requirements within 60 days; and (4) report implementation to Commission within 1 week of completion. ABSM directed to: (1) establish reasonable security arrangements and policies for CCTV data protection within 60 days; and (2) report implementation to Commission within 1 week. SPMS found not in breach as CCTV footage was outside its control and responsibility. MCST 4375 had already replaced SPMS and issued internal memorandum restricting unauthorized distribution of media materials.
companyNow: Following the 2020 enforcement decision, MCST 4375 replaced its managing agent and implemented mandatory data protection policies and approval procedures for media distribution.
dataType: Video footage, biometric data (image/appearance of individuals captured in CCTV)
legalBasisViolated: Singapore PDPA Section 12 (Developing and implementing data protection policies)
Singapore PDPA Section 24 (Ensuring reasonable security arrangements for personal data)

company: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 3593
companyDescription: Management Corporation Strata Title Plan No. 3593 (MCST 3593) is a condominium management corporation responsible for overseeing Marina Bay Residences in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: MCST 3593 is a management corporation for a residential condominium in Singapore. It appointed Edmund Tie & Company Property Management Services Pte Ltd as its managing agent in 2012 and New-E Security Pte Ltd to provide security services since November 2014. As an organization under Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act 2012, MCST 3593 held responsibility for protecting residents' personal data captured in the condominium's CCTV systems.
caseDescription: A condominium management corporation failed to implement data protection policies and contractual safeguards when engaging a security company to manage CCTV systems. A security supervisor unauthorized­ly disclosed CCTV footage containing personal data of residents to a requesting unit owner via WhatsApp and the footage was subsequently posted on Facebook, exposing identifiable individuals.
violationSummary: The unauthorized disclosure of CCTV footage containing identifiable personal data to unauthorized parties (resident and via social media) represents a breach of confidentiality obligations. The organization failed to maintain reasonable security arrangements and contractual protections required under the PDPA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: MCST 3593 failed to implement data protection policies, appoint a Data Protection Officer, or include data protection clauses in its contract with a security company managing CCTV systems.
whyTheyWereWrong: Without written safeguards, a security supervisor was able to unlock and share CCTV footage of identifiable residents via WhatsApp, which was then posted on Facebook.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCST 3593 claimed it had appointed ETCPM to advise on PDPA obligations and that measures and safeguards had already been put in place to ensure compliance with the PDPA.
claimsVsReality.reality: MCST 3593 had not appointed a Data Protection Officer, had not developed any data protection policies, and the contract with New-E contained no data protection clauses or references to the PDPA whatsoever.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCST 3593 argued that the Security Supervisor's disclosure was a rogue act that no measures could have prevented, as he acted against the Residence Manager's instructions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Security Supervisor was able to disclose the footage precisely because there were no written policies, no data protection training, and no contractual safeguards governing how CCTV footage could be accessed, recorded on mobile devices, or shared.

claimsVsReality.claim: MCST 3593 had standard operating procedures in place to govern CCTV footage release.
claimsVsReality.reality: New-E had only a verbal practice of releasing footage to ETCPM representatives, with no written policies to guide employees on their obligations under the PDPA or procedures for handling CCTV footage.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 11(3) – Requirement to appoint a Data Protection Officer
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 3593 failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer prior to the incident, in breach of statutory requirement
violations: MCST 3593 failed to appoint a Data Protection Officer prior to the incident, in breach of statutory requirement

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Requirement to develop and implement data protection policies
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 3593 had not developed or implemented any data protection policies or standard operating procedures as required by the PDPA
violations: MCST 3593 had not developed or implemented any data protection policies or standard operating procedures as required by the PDPA

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Requirement to put in place reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: MCST 3593 failed to include data protection clauses in its contract with security services provider New-E and provided no written instructions regarding CCTV footage protection
violations: MCST 3593 failed to include data protection clauses in its contract with security services provider New-E and provided no written instructions regarding CCTV footage protection
MCST 3593 did not communicate any data protection requirements to its managing agent or security provider
New-E failed to implement written policies regarding CCTV footage disclosure procedures and relied only on verbal instructions
New-E did not provide data protection training to its employees, allowing a security supervisor to improperly disclose footage using personal mobile phone

outcome: MCST 3593 directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $5,000 within 30 days. MCST 3593 has appointed a Data Protection Officer, implemented a Personal Data Protection Policy and Standard Operating Procedures, and plans to include additional data processing provisions in contracts with service providers. New-E directed to implement a data protection policy and internal guidelines for CCTV management and access control within 30 days and report completion to the Commission within 7 days. ETCPM found not to be in breach of PDPA obligations.
companyNow: Following the incident and enforcement action, MCST 3593 appointed a Data Protection Officer, implemented a Personal Data Protection Policy and Standard Operating Procedures, and amended contracts with service providers to include data protection provisions.
dataType: CCTV footage, biometric/video imagery of identifiable individuals
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 11(3) – Failure to appoint Data Protection Officer
PDPA Section 12 – Failure to develop and implement data protection policy
PDPA Section 24 – Failure to put in place reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data

companyDescription: SPH Magazines is a Singapore-based media company that operates HardwareZone, a popular online forum for technology discussions and community engagement.
companyLongDescription: SPH Magazines Pte Ltd is a subsidiary of Singapore Press Holdings, one of Singapore's largest media organizations. The company operates HardwareZone, an online community portal where members discuss technology topics and share professional information. The forum requires members to register with personal data including usernames, emails, full names, and optional profile information such as job roles, industry, and income ranges. Senior moderators, who are volunteers from the member community, are granted access to member profiles to enforce forum rules and maintain community standards.
caseDescription: SPH Magazines failed to implement reasonable password security requirements for senior moderators of its HardwareZone forum. A hacker compromised a senior moderator's credentials (obtained from a public credential leak database) and used them to access personal data of approximately 685,393 forum members over a two-year period. The organization discovered the breach only after the hacker used a stolen administrator account to post unauthorized content.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements (as required by PDPA section 24) by not enforcing password security requirements on senior moderator accounts, including absence of mandatory password changes, length/complexity standards, or regular expiration policies. Additionally, no security testing was conducted to identify vulnerabilities.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SPH Magazines failed to implement password security requirements for senior moderators of its HardwareZone forum.
whyTheyWereWrong: Forum members' personal information including usernames, email addresses, names, and optional profile data were exposed to unauthorized access for approximately two years without the company's.

claimsVsReality.claim: Senior moderator passwords were subject to the same security requirements as employee passwords.
claimsVsReality.reality: Senior moderator accounts had no password expiration requirements or complexity standards; the compromised moderator's password had not been changed in 10 years and did not meet minimum length/complexity standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had adequate security measures to protect member data in the forum.
claimsVsReality.reality: No security testing was performed on the forum website, leaving the organization unaware of its security vulnerabilities and unable to detect unauthorized access for approximately two years.

claimsVsReality.claim: MD5 hashing of passwords provided sufficient protection for member data.
claimsVsReality.reality: MD5 is an outdated algorithm known to be easily circumvented, and the decision not to apply password policies to senior moderators created a critical vulnerability regardless of hashing method.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement reasonable password security requirements for senior moderator accounts (no mandatory expiration, length, or complexity standards)
violations: Failed to implement reasonable password security requirements for senior moderator accounts (no mandatory expiration, length, or complexity standards)
Password used by compromised senior moderator was not changed for 10 years and did not meet complexity standards
Senior moderators had access rights to member profiles without adequate security controls
No security testing was conducted on the Forum website to identify vulnerabilities
Unauthorized access to personal data of 685,393 member profiles remained undetected for approximately 2 years

outcome: The Commissioner directed SPH Magazines to pay a financial penalty of SGD 26,000 within 30 days. The organization was not subject to additional directions given the remedial measures already undertaken, which included: temporary suspension of senior moderator access (19 February 2018), member notification and password change advisories, implementation of two-factor authentication for senior moderator accounts (April 2018), enhanced password policy (minimum 8 characters, alphanumeric, upper/lower case, 3-month expiration), captcha implementation, and removal and purging of sensitive fields (full names and optional profile information) from the database.
companyNow: SPH Magazines continues to operate HardwareZone as part of Singapore Press Holdings' media portfolio, which has diversified into digital and online platforms in recent years.
dataType: Username, email address, full name, password hash, year of birth, gender, country, education, job scope, occupation, industry, company size, monthly income range, area of interest, homepage URL, instant messaging handles

companyDescription: SCAL Academy is a Singapore-based education and training provider that offers courses, seminars, and workshops for professional development.
companyLongDescription: SCAL Academy is a Singapore-registered training organization that delivers educational courses, seminars, and workshops to individuals seeking professional development. The company collects participant registration data through its website to manage enrollments and course administration. In 2018, it engaged a freelance vendor to develop a document upload feature to streamline the registration process, but inadequate security specifications resulted in a significant data protection failure.
caseDescription: SCAL Academy failed to implement adequate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal data of 3,628 participants uploaded to its website. A vendor hired to develop a document upload feature omitted to require authentication for access and failed to implement search engine blocking, resulting in scanned registration documents being publicly discoverable and accessible via Google search.
violationSummary: The organization failed to take reasonable security steps to protect personal data in its possession and control. Specifically, it did not verify with the vendor what security arrangements were implemented, did not conduct or verify testing of security measures, and failed to ensure authentication requirements and search engine blocking were in place before deployment.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SCAL Academy failed to implement authentication requirements and search engine blocking on its document upload feature.
whyTheyWereWrong: Participants' sensitive personal data including names, ID numbers, addresses, and employment details were exposed to the public without their knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Incident neither impacted nor caused significant harm to the affected individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: 3,628 participants had sensitive personal data including names, NRIC/work permit numbers, dates of birth, addresses, nationalities, and employment information publicly discoverable via Google search for an extended period.

claimsVsReality.claim: The vendor was responsible for the security failure and the organization issued appropriate instructions.
claimsVsReality.reality: SCAL Academy failed to specify detailed security requirements, did not verify what measures the vendor actually implemented, and conducted no testing to confirm the security arrangements were effective before deployment.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 — Organisation must protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to verify security arrangements with vendor before implementation
violations: Failed to verify security arrangements with vendor before implementation
Did not conduct or verify testing of security measures
Failed to implement authentication requirements for document access
Failed to implement search engine blocking recommendations
Did not articulate business requirements or agree on specific technical measures with vendor
Did not conduct user acceptance testing or risk-based security scenarios

outcome: The Commissioner found the Organisation in breach of PDPA Section 24 and directed payment of a financial penalty of $15,000 within 30 days. The Organisation was not issued further directions given its cooperative investigation conduct and swift remedial actions including implementing access controls, search engine blocking, document removal, and disabling upload functionality. The Organisation also strengthened vendor communication protocols and provided PDPA compliance education.
companyNow: SCAL Academy continues to operate in Singapore as an education and training provider, having implemented stronger vendor management practices and PDPA compliance procedures following the 2020 enforcement action.
dataType: Name, race, nationality, date of birth, gender, country of birth, NRIC/work permit number, address, occupation, employer name

companyDescription: Royal Caribbean Cruises is a major cruise line operator offering vacation and holiday bookings globally. The company operates a fleet of cruise ships serving millions of passengers annually.
companyLongDescription: Royal Caribbean Cruises is one of the world's largest cruise line companies, providing vacation experiences with a fleet of modern ships serving international markets. The company operates booking systems, onboard services, and payment processing for customers worldwide. In 2020, the Singapore subsidiary (Royal Caribbean Cruises (Asia) Pte. Ltd.) was operating an electronic receipt system to manage customer payments for cruise bookings and holiday packages. The company is a major player in the cruise and vacation industry with significant customer reach.
caseDescription: Royal Caribbean Cruises' electronic receipt system hosted on an AWS server was compromised in a cyber-attack, exposing personal data of 6,004 customers and 25 employees. The organisation failed to implement basic security measures including unpatched software vulnerabilities and inadequately protected administrative credentials. The Commissioner found the organisation liable for failing to meet reasonable security standards under section 24 of the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data. Specific failures included: (1) storing unencrypted administrative credentials in publicly accessible files without access controls, and (2) failing to patch known security vulnerabilities in phpMyAdmin software. These fundamental security omissions allowed an attacker to gain unauthorised access and delete/expose customer and employee data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Royal Caribbean Cruises hosted an electronic receipt system on an AWS server without implementing basic security measures, leaving administrative credentials publicly accessible.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposed system allowed attackers to access and ransom the personal data of 6,004 customers and 25 employees, placing sensitive information including names, addresses, email.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT Vendor was responsible for security measures and patching of the Receipt System
claimsVsReality.reality: Royal Caribbean Cruises (Asia) Pte. Ltd. had never engaged the IT Vendor to provide security maintenance or patching services; the organisation was contractually responsible as data controller

claimsVsReality.claim: Administrative credentials were adequately protected
claimsVsReality.reality: Administrator usernames and passwords were stored in plaintext files within the same server with no access controls, making them publicly accessible to anyone with network access

claimsVsReality.claim: The Receipt System maintained current security standards
claimsVsReality.reality: The phpMyAdmin tool version in use contained known, publicly-disclosed security vulnerabilities that were never patched, creating easy exploitation pathways for attackers

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Organisations must protect personal data in their possession or control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement access controls for administrative credentials, storing them in plaintext in files on the same server with public accessibility
violations: Failed to implement access controls for administrative credentials, storing them in plaintext in files on the same server with public accessibility
Failed to patch known security vulnerabilities in phpMyAdmin tool, despite patching being a critical and common security requirement
Absent security maintenance processes and lack of clarity regarding vendor security responsibilities resulted in unpatched system vulnerable to cyber-attack
Overall security standard for Receipt System fell far short of reasonable requirements

outcome: The Commissioner found Royal Caribbean Cruises in breach of PDPA section 24 for failing to implement reasonable security measures. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $16,000 within 30 days. No further directions were imposed given the remediation measures the organisation had already undertaken, including taking the Receipt System offline permanently, engaging cybersecurity consultants for forensic investigation, implementing IP address restrictions, and notifying affected customers.
companyNow: Royal Caribbean Cruises remains a major global cruise operator and publicly traded company. The company continues to operate cruise services internationally despite challenges in the sector.
dataType: Financial data (credit/debit card numbers, payment information), personal identifiers (name, date of birth, nationality, marital status, passport details), contact information (address, email, mobile number, emergency contacts), employee credentials (usernames, passwords)

companyDescription: Creative Technology Ltd is a Singaporean technology company that manufactures audio and music products, including Sound Blaster sound cards and gaming peripherals.
companyLongDescription: Creative Technology Ltd is a Singapore-based technology company founded in 1981 that specializes in digital entertainment products and services. The company is known for its Sound Blaster audio card line and gaming peripherals. In this case, the company operated an online support forum established in 2004 to help users discuss and share information about Creative's products. The forum was breached in 2018 due to inadequate security maintenance.
caseDescription: Creative Technology's online support forum was hacked in mid-2018 due to unpatched vBulletin software containing a known SQL injection vulnerability. Approximately 484,512 user accounts were compromised, exposing usernames, hashed passwords, email addresses, and IP addresses. The organization failed to implement security patches released in 2016 and used outdated MD5 password hashing instead of more secure algorithms.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by not patching known vulnerabilities in vBulletin software for three years and using insufficiently secure MD5 password hashing, leading to unauthorized access and disclosure of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Creative Technology failed to patch known SQL injection vulnerabilities in vBulletin forum software for three years.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users' usernames, email addresses, IP addresses, and hashed passwords were exposed to attackers, creating risk of account compromise and identity theft if users reused credentials elsewhere.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation stated the disclosure was unlikely to have caused serious or substantial harm because most email addresses were 'disposable' and only ~2,600 accounts had identifiable user information.
claimsVsReality.reality: All 484,512 user accounts had credentials exposed (usernames, hashed passwords, email addresses, IP addresses), and users who reused passwords faced additional risk of compromise to other online accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation deleted the user database to comply with section 25 of the PDPA's data retention minimisation obligation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation deleted the database within 2 weeks of discovering the breach without considering that an investigation could be anticipated given the scale of the breach affecting 484,512 users, and thereby destroyed evidence needed to verify the scope of harm.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to patch or update vBulletin software for three years despite security patches being available since 2016
violations: Failed to patch or update vBulletin software for three years despite security patches being available since 2016
Used MD5 algorithm for password hashing which is no longer sufficiently secure compared to alternatives like bcrypt
Did not implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent SQL injection attacks

outcome: The Commissioner found Creative Technology in breach of PDPA Section 24 and directed the organization to pay a financial penalty of $15,000 SGD within 30 days. The Commissioner did not impose additional directions as the organization had already ceased operating the forum and deleted the user database. The organization had implemented remedial actions including notifying affected users, conducting system reviews, and permanently shutting down the forum.
companyNow: Creative Technology remains active as a manufacturer of audio solutions and gaming peripherals. The support forum at the center of this case was permanently shut down following the 2018 breach.
dataType: usernames, hashed passwords, email addresses, IP addresses, age, date of birth, contact details, location, occupation

companyDescription: Global Data Vault, LLC is a Texas-based limited liability corporation providing data storage and recovery services, headquartered at 900 Jackson St, Ste 220, Dallas, TX 75202.
companyLongDescription: Global Data Vault, LLC is a Texas-based limited liability corporation providing data storage and recovery services, headquartered at 900 Jackson St, Ste 220, Dallas, TX 75202.
caseDescription: Global Data Vault claimed to comply with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework but failed to renew its certification and continued making false Privacy Shield claims on its website for nearly a year. The company also failed to obtain required annual verification statements during its actual participation period and did not affirm continuing obligations after ceasing participation.
violationSummary: The company failed to maintain required compliance verification and made false claims about Privacy Shield participation, undermining the security framework designed to protect personal data in international transfers.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Global Data Vault claimed on its website from July 2018 to May 2019 that it was a current certified participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU residents and customers transferred personal data to Global Data Vault based on false assurances that their information would receive Privacy Shield protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: GDV complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: GDV obtained Privacy Shield certification in June 2017 but did not renew it in 2018 and was not a current participant when making these claims from July 2018 to May 2019

claimsVsReality.claim: GDV is subject to investigatory and enforcement powers of the FTC regarding Privacy Shield compliance
claimsVsReality.reality: GDV was not in compliance with Privacy Shield Principles during the time it made this claim, having failed to obtain required annual verification statements

claimsVsReality.claim: GDV complies with all Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: GDV failed to comply with Supplemental Principle 7 verification requirement and failed to affirm continuing obligations after ceasing participation

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented that it was a current participant in Privacy Shield after certification lapsed in 2018, continuing this false representation through May 2019
violations: Represented that it was a current participant in Privacy Shield after certification lapsed in 2018, continuing this false representation through May 2019
Represented compliance with Privacy Shield principles while having failed to obtain required annual verification statements during 2017-18 certification period
Represented compliance with Privacy Shield principles while failing to affirm continuing obligations to protect personal information after ceasing participation

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Shield Principles Supplemental Principle 7 requires annual verification through self-assessment or outside compliance review that assertions about Privacy Shield privacy practices are true and implemented.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to obtain attested verification statement during the 2017-18 period when certified to participate in Privacy Shield
violations: Failed to obtain attested verification statement during the 2017-18 period when certified to participate in Privacy Shield

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Shield framework requires companies that cease participation to affirm to Commerce that they will continue protecting personal information received during participation.
regulatoryFindings.description: Did not affirm commitment to continue applying Privacy Shield principles to personal data received during participation period
violations: Did not affirm commitment to continue applying Privacy Shield principles to personal data received during participation period

outcome: FTC issued a complaint on January 23, 2020 alleging three counts of deceptive practices under Section 5 of the FTC Act. The complaint alleges Privacy Shield misrepresentation, failure to comply with verification requirements, and failure to affirm continuing obligations. Commerce warned the company to take down false Privacy Shield claims, which the company failed to do. The document does not include final settlement terms or remediation requirements, indicating this is the complaint stage initiating formal enforcement proceedings.
dataType: Personal data transferred from European Union under Privacy Shield framework
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles – Supplemental Principle 7 (verification requirement)
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework – Continuing obligations requirement

companyDescription: The Metropolitan Police Service is the territorial police force responsible for law enforcement across London and surrounding areas, operating since 1829. It maintains the Police National Database (PND) for recording and sharing criminal intelligence across UK law enforcement agencies.
companyLongDescription: The Metropolitan Police Service is the territorial police force responsible for law enforcement across London and surrounding areas, operating since 1829. It maintains the Police National Database (PND) for recording and sharing criminal intelligence across UK law enforcement agencies.
caseDescription: The Metropolitan Police Service failed to ensure accuracy of sensitive criminal records uploaded to the Police National Database (PND). For nearly a decade, records could not be correctly uploaded, amended, or deleted without detection. MPS lacked automated quality checks despite processing vast daily volumes, leaving partner agencies with potentially inaccurate information that could have compromised investigations.
violationSummary: MPS failed to implement adequate technical and organisational measures to ensure the accuracy and integrity of sensitive criminal data in their control, resulting in system failures that prevented proper data management for an extended period.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: The Metropolitan Police Service operated the Police National Database since 2011 without automated systems to verify that sensitive criminal records were correctly uploaded, amended.
whyTheyWereWrong: Partner law enforcement agencies and criminal justice organizations received inaccurate, incomplete, or outdated criminal records without knowing the data was corrupted.

claimsVsReality.claim: MPS described its record-checking system at the time of incident discovery as functional and appropriate
claimsVsReality.reality: MPS itself described the checking system as 'immature,' lacking automated verification despite nine years of PND operation and daily processing of thousands of records

claimsVsReality.claim: Data integrity issues may not have been foreseeable
claimsVsReality.reality: An automated checking system was successfully deployed post-incident as a remedial measure, demonstrating that such a system could have been implemented at any time and would have likely prevented the incident entirely

claimsVsReality.claim: Incident had limited impact because MPS's own systems retained accurate records
claimsVsReality.reality: Partner agencies and other law enforcement organisations relying on PND were unaware of inaccurate updates and lacked access to correct information for investigations, potentially compromising operational decisions

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 38(4) of Part 3 of the Data Protection Act 2018 requires all reasonable steps to be taken to ensure that personal data which is inaccurate, incomplete or no longer up to date is not transmitted or made available for any of the law enforcement purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: MPS failed to take reasonable steps to ensure inaccurate, incomplete, or outdated criminal records were not transmitted to partner agencies via PND
violations: MPS failed to take reasonable steps to ensure inaccurate, incomplete, or outdated criminal records were not transmitted to partner agencies via PND
MPS did not develop automated quality assurance systems despite operating PND for nearly a decade, allowing data integrity failures to persist undetected
Criminal records could not be reliably uploaded, amended, or deleted, compromising the accuracy of information available to law enforcement partners

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to MPS. MPS has since addressed all identified issues and implemented enhanced monitoring frameworks locally and via support functions. The Commissioner recommended MPS review codebase management practices, implement proper protection of deployment code branches, conduct mandatory code reviews before deployment including regression testing, and document testing, review, and deployment best practices for all software processing sensitive data. Ongoing oversight from MPS Senior Responsible Officer and technical teams ensures reduced recurrence risk.
companyNow: The Metropolitan Police Service remains the primary law enforcement agency for London and the surrounding areas. Following this enforcement action, MPS has implemented enhanced data quality controls and monitoring frameworks for the Police National Database.
dataType: Criminal records, organised crime group intelligence, sensitive personal data

companyDescription: Cosmetic Medical Limited is a cosmetic medical services provider registered in the Isle of Man at 34 Victoria Street, Douglas, IM1 2LD.
companyLongDescription: Cosmetic Medical Limited is a cosmetic medical services provider registered in the Isle of Man at 34 Victoria Street, Douglas, IM1 2LD.
caseDescription: Cosmetic Medical Limited failed to cooperate with the Information Commissioner's investigation into a data subject's complaint regarding a Subject Access Request. The company repeatedly failed to provide required information despite multiple requests, an Information Notice, and explicit warnings of consequences. The Commissioner imposed a penalty for violations of cooperation obligations under Article 31 and information notice requirements under Regulation 101.
violationSummary: The company's failure to cooperate with the supervisory authority and refusal to provide information required for the investigation represents exclusion of the individual from accessing their own data and from meaningful investigation of their complaint.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Cosmetic Medical Limited failed to cooperate with the Information Commissioner's investigation.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's non-cooperation prevented the Commissioner from investigating a data subject's complaint about access to their personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: CML assured the Commissioner on 14 September 2020 that it would provide information relating to the SAR investigation.
claimsVsReality.reality: CML failed to provide relevant information and supplied only details about events preceding the SAR.

claimsVsReality.claim: CML asserted over 14 days following 14 September that information would be submitted.
claimsVsReality.reality: No further information was provided despite these assurances.

claimsVsReality.claim: CML asserted it would provide additional information following the Information Notice and initial response on 30 October 2020.
claimsVsReality.reality: No additional information was provided by the 4 November 2020 deadline.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 31 requires controllers to cooperate with supervisory authorities on request in the performance of their tasks.
regulatoryFindings.description: CML failed to respond to the Commissioner's cooperation request of 27 August 2020 until 14 September 2020 and provided only partial, non-responsive information.
violations: CML failed to respond to the Commissioner's cooperation request of 27 August 2020 until 14 September 2020 and provided only partial, non-responsive information.
CML provided information relating to events before the SAR was received rather than information about SAR compliance.
CML gave assurances that information would be provided but failed to deliver within the specified timeframe and beyond.

regulatoryFindings.act: Regulation 101 (Information Notices) empowers the Commissioner to order controllers to provide information required for the performance of tasks.
regulatoryFindings.description: An Information Notice was issued on 29 September 2020 requiring compliance by 29 October 2020; CML did not respond until 30 October 2020.
violations: An Information Notice was issued on 29 September 2020 requiring compliance by 29 October 2020; CML did not respond until 30 October 2020.
CML provided only partial information on 30 October 2020 and provided no additional information by the 4 November 2020 deadline despite assurances of action.
CML demonstrated a pattern of non-compliance with formal information requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: Articles 12 and 15 require controllers to respond to Subject Access Requests in compliance with prescribed timeframes and provide access to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: CML failed to properly comply with the SAR submitted on 7 July 2020, triggering the investigation.
violations: CML failed to properly comply with the SAR submitted on 7 July 2020, triggering the investigation.

outcome: The Information Commissioner imposed an administrative fine of £3,250.00 on Cosmetic Medical Limited, payable by 22 January 2021 via BACS transfer or cheque. The fine addresses failures to cooperate with the Commissioner's investigation and non-compliance with an Information Notice. CML has a right of appeal to the Isle of Man Data Protection Tribunal under Regulation 120. The Commissioner decided not to certify the failure to comply with the Information Notice to the High Court in addition to the penalty.
dataType: Personal data subject to Subject Access Request (SAR)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR and LED Implementing Regulations 2018, Regulation 101 (Information notices)
GDPR Articles 12 and 15 (Subject Access Request compliance)

companyDescription: University College Dublin is a public research university and constituent university of the National University of Ireland, founded in 1854. It is one of Ireland's leading academic institutions.
companyLongDescription: University College Dublin is a public research university and constituent university of the National University of Ireland, founded in 1854. It is one of Ireland's leading academic institutions.
caseDescription: University College Dublin failed to implement adequate security measures on its email service, resulting in 7 data breaches where unauthorised parties accessed UCD email accounts. The university also stored personal data longer than necessary and failed to notify one breach to the DPC within the required timeframe.
violationSummary: UCD failed to implement appropriate security measures (technical and organisational) required by GDPR Article 32, directly resulting in multiple breaches where unauthorised parties accessed email accounts containing personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: University College Dublin failed to implement appropriate security measures on its email service, stored personal data longer than necessary.
whyTheyWereWrong: Unauthorised third parties accessed thousands of UCD staff and student email accounts containing sensitive personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security using appropriate technical and organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: UCD failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data on its email service, allowing unauthorised third parties to access email accounts
violations: UCD failed to ensure appropriate security of personal data on its email service, allowing unauthorised third parties to access email accounts

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32(1) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure appropriate security of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: UCD did not implement adequate security measures to protect email accounts from unauthorised access
violations: UCD did not implement adequate security measures to protect email accounts from unauthorised access

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(e) requires personal data be stored in a form which permits identification of data subjects no longer than necessary for processing purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: UCD stored certain personal data in email accounts for longer than necessary
violations: UCD stored certain personal data in email accounts for longer than necessary

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33(1) requires data controllers to notify the supervisory authority of a personal data breach without undue delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: UCD notified one personal data breach 13 days after becoming aware of it, exceeding the 'without undue delay' requirement
