violations: UCD notified one personal data breach 13 days after becoming aware of it, exceeding the 'without undue delay' requirement

outcome: The Data Protection Commission imposed an administrative fine of €70,000 on UCD, issued a reprimand, and ordered UCD to bring its email service processing operations into full compliance with GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1) through implementation of appropriate technical and organisational security measures.
companyNow: University College Dublin continues to operate as Ireland's largest university. The institution has implemented enhanced cybersecurity measures and data protection protocols following the DPC enforcement action.
dataType: Email account credentials, email content, personal identifiers

companyDescription: A Hungarian warehouse and logistics operator managing dry goods storage (telecommunications equipment, hardware, cables) with approximately 37 employees at the monitored facility.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian warehouse and logistics operator managing dry goods storage (telecommunications equipment, hardware, cables) with approximately 37 employees at the monitored facility.
caseDescription: A warehouse operator installed surveillance cameras ostensibly for asset protection but positioned them to monitor employees' work intensity and break-room usage. The company failed to provide adequate, timely notice about the camera system to employees for months after deployment began. Camera angles captured both protected valuables and employee workstations, enabling unauthorized workplace monitoring.
violationSummary: The company deployed electronic surveillance systems with camera angles that were capable of monitoring employees' work activity and break-room usage, not limited to asset protection as claimed. This constitutes unauthorized workplace surveillance—a classic privacy invasion through persistent monitoring.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed warehouse surveillance cameras with viewing angles capturing both high-value assets and employee workstations.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees had no clear understanding that their administrative work areas and break patterns were being monitored, enabling managers to track work intensity.

claimsVsReality.claim: Cameras were installed solely for asset protection and building security (vagyonvédelem és épületek biztonsága).
claimsVsReality.reality: Camera angles were configured to capture employee workstations and break areas, making them equally capable of monitoring work intensity and employee presence during non-working periods.

claimsVsReality.claim: The storeroom area was not designated as a break-room and only involved brief administrative tasks with no continuous employee presence.
claimsVsReality.reality: Employees used the storeroom during breaks; supervisors explicitly instructed employees (including the complainant) to limit their time there, indicating the system was being used to monitor employee behavior during non-work periods.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees were informed about camera operations through a data protection notice provided at hire and through a general policy available on the internal network.
claimsVsReality.reality: The initial notice was generic and non-specific; the detailed operational policy was not issued until April 3, 2020—more than 4.5 months after cameras began recording on November 18, 2019. No location-specific warnings were posted at the monitored areas during the gap period.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires that personal data shall be 'collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes.'
regulatoryFindings.description: Camera in the warehouse storeroom was configured to capture both high-value tools/parts (the stated purpose) and the administrative workstation where employees performed brief clerical tasks, rendering it capable of monitoring work intensity contrary to the stated asset-protection purpose.
violations: Camera in the warehouse storeroom was configured to capture both high-value tools/parts (the stated purpose) and the administrative workstation where employees performed brief clerical tasks, rendering it capable of monitoring work intensity contrary to the stated asset-protection purpose.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data shall be 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed' (data minimization).
regulatoryFindings.description: The camera's field of view encompassed far more than the protected assets—it captured the entire workstation area and employee movements, going beyond what was necessary for asset protection.
violations: The camera's field of view encompassed far more than the protected assets—it captured the entire workstation area and employee movements, going beyond what was necessary for asset protection.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(1) requires the controller to provide data subjects with specified information at the time personal data are obtained from them, including the identity of the controller, the purpose of processing, the legal basis, and other details enabling fair and transparent processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: For approximately 5.5 months (November 18, 2019 – April 3, 2020), employees received no specific notice about the camera system's operation at their worksite. A generic one-page statement provided at hire mentioned cameras only in passing; the detailed operational policy was not issued until months after recording began. No location-specific signage was posted at the monitored areas during this period.
violations: For approximately 5.5 months (November 18, 2019 – April 3, 2020), employees received no specific notice about the camera system's operation at their worksite. A generic one-page statement provided at hire mentioned cameras only in passing; the detailed operational policy was not issued until months after recording began. No location-specific signage was posted at the monitored areas during this period.

outcome: The Nemzeti Adatvédelmi és Információszabadság Hatóság (National Data Protection Authority) found two substantive violations: (1) violations of GDPR Articles 5(1)(b) and 5(1)(c) for improper camera positioning enabling unauthorized employee monitoring, and (2) violation of GDPR Art. 13(1) for failure to provide timely, specific notice to affected employees. The Authority ordered the company to: (a) reposition the storeroom camera to eliminate its capability to monitor employee work activity and restrict its field of view to protected assets only, and (b) pay a fine of 700,000 HUF (approximately €2,360 / $2,600 USD). The decision was also ordered to be published in anonymized form. The company was required to comply within 30 days of the decision becoming final. The decision is subject to administrative court review within 30 days of service.
companyNow: Unknown – company identity redacted in published decision. Likely still operating warehouse/logistics operations in Hungary.
dataType: Biometric data (facial recognition/video surveillance), location data, work activity patterns
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13(1) – Transparency/Information to be Provided to Data Subject

companyDescription: A debt collection agency operating in Hungary that specializes in pursuing outstanding debts through payment demands and collection activities.
companyLongDescription: A debt collection agency operating in Hungary that specializes in pursuing outstanding debts through payment demands and collection activities.
caseDescription: A debt collection agency unlawfully processed a complainant's phone number by recording it under a different person's account without consent. The agency failed to adhere to data accuracy principles and could not demonstrate lawful basis for the data processing. The phone number was subsequently deleted after the authority's intervention.
violationSummary: The agency collected and recorded the complainant's phone number during a call without consent or notification, treating contact information as belonging to the debtor. This constitutes surveillance-like collection of personal data without proper legal basis or individual awareness.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A collection agency recorded a person's phone number in another person's debt file without consent, then sent repeated SMS payment demands to that number.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant received multiple threatening SMS messages about a debt that was not theirs, had their phone number tied to another person's file without permission.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agency claimed it did not process the complainant's personal data, only stored the phone number as a contact number for reaching the debtor.
claimsVsReality.reality: The phone number unequivocally belonged to and identified the complainant, constituting personal data under GDPR; it was stored under the debtor's account without consent, making it unlawfully processed personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Agency stated the phone number was provided voluntarily by the complainant during a telephone conversation as a means to contact the debtor.
claimsVsReality.reality: No explicit consent or notification was given during the call regarding data processing, retention, or storage; the agency failed to provide transparency about how the data would be used or kept.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires that personal data shall be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; reasonable measures must be taken to erase or rectify inaccurate personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency recorded complainant's phone number under debtor's account despite knowing it was the complainant's contact number, not the debtor's, creating inaccurate records.
violations: Agency recorded complainant's phone number under debtor's account despite knowing it was the complainant's contact number, not the debtor's, creating inaccurate records.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing is lawful only if it has a valid legal basis, such as explicit consent from the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency processed complainant's phone number without demonstrating valid legal basis or obtaining explicit consent from the complainant, only implicit agreement to facilitate debt communication.
violations: Agency processed complainant's phone number without demonstrating valid legal basis or obtaining explicit consent from the complainant, only implicit agreement to facilitate debt communication.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires data controllers to facilitate individuals' rights under Articles 15–22 and provide responses within one month of request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency initially denied access to data claimed to be under a different person's account, violating transparency obligations despite the data being the complainant's personal information.
violations: Agency initially denied access to data claimed to be under a different person's account, violating transparency obligations despite the data being the complainant's personal information.

outcome: The authority found the collection agency violated GDPR Articles 5(1)(d) and 6(1) through unlawful and inaccurate processing of the complainant's phone number. The agency was ordered to pay 300,000 HUF in administrative fines. The phone number was already deleted from the agency's system prior to the authority's intervention. The complainant's request to delete address and email data was rejected as those data were not unlawfully processed. The authority also awarded 10,000 HUF to the complainant for exceeding processing deadlines. The decision is subject to judicial review at the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
dataType: Telephone number, residential address, email address

companyDescription: Innovasjon Norge is a public enterprise owned by the Norwegian Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, established to promote innovation, entrepreneurship, and business development in Norway. The agency provides financing, advisory services, and support to businesses and entrepreneurs.
companyLongDescription: Innovasjon Norge is a public enterprise owned by the Norwegian Ministry of Trade, Industry and Fisheries, established to promote innovation, entrepreneurship, and business development in Norway. The agency provides financing, advisory services, and support to businesses and entrepreneurs.
caseDescription: Innovasjon Norge processed credit application data for individuals without a lawful basis under GDPR Article 6. The company obtained and stored personal and financial information from multiple credit inquiries between January and April 2020, failing to document legal grounds for processing and mishandling sensitive credit data internally.
violationSummary: The company processed sensitive personal data (credit inquiries) without establishing a valid legal basis under GDPR Article 6, compounded by inadequate security measures and internal data handling protocols, creating systemic insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Innovasjon Norge processed personal credit application data for multiple individuals without a documented legal basis.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals' sensitive financial and credit information was handled internally by Innovasjon Norge without lawful authorization, exposing their creditworthiness.

claimsVsReality.claim: Innovasjon Norge claimed that credit inquiries were necessary to evaluate customer financing applications.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no documented lawful basis under GDPR Article 6 to process the data. No consent was obtained, no legitimate interest was established, and the processing was not linked to an actual contractual relationship with the individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted that it had functional safeguards for handling sensitive financial data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Passwords and access credentials were shared among employees, there was no audit trail, and data was retained without clear deletion policies or access controls—indicating inadequate security measures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data is lawful only if it is based on one of six enumerated legal bases (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge processed credit application data of 4-6 individuals from January–April 2020 without documenting a lawful basis under Article 6(1). No consent was obtained, no contractual relationship existed, and no other legal basis was established or recorded.
violations: Innovasjon Norge processed credit application data of 4-6 individuals from January–April 2020 without documenting a lawful basis under Article 6(1). No consent was obtained, no contractual relationship existed, and no other legal basis was established or recorded.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Credit inquiries were stored and handled internally without adequate security safeguards or access controls. Data was shared among Innovasjon Norge staff without documented authorization or need-to-know restrictions, creating risk of unauthorized disclosure.
violations: Credit inquiries were stored and handled internally without adequate security safeguards or access controls. Data was shared among Innovasjon Norge staff without documented authorization or need-to-know restrictions, creating risk of unauthorized disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires that controllers implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge failed to maintain secure routines for handling credit data. Passwords and access credentials were shared among employees; there was no documented audit trail or monitoring of data access; and credit inquiries were retained without clear retention or deletion policies.
violations: Innovasjon Norge failed to maintain secure routines for handling credit data. Passwords and access credentials were shared among employees; there was no documented audit trail or monitoring of data access; and credit inquiries were retained without clear retention or deletion policies.

regulatoryFindings.act: Norwegian Personal Data Act § 6 requires that any processing of personal data by a public body must have a documented lawful basis under the applicable regulations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Innovasjon Norge, as a public institution, processed credit data without documented legal basis or treatment ground (behandlingsgrunnlag) as required by domestic law.
violations: Innovasjon Norge, as a public institution, processed credit data without documented legal basis or treatment ground (behandlingsgrunnlag) as required by domestic law.

outcome: Datatilsynet issued an administrative penalty of NOK 1,000,000 under GDPR Article 83. Innovasjon Norge was ordered to cease processing of the affected individuals' credit data and to document lawful basis for any future personal data processing. The company must implement enhanced security measures, including restricted access controls, audit logging, and employee training on data protection obligations. Compliance must be demonstrated by 25 January 2021. The penalty reflects the systematic nature of the violation, involving multiple individuals and extended duration (January–April 2020), but was moderated due to lack of evidence that damage was caused and absence of intentional misconduct.
companyNow: Innovasjon Norge remains a Norwegian government development agency. As of 2020, it has been required to strengthen data protection practices and implement documented consent and lawful-basis frameworks for all personal data processing.
dataType: Financial data, personal identifiers, credit information

companyDescription: LotaData, Inc. is a Delaware-based company located in San Francisco that provides analysis and insights derived from mobile users' location data.
companyLongDescription: LotaData, Inc. is a Delaware-based company located in San Francisco that provides analysis and insights derived from mobile users' location data.
caseDescription: LotaData falsely claimed on its privacy policy that it was certified and compliant with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks. The company initiated an application in November 2017 but never completed certification, yet continued to represent itself as a Privacy Shield participant. This deceptive practice violated FTC Act Section 5.
violationSummary: LotaData deliberately misrepresented its Privacy Shield compliance status on its publicly accessible privacy policy, creating false impressions about legal certifications and data protection safeguards.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: LotaData falsely claimed on its privacy policy that it was certified and compliant with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, despite never completing certification with the U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: European users and customers relied on LotaData's false Privacy Shield claims when deciding to transfer their personal location data to the United States.

claimsVsReality.claim: LotaData complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and the Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce.
claimsVsReality.reality: LotaData initiated an application to Commerce for Privacy Shield certification in November 2017 but never completed the necessary steps to participate in either framework and was never certified.

claimsVsReality.claim: LotaData has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: LotaData was not certified to participate in either the EU-U.S. or the Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: LotaData represented itself as certified under EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks when it had never completed certification with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
violations: LotaData represented itself as certified under EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks when it had never completed certification with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
The company continued making false Privacy Shield compliance statements in its privacy policy despite only initiating an application in November 2017 without completing required certification steps.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint (January 13, 2020) against LotaData alleging deceptive acts in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint seeks to compel removal of false Privacy Shield certification claims and require compliance with applicable data protection frameworks. No monetary penalty is specified in the complaint.
dataType: Location data, mobile user data

companyDescription: MASMOVIL is a Spanish telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and converged services to residential and business customers.
companyLongDescription: MASMOVIL is a Spanish telecommunications company providing mobile, fixed-line, broadband, and converged services to residential and business customers.
caseDescription: MASMOVIL failed to properly cancel a customer's telephone service after she exercised her contractual right to terminate. The company continued billing her account for 4 months and sent a payment demand threatening inclusion in credit blacklists, treating her personal data without legitimate basis after the contract ended.
violationSummary: The company's operational failure to properly execute contract termination resulted in unlawful continued processing of personal data (billing, payment demands, credit file threats) lacking any lawful basis under GDPR Article 6.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: MASMOVIL continued processing a customer's personal data for billing and debt collection four months after the customer terminated her contract, culminating in a threatening payment demand.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer received a payment demand for €197.01 in January 2019 with threats of credit blacklisting inclusion, despite her contract having ended in September 2018.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed the service of fixed-line telephony was given de alta (activated) and functioning normally, with evidence of traffic shown in invoices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer had made four complaints between May and July 2017 that the line was non-functional; a government regulator (SESIAD) confirmed the service was never effectively activated, estimating damages in the customer's favor.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated it processed the customer's data legitimately under Article 6(1)(b) based on an active contract and Article 6(1)(f) legitimate interest in debt collection.
claimsVsReality.reality: By September 21, 2018, the company had acknowledged contract termination and paid refunds; processing from that date onward—particularly billing and credit threats in January 2019—lacked any lawful ground.

claimsVsReality.claim: MASMOVIL claimed the data was merely 'blocked' for legal obligations and caused no harm since the customer was never actually reported to credit files.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer received an explicit threat of credit blacklist inclusion on January 28, 2019, causing distress; the threat itself was unlawful processing regardless of whether it was executed.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires that personal data processing be lawful and based on one of six specified grounds (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: MASMOVIL processed the customer's personal data for billing and debt collection from September 21, 2018 to January 31, 2019 without any lawful basis, as the contract had terminated and no other ground existed.
violations: MASMOVIL processed the customer's personal data for billing and debt collection from September 21, 2018 to January 31, 2019 without any lawful basis, as the contract had terminated and no other ground existed.
The company sent a payment demand on January 28, 2019 threatening credit blacklist inclusion while processing personal data unlawfully after contract termination.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Continuing to bill and threaten credit file inclusion for a service the company admitted had not been properly deactivated violated transparency and fairness principles.
violations: Continuing to bill and threaten credit file inclusion for a service the company admitted had not been properly deactivated violated transparency and fairness principles.

outcome: MASMOVIL was ordered to pay €60,000. The company was required to cease unlawful processing, block the customer's data (which occurred January 31, 2019), cancel all illegitimate invoices, and implement proper contract termination procedures. The customer was informed that no debt remained and her data had been blocked.
companyNow: MASMOVIL (XFERA MÓVILES, S.A.) remains a major Spanish mobile operator. The company acknowledged the error, cancelled the disputed debt on January 31, 2019 within 48 hours of the customer's complaint, and blocked the customer's data.
dataType: Identification data, contact information

companyDescription: TDARX, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing IT management and security services through the websites tdarx.com and nocdoc.com, with principal office in Winston Salem, North Carolina.
companyLongDescription: TDARX, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing IT management and security services through the websites tdarx.com and nocdoc.com, with principal office in Winston Salem, North Carolina.
caseDescription: TDARX, Inc. falsely claimed to be certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework after its certification lapsed in 2018. The company failed to comply with mandatory annual verification requirements while participating in the program and failed to affirm continued data protection commitments to Commerce after its certification expired.
violationSummary: TDARX made false and misleading representations about Privacy Shield compliance, creating risk of unauthorized or inadequately protected disclosure of personal data to third parties who relied on those false certifications.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: TDARX claimed on its website that it participated in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework and complied with its principles, even after its certification lapsed in 2018.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU individuals who transferred personal data to TDARX relied on false claims of Privacy Shield protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: TDARX represented that it was a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework and complied with Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: TDARX's Privacy Shield certification lapsed in 2018, one year after initial certification in 2017, and the company was no longer a valid participant.

claimsVsReality.claim: TDARX represented that it would cooperate with EU data protection authorities regarding Privacy Shield complaints and resolve complaints in compliance with Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: TDARX failed to obtain the mandatory annual verification statement required by Supplemental Principle 7 during its 2017-18 certification period and did not affirm continuing data protection obligations after certification lapsed.

claimsVsReality.claim: TDARX maintained on its website statements committing to Privacy Shield compliance and recourse mechanisms.
claimsVsReality.reality: After being warned by Commerce to remove Privacy Shield claims, TDARX continued disseminating the false statements without timely withdrawal or affirmation of continuing protection obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: TDARX represented it was a current participant in EU-U.S. Privacy Shield when its certification had lapsed in 2018, making the representation false or misleading.
violations: TDARX represented it was a current participant in EU-U.S. Privacy Shield when its certification had lapsed in 2018, making the representation false or misleading.
TDARX represented compliance with Privacy Shield principles while failing to obtain required annual verification statements signed by a corporate officer or outside reviewer.
TDARX represented compliance with Privacy Shield continuing obligations while failing to affirm to Commerce that it would continue protecting personal data received during program participation.

regulatoryFindings.act: EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Supplemental Principle 7 requires participating companies to verify annually through self-assessment or outside compliance review that Privacy Shield practice assertions are true and implemented.
regulatoryFindings.description: During 2017-18 certification period, TDARX failed to obtain any attested verification statement required by Supplemental Principle 7.
violations: During 2017-18 certification period, TDARX failed to obtain any attested verification statement required by Supplemental Principle 7.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Shield framework requires companies that cease participation to affirm to Commerce they will continue applying Privacy Shield principles to personal data received during program participation.
regulatoryFindings.description: TDARX failed to affirm continuing data protection commitments to Commerce when its certification lapsed in 2018, despite retaining personal data collected during participation.
violations: TDARX failed to affirm continuing data protection commitments to Commerce when its certification lapsed in 2018, despite retaining personal data collected during participation.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against TDARX alleging three counts: misrepresentation regarding current Privacy Shield participation, misrepresentation regarding verification compliance, and misrepresentation regarding continuing obligations. The document is a complaint issued January 23, 2020; no settlement or final order terms are included in this document. Typical FTC outcomes in such cases include cease-and-desist orders and compliance directives to remove false claims and implement adequate data protection measures.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types); EU personal data subject to GDPR
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive Acts or Practices
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles – Supplemental Principle 7 (Verification Requirement)
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles – Continuing Obligations

companyDescription: Medable, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing technology solutions to business customers in pharmaceutical, biotechnology, and research industries, headquartered in Palo Alto, California.
companyLongDescription: Medable, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing technology solutions to business customers in pharmaceutical, biotechnology, and research industries, headquartered in Palo Alto, California.
caseDescription: Medable falsely claimed to be certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework in its privacy policy from December 2017 to October 2018, despite never completing the certification process. The company represented to users transferring personal data from the EEA that it adhered to Privacy Shield Principles, when in fact it had no such certification. This deceptive practice violated Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.
violationSummary: Company made deceptive claims about how personal data would be protected, misleading individuals about the legal framework governing their information transfer.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Medable falsely stated in its privacy policy from December 2017 to October 2018 that it was EU/US Privacy Shield certified.
whyTheyWereWrong: European users transferred personal data to Medable based on false Privacy Shield certification claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: Medable is EU/US Privacy Shield certified
claimsVsReality.reality: Medable was never certified; it only initiated an application in December 2017 but did not complete the steps necessary to participate

claimsVsReality.claim: Medable adheres to Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: Without certification, Medable could not legally claim adherence to Privacy Shield Principles

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Medable represented in its privacy policy that it was EU/US Privacy Shield certified when it had never completed certification
violations: Medable represented in its privacy policy that it was EU/US Privacy Shield certified when it had never completed certification
Company claimed adherence to Privacy Shield Principles while lacking actual certification
Misrepresentations continued from December 2017 to October 2018 despite only initiating the application process

outcome: FTC issued a complaint against Medable for deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint was issued on January 6, 2020. Respondent was required to cease the deceptive practices and comply with FTC directives regarding accurate privacy representations.
dataType: Personal data from European Economic Area residents, including health/research data

companyDescription: T&M Protection Resources, LLC is a Delaware limited liability corporation based in New York that provides background check, security, and investigative services. The company obtained EU resident personal data in connection with its background check services.
companyLongDescription: T&M Protection Resources, LLC is a Delaware limited liability corporation based in New York that provides background check, security, and investigative services. The company obtained EU resident personal data in connection with its background check services.
caseDescription: T&M Protection Resources claimed to comply with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework on its website but failed to renew its certification in 2018. After certification lapsed, the company continued making false claims about Privacy Shield participation and failed to obtain required annual verification statements. The company also did not affirm its commitment to protect personal data previously collected under the framework.
violationSummary: The company made deceptive representations about Privacy Shield participation when marketing background check services to EU residents, misrepresenting the legal safeguards protecting their personal data transfers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: T&M Protection Resources claimed on its website that it complied with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU residents whose personal data T&M collected for background checks lost legal protections they believed they had.

claimsVsReality.claim: T&M Protection Resources, LLC complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce.
claimsVsReality.reality: T&M's Privacy Shield certification expired in 2018 and was never renewed; the company was not a current Privacy Shield participant when making this claim.

claimsVsReality.claim: T&M Protection Resources, LLC has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: T&M obtained certification in 2017 but did not complete renewal steps when certification expired in 2018, and did not affirm its commitment to protect previously collected data.

claimsVsReality.claim: If there is any conflict between the terms in this privacy policy and the Privacy Shield Principles, the Privacy Shield Principles shall govern.
claimsVsReality.reality: T&M made no effort to ensure Privacy Shield Principle compliance, failing annual verification requirements and failing to affirm continuing obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: T&M made express representations on its privacy policy that it complied with EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework and had certified to the Department of Commerce, when in fact its certification had lapsed in 2018 and it did not complete renewal steps.
violations: T&M made express representations on its privacy policy that it complied with EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework and had certified to the Department of Commerce, when in fact its certification had lapsed in 2018 and it did not complete renewal steps.
T&M continued claiming Privacy Shield participation after Commerce warned the company to remove such claims unless it completed renewal steps.
T&M failed to comply with Privacy Shield Principle 7 verification requirement during its 2017-18 participation period, failing to obtain attested verification statements.
T&M failed to affirm to Commerce its continuing commitment to protect personal information received during its Privacy Shield participation period, as required by Privacy Shield principles.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on 16 March 2020 alleging three counts of deceptive practices under Section 5 of the FTC Act. The document is the complaint itself and does not indicate final resolution, penalty amount, or specific remediation order terms beyond alleging violations.
dataType: Personal data from EU residents (specific types not detailed but includes background check information)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles – Supplemental Principle 7 (verification requirement)
EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework – Continuing obligations upon cessation of participation

companyDescription: Hungarian employer providing cafeteria (non-wage) employee benefits including subsidised leisure cards. Operates payroll, human resources, and benefits administration with hundreds of employees.
companyLongDescription: Hungarian employer providing cafeteria (non-wage) employee benefits including subsidised leisure cards. Operates payroll, human resources, and benefits administration with hundreds of employees.
caseDescription: An employer failed to delete an employee's obsolete temporary residential address from payroll records after the employee requested deletion in 2018, violating data accuracy and deletion rights under GDPR. The employer also transmitted employee personal data to a benefits administrator without proper legal basis or adequate disclosure, and failed to respond to data subject requests within statutory timeframes.
fineDisplay: €1,800,000 (approx. 600,000 HUF data protection fine + 10,000 HUF procedural compensation)
violationSummary: The employer failed to maintain accurate personal data and implement proper data management procedures. Retention of demonstrably obsolete data and transmission without adequate safeguards/disclosure reflects systemic failure to protect data integrity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Retained an employee's outdated temporary address in payroll records for 19 years after the employee notified the employer it had expired in 1999.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's inaccurate address remained in active use in the employer's systems, exposing her to misdirected communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employer claimed employee obligation to self-report address changes to payroll department under Labour Code.
claimsVsReality.reality: Employee provided multiple documented notifications (1999, 2007, 2014, 2016, 2018) to various employer departments; employer failed to consolidate or act on any notification. Employer's argument that employee bore sole responsibility contradicted by employer's duty under GDPR to maintain accurate data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employer claimed data transfer to benefits administrator pursued legitimate interest to facilitate seamless benefits enrollment transition.
claimsVsReality.reality: Legitimate interest doctrine under GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) protects controller or third-party interests, not data subject interests. Facilitating optional benefits access for employee benefit is not a legitimate interest of controller or administrator; it is interest of employee/subject.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employer claimed general employee information handbook provided adequate transparency about data processing and transfer.
claimsVsReality.reality: Generic handbook did not separately address or disclose specific data processing for benefits administration, did not mention transfer to external administrator, and did not constitute GDPR Art. 13 compliant notice at time of data collection/transfer.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(d): Personal data shall be accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date; reasonable measures must be taken to erase or rectify inaccurate data without undue delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer retained employee's temporary residential address marked as ceased in June 1999 for over 19 years despite employee notification in 2016, 2018, and multiple prior occasions. No corrective action taken until regulator intervention in 2020.
violations: Employer retained employee's temporary residential address marked as ceased in June 1999 for over 19 years despite employee notification in 2016, 2018, and multiple prior occasions. No corrective action taken until regulator intervention in 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 17(1)(a): Data subject has right to erasure when personal data no longer necessary for the purposes for which collected or processed.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer failed to delete temporary address after employee's written request on 25 September 2018, citing only that employee had not formally reported change to payroll department—despite employee providing documented notification.
violations: Employer failed to delete temporary address after employee's written request on 25 September 2018, citing only that employee had not formally reported change to payroll department—despite employee providing documented notification.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1): Processing lawful only if legal basis exists (e.g. consent, contract, legitimate interest of controller/third party).
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer transferred employee name, tax ID, birth details, and permanent address to benefits administrator without employee consent, claiming 'legitimate interest' to facilitate benefits enrollment, but legitimate interest doctrine does not encompass interests of data subject or employer assisting employee access to optional benefits.
violations: Employer transferred employee name, tax ID, birth details, and permanent address to benefits administrator without employee consent, claiming 'legitimate interest' to facilitate benefits enrollment, but legitimate interest doctrine does not encompass interests of data subject or employer assisting employee access to optional benefits.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13: Where data collected from data subject, controller must provide specified information at time of collection, including purposes, legal basis, and recipient categories.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer transmitted personal data to benefits administrator without providing employee prior notice, information about data transfer, or data processing consent form signed by employee; generic employee handbook insufficient.
violations: Employer transmitted personal data to benefits administrator without providing employee prior notice, information about data transfer, or data processing consent form signed by employee; generic employee handbook insufficient.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(1)-(4): Controller must respond to data subject requests regarding rights (access, deletion, etc.) within one month without undue delay, confirming action taken.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employer received employee's 25 September 2018 email requesting deletion of temporary address and did not acknowledge request or provide any information about actions taken; no response within statutory one-month deadline.
violations: Employer received employee's 25 September 2018 email requesting deletion of temporary address and did not acknowledge request or provide any information about actions taken; no response within statutory one-month deadline.

outcome: Authority established three violations: (1) failure to delete/rectify obsolete temporary address in violation of Articles 5(1)(d), 16, 17(1)(a); (2) failure to respond to deletion request in violation of Article 12(1)-(4); (3) unlawful data transfer without lawful basis or disclosure in violation of Articles 6(1), 13. Employer ordered to cease processing; temporary address deleted on 17 January 2020 after regulator notification. Data protection fine of 600,000 HUF imposed; separate administrative penalty of 10,000 HUF for exceeding statutory response deadline. Employer required to establish internal processes for handling data subject requests. Decision final; administrative review available within 30 days to Budapest Metropolitan Court.
companyNow: Unknown; employer appears to be a large Hungarian industrial/energy company with 2019 revenue ~20 billion HUF. Current status unknown.
dataType: Name, tax identification number, mother's name, birth place, birth date, permanent address, temporary residential address
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 17(1)(a) – Right to erasure (right to be forgotten)
GDPR Art. 6(1) – Lawfulness of processing (lack of valid legal basis)
GDPR Art. 13 – Information to be provided where data collected from subject
GDPR Art. 12(1)-(4) – Transparent communication and facilitation of data subject rights

companyDescription: Glovo is a Spanish-founded on-demand delivery platform operating in multiple countries, connecting users with restaurants, supermarkets, and local merchants. The company processes personal data of millions of users, couriers, and merchants.
companyLongDescription: Glovo is a Spanish-founded on-demand delivery platform operating in multiple countries, connecting users with restaurants, supermarkets, and local merchants. The company processes personal data of millions of users, couriers, and merchants.
caseDescription: Glovo failed to designate a Data Protection Officer (DPO) as required by GDPR Article 37(1)(b) despite conducting large-scale personal data processing. The company acknowledged the absence of a formally designated DPO but claimed a Data Protection Committee performed equivalent functions. Only after enforcement proceedings began did Glovo formally appoint a DPO in January 2020.
violationSummary: Failure to designate required Data Protection Officer represents inadequate organizational governance and safeguarding mechanisms for personal data processing, creating systemic insecurity in data protection compliance framework.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: GLOVOAPP23 failed to designate a Data Protection Officer despite conducting large-scale personal data processing operations involving systematic monitoring of millions of food delivery users.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of users and drivers had their personal data routinely collected and monitored without a designated officer to safeguard their rights, investigate complaints.

claimsVsReality.claim: Glovo stated it was exempt from DPO designation requirements under Articles 37 RGPD and 34 LOPGDD because its data processing activities did not fall within mandatory designation thresholds.
claimsVsReality.reality: Glovo's large-scale food delivery operations involving systematic monitoring of millions of users and couriers clearly met GDPR Article 37(1)(b) criteria requiring mandatory DPO designation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Glovo's Data Protection Committee, Subcommittee, and Legal Department performed DPO functions effectively and with full guarantees of data subject rights.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ad hoc internal committees lack the formal independence, legal status, and dedicated accountability required of a designated DPO under GDPR Article 39, and were not accessible to data subjects as a point of contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: Glovo had internally designated a DPO as early as May 23, 2019.
claimsVsReality.reality: Glovo only formally notified the AEPD DPD Registry of DPO appointment on January 31, 2020, nearly eight months later and only after enforcement proceedings commenced, indicating no genuine prior designation.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 37(1)(b) requires data controllers and processors to designate a Data Protection Officer when principal activities consist of systematic monitoring of data subjects at large scale.
regulatoryFindings.description: Glovo conducted large-scale personal data processing of millions of users and drivers but failed to designate a DPO, instead attempting to substitute a Data Protection Committee lacking formal legal status and independence.
violations: Glovo conducted large-scale personal data processing of millions of users and drivers but failed to designate a DPO, instead attempting to substitute a Data Protection Committee lacking formal legal status and independence.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83(4) provides for administrative fines up to €10,000,000 or 2% of annual global turnover for violations of DPO designation obligations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Glovo's failure constituted a grave infraction under GDPR Article 83(4), warranting administrative penalty.
violations: Glovo's failure constituted a grave infraction under GDPR Article 83(4), warranting administrative penalty.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 34 requires notification to Spanish data protection authority of DPO designations within ten days.
regulatoryFindings.description: Glovo did not formally notify the AEPD of DPO designation until January 31, 2020, only after enforcement proceedings commenced on January 13, 2020.
violations: Glovo did not formally notify the AEPD of DPO designation until January 31, 2020, only after enforcement proceedings commenced on January 13, 2020.

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed a €25,000 administrative fine for violation of GDPR Article 37(1)(b). Glovo was required to comply with DPO designation obligations and notify the AEPD of the appointment. The company subsequently formalized the designation of C.C.C. as DPO in February 2020. The resolution became enforceable after notification, with payment due within specified voluntary payment periods or subject to executive collection proceedings.
companyNow: Glovo remains an active food delivery platform operating across Europe and other regions. The company completed DPO designation following the enforcement action and incorporated enhanced data governance structures.
dataType: Personal identifiers, contact information, location data, transaction data

companyDescription: A transportation or logistics company operating in Finland with approximately 47 employees, using commercial vehicle fleet management systems to track work hours and driving activity for VAT compliance purposes.
companyLongDescription: A transportation or logistics company operating in Finland with approximately 47 employees, using commercial vehicle fleet management systems to track work hours and driving activity for VAT compliance purposes.
caseDescription: A transportation company deployed an electronic driving log system to track employee work hours and collected location data via GPS without conducting a required data protection impact assessment (DPIA). The company failed to implement adequate privacy-by-design measures and did not document compliance with GDPR requirements, exposing approximately 47 employees to systematic location monitoring without proper risk assessment.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected and processed location data on employees through GPS-enabled driving logs without prior Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA) as required by GDPR Art. 35, nor did it implement privacy-by-design safeguards. This constitutes systematic surveillance of workers.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A transportation company deployed an electronic driving log system that continuously tracked GPS location data of approximately 47 employees to monitor work hours starting in 2017.
whyTheyWereWrong: Workers had no meaningful choice to refuse location monitoring due to employment dependency, exposing them to continuous surveillance of their movements.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it conducted 'careful evaluation' of the driving log system during procurement and handled it with workers through discussion.
claimsVsReality.reality: No formal DPIA was documented; company failed to identify high-risk processing (location monitoring of subordinate workers) or implement required privacy safeguards before deployment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company argued the system served only to record vehicle locations for VAT deduction compliance, not employee monitoring.
claimsVsReality.reality: System was explicitly used to monitor employee work hours and track employee location via GPS, creating systematic surveillance with high privacy risks regardless of stated business purpose.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company asserted that data protection law guidance was ambiguous and only WP29 guidance (issued April 2017) clarified DPIA requirements for location data.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Finnish DPA published clear guidance on DPIA requirements for location processing in December 2018; company had adequate time and opportunity to understand obligations before implementing the system in 2018.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 35(1) requires data controllers to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment before processing that is likely to result in high risk to individuals' rights and freedoms, particularly when using new technologies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to conduct DPIA despite implementing GPS-based location tracking of employees, which constitutes high-risk processing of workers in subordinate position.
violations: Company failed to conduct DPIA despite implementing GPS-based location tracking of employees, which constitutes high-risk processing of workers in subordinate position.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 24(1) requires controllers to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure compliance and demonstrate compliance with GDPR, considering the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company did not establish documented compliance procedures, risk assessments, or demonstrate technical/organisational safeguards for location data collection on employees.
violations: Company did not establish documented compliance procedures, risk assessments, or demonstrate technical/organisational safeguards for location data collection on employees.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 25(1) requires controllers to implement data protection by design and by default, integrating privacy principles into the processing method itself.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company deployed location tracking system without embedding privacy safeguards, data minimization, or impact assessment into the design and implementation process.
violations: Company deployed location tracking system without embedding privacy safeguards, data minimization, or impact assessment into the design and implementation process.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 35(3)(c) specifically identifies systematic monitoring of publicly accessible areas on a large scale as requiring DPIA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company implemented systematic work hour monitoring through GPS location tracking, meeting criteria for mandatory DPIA assessment.
violations: Company implemented systematic work hour monitoring through GPS location tracking, meeting criteria for mandatory DPIA assessment.

outcome: The Finnish Data Protection Ombudsman determined the company violated GDPR Articles 24, 25, and 35 by failing to conduct a mandatory Data Protection Impact Assessment and implement privacy-by-design safeguards for employee location monitoring. The Penalty Committee imposed a €16,000 administrative fine and issued a formal warning (reprimand) under GDPR Article 58(2)(b). The company was required to halt use of the location monitoring feature pending completion of a proper DPIA. The company began conducting the required DPIA after receiving the investigation notice.
companyNow: Unknown. The company suspended use of the GPS location monitoring feature during the investigation and initiated a proper Data Protection Impact Assessment in response to regulatory pressure.
dataType: Location data, employee location information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 24 - Accountability and demonstration of compliance
GDPR Art. 25 - Data protection by design and default
GDPR Art. 35 - Data Protection Impact Assessment requirement

companyDescription: Anthem, Inc. is a major diversified healthcare company and insurance provider headquartered in Indianapolis, Indiana. It operates as a covered entity and business associate under HIPAA, serving millions of individuals across multiple states through health insurance plans and related healthcare services.
companyLongDescription: Anthem, Inc. is a major diversified healthcare company and insurance provider headquartered in Indianapolis, Indiana. It operates as a covered entity and business associate under HIPAA, serving millions of individuals across multiple states through health insurance plans and related healthcare services.
caseDescription: Anthem suffered a massive data breach exposing 78.8 million individuals' sensitive health and personal data due to inadequate cybersecurity safeguards. The breach resulted from spearphishing and exploited multiple security weaknesses including poor network segmentation, inadequate logging and monitoring, failure to implement encryption, and non-implementation of security policies such as multi-factor authentication. The company failed to comply with HIPAA Privacy and Security Rules and California's unfair competition law.
violationSummary: Anthem failed to implement and maintain adequate administrative, physical, and technical safeguards required by HIPAA and California law to protect sensitive health information from unauthorized access and breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Anthem failed to implement adequate security safeguards, properly segment its network, monitor system activity, encrypt sensitive data, or follow its own security policies.
whyTheyWereWrong: An unauthorized party accessed unencrypted sensitive data of 78.8 million individuals, including 13.5 million California residents, exposing their names, Social Security numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Anthem maintained adequate safeguards to protect sensitive health and personal information of its members and covered individuals.
claimsVsReality.reality: Anthem failed to implement basic security controls including network segmentation, encryption, audit logging, access controls, multi-factor authentication, and security monitoring; it also failed to follow existing security policies and failed to respond to security alerts for over a year, allowing attackers to access unencrypted health data for approximately 12 months before discovery.

claimsVsReality.claim: Anthem's security program was updated and maintained to address known cybersecurity threats.
claimsVsReality.reality: Anthem failed to update its security program to protect against known cybersecurity threats, did not properly configure security tools to detect unauthorized activity, and ignored alerts indicating breach indicators such as backdoor installation and malware execution.

regulatoryFindings.act: HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 C.F.R. Part 164, Subparts A, C, E) requires covered entities and business associates to maintain standards governing the privacy and security of PHI and ePHI.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem failed to implement and maintain administrative, physical, and technical safeguards required to protect PHI and ePHI from unauthorized access and disclosure
violations: Anthem failed to implement and maintain administrative, physical, and technical safeguards required to protect PHI and ePHI from unauthorized access and disclosure

regulatoryFindings.act: HIPAA Security Rule (45 C.F.R. § 164.306–.312, .316) requires covered entities to implement administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to protect ePHI including risk assessment, access controls, encryption, audit controls, and integrity controls.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem failed to properly segment its network, implement encryption, establish access controls, maintain adequate audit logging and monitoring, implement multi-factor authentication for remote access, enforce anti-virus protections, and maintain secure password practices
violations: Anthem failed to properly segment its network, implement encryption, establish access controls, maintain adequate audit logging and monitoring, implement multi-factor authentication for remote access, enforce anti-virus protections, and maintain secure password practices
Anthem failed to regularly and accurately assess and mitigate risks to ePHI

Anthem failed to properly configure security tools to generate alerts and failed to respond to alerts regarding backdoor installation, unauthorized device scanning, malware execution, and unauthorized queries

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair, unlawful, or fraudulent acts or practices in commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem engaged in unlawful practice by violating HIPAA and failing to implement, maintain, and follow reasonable security procedures and practices to protect personal information
violations: Anthem engaged in unlawful practice by violating HIPAA and failing to implement, maintain, and follow reasonable security procedures and practices to protect personal information

outcome: California Attorney General filed complaint on September 30, 2020, seeking injunctive relief to prevent Anthem from engaging in unfair competition and data security violations; civil penalties of $2,500 per Business & Professions Code § 17200 violation and $100 per HIPAA violation (capped at $25,000 per calendar year); and recovery of investigation costs. The case sought court orders compelling compliance with HIPAA and California privacy laws and preventing recurrence of similar violations.
companyNow: Anthem, Inc. is one of the largest health insurance companies in the United States. It remains a major player in the health insurance industry and continues to be subject to enhanced regulatory scrutiny regarding data security and privacy compliance.
dataType: Protected health information (PHI), electronic personal health information (ePHI), names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, healthcare identification numbers, home addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, employment information, income data
legalBasisViolated: HIPAA Privacy Rule (45 C.F.R. Part 164, Subparts A, C, E)
California Business & Professions Code § 17200 (Unfair Competition Law)

companyDescription: The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) is a government department of the Isle of Man located in Douglas, responsible for administering data protection law and related government functions.
companyLongDescription: The Department of Home Affairs (DHA) is a government department of the Isle of Man located in Douglas, responsible for administering data protection law and related government functions.
caseDescription: The Department of Home Affairs failed to comply with data subject access requests under GDPR Articles 12 and 15, providing personal data piecemeal over five months instead of within one month as required. The department also failed to comply with a prior 2015 enforcement notice ordering timely compliance with access requests, and attempted to improperly restrict disclosures without proper justification.
violationSummary: The department systematically excluded the data subject from access to personal data they were lawfully entitled to receive, violating the transparency principle and data subject rights under GDPR.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The Department of Home Affairs failed to provide a data subject with complete personal data for five months after receiving a request.
whyTheyWereWrong: An employee seeking to understand their personnel records and work-related complaints was left unable to properly defend themselves in employment disputes because the department withheld their.

claimsVsReality.claim: DHA stated that restrictions based on Schedule 9 (redaction of third-party data) prevented disclosure of all personal data
claimsVsReality.reality: The commissioner found DHA was not entitled to rely on that restriction broadly; controllers must demonstrate necessity and proportionality case-by-case; DHA provided scant information about what restrictions were actually needed

claimsVsReality.claim: DHA represented that the context of access requests related to employment matters was 'unprecedented in the Isle of Man'
claimsVsReality.reality: There are Employment and Equality Tribunal cases demonstrating such requests are common practice in relation to employment matters (e.g., Versluijs v DHA Fire & Rescue Service)

claimsVsReality.claim: DHA claimed the 2015 enforcement notice had been issued 'some time ago' and was no longer applicable
claimsVsReality.reality: The 2015 EN remained valid and in effect; the commissioner advised DHA of its continuance in various communications; DHA was bound by its terms requiring compliance with subject access requests

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12 requires controllers to provide transparent information and facilitate communication regarding the exercise of data subject rights without undue delay or within one month of receipt.
regulatoryFindings.description: DHA provided personal data piecemeal over five months instead of within one month, failing to communicate a complete response without undue delay
violations: DHA provided personal data piecemeal over five months instead of within one month, failing to communicate a complete response without undue delay

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 establishes the right of access whereby data subjects may obtain confirmation of whether processing is occurring and access to their personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: DHA initially withheld data, then provided it incrementally over 5 months; data subject did not receive complete data to which entitled until January 2020, five months after August 2019 request
violations: DHA initially withheld data, then provided it incrementally over 5 months; data subject did not receive complete data to which entitled until January 2020, five months after August 2019 request

regulatoryFindings.act: Controllers may restrict the right of access only in limited circumstances prescribed by law, and must demonstrate necessity and proportionality.
regulatoryFindings.description: DHA applied Schedule 9 restriction (redaction of third-party data) without proper justification or demonstrating it was necessary and proportionate; failed to apply own policy on such restrictions; provided no information to commissioner regarding restriction analysis
violations: DHA applied Schedule 9 restriction (redaction of third-party data) without proper justification or demonstrating it was necessary and proportionate; failed to apply own policy on such restrictions; provided no information to commissioner regarding restriction analysis

regulatoryFindings.act: An enforcement notice issued under predecessor data protection law has effect after GDPR implementation and controllers must comply as if it were issued under GDPR regulatory powers.
regulatoryFindings.description: DHA failed to comply with 2015 enforcement notice ordering compliance with subject access requests; failure to comply with that order was basis for additional penalty under Article 58(2)(c)
violations: DHA failed to comply with 2015 enforcement notice ordering compliance with subject access requests; failure to comply with that order was basis for additional penalty under Article 58(2)(c)

outcome: The Information Commissioner imposed a penalty of £12,250.00 and issued a compliance order. The DHA is required to comply with all future data subject access requests within the statutory timeframe and without undue delay, in accordance with Articles 12 and 15 of GDPR. The commissioner considered the DHA's negligent character (knowing or should have known its obligations; had appointed a data protection officer), prior relevant enforcement action (2015 EN), and failure to mitigate damage. The DHA did eventually provide all requested data on 15 January 2020 following the 2019 enforcement notice, but this late compliance did not mitigate the failures.
companyNow: The Department of Home Affairs is the government department responsible for home affairs, immigration, and public safety in the Isle of Man. It remains a public authority subject to data protection oversight.
dataType: Staff records, employment data, work-related complaints
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 12 (transparent information, communication and modalities for the exercise of rights)
GDPR Art. 15 (right of access by the data subject)
Data Protection Act 2002 s.36 (subject access rights)
GDPR and LED Implementing Regulations 2018, Regulation 106 (enforcement notice compliance)

companyDescription: MIRACLIA TELECOMUNICACIONES, S.L. is a Spanish microenterprise that developed and operated a mobile application enabling users to make automated prank calls to others. The app included functionality to record, download, and share call recordings.
companyLongDescription: MIRACLIA TELECOMUNICACIONES, S.L. is a Spanish microenterprise that developed and operated a mobile application enabling users to make automated prank calls to others. The app included functionality to record, download, and share call recordings.
caseDescription: MIRACLIA operated a prank call application that recorded users' voice data and phone numbers without their knowledge or consent. The company failed to provide mandatory transparency disclosures before collecting personal data and could not establish a lawful basis for the treatment. Users receiving calls had no prior information they were being recorded or how their data would be used.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected voice and phone data through calls without notice or consent, which constitutes hidden surveillance of personal communications.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: MIRACLIA operated a prank call application that automatically recorded voice conversations from recipients' phones.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of prank call recipients had their voices secretly recorded and their phone numbers stored in MIRACLIA's systems without any advance notice, consent, or opportunity to refuse.

claimsVsReality.claim: MIRACLIA claimed it does not collect or store personal data of prank call recipients and only facilitates communication between the prank caller and recipient.
claimsVsReality.reality: MIRACLIA stored phone numbers of recipients in its systems until the time of call and generated and hosted audio recordings of calls in its cloud infrastructure, along with URLs accessible by the prank caller. It did collect and process personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: MIRACLIA asserted that recipients' phone data remained on the user's (prank caller's) device only and was not retained by MIRACLIA.
claimsVsReality.reality: Inspection found that phone numbers were stored in MIRACLIA's systems until the moment the call was placed (for scheduled calls, they could be stored for days/months). Only after the call was made did data leave MIRACLIA's direct control.

claimsVsReality.claim: Recipients were informed via post-call message and had the option to press '5' to delete recordings and block future calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: Recipients had no prior notice that recording would occur, no identification of MIRACLIA or its purposes, and the post-call message was insufficient to satisfy transparency requirements. Many callers experienced technical issues with the deletion mechanism (described as 'unstable' in testing).

claimsVsReality.claim: MIRACLIA acts only as an intermediary facilitating private communication between consenting adults.
claimsVsReality.reality: Recipients never consented; prank callers consented only for themselves. MIRACLIA actively designed, hosted, recorded, and enabled distribution of calls—it was not a passive conduit.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: MIRACLIA processed voice recordings and phone numbers of call recipients without transparency—they received no notification before or during calls that recording was occurring, no identity of the responsible party, and no information about their rights
violations: MIRACLIA processed voice recordings and phone numbers of call recipients without transparency—they received no notification before or during calls that recording was occurring, no identity of the responsible party, and no information about their rights

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1) requires that processing be based on at least one lawful basis (e.g. consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interest).
regulatoryFindings.description: MIRACLIA claimed legitimate interest but failed to inform data subjects, preventing them from understanding or objecting to the claimed interest. The company also relied on a contract between itself and the prank caller, but the call recipient was not party to that contract and could not consent. No valid consent was ever sought from call recipients.
violations: MIRACLIA claimed legitimate interest but failed to inform data subjects, preventing them from understanding or objecting to the claimed interest. The company also relied on a contract between itself and the prank caller, but the call recipient was not party to that contract and could not consent. No valid consent was ever sought from call recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13 requires that when personal data is obtained directly from the data subject, the controller must provide information including identity, purposes, legal basis, recipients, and retention period at the time of collection.
regulatoryFindings.description: Call recipients learned nothing during the call—no identification of MIRACLIA, no statement of purposes, no basis for processing, no retention periods, and no information about their data rights. The only 'information' provided was a brief post-call message offering to press '5' to delete—insufficient and far too late.
violations: Call recipients learned nothing during the call—no identification of MIRACLIA, no statement of purposes, no basis for processing, no retention periods, and no information about their data rights. The only 'information' provided was a brief post-call message offering to press '5' to delete—insufficient and far too late.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 14 requires that when personal data is obtained from sources other than the data subject, the controller must provide equivalent information within a reasonable timeframe or upon first communication with the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: When phone numbers were provided by the prank caller (third party), MIRACLIA never notified the call recipient of processing, never identified itself, and never provided the required disclosures. The post-call message did not satisfy Art. 14 requirements.
violations: When phone numbers were provided by the prank caller (third party), MIRACLIA never notified the call recipient of processing, never identified itself, and never provided the required disclosures. The post-call message did not satisfy Art. 14 requirements.

outcome: MIRACLIA was ordered to pay €40,000 in administrative penalties for violations of GDPR Arts. 5, 6, 13, and 14. The company was required within three months to: (1) revise all data processing operations to comply with GDPR; (2) overhaul information provided to users and obtain valid informed consent before any data collection; (3) implement mechanisms to ensure data subjects receive and access information; and (4) cease unlawful processing of data from individuals who did not provide consent. These measures must apply across all EEA countries where MIRACLIA operates the application. Failure to comply may result in additional administrative penalties for non-cooperation with the authority.
companyNow: MIRACLIA remains a small operator (2 employees as of 2018, €475k revenue, €6k capital). The company received the enforcement decision in 2020. Status post-compliance is unknown, though the decision mandated operational changes by 2020.
dataType: Phone numbers, voice recordings, personal communications
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Lack of lawful basis (no valid consent or legitimate interest)
GDPR Art. 13 – Failure to provide information when data obtained from data subject
GDPR Art. 14 – Failure to provide information when data obtained from third party

company: Mediarey Hungary Services Zártkörűen Működő Részvénytársaság (Forbes Hungary)
companyDescription: Mediarey Hungary Services is the Hungarian publisher of Forbes magazine, which produces annual rankings of the wealthiest individuals and largest family businesses in Hungary, distributed in print and online.
companyLongDescription: Mediarey Hungary Services is the Hungarian publisher of Forbes magazine, which produces annual rankings of the wealthiest individuals and largest family businesses in Hungary, distributed in print and online.
caseDescription: Forbes Hungary published wealthy individuals' names and estimated wealth in printed and online 'richest Hungarians' lists without proper prior notice, failing to conduct or communicate legitimate interest assessments, and ignoring data subjects' objections and access requests.
