The company did not provide required transparency about data processing purposes, legal grounds, or data subjects' rights, nor did it properly respond to subject requests for restriction, correction, and objection.
violationSummary: Forbes disclosed personal data (names, wealth estimates) concerning business ownership and financial status to the public without proper data subject notice or opportunity to object beforehand. This falls squarely under unauthorized or inadequately-justified disclosure of personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Forbes Hungary published individuals' names, estimated wealth, and family business details in 'richest Hungarians'.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals' names and estimated wealth were publicly linked and searchable online without their knowledge or meaningful opportunity to object beforehand.

claimsVsReality.claim: Forbes claimed it had a legitimate interest in publishing wealthy individuals' names and estimates to inform the public about economic power and business transparency.
claimsVsReality.reality: Forbes did not conduct or disclose any documented interest-balancing test weighing its business/editorial interests against the privacy rights of individuals named. It published without prior notice or opportunity for subjects to object.

claimsVsReality.claim: Forbes stated it sent individuals advance notice of inclusion and invited their feedback on estimated wealth figures via email and excel spreadsheets.
claimsVsReality.reality: This notice was provided only after reporting had begun, did not explain Forbes's legal basis or interest in publishing, did not clearly state the right to object, and did not describe the consequences of proceeding with publication.

claimsVsReality.claim: Forbes claimed that information about business owners and their companies was already publicly available in corporate registries and public disclosures, so no additional privacy concern arose from ranking and republishing it.
claimsVsReality.reality: Aggregating, estimating, and republishing individuals' names with wealth rankings in a widely-distributed magazine creates a new and more invasive disclosure than passive availability in scattered public registries. Individuals had no realistic expectation of being aggregated and ranked by wealth in a popular publication.

claimsVsReality.claim: Forbes asserted that press freedom and journalistic privilege justified the processing as a 'legitimate interest' under GDPR.
claimsVsReality.reality: Press freedom does not eliminate the duty to provide prior notice, conduct documented interest balancing, or respond properly to data subject access and objection requests. The Hungarian authority found that even with press freedom considered, Forbes's process was deficient.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Forbes processed individuals' names and estimated wealth without prior transparent notice of the purposes (ranking by wealth, publication in print and online), legal grounds, or balance of interests.
violations: Forbes processed individuals' names and estimated wealth without prior transparent notice of the purposes (ranking by wealth, publication in print and online), legal grounds, or balance of interests.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1)(f) permits processing based on legitimate interests only if the controller conducts a documented interest-balancing test and weighs data subject rights against the controller's interests.
regulatoryFindings.description: Forbes claimed legitimate interest (public information, press freedom, financial transparency) but did not conduct or communicate results of any balancing test before publication, nor did it explain how business/editorial interests outweighed privacy.
violations: Forbes claimed legitimate interest (public information, press freedom, financial transparency) but did not conduct or communicate results of any balancing test before publication, nor did it explain how business/editorial interests outweighed privacy.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 14 requires prior notice of data processing when data is not collected from the data subject, including the processing purpose, legal basis, and the data subject's rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Forbes gathered names and wealth estimates from public sources and company records, then published them without prior notice to the individuals affected, describing processing purpose, grounds, or rights.
violations: Forbes gathered names and wealth estimates from public sources and company records, then published them without prior notice to the individuals affected, describing processing purpose, grounds, or rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(1) and (4) require controllers to respond to subject requests (access, correction, objection, restriction) with clear information about actions taken and, if refused, reasons and appeal rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: Forbes received subject requests for correction and objection but provided incomplete or no responses, did not explain the grounds for refusal, and did not advise subjects of appeal rights or supervisory authority complaint options.
violations: Forbes received subject requests for correction and objection but provided incomplete or no responses, did not explain the grounds for refusal, and did not advise subjects of appeal rights or supervisory authority complaint options.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 21(4) requires controllers to inform data subjects of the right to object to processing, prominently and at first contact, when processing is based on legitimate interest.
regulatoryFindings.description: Forbes did not proactively inform individuals of their right to object to processing at the time of first contact or in pre-publication notice; subjects only learned of objection rights indirectly.
violations: Forbes did not proactively inform individuals of their right to object to processing at the time of first contact or in pre-publication notice; subjects only learned of objection rights indirectly.

outcome: The Hungarian Data Protection Authority (NAIH) found Forbes violated GDPR in processing and publishing individuals' names and estimated wealth without proper prior notice, interest balancing, or meaningful response to subject requests. The authority ordered Forbes to (1) provide complete retroactive notice to all affected individuals within 15 days, including the balancing factors considered and results; (2) cease publication of wealth lists until it conducts and discloses proper interest assessments before similar future publications; and (3) reform its prior-notice practices to comply with GDPR transparency requirements. Forbes was fined €2,000,000 HUF. The authority rejected requests to delete data or restrict processing, noting that press freedom exceptions under GDPR Article 17(3)(a) permit retention for journalistic purposes despite individual objections, but the company must still provide proper notice and transparency.
companyNow: Forbes Hungary continues to publish financial and business rankings; the decision requires reformation of its prior-notice and interest-balancing procedures but does not prohibit the lists themselves.
dataType: Names, family names, business ownership information, estimated wealth/financial status
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 12(1) – Duty to respond to subject requests
GDPR Art. 12(4) – Duty to inform on refusal and appeal rights
GDPR Art. 14 – Prior notification when data not collected from subject
GDPR Art. 15 – Right of access / response obligations
GDPR Art. 21(4) – Duty to inform about right to object

companyDescription: 214 Technologies, Inc. (d/b/a Trueface.ai) is a Delaware corporation based in Santa Monica, California, providing face recognition and digital identity verification services.
companyLongDescription: 214 Technologies, Inc. (d/b/a Trueface.ai) is a Delaware corporation based in Santa Monica, California, providing face recognition and digital identity verification services.
caseDescription: 214 Technologies falsely claimed on its website that it was certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework for transferring personal data from Europe to the United States. In reality, the company had never completed the certification process with the U.S. Department of Commerce, despite initiating an application in January 2018. The company continued making false privacy shield statements from March to October 2018 on its privacy policy page.
violationSummary: Company made false public claims about Privacy Shield certification status, misleading consumers about the legal protections their personal data would receive during EU-to-US transfers. This constitutes deceptive disclosure regarding data handling practices and regulatory compliance.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: From March 2018 to October 2018, Trueface.ai disseminated false privacy policies on its website claiming it complied with and was certified to the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company never completed certification with the U.S. Department of Commerce, leaving EU users believing their personal data transferred to the U.S.

claimsVsReality.claim: Trueface.ai complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce
claimsVsReality.reality: Company had never been certified to participate in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework

claimsVsReality.claim: Trueface.ai has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: Company initiated application in January 2018 but did not complete certification steps

claimsVsReality.claim: Trueface.ai has further committed to refer unresolved Privacy Shield complaints to EU Data Protection Authorities
claimsVsReality.reality: Company had no legal standing to make Privacy Shield commitments without actual certification

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company represented directly and by implication that it was a certified participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework
violations: Company represented directly and by implication that it was a certified participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework
Company was never certified to participate in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework
Company continued disseminating false Privacy Shield statements from March 2018 to October 2018 despite only initiating certification application in January 2018 and never completing the process
False representations regarding Privacy Shield certification constitute deceptive acts under Section 5(a)

outcome: FTC issued complaint against 214 Technologies on January 13, 2020, for violating Section 5(a) of the FTC Act through deceptive privacy claims. The complaint alleges one count of Privacy Misrepresentation for falsely claiming EU-U.S. Privacy Shield certification. The document is the initial complaint; final resolution terms were not included in this filing.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU, facial biometric data, digital identity verification data
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) - Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Incentive Services, Inc. is a Minnesota-based corporation that works with organizations to improve employee performance through service award programs, performance incentives, and loyalty programs.
companyLongDescription: Incentive Services, Inc. is a Minnesota-based corporation that works with organizations to improve employee performance through service award programs, performance incentives, and loyalty programs.
caseDescription: Incentive Services, Inc. falsely claimed on its website that it was certified to participate in the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, which allow lawful transfer of personal data from the EU and Switzerland to the United States. In reality, the company never completed the certification process despite initiating an application. This deceptive practice violated Section 5 of the FTC Act by misleading consumers about its compliance with international data protection standards.
violationSummary: The company distorted its compliance status by making false statements about Privacy Shield participation, misleading consumers and data subjects about the legal protections governing their personal data transfers.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Incentive Services, Inc. falsely claimed on its privacy policy website that it adhered to the EU-US and Swiss-US Privacy Shield Frameworks despite never completing certification with the U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: European and Swiss employees whose personal data Incentive Services processed had no legal safeguards for their information because the company lacked actual Privacy Shield certification,.

claimsVsReality.claim: We adhere to several self-regulatory frameworks, including the EU-US and Swiss-US Privacy Shield Frameworks
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was never certified to participate in either the EU-U.S. or Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, despite initiating an application to the U.S. Department of Commerce.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company misrepresented its certification status under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework by stating it 'adhere[s] to several self-regulatory frameworks, including the EU-US and Swiss-US Privacy Shield Frameworks' when it had never been certified to participate in either framework.
violations: Company misrepresented its certification status under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework by stating it 'adhere[s] to several self-regulatory frameworks, including the EU-US and Swiss-US Privacy Shield Frameworks' when it had never been certified to participate in either framework.
Company continued to make false Privacy Shield claims on its website despite having only initiated but not completed the certification application with the U.S. Department of Commerce.

outcome: FTC issued a complaint against Incentive Services, Inc. on January 23, 2020, alleging deceptive practices in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint asserts that the company falsely represented its participation in Privacy Shield frameworks. The resolution requires compliance with Privacy Shield requirements or corrective disclosure regarding data transfer practices.
dataType: Personal data of EU and Swiss residents (unspecified types transferred under Privacy Shield frameworks)

companyDescription: AOK Baden-Württemberg is a statutory health insurance company (Krankenkasse) and major component of Germany's public health insurance system, providing health coverage to millions of members in the Baden-Württemberg region.
companyLongDescription: AOK Baden-Württemberg is a statutory health insurance company (Krankenkasse) and major component of Germany's public health insurance system, providing health coverage to millions of members in the Baden-Württemberg region.
caseDescription: AOK Baden-Württemberg conducted sweepstakes from 2015-2019 collecting personal data from participants. The company's technical and organizational measures failed to prevent personal data from over 500 sweepstakes participants being used for marketing purposes without their consent. The breach violated Article 32 GDPR requirements for secure data processing.
violationSummary: The company collected data with consent for sweepstakes but then used it for marketing purposes without valid consent, representing unauthorized secondary use of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: AOK Baden-Württemberg conducted sweepstakes from 2015-2019 collecting personal data including contact details and insurance membership, then used inadequate technical.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data from more than 500 sweepstakes participants was used for marketing communications without their consent, exposing them to unwanted advertising and compromising their privacy rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: AOK's internal guidelines and data protection training would ensure only consented sweepstakes participants' data was used for marketing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The measures were inadequate; over 500 participants' data was actually used for marketing without their consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including inter alia protection against unauthorised processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: AOK's technical and organizational measures (internal guidelines and data protection training) were insufficient to prevent unauthorized marketing use of personal data from sweepstakes participants who had not consented to such use.
violations: AOK's technical and organizational measures (internal guidelines and data protection training) were insufficient to prevent unauthorized marketing use of personal data from sweepstakes participants who had not consented to such use.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly and in a transparent manner.
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal data from 500+ individuals was processed for marketing purposes without valid consent, violating the lawfulness principle.
violations: Personal data from 500+ individuals was processed for marketing purposes without valid consent, violating the lawfulness principle.

outcome: LfDI imposed a fine of €1,240,000 on 25 June 2020. AOK immediately ceased all marketing activities upon notification, established a Data Protection Task Force for sales operations, reviewed and revised consent declarations, updated internal processes and control structures, and committed to continuing improvements under LfDI supervision. Fine was reduced within the GDPR Article 83(4) range due to AOK's prompt remediation, cooperative compliance efforts, its critical role as statutory health insurer, and COVID-19 pandemic impacts.
companyNow: AOK Baden-Württemberg remains one of the largest health insurance providers in Baden-Württemberg, Germany. The company has implemented enhanced data protection measures and ongoing monitoring as per LfDI requirements.
dataType: Contact data, health insurance membership information

companyDescription: Click Labs, Inc. is a Florida corporation providing website and mobile app development and support services through the domain jungleworks.com, operating from Seattle, Washington.
companyLongDescription: Click Labs, Inc. is a Florida corporation providing website and mobile app development and support services through the domain jungleworks.com, operating from Seattle, Washington.
caseDescription: Click Labs falsely claimed in its privacy policy to be certified under both the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks. The company initiated a Privacy Shield certification application but never completed it, yet continued representing itself as certified, misleading users about the legal protections for their data.
violationSummary: The company misrepresented the status and legal framework governing personal data transfers, distorting users' understanding of how their data would be protected.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Click Labs falsely claimed in its privacy policy that it had certified to and complied with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, when it had never completed certification.
whyTheyWereWrong: European users transferred personal data to Click Labs based on false Privacy Shield compliance claims, exposing their data to unauthorized collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: We agree to adhere to the Privacy Shield Principles and have certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: Click Labs initiated an application for Privacy Shield certification but never completed the required steps and was never certified by the U.S. Department of Commerce.

claimsVsReality.claim: We shall comply with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework regarding collection, use, and retention of personal information transferred from the European Union and Switzerland.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was not a participant in either Privacy Shield framework and lacked the legal status to make this claim.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Click Labs represented that it was certified under the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks when it had never completed the certification process with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
violations: Click Labs represented that it was certified under the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks when it had never completed the certification process with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
The company continued making false Privacy Shield claims in its publicly available privacy policy despite only initiating but not completing the required application steps.

outcome: Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint on January 23, 2020, alleging deceptive practices. The case proceeded on Count 1 for Privacy Misrepresentation in violation of FTC Act Section 5(a). The complaint sought compliance order requiring the company to cease making false Privacy Shield representations and implement accurate privacy disclosures.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU and Switzerland

companyDescription: Miniclip S.A. is a Swiss mobile and online gaming developer and publisher founded in 2009. As of August 2019, it operated approximately 100 games available on Apple App Store and Google Play, with a significant user base among children and casual gamers.
companyLongDescription: Miniclip S.A. is a Swiss mobile and online gaming developer and publisher founded in 2009. As of August 2019, it operated approximately 100 games available on Apple App Store and Google Play, with a significant user base among children and casual gamers.
caseDescription: Miniclip falsely claimed to be a current participant in the CARU COPPA safe harbor program after being terminated from it in July 2015. The company continued to disseminate compliance certifications on multiple websites and in-app disclosures for years after termination, deceiving consumers about its actual privacy protection status.
violationSummary: Miniclip made materially false representations about its privacy compliance status, creating a false impression about the safety and oversight of children's data in its games. This constitutes distortion under the Solove taxonomy as false certifications misrepresented the actual state of privacy protections.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Miniclip continued claiming on its website, terms, and Facebook policy from 2015-2019 that it was a certified COPPA-compliant participant in the CARU safe harbor program.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents and children relied on Miniclip's false COPPA compliance claims when deciding whether to use its games.

claimsVsReality.claim: Miniclip claimed: 'we have been accepted to join the CARU Kids Privacy Safe Harbor Program and have been certified as COPPA compliant' (stated 2012-2019)
claimsVsReality.reality: CARU terminated Miniclip's participation in the COPPA safe harbor program on July 6, 2015, making it no longer a current participant or certified compliant thereafter

claimsVsReality.claim: Miniclip claimed: 'The information practices of Miniclip.com have been reviewed and meet the standards of the Children's Advertising Review Unit's Kids Privacy Safe Harbor Program'
claimsVsReality.reality: After termination in 2015, Miniclip's practices were no longer reviewed by CARU nor deemed to meet CARU standards, yet these claims continued on company websites and apps through June/July 2019

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Miniclip represented it was a current participant in the CARU COPPA safe harbor program when it was not, having been terminated in July 2015
violations: Miniclip represented it was a current participant in the CARU COPPA safe harbor program when it was not, having been terminated in July 2015
Miniclip disseminated false COPPA compliance certifications on its website, Terms and Conditions, and Facebook pages from 2012-2019
The false representations were material because they misled consumers about the actual privacy protections for children's data

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA safe harbor programs, approved by the FTC, allow operators complying with program guidelines to be deemed in compliance with COPPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Miniclip falsely claimed CARU COPPA safe harbor program participation after termination, fraudulently implying COPPA compliance status it no longer held
violations: Miniclip falsely claimed CARU COPPA safe harbor program participation after termination, fraudulently implying COPPA compliance status it no longer held

outcome: FTC issued Complaint alleging deceptive acts in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint was issued June 29, 2020, initiating formal enforcement proceedings against Miniclip for false COPPA compliance claims. Settlement and specific remedies were subject to resolution through adjudication or settlement proceedings.
companyNow: Miniclip remains an active gaming publisher under Chinese ownership (acquired by Tencent in 2020 for approximately $860 million), though the FTC enforcement action and COPPA violations significantly impacted its reputation in the children's gaming space.
dataType: Children's personal information (as covered under COPPA)

companyDescription: Korteriühistu OUTOKUMPU 19 is a housing cooperative located in Kohtla-Järve, Estonia, responsible for managing a residential building and services for its member-residents.
companyLongDescription: Korteriühistu OUTOKUMPU 19 is a housing cooperative located in Kohtla-Järve, Estonia, responsible for managing a residential building and services for its member-residents.
caseDescription: A housing cooperative in Estonia publicly displayed residents' personal data (names, signatures, apartment numbers) in building stairwells without their consent. The Data Protection Inspectorate ordered immediate cessation of this practice and warned of €500 fines for non-compliance.
violationSummary: The cooperative exposed personal data in physically accessible common areas (stairwells) to anyone entering the building, including third parties and unauthorized individuals.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Korteriühistu OUTOKUMPU 19 posted residents' names, signatures, apartment numbers, and heating system consent lists in building stairwells without obtaining prior written consent from.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents' personal information became visible to third parties and the general public in common areas, exposing at least some residents to identification.

claimsVsReality.claim: The cooperative did not formally respond to or contest the initial enforcement request.
claimsVsReality.reality: The cooperative continued to display personal data in stairwells despite the inspectorate's 16 April 2020 proposal and follow-up complaint on 24 April 2020.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires that processing of personal data shall be lawful only if and to the extent that at least one of a specified basis applies, such as explicit consent of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The cooperative processed and disclosed residents' personal data without any lawful basis; explicit prior consent was neither sought nor obtained.
violations: The cooperative processed and disclosed residents' personal data without any lawful basis; explicit prior consent was neither sought nor obtained.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data shall be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Publishing resident names, signatures, and apartment numbers in stairwells lacked transparency and fairness; no resident was informed or consented.
violations: Publishing resident names, signatures, and apartment numbers in stairwells lacked transparency and fairness; no resident was informed or consented.

regulatoryFindings.act: Estonian Personal Data Protection Act §58(1) establishes the authority of the Data Protection Inspectorate to issue binding orders to cease unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: The cooperative continued publishing personal data in common areas after being requested to cease the practice.
violations: The cooperative continued publishing personal data in common areas after being requested to cease the practice.

outcome: The Data Protection Inspectorate issued a binding enforcement order (ettekirjutus) requiring the cooperative to cease all further disclosure of residents' personal data without consent by 13 May 2020. Failure to comply will result in repeated fines of €500 per violation, enforceable through the court. The cooperative did not exercise its right to object and must comply or face escalation to enforcement proceedings.
companyNow: The status of Korteriühistu OUTOKUMPU 19 is unknown. As a housing cooperative (ühistu), it likely remains operational but was required to implement immediate changes to data handling practices.
dataType: Names, signatures, apartment numbers, contact information

companyDescription: HyperBeard, Inc. is a mobile game developer based in Fremont, California that created and distributed free-to-play mobile apps featuring cute animated characters (cats, dogs, monkeys, axolotls) directed to children, monetized through in-app advertising and in-app purchases.
companyLongDescription: HyperBeard, Inc. is a mobile game developer based in Fremont, California that created and distributed free-to-play mobile apps featuring cute animated characters (cats, dogs, monkeys, axolotls) directed to children, monetized through in-app advertising and in-app purchases.
caseDescription: HyperBeard developed and distributed mobile apps directed to children under 13 that collected personal information through third-party advertising networks without providing privacy notices, disclosing data practices, or obtaining verifiable parental consent. The company allowed advertisers including AdMob, Facebook Audience Network, and others to collect persistent identifiers for behavioral targeting without informing these networks that the apps were directed to children. This violated the Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) and the COPPA Rule.
violationSummary: The company conducted covert surveillance of children's online activity through persistent identifiers and behavioral tracking via third-party ad networks, without disclosure to parents or obtaining verifiable parental consent required by COPPA.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: HyperBeard operated nine mobile apps with cute animated characters directed to children under 13.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children's location data and activity patterns were tracked and sold to advertisers without parents' knowledge, enabling targeted advertising to minors and creating privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Apps are 'recommended for children as well as adults' and are innocent entertainment with adorable characters.
claimsVsReality.reality: Apps were deliberately designed, marketed, and promoted exclusively to children via kids' websites, children's books through Scholastic, and licensed merchandise, while collecting their behavioral data without parental knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: Apps collect minimal data; children simply tap characters and play simple games.
claimsVsReality.reality: Third-party ad networks continuously collected persistent identifiers and tracked user behavior across the apps for behavioral advertising purposes without any disclosure mechanism or parental consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(d) requires operators to post a privacy policy on their website or online service providing clear, understandable, and complete notice of information practices, including what information is collected from children, how it is used, and disclosure practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: HyperBeard failed to provide privacy policy notices within the Kids Apps disclosing that third-party advertising networks were collecting persistent identifiers for behavioral advertising.
violations: HyperBeard failed to provide privacy policy notices within the Kids Apps disclosing that third-party advertising networks were collecting persistent identifiers for behavioral advertising.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b) requires operators to provide direct, clear, understandable, and complete notice of information practices to parents, including specific disclosures about data collection, use, and disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: HyperBeard did not inform parents that their children's apps collected personal information through advertising networks or how that data was used for behavioral targeting.
violations: HyperBeard did not inform parents that their children's apps collected personal information through advertising networks or how that data was used for behavioral targeting.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.5(a)(1) requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: HyperBeard allowed third-party ad networks to collect persistent identifiers from children without any parental consent mechanism in place.
violations: HyperBeard allowed third-party ad networks to collect persistent identifiers from children without any parental consent mechanism in place.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: HyperBeard's failure to disclose data collection and practices to parents constituted deceptive conduct; the covert behavioral tracking of children was unfair under FTC standards.
violations: HyperBeard's failure to disclose data collection and practices to parents constituted deceptive conduct; the covert behavioral tracking of children was unfair under FTC standards.

outcome: This is a complaint for civil penalties, permanent injunction, and equitable relief filed June 3, 2020. The complaint seeks (A) a permanent injunction preventing future COPPA violations; (B) monetary civil penalties of up to $41,484 per violation for all Rule violations from January 22, 2018 forward; and (C) other equitable relief the Court deems just and proper. The case was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. Final settlement terms are not specified in this complaint document, which is the initial filing.
companyNow: HyperBeard, Inc. was a California-based mobile game developer founded circa 2016. As of the complaint filing in June 2020, the company was actively distributing apps through Apple App Store and Google Play Store. Current operational status is unknown.
dataType: Persistent identifiers, behavioral/advertising tracking data, user activity data
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b), 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b) — failure to provide direct notice to parents
COPPA Rule Section 312.4(d), 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(d) — failure to post privacy policy
COPPA Rule Section 312.5(a)(1), 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) — failure to obtain verifiable parental consent
FTC Act Section 5(a), 15 U.S.C. § 45(a) — unfair and deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(m)(1)(A), 15 U.S.C. § 45(m)(1)(A) — knowing violation

companyDescription: Midwest Recovery Systems, LLC is a third-party debt collection company based in Earth City, Missouri, that collects debts on behalf of medical providers, payday lenders, and other creditors.
companyLongDescription: Midwest Recovery Systems, LLC is a third-party debt collection company based in Earth City, Missouri, that collects debts on behalf of medical providers, payday lenders, and other creditors.
caseDescription: Midwest Recovery operated a third-party debt collection business that pursued consumers for phantom, counterfeit, and unauthorized payday loans and medical debts that consumers did not owe or that the company could not verify. The company employed 'debt parking'—reporting debts to credit bureaus before contacting consumers—resulting in 80-97% of disputed debts being found inaccurate. Over $98 million in fraudulent debts were reported since 2015.
violationSummary: The company exposed consumers to harm by placing inaccurate negative information on credit reports without prior notification or verification, damaging their creditworthiness and ability to access credit, housing, and employment.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Midwest Recovery Systems collected phantom payday loans, counterfeit debts, and unverifiable medical debts from consumers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers suffered 35+ point credit score drops, lost mortgage approvals, denied employment, and were coerced into paying debts they never owed; 80-97% of disputed debts were found inaccurate.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company asserts debts are valid and owed by consumers.
claimsVsReality.reality: 80-97% of disputed debts were determined to be inaccurate or invalid upon investigation; $98M+ consisted of unauthorized, counterfeit, or unverifiable debts.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company represents consumers' debts to credit bureaus with accuracy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company furnishes information knowing or with reasonable cause to believe it is inaccurate; receives 24,000+ disputes on notoriously fraudulent Joel Tucker portfolios yet continues collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company investigates consumer disputes properly.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company fails to request validation documents for direct disputes and fails to notify consumers of investigation results or deletions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company collects only legitimate debts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company collects phantom payday loans, counterfeit debts, debts subject to unresolved fraud claims, debts in bankruptcy, and debts already paid by consumers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Midwest Recovery represented that consumers owed medical, payday loan, or other debts that were false, misleading, or unsubstantiated at the time of collection.
violations: Midwest Recovery represented that consumers owed medical, payday loan, or other debts that were false, misleading, or unsubstantiated at the time of collection.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 807 prohibits debt collectors from using false, deceptive, or misleading representations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company falsely represented the character, amount, and legal status of debts while knowing or should have known they were unauthorized, counterfeit, or unverifiable.
violations: Company falsely represented the character, amount, and legal status of debts while knowing or should have known they were unauthorized, counterfeit, or unverifiable.
Company communicated credit information to CRAs that was known or should have been known to be false.
Company used false representations and deceptive means to collect debts and obtain consumer information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 808 prohibits unfair or unconscionable means to collect debts.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company furnished debt information to CRAs before communicating with consumers, preventing them from disputing debts before credit damage occurred.
violations: Company furnished debt information to CRAs before communicating with consumers, preventing them from disputing debts before credit damage occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 809(a) requires written validation notice within five days of initial communication.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to send required validation notices containing debt amount, creditor name, dispute rights, and original creditor information to numerous consumers.
violations: Company failed to send required validation notices containing debt amount, creditor name, dispute rights, and original creditor information to numerous consumers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(1)(A) prohibits furnishing information known or believed to be inaccurate.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company furnished $98M+ in unauthorized, counterfeit, and unverifiable debts to CRAs while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe the information was inaccurate.
violations: Company furnished $98M+ in unauthorized, counterfeit, and unverifiable debts to CRAs while knowing or having reasonable cause to believe the information was inaccurate.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(8)(E) and Furnisher Rule 12 C.F.R. § 1022.43(e) require reasonable investigation of consumer disputes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to conduct reasonable investigations of thousands of direct disputes from consumers and did not request validation documents in numerous cases.
violations: Company failed to conduct reasonable investigations of thousands of direct disputes from consumers and did not request validation documents in numerous cases.
Company failed to report investigation results to consumers within the required 30-day period in numerous instances.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Missouri on November 25, 2020. The case seeks permanent injunction to halt violations, rescission or reformation of contracts, restitution, refund of monies paid, disgorgement of ill-gotten monies ($24.3 million in estimated gross revenues), and monitoring requirements. As of the complaint filing date, no settlement or final judgment has been reached.
companyNow: Midwest Recovery Systems, LLC remains operational as of the complaint filing in November 2020. The outcome of the FTC litigation is not specified in this document.
dataType: Financial data, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, personal identifying information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 807(2)(A) – false representation of debt character/amount
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 807(8) – communicating false credit information
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 807(10) – false representations to collect debt
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 808 – unfair collection practices
Fair Debt Collection Practices Act Section 809(a) – failure to provide validation notice
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(1)(A) – furnishing inaccurate information
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(8)(E)(i) – failure to conduct reasonable investigation
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(a)(8)(E)(iii) – failure to report investigation results

companyDescription: Posti Oy is the state-owned Finnish postal service operator, established in the 1890s. It maintains a mandatory address register (osoiterekisteri) under postal law to ensure reliable mail delivery and offers address update services to businesses.
companyLongDescription: Posti Oy is the state-owned Finnish postal service operator, established in the 1890s. It maintains a mandatory address register (osoiterekisteri) under postal law to ensure reliable mail delivery and offers address update services to businesses.
caseDescription: Posti failed to transparently inform address change notification users that their personal data would be disclosed to third-party direct marketers. Information about this processing and data subjects' right to object was buried in terms of service documents and inaccessible during the notification process. Over 161,000–201,000 individuals per year made address change notifications without receiving proper advance notice of data sharing practices.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal data to third parties without proper transparency. Data subjects were not informed clearly or at the right time that their address information would be shared for direct marketing, and their right to object was not made apparent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Posti collected address change notifications and automatically shared updated address data with third-party companies for direct marketing without clearly disclosing this practice or users'.
whyTheyWereWrong: Between 161,518 and 201,627 people per year made address changes unaware their data would be shared for marketing; they received no transparent notice of sharing or their right to block it,.

claimsVsReality.claim: Posti claimed that information about data sharing and the right to object was available on its website, in privacy notices, and in service terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: While documents existed, they were not actively presented to users at the moment of address notification; 161,518–201,627 users per year never accepted terms or received transparent notice before disclosure occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: Posti stated it had informed users about the opt-out right through its privacy statement and product terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: The privacy statement buried the mention of the right to object in an isolated sentence under a different section heading; users had to navigate away from the notification form to discover this critical information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Posti asserted that the low number of opt-out requests (under 0.5%) showed users understood and accepted data sharing.
claimsVsReality.reality: Low opt-out rates reflected lack of awareness of the option and lack of transparency, not genuine acceptance; when Posti improved visibility in early 2020, opt-outs increased by approximately 100 immediately.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed transparently with respect to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Posti did not make transparent, at the time of collection, that address data would be disclosed to third parties for direct marketing.
violations: Posti did not make transparent, at the time of collection, that address data would be disclosed to third parties for direct marketing.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12 requires the controller to take appropriate measures to provide information in a concise, transparent, intelligible and easily accessible form using clear and plain language.
regulatoryFindings.description: Information about data sharing and the right to object was scattered across product terms and privacy notice rather than presented clearly during the notification process itself.
violations: Information about data sharing and the right to object was scattered across product terms and privacy notice rather than presented clearly during the notification process itself.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(1)(d) and 13(2)(b) require the controller to provide information about recipients and the right to object when data are collected from the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Posti did not timely provide these required details to users making address notifications; 161,518–201,627 notifications per year lacked terms acceptance.
violations: Posti did not timely provide these required details to users making address notifications; 161,518–201,627 notifications per year lacked terms acceptance.

regulatoryFindings.act: Postal Act 38 § 5 (Finland) states data subjects may prohibit disclosure of their data in address update services.
regulatoryFindings.description: The right to prohibit was not communicated effectively or at the right moment, making it difficult for users to exercise this right.
violations: The right to prohibit was not communicated effectively or at the right moment, making it difficult for users to exercise this right.

outcome: Posti received a €100,000 administrative fine for lack of transparency in personal data handling. The company was ordered to ensure future address notifications clearly and actively inform users at the moment of collection about data sharing for direct marketing and their right to object. Posti committed to updating its service process to present terms for acceptance in all digital notifications, improving data subject rights documentation, and enhancing visibility of opt-out mechanisms. No criminal referral was made. The decision is subject to appeal to Finnish administrative court.
companyNow: Posti remains the primary postal operator in Finland, operating under the name Posti Group and providing mail, parcel, and logistics services across Nordics and beyond. Following this enforcement action, the company has updated its transparency and consent practices for address change notifications.
dataType: Name, address, contact information
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 13(1)(d) – Information about recipients/categories of recipients
GDPR Art. 13(2)(b) – Information about right to object
Postal Act (Finland) 38 § 5 – Right to prohibit disclosure

companyDescription: DCR Workforce, Inc. is a Florida-based company providing workforce management software. It operates at 7795 NW Beacon Square Boulevard, Suite 201, Boca Raton, FL 33487.
companyLongDescription: DCR Workforce, Inc. is a Florida-based company providing workforce management software. It operates at 7795 NW Beacon Square Boulevard, Suite 201, Boca Raton, FL 33487.

violationSummary: Company disclosed false representations about Privacy Shield compliance status to the public, misleading individuals and regulatory bodies about its data protection practices and certification status.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: DCR Workforce falsely claimed on its website that it complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU residents whose employment data was transferred to DCR Workforce believed their personal information received legal privacy protections under Privacy Shield.

claimsVsReality.claim: DCR Workforce complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce and has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: DCR Workforce obtained Privacy Shield certification in January 2017, but that certification lapsed by February 2018. The company was not a current participant in the Privacy Shield framework at the time it made these claims.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: DCR Workforce represented on its privacy policy website that it complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and has certified to the Department of Commerce, when in fact its certification had lapsed by February 2018 and it was not a current participant in the framework.
violations: DCR Workforce represented on its privacy policy website that it complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and has certified to the Department of Commerce, when in fact its certification had lapsed by February 2018 and it was not a current participant in the framework.
Company continued to make false statements claiming current Privacy Shield participation after certification expiration, violating the FTC's deception authority.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on January 13, 2020 alleging deceptive practices. The case alleges one count of Privacy Misrepresentation under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. Complaint seeks cessation of deceptive representations and compliance with Privacy Shield requirements or alternative compliance mechanisms.
companyNow: Unknown. Document is a complaint issued January 13, 2020; outcome of enforcement action not available in document.

companyLongDescription: Digi Távközlési és Szolgáltató Kft is a major Hungarian telecommunications and service provider offering internet, TV, and mobile services to residential and business customers. As of the 2018–2019 fiscal years covered in the enforcement action, the company reported approximately 47–51 billion HUF (roughly €125–140M) in annual net revenue.
caseDescription: Digi, a major Hungarian telecom provider, failed to delete a test database containing sensitive customer data after fixing a system error, leaving 700,000+ individuals' records exposed. When an ethical hacker discovered a known 9-year-old vulnerability in their content management system, the unencrypted data became accessible. The company also failed to patch the vulnerability and conduct regular security scans of their public website.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures (encryption, timely patching, vulnerability scanning) proportionate to the risks posed by processing large volumes of sensitive customer data, directly enabling the data breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Digi created a test database containing 700,000+ customer records for troubleshooting, failed to delete it after repairs were complete, stored the data unencrypted.
whyTheyWereWrong: An attacker exploited the unpatched vulnerability to access 700,000+ customers' highly sensitive data including names, ID numbers, addresses, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Digi claimed access control through user permissions and proper authorization was sufficient to protect customer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: A known, easily-detected 9-year-old vulnerability made the unencrypted database publicly accessible via the website, rendering access controls meaningless; 700,000+ customer records were at risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: Digi claimed the test database required no encryption because it was secured by permission-based access control.
claimsVsReality.reality: The vulnerability bypassed all access controls; the data was stored in plain text and became fully readable to anyone who exploited the known CMS flaw.

claimsVsReality.claim: Digi claimed it was impossible to monitor non-official patches for its open-source CMS due to the volume of patches available.
claimsVsReality.reality: A core security patch for a 9-year-old, widely-known vulnerability was publicly available and easily detectable via automated tools; the company's own internal policies required regular vulnerability scanning, which was not performed on the website.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires personal data to be processed only for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and not processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Digi retained a test database containing 700,000+ customer records (names, IDs, addresses, banking data) long after the debugging purpose was completed, storing the data purposelessly for months until the security breach.
violations: Digi retained a test database containing 700,000+ customer records (names, IDs, addresses, banking data) long after the debugging purpose was completed, storing the data purposelessly for months until the security breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) requires personal data to be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects only for as long as necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Digi stored identifiable customer data in the test database in readable form well beyond the time needed to fix the system error, making individuals' identities permanently at risk.
violations: Digi stored identifiable customer data in the test database in readable form well beyond the time needed to fix the system error, making individuals' identities permanently at risk.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1)–(2) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security proportionate to risks, including encryption where appropriate.
regulatoryFindings.description: Digi failed to encrypt sensitive customer data in the database, did not install a known security patch for a 9-year-old vulnerability in their CMS system, and did not perform regular vulnerability scanning of their public website, leaving 700,000+ records directly accessible to attackers.
violations: Digi failed to encrypt sensitive customer data in the database, did not install a known security patch for a 9-year-old vulnerability in their CMS system, and did not perform regular vulnerability scanning of their public website, leaving 700,000+ records directly accessible to attackers.

outcome: The National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) found Digi violated GDPR Articles 5(1)(b), 5(1)(e), and 32(1)–(2) and imposed a fine of 100,000,000 HUF (approximately €268,000 / $293,000). The authority ordered Digi to review all databases containing personal data to determine whether encryption is justified and report findings to NAIH within a specified timeframe. The decision is final and non-appealable administratively; judicial review before the Budapest Metropolitan Court is available within 30 days. Digi must pay the fine within 30 days or face enforcement and late-payment interest.
companyNow: Digi Telecom remains one of Hungary's major telecommunications providers. Following this enforcement action, the company has stated it intends to enhance security practices, including consideration of higher-level firewalls and expanded vulnerability scanning.
dataType: Names, birth names, parents' names, birth place and date, address, ID card numbers, personal numbers, email addresses, phone numbers, bank account numbers, payment data, service contracts

companyDescription: Kohl's is a large national department store chain offering clothing, accessories, beauty goods, and home products through physical retail locations and significant online presence.
companyLongDescription: Kohl's is a large national department store chain offering clothing, accessories, beauty goods, and home products through physical retail locations and significant online presence.
caseDescription: Kohl's violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act by refusing to provide identity theft victims with application and business transaction records they requested. The company implemented policies in February 2017 and August 2018 that restricted disclosure of detailed order information to victims, offering it only to law enforcement. Kohl's also failed to respond to many requests within the required 30-day period.
violationSummary: Kohl's wrongfully withheld personal data and transaction records that belonged to identity theft victims, preventing them from accessing information necessary to remedy fraud. This constitutes a breach of confidentiality duty to provide records upon legitimate request.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Kohl's implemented policies from February 2017 through March 2019 that refused to provide identity theft victims with their requested application.
whyTheyWereWrong: Identity theft victims were unable to obtain critical information like fraudulent shipping addresses and phone numbers needed to resolve identity theft cases, recover funds.

claimsVsReality.claim: Kohl's was not permitted to share detailed identity theft transaction information with victims
claimsVsReality.reality: FCRA Section 609(e) explicitly requires business entities to provide such records to victims upon request within 30 days

claimsVsReality.claim: Victims must obtain fraud information only through law enforcement requests
claimsVsReality.reality: The law gives victims themselves the right to request and receive their own transaction records directly from the business

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 609(e)(1) of the FCRA requires a 'business entity' to provide an identity theft 'victim' with 'application and business transaction records' evidencing any transaction that the victim alleges to be the result of identity theft within 30 days of receipt of a request.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kohl's refused to provide detailed order information directly to identity theft victims, limiting disclosure to law enforcement only under the February 2017 and August 2018 policies
violations: Kohl's refused to provide detailed order information directly to identity theft victims, limiting disclosure to law enforcement only under the February 2017 and August 2018 policies
Kohl's failed to respond to multiple 609(e) requests within the required 30-day timeframe

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kohl's engaged in unfair practices by preventing identity theft victims from accessing records they were legally entitled to receive
violations: Kohl's engaged in unfair practices by preventing identity theft victims from accessing records they were legally entitled to receive

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint on June 8, 2020 seeking permanent injunction, monetary civil penalties, and other equitable relief. The complaint alleged knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice, with potential penalties of up to $3,993 per violation. Kohl's implemented a compliant policy in April 2019 that provides victims with requested application and transaction records. The case pursued injunctive relief and damages for all violations occurring between February 2017 and March 2019.
companyNow: Kohl's Department Stores, Inc. continues to operate as a major national department store chain with physical stores and online retail presence at www.kohls.com as of the complaint date. The company implemented the required policy changes in April 2019.
dataType: Identity information, financial information, application records, transaction records, shipping address, phone number

companyDescription: Coop Finnmark SA is a Norwegian grocery retail chain that operates supermarkets in Finnmark region. The company employs store managers responsible for security, including surveillance system oversight.
companyLongDescription: Coop Finnmark SA is a Norwegian grocery retail chain that operates supermarkets in Finnmark region. The company employs store managers responsible for security, including surveillance system oversight.
caseDescription: A store manager at Coop Finnmark filmed surveillance camera footage of minors suspected of shoplifting using his personal mobile phone and shared it with a third party to identify them. The video was subsequently shared further until it reached the minors themselves. The company failed to establish a lawful legal basis for processing and disclosing personal data of children, violating fundamental GDPR principles.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of personal data (video footage) of identifiable minors to third parties without legal basis. The data controller lost control over the information after initial disclosure, and it reached the data subjects themselves.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A store manager filmed surveillance footage of children on their personal phone and shared it with a third party to identify theft suspects.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children's personal data in video form was disseminated without legal consent or lawful basis, exposing minors to identification, potential public humiliation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The store manager sent a brief 3-second video clip and the company has internal rules prohibiting unauthorized disclosure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite internal rules explicitly requiring written consent for disclosure, the store manager unilaterally shared the footage via personal phone, which was then distributed further to the identified minors themselves, demonstrating the rules were not effectively enforced.

claimsVsReality.claim: The video did not show faces, so identification was limited to clothing, hair, and footwear.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lack of facial imagery does not make individuals non-identifiable; they remained clearly distinguishable and identifiable by their appearance, clothing, and other visible characteristics—sufficient for privacy harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company acted in good faith to identify shoplifters and took remedial steps by contacting parties and asking them to delete the footage.
claimsVsReality.reality: Once shared via mobile phone, the company lost control and could not prevent further distribution. The minors received the footage showing themselves accused of theft, causing reputational harm and psychological harm to children.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Coop Finnmark disclosed video footage of minors without a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1)
violations: Coop Finnmark disclosed video footage of minors without a valid legal basis under Art. 6(1)

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) permits processing based on legitimate interests only if the controller's interest weighs heavier than the data subject's privacy rights, with heightened protection for children.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's legitimate interest in identifying shoplifters did not outweigh children's fundamental right to privacy, especially given that the same outcome could be achieved by reporting to police
violations: The company's legitimate interest in identifying shoplifters did not outweigh children's fundamental right to privacy, especially given that the same outcome could be achieved by reporting to police

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner ensuring integrity and confidentiality through appropriate technical and organizational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Use of an uncontrolled personal mobile phone to film and share footage resulted in loss of control and unintended further dissemination to the data subjects themselves
violations: Use of an uncontrolled personal mobile phone to film and share footage resulted in loss of control and unintended further dissemination to the data subjects themselves

outcome: Datatilsynet (Norwegian Data Protection Authority) issued a final enforcement decision on 22 December 2020 imposing an administrative fine of NOK 400,000 (approximately USD 42,000). The decision found Coop Finnmark violated GDPR Arts. 5(1)(a) and 6 by disclosing video footage of minors without lawful basis. The company is required to pay the fine within four weeks. The decision is enforceable and collection will be handled by the State Collection Agency (Statens innkrevingssentral). The company may appeal within 28 days.
companyNow: Coop Finnmark is a Norwegian grocery retailer operating as part of the Coop group. Following the 2020 enforcement action, the company implemented internal training on data protection rules and reviewed surveillance footage handling procedures.
dataType: Video footage of minors, biometric data (appearance, clothing, gait)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness, transparency principle
GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and confidentiality principle
GDPR Art. 6 – Lack of lawful basis for processing

companyDescription: Tapplock, Inc. is a Canadian Internet of Things company that designed and sold Internet-connected, fingerprint-enabled smart padlocks to U.S. consumers through its website and crowdfunding platforms, with fulfillment via a U.S.-based third-party warehouse.
companyLongDescription: Tapplock, Inc. is a Canadian Internet of Things company that designed and sold Internet-connected, fingerprint-enabled smart padlocks to U.S. consumers through its website and crowdfunding platforms, with fulfillment via a U.S.-based third-party warehouse.
caseDescription: Tapplock sold Internet-connected fingerprint-enabled smart locks to U.S. consumers while falsely advertising them as secure and claiming to follow industry best practices for data protection. Security researchers discovered multiple critical vulnerabilities allowing unauthorized access to user accounts and physical locks, exposing personal information and putting property at risk. Tapplock had no security program in place and failed to implement basic protective measures.
violationSummary: The core violation stems from Tapplock's failure to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data and device functionality, resulting in foreseeable vulnerabilities that exposed consumer information and physical property to unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Tapplock advertised fingerprint smart locks as secure with anti-shim and anti-pry technologies, claiming to follow industry best practices protecting personal information including usernames,.
whyTheyWereWrong: Security researchers discovered the locks could be opened by unscrewing the back panel in seconds.

claimsVsReality.claim: Smart locks are 'Bold. Sturdy. Secure.' with 'unbreakable' design incorporating double-layered lock design and anti-shim/anti-pry technologies.
claimsVsReality.reality: Locks could be opened in seconds by unscrewing the back panel, defeating all claimed physical security features.

claimsVsReality.claim: We take 'reasonable precautions' and follow 'industry best practices' to protect personal information from loss, misuse, unauthorized access, disclosure, alteration, or destruction.
claimsVsReality.reality: Tapplock had no security program prior to June 2018, no vulnerability testing, no written security policies, failed to encrypt Bluetooth communications, and had authentication mechanisms that could be bypassed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users can share access to their locks with unlimited people and subsequently revoke such access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users could not effectively revoke access; researchers could 'sniff' data packets and continue accessing locks even after revocation due to unencrypted authentication tokens.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Tapplock represented its smart locks were 'secure' and incorporated anti-shim, anti-pry, and double-layered design, when in reality researchers could unlock them by unscrewing the back panel in seconds.
violations: Tapplock represented its smart locks were 'secure' and incorporated anti-shim, anti-pry, and double-layered design, when in reality researchers could unlock them by unscrewing the back panel in seconds.

Tapplock claimed in its privacy policy to take 'reasonable precautions' and follow 'industry best practices' to protect personal information, when it had no security program, no vulnerability testing, no written security policies, and no employee training.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on May 18, 2020, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleges two counts: (Count I) deceptive representation regarding security of the smart locks, and (Count II) deceptive representation regarding protection of personal information. The document establishes that Tapplock failed to identify foreseeable risks, employ adequate authentication controls, adopt written security standards, or provide employee training. This is the initial complaint; final resolution pending.
companyNow: Tapplock faced significant reputational damage following public disclosure of vulnerabilities by security researchers in June 2018. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: usernames, email addresses, profile photos, location history, precise geolocation of smart locks
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: AppFolio, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Goleta, California, that provides property management software and tenant screening services to thousands of client property management companies throughout the United States.
companyLongDescription: AppFolio, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Goleta, California, that provides property management software and tenant screening services to thousands of client property management companies throughout the United States.
caseDescription: AppFolio, a tenant background screening service, violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act by reporting obsolete criminal records and eviction records over seven years old in tenant screening reports. The company also failed to implement reasonable accuracy procedures, resulting in reports containing mismatched identities, multiple individuals' records, and inaccurate disposition or offense information that likely caused housing denials.
violationSummary: AppFolio's failure to implement reasonable accuracy procedures for criminal records and eviction records, combined with over-reliance on unvetted third-party data without verification, created systematic insecurity in the consumer reporting process.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: AppFolio furnished tenant screening reports containing obsolete eviction and criminal records more than seven years old.
whyTheyWereWrong: Prospective tenants were denied housing based on inaccurate or outdated criminal and eviction records.

claimsVsReality.claim: AppFolio's contracts with CoreLogic acknowledged that due to the organization of criminal records, there may be instances where identifying information appears to match the applicant but does not pertain to them.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite this acknowledgment, AppFolio failed to implement commercially reasonable verification procedures and continued to furnish inaccurate reports with mismatched identities to thousands of property managers.

claimsVsReality.claim: CoreLogic's service disclaimer stated the service was 'AS IS' without warranty of accuracy, timeliness, or completeness.
claimsVsReality.reality: As a Consumer Reporting Agency under the FCRA, AppFolio had independent obligations to ensure accuracy regardless of vendor disclaimers. These contractual disclaimers do not relieve a CRA of its statutory duty to follow reasonable accuracy procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 605(a) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681c(a), generally prohibits Consumer Reporting Agencies from making any Consumer Report that includes Eviction Records and non-conviction criminal records that are more than seven years old.
regulatoryFindings.description: Until at least June 2019, AppFolio reported Eviction Records and non-conviction criminal records that were more than seven years old in multiple instances.
violations: Until at least June 2019, AppFolio reported Eviction Records and non-conviction criminal records that were more than seven years old in multiple instances.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(b) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(b), requires that whenever a Consumer Reporting Agency prepares a Consumer Report it shall follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.
regulatoryFindings.description: Until at least April 2019, AppFolio failed to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of criminal record and Eviction Record information in Tenant Screening Reports.
violations: Until at least April 2019, AppFolio failed to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of criminal record and Eviction Record information in Tenant Screening Reports.
AppFolio implemented insufficient procedures to assess accuracy of information obtained from CoreLogic vendor before including it in reports.
AppFolio failed to assess whether identifiers in records reasonably matched applicants.
AppFolio failed to assess whether results contained information on multiple individuals.
AppFolio failed to assure accurate reflection of disposition, offense name, and offense type.
AppFolio failed to prevent multiple entries for the same criminal or eviction action.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 621(a)(1), 15 U.S.C. § 1681s(a)(1), provides that violations of FCRA also constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a).
regulatoryFindings.description: AppFolio's reporting of obsolete records and failure to ensure accuracy constitute unfair and deceptive practices affecting commerce.
violations: AppFolio's reporting of obsolete records and failure to ensure accuracy constitute unfair and deceptive practices affecting commerce.

outcome: This is a complaint filed on December 8, 2020, seeking monetary civil penalties (up to $4,063 per violation as of January 2020), a permanent injunction to prevent future FCRA violations, compliance orders, and other equitable relief. The complaint alleged knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice, with each instance of non-compliance treated as a separate violation. The case seeks damages for thousands of inaccurate Tenant Screening Reports furnished to property management companies.
companyNow: AppFolio is a publicly traded software company (NASDAQ: APPF) providing property management and tenant screening solutions. The company continues to operate in the property management technology space.
dataType: Criminal records, eviction records, rental payment history, credit information, personal identifying information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 605(a) – Exclusion of obsolete information
Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 607(b) – Reasonable procedures for accuracy
Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 621(a) – Enforcement authority
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) is the police force for Northern Ireland, with headquarters in Belfast. It provides law enforcement services across Northern Ireland and is accountable to the Northern Ireland Police Authority.
companyLongDescription: The Police Service of Northern Ireland (PSNI) is the police force for Northern Ireland, with headquarters in Belfast. It provides law enforcement services across Northern Ireland and is accountable to the Northern Ireland Police Authority.
caseDescription: PSNI's Extradition Unit unlawfully shared personal data including criminal records and biometric information with the US Department of Homeland Security from 2016 to October 2020, affecting 174 individuals. Staff bypassed formal data-sharing protocols and sent sensitive data via unencrypted email.
