The organization lacked adequate oversight, security measures, and documented lawful basis for the proactive sharing that disrupted travel arrangements and led to entry refusals.
violationSummary: PSNI failed to maintain confidentiality of sensitive personal data through unauthorized disclosure to a third country (US DHS) without proper safeguards, consent, or lawful basis. The systematic, unregulated sharing of criminal records and biometric data outside formal channels constitutes breach of confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: PSNI's Extradition Unit staff proactively shared 174 individuals' criminal conviction data, biometric data.
whyTheyWereWrong: 174 data subjects' sensitive personal data including criminal records and biometrics were transferred to a foreign government without their consent or knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSNI had formal data-sharing arrangements and policies regulating Extradition Unit staff access to systems and data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Staff bypassed these formal processes and engaged in informal, proactive sharing of personal data outside documented protocols without clear understanding that practices violated policy.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSNI has appropriate security measures in place for handling sensitive personal data in law enforcement contexts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive criminal conviction and biometric data were routinely transmitted to the US via unencrypted email without password protection, exposing data to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data sharing with DHS serves documented law enforcement purposes with appropriate safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: The sharing was proactive and intended merely to alert DHS to possible future travel, not to prevent/detect crime; no documented lawful basis, safeguards, or Schedule 8 conditions supported the processing.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 34(3) DPA 2018: The controller is responsible for and must be able to demonstrate compliance with data protection legislation.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI lacked effective managerial oversight and governance structures to demonstrate accountability; a culture evolved where staff shared data outside established policies without clear evidence they understood those practices violated policy.
violations: PSNI lacked effective managerial oversight and governance structures to demonstrate accountability; a culture evolved where staff shared data outside established policies without clear evidence they understood those practices violated policy.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 35(1) DPA 2018: Processing of personal data for law enforcement purposes must be lawful and fair.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI engaged in proactive, informal sharing of criminal conviction data outside formal arrangements; no documented lawful reason or formal request justified the sharing; data subjects could not reasonably expect their data to be used to disrupt travel arrangements.
violations: PSNI engaged in proactive, informal sharing of criminal conviction data outside formal arrangements; no documented lawful reason or formal request justified the sharing; data subjects could not reasonably expect their data to be used to disrupt travel arrangements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 40 DPA 2018: Personal data for law enforcement must be processed with appropriate security using technical/organizational measures protecting against unauthorized processing and accidental loss/destruction/damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI routinely transmitted sensitive personal data to the US via unencrypted email without password protection, despite having policies/guidance on secure handling; data was processed without appropriate security safeguards.
violations: PSNI routinely transmitted sensitive personal data to the US via unencrypted email without password protection, despite having policies/guidance on secure handling; data was processed without appropriate security safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 42(1) DPA 2018: When processing sensitive personal data, a controller must have an appropriate policy document and either consent or satisfy a Schedule 8 condition.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI shared biometric data (sensitive processing) without data subject consent or awareness; lacked appropriate policy documents; processing was for disrupting travel (not law enforcement crime prevention); failed to satisfy Schedule 8 conditions.
violations: PSNI shared biometric data (sensitive processing) without data subject consent or awareness; lacked appropriate policy documents; processing was for disrupting travel (not law enforcement crime prevention); failed to satisfy Schedule 8 conditions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 73(1) DPA 2018: A controller may not transfer personal data to a third country unless specified conditions and safeguards are met.
regulatoryFindings.description: PSNI lacked appropriate safeguards and did not establish a lawful basis prior to proactive sharing with US DHS; transfer was not necessary for law enforcement purposes and was not for specified special circumstances.
violations: PSNI lacked appropriate safeguards and did not establish a lawful basis prior to proactive sharing with US DHS; transfer was not necessary for law enforcement purposes and was not for specified special circumstances.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to PSNI. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps already taken by PSNI, including stricter controls requiring future data sharing within formal arrangements, revised guidance/policies, and standard operating procedures for data transfers. PSNI was recommended to: (1) establish clear lawful basis documented prior to sharing via formal arrangements only; (2) review access controls and increase managerial oversight through regular audits; (3) implement higher security levels and management checks; (4) ensure consent or Schedule 8 conditions for sensitive processing with appropriate policy documents; (5) identify lawful bases for third-country transfers within appropriate data protection frameworks. PSNI informed the ICO it had already taken steps to address all recommendations.
companyNow: The Police Service of Northern Ireland remains the primary law enforcement agency for Northern Ireland. Following this enforcement action, PSNI implemented stricter data governance controls and continues to operate under enhanced data protection oversight.
dataType: Criminal conviction data, biometric data, basic personal identifiers (name, contact details), travel authorization data (ESTA/VISA), missing persons information

companyDescription: EmpiriStat, Inc. is a Delaware corporation located in Mount Airy, Maryland that provides statistical analysis and clinical trial support services.
companyLongDescription: EmpiriStat, Inc. is a Delaware corporation located in Mount Airy, Maryland that provides statistical analysis and clinical trial support services.
caseDescription: EmpiriStat falsely claimed to be a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework after its certification lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed. The company failed to obtain required annual verification statements and did not affirm its commitment to continue protecting personal data received during its participation. These misrepresentations violated FTC Act Section 5.
violationSummary: Company made false public statements about Privacy Shield participation and compliance, misleading individuals and regulators about the protection of their personal data transferred internationally.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: EmpiriStat claimed on its website that it currently participated in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework even though its certification lapsed in 2018 and was never renewed.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU individuals and organizations transferred personal data to EmpiriStat believing it met Privacy Shield adequacy standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: EmpiriStat has certified to the Department of Commerce and complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework.
claimsVsReality.reality: Certification was obtained in February 2017 but lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed. Company continued making Privacy Shield claims after certification lapsed.

claimsVsReality.claim: EmpiriStat's practices comply with the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: EmpiriStat failed to obtain required annual verification statements for 2017-18 period and failed to provide them to FTC as mandated by Supplemental Principle 7.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data received from EU is protected under Privacy Shield framework standards.
claimsVsReality.reality: After allowing certification to lapse, EmpiriStat did not affirm to Commerce its commitment to continue protecting personal data previously received, as required by Privacy Shield framework.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: EmpiriStat represented it was a current Privacy Shield participant when certification had lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed.
violations: EmpiriStat represented it was a current Privacy Shield participant when certification had lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed.
EmpiriStat claimed compliance with Privacy Shield Principles without obtaining required annual verification statements during 2017-18 certification period.
EmpiriStat did not affirm to Commerce its commitment to continue protecting personal data received during Privacy Shield participation after allowing certification to lapse.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Shield Supplemental Principle 7 requires annual verification through self-assessment or outside compliance review that Privacy Shield assertions are true and practices implemented.
regulatoryFindings.description: EmpiriStat failed to obtain attested verification statement for 2017-18 certification period.
violations: EmpiriStat failed to obtain attested verification statement for 2017-18 certification period.
EmpiriStat failed to provide verification statement to FTC as required.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Shield framework requires companies withdrawing from program to affirm to Commerce they will continue applying principles to personal data received during participation.
regulatoryFindings.description: EmpiriStat did not affirm continuing obligations after allowing certification to lapse in 2018.
violations: EmpiriStat did not affirm continuing obligations after allowing certification to lapse in 2018.
EmpiriStat did not take down Privacy Shield claims despite Commerce warning.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on January 13, 2020, alleging three counts of deceptive practices under Section 5 of the FTC Act. Case resolved through enforcement action; document indicates complaint issued but does not specify settlement terms or final order details beyond the charges.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU to US under Privacy Shield framework
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive Acts or Practices
Privacy Shield Principles – Supplemental Principle 7 (Verification requirement)
Privacy Shield Framework – Continuing Obligations (post-withdrawal affirmation requirement)

companyDescription: A bar operator in Budapest VII district operating an establishment with security cameras. The operator manages camera surveillance and handles personal data of patrons and others captured on video.
companyLongDescription: A bar operator in Budapest VII district operating an establishment with security cameras. The operator manages camera surveillance and handles personal data of patrons and others captured on video.
caseDescription: A bar operator failed to properly inform a data subject about their right to restrict data processing after the subject requested camera footage be locked for a police investigation. The operator deleted the locked footage after 30 days without notifying the subject, and subsequently ignored multiple requests for access to the footage and information about its deletion.
violationSummary: The operator failed to provide adequate transparency about data restriction and deletion, and failed to respond to data subject requests, undermining the security and proper handling of personal data (video footage).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The bar operator locked camera footage per a patron's request but failed to notify them of the lock, then deleted the locked footage after 30 days without advance notice or explanation.
whyTheyWereWrong: The patron lost permanent access to critical evidence of their assault by security guards because the operator destroyed their restricted data without warning.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator claimed camera footage was locked upon request and would be managed according to law.
claimsVsReality.reality: The operator locked footage but never informed the subject, then deleted it after 30 days without notice, violating the subject's right to restrict processing.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator stated only official police requests could result in footage release.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under GDPR Article 15(3), data subjects have a right to copies of their own personal data; the operator's policy was overly restrictive and not aligned with GDPR.

claimsVsReality.claim: The operator claimed earlier legislation (Szvtv.) permitted deletion after 30 days of no authority request.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR, applicable from May 25, 2018, permits restriction of processing for legal proceedings duration; old Hungarian law did not override GDPR subject rights.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(2) requires that the controller be responsible for and able to demonstrate compliance with data protection principles (Accountability Principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator failed to maintain dated records of data processing policies and could not prove that camera monitoring complied with GDPR requirements during the relevant period.
violations: The operator failed to maintain dated records of data processing policies and could not prove that camera monitoring complied with GDPR requirements during the relevant period.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(1)-(4) requires controllers to provide clear, transparent communication about data processing in response to data subject requests within one month.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator did not respond to four separate requests from the subject between November 2018 and April 2019, providing information only on April 23, 2019—months after some requests.
violations: The operator did not respond to four separate requests from the subject between November 2018 and April 2019, providing information only on April 23, 2019—months after some requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15 grants data subjects the right to access personal data held by controllers.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator failed to fulfill the subject's March 1, 2019 access request and provided no explanation for the omission until April 23, 2019.
violations: The operator failed to fulfill the subject's March 1, 2019 access request and provided no explanation for the omission until April 23, 2019.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 18(1)(c) permits subjects to restrict processing when the controller no longer needs the data but the subject requires it for legal proceedings.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator deleted the locked footage after 30 days despite the subject's ongoing need for it in a criminal investigation, violating the restriction right.
violations: The operator deleted the locked footage after 30 days despite the subject's ongoing need for it in a criminal investigation, violating the restriction right.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 18(3) requires controllers to inform subjects before lifting a processing restriction.
regulatoryFindings.description: The operator deleted the restricted footage without prior notice to the subject, preventing them from being aware of the action.
violations: The operator deleted the restricted footage without prior notice to the subject, preventing them from being aware of the action.

outcome: The NAIH (Hungarian National Data Protection Authority) partially upheld the complainant's request. The authority established that the operator failed to provide adequate information about the restriction of processing, the lifting of that restriction, and deletion of footage. The operator was ordered to fulfill the subject's outstanding access request within 30 days and provide written proof. A data protection fine of 2,000,000 Hungarian Forint was imposed by the authority ex officio. The operator was found to have violated the accountability principle regarding the general camera surveillance practice. Appeal is possible to the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
dataType: Video surveillance footage, personal data of individuals captured on camera
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 18 – Right to restrict processing
GDPR Art. 18(3) – Obligation to inform about lifting of restriction

companyDescription: Retina-X Studios, LLC, a Florida-based software company, developed and sold mobile device monitoring applications marketed ostensibly for parental control and employee monitoring. The company operated from 2007 to 2018 and sold over 15,000 licenses across three main products before discontinuing sales.
companyLongDescription: Retina-X Studios, LLC, a Florida-based software company, developed and sold mobile device monitoring applications marketed ostensibly for parental control and employee monitoring. The company operated from 2007 to 2018 and sold over 15,000 licenses across three main products before discontinuing sales.
caseDescription: Retina-X Studios sold mobile device monitoring software (MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, TeenShield) marketed for child/employee monitoring but enabled surreptitious surveillance of unsuspecting victims without their knowledge or consent. The company failed to implement reasonable security measures, resulting in at least two data breaches that exposed sensitive personal information including messages, locations, and photos. The software was heavily marketed as a tool for stalking and abuse, and the company collected personal data from children under 13 without proper safeguards.
violationSummary: The primary harm stems from enabling large-scale surreptitious surveillance of unwitting individuals. Secondary violations include data insecurity and breach of confidentiality. The surveillance capability is foundational to all other harms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: Retina-X Studios sold mobile monitoring software (MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, TeenShield) allowing purchasers to secretly track another person's texts, locations, photos.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 15,000 licenses enabled stalkers and domestic abusers to obtain victims' intimate communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: Monitoring products are designed for legitimate purposes such as monitoring children and employees.
claimsVsReality.reality: The products were heavily marketed and used by domestic abusers and stalkers to surreptitiously track victims without knowledge or consent. The requirement to jailbreak/root devices to install the software is atypical of legitimate parental control tools, which have non-invasive alternatives.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer databases remain confidential and private. 'Your private information is safe with us.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Unencrypted credentials were stored in the application code, allowing hackers to access databases in both February 2017 and February 2018. Respondents were unaware of the first breach for two months until a journalist contacted them. Collected data including login credentials, text messages, GPS locations, contact lists, browser history, photos, and children's personal information was exposed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Products are installed with physical access but operate transparently with visible monitoring icons.
claimsVsReality.reality: Respondents provided customers with explicit instructions on how to hide the monitoring icon, enabling surreptitious monitoring of device users who had no knowledge they were being tracked and no way to remove the software.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents sold surveillance software without reasonable safeguards against misuse by abusers and stalkers, causing substantial, unavoidable consumer injury.
violations: Respondents sold surveillance software without reasonable safeguards against misuse by abusers and stalkers, causing substantial, unavoidable consumer injury.
Respondents falsely represented that customer data was 'confidential, private, and safe' while maintaining inadequate security controls that permitted unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.8 requires operators with actual knowledge of collecting children's personal information to establish and maintain reasonable procedures to protect the confidentiality, security, and integrity of that information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents collected approximately 950 dates of birth through TeenShield, approximately one-third identifying children under 13, with actual knowledge that children were being monitored. Respondents failed to implement security standards, policies, or procedures and did not adequately oversee third-party service providers handling children's data.
violations: Respondents collected approximately 950 dates of birth through TeenShield, approximately one-third identifying children under 13, with actual knowledge that children were being monitored. Respondents failed to implement security standards, policies, or procedures and did not adequately oversee third-party service providers handling children's data.

outcome: FTC filed a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices under FTC Act Section 5(a) and violations of COPPA Rule. The complaint identifies five counts: (I) Unfairness for selling surveillance tools without safeguards; (II–IV) Deception regarding data security and privacy for MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, and TeenShield; and (V) COPPA violation for failing to protect children's personal information. MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, and TeenShield have not been available for purchase since April 2018, though product websites remain online. The case was filed March 26, 2020. Final consent order or settlement terms would be determined in subsequent proceedings.
companyNow: Retina-X Studios' monitoring products (MobileSpy, PhoneSheriff, TeenShield) have been unavailable for purchase since April 2018. The company's websites remain online. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Text messages, email, GPS location, photos, browser history, contact lists, call history, keystroke logs, financial account information, children's personal information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 312, Section 312.8 – Failure to establish and maintain reasonable procedures to protect confidentiality, security, and integrity of children's personal information

companyDescription: Google Ireland Ltd is a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. and serves as the European contracting entity for Google advertising and digital services, including Google AdWords (now Google Ads), the primary global advertising platform for search, display, and video advertising.
companyLongDescription: Google Ireland Ltd is a subsidiary of Alphabet Inc. and serves as the European contracting entity for Google advertising and digital services, including Google AdWords (now Google Ads), the primary global advertising platform for search, display, and video advertising.
caseDescription: Google Ireland Ltd failed to respond within the statutory one-month deadline to a data subject's access request under GDPR Article 15 regarding how their name was processed in Google AdWords. The company did not provide substantive information about the lawful basis for processing, algorithmic decision-making, or how the data was used for ad targeting, violating the controller's obligation to respond to access requests promptly and completely.
violationSummary: Google excluded the data subject from access to information about their personal data processing by failing to provide required transparency and access disclosures within statutory deadlines, effectively denying the controller's information obligations.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Google Ireland Ltd failed to respond substantively within one month to a data subject's request for information about how their name was processed in Google AdWords.
whyTheyWereWrong: The data subject was left in the dark for months about whether their name was being used as an advertising keyword, which ads appeared when searching their name.

claimsVsReality.claim: Google's internal processes would route access requests submitted through the correct AdWords contact channels to the appropriate team
claimsVsReality.reality: An access request submitted through the AdWords web form was misdirected and not forwarded to the competent department for over three months, despite multiple follow-ups

claimsVsReality.claim: Google does not use the data subject's name as an advertising keyword or target for automated decision-making in AdWords
claimsVsReality.reality: Google's actual practices regarding how personal names are processed, profiled, and used algorithmically in ad targeting decisions were not transparently disclosed until compelled by the regulator

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires the controller to provide information on action taken on a request without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt of the request, extendable by two months in complex cases with notice.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google failed to respond within the one-month deadline to the data subject's access request submitted in 2018
violations: Google failed to respond within the one-month deadline to the data subject's access request submitted in 2018
No extension notice was issued indicating the need for additional time
Response was not provided until after the extended three-month period had passed

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing, access to personal data, and detailed information including processing purposes, data categories, recipients, storage duration, and information about automated decision-making.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google did not provide substantive information about how the data subject's name was processed in AdWords
violations: Google did not provide substantive information about how the data subject's name was processed in AdWords
No explanation of algorithmic logic or search-triggered ad targeting mechanisms was disclosed
Information regarding profiling and automated decision-making related to the data subject was not provided

outcome: The Hungarian Data Protection Authority (NAIH) found that Google Ireland Ltd violated GDPR Articles 12(3) and 15(1) by failing to respond timely and substantively to the data subject's access request regarding name processing in Google AdWords. The authority terminated the own-initiative investigation into general AdWords practices due to lack of systemic evidence. The authority did not impose an administrative fine, finding the violation did not warrant further enforcement beyond the finding of non-compliance. Google did subsequently provide the requested information. The authority compensated the requester 10,000 HUF for exceeding the processing deadline and ordered Google to bear 6,100 HUF in procedural costs for document access. The decision is subject to judicial review at the Budapest Metropolitan Court.
companyNow: Google Ireland Ltd remains the primary EMEA contracting entity for Google services including Google Ads. The company continues to be subject to GDPR enforcement by EU data protection authorities.
dataType: Name, search history, behavioral data, advertising profile

companyDescription: Thru, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Irving, Texas that provides cloud-based file transfer software for enterprises.
companyLongDescription: Thru, Inc. is a Delaware corporation based in Irving, Texas that provides cloud-based file transfer software for enterprises.
caseDescription: Thru, Inc. falsely claimed on its website that it was certified to participate in the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, while never actually completing certification. The company initiated a Privacy Shield application in June 2017 but failed to finalize the process, yet continued making false compliance statements in its privacy policy.
violationSummary: The company made deceptive public disclosures about Privacy Shield participation that misrepresented the legal status and protection level of personal data transfers, violating FTC deception authority.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Thru, Inc. falsely claimed on its website that it complied with the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks, despite never completing certification with the U.S. Department of Commerce.
whyTheyWereWrong: European and Swiss users who transferred personal data to Thru believed their information was legally protected under Privacy Shield adequacy standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Thru Inc. complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce.
claimsVsReality.reality: Thru never completed Privacy Shield certification steps with the U.S. Department of Commerce, despite initiating an application in June 2017.

claimsVsReality.claim: Thru is a participant in both EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Thru was never certified to participate in either framework and did not appear on the Department of Commerce's public list of certified companies.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Thru represented directly and by implication that it was a certified participant in both EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks on its privacy policy website.
violations: Thru represented directly and by implication that it was a certified participant in both EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks on its privacy policy website.
Thru had not been certified to participate in either framework despite initiating an application in June 2017 and not completing the certification steps.
Thru continued to disseminate false Privacy Shield compliance statements in its privacy policy despite the absence of certification.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against Thru, Inc. on January 13, 2020, for deceptive practices. The complaint alleges violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act based on false Privacy Shield certification claims. The document represents the initial complaint; final settlement or consent order terms are not provided in this document.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU and Switzerland (unspecified types)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: CALLESGARCIA S.C. is a photography/event services business (likely a wedding photography enterprise) that operated in Spain. The company was engaged to provide wedding reportage photography services.
companyLongDescription: CALLESGARCIA S.C. is a photography/event services business (likely a wedding photography enterprise) that operated in Spain. The company was engaged to provide wedding reportage photography services.
caseDescription: A wedding photography business used a photograph from a client's wedding reportage for commercial advertising without the client's consent. The Spanish Data Protection Authority found this violated GDPR Article 6 by processing personal data (the client's image) without a lawful basis. The company was fined €4,000 and ordered to notify the complainant and comply with privacy regulations.
violationSummary: The company collected personal data (photograph) for a specific purpose (wedding photography) but reused it for a materially different secondary purpose (commercial advertising) without consent, which is a classic secondary use violation.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: CALLESGARCIA S.C. used wedding photographs featuring the complainant's image for commercial advertising and business promotion without obtaining the complainant's consent or authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's facial image was publicly displayed in advertising materials without permission, exposing their likeness to commercial use.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company implied it had the right to use wedding photographs for its own commercial advertising and business promotion.
claimsVsReality.reality: Without explicit consent from the individuals pictured, the company had no lawful basis under GDPR Article 6 to process and reuse the photographs for secondary commercial purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) requires that processing of personal data is lawful only if at least one of the specified conditions applies, including explicit consent of the data subject for specific purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: CALLESGARCIA S.C. processed the complainant's facial image (personal data) for commercial advertising without obtaining prior consent, thereby failing to satisfy any lawful basis under Article 6.
violations: CALLESGARCIA S.C. processed the complainant's facial image (personal data) for commercial advertising without obtaining prior consent, thereby failing to satisfy any lawful basis under Article 6.

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72.1(c) classifies as very serious the processing of personal data without any of the lawfulness conditions in GDPR Article 6.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's use of the wedding photograph for business promotion lacked any lawful basis and constituted a serious violation of the framework.
violations: The company's use of the wedding photograph for business promotion lacked any lawful basis and constituted a serious violation of the framework.

outcome: The Director of the Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) imposed a fine of €4,000 on CALLESGARCIA S.C. (NIF J10460640) and ordered notification to the complainant. The company was instructed to adapt its privacy practices to GDPR Article 13 and cease unlawful processing. The fine is enforceable via bank transfer to the AEPD's account. The respondent may file a repositioning appeal within one month or seek judicial review before the National Court within two months.
companyNow: Unknown. The company's current status and operations cannot be determined from the document.
dataType: Biometric data (facial image/photograph)

companyDescription: A Hungarian bookkeeping and accounting firm that serves clients by managing their government-related financial transactions and compliance, including handling their ügyfélkapu (centralized government citizen portal) access credentials for online filing and communication.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian bookkeeping and accounting firm that serves clients by managing their government-related financial transactions and compliance, including handling their ügyfélkapu (centralized government citizen portal) access credentials for online filing and communication.
caseDescription: A bookkeeping firm stored client ügyfélkapu (Hungarian government portal) credentials—including usernames and plaintext passwords—in both electronic and paper formats without adequate security safeguards. The paper-based file was blown away and found by a third party, exposing approximately 100 individuals' sensitive government access credentials and personal identification data. The firm failed to implement proper technical and organizational security measures and lacked procedures for reporting data breaches to the supervisory authority.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate technical and organizational security measures (GDPR Art. 32) to protect sensitive personal data, particularly government portal credentials. Storing plaintext passwords and printing sensitive data to paper that could be easily lost constitutes inadequate safeguarding of data integrity and confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: An accounting firm stored unencrypted ügyfélkapu (Hungarian government portal) login credentials along with citizens' full names, tax IDs, social security numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 100 citizens' unencrypted government portal passwords and personal identity data were exposed when a printed list blew away in the wind, enabling identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed that only 9 employees and an authorized IT person could access the server and client data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite claims of password protection and authorized access controls, a printed copy containing unencrypted credentials and sensitive personal data was lost and found by a third party, demonstrating that security controls were inadequate and the paper-based storage practice created an uncontrolled exposure risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company stated it had put appropriate security measures in place by encrypting server access and maintaining locked folders for paper documents.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's security was insufficient because plaintext passwords were stored and repeatedly printed, and paper documents were stored in an unlocked folder that allowed a copy to be blown away and lost, proving the claimed measures were inadequate.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32(1) requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, considering the state of the art, implementation costs, and the nature and scope of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company stored ügyfélkapu access credentials (usernames and unencrypted passwords) on a server and routinely printed sensitive data to paper, stored in unlocked folders, enabling unauthorized access and loss of approximately 100 individuals' credentials.
violations: Company stored ügyfélkapu access credentials (usernames and unencrypted passwords) on a server and routinely printed sensitive data to paper, stored in unlocked folders, enabling unauthorized access and loss of approximately 100 individuals' credentials.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 24(1)-(2) requires controllers to implement appropriate internal data protection policies, including procedures for incident handling and reporting obligations to supervisory authorities.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company's internal data protection incident handling policy failed to address when breaches must be reported to the supervisory authority, leaving no clear obligation to notify authorities of data incidents.
violations: Company's internal data protection incident handling policy failed to address when breaches must be reported to the supervisory authority, leaving no clear obligation to notify authorities of data incidents.

outcome: The Nemzeti Adatvédelmi és Információszabadság Hatóság (NAIH) found the company violated GDPR Articles 32 and 24. The company was ordered to: (1) cease paper-based storage of client government portal credentials and maintain only electronic copies with electronic backups; (2) amend its internal incident handling policy to include clear procedures for notifying the supervisory authority when required by GDPR Art. 33. The company was fined 500,000 HUF (approximately €1,685 or $1,848 USD at 2020 rates) payable within 30 days of finality. The decision was ordered published without the company's identifying details. The company may appeal to the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
companyNow: Unknown; the company's identity was withheld from public disclosure per the authority's order.
dataType: National ID numbers, tax identification numbers, social security numbers, birth dates, parental names, ügyfélkapu (government portal) usernames and unencrypted passwords
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 32(1) – Inadequate technical and organizational security measures
GDPR Art. 24(1)-(2) – Inadequate internal data protection incident handling policy

companyDescription: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. is a medical device and in vitro diagnostics company headquartered in Raritan, New Jersey. It provides diagnostic testing services and products for clinical laboratories and healthcare providers.
companyLongDescription: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. is a medical device and in vitro diagnostics company headquartered in Raritan, New Jersey. It provides diagnostic testing services and products for clinical laboratories and healthcare providers.
caseDescription: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics claimed to comply with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework in its privacy policy, but allowed its Privacy Shield certification to lapse in 2018. After Commerce warned the company to remove Privacy Shield claims in August 2018, the company continued to falsely represent on its website that it participated in Privacy Shield and complied with the framework's principles, including a verification requirement it never satisfied.
violationSummary: The company disclosed false claims about Privacy Shield participation and compliance on its public-facing privacy policy, misleading consumers and data subjects about the legal basis and protections for their personal data transfers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics falsely claimed on its website that it participated in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework even after its certification lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU and Swiss residents whose personal data was transferred to the United States relied on Ortho-Clinical's false Privacy Shield certification claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. (and its parent/subsidiary company, Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics Bermuda Co. Ltd.) participates in and has certified its compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework
claimsVsReality.reality: The company obtained Privacy Shield certification in April 2017, but that certification lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed. By 2018 and 2019, the company was not a current participant in Privacy Shield.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. is committed to subjecting all personal data received from the European Union (EU) member countries and Switzerland, respectively, in reliance on each Privacy Shield Framework, to the Framework's applicable Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to comply with Privacy Shield Supplemental Principle 7, which requires annual verification through self-assessment or outside compliance review. During the 2017-18 period when certified, the company failed to obtain any attested verification statement and did not provide it to the FTC as required.

claimsVsReality.claim: To learn more about the Privacy Shield Frameworks, and to view our certification visit the U.S. Department of Commerce's Privacy Shield List
claimsVsReality.reality: When individuals consulted the Commerce Privacy Shield list after the company's August 2018 certification lapse, they would not find Ortho-Clinical listed as a current participant, contradicting the company's ongoing claims.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ortho-Clinical represented on its privacy policy website that it 'participates in and has certified its compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework' when its certification had lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed
violations: Ortho-Clinical represented on its privacy policy website that it 'participates in and has certified its compliance with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework' when its certification had lapsed in 2018 and was not renewed

Ortho-Clinical represented that it 'subjecting[s] all personal data received from the European Union (EU) member countries and Switzerland...to the Framework's applicable Principles' despite not being a current participant
Ortho-Clinical failed to comply with Privacy Shield Supplemental Principle 7 by not obtaining annual attested verification statements during 2017-18 that it was certified
Ortho-Clinical failed to affirm to Commerce its commitment to continue protecting personal information it received during participation after its certification lapsed

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging three counts of deceptive practices: (1) Privacy Misrepresentation – claiming current Privacy Shield participation when certification had lapsed; (2) Misrepresentation Regarding Verification – representing compliance with Privacy Shield principles while failing to obtain required annual verification statements; (3) Misrepresentation Regarding Continuing Obligations – representing compliance while failing to affirm continuing protection obligations to Commerce. As a complaint, this initiated formal enforcement proceedings under FTC authority; the document does not contain final settlement terms, but FTC enforcement typically results in cease-and-desist orders and compliance monitoring.
companyNow: Ortho-Clinical Diagnostics, Inc. continues to operate as a medical device and in vitro diagnostics provider. The company is owned by Carlyle Group and remains active in clinical diagnostics.
dataType: Personal data from EU and Swiss residents (types not specified but potentially health-related given medical device/diagnostics services)
legalBasisViolated: EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework (Supplemental Principle 7 – Verification requirement)

companyDescription: Statistics Canada is Canada's national statistical office mandated to collect, compile, and publish statistical information on commercial, industrial, financial, social, economic and general activities of the Canadian population.
companyLongDescription: Statistics Canada is a federal government agency that serves as the country's primary source of official statistics. Operating under the Statistics Act, it collects data through direct surveys and increasingly through administrative data from both government and private sector sources. The agency operates research data centres across Canada and employs statistical experts to analyze economic, social, and demographic trends. It has expanded its use of private sector data sources as part of a modernization initiative.
caseDescription: Statistics Canada collected detailed credit information from TransUnion on approximately 24 million Canadians and proposed to collect comprehensive financial transaction data from 500,000 households without prior individual consent. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the Credit Information Project fell within legal authority but identified significant privacy concerns regarding necessity, proportionality, transparency, and internal security monitoring for both projects.
violationSummary: The projects involved systematic collection of detailed personal financial and credit information from large populations without individual knowledge or consent, constituting surveillance-type data collection from administrative sources.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Statistics Canada collected detailed credit information on approximately 24 million Canadians from TransUnion.
whyTheyWereWrong: Canadians had their sensitive financial and credit data secretly extracted and linked with other personal information by the government without knowing it was happening.

claimsVsReality.claim: Statistics Canada had appropriate safeguards to protect personal information and would keep it confidential.
claimsVsReality.reality: The agency had significant internal security vulnerabilities and insufficient monitoring for unauthorized internal access to sensitive data containing direct identifiers and linkage keys.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Credit Information Project was protective of privacy and necessary in its current form.
claimsVsReality.reality: Statistics Canada failed to demonstrate that all the personal information collected (600 elements per person) was necessary, and did not adequately consider less invasive alternatives or proportionality to the invasion of privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Canadians were adequately informed about the collection via consumer reporting legislation notices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Statistics Canada failed to be adequately transparent with the public about these data collection initiatives, with most Canadians unaware their detailed credit and financial information was being secretly collected and linked across multiple government databases.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 - Government institutions must collect personal information relating directly to authorized operating programs or activities
regulatoryFindings.description: Credit Information Project: Found to be within authority under Statistics Act Section 13 as TransUnion maintained data in existing database; no violation found
violations: Credit Information Project: Found to be within authority under Statistics Act Section 13 as TransUnion maintained data in existing database; no violation found
Financial Transactions Project: Strong concerns that compiling data from separate databases would exceed Section 13 authority by requiring creation of new records

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act and TBS Directive - Collection of personal information must be demonstrably necessary and proportional to privacy intrusion
regulatoryFindings.description: Statistics Canada did not demonstrate necessity of all 600+ data elements collected on 44 million records
violations: Statistics Canada did not demonstrate necessity of all 600+ data elements collected on 44 million records
Financial transaction line-by-line collection characterized as akin to total state surveillance, disproportionate to stated objectives
Failure to adequately consider less privacy-invasive alternatives such as aggregated data, surveys, or hybrid methods
Retention of linkage keys enabling indefinite re-identification for undefined future purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act and TBS Directive - Transparency requirements regarding personal information collection
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to adequately engage public or affected individuals about projects prior to collection
violations: Failed to adequately engage public or affected individuals about projects prior to collection
Reliance on post-collection notices from third parties (TransUnion) rather than proactive direct notification
Notices required individuals to request credit file access to discover disclosure had occurred

regulatoryFindings.act: TBS Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.2.21 - Access to personal information must be monitored and documented
regulatoryFindings.description: Logging and audit trails reviewed only upon request rather than proactively monitored
violations: Logging and audit trails reviewed only upon request rather than proactively monitored
Lack of centralized logging and monitoring solution preventing comprehensive detection of unauthorized activity
Inadequate measures to address internal threat vulnerabilities despite holding extremely sensitive high-value data

regulatoryFindings.act: Statistics Act Section 17(2)(a) - Discretionary disclosure of identifying information
regulatoryFindings.description: Directive on Discretionary Disclosures does not expressly require weighing of individual privacy interests when deciding to disclose identifiable information to other agencies
violations: Directive on Discretionary Disclosures does not expressly require weighing of individual privacy interests when deciding to disclose identifiable information to other agencies

outcome: Statistics Canada agreed to implement all six recommendations: halt both projects in their original form; redesign projects to respect necessity and proportionality principles in collaboration with the Office of the Privacy Commissioner; increase transparency through improved website and direct notification to affected individuals; implement proactive internal access monitoring; and commit to legislative reform discussions. Statistics Canada placed both projects on hold pending investigation completion and committed to working with the OPC on redesign. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner noted significant privacy concerns despite finding no technical violation of the Privacy Act for the Credit Information Project, and declined to make a finding on the Financial Transactions Project as no data was collected.
companyNow: Statistics Canada continues to operate as Canada's national statistics agency. Following this enforcement action, it has committed to redesigning its data collection projects with enhanced privacy safeguards and transparency measures.
dataType: Credit information, financial transaction data, name, age, date of birth, social insurance number, address, mortgage information, account balances, transaction details
legalBasisViolated: Statistics Act Section 13 (scope of access to records)
TBS Directive on Privacy Practices (necessity and proportionality)
TBS Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.2.21 (monitoring and documentation of access)

companyDescription: Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) is a federal government department responsible for administering social programs, employment services, and volunteer recognition initiatives for the Government of Canada.
companyLongDescription: ESDC administers major Canadian federal programs including Employment Insurance, Canada Pension Plan services, and various volunteer and community recognition programs such as the Prime Minister's Volunteer Awards (now Canada's Volunteer Award Program). As a federal institution, ESDC is subject to the Privacy Act and must comply with strict requirements governing the collection, use, and retention of personal information. The department operates through various regional offices and service delivery channels across Canada.
caseDescription: Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) collected a complainant's personal information for the second time through a third-party vendor (Grey House Publishing) for the Prime Minister's Volunteer Awards program, despite the complainant's prior explicit request to be removed from the distribution list in 2014. ESDC failed to ensure that the third-party vendor obtained the information with proper consent and did not have mechanisms in place to honor opt-out requests across multiple years.
violationSummary: ESDC engaged in repeated collection of personal information for promotional purposes without proper consent and in disregard of the individual's express objection, constituting unauthorized surveillance through third-party data acquisition.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: ESDC collected a complainant's name, email, and phone number through a third-party vendor for the Prime Minister's Volunteer Awards program despite the complainant's explicit 2014 request to be.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant received unwanted promotional emails years after requesting removal, exposing him to continued contact he had explicitly rejected.

claimsVsReality.claim: ESDC acquired the distribution list in a compliant manner and did not collect the complainant's personal information without authorization.
claimsVsReality.reality: Grey House obtained the complainant's information without his consent in violation of PIPEDA, and ESDC failed to verify that its vendor had obtained proper consent despite contractually requiring it.

claimsVsReality.claim: ESDC had no mechanism to track opt-out requests across multiple years because it receives new distribution lists annually.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant explicitly requested removal in 2014, and ESDC re-collected and re-used his information in 2015 without verifying his prior opt-out status or implementing tracking systems.

claimsVsReality.claim: The contact information constituted business contact information that could be collected without consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant was not an executive, director, or employee of the club and did not hold a position of responsibility; the information was personal contact information, not legitimate business contact data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 – Collection Limits
regulatoryFindings.description: ESDC collected personal information that exceeded the framework of its program parameters by failing to ensure third-party vendor compliance with consent requirements
violations: ESDC collected personal information that exceeded the framework of its program parameters by failing to ensure third-party vendor compliance with consent requirements
Collection occurred despite contractual requirements that lists be obtained 'in accordance with Canadian legislation' with 'all necessary consents'

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 5 – Direct Collection Preference
regulatoryFindings.description: While Section 5 did not strictly apply (as the information was not for administrative purposes directly affecting the individual), ESDC's approach did not respect the spirit of the Act
violations: While Section 5 did not strictly apply (as the information was not for administrative purposes directly affecting the individual), ESDC's approach did not respect the spirit of the Act

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA)
regulatoryFindings.description: Third-party vendor Grey House collected personal information without consent, in violation of PIPEDA requirements
violations: Third-party vendor Grey House collected personal information without consent, in violation of PIPEDA requirements

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. ESDC violated Section 4 of the Privacy Act by collecting personal information through a third party without ensuring compliance with consent requirements and by disregarding the complainant's explicit opt-out request from 2014. Following the complaint, ESDC implemented procedural changes to verify new distribution lists and remove individuals who no longer wish to receive emails about the program. The Commissioner recommended that ESDC ensure third-party vendors comply with contractual obligations related to privacy responsibilities.
companyNow: ESDC continues to operate as a major federal department, now operating under the expanded mandate as Employment and Social Development Canada following departmental reorganizations. The department has implemented enhanced privacy procedures following complaints like this one.
dataType: Name, email address, telephone number

companyDescription: The Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA) is a federal government institution responsible for regulating air, rail, and maritime transportation in Canada, including adjudicating passenger rights complaints.
companyLongDescription: The Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA) is a Crown corporation that serves as Canada's independent transportation regulator. It handles air passenger rights complaints, rail and maritime transportation regulatory matters, and adjudicates disputes between stakeholders and regulated entities. The CTA operates under federal legislation including the Canada Transportation Act and is subject to the Privacy Act for handling personal information requests.
caseDescription: The Canadian Transportation Agency (CTA) improperly withheld personal information about an air passenger rights advocate by claiming it did not constitute his personal information under the Privacy Act. The CTA incorrectly applied exemptions under paragraphs 12(1)(b), sections 26 and 27, and subsection 70(1) to refuse disclosure of records containing the complainant's name accompanied by information about him, his conduct, and the CTA's handling of his submissions.
violationSummary: The CTA violated the complainant's right to access his own personal information by improperly excluding it from disclosure. This is exclusion under the Solove taxonomy because the violation involves denying an individual access to information about themselves that they are legally entitled to receive.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The Canadian Transportation Agency withheld 760 pages of records about an air passenger rights advocate, claiming his name.
whyTheyWereWrong: The advocate was denied access to records containing his name alongside information about his conduct, submissions.

claimsVsReality.claim: References to the complainant's name in internal deliberations about regulatory matters he brought before the CTA do not constitute his personal information because they relate to his representative capacity on behalf of an unincorporated organization.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant filed all complaints and litigation under his own name as the organization was not a separate legal entity; records contained his name accompanied by information about his conduct, views about his submissions, and details about how the CTA handled his case—all of which qualify as his personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The information does not engage privacy rights because it involves deliberations on regulatory or adjudicative matters rather than matters of personal intimacy, identity, dignity and integrity.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal agency discussions evaluating the complainant's conduct and submissions directly concern his identity and how he is perceived by a government institution, engaging the privacy rights the Act is intended to protect.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 3 defines personal information as information about an identifiable individual, including information about race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, marital status, education, medical, criminal or employment history, financial transactions, identifying numbers, fingerprints, blood type, personal opinions, views or opinions of another individual about the individual, and the name of an individual where it appears with other personal information relating to the individual or where disclosure of the name itself would reveal information about the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: The CTA incorrectly withheld records containing the complainant's name accompanied by information about him, his conduct, views about his submissions, and information the CTA collected about him from news articles, claiming this did not constitute his personal information.
violations: The CTA incorrectly withheld records containing the complainant's name accompanied by information about him, his conduct, views about his submissions, and information the CTA collected about him from news articles, claiming this did not constitute his personal information.

The CTA took the position that the complainant's name should not be considered his personal information when it related to regulatory or adjudicative matters brought before the CTA on behalf of an organization, despite the organization not being a separate legal entity.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act paragraph 12(1)(b) provides a right of access for individuals to any personal information about themselves under the control of a government institution.
regulatoryFindings.description: The CTA incorrectly applied paragraph 12(1)(b) as an exemption rather than recognizing it as a provision that sets out the right of access, and wrongly denied the complainant access to his personal information by claiming it fell outside the scope of accessible information.
violations: The CTA incorrectly applied paragraph 12(1)(b) as an exemption rather than recognizing it as a provision that sets out the right of access, and wrongly denied the complainant access to his personal information by claiming it fell outside the scope of accessible information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 26 permits withholding of personal information about an individual other than the requester, but excludes from the definition of personal information details about individuals performing services under contract for a government institution, including their name and opinions given in the course of performance of those services.
regulatoryFindings.description: The CTA withheld the name and business contact information of a contractor on page 463 under section 26, which should have been disclosed as the contractor's identifying information relating to services performed is excluded from the definition of personal information.
violations: The CTA withheld the name and business contact information of a contractor on page 463 under section 26, which should have been disclosed as the contractor's identifying information relating to services performed is excluded from the definition of personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 27 permits withholding of personal information subject to solicitor-client privilege.
regulatoryFindings.description: The CTA withheld entire records under section 27, including names and email addresses of senders and recipients as well as date and time of transmission, which do not normally qualify for privilege exemption as they do not reveal the contents of communications and are not privileged information.
violations: The CTA withheld entire records under section 27, including names and email addresses of senders and recipients as well as date and time of transmission, which do not normally qualify for privilege exemption as they do not reveal the contents of communications and are not privileged information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act subsection 70(1) exempts records containing confidences of the Queen's Privy Council for Canada (cabinet confidences), including discussion papers intended to present background explanations, analyses of problems or policy options to Council for consideration in making decisions.
regulatoryFindings.description: The CTA withheld an email on page 254 under subsection 70(1), claiming it constituted a cabinet confidence discussion paper, but there was no evidence the email was submitted or intended to be submitted to Cabinet, no reference to a document intended for Cabinet, and no mandatory consultation with the Privy Council Office as required by Treasury Board policy.
violations: The CTA withheld an email on page 254 under subsection 70(1), claiming it constituted a cabinet confidence discussion paper, but there was no evidence the email was submitted or intended to be submitted to Cabinet, no reference to a document intended for Cabinet, and no mandatory consultation with the Privy Council Office as required by Treasury Board policy.

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. The Privacy Commissioner recommended that the CTA disclose: (1) information withheld under section 12(1)(b) where the complainant's name or organization is mentioned; (2) contractor information on page 463; (3) sender, recipient, date and time information withheld under section 27 that is not privileged; and (4) the portion of email correspondence withheld under subsection 70(1) referring to the complainant by name. The CTA agreed to implement all recommendations and to release this information to the complainant on or before March 1, 2019. The matter was deemed conditionally resolved pending the CTA's compliance with the disclosure deadline.
companyNow: The CTA continues to operate as Canada's federal transportation regulator, handling passenger rights advocacy matters and regulatory decisions.
dataType: Name, personal opinions, views about conduct, information collected from news articles
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act section 3 (definition of personal information)
Privacy Act paragraph 12(1)(b) (right of access to personal information)
Privacy Act section 26 (third party personal information exemption)

companyDescription: Global Affairs Canada is the Canadian federal department responsible for diplomatic relations, international development, and consular services.
companyLongDescription: Global Affairs Canada (GAC) is the Government of Canada department that manages Canada's international relations, including diplomatic missions, development assistance, and consular services for Canadian citizens abroad. The department employs diplomats and staff who are issued special diplomatic passports to facilitate their official work. Under departmental policy, certain posted employees are authorized to use diplomatic passports for personal travel while on international posting.
caseDescription: Global Affairs Canada requested an employee's diplomatic passport as evidence during an administrative investigation, but the passport contained personal travel information collected under a policy permitting employees to use diplomatic passports for personal travel. GAC failed to demonstrate it had authority under the Privacy Act to collect this personal information, as it could not establish the collection related directly to its operating programs or activities.
violationSummary: GAC attempted to collect personal information (travel history) from a diplomatic passport without establishing legal authority or necessity. The collection was sought as evidence in an administrative investigation, but GAC could not demonstrate the personal travel data related directly to its operating programs or activities, violating the foundational requirement of the Privacy Act.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Global Affairs Canada requested an employee's diplomatic passport as evidence during an administrative investigation.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees used diplomatic passports for personal travel under GAC policy, creating a record of personal travel history; GAC demanded the original passport to access this information.

claimsVsReality.claim: GAC has authority to collect the personal travel information contained in diplomatic passports because the passports are government property and can be requested at any time.
claimsVsReality.reality: GAC failed to demonstrate that the collection of personal travel information related directly to any operating program or activity, and therefore lacked legal authority under the Privacy Act to collect personal travel data from diplomatic passports used for authorized personal travel.

claimsVsReality.claim: The administrative investigation necessitated collection of the complainant's complete personal travel history contained in the diplomatic passport.
claimsVsReality.reality: GAC refused to provide the Office with information about the nature of the administrative investigation or how personal travel information was linked to the investigation, preventing any demonstration that the collection was necessary or authorized.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4
regulatoryFindings.description: GAC collected personal travel information without demonstrating it related directly to an operating program or activity of the institution
violations: GAC collected personal travel information without demonstrating it related directly to an operating program or activity of the institution
GAC failed to provide information regarding the nature of the administrative investigation or how the personal travel data was necessary to it
GAC did not establish authority to collect personal information from diplomatic passport use for personal travel

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3
regulatoryFindings.description: GAC sought to collect personal information (name, date of birth, citizenship, travel history) without legal basis
violations: GAC sought to collect personal information (name, date of birth, citizenship, travel history) without legal basis

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. GAC was directed to clarify its policy and practices related to personal use of diplomatic passports and privacy implications. GAC must disseminate clarified terms to users and affected individuals, and advise users of the purposes for which it may collect personal travel information. GAC was required to report to the Privacy Commissioner within 30 days of actions taken or proposed to implement these recommendations.
companyNow: Global Affairs Canada continues to operate as the primary federal department managing Canada's international affairs and diplomatic relations. The department remains responsible for the management and oversight of diplomatic passport issuance and use policies.
dataType: Personal travel history, passport information, visa records, border crossing stamps, date of birth, citizenship
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 4 (no personal information shall be collected unless it relates directly to an operating program or activity)
Privacy Act Section 3 (definition of personal information)

companyDescription: Correctional Service Canada is the federal government agency responsible for managing penitentiaries and supervising federal inmates in Canada.
companyLongDescription: Correctional Service Canada (CSC) is a federal Crown corporation within the Department of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness that operates the Canadian federal penitentiary system. It is responsible for the custody, supervision, and rehabilitation of federally sentenced offenders, managing institutions across the country and maintaining security operations to protect inmates, staff, and the public.
caseDescription: Three employees of Correctional Service Canada complained that video surveillance footage collected for security purposes was being improperly used to monitor their individual performance. After investigation, the Privacy Commissioner determined the use was consistent with the stated purpose of maintaining institutional security and preventing inmate deaths, not employee performance monitoring.
violationSummary: The complainants alleged secondary use of video data collected for security purposes, claiming it was being repurposed to monitor employee performance without consent. However, the Commissioner found the actual use was consistent with the original security collection purpose.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Correctional Service Canada reviewed video surveillance footage of employee patrols and provided feedback to employees after an inmate death.
whyTheyWereWrong: The Privacy Commissioner determined the video review was not employee performance monitoring but was legitimately used to identify systemic patrol deficiencies that contributed to an inmate's.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC was using video footage to monitor employee performance in violation of the Privacy Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: CSC was using video footage to investigate systemic patrol deficiencies after an inmate death and to prevent future deaths, which is consistent with the stated security purpose of collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: The video review and feedback constituted improper employee performance monitoring.
claimsVsReality.reality: The video review was a one-time response to identify institutional security issues related to patrol quality following an inmate death, not ongoing performance monitoring of staff.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 7(a) — personal information shall not be used without consent except for the purpose for which it was obtained or compiled, or for a use consistent with that purpose
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainants alleged video footage was used for employee performance monitoring rather than security purposes
violations: Complainants alleged video footage was used for employee performance monitoring rather than security purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 — definition of personal information includes recorded information about identifiable individuals, including appearance and mannerisms
regulatoryFindings.description: Video footage captured complainants' appearance and mannerisms, constituting personal information under the Act
violations: Video footage captured complainants' appearance and mannerisms, constituting personal information under the Act

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner determined the complaints were not well-founded. CSC's use of video footage to review patrol quality and identify systemic deficiencies following an inmate death was consistent with the security collection purpose. No violation of the Privacy Act was found. No remediation or compliance orders were issued.
companyNow: Correctional Service Canada continues to operate as Canada's federal penitentiary system, managing multiple security-level institutions and inmate populations across the country.
dataType: Video footage, appearance, mannerisms, employment information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 7(a) — use of personal information without consent
Privacy Act Section 3 — definition of personal information

companyDescription: Equifax Inc. is a major credit reporting and data analytics company headquartered in the United States, with a Canadian subsidiary Equifax Canada Co. providing credit reporting and consumer information services to Canadian customers.
companyLongDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the largest credit reporting agencies globally, maintaining credit files and personal financial information on millions of consumers. The company offers direct-to-consumer products including credit reports, credit monitoring, and fraud alert services, as well as enterprise solutions for financial institutions and other organizations. Equifax Canada Co. is its Canadian subsidiary, responsible for credit reporting and related services in Canada while coordinating with the US parent company for product delivery. The company processes highly sensitive personal information including social insurance numbers, payment card data, and detailed credit histories.
caseDescription: Equifax Inc. and Equifax Canada Co. failed to implement adequate security safeguards, retention practices, and accountability measures for Canadian personal information. A 2017 breach exposed data of approximately 19,000 Canadians due to unpatched vulnerabilities, inadequate network segregation, and poor security practices. The companies also failed to obtain valid consent for disclosure of sensitive information to Equifax Inc. in the US.
violationSummary: The companies failed to implement security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of personal information held, including inadequate vulnerability management, network segregation, basic security practices, and oversight mechanisms.
