This constitutes a systemic failure to protect against unauthorized access, disclosure, and use of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Equifax Inc. and Equifax Canada Co. failed to patch a known software vulnerability for over two months, implement adequate network segregation.
whyTheyWereWrong: The 19,000 affected Canadians had their social insurance numbers, payment card information, and credit file details exposed to attackers, creating severe risk of identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax had adequate security safeguards in place to protect sensitive Canadian personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to patch a known vulnerability for 2+ months, had inadequate network segregation that allowed broad database access, and lacked basic security practices—allowing attackers to access hundreds of database tables and 11,000 undeleted IT staff files containing personal data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax properly managed data retention and destruction practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company retained IT staff file shares containing Canadian personal information for years after they were created (April 2010 to September 2016), with some files never deleted, allowing attackers to access approximately 8,000 Canadians' data from outdated archived files.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax Canada maintained adequate accountability for personal information processed by parent company Equifax Inc.
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax Canada had minimal oversight of Equifax Inc.'s security practices despite transferring full Canadian credit files to the US parent company; security policies and direction were largely managed by Equifax Inc. without meaningful Canadian subsidiary accountability.

claimsVsReality.claim: Canadians provided informed consent for disclosure of their personal information to Equifax Inc. in the US.
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax Canada failed to obtain valid consent from Canadians for the collection and disclosure of their sensitive personal information to the US parent company, particularly regarding the transfer of full credit files needed for product delivery.

claimsVsReality.claim: Post-breach mitigation measures adequately protected affected Canadians from identity theft and unauthorized use.
claimsVsReality.reality: The offered post-breach protections were inadequate to address the severe ongoing risk created by the exposure of social insurance numbers, payment card information, and detailed credit files to attackers.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Security safeguards must be appropriate to the sensitivity of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to patch known Apache Struts vulnerability for over 2 months after notification
violations: Failed to patch known Apache Struts vulnerability for over 2 months after notification
Inadequate network segregation allowing attackers to access hundreds of database tables
Poor implementation of basic security practices including unencrypted passwords in file shares
Inadequate oversight mechanisms with disconnect between policies and practices
Canadian credit card information not included in PCI-DSS certification scope

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5 – Personal information no longer required must be destroyed according to retention schedules
regulatoryFindings.description: No deletion process in place for Canadian personal information in GCS databases despite retention periods expiring
violations: No deletion process in place for Canadian personal information in GCS databases despite retention periods expiring
No Canadian data had been deleted since at least 2010
Key staff unaware of retention policy and accountability unclear
No monitoring of compliance with retention practices

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1 and Section 4.1.3 – Organization responsible for personal information under its control, including information transferred to third parties
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax Canada failed to maintain adequate accountability for Canadian personal information held by Equifax Inc.
violations: Equifax Canada failed to maintain adequate accountability for Canadian personal information held by Equifax Inc.
No formal written agreement between Equifax Canada and Equifax Inc. at time of breach
Inadequate monitoring of Equifax Inc.'s compliance with Canadian privacy requirements
Lack of clarity about scope and roles/responsibilities for handling Canadian data
Breach response failures and inadequate post-breach communications to affected individuals

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 and Section 6.1 – Valid consent requires knowledge of nature, purpose and consequences of collection, use or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate disclosure that sensitive information was being collected by Equifax Inc. in the US
violations: Inadequate disclosure that sensitive information was being collected by Equifax Inc. in the US
GCS portal presented as operated by Equifax Canada directly despite US operation by Equifax Inc.
No clear explanation of subsequent disclosures of credit reports and alerts to Equifax Inc.
No communication of alternative options (e.g., postal-based free credit reports) that avoid Equifax Inc. transfer
Reliance on general Privacy Policy language insufficient for sensitive data transfer consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Security safeguards must be appropriate to sensitivity of information held by Equifax Canada
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate oversight mechanisms including limited-scope ISO 27001 sampling and lack of comprehensive external security audits
violations: Inadequate oversight mechanisms including limited-scope ISO 27001 sampling and lack of comprehensive external security audits
Internal penetration testing conducted only annually with very limited tools and techniques
PCI-DSS certification not conducted since September 2016
Vulnerability management highly integrated with Equifax Inc. without independent controls
External penetration tests identified serious systemic vulnerabilities remaining unaddressed
Inadequate training for staff on data handling and security practices

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1 – Organizations must implement safeguards to protect against unauthorized use of compromised personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Offered only one year of credit monitoring when enduring risk of identity theft exists
violations: Offered only one year of credit monitoring when enduring risk of identity theft exists
Failed to offer credit freeze product 'for life' as offered to US consumers despite identical risks
Reliance on fraud alerts insufficient as they do not prevent fraudulent credit checks

outcome: Equifax Canada signed a compliance agreement committing to undertake corrective measures including: (1) implementing a formal written arrangement with Equifax Inc. covering all Canadian personal information; (2) instituting robust monitoring programs against the arrangement requirements; (3) identifying and deleting Canadian personal information no longer required; (4) providing bi-annual audit reports and certifications for six years covering all Canadian data processed by Equifax Inc.; (5) providing detailed security audit reports and certifications every two years for six years; (6) providing extended credit monitoring of at least 4 years to affected individuals. The matter was found well-founded and conditionally resolved except for Section 6 (post-breach safeguards) which was found well-founded and partially resolved as Equifax Canada did not agree to provide a free or low-cost credit freeze product.
companyNow: Equifax remains a major credit reporting agency operating globally. Following the 2017 breach and subsequent regulatory actions, the company has invested significantly in cybersecurity improvements and continues to operate its credit reporting and consumer information services.
dataType: Social insurance numbers, payment card information, credit report data, account information, names, addresses, dates of birth

companyDescription: Facebook is a social media platform founded in 2004 that allows users to connect, share content, and integrate third-party applications. It operates a platform ecosystem with over 40 million integrated apps and sites.
companyLongDescription: Facebook is a major social media company that provides a platform for users to create profiles, share information, and connect with others. Since 2007, Facebook has allowed third-party developers to integrate apps and services through its Platform, using APIs like Graph API to access user data. The company processes personal information from hundreds of millions of users worldwide and provides developers with access to user data through various permission models and integrations.
caseDescription: Facebook failed to obtain valid and meaningful consent from both users who installed the 'thisisyourdigitallife' app and their friends whose data was disclosed to the app. The platform also had inadequate safeguards to prevent unauthorized access and use of user information by third-party apps, and failed to take responsibility for protecting personal information under its control, ultimately leading to the unauthorized disclosure of approximately 87 million users' data worldwide (622,000 in Canada) for political micro-targeting purposes.
violationSummary: Facebook disclosed massive amounts of personal information to third-party apps without obtaining meaningful consent from users or their friends. The disclosure occurred without users understanding the purposes, consequences, or which specific apps would receive their data, constituting improper information dissemination.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Facebook failed to obtain valid and meaningful consent from users and their friends before disclosing their personal information to third-party apps.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Canadians' personal information was accessed and used by Cambridge Analytica for political profiling without their knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook stated it shared the goal of ensuring user privacy in connection with third-party applications and that application developers behave responsibly with user data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Facebook had inadequate safeguards, relied on superficial and reactive monitoring, and provided no evidence of enforcement actions against apps that violated privacy contractual terms.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook's consent mechanisms and privacy communications adequately protected user information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Facebook used overbroad and conflicting language presented at registration for disclosures occurring years later to unknown apps for unknown purposes, insufficient to support meaningful consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook took responsibility for protecting personal information under its control.
claimsVsReality.reality: Facebook abdicated responsibility by shifting it almost exclusively to users and apps, creating an empty privacy protection framework that failed to prevent unauthorized access and use.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Clause 4.3 and PIPA Section 10 require knowledge and consent of individuals for collection, use, or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Facebook failed to obtain meaningful consent from Installing Users; consent was based on overly broad, generic language in terms of service presented years before disclosure, without specific information about which apps would access data or for what purposes
violations: Facebook failed to obtain meaningful consent from Installing Users; consent was based on overly broad, generic language in terms of service presented years before disclosure, without specific information about which apps would access data or for what purposes
Facebook relied on third-party apps to obtain consent without verifying that meaningful consent was actually obtained
Facebook was unable to demonstrate that the TYDL App obtained meaningful consent for its purposes, including potentially political purposes
For Installing Users, the installation dialog box did not describe purposes for which information was requested, how it would be used, or potential consequences

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Clause 4.3.2 and PIPA Section 10 require organizations to make reasonable efforts to ensure individuals are advised of purposes and that consent is meaningful
regulatoryFindings.description: Facebook failed to obtain meaningful consent from Affected Users (friends of app installers) for disclosure of their information
violations: Facebook failed to obtain meaningful consent from Affected Users (friends of app installers) for disclosure of their information
Affected Users had no knowledge their information would be disclosed to the TYDL App and could not have provided informed consent
Language in Data Use Policy was overbroad and conflicting, referring to disclosures to 'unknown apps for unknown purposes' without specific app-by-app notice
Consent mechanisms relied upon Installing Users to consent on behalf of hundreds of their friends without those friends' knowledge
Information shared with 'friends only' was still disclosed to third-party apps without express app-by-app consent for sensitive data

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Clauses 4.7 and 4.7.1 and PIPA Section 34 require appropriate security safeguards to protect personal information from unauthorized access, use, and disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Facebook had superficial and largely reactive monitoring of third-party app compliance with Platform Policy
violations: Facebook had superficial and largely reactive monitoring of third-party app compliance with Platform Policy
Facebook's monitoring only covered top 500 apps; the TYDL App with 300,000 installing users was not a 'top app' and went unmonitored despite accessing data of 87 million individuals
Facebook relied on user and media reports rather than proactive monitoring to detect violations
Facebook did not review the TYDL App's privacy policy or verify that it was obtaining meaningful consent despite concerns

After rejecting the TYDL App's request for extended permissions in May 2014 based on over-requesting data, Facebook failed to review whether the app was then in compliance with existing Platform Policy
Facebook took no enforcement action against the TYDL App until December 2015, 18 months after it should have been apparent the app was violating policies
Facebook failed to provide evidence that monitoring and enforcement resulted in meaningful prevention of unauthorized access to and use of user information
Facebook did not proactively monitor whether apps were planning to use information in line with Platform Policy before disclosure occurred (pre-App Review)

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Clause 4.1.4(a) and PIPA Section 4(2) require organizations to implement policies and practices to give effect to privacy principles and take responsibility for personal information under their control
regulatoryFindings.description: Facebook abdicated responsibility for personal information under its control, shifting responsibility to users and apps
violations: Facebook abdicated responsibility for personal information under its control, shifting responsibility to users and apps
Facebook's purported safeguards were superficial and ineffective; the consent and safeguard regimes resulted in unauthorized access to millions of users' information
Facebook did not implement meaningful policies and practices despite previous 2009 OPC investigation findings and commitments
Facebook did not take real responsibility for the vast amounts of sensitive personal information within its control
Facebook only investigated the TYDL App and alerted users in 2018 following media coverage, not when violations should have been apparent or detected
Facebook did not notify users of the TYDL App's violation of contractual safeguards or the unauthorized access to 87 million users' information until forced by media and regulatory investigations

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada and the Information and Privacy Commissioner for British Columbia jointly concluded that Facebook violated PIPEDA and PIPA in multiple respects. The regulators found that Facebook: (1) failed to obtain meaningful consent from Installing Users; (2) failed to obtain adequate consent from Affected Users (friends of app installers); (3) had inadequate safeguards to protect user information from unauthorized access and use; and (4) failed to implement policies and practices to give effect to privacy principles, demonstrating a lack of accountability. The investigation revealed that approximately 300,000 Installing Users and 87 million Affected Users worldwide (including 622,000 users in Canada) had their personal information disclosed to the TYDL App, which subsequently used the data for political micro-targeting purposes through Cambridge Analytica. The report expressed serious concerns about Facebook's failure to implement meaningful recommendations from the OPC's 2009 investigation and found that the privacy protection framework was fundamentally empty and ineffective. While Facebook made recommendations for compliance, Facebook rejected or refused to implement the regulators' recommendations in any acceptable manner. The regulators emphasized the high risk that Canadians' personal information would continue to be disclosed to apps and used in ways users do not expect or know about.
companyNow: Facebook (now Meta Platforms, Inc.) remains one of the world's largest social media companies with billions of users, though it has faced increased regulatory scrutiny and rebranded to Meta in 2021 to reflect its focus on metaverse development.
dataType: Profile information (name, gender, Facebook ID, profile pictures, cover photos, networks), birthdate, current city, pages liked, friends list, private messages, email addresses, photos, posts, behavioural data
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Clause 4.3.2 (Reasonable Effort to Advise of Purposes)

companyDescription: Loblaw Companies Limited is Canada's largest retailer, operating grocery stores and pharmacies across the country. The company is a major player in Canadian retail and food distribution.
companyLongDescription: Loblaw Companies Limited is Canada's leading food and pharmacy retailer, with a network of stores operating under banners including Loblaws, No Frills, Shoppers Drug Mart, and others. Founded in 1919, Loblaw operates across Canada with hundreds of locations and millions of customers. The company provides grocery, pharmacy, and general merchandise retail services to Canadian consumers and is a major employer and economic force in the country.
caseDescription: Loblaw collected excessive personal information from gift card registrants by requesting full copies of identification documents when only name and address were necessary for fraud prevention and eligibility verification. While the company subsequently clarified its requirements to allow redaction of sensitive information, the initial over-collection violated PIPEDA's minimization principle. The complaint regarding cross-border data transfers to a U.S. processor was found to have adequate contractual safeguards and sufficient transparency.
violationSummary: Loblaw's initial failure to specify what information could be redacted from identification documents resulted in collection of more personal information than necessary for the stated purposes of eligibility verification and fraud prevention, constituting unnecessary interrogation and collection beyond what the program required.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Loblaw requested full unredacted copies of identification documents from gift card registrants without clearly specifying that sensitive information could be removed.
whyTheyWereWrong: Canadians submitting identification documents were unknowingly providing driver's license numbers, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: Registrants were informed they could redact sensitive information from identification documents
claimsVsReality.reality: Initial communications did not clearly specify what could be redacted, resulting in many registrants submitting full unredacted documents with unnecessary sensitive identifiers

claimsVsReality.claim: The company only needed name and address for verification purposes
claimsVsReality.reality: Loblaw collected complete driver's licenses and utility bills containing information beyond what was necessary, including driver's license numbers and other identifying details

claimsVsReality.claim: Cross-border transfers to U.S. processor had adequate safeguards
claimsVsReality.reality: While contractual protections were deemed sufficient by the regulator, registrants were not clearly informed upfront about data transfers to the United States and El Salvador before being asked to provide identification

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.4 - Collection of personal information shall be limited to that which is necessary for the purposes identified by the organization
regulatoryFindings.description: Loblaw initially requested full unredacted copies of identification documents (including driver's licence numbers and photographs) when only name and residential address were necessary to verify eligibility and prevent fraud
violations: Loblaw initially requested full unredacted copies of identification documents (including driver's licence numbers and photographs) when only name and residential address were necessary to verify eligibility and prevent fraud

Loblaw failed to inform registrants that sensitive information such as driver's licence numbers could be redacted, resulting in unnecessary collection of excess personal data from individuals who submitted full document scans

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.1.3 - Organizations are responsible for personal information transferred to third parties and must use contractual means to provide comparable level of protection
regulatoryFindings.description: Investigation found no violation; Loblaw had detailed contractual safeguards with Program Administrator including encryption, access controls, incident response procedures, and audit rights
violations: Investigation found no violation; Loblaw had detailed contractual safeguards with Program Administrator including encryption, access controls, incident response procedures, and audit rights

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.8 - Organizations must make readily available specific information about policies and practices relating to personal information management
regulatoryFindings.description: Investigation found no violation; Loblaw's Program Privacy Policy adequately disclosed cross-border transfers to United States and other jurisdictions, including notice about potential law enforcement access
violations: Investigation found no violation; Loblaw's Program Privacy Policy adequately disclosed cross-border transfers to United States and other jurisdictions, including notice about potential law enforcement access

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.3 - Knowledge and consent of individual required for collection, use or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: While initial over-collection occurred, Loblaw obtained express consent for collection of name and address information for stated purposes; no violation found for transfer of legitimately consented-to information for consistent purposes
violations: While initial over-collection occurred, Loblaw obtained express consent for collection of name and address information for stated purposes; no violation found for transfer of legitimately consented-to information for consistent purposes

outcome: The investigation found the collection of excess identification information to be well-founded and resolved after Loblaw publicly clarified that only name and address were required and that other information could be redacted. Loblaw revised its communication to registrants and updated its Q&A website accordingly. The complaints regarding cross-border data transfers and transparency were found to be not well-founded, as Loblaw demonstrated adequate contractual protections with third-party processors and sufficient disclosure of its data handling practices in its Program Privacy Policy.
companyNow: Loblaw remains Canada's largest retailer and continues to operate extensive grocery and pharmacy networks across the country. The company has expanded its digital presence and e-commerce offerings in recent years.
dataType: Name, residential address, date of birth, telephone number, email address, government-issued identification (driver's licence, utility bills)
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.1.3 (Accountability for third-party processing)

companyDescription: AggregateIQ Data Services Ltd. is a British Columbia-based political data services company that provided election and campaign-oriented software, website development, and digital advertising services to political campaigns globally.
companyLongDescription: Founded in 2013 and incorporated in Victoria, British Columbia, AggregateIQ specialized in providing targeted advertising, data processing, and database management services for political campaigns in multiple jurisdictions including Canada, the UK, and the US. The company worked with high-profile campaigns including Brexit referendum campaigns and US presidential campaigns, utilizing personal information including psychographic profiles derived from Facebook data obtained through third-party apps and intermediaries like Cambridge Analytica and SCL Elections.
caseDescription: AggregateIQ, a British Columbia-based political data services company, failed to obtain adequate consent for its collection, use, and disclosure of personal information on behalf of multiple political campaigns globally. The company processed personal information including sensitive political opinions and psychographic profiles derived from Facebook data without ensuring meaningful consent, and maintained inadequate security measures resulting in exposure of data on an unsecured GitLab repository affecting approximately 35 million individuals.
violationSummary: AggregateIQ used personal information for purposes beyond those for which individuals originally consented. Specifically, it disclosed voter information to Facebook for targeted advertising and lookalike audience analytics without consent addressing these secondary uses, and used psychographic and sensitive data from disparate sources (including improperly obtained Facebook data) for political microtargeting without verifying consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: AggregateIQ collected, used, and disclosed personal information including political opinions.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 35 million people's personal information—including their political opinions and psychographic profiles—was exposed to unauthorized access because AggregateIQ failed to secure it.

claimsVsReality.claim: AggregateIQ relied on consent provided by individuals to their political campaign clients for all uses of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: For most campaigns examined, either the consent did not address all of AggregateIQ's work or AggregateIQ was unaware of whether or how individuals had consented; for US campaigns, AggregateIQ did not even attempt to determine whether consent existed.

claimsVsReality.claim: AggregateIQ maintained adequate security measures to protect personal information in its custody.
claimsVsReality.reality: AggregateIQ stored sensitive data including personal information, encryption keys, and login credentials for 35 million people on an unsecured GitLab repository, exposing it to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: AggregateIQ's use of voter information aligned with the purposes for which individuals originally consented.
claimsVsReality.reality: For Vote Leave and US campaigns, AggregateIQ disclosed personal information to Facebook for custom audiences advertising and lookalike audience analysis without adequate consent covering these specific uses.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPA Section 6 and PIPEDA Principle 4.3: Organizations must obtain knowledge and consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information. Consent must be meaningful and address the specific purposes for which information will be used.
regulatoryFindings.description: AggregateIQ used and disclosed Vote Leave supporter data to Facebook for custom audiences and lookalike audience targeting without adequate consent covering these secondary uses
violations: AggregateIQ used and disclosed Vote Leave supporter data to Facebook for custom audiences and lookalike audience targeting without adequate consent covering these secondary uses
AggregateIQ collected and used personal information from SCL Elections for US political campaigns without any verification that consent had been obtained from individuals
AggregateIQ used personally identifiable information for social media advertising disclosure without individuals having consented to disclosure to third-party platforms
AggregateIQ processed psychographic and sensitive data (ethnicity, religion, political opinions) derived from Facebook without verifying consent from data subjects
For Canadian campaigns, AggregateIQ performed social media advertising and analytics using lookalike audiences without consent extending beyond campaign communication purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPA Sections 12(2), 15(2), 18(2) and PIPEDA Principle 4.3: When processing personal information on behalf of another organization, the service provider must take reasonable measures to ensure the consent obtained by the original organization is adequate and covers the service provider's intended uses and disclosures.
regulatoryFindings.description: AggregateIQ relied on broad contractual clauses stating compliance with data protection laws rather than verifying actual consent from individuals for its specific data uses
violations: AggregateIQ relied on broad contractual clauses stating compliance with data protection laws rather than verifying actual consent from individuals for its specific data uses
AggregateIQ did not review consent language used by clients to verify third-party consent adequately covered its activities
AggregateIQ did not attempt to determine whether consent existed for its work with SCL and US campaigns
AggregateIQ failed to ensure express consent for sensitive information uses in political contexts where ethnicity, religion, and psychographic profiles were involved

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPA Section 34 and PIPEDA Principles 4.7 and 4.7.1: Organizations must make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal information in their custody from unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, modification, or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: AggregateIQ stored encryption keys, login credentials, and personal information of 35 million people in an unprotected and publicly accessible GitLab repository
violations: AggregateIQ stored encryption keys, login credentials, and personal information of 35 million people in an unprotected and publicly accessible GitLab repository
AggregateIQ failed to implement access controls, allowing a cybersecurity researcher to register with only an email address and download over 20,000 folders and 113,000 files
AggregateIQ failed to adequately segregate sensitive personal information from development repositories and backup systems
AggregateIQ did not conduct regular security audits to prevent unnecessary personal information storage in internet-accessible locations
AggregateIQ's security practices resulted in unauthorized exposure of US voter data including names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and dates of birth

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPA Section 35 and PIPEDA Principle 4.5: Organizations must delete personal information that is no longer necessary for legal or business purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: AggregateIQ retained personal information in the GitLab repository longer than necessary for business purposes, creating unnecessary vulnerability
violations: AggregateIQ retained personal information in the GitLab repository longer than necessary for business purposes, creating unnecessary vulnerability

outcome: AggregateIQ's investigation was found to be well-founded. The company was ordered to implement compliance measures including: (1) taking reasonable measures to verify that third-party consent relied upon for collection, use, and disclosure of personal information complies with PIPA and PIPEDA, including reviewing client consent language; (2) ensuring express consent is obtained for sensitive personal information and uses beyond reasonable expectations; (3) implementing and maintaining reasonable security measures to protect personal information, including the specific remedial measures outlined (improved employee training, technical safeguards, regular audits, new post-project removal policies, enhanced server and repository security); and (4) deleting all personal information no longer necessary for legal or business purposes. AggregateIQ committed to implementing all recommendations. The Privacy Commissioners agreed to engage with AggregateIQ in approximately 6 months to obtain evidence of implementation. The matter was conditionally resolved pending verification of compliance.
companyNow: AggregateIQ agreed to implement the privacy regulators' recommendations following the 2019 investigation, including measures to ensure adequate consent and implement reasonable security measures. The company's current operational status is not specified in the document.
dataType: Names, email addresses, postal codes, phone numbers, donation history, political opinions, ethnicity, gun ownership, religious affiliation, marital/parental status, vehicle ownership, psychographic profiles (OCEAN personality traits), voter intention data, IP addresses
legalBasisViolated: PIPA Section 12(2) (collection on behalf of another organization)
PIPA Section 15(2) (use on behalf of another organization)
PIPA Section 18(2) (disclosure on behalf of another organization)
PIPEDA Principle 4.3.6 (express consent for sensitive information)
PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1 (safeguards against loss, theft, unauthorized access)

companyDescription: TransUnion is a major consumer credit reporting agency that maintains credit files and histories for Canadian consumers and provides credit information to financial institutions and authorized parties.
companyLongDescription: TransUnion is a global provider of credit information, analytics, and identity verification services. In Canada, it operates as a consumer credit reporting agency maintaining credit files and credit histories for millions of Canadian consumers. The company provides credit reports and related services to financial institutions, employers, landlords, and other authorized users. TransUnion manages sensitive personal financial data including payment history, debt levels, and contact information.
caseDescription: TransUnion disclosed a consumer's credit file information to Statistics Canada without the consumer's consent. The consumer alleged that Statistics Canada subsequently shared this information with other government institutions and used it to initiate debt collection efforts. The investigation found that TransUnion's disclosure was lawful under PIPEDA exemptions and that there was no evidence Statistics Canada improperly shared the information.
violationSummary: While the disclosure occurred, it was found to be authorized under PIPEDA section 7(3)(c.1)(iii), which permits disclosure to government institutions without consent when the institution has lawful authority and the disclosure is to administer a law. The allegation of improper secondary disclosure by Statistics Canada was not substantiated.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: TransUnion disclosed a consumer's credit file information to Statistics Canada without the consumer's consent under a legal request authorized by the Statistics Act.
whyTheyWereWrong: The consumer's credit information was accessed and he subsequently received debt collection calls, raising concerns that his data was misused despite contractual safeguards meant to protect it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Statistics Canada would use the information for statistical purposes only and would not impact any individual's credit score
claimsVsReality.reality: The consumer received debt collection calls approximately two months after Statistics Canada first accessed his file, suggesting potential misuse despite claimed contractual safeguards

claimsVsReality.claim: TransUnion did not create a new technical process to provide the information to Statistics Canada; it used existing systems
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of the system used, the disclosure occurred without the consumer's knowledge or consent, raising privacy concerns about the ease of access

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA section 7(3)(c.1)(iii) authorizes disclosure of personal information without knowledge or consent to a government institution that has made a request, identified lawful authority, and indicated the disclosure is to administer a law of Canada
regulatoryFindings.description: Complaint alleged unauthorized disclosure without consent, but investigation found disclosure was authorized under the exemption as Statistics Canada identified its lawful authority under section 13 of the Statistics Act and the purpose related to administering the Statistics Act
violations: Complaint alleged unauthorized disclosure without consent, but investigation found disclosure was authorized under the exemption as Statistics Canada identified its lawful authority under section 13 of the Statistics Act and the purpose related to administering the Statistics Act

regulatoryFindings.act: Statistics Act section 13 authorizes the Chief Statistician to obtain documents or records from organizations for statistical purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Statistics Canada lawfully accessed credit information from TransUnion pursuant to this authority; no violation found
violations: Statistics Canada lawfully accessed credit information from TransUnion pursuant to this authority; no violation found

outcome: The complaint was determined to be not well-founded. The Office concluded that TransUnion's disclosure of personal information to Statistics Canada was authorized under PIPEDA section 7(3)(c.1)(iii) because Statistics Canada identified its lawful authority under section 13 of the Statistics Act and indicated the disclosure was to administer that Act. The allegation that Statistics Canada improperly disclosed the information to other institutions for debt collection was not substantiated; no evidence supported this claim. Statistics Canada confirmed it did not share the complainant's information with other government institutions or private organizations. The Office noted concerns regarding Statistics Canada's transparency and proportionality in collecting the information, and Statistics Canada committed to implementing recommendations for redesigning its Credit Information Project.
companyNow: TransUnion continues to operate as one of Canada's major credit reporting agencies, providing credit information and analytics services to the financial services industry and authorized third parties.
dataType: Credit file information, financial history, contact information

companyDescription: Grey House Publishing Canada is a publishing company that produces annual print directories and maintains electronic databases containing business and organizational contact information for various sectors.
companyLongDescription: Grey House Publishing Canada compiles and markets annual print directories covering business, health, statistical and demographic fields, alongside electronic databases collectively called Canada's Resource Information Centre (CIRC). The company uses various methods including manual online research, questionnaires, and telephone communications to gather organizational and contact information. Grey House sells its directories, CIRC subscriptions, and data products to clients, including government departments.
caseDescription: Grey House Publishing Canada collected a complainant's personal information from a local association webpage and included it in its Associations Canada directory and database without obtaining consent. The company then sold an email distribution list containing this information to a federal government department, which used it to send unsolicited award promotion emails to the complainant.
violationSummary: Grey House engaged in systematic collection of personal information from publicly accessible websites through manual research and compilation, then used and disclosed that information without adequate consent, constituting surveillance-like collection practices.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Grey House Publishing Canada manually collected a complainant's contact information from a local association webpage without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant received unsolicited award promotion emails from a federal agency based on his information being sold without his knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant's information was 'business contact information' exempt from PIPEDA jurisdiction because he was the primary contact for the association.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant was no longer a director when his information was sold and was listed on the webpage solely for general inquiries, making it personal information subject to PIPEDA.

claimsVsReality.claim: Grey House was not conducting commercial activity; the information was collected for research purposes and provided to ESDC for non-commercial award promotion.
claimsVsReality.reality: Grey House sold directories and database access, and entered into a fee-based contract with ESDC to provide the email distribution list, making it a commercial activity.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant's information was 'publicly available' and Grey House could rely on implied consent without express authorization.
claimsVsReality.reality: The information being publicly available on a local webpage did not constitute consent for a third-party publisher to collect and resell it nationally, and no regulatory exception applied.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant had subscribed to Grey House's email distribution list, as stated by ESDC when sending award promotion emails.
claimsVsReality.reality: Grey House confirmed the complainant had never subscribed to any of its lists and his information was included without his knowledge.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Consent Requirement
regulatoryFindings.description: Grey House collected the complainant's personal information without express consent
violations: Grey House collected the complainant's personal information without express consent
Company relied on invalid implied consent based on information being 'publicly available'
The publicly available information exceptions in PIPEDA Regulations did not apply to the circumstances
The complainant could not reasonably expect his information would be collected, included in a national directory, and sold to third parties

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.8.1 – Openness
regulatoryFindings.description: Grey House's Privacy Statement contained only limited information
violations: Grey House's Privacy Statement contained only limited information
The statement did not adequately reflect the organization's actual privacy practices
Individuals could not easily acquire information about the company's collection and use practices

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 4(1)(a) – Commercial Activity
regulatoryFindings.description: Grey House was conducting commercial activity by compiling, marketing, and selling directories and database access
violations: Grey House was conducting commercial activity by compiling, marketing, and selling directories and database access
The company charged fees for email distribution lists provided to government departments
PIPEDA applied to the organization's collection, use, and disclosure of personal information

outcome: Grey House was found to have violated PIPEDA Principle 4.3 by collecting and using the complainant's personal information without adequate consent, and violated Principle 4.8.1 by maintaining an inadequate Privacy Statement. The company immediately removed the complainant's information from its database and agreed to revise its Privacy Statement to better reflect its privacy practices. The complainant confirmed receipt of no subsequent award mailings. Both matters were resolved through corrective action.
dataType: Name, email address, telephone number, business contact information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Section 2(1) – definition of personal information
PIPEDA Regulations Specifying Publicly Available Information – exceptions inapplicable

companyDescription: 411Numbers operates online telephone directory websites providing free access to names, addresses, and telephone numbers of individuals in Canada and other countries, generating revenue through advertising and removal fees.
companyLongDescription: 411Numbers is a telephone directory service operator incorporated in Hong Kong but owned and operated from Quebec, Canada. The company maintained databases of personal information sourced from third-party data brokers and published this information on country-specific websites (411numbers.ca, 411numbers-canada.com, and similar sites for 12+ other countries). It generated revenue primarily through advertising and secondarily through a paid removal service that charged individuals fees to de-index or remove their personal information from the websites.
caseDescription: 411Numbers operated online telephone directory websites that published personal information of individuals, including unlisted telephone numbers, without consent. The company also charged fees for removal services and required excessive documentation (passport, driver's license, utility bill) to remove information. 411Numbers was unresponsive to privacy complaints and maintained an inaccurate privacy policy.
violationSummary: 411Numbers systematically collected and published personal information including unlisted phone numbers without individual knowledge or consent, and made this information searchable and accessible to the public through its websites.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: 411Numbers published unlisted telephone numbers and personal information of individuals on its websites without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals' unlisted numbers were exposed online without permission, putting personal safety at risk—including a Canadian judge whose family faced security threats from the disclosure of his.

claimsVsReality.claim: 411Numbers stated the fee was only for Google de-indexing, not for removal from its database, which was always free.
claimsVsReality.reality: Screenshots of the 'Express Removal' service advertised immediate removal from the database for $19.99, plus Google de-indexing and ancillary services.

claimsVsReality.claim: 411Numbers claimed it obtained information exclusively from foreign-based companies and did not know how those companies obtained the data.
claimsVsReality.reality: 411Numbers purchased data from a US data broker with an 'F' rating from the Better Business Bureau, demonstrating poor due diligence on data source quality.

claimsVsReality.claim: 411Numbers asserted it was not subject to PIPEDA jurisdiction because it was incorporated in Hong Kong with servers outside Canada.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was owned and operated by an individual residing in Quebec, Canada, with a Quebec mailing address listed as its contact point, establishing a real and substantial connection to Canada.

claimsVsReality.claim: 411Numbers maintained that name, address, and telephone number information did not require consent because it was 'publicly available' information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Unlisted telephone numbers (which individuals had specifically requested not be published) do not qualify as publicly available information and required consent to collect and disclose.

claimsVsReality.claim: 411Numbers stated it used sampling processes to screen databases for unlisted numbers, involving approximately 1,000 manual samples and 100,000 automated samples.
claimsVsReality.reality: These sampling processes were undocumented and unverified, and the company admitted it could not fully update its database to ensure no unlisted numbers were provided.

claimsVsReality.claim: 411Numbers stated individuals could easily request removal of their information at no cost.
claimsVsReality.reality: Individuals faced great difficulty contacting the company, with unresponsive email addresses and were required to provide copies of passports, driver's licenses, and utility bills to verify their identity for removal requests.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires knowledge and consent for collection, use or disclosure of personal information except where inappropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: Published unlisted telephone numbers and associated personal information (name, address) without individual consent
violations: Published unlisted telephone numbers and associated personal information (name, address) without individual consent
Did not obtain consent despite unlisted numbers not being publicly available under the Regulations
Published information of Canadian judge and other individuals with unlisted numbers

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.3 prohibits requiring more information than necessary to fulfill explicitly specified and legitimate purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Required passport, driver's license, and utility bill copies for removal requests (May-September 2015)
violations: Required passport, driver's license, and utility bill copies for removal requests (May-September 2015)
Information required was excessive for purpose of verifying name and address
Later reduced requirement to utility bill only, then eliminated proof of identity requirement

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 5(3) requires organizations only collect, use or disclose personal information for purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: Used publication of personal information as mechanism to encourage paid removal fees
violations: Used publication of personal information as mechanism to encourage paid removal fees
Charged for removal of information that was posted without requisite consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principles 4.1, 4.1.2, 4.1.4, 4.8, 4.10 require accountability, openness, and ability to challenge compliance
regulatoryFindings.description: Sole owner/employee insufficiently aware of obligations under PIPEDA
violations: Sole owner/employee insufficiently aware of obligations under PIPEDA
Did not designate individual responsible for privacy compliance
Privacy policy contained multiple factual errors and inaccuracies
Unresponsive to privacy complaints and inquiries from individuals and regulator
Inadequate complaint handling procedures and staff training

outcome: 411Numbers agreed to: (1) remove personal information of all individuals with unlisted phone numbers from all websites within specified timeframes (90 days for Canadian sites, 45 days for France/Germany/Italy/Netherlands/Spain/US, 30 days for Australia/Belgium); (2) implement due diligence measures to ensure future listings from third parties do not contain unlisted numbers; (3) verify listings against Whitepages; (4) revise privacy policy to accurately describe personal information handling; (5) establish procedures to receive and handle privacy complaints; (6) provide PIPEDA training to all employees; (7) submit proof of compliance including list of removed numbers and computer algorithm used. The Office will monitor and review corrective actions on agreed timeline.
companyNow: 411Numbers ceased its paid removal service practice and agreed to remove all data associated with unlisted numbers from its websites following the PIPEDA investigation.
dataType: Name, address, telephone number (including unlisted numbers)

companyDescription: Idameneo (No.123) Pty Limited is an Australian private company. Limited public information is available about its operations.
companyLongDescription: Idameneo (No.123) Pty Limited is a private Australian entity that became subject to a privacy complaint under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth). The company was involved in a dispute regarding access to personal information held by it. The determination by the Office of the Australian Information Commissioner (OAIC) found that while the company refused access, no breach of APP 12 occurred because either an exception to access obligations applied or alternative means of access were available to the complainants.
caseDescription: A complaint was filed regarding refusal to provide access to personal information under APP 12 of the Australian Privacy Principles. The OAIC determined that the entity did not breach APP 12 because an exception to access obligations applied or alternative means of access were available.
violationSummary: The complaint alleged a breach of access rights, which falls under the Exclusion category as it concerns the individual's ability to access information held about them.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Idameneo refused to provide access to personal information held about two individuals in response to access requests under APP 12 of the Australian Privacy Principles.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individuals were denied access to their own personal information without a valid legal basis, preventing them from knowing what data was held about them and by whom.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 12 – Australian Privacy Principles requiring organisations to provide individuals with access to personal information held about them, with exceptions for certain circumstances

outcome: The OAIC determined no breach of APP 12. The entity's refusal to provide access was justified under an exception to the access obligation, or alternative means of access were available to the complainants.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified type)

companyDescription: Spotless Group is an Australian contract services company providing facilities management, cleaning, and hospitality services across commercial and institutional sectors.
companyLongDescription: Spotless Group Limited is a major Australian contractor specializing in facilities management, cleaning services, and hospitality operations for commercial, healthcare, and institutional clients. The company manages significant volumes of customer and employee personal information as part of its service delivery. Spotless operates multiple business lines and subsidiaries across Australia, serving large enterprise clients and government institutions.
caseDescription: Spotless Group breached Australian privacy principles NPP 2 (disclosure) and NPP 4 (security) when handling personal information. The OAIC determined the company improperly disclosed personal data and failed to adequately secure it. The company was ordered to pay compensation and undertake independent privacy compliance reviews.
violationSummary: The primary breach involves unauthorized or improper disclosure of personal information under NPP 2, combined with security failures under NPP 4, which constitutes both a disclosure and insecurity violation.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Spotless Group improperly disclosed personal information and failed to implement adequate security measures to protect customer data from unauthorized access or loss.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' personal information was exposed to unauthorized disclosure and insufficient security protections, leaving their sensitive data vulnerable to misuse and breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: Spotless Group maintained adequate privacy protections and secure handling of personal information in accordance with Australian Privacy Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company breached NPP 2 by improperly disclosing personal information and breached NPP 4 by failing to implement adequate security measures to protect data.

regulatoryFindings.act: NPP 2 – Personal information must not be disclosed without consent or as required/authorized by law
regulatoryFindings.description: Improper disclosure of personal information held by Spotless Group
violations: Improper disclosure of personal information held by Spotless Group

regulatoryFindings.act: NPP 4 – Personal information must be protected by reasonable security safeguards
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate security measures failed to prevent unauthorized access or disclosure of personal data
violations: Inadequate security measures failed to prevent unauthorized access or disclosure of personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: NPP 1.3 – Individuals must be notified when personal information is collected
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to provide adequate notice of collection practices
violations: Failure to provide adequate notice of collection practices

outcome: The OAIC determined breaches of NPP 2 and NPP 4. Spotless Group was ordered to provide a written apology, pay compensation of $3,000–$6,000 per affected individual for non-economic loss (including aggravation), and commission an independent review of current privacy compliance across the organization including all subsidiaries. Implementation of recommendations is to be independently assessed after 6 months.
companyNow: Spotless Group remains a significant player in Australian facilities management, though the company has undergone restructuring and ownership changes since the 2019 enforcement action.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified types)
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) – NPP 2 (Disclosure of personal information)
Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) – NPP 4 (Security of personal information)
Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) – NPP 1.3 (Notice of collection of personal information)

companyDescription: Commonwealth Bank of Australia is Australia's largest bank by market capitalisation and a major financial services provider.
companyLongDescription: Commonwealth Bank of Australia Limited is Australia's largest bank by assets and market capitalisation, providing retail banking, business banking, institutional banking, and wealth management services. The bank serves millions of customers across Australia and internationally. CBA is a publicly listed company on the Australian Securities Exchange and is a systemically important financial institution in Australia.
caseDescription: Commonwealth Bank of Australia breached APP 10.2 by failing to ensure the quality of personal information it disclosed. The bank provided inaccurate or unreliable personal information, causing non-economic loss to the complainant. The OAIC ordered the bank to pay damages and implement remedial measures.
violationSummary: APP 10.2 requires Australian Privacy Principles entities to take reasonable steps to ensure personal information is accurate, up-to-date, and complete. The bank's breach involved disclosing information that did not meet these quality standards, constituting an insecurity violation where personal information was not properly maintained.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies

claimsVsReality.reality: The bank disclosed inaccurate and unreliable personal information to the complainant, causing non-economic loss

outcome: Commonwealth Bank of Australia ordered to pay damages of AUD $15,000 for non-economic loss, issue an apology, undertake changes to its policies and operational processes and procedures, obtain independent assessment of the effectiveness of amended policies, and provide an independent report to the OAIC.

companyDescription: TICA Default Tenancy Control is an Australian property management company specializing in tenancy control and rental compliance services.
companyLongDescription: TICA Default Tenancy Control operates in the Australian hospitality and property management sector, providing tenancy control services to landlords and property managers. The company collects and maintains tenant personal information as part of its core business operations. In 2019, the company was found to have breached privacy obligations by failing to maintain adequate data quality standards for personal information it held.
caseDescription: TICA Default Tenancy Control breached Australian Privacy Principle 1.5 by collecting and handling tenant personal information without proper data quality standards. The company failed to take reasonable steps to ensure the accuracy, completeness, and currency of personal information collected from tenants.
violationSummary: The breach of NPP 1.5 and APP 10 relates to failure to maintain data quality and security standards, which falls under insecurity in the Solove taxonomy—the company did not adequately protect or maintain the integrity of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: TICA Default Tenancy Control collected and retained tenant personal information without implementing adequate data quality controls to ensure the information remained accurate.
whyTheyWereWrong: A tenant's personal information was retained inaccurately, exposing them to potential misuse, incorrect dealings, and loss of control over how their data was used by the company.

claimsVsReality.claim: TICA Default Tenancy Control maintained reasonable data quality standards for tenant information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to take reasonable steps to ensure personal information was accurate, complete, and current, resulting in a tenant's data being retained inaccurately.

regulatoryFindings.act: NPP 1.5 / APP 10 – Data Quality: Personal information must be accurate, complete, up-to-date, and relevant
regulatoryFindings.description: TICA Default Tenancy Control failed to take reasonable steps to ensure personal information collected from tenants was accurate and current
violations: TICA Default Tenancy Control failed to take reasonable steps to ensure personal information collected from tenants was accurate and current

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 5.2 – Notification: Collection of personal information must be accompanied by a privacy notice in an accessible location
regulatoryFindings.description: Company did not maintain a compliant privacy notice in a tenant-accessible section of its website
violations: Company did not maintain a compliant privacy notice in a tenant-accessible section of its website

outcome: The OAIC determined a breach of NPP 1.5 was substantiated. TICA Default Tenancy Control was ordered to: (1) provide a written apology, (2) pay $1,500 in compensation for non-economic loss, and (3) produce or update a privacy notice compliant with APP 5.2 in a tenant-accessible section of its website.
