companyDescription: Novelship is a Singapore-based e-commerce platform specializing in the buying and selling of luxury streetwear brands. The platform connects buyers and sellers while facilitating payment processing.
companyLongDescription: Novelship operates an online marketplace focused on luxury streetwear transactions, requiring users to create accounts and provide personal data for buyer or seller registration. The company acts as a facilitator, processing payments on behalf of transacting parties through an external payment processor. Novelship collects and processes sensitive seller information including names, addresses, email addresses, and banking details. The platform was launched without adequate pre-launch security testing, exposing it to critical vulnerabilities.
caseDescription: Novelship, an e-commerce platform for luxury streetwear, failed to conduct adequate security testing before launching its website, resulting in a vulnerability that allowed an unauthorized seller to access the personal data of six other sellers. The organization did not perform vulnerability scanning for OWASP Top Ten vulnerabilities, which would have detected the URL manipulation vulnerability exploited in the incident. Upon discovery, Novelship implemented remedial measures including fixing the vulnerability and redacting bank information.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement adequate security measures and testing protocols to protect personal data from unauthorized access, resulting in actual breach of six individuals' sensitive information including financial details.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Novelship failed to conduct adequate security testing before launching its e-commerce website, omitting vulnerability scanning for OWASP Top Ten vulnerabilities that would have detected the URL.
whyTheyWereWrong: A malicious seller used the undetected URL vulnerability to access the personal data—including names, email addresses, shipping addresses, hashed passwords.

claimsVsReality.claim: Novelship conducted adequate security testing before website launch.
claimsVsReality.reality: Testing was limited to design and functionality issues; no vulnerability scanning for OWASP Top Ten vulnerabilities was performed, allowing a URL manipulation vulnerability to remain undetected for eight months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Seller personal data was adequately protected on the platform.
claimsVsReality.reality: An unauthorized seller exploited the undetected URL vulnerability to access the personal data of six other sellers, including names, emails, addresses, hashed passwords, and bank account numbers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24 - Protection Obligation requires organisations to protect personal data from unauthorised access through reasonable security measures
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct adequate security testing before website launch
violations: Failed to conduct adequate security testing before website launch
Limited testing to design and functionality only, excluding vulnerability scanning
Did not scan for OWASP Top 10 vulnerabilities
URL manipulation vulnerability was not detected and remained exploitable for eight months
Six sellers' personal data including names, emails, addresses, hashed passwords, and bank account numbers were accessed without authorization

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found Novelship in breach of the Protection Obligation under Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012. The organization was directed to pay a financial penalty of S$4,000 within 30 days. No other directions were required as Novelship had already implemented necessary remedial measures including fixing the vulnerability, redacting bank information, and committing to develop a new website.
companyNow: Novelship continues to operate as a luxury streetwear e-commerce platform in Southeast Asia. Following the 2019 breach, the company committed to developing a new website and implemented enhanced security measures including vulnerability fixes and banking data redaction.
dataType: Names, email addresses, shipping addresses, hashed passwords, bank account numbers
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24 (Protection Obligation)

companyDescription: Interauct! operated an online mobile number auction platform for a telecommunications provider from 2000 to 2018. The company engaged a vendor for web hosting services.
companyLongDescription: Interauct! Pte Ltd was a Singapore-based technology company that operated an online mobile number auction system for a major telecommunications provider, starting in 2000 and concluding operations in 2018. The company relied on third-party vendor infrastructure for web hosting and server management. During server migrations in 2012 and 2016, Interauct! created backup files containing participant personal data but failed to delete these backups after migrations were complete, resulting in unnecessary data retention.
caseDescription: Interauct! operated an online mobile number auction and retained backup files containing personal data of auction participants long after server migrations were complete. In April 2019, a vendor misconfiguration exposed approximately 8,750 individuals' personal data on an internet sub-domain, though access required complex URLs and only the telecommunications provider actually accessed the files. The organisation deleted the files within three hours of discovery and remediated the vendor's misconfiguration within six hours.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to delete personal data after it was no longer needed (retention limitation breach), creating unnecessary risk. While reasonable security measures were in place, the primary violation stems from improper data retention practices that exposed sensitive personal data to potential unauthorised access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Interauct! retained backup files containing personal data of 8,750 auction participants long after server migrations were complete.
whyTheyWereWrong: The prolonged retention of unnecessary backup files exposed sensitive personal data including names, ID numbers, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: The backup files needed to be retained on vendor servers for operational purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Organisation admitted there was no reason to retain the Files after migration exercises were completed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The exposed files were protected by reasonable security measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: While URL complexity provided some protection, the files remained unnecessarily accessible on internet-facing infrastructure due to vendor misconfiguration, and only remained uncompromised because the complex URLs happened not to be discovered by unauthorized parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 25 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 – Retention Limitation Obligation requires organisations to retain personal data only as long as necessary for the purposes for which it was collected.
regulatoryFindings.description: Interauct! retained backup files containing personal data of auction participants after server migration exercises were completed in 2012 and 2016, with no legitimate reason to continue storing them
violations: Interauct! retained backup files containing personal data of auction participants after server migration exercises were completed in 2012 and 2016, with no legitimate reason to continue storing them
The files remained on vendor servers until discovered in April 2019, unnecessarily prolonging exposure risk for approximately 8,750 individuals

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to Interauct! for breach of the Retention Limitation Obligation under Section 25 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012. No monetary penalty was imposed. The organisation remedied the breach by deleting all files within three hours of discovery and ensuring the vendor fixed the server misconfiguration within six hours. No further directions were required as the breach had been fully remedied.
companyNow: Interauct! ceased operating the auction in 2018 and was under investigation by Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission in 2019. The company's current status is unknown.
dataType: Name, ID number (passport/NRIC), mobile number, address, date of birth, email address
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 25 (Retention Limitation Obligation)

companyDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club is a private country club located in Singapore offering recreational and hospitality facilities to members.
companyLongDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club is a membership-based private country club in Singapore providing hospitality, recreational facilities, and amenities to its members. The club operates various facilities and maintains an electronic direct mail system for member communications. As a private club, it collects and maintains personal data of its members for operational and communication purposes.
caseDescription: Tanah Merah Country Club's electronic direct mail system was compromised due to weak password controls, allowing unauthorised access and spam emails to be sent. The organisation used a weak, unchanging password shared across multiple staff and vendors since 2010, with no password management protocols in place.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal data in its EDM system. Weak password controls, password sharing, and lack of password expiry/strength enforcement constitute failures in organisational and technical security measures required under PDPA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Tanah Merah Country Club's electronic direct mail system was compromised due to a weak, unchanging password (the organisation's initials.
whyTheyWereWrong: The weak password controls allowed unauthorised access to the EDM system, resulting in spam emails being sent to members.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation maintained secure access controls for its electronic direct mail system.
claimsVsReality.reality: The EDM system used a single weak password (initials + '2010') shared among multiple staff and a vendor, unchanged since 2010, with no password management protocols.

claimsVsReality.claim: The means of unauthorised access could not be determined.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the specific attacker was not identified, investigation evidence pointed directly to the weak password control as the cause of the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to put in place reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised or accidental access, processing, alteration, loss or destruction
regulatoryFindings.description: Weak password using only organisation initials and year 2010
violations: Weak password using only organisation initials and year 2010
Password not changed since 2010
Password shared among at least 3 persons without access controls
No arrangements in place to enforce password strength, expiry, or protection
Failure to implement adequate access controls to the EDM system

outcome: The Organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of $4,000 (reduced on reconsideration from $8,000) within 30 days. The penalty was reduced based on the Organisation's prompt cooperation with the investigation and swift remedial measures. No further directions were issued given the remediation undertaken.
dataType: Email addresses, personal contact information

companyDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry is a Singapore-based ferry operator providing fast ferry services. The company operates passenger transport services in the Singapore region.
companyLongDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry Pte. Ltd. is a transportation company based in Singapore that provides fast ferry services to customers in the region. The company handles customer bookings and personal data including names, contact information, and travel preferences. Despite claiming to implement security measures such as regular anti-virus updates, the organization failed to implement fundamental password management practices, leaving customer data vulnerable to compromise.
caseDescription: Horizon Fast Ferry's email account was compromised by malware and used to send phishing emails to three customers. The organization failed to implement adequate security measures, including sharing an unchanged password among 11 employees for nearly 3 years. The breach resulted in disclosure of customers' personal booking data through fraudulent emails.
violationSummary: The organization failed to maintain reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession. The shared, unchanged password and inadequate security practices created vulnerability to malware infection and unauthorized access, directly enabling the phishing incident.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Horizon Fast Ferry's email account was compromised by malware and used to send phishing emails to three customers after the organization shared an unchanged password among 11 employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers received fraudulent phishing emails containing their own personal booking data, exposing them to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had implemented various security measures including updating anti-virus software regularly.
claimsVsReality.reality: The email account password was shared by 11 employees and had not been changed for almost 3 years, representing a critical security failure that undermined any other protective measures.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organizations to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or control
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement reasonable password management practices by allowing 11 employees to share a single email account password
violations: Failed to implement reasonable password management practices by allowing 11 employees to share a single email account password
Failed to rotate the shared password for approximately 3 years
Failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to prevent malware infection and unauthorized access to customer data

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection issued a warning to Horizon Fast Ferry Pte. Ltd. for breach of the Protection Obligation under PDPA Section 24. The organization was required to implement stronger security measures, including proper password management protocols and enhanced malware protection.
dataType: Email addresses, booking information, personal identifiers

companyDescription: Chan Brothers Travel is a Singapore-based travel and tourism company that operates a customer-facing website for tour enquiries and bookings.
companyLongDescription: Chan Brothers Travel Pte Ltd is a Singapore travel and tourism operator that provides tour packages and travel services to customers. The company hosted its website on Salesforce Community Cloud to manage customer enquiries and feedback through online forms. In 2018, the company engaged a vendor to maintain the website but failed to properly assess the security implications of software updates.
caseDescription: Chan Brothers Travel's website automatically indexed and exposed personal data of approximately 5,593 individuals through search engines due to a misconfigured SEO feature introduced in a Salesforce software update. The organisation failed to understand the security implications of the 'Public' website setting and did not properly assess the new feature's impact on data protection.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security measures by not configuring security settings appropriately for the SEO feature and not assessing the implications of the public website access setting. This resulted in personal data being exposed through web search engines, representing a failure to maintain reasonable security safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Chan Brothers Travel's website automatically indexed and exposed personal data of 5,593 individuals through search engines after a Salesforce software update enabled a public SEO feature.
whyTheyWereWrong: Travel customers' names, email addresses, phone numbers, and some national ID numbers were searchable and cached on the internet, exposing them to identity theft, spam, phishing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Chan Brothers Travel claimed they did not receive notification from Salesforce about the SEO feature software release in March 2018.
claimsVsReality.reality: Salesforce published release notes on its website and the vendor Aodigy had received information about the release, making it unlikely that Salesforce would have omitted to notify the organisation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation may have tasked its vendor Aodigy with reviewing security configurations as part of general maintenance services.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation did not provide clear written instructions to Aodigy to assess the security configuration of the IT system, leaving the responsibility ambiguous.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organisations must implement and maintain reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to assess the security implications of the 'Public' website configuration
violations: Failed to assess the security implications of the 'Public' website configuration
Failed to understand the function and operation of the SEO feature introduced in the March 2018 software update
Did not configure security settings appropriately when the SEO feature was automatically enabled
Failed to provide clear instructions to the outsource vendor regarding security configuration review

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a Warning to Chan Brothers Travel for breaching Section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation took immediate steps to prevent recurrence of the incident. No compliance directions were required as the organisation demonstrated prompt voluntary notification and cooperation with the Commission's investigation.
dataType: Names, email addresses, mobile phone numbers, NRIC numbers

companyDescription: Zero1 Pte. Ltd. was a licensed Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) in Singapore providing mobile services to subscribers.
companyLongDescription: Zero1 was a Mobile Virtual Network Operator licensed to provide mobile telecommunications services in Singapore. The company partnered with Singtel and used third-party platforms to manage subscriber billing and account services. In 2019, during a platform migration to a new billing system, a technical error caused subscriber invoices to be sent to incorrect email addresses, affecting 118 customers.
caseDescription: Zero1, a Mobile Virtual Network Operator, suffered a data breach affecting 118 subscribers when invoices containing personal data were sent to unintended recipients. The incident was caused by Batch ID duplication during platform migration, resulting from inadequate pre-launch testing and insufficient controls to ensure unique Batch ID generation.
violationSummary: Personal data (invoices containing names, addresses, subscriber IDs, mobile numbers, charges, and call details) was exposed to unintended recipients due to system errors. This falls under Exposure in the Dissemination category, as the data became accessible to individuals not intended to receive it.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Zero1 sent 118 invoices containing subscriber personal data (names, addresses, phone numbers, call details) to wrong email addresses due to Batch ID duplication errors during platform migration.
whyTheyWereWrong: Subscribers received other customers' invoices exposing their names, addresses, mobile numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pre-launch testing was conducted to ensure the New Platform would function correctly.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only two test accounts were used instead of simulating the actual staggered migration scenario with high volumes of subscriber data, failing to detect the Batch ID duplication issue.

claimsVsReality.claim: Batch ID generation processes were designed to ensure unique identifiers.
claimsVsReality.reality: No safeguards like date/time stamps were included in Batch ID generation, allowing duplicate IDs to be issued when incomplete deletion occurred during data migration.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA 2012 Protection Obligation – Organisations must protect personal data in their possession against unauthorised or accidental access, processing, loss, destruction, or other forms of misuse
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to scope pre-launch testing adequately to simulate the staggered migration scenario
violations: Failed to scope pre-launch testing adequately to simulate the staggered migration scenario
Used only two test accounts instead of simulating expected high-volume usage patterns
Failed to implement adequate processes to ensure unique Batch ID generation (e.g., date/time stamps)
Did not identify and prevent Batch ID duplication that resulted in invoices being sent to wrong subscribers

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found both Zero1 and IP Tribe Pte Ltd in breach of the Protection Obligation under the PDPA 2012 and issued a Warning to each party. Both organisations had already taken remedial actions to address gaps in security arrangements, including implementation of date/time stamps in Batch ID generation. No further directions were required.
dataType: Name, address, subscriber ID, mobile number, mobile charges, international call details

companyDescription: Singapore Accountancy Commission is the regulatory body responsible for accountancy education and professional standards in Singapore, administering the Singapore Chartered Accountant Qualification programme.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Accountancy Commission (SAC) is a statutory board and professional regulator in Singapore that oversees accountancy education, training, and professional standards. It administers the Singapore Chartered Accountant Qualification (SCAQ) programme and maintains the register of Singapore Chartered Accountants. The organisation is responsible for ensuring compliance with accounting standards and professional ethics among its members and candidates.
caseDescription: Singapore Accountancy Commission mistakenly sent emails containing personal data of 6,541 SCAQ programme personnel and candidates to 41 unintended recipients between June and October 2019. The organization lacked robust processes, supervisory checks, and technical measures to prevent sending emails with personal data to unauthorized parties. Staff were not trained on data protection policies during induction.
violationSummary: The organization failed to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data against unauthorized access, demonstrating inadequate technical and administrative safeguards in email handling procedures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Singapore Accountancy Commission mistakenly sent emails containing personal data of 6,541 SCAQ programme personnel and candidates to 41 unintended recipients between June and October 2019.
whyTheyWereWrong: The organisation's lack of supervisory checks, technical measures, and staff training on data protection policies exposed sensitive information including National Registration numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data was being handled securely and staff were trained on data protection policies.
claimsVsReality.reality: Staff involved in sending emails had received no data protection training during induction, and there were no second-tier supervisory checks or technical measures to prevent accidental disclosure.

claimsVsReality.claim: Robust processes were in place to protect personal data when sending emails.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation lacked basic procedural safeguards, with data protection policies not translated into actual security arrangements or technical controls.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data in their possession or under their control against unauthorised access, processing, use, modification, disclosure or loss.
regulatoryFindings.description: No second-tier or supervisory checks implemented for email handling
violations: No second-tier or supervisory checks implemented for email handling
No technical measures in place to prevent sending personal data to unintended recipients
Staff not informed of personal data protection policies during induction training
Data protection policies not translated into practical security arrangements

outcome: Singapore Accountancy Commission was directed to pay a financial penalty of $5,000 within 30 days. The organization had admitted the breach, cooperated with the investigation, and undertaken remedial actions including cybersecurity training for all employees and revision of data handling policies and procedures. No further directions were issued in view of the remedial actions taken.
companyNow: Singapore Accountancy Commission continues to operate as the primary regulator of the accountancy profession in Singapore, now with enhanced data protection and cybersecurity measures following this incident.
dataType: Names, National Registration Identification Card numbers, dates of birth, contact details, education and employment information, examination results

companyDescription: FWD Singapore is a life insurance company operating in Singapore, offering insurance products and financial protection solutions.
companyLongDescription: FWD Singapore Pte Ltd is a subsidiary of FWD Group, a major insurance and financial services provider in Asia. The company provides life insurance, general insurance, and investment-linked products to customers across Singapore. FWD operates as part of a larger regional insurance group with significant operations throughout Asia-Pacific.
caseDescription: FWD Singapore unintentionally disclosed personal data of 71 individuals through 42 payment advice letters sent to incorrect recipients due to a logic error introduced during a system fix. The company failed to conduct adequate manual code review and unit testing. The data breach occurred between June and July 2019 and was voluntarily reported to the Commission.
violationSummary: The personal data (names and identification numbers) was exposed to unintended recipients through misdirected payment advice letters, making the information accessible to parties who should not have had access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: FWD Singapore sent 42 payment advice letters containing names and identification numbers of 71 individuals to incorrect recipients due to a logic error introduced during a system fix between.
whyTheyWereWrong: The personal data of 71 individuals was exposed to unintended recipients, compromising their privacy and exposing sensitive financial information without their consent or knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: The system fix was properly tested and deployed safely.
claimsVsReality.reality: A logic error introduced during the fix was not detected because manual code review and unit testing were not conducted to a reasonable standard.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's development processes were adequate to prevent data disclosure incidents.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's development processes failed to catch a logic error that caused personal data of 71 individuals to be sent to wrong recipients, requiring process improvements after the incident.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organisations must take reasonable steps to protect personal data in their possession or under their control against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct manual code review and unit testing to a reasonable standard when deploying a fix for a logic error, resulting in a second logic error that caused incorrect mailing addresses to be extracted and personal data to be sent to wrong recipients
violations: Failed to conduct manual code review and unit testing to a reasonable standard when deploying a fix for a logic error, resulting in a second logic error that caused incorrect mailing addresses to be extracted and personal data to be sent to wrong recipients

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to FWD Singapore. No monetary penalty was imposed. The organisation voluntarily notified the Commission of the incident and had successfully retrieved 67 out of 71 affected letters. The company implemented improvements to its development processes to prevent recurrence, and no further directions were required.
companyNow: FWD Singapore continues to operate as an insurance provider in Singapore, now part of the broader FWD Group which has expanded significantly across Asia since the 2019 incident.
dataType: Names, identification numbers, mailing addresses

companyDescription: Actstitude is a Singapore-based social media marketing agency that operates a resume upload platform for job applicants.
companyLongDescription: Actstitude Pte Ltd is a social media platform marketing agency based in Singapore that maintains a webpage for candidates to upload resumes as part of their recruitment process. The company failed to implement basic security controls on this resume repository, resulting in widespread exposure of personal data. Despite operating in a digital marketing space, the organization did not implement standard security practices such as pre-launch vulnerability scanning or periodic security reviews.
caseDescription: Actstitude, a social media marketing agency, failed to implement access controls on a resume upload webpage, allowing URLs to be manipulated to access other users' resumes. The lack of security testing and vulnerability scanning resulted in Google indexing the URLs, exposing the resumes of over 160 individuals.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data against unauthorised disclosure by not implementing access controls or conducting security testing, directly violating the protection obligation under PDPA.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Actstitude failed to implement access controls on its resume upload webpage, allowing URLs to be manipulated to access other users' resumes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 160 job applicants' resumes containing personal data were exposed through Google search results, allowing anyone to manipulate URLs and access sensitive employment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Actstitude maintained a secure resume upload service for job applicants.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no access controls on resume files, URLs could be manipulated to access other applicants' resumes, and over 160 resumes were indexed by Google and exposed publicly.

claimsVsReality.claim: Actstitude conducted appropriate security testing before launching the resume webpage.
claimsVsReality.reality: No vulnerability scanning was performed as part of pre-launch testing, and no periodic security reviews were conducted after the July 2018 launch.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation requires organisations to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data in their possession against unauthorised disclosure and other misuse
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement access controls on resume files
violations: Failed to implement access controls on resume files
Failed to conduct vulnerability scanning prior to website launch
Failed to conduct periodic security reviews
URLs were manipulable, allowing unauthorised access to other individuals' resumes
Google indexed the URLs, resulting in public disclosure of personal data

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection issued a warning to the Organisation. No directions were required as the Organisation had already taken corrective action to address the security gaps in its systems.
dataType: Resume data, personal identifiers (names)

companyDescription: Jean Yip Salon is a hair salon chain operating in Singapore. The company operates customer appointment booking systems and internal employee management systems.
companyLongDescription: Jean Yip Salon Pte Ltd is a retail hair and beauty salon business based in Singapore. The company maintains both customer-facing systems for appointment booking and internal employee systems for staff management. In 2019, the company's inadequate server configuration and weak security controls led to unintended public exposure of sensitive employee personal data, resulting in an enforcement action by Singapore's Personal Data Protection Commission.
caseDescription: Jean Yip Salon's employee system was publicly accessible on the internet due to inadequate server configuration and weak security controls, exposing the personal data of 28 individuals including NRIC numbers and residence status. The organisation failed to implement reasonable security measures including password policies, account management processes, and proper access controls. The breach was discovered via complaint and the organisation had already implemented corrective measures by the time of enforcement.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to adopt reasonable measures to protect personal data against unauthorised access, including lack of password policies, inadequate access controls, and poor server configuration management.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Jean Yip Salon publicly exposed an internal employee system on the internet without proper access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees' sensitive identity documents and residential information were accessible to the public, putting 28 individuals at risk of identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had secure systems protecting employee data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Opening a server to public access was intentional and limited to the customer booking system.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation opened public access without ascertaining what the server hosted, inadvertently exposing the internal employee system on the same server.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24 – Organisations must adopt reasonable measures to protect personal data against risks of unauthorised access

violations: Opened public access to server without ascertaining what data it hosted
Inadvertently exposed internal employee system due to poor access controls
Failed to implement password policies for user accounts
No processes to remove or deactivate unnecessary user accounts
Allowed access using default username and password credentials

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the Organisation in breach of section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 and issued a warning. No formal directions were required as the Organisation had already implemented corrective measures addressing the security gaps identified.
companyNow: Jean Yip Salon continues to operate in Singapore. Following the 2019 enforcement action, the company implemented corrective security measures to address the identified gaps.

companyDescription: SSA Group International is a Singapore-based training and course registration service provider. The company maintains a web-based system for managing course registrations and participant information.
companyLongDescription: SSA Group International is a Singapore-based educational services organization that offers course registration and training programs. The company operates a web-based platform where individuals register for courses and provide personal information during the enrollment process. The organization maintains databases of course registrants and their associated personal and transaction data. SSA Group International's primary business involves managing course registrations and coordinating training delivery for its client base.
caseDescription: SSA Group International publicly exposed 53 individuals' course registration information via an unprotected webpage that was indexed by search engines. The organisation failed to implement authentication mechanisms, provide security instructions to developers, or conduct security reviews, leaving the data accessible for over a year.
violationSummary: The personal data was exposed to the public without authorisation due to inadequate security controls. The webpage was freely accessible and indexed by search engines, making the data broadly discoverable.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: SSA Group International left a webpage containing 53 individuals' course registration information, names.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal data including names and course registration details of 53 individuals were exposed to anyone online for over a year, allowing potential identity misuse, targeted marketing.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Webpage had not been easy to locate.
claimsVsReality.reality: An online search of the names of the 53 affected individuals directly produced the Webpage's URL, making it easily discoverable.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Organization implemented adequate security measures to protect personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: No authentication mechanisms, no formal security instructions to developers, and no security reviews or vulnerability scanning were conducted for over a year after the webpage's creation in April 2018.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to adopt reasonable steps to protect personal data against unauthorised access
regulatoryFindings.description: No authentication mechanisms implemented to restrict access to the webpage
violations: No authentication mechanisms implemented to restrict access to the webpage
No formal security instructions provided to the webpage developer
No security reviews or vulnerability scanning conducted since webpage creation in April 2018
Webpage remained publicly accessible and searchable for over one year

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner issued a warning to the organisation. No formal directions were required as SSA Group International had already implemented corrective measures to address the security gaps, including implementation of authentication controls and security protocols.
dataType: Names, course registration information, course titles, sponsorship type, referral source, transaction dates

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited is a major telecommunications provider in Singapore offering mobile, broadband, and fixed-line services to consumers and businesses.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (now part of Singtel) is Singapore's largest integrated telecommunications company, providing mobile, broadband, fixed-line, and ICT services. The company has been a dominant player in Singapore's telecommunications sector since its founding. It serves millions of subscribers across Singapore and operates regional networks throughout Asia.
caseDescription: Singapore Telecommunications failed to adequately test its database migration system, resulting in a technical issue that exposed personal data of 750 mobile subscribers to unauthorized access for approximately 11 hours. The personal data of 39 subscribers were actually accessed by other subscribers, including mobile numbers, account details, and usage information. The incident occurred due to inadequate testing of timeout scenarios and failure to anticipate the risks posed by reassigned historical mobile numbers.
violationSummary: The organization failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access to personal data, specifically by not conducting thorough testing of the database migration system to identify and prevent the timeout-related routing flaw that allowed subscribers to view each other's data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Singapore Telecommunications failed to adequately test its database migration system, allowing 750 mobile subscribers to view other subscribers' personal data for approximately 11 hours on 20.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company's inadequate testing of timeout scenarios and failure to anticipate risks from reassigned historical numbers resulted in 39 real subscribers having their mobile numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The combination of factors causing the data breach was obscure and unforeseeable.
claimsVsReality.reality: Session timeouts were an anticipated scenario, and the company had full knowledge of how dummy numbers for porting were eventually reassigned to other subscribers—making the risk combination foreseeable and not obscure.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's system design properly intended to display an error message during timeouts.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system lacked adequate testing of timeout scenarios, which would have revealed that the Master Routing Database defaulted to querying the Existing System and retrieving unauthorized data instead of displaying an error message.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to carry out thorough testing to identify potential unintended effects of dummy numbers during system migration
violations: Failed to carry out thorough testing to identify potential unintended effects of dummy numbers during system migration
Test plan did not anticipate likely failure scenarios such as session timeouts
Inadequate security measures during database migration resulted in unauthorized disclosure of 39 subscribers' personal data and exposure of 750 subscribers' data to access risk

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found Singapore Telecommunications in breach of PDPA Section 24 and directed the organization to pay a financial penalty of SGD 9,000 within 30 days. No further remedial directions were imposed as the organization had completed its system migration on 19 August 2018 and implemented temporary fixes to prevent further unauthorized access.
companyNow: Singapore Telecommunications continues to operate as a major telecom provider in Singapore and the region, now part of the Singtel group, delivering integrated telecommunications services to millions of customers.
dataType: Mobile numbers, mobile plans, usage details, account numbers, add-on services

companyDescription: NTUC Income Insurance is a cooperative insurance company in Singapore providing various insurance products including life, health, and general insurance to customers.
companyLongDescription: NTUC Income Insurance Co-Operative Limited is a Singapore-based insurance provider offering a range of insurance solutions. The company operates a digital platform allowing customers to submit online enquiries and upload supporting documents. As a cooperative insurer, it operates under the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 in Singapore and is subject to regulatory oversight by the Personal Data Protection Commission.
caseDescription: NTUC Income Insurance failed to adequately protect personal data due to a coding error in its website's online enquiry application. The defect caused supporting documents uploaded by 17 users to be attached to acknowledgement emails sent to 123 other users, disclosing sensitive insurance information. The organization's manual code review and testing procedures failed to detect the vulnerability before deployment.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures to protect personal data, resulting in unintended disclosure through poor code quality and insufficient testing protocols.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: NTUC Income Insurance deployed a website application with a coding error that attached uploaded insurance documents from 17 users to acknowledgement emails sent to 123 other users.
whyTheyWereWrong: Insurance customers received emails containing other people's names, policy numbers, premium amounts, and addresses, exposing their financial and personal details without consent or knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: Manual code review and testing procedures would adequately detect vulnerabilities before deployment.
claimsVsReality.reality: A coding error that applied one user's file variable to another user's submission went undetected through manual review and was only caught after 17 users' documents were sent to 123 others.

claimsVsReality.claim: Test scenarios covered the various usage patterns customers would encounter.
claimsVsReality.reality: Tests did not simulate the scenario where some users upload files while others do not, which was the exact situation that triggered the vulnerability.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 requires organisations to implement administrative, physical and technical measures to protect personal data against unauthorised access, processing, use, modification, disclosure or loss.
regulatoryFindings.description: Poor quality code with a variable assignment bug that was not detected during manual code review
violations: Poor quality code with a variable assignment bug that was not detected during manual code review
Inadequate test scenarios that did not simulate real-world usage patterns where some users upload files and others do not
Lack of adequate quality assurance processes before deployment of the enhanced website application

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found the Organisation in breach of the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 and issued a warning. No formal directions were required as the Organisation has implemented corrective measures, including replacing manual code review with automated tools (Crucible and SonarQube) and establishing adequate test scenarios and reviews before IT system changes are deployed.
companyNow: NTUC Income Insurance continues to operate as a major cooperative insurer in Singapore, having implemented enhanced code review and testing procedures following the 2019 incident.
dataType: Names, policy numbers, premium amounts, sum assured, period of coverage, email addresses, mailing addresses
legalBasisViolated: Personal Data Protection Act 2012, Section 24 (Protection Obligation)

companyDescription: AXA Insurance is a major global insurance provider offering life, health, general and investment insurance products. In Singapore, it operates as AXA Insurance Pte. Ltd., serving thousands of policyholders.
companyLongDescription: AXA is one of the world's largest insurance groups, with operations across Europe, Asia-Pacific, and other regions. AXA Insurance Singapore offers comprehensive insurance solutions including motor, travel, home, and life insurance. The company manages significant customer data and policyholder information as part of its core insurance operations. In Singapore, it operates under the regulatory framework of the Monetary Authority of Singapore and the Personal Data Protection Commission.
caseDescription: AXA Insurance inadvertently disclosed personal data of 87 policyholders to an unintended recipient via email. The disclosure occurred because the organisation lacked proper processes to segregate internal documents from customer documents during scanning, and failed to verify attachments before sending. The Commission found the organisation breached its obligation to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement adequate security controls and processes to prevent inadvertent disclosure of personal data to unintended recipients, resulting in exposure of sensitive policyholder information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: AXA Insurance emailed personal data of 87 policyholders including names, NRIC numbers, and policy details to an unintended recipient due to lack of document segregation processes during scanning.
whyTheyWereWrong: Policyholders' sensitive identification numbers and policy information were exposed to an unauthorized person, creating risk of identity theft and unauthorized access to their insurance accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: AXA had processes in place to protect customer personal data during document scanning.
claimsVsReality.reality: AXA had no process to segregate internal documents from customer documents during scanning, allowing sensitive policyholder data to be mixed with other materials.

claimsVsReality.claim: AXA employees verified attachments before sending emails to customers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer care specialist failed to check the attachment before sending the email, resulting in unintended disclosure of 87 policyholders' personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24 - Protection Obligation: An organisation must make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement process to segregate documents intended for internal record purposes from documents for customers during scanning
violations: Failed to implement process to segregate documents intended for internal record purposes from documents for customers during scanning
Failed to verify Attachment contents before sending email to customer
Inadequate security arrangements enabled inadvertent disclosure of personal data of 87 policyholders

outcome: The Commission issued a warning to AXA Insurance. The organisation admitted liability and had taken corrective measures to address the lapses in processes that led to the breach.
companyNow: AXA remains a leading global insurer and continues operations in Singapore with enhanced data protection practices. The company has implemented corrective measures following this incident.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, insurance policy numbers, servicing agent details

company: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association
companyDescription: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association is a registered volunteer organisation comprising parents of students at Henry Park Primary School in Singapore.
companyLongDescription: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association is a registered society of parent volunteers serving the Henry Park Primary School community. The organisation operated a website built using WordPress by a parent volunteer to allow members to view their account information. The organisation collected and stored members' personal data including names, contact numbers, child names, and child class information on this website.
caseDescription: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association's website exposed members' personal data (names, contact numbers, child names and classes) to public search engines due to inadequate access controls and security testing. The data was crawled and indexed by Google despite the Organisation's belief that it was only accessible to logged-in members. The Organisation lacked adequate security arrangements, had not appointed a data protection officer, and had not implemented PDPA compliance policies.
violationSummary: The Organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements, resulting in unintended exposure of personal data to the public via Google search indexing. This represents a failure of information processing security controls leading to uncontrolled dissemination.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Henry Park Primary School Parents' Association's website exposed members' personal data including names, contact numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents and children's personal information became publicly searchable on Google, exposing families to potential contact by unknown third parties and creating privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation verified that account particulars could not be viewed by public users accessing the website.
claimsVsReality.reality: The personal data was successfully crawled, indexed, and made searchable by Google search engines despite these tests, indicating the access control protections were ineffective.

claimsVsReality.claim: Members' data was intended to be accessible only to logged-in members through user ID and password authentication.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data became publicly searchable online and was discovered by a member performing a routine Google search of her own name.

claimsVsReality.claim: Rudimentary login testing was sufficient to ensure data security.
claimsVsReality.reality: Proper security testing such as vulnerability scans would have identified the access control weakness before the website was launched.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 11(3) – Reasonable Security Arrangements
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct adequate security testing (e.g., vulnerability scans) before launching the website
violations: Failed to conduct adequate security testing (e.g., vulnerability scans) before launching the website
Access control weakness allowed Google to crawl and index member personal data despite intended login-only access
Rudimentary testing (manual verification of member and public access) was insufficient to identify the security flaw

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Appointment of Data Protection Officer
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to appoint any individual responsible for ensuring PDPA compliance
violations: Failed to appoint any individual responsible for ensuring PDPA compliance

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Data Protection Policies and Practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations
violations: Failed to develop and implement policies and practices necessary to meet PDPA obligations
No data protection training program for volunteers handling personal data

outcome: The Organisation was directed to: (1) appoint one or more individuals responsible for PDPA compliance within 60 days; (2) develop and implement internal data protection and training policies; and (3) provide data protection training to all volunteers handling personal data. The Organisation took remedial action by taking the website offline immediately after the incident and launching a new website on 14 November 2019 that no longer permitted online access to the members' database and included a data protection notice.
companyNow: The organisation took its original website offline after the March 2019 incident and launched a new website in November 2019 that no longer allows online database access, with added data protection notices.
dataType: Names, contact numbers, child names, child class information

companyDescription: SAFRA National Service Association is a Singapore-based membership organisation that operates recreational facilities including a shooting club for its members.
companyLongDescription: SAFRA (Singapore Armed Forces Association) National Service Association is a Singapore-based recreational and social organisation that provides facilities and programmes for members. The organisation operates various clubs and activities including a shooting club. At the time of the incident, SAFRA maintained digitalised membership records containing sensitive personal data of thousands of members.
caseDescription: An employee of SAFRA National Service Association accidentally disclosed personal data of 780 shooting club members to 491 members by failing to delete an Excel spreadsheet containing member information before sending mass emails. The Organisation had no documented process for sending mass emails and relied on verbal instructions, creating a manual process vulnerable to human error that had been in place since at least September 2016.
violationSummary: The Organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to prevent accidental disclosure of personal data. The manual email process with spreadsheet attachments created a foreseeable risk of exposure, and the Organisation's lack of documented procedures and process automation enabled the data breach.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: An employee sent two batches of mass emails with an Excel spreadsheet containing 780 members' full personal data (names, NRIC numbers, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 780 shooting club members had their sensitive personal data including NRIC numbers, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: A software glitch in the webmail system prevented the employee from deleting the spreadsheet attachment despite multiple attempts.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organisation's webmail service provider confirmed they had never encountered such an issue, and the Commission found on balance of probabilities that the employee simply failed to delete the attachment before sending the emails.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had provided verbal instructions to staff on data protection practices including checking for unnecessary attachments before sending emails.
claimsVsReality.reality: No documented processes existed for the monthly mass email task that had been ongoing since at least September 2016, and the organisation was unaware of the manual process the employee had actually been using.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, disclosure, copying, modification, and similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Organisation failed to implement documented procedures for mass email sending
violations: Organisation failed to implement documented procedures for mass email sending
Relied on verbal instructions only, which are insufficient for regular recurring tasks
Used manual process instead of available automation tools like mail-merge functions
Did not provide adequate training or oversight of the email process despite it occurring monthly since at least September 2016
Failed to implement process safeguards and technical solutions to prevent accidental disclosure

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found the Organisation had contravened PDPA Section 24. The Organisation was directed to: (1) pay a financial penalty of SGD $10,000 within 30 days; and (2) conduct a review of its email system and processes to implement process safeguards and written standard operating procedures to protect personal data within 120 days. The Organisation had already implemented remedial measures including masking NRIC numbers, circulating data protection guidelines, notifying affected members, setting up an incident response team, and planning to automate mass email sending.
companyNow: SAFRA continues to operate in Singapore as a major recreational organisation. Following this enforcement action, the organisation has implemented enhanced data protection measures, automated mass email systems, and stricter access controls to its databases.
dataType: Name, NRIC number, date of birth, address, telephone number, email address

companyDescription: PeopleSearch Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based subsidiary of a listed company providing professional recruitment and flexible staffing services in Asia, including outsourced payroll management.
companyLongDescription: PeopleSearch Pte. Ltd. operates as a business division of a Singapore-listed recruitment and staffing company, offering outsourced payroll management services to clients across Asia. The organization managed sensitive employee data including NRIC numbers, bank accounts, and salary information on a virtual machine server. In March 2019, the company suffered a ransomware attack that encrypted personal data of 944 individuals due to unaddressed security vulnerabilities. The company maintained good backup practices and promptly restored operations from a backup.
caseDescription: PeopleSearch suffered a ransomware attack on 1-2 March 2019 that encrypted personal data of 944 individuals (472 employees and 472 next of kin members) stored in a payroll software database. The organisation had failed to conduct security scans, penetration testing, or patching of the server for at least 12 months prior to the incident, leaving critical vulnerabilities that were exploited by the attacker.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements as required by Section 24 of the PDPA. Specifically, the absence of regular security testing, penetration testing, and patching of the VM Server for at least 12 months resulted in unpatched vulnerabilities that were exploited by the ransomware attack, causing unauthorised modification of sensitive personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: PeopleSearch failed to conduct security scans, penetration testing, or patching of its payroll server for at least 12 months.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unpatched server exposed sensitive personal data of 944 individuals including NRIC numbers, bank account numbers, salary details, and next-of-kin information to encryption.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ransomware attack was an unavoidable external security incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: Critical vulnerabilities existed because PeopleSearch had not conducted any security scans, penetration testing, or patching for at least 12 months—a failure of internal security governance, not an unpreventable external attack.

claimsVsReality.claim: The departure of an employee responsible for VM Server oversight excuses the security failures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Deputy Commissioner explicitly rejected this explanation, finding that organizations must have processes in place to ensure continuous security maintenance regardless of personnel changes.

claimsVsReality.claim: No harm occurred because there was no evidence of data exfiltration.
claimsVsReality.reality: 944 individuals' sensitive personal data (NRIC numbers, bank account numbers, salary details) was rendered inaccessible and vulnerable during the encryption, exposing them to identity theft and financial fraud regardless of whether exfiltration actually occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – An organisation must protect personal data in its possession or under its control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct any security scans, penetration testing, or patching of the VM Server for at least 12 months prior to the incident
violations: Failed to conduct any security scans, penetration testing, or patching of the VM Server for at least 12 months prior to the incident
No documented process in place to ensure regular security testing and patching
Vulnerabilities in the VM Server were exploited by ransomware attack resulting in unauthorised modification of personal data
Failure to implement adequate security measures for sensitive data including NRIC numbers and financial information (bank account numbers and salary details)

outcome: PeopleSearch was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 5,000 within 30 days. The organisation had already taken remedial actions including disabling remote desktop accounts, changing passwords, installing latest Windows server updates, and decommissioning the affected VM Server. The relatively modest penalty reflects mitigating factors including the organisation's regular backup practices (which allowed recovery within 2 days), prompt remedial actions, full cooperation with the Commission, absence of evidence of data exfiltration, and no reported harm to affected individuals.
companyNow: PeopleSearch incorporated its payroll business division into a separate legal entity on 1 April 2019 and decommissioned the affected server, continuing operations with improved security practices.
dataType: NRIC numbers, residential addresses, contact numbers, email addresses, bank account numbers, salary details, next of kin information (names, ages, contact numbers, relationship)

companyDescription: National Healthcare Group Pte Ltd is Singapore's leading public healthcare shared services provider, managing and coordinating clinical and administrative services across multiple healthcare institutions.
companyLongDescription: National Healthcare Group Pte Ltd is a Singapore-based healthcare organization that serves as an appointed public healthcare shared services provider. The organization operates websites and IT systems to support its partner doctors and public engagement. NHG contracted external vendors for website development and IT support services but maintained responsibility for data protection and security oversight of its systems.
caseDescription: National Healthcare Group failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data of 129 partner doctors and 5 members of the public contained in a website list that was accessible to the public via the Internet. A penetration test conducted in mid-2016 had identified the vulnerability and recommended remediation, but the organization failed to act on it for over a year until a doctor discovered the exposed list through a Google search in February 2018. The organization's failure to exercise adequate oversight regarding the penetration test findings and to ensure proper web configuration security measures constituted a breach of the Protection Obligation under the PDPA.
violationSummary: The violation involves failure to maintain reasonable security steps and arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and disclosure of personal data. The web configuration file lacked necessary access restrictions despite a vendor's explicit penetration test report identifying and recommending remediation of this vulnerability over a year before the unauthorized disclosure occurred.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: National Healthcare Group failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data of 129 partner doctors.
whyTheyWereWrong: The exposed list containing doctors' NRIC numbers, dates of birth, mobile numbers, email addresses, clinic addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT Services Provider and Website Developer were responsible for managing security vulnerabilities and the organization had appropriately delegated responsibility to them.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization retained legal responsibility under PDPA Section 24 regardless of vendor engagement; the penetration test report was available to the organization but remained unacted upon for over a year.

claimsVsReality.claim: The vulnerability was not sufficiently highlighted in the Penetration Test Report to warrant urgent action.
claimsVsReality.reality: The vulnerability was the first item in the report with clear language requiring no technical expertise to understand, and specific remediation steps were provided.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization could not understand the findings and lacked sufficient IT expertise to act on them.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization should have consulted the Vendor for clarifications if needed, and in fact employed a Chief Information Officer and Cluster Information Security Officer (seconded from the IT Services Provider) who should have understood the report.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation: Organizations must protect personal data in their possession or control by taking reasonable security steps or arrangements to prevent unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement access restrictions in web configuration file prior to website going live in December 2015
violations: Failed to implement access restrictions in web configuration file prior to website going live in December 2015
Failed to exercise reasonable oversight and timely action on penetration test report findings issued in June/July 2016 identifying the vulnerability
Allowed the vulnerability to remain unfixed for over 12 months despite explicit identification and remediation recommendations
Improperly delegated responsibility for addressing security vulnerabilities without maintaining adequate organizational oversight

outcome: National Healthcare Group was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 6,000 within 30 days. The organization had already implemented comprehensive remedial measures including: (1) immediately taking the website offline and fixing the configuration issue; (2) requesting Google to remove cached copies of the exposed list; (3) contacting all 129 affected GPs to inform them of the incident; and (4) implementing enhanced security practices including additional configuration checks during user acceptance testing and prior to going live, as well as conducting penetration tests before websites go live. No further directions were imposed given the remediation measures already undertaken.
companyNow: National Healthcare Group continues to operate as a major healthcare services provider in Singapore, now with enhanced security protocols and penetration testing requirements in place.
dataType: Names, mobile numbers, email addresses, mailing addresses, clinic addresses, medical registration numbers, NRIC numbers, dates of birth, photographs

companyDescription: Globalsign.in Pte Ltd is an email marketing service provider that operated the Global2Mail Online Marketing Web Application platform, which helped businesses send mass marketing emails to customer lists.
companyLongDescription: Globalsign.in Pte Ltd provided email marketing services through its Global2Mail platform, enabling organizations like MSIG Insurance to conduct mass email campaigns. The company stored customer email addresses and names on its servers for clients. In August 2017, the platform suffered a significant security breach when an unauthorized user gained access to the administrator account, compromising personal data and resulting in spam emails being sent to hundreds of thousands of recipients.
caseDescription: Globalsign.in's email marketing platform was compromised when an administrator account was accessed without authorization, allowing an intruder to send spam emails to 359,364 stored email addresses, including 149,172 email addresses of MSIG Insurance customers. The breach exposed personal data (email addresses and names) and resulted in spam emails with lottery phishing links sent to impacted customers. Globalsign.in failed to implement adequate security controls including password management, two-factor authentication, security scanning, and proper data retention practices.
violationSummary: Globalsign.in failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, specifically lacking password change requirements, account sharing controls, security scanning, and proper logging mechanisms. The unauthorized access to the administrator account and subsequent misuse exemplifies insecurity of personal data processing systems.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Globalsign.in failed to implement adequate security controls on its email marketing platform, allowing an unauthorized intruder to access the administrator account.
whyTheyWereWrong: The breach exposed the email addresses and names of 149,172 MSIG Insurance customers to unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: GSI claimed it had complied with MSIG's express instructions to delete and purge data after each marketing campaign.
claimsVsReality.reality: The G2M platform still retained at least 149,172 email addresses provided by MSIG that had been used in prior campaigns, contradicting GSI's claim of compliance.

claimsVsReality.claim: GSI implemented password management practices to protect administrator and client accounts.
claimsVsReality.reality: GSI had not implemented mechanisms to require regular password changes, did not log password changes to the administrator account, did not enforce password strength requirements, and allowed multiple users to share the same administrator credentials.

claimsVsReality.claim: The spam emails contained phishing or malware content that posed a threat to recipients.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cyber-security investigations concluded the spam emails did not contain phishing or malware content; users were simply redirected to a video on lotterydominator.com with no complaints of further negative consequences.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Requirement to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement mandatory password change mechanisms for administrator and client accounts
violations: Failed to implement mandatory password change mechanisms for administrator and client accounts
Failed to maintain logs when administrator account passwords were changed
Did not enforce password strength requirements
Multiple users shared the same administrator account and login credentials, preventing audit trails
Did not conduct security scans for 12 months prior to the incident
Failed to implement two-factor authentication (only implemented post-incident)
Did not use encrypted database storage (only implemented post-incident)

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 25 – Requirement to cease retaining documents containing personal data once the purpose for retention is no longer served and retention is no longer necessary
regulatoryFindings.description: Retained 149,172 email addresses provided by MSIG beyond the completion of marketing campaigns despite explicit contractual obligation to delete after each campaign
violations: Retained 149,172 email addresses provided by MSIG beyond the completion of marketing campaigns despite explicit contractual obligation to delete after each campaign
Failed to promptly purge customer data from previous campaigns despite repeated requests from MSIG
June 5, 2017 email showed GSI was still in the process of purging data, indicating delays and incomplete compliance

outcome: Globalsign.in directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $34,000 within 30 days. No further compliance orders required given remedial actions already taken by both MSIG and Globalsign.in post-incident, including implementation of two-factor authentication, encrypted database storage, HTTPS enforcement, improved access logging, and transition to ISO 27001 compliant security measures.
dataType: Email addresses, names (first and last names of insurance customers)

companyDescription: The Society of Tourist Guides (Singapore) is a non-profit organization that works with Singapore's Tourism Board to promote professionalism among tourist guides and maintains a registry of qualified tourism ambassadors.
companyLongDescription: Founded to enhance the professionalism of Singapore's tourism industry, the Society of Tourist Guides operates as a non-profit membership organization working in partnership with the Singapore Tourism Board. It maintains a publicly accessible directory of registered tourist guides to help members of the public find guides with specific expertise and services. The organization collects member profile data for public directory purposes and sensitive identity documents for administrative functions including training grant applications and access verification.
caseDescription: The Society of Tourist Guides (Singapore) failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive personal data of 111 members, including identity documents and biometric information, which were exposed through publicly accessible web directories. The organisation did not specify data protection requirements to its IT vendor, conduct security testing, or appoint a data protection officer, in violation of Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to implement adequate security controls resulted in sensitive identification documents and biometric data becoming accessible to the public through web directories, enabling unauthorised disclosure without consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The Society of Tourist Guides failed to implement security measures protecting 111 members' sensitive identity documents.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' passport numbers, NRICs, driving licenses, fingerprints, addresses and photographs were exposed to anyone on the internet, enabling identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization's website was secure and suitable for collecting sensitive identity documents from members.
claimsVsReality.reality: The website stored 111 members' NRIC images, driving licenses, fingerprints, and photographs in publicly accessible directories with no password protection, allowing anyone to download these documents via direct links.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT vendor was responsible for protecting the personal data on the website.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization owned and controlled the website and data; the vendor merely provided ad-hoc technical assistance and had no data processing responsibility. The organization failed to specify any data protection requirements to the vendor.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization lacked sufficient expertise to manage data security.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the organization cited inexperience, it could have simply instructed its vendor to use basic, standard security measures like non-public folders or .htaccess file restrictions—techniques the Commissioner identified as common and direct methods to prevent unauthorized access.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 24 – Security of Personal Data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to specify data protection and storage requirements to IT vendor
violations: Failed to specify data protection and storage requirements to IT vendor
Did not conduct security testing since website launch
Failed to implement reasonable technical security measures such as non-public folders, access controls, or .htaccess restrictions
Did not ensure separation between publicly accessible profile data and sensitive identification documents intended for administrative use only

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 11(3) – Designation of Data Protection Officer
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to appoint a data protection officer before the data breach incident occurred
violations: Failed to appoint a data protection officer before the data breach incident occurred

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA section 12 – Data Protection Policies and Practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to develop and implement written data protection policies and practices
violations: Failed to develop and implement written data protection policies and practices
