Failed to communicate data protection information to staff

outcome: The Commissioner directed the Society of Tourist Guides to pay a financial penalty of SGD 20,000 in 8 equal monthly instalments from February to September 2020. The organisation must complete within 60 days: (1) review and implement appropriate security arrangements for the website; (2) develop written internal policies and practices compliant with PDPA section 12; (3) develop and implement a training policy for employees handling personal data; and (4) require all existing employees to attend such training.
companyNow: The organization continues to operate as a non-profit tourism industry body in Singapore, now with enhanced data protection governance following the 2019 enforcement action.
dataType: Identity documents (NRIC, driving licence, vocational licence, employment pass), photographs, names, contact numbers, email addresses, biometric data (thumbprints, fingerprints), date of birth, address, gender, race, country of birth, occupation, military rank, blood group, religion
legalBasisViolated: PDPA section 11(3) (Designation of Data Protection Officer)
PDPA section 12 (Data Protection Policies and Practices)

companyDescription: Learnaholic Pte. Ltd. is an IT vendor that provides attendance-taking and e-learning systems to schools in Singapore, operating under contract with the Ministry of Education.
companyLongDescription: Learnaholic Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based IT services company specializing in the design, installation, and maintenance of attendance and e-learning management systems for educational institutions. The company provides critical infrastructure to schools, managing systems that track student attendance and facilitate digital learning. As a service provider to the Ministry of Education, Learnaholic handled sensitive personal data of students, parents, and school staff across multiple institutions.
caseDescription: Learnaholic, an IT vendor providing attendance and e-learning systems to schools, failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data of approximately 47,802 students, parents, and staff. The company opened a firewall port for remote troubleshooting, disabled password protection on remote access software, and forgot to close the port after completion, creating a vulnerability that was exploited by a hacker for approximately 1-11 months. The attacker obtained login credentials from a configuration file and accessed the company representative's work email containing unencrypted personal data, including medical information of 372 minors.
violationSummary: The violation is categorized as Information Processing – Insecurity because the organization failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, resulting in unauthorized access and exfiltration. Multiple security failures (open port, disabled passwords, unencrypted storage, inadequate access controls) created conditions enabling breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Learnaholic opened a firewall port for remote troubleshooting, disabled password protection on remote access software, forgot to close the port after completion.
whyTheyWereWrong: A hacker exploited these security failures to steal personal data including names, ID numbers, contact information, addresses, and medical records of nearly 48,000 students, parents.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation disabled the input feature at the client side of VNC Viewer, preventing unauthorized changes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Client-side disabling only prevented the organization from making changes; a hacker could still make modifications from the server side, and the vulnerability remained fully exploitable.

claimsVsReality.claim: The credentials in the configuration file were stored in a jumbled or random manner, making them difficult to match.
claimsVsReality.reality: The obfuscation was trivial and a basic brute-force attack with trial-and-error could easily match email accounts to passwords in minutes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Retaining the personal data in the employee's email was useful for future reference.
claimsVsReality.reality: No valid legal or business purpose justified storing 47,802 individuals' unencrypted sensitive records including ID numbers and medical data in an employee email account indefinitely.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: Organizations must make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or control by preventing unauthorized access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Opened firewall port and reconfigured intranet firewall to allow remote access without informing the school
violations: Opened firewall port and reconfigured intranet firewall to allow remote access without informing the school
Disabled password protection on remote access software (VNC Server)
Failed to close the firewall port after remote troubleshooting was completed, leaving vulnerability exposed for 1-11 months
Stored configuration file containing login credentials in a folder that was synced to Guard Post Cluster, making it accessible to attackers
Stored login credentials in unsecured, jumbled manner susceptible to brute-force attacks
Retained unencrypted personal data in work email account indefinitely instead of deleting after use
Failed to encrypt sensitive personal data, especially medical information of minors, sent in bulk

outcome: The Commissioner found Learnaholic in breach of Section 24 of the PDPA and directed the company to pay a financial penalty of S$60,000.00 within 30 days. The company was required to implement comprehensive remedial measures including changing all work email passwords, activating two-factor authentication, deleting all emails containing personal data, implementing scripts to prevent non-essential files from being copied to Guard Post Clusters, and establishing new practices for prompt deletion of emails containing personal data after completion of tasks. The penalty was adjusted downward from initial calculations to account for the company's swift remedial actions after discovery and clarification regarding the duration of the vulnerability exposure.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, contact numbers, email addresses, home addresses, medical information (health conditions)

companyDescription: i-vic International is a Singapore-based data intermediary and IT service provider that processes personal data and manages IT infrastructure for client organizations.
companyLongDescription: i-vic International Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-incorporated company specializing in data processing and IT infrastructure management services. The organization was engaged by the Employment and Employability Institute (e2i) to manage mailbox operations, develop and maintain CRM software, and handle customer queries for Singapore's work trial programme administered by Workforce Singapore. As a data intermediary, i-vic processed sensitive personal data on behalf of its clients.
caseDescription: i-vic International, a data intermediary processing personal data for e2i's work trial programme, inadvertently attached documents containing sensitive personal data of three individuals to emails sent to nine unintended recipients due to a code error in the automated email generation system. The organisation failed to conduct diligent and properly scoped testing of the system, particularly testing scenarios where email instructions were queued during concurrent batch processes, which violated the Protection Obligation under section 24 of the PDPA.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements by not conducting adequate testing of the automated email system, particularly under the specific conditions where email generation instructions would be queued while another batch process ran. This inadequate security testing resulted in unauthorised disclosure of personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: i-vic International failed to properly test its automated email generation system, allowing a code error during concurrent batch processing to attach sensitive personal documents to emails sent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Three individuals had their names, NRIC numbers, signatures, addresses, phone numbers, emails, ages, races, bank account numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: i-vic had tested the code of the Automated Email Generation Process
claimsVsReality.reality: i-vic did not test scenarios where email instructions were queued during concurrent batch processes, which directly caused the incident

claimsVsReality.claim: Emails would be processed and sent individually and not queued during the Reward Programme Process
claimsVsReality.reality: The system queued emails during the Reward Programme Process on the 1st of every month, and a code error caused wrong documents to be attached to these queued emails

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection Obligation: An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or under its control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to conduct diligent and properly scoped testing of the automated email generation process code
violations: Failure to conduct diligent and properly scoped testing of the automated email generation process code
Failure to test how the system behaved when email instructions were queued during the concurrent reward programme batch process

Inadequate security arrangements in the form of insufficient code testing despite knowing that the automated email generation process was unable to run while the reward programme process was executing monthly

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner found that i-vic International contravened section 24 of the PDPA due to failure to implement reasonable security arrangements through adequate testing. The organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $6,000 within 30 days. No further directions were issued as the organisation had already taken remedial actions, including fixing the code error, rewriting the code to enable automated encryption of attachments, and ensuring wrong files would not be attached to emails.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, signatures, residential addresses, mobile numbers, email addresses, age, race, bank account numbers, academic qualifications, work trial company details, work experience details

companyDescription: Honestbee is an online food and grocery delivery service that connected merchants with customers through a logistics platform.
companyLongDescription: Honestbee Pte Ltd was a Singapore-based online delivery platform that enabled third-party merchants to offer food and grocery delivery services. The company accepted personal data from merchants and their customers to facilitate logistics and service delivery. The company operated in the competitive food delivery sector in Southeast Asia during the late 2010s.
caseDescription: Honestbee, an online food and grocery delivery service, stored personal data from approximately 8,000 individuals in an unsecured AWS file repository without access restrictions, making it publicly accessible. The company failed to implement basic security measures such as access controls or verification checks for test data. The breach was discovered on 2 May 2019 and the company promptly remediated by restricting access and implementing security improvements.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data, leaving it accessible to the public. This directly falls under the Solove category of insecurity — inadequate safeguards and controls that exposed sensitive personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Honestbee stored approximately 8,000 individuals' personal data including names, email addresses, residential addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive personal information including home addresses and contact details were exposed to the public, allowing anyone with basic technical knowledge to access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Test data was stored securely in accordance with security best practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Test data containing real customers' personal information was stored in an unsecured AWS bucket with no access restrictions, accessible to anyone with basic AWS knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: Appropriate access controls and verification checks were in place for test data storage.
claimsVsReality.reality: No access controls, verification checks, or security measures were implemented; the bucket was configured without any restrictions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Data Protection Act 2012 Section 24 — Organisations must implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement access restrictions on AWS bucket storing personal data
violations: Failed to implement access restrictions on AWS bucket storing personal data
Omitted rudimentary security measures such as checks to confirm test data was stored with appropriate access controls
Allowed public access to personal data containing names, email addresses, residential addresses, and mobile numbers

outcome: The Organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $8,000 within 30 days. The organisation has blocked public access to the personal data, circulated a report to its engineering team to prevent similar mistakes in code reviews, and is in discussions with cybersecurity companies to perform regular security audits. No other directions were imposed in light of the remedial measures taken.
companyNow: Honestbee ceased operations and is no longer active. The company struggled financially and shut down its operations in multiple markets including Singapore.
dataType: Names, email addresses, residential addresses, mobile numbers

companyDescription: Chizzle Pte. Ltd. is a mobile application platform that connects learners and teachers across Singapore, Australia, and India for educational purposes.
companyLongDescription: Chizzle Pte. Ltd. operates a mobile application designed to facilitate connections between students and teachers in Singapore, Australia, and India. The company ran the application on a LAMP stack infrastructure since 2016. Despite operating a user-facing educational platform handling personal data, the company failed to implement basic security governance practices, including security audits or awareness of its own system components.
caseDescription: Chizzle, a mobile application connecting learners and teachers, suffered a cyberattack in July 2018 that compromised personal data of approximately 2,213 users. An unauthorised party gained access to the company's database through an improperly secured phpMyAdmin tool and deleted the database while demanding ransom. The company had failed to conduct any security review of its system and was unaware the phpMyAdmin tool even existed on its infrastructure.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data as required by section 24 of the PDPA. Specifically, it did not conduct security reviews of its web-connected systems, left a database administration tool (phpMyAdmin) exposed to remote internet access without proper safeguards, and failed to implement basic security controls that would have prevented unauthorised access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Chizzle failed to conduct any security review of its system, leaving a phpMyAdmin database administration tool exposed to remote internet access.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users' names, dates of birth, genders, email addresses, mobile numbers and residential addresses were deleted by attackers who gained full database control.

claimsVsReality.claim: Chizzle was not aware that phpMyAdmin was part of its system and had no need for it.
claimsVsReality.reality: phpMyAdmin had been installed as part of the LAMP stack since 2016 and was configured to allow remote internet access, making it discoverable and exploitable by attackers through brute force attacks.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organisation had adequate security measures in place to protect user data.
claimsVsReality.reality: No security review had ever been conducted, and the company had no logs to even verify how the unauthorised access occurred, demonstrating complete absence of security monitoring and governance.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct any security review of its IT system
violations: Failed to conduct any security review of its IT system
Did not identify or assess the security risks posed by phpMyAdmin tool with remote internet access
Permitted remote access to database administration tool without proper controls or authentication
Did not implement reasonable safeguards against brute force attacks on database administration interfaces
Lacked awareness of critical components in its own IT infrastructure

outcome: The Commissioner found a breach of section 24 of the PDPA and imposed a financial penalty of SGD $8,000 (reduced from a higher amount due to the organisation's dire financial circumstances). The organisation was directed to: (1) engage qualified personnel to conduct a security audit of its mobile application and IT system; (2) furnish an audit schedule within 30 days; (3) rectify identified security gaps; (4) develop an IT security policy within 60 days of audit completion; (5) review and revise developmental processes to adopt a data protection by design approach within 120 days; and (6) report completion of each directive to the Commission within one week of completion.
companyNow: Following the 2019 enforcement action, Chizzle was required to engage qualified security personnel, conduct a full security audit, and adopt a data protection by design approach. The company's current operational status is unclear from public sources.
dataType: Names, dates of birth, genders, email addresses, mobile numbers, residential addresses

companyDescription: The Travel Corporation is a Singapore-based travel company that offers travel packages directly to customers and through third-party travel agencies.
companyLongDescription: The Travel Corporation (2011) Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore travel services company that provides travel packages to both direct customers and via third-party travel agencies. The company operates in the hospitality and travel sector, serving customers throughout Singapore. It maintains a database of customer, prospective customer, employee, and supplier information as part of its business operations.
caseDescription: The Travel Corporation lost an unencrypted portable hard disk containing personal data of 18,630 customers, prospective customers, employees, and suppliers after an employee misplaced it in July 2018. The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements such as encryption, password protection, and proper policies governing portable storage devices. The company also failed to appoint a data protection officer prior to the breach.
violationSummary: The company failed to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data by not implementing encryption, password protection, or effective operational frameworks for portable storage device management, resulting in the loss of an unencrypted hard disk.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The Travel Corporation lost an unencrypted portable hard disk containing personal data of 18,630 customers, prospective customers, employees.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' personal information including names, email addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, postal addresses, passport numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had a Portable Computer and Storage Devices Policy stipulating that portable computing and storage devices must have designated custodians.
claimsVsReality.reality: The policy existed only on paper; there were no operational frameworks or procedures to implement it, and employees received only verbal instructions not to remove devices from the office.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had clear guidelines in its Acceptable User Policy and Information Sensitivity Policy requiring password protection and data encryption for portable storage devices.
claimsVsReality.reality: No password protection or encryption policies were actually implemented on the hard disk or other portable storage devices, leaving sensitive customer data completely unprotected.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company could not appoint a data protection officer because no employees had passed the CIPM certification exams.
claimsVsReality.reality: The PDPA does not require DPO certification; organizations may appoint a DPO and then provide training, making the company's failure to appoint someone prior to the breach a breach of mandatory law.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection of Personal Data: Organisations must protect personal data in their possession by making reasonable security arrangements.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement encryption policies for portable storage devices despite having guidelines requiring this
violations: Failed to implement encryption policies for portable storage devices despite having guidelines requiring this
Failed to implement password protection policies for portable storage devices
Did not have operational frameworks or procedures to effectively implement the Portable Computer and Storage Devices Policy
Relied only on verbal instructions rather than enforced policies to prevent removal of portable storage devices from office premises
An unencrypted hard disk containing 18,630 individuals' personal data was lost due to inadequate security measures

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 11(3) – Designation of Data Protection Officer: Organisations must designate one or more individuals responsible for ensuring compliance with the PDPA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to appoint a data protection officer prior to the data breach incident on 25 July 2018
violations: Failed to appoint a data protection officer prior to the data breach incident on 25 July 2018
Only appointed a DPO on 22 October 2018, after the breach had occurred

outcome: The Commissioner found The Travel Corporation in breach of PDPA Section 24 (Protection of Personal Data) and PDPA Section 11(3) (Designation of Data Protection Officer). The Organisation was directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD 12,000 within 30 days. The penalty was mitigated based on the company's prompt notification of the breach, full cooperation with investigations, immediate remedial measures (ceasing use of portable storage devices, implementing cloud-based storage, appointing a DPO), and the absence of complaints. No other directions were imposed given the remediation measures taken.
companyNow: The Travel Corporation continues to operate in Singapore. Following the 2019 enforcement action, the company implemented cloud-based storage systems, appointed a data protection officer, and enhanced its PDPA compliance policies and employee training programs.
dataType: Name, email address, phone number, date of birth, postal address, passport number, NRIC number, office contact information
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 11(3) (Designation of Data Protection Officer)

companyDescription: Saturday Club Pte Ltd is a hospitality venue operator in Singapore offering membership-based social and dining facilities.
companyLongDescription: Saturday Club Pte Ltd operates as a hospitality establishment in Singapore, providing membership-based club services including dining, events, and social amenities. The organization serves a membership base requiring collection and retention of personal data including names, contact information, and payment details. In 2019, the company came under regulatory scrutiny following a data breach incident that revealed systemic gaps in data protection governance and compliance infrastructure.
caseDescription: Saturday Club Pte Ltd failed to develop internal policies and practices necessary to comply with the Personal Data Protection Act 2012. The organisation was found in breach of section 12 of the PDPA following an investigation into a suspected data breach.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to establish internal policies and practices to meet PDPA obligations constitutes inadequate security and governance measures for personal data protection.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Saturday Club Pte Ltd failed to develop any internal policies and practices necessary to comply with the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 following a suspected data breach.
whyTheyWereWrong: Members' personal data was exposed to risk because the company had no internal safeguards, policies, or procedures in place to protect their information after the breach occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: Saturday Club operated with standard data protection practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization had not developed ANY internal policies or practices for data protection, leaving member data vulnerable during and after the breach.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 requires organisations to develop and maintain internal policies and practices necessary to meet obligations under the PDPA
regulatoryFindings.description: Saturday Club Pte Ltd had not developed any internal policies and practices required by the PDPA
violations: Saturday Club Pte Ltd had not developed any internal policies and practices required by the PDPA

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection issued directions to the Organisation to ensure compliance with section 12 of the PDPA and to establish necessary internal policies and practices.
companyNow: Saturday Club Pte Ltd continues to operate in Singapore as a membership-based hospitality venue, operating under the compliance obligations imposed by the PDPC in 2019.
dataType: Personal data (type not specified)

companyDescription: Tan Tock Seng Hospital is a major public tertiary hospital in Singapore providing acute care, infectious disease treatment, and specialist medical services.
companyLongDescription: Tan Tock Seng Hospital is one of Singapore's leading public healthcare institutions, established to provide comprehensive acute care and specialist medical services. It is particularly renowned for its infectious disease management and serves as a key government healthcare facility. The hospital handles hundreds of thousands of patient interactions annually and maintains extensive patient records and personal data.
caseDescription: Tan Tock Seng Hospital sent appointment reschedule letters containing patient names, NRIC numbers, and appointment details to 85 wrong addresses due to a manual mail merge error where staff sorted only the address field in a spreadsheet without updating corresponding patient records. The hospital failed to implement quality checks or random sampling to catch the misdirected letters before distribution.
violationSummary: Personal data containing sensitive identifiers (NRIC numbers) and health appointment information was exposed to unintended recipients as a result of inadequate data handling procedures and lack of security controls during manual data processing.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Tan Tock Seng Hospital manually generated appointment reschedule letters using a mail merge function that sent patient names, NRIC numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients' sensitive personal data including national identification numbers and appointment information were exposed to 85 unintended recipients, violating their privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: The hospital's mail merge process was reliable and secure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Manual mail merge operation caused patient data to be sent to 85 wrong addresses due to lack of quality control checks or random sampling verification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Patient data was adequately protected during the letter generation process.
claimsVsReality.reality: The hospital failed to implement any verification procedures, allowing 85 individuals' sensitive NRIC numbers and health appointment details to be misdirected to unknown recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or disposal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to conduct quality checks on letter generation and printing
violations: Failed to conduct quality checks on letter generation and printing
No random sampling or verification process implemented
Inadequate oversight of manual mail merge process
Manual data handling without proper controls or validation

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection issued a warning to the organisation. No formal directions were required as Tan Tock Seng Hospital had already implemented corrective measures addressing the security gaps, including improved controls over manual data processing procedures.
companyNow: Tan Tock Seng Hospital remains an active major public hospital in Singapore and continues to provide acute and specialist care services.
dataType: Names, NRIC numbers, appointment details

companyDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited (Singtel) is a major telecommunications company in Singapore providing mobile, fixed-line, and broadband services to millions of customers.
companyLongDescription: Singapore Telecommunications Limited is Singapore's largest integrated telecommunications company, offering mobile, fixed-line, internet, and pay-TV services. The company operates the My Singtel mobile app which allows customers to manage their accounts and track usage. As a leading telecom provider, Singtel serves millions of customers across Singapore and has regional operations. The company is majority-owned by Temasek Holdings.
caseDescription: Singapore Telecommunications' mobile app contained a design flaw (Direct Object Reference Vulnerability) in its API that allowed unauthorized access to customer account details. An anonymous informant demonstrated the vulnerability by accessing four customer billing accounts, putting approximately 330,000 customers' personal data at risk of disclosure. The company had engaged third-party security vendors for penetration testing but failed to implement proper input validation and parameter verification.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data by not validating API parameters against login credentials, allowing unauthorized manipulation of request parameters to access other customers' data. This is a fundamental security design flaw in data processing.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Singapore Telecommunications' My Singtel mobile app contained a Direct Object Reference Vulnerability in its API that allowed unauthorized access to customer account details when parameters were.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 330,000 customers' personal data including names, billing addresses, account numbers, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The vulnerability exploitation was 'not something that a normal user would attempt' and required someone to be 'technically competent' with specialized workstation access
claimsVsReality.reality: Anyone with basic working knowledge of how mobile apps communicate with servers via APIs could exploit the vulnerability using freely available online tools

claimsVsReality.claim: The 2015 penetration test identified only input field vulnerabilities, so non-input field vulnerabilities would not have been caught by the same code review
claimsVsReality.reality: The 2015 Penetration Test Report showed that both input and non-input fields were affected by Direct Object Reference vulnerabilities, contradicting the company's representation

claimsVsReality.claim: Third-party security penetration testing was sufficient to protect customer data
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite regular penetration tests by a third-party security vendor, the Direct Object Reference Vulnerability remained undetected until an anonymous informant demonstrated it

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks to personal data in their possession or control
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement parameter validation in API design – application input was not validated against login credentials before processing requests
violations: Failed to implement parameter validation in API design – application input was not validated against login credentials before processing requests
Did not implement input and non-input field validation despite knowing of Direct Object Reference vulnerabilities from 2015 penetration test
Failed to conduct thorough code review of API accepting both input and non-input fields after receiving professional security advice
Inadequate security design allowed authenticated users to intercept and modify API request parameters to access other customers' data
330,000 customers' personal data was put at risk despite only 4 accounts being directly accessed

outcome: The Commissioner found Singapore Telecommunications in breach of PDPA Section 24 for failing to implement reasonable security arrangements. The company was directed to pay a financial penalty of S$25,000 within 30 days. No additional directions were issued as the organisation had already remediated the vulnerability by tightly coupling Mobile App user identifiers to authenticated sessions and implementing parameter validation to prevent unauthorized access.
companyNow: Singtel remains Singapore's leading telecommunications provider and continues to operate the My Singtel app with enhanced security measures post-2019 remediation.
dataType: Mobile phone number, billing address, billing account number, customer name, service plan information (data usage, talk time, SMS usage), bill amount, payment due date
legalBasisViolated: PDPA Section 24 – Obligation to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements

companyDescription: SearchAsia Consulting is a Singapore-based recruitment company that matches job seekers with employers seeking to fill specific roles.
companyLongDescription: SearchAsia Consulting Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-incorporated recruitment firm that provides job matching services between job seekers and hiring organizations. The company operated a website allowing job seekers to upload their résumés for assessment and matching with available positions. In 2018, the company suffered a significant data security failure when résumés were inadvertently exposed to public access through search engine indexing.
caseDescription: SearchAsia Consulting, a Singapore-based recruitment company, failed to implement adequate security measures to protect résumés uploaded by job seekers on its website. The résumés were stored in an unsecured folder without access controls, allowing search engine crawlers to index and expose them to the public. The company did not provide proper instructions to its third-party developer or conduct security tests to verify protection of the personal data.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data from unauthorised access and disclosure, resulting in the indexing and public accessibility of sensitive résumés through search engines.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: SearchAsia Consulting stored job seeker résumés in an unsecured folder without access controls, allowing search engine crawlers to index and publicly expose them online.
whyTheyWereWrong: Job seekers' personal data including names, phone numbers, employment history, qualifications, and in some cases nationality, date of birth, marital status.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company instructed its third-party web developer to restrict access to the folder containing résumés to only one employee and that the developer confirmed résumés would be encrypted and 'safe'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The developer denied receiving any security specifications from the company, provided no written security instructions were documented, no testing was conducted to verify access controls or encryption, and the folder remained publicly accessible to search engine crawlers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company relied on its web hosting provider to ensure adequate security features on the website.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company never informed the web host that the folder contents needed protection, so the web host's security reviews did not address protection of the personal data stored in the résumé folder.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Organisations must make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in their possession or control from unauthorised access, disclosure and similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement access controls on the folder containing résumés
violations: Failed to implement access controls on the folder containing résumés
Did not provide documented security instructions to third-party web developer
Did not inform web hosting provider that the folder contents required protection
Failed to conduct security tests or checks to verify protection measures were in place
Allowed search engine crawlers to index and publicly expose personal data

outcome: The organisation was found in breach of Section 24 of the PDPA and directed to pay a financial penalty of SGD $7,000 within 30 days. No other directions were issued given the organisation's remedial actions, which included disabling directory listing, adding search engine crawler prevention mechanisms, removing public access permissions from sensitive directories, and requesting Google to remove cached résumés from search results.
companyNow: Following the 2019 enforcement action, SearchAsia Consulting implemented remedial security measures including disabling directory listing, adding search engine crawler prevention mechanisms, and removing public access permissions from sensitive file directories.
dataType: Name, phone numbers, employment history, educational qualifications, achievements, skillset, nationality, date of birth, marital status, current salary

companyDescription: Ninja Logistics is a Singapore-based logistics company providing package delivery and tracking services on behalf of retailers to end customers.
companyLongDescription: Ninja Logistics Pte Ltd is a logistics provider that handles packaging, delivery, and order tracking services for retailers. The company operated a web-based tracking function allowing customers to check delivery status and confirm parcel collection. The company's primary business involves last-mile delivery and logistics management for e-commerce retailers in Singapore and the broader region.
caseDescription: Ninja Logistics operated a package tracking function that exposed customer personal data due to inadequate security controls. Tracking IDs could be manipulated by changing digits to access other customers' information including names, addresses, and signatures. The company was aware of this vulnerability for nearly 2 years but failed to implement effective secondary authentication or data retention limits.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in its possession, specifically by using Tracking IDs as the sole authentication method despite knowing they could be manipulated, and by retaining personal data indefinitely after delivery completion.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Ninja Logistics operated a package tracking website that exposed customer names, addresses, and signatures because tracking IDs could be accessed by simply changing a few digits.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 1.2 million customers' names, addresses, and signatures were exposed to unauthorized access for nearly 2 years, allowing anyone to retrieve delivery information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company archived 2.6 million tracking IDs on 31 August 2016, so data was only exposed for less than 2 years
claimsVsReality.reality: Even after archiving 2.6 million records, 1,262,861 affected individuals' tracking data accumulated after that date and remained accessible for close to 2 years

claimsVsReality.claim: Keeping tracking data accessible was a well-meaning feature to differentiate from competitors and avoid burdening retailers and customers
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement any data retention limits or expiration procedures, despite being aware from launch in 2014 that tracking IDs could be manipulated by changing digits

claimsVsReality.claim: There was no evidence of actual unauthorized access or data exfiltration
claimsVsReality.reality: The vulnerability created a foreseeable and significant risk of unauthorized access to sensitive personal data (names, addresses, signatures) for over 1.2 million individuals over nearly 2 years

claimsVsReality.claim: The company attempted secondary authentication methods using mobile numbers and surnames for 3 months starting in 2014
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite knowing about the manipulation risk, the company abandoned authentication efforts in 2015 and implemented no alternative security measures for nearly 2 years until notified of the breach

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organisations to protect personal data by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification, disposal or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement effective secondary authentication despite being aware that Tracking IDs could be manipulated
violations: Failed to implement effective secondary authentication despite being aware that Tracking IDs could be manipulated
Did not establish procedures to remove or expire personal data after delivery completion
Maintained exposed personal data (names, addresses, signatures) of 1.26 million individuals for approximately 2 years despite known security vulnerabilities

outcome: The Commissioner found Ninja Logistics contravened Section 24 of the PDPA. The organisation was directed to: (1) pay a financial penalty of $90,000 within 30 days; and (2) implement a reasonable validity period for Tracking IDs after delivery completion, set as short as possible while meeting business needs. The organisation implemented remedial measures including removing customer addresses from certain delivery statuses, setting Tracking ID expiration at 14 days post-delivery, engaging security consultants for a one-year security framework program, and improving data protection policies with legal assistance.
dataType: Customer names, addresses, signatures

companyDescription: Marshall Cavendish Education is an educational technology and publishing company that provides learning management systems and digital educational content to schools in Singapore and internationally.
companyLongDescription: Marshall Cavendish Education is a subsidiary of Marshall Cavendish International, a major educational publishing and content company. The company developed and operated a learning management system (mconline.com.sg) used by Ministry of Education schools in Singapore. It provides digital learning platforms, educational software, and teaching materials to educational institutions across multiple countries.
caseDescription: Marshall Cavendish Education failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal data on its learning management system. A ransomware attack in February 2017 encrypted files containing data of over 250,000 users after a system engineer made unauthorized firewall changes that were never reversed. The company lacked proper supervisory controls and monitoring procedures over IT system changes.
violationSummary: The organization failed to make reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorized access and modification of personal data, specifically: (1) failure to reverse a temporary firewall rule change that exposed the backup server to internet access; (2) inadequate supervision over IT staff installations of remote access software; (3) lack of monitoring and approval processes for firewall configuration changes; (4) unnecessary number of remote access accounts with minimal oversight.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Marshall Cavendish Education failed to reverse a firewall rule change that temporarily exposed its backup server to the internet.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 250,000 students and users had their personal data including names, birth certificate numbers, NRIC numbers, school details, and family contact information encrypted.

claimsVsReality.claim: The firewall rule change was intended to be temporary to fix an antivirus update issue.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system engineer failed to reverse the firewall rule change after completing the investigation, leaving the backup server continuously exposed to internet access for an extended period.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization had adequate supervision over IT system changes by the IT Manager.
claimsVsReality.reality: The IT Manager exercised no competent supervision—there were no standard operating procedures for firewall changes, no monitoring of unauthorized software installation, and no approval process for remote access software deployment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal data was adequately protected by reasonable security arrangements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization lacked basic controls such as documented firewall change logs, approval requirements for system changes, records of remote access software installation, and timely removal of former employee accounts (one dating back to 2014).

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 - Protection Obligation: An organisation shall protect personal data in its possession or control by making reasonable security arrangements to prevent unauthorised access, collection, use, disclosure, copying, modification or similar risks
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to reverse a temporary firewall rule change that exposed the backup server to unrestricted internet access for approximately one year
violations: Failed to reverse a temporary firewall rule change that exposed the backup server to unrestricted internet access for approximately one year
Inadequate supervision of IT staff who installed unauthorized remote access software on the backup server without proper approval or monitoring
Absence of standard operating procedures to document and monitor firewall configuration changes
Lack of measures to prevent installation of unauthorized software
Insufficient monitoring of remote access accounts (15 accounts found, reduced to 5)
Failure to implement adequate approval processes and supervisory oversight for critical IT security decisions
Unauthorized encryption of personal data by ransomware due to inadequate network security controls

outcome: Marshall Cavendish Education was found in breach of Section 24 of the PDPA. The Commissioner directed the organization to pay a financial penalty of S$40,000 within 30 days. The penalty was imposed despite mitigating factors (cooperation, no misuse of data, remedial measures taken) because the breach resulted in loss of access to and control of personal data, and the company failed to implement reasonable security arrangements and adequate supervision. No further directions were deemed necessary given the comprehensive remedial measures already implemented, including hiring an IT security officer, conducting external security audits, implementing approval processes for system changes, and establishing monthly reviews of user access rights.
companyNow: Marshall Cavendish Education remains active in educational technology and publishing, now operating under stronger cybersecurity governance following the 2017 incident and subsequent remedial measures.
dataType: Personal identification data (NRIC, birth certificate numbers, names), school information, contact details (email, address, phone numbers), parent/guardian information

companyDescription: EU Holidays Pte. Ltd. is a travel agency based in Singapore that arranges tour packages and travel reservations for customers.
companyLongDescription: EU Holidays Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-based travel agency that specializes in organizing tour packages and travel reservations for customers. The company operates an e-commerce website that allows customers to make online reservations either directly or through partner agents. The company collects and stores personal data from customers as part of its core business operations, including names, contact information, passport details, and travel itineraries.
caseDescription: EU Holidays failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect customer personal data collected through its website, resulting in 1,077 customers' tax invoices being publicly accessible through unprotected web directories from December 2017 to January 2019. The company also failed to develop or implement any internal data protection policies required under Singapore's PDPA. Upon discovery of the breach, the company took prompt remedial action by deleting and disabling access to the exposed data.
violationSummary: The organisation failed to take reasonable security steps to prevent unauthorised access to personal data in its possession. The data was stored in publicly accessible web directories without proper access controls (no folder permissions, authentication mechanisms, or password protections), violating the core security obligation under PDPA section 24.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: EU Holidays failed to implement access controls on its website, leaving tax invoices containing 1,077 customers' personal data publicly accessible through unprotected web directories.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' sensitive information including names, addresses, passport details, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: EU Holidays intended for tax invoices from direct reservations to be stored in a backend Content Management System accessible only to authorized staff.
claimsVsReality.reality: Tax invoices were stored in Web Directory 1, which was publicly accessible to anyone on the internet without password protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: EU Holidays did not intend for Web Directory 2 to be publicly accessible and expected it to be protected by partner agent email and password access controls.
claimsVsReality.reality: Web Directory 2 had no access controls implemented because the company failed to provide any instructions to the IT vendor about security requirements, leaving it publicly accessible.

claimsVsReality.claim: The IT vendor was responsible for implementing appropriate security measures for the website.
claimsVsReality.reality: The contract with the IT vendor contained no requirements regarding data protection or security, and the company failed to review or verify the security standards after the website launched.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 – Protection of Personal Data
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to assess risks to personal data collected through website
violations: Failed to assess risks to personal data collected through website
Did not specify security requirements in IT vendor contract
Left security arrangements entirely to vendor without oversight or review
Stored tax invoices in publicly accessible web directories without access controls
Did not implement folder permissions, authentication, or password protections
Did not implement reasonable technical security measures such as .htaccess files or access control restrictions

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Policies and Practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to develop any internal data protection policies
violations: Failed to develop any internal data protection policies
Did not implement written policies to guide employees on handling personal data
No staff communication or training on PDPA obligations

outcome: The Commissioner directed EU Holidays to: (1) pay a financial penalty of $15,000 within 30 days; (2) within 60 days, review website security and implement appropriate security arrangements to protect personal data; (3) develop a comprehensive data protection policy with written internal policies compliant with PDPA; and (4) develop and conduct a mandatory employee training programme on PDPA obligations for all staff.
dataType: Name, email address, postal address, contact number, date of birth, gender, passport details, travel destination, departure date, booking date, rooming arrangement, amount payable

companyDescription: iClick Media is a Singapore-based IT vendor that provided technology services to travel and holiday companies, including data handling responsibilities.
companyLongDescription: iClick Media Pte. Ltd. is a Singapore-incorporated IT services company that operated as a data processor for client organisations in the travel and hospitality sector. The company handled personal data on behalf of clients such as EU Holidays but failed to implement basic data protection governance. Despite processing sensitive customer information, iClick Media had no formal data protection policies, procedures, or employee training in place to ensure compliance with Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act.
caseDescription: iClick Media, an IT vendor to EU Holidays, failed to develop internal policies and practices necessary to comply with Singapore's Personal Data Protection Act. The organisation had no data protection policies or employee training programmes in place despite handling personal data on behalf of its client.
violationSummary: The organisation's failure to establish data protection policies and internal practices constitutes inadequate safeguards and governance for personal data handling, directly impacting the security and proper processing of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: iClick Media, an IT vendor to EU Holidays, failed to develop any internal data protection policies or employee training programmes despite handling personal data on behalf of its client.
whyTheyWereWrong: The absence of data protection policies and training left personal data vulnerable to mishandling, unauthorised access.

claimsVsReality.claim: iClick Media was operating as a compliant IT vendor handling personal data.
claimsVsReality.reality: iClick Media had zero data protection policies, procedures, or employee training in place, making it non-compliant with the PDPA from the outset.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 12 – Organisations must develop and maintain internal policies and practices necessary to comply with the PDPA
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to develop any data protection policy
violations: Failed to develop any data protection policy
Failed to establish written internal policies for PDPA compliance
Failed to implement employee training on data protection obligations

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner directed iClick Media to, within 60 days: (1) put in place a comprehensive data protection policy and written internal policies compliant with PDPA provisions; (2) develop and deliver a mandatory training programme for all employees on their PDPA obligations when handling personal data; and (3) submit a written update to the Commission within 7 days of completing the above actions.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified types)

companyDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. is the Spanish subsidiary of Vodafone Group, one of Europe's largest multinational telecommunications companies providing mobile, broadband, and digital services to millions of customers.
companyLongDescription: Vodafone España, S.A.U. is the Spanish subsidiary of Vodafone Group, one of Europe's largest multinational telecommunications companies providing mobile, broadband, and digital services to millions of customers.
caseDescription: Vodafone sent customer invoices containing one person's personal data to a neighbor's address, with the envelope addressed to the neighbor but the invoice containing the customer's full details. The company failed to respond to the data protection authority's initial investigation request. Although Vodafone later corrected the error, the initial security lapse and lack of cooperation resulted in a €50,000 fine for violation of GDPR data security principles.
violationSummary: The company's failure to maintain adequate security measures resulted in unauthorized exposure of personal data (customer invoice details) to third parties (the neighbor), meeting the definition of Information Dissemination – Exposure under Solove taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Vodafone sent customer invoices containing full personal data including name, DNI, and address to a neighbor's address.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's sensitive personal data was exposed to an unauthorized third party due to a data migration error and lack of adequate security controls, compromising confidentiality.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone claimed the data duplication and delivery error were the result of a 'punto error' (one-time mistake) and a data migration problem between systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The error exposed customer personal data to a third party for an extended period, demonstrating systemic failures in data quality control and security management, not a minor isolated incident.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone argued that no culpability or negligence could be proven and therefore no sanction should be imposed, citing principles of 'nullum poena sine culpa'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement adequate security measures, controls, and verification procedures required by GDPR Article 5(1)(f), demonstrating significant negligence in data protection practices, regardless of intent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Vodafone contended the error was immediately corrected once discovered, mitigating any harm.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to respond to the data protection authority's initial investigation request for one month, delaying identification of systemic issues and extending the period during which personal data remained at risk.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be treated with integrity and confidentiality, ensuring adequate security of personal data including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing, accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone failed to implement adequate technical or organisational measures to prevent personal data (customer invoice details) from being sent to an unauthorized third party (neighbor's address)
violations: Vodafone failed to implement adequate technical or organisational measures to prevent personal data (customer invoice details) from being sent to an unauthorized third party (neighbor's address)
The company's data management systems contained a data duplication error linking the customer's data to the neighbor's contact information, demonstrating insufficient data processing controls
No preventive measures were in place to verify envelope recipient against invoice data before mailing

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5(a) establishes that violations of basic treatment principles (Article 5) are sanctionable with administrative fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: Vodafone's violation of Article 5(1)(f) regarding data security and confidentiality triggered liability for administrative sanctions as a 'very grave' infraction
violations: Vodafone's violation of Article 5(1)(f) regarding data security and confidentiality triggered liability for administrative sanctions as a 'very grave' infraction

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 72(1)(a) classifies as 'very grave' any treatment of personal data that violates the principles and guarantees established in GDPR Article 5.
regulatoryFindings.description: The data exposure incident constituted a substantive violation of GDPR Article 5, classified as a very grave infraction under Spanish data protection law
violations: The data exposure incident constituted a substantive violation of GDPR Article 5, classified as a very grave infraction under Spanish data protection law

outcome: AEPD imposed an administrative fine of €50,000 on Vodafone España, S.A.U. for violation of GDPR Article 5(1)(f). The company must pay the fine within the voluntary payment period established by Spanish administrative procedures. The fine is classified as 'very grave' with a prescription period of three years. Vodafone confirmed during the proceedings that the error has been corrected and the neighbor's data has been de-linked from the customer's account. The resolution is final at the administrative level; Vodafone may file a motion for reconsideration within one month or pursue contentious-administrative appeal before the National Court within two months.
companyNow: Vodafone España remains a major telecommunications provider in Spain as part of the Vodafone Group, a multinational telecom company. The company continues operating under enhanced data security scrutiny following this enforcement action.
dataType: Name, address, DNI (national ID number), invoice/billing information

companyDescription: Delivery Hero Germany GmbH operated online food delivery platforms (Lieferheld, Pizza.de) before acquisition by Takeaway.com. The company processes customer data including contact information, account credentials, and order history.
companyLongDescription: Delivery Hero Germany GmbH operated online food delivery platforms (Lieferheld, Pizza.de) before acquisition by Takeaway.com. The company processes customer data including contact information, account credentials, and order history.
caseDescription: Delivery Hero failed to delete inactive customer accounts for years, including one dormant since 2008, and ignored data subject rights requests for account information and deletion. The company also continued sending marketing emails to customers who explicitly objected, with one individual receiving 15 unwanted emails after opting out. These failures reflected systemic organizational problems despite repeated warnings from the regulator.
violationSummary: Delivery Hero systematically failed to honor data subject rights to deletion, access, and objection, excluding individuals from meaningful control over their personal data processing in violation of GDPR Chapter III.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Delivery Hero Germany GmbH failed to delete 10 inactive customer accounts despite years of inactivity, ignored 5 data subject access requests.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' personal data was retained indefinitely without consent and used for marketing against their explicit wishes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Delivery Hero claimed technical errors and staff oversights caused the data handling failures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The high volume and repetition of violations across multiple categories revealed systemic organizational problems, not isolated technical errors. Despite repeated regulatory warnings over an extended period, the company failed to implement adequate safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) requires that personal data be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than necessary (Storage Limitation Principle).
regulatoryFindings.description: Delivery Hero retained 10 inactive customer accounts without justification, including one dormant since 2008, failing to delete data when retention was no longer necessary.
violations: Delivery Hero retained 10 inactive customer accounts without justification, including one dormant since 2008, failing to delete data when retention was no longer necessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15 grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing and access to their personal data without undue delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: In 5 cases, Delivery Hero failed to provide data subject access requests or only complied after regulatory intervention by Berlin DPA.
violations: In 5 cases, Delivery Hero failed to provide data subject access requests or only complied after regulatory intervention by Berlin DPA.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 17 grants data subjects the right to erasure when data is no longer necessary or consent is withdrawn.
regulatoryFindings.description: Delivery Hero did not delete accounts of former customers who had not used the platform for years, violating the right to erasure.
violations: Delivery Hero did not delete accounts of former customers who had not used the platform for years, violating the right to erasure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 21 grants data subjects the right to object to direct marketing processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: One customer who explicitly objected to marketing received 15 additional promotional emails; 8 customers complained about unsolicited marketing that continued unabated.
violations: One customer who explicitly objected to marketing received 15 additional promotional emails; 8 customers complained about unsolicited marketing that continued unabated.

outcome: Berlin DPA issued fines totaling €195,407 in August 2019 in two administrative decisions (covering violations under pre-GDPR law and GDPR proper). The decision is final. On 1 April 2019, Takeaway.com acquired Delivery Hero's German brands (Lieferheld, Pizza.de, foodora). The new owner accepted the fines without legal challenge and committed to comprehensive process reviews and data protection improvements.
companyNow: Delivery Hero's German operations were acquired by Dutch-based Takeaway.com in April 2019. Takeaway accepted the fines and implemented data protection remediation measures including staff training and process reviews.
dataType: Email addresses, customer account data, personal identifiers

companyDescription: Financial services company offering vehicle financing, leasing, and credit products. Inherited customer base through a 2010 merger/absorption of predecessor company.
companyLongDescription: Financial services company offering vehicle financing, leasing, and credit products. Inherited customer base through a 2010 merger/absorption of predecessor company.
caseDescription: A financial services company refused to delete a customer's phone number after the customer withdrew consent and requested deletion. The company claimed a 'legitimate interest' in debt collection via phone calls, but performed an inadequate and legally deficient balancing test. The authority found the data processing had no proper legal basis and violated GDPR principles on data minimisation and purpose limitation.
violationSummary: Company processed phone number for debt collection (secondary purpose beyond original contract) without demonstrating compatibility with original collection purpose, and without valid legal basis under GDPR Art. 6(1)(f).
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The company refused to delete a customer's phone number after the customer withdrew consent, claiming a legitimate interest in contacting the customer about overdue debt collection.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer lost the ability to control unwanted telephone contact about a resolved financial matter.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company claimed it performed a proper GDPR balancing test and that legitimate interest in debt collection via phone superseded customer's right to erasure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Authority found the balancing test legally deficient in six critical respects: failed to separate processing purposes, weighted company convenience over data subject rights, provided no evidence phone contact was necessary, ignored alternative communication methods, and did not address data subject expectations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated it needed phone number for 'debt recovery via telephone contact' and 'customer service development,' citing financial efficiency and consent-independent processing rights.
claimsVsReality.reality: Phone contact was not necessary for debt recovery (postal address sufficed); customer service development was never formally identified as a processing purpose; no valid interest balancing supported either use; and customer had withdrawn consent, terminating the only lawful basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b): Personal data shall be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes, and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company processed phone number for debt collection via phone calls without demonstrating the secondary purpose was compatible with the original contract purpose (vehicle financing), and without prior notification to customer of this different use.
violations: Company processed phone number for debt collection via phone calls without demonstrating the secondary purpose was compatible with the original contract purpose (vehicle financing), and without prior notification to customer of this different use.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c): Personal data shall be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed ('data minimisation').
regulatoryFindings.description: Company retained phone number despite customer's explicit request for deletion and withdrawal of consent. Retention was not necessary as customer's postal address provided sufficient alternative for debt communications.
violations: Company retained phone number despite customer's explicit request for deletion and withdrawal of consent. Retention was not necessary as customer's postal address provided sufficient alternative for debt communications.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f): Processing is lawful only if necessary for the purposes of legitimate interests pursued by the controller or a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company claimed legitimate interest in debt collection via phone but failed to conduct a proper balancing test. Balancing was defective: weighted company cost-saving and convenience above customer's explicit rejection of phone contact; failed to consider that written communication sufficed; and did not evidence that phone contact was necessary for debt recovery.
violations: Company claimed legitimate interest in debt collection via phone but failed to conduct a proper balancing test. Balancing was defective: weighted company cost-saving and convenience above customer's explicit rejection of phone contact; failed to consider that written communication sufficed; and did not evidence that phone contact was necessary for debt recovery.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(4): If processing for a purpose different from that for which the personal data were collected, the controller shall determine compatibility by reference to multiple factors including the relationship between original and new purposes, expectations of the data subject, and whether appropriate safeguards exist.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company did not perform a proper compatibility assessment for the secondary purpose (debt collection calls). The assessment omitted goal-by-goal balancing, failed to identify debt collection as a separate processing purpose, and did not address whether customer could have reasonably expected phone-based collection efforts.
violations: Company did not perform a proper compatibility assessment for the secondary purpose (debt collection calls). The assessment omitted goal-by-goal balancing, failed to identify debt collection as a separate processing purpose, and did not address whether customer could have reasonably expected phone-based collection efforts.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(3): Where personal data are processed for a purpose different from that for which they were collected, the controller shall inform the data subject before such processing about that different purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customer was never informed that their phone number would be used for unsolicited debt collection calls, only for original financing contract purposes.
violations: Customer was never informed that their phone number would be used for unsolicited debt collection calls, only for original financing contract purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 17(1)(b): The data subject has the right to obtain erasure of personal data without undue delay where the data subject withdraws consent on which processing is based and there is no other legal basis for the processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customer withdrew consent and requested deletion. Company refused, claiming legitimate interest, but that interest was not legally established via valid balancing. Company therefore violated the erasure right by refusing deletion.
violations: Customer withdrew consent and requested deletion. Company refused, claiming legitimate interest, but that interest was not legally established via valid balancing. Company therefore violated the erasure right by refusing deletion.

outcome: Authority partially granted customer's complaint. Found violation of right to erasure, purpose limitation, data minimisation, and failure to conduct valid legitimate interest balancing. Ordered company to delete phone number from all records and notify customer of deletion. Imposed 1,000,000 HUF administrative fine for the processing violations. Company must provide proof of deletion within 30 days. Decision is final subject to administrative court review within 30 days.
dataType: Telephone number, address/residential data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6(4) – Compatibility Test for Secondary Purpose
GDPR Art. 13(3) – Information for Secondary Processing

companyDescription: The Magyar Nemzeti Bank is Hungary's central bank and primary financial regulatory authority, responsible for monetary policy, payment system oversight, and banking supervision. It maintains extensive customer financial records and transactional data from its banking operations and regulatory functions.
companyLongDescription: The Magyar Nemzeti Bank is Hungary's central bank and primary financial regulatory authority, responsible for monetary policy, payment system oversight, and banking supervision. It maintains extensive customer financial records and transactional data from its banking operations and regulatory functions.
caseDescription: The Hungarian National Bank failed to respond timely to multiple data subject access requests submitted between June–November 2018, and unlawfully deleted camera footage after the data subject requested processing restrictions. The bank also denied access to camera footage copies, failed to provide statutory legal references, and did not provide copies of internal circulars.
violationSummary: The bank's failure to implement processing restrictions and subsequent deletion of personal data (camera footage) demonstrates insecurity in data handling. The delayed responses and withholding of mandatory information also constitute failures to provide transparency and access as required.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Magyar Nemzeti Bank failed to respond within one month to three data subject access requests submitted in June, August.
whyTheyWereWrong: A bank customer lost irreplaceable evidence of her interactions at bank branches because the bank destroyed video.

claimsVsReality.claim: MNB stated it was implementing a court-ordered interim measure restricting all communications with the subject regarding contractual disputes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The interim measure applied only to communications about prior contractual matters, not to data protection access requests, which MNB should have treated separately and answered on time.

claimsVsReality.claim: MNB claimed camera footage deletion followed standard security industry practice under the then-applicable Hungarian law (Szvtv.), requiring deletion 30 days after a restriction request without authority action.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR (effective May 2018) imposed no such automatic deletion requirement; controllers must maintain restricted data until the legal claim is resolved, and national law cannot override this fundamental GDPR obligation.

claimsVsReality.claim: MNB stated it could not provide redacted camera footage because footage contained both third-party images and business secrets.
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR explicitly permits redaction of third-party personal data and legitimate trade secrets; the subject's presence in footage and general bank operations are not protected secrets, and redaction was both lawful and feasible.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12(3) requires data controllers to provide information on actions taken in response to subject rights requests within one month of receipt, or extend by two months with notice of reasons.
regulatoryFindings.description: MNB failed to respond to requests submitted 14 June 2018, 22 August 2018, and 5 November 2018 until 8 February 2019 (more than three months for the last request), without timely notification of extension or reasons.
violations: MNB failed to respond to requests submitted 14 June 2018, 22 August 2018, and 5 November 2018 until 8 February 2019 (more than three months for the last request), without timely notification of extension or reasons.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 12(4) requires controllers to inform subjects of reasons when denying action on a request.
regulatoryFindings.description: MNB's 18 December 2018 response did not identify which specific requests were denied or why, merely stating some requests were repetitive without clear designation.
violations: MNB's 18 December 2018 response did not identify which specific requests were denied or why, merely stating some requests were repetitive without clear designation.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 15(1) and (3) grant subjects the right to access personal data and obtain a copy thereof, with exceptions only for third-party confidentiality and trade secrets that can be redacted.
