regulatoryFindings.description: MNB refused to provide redacted copies of camera footage containing third persons and business secrets, despite the clear lawfulness of redaction; withheld precise statutory citations for data retention; failed to disclose whether personal data processing was ongoing with security services.
violations: MNB refused to provide redacted copies of camera footage containing third persons and business secrets, despite the clear lawfulness of redaction; withheld precise statutory citations for data retention; failed to disclose whether personal data processing was ongoing with security services.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 18(1)(c) permits subjects to request restriction of processing when data is no longer needed for processing purposes but is required for legal claims.
regulatoryFindings.description: MNB deleted at least three camera recordings within the necessary timeframe for legal proceedings despite the subject's explicit restriction request, destroying evidence the subject needed for potential litigation.
violations: MNB deleted at least three camera recordings within the necessary timeframe for legal proceedings despite the subject's explicit restriction request, destroying evidence the subject needed for potential litigation.

outcome: The authority partially granted the subject's complaint. MNB was ordered to: (1) provide redacted copies of camera footage with third-party and trade secret information masked within 30 days; (2) provide a copy of the 2017 June 30 internal circular (or redacted version) within 30 days; (3) pay a administrative penalty of 700,000 HUF (approximately USD 1.96 million). The authority found MNB violated Articles 12, 15, and 18 of the GDPR. The decision became final upon service and is subject to judicial review before the Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: The Magyar Nemzeti Bank (National Bank of Hungary) continues to operate as Hungary's central bank and financial supervisory authority. It remains responsible for monetary policy, banking regulation, and data protection compliance.
dataType: Financial records, contract details, personal identification data, biometric data (signature samples), camera footage, audio recordings of calls

companyDescription: LightYear Dealer Technologies is a Missouri-based software company founded in 1996 with approximately 80 employees. It develops and operates a dealer management system (DMS) that tracks sales, finance, inventory, payroll, and customer information for automotive dealerships nationwide.
companyLongDescription: LightYear Dealer Technologies is a Missouri-based software company founded in 1996 with approximately 80 employees. It develops and operates a dealer management system (DMS) that tracks sales, finance, inventory, payroll, and customer information for automotive dealerships nationwide.
caseDescription: LightYear Dealer Technologies operated a dealer management system that stored highly sensitive personal information about 14+ million consumers and 39,000 employees in unencrypted clear text with no access controls. An unsecured storage device attached to the backup network in April 2015 created an open port that remained undetected for 18 months, enabling a hacker to breach and download personal information of 12.5 million consumers between October and November 2016. The company failed to develop written security policies, conduct risk assessments, monitor systems, or implement basic safeguards required by law.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable data security safeguards (encryption, access controls, monitoring, risk assessment) required under the Safeguards Rule, resulting in a massive breach. This is a core insecurity violation — the data was collected but not adequately protected.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: DealerBuilt stored personal data for 14+ million consumers and 39,000 employees in unencrypted clear text without access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: A hacker exploited the unsecured device and stole personal information including Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: LightYear's backup service was secure and appropriately protected customer data
claimsVsReality.reality: Customer data was stored in unencrypted clear text with no access controls; a storage device with an open port remained undetected for 18 months, exposing 12.5 million consumers' data to breach

claimsVsReality.claim: The company maintained adequate security monitoring and device management procedures
claimsVsReality.reality: LightYear performed no vulnerability scanning, penetration testing, device inventory, or system monitoring; the open port was discovered only when a customer called about publicly accessible data

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: LightYear's failure to employ reasonable security measures to protect personal information caused substantial injury to consumers (identity theft, fraud, financial loss) not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves.
violations: LightYear's failure to employ reasonable security measures to protect personal information caused substantial injury to consumers (identity theft, fraud, financial loss) not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers themselves.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314), implementing GLB Act Section 501(b), requires financial institutions to protect security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information by developing, implementing, and maintaining a comprehensive information security program.
regulatoryFindings.description: LightYear failed to develop, implement, and maintain a written organizational information security policy.
violations: LightYear failed to develop, implement, and maintain a written organizational information security policy.
LightYear failed to designate employees to coordinate the information security program.
LightYear failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks through periodic risk assessments or vulnerability testing.
LightYear failed to design and implement basic safeguards (encryption, access controls, authentication, monitoring) to control identified risks.
LightYear failed to regularly test or monitor the effectiveness of safeguards' key controls, systems, and procedures.
LightYear stored consumers' personal information in clear text without access controls or authentication protections.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against LightYear Dealer Technologies alleging violations of the FTC Act and the Safeguards Rule. The complaint seeks a compliance order requiring the company to implement reasonable security safeguards. No monetary penalty is specified in the complaint document; enforcement would proceed through settlement negotiations or administrative proceedings.
companyNow: LightYear Dealer Technologies (DealerBuilt) continues to operate its dealer management system software. The company has approximately 180 customers comprising nearly 320 dealership locations. Status following this enforcement action is not disclosed in the complaint.
dataType: Consumer personal information (name, address, phone, email, SSN, driver's license, DOB, credit card numbers, vehicle identifiers), employee payroll data (name, address, phone, email, SSN, wages, bank account information)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a)(1) - Section 5(a) prohibition on unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information Rule (Safeguards Rule), 16 C.F.R. Part 314

companyDescription: The Budapest Police Headquarters is Hungary's largest regional police authority, responsible for law enforcement operations, crime prevention, and public safety across Budapest and surrounding areas. It maintains large databases of sensitive law enforcement and personnel data.
companyLongDescription: The Budapest Police Headquarters is Hungary's largest regional police authority, responsible for law enforcement operations, crime prevention, and public safety across Budapest and surrounding areas. It maintains large databases of sensitive law enforcement and personnel data.
caseDescription: Budapest Police Headquarters lost a 4GB USB drive containing unencrypted personnel data for 1,733 employees during an off-site management meeting. The drive included sensitive employment records and personal identifiers. The organization failed to report the incident to the National Data Protection Authority within the mandatory 72-hour window, instead waiting 45 days, citing the need for internal investigation and risk assessment.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement basic technical and organizational measures to protect personal data (encryption, access controls), creating vulnerability to unauthorized access and disclosure. Additionally, they failed the mandatory incident notification obligation under GDPR Article 33(1).
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Budapest Police Headquarters lost an unencrypted USB drive containing 1,733 employees' full personnel records with birth dates, mothers' names.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,733 police officers' sensitive personal data including birth dates, mothers' names, and TAJ numbers remained exposed on unencrypted media indefinitely, enabling identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization claimed delay was necessary to complete internal investigation and obtain risk assessment from parent organization (ORFK) before reporting.
claimsVsReality.reality: All material facts regarding the incident, affected data, and personal identifiers were known to management on January 11, 2019, and the mandatory 72-hour reporting window was 15 times longer than the actual 45-day delay. Risk assessment could have been conducted in parallel with notification.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization stated personnel data lacked sensitive information and were primarily publicly accessible.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data included birth dates, mother's names, and TAJ identification numbers—highly sensitive personal identifiers enabling identity theft—stored on an unencrypted device creating ongoing confidentiality breach risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization claimed proper internal incident procedures were followed.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal procedures (ORFK Directive 15/2018) required immediate notification of the data protection officer within 72 hours. The officer was not notified until January 28 at 07:30—well outside the mandatory window.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 33(1) requires data controllers to notify the supervisory authority without undue delay and, where feasible, no later than 72 hours after becoming aware of a personal data breach that risks the rights and freedoms of individuals.
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization delayed notification for 45 days (until February 25, 2019) despite becoming aware of the incident on January 11, 2019, exceeding the 72-hour deadline by fifteen times.
violations: The organization delayed notification for 45 days (until February 25, 2019) despite becoming aware of the incident on January 11, 2019, exceeding the 72-hour deadline by fifteen times.
Justifications for delay (completion of internal investigation, awaiting risk assessment from parent organization) were rejected as insufficient under GDPR requirements.
The data protection officer was not notified until January 28 at 07:30, well beyond the 72-hour window from incident discovery.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including protection against unauthorized access and disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: The USB drive was stored on a private device without any password protection, encryption, or access controls.
violations: The USB drive was stored on a private device without any password protection, encryption, or access controls.
Personnel data including sensitive identifiers (TAJ numbers, birth dates) were copied to an unencrypted portable storage device in violation of internal IT security policies.
No data loss prevention or centralized encryption management systems were implemented despite availability of such technology.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) (Integrity and Confidentiality) requires personal data be processed securely, with appropriate protection against unauthorized processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: 1,733 employees' birth data, mother's names, and TAJ identification numbers were exposed to ongoing confidentiality breach risk through an unencrypted, uncontrolled storage device.
violations: 1,733 employees' birth data, mother's names, and TAJ identification numbers were exposed to ongoing confidentiality breach risk through an unencrypted, uncontrolled storage device.
The organization created conditions enabling identity theft and misuse of sensitive personal identifiers through inadequate safeguarding.

outcome: The Hungarian National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) issued a decision on June 25, 2019, finding the Budapest Police Headquarters violated GDPR Article 33(1) by failing to report the data breach within 72 hours. The Authority imposed a 5,000,000 HUF fine and ordered the organization to implement necessary measures to ensure future incidents are reported within the required timeframe, with compliance documentation required within 30 days. The decision has been ordered published with the organization's identifying information. The fine is enforceable unless challenged through administrative court proceedings within 30 days.
companyNow: The Budapest Police Headquarters (Budapesti Rendőr-főkapitányság) continues to operate as Hungary's primary law enforcement authority for Budapest. The authority has since implemented enhanced data protection procedures and incident reporting protocols as required by the enforcement order.
dataType: Personnel data (full names, birth dates, mother's names, TAJ numbers, job titles, employment records)

company: Office Depot, Inc. and Support.com, Inc.
companyDescription: Office Depot is a nationwide office supply retailer operating over 1,000 stores selling office supplies, furniture, print services, and technical support services. Support.com is a technology services company providing cloud-based software and technical support services directly and indirectly to consumers through retail partners.
companyLongDescription: Office Depot is a nationwide office supply retailer operating over 1,000 stores selling office supplies, furniture, print services, and technical support services. Support.com is a technology services company providing cloud-based software and technical support services directly and indirectly to consumers through retail partners.
caseDescription: Office Depot and Support.com deceived millions of consumers by using a deceptive software tool (PC Health Check Program) that falsely reported malware infections and security problems on computers, regardless of actual system status. The program was deliberately configured to show 'malware found' whenever employees checked initial symptom boxes, not based on actual scans. This deception was used to convince consumers to purchase expensive diagnostic and repair services costing $300+.
violationSummary: The deception involved misrepresenting the results of security diagnostics through deliberately flawed software logic, constituting insecurity in information processing by providing false threat assessments designed to manipulate consumer purchasing decisions.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Office Depot and Support.com programmed the PC Health Check software to automatically report false malware infections whenever store employees checked initial problem checkboxes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Tens of millions of consumers were deceived into purchasing expensive computer repair services costing over $300 each based on fabricated malware findings, causing financial harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The PC Health Check Program is a free diagnostic service that scans computers for viruses and security problems.
claimsVsReality.reality: The program did not perform genuine scans; results were predetermined based solely on whether initial checkbox statements were selected, not on actual system conditions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Results showed 'Malware Symptoms Found' and 'infections detected' based on scan findings.
claimsVsReality.reality: These results were automatically generated whenever any of four initial symptom checkboxes were checked, regardless of actual malware presence or the results of the actual 'Quick Malware Scan'.

claimsVsReality.claim: Store employees run 'complete diagnostics' and the program will 'check for viruses' and make PCs 'run faster'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The program ran brief, limited scans that had no connection to the malware findings displayed. Results were triggered by checkbox selection, not diagnostic logic.

claimsVsReality.claim: Support.com presented the tool as using 'heuristic questions to identify likely malware infestations' running in 'a few minutes'.
claimsVsReality.reality: The tool assumed infection based on symptom questions asked, not on actual malware detection, and the questions themselves were the sole trigger for malware findings.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Office Depot falsely represented that the PC Health Check Program detected actual malware infections and security problems on consumers' computers when results were predetermined solely by checkbox selection.
violations: Office Depot falsely represented that the PC Health Check Program detected actual malware infections and security problems on consumers' computers when results were predetermined solely by checkbox selection.
Support.com provided the deceptive software as a means and instrumentality for Office Depot to commit these deceptive practices, knowing it would be used to deceive consumers.
The companies knew since 2012 that checking any initial symptom box would automatically trigger malware findings regardless of actual system status, yet continued the practice.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief. The complaint seeks permanent injunctive relief, restitution and refund of monies paid, disgorgement of ill-gotten monies, rescission or reformation of contracts, and other equitable remedies. As of the complaint filing (March 2019), the case was pending in the Southern District of Florida. Office Depot suspended use of the PC Health Check Program in November 2016 following media investigation by KIRO 7.
companyNow: Office Depot continues operations as a major office supply retailer with over 1,000 stores. The company severed its relationship with Support.com around 2017 and acquired its own tech-support services company to continue offering computer diagnostic and repair services.
dataType: Computer system information, security diagnostics
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce
FTC Act Section 13(b) – authority to seek injunctive relief

companyDescription: InfoTrax Systems, L.C. is a technology company founded in 1998 that provides backend operations systems and online distributor tools for the direct sales and multi-level marketing industry. The company manages critical business functions including compensation, inventory, orders, accounting, and data security for major clients like dōTERRA, XanGo, and LifeVantage.
companyLongDescription: InfoTrax Systems, L.C. is a technology company founded in 1998 that provides backend operations systems and online distributor tools for the direct sales and multi-level marketing industry. The company manages critical business functions including compensation, inventory, orders, accounting, and data security for major clients like dōTERRA, XanGo, and LifeVantage.
caseDescription: InfoTrax Systems failed to implement reasonable data security measures to protect approximately 11.8 million consumers' personal information. Attackers exploited vulnerabilities over nearly two years (May 2014–February 2016), accessing sensitive data including SSNs, payment card numbers, and credentials. The company stored unencrypted sensitive data and lacked intrusion detection systems, code review processes, and network segmentation.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security safeguards and encryption for sensitive personal data directly enabled unauthorized access and exposure of consumer information on a massive scale.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: InfoTrax operated backend systems for multi-level marketers while failing to implement code reviews, penetration testing, input validation, network segmentation, intrusion detection.
whyTheyWereWrong: Intruders accessed personal information of approximately 11.8 million consumers undetected for 21 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: InfoTrax purported to ensure that all personal information was adequately protected by contract.
claimsVsReality.reality: InfoTrax stored 11.8 million consumers' SSNs, payment cards, bank details, and passwords in unencrypted text, lacked intrusion detection, and remained unaware of attacker access for 21 months.

claimsVsReality.claim: Respondents assumed responsibility for the security and confidentiality of consumers' personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Respondents failed to conduct code reviews, penetration testing, implement network segmentation, or maintain inventory of stored data, leaving systems vulnerable to compromise.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents failed to employ reasonable data security practices to protect personal information (names, addresses, SSNs, financial account information) from unauthorized access and exfiltration.
violations: Respondents failed to employ reasonable data security practices to protect personal information (names, addresses, SSNs, financial account information) from unauthorized access and exfiltration.
Respondents failed to conduct adequate code reviews and penetration testing to assess cybersecurity risks.
Respondents failed to implement input validation, malicious file upload protections, and network segmentation.
Respondents failed to implement intrusion detection/prevention systems, file integrity monitoring, or data loss prevention tools.
Respondents failed to maintain a systematic inventory and deletion process for unnecessary consumer personal information.
Respondents stored sensitive personal information (SSNs, payment card data, bank account information, authentication credentials) in clear, readable text without encryption.

As a result, attackers accessed the systems undetected for 21 months (May 2014–February 2016), compromising data of approximately 1 million consumers on March 2, 2016 alone, and over 2,300 unique payment card numbers on subsequent intrusions.

Breached information was used to commit identity theft and fraud, resulting in 238 unauthorized credit card charges, 34 new fraudulent credit lines, 15 tax fraud cases, and ongoing financial harm to distributors and consumers.

outcome: On December 30, 2019, the FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document is the initial complaint, not a final settlement. Respondents were required to cease the alleged practices and implement comprehensive data security measures, subject to FTC monitoring and compliance reviews. The case initiated enforcement action against both the company and CEO Mark Rawlins individually.
companyNow: InfoTrax Systems continues to operate as a technology service provider for multi-level marketers. The company was required to implement extensive data security improvements and remediation measures under FTC oversight.
dataType: Full names, dates of birth, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, Social Security numbers, government identification numbers, payment card information (credit/debit card numbers, CVVs, expiration dates), bank account information (account and routing numbers), user IDs and passwords
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Deutsche Wohnen SE is one of Germany's largest residential real estate companies, managing hundreds of thousands of apartments across the country. The company provides residential rental housing and related property management services.
companyLongDescription: Deutsche Wohnen SE is one of Germany's largest residential real estate companies, managing hundreds of thousands of apartments across the country. The company provides residential rental housing and related property management services.
caseDescription: Deutsche Wohnen SE maintained an archive system that stored tenant personal data indefinitely without ability to delete obsolete records. Data including salary statements, tax records, and financial information from years past remained accessible despite no longer serving their original purpose. Despite a 2017 regulatory warning, the company failed to remediate the unlawful storage system for over 18 months.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate technical and organizational measures (Art. 32 equivalent) to manage data retention and deletion. The archive system's design prevented lawful data management, creating ongoing exposure of sensitive tenant financial information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Deutsche Wohnen SE used an archive system that stored tenant personal data including salary statements, tax records, and bank details without any capability to delete outdated information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of tenants had years-old sensitive financial and personal information left accessible in company systems indefinitely.

claimsVsReality.claim: Deutsche Wohnen claimed to have made preparations to remedy the identified data storage deficiencies after the 2017 regulatory warning.
claimsVsReality.reality: By March 2019 (18+ months later), no actual data cleanup had occurred and no lawful justification for continued storage could be demonstrated; preparatory measures had not resulted in legal compliance.

claimsVsReality.claim: The archive system was a neutral storage mechanism for tenant records.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system was deliberately designed without any deletion capability, embedding non-compliance into its core architecture and making lawful data management structurally impossible.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(e) requires that personal data be kept in a form which permits identification of data subjects for no longer than necessary (Storage Limitation).
regulatoryFindings.description: Deutsche Wohnen retained tenant salary statements, tax records, insurance data, and bank statements for years beyond their original collection purpose, with no mechanism to delete obsolete records.
violations: Deutsche Wohnen retained tenant salary statements, tax records, insurance data, and bank statements for years beyond their original collection purpose, with no mechanism to delete obsolete records.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing (Integrity and Confidentiality).
regulatoryFindings.description: The archive system offered no controls to prevent unauthorized viewing of years-old sensitive financial data; multiple archived records were accessible to staff without legitimate need.
violations: The archive system offered no controls to prevent unauthorized viewing of years-old sensitive financial data; multiple archived records were accessible to staff without legitimate need.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 25(1) requires data protection by design and by default, including technical and organizational measures to implement data protection principles effectively.
regulatoryFindings.description: Deutsche Wohnen deliberately designed an archive structure incapable of data deletion, embedding non-compliance into its system architecture from inception.
violations: Deutsche Wohnen deliberately designed an archive structure incapable of data deletion, embedding non-compliance into its system architecture from inception.

outcome: Fine of €14.5 million imposed on 30 October 2019 for violations between May 2018 and March 2019. Additional fines of €6,000–€17,000 imposed for 15 individual cases of unlawful data retention. Decision not yet final as of press release date; Deutsche Wohnen SE entitled to appeal. Regulatory expectation that company will restructure archive systems and implement proper data deletion protocols. Berlin DPA publicly recommended all data processors review archive compliance with GDPR.
companyNow: Deutsche Wohnen SE remains a major German residential property manager, operating hundreds of thousands of rental units across Germany. The company is subject to ongoing regulatory scrutiny regarding data protection compliance.
dataType: Financial data, employment records, salary information, tax records, social insurance data, bank account information, personal identification documents
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality Principle
GDPR Art. 25 Abs. 1 – Data Protection by Design and by Default

companyDescription: Cambridge Analytica was a private data analytics and consulting company that provided voter-profiling, microtargeting, and political marketing services. The company operated as part of the SCL Group family of companies and was based in New York. It described itself as 'politically neutral' on its website.
companyLongDescription: Cambridge Analytica was a private data analytics and consulting company that provided voter-profiling, microtargeting, and political marketing services. The company operated as part of the SCL Group family of companies and was based in New York. It described itself as 'politically neutral' on its website.
caseDescription: Cambridge Analytica and its executives harvested Facebook profile data from approximately 250,000–270,000 app users and 50–65 million of their friends through a deceptive app (GSRApp). They falsely represented that the app would not collect any identifiable information, but actually collected persistent Facebook User IDs and other identifiable data. The data was used for political microtargeting and voter profiling.
violationSummary: The company made false representations about what data would be collected (claiming no identifiable information) when in fact persistent User IDs and other identifiable information were harvested and used to identify and profile individuals for political purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Cambridge Analytica and its executives developed and operated the GSRApp that secretly harvested Facebook profile data including persistent user IDs from approximately 250,000–270,000 direct.
whyTheyWereWrong: The company falsely told users the app would not collect identifiable information, but it harvested Facebook User IDs and personal details from at least 30 million identifiable U.S.

claimsVsReality.claim: The GSRApp will NOT download your name or any other identifiable information—we are interested in your demographics and likes
claimsVsReality.reality: The GSRApp collected Facebook User IDs (persistent, unique identifiers linking users to their profiles) along with demographics, birthdate, location, friends list, and likes data

claimsVsReality.claim: Cambridge Analytica was politically neutral
claimsVsReality.reality: The company actively provided voter-profiling and microtargeting services to U.S. political campaigns and clients, with specific interest in questions about national security and political orientation

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents represented that GSRApp did not collect any identifiable information from Facebook users who authorized it, when in fact it collected Facebook User IDs and other identifiable profile data
violations: Respondents represented that GSRApp did not collect any identifiable information from Facebook users who authorized it, when in fact it collected Facebook User IDs and other identifiable profile data
They made this false representation knowing that approximately half of survey participants initially refused to grant permission, and only after the false claim was added did participation increase

outcome: FTC issued a complaint against Aleksandr Kogan and Alexander Nix on December 18, 2019, alleging deceptive practices. The complaint seeks to hold respondents responsible for their deceptive acts in harvesting personal information from Facebook users through false representations about data collection. The proceedings indicate compliance orders and monitoring were the enforcement mechanism rather than a monetary fine.
companyNow: Cambridge Analytica filed for bankruptcy in May 2018 and proceedings were ongoing at time of complaint. The company is now defunct. SCL Elections, the related U.K. entity, was placed into liquidation on April 17, 2019.
dataType: Facebook profile data including User IDs, name, gender, birthdate, location, friends list, public page likes
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices
FTC Act Section 5 – Deceptive acts or practices involving foreign commerce

companyDescription: Unrollme was an email management service offering two features: unsubscribing users from unwanted emails and consolidating wanted subscription emails into a daily 'Rollup' digest. It operated via website, iOS app, and Android app.
companyLongDescription: Unrollme was an email management service offering two features: unsubscribing users from unwanted emails and consolidating wanted subscription emails into a daily 'Rollup' digest. It operated via website, iOS app, and Android app.
caseDescription: Unrollme, an email management service, obtained full access to users' email accounts under the guise of removing unwanted subscription emails. However, its parent company Slice secretly accessed and harvested e-receipts and personal data from those inboxes for market research and sale to third parties. Unrollme deceived users through misleading messages claiming it would 'not touch personal stuff' and failed to disclose the secondary data collection.
violationSummary: Unrollme collected email data ostensibly for subscription management but secretly repurposed it for market research and commercial sale without user knowledge or consent, constituting prohibited secondary use.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Unrollme granted its parent company Slice full access to users' email accounts and failed to disclose that Slice would extract entire e-receipts containing names, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 55,000 consumers granted email access after Unrollme falsely promised their personal data would not be touched, exposing their credit card numbers, billing addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Unrollme stated 'we won't touch your personal stuff' and required email access only to monitor and manage subscription emails.
claimsVsReality.reality: Parent company Slice used automated crawlers to capture and store entire e-receipt bodies (including full personal data, credit card info, health product purchases) for market research and commercial sale.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer support represented: 'we are not reading your personal emails' and 'our algorithm only looks at subscription emails and does not touch your private emails.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Slice accessed and preserved all e-receipts without removing personal or sensitive information before storage in its Data Warehouse for analytics and sale to third parties.

claimsVsReality.claim: Access to email was necessary for core service delivery (unsubscribing and creating Rollup consolidation).
claimsVsReality.reality: Access enabled Slice to conduct undisclosed secondary data collection and monetization of user purchase history and sensitive financial/health information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Unrollme represented it would not touch users' personal emails (Paragraphs 11–12) but granted Slice access to harvest entire e-receipts containing personal financial and health data.
violations: Unrollme represented it would not touch users' personal emails (Paragraphs 11–12) but granted Slice access to harvest entire e-receipts containing personal financial and health data.
Unrollme represented access was required only to scan for subscriptions (Paragraph 13) but failed to disclose it also enabled Slice to collect and sell personal purchase data to third parties.

Customer support provided false assurances that Unrollme only accessed subscription emails and did not see personal content, despite knowing Slice was capturing full e-receipt bodies with sensitive information.

outcome: FTC issued Complaint against Unrollme alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleges two counts: (1) false representation that Unrollme would not touch personal emails, and (2) failure to disclose material information about secondary data use by Slice. The case alleges that over 20,000 consumers were deceived by early messages and over 35,000 by later messages into granting email access. Unrollme was required to comply with FTC orders; final settlement details are not included in this complaint document.
companyNow: Unrollme remained operational under Slice Technologies ownership following the FTC complaint. The company made privacy disclosures more explicit after May 2017 in response to FTC concerns.
dataType: Email content, e-receipts, billing addresses, shipping addresses, credit card information, health-related product/service purchases
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the three major nationwide consumer reporting agencies in the United States, operating since 1899. It collects, processes, and maintains credit and personal information on over 200 million U.S. consumers, providing credit reports, credit scores, and related services to businesses and direct consumers.
companyLongDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the three major nationwide consumer reporting agencies in the United States, operating since 1899. It collects, processes, and maintains credit and personal information on over 200 million U.S. consumers, providing credit reports, credit scores, and related services to businesses and direct consumers.
caseDescription: Equifax failed to patch a known critical vulnerability in its ACIS Dispute Portal system for over four months, allowing attackers to steal personal information from approximately 147 million consumers. The company's security practices were inadequate across patch management, network segmentation, access controls, encryption, and intrusion detection. Equifax also made false claims about its security safeguards in privacy policies.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security safeguards—including patch management, encryption, access controls, network segmentation, and intrusion detection—resulted in unauthorized access and massive personal data breach, fitting the Solove category of inadequate information security controls.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: Equifax failed to patch a critical Apache Struts vulnerability for over four months despite receiving alerts.
whyTheyWereWrong: Attackers exploited the unpatched vulnerability to steal personal information from 147 million consumers including SSNs, names, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, emails.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax maintains privacy policies stating 'We are committed to protecting the security of your information through procedures and technologies designed for this purpose' and 'We limit access to your personal information to employees having a reasonable need to access this information.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax failed to patch known critical vulnerabilities for months, stored sensitive data in plain text, did not segment databases, left credentials unencrypted in accessible file shares, and allowed widespread employee and contractor access to sensitive data without business justification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax maintains 'reasonable physical, technical, and procedural safeguards to help protect your personal information.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax lacked patch management enforcement, relied on misconfigured vulnerability scanners, had no network segmentation, no encryption for SSNs, minimal intrusion detection on legacy systems, and no file integrity monitoring—enabling a 4-month undetected breach affecting 147 million consumers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. Acts are unfair if they cause or are likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that consumers cannot reasonably avoid and that is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax failed to implement reasonable security measures (patch management, encryption, network segmentation, access controls, intrusion detection) to protect 147 million consumers' sensitive personal information, causing substantial injury through identity theft risk.
violations: Equifax failed to implement reasonable security measures (patch management, encryption, network segmentation, access controls, intrusion detection) to protect 147 million consumers' sensitive personal information, causing substantial injury through identity theft risk.

Equifax represented in privacy policies that it limits access to personal information to employees with reasonable need and maintains reasonable physical, technical, and procedural safeguards, when in fact it did neither.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop a comprehensive written information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including identifying risks, designing safeguards to control risks, and regularly testing/monitoring effectiveness.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax failed to implement reasonable patch management procedures, resulting in a critical vulnerability remaining unpatched for 4+ months despite receiving government alerts.
violations: Equifax failed to implement reasonable patch management procedures, resulting in a critical vulnerability remaining unpatched for 4+ months despite receiving government alerts.
Equifax failed to implement network segmentation, allowing attackers who breached ACIS to easily access dozens of unrelated databases.
Equifax stored 145+ million SSNs and other sensitive data in plain text instead of encrypted form, contrary to its own policies.
Equifax failed to implement intrusion detection controls on legacy ACIS systems, preventing discovery of attackers on the network for months.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Relief against Equifax Inc., alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act and the Safeguards Rule. The complaint sought permanent injunctive relief, restitution, refund of monies paid, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The document filed on July 22, 2019, initiates the enforcement action; the final settlement and specific remedial requirements would be determined through subsequent proceedings.
companyNow: Equifax remains one of the three major consumer reporting agencies in the United States. Following the 2017 breach and subsequent enforcement actions, the company has implemented significant remediation and security improvements, though it continues to face litigation and regulatory oversight.
dataType: Names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, physical addresses, telephone numbers, email addresses, payment card numbers and expiration dates
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act, Section 5(a) – Unfair acts or practices

company: Zala Megyei Kormányhivatal Keszthelyi Járási Földhivatall (Keszthely Land Registry Office)
companyDescription: The Keszthely Land Registry Office is a government agency responsible for managing property registrations and land records in Keszthely, Hungary, operating under the Zala County Government Administration.
companyLongDescription: The Keszthely Land Registry Office is a government agency responsible for managing property registrations and land records in Keszthely, Hungary, operating under the Zala County Government Administration.
caseDescription: A Hungarian land registry office distributed a single property registration decision to 41 property owners, each containing the full decision with personal data of all others affected. This exposed sensitive financial and personal data of property owners to unauthorized third parties, violating data minimization and transparency principles.
violationSummary: The defendant unlawfully increased the accessibility of personal data by sending comprehensive decision documents containing third-party personal data to unrelated property owners, violating data minimization and transparency principles.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Keszthely Land Registry Office distributed a single decision document to all 41 affected property owners containing the full personal.
whyTheyWereWrong: Forty property owners' sensitive personal and financial information—including names, addresses, birth years, borrowed amounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: The office claimed that applicable regulations contained no detailed requirements for delivery of decisions ('a vonatkozó jogszabályok nem tartalmaznak részlet-rendelkezéseket').
claimsVsReality.reality: FVM Regulation §99 explicitly required excerpt-based delivery when a decision contained multiple measures not affecting all parties.

claimsVsReality.claim: The office claimed it could not extract excerpts from the computerized decision ('a számítógép generálja, így az ilyen formátumú döntésből nem lehet kivonatos határozatot nyomtatni').
claimsVsReality.reality: The system manual made no provision for automated excerpt generation in multi-property decisions, but the regulation explicitly required excerpt delivery regardless of technical constraints.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently with respect to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: The land registry provided misleading information to complainants, stating that regulations contained no detailed delivery requirements when FVM Regulation §99 explicitly required excerpt delivery.
violations: The land registry provided misleading information to complainants, stating that regulations contained no detailed delivery requirements when FVM Regulation §99 explicitly required excerpt delivery.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes of processing ('data minimization').
regulatoryFindings.description: The office sent complete decisions containing all 41 property owners' personal data to each recipient when only individual excerpts were necessary and legally required.
violations: The office sent complete decisions containing all 41 property owners' personal data to each recipient when only individual excerpts were necessary and legally required.

regulatoryFindings.act: FVM Regulation §99 requires that when a decision contains multiple measures not affecting all parties, only the relevant excerpt must be delivered to each affected party.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office delivered the complete 41-property decision to all recipients instead of extracting and sending individual property excerpts as required.
violations: The office delivered the complete 41-property decision to all recipients instead of extracting and sending individual property excerpts as required.

outcome: The National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) upheld the complainants' request, finding the land registry violated data minimization and transparency principles under GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 5(1)(c). The office was ordered to pay a 600,000 HUF administrative fine and 10,000 HUF compensation for exceeding the 120-day processing deadline. The authority found the violation resulted from negligent staff error and improper software use rather than systemic policy, but mandated compliance with excerpt delivery requirements going forward. The decision is subject to administrative review before the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days.
companyNow: The Keszthely Land Registry Office remains part of Hungary's Zala County Government Administration, operating under land registration oversight. The office has acknowledged the violation and modified practices to comply with excerpt-based delivery requirements.
dataType: Names, birth years, mothers' names, addresses, loan amounts, loan currency, loan purpose
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) – Lawfulness, fairness and transparency
GDPR Art. 58(2)(b) – Corrective power to admonish

companyDescription: XFERA MÓVILES, S.A., operating under the brand MASMOVIL, is a Spanish virtual mobile network operator and broadband service provider offering combined telecommunications services including landline, mobile, and internet access to residential and business customers.
companyLongDescription: XFERA MÓVILES, S.A., operating under the brand MASMOVIL, is a Spanish virtual mobile network operator and broadband service provider offering combined telecommunications services including landline, mobile, and internet access to residential and business customers.
caseDescription: XFERA modified a customer's service contract without consent, replacing her personal details with those of an unknown third party while retaining her bank account for billing. The unauthorized change disabled her landline and internet access. The company failed to verify identity during the modification process, indicating lax security procedures.
violationSummary: Company failed to implement reasonable security measures to verify identity before altering personal data in customer contracts. Lack of procedural safeguards allowed unauthorized modification of sensitive personal information linked to financial accounts.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: XFERA modified a customer's contract without consent, changing the account holder's name and address to a third party while keeping her bank account.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer lost access to essential services for months, experienced unauthorized charges to her bank account, and suffered financial.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company asserted that a third party acting with fraudulent intent caused the identity change, making the infraction attributable to external bad faith rather than company negligence.
claimsVsReality.reality: Internal incident documentation showed the operator directly modified customer data in the system without verifying identity, despite receiving different information from the customer during the call—indicating company operational failure, not external fraud alone.

claimsVsReality.claim: XFERA invoked pendency of criminal proceedings as grounds to suspend the administrative procedure due to 'prejudicial' penal jurisdiction.
claimsVsReality.reality: The administrative violation (unlawful data processing without consent) and potential criminal charges (fraud, forgery) involve different legal goods, different actors, and different standards—no true identity of subject, fact, and legal ground exists to require suspension.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6.1(a) requires that personal data treatment be lawful and based on at least one legal ground, including explicit informed consent of the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: XFERA processed and modified the complainant's personal data (name, address, DNI, bank details) without her knowledge or consent, associating her financial account with a third party's identity.
violations: XFERA processed and modified the complainant's personal data (name, address, DNI, bank details) without her knowledge or consent, associating her financial account with a third party's identity.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently in relation to the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: XFERA altered contract terms and personal data without any transparent communication or authorization from the customer, creating a substantial imbalance in the contractual relationship.
violations: XFERA altered contract terms and personal data without any transparent communication or authorization from the customer, creating a substantial imbalance in the contractual relationship.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 32 requires implementation of appropriate technical and organizational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company operator made direct changes to customer records based on unverified telephone information, failing to implement identity verification procedures before processing modifications to sensitive personal data.
violations: Company operator made direct changes to customer records based on unverified telephone information, failing to implement identity verification procedures before processing modifications to sensitive personal data.

outcome: AEPD imposed an administrative fine of €60,000 on XFERA for violation of GDPR Article 6.1(a). The decision became final and executable. The company was required to make payment within the prescribed voluntary payment period. The decision is subject to appeal before the National Court (Audiencia Nacional) within two months.
companyNow: MASMOVIL/XFERA continues operating as a Spanish telecommunications provider. The 2019 enforcement action prompted internal implementation of training measures and external advisory services for staff involved in commercial processes.
dataType: Personal identifiers, financial data, address, email, phone number, DNI, bank account details

companyDescription: ClixSense was a crowdsourced task and survey platform owned by James V. Grago Jr. and operating as a sole proprietorship in Hampstead, North Carolina. Users earned money by viewing advertisements, completing online surveys, and performing microtasks. The company generated $6.7 million in revenue in 2015 and $9.1 million in 2016.
companyLongDescription: ClixSense was a crowdsourced task and survey platform owned by James V. Grago Jr. and operating as a sole proprietorship in Hampstead, North Carolina. Users earned money by viewing advertisements, completing online surveys, and performing microtasks. The company generated $6.7 million in revenue in 2015 and $9.1 million in 2016.
caseDescription: ClixSense operated a platform where users earned money viewing ads and completing surveys. The company publicly promised to use 'latest security and encryption techniques' but actually stored 6.6 million consumers' personal data—including Social Security numbers—in clear text with no encryption. A 2016 data breach exposed 2.7 million users' records after hackers exploited unreasonable security practices.
violationSummary: ClixSense failed to implement reasonable and necessary security measures to protect personal data at rest and in transit. Data was stored unencrypted despite promises of encryption. This constitutes insecurity under the Solove taxonomy because the company's negligent security practices created unreasonable risk of unauthorised access and exposure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: ClixSense stored 6.6 million users' personal data including Social Security numbers in unencrypted clear text, lacked network segregation, access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers accessed and publicly posted personal information for 2.7 million consumers including 500,000 U.S.

claimsVsReality.claim: ClixSense utilizes the latest security and encryption techniques to ensure the security of your account information.
claimsVsReality.reality: ClixSense stored all personal information—names, addresses, dates of birth, Social Security numbers, passwords—in clear text with zero encryption from at least 2011 through 2016.

claimsVsReality.claim: We view protection of users' privacy as a very important community principle.
claimsVsReality.reality: ClixSense failed to perform basic security measures, did not test for vulnerabilities, lacked intrusion detection, did not segregate networks, and allowed employees to store credentials in plain text on personal devices.

claimsVsReality.claim: You and your information are one of our most important assets.
claimsVsReality.reality: 6.6 million consumers' sensitive personal information was exposed in a data breach; approximately 2.7 million records including Social Security numbers were publicly posted on a hacking forum.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ClixSense represented it utilized 'latest security and encryption techniques' but stored all personal data in clear text with zero encryption
violations: ClixSense represented it utilized 'latest security and encryption techniques' but stored all personal data in clear text with zero encryption
ClixSense failed to implement vulnerability testing, intrusion detection, access controls, or network segregation—basic industry standards since 2013

ClixSense engaged in unreasonable security practices including storing plain-text credentials in employee email, failing to change default credentials, and downloading untrusted software without isolation

outcome: On June 19, 2019, the FTC issued a complaint alleging deceptive and unfair practices. The document is the initial complaint filed; no final settlement or order is shown in this complaint document itself. Typical FTC outcomes in such cases involve consent orders requiring reasonable security safeguards, data minimisation, privacy policy updates, and ongoing compliance monitoring. Final resolution would be documented in a separate order.
companyNow: ClixSense was operational as of the complaint date (June 2019). No public information provided in this document regarding current status post-enforcement.
dataType: Full names, physical addresses, dates of birth, gender, email addresses, usernames, passwords, security question answers, Social Security numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Count I: Deception – Misrepresentation about encryption
Count II: Deception – Misrepresentation about latest security techniques
Count III: Unfairness – Failure to employ reasonable security practices

companyDescription: SecurTest, Inc. is a Florida-based background screening services company that processes personal data for employment and HR purposes, including transfers from European jurisdictions.
companyLongDescription: SecurTest, Inc. is a Florida-based background screening services company that processes personal data for employment and HR purposes, including transfers from European jurisdictions.
caseDescription: SecurTest falsely claimed to be certified under the EU-U.S. and Swiss-U.S. Privacy Shield frameworks on its website from September 2017 to July 2018, despite not having completed the certification process. The company initiated an application in September 2017 but did not finish the required steps until August 2018, after FTC staff contacted them about the deceptive statements.
violationSummary: The misrepresentation disclosed false information about Privacy Shield certification, directly affecting how consumers understood the protections for their cross-border data transfers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: SecurTest falsely claimed on its website from September 2017 to July 2018 that it was certified under the EU-U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union and Swiss residents transferred their personal data to SecurTest under the mistaken belief their information would receive legally-mandated privacy protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: SecurTest, Inc. has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: SecurTest had not completed the certification process and did not self-certify to Commerce until August 31, 2018, despite these claims made from September 2017 to July 2018.

claimsVsReality.claim: SecurTest complies with the EU-US Privacy Shield Framework and the Swiss-US Privacy Shield Framework.
claimsVsReality.reality: SecurTest was not a participant in either framework during the period it made these claims, though it had initiated an application in September 2017.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SecurTest represented that it had self-certified to the Privacy Shield frameworks when it had not completed certification, making material misrepresentations about the legal framework protecting personal data transfers from the EU and Switzerland.
violations: SecurTest represented that it had self-certified to the Privacy Shield frameworks when it had not completed certification, making material misrepresentations about the legal framework protecting personal data transfers from the EU and Switzerland.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. SecurTest corrected its website statements and completed Privacy Shield certification on August 31, 2018, after FTC staff intervention. The complaint was issued on August 12, 2019.
companyNow: Unknown current status; company achieved Privacy Shield certification in August 2018 and appears to continue offering background screening services.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU and Switzerland (unspecified types)

companyDescription: NHS Highland is a territorial health authority in Scotland providing healthcare services to the Highland region. It operates multiple clinical services including specialist and community health provision.
companyLongDescription: NHS Highland is a territorial health authority in Scotland providing healthcare services to the Highland region. It operates multiple clinical services including specialist and community health provision.
caseDescription: NHS Highland sent an email to 37 patients without using BCC, exposing all email addresses to all recipients. The email list revealed individuals connected to HIV services, allowing recipients to infer sensitive health status. The organisation lacked adequate technical and organisational measures to prevent such disclosure and had not obtained proper consent for sending emails on behalf of patient groups.
violationSummary: Email addresses were exposed to unintended recipients through failure to use adequate security measures (BCC), resulting in unauthorised disclosure of personal data linked to sensitive health information.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: NHS Highland sent a group email to 37 patients without using the Blind Carbon Copy option, revealing all recipients' email addresses (which included names) to every recipient.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients' email addresses and names were exposed to all other recipients, allowing them to identify which individuals were accessing HIV services.

claimsVsReality.claim: BCC is accepted best practice for group communications
claimsVsReality.reality: BCC provided insufficient security; email recall failed, exposing 37 recipients' addresses and enabling identification of individuals accessing HIV services

claimsVsReality.claim: Standard email policy adequately addressed group communication security
claimsVsReality.reality: Policy was insufficient for sensitive patient communications; no consent was in place, and the sensitivity of health-related email exposure was not considered

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) UK GDPR requires personal data be processed in a manner ensuring appropriate security, including protection against unauthorised processing and accidental loss or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: NHS Highland relied on BCC for group communications without considering it the most secure method; email recall attempts failed, leaving data permanently exposed
violations: NHS Highland relied on BCC for group communications without considering it the most secure method; email recall attempts failed, leaving data permanently exposed

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) UK GDPR requires controllers and processors implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: BCC was standard practice in induction materials but not the most appropriate way to manage emails to sensitive patient groups; no alternative secure methods were implemented
violations: BCC was standard practice in induction materials but not the most appropriate way to manage emails to sensitive patient groups; no alternative secure methods were implemented

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 25 UK GDPR requires controllers implement appropriate technical and organisational measures at determination and time of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent for NHS Highland to send emails on behalf of patient groups was not in place and did not explicitly cover non-medical communications; sensitivity of HIV-related email addresses was not considered when arrangement was established
violations: Consent for NHS Highland to send emails on behalf of patient groups was not in place and did not explicitly cover non-medical communications; sensitivity of HIV-related email addresses was not considered when arrangement was established

outcome: ICO issued a reprimand to NHS Highland for violations of Articles 5(1)(f), 25, and 32(1) of UK GDPR. No administrative penalty was imposed under the ICO's revised public sector enforcement approach (June 2022). NHS Highland was required to provide progress updates within three months on recommendations including: reviewing data protection and email policies; conducting Data Protection Impact Assessments for group emails containing special category data; and implementing regular UK GDPR training. NHS Highland has ceased sending group emails to patients and added recommendations to its Information Governance action plan.
companyNow: NHS Highland continues to operate as a territorial health authority in the Scottish NHS. Following the incident, it has ceased the practice of sending group emails to patients and implemented enhanced information governance measures.
dataType: email addresses, special category data (health data relating to HIV services)
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality
UK GDPR Article 25 – Data Protection by Design and Default
UK GDPR Article 32(1) – Security of Processing

companyDescription: The Baden-Württemberg Police Department is a state law enforcement agency responsible for policing in the German state of Baden-Württemberg. It operates under the Data Protection Authority (LfDI) of the state.
companyLongDescription: The Baden-Württemberg Police Department is a state law enforcement agency responsible for policing in the German state of Baden-Württemberg. It operates under the Data Protection Authority (LfDI) of the state.
caseDescription: A police officer unlawfully accessed vehicle registration data and telecommunications contact information from government databases using his official credentials for private purposes—to locate and contact a casual acquaintance without authorization. The LfDI imposed a fine on the officer personally, establishing that public sector employees are not immune from data protection sanctions when abusing access for private gain.
violationSummary: The officer obtained personal data through authorized government systems but repurposed it for an entirely unauthorized private purpose (locating and contacting a casual acquaintance), constituting secondary use without any valid legal basis or consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A police officer used his official credentials to query government databases (ZEVIS and SARS) to obtain a private acquaintance's vehicle registration, personal details.
whyTheyWereWrong: The officer obtained and used personal data from government databases for private contact purposes without consent, exposing the victim to unsolicited contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: Public sector employees are exempt from GDPR sanctions under LDSG §28.
claimsVsReality.reality: The exemption applies only to the employer authority itself; individual employees remain personally liable when acting outside official duties for purely private purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly, and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: Officer processed personal data without any lawful basis or transparency, purely for private purposes unrelated to police duties.
violations: Officer processed personal data without any lawful basis or transparency, purely for private purposes unrelated to police duties.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires personal data collected for specified purposes to be processed only in ways compatible with those original purposes (purpose limitation).
regulatoryFindings.description: Data obtained through official police access was repurposed for private contact without any connection to law enforcement objectives.
violations: Data obtained through official police access was repurposed for private contact without any connection to law enforcement objectives.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6 requires a valid legal basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests) for any processing of personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Officer had no legal basis; the private contact was neither authorized nor consented to by the data subject.
violations: Officer had no legal basis; the private contact was neither authorized nor consented to by the data subject.

regulatoryFindings.act: LDSG §28 establishes that sanctions under GDPR may not be applied to public authorities themselves, but this exemption does not protect individual employees acting outside their official duties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Officer acted in purely personal capacity, not as an agent of the police authority, so the exemption for public authorities did not apply and personal liability was appropriate.
violations: Officer acted in purely personal capacity, not as an agent of the police authority, so the exemption for public authorities did not apply and personal liability was appropriate.

outcome: The LfDI imposed a fine of €1,400 on the police officer on 9 May 2019. The decision is legally final. The case establishes precedent that public sector employees cannot claim immunity when they abuse official data access for purely private purposes. The fine was calculated as a first offense affecting only one individual, within the maximum penalty framework of GDPR Art. 83(5). No remediation or monitoring was specified beyond the fine itself.
companyNow: The Baden-Württemberg Police Department continues as an operating law enforcement agency in Germany. This enforcement action prompted internal policy review regarding data access controls and employee training on data protection obligations.
dataType: Vehicle registration data, personal contact information, phone numbers (landline and mobile)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 6 – Lack of valid legal basis
LDSG §28 – Prohibition on unauthorized processing by public sector employees

companyDescription: Aetna Inc. is a major health care insurance company headquartered in Hartford, Connecticut, providing health care services across the United States. The company was acquired by CVS Health Corporation in 2018 for approximately $70 billion.
companyLongDescription: Aetna Inc. is a major health care insurance company headquartered in Hartford, Connecticut, providing health care services across the United States. The company was acquired by CVS Health Corporation in 2018 for approximately $70 billion.
caseDescription: Aetna mailed settlement letters to approximately 1,991 California residents revealing HIV medication status through a transparent envelope window. The company failed to adequately protect the confidentiality of sensitive health information when transmitting it to a settlement administrator, causing unlawful disclosure of protected medical data.
violationSummary: The company breached its duty to maintain confidentiality of protected health information by disclosing HIV status through transparent envelope windows, directly compromising patient privacy.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Aetna mailed settlement letters to 1,991 Californians in envelopes with enlarged, clear windows that visibly revealed through the window that recipients were taking HIV-related medication.
whyTheyWereWrong: 1,991 individuals had their sensitive HIV medication status involuntarily exposed to postal workers, mail handlers, family members.

claimsVsReality.claim: Aetna's settlement letters would inform members about alternative pharmacy options for HIV medications in a manner consistent with legal compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The envelopes used transparent windows that exposed recipients' HIV medication use to anyone handling the mail, violating California's medical privacy laws.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 56.101(a) requires health care service plans to preserve the confidentiality of medical information they create, maintain, preserve, store, abandon, destroy, or dispose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aetna failed to maintain and preserve medical information in a manner that preserved confidentiality by providing HIV medication information without adequate protective measures to the settlement administrator
violations: Aetna failed to maintain and preserve medical information in a manner that preserved confidentiality by providing HIV medication information without adequate protective measures to the settlement administrator

regulatoryFindings.act: California Health & Safety Code § 120980 penalizes any person who negligently discloses results of an HIV test in a way that identifies the taker of the test.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aetna negligently disclosed HIV test results and medication information through transparent envelope windows in a manner that identified recipients to postal workers and others handling the mail
violations: Aetna negligently disclosed HIV test results and medication information through transparent envelope windows in a manner that identified recipients to postal workers and others handling the mail

regulatoryFindings.act: California Constitution Article 1 § 1 provides for a fundamental right of privacy, including protection of a person's HIV status.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aetna violated individuals' constitutional privacy rights by exposing HIV medication status through envelope design
violations: Aetna violated individuals' constitutional privacy rights by exposing HIV medication status through envelope design

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair, unlawful, or fraudulent business practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aetna engaged in unfair business practices by failing to implement basic confidentiality measures when mailing sensitive health information
violations: Aetna engaged in unfair business practices by failing to implement basic confidentiality measures when mailing sensitive health information

outcome: The complaint seeks injunctive relief to prevent future violations, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation of Civil Code § 56.101 and § 17200, recovery of investigation costs, and other equitable relief. The case was filed January 28, 2019 in San Bernardino Superior Court seeking to establish liability and obtain remedies for the privacy breach.
companyNow: Aetna Inc. continues to operate as a major health insurance provider and subsidiary of CVS Health Corporation (acquired 2018). The company remains subject to HIPAA and state privacy law compliance requirements.
dataType: HIV medication status, health data

company: Kecskemét Megyei Jogú Város Polgármesteri Hivatala (Mayor's Office of Kecskemét)
companyDescription: Kecskemét Megyei Jogú Város Polgármesteri Hivatala is the mayor's office and primary administrative authority for Kecskemét, a major Hungarian city. It handles government functions, whistleblower complaints, and public administration duties for the local municipality.
companyLongDescription: Kecskemét Megyei Jogú Város Polgármesteri Hivatala is the mayor's office and primary administrative authority for Kecskemét, a major Hungarian city. It handles government functions, whistleblower complaints, and public administration duties for the local municipality.
caseDescription: A Hungarian local government office illegally disclosed a whistleblower's personal data to the institution being reported, without legal basis or consent. The disclosure resulted in the whistleblower's wrongful termination from employment. The authority failed to protect the confidentiality of the whistleblower report as required by law.
violationSummary: The government office disclosed confidential whistleblower personal data to an unauthorized third party (the institution under investigation), violating explicit statutory protections for whistleblower anonymity and the requirement for legal basis under GDPR Article 6.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Shared a confidential whistleblower report containing the reporter's full personal data (name, email, phone) with the institution being reported, without anonymization or legal justification.
whyTheyWereWrong: The whistleblower lost their job after the employer learned of the complaint through this illegal disclosure, suffering severe financial.
