claimsVsReality.claim: The office claimed the report could be shared under the Whistleblower Protection Act §3(4)(b) because information validity had not been questioned.
claimsVsReality.reality: The statute's exception for demonstrably malicious or false reports applies only when bad faith and falsity have been established through proper investigation—not merely when they have not been questioned. No such determination was made.

claimsVsReality.claim: The office stated the whistleblower's personal data were already known to the institution as the whistleblower's employer, so no unauthorized disclosure occurred.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the employer knew the individual, it did not previously know that person was the source of the confidential whistleblower complaint, nor did it have authorization to receive that sensitive report.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires personal data to be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office unlawfully disclosed whistleblower personal data without legal basis (Article 6 grounds missing) and without transparency to the data subject.
violations: The office unlawfully disclosed whistleblower personal data without legal basis (Article 6 grounds missing) and without transparency to the data subject.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6 requires a lawful basis (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interest, public task, or legitimate interest) for any data processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office had no lawful basis to share the whistleblower's name, email, and phone with the investigated institution. The exception for demonstrably malicious or false reports was not applicable here.
violations: The office had no lawful basis to share the whistleblower's name, email, and phone with the investigated institution. The exception for demonstrably malicious or false reports was not applicable here.

regulatoryFindings.act: Hungarian Whistleblower Protection Act §3(2)-(3) restricts sharing whistleblower personal data only to authorities with legal jurisdiction and duty of care, with explicit consent exception.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office shared the report with the institution under investigation (the whistleblower's own employer), which had no statutory authorization to receive it and was the subject of the complaint.
violations: The office shared the report with the institution under investigation (the whistleblower's own employer), which had no statutory authorization to receive it and was the subject of the complaint.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Articles 33-34 require notification of high-risk incidents and timely notice to affected individuals.
regulatoryFindings.description: The office complied with incident reporting to authorities but initially failed to understand and properly manage the severity of the breach until the employee inquired about data exposure.
violations: The office complied with incident reporting to authorities but initially failed to understand and properly manage the severity of the breach until the employee inquired about data exposure.

outcome: The National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) found the office unlawfully disclosed whistleblower personal data without legal basis, breaching GDPR Articles 5(1)(a) and 6, as well as Hungarian whistleblower protection laws. The authority imposed a 1,000,000 HUF fine payable within 30 days, ordered compliance measures, and mandated public disclosure of the decision with the office's identifying information. The office must ensure proper handling of future whistleblower reports and implement training and internal controls. Administrative appeal available to Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: The Mayor's Office of Kecskemét continues to function as the local government administrative body for the city. Following this decision, it is required to implement revised internal procedures for handling whistleblower reports and protect such data from further unauthorized disclosure.
dataType: Personal data from whistleblower report: name, email address, phone number, identification of whistleblower status

companyDescription: Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting and data analytics firm founded in 2013 that specialized in voter profiling and targeted political advertising using personal data harvested from millions of social media users.
companyLongDescription: Cambridge Analytica was a political consulting and data analytics firm founded in 2013 that specialized in voter profiling and targeted political advertising using personal data harvested from millions of social media users.
caseDescription: Cambridge Analytica, a political data firm, engaged in the unauthorized collection and misuse of Facebook user data without informed consent. The company weaponized psychological profiling and behavioral targeting of millions of users for political campaigns. The FTC moved for summary judgment after Cambridge Analytica failed to oppose the complaint during bankruptcy proceedings.
violationSummary: Cambridge Analytica covertly harvested vast quantities of personal data through third-party apps and without clear disclosure of collection scope or political targeting purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Cambridge Analytica collected and retained personal data from millions of Facebook users without authorization and used psychological profiling to manipulate political behavior.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Facebook users had their personal data harvested and weaponized for political manipulation without their knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company claimed to provide legitimate political consulting and voter targeting services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cambridge Analytica harvested personal data without authorization, used psychological profiling to manipulate voters, and engaged in deceptive data practices that violated user privacy and election integrity.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users consented to data collection through Facebook app terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users were not informed that third-party apps shared their data with Cambridge Analytica or how their data would be used for voter manipulation and political targeting.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Cambridge Analytica deceived millions of users by collecting personal and psychological data without informed consent or clear disclosure of political targeting purposes.
violations: Cambridge Analytica deceived millions of users by collecting personal and psychological data without informed consent or clear disclosure of political targeting purposes.
The company engaged in unfair practices by weaponizing personal data for voter manipulation without user knowledge or authorization.

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint for summary decision against Cambridge Analytica. Cambridge Analytica, then in bankruptcy, did not file opposition within the 14-day period required under FTC Rules of Practice 3.24(a)(2). The FTC found no material facts in dispute and sought final judgment and order. The company ceased operations in 2018 and entered bankruptcy, with assets liquidated.
companyNow: Cambridge Analytica shut down in May 2018 following the data privacy scandal. The company is now defunct, with remaining assets handled through bankruptcy proceedings.
dataType: Personal data, behavioral data, political preferences, psychological profiles
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Privacy violations through unauthorized data collection and use

companyDescription: The Budapest Regional Court is the appellate court serving the Budapest metropolitan region in Hungary's judicial system, overseeing cases from district courts and handling judicial administration for subordinate courts.
companyLongDescription: The Budapest Regional Court is the appellate court serving the Budapest metropolitan region in Hungary's judicial system, overseeing cases from district courts and handling judicial administration for subordinate courts.
caseDescription: The Budapest Regional Court illegally extracted a list of 51 judges who were members of the Hungarian Judges' Association (MABIE) from payroll records, compiled them for a different purpose than salary deduction, and distributed the list to court leaders without consent. The data included tax identification numbers and membership details. The court violated GDPR principles by processing special category data without legal basis and sharing it with unauthorized recipients.
violationSummary: The core harm was unauthorized disclosure of special category data (union membership) to third parties (court supervisors) without legal basis, combined with purpose creep from legitimate payroll processing to political organizing.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The court president compiled a list of 51 judges' union membership data including names, tax identification numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Fifty-one judges had their sensitive union membership and tax identification data exposed to their supervisors without authorization, chilling their freedom of association.

claimsVsReality.claim: The data extraction was necessary for administrative purposes to determine how many MABIE members served at the court.
claimsVsReality.reality: The actual purpose was to encourage judges to withdraw from the union by distributing the membership list to supervisory staff for political persuasion, a purpose incompatible with the original payroll deduction authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: The court only distributed the list to inquiring leaders seeking confirmation of their own membership.
claimsVsReality.reality: The court distributed detailed membership data on 51 judges to 18 court leaders during a mandatory meeting, including members not present and data beyond what any individual leader could legitimately need.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tax identification numbers appeared in the list accidentally.
claimsVsReality.reality: The tax IDs were extracted from payroll records alongside union data, demonstrating systematic data aggregation beyond the stated purpose, and their inclusion in the distributed list served no legitimate administrative function.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires personal data be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: The court extracted union membership data from payroll systems originally authorized only for salary deduction, then used it to identify members for political persuasion purposes without consent or lawful basis.
violations: The court extracted union membership data from payroll systems originally authorized only for salary deduction, then used it to identify members for political persuasion purposes without consent or lawful basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1) provides lawful processing requires consent, contractual necessity, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests; for public authorities, legitimate interests are excluded.
regulatoryFindings.description: The court had no consent, no legal obligation, and no valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) for extracting and compiling the membership list for the stated political purpose.
violations: The court had no consent, no legal obligation, and no valid lawful basis under Art. 6(1) for extracting and compiling the membership list for the stated political purpose.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 9(1) prohibits processing special category data including data revealing trade union membership.
regulatoryFindings.description: Union membership is a special category; the court processed it outside the narrow exceptions in Art. 9(2), particularly 9(2)(d) which requires organization activity and does not apply to employer use.
violations: Union membership is a special category; the court processed it outside the narrow exceptions in Art. 9(2), particularly 9(2)(d) which requires organization activity and does not apply to employer use.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 13(3) requires data controllers to inform data subjects of processing for new purposes before processing occurs.
regulatoryFindings.description: The court disclosed data for political persuasion without informing the 51 judges of this secondary use or obtaining new consent.
violations: The court disclosed data for political persuasion without informing the 51 judges of this secondary use or obtaining new consent.

outcome: The Hungarian National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) found the court violated GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) and Art. 6(1) by processing union membership data outside its original purpose without lawful basis and sharing it with unauthorized recipients. The authority ordered the court to: (1) notify all 18 meeting attendees within 15 days about the unlawful disclosure and demand deletion of the list; (2) ensure deletion is documented and reported within 15 days; and (3) pay 3,000,000 HUF administrative fine within 30 days. The authority also ordered public disclosure of the court's identity on its website. The decision is final and enforceable; the court may appeal to the Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days. Data deletion remains prohibited until appeal deadlines expire.
companyNow: The Budapest Regional Court (Fővárosi Törvényszék) continues to operate as Hungary's primary appellate court. Following this 2019 decision, the court would have been required to implement data protection compliance measures and delete the unlawfully processed membership list.
dataType: Trade union/interest representation membership, tax identification numbers, employment data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 9(1) – Prohibition on Processing Special Category Data
GDPR Art. 9(2)(d) – Exception for Associations (not applicable)

companyDescription: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000, S.L. is a Spanish mobile phone retailer that operated an e-commerce website collecting customer data through registration, contact, and newsletter subscription forms.
companyLongDescription: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000, S.L. is a Spanish mobile phone retailer that operated an e-commerce website collecting customer data through registration, contact, and newsletter subscription forms.
caseDescription: A Spanish mobile phone retailer collected personal data through website registration, contact, and newsletter subscription forms without providing the mandatory privacy information required by GDPR Article 13. The company failed to identify itself in the legal notice and lacked a privacy policy, leaving users in the dark about how their data would be handled.
violationSummary: The company excluded data subjects from essential information required by law, preventing them from understanding their rights and the processing of their personal data.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000 operated a website collecting users' names, email addresses, and passwords through registration.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users submitting personal data through the website had no way to learn who controlled their information, why it was being collected, how long it would be kept.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company operated a website with legitimate data collection mechanisms (registration forms, contact forms, newsletter signup)
claimsVsReality.reality: No privacy policy existed and the company failed to identify itself or disclose any information about data processing to users, violating fundamental GDPR transparency requirements

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 13 requires that when personal data is obtained from a data subject, the controller must provide at the moment of collection the identity and contact details of the controller, purposes of processing, legal basis, recipients, data retention period, and rights of the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000 failed to provide any privacy policy on its website
violations: MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000 failed to provide any privacy policy on its website
The company did not identify itself as the data controller in its legal notice
Users collecting data had no access to mandatory information about processing purposes, retention, or their rights
No information was provided about the legal basis, recipients, or data retention criteria

regulatoryFindings.act: LOPDGDD Article 11 permits satisfaction of Article 13 duties by providing basic information and directing users to additional information via an electronic address, but basic information must include controller identity, processing purpose, and rights information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Website lacked even basic privacy information in accessible format
violations: Website lacked even basic privacy information in accessible format
No electronic direction to privacy policy or additional information was provided

outcome: The Director of AEPD imposed a fine of €1,500 on MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000, S.L. for violation of GDPR Article 13. The company was ordered to make the sanction effective within the payment term specified by Spanish administrative procedure law. The resolution is executable and subject to administrative and judicial appeal within the specified timeframes. No evidence of post-decision compliance improvements was documented.
companyNow: Unknown. No information regarding the current operational status of MYMOVILES EUROPA 2000, S.L. is provided in the document.
dataType: Name, surname, email address, password, contact information

companyDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the three largest consumer reporting agencies in the United States. It owns, licenses, and maintains personal information on hundreds of millions of consumers and businesses globally, generating credit reports and analytics sold to financial institutions, retailers, insurers, and government agencies.
companyLongDescription: Equifax Inc. is one of the three largest consumer reporting agencies in the United States. It owns, licenses, and maintains personal information on hundreds of millions of consumers and businesses globally, generating credit reports and analytics sold to financial institutions, retailers, insurers, and government agencies.
caseDescription: Equifax failed to patch a known critical vulnerability in Apache Struts software for months, allowing intruders to access and exfiltrate personal information on over 147 million U.S. consumers (15.8 million California residents) from May-July 2017. The company's inadequate security infrastructure, outdated asset inventories, misconfigured scanning tools, and poor breach notification practices violated California data protection laws.
violationSummary: Equifax failed to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures to protect personal information from unauthorized access, and failed to detect and remediate a known, critical vulnerability in timely fashion, allowing massive data exfiltration.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Equifax failed to patch a critical Apache Struts vulnerability in its public-facing dispute portal for months after being alerted on March 8, 2017, despite having a documented patching process.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 147 million consumers, including 15.8 million California residents, had their Social Security numbers, birth dates, addresses, driver's license numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax represents via its website that it takes reasonable steps to protect the security of consumers' personal information and uses technical, administrative, and physical security measures that comply with applicable federal and state laws.
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax failed to patch a known critical vulnerability for 4+ months, lacked comprehensive IT asset inventory, used outdated employee contact lists, misconfigured security scanning tools, and allowed intruders to access and exfiltrate 147+ million consumers' sensitive personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.81.5(b) requires entities to implement and maintain reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of personal information owned, licensed, or maintained, to protect personal information from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax failed to implement reasonable security procedures by not patching a known critical vulnerability in Apache Struts for over 4 months after notification.
violations: Equifax failed to implement reasonable security procedures by not patching a known critical vulnerability in Apache Struts for over 4 months after notification.
Equifax lacked a comprehensive inventory of its IT assets, preventing timely identification and patching of vulnerable systems.
Equifax misconfigured its vulnerability scanning tools, which failed to detect or alert staff that the Apache Struts vulnerability had not been patched.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.82 requires entities to disclose a breach of security of unencrypted personal information of California residents in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax discovered suspicious activity on July 29, 2017, but delayed public announcement until September 7, 2017 (over one month later).
violations: Equifax discovered suspicious activity on July 29, 2017, but delayed public announcement until September 7, 2017 (over one month later).
The delayed announcement caused widespread confusion and burdened consumers with identity protection costs and time.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair competition, including unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business acts or practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by publicly representing that it takes reasonable steps to protect consumer personal information while maintaining inadequate security infrastructure.
violations: Equifax engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by publicly representing that it takes reasonable steps to protect consumer personal information while maintaining inadequate security infrastructure.
Equifax made unfair, deceptive, untrue, and misleading statements regarding its data security practices at the time of the breach.

outcome: Complaint for injunction, civil penalties, and other equitable relief filed July 22, 2019. Plaintiff seeks court orders to prevent further unfair competition violations, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation under Business & Professions Code § 17206, recovery of investigation costs, and such other relief as the court deems just and proper. The complaint alleges violations of California Civil Code §§ 1798.81.5(b) and 1798.82, as well as § 17200 UCL.
companyNow: Equifax remains one of the three largest consumer reporting agencies in the United States as of the complaint filing. The company continues to collect and maintain personal information on over 820 million consumers and 91 million businesses worldwide.
dataType: Social Security numbers, birth dates, addresses, driver's license numbers, credit card numbers, credit history, financial account information, credit inquiry records, public records (bankruptcies, tax liens, civil judgments)
legalBasisViolated: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 (Unfair Competition Law)

companyDescription: GRUPO VALSOR Y LOSAN, S.L. is a real estate management company (gestora inmobiliaria) based in Spain that handles property transactions and sales.
companyLongDescription: GRUPO VALSOR Y LOSAN, S.L. is a real estate management company (gestora inmobiliaria) based in Spain that handles property transactions and sales.
caseDescription: A real estate management company disclosed personal data of third parties (names, surnames, addresses) in property purchase contract emails sent to prospective buyers. The company failed to maintain the integrity and confidentiality of personal data and did not respond to the data protection authority's investigation request.
violationSummary: The company breached the confidentiality of personal data by disclosing third parties' identifiers to unauthorized recipients (prospective buyers). This constitutes a breach of confidentiality under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: GRUPO VALSOR Y LOSAN disclosed personal data of third parties including names, surnames, and home addresses in property purchase contract emails sent to prospective buyers without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two individuals' complete personal identifiers were exposed to an unauthorized third party during a real estate transaction, compromising their privacy.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that guarantees adequate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, through appropriate technical or organizational measures ('integrity and confidentiality').
regulatoryFindings.description: The company facilitated disclosure of personal identifiers (names, surnames, addresses) in property purchase contract emails sent to prospective buyers without authorization, violating the integrity and confidentiality principle.
violations: The company facilitated disclosure of personal identifiers (names, surnames, addresses) in property purchase contract emails sent to prospective buyers without authorization, violating the integrity and confidentiality principle.
The company failed to demonstrate proactive responsibility for compliance with data protection obligations when required to respond to the data protection authority's investigation request.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 83.5 establishes that violations of Article 5(1)(f) constitute very serious infringements subject to administrative fines up to €20,000,000 or 4% of annual global turnover.
regulatoryFindings.description: The breach of Article 5(1)(f) triggered enforcement action under Article 83.5, making the company subject to administrative fines.
violations: The breach of Article 5(1)(f) triggered enforcement action under Article 83.5, making the company subject to administrative fines.

outcome: The Spanish Data Protection Authority (AEPD) Director imposed an administrative fine of €2,500 on GRUPO VALSOR Y LOSAN, S.L. for violating GDPR Article 5(1)(f) regarding integrity and confidentiality of personal data. The company must pay the fine within the specified voluntary payment period. The decision is final but subject to administrative review or contentious-administrative appeal before the National Court within two months of notification.
dataType: Personal identifiers (names, surnames, home address)

company: Landesbeauftragter für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit (LfDI) Baden-Württemberg
companyDescription: The LfDI Baden-Württemberg is the state data protection authority responsible for enforcing GDPR and data protection legislation in the state of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. It investigates complaints, enforces compliance, and issues guidance on data protection matters.
companyLongDescription: The LfDI Baden-Württemberg is the state data protection authority responsible for enforcing GDPR and data protection legislation in the state of Baden-Württemberg, Germany. It investigates complaints, enforces compliance, and issues guidance on data protection matters.
caseDescription: This is a press release by the Baden-Württemberg data protection authority reporting a ten-fold increase in data breach notifications since GDPR came into effect. The authority highlights pervasive failures in data handling, particularly in medical practices, caused by negligence, ransomware attacks, and misdirected communications.
violationSummary: The violations stem from inadequate security measures, lack of internal controls, and organisational failures to properly safeguard personal data. Both technical insecurity (ransomware) and process failures (misdirection) fall under insecurity.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Multiple organizations across Baden-Württemberg reported nearly 1,000 data breaches in 2019, including postal misdirection, hacking attacks, email misdirection.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients' extremely sensitive health records including medical reports, prescriptions, and X-rays were exposed to unauthorized recipients or encrypted by ransomware.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed with integrity and confidentiality, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Multiple organisations failed to maintain confidentiality by misdirecting sensitive health data via post, email and fax to unauthorised recipients
violations: Multiple organisations failed to maintain confidentiality by misdirecting sensitive health data via post, email and fax to unauthorised recipients
Organisations lacked adequate encryption and ransomware protections, allowing hackers to access personal data

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure security of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Medical practices lacked adequate internal control mechanisms to prevent accidental disclosure of health data
violations: Medical practices lacked adequate internal control mechanisms to prevent accidental disclosure of health data
Organisations failed to implement encryption, employee training, and data security procedures
No adequate measures to protect against ransomware attacks

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33 requires notification of data breaches to the supervisory authority without undue delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Nearly 1,000 breach notifications received in 2019 alone, with 177 in May, indicating widespread organisational failure to prevent breaches in the first instance
violations: Nearly 1,000 breach notifications received in 2019 alone, with 177 in May, indicating widespread organisational failure to prevent breaches in the first instance

outcome: The LfDI issued monetary penalties totalling €207,140 for data handling failures. The highest penalties were two fines of €80,000 each: one for a digital publication that published health data due to inadequate internal controls, and one for a financial company that improperly disposed of personal data. The authority issued compliance guidance and emphasised mandatory notification of affected individuals for health data breaches, in addition to authority notification.
companyNow: The Landesbeauftragter für den Datenschutz und die Informationsfreiheit (LfDI) Baden-Württemberg continues to function as the state-level data protection authority in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, overseeing GDPR compliance and investigating data protection violations.
dataType: Health data, patient records, prescriptions, X-ray images, general personal data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 33 - Notification of a personal data breach

company: Budapesti Műszaki és Gazdaságtudományi Egyetem (Budapest University of Technology and Economics)
companyDescription: Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) is Hungary's oldest and largest technical university, founded in 1782, providing engineering and technical education and research.
companyLongDescription: Budapest University of Technology and Economics (BME) is Hungary's oldest and largest technical university, founded in 1782, providing engineering and technical education and research.
caseDescription: A university failed to provide an employee access to their personal data and employment records within the legally required one-month deadline. The university delayed responding to the access request for over three months and did not provide complete information even after regulatory intervention. This violated the employee's right to access their own personal data under GDPR.
violationSummary: The university denied the data subject effective access to their own personal data for an extended period without valid grounds, violating the right to access guaranteed under GDPR Article 15.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Budapest University of Technology and Economics failed to provide an employee's requested personal data within the required one-month deadline.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee was denied timely access to their own employment records, including tax withholding details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The university stated it would respond to the data request and requested the employee's patience (November 20, 2018 email).
claimsVsReality.reality: The university did not respond substantively for over three months until after regulatory intervention; the response was incomplete.

claimsVsReality.claim: The university claimed the employee already had certain information like M30 tax documents, so this satisfied the access request.
claimsVsReality.reality: Receiving information through employment processes does not discharge GDPR obligations; the university must provide complete personal data files upon request.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 12(3) requires the controller to provide information on action taken on a data subject's request without undue delay and in any case within one month of receipt, extendable by two months for complex or numerous requests if the controller notifies the data subject.
regulatoryFindings.description: University failed to respond to the data access request within one month of receipt (October 10, 2018) without providing notice of extension or justification
violations: University failed to respond to the data access request within one month of receipt (October 10, 2018) without providing notice of extension or justification
First substantive response only provided after regulatory intervention, in January 2019, over three months later
Response was incomplete and the data subject had to request additional clarification

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(1) grants data subjects the right to obtain confirmation of processing and access to a copy of their personal data along with specified metadata.
regulatoryFindings.description: University did not provide complete personal data copies and supporting documents as required, including employment records and work descriptions
violations: University did not provide complete personal data copies and supporting documents as required, including employment records and work descriptions
University claimed certain information had already been provided to the employee, but this does not satisfy the GDPR access right obligation to provide complete records on demand

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 15(3) requires the controller to provide a copy of personal data being processed in a commonly used electronic format when requested electronically.
regulatoryFindings.description: University did not provide data in accessible format within required timeframe
violations: University did not provide data in accessible format within required timeframe
Incidentally transmitted M30 tax form containing personal data of another individual (data breach/additional violation)

outcome: The Hungarian Data Protection Authority (NAIH) found the university violated GDPR Articles 12(3)-(4) and 15(1)-(3). The authority ordered the university to: (1) fulfill the employee's data access request within 8 days of the decision; (2) prove compliance within 8 days after fulfillment; (3) pay 600,000 HUF administrative fine; (4) allow publication of the decision with the university's identifying data on the authority's website. The decision is subject to judicial review within 30 days. The case highlights institutional failures in handling data subject rights even at an academic institution.
companyNow: The Budapest University of Technology and Economics remains a leading Hungarian technical university and continues its operations as a public higher education institution.
dataType: Employment records, social security registration details, tax information, work-related documentation

companyDescription: An unnamed private entity engaged in unauthorized debt claim purchasing and collection without Magyar Nemzeti Bank licensing. It processed personal data of bank loan borrowers in connection with unlicensed financial services.
companyLongDescription: An unnamed private entity engaged in unauthorized debt claim purchasing and collection without Magyar Nemzeti Bank licensing. It processed personal data of bank loan borrowers in connection with unlicensed financial services.
caseDescription: An unlicensed financial entity engaged in unauthorized debt claim purchasing activity without Magyar Nemzeti Bank (MNB) approval and unlawfully processed personal data of loan borrowers. The entity obtained personal data through an assignment agreement and continued processing it for debt collection purposes without proper legal basis, in violation of GDPR principles of lawful processing, purpose limitation, and data minimization.
violationSummary: The entity processed personal data pursuant to an activity (unlicensed debt purchasing) that was itself unauthorized under financial services law, violating GDPR Article 5(1)(a) lawfulness requirement and Article 6 legal basis requirements. The processing was insecure in the sense of lacking proper legal authority.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Purchased bank loan debt claims without Magyar Nemzeti Bank authorization and processed borrowers' personal data including names, birth details, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Borrowers had their personal data illegally processed and shared to an unauthorized debt collector.

claimsVsReality.claim: The entity claimed it had a valid legal basis to process personal data under the contract performance provision and prior consent, and that it could continue processing even after consent withdrawal due to legal obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The underlying loan contract had terminated and been assigned; no valid legal basis existed under GDPR Article 6. The entity was unlicensed to purchase claims, making the processing itself illegal. Prior consent obtained under the loan contract did not transfer to the debt purchaser.

claimsVsReality.claim: The entity claimed it implemented a data protection policy as of 25 May 2018 and was compliant thereafter.
claimsVsReality.reality: A policy does not create legal basis or lawfulness; the entity continued to process data without proper GDPR Article 6 grounds and in violation of Article 5 principles, regardless of internal procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(a) requires that personal data be processed lawfully, fairly and transparently.
regulatoryFindings.description: The entity processed personal data in connection with unlicensed debt purchasing activity, which itself violated Hungarian financial services law (MNB authorization requirement), making the processing inherently unlawful.
violations: The entity processed personal data in connection with unlicensed debt purchasing activity, which itself violated Hungarian financial services law (MNB authorization requirement), making the processing inherently unlawful.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 5(1)(b) requires that personal data be collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not processed in a manner incompatible with those purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Data collected under an original loan contract with the bank was processed for debt collection purposes after the underlying contract terminated and was assigned to an unlicensed third party, violating purpose limitation and the incompatibility of purposes.
violations: Data collected under an original loan contract with the bank was processed for debt collection purposes after the underlying contract terminated and was assigned to an unlicensed third party, violating purpose limitation and the incompatibility of purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 6(1) provides that processing is lawful only if one of six legal bases is satisfied (consent, contract, legal obligation, vital interests, public task, or legitimate interests).
regulatoryFindings.description: The entity relied on contract performance (Article 6(1)(b)), but the underlying contract (the bank loan) had terminated before assignment; it also incorrectly relied on prior consent and a legal obligation basis that did not apply under GDPR.
violations: The entity relied on contract performance (Article 6(1)(b)), but the underlying contract (the bank loan) had terminated before assignment; it also incorrectly relied on prior consent and a legal obligation basis that did not apply under GDPR.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Article 58(2) empowers supervisory authorities to censure and restrict processing where violations occur.
regulatoryFindings.description: The authority found violations of Articles 5 and 6 and exercised its authority to restrict and prohibit debt-related processing of the individuals' data.
violations: The authority found violations of Articles 5 and 6 and exercised its authority to restrict and prohibit debt-related processing of the individuals' data.

outcome: The National Data Protection and Information Freedom Authority (NAIH) partially upheld the individuals' complaint. The Authority found the entity unlawfully processed the individuals' personal data in connection with unauthorized debt claim purchasing. The Authority: (1) censured the entity for violating GDPR Articles 5(1)(a)–(b) and 6(1); (2) ordered restriction of the individuals' personal data processing and prohibited their use for debt claim collection purposes; (3) rejected the individuals' request for a specific fine amount but imposed an administrative fine of 1,000,000 HUF (approximately €3,400) on the entity due diligence grounds. The Authority noted that data stored in connection with proceedings before other authorities (tax, central bank, bankruptcy, police, land registry) may be retained for purposes of defending legal claims, consistent with GDPR Article 17(3)(e). The decision is final subject to judicial review before the Budapest Metropolitan Court within 30 days.
companyNow: Unknown. The entity was unlicensed and operating illegally; no information provided on current operational status. The MNB prohibited it from engaging in debt claim purchasing activity as of January 2019.
dataType: Personal identification data (name, birth name, birthplace, date of birth, mother's name, address), financial data (loan amounts, collateral information)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Article 6(1) – Legal basis for processing
GDPR Article 58(2)(b) – Supervisory authority power to censure
GDPR Article 83(5)(a) – Administrative fines for principles violations

companyDescription: A Hungarian debt collection company engaged in credit recovery and vehicle repossession services, processing personal data including contact information for enforcement purposes.
companyLongDescription: A Hungarian debt collection company engaged in credit recovery and vehicle repossession services, processing personal data including contact information for enforcement purposes.
caseDescription: A debt collection company continued to process a debtor's telephone numbers after the debtor withdrew consent and requested deletion. The company claimed a legitimate interest basis under GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) for debt collection, but the interest assessment was flawed and did not override the data subject's right to erasure. The authority found the processing unlawful and imposed a fine.
violationSummary: The company repurposed telephone numbers originally collected with consent for debt collection under an asserted but inadequately justified legitimate interest, continuing processing after withdrawal of the original legal basis.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The debt collection company retained and processed a customer's telephone numbers after the customer explicitly withdrew consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer lost the ability to control contact with the company and faced continued unwanted phone calls for debt collection purposes after clearly requesting all communications cease,.

claimsVsReality.claim: We must retain telephone numbers because processing is necessary for legal proceedings (Art. 17(3)(e)) and for the purposes of legitimate interests (Art. 6(1)(f)).
claimsVsReality.reality: Debt collection is not a legal proceeding—it is a pre-legal settlement effort. No court case had been filed. The company's own interest assessment was contradictory and incomplete, failing to prove telephone contact was necessary when postal contact was available and the data subject had explicitly requested postal-only contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: We have conducted a proper interest balancing test (Érdekmérlegelés) that justifies retention of telephone numbers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The interest assessment contained multiple fundamental flaws: it was internally contradictory, it focused narrowly only on vehicle withdrawal scenarios while ignoring other debt collection purposes, it generalized about data subject preferences, and it entirely failed to address what happens when an individual objects to or refuses telephone contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: We must notify the data subject about vehicle withdrawal consequences via telephone because the administrative decision does not contain full details.
claimsVsReality.reality: Administrative decisions that comply with statutory requirements and produce legal effect do not require supplementary telephone notification. The data subject is presumed to know traffic law (Road Traffic Act) requirements for vehicle operation, and explanation of legal consequences is not the company's obligation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Processing is restricted to third-party collection and vehicle withdrawal notification only.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's response letter explicitly stated it retained telephone numbers 'as long as the debt remains unpaid' and used them for general debt collection communication—far broader than the narrow restriction it later claimed.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) requires that personal data be 'collected for specified, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes.'
regulatoryFindings.description: The company collected telephone numbers with consent for loan assessment and contact during the contractual relationship, then continued processing for debt collection purposes after consent was withdrawn, without a valid legal basis.
violations: The company collected telephone numbers with consent for loan assessment and contact during the contractual relationship, then continued processing for debt collection purposes after consent was withdrawn, without a valid legal basis.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(c) requires that personal data be 'adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed' (data minimisation).
regulatoryFindings.description: Telephone numbers were retained and processed for debt collection despite the data subject's explicit request for deletion and despite postal address being available for contact, making telephone data unnecessary.
violations: Telephone numbers were retained and processed for debt collection despite the data subject's explicit request for deletion and despite postal address being available for contact, making telephone data unnecessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 17(1)(b) grants the data subject the right to erasure when 'the data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based, and there is no other legal ground for the processing.'
regulatoryFindings.description: The company refused the erasure request, claiming a legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) without conducting a proper, balanced interest assessment that demonstrated necessity or proportionality.
violations: The company refused the erasure request, claiming a legitimate interest under Art. 6(1)(f) without conducting a proper, balanced interest assessment that demonstrated necessity or proportionality.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) permits processing only if 'necessary for the purposes of the legitimate interests pursued by the controller or by a third party, except where such interests are overridden by the interests or fundamental rights and freedoms of the data subject.'
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's interest assessment was contradictory, incomplete, failed to address the data subject's explicit objection, did not justify why telephone contact was necessary given postal contact availability, and did not properly weigh the company's interest against the data subject's right to erasure.
violations: The company's interest assessment was contradictory, incomplete, failed to address the data subject's explicit objection, did not justify why telephone contact was necessary given postal contact availability, and did not properly weigh the company's interest against the data subject's right to erasure.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 47 Recital establishes that when legitimate interest is the legal basis, a balancing test must be conducted beforehand, determining the legitimate interest, the impact on the data subject, necessity, and proportionality.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company's interest balancing document contained fundamental gaps: it was contradictory (claiming both equal balance and superiority of the company's interest), narrowly focused only on vehicle withdrawal notifications, generalized about data subject preferences, and failed to address what happens when an individual objects.
violations: The company's interest balancing document contained fundamental gaps: it was contradictory (claiming both equal balance and superiority of the company's interest), narrowly focused only on vehicle withdrawal notifications, generalized about data subject preferences, and failed to address what happens when an individual objects.

outcome: The authority granted the data subject's request, ordering immediate erasure of both telephone numbers from all records and prohibiting further processing. The company was required to confirm deletion and notify the data subject within 30 days. The authority rejected the data subject's request for an administrative fine initially, but then exercised official discretion to impose an administrative fine of 1,000,000 Ft (approximately €1,000,000) for the unlawful processing. The decision is subject to judicial review before the Metropolitan Court of Budapest within 30 days. Disputed data may not be deleted or destroyed pending court resolution.
dataType: Telephone numbers (landline and mobile)
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 5(1)(b) – Purpose Limitation (Purpose Limitation Principle)
GDPR Art. 6(1)(f) – Legitimate Interest (inadequate or absent interest assessment)
GDPR Art. 13(3) – Transparency of purpose changes
GDPR Art. 47 Recital – Necessity of interest balancing

companyDescription: Health Canada is the federal department responsible for helping Canadians maintain and improve their health, including administering the Non-Insured Health Benefits Program for First Nations and Inuit residents.
companyLongDescription: Health Canada is a federal government department that develops health policies, enforces health regulations, and administers health programs for Canadian residents. The Non-Insured Health Benefits Program provides coverage for medically necessary health services such as prescription drugs, dental care, vision care, and medical transportation for registered First Nations and recognized Inuit residents not covered by private or provincial plans. The program uses expert drug-review committees to establish evidence-based clinical criteria for determining drug eligibility.
caseDescription: Physicians complained that Health Canada collected excessive personal information from patients applying for Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) drug coverage, requiring exact diagnostic details when general ranges would suffice. Health Canada demonstrated that all collected information was necessary for adjudicating drug benefit claims based on evidence-based clinical criteria established by expert committees. The complaint was found to be not well-founded.
violationSummary: The complaint alleged unnecessary interrogation through excessive information collection requirements on Limited Use drug benefit forms, though the investigation ultimately found the collection justified by clinical necessity.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Health Canada collected detailed personal medical information from physicians on Limited Use drug benefit forms for First Nations.
whyTheyWereWrong: First Nations and Inuit patients unnecessarily disclosed sensitive diagnostic details and experienced delayed access to medically necessary treatments while Health Canada adjudicated their drug.

claimsVsReality.claim: Physicians argued that Health Canada requests exact diagnostic information when general ranges would suffice to demonstrate eligibility.
claimsVsReality.reality: Health Canada's expert committees required exact clinical parameters (e.g., specific number of swollen joints) to calculate percentage improvements, monitor treatment efficacy, and ensure cost-effective use of biologic therapies—information ranges cannot provide these calculations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Collection of detailed personal information caused unnecessary delays in patient access to treatment.
claimsVsReality.reality: While Health Canada collected information based on evidence-based clinical criteria, physicians confirmed that patients experienced delays; Health Canada subsequently implemented expedited review processes for some drugs in response.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 - Personal information collected by a government institution must relate directly to an operating program or activity of the institution
Privacy Act Section 3 - Definition of personal information as information about an identifiable individual recorded in any form
regulatoryFindings.description: Health Canada collects names and medical information of NIHB beneficiaries
violations: Health Canada collects names and medical information of NIHB beneficiaries

outcome: The complaint was determined to be not well-founded. Health Canada demonstrated that the personal information collected on Limited Use drug benefit forms relates directly to the administration of the NIHB Program and is necessary for adjudicating drug benefit claims. The investigation confirmed that all data fields requested correspond to clinical criteria and eligibility requirements established by evidence-based expert drug-review committees. While the complaint was dismissed, Health Canada was encouraged to implement expedited review processes and improve transparency with beneficiaries regarding information-handling practices, particularly regarding sensitive mental health information.
companyNow: Health Canada continues to administer the NIHB Program and other federal health initiatives. Following this investigation, the department committed to expanding expedited review processes and improving transparency in its information-handling practices with beneficiary communities.
dataType: Health data, diagnostic information, medical history, prescription drug information, mental health information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 4 (requirement that collected information relate directly to operating program)

companyDescription: Correctional Service Canada (CSC) is the federal government agency responsible for managing federal penitentiaries and offender rehabilitation across Canada. It operates correctional institutions housing inmates serving sentences of two years or more.
companyLongDescription: Correctional Service Canada is a federal Crown corporation under the jurisdiction of the Canadian Department of Public Safety. It manages the federal correctional system, operating institutions ranging from minimum to maximum security facilities. CSC is responsible for custody, security, and rehabilitation of federal offenders. The agency must comply with federal privacy legislation, including the Privacy Act, which grants inmates and other individuals the right to access personal information held by government institutions.
caseDescription: Correctional Service Canada (CSC) violated the Privacy Act by failing to provide a federal inmate with timely access to video and audio recordings he requested, despite a previous 2012 finding of similar violations. CSC failed to retrieve and retain video recordings before they were overwritten due to processing delays exceeding the 108-hour retention period, and left four requests unanswered for over two and a half years.
violationSummary: CSC failed to implement adequate retention and retrieval processes for personal information (video/audio recordings) with short retention periods, resulting in loss of records before the complainant could access them. This constitutes insecurity in information processing and handling.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: CSC failed to process video access requests within the 108-hour retention period, causing recordings to be overwritten, and left four requests unanswered for over two.
whyTheyWereWrong: An inmate seeking evidence of officer misconduct, assault, and corruption lost access to video recordings that could have proven his innocence because CSC's processing delays exceeded.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC claimed it was unable to locate video recordings from October 2015 incidents when it advised the complainant on December 11, 2015.
claimsVsReality.reality: CSC later determined the recordings were in fact retained and only then disclosed they were being withheld under exemptions on February 22, 2017—over two months later.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC's internal processes adequately handled requests for records with short retention periods following the 2012 Privacy Commissioner recommendation.
claimsVsReality.reality: CSC failed to implement any new processes and repeated the identical violation: video requests were delayed 6-7 days reaching ATIP, then another 7-14 days before retrieval was tasked back to the institution, causing videos to be overwritten before retrieval.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC could have retrieved the November 2015 video recordings that the complainant requested on the same day the incidents occurred.
claimsVsReality.reality: Due to processing delays exceeding the 108-hour retention window, both requested recordings were overwritten before retrieval was even attempted, leaving the complainant without evidence of the incidents.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Subsection 6(1) and Privacy Regulations Section 4(1)
regulatoryFindings.description: CSC failed to retain video recordings for the required retention period before they were overwritten
violations: CSC failed to retain video recordings for the required retention period before they were overwritten
CSC did not make reasonable efforts to secure and preserve video recordings prior to destruction

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Subsection 12(1)
regulatoryFindings.description: CSC denied the complainant access to personal information (video recordings) about himself that was under CSC's control
violations: CSC denied the complainant access to personal information (video recordings) about himself that was under CSC's control
The complainant provided sufficiently specific information to render the recordings reasonably retrievable, but CSC failed to retrieve them in time

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Subsection 16(3)
regulatoryFindings.description: CSC failed to respond to four access requests within the required time limits, resulting in a deemed refusal to provide access
violations: CSC failed to respond to four access requests within the required time limits, resulting in a deemed refusal to provide access

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. CSC was ordered to implement appropriate processes to ensure that personal information access requests for records with short retention periods are expeditiously forwarded and retrieved before destruction. CSC was directed to provide complete responses to the four outstanding requests as soon as possible. CSC's Interim Commissioner accepted the recommendations and committed to ensuring immediate retrieval and preservation of videos when access requests are received, with formal follow-up reporting to the Privacy Commissioner within six months.
companyNow: CSC continues to operate as Canada's federal correctional agency. Following this 2018 finding, the agency committed to implementing improved processes for handling access requests involving records with short retention periods.
dataType: Video recordings, audio recordings, institutional records, grievance files, personal identifying information

companyDescription: The Department of National Defence (DND) is Canada's federal government agency responsible for defence and military operations, including the Canadian Armed Forces.
companyLongDescription: The Department of National Defence (DND) is the primary federal government institution in Canada responsible for defence policy, military operations, and the administration of the Canadian Armed Forces (CAF). It manages military personnel, defence infrastructure, and security operations across Canada. The Directorate of Access to Information and Privacy (DAIP) within DND handles privacy and access to information requests for military records and investigations.
caseDescription: The Department of National Defence (DND) disclosed deceased Canadian Forces members' medical records to military investigators under Privacy Act section 8(2)(e) for suicide investigations. While the disclosures were found to be authorized, the investigation identified deficiencies in DND's record retention practices and recommended improvements to ensure statutory compliance and best practices.
violationSummary: The disclosure of sensitive medical records without explicit consent, though authorized under section 8(2)(e), involved the dissemination of particularly sensitive personal health information. The violation relates to how DND managed the disclosure process and record-keeping rather than the authorization itself.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: DND disclosed deceased Canadian Forces members' complete medical records to military investigators for suicide investigations based on requests that often sought full medical histories rather.
whyTheyWereWrong: Families of deceased service members had their relatives' sensitive mental health and medical information disclosed without clear necessity, causing distress to grieving families.

claimsVsReality.claim: DND claimed that section 8(2)(e) of the Privacy Act authorizes full disclosure of medical records to military investigators for suicide investigations without additional justification.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the legal authority existed, the investigation found DND routinely disclosed complete medical histories when investigating officers' own procedures stated they only needed to determine if injuries were self-inflicted, making full disclosure unnecessary.

claimsVsReality.claim: DND stated it had no formal operating procedure for 8(2)(e) disclosure decisions, with authority limited only to the Director and Deputy Director of Privacy Operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite this claim of centralized control, the investigation found inconsistent record-keeping, missing request forms, illegible handwritten notations, and inadequate documentation of the necessity assessment required before disclosure.

claimsVsReality.claim: Investigators needed complete medical files including mental health history, family medical history, and medication records to conduct suicide investigations.
claimsVsReality.reality: CF-NIS's own Standard Operating Procedures stated that suicide investigations should focus only on determining whether wounds were self-inflicted, with administrative details about mental state or medications explicitly noted as unnecessary to pursue.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act subsection 8(4) and Privacy Regulations section 7
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to retain copies of 8(2)(e) request forms in 3 of 6 cases reviewed
violations: Failed to retain copies of 8(2)(e) request forms in 3 of 6 cases reviewed
Inadequate documentation of disclosures across multiple locations
Failure to maintain comprehensive records of information disclosed

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Secretariat Directive on Privacy Practices - Appendix C
regulatoryFindings.description: Requests did not specify the section of statute under which investigative activity was undertaken
violations: Requests did not specify the section of statute under which investigative activity was undertaken
Incomplete documentation of disclosure authorization and scope

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 8(2)(e) - disclosure authorization criteria
regulatoryFindings.description: Insufficient documentation of necessity assessment for sensitive medical information
violations: Insufficient documentation of necessity assessment for sensitive medical information
Lack of explicit verification that investigative body operated under proper statutory authority

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found that the disclosures were authorized under section 8(2)(e) but identified significant record-keeping deficiencies. The Commissioner recommended that DND: (1) retain copies of all 8(2)(e) request forms as required by law; (2) verify that requests reference the statutory authority for the investigation; and (3) maintain comprehensive records of all disclosures. DND's Deputy Minister committed to reviewing policies and procedures within six months and reporting back to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner on implementation.
companyNow: The Department of National Defence continues to operate as Canada's primary defence ministry, managing CAF operations and military personnel affairs.
dataType: Medical records, mental health information, personal health information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act section 8(4) - failure to retain copies of requests
Privacy Regulations section 7 - inadequate record retention periods
Privacy Act section 8(2)(e) - disclosure procedures and documentation requirements
Treasury Board Secretariat Directive on Privacy Practices - incomplete request documentation

companyDescription: Correctional Service Canada is a federal government agency responsible for managing correctional institutions across Canada and overseeing the custody and supervision of offenders.
companyLongDescription: Correctional Service Canada (CSC) is a federal government agency within the Department of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness. It operates a network of correctional institutions ranging from minimum to maximum security levels and supervises offenders in the community. CSC's mandate includes managing inmate populations, ensuring institutional safety and security, and supporting offender rehabilitation and reintegration.
caseDescription: Correctional Service Canada used a cell-site simulator device at Warkworth Institution from May to September 2015 to detect unauthorized inmate cell phone use, which resulted in the interception and collection of six text messages and metadata from staff and public cell phones without explicit authorization. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found that while metadata collection was proportionate to CSC's security mandate, the interception and collection of text message content violated the Privacy Act's collection provisions because it was not authorized.
violationSummary: The use of a cell-site simulator to intercept cell phone metadata and text messages without explicit authorization constitutes unauthorized surveillance of personal communications. This involves systematic collection of communications data from identifiable individuals without their knowledge or consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Correctional Service Canada used a cell-site simulator device at Warkworth Institution from May to September 2015 that intercepted and collected six text messages.
whyTheyWereWrong: Staff members and members of the public had their private text messages and cell phone metadata collected without their knowledge or consent, exposing their personal communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC authorized the contractor only to collect cell phone metadata, not message content.
claimsVsReality.reality: The contractor intercepted and recorded six text messages while operating the cell-site simulator, and CSC was found responsible for this interception despite not explicitly authorizing it.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC did not intercept or record any cell phone conversations.
claimsVsReality.reality: While CSC was correct about conversations, it did intercept six text messages containing personal information from staff and public cell phones.

claimsVsReality.claim: The warden's email accurately described what the cell-site simulator would do.
claimsVsReality.reality: The warden's email contained inaccuracies about the device's capabilities and authorization; CSC later claimed it had not authorized content interception despite the device being capable of and performing such interception.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 – Personal information collected by a government institution must relate directly to an operating program or activity of the institution
regulatoryFindings.description: Interception and collection of six text messages without explicit authorization by CSC
violations: Interception and collection of six text messages without explicit authorization by CSC
Collection of metadata from all cell phones in range of simulator, including staff and public phones not authorized for collection

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Definition of personal information as information about identifiable individuals
regulatoryFindings.description: Cell phone metadata (IMEI, IMSI, location, communication patterns) collected constitutes personal information of identifiable individuals
violations: Cell phone metadata (IMEI, IMSI, location, communication patterns) collected constitutes personal information of identifiable individuals
Text messages containing information about senders, receivers, and third parties collected without authorization

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found the complaints well-founded. While the collection of cell phone metadata was determined to be proportionate and consistent with CSC's security mandate, the interception and collection of six text messages violated the Privacy Act's collection provisions because it was not explicitly authorized. CSC was held responsible for the contractor's actions in intercepting text messages, as the contractor was acting on behalf of CSC. CSC has committed to not using cell-site simulators in the future and was advised that any future use would require completion of a Privacy Impact Assessment and threat risk assessment.
companyNow: Correctional Service Canada continues to operate as the primary federal incarceration agency in Canada. Following this case, CSC committed to not using cell-site simulators in the future.
dataType: Cell phone metadata (IMEI, IMSI, carrier network, location, communication timing/duration), text message content, identifying information (nicknames, phone identifiers)
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 3 (definition of personal information)
Privacy Act Section 4 (collection of personal information must relate directly to operating program or activity)

companyDescription: Transport Canada is the federal department responsible for aviation safety, transportation infrastructure, and regulatory oversight in Canada under the Aeronautics Act.
companyLongDescription: Transport Canada is a federal government institution that develops and enforces aviation regulations through the Canadian Aviation Regulations (CARs). The department is responsible for aviation safety, including oversight of both commercial and recreational aircraft operations. In response to a 200% increase in unmanned aircraft incidents since 2014, Transport Canada issued an Interim Order in March 2017 requiring recreational drone operators to display personal identification on their devices as an interim safety measure pending new permanent regulations.
caseDescription: Four complainants alleged that Transport Canada's Interim Order requiring owners of unmanned aircraft to display their names, addresses, and telephone numbers on the device violated the Privacy Act's disclosure provisions. Complainants argued this mandatory public display of personal information without consent exposed operators to harassment and identity theft risks. Transport Canada defended the requirement as a temporary safety measure to identify recreational UAV operators and reduce aviation incidents.
violationSummary: The complainants alleged that the requirement to display personal contact information on unmanned aircraft exposed individuals' personal information to the general public and other institutions without consent, creating risk of harassment and identity theft. However, the investigator found no actual violation because Transport Canada did not collect the personal information—the regulation merely required operators to display it.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Invasion of Seclusion
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Transport Canada required owners of recreational unmanned aircraft to display their personal name, address, and telephone number on the exterior of the device.
whyTheyWereWrong: Operators faced exposure to harassment and identity theft if their aircraft went missing or were located.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Interim Order requirement does not trigger collection of personal information by Transport Canada because the requirement only places an onus on operators to mark their devices with contact information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Operators were forced to publicly expose their personal names, addresses, and telephone numbers on devices that could be lost, recovered, or located by anyone, creating real harassment and identity theft risks without consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The identification requirement is in line with other federal transportation regulations and international obligations (ICAO).
claimsVsReality.reality: All other federally and provincially regulated forms of transport in Canada use registration numbers rather than requiring public display of personal contact information, making this approach uniquely invasive.

claimsVsReality.claim: The requirement places greater accountability on recreational users and will reduce incidents.
claimsVsReality.reality: Privacy concerns were raised by the public and stakeholders during consultations, leading Transport Canada to redraft the regulations, suggesting the initial approach was problematic.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 8(1) – Personal information can only be disclosed with consent or under permitted categories
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainants alleged mandatory display of personal contact information violated disclosure provisions by forcing exposure without consent
violations: Complainants alleged mandatory display of personal contact information violated disclosure provisions by forcing exposure without consent

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 4 – Personal information collected by government institutions must relate directly to an operating program
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainants argued Transport Canada collected personal information through the requirement
violations: Complainants argued Transport Canada collected personal information through the requirement

regulatoryFindings.act: Aeronautics Act subsection 6.41(1) – Minister authority to make interim orders for aviation safety
regulatoryFindings.description: No violation found; Minister had authority to issue the interim order
violations: No violation found; Minister had authority to issue the interim order

outcome: The complaints were found not well-founded. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner determined that although names, addresses, and telephone numbers are personal information under the Privacy Act, the Interim Order did not trigger a collection of personal information by Transport Canada because the requirement only places an obligation on UAV operators to mark their devices—it does not result in Transport Canada collecting that information. The disclosure provisions of the Privacy Act therefore do not apply. However, the Commissioner acknowledged the broader privacy implications and noted satisfaction with Transport Canada's commitment to rework identification and registration requirements in final regulations to address privacy concerns, with monitoring of future regulatory developments.
companyNow: Transport Canada remains the federal aviation regulator in Canada, overseeing all aircraft operations and aeronautical safety. The department subsequently redrafted its regulations in response to privacy concerns raised during public consultations on the unmanned aircraft requirements.
dataType: Name, address, telephone number
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act section 8(1) – disclosure of personal information
Privacy Act section 5 – collection of personal information
Privacy Act section 4 – personal information relating to operating programs

companyDescription: Statistics Canada is the official statistical agency of the Canadian federal government, responsible for collecting, analyzing, and publishing statistical data on Canadian economic, social, and demographic activities.
companyLongDescription: Statistics Canada (StatCan) is a Crown corporation mandated under the Statistics Act to collect and disseminate official statistical information about Canada. It operates multiple statistical programs including the decennial Census of Population and ongoing social and economic statistics programs. StatCan collects sensitive personal information from millions of Canadian households and businesses under legal authority requiring strict confidentiality. The agency is responsible for protecting respondent confidentiality and preventing unauthorized disclosure of census data and other statistical information.
caseDescription: A complainant alleged that Statistics Canada improperly disclosed confidential census data to Shared Services Canada (SSC) when transferring its IT infrastructure, and that SSC's shared data centres created risks of unauthorized disclosure.
