The Office of the Privacy Commissioner investigated and found that Statistics Canada did not violate the Privacy Act, as the transfer was legally required and reasonable safeguards were implemented.
violationSummary: The complaint alleged risks of unauthorized disclosure and insecurity in the handling of census data stored in shared data centres with decryption vulnerabilities, though the investigation concluded safeguards were adequate.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Statistics Canada transferred IT infrastructure management and census data storage to Shared Services Canada (SSC), a shared federal data centre serving 43 government institutions.
whyTheyWereWrong: Census respondents faced unauthorized disclosure risk when their confidential census data was stored in SSC shared data centres accessible to other federal institutions.

claimsVsReality.claim: SSC has taken ownership of all Government of Canada data centres and the census infrastructure is physically segregated from other partners' infrastructure with locked cabinets preventing unauthorized physical access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Census data was stored in SSC shared data centres also serving 42 other federal institutions; physical segregation and locks did not prevent SSC employees from other institutions from accessing infrastructure in shared facilities.

claimsVsReality.claim: All SSC employees with access to census infrastructure are deemed employees under the Statistics Act, sworn to confidentiality, and cleared to secret level, exceeding census information classification.
claimsVsReality.reality: Deemed employee status and security clearances do not eliminate the structural risk that employees from other government departments with legitimate access to shared data centre infrastructure could access or be exposed to census data during decryption for processing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Census data is neither used by nor disclosed to SSC; the arrangement focuses only on IT infrastructure integrity and availability.
claimsVsReality.reality: SSC employees and other federal institutions had infrastructure-level access to the physical and logical systems containing unencrypted census data during processing and operations, creating practical disclosure exposure regardless of formal authorization restrictions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8 - Personal information shall not be disclosed without consent except in permitted categories
regulatoryFindings.description: Allegation that transfer of census data to SSC constituted unauthorized disclosure - Found NOT VIOLATED as transfer was legally required and control remained with StatCan
violations: Allegation that transfer of census data to SSC constituted unauthorized disclosure - Found NOT VIOLATED as transfer was legally required and control remained with StatCan

regulatoryFindings.act: Statistics Act Section 5 - Minister may use services of employees of federal public administration as deemed employees
regulatoryFindings.description: Allegation that SSC employees could not be properly sworn as deemed employees - Found NOT VIOLATED as StatCan has authority and has implemented monitoring
violations: Allegation that SSC employees could not be properly sworn as deemed employees - Found NOT VIOLATED as StatCan has authority and has implemented monitoring

regulatoryFindings.act: Shared Services Canada Act Section 16 - Personal information collected by other institutions and contained in SSC's IT systems is not under SSC's control
regulatoryFindings.description: No violation found; personal information retained under StatCan's control despite being housed on SSC infrastructure
violations: No violation found; personal information retained under StatCan's control despite being housed on SSC infrastructure

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the complaint not well-founded. Statistics Canada was determined to have taken appropriate and reasonable steps to safeguard census data transferred to Shared Services Canada's IT infrastructure, including: establishing Business Arrangements and Complementary Agreements defining roles and responsibilities; ensuring all SSC employees with access to census data were deemed employees sworn under the Statistics Act; implementing physical segregation of census infrastructure (census enclave); requiring security clearances exceeding census data classification; conducting Threat Risk Assessments and Security Authorization and Accreditation processes; and establishing monitoring procedures for SSC employees with access to sensitive data. No violation of the Privacy Act was found.
companyNow: Statistics Canada continues to operate as Canada's national statistical agency, conducting the 2021 and upcoming 2026 Census of Population and managing numerous ongoing statistical programs. The agency remains responsible for census data collection and dissemination.
dataType: Census data, personal information including race, national or ethnic origin, colour, religion, age, marital status, education, medical, criminal or employment history, financial transactions, identifying numbers
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 8 (disclosure of personal information)
Statistics Act Section 5 (use of deemed employees)
Statistics Act Section 6 (oath of office requirement)
Shared Services Canada Act Section 6 (provision of IT services)
Shared Services Canada Act Section 16 (control of personal information)

company: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada
companyDescription: Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) is a Canadian federal government department responsible for research, science policy, and economic development programs.
companyLongDescription: ISED is a department of the Government of Canada that develops policies, programs, and services to advance science, research, innovation, and economic development. It manages various federal initiatives and funding programs across multiple sectors. Like other Canadian government institutions, ISED is subject to the Privacy Act and must ensure accurate handling of personal information in human resources and administrative functions.
caseDescription: ISED used inaccurate personal information when staffing a position, selecting the complainant's profile from the MyGCHR human resources system instead of the intended candidate with the same name. Due to this error, the complainant was incorrectly terminated from his position at PSPC and missed pay periods. ISED failed to take all reasonable steps to ensure accuracy by not validating identity using additional data fields such as PRI or date of birth.
violationSummary: ISED failed to implement adequate data validation procedures when accessing personal information in the MyGCHR system. The institution did not take all reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of personal information used for an administrative purpose (staffing decision), resulting in the wrong individual being selected due to insufficient identity verification protocols.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: ISED selected the complainant's profile from the MyGCHR human resources system instead of the intended candidate with the same name when staffing a position, using only first.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant was incorrectly terminated from his position at PSPC and missed pay periods as a result of ISED's failure to use additional identity validation fields such as PRI or date.

claimsVsReality.claim: Searching MyGCHR by first and last name only was sufficient to identify and select the correct employee for staffing purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The search identified and selected the wrong person with the same name, resulting in incorrect termination and lost pay for the actual complainant.

claimsVsReality.claim: HR officials had adequate procedures in place to ensure accurate identity verification during the hiring process.
claimsVsReality.reality: HR officials lacked instructions to use additional data fields like PRI or date of birth, making the system vulnerable to name-matching errors.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 6(2) – institutions must take all reasonable steps to ensure that personal information used for an administrative purpose is as accurate, up-to-date and complete as possible
regulatoryFindings.description: ISED used inaccurate information about the complainant when staffing a position by selecting his profile from MyGCHR instead of the intended candidate
violations: ISED used inaccurate information about the complainant when staffing a position by selecting his profile from MyGCHR instead of the intended candidate
HR officials searched MyGCHR using only first and last name without validating identity through additional data fields such as PRI or date of birth
The error resulted in the complainant being incorrectly 'hired' and 'terminated' in the system, causing financial harm (missed pay periods)

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. ISED acknowledged the breach and took corrective action by creating a document reminding staff to validate employee identity using multiple data fields (PRI, date of birth) when selecting profiles from MyGCHR. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner determined that ISED has taken reasonable steps to ensure accuracy going forward and issued no further recommendations. No monetary penalty was imposed.
companyNow: ISED continues to operate as a Canadian federal department managing science, research, and economic development initiatives. The department has implemented additional safeguards for identity validation in HR systems following this incident.
dataType: Employment history, name, identifying numbers (Personal Record Identifier), financial information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 6(2) – duty to take all reasonable steps to ensure personal information used for administrative purposes is as accurate, up-to-date and complete as possible
Privacy Act Section 3 – definition of personal information

companyDescription: VTech Holdings Limited is a Hong Kong-headquartered manufacturer of electronic learning products for children and the world's largest manufacturer of cordless phones, with operations in 13 countries.
companyLongDescription: VTech Holdings Limited is a major consumer electronics company specializing in interactive learning toys, web-enabled children's products, and cordless communication devices. Headquartered in Hong Kong, the company operates globally through subsidiaries including VTech Technologies Canada Ltd. The company's product lines include the V.Reader Interactive E-Reading System, Tote & Go Laptop WEB, and cloud-based platforms like Learning Lodge, Planet VTech, and Kid Connect that enable parents and children to interact across devices.
caseDescription: VTech suffered a major data breach affecting over 316,000 Canadian children and 237,000 Canadian adults due to inadequate information security safeguards. The attacker exploited a well-known SQL injection vulnerability and leveraged poor administrative access controls to access and exfiltrate sensitive personal information including children's photos, voice recordings, and chat logs. Following the breach, VTech implemented comprehensive remedial measures to strengthen its security infrastructure and was found to have resolved the matter through timely corrective action.
violationSummary: VTech failed to implement adequate technological and organizational safeguards to protect highly sensitive personal information of children and parents. Specific failures included lack of testing and maintenance to identify vulnerabilities, inadequate administrative access controls, cryptographic deficiencies, absence of security monitoring and logging, and no comprehensive security management program. These failures directly enabled unauthorized access and compromise of data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: VTech failed to implement adequate security safeguards for its children's web-based products, allowing an attacker to exploit a well-known SQL injection vulnerability.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children's intimate personal data including photos, voice recordings, and chat logs were exposed to an attacker.

claimsVsReality.claim: VTech claimed it had identified the need to conduct a risk assessment in advance of the breach and that certain aspects had been scheduled.
claimsVsReality.reality: No comprehensive risk assessments were completed before the breach; the company lacked an overarching security management program and had not implemented planned intrusion detection systems.

claimsVsReality.claim: VTech claimed to have safeguards in place to protect personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: VTech had significant safeguard deficiencies including no regular vulnerability testing, inadequate access controls, plaintext storage of sensitive data, unencrypted transmission of communications, and absence of security monitoring to detect unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: VTech claimed the attacker intended only to highlight vulnerabilities.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of intent, the attacker successfully exfiltrated and publicly disclosed intimate personal information of over half a million individuals, including children's photos and voice recordings.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Personal information shall be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: VTech failed to implement adequate organizational and technological safeguards commensurate with the sensitivity of children's personal information and the number of individuals affected
violations: VTech failed to implement adequate organizational and technological safeguards commensurate with the sensitivity of children's personal information and the number of individuals affected
VTech did not have a program of regular testing and maintenance to identify and mitigate system vulnerabilities, allowing attackers to exploit a well-known SQL injection vulnerability
VTech had inadequate administrative-level access controls, including storage of production passwords in test environments and sharing of accounts between staff
VTech stored sensitive information in plaintext and transmitted customer communications unencrypted; password cryptography was weak and encryption keys were inadequately protected
VTech lacked sufficient host and network security logging and monitoring to detect unauthorized activity or data exfiltration
VTech lacked a comprehensive overarching data security policy, associated training, and program for regular risk assessments and policy reviews

outcome: The matter was determined to be well-founded and resolved. VTech implemented comprehensive remedial measures including: (1) regular multifaceted testing protocols and patch management to identify and mitigate vulnerabilities; (2) enhanced administrative access controls with limited scope and stronger authentication; (3) enhanced encryption for stored information and information in transit; (4) increased and centralized logging and monitoring with restricted outgoing traffic monitoring; and (5) a new comprehensive data security policy with a Data Security Governance Board, annual staff training, compliance monitoring, and annual risk assessments. VTech also entered into a settlement with the U.S. Federal Trade Commission requiring implementation of a comprehensive data security program subject to ongoing audits.
companyNow: VTech continues to operate as a leading children's electronics manufacturer. Following the 2015 breach and subsequent remediation, the company implemented comprehensive security governance improvements including a Data Security Governance Board, annual risk assessments, and enhanced encryption protocols.
dataType: Children's personal information (name, gender, date of birth, profile pictures, voice recordings, chat logs), parent information (name, email, IP address, mailing address, billing address, last 4 digits of credit card, expiration date, password, security questions)
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – personal information shall be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1 – security safeguards shall protect personal information against loss or theft, unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use, or modification
PIPEDA Principle 4.7.2 – nature of safeguards must vary depending on sensitivity of information and amount affected
PIPEDA Principle 4.7.3 – methods of protection must include physical, organizational, and technological measures

companyDescription: Profile Technology Ltd. is a New Zealand-based company that operated The Profile Engine, a social networking and search website.
companyLongDescription: Profile Technology Ltd., a New Zealand-based company, operated www.profileengine.com (The Profile Engine), a website that initially claimed to function as a search engine for Facebook profiles. The company collected approximately 420 million profiles from Facebook and indexed them on its own platform. By 2011, the company repositioned itself as a full social network offering features including profile browsing, dating search, music streaming, games, and research tools. The company scraped and repurposed user data without valid consent and resisted deletion requests and regulatory compliance.
caseDescription: Profile Technology, a New Zealand-based company, collected millions of Canadian Facebook user profiles without consent and republished them on its own social networking website (The Profile Engine). The company initially claimed to operate as a search engine but subsequently repurposed the copied profile data to develop and populate its own social network. When users discovered their information and requested deletion, the company imposed burdensome procedures and retained helpdesk ticket information indefinitely.
violationSummary: Profile Technology disclosed individuals' personal information by copying Facebook profiles and posting them on its website without consent. This constitutes unauthorized disclosure of personal information obtained from a third party and repurposed without meaningful consent from affected individuals.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Profile Technology collected millions of Canadian Facebook user profiles without consent and republished them on its own social networking website, The Profile Engine.
whyTheyWereWrong: Canadians discovered their outdated personal information—including photos, birthdates, relationship status, and locations—publicly displayed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook contracted with us to provide Advanced Search functions and agreed to provide us with unlimited access to information which their users had consented to make public.
claimsVsReality.reality: Profile Technology collected profiles with Facebook's permission but subsequently repurposed the data for its own social networking website without obtaining user consent for that new purpose.

claimsVsReality.claim: We are simply a search engine indexing publicly available information from Facebook, similar to how Google operates.
claimsVsReality.reality: Profile Technology evolved into a full social network by 2011, displaying copied profiles, offering dating search, music streaming, and other social features—not merely indexing.

claimsVsReality.claim: We cannot identify which profiles are associated with Canadians and therefore cannot comply with deletion recommendations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Profile Technology failed to adequately explain why it could not identify Canadian users and did not propose reasonable measures to address privacy concerns, demonstrating unwillingness rather than inability.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users gave permission for their profiles when they ticked 'Allow my profile to be indexed by search engines' in Facebook privacy settings.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users who checked that box consented only to search engine indexing, not to collection for Profile Technology's proprietary social network or indefinite retention after privacy settings changed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Profile information we use is kept current and reflects user preferences.
claimsVsReality.reality: Profile Technology retained outdated information without updating it to reflect changes users made to their Facebook privacy settings or account deletions after the initial scrape.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires knowledge and consent of the individual for collection, use or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Profile Technology collected and used personal information from Facebook profiles without the knowledge or consent of individuals
violations: Profile Technology collected and used personal information from Facebook profiles without the knowledge or consent of individuals
Individuals were not informed that their profile information would be copied and displayed on The Profile Engine website
The company repurposed profile information from a search engine function to populate its own social networking website without obtaining fresh consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 5(3) limits collection, use or disclosure to purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate in the circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: Profile Technology used profile information to create a static replica of Facebook profiles on its own website without individuals' knowledge or control
violations: Profile Technology used profile information to create a static replica of Facebook profiles on its own website without individuals' knowledge or control
The company used outdated profile information that individuals had deleted or modified on Facebook
Profile Technology knowingly used information that was no longer public on Facebook and did not reflect users' current privacy settings or content changes
The repurposing of information from search engine functionality to social network development was not a purpose a reasonable person would consider appropriate

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5 requires personal information be retained only as long as necessary for fulfillment of purposes and organizations must develop retention guidelines with minimum and maximum retention periods
regulatoryFindings.description: Profile Technology indefinitely retained helpdesk ticket information (names, email addresses, redacted photo identification) provided by individuals requesting profile deletion
violations: Profile Technology indefinitely retained helpdesk ticket information (names, email addresses, redacted photo identification) provided by individuals requesting profile deletion
The company did not establish reasonable retention periods for helpdesk system information
Indefinite retention was not justified by potential future regulatory investigation

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Regulations Specifying Publicly Available Information section 1(e) exempts only personal information appearing in publications (magazines, books, newspapers in printed or electronic form) where the individual provided the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Profile Technology claimed Facebook profiles constitute 'publications' exempting them from consent requirements
violations: Profile Technology claimed Facebook profiles constitute 'publications' exempting them from consent requirements
Facebook profiles are dynamic and individuals maintain control over content and accessibility, unlike traditional publications
Profile information included content provided by third parties (e.g., group membership information, friend network data) not provided by the subject individual
Facebook profiles contained outdated information no longer accurate or public on the source platform

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada issued a Report of Findings determining the complaints to be well-founded. The OPC recommended that Profile Technology: (1) remove from its website and delete from its records all individual profiles and groups associated with Canadian residents (excluding profiles created independently or claimed by users who have not requested deletion); and (2) implement a reasonable retention policy for helpdesk system information and delete past records. Profile Technology refused to comply with these recommendations, claiming inability to identify which profiles were associated with Canadians and proposing no alternative measures. Prior to report issuance, Profile Technology removed profiles from its website and uploaded much of the database to the Internet Archive as torrent files, making the information available for peer-to-peer download. The company claimed to have 'anonymized' the data by removing certain identifiers and encrypting others, but the OPC determined this did not adequately address privacy risks given the extensive personal information (including images) in the profiles and the undefined encryption protections. The OPC continues to monitor the situation for any future use or disclosure of Canadian profile information.
companyNow: Profile Technology appears to have faced significant regulatory pressure following the 2018 PIPEDA investigation. The company's status today is unclear, though the investigation revealed it transferred data to the Internet Archive after initial regulatory contact.
dataType: Name, gender, date of birth, username, photo, relationship status, political affiliation, location, education history, friend lists, group memberships, music preferences, estimated IQ, social influence metrics, behavioral allegations
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA paragraphs 7(1)(d) and 7(2)(c.1) (publicly available information exemption)
PIPEDA Regulations Specifying Publicly Available Information section 1(e)

companyDescription: Facebook is a global social media platform founded in 2004 that enables users to connect, share content, and communicate with friends and family online.
companyLongDescription: Facebook is a leading social media company that operates the world's largest social network, connecting billions of users across personal computers and mobile devices. The platform provides free services funded by targeted advertising and has expanded to include messaging, photo sharing, video, and marketplace features. Facebook went public in 2012 and is now part of Meta Platforms, Inc., a technology conglomerate.
caseDescription: Facebook's Contact Importer tool and matching process across address books resulted in unauthorized disclosure of contact information during a 2013 breach affecting approximately 1.1 million user downloads. Facebook collected, stored, and matched contact information of both users and non-users without obtaining meaningful consent from non-users and without adequately disclosing its practices to users.
violationSummary: The breach exposed contact information to unauthorized recipients through the Download Your Information tool due to a coding error. Additionally, Facebook's practice of matching contact information across address books and storing non-user data constitutes unauthorized exposure and processing of personal information without proper consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Facebook's Contact Importer tool and address book matching process disclosed approximately 14 million pieces of contact information belonging to non-users.
whyTheyWereWrong: Non-users whose contact details were collected, matched, and exposed had no opportunity to consent or even know their information was being processed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook had comprehensive safeguards and rigorous engineering processes to protect contact information.
claimsVsReality.reality: A coding error in Facebook's address book matching process caused matched contact data to be improperly stored alongside user-imported contacts, exposing non-user information through the Download Your Information tool for over one year.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook was only collecting contact information from its users with their consent through the Contact Importer tool.
claimsVsReality.reality: Facebook was systematically collecting, matching, and using contact information of non-users (people who had never agreed to Facebook's terms) without any consent or knowledge that their data was being processed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The breach was an isolated mistake that could not have been detected easily.
claimsVsReality.reality: The breach persisted undetected for over 13 months (May 2012–June 2013) until an external security researcher reported it, affecting 1.1 million downloads and exposing personal information of approximately 6.1 million individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook provided affected users with appropriate notice and transparency about the breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: Facebook chose not to disclose which other Facebook users had received the personal information of affected individuals, severely limiting victims' ability to understand the scope of exposure or take protective action.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 and 4.7.1 – Personal information must be protected by appropriate security safeguards
regulatoryFindings.description: Facebook did not have appropriate safeguards in place prior to the breach to protect contact information of users and non-users
violations: Facebook did not have appropriate safeguards in place prior to the breach to protect contact information of users and non-users
Testing conducted on the Download Your Information tool update was inadequate and did not verify that information displayed was equivalent to that in the user's address book
Inadequate synthetic testing data did not accurately mirror how proposed code changes would function with real data

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 and Section 6.1 – Meaningful consent required for collection and use of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Facebook used personal information of non-users during the matching across address books process without obtaining their meaningful consent
violations: Facebook used personal information of non-users during the matching across address books process without obtaining their meaningful consent
Facebook's notices to non-users did not adequately explain the matching process or allow reasonable understanding of how their personal information would be used
Non-users may never receive notice or opt-out opportunity if no Facebook user sends them an invitation

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.8 – Organizations must be open about policies and practices relating to personal information management
regulatoryFindings.description: Facebook failed to adequately explain to users what 'others' means in notices about contact information being used to help 'you and others' find friends
violations: Facebook failed to adequately explain to users what 'others' means in notices about contact information being used to help 'you and others' find friends
The matching across address books process was not sufficiently described to Facebook users in an open and transparent fashion
Notices did not explain how Facebook combines and matches contact information across different users' address books

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9, 4.9.1 and 4.9.5 – Individuals have right to access and correct their personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Facebook did not provide users with access to contact information matched to them through the address book matching process
violations: Facebook did not provide users with access to contact information matched to them through the address book matching process
Facebook did not allow users to correct or amend matched contact information associated with their accounts
Users were unable to learn about or dispute additional email addresses and phone numbers Facebook associated with them

outcome: Facebook agreed to implement multiple remedial measures: (1) Implemented a Privacy Framework based on 'least privilege' principle to prevent inadvertent disclosure of matched contact data; (2) Deprecated the repository of hashed contact points containing non-user data; (3) Revised the 'User Matches' data set to exclude contact information not associated with known Facebook accounts; (4) Updated notices to Facebook users regarding the contact importer and matching process by May 25, 2018; (5) Implemented an interim solution allowing users to request access to their matched contact information and request deletion of specific matches through a Personal Data Request form; (6) Updated help documentation to make the process for accessing matched contact information transparent and accessible; (7) Committed to developing a longer-term permanent solution for access to and correction of matched data as part of GDPR compliance efforts. The Office will continue to follow up on implementation of these commitments.
companyNow: Facebook remains one of the world's most widely used social platforms with approximately 3 billion monthly active users. The company now operates under parent company Meta Platforms, Inc., which also owns Instagram, WhatsApp, and other digital properties.
dataType: Email addresses, telephone numbers, contact information, address book data
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Consent for collection and use of personal information
PIPEDA Principle 4.7 – Security safeguards appropriate to data sensitivity
PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1 – Protection against unauthorized access and disclosure
PIPEDA Principle 4.8 – Openness about policies and practices
PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – Right of access to personal information
PIPEDA Principle 4.9.5 – Correction of inaccurate information
PIPEDA Section 6.1 – Valid consent requires understanding of nature, purpose and consequences
PIPEDA Subsection 9(1) – Exemption for disclosure of third-party information

companyDescription: A courier and parcel delivery service operating in Canada that transports packages for individuals and businesses.
companyLongDescription: The company is a courier service that handles package delivery for customers across Canada. It operates a driver network that attempts to deliver parcels to specified addresses and, when recipients are unavailable, has historically offered a 'delivery to a neighbour' option. The company serves both individual recipients and institutional shippers such as financial institutions, managing the logistics of transporting sensitive documents and parcels.
caseDescription: A courier company disclosed a complainant's personal information without consent by delivering a package addressed to her to a neighbour instead of the intended address. The package contained sensitive financial documents from a financial institution. The courier lacked adequate consent procedures and failed to ensure that the shipper (financial institution) had obtained valid consent for the 'delivery to a neighbour' practice.
violationSummary: The courier disclosed the complainant's personal information (name, address, unlisted phone number, and the fact that she was receiving financial documents) to a neighbour without her knowledge or consent, constituting unauthorized disclosure of personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The courier company delivered a package containing sensitive financial documents to the complainant's neighbour without obtaining her consent, relying instead on vague terms.
whyTheyWereWrong: A woman's unlisted phone number and confidential financial documents were exposed to her neighbour without her knowledge or agreement, putting her sensitive personal.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers are well acquainted with the availability of shipping options, including 'delivery to a neighbour,' and can opt out via terms and conditions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The shipper (financial institution) was unaware that 'delivery to a neighbour' was a common practice, and the complainant had no direct contact with the courier and never had a chance to choose options; the privacy statement did not explicitly mention this practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: The courier obtained consent from the shipper for the 'delivery to a neighbour' practice through general terms and conditions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The shipper stated it was not aware of the practice, and the courier's terms and conditions did not specifically require or verify that the shipper understood the practice or obtained valid consent from recipients.

claimsVsReality.claim: Delivery to a neighbour is convenient for customers who prefer to avoid separate pick-up locations.
claimsVsReality.reality: For sensitive financial documents, recipients would not reasonably expect their financial institution to have such packages delivered to a neighbour without express consent, especially when they were unaware a package was being sent.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Organizations must obtain informed consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information, except where otherwise permitted by law. Consent must be meaningful and individuals should be given choice regarding their personal information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Courier did not obtain consent directly from the complainant for delivering packages to a neighbour
violations: Courier did not obtain consent directly from the complainant for delivering packages to a neighbour
Courier failed to exercise due diligence to verify that the shipper (financial institution) had obtained valid consent from the complainant
Courier's privacy statement did not explicitly mention the 'delivery to a neighbour' practice
Courier's terms and conditions did not clearly indicate how individuals could avoid the 'delivery to a neighbour' practice
Courier did not ensure shippers understood the nature of the practice and their responsibility to obtain valid consent

outcome: The Commissioner found the complaint well-founded. In response to the office's recommendations, the courier committed to discontinue the practice of delivering packages to neighbours without explicit consent. The office confirmed that the 'delivery to a neighbour' practice has ended as a result of this commitment.
dataType: Personal financial documents, name, address, unlisted telephone number

companyDescription: Microsoft is a multinational technology corporation that develops and licenses software, cloud services, and hardware products including the Windows operating system.
companyLongDescription: Microsoft is a leading global technology company founded in 1975 that develops and sells software, cloud computing services, and hardware devices. The company's Windows operating system is one of the most widely used desktop operating systems in the world, with hundreds of millions of users. Windows 10, released in 2015, was designed as a unified cloud-based platform across multiple device types including desktops, tablets, and smartphones. The company also provides enterprise services, productivity software, and cloud infrastructure through its Azure platform.
caseDescription: Microsoft set multiple privacy settings to 'on' by default during Windows 10 installation without obtaining meaningful consent from users. The default settings collected sensitive diagnostic data, location information, and voice recordings with unclear explanations of purposes and consequences. Users could not reasonably understand the nature and scope of data collection or how to meaningfully opt out.
violationSummary: Microsoft engaged in extensive default surveillance of user activities (browsing, typing, voice, location) without meaningful opt-in consent. The collection was presented with unclear/conflicting explanations that prevented users from understanding the scope and sensitivity of data being collected.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Microsoft set multiple Windows 10 privacy settings to 'on' by default during installation, including location tracking, diagnostics, tailored experiences.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hundreds of millions of users could not reasonably understand what data Microsoft would collect, how it would be used, or how to meaningfully opt out.

claimsVsReality.claim: Express settings reflected what the average user reasonably expects from a modern operating system.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users could not reasonably understand the nature and scope of data collection or the consequences of accepting these settings without additional research.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Location setting could be on by default because apps must ask users separately for permission before accessing location.
claimsVsReality.reality: Microsoft and third-party apps could still determine precise device location through Windows data collection even when the Location setting was off.

claimsVsReality.claim: Full Diagnostics collection was an appropriate default setting.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users would not reasonably expect Microsoft to collect the vast amounts of sensitive diagnostic information associated with Full Diagnostics, which should have been set to 'Basic' by default.

claimsVsReality.claim: Relevant Ads setting provided users adequate control over advertising practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Turning on Relevant Ads did not constitute informed consent to Microsoft's own advertising practices, which required a separate control mechanism.

claimsVsReality.claim: Speech Recognition as a default setting was reasonable for Windows 10.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users who had previously declined Cortana would not reasonably expect Speech Recognition to be enabled by default, collecting vast amounts of potentially sensitive voice instruction data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 6.1 – Valid consent requires that individuals reasonably understand the nature, purpose and consequences of collection, use or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Confusing explanations of Advertising ID that conflated Microsoft's own advertising practices with the OS-level identifier disclosure, preventing users from understanding what they were consenting to
violations: Confusing explanations of Advertising ID that conflated Microsoft's own advertising practices with the OS-level identifier disclosure, preventing users from understanding what they were consenting to
Speech Recognition setting defaulted to 'on' with unclear explanation that turning it 'off' only disables cloud-based services, not device-based recognition
Diagnostics set to Full by default with vast breadth of sensitive data collected (browser history, app usage, typing/inking) without clear explanation of purposes or sensitivity
Location setting explanations did not clarify exceptions (that precise location could still be determined when setting is off via WiFi/Bluetooth)

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.3.2 – Organizations must advise individuals of purposes for collection in manner that allows reasonable understanding
regulatoryFindings.description: Diagnostics explanations did not adequately disclose that Full telemetry would be used for 'Tailored Experiences' (targeted marketing), conflating product improvement with marketing
violations: Diagnostics explanations did not adequately disclose that Full telemetry would be used for 'Tailored Experiences' (targeted marketing), conflating product improvement with marketing
De-identified location data sharing with third party HERE was not clearly explained during installation
Speech Recognition collection purposes and extent of voice data retention were not clearly communicated

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.3.6 – Organizations should generally seek express/opt-in consent when information is sensitive
regulatoryFindings.description: Full Diagnostics set to on by default (opt-out) despite collecting highly sensitive data including browser searches, medical/dating app usage, and crash memory states
violations: Full Diagnostics set to on by default (opt-out) despite collecting highly sensitive data including browser searches, medical/dating app usage, and crash memory states
Speech Recognition set to on by default (opt-out) despite collecting voice content that could include sensitive personal information (medical appointments, private messages)
Location set to on by default for de-identified sharing with third parties without opt-in consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.1.4 – Organizations must implement policies and practices to give effect to privacy principles
regulatoryFindings.description: No written policies or documented procedures to ensure sensitive diagnostic information was not used for Tailored Experiences (targeted marketing)
violations: No written policies or documented procedures to ensure sensitive diagnostic information was not used for Tailored Experiences (targeted marketing)
Speech Recognition setting not functioning properly—user's choice to turn off Speech Recognition was being overridden by prior Cortana choice, failing to give effect to user choices

outcome: Matter found to be well-founded and conditionally resolved. Microsoft committed to: (1) Implement opt-in consent (no pre-selected defaults) for all seven installation privacy settings by end of 2018, with separate pages for each setting; (2) Set Diagnostics to Basic by default instead of Full; (3) Set Speech Recognition to off by default instead of on; (4) Enhance transparency for Location, Diagnostics, Relevant Ads (Advertising ID), and Speech Recognition settings with clearer 'Learn more' explanations; (5) Add prohibition in Microsoft Store App Policies and Windows SDK forbidding third-party apps from determining precise location when Location is off without separate consent; (6) Implement and document formal procedures to prevent use of sensitive diagnostic data for Tailored Experiences; (7) Fix Speech Recognition setting malfunction and delete improperly collected voice data by August 31, 2018; (8) Obtain meaningful consent for ongoing speech data retention. Office to conduct monthly follow-ups through end of 2018 to verify implementation of all commitments.
companyNow: Microsoft remains one of the world's largest technology companies, with a dominant position in enterprise software and cloud computing through Azure. The company continues to develop and update Windows as a core product serving millions of users globally.
dataType: Location data, diagnostic/telemetry data, speech/voice data, typing and inking input, browsing history, advertising ID, calendar and contact information

companyDescription: The World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) is an international independent agency established in 1999 to oversee anti-doping activities and manage compliance with the World Anti-Doping Code across global sports organizations.
companyLongDescription: WADA is a non-profit international agency headquartered in Montreal, Quebec, composed of and funded by sports organizations and governments worldwide. It manages the ADAMS (Anti-Doping Administration and Management System) database, which serves as a clearing-house for anti-doping information used by approximately 130 International Federations, over 220 National Anti-Doping Organizations, 35 laboratories, and 20,000 athletes globally. ADAMS coordinates anti-doping activities, stores laboratory results, therapeutic use exemptions, athlete whereabouts information, and doping control records. The agency conducts scientific research, provides education, develops anti-doping capacities, and monitors compliance with anti-doping codes across international and national sporting bodies.
caseDescription: WADA's ADAMS anti-doping database was breached by the 'Fancy Bear' hacking group in August–September 2016, exposing sensitive personal and health information of 127 athletes published online and potentially affecting 11,837 athletes' records. The breach resulted from compromised email accounts leading to unauthorized access via legitimate credentials, compounded by insufficient security safeguards including weak access controls, lack of two-factor authentication, inadequate monitoring, and missing encryption at rest.
violationSummary: WADA failed to implement security safeguards appropriate to the high sensitivity of personal health and anti-doping information, as required by PIPEDA Principles 4.7, 4.7.1, 4.7.2, and 4.7.3. Specific deficiencies included lack of mandatory password resets, absence of two-factor authentication, inadequate logging and anomaly detection, missing encryption at rest, insufficient access control oversight, lack of documented incident response procedures, and inadequate staff training.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: WADA failed to implement adequate security safeguards for the ADAMS anti-doping database, including weak access controls, no two-factor authentication.
whyTheyWereWrong: 127 athletes had their personal medical information, including prohibited substances prescribed to them and underlying medical conditions, publicly exposed online.

claimsVsReality.claim: ADAMS has a multi-level access system that protects security and confidentiality with a level of security typically used by financial institutions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system lacked two-factor authentication, had weak password complexity requirements (only changed on August 19 after the breach began on August 4), inadequate monitoring of access, and compromised credentials allowed attackers to access administrator and athlete data for weeks undetected.

claimsVsReality.claim: WADA oversees the ADAMS database and is responsible for regulating access and ensuring safeguarding of information.
claimsVsReality.reality: WADA failed to detect the compromise of three employee email accounts for 31-72 minutes, failed to detect unauthorized access to the IOC administrator account for days, and did not discover the breach until September 12 when attackers publicly published stolen data online.

claimsVsReality.claim: The granting of permissions is based on the need-to-know principle to limit data exposure.
claimsVsReality.reality: The IOC administrator account created for the Rio Games retained access to athlete test results from up to eight years of previous Olympics, and attackers using this account were able to access thousands of athlete records beyond the 127 whose data was published.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 — Personal information shall be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: WADA failed to implement security safeguards commensurate with the highly sensitive nature of athlete health data, anti-doping information, and whereabouts data stored in ADAMS
violations: WADA failed to implement security safeguards commensurate with the highly sensitive nature of athlete health data, anti-doping information, and whereabouts data stored in ADAMS
Inadequate authentication mechanism (single-factor password-only access instead of two-factor authentication) for a publicly-facing web interface managing sensitive health and anti-doping information
No encryption at rest for data in ADAMS despite encryption in transit
Inadequate monitoring and logging capabilities failed to detect thousands of attacker-generated events during the breach period

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1 — Security safeguards must protect personal information against loss or theft, and unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use, or modification
regulatoryFindings.description: Weak password management practices (non-mandatory password resets for new accounts, no password expiry periods for temporary credentials) allowed credentials to persist indefinitely in email accounts, facilitating unauthorized access
violations: Weak password management practices (non-mandatory password resets for new accounts, no password expiry periods for temporary credentials) allowed credentials to persist indefinitely in email accounts, facilitating unauthorized access
Credentials for the independent observer account and IOC administrator account were compromised via email account breaches and used to gain ADAMS access
Lack of account activity notifications meant the IOC employee was unaware their administrator account had been used to create additional accounts and extract data for several days

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.2 — Nature of safeguards shall vary based on sensitivity of information, amount, distribution, format, and storage method
regulatoryFindings.description: WADA did not conduct threat or vulnerability assessments to determine appropriate safeguards tailored to its high-value target status and the sophisticated threat environment
violations: WADA did not conduct threat or vulnerability assessments to determine appropriate safeguards tailored to its high-value target status and the sophisticated threat environment
No documented risk-management framework guided selection of security measures; WADA used an ad hoc 'fluid approach' inappropriate for an organization handling highly sensitive data
Overly broad administrative rights granted to ADOs (e.g., IOC administrator account could create additional administrator accounts) without corresponding oversight or audit capabilities

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.3 — Methods of protection shall include physical, organizational, and technological measures
regulatoryFindings.description: Organizational measures deficient: No incident response plan at time of breach; ad hoc response to phishing campaign (e.g., decision not to force immediate password resets due to convenience concerns); lack of contractual audit and inspection rights over ADOs
violations: Organizational measures deficient: No incident response plan at time of breach; ad hoc response to phishing campaign (e.g., decision not to force immediate password resets due to convenience concerns); lack of contractual audit and inspection rights over ADOs
Technological measures deficient: Single-factor authentication, no encryption at rest, inadequate logging configuration, no account activity alerts
Lack of documented security policies and procedures to enforce ISO standards referenced in WADA's IS Corporate Policy

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4 — Organizations shall implement policies and practices including procedures to protect personal information, training staff, and communicating policies
regulatoryFindings.description: WADA lacked comprehensive written policies and procedures for information security; IS Corporate Policy referenced ISO standards but critical requirements were not documented or enforced
violations: WADA lacked comprehensive written policies and procedures for information security; IS Corporate Policy referenced ISO standards but critical requirements were not documented or enforced

Insufficient staff training and awareness: Little evidence of security awareness communication; non-mandatory password reset practice communicated verbally rather than in writing; no ongoing privacy and security training program for employees
ADAMS user training focused on system usage rather than security safeguards and account creation best practices; limited security awareness among stakeholders granted administrative rights

outcome: WADA was found in breach of PIPEDA Principles 4.1.4, 4.7, 4.7.1, 4.7.2, and 4.7.3. The Privacy Commissioner concluded the matter was well-founded and conditionally resolved. WADA agreed to implement comprehensive recommendations including: developing a documented Information Security framework with risk assessment and safeguard testing; implementing mandatory password resets and expiry periods; making two-factor authentication mandatory for non-athletes (optional for athletes with active promotion); updating contracts to permit audit and inspection of ADOs; restricting administrator account creation to WADA; implementing account activity notifications; encrypting data at rest; and improving logging and monitoring. WADA submitted to a compliance agreement under PIPEDA Section 17.1(1), with the OPC retaining ongoing monitoring authority to ensure full implementation.
companyNow: WADA continues to operate as the international anti-doping authority, managing the ADAMS database and anti-doping oversight for global sports organizations, though it has since enhanced security practices following the 2016 breach.

companyDescription: A large online marketplace platform that facilitates buying and selling between users, with a separate grassroots advocacy network for government relations messaging.

caseDescription: An online marketplace sent unsolicited mass emails to Canadian members inviting them to sign a petition on public policy matters without obtaining proper consent or providing opt-out mechanisms. outcome: The online marketplace was required to: (1) implement measures to recognize and appropriately escalate privacy-related customer complaints to designated privacy compliance personnel, including staff training; (2) provide users with an easily accessible unsubscribe link/opt-out function embedded in all public policy and petition emails; (3) amend its privacy policy to clearly indicate it sends public policy and petition notices and explain how users can opt out; and (4) limit future public policy and petition messaging to matters relevant to the underlying commercial relationship. companyDescription: MRI Diagnostics is a medical centre operating in Singapore that provides magnetic resonance imaging and X-Ray services to patients.
companyLongDescription: MRI Diagnostics (trading as NovenaMRI) operates a medical imaging centre in Singapore providing MRI and X-Ray diagnostic services. The company collects and maintains sensitive patient personal data including names, identification numbers, and medical imaging records. caseDescription: MRI Diagnostics subscribed to a cloud-based teleradiology system operated by Clarity Radiology. An IT vendor maintaining the system removed access restrictions during patching and failed to reinstate them, causing three Excel spreadsheets containing approximately 4,099 patients' personal data to be indexed by Google and exposed to unauthorized access. MRI Diagnostics was found to have inadequate vendor management and security oversight, and failed to implement proper data protection arrangements.
violationSummary: The core violation involved failure to implement reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data in possession or under control. The organization failed to establish proper vendor specifications, conduct due diligence on vendor security standards, verify data protection implementations, and maintain written agreements with security obligations—all contributing to unauthorized access and exposure of sensitive health data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: MRI Diagnostics subscribed to a cloud-based teleradiology system operated by Clarity Radiology without proper vendor due diligence, written agreements.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 4,099 patients had their names, NRIC numbers, and radiology scan types indexed by Google search engines.

claimsVsReality.reality: MRI Diagnostics took no steps to verify or assess Clarity's data protection arrangements, security standards (such as ISO 27001 compliance), or security measures before subscribing to the cloud-based service.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clarity was responsible for protecting the patient data exposed in the incident.
claimsVsReality.reality: Clarity was classified as a vendor providing Software-as-a-Service, not a data processor, so responsibility for data protection remained with MRI Diagnostics as the data controller.

caseDescription: BLU Products preinstalled ADUPS spyware on mobile devices that secretly collected and transmitted sensitive personal data including full text message contents, real-time location, call logs, and contact lists to Chinese servers without user knowledge or consent. Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
