regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: BLU represented in its privacy policy that it limits disclosure of consumer information to third-party service providers only to the extent necessary to perform their functions, but in fact ADUPS collected and transmitted text messages, location data, call logs, contacts, and app lists that were not needed for firmware updates.
violations: BLU represented in its privacy policy that it limits disclosure of consumer information to third-party service providers only to the extent necessary to perform their functions, but in fact ADUPS collected and transmitted text messages, location data, call logs, contacts, and app lists that were not needed for firmware updates.

BLU represented that it implements appropriate physical, electronic, and managerial security procedures to protect personal information, but failed to perform due diligence on ADUPS, lacked written security standards for service provider oversight, failed to contractually require data security standards, and failed to assess security risks of third-party software.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on 6 September 2018 alleging two counts of deceptive practices. The complaint alleges violations of FTC Act Section 5 regarding both deceptive disclosure practices and deceptive security claims. Resolution included compliance orders requiring BLU to implement comprehensive information security measures, maintain security controls over third-party vendors, obtain consumer consent for data collection beyond necessary functions, and submit to ongoing compliance monitoring.
companyNow: BLU Products continues to operate as a mobile device manufacturer, but the company faced significant reputational damage from the ADUPS scandal and regulatory enforcement action.
dataType: Text messages, location data, call logs, contact lists, application usage
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair and deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive privacy and security representations

company: Landesbeauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit Mecklenburg-Vorpommern (Data Protection Authority of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern)
companyDescription: The Landesbeauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is an independent data protection supervisory authority responsible for monitoring GDPR/privacy law compliance across the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It provides guidance, conducts investigations, mediates complaints, and issues enforcement actions.
companyLongDescription: The Landesbeauftragte für Datenschutz und Informationsfreiheit Mecklenburg-Vorpommern is an independent data protection supervisory authority responsible for monitoring GDPR/privacy law compliance across the German state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. It provides guidance, conducts investigations, mediates complaints, and issues enforcement actions.
caseDescription: This is the 2018 activity report of the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern data protection authority documenting enforcement actions, consultations, and guidance. The report addresses GDPR implementation challenges, data breach notifications, and privacy violations across multiple sectors including police bodycams, healthcare, education, and municipal administration.
violationSummary: Systemic failures in encryption, access control, secure transmission protocols, and data protection infrastructure across multiple enforced entities. Organizations failed to implement or maintain security standards required by GDPR Art. 32.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Multiple organizations under their oversight failed to implement basic data security measures, including unencrypted email transmission of sensitive personal data.
whyTheyWereWrong: A 15-year-old sexual abuse victim had her contact information illegally obtained by a police officer who then solicited her via SMS; another 13-year-old witness was contacted by an investigator.

claimsVsReality.claim: Organizations claimed uncertainty about GDPR encryption requirements and legitimate business justifications for unencrypted transmission
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR Art. 32 explicitly requires encryption as a standard technical measure; legitimate business needs do not justify exposing sensitive data to interception. Unencrypted fax transmission to wrong recipient, unencrypted email with health/financial data, and unencrypted smart meter readings all violated established standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: Police and justice sector actors claimed lack of awareness about GDPR restrictions on access to personal data
claimsVsReality.reality: Police officers knowingly exploited access to contact databases for sexual coercion of minors and extortion. This constituted deliberate misuse rather than ignorance; discipline and criminal referral were appropriate.

claimsVsReality.claim: Educational institutions claimed uncertainty about photo permissions and media release forms required under GDPR Art. 13
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR Art. 13 requires explicit, granular consent for each use (e.g., homepage vs. press vs. distribution to other parents). Silent consent and blanket permissions violate the standard.

claimsVsReality.claim: Health sector entities claimed insufficient time/resources to implement GDPR compliance measures
claimsVsReality.reality: GDPR became enforceable May 25, 2018. Organizations had 24 months from adoption (May 2016) to prepare. Late implementation reflects priority failure, not impossibility.

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 5(1)(f) requires that personal data be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: OLG Rostock sent confidential criminal case documents via unencrypted fax to wrong recipient, exposing defendant and case details to third parties
violations: OLG Rostock sent confidential criminal case documents via unencrypted fax to wrong recipient, exposing defendant and case details to third parties
Public authority transmitted sensitive social data via unencrypted email to employee's work address, visible to colleagues and sent without authorization to mayor
Municipal ratsinformation system was compromised for 6+ years (2012-2018) with unencrypted resident data stored and exposed in procurement documents

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, including encryption of personal data and the ability to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems.
regulatoryFindings.description: Smart meters transmitted consumption data unencrypted, enabling behavioral profiling through second-by-second granularity instead of monthly consolidated readings
violations: Smart meters transmitted consumption data unencrypted, enabling behavioral profiling through second-by-second granularity instead of monthly consolidated readings
Email communications lacked end-to-end encryption (S/MIME or OpenPGP) despite transport of sensitive health data, financial records, and legal documents
Fax-based transmission of sensitive documents lacked error detection; manual typos in recipient numbers resulted in misdirection to third parties

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 33 requires notification of a personal data breach to the supervisory authority without undue delay and in any case within 72 hours.
regulatoryFindings.description: Municipal authority delayed breach notification by 14 days after discovery of ratsinformation system compromise affecting 6 years of council records
violations: Municipal authority delayed breach notification by 14 days after discovery of ratsinformation system compromise affecting 6 years of council records
Organization failed to conduct timely security assessment following system compromise, delaying identification of scope of exposed data

regulatoryFindings.act: GDPR Art. 32 requires measures to prevent unauthorized persons from gaining access to personal data processing systems and data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Police officer misused position to access contact details of minors, using obtained numbers to sexually solicit a 15-year-old witness via SMS
violations: Police officer misused position to access contact details of minors, using obtained numbers to sexually solicit a 15-year-old witness via SMS
Criminal investigator accessed witness contact information and subsequently contacted 13-year-old witness via WhatsApp with sexual advances
Police officer used access to arrest records to identify and contact witness to extort withdrawal of domestic violence complaint against his son

outcome: The authority issued warnings and compliance orders to violating organizations. For police abuses, formal disciplinary proceedings were initiated against officers who misused access. Municipalities were required to cease operation of insecure systems (e.g., ratsinformation platform), notify affected residents, and implement enhanced security protocols. Organizations were directed to implement encryption standards (TLS 1.2+, S/MIME, OpenPGP), conduct data protection impact assessments using Standard-Datenschutzmodell, and appoint data protection officers. Ongoing monitoring and consultation services provided to healthcare, education, and municipal sectors.
companyNow: The Mecklenburg-Vorpommern Data Protection Authority continues operation as an independent regulatory body. In 2018, the authority reported severe personnel constraints (insufficient staff relative to workload following GDPR implementation) and continued advocacy for additional resources to fulfill enforcement mandates.
dataType: Multiple types including health data, financial data, biometric data, personal identifiers, location data
legalBasisViolated: GDPR Art. 35 - Data protection impact assessment
GDPR Art. 37 - Data protection officer designation
GDPR Art. 4 Nr. 14 - Biometric data definition

company: Prime Sites, Inc. (doing business as Explore Talent)
companyDescription: Explore Talent (Prime Sites, Inc.) operated an online talent search network allowing aspiring actors, models, and artists to search for auditions and casting calls. The company charged users for premium 'pro' memberships to access and apply for listed opportunities.
companyLongDescription: Explore Talent (Prime Sites, Inc.) operated an online talent search network allowing aspiring actors, models, and artists to search for auditions and casting calls. The company charged users for premium 'pro' memberships to access and apply for listed opportunities.
caseDescription: Explore Talent collected personal information from over 100,000 children under 13 without parental consent or adequate notice, in violation of COPPA. The company made false privacy claims and misrepresented casting opportunities to deceive users into paying for premium memberships.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected and disclosed personal information from children under 13 without parental knowledge or consent, enabling surveillance and exposure of minors' identities and photographs online.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Explore Talent collected personal information from over 100,000 children under 13 without obtaining parental consent, made their profiles publicly visible with names and photographs.
whyTheyWereWrong: More than 100,000 children's names, photos, email addresses, mailing addresses, and phone numbers were made publicly searchable.

claimsVsReality.claim: Explore Talent stated in its Privacy Policy: 'We do not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13.'
claimsVsReality.reality: More than 100,000 users who registered as under age 13 had their personal information collected, including names, emails, addresses, phone numbers, birthdates, and photographs, which became publicly visible on user profiles.

claimsVsReality.claim: Casting directors and agents were interested in specific Explore Talent users for particular roles, as represented by telemarketers in sales calls.
claimsVsReality.reality: When one user directly contacted a casting director for 'Jack Reacher 2,' the director stated the film was not working with Explore Talent and all speaking roles were already cast. Another user promised a role in 'Fast and Furious' received no contact despite paying for pro membership.

claimsVsReality.claim: Explore Talent is the 'world's largest talent resource' with opportunities to connect users with industry professionals.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company systematically targeted vulnerable minors with false casting opportunities, charged them money based on unfounded claims, and exposed their personal data and photographs to predatory contact.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(d) requires an operator to provide sufficient notice on its Web site or online services of the information it collects online from children, how it uses such information, and its disclosure practices for such information, among other required content.
regulatoryFindings.description: Explore Talent maintained a fine-print Privacy Policy buried at the bottom of the homepage among a dozen other hyperlinks, not prominently displayed or required to be reviewed or agreed to by registrants.
violations: Explore Talent maintained a fine-print Privacy Policy buried at the bottom of the homepage among a dozen other hyperlinks, not prominently displayed or required to be reviewed or agreed to by registrants.
The Policy falsely stated the company did not knowingly collect information from children under 13, despite routinely collecting personal information from 100,000+ child users.
The Policy did not provide adequate substantive notice about what information was collected from children, how it was used, or how it was disclosed.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b) requires an operator to provide direct notice to parents of the information collected online from children, how it is used, and its disclosure practices, among other required content.
regulatoryFindings.description: Explore Talent provided no direct notice to parents of the personal information collected from child users.
violations: Explore Talent provided no direct notice to parents of the personal information collected from child users.
Parents were not notified about collection of full names, email addresses, mailing addresses, phone numbers, birthdates, photographs, and physical measurements.
Parents were not informed that children's profiles would be publicly visible to other users and unregistered visitors.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) requires an operator to obtain verifiable parental consent before any collection, use, and/or disclosure of personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Explore Talent collected personal information from children under 13 without obtaining any verifiable parental consent.
violations: Explore Talent collected personal information from children under 13 without obtaining any verifiable parental consent.
The company did not verify that profiles indicating an age under 13 were created by legal guardians.
Users indicating age 12 or younger were only presented with a confirmation message asking them to verify their birthdate, not blocked from registration or required to provide parental consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) / 15 U.S.C. § 45(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Explore Talent made false and misleading representations in its Privacy Policy that it 'does not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13,' while knowingly collecting such information from 100,000+ child users.
violations: Explore Talent made false and misleading representations in its Privacy Policy that it 'does not knowingly collect personal information from children under 13,' while knowingly collecting such information from 100,000+ child users.

Defendant's telemarketers made false representations to users that casting directors had chosen them for specific roles in major motion pictures (e.g., 'Jack Reacher' sequel, 'Fast and Furious' films) without any basis in fact.
Users who paid for pro memberships based on these false casting representations received no contact about promised opportunities.

outcome: Complaint filed seeking permanent injunction against future COPPA and FTC Act violations, monetary civil penalties (up to $16,000 per violation), and other equitable relief. The document indicates this is the initial complaint stage; no final settlement or judgment amount is specified in the complaint itself.
companyNow: As of the complaint filing date (February 5, 2018), Explore Talent was operating ExploreTalent.com with over 10 million members. No resolution information is provided in this complaint document.
dataType: Children's personal information including full names, email addresses, telephone numbers, mailing addresses, photographs, birthdates, physical measurements
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) (verifiable parental consent requirement)
FTC Act Section 5(a) / 15 U.S.C. § 45(a) (unfair or deceptive acts)

companyDescription: Integrated Flight Solutions LLC operated NoveltyExcuses.com, an e-commerce website that sold customizable fake financial documents, identity documents, and medical absence notes. The site marketed products as novelties but made clear they looked authentic and were 'proven to work' for deceiving recipients.
companyLongDescription: Integrated Flight Solutions LLC operated NoveltyExcuses.com, an e-commerce website that sold customizable fake financial documents, identity documents, and medical absence notes. The site marketed products as novelties but made clear they looked authentic and were 'proven to work' for deceiving recipients.
caseDescription: NoveltyExcuses.com sold customizable fake documents (pay stubs, utility bills, insurance cards, doctor's notes) advertised as authentic-looking novelties. The FTC alleged defendants knew these documents would be used for identity theft, loan fraud, and housing fraud. Documents were designed to deceive recipients and lacked permanent markings identifying them as fake, despite disclaimers.
violationSummary: Defendants facilitated the misappropriation of personal information by selling tools designed to create fake identity and financial documents that would deceive third parties (lenders, landlords, employers) into believing false information about consumers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Operated NoveltyExcuses.com selling over 50 customizable fake financial, identity, and medical documents including pay stubs, utility bills, insurance cards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Identity thieves used fake pay stubs and utility bills from the site to fraudulently obtain credit cards, mortgages.

claimsVsReality.claim: Products are novelties and entertainment items for gags, tricks, and fooling friends/family/colleagues
claimsVsReality.reality: Documents were designed to deceive third parties (lenders, landlords, employers) into believing false information, and were actively used for identity theft, loan fraud, and housing fraud

claimsVsReality.claim: Small-print disclaimers identify products as 'For Entertainment Purpose Only'
claimsVsReality.reality: Disclaimers were easily deleted from electronic files by customers; many documents contained no permanent, visible marking indicating they were fake

claimsVsReality.claim: Website states it is 'a great alternative to illegal document mills'
claimsVsReality.reality: The products and their functionality were functionally equivalent to illegal document mills, enabling the same fraud schemes

claimsVsReality.claim: Forms are so authentic-looking that 'trained professionals may have a hard time telling the difference'
claimsVsReality.reality: This marketing language made clear defendants knew documents would deceive recipients and be presented as genuine

claimsVsReality.claim: 100% guarantee and 'proven to work'
claimsVsReality.reality: Guarantee of effectiveness at deceiving recipients; 'proven to work' for fraudulent purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants sold fake financial, identity, and medical documents that are used to commit identity theft and loan fraud, knowing these documents would be presented to third parties as genuine
violations: Defendants sold fake financial, identity, and medical documents that are used to commit identity theft and loan fraud, knowing these documents would be presented to third parties as genuine
Despite labeling products as 'novelties' for 'entertainment' purposes, defendants did not clearly and prominently mark documents as fake or prevent removal of disclaimers
Defendants marketed documents as 'authentic looking' and 'proven to work,' knowing they would deceive recipients such as lenders, landlords, and employers

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(n) defines unfairness as substantial injury to consumers that cannot be reasonably avoided and is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sale of fake documents causes substantial injury to identity theft victims whose personal information is misused, and to lenders and landlords defrauded by false application documents
violations: Sale of fake documents causes substantial injury to identity theft victims whose personal information is misused, and to lenders and landlords defrauded by false application documents
Consumers cannot reasonably avoid this injury as victims of third parties' use of fake documents provided by defendants
No legitimate consumer benefit outweighs the substantial harms of identity fraud, loan fraud, and housing fraud

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint for permanent injunction and other equitable relief under Section 13(b) of the FTC Act. Sought remedies include permanent injunction against future violations, disgorgement of ill-gotten monies, restitution, refund of monies paid, and rescission or reformation of contracts. Case status from document: complaint filed 09/13/2018; final resolution not specified in complaint.
companyNow: Unknown. Integrated Flight Solutions LLC operated NoveltyExcuses.com as of October 2017. Current operational status unknown.
dataType: Financial data, identity information, employment and residency verification documents
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) - Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce
FTC Act Section 5(n) - Standard for unfairness (substantial injury to consumers)

companyDescription: IDmission LLC is a Delaware corporation offering a cloud-based technology platform to help business clients engage with their customers, with principal offices in Boulder, Colorado.
companyLongDescription: IDmission LLC is a Delaware corporation offering a cloud-based technology platform to help business clients engage with their customers, with principal offices in Boulder, Colorado.
caseDescription: IDmission LLC falsely claimed to be certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework on its website and privacy policy. Although the company initiated an application for certification in October 2017, it never completed the required steps to actually participate in the framework. The company continued making the false claims even after the U.S. Department of Commerce warned it to take down the statements.
violationSummary: IDmission distorted the reality of its data protection status by falsely representing Privacy Shield certification, creating a misleading impression of compliance that was essential to consumer trust in cross-border data transfers.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: IDmission LLC published false statements in its privacy policy claiming it had certified to and complied with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU residents transferred personal data to IDmission believing their information would receive legal protections equivalent to EU standards.

claimsVsReality.claim: IDmission, LLC complies with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Framework and has certified to the Department of Commerce that it adheres to the Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: IDmission initiated an application for Privacy Shield certification in October 2017 but did not complete the necessary steps to participate in the framework or achieve actual certification

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers can view IDmission's Privacy Shield certification on the official privacyshield.gov website
claimsVsReality.reality: IDmission was not listed on the Privacy Shield registry because it never completed the certification process

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: IDmission represented that it was a participant in and certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework when it had not completed the certification process and was not actually certified
violations: IDmission represented that it was a participant in and certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework when it had not completed the certification process and was not actually certified

IDmission continued to make these false representations on its website after the U.S. Department of Commerce specifically warned the company to remove the claims unless and until certification was completed

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on November 15, 2018, against IDmission LLC alleging deceptive acts or practices in violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint establishes that IDmission falsely claimed Privacy Shield certification while never completing the required certification steps. The complaint serves as the formal charging document initiating enforcement proceedings; the final resolution would be determined through subsequent settlement or litigation.
dataType: Personal data transferred from EU to United States

companyDescription: RealPage, Inc. is a property management software company providing tenant screening, rental management, and business intelligence tools to residential property owners and managers throughout the United States. The company compiled criminal records, eviction histories, and credit information into automated tenant background reports.
companyLongDescription: RealPage, Inc. is a property management software company providing tenant screening, rental management, and business intelligence tools to residential property owners and managers throughout the United States. The company compiled criminal records, eviction histories, and credit information into automated tenant background reports.
caseDescription: RealPage operated tenant screening services that provided inaccurate criminal background reports to landlords and property managers. The company used overly broad matching criteria with insufficient filters, resulting in criminal records belonging to different individuals being included in tenant screening reports. This led to prospective tenants being denied housing based on inaccurate information.
violationSummary: RealPage failed to implement reasonable procedures to ensure accuracy of consumer reports, instead operating an inherently insecure matching system that predictably generated false positives identifying wrong individuals. This constitutes a systemic failure to secure and verify personal data before transmission to third parties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: RealPage used overly broad matching criteria with soft phonetic matching and partial name matches to compile tenant screening reports without adequate filtering or manual verification.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of applicants were denied housing based on criminal records belonging to other individuals, including people with completely different names, birthdates, genders, and races.

claimsVsReality.claim: RealPage's proprietary matching algorithm provided accurate criminal background information for tenant screening.
claimsVsReality.reality: The algorithm's broad soft-matching criteria produced significant false positives, matching individuals with different names (not nicknames), different birth dates, different genders, and different races to the same search query, with no filtering or manual review to catch these errors.

claimsVsReality.claim: RealPage filtered results to ensure only accurate records were reported.
claimsVsReality.reality: RealPage's filtering was minimal and inconsistent: it only excluded records without exact middle name matches if middle name was available, only partially filtered by state/gender if that data was provided, and had no procedures to identify when multiple different individuals appeared in a single report.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(b) requires that whenever a consumer reporting agency prepares a consumer report, it shall follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of the information concerning the individual about whom the report relates.
regulatoryFindings.description: RealPage used broad matching criteria (soft name matches, phonetic matching, flexible date of birth ranges) without adequate filtering to identify correct individuals
violations: RealPage used broad matching criteria (soft name matches, phonetic matching, flexible date of birth ranges) without adequate filtering to identify correct individuals
RealPage did not implement procedures to assess accuracy of results, particularly when records contained internal inconsistencies or clearly referenced multiple individuals
RealPage continued reporting inaccurate criminal records despite receiving disputes throughout the relevant period (2012-2017)

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act defines a consumer reporting agency as any person that regularly engages in assembling or evaluating consumer information for furnishing consumer reports to third parties.
regulatoryFindings.description: RealPage qualified as a consumer reporting agency by regularly selling tenant screening reports containing criminal records, credit information, and other personal data to rental property owners and management companies
violations: RealPage qualified as a consumer reporting agency by regularly selling tenant screening reports containing criminal records, credit information, and other personal data to rental property owners and management companies

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: RealPage's failure to implement reasonable accuracy procedures constituted unfair practices that caused substantial injury to consumers seeking housing
violations: RealPage's failure to implement reasonable accuracy procedures constituted unfair practices that caused substantial injury to consumers seeking housing

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint against RealPage seeking monetary civil penalties (up to $3,500-$3,817 per violation depending on violation date), permanent injunction against future FCRA and FTC Act violations, and other equitable relief. The complaint does not indicate a final settlement amount as this was the initial complaint filing on October 16, 2018.
companyNow: RealPage is owned by Thoma Bravo private equity firm (acquired 2019). The company continues as a leading property management software provider but has undergone regulatory compliance changes following this FTC action.
dataType: Criminal records, eviction history, rental history, credit information, personal identifiers (name, date of birth, address, gender, race), photographs
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 607(b) (15 U.S.C. § 1681e(b))
Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 621(a) (15 U.S.C. § 1681s(a))

companyDescription: SmartStart Employment Screening, Inc. is a Delaware-based background and employment screening services company operating from Clearwater, Florida. The company serves businesses requiring employment verification and background check services.
companyLongDescription: SmartStart Employment Screening, Inc. is a Delaware-based background and employment screening services company operating from Clearwater, Florida. The company serves businesses requiring employment verification and background check services.
caseDescription: SmartStart falsely claimed to participate in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework on its website through at least June 2018, even after its certification expired in September 2017. The company obtained Privacy Shield certification in September 2016 but failed to renew it and did not complete the required steps to affirm continued protection of personal data received during participation.
violationSummary: The company's deceptive claims about Privacy Shield participation constitute disclosure violations because they misrepresented the legal protections and oversight applicable to personal data, undermining individuals' ability to make informed decisions about data transfers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: SmartStart Employment Screening falsely claimed on its website through June 2018 that it was a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: EU citizens and job applicants submitted sensitive personal background data to SmartStart believing it would receive Privacy Shield protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: SmartStart complies with the EU-US Privacy Shield Framework and has certified adherence to Privacy Shield Principles
claimsVsReality.reality: SmartStart obtained Privacy Shield certification in September 2016 but allowed it to expire in September 2017 without renewal and did not complete required steps to affirm continued protection of previously received personal data

claimsVsReality.claim: SmartStart has joined the EU Privacy Shield Program
claimsVsReality.reality: SmartStart is not a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework as of at least June 2018 when false statements were still being disseminated

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SmartStart represented directly and by implication that it was a current participant in EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles when in fact its certification had expired in September 2017 and was not renewed.
violations: SmartStart represented directly and by implication that it was a current participant in EU-U.S. Privacy Shield Principles when in fact its certification had expired in September 2017 and was not renewed.

SmartStart represented that it would abide by Privacy Shield framework principles requiring affirmation to Commerce of continued protection of personal data upon ceasing participation, but failed to make such affirmation.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on November 15, 2018 alleging two counts of deceptive practices. The complaint seeks cessation of false Privacy Shield claims and compliance with Privacy Shield requirements or alternative protective measures. Final resolution pending or subject to consent order requiring removal of deceptive statements and implementation of compliant data protection practices.
companyNow: SmartStart Employment Screening, Inc. remains an employment screening services provider. Current Privacy Shield status and resolution of this enforcement action unknown.
dataType: Personal data from EU residents including identification, employment, and background check information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Innovative Paycheck Solutions (operating as FakePayStubOnline.com) was a document forgery service operated by Katrina Moore that sold counterfeit financial documents including pay stubs, tax forms, and bank statements, along with services to falsify genuine bank statements.
companyLongDescription: Innovative Paycheck Solutions (operating as FakePayStubOnline.com) was a document forgery service operated by Katrina Moore that sold counterfeit financial documents including pay stubs, tax forms, and bank statements, along with services to falsify genuine bank statements.
caseDescription: Katrina Moore operated a website selling fake pay stubs, tax forms, bank statements, and document falsification services since 2013. The company knew these documents would be presented as genuine to lenders, landlords, and government agencies, facilitating identity theft, tax fraud, and loan fraud. The FTC sued for unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.
violationSummary: The company's sale of forged financial documents and services to falsify real documents enabled widespread disclosure of personal information to fraudsters and misuse of stolen identities in financial crimes against third parties.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Sold fake financial documents including pay stubs, W-2s, 1099s, and bank statements, and offered services to edit real bank statements.
whyTheyWereWrong: Purchasers used the fake documents to commit identity theft and loan fraud, causing victims to experience damaged credit, fraudulent loan applications, delayed tax refunds.

claimsVsReality.claim: All items sold on this site are for novelty and entertainment purposes only.
claimsVsReality.reality: Documents were designed to look authentic and were marketed as such, with customers able to populate them with any personal or financial information and used to commit fraud against lenders, landlords, and government agencies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Products are 'fake' but look 'authentic' and contain 'accurate' calculations, and we do not use watermarks.
claimsVsReality.reality: The authentic appearance and lack of watermarks facilitated use of forged documents in fraudulent loan applications, rental agreements, and tax filings, directly enabling identity theft and financial crime.

claimsVsReality.claim: The term 'fake' is used for search engine optimization purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Documents were sold specifically because they appeared genuine enough to deceive financial institutions and government agencies into processing fraudulent applications based on stolen personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendant advertised and sold fake financial documents knowing they would be presented as genuine to third parties such as lenders and landlords, deceiving recipients about their authenticity and origin.
violations: Defendant advertised and sold fake financial documents knowing they would be presented as genuine to third parties such as lenders and landlords, deceiving recipients about their authenticity and origin.
Defendant did not clearly mark fake documents as inappropriate for use beyond novelty purposes, instead emphasizing their authentic appearance and accurate tax calculations, facilitating fraud.

Defendant's practices caused substantial injury to consumers (identity theft victims and fraud victims) who could not reasonably avoid the harm, with no countervailing consumer or competitive benefits.

outcome: The FTC obtained a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief against Katrina Moore. The case sought permanent injunction to halt future violations, disgorgement of ill-gotten monies, rescission or reformation of contracts, restitution, and refund of monies paid. The document filed on September 13, 2018 represents the initial complaint; final resolution and remediation requirements would be determined by subsequent court orders.
companyNow: Status unknown. The complaint was filed in September 2018 seeking permanent injunction and equitable relief against the operator and the business.
dataType: Personal identification information, Social Security numbers, employment history, financial information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce
FTC Act Section 5(n) – Substantial injury to consumers that cannot be reasonably avoided

companyDescription: mResource LLC, operating as Loop Works LLC, is a recruitment and talent management services provider based in Chicago, Illinois offering staffing and recruitment solutions.
companyLongDescription: mResource LLC, operating as Loop Works LLC, is a recruitment and talent management services provider based in Chicago, Illinois offering staffing and recruitment solutions.
caseDescription: mResource LLC, operating as Loop Works, falsely claimed on its website that it was a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework, a data protection mechanism for transferring personal data from the EU to the US. In reality, the company obtained Privacy Shield certification in December 2016 but failed to renew it after it expired in December 2017, yet continued to represent itself as compliant.
violationSummary: The company's false claim of Privacy Shield participation masked the true absence of adequate data protection mechanisms, creating insecurity regarding how personal data of EU individuals was actually protected.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: mResource LLC falsely claimed on its website through at least June 2018 that it was a current participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework.

The company continued making false claims of Privacy Shield participation for at least eight months after certification expired, violating FTC deception authority.
violationSummary: VenPath's deceptive statements about Privacy Shield participation and compliance constitute misrepresentation regarding the safeguards applied to EU residents' personal data, enabling unlawful transfers and inadequate protection.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling

whyTheyWereWrong: VenPath's Privacy Shield certification expired in October 2017 and was never renewed, meaning EU residents' personal data lacked the legal protections VenPath falsely promised.

companyDescription: PayPal is a Delaware corporation headquartered in San Jose, California, operating as a leading digital payments platform. The company provides payment and social networking services, including the Venmo peer-to-peer mobile payment application acquired in 2013.
companyLongDescription: PayPal is a Delaware corporation headquartered in San Jose, California, operating as a leading digital payments platform. The company provides payment and social networking services, including the Venmo peer-to-peer mobile payment application acquired in 2013.
caseDescription: PayPal's Venmo payment service misrepresented fund availability and transfer timelines, delayed or reversed transactions without disclosure, and failed to implement adequate privacy controls and security safeguards. Millions of consumers relied on misleading claims about overnight fund transfers and private transaction settings, suffering financial losses when funds were frozen or removed without warning.
violationSummary: PayPal made false or misleading representations about fund transfer timelines and privacy settings, withheld material facts about transaction holds/reversals and retroactive sharing capabilities, and failed to implement promised 'bank-grade' security, resulting in unauthorized account access and financial loss.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Venmo represented that funds were credited to accounts and could transfer to bank accounts overnight.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers suffered financial hardship unable to access expected funds for rent and bills; some lost thousands of dollars when Venmo reversed transactions after customers had already.

claimsVsReality.claim: Money credited to your Venmo balance. Transfer to your bank overnight.
claimsVsReality.reality: Funds could be frozen or reversed during hidden fraud reviews; overnight transfers were not guaranteed and often delayed or failed without disclosure to consumers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Use Venmo with anyone and for purchases; cash out to any bank overnight.
claimsVsReality.reality: Transactions were frequently delayed or reversed, particularly involving new users or business transactions, contradicting claims that 'anyone' could transact and receive funds immediately.

claimsVsReality.claim: Setting your default audience to 'Participants Only' will ensure your payments are only visible to you and the other participant.
claimsVsReality.reality: The other transaction participant could retroactively override the privacy setting and publish the transaction publicly at any time without notice to the user.

claimsVsReality.claim: Venmo uses bank-grade security systems and data encryption to protect your financial information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Venmo lacked basic security safeguards; it did not notify users of password changes, email address changes, or new devices added to accounts, enabling unauthorized account takeovers and fund withdrawals without any user notification.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Venmo represented that money credited to a Venmo account could be transferred to an external bank account overnight, but failed to disclose that funds could be frozen or removed during hidden fraud review processes, in numerous instances causing delays or reversals.
violations: Venmo represented that money credited to a Venmo account could be transferred to an external bank account overnight, but failed to disclose that funds could be frozen or removed during hidden fraud review processes, in numerous instances causing delays or reversals.

Venmo represented that the Default Audience Setting and Individual Audience Setting would restrict transaction visibility to specified groups (e.g., 'Participants Only' or 'Friends'), but failed to disclose that another transaction participant could retroactively override privacy settings and publish previously private transactions without notice.

Venmo represented it used 'bank-grade security systems and data encryption' to protect financial information, but failed to implement basic safeguards including security notifications for account changes, resulting in unauthorized account takeovers where funds were withdrawn without consumer notification.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) and Regulation P (12 C.F.R. Part 1016) require financial institutions to provide customers with a clear and conspicuous initial privacy notice that accurately reflects the institution's privacy policies and practices, and to deliver the notice so each consumer receives actual notice.
regulatoryFindings.description: Venmo failed to provide a clear and conspicuous initial privacy notice; the signup screen displayed the disclosure in grey text on a light grey background, insufficient to call attention to the nature and significance of the information.
violations: Venmo failed to provide a clear and conspicuous initial privacy notice; the signup screen displayed the disclosure in grey text on a light grey background, insufficient to call attention to the nature and significance of the information.

Venmo's privacy notice was not accurate; it claimed information was shared only with a user's 'social web' for 'public' or 'friends-only' transactions, but Venmo actually shared all transactions by default with 'everyone on the Internet,' including non-account holders.

Venmo failed to deliver the initial privacy notice so consumers could reasonably expect to receive actual notice; users could click a link to the Privacy Policy but the company did not require acknowledgement of receipt as a condition of service access.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop a comprehensive written information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including risk assessment, safeguard implementation, and regular testing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Until at least August 2014, Venmo failed to maintain a written comprehensive information security program.
violations: Until at least August 2014, Venmo failed to maintain a written comprehensive information security program.
Until at least September 2014, Venmo failed to assess reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information.

Until approximately March 2015, Venmo failed to implement basic safeguards including security notifications to consumers of password/email changes or new device additions to accounts, and failed to maintain adequate customer support to investigate and respond to unauthorized transaction reports, resulting in account takeovers where funds were withdrawn without notification.

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a Complaint on May 23, 2018, alleging violations of FTC Act Section 5, the Privacy Rule, Regulation P, and the Safeguards Rule. The complaint seeks a Consent Order requiring PayPal/Venmo to implement comprehensive remedial measures including: clear and accurate disclosures about fund transfer timing and conditions, accurate privacy notices and settings, implementation of adequate security safeguards including security notifications and customer support, and ongoing compliance monitoring.
companyNow: PayPal remains a major global fintech company and continues to operate Venmo as a peer-to-peer payment service. Following this enforcement action, PayPal implemented corrective measures to its privacy controls and security practices.
dataType: financial information, payment transaction details, account information, personal information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

GLB Safeguards Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 314 – Information security program requirements
GLB Safeguards Rule 16 C.F.R. § 314.3 – Risk assessment

companyDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a San Francisco-based transportation network company providing ride-sharing, delivery, and mobility services globally. Founded in 2009, it operates in over 70 countries.
companyLongDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a San Francisco-based transportation network company providing ride-sharing, delivery, and mobility services globally. Founded in 2009, it operates in over 70 countries.
caseDescription: In November 2016, Uber discovered hackers had accessed personal data of millions of customers and over 174,000 California drivers. Rather than notifying affected individuals and regulators as required by law, Uber paid hackers $100,000 for silence and deletion. Notification was only issued over a year later in November 2017.
violationSummary: Hackers breached Uber's cloud storage containing personal data, causing loss of confidentiality. Uber then compounded the breach by intentionally concealing it and suppressing notification to affected individuals.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Concealed a data breach affecting millions of users by paying hackers $100,000 to delete stolen data and remain silent, delaying notification to regulators and victims for over 13 months.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 174,000 California drivers' unencrypted names and driver's license numbers were stolen, along with names, emails.

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber maintained reasonable security procedures to protect personal information
claimsVsReality.reality: Uber published cloud storage credentials in plain text, lacked multi-factor authentication, and allowed personal credentials for GitHub access

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber would notify affected individuals of breaches expeditiously
claimsVsReality.reality: Uber concealed the breach for 13+ months, notifying regulators only in November 2017, 11 months after hackers were paid

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber's systems were adequately secured against unauthorized access
claimsVsReality.reality: Hackers easily exploited a 'major vulnerability' in Uber's security system via GitHub access and plaintext credentials

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.82(a) requires disclosure of a breach of security of a system and issuance of security breach notification to affected individuals in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Uber failed to notify affected drivers and users until November 2017, more than 13 months after the November 2016 breach, violating the requirement for expedient notification.
violations: Uber failed to notify affected drivers and users until November 2017, more than 13 months after the November 2016 breach, violating the requirement for expedient notification.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.81.5(b) requires implementation and maintenance of reasonable security procedures and practices appropriate to the nature of personal information to protect it from unauthorized access, destruction, use, modification, or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Uber failed to implement reasonable security by: (1) allowing employees to use personal usernames/passwords for GitHub access without multi-factor authentication; (2) publishing cloud storage credentials in plain text in computer code; (3) inadequate access controls on its private GitHub workspace.
violations: Uber failed to implement reasonable security by: (1) allowing employees to use personal usernames/passwords for GitHub access without multi-factor authentication; (2) publishing cloud storage credentials in plain text in computer code; (3) inadequate access controls on its private GitHub workspace.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair competition, including unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business acts or practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Uber engaged in unlawful and fraudulent conduct by deliberately concealing the breach, paying hackers to suppress evidence, and intentionally delaying notification to regulators and victims.
violations: Uber engaged in unlawful and fraudulent conduct by deliberately concealing the breach, paying hackers to suppress evidence, and intentionally delaying notification to regulators and victims.

outcome: The complaint sought permanent injunction preventing Uber from engaging in unfair competition, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation, and recovery of costs of suit. The document is the initial complaint filed September 25, 2018; final resolution and settlement terms are not reflected in this document.
companyNow: Uber Technologies remains a major global ride-sharing platform. The company subsequently settled related investigations and implemented enhanced security and compliance programs following the 2016 breach disclosure.
dataType: Names, driver's license numbers, email addresses, mobile phone numbers

company: EMP Media, Inc. (d/b/a MyEx.com, Post My Ad, T & A Media, Internet Secrets)
companyDescription: EMP Media, Inc. was a Nevada corporation founded in 2008 that operated multiple online properties including MyEx.com, a revenge porn website dedicated to publishing intimate images and personal information without consent.
companyLongDescription: EMP Media, Inc. was a Nevada corporation founded in 2008 that operated multiple online properties including MyEx.com, a revenge porn website dedicated to publishing intimate images and personal information without consent.
caseDescription: EMP Media operated MyEx.com, a revenge porn website that solicited and published intimate images of individuals without consent, along with their personal information. The company charged victims $499–$2,800 to remove their images and data. The FTC and Nevada alleged unfair and deceptive practices causing substantial consumer harm.
violationSummary: The company publicly disclosed intimate images and personal information without consent, enabling identification and contact of individuals. This falls squarely within 'Disclosure' – the unauthorized revelation of sensitive personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: EMP Media operated MyEx.com, a revenge porn website that solicited intimate images without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 12,620 victims had explicit images published without consent, causing job loss, depression, anxiety, unwanted contact from strangers.

claimsVsReality.reality: The site actively solicited intimate images, demanded $499–$2,800 from victims to remove them, and operated as an extortion scheme

claimsVsReality.claim: Defendant Applegate told GoDaddy that the Netherlands address and 'Eun Kim' contact were fabricated: 'it's a made up name for the address'
claimsVsReality.reality: These false identities were used to evade law enforcement after GoDaddy informed Applegate of child exploitation reports and contact from internet crimes task forces

claimsVsReality.reality: These services were controlled or affiliated with EMP and the defendants, routing funds through Western Union to the Philippines in the name of 'Sheila Garcia' – an apparent front

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: EMP solicited intimate images without consent from individuals and published them alongside personal information on a publicly accessible website
violations: EMP solicited intimate images without consent from individuals and published them alongside personal information on a publicly accessible website
EMP charged victims $499–$2,800 to remove non-consensual intimate images and personal data, constituting extortion

Victims could not avoid the harm as individuals had no control over whether their images were submitted or published

violations: EMP demanded payment from consumers under threat of continued public display of intimate images and personal information

The court was asked to suspend the website, freeze assets, and enforce compliance monitoring. The complaint documents that EMP took in over $4 million from January 2014 through April 2016 alone, partially through removal fees.
companyNow: EMP Media was dissolved July 7, 2016. MyEx.com continues to operate behind anonymized domain registration through Yeicox Limited (British Virgin Islands), registered via Panama-based privacy services, evading enforcement.

companyDescription: Apartment Hunters, Inc. operated prepaid rental listing websites targeting housing-vulnerable populations, including Section 8 voucher recipients. The company charged subscription fees for access to rental property contact information while making deceptive claims about listing accuracy and housing search success rates.
companyLongDescription: Apartment Hunters, Inc. operated prepaid rental listing websites targeting housing-vulnerable populations, including Section 8 voucher recipients. The company charged subscription fees for access to rental property contact information while making deceptive claims about listing accuracy and housing search success rates.
caseDescription: Apartment Hunters operated prepaid rental listing websites (WeTakeSection8.com, ApartmentHunterz.com, FeaturedRentals.com) that charged consumers fees to access contact information for property managers. The company made false and unsubstantiated claims about listing accuracy, availability, exclusivity, and how quickly consumers would find housing. The majority of listings were unavailable or did not accept the vouchers advertised, particularly on the Section 8 site targeting low-income families with strict housing deadlines.
violationSummary: Defendants misrepresented material facts about rental listings (accuracy, availability, exclusivity, and search outcomes), deceiving consumers into purchasing subscriptions under false pretenses.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Apartment Hunters charged consumers $14.99–$49 for access to rental listings on WeTakeSection8.com, ApartmentHunterz.com.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers—particularly vulnerable Section 8 voucher holders with only 60–120 days to secure housing—lost subscription fees.

claimsVsReality.claim: 500,000+ Section 8 approved or low-priced apartments and homes available for rent nationwide with most up-to-date listings updated daily
claimsVsReality.reality: Majority of listings were unavailable for rent; most available units did not accept Section 8 vouchers; company did not verify availability in timely manner

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers find a place within 5–7 business days (WeTakeSection8.com) or 3–5 days (ApartmentHunterz.com)
claimsVsReality.reality: No substantiation provided; company knew claims were inaccurate; actual consumer outcomes differed significantly; defendants received hundreds of complaints about unavailable properties

claimsVsReality.claim: Exclusive rights to list thousands of Section 8 and other rental listings not found on free websites
claimsVsReality.reality: No exclusive rights existed; company did not verify whether listings appeared on free websites; same listings appeared across multiple platforms

claimsVsReality.claim: Listings are validated and phone numbers, email addresses, and availability are confirmed
claimsVsReality.reality: Company did little verification and received listings from third-party data partners with known inaccuracies in description, price, availability, and address

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants represented that rental listings were accurate, up-to-date, and available for rent when in fact the majority were unavailable or did not match advertised criteria (particularly Section 8 acceptance).
violations: Defendants represented that rental listings were accurate, up-to-date, and available for rent when in fact the majority were unavailable or did not match advertised criteria (particularly Section 8 acceptance).
Defendants claimed consumers would find housing within 3–7 business days; in reality, no substantiation supported these claims and complaints showed actual outcomes differed significantly.

Defendants claimed to have exclusive rights to thousands of listings and that consumers could not find these on free websites, when they had no exclusive rights and did not verify whether listings appeared elsewhere.
Defendants claimed to validate listings and update them daily in real-time when they did little verification and received listings from third-party data partners with known inaccuracies.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief seeking temporary, preliminary, and permanent injunctive relief; rescission or reformation of contracts; restitution; refund of monies paid; disgorgement of ill-gotten monies; and costs. The document filed 09/11/18 initiated the case. Final resolution and settlement terms would be determined in subsequent court proceedings or settlement agreements.
companyNow: Apartment Hunters continued operating prepaid rental listing services after its California PRLS license was revoked in 2015 for similar deceptive practices. The company remained subject to FTC enforcement action as of the September 2018 complaint.
dataType: Personal contact information (phone numbers, email addresses), rental history information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a multinational transportation and delivery company founded in 2009 that operates a mobile application connecting drivers with riders seeking transportation services. As of the complaint period, Uber had over 160,000 active drivers and more than 1 billion completed rides with over $1.5 billion in annual revenues.
companyLongDescription: Uber Technologies, Inc. is a multinational transportation and delivery company founded in 2009 that operates a mobile application connecting drivers with riders seeking transportation services. As of the complaint period, Uber had over 160,000 active drivers and more than 1 billion completed rides with over $1.5 billion in annual revenues.
caseDescription: Uber falsely represented that it closely monitored and audited employee access to consumer data and provided reasonable security for personal information stored in databases. In reality, Uber failed to implement basic security controls, stored sensitive data unencrypted, and suffered two major breaches exposing millions of riders' and drivers' personal information, which it concealed for over a year.
violationSummary: Two major data breaches resulted directly from Uber's inadequate security practices and deceptive representations. Millions of consumers' confidential personal information was exposed to unauthorized access despite Uber's public promises of strong protections.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Uber falsely promised that internal employee access to riders' and drivers' personal data was continuously monitored.
whyTheyWereWrong: In reality, Uber stored millions of consumers' unencrypted names, phone numbers, driver's license numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Uber has a strict policy prohibiting all employees from accessing rider or driver data, with close monitoring and auditing by data security specialists on an ongoing basis
claimsVsReality.reality: From August 2015 to May 2016, Uber ceased timely follow-up on automated alerts and only monitored high-profile executive accounts, not general employee access. No continuous monitoring occurred during this period unless employees self-reported.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information is securely stored with standard, industry-wide, commercially reasonable security practices such as encryption, firewalls and SSL
claimsVsReality.reality: Sensitive personal information including names, license numbers, SSNs, and bank account data were stored in plain, unencrypted text in database backups until at least November 2016

claimsVsReality.claim: Information will be kept secure and encrypted to the highest security standards available
claimsVsReality.reality: Engineers posted AWS access keys in plain text to GitHub repositories, and Uber did not require multi-factor authentication for programmatic service account access until November 2016, allowing 2016 breach of 57M+ people

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented that internal access to consumer personal information is closely monitored and audited by data security specialists on an ongoing basis, when in fact Uber failed to closely monitor or audit such access from August 2015 to May 2016
violations: Represented that internal access to consumer personal information is closely monitored and audited by data security specialists on an ongoing basis, when in fact Uber failed to closely monitor or audit such access from August 2015 to May 2016

Represented that consumers' personal information would be securely stored with reasonable security practices such as encryption, when in fact Uber stored sensitive personal information in plain text, failed to implement multi-factor authentication until September 2015, and failed to require multi-factor authentication for programmatic access until November 2016

Represented through customer service that information would be kept 'secure and encrypted to the highest security standards available,' when in fact Uber's actual practices left data vulnerable to unauthorized access

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices under FTC Act Section 5(a). The case proceeded based on Uber's false claims about data security and access monitoring, combined with actual breaches exposing millions of consumers' sensitive personal information. Uber was required to implement comprehensive information security improvements, including mandatory encryption, multi-factor authentication, access controls, ongoing auditing, and third-party security assessments.
companyNow: Uber Technologies remains a major global ride-sharing and delivery platform operating in hundreds of cities worldwide. The company continues operations while under FTC enforcement oversight and compliance obligations.
dataType: Names, email addresses, phone numbers, postal addresses, Social Security numbers, driver's license information, bank account and routing numbers, vehicle registration, insurance information, precise geolocation data, trip records
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Failure to provide reasonable and appropriate data security

companyDescription: The Privy Council Office (PCO) is the central agency of the Government of Canada, responsible for supporting the Prime Minister and Cabinet. The MyDemocracy.ca initiative was a civic engagement platform launched to gather public opinion on electoral reform.
companyLongDescription: The Privy Council Office is a federal government institution that serves as the principal policy advisory body to Canada's Prime Minister and Cabinet. In 2016, it launched MyDemocracy.ca, an online civic engagement platform designed to invite Canadians to share their views on electoral reform and learn how their democratic values compared to others. The website promised anonymous participation but was technically configured to share user data with third-party tracking services. The initiative ran until January 15, 2017, and gathered feedback from approximately 360,000 Canadian participants.
caseDescription: The Privy Council Office (PCO) operated the MyDemocracy.ca website, a civic engagement platform that promised anonymous survey responses about electoral reform. However, the website's design automatically shared users' IP addresses, browser characteristics, and unique results identifiers with Facebook and Google Analytics when users visited the homepage, before they could consent. For users logged into Facebook, identifying information including Facebook ID was also disclosed, compromising anonymity despite PCO's public assurances.
violationSummary: The website design facilitated unauthorized disclosure of personal information (IP addresses, browser characteristics, unique results URLs, and Facebook IDs) to third parties (Facebook and Google Analytics) without meaningful prior consent, in violation of section 8 of the Privacy Act. The disclosure occurred automatically upon page load, before users could make informed decisions about participation.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Privy Council Office operated MyDemocracy.ca, a civic engagement website that automatically disclosed users' IP addresses, browser characteristics.
whyTheyWereWrong: Citizens believed their survey responses about electoral reform were anonymous, but the website's design exposed their IP addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Responses would be anonymous and privacy protection was a core consideration in the website's development.
claimsVsReality.reality: The website automatically disclosed IP addresses, browser characteristics, unique identifiers, and Facebook IDs to third-party services (Facebook and Google Analytics) as soon as users loaded the homepage, before any consent or opt-in action.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information was only collected and disclosed to the PCO in aggregate, anonymized form.
claimsVsReality.reality: Individual user data including unique result URLs, voter archetypes, and identifying information were automatically shared with Facebook servers, and users logged into Facebook had their Facebook IDs disclosed to Facebook.

claimsVsReality.claim: Steps were taken prior to implementation to ensure potential privacy risks were identified and mitigated before launch.
claimsVsReality.reality: The website design allowed third-party tracking components to execute automatically on page load without user action, exposing personal information before participants could even view the survey questions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 8 – Personal information under the control of a government institution shall not be disclosed without consent of the individual, except in accordance with permitted categories
regulatoryFindings.description: PCO disclosed IP addresses, browser characteristics, and MyDemocracy URLs to Facebook when the homepage was loaded, before users could consent
violations: PCO disclosed IP addresses, browser characteristics, and MyDemocracy URLs to Facebook when the homepage was loaded, before users could consent
PCO disclosed unique results URLs and participant archetypes to Facebook when users initiated social sharing, without explicit prior consent
PCO disclosed Facebook ID (identifying information) to Facebook for logged-in users, linking personal information to identifiable individuals
PCO disclosed IP addresses and browsing data to Google Analytics without adequate consent framework
PCO did not obtain meaningful consent at the point of disclosure; Privacy Policy notice came too late (after homepage load)

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act section 3 – Personal information is information about an identifiable individual; identifiable when there is a serious possibility an individual could be identified through that information alone or in combination with other information
regulatoryFindings.description: IP addresses, browser characteristics, and unique results URLs, when combined, constitute personal information capable of identifying individuals (recognized in government policy and academic research showing 75-90% recognition rate for repeat visitors)
violations: IP addresses, browser characteristics, and unique results URLs, when combined, constitute personal information capable of identifying individuals (recognized in government policy and academic research showing 75-90% recognition rate for repeat visitors)
For logged-in Facebook users, Facebook IDs explicitly identify individuals, linking all disclosed information to identifiable persons
Even for non-logged-in users, the combination of IP address and browser characteristics presents serious possibility of individual identification

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Directive on Privacy Impact Assessment – PIAs required for new or modified programs that may impact privacy
regulatoryFindings.description: PCO failed to conduct a Privacy Impact Assessment for the MyDemocracy initiative despite collecting personal data and integrating third-party tracking components
violations: PCO failed to conduct a Privacy Impact Assessment for the MyDemocracy initiative despite collecting personal data and integrating third-party tracking components

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Standard on Privacy and Web Analytics – appropriate privacy safeguards required for web analytics use
regulatoryFindings.description: PCO's use of Google Analytics did not clearly comply with TBS standard requirements for privacy-protective web analytics implementation
violations: PCO's use of Google Analytics did not clearly comply with TBS standard requirements for privacy-protective web analytics implementation

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded. PCO did not meet section 8 requirements of the Privacy Act. The OPC issued four recommendations: (1) conduct Privacy Impact Assessments for future initiatives; (2) ensure third-party component use does not create privacy risks and obtain consent before information sharing; (3) inform individuals of all collection and disclosure purposes at or before collection, presented at key decision points; (4) ensure Web Analytics compliance with TBS standards. PCO acknowledged the findings as a valuable reminder about the need to understand online tools and committed to undertaking PIAs on design and privacy implications of future projects. PCO made certain design modifications during investigation (including delaying Facebook Connect activation until after user action and amending Privacy Policy), but the OPC remained concerned about the initial design approach and noted alternative architectures could have prevented premature disclosure.
companyNow: The Privy Council Office continues to operate as a core government institution supporting Canada's Prime Minister and Cabinet on policy matters. The MyDemocracy.ca initiative has concluded and is no longer operational.
dataType: IP addresses, browser characteristics, web browsing behavior, demographic information (gender, age, education, income, postal code), Facebook ID, unique survey results URL
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) section 8 – unauthorized disclosure of personal information without consent
Privacy Act (Canada) section 3 – definition of personal information (IP addresses and browser characteristics in combination constitute identifiable information)
Treasury Board Directive on Privacy Impact Assessment – failure to conduct PIA
Treasury Board Standard on Privacy and Web Analytics – inadequate compliance

companyDescription: Public Services and Procurement Canada (PSPC) is a federal government department responsible for administering pay and procurement services for over 100 Canadian government departments, agencies, and Crown Corporations serving approximately 290,000 public servants.
companyLongDescription: PSPC manages the centralized pay administration system for the Canadian federal public service. In 2016, it launched the Phoenix pay system, a modernized platform based on PeopleSoft software designed to automate administrative processes and improve pay services delivery. The system integrates with the government's Human Resources Management System and serves diverse user roles including compensation advisors, financial officers, managers, and individual employees across multiple organization types.
caseDescription: Public Services and Procurement Canada's Phoenix pay system contained at least 11 privacy breaches and multiple vulnerabilities that exposed the personal information of approximately 290,000 federal public service employees to unauthorized access. The breaches resulted from inadequate row-level security implementation, custom coding errors, and user input errors that allowed employees in various roles to access personal information beyond their authorized scope. PSPC was aware of privacy vulnerabilities before Phoenix's launch in February 2016 but failed to resolve them, and provided insufficient notification to affected individuals.
