violationSummary: The primary violation involved systemic security failures in the design and maintenance of the Phoenix system, including failure to properly implement row-level security controls, custom coding defects, and inadequate access monitoring. These technical and procedural failures created conditions for unauthorized disclosure of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: PSPC deployed the Phoenix pay system with at least 11 privacy breaches affecting 290,000 federal employees, caused by inadequate row-level security, custom coding errors.
whyTheyWereWrong: Federal employees had their names, pay identification numbers, and salary information exposed to colleagues.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSPC stated the breaches involved only a limited number of departments and only employee names and Personal Record Identifier numbers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The investigation revealed at least 11 breaches affecting most government-wide departments, with exposed data including employee names, PRI numbers, and salary information.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSPC claimed the risk to affected individuals was 'very low' and information was only available to a limited number of federal public servants.
claimsVsReality.reality: Most vulnerabilities were government-wide, meaning personal information of all 290,000 employees in the Phoenix system was at risk to up to 70,000 users in various roles, and for some breaches information could be changed and transactions conducted.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSPC assured the Office that according to its audits, no inappropriate transactions associated with the breaches had taken place.
claimsVsReality.reality: Upon review of audit logs, at least one inappropriate transaction was confirmed (IR 03685524), contradicting PSPC's initial assurances.

claimsVsReality.claim: PSPC took measures to address known vulnerabilities before Phoenix launched.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite pre-launch identification and mitigation attempts, Phoenix had privacy vulnerabilities from the day it launched on February 24, 2016, with persistent vulnerabilities remaining that could lead to future breaches.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 and 8(1) – Personal information can only be disclosed with individual consent or in accordance with permitted categories
regulatoryFindings.description: Unauthorized disclosure of employee names, PRI numbers, and salary information to employees without a 'need to know'
violations: Unauthorized disclosure of employee names, PRI numbers, and salary information to employees without a 'need to know'
Disclosure occurred across 11 documented breach incidents affecting system-wide scope in most cases
No consent obtained from affected individuals prior to disclosure

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Secretariat Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.2.21 – Departments must monitor and document access and use of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: PSPC did not audit or monitor viewing access to personal information held in Phoenix
violations: PSPC did not audit or monitor viewing access to personal information held in Phoenix
PSPC relied on ad hoc user reporting rather than systematic monitoring
PSPC acknowledged it lacked practical solutions to monitor pages viewed by users

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Secretariat Directive on Privacy Practices Section 17 – IT systems must include security audit log functions and automated incident tools
regulatoryFindings.description: PSPC limited use of audit capabilities to specific data items due to performance concerns
violations: PSPC limited use of audit capabilities to specific data items due to performance concerns
Insufficient real-time security incident monitoring and documentation
Response to security incidents managed via email chain rather than formal incident management system

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Secretariat Guidelines for Privacy Breaches – Institutions should notify affected individuals as soon as possible when breaches involve sensitive data or identity theft risks
regulatoryFindings.description: PSPC delayed notification until July 21, 2016, months after vulnerabilities were discovered in February 2016
violations: PSPC delayed notification until July 21, 2016, months after vulnerabilities were discovered in February 2016
Notifications were incomplete and used language suggesting limited scope when vulnerabilities were system-wide
PSPC failed to provide affected employees with sufficient information to assess risk and take protective measures

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the complaints well-founded and issued six recommendations to PSPC: (1) develop and implement controls to monitor and document access to personal information; (2) improve testing procedures to proactively address privacy vulnerabilities; (3) conduct necessary security risk assessments (Privacy Impact Assessment and Threat and Risk Assessment) by April 2018; (4) implement measures to mitigate social engineering risks at the Public Service Pay Centre and Pension Centre; (5) review breach notification practices and provide comprehensive notification of breaches and vulnerabilities to affected individuals; and (6) complete review of all pages with row-level security by June 30, 2017. PSPC agreed to all recommendations on May 15, 2017, with implementation timelines ranging from June 30, 2017 to March 31, 2018. The OPC requested follow-up reporting within 6 months on implementation progress. No monetary penalty was imposed; the enforcement was through compliance orders and monitoring requirements.
companyNow: PSPC continues to operate the Phoenix pay system with ongoing remediation efforts. The department remains responsible for federal government pay administration and procurement services.
dataType: Employee names, Personal Record Identifier (PRI) numbers, salary information, date of birth, home address
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 3 (definition of personal information)
Privacy Act Section 8(1) (unauthorized disclosure without consent)
Treasury Board Secretariat Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.2.21 (monitoring and documenting access)
Treasury Board Secretariat Directive on Privacy Practices Section 17 (security audit log requirements)

companyDescription: Health Canada is the federal department responsible for administering the Non-Insured Health Benefits (NIHB) Program, which provides healthcare coverage to registered First Nations and recognized Inuit residents across Canada.
companyLongDescription: Health Canada's Non-Insured Health Benefits Program is a national healthcare initiative providing medically necessary services—including prescription drugs, dental and vision care, medical supplies, mental health counselling, and transportation to specialized health services—to registered First Nations and recognized Inuit residents in Canada who lack access to private plans or provincial/territorial programs. The program collects personal health information from healthcare providers on behalf of patients to adjudicate claims and coordinate processing with other health programs.
caseDescription: Health Canada's Non-Insured Health Benefits Program collected diagnostic information about First Nations and Inuit patients beyond what was necessary for adjudicating medical transportation and specialist referral claims. The 'Reason for Appointment' field on claim forms resulted in the unintentional over-collection of sensitive health information from physicians. Health Canada acknowledged the issue and removed the problematic field from its forms in October 2016.
violationSummary: Health Canada systematically collected personal health information (diagnostic details) through a prescribed form field beyond what was legitimately required for its stated purpose of administering benefits. This constitutes surveillance-like collection of sensitive personal health data that individuals did not intend to disclose and that was not necessary for the transaction.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Health Canada's Non-Insured Health Benefits Program collected diagnostic information about First Nations.
whyTheyWereWrong: First Nations and Inuit patients were forced to disclose sensitive diagnostic information as a condition for accessing medically necessary travel.

claimsVsReality.claim: The 'Reason for Appointment' field was intended only to establish or confirm core policy requirements for travel approval—specifically that medical services are not available locally and that the referred provider is the nearest available.
claimsVsReality.reality: The field resulted in the unintentional but systematic collection of sensitive diagnostic information from physicians, which was neither necessary for claims adjudication nor legitimately required under NIHB policies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Health Canada's collection of personal information is limited to that which is required for review and processing of claims, with only the minimum information needed to assess benefit needs.
claimsVsReality.reality: Health Canada collected diagnostic details about patients that went beyond transaction-based information necessary for adjudication, violating the principle of minimum necessary collection.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 requires that personal information collected by a government institution must relate directly to an operating program and be demonstrably necessary to achieve a specific and legitimate purpose
regulatoryFindings.description: Health Canada collected diagnostic information through the 'Reason for Appointment' field that was not necessary for adjudicating Non-Insured Health Benefits claims
violations: Health Canada collected diagnostic information through the 'Reason for Appointment' field that was not necessary for adjudicating Non-Insured Health Benefits claims
The collection exceeded what was required for the legitimate purpose of confirming policy requirements (local availability of services and nearest provider)

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 defines personal information broadly as information about identifiable individuals that relates to or concerns that person
regulatoryFindings.description: Diagnostic information collected about patients constitutes personal information under this definition
violations: Diagnostic information collected about patients constitutes personal information under this definition
Health service providers were required to disclose intimate details about patients' medical conditions

regulatoryFindings.act: Treasury Board Directive on Privacy Practices requires collection to be demonstrably necessary and proportionate
regulatoryFindings.description: The 'Reason for Appointment' field created unnecessary collection of detailed diagnostic information beyond the policy requirement to verify local service availability
violations: The 'Reason for Appointment' field created unnecessary collection of detailed diagnostic information beyond the policy requirement to verify local service availability

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. Health Canada removed the 'Reason for Appointment' field from the Non-Insured Health Benefits Medical Transportation and Specialist Referral Form, with NIHB clerks directed not to request diagnostic information as of June 2016 and the new form officially introduced in October 2016. Health Canada was directed to: (1) develop a plan for retention or secure destruction of over-collected information; (2) continue consultations with First Nations and Inuit communities and health service providers to minimize privacy impacts; (3) develop clear guidelines for health service providers specifying what information is required for each form field; and (4) report progress within 6 months.
companyNow: Health Canada continues to administer the NIHB Program and other federal health services. Following this investigation, the department removed the problematic 'Reason for Appointment' field from its claim forms and committed to better privacy protections for First Nations and Inuit communities.
dataType: Health data, diagnostic information, medical history, personal identifiers
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 4 (collection must relate directly to operating program)
Privacy Act Section 3 (definition of personal information)
Treasury Board Directive on Privacy Practices Section 6.2.8 (collection must be demonstrably necessary)

companyDescription: Wajam Internet Technologies Inc. was a Montreal-based software company that developed a social search engine application bundled with other software. The company generated revenue through contextual advertising based on users' search queries.
companyLongDescription: Wajam Internet Technologies Inc., incorporated federally with headquarters in Montreal, developed browser-based software called 'Wajam' and 'Social2Search' that claimed to enhance search results by overlaying content from users' social media networks. The software was distributed primarily through third-party bundlers that packaged it with unrelated free software. The company's primary revenue model relied on displaying contextual advertisements based on captured user search queries and browsing behavior. Prior to 2017, Wajam sold its assets to Hong Kong-based Iron Mountain Technology Limited and ceased Canadian operations.
caseDescription: Wajam developed adware that tracked users' online search queries and displayed targeted ads without meaningful consent. The software was distributed via third-party bundlers with other free software, often using deceptive installation screens and making it difficult for users to uninstall. The company failed to encrypt sensitive personal data, retained user information indefinitely without clear policies, and lacked a privacy accountability framework.
violationSummary: Wajam systematically collected and monitored users' search queries, browsing history, and online behavior through software installed without meaningful consent. The surveillance was the primary business model to serve targeted advertising.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Wajam distributed adware that tracked users' search queries and displayed targeted ads without meaningful consent, bundled deceptively with free software and made difficult to uninstall.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users' search queries and browsing behavior were captured and transmitted to Wajam servers in unencrypted plain text.

claimsVsReality.claim: Social2Search is a social search engine that gives you access to your friends' knowledge and recommendations from Facebook, LinkedIn, Google+, and other major social networks.
claimsVsReality.reality: By 2017, the software could only link to Twitter; Facebook linking was disabled in 2014, LinkedIn in 2013, and Google+ in 2012. The websites contained outdated and inaccurate information for years.

claimsVsReality.claim: The software requires user consent and provides clear, transparent installation and control options.
claimsVsReality.reality: The software was installed silently by third-party distributors, presented confusing or missing consent screens with broken decline buttons, and made uninstallation difficult with malicious ads and fake software redirects.

claimsVsReality.claim: User data is safeguarded and retained according to transparent policies.
claimsVsReality.reality: All raw user data was stored in unencrypted plain text on Wajam's servers and retained indefinitely, even after users uninstalled the software. User identifiers persisted on devices post-uninstallation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4 – Accountability: Organizations must implement policies and procedures to protect personal information, establish complaint procedures, train staff, and develop information about their policies.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent had no demonstrable privacy management framework
violations: Respondent had no demonstrable privacy management framework
Unable to provide evidence of written policies and procedures for protecting personal information
No documentation of privacy training provided to employees
No overall data retention and destruction policy or procedures in place

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 and 4.3.2 – Consent: Organizations must obtain knowledge and consent of individuals for collection, use, and disclosure of personal information. Consent must be meaningful and individuals must understand the nature, purpose, and consequences.
regulatoryFindings.description: Software installed through bundling with free software without meaningful consent
violations: Software installed through bundling with free software without meaningful consent
Consent screens displayed by third-party distributors were unclear, confusing, and sometimes presented outdated information
Evidence of silent installations by distributors despite Distribution Agreement prohibitions
Multiple-offer consent screens designed to bias toward installation rather than informed choice
Pre-checked boxes and greyed-out decline options in installation screens

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.5 – Consent Without Deception: Consent should not be obtained through deception.
regulatoryFindings.description: Websites claimed software could link to Google+, Facebook, LinkedIn, and Twitter when these integrations had ceased years earlier
violations: Websites claimed software could link to Google+, Facebook, LinkedIn, and Twitter when these integrations had ceased years earlier
Privacy Policy claimed use of 'modern cryptography' for data transmission and storage when data was actually transmitted unencrypted
Privacy Policy misleadingly stated data retention was limited when raw user data was retained indefinitely
Certain information was mislabeled as 'Non-Personal Information' despite being linked to specific users

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.8 – Withdrawal of Consent: Individuals may withdraw consent at any time. Organizations must inform individuals of implications of withdrawal.
regulatoryFindings.description: Uninstallation process did not fully function for many users despite stated availability
violations: Uninstallation process did not fully function for many users despite stated availability
Software code remnants remained in browser cache after uninstallation, continuing to collect data
Unique user identifiers were not deleted from users' computers after uninstallation
Uninstallation landing page served unsolicited ads and potentially unwanted programs, creating barriers to withdrawal

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5 and 4.5.2 – Retention and Destruction: Personal information shall be retained only as long as necessary. Organizations must develop guidelines and implement procedures for retention with minimum and maximum retention periods.
regulatoryFindings.description: Primary database containing 400 terabytes of raw user data retained indefinitely even after users uninstalled software
violations: Primary database containing 400 terabytes of raw user data retained indefinitely even after users uninstalled software
No overall data retention and destruction policy or procedures in place
Retention of user information for indefinite period to prevent fraudulent repeat payments was excessive and unreasonable for stated purpose
Privacy Policy did not explain purposes for retaining user data after uninstallation or deletion timelines

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1, 4.7.2, 4.7.3 – Safeguards: Organizations must protect personal information against unauthorized access, disclosure, use, or modification. Safeguards must be appropriate to the sensitivity of information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Initial collection and transmission of user information occurred in unencrypted format despite being linked to individual users
violations: Initial collection and transmission of user information occurred in unencrypted format despite being linked to individual users
User search keyword queries transmitted unencrypted and stored unencrypted despite potential sensitivity
Primary database containing hundreds of terabytes of personal information remained unencrypted throughout investigation
Lack of accountability framework meant inadequate monitoring and protection of website integrity against malicious code

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the respondent contravened multiple PIPEDA principles regarding accountability, consent, retention, and safeguards. The respondent agreed to cease operations in Canada and sell its assets to Hong Kong-based company Iron Mountain Technology Limited (IMTL). The respondent committed to stop collecting personal information from Canadian users and to securely destroy all Canadian user data held on its hard drives. The preliminary report issued 12 recommendations including establishing a privacy accountability framework, ceasing use of third-party bundled distributors, amending misleading website and privacy policy content, fixing uninstallation bugs, implementing encryption, and obtaining explicit consent from affected users or ceasing collection. The respondent stated it could not comply with recommendations due to asset transfer, but agreed to destruction of records.
companyNow: Wajam ceased operations in Canada in 2017 after selling its assets to Iron Mountain Technology Limited. The company agreed to destruction of all user data in its possession.
dataType: Search queries, browsing history, IP addresses, device identifiers, geolocation, unique user identifiers, social media account information

companyDescription: A Canadian property history report provider that sold online reports to home buyers, sellers, real estate agents, and home inspectors containing information about residential properties.
companyLongDescription: An Ontario-based corporation operating online that compiled and sold property history reports across Canada. The company offered two principal report types (Essential and Comprehensive) containing information such as sales history, drug activity linked to addresses, insurance claims, building permits, and construction dates. The company marketed its reports as tools to protect consumers with legal disclosure and due diligence information, positioning itself similarly to vehicle history report providers.
caseDescription: A property history report company collected and disclosed drug activity information (police records of marijuana grow operations and methamphetamine labs) linked to residential properties without obtaining consent from current or past owners and occupants. The company claimed this information was publicly available and not personal information, but the Privacy Commissioner determined drug activity data constitutes personal information about identifiable individuals and does not fall within the publicly available information exemption under PIPEDA.
violationSummary: The company disclosed personal information (drug activity linked to identifiable individuals via property ownership/occupancy records) without consent, and mischaracterized the data as non-personal and publicly available to avoid consent requirements.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The company collected and disclosed drug activity information (police records of marijuana grow operations.
whyTheyWereWrong: People's names could be linked to drug activity records through property ownership registries, creating a false perception or assumption that they were personally involved in illegal drug.

claimsVsReality.claim: Drug activity information is restricted to data about the property and does not include identifiable personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Drug activity data could be directly linked to identifiable individuals (current and past owners/occupants) through provincial land registries and online databases, creating risk of reputational harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: Drug activity information falls within publicly available information under PIPEDA regulations because it comes from police records accessible via access-to-information requests and police websites.
claimsVsReality.reality: Police records obtained via access-to-information requests and police websites do not constitute any of the specified categories of publicly available information under the Regulations (telephone directories, professional directories, statutory registries with public access rights, judicial records, or publications where individuals provided the information).

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's business model is equivalent to vehicle history reports and provides necessary consumer protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: Unlike vehicle history reports, drug activity information about properties inherently links to specific individuals and creates significant reputational risk by implying personal involvement in illegal activity, requiring explicit individual consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA s. 2(1) and Schedule 1 Principle 4.3 – Organizations must obtain knowledge and consent for collection, use and disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent collected drug activity information without consent from affected individuals
violations: Respondent collected drug activity information without consent from affected individuals
Respondent used and disclosed drug activity information in property history reports without consent
Respondent failed to obtain meaningful consent with clear explanation of purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA s. 7(1)(d), 7(2)(c.1), 7(3)(h.1) and Regulations Specifying Publicly Available Information – Exemption applies only to information in specified publicly available sources (directories, registries, judicial records, publications)
regulatoryFindings.description: Drug activity information from police services and access to information requests does not constitute a specified publicly available source
violations: Drug activity information from police services and access to information requests does not constitute a specified publicly available source
Information on police websites does not qualify as a statutory registry, judicial record, or publication under the Regulations
Respondent misclassified drug activity information as falling within the publicly available exemption

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA s. 2(1) – Personal information is information about an identifiable individual
regulatoryFindings.description: Drug activity information could be linked to identifiable individuals (property owners/occupants) through provincial land registries and online databases
violations: Drug activity information could be linked to identifiable individuals (property owners/occupants) through provincial land registries and online databases
Information raises significant possibility that identified individual was involved in or associated with drug activity, making it 'about' that individual

outcome: The respondent committed to cease inclusion of drug activity information in its property history reports. The respondent halted distribution of reports pending compliance. The Privacy Commissioner accepted these commitments as resolving the complaint. The respondent also clarified that insurance claims information (limited to structural damage where payment went to contractors, not claimants) does not constitute personal information and does not require consent.
dataType: Drug activity records, sales history, insurance claims, property ownership information, occupancy information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA s. 2(1) – Definition of personal information
PIPEDA s. 7(1)(d), 7(2)(c.1), 7(3)(h.1) – Consent requirement for collection, use and disclosure
PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.3 – Knowledge and consent requirement
PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.3.2 – Meaningful consent requirement
Regulations Specifying Publicly Available Information s. 1 – Exemption for publicly available information

companyDescription: A FinTech organization providing online digital financial services and investment account management to Canadian clients.
companyLongDescription: An early-stage financial technology company operating in Canada that offered investment account management services through a digital platform. The company collected personal information from website visitors before allowing them to review account terms, citing regulatory requirements as justification. The organization was subject to PIPEDA privacy obligations and engaged with the OPC's early resolution process.
caseDescription: A FinTech company required prospective clients to provide personal information, including sensitive data, before they could review the company's investment account management agreement and terms. The complainant was unable to review the agreement first to make an informed decision about opening an account. The company incorrectly cited regulatory requirements as justification for collecting information from non-clients.
violationSummary: The company collected personal information without obtaining valid, informed consent. The complainant was required to disclose sensitive personal data before understanding the privacy implications or terms of service, preventing meaningful consent and violating PIPEDA's requirement to identify collection purposes at or before the time of collection.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The FinTech company required prospective clients to provide personal information, including sensitive data, before they could access.
whyTheyWereWrong: Prospective clients were unable to make informed decisions about whether to open an account because they had to disclose personal information before reviewing the terms.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company cited 'regulatory requirements' as justification for collecting personal information from non-clients before they could view the account agreement.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regulatory requirements for personal information collection only apply once an individual becomes a client, not during the prospect stage when reviewing terms.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information must be collected before prospects can access the investment account management agreement.
claimsVsReality.reality: Prospective clients must be able to review the management agreement without providing personal information first to enable informed decision-making and valid consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.2.1 — An organization shall identify the purposes for which personal information is collected at or before the time of collection.
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization did not clearly identify collection purposes before requiring disclosure of personal information from prospective clients
violations: Organization did not clearly identify collection purposes before requiring disclosure of personal information from prospective clients
Prospective clients could not review the management agreement (which would detail purposes) without first providing personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 3.2 — An organization shall obtain an individual's consent before or at the time of collecting, using or disclosing personal information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent was not meaningful or informed — individuals could not review terms before deciding whether to proceed
violations: Consent was not meaningful or informed — individuals could not review terms before deciding whether to proceed
Collection of sensitive personal information from non-clients without valid legal basis (regulatory requirements apply only to clients)

outcome: The organization agreed to revise its website and Privacy Policy to allow prospective clients to review the management agreement and terms of conditions without first providing personal information. This enables individuals to make informed decisions about whether to proceed and to understand the privacy implications before disclosing sensitive data. The complainant was satisfied with the early resolution outcome.
dataType: Financial information, investment account details, sensitive personal information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 3.2 (consent requirement — informed and voluntary)
PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.2.1 (purposes must be identified at or before time of collection)

companyDescription: A Canadian auto insurance company that collects personal information including credit scores from policyholders during the claims process.
companyLongDescription: The insurance company operates in Canada under PIPEDA jurisdiction and collects credit score information from accident benefit claimants as part of its standard claims assessment procedure. The company maintained that credit score collection was routine and voluntary, conducted through scripted telephone interviews by claims advisors. However, the company failed to demonstrate legal authority or direct business necessity for this practice and did not clearly communicate that consent was optional.
caseDescription: An insurance company collected and used consumers' credit scores during auto insurance claims assessment without meaningful consent and without clearly disclosing that providing consent was optional. The company failed to demonstrate that credit score collection was appropriate for fraud detection purposes during claims assessment, contrary to privacy law requirements.
violationSummary: The company conducted systematic collection of credit scores from all claimants during the claims assessment process without adequately informing them the practice was optional. This constitutes surveillance of financial information during a claims process where it was not legally authorized or appropriately disclosed.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: An insurance company collected and used consumers' credit scores during auto insurance claims assessment without obtaining truly informed consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Claimants were pressured into providing credit scores during aggressive telephone interviews without understanding the practice was optional.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consent to collect credit scores is voluntary and clearly communicated as optional through scripted telephone questions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's telephone script did not clearly indicate consent was optional, and claimants felt pressured to consent during aggressive interviews to 'maintain peace' rather than understanding they could refuse.

claimsVsReality.claim: Obtaining credit scores helps detect and prevent fraud, which controls costs and keeps insurance premiums low.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company could not demonstrate to regulators that it had legal authority under Ontario's Consumer Reporting Act to collect credit scores for fraud detection during claims assessment, nor could it show such scores are effective for this purpose.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's privacy notifications adequately explain the purposes for collecting credit score information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's notifications used vague language ('to offer you insurance products and service that best meet your needs') that did not specifically help individuals understand how credit score data would be used in claims assessment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Claims would be handled the same way regardless of whether claimants provide consent to credit score collection.
claimsVsReality.reality: Claims without credit score consent were actually handled differently than those with consent, but employee scripts provided inaccurate information about this distinction.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 — Organizations must make reasonable effort to advise individuals of purposes and ensure consent is meaningful by stating purposes clearly
regulatoryFindings.description: Advisor script marked '(Mandatory)' gave appearance that consent was required, not optional
violations: Advisor script marked '(Mandatory)' gave appearance that consent was required, not optional
Failed to clearly advise consumers that providing consent was voluntary

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Subsection 5(3) — Organizations may only collect personal information for purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection of credit scores for fraud detection during claims assessment is not appropriate — company failed to demonstrate 'direct business need' under Ontario Consumer Reporting Act
violations: Collection of credit scores for fraud detection during claims assessment is not appropriate — company failed to demonstrate 'direct business need' under Ontario Consumer Reporting Act
Company could not prove credit scores are necessary or effective for fraud detection in claims assessment

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.8.1 — Organizations must be open about policies and practices; individuals must be able to acquire information without unreasonable effort
regulatoryFindings.description: Privacy notifications did not specify types of information obtained from credit reporting agencies
violations: Privacy notifications did not specify types of information obtained from credit reporting agencies
Purposes stated too vaguely ('offer products that best meet your needs' instead of specific fraud detection purpose)
Script incorrectly told clients refusing consent their claim would be handled same as others when this was false

outcome: Matter found well-founded and conditionally resolved. Insurance company agreed to: (1) cease collecting and using credit scores for auto insurance claims assessment effective end of April 2017; (2) conduct comprehensive review of credit score collection for other insurance types and purposes by end of June 2017 (or December 2017 if major system changes required); (3) ensure compliance with recommendations regarding notification, voluntariness disclosure, and consequences explanation. Office confirmed satisfaction with proposed changes.
companyNow: Following the 2017 PIPEDA enforcement action, the company agreed to cease collecting credit scores for accident benefit claim assessments by April 2017 and to review and remediate its credit score collection practices across all insurance types by June-December 2017.
dataType: Credit score, credit file, financial information

companyDescription: A commercial insurance company that provides coverage for retail stores and other businesses. The company processes insurance claims and maintains detailed documentation related to incidents.
companyLongDescription: This is a commercial insurance provider serving retail and other business sectors in Canada. The company handles insurance claims, conducts investigations, and maintains case files including incident documentation, video evidence, and internal case management notes. Like most insurers, it manages sensitive information involving multiple parties including claimants, witnesses, and employees.
caseDescription: An insurance company refused to provide an individual with access to personal information held in her insurance claim file, including case management notes and incident video, claiming confidentiality and third-party privacy concerns. Through early resolution, the company agreed to allow the individual to view the video and provided redacted case management notes that removed confidential commercial information and third-party personal data.
violationSummary: The company improperly excluded the individual from access to their own personal information by refusing to provide or allow access to records, failing to explore alternative solutions such as redaction or in-person viewing that would balance privacy concerns with access rights.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The insurance company initially refused to provide an individual with access to her personal information from an insurance claim file, including case management notes.
whyTheyWereWrong: By refusing access to the video and complete case management notes, the insurance company prevented an injured claimant from understanding the full details of her own incident.

claimsVsReality.claim: Case management notes are confidential internal documents that cannot be released to claimants.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under PIPEDA, case management notes must be provided to the individual, with only truly confidential commercial information and third-party personal data redacted; the individual is entitled to access information about their own claim.

claimsVsReality.claim: The video cannot be provided because it contains images of store employees and customers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The video could be made accessible to the claimant through viewing (without providing a copy) or by redacting identifiable information of third parties; the presence of third-party images does not justify complete denial of access.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to provide individuals access to their personal information, subject only to specific exemptions including confidential commercial information and third-party personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Insurance company refused to provide access to case management notes citing confidentiality without exploring redaction alternatives
violations: Insurance company refused to provide access to case management notes citing confidentiality without exploring redaction alternatives
Insurance company refused to provide video access citing presence of third-party images without offering alternative access methods like supervised viewing

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA exemptions for confidential commercial information and third-party data must be applied narrowly, and organizations must sever or redact exempt portions to provide maximum access to the individual's own personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to consider redaction or alternative solutions to balance competing privacy interests
violations: Company failed to consider redaction or alternative solutions to balance competing privacy interests

outcome: The complaint was early resolved through alternative solutions negotiated with the Early Resolution Officer. The insurance company agreed to allow the individual to view the incident video in person at a neutral location with transportation assistance. The company also provided a redacted copy of case management notes with confidential commercial information and third-party personal data removed. The organization received guidance on proper procedures for providing access to personal information while protecting exempted content.
dataType: Personal injury claim information, incident video, case management notes, third-party personal information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Section 9(3)(b) - confidential commercial information exemption
PIPEDA - access to personal information obligation

companyDescription: A Canadian financial institution operating as an online bank providing savings accounts and banking services to customers.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian online bank that offers savings accounts and related banking services without face-to-face customer contact. The institution was found to have unlawfully required customers to consent to sharing their Social Insurance Numbers with credit reporting agencies for identity verification purposes. While the company justified this practice as beneficial for maintaining data integrity, the OPC determined this practice violated PIPEDA principles and ordered the institution to make SIN use optional.
caseDescription: A financial institution required customers to provide their Social Insurance Number (SIN) to credit reporting agencies for identity verification as a mandatory condition of opening a savings account. The institution unlawfully conditioned service on consent to this practice, despite SIN being required only for income reporting obligations. The OPC found this violated PIPEDA Principle 4.3.3 and ordered the institution to make SIN use for identity verification optional rather than mandatory.
violationSummary: The financial institution used SIN beyond its legally required purpose (income reporting) for secondary purposes (identity verification with credit agencies) and made this secondary use a mandatory condition of service, violating the principle that organizations must limit collection and use of personal information to necessary purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The financial institution required customers to provide their Social Insurance Number (SIN) to credit reporting agencies for identity verification as a mandatory condition of opening a savings.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers were forced to share their SIN with third-party credit reporting agencies against their wishes, exposing sensitive personal identifiers to unnecessary entities.

claimsVsReality.claim: Using SIN for identity verification helps maintain the integrity and accuracy of customer personal information and is appropriate for online banking.
claimsVsReality.reality: SINs are only legally required for income reporting purposes; they are not necessary for identity verification and government guidance documents do not recommend or require their use for this purpose.

claimsVsReality.claim: FINTRAC guidelines and Government of Canada standards support requiring SIN use for identity verification in online banking.
claimsVsReality.reality: FINTRAC guidelines on identity verification methods and ESDC's SIN protection guidance make no requirement for or suggestion of using individual SINs for identity verification purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.3.3 requires that organizations limit the collection and use of personal information to purposes that are appropriate and necessary, and that individuals cannot be required to consent to inappropriate uses as a condition of service.
regulatoryFindings.description: Financial institution required SIN disclosure to credit reporting agencies for identity verification purposes as a mandatory condition of service
violations: Financial institution required SIN disclosure to credit reporting agencies for identity verification purposes as a mandatory condition of service
SIN use for identity verification was not legally required and went beyond the necessary purpose of income reporting
Institution did not allow customers to opt out of this secondary use while still accessing banking services

outcome: The OPC found the matter well-founded and conditionally resolved. The financial institution agreed to make SIN use for identity verification optional rather than a mandatory condition of service, and to implement changes to its online application process and privacy communications by February 15, 2018. Follow-up confirmation in March 2018 verified full compliance with the recommendations.
dataType: Social Insurance Number (SIN), financial/identity verification data

companyDescription: A Canadian automobile insurance company that collects and maintains customer personal information for underwriting and insurance history purposes.
companyLongDescription: An automobile insurance provider operating in Canada under PIPEDA jurisdiction. The company collected customer information through standard insurance application forms and retained personal data to share insurance history with other insurers evaluating customers' future applications. The company failed to properly document and manage its disclosures of personal information to third-party databases, lacking clear policies on data sharing practices.
caseDescription: An insurance company refused to delete a customer's personal information after the customer withdrew consent, citing retention for insurance history purposes. The company was found to have violated PIPEDA by failing to respect the withdrawal of consent for continued use of personal data, though it was not required to delete information from third-party databases to which it had lawfully disclosed the data.
violationSummary: The company violated the individual's right to withdraw consent and have their information deleted from the company's own records. This represents a failure to respect data subject control and exclusion rights under PIPEDA.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: The insurance company refused to delete a customer's personal information after the customer withdrew consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: By refusing to delete the customer's data after consent withdrawal, the company prevented the individual from controlling their own personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company must retain the customer's personal information to provide insurance history to other insurers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no legal requirement to retain the information; it chose to do so for competitive advantage in the insurance market.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company cannot delete personal information from third-party databases to which it has disclosed data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under PIPEDA, the company is not required to delete from third-party records, but it should have removed the data from its own records upon consent withdrawal regardless of third-party copies.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had clear policies and procedures for tracking personal information disclosures to third parties.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked readily available documentation explaining its disclosure practices, requiring it to develop new tracking procedures following the investigation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1 – Individual's right to withdraw consent for collection, use and disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Company refused to treat deletion request as withdrawal of consent
violations: Company refused to treat deletion request as withdrawal of consent
Company continued use of personal information without valid consent after individual's withdrawal request

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4(d) – Organization must develop information explaining policies and procedures for disclosure to third parties
regulatoryFindings.description: Company lacked readily available explanation or clear understanding of its disclosure of personal information to third-party organizations
violations: Company lacked readily available explanation or clear understanding of its disclosure of personal information to third-party organizations
Company could not readily explain why and to whom personal information was being disclosed

outcome: The complaint was partially upheld. The company was required to delete the individual's personal information from its own records following the withdrawal of consent, though it was not required to demand deletion from third-party databases where information had been lawfully disclosed. The company was also required to develop and implement improved documentation and policies explaining its disclosure practices to third parties, which it subsequently provided to the Office.
dataType: Insurance history, personal information (name, contact details, driving/insurance records)
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4(d) (Accountability – documentation and explanation of disclosure)

companyDescription: Public Executions Inc. operated publicexecutions.ca, a for-profit online database that allowed judgment creditors to post details about debtors for a fee, including personal information like addresses and photographs, to increase collection pressure through public exposure.
companyLongDescription: Public Executions Inc. ran a commercial website called publicexecutions.ca dedicated to publishing personal information about judgment debtors without their consent. The platform allowed creditors to post court judgment details, debtors' names, addresses, photographs, and other personal information for a fee, with the explicit goal of shaming debtors into paying through public humiliation and reputational damage. The website featured a searchable database and Canada-wide map of debtors, with entries appearing prominently in Google search results. The company did not verify the accuracy of posted information and allowed creditors to offer rewards for 'tips' about debtors' assets.
caseDescription: Public Executions Inc. operated publicexecutions.ca, a website that published personal information about judgment debtors without consent, charging creditors a fee to post details including names, addresses, and photographs to shame debtors into paying court-ordered debts. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada found this violated PIPEDA's requirement that personal information collection and disclosure be appropriate, and initiated Federal Court proceedings; the operator subsequently took down the website.
violationSummary: The company publicly exposed sensitive personal information (names, addresses, photographs, financial details) about individuals to the world at large via the internet and search engines for coercive and commercial purposes, causing reputational and other harms.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Public Executions Inc. operated a website that published judgment debtors' personal information including names, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: The public shaming and exposure of debtors' personal information caused real harm to people—one debtor reported that publication of his home address.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website complies with all Canadian law regarding privacy and operates under PIPEDA section 7 which permits disclosure of personal information for debt collection purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found that PIPEDA does not permit indiscriminate disclosure to the world at large; section 7(3)(b) only allows disclosure to debt collection agencies and legal mechanisms, not public posting for commercial gain and coercion.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website is a journalistic platform exempt from PIPEDA consent requirements because it is not a vendor-consumer relationship.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OPC determined PIPEDA clearly applies because the website engages in commercial activity by collecting fees from creditors, and the content is not journalistic—it simply republishes information provided by others without original production.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website merely offers a neutral platform where creditors post facts; the respondent is not collecting or disclosing personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The respondent actively solicits, organizes, makes searchable, and profits from the disclosure of personal information, and the information appears prominently in Google search results, creating widespread public exposure.

claimsVsReality.claim: A reasonable person would consider it appropriate to publicize debtors' failure to pay broadly for financial gain and to coerce payment.
claimsVsReality.reality: The OPC found that a reasonable person would not consider such public shaming appropriate, especially given strict regulations on consumer reporting agencies and collection agencies that prohibit such practices.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website serves the public interest by promoting access to justice and correcting legal system failings in debt enforcement.
claimsVsReality.reality: The website caused documented harm to debtors—including physical safety risks to families—and operated in direct violation of Ontario's Consumer Reporting Act after being ordered to register as a consumer reporting agency.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA s. 4(1)(a) - Application to commercial activities
regulatoryFindings.description: Company collected fees from creditors to post debtor information, constituting commercial activity subject to PIPEDA
violations: Company collected fees from creditors to post debtor information, constituting commercial activity subject to PIPEDA

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA s. 5(3) - Appropriateness of purpose
regulatoryFindings.description: Publishing debtor personal information for coercion and financial gain is not appropriate; violates spirit of regulated debt collection and consumer reporting agency restrictions
violations: Publishing debtor personal information for coercion and financial gain is not appropriate; violates spirit of regulated debt collection and consumer reporting agency restrictions
Disclosed sensitive information (addresses, photographs, family details) broadly to world via search engines without consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA s. 4(2)(c) - Journalistic exemption
regulatoryFindings.description: Website does not qualify as journalism: lacks original production, serves coercive rather than informational purpose, lacks accurate fact-checking discipline
violations: Website does not qualify as journalism: lacks original production, serves coercive rather than informational purpose, lacks accurate fact-checking discipline

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA s. 7(3)(b) - Debt collection disclosure exemption
regulatoryFindings.description: Exemption does not permit indiscriminate disclosure to world at large; applies only to lawful debt collection mechanisms
violations: Exemption does not permit indiscriminate disclosure to world at large; applies only to lawful debt collection mechanisms

regulatoryFindings.act: Ontario Consumer Reporting Act
regulatoryFindings.description: Operated as unregistered consumer reporting agency; disclosed credit information to world at large contrary to restrictions limiting disclosure to specified circumstances
violations: Operated as unregistered consumer reporting agency; disclosed credit information to world at large contrary to restrictions limiting disclosure to specified circumstances

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found the complaints well-founded. Initial recommendations to delete all debtor information from the website and remove from search engine caches were refused by the operator. The OPC initiated legal proceedings in Federal Court on November 16, 2017. The website operator subsequently took down the website and advised the OPC of no current plans to reinstate it. The OPC discontinued its Federal Court application on December 22, 2017, but reserved the right to reinstitute or commence new proceedings should the website reappear, and indicated ongoing monitoring.
companyNow: The website was taken down in December 2017 after the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada initiated Federal Court proceedings, and the operator indicated no plans to reinstate it.
dataType: Name, address, date of birth, occupation, photograph, financial information (debt amounts), business information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA s. 7(3)(b) - Misapplication of debt collection exemption
Ontario Collection and Debt Settlement Services Act

companyDescription: A Canadian bank that conducted unauthorized credit inquiries on former customers through its marketing department.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian financial institution that engaged in a practice of performing soft credit inquiries on customers' credit files even after their business relationships had terminated. The bank's marketing department continued to monitor the credit profiles of closed accounts without explicit ongoing consent. After investigation, the bank acknowledged the practice violated privacy principles and agreed to update its policies to prohibit post-relationship credit checks.
caseDescription: A bank performed approximately 15 credit inquiries on a former customer without her consent over several years after her business relationship with the bank had ended. The customer discovered the unauthorized checks when reviewing her credit report and filed a complaint. The bank agreed to cease the practice and update its privacy policy to prohibit credit checks after relationship termination.
violationSummary: The bank continued to collect and use credit information for purposes beyond the original transaction (marketing) after the business relationship ended, without adequate legal basis or fresh consent for the secondary use.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The bank performed approximately 15 credit inquiries on a former customer without her consent over several years after she had terminated her business relationship with the institution.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's sensitive credit information was accessed repeatedly without authorization after the business relationship ended, exposing her to unauthorized monitoring.

claimsVsReality.claim: The credit inquiries were 'soft hits' with no impact on the customer's credit rating.
claimsVsReality.reality: Even soft inquiries constitute unauthorized collection and use of sensitive personal information without consent, violating the customer's privacy rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank's privacy policy authorized credit checks upon service registration and retention of the ability to perform inquiries after service ending.
claimsVsReality.reality: The policy language did not constitute valid consent for continued inquiries years after the relationship terminated, especially when the services were never even activated.

claimsVsReality.claim: The inquiries originated from the bank's marketing group.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank's internal investigation revealed the marketing department was not the actual source, indicating internal communication failures and lack of proper oversight.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires that organizations obtain meaningful consent before collecting, using or disclosing personal information, and consent must be informed and voluntary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank performed soft credit inquiries without valid consent after the business relationship ended
violations: Bank performed soft credit inquiries without valid consent after the business relationship ended
Bank did not obtain fresh consent for the secondary use of credit information for marketing purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5 requires that organizations limit collection, use, disclosure and retention of personal information to purposes that are appropriate.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank retained and continued to use credit information after the business relationship ended without a legal requirement to do so
violations: Bank retained and continued to use credit information after the business relationship ended without a legal requirement to do so
Bank collected sensitive credit data for marketing purposes after services were closed and never activated

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.4 requires that organizations make reasonable efforts to ensure that personal information is accurate, complete and up-to-date.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank did not provide complete and accurate information to the individual about why credit checks were being performed or the consent basis for them
violations: Bank did not provide complete and accurate information to the individual about why credit checks were being performed or the consent basis for them

outcome: The bank agreed to cease performing credit inquiries on former customers after the termination of their business relationship and updated its privacy policy accordingly. The bank confirmed the practice ended and the policy was updated. The complainant was satisfied with the resolution.
dataType: Credit information, financial data, credit history

companyDescription: A commercial airline operating international flights and subject to Canadian privacy law (PIPEDA).
companyLongDescription: A commercial airline that operates passenger transportation services, including international flights. The airline is subject to the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA), Canada's federal private sector privacy law. In this case, the airline denied a passenger boarding based on immigration documentation requirements and subsequently withheld records about the incident when the passenger requested access to his personal information.
caseDescription: A traveler denied boarding due to lack of appropriate documentation requested access to all documents, notes, and correspondence relating to the incident. The airline refused to provide certain documents and correspondence with third parties, citing exemptions under PIPEDA for collection and disclosure without consent when investigating potential breaches of immigration law.
violationSummary: The complainant alleged the airline improperly excluded him from access to his personal information by refusing to disclose documents and correspondence exchanged with third parties, thereby denying him the right to be informed of the use and disclosure of his personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The airline refused to provide a passenger with documents, notes, and correspondence relating to his denied boarding, citing PIPEDA exemptions for law enforcement investigations.
whyTheyWereWrong: The passenger was denied complete transparency about why he was refused boarding and what information the airline held about him.

claimsVsReality.claim: The airline claimed it needed to collect and withhold the passenger's information without consent to investigate potential breaches of Canadian immigration law.
claimsVsReality.reality: The airline withheld documents, notes and correspondence that would have provided the passenger transparency about why he was denied boarding, preventing him from understanding or contesting the decision.

claimsVsReality.claim: The airline stated that disclosing the information to the passenger would compromise the investigation into the passenger's travel status and immigration compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The government institution itself refused to release the information; the airline used this third-party refusal as justification for complete non-disclosure to the passenger.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 — Knowledge and consent of individuals are required for collection, use, or disclosure of personal information except where inappropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: The airline collected personal information without the complainant's knowledge or consent
violations: The airline collected personal information without the complainant's knowledge or consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Paragraph 7(1)(b) — Organizations may collect personal information without consent if reasonable to expect that collection with consent would compromise accuracy and collection is reasonable for investigating breach of agreement or contravention of law
regulatoryFindings.description: The airline invoked exemption to collect information to investigate potential non-compliance with Immigration and Refugee Protection Act
violations: The airline invoked exemption to collect information to investigate potential non-compliance with Immigration and Refugee Protection Act

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 — Individuals have right of access to personal information and right to be informed of existence, use and disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: The airline refused to provide access to documents, notes, and correspondence with third parties relating to the denied boarding
violations: The airline refused to provide access to documents, notes, and correspondence with third parties relating to the denied boarding

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Subsections 9(2.1) to 9(2.4) — Scheme protecting integrity of lawful investigations where disclosure to government institutions occurs; organization must request government institution's objection
regulatoryFindings.description: The airline properly followed the scheme by seeking government institution's permission before disclosure; government refused release of information
violations: The airline properly followed the scheme by seeking government institution's permission before disclosure; government refused release of information

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner concluded that both the collection and disclosure complaints were not well-founded. The airline was permitted under PIPEDA exemptions to collect the complainant's personal information without his knowledge or consent under paragraph 7(1)(b) because the collection was reasonable for investigating potential non-compliance with the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act. The disclosure to the government institution was also permitted under subparagraph 7(3)(c.1)(ii). The airline properly followed the mandatory scheme under subsections 9(2.1) to 9(2.4) by requesting the government institution's permission before disclosing information; since the government institution objected, the airline was not required to provide the complainant with access to the disclosed information.
dataType: Passenger Name Record (PNR), identification, passport details, travel documentation
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Paragraph 7(1)(b) (Collection without Knowledge or Consent)
PIPEDA Subparagraph 7(3)(c.1)(ii) (Disclosure without Knowledge or Consent)

companyDescription: Jet Airways was an Indian airline based in Mumbai that operated passenger flights to and from Canada and other international destinations.
companyLongDescription: Jet Airways was a full-service airline headquartered in Mumbai, India, that operated scheduled passenger flights across India and internationally, including routes to and from Canada. The airline was registered as an extra-provincial company in British Columbia. It provided standard airline services including passenger bookings, in-flight services, and customer relations support.
caseDescription: Jet Airways failed to respond to a disabled passenger's access request within the statutory 30-day timeframe under PIPEDA and improperly withheld personal information relating to a service dog incident using overbroad claims of solicitor-client and litigation privilege. The airline refused to provide incident documents, internal notes, and correspondence despite the complainant's legal right to access her personal information.
violationSummary: The airline wrongfully excluded the complainant from access to her personal information by invoking blanket privilege claims and failing to respond within prescribed timeframes, preventing her from obtaining records about an incident affecting her fundamental rights.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Jet Airways failed to respond to a disabled passenger's access request within the statutory 30-day timeframe and then improperly withheld incident documents.
whyTheyWereWrong: A disabled passenger and her companion were illegally removed from a flight after refusing to muzzle their service dogs, then denied access to records of what happened to them.

claimsVsReality.claim: Jet Airways claimed that all documents related to the incident were protected by solicitor-client privilege and litigation privilege because the matter could potentially result in legal proceedings.
claimsVsReality.reality: The documents were created immediately after the incident as part of normal incident handling and guest relations procedures, not as part of communications with or advice from legal counsel. The airline only involved its legal department after the passenger's compensation demand and threat of regulatory complaints.

claimsVsReality.claim: Jet Airways claimed that it had a policy to treat every incident with the assumption that litigation could occur and to immediately transfer such documents to counsel as privileged.
claimsVsReality.reality: When our Office reviewed the respondent's policy, there was no such documented policy, and the respondent could not produce written evidence of this procedure. The respondent later admitted it did not explicitly label documents as privileged in its communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: Jet Airways claimed that the documents were part of a formal dispute resolution process under paragraph 9(3)(d) of PIPEDA and therefore exempt from disclosure.
claimsVsReality.reality: The documents at issue were generated on or around the date of the incident, before any formal dispute resolution process had begun. Internal email exchanges between guest relations and airport teams about an incident do not constitute a formal dispute resolution process.

claimsVsReality.claim: Jet Airways claimed it could not respond to the access request within 30 days because a staff member was on medical leave and because it believed the information was confidential and privileged.
claimsVsReality.reality: The airline never notified the passenger of any extension within the 30-day period, as required by law. The medical leave explanation was only provided after the Office issued its preliminary report. PIPEDA requires a timely response regardless of internal staffing or anticipated litigation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Subsection 8(3) – Organization must respond to access requests with due diligence, no later than 30 days after receipt
regulatoryFindings.description: Jet Airways failed to respond to the complainant's access request within the 30-day statutory timeframe
violations: Jet Airways failed to respond to the complainant's access request within the 30-day statutory timeframe
No notice of extension was provided within 30 days as required by Subsection 8(4)
The airline's excuse of staff medical leave does not justify failure to comply with legal obligations

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Paragraph 9(3)(a) – Organization may refuse access if information is protected by solicitor-client privilege
regulatoryFindings.description: Jet Airways applied a blanket policy treating all incident documents as privileged, which is overbroad and does not meet the test for privilege
violations: Jet Airways applied a blanket policy treating all incident documents as privileged, which is overbroad and does not meet the test for privilege
The airline claimed privilege retroactively once a 'legal notice' was issued, for documents created before litigation was contemplated
Jet Airways refused to provide basic document details (author, date, recipient, purpose) to support privilege claims
Not every document prepared in response to an incident was created for the dominant purpose of litigation

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Paragraph 9(3)(d) – Organization may refuse access if information was generated during a formal dispute resolution process
regulatoryFindings.description: Jet Airways characterized routine internal correspondence between departments as a 'formal dispute resolution process'
violations: Jet Airways characterized routine internal correspondence between departments as a 'formal dispute resolution process'
The airline's grievance redressal mechanism is merely an informal internal complaint escalation process, not a legislated or agreed formal framework with recognized rules
Documents were generated on or around the incident date, before any formal dispute resolution process had begun

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4 – Organizations must implement policies and practices to give effect to principles in Schedule 1, including procedures to respond to complaints and inquiries
regulatoryFindings.description: Jet Airways failed to adopt policies clearly defining when solicitor-client and litigation privilege apply
violations: Jet Airways failed to adopt policies clearly defining when solicitor-client and litigation privilege apply
The airline's broad policy claiming privilege for all incident documents contradicts the requirements of Principle 4.9 regarding access to personal information
The organization did not revise its overly broad privilege claims despite Office recommendations

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – Individuals have the right to be informed of the existence and disclosure of their personal information and to be given access upon request
regulatoryFindings.description: Jet Airways withheld the complainant's personal information relating to the incident, including Departure Control System Report, police involvement materials, hotel accommodation details, and internal investigation materials
violations: Jet Airways withheld the complainant's personal information relating to the incident, including Departure Control System Report, police involvement materials, hotel accommodation details, and internal investigation materials
The airline failed to release any documents beyond the PNR despite the complainant's legal entitlement to access her personal information

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded with respect to Subsection 8(3) (failure to respond timely) and Principle 4.1.4 (inadequate policies). The complaint was also found well-founded regarding improper application of Paragraph 9(3)(d) (formal dispute resolution exemption). An impasse over Paragraph 9(3)(a) privilege claims was reported, preventing a definitive finding on whether documents were properly withheld under solicitor-client privilege. The Office recommended that Jet Airways: (1) implement procedures to respond to access requests in accordance with PIPEDA timeframes and requirements; (2) release documents not properly covered by privilege; (3) revise its policy for applying privilege claims to ensure they are not overbroad; (4) properly apply the formal dispute resolution exemption; and (5) recognize and respect its obligations under the Act. The Office indicated it would have a continuing interest in the respondent's compliance and would consult on authorities under the Act towards achieving compliance.
companyNow: Jet Airways ceased operations in 2019 and filed for insolvency. The airline was grounded after running out of cash and failing to secure additional funding.
dataType: Passenger Name Record (PNR), booking information, incident documentation, correspondence
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Subsection 8(3) – failure to respond within 30 days
PIPEDA Subsection 8(5) – deemed refusal due to missed deadline
PIPEDA Subsection 8(7) – failure to provide written reasons for refusal
PIPEDA Paragraph 9(3)(a) – improper application of solicitor-client privilege
PIPEDA Paragraph 9(3)(d) – improper application of formal dispute resolution exemption
PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4 – failure to implement adequate policies and practices
PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – failure to provide access to personal information upon request

companyDescription: An unnamed retail store operating in Canada that processes customer credit card transactions and maintains transaction records.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian retail merchant that processes customer payments via credit card and maintains transaction records. The store is subject to both contractual obligations imposed by credit card networks and legal requirements under the Excise Tax Act for tax compliance and audit purposes. The store's data retention practices were challenged when a customer requested deletion of her transaction history.
caseDescription: A retail store refused to delete customer credit card transaction records following a withdrawal of consent request, initially citing contractual obligations to credit card companies.
