The store later explained it was also legally obliged to retain the data under the Excise Tax Act. After the Privacy Commissioner clarified the legal and contractual basis for retention, the complainant accepted the explanation.
violationSummary: The company failed to provide adequate transparency and explanation regarding why personal data could not be deleted upon consent withdrawal, limiting the individual's meaningful right to control their information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: The retail store refused to delete customer credit card transaction records after the customer withdrew consent, citing contractual and legal retention obligations.
whyTheyWereWrong: The store initially failed to clearly explain its legal and contractual basis for retention, leaving the customer without adequate transparency about why her data could not be deleted despite.

claimsVsReality.claim: The retail store is contractually required to retain credit card transaction records for a certain period.
claimsVsReality.reality: The store was contractually required by credit card companies AND legally required under the Excise Tax Act to retain transaction data—both restrictions applied simultaneously.

claimsVsReality.claim: The customer's withdrawal of consent meant her data should be deleted immediately.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under PIPEDA, the right to withdraw consent is limited by legal and contractual restrictions that may require data retention regardless of consent withdrawal.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2 – Consent: An individual may withdraw consent at any time, subject to legal or contractual restrictions
regulatoryFindings.description: Retail store initially failed to explain valid legal and contractual reasons for data retention, preventing the complainant from understanding legitimate limitations on her right to withdrawal
violations: Retail store initially failed to explain valid legal and contractual reasons for data retention, preventing the complainant from understanding legitimate limitations on her right to withdrawal

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – Accountability: Organizations must be transparent about their practices and limitations
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate initial explanation of retention obligations under Excise Tax Act and credit card company contracts
violations: Inadequate initial explanation of retention obligations under Excise Tax Act and credit card company contracts

outcome: The retail company clarified its legal obligations under the Excise Tax Act and contractual obligations to credit card companies for retaining transactional data. The Privacy Commissioner communicated this explanation to the complainant, who accepted it and considered the matter resolved. No monetary penalty was imposed. The complainant indicated that earlier provision of this information would have prevented the need for complaint escalation.
dataType: Credit card transaction records

companyDescription: A Canadian financial institution that issues credit cards and provides dispute resolution services to cardholders.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian financial institution operating under PIPEDA jurisdiction, issuing credit cards and providing chargeback and dispute resolution services. The institution manages customer disputes by initiating chargeback requests with merchant banks and conducting pre-arbitration processes. The institution processes customer access requests for personal information held in its systems.
caseDescription: A financial institution improperly withheld personal information from a complainant's access request by citing a confidential commercial information exemption under PIPEDA section 9(3)(b). The institution refused to disclose documents related to a disputed credit card transaction and chargeback process. After investigation, the Privacy Commissioner determined the exemption was inappropriately applied and that the institution failed to respond within required timelines.
violationSummary: The financial institution improperly excluded personal information from disclosure by invoking an exemption for confidential commercial information without meeting the very high legal standard required under PIPEDA section 9(3)(b). This constitutes exclusion of lawfully requested personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The financial institution improperly withheld personal information from an access request by citing a confidential commercial information exemption under PIPEDA section 9(3)(b).
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant was unable to understand the full details of how his disputed transaction was handled.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pre-arbitration documents are confidential commercial information exempt from disclosure under PIPEDA section 9(3)(b).
claimsVsReality.reality: The documents contained the complainant's personal transactional information and information about his dispute, which he was entitled to access; the financial institution could not provide a compelling explanation for the exemption's application.

claimsVsReality.claim: The financial institution would respond to the access request within 30 days as required by PIPEDA.
claimsVsReality.reality: The financial institution failed to respond within the 30-day timeframe and did not send a notice of extension within 30 days as required, causing significant delay in the complainant receiving his information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – An individual shall be given access to their personal information upon request
regulatoryFindings.description: Financial institution withheld personal information pertaining to the complainant's disputed credit card transaction and chargeback process without valid legal justification
violations: Financial institution withheld personal information pertaining to the complainant's disputed credit card transaction and chargeback process without valid legal justification

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 8(3) – Organizations must respond to access requests within 30 days
regulatoryFindings.description: Financial institution failed to respond within the required 30-day timeframe
violations: Financial institution failed to respond within the required 30-day timeframe

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 8(4) – Organizations must send notice of extension within 30 days if unable to meet deadline
regulatoryFindings.description: Financial institution did not send a notice of extension within 30 days as required
violations: Financial institution did not send a notice of extension within 30 days as required

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 9(3)(b) – Confidential commercial information exemption applies only where the standard is very high
regulatoryFindings.description: Financial institution invoked the confidential commercial information exemption without providing compelling evidence that disclosure would cause irreparable harm or meet the very high standard required by law
violations: Financial institution invoked the confidential commercial information exemption without providing compelling evidence that disclosure would cause irreparable harm or meet the very high standard required by law

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner determined the matter was well-founded and resolved. The financial institution was required to correct its application of the exemptions and provide the complainant with access to his personal information from the Acquirer Representment Form, Pre-Arbitration Questionnaire, and Chargeback Questionnaire. The Commissioner encouraged the institution to prioritize responsiveness, timeliness, and quality in handling future access requests.
dataType: Credit card transaction data, account statements, correspondence, telephone call recordings, chargeback and dispute documentation
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – Right to access personal information
PIPEDA Section 8(4) – Notice of extension requirement
PIPEDA Section 9(1) – Third party information severability
PIPEDA Section 9(3)(b) – Confidential commercial information exemption

companyDescription: A Canadian financial institution that provides banking and registered savings account services to customers.
companyLongDescription: A regulated Canadian financial institution offering consumer banking services including Registered Education Savings Plan (RESP) accounts and other deposit products. The institution operates under PIPEDA privacy requirements and maintains internal procedures for responding to law enforcement requests. The company holds sensitive financial information on behalf of customers spanning multiple decades.
caseDescription: A financial institution disclosed personal financial information from a customer's RESP account dating back to 1999 to police in response to a production order, but the disclosed information extended beyond the scope specified in the order. The institution provided transactional data from 1999 without a valid legal basis, as the production order only requested supporting documents for deposits between October and December 2010.
violationSummary: The financial institution improperly disclosed personal financial information beyond the scope of the production order. Although disclosure pursuant to a court order is permitted under PIPEDA paragraph 7(3)(c), the institution exceeded the specific date range and nature of documents requested, constituting an unauthorized disclosure of sensitive financial information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The financial institution disclosed RESP account transaction data from 1999 to police in response to a production order that only requested supporting documents for deposits between October.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's sensitive financial information spanning 14 years was exposed to law enforcement without legal justification, exceeding the scope of the court order.

claimsVsReality.claim: The financial institution could disclose all RESP account information because the 2013 production order did not specify a timeframe, so we provided what we believed was necessary to comply.
claimsVsReality.reality: The 2013 production order explicitly specified in Appendix B that supporting documents were required only for transactions between October 1 and December 31, 2010, to account for deposits made during that period. Transactions from 1999 fell entirely outside this scope.

claimsVsReality.claim: The customer consented to disclosure of his financial information to law enforcement through the broad privacy policy clause permitting disclosure for prevention and detection of criminal activity.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer could not reasonably be expected to understand that vague general language in a privacy policy constituted informed consent to disclosure of 14 years of sensitive account data to police without specificity about scope, timing, or nature of the disclosure.

claimsVsReality.claim: The subsequent informal request from the detective for RESP account opening details in 1999 was a valid extension of the production order.
claimsVsReality.reality: The financial institution's own internal procedures explicitly state that requests for information outside the original scope of a production order require an additional production order to be issued—the detective's informal request did not meet this requirement.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 and subsection 6(1) – Knowledge and Consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Financial institution disclosed personal information without valid consent. Privacy policy language was too general and broad to constitute informed consent for sensitive financial information disclosure to law enforcement.
violations: Financial institution disclosed personal information without valid consent. Privacy policy language was too general and broad to constitute informed consent for sensitive financial information disclosure to law enforcement.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA paragraph 7(3)(c) – Court Orders
regulatoryFindings.description: Financial institution disclosed personal information beyond the scope of the production order issued in 2013. Transactional information from 1999 was not covered by the order, which specifically requested supporting documents only for the period October 1 to December 31, 2010.
violations: Financial institution disclosed personal information beyond the scope of the production order issued in 2013. Transactional information from 1999 was not covered by the order, which specifically requested supporting documents only for the period October 1 to December 31, 2010.

outcome: The complaint was found well-founded and resolved. Following the Office's Preliminary Report of Investigation, the financial institution agreed to review and clarify its procedures for complying with production orders. The institution committed to providing 'job aids' and dedicated training to staff responsible for disclosures pursuant to production orders to ensure only information within the scope of orders is disclosed. The financial institution acknowledged responsibility to ensure employees understand they must provide personal information only within the scope of production orders.
dataType: Financial account information, RESP (Registered Education Savings Plan) account statements, transaction history

companyDescription: The Australian Department of Defence is the military and defence agency responsible for protecting Australia's sovereignty and interests.
companyLongDescription: The Department of Defence is a major government agency within Australia's defence sector. It operates military forces and manages sensitive national security information. As a government entity, it is subject to the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and Information Privacy Principles. The department handles vast quantities of sensitive personal and classified information.
caseDescription: The Department of Defence breached Information Privacy Principles 4 and 10 by failing to protect sensitive personal information and unauthorised use of that data. The breach resulted from data security failures that exposed an individual's private information to unauthorised access or use.
violationSummary: The Department of Defence failed to implement adequate security measures to protect sensitive personal information, resulting in a breach of IPP 4 (data security obligation). Additionally, the information was used in an unauthorised manner in violation of IPP 10.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The Department of Defence failed to secure sensitive personal information and allowed unauthorised access or use of an individual's private data due to data security failures.
whyTheyWereWrong: An individual's private information was exposed to unauthorised access, causing non-economic loss and requiring them to incur $3,000 in expenses to remediate the harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Department of Defence had adequate data security measures in place to protect sensitive personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data security failures allowed unauthorised access or use of an individual's private sensitive information, resulting in actual harm and expenses incurred by the affected person.

regulatoryFindings.act: Information Privacy Principle 4 – Personal information must be protected by security safeguards against misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Department of Defence failed to implement adequate data security measures, allowing unauthorised access to sensitive personal information
violations: Department of Defence failed to implement adequate data security measures, allowing unauthorised access to sensitive personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: Information Privacy Principle 10 – Personal information shall not be used or disclosed for a purpose other than that for which it was collected
regulatoryFindings.description: Sensitive personal information was used in an unauthorised manner inconsistent with the original collection purpose
violations: Sensitive personal information was used in an unauthorised manner inconsistent with the original collection purpose

outcome: The OAIC found breaches of IPP 4 and IPP 10. The Department of Defence was ordered to: review and report on remedial procedures within nine months, provide a formal apology, pay compensation of AUD $10,000 for non-economic loss, and reimburse AUD $3,000 in reasonably incurred expenses. The matter is under review by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal.
companyNow: The Department of Defence continues to operate as Australia's primary defence agency. It remains subject to privacy law oversight by the OAIC.
dataType: Sensitive personal information (unspecified type)

companyDescription: The Westin Sydney is a luxury 5-star hotel located in Sydney, Australia, part of the Marriott International Westin brand portfolio.
companyLongDescription: The Westin Sydney is a high-end hotel property in Australia operated under the Westin brand, which is part of Marriott International. The Westin brand specializes in luxury hospitality services with properties worldwide. The Sydney location offers premium accommodation and guest services in Australia's largest city.
caseDescription: The Westin Sydney recorded a phone call without the participant's knowledge or consent, violating APP 3.5 which requires personal information collection by lawful and fair means. The hotel also failed to provide timely access to the call recording in breach of APP 12. The OAIC determined the collection was unfair and ordered a written apology and $1,500 in damages for non-economic loss.
violationSummary: The unauthorized recording of a phone call without participant knowledge constitutes covert surveillance and collection of personal information by unfair means, directly falling under the Surveillance category of Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: The Westin Sydney recorded a guest's phone call without their knowledge or consent and then failed to provide timely access to the recording when requested.
whyTheyWereWrong: The guest was secretly recorded during a private phone call, violating their reasonable expectation of privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: The hotel had authority to record the guest's phone call as part of normal business operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The guest was never informed of or consented to the recording, making the collection unfair and unlawful under Australian privacy law.

claimsVsReality.claim: Three days was a reasonable timeframe to provide the guest access to their call recording.
claimsVsReality.reality: The delay in providing access breached APP 12 obligations, which require timely provision of personal information upon request.

regulatoryFindings.act: Australian Privacy Principle 3.5 - Personal information must be collected by lawful and fair means
regulatoryFindings.description: Recording of telephone call without the knowledge or consent of the participant
violations: Recording of telephone call without the knowledge or consent of the participant
Collection of personal information (call content) through covert surveillance without fair notice

regulatoryFindings.act: Australian Privacy Principle 12 - Individuals have the right to access their personal information within a reasonable timeframe
regulatoryFindings.description: Providing access to the call recording within three days was determined to be an unreasonable delay
violations: Providing access to the call recording within three days was determined to be an unreasonable delay

outcome: The OAIC found a breach of APP 3.5 for unfair collection means. The Westin Sydney was ordered to provide a written apology to the complainant and pay $1,500 in damages for non-economic loss. The Federal Court subsequently dismissed the hotel's review application in 2018.
companyNow: The Westin Sydney continues to operate as a luxury hotel property in Australia. This 2017 privacy breach case resulted in increased awareness of recording practices in Australian hospitality venues.
dataType: Audio recordings, phone call content
legalBasisViolated: Australian Privacy Principle 3.5 (collection by lawful and fair means)
Australian Privacy Principle 12 (access to personal information)

companyDescription: Comcare is the Australian workers' compensation authority, providing workers' compensation insurance and services to the Australian public sector and employees.
companyLongDescription: Comcare is a statutory authority in Australia established under the Comcare Act 1988, responsible for workers' compensation insurance and rehabilitation services for the Australian public sector workforce and eligible employees. It operates as the national workers' compensation insurer, managing claims and providing injury management services across Commonwealth authorities and prescribed employers. The organization handles sensitive personal and medical information as part of its core function.
caseDescription: Comcare breached Information Privacy Principles by failing to adequately secure personal information (IPP 4) and unauthorisedly disclosing it (IPP 11). The Australian Information Commissioner found the organisation liable for data security failures resulting in unauthorised disclosure of personal information belonging to the complainant.
violationSummary: The primary violation was a data security failure under IPP 4, which led to unauthorised disclosure under IPP 11. This fits the Insecurity category as the organisation failed to implement appropriate security measures to protect personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Comcare failed to adequately secure personal information and unauthorisedly disclosed it, breaching Information Privacy Principles 4 and 11.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's personal information was exposed due to inadequate security measures, causing non-economic harm and requiring them to incur $3,000 in expenses to mitigate the breach.

claimsVsReality.claim: Comcare maintained adequate security over personal information in its possession.
claimsVsReality.reality: Comcare failed to implement adequate security measures, resulting in unauthorised disclosure of the complainant's personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information held by Comcare was protected from unauthorised access and disclosure.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information belonging to the complainant was unauthorisedly disclosed due to security failures.

regulatoryFindings.act: IPP 4 - Data Security: An organisation must take reasonable steps to protect personal information from misuse and loss, and from unauthorised access, modification or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Comcare failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal information
violations: Comcare failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal information
The security failure resulted in unauthorised access and disclosure of personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: IPP 11 - Unauthorised Disclosure: Personal information must not be disclosed to a third party without consent unless authorised by law
regulatoryFindings.description: Comcare unauthorisedly disclosed personal information to unauthorised parties
violations: Comcare unauthorisedly disclosed personal information to unauthorised parties
The disclosure occurred as a result of the security breach

outcome: The Administrative Appeals Tribunal upheld the OAIC determination. Comcare was ordered to pay $20,000 in non-economic loss damages to the complainant for breach of IPP 4 and IPP 11, plus $3,000 reimbursement for reasonably incurred expenses. Economic loss and aggravated damages were not awarded. The case remained under review by the Administrative Appeals Tribunal at the time of this determination.
companyNow: Comcare continues to operate as Australia's workers' compensation authority, managing worker claims and rehabilitation services for the Commonwealth sector.
dataType: Personal information (specific types not detailed in document)

companyDescription: The Department of Defence is Australia's federal military and defence organisation responsible for national security, military operations, and defence policy.
companyLongDescription: The Australian Department of Defence is a government agency accountable for Australia's military forces, defence capability, and national security strategy. It operates under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) and the Australian Privacy Principles, which regulate the handling of personal information collected and held by the department. The department manages sensitive defence and personal information related to military personnel, defence contractors, and the public.
caseDescription: The Department of Defence unauthorisedly disclosed personal information of an individual ('LA'), breaching APP 6 of the Australian Privacy Principles. The OAIC found a breach and awarded compensation for non-economic loss and reimbursement of reasonably incurred expenses.
violationSummary: Unauthorised disclosure of personal information directly constitutes a breach of confidentiality under the Information Dissemination category.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Department of Defence unauthorisedly disclosed personal information of an individual ('LA') in breach of APP 6 of the Australian Privacy Principles.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individual suffered non-economic loss and was forced to incur expenses totalling $3,420 to address the unauthorised disclosure of their personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Department of Defence appropriately managed and protected personal information under APP 6.
claimsVsReality.reality: The department unauthorisedly disclosed personal information of an individual, breaching APP 6 and causing non-economic loss and expenses of $3,420.

regulatoryFindings.act: APP 6 – Australian Privacy Principles – entities must take reasonable steps to ensure personal information they hold is accurate, up to date, complete, relevant and not misleading, and is protected by reasonable security measures from misuse, loss, unauthorised access, modification or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Unauthorised disclosure of personal information held by the Department of Defence
violations: Unauthorised disclosure of personal information held by the Department of Defence

outcome: The OAIC determined a breach of APP 6 and awarded damages of $12,000 for non-economic loss and reimbursement of $3,420 in reasonably incurred expenses. Aggravated damages were not awarded.
companyNow: The Department of Defence continues to operate as Australia's primary defence agency, responsible for military operations, defence policy, and national security under successive governments.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified types)

companyDescription: Md7, LLC is a Delaware-based limited liability company that assists wireless operators in managing real estate-related issues. The company operates from San Diego, California.
companyLongDescription: Md7, LLC is a Delaware-based limited liability company that assists wireless operators in managing real estate-related issues. The company operates from San Diego, California.
caseDescription: Md7, LLC falsely claimed on its website to be certified under the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework, which governs compliant transfer of personal data from Europe to the US. The company initiated an application but never completed certification, making deceptive statements about its participation to consumers and business partners.
violationSummary: The company made false representations about certification status that would affect how consumers understood privacy protections for their personal data, constituting deceptive disclosure under FTC standards.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Md7, LLC published privacy policies on its website falsely claiming it was certified and compliant with the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework when it had not completed certification with the U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union and Swiss customers transferred personal data to Md7 believing their information would receive Privacy Shield-level legal protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: Md7, LLC complies with the US-EU Privacy Shield Framework and has certified that it adheres to Privacy Shield principles
claimsVsReality.reality: Although Md7 initiated an application for Privacy Shield certification to the U.S. Department of Commerce, it did not complete the necessary steps and is not listed as a certified participant on the Privacy Shield directory maintained by Commerce.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers can view our Privacy Shield certification page at privacyshield.gov
claimsVsReality.reality: No certification page exists for Md7, LLC because the company never completed the certification process and therefore has no listing on the Privacy Shield website.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Md7, LLC represented expressly and by implication that it was a participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework through statements in its privacy policy and website, when in fact it had not completed certification and was not a certified participant.
violations: Md7, LLC represented expressly and by implication that it was a participant in the EU-U.S. Privacy Shield framework through statements in its privacy policy and website, when in fact it had not completed certification and was not a certified participant.
The company claimed to comply with Privacy Shield principles and directed customers to view its certification page on privacyshield.gov, creating a false impression of regulatory compliance.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on November 20, 2017, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint seeks compliance order to cease false Privacy Shield claims and correct misleading statements. Document indicates this is the initial complaint filing; final resolution terms not yet specified in this document.
dataType: Personal data from EU/EEA individuals and employees

companyDescription: TaxSlayer, LLC is a Georgia-based tax return preparation and electronic filing service founded over 50 years ago. The company developed browser-based software and mobile applications to help consumers prepare and file federal and state income tax returns, serving over 950,000 users in 2016.
companyLongDescription: TaxSlayer, LLC is a Georgia-based tax return preparation and electronic filing service founded over 50 years ago. The company developed browser-based software and mobile applications to help consumers prepare and file federal and state income tax returns, serving over 950,000 users in 2016.
caseDescription: TaxSlayer failed to protect over 950,000 users' sensitive financial and tax data by omitting clear privacy notices and implementing inadequate security controls. A list validation attack from October 2015 to December 2015 compromised 8,882 accounts, enabling attackers to file fraudulent tax returns and divert refunds. Victims suffered identity theft, requiring extensive remediation efforts.
violationSummary: TaxSlayer failed to design and implement adequate safeguards for sensitive financial information entrusted by 950,000+ users. The company did not conduct risk assessments, had no written security program until November 2015, lacked strong authentication controls, and did not notify users when critical account details were altered. This directly enabled credential-based account takeover and tax identity theft.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: TaxSlayer failed to provide clear privacy notices to customers, did not require strong passwords, lacked multi-factor authentication.
whyTheyWereWrong: Attackers exploited these security gaps to breach 8,882 accounts and commit tax identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: TaxSlayer advertised secure, reliable tax preparation and refund services
claimsVsReality.reality: TaxSlayer had no written security program, weak password policies, and no multi-factor authentication until after the breach, allowing attackers to compromise 8,882 accounts and commit tax identity theft

claimsVsReality.claim: TaxSlayer's privacy policy informed customers of data handling practices
claimsVsReality.reality: The privacy policy was buried in a lengthy license agreement without clear presentation, and TaxSlayer did not require customers to acknowledge it before using the service

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) and Regulation P (12 C.F.R. Part 1016) require financial institutions to provide consumers with a clear and conspicuous initial and annual privacy notice that accurately reflects the institution's privacy policies and practices, and deliver the notice so each consumer can reasonably be expected to receive actual notice.
regulatoryFindings.description: TaxSlayer's privacy policy was embedded at the end of a long license agreement without conveying its importance or relevance to customers
violations: TaxSlayer's privacy policy was embedded at the end of a long license agreement without conveying its importance or relevance to customers
TaxSlayer did not require customers to acknowledge receipt of the privacy notice as a necessary step to obtaining the service

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive information security program with administrative, technical, and physical safeguards appropriate to the institution's size, complexity, and the sensitivity of customer information.
regulatoryFindings.description: TaxSlayer had no written information security program until November 2015, despite collecting highly sensitive tax and financial data from 950,000+ users since the 1990s
violations: TaxSlayer had no written information security program until November 2015, despite collecting highly sensitive tax and financial data from 950,000+ users since the 1990s
TaxSlayer failed to conduct risk assessments identifying reasonably foreseeable threats such as credential-stuffing attacks
TaxSlayer did not require strong passwords (only 8-16 character requirement with no complexity standards), enabling dictionary and brute-force attacks
TaxSlayer failed to implement multi-factor authentication until December 21, 2015, after the breach occurred
TaxSlayer did not require email address validation at account creation to verify accuracy and communicate security issues
TaxSlayer failed to notify users when material changes were made to mailing address, password, security question, bank routing number, or refund method
TaxSlayer did not use rate-limiting or IP/device blocking tools to prevent rapid-succession credential-stuffing attacks

outcome: The FTC issued a Complaint against TaxSlayer on October 20, 2017, alleging violations of the FTC Act, Privacy Rule, Regulation P, and Safeguards Rule. The complaint details two counts: Count I (Privacy Rule/Reg. P violations for inadequate privacy notices) and Count II (Safeguards Rule violations for failure to implement comprehensive security controls). The document does not indicate a final settlement or penalty amount; it represents the initial enforcement action. TaxSlayer was required to address the failures and implement compliance measures.
companyNow: TaxSlayer continues to operate as a tax preparation software provider. The company has since implemented multi-factor authentication and enhanced security controls in response to the enforcement action and breach.
dataType: Financial data, tax information, Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, payment card numbers, personal identification, income, employment status, government benefits, health insurance information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 313 (Regulation P 12 C.F.R. Part 1016)

companyDescription: VIZIO, Inc. is a television manufacturer founded in 2002 that designs and sells internet-connected televisions in the United States. Since 2010, the company has sold over 11 million smart TVs with built-in streaming and interactive features.
companyLongDescription: VIZIO, Inc. is a television manufacturer founded in 2002 that designs and sells internet-connected televisions in the United States. Since 2010, the company has sold over 11 million smart TVs with built-in streaming and interactive features.
caseDescription: VIZIO manufactured smart TVs with automated content recognition (ACR) software that secretly collected second-by-second viewing data from over 11 million households without informed consent. The company sold this viewing history to third parties for audience measurement, advertising analytics, and targeted advertising. Consumers received inadequate notice and were misled about the extent of data collection and sale.
violationSummary: VIZIO engaged in comprehensive, second-by-second surveillance of consumer television viewing across multiple content sources without consumers' knowledge or informed consent. The default-enabled tracking and surreptitious transmission of pixel-level viewing data to company servers exemplifies unlawful surveillance.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: VIZIO installed automated content recognition (ACR) software by default on smart televisions to continuously track second-by-second viewing habits.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 11 million households had their detailed television viewing behavior harvested and sold to third parties for advertising targeting.

claimsVsReality.claim: Smart Interactivity enables program offers and suggestions about what to watch.
claimsVsReality.reality: Smart Interactivity was primarily used to track viewing habits and monetize viewing data; program offers/suggestions were rarely or never provided.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers received notice of ACR tracking and had the ability to easily disable it.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumers received no on-screen notice (post-August 2014) or inadequate notice (February 2014 pop-up with no data collection disclosure). March 2016 notice timed out in 30 seconds without easy menu access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Viewing data was collected for audience measurement and analytics purposes only.
claimsVsReality.reality: Viewing data was sold to third parties for audience measurement, advertising effectiveness analysis, and targeted ad placement across devices based on household IP addresses.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: VIZIO collected second-by-second viewing data from 11+ million TVs via default-enabled ACR software without obtaining informed consumer consent.
violations: VIZIO collected second-by-second viewing data from 11+ million TVs via default-enabled ACR software without obtaining informed consumer consent.
VIZIO represented 'Smart Interactivity' as enabling 'program offers and suggestions' but actually used it for comprehensive viewing surveillance and data monetization.
VIZIO failed to adequately disclose that viewing data was collected, stored indefinitely, and sold to third parties for audience measurement, advertising analytics, and targeted ad placement.
Initial on-screen notices (2014) made no mention of data collection. Later notifications (2016) timed out in 30 seconds and did not provide easy access to disable tracking.

regulatoryFindings.act: New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act § 56:8-2 prohibits unconscionable commercial practices, misrepresentation, and knowing omission of material facts in connection with sale of merchandise.
regulatoryFindings.description: VIZIO marketed televisions with vague descriptions of 'Smart Interactivity' that concealed the extent of tracking and data commercialization.
violations: VIZIO marketed televisions with vague descriptions of 'Smart Interactivity' that concealed the extent of tracking and data commercialization.
VIZIO omitted material facts about viewing data collection and third-party sale despite this information being essential to consumer decision-making.
VIZIO did not provide promised 'program offers or suggestions' for over two years yet continued marketing 'Smart Interactivity' feature.

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint seeking permanent injunctive relief and equitable remedies including rescission, restitution, civil penalties, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. VIZIO was required to obtain affirmative informed consent before collecting and sharing viewing data, provide clear and prominent disclosures, and cease deceptive representations. The company must implement reasonable data security measures and allow consumers to delete viewing data.
companyNow: VIZIO continues to manufacture and sell smart televisions. The company is now owned by LeEco (as of 2016) and later by Walmart (2024), operating under enhanced FTC compliance obligations and privacy requirements.
dataType: Television viewing history, IP addresses, MAC addresses, WiFi data, demographic information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair and deceptive practices
New Jersey Consumer Fraud Act § 56:8-2 – Misrepresentation and omission of material fact

company: Credit Bureau Center, LLC (formerly MyScore LLC)
companyDescription: Credit Bureau Center, LLC (formerly MyScore LLC) operated websites including eFreeScore.com, CreditUpdates.com, and FreeCreditNation.com that advertised free credit scores and reports but enrolled consumers in unauthorized negative option credit monitoring services.
companyLongDescription: Credit Bureau Center, LLC (formerly MyScore LLC) operated websites including eFreeScore.com, CreditUpdates.com, and FreeCreditNation.com that advertised free credit scores and reports but enrolled consumers in unauthorized negative option credit monitoring services.
caseDescription: Defendants operated a scheme using fake rental property ads on Craigslist and fraudulent landlord emails to lure consumers to websites offering 'free' credit reports. Consumers were deceived into enrolling in a negative option credit monitoring service charging $29.94 monthly without clear disclosure or authorization. Over 500 complaints were filed, causing millions in consumer losses.
violationSummary: The company deliberately deceived consumers through fake rental ads and fraudulent landlord emails, then obtained personal information including SSNs under false pretenses. This constitutes both deception in advertising and improper data collection.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Credit Bureau Center placed fake rental property advertisements on Craigslist and sent fraudulent landlord emails to lure consumers to their websites.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 500 consumers were deceived into believing they needed credit reports to rent non-existent properties, then charged $29.94 monthly without authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers can view rental properties by obtaining their credit reports from our websites
claimsVsReality.reality: The rental properties advertised did not exist or were not available for rent; the ads were solely designed to drive traffic to credit monitoring service enrollment pages

caseDescription: Jerk, LLC operated a reputational/social media website (jerk.com) where it misrepresented the source of user-generated content. The FTC pursued enforcement with a Compliance Monitoring provision that respondent John Fanning argued was overbroad, unreasonably related to the violations, and violated due process. On remand from the First Circuit Court of Appeals, the parties disputed the appropriate scope of ongoing monitoring obligations.

Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC compliance monitoring provisions must bear a reasonable relation to the unlawful practices found to exist.
regulatoryFindings.description: The proposed blanket Compliance Monitoring provision was overbroad and not reasonably tailored to the specific violations involving content source misrepresentation on a reputation/social media website
violations: The proposed blanket Compliance Monitoring provision was overbroad and not reasonably tailored to the specific violations involving content source misrepresentation on a reputation/social media website

outcome: On remand from the First Circuit Court of Appeals (Fanning v. FTC, 821 F.3d 164, 1st Cir. 2016), John Fanning challenged the scope of the Compliance Monitoring Provision as overbroad and violating due process. The First Circuit found that the original scope was unreasonable—noting it would require Fanning to report even if he became a waiter at a restaurant, which was unrelated to the actual violations. Fanning argued the monitoring must be limited to business affiliations or employment involving reputational/social media websites where similar content-source misrepresentation could occur. The final resolution required narrowing the compliance monitoring to activities reasonably related to the original violations.

companyDescription: Upromise was a FinTech company that offered free memberships allowing consumers to earn cash-back rewards on eligible online and in-store purchases, directing rewards to college savings plans or student loan paydown. The company offered the RewardU toolbar to remind members of cash-back opportunities while browsing.
companyLongDescription: Upromise was a FinTech company that offered free memberships allowing consumers to earn cash-back rewards on eligible online and in-store purchases, directing rewards to college savings plans or student loan paydown. The company offered the RewardU toolbar to remind members of cash-back opportunities while browsing.
caseDescription: Upromise distributed the RewardU toolbar that collected extensive browsing and search data from consumers, but failed to disclose this data collection clearly and prominently as required by a prior FTC consent order. The company also submitted inadequate third-party assessments that did not properly evaluate the toolbar's security safeguards.
violationSummary: Upromise used RewardU to record and transmit detailed information about consumer online activity including searches, browsing, and transactions without adequate, conspicuous disclosure. This constitutes surveillance through a targeting tool installed on consumer computers.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Upromise distributed the RewardU toolbar from 2013-2016 that collected consumers' search queries, browsing activity.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Upromise members downloaded RewardU believing it only reminded them of cash-back offers, but the toolbar secretly monitored all their online activity.

claimsVsReality.claim: RewardU is a helpful tool that reminds members of cash-back opportunities with no mention of extensive data collection.
claimsVsReality.reality: RewardU collected search queries, browsing URLs, IP addresses, unique identifiers, and website visit information from consumer computers, with no meaningful way for consumers to discover the extent of collection without special software.

claimsVsReality.claim: Upromise disclosed what data RewardU collects and how it is used when consumers download the toolbar.
claimsVsReality.reality: Disclosures were buried in 633-word footnotes in small font, light gray text, and contradictory across three different privacy policies, making it impossible for ordinary consumers to notice or understand them.

claimsVsReality.claim: Upromise obtained qualified independent assessments confirming RewardU safeguards adequately protect consumer data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Fishnet Security assessments barely mentioned RewardU, misidentified the vendor, and contained no evaluation of the toolbar's specific administrative, technical, or physical safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(l) and 16(a)(1) authorize civil penalties for violations of a prior FTC Commission Order.
regulatoryFindings.description: Upromise failed to clearly and prominently disclose all types of data collected by the RewardU targeting tool prior to download, in violation of the Commission Order Section I(A)(1).
violations: Upromise failed to clearly and prominently disclose all types of data collected by the RewardU targeting tool prior to download, in violation of the Commission Order Section I(A)(1).

Disclosures were presented in small font, footnote style, light gray text on white background, and contradictory across multiple privacy policies, violating the 'clearly and prominently' standard requiring noticeable size, high contrast, understandable language, and nothing contrary or mitigating.

Upromise failed to obtain compliant third-party assessments of the RewardU targeting tool as required by the Commission Order Section VI, instead submitting assessments that barely mentioned RewardU and did not evaluate the toolbar's safeguards.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Commission Order (March 27, 2012, Docket No. C-4351) Definition 10 defines 'Targeting Tool' as any software installed on a consumer's computer used to record or transmit information about online activity.
regulatoryFindings.description: RewardU qualifies as a targeting tool because it records and transmits search queries, browsing URLs, IP addresses, unique identifiers, and website visit information from consumer computers in the background without clear notice.
violations: RewardU qualifies as a targeting tool because it records and transmits search queries, browsing URLs, IP addresses, unique identifiers, and website visit information from consumer computers in the background without clear notice.
Upromise acknowledged RewardU was a targeting tool for purposes of the assessment requirement but failed to treat it as such for disclosure requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Commission Order Section I(A) requires clear, prominent, separate disclosure prior to download, with disclosures in type and size noticeable for ordinary consumers, high contrast print, separate from EULA/privacy policy, understandable language, and nothing contrary or inconsistent.
regulatoryFindings.description: Upromise disclosed RewardU data collection in a 633-word footnote in small font after consumers clicked links or scrolled past extensive marketing content, making it unavoidable but obscure.
violations: Upromise disclosed RewardU data collection in a 633-word footnote in small font after consumers clicked links or scrolled past extensive marketing content, making it unavoidable but obscure.
Text was in light gray on white background with poor contrast and complex language about search providers, Toolbar IDs, and shared data.
The popup at installation linked to three different contradictory privacy policies (Upromise, RewardU, Rakuten toolbar, and Rakuten general), leaving consumers uncertain which terms applied.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Commission Order Section VI requires biennial third-party assessments from qualified professionals (CISSP, CISA, or GIAC certified) that set forth specific administrative, technical, and physical safeguards and certify the security program protects personal information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Fishnet Security assessments submitted in 2013 and later mentioned RewardU only once in 133 pages, incorrectly identifying the vendor as Compete instead of Rakuten, and merely stating the vendor contract 'includes all three criteria' without evaluating the toolbar itself.
violations: Fishnet Security assessments submitted in 2013 and later mentioned RewardU only once in 133 pages, incorrectly identifying the vendor as Compete instead of Rakuten, and merely stating the vendor contract 'includes all three criteria' without evaluating the toolbar itself.
Assessments did not set forth specific safeguards for RewardU, explain how safeguards protect consumers, or certify the toolbar's security compliance with the Order.

outcome: The FTC filed a civil complaint for civil penalties, injunction, and other equitable relief. The complaint alleges violations of the March 2012 Commission Order through both inadequate RewardU data collection disclosures (First Cause of Action) and failure to obtain compliant assessments (Second Cause of Action). Relief sought includes judgment on each violation, civil penalties up to $40,654 per violation, permanent injunction from violating the Order, and costs and attorneys' fees. The document requests the Court deem appropriate under its equitable powers. As this is a complaint filed March 16, 2017, the case outcome is not yet decided in this document.
companyNow: Upromise is now part of Sallie Mae Student Loan Corporation (as stated in the disclosure text). The company ceased distribution of RewardU in January 2016.
dataType: Search queries, browsing behavior, IP address, unique identifiers, financial transaction data, personal identifiable information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Order Docket No. C-4351, Section I(A)(1) – Targeting Tool Disclosures
FTC Order Section VI – Assessment Requirements

companyDescription: Lenovo (United States) Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Morrisville, North Carolina. As a subsidiary of the Chinese conglomerate Lenovo Group, it manufactures and sells personal computers, laptops, and related hardware to U.S. consumers.
companyLongDescription: Lenovo (United States) Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Morrisville, North Carolina. As a subsidiary of the Chinese conglomerate Lenovo Group, it manufactures and sells personal computers, laptops, and related hardware to U.S. consumers.
caseDescription: Lenovo preinstalled adware called VisualDiscovery on laptops without adequate disclosure. The software acted as a man-in-the-middle to intercept encrypted communications, inject pop-up ads, and collect browsing data. Lenovo failed to implement basic security measures and left over 750,000 consumers exposed to security vulnerabilities.
violationSummary: VisualDiscovery conducted continuous surveillance of all consumer internet activity, including encrypted communications, without meaningful disclosure or consent. The man-in-the-middle interception of HTTPS traffic represents systematic surveillance of sensitive personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Lenovo preinstalled VisualDiscovery adware on over 750,000 laptops without adequately disclosing that it would inject pop-up ads, intercept encrypted communications, and collect browsing data.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' encrypted communications were decrypted and re-encrypted without their knowledge, their browsers lost security protections against spoofed websites.

claimsVsReality.claim: Lenovo represented that its personal computers contained certain quality software (Windows OS, McAfee security, internet browsers) that would function normally
claimsVsReality.reality: The preinstalled VisualDiscovery adware undermined and compromised these software programs, causing them to function in an inferior manner and exposing consumers to security risks

claimsVsReality.claim: A one-time pop-up window disclosed that VisualDiscovery would help consumers 'discover visually similar products and best prices while you shop'
claimsVsReality.reality: VisualDiscovery injected unlimited pop-up ads, intercepted all encrypted HTTPS communications as a man-in-the-middle, and collected and transmitted sensitive browsing data to Superfish servers without meaningful disclosure

claimsVsReality.claim: The opt-out link in the pop-up window provided an effective way to disable VisualDiscovery
claimsVsReality.reality: Clicking the opt-out link only stopped the display of pop-up ads; the software remained active as a man-in-the-middle, continuing to intercept encrypted communications and collect browsing data

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair competition, including unlawful, unfair, deceptive, or misleading business acts or practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to disclose that VisualDiscovery would inject unlimited pop-up ads, act as a man-in-the-middle intercepting encrypted communications, and collect browsing data without meaningful consent
violations: Failed to disclose that VisualDiscovery would inject unlimited pop-up ads, act as a man-in-the-middle intercepting encrypted communications, and collect browsing data without meaningful consent
Affirmatively represented that preinstalled software (Windows OS, McAfee, browsers) functioned normally when VisualDiscovery's preinstallation undermined and compromised their operation
Failed to follow reasonable security and privacy protocols for third-party software, including failing to adequately assess security risks prior to preinstallation
Failed to provide an effective way to remove or opt out of preinstalled software; clicking the opt-out link only stopped pop-ups but left the man-in-the-middle spyware active

outcome: The complaint seeks a permanent injunction prohibiting Lenovo from engaging in unfair competition as defined in Business & Professions Code § 17200. The People seek court orders to restore money or property acquired through unfair competition, assessment of civil penalties of $2,500 per violation, recovery of investigative costs, and other relief deemed just and proper. The document is a complaint filed September 5, 2017; final judgment and monetary outcome are not yet determined at this stage.
companyNow: Lenovo remains one of the world's largest personal computer manufacturers. The company subsequently discontinued VisualDiscovery and implemented improved security and transparency practices for preinstalled software.
dataType: Internet browsing data, encrypted HTTPS communications, sensitive personal information transmitted over the Internet
legalBasisViolated: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 (Unfair Competition Law)
California Business & Professions Code § 17203 (Corrective Advertising / Restitution)

caseDescription: Target failed to implement reasonable security procedures to protect personal information of California residents, resulting in unauthorized access to payment card data for over 40 million consumers (7.75 million California residents) and contact information for 70 million individuals (8.33 million California residents). violations: Target failed to implement reasonable security procedures despite owning payment card information and contact information for millions of California residents

caseDescription: Lenovo preinstalled adware called VisualDiscovery on over 750,000 laptops without adequate disclosure. violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Lenovo preinstalled VisualDiscovery adware on over 750,000 laptops that secretly intercepted all encrypted website traffic.

claimsVsReality.claim: VisualDiscovery enables users to 'discover visually similar products and best prices while you shop'

claimsVsReality.reality: Komodia tool created two critical security vulnerabilities: failed to validate certificates properly and used weak shared encryption key ('komodia') crackable in under one hour, enabling attackers to compromise all affected devices

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent made representations that VisualDiscovery would enable consumers to discover similar products and best prices but failed to disclose that it would act as a man-in-the-middle intercepting all communications including encrypted HTTPS websites and collecting browsing data transmitted to Superfish servers.
violations: Respondent made representations that VisualDiscovery would enable consumers to discover similar products and best prices but failed to disclose that it would act as a man-in-the-middle intercepting all communications including encrypted HTTPS websites and collecting browsing data transmitted to Superfish servers.

Respondent's preinstallation of software without adequate notice or informed consent that intercepted sensitive encrypted communications and collected browsing data caused substantial injury to consumers not offset by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable.

Respondent failed to implement reasonable security measures to assess and address security risks created by third-party software, resulting in critical vulnerabilities that exposed consumer personal information to unauthorized access including fraudulent certificate issuance and man-in-the-middle attacks.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging three counts of violation: (1) deceptive failure to disclose VisualDiscovery's man-in-the-middle functionality and data collection; (2) unfair preinstallation of man-in-the-middle software without adequate notice or consent; (3) unfair security practices in failing to reasonably assess third-party software risks. The document is the complaint; ultimate resolution through consent order or settlement would follow.
companyNow: Lenovo continues as one of the world's largest PC manufacturers. The company has since implemented enhanced security review procedures for preinstalled software following this enforcement action.
dataType: Login credentials, Social Security numbers, financial account information, medical information, web-based email communications, URLs visited, IP addresses, shopping browsing behavior
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair acts or practices

companyDescription: A voluntary industry charter signed by Belgian and Luxembourg media organisations (print, audiovisual, and magazine publishers) establishing procedures for citizens to request rectification, updates, or de-indexing of online publications mentioning them.
companyLongDescription: A voluntary industry charter signed by Belgian and Luxembourg media organisations (print, audiovisual, and magazine publishers) establishing procedures for citizens to request rectification, updates, or de-indexing of online publications mentioning them.
caseDescription: This is a voluntary charter establishing rights for citizens mentioned in online publications. It balances privacy rights against press freedom by allowing citizens to request rectification, judicial information updates, or de-indexing of inaccurate or outdated content from search engines and media archives.
companyWorth: Multiple organizations (combined revenue in hundreds of millions EUR for major signatories like VRT, RTBF, Mediahuis, Rossel)
violationSummary: The charter recognizes that permanent online accessibility of archived content (particularly judicial/criminal information) creates persistent visibility via search engines, increasing accessibility and privacy harm despite original publication being lawful.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Multiple Belgian media organizations signed a voluntary charter establishing procedures for citizens cited in online publications to request rectification of factual errors.
whyTheyWereWrong: This document does not describe wrongdoing by the signatory companies.
outcome: This is a voluntary charter establishing procedures for media organisations to handle citizen requests regarding online publications. It does not constitute an enforcement action or penalty. Signatories commit to: (1) rectifying factual errors upon sufficient proof; (2) updating judicial information when cases conclude (acquittal, dismissal, rehabilitation, pardon, amnesty); (3) de-indexing from search engines only after the search engine has refused the request, via technical means (robots.txt, noindex tag) while keeping content accessible on the media site. Decisions must be made within three months. The charter balances archival preservation and collective memory against individual privacy, maintaining that archived press content should remain accessible as a matter of democratic importance.
companyNow: This charter represents a collective commitment by major Belgian and Luxembourg media organisations (Vlaamse Nieuwsmedia, LA PRESSE.be, The Ppress, Medialaan, RTBF, RTL Belux, VRT, and Fédération des télés Locales) to establish privacy-respecting procedures for handling online publication requests.
dataType: Personal names, judicial information, criminal records, accident details

companyDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is a Canadian federal agency responsible for border management, immigration enforcement, and customs operations at Canada's borders.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is a Canadian federal department established in 2003, responsible for collecting revenue, facilitating trade and travel, and enforcing laws at the Canada-US border and international ports of entry. The agency operates under the Department of Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness and employs thousands of officers across the country. In 2013-2016, the CBSA partnered with Force Four Productions to permit filming of border enforcement operations for the National Geographic series 'Border Security: Canada's Front Line.' The agency exercises federal law enforcement powers including detention authority.
caseDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) participated in a television documentary series by allowing a production company (Force Four) to film enforcement operations at border crossings and during immigration enforcement activities. The CBSA failed to obtain valid informed consent from individuals who were filmed and detained, and disclosed personal information about enforcement targets without authorization. The consent process was fundamentally flawed due to the coercive context of detention and arrest, and facial blurring used to protect non-consenting individuals was inadequate.
violationSummary: The CBSA disclosed personal information of detained individuals to Force Four for commercial television production purposes without valid informed consent. The disclosure occurred in real-time during filming and individuals could not provide meaningful consent given the coercive context of CBSA detention and questioning. Additionally, personal information about an enforcement target was disclosed to production crew members in advance of filming without authorization.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The CBSA allowed a television production company to film enforcement operations and immigration detentions without obtaining valid informed consent from individuals.
whyTheyWereWrong: Detainees signed consent forms under coercive conditions—while frightened and detained—without understanding what they were agreeing to, resulting in their identities.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CBSA stated it had a 'solid process for protecting the privacy rights of individuals' and that consent was being properly obtained.
claimsVsReality.reality: Individuals were asked to sign consent forms while detained and afraid, with minimal or no explanation of how their personal information would be used or broadcast internationally.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CBSA claimed it was not responsible for consent collection because Force Four was 'responsible for seeking any consent necessary' under the Agreement.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CBSA could not contract out of its obligations under the Privacy Act and remained responsible for personal information under its control, including individuals filmed during CBSA enforcement operations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CBSA represented that individuals had alternatives and could refuse consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: No meaningful alternatives were offered to detainees, and the coercive context of detention made any consent inherently involuntary and uninformed.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 – Personal information shall only be collected by government institutions if it directly relates to an operating program or activity
regulatoryFindings.description: While CBSA's collection of information for enforcement was lawful, the subsequent disclosure to Force Four for commercial television production purposes was not directly related to CBSA operating programs
violations: While CBSA's collection of information for enforcement was lawful, the subsequent disclosure to Force Four for commercial television production purposes was not directly related to CBSA operating programs
CBSA facilitated personal information collection by allowing Force Four filming of enforcement activities without ensuring compliance with section 4 for the disclosed purpose

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Personal information can only be disclosed with individual's consent or in accordance with permitted disclosure categories
regulatoryFindings.description: CBSA disclosed personal information of detained individuals to Force Four without obtaining valid informed consent
violations: CBSA disclosed personal information of detained individuals to Force Four without obtaining valid informed consent
Consent obtained was not meaningful – individuals were under duress during detention and arrest, could not freely consent
Individuals were not properly informed of the purpose for which their information would be disclosed (commercial television production)
CBSA disclosed personal information about enforcement target (name, nationality, warrant details, deportation history) to production crew in advance of raid without consent or valid legal basis
Facial blurring used to protect non-consenting individuals was inadequate and did not prevent identification

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the complaint well-founded. The CBSA was required to cease its participation in the TV Program. The CBSA accepted the recommendation and terminated involvement in the documentary series as of May 2016. The CBSA was also directed to conduct Privacy Impact Assessments (PIAs) before undertaking future initiatives involving personal information collection and disclosure. No monetary penalty was imposed; the enforcement mechanism was a compliance order and cessation of the problematic activity.
companyNow: The CBSA continues to operate as a federal border enforcement agency. Following this investigation, it ceased participation in the TV series and committed to conducting Privacy Impact Assessments before undertaking similar public-facing initiatives.
dataType: Identity information (name, immigration status), location data, video/biometric data (facial features, voice)
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) Section 4 – Unlawful collection of personal information not directly related to operating programs
Privacy Act (Canada) Section 8(1) – Disclosure without valid consent

companyDescription: Mobilshred Inc. is a Canadian records management and document storage company operating under the Recall brand, providing secure storage and destruction services for sensitive information.
companyLongDescription: Mobilshred Inc. (operating as Recall) is a Canadian subsidiary of Recall Canada Holdings, which is ultimately owned by Australian-listed Recall Holdings Limited. The company provides records management services including document storage, digital solutions, data protection, and secure destruction across Canada. Mobilshred Inc. operates exclusively in Canada with no U.S. facilities, and serves approximately 80,000 customers globally.
caseDescription: A complainant raised concerns that the Canada Revenue Agency's contract with Mobilshred Inc. for outsourced storage of Canadian taxpayer information could expose personal data to U.S. authorities under the USA PATRIOT Act. The Privacy Commissioner investigated whether the CRA had adequately safeguarded personal information and found that the CRA implemented appropriate contractual and operational measures to keep all taxpayer records in Canada, rendering the complaint not well-founded.
violationSummary: The alleged risk was potential unauthorized exposure of personal taxpayer information to foreign authorities (U.S. government) through cross-border data transfer or storage. Although no actual violation was found, the concern fell within the Information Dissemination – Exposure category due to the risk of unauthorized access by third parties.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Mobilshred Inc. contracted with Canada's Revenue Agency to store Canadian taxpayer records, raising concerns that personal information could be exposed to U.S. authorities under the USA PATRIOT.
whyTheyWereWrong: The investigation found no actual harm; the CRA implemented adequate contractual safeguards requiring all taxpayer records remain physically in Canada.

claimsVsReality.claim: Mobilshred Inc. could expose Canadian taxpayer data to U.S. authorities under the USA PATRIOT Act because its parent company Recall has U.S. operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Mobilshred Inc. is a wholly Canadian entity with no U.S. operations; the CRA contractually required all taxpayer records remain physically in Canada; Recall Holdings Limited is Australian-based, not U.S.-based.

claimsVsReality.claim: Mobilshred Inc. is a division of U.S.-based Recall Corporation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Mobilshred Inc. is owned by Recall Canada Holdings (Canadian entity), which is owned by Recall Holdings Limited (Australian entity); Recall Corporation (U.S.) is a completely separate subsidiary.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8 – Protection of personal information from unauthorized disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: No violation found; CRA demonstrated adequate safeguards to prevent unauthorized disclosure of taxpayer personal information to foreign authorities
violations: No violation found; CRA demonstrated adequate safeguards to prevent unauthorized disclosure of taxpayer personal information to foreign authorities

outcome: The complaint was found to be not well-founded. The Privacy Commissioner determined that the CRA had taken appropriate steps to mitigate privacy risks by requiring that all taxpayer information remain in Canada at all times, incorporating detailed physical and technological security requirements into the Mobilshred Inc. contract, and verifying that Mobilshred Inc. is a wholly Canadian entity with no U.S. operations. No remedial action was required.
companyNow: Mobilshred Inc. continues to operate as a Canadian records management provider under the Recall brand, serving government and private sector clients.
dataType: Tax information, taxpayer personal information

companyDescription: The Parole Board of Canada (PBC) is a federal government agency responsible for making parole decisions and managing offenders in the community under the Corrections and Conditional Release Act.
companyLongDescription: The Parole Board of Canada is a Crown corporation and independent administrative tribunal that conducts parole hearings, makes release decisions on federal offenders, and oversees conditional release supervision. As a government agency, it handles sensitive personal information including offender records, victim statements, and employee personnel files. The PBC operates under strict privacy and access to information legislation governed by the Privacy Act.
caseDescription: The Parole Board of Canada disclosed an employee's medical information to individuals involved in a Public Service Staffing Tribunal hearing without consent. The medical information was included in materials sent on March 19, 2014, despite the PSST's explicit order to remove such sensitive health data. The disclosure was acknowledged as a mistake by the PBC, which apologized, ensured recipients deleted the information, and reported the breach to its Access to Information and Privacy division.
violationSummary: The PBC improperly disclosed personal medical information without the employee's consent and contrary to tribunal-mandated restrictions. This constitutes unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal information to third parties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A Parole Board of Canada human resources employee disclosed an employee's confidential medical information to individuals involved in a Public Service Staffing Tribunal hearing without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's sensitive medical data was exposed to external parties in a legal proceeding where it was explicitly prohibited, violating her privacy rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: The PBC would remove all sensitive personal information including medical/health data from materials provided to the Public Service Staffing Tribunal.
claimsVsReality.reality: A PBC HR employee failed to remove the complainant's medical information from the submitted materials, inadvertently disclosing confidential health data to tribunal participants despite explicit instructions to exclude such information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The PBC protects employee personal information in accordance with the Privacy Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: The PBC contravened the disclosure provisions of the Privacy Act by sharing an employee's medical information without consent and without authorization under any permitted disclosure category.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Personal information can only be disclosed with individual's consent or in accordance with permitted categories under Section 8(2)
regulatoryFindings.description: Medical information was disclosed without employee consent
violations: Medical information was disclosed without employee consent
Disclosure was not in accordance with any permitted category under Section 8(2)
Medical information was included despite explicit PSST order to remove it

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Defines personal information as information about an identifiable individual recorded in any form
regulatoryFindings.description: Medical information constitutes personal information and was subject to disclosure protections
violations: Medical information constitutes personal information and was subject to disclosure protections

outcome: The complaint was determined to be well-founded. The PBC acknowledged the breach, apologized to the complainant, ensured all recipients disposed of the disclosed medical information, and filed a breach report with its Access to Information and Privacy division. The investigating authority expressed satisfaction with these remedial measures and made no further recommendations.
companyNow: The Parole Board of Canada continues to operate as a federal agency responsible for parole decisions and offender management, having implemented improved information handling procedures following privacy breaches.
dataType: Medical/health information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 3 (definition of personal information)
Privacy Act Section 8(1) (requirement for consent for disclosure)
Privacy Act Section 8(2) (permitted categories of disclosure)
