regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement adequate controls to prevent unauthorized disclosure of customer contact information
violations: Failed to implement adequate controls to prevent unauthorized disclosure of customer contact information
Insufficient employee training to recognize and resist deceptive impersonation techniques
Inadequate verification procedures before disclosing customer personal information to unknown parties

outcome: The financial institution reported the breach to the Privacy Commissioner of Canada, investigated the scope of the incident, notified all 100 affected customers, provided complimentary third-party credit protection monitoring, enhanced controls to prevent recurrence, and conducted additional staff training. No fraud was ultimately reported by affected customers.
dataType: Contact information, personal identifying information, financial account details
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1 Principle 4.2 (Protection of Personal Information)

companyDescription: A Canadian bank operating in partnership with a retailer to offer co-branded credit cards and loyalty programs.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian financial institution that operates credit card programs in partnership with retail stores, offering customers the ability to join loyalty programs and apply for credit products. The bank processes customer applications and conducts credit inquiries through in-store sales personnel. It is subject to PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) regulations governing the collection, use, and disclosure of personal information in Canada.
caseDescription: A customer was enrolled in a retailer credit card without his knowledge or consent while signing up for a loyalty program. The bank collected sensitive financial and personal information including a hard pull credit inquiry without express consent, and filled the application with inaccurate information the customer never provided.
violationSummary: The bank interrogated the individual for personal financial information (income, rent) under the guise of a loyalty program without clear disclosure or consent that this data would be used for a credit application and credit inquiry.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A bank enrolled a customer in a retail credit card without his knowledge or consent while he was signing up for a loyalty program.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's credit was pulled without authorization, leaving him exposed to potential identity fraud and damaging his credit history with a false inquiry and account he never applied for.

claimsVsReality.claim: The individual had knowingly provided his personal information for the purpose of obtaining a credit card.
claimsVsReality.reality: The individual was told by the salesperson that the application had nothing to do with a credit card and never saw the electronic tablet or understood he was applying for credit.

claimsVsReality.claim: The individual provided all the information included in the application and clicked the requisite consent box for a credit check.
claimsVsReality.reality: The investigation found no evidence the complainant ever saw the tablet screen, provided most of the information (only driver's license details were accurate), or actually clicked any consent box—the salesperson likely clicked it instead.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Organizations must obtain informed consent for collection, use or disclosure of personal information, with express consent required for sensitive information
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank failed to obtain consent for collection of personal financial data (income, rent)
violations: Bank failed to obtain consent for collection of personal financial data (income, rent)
Bank failed to obtain express consent for hard pull credit inquiry
Salesperson misrepresented that the application was not for a credit card
No evidence customer saw or agreed to tablet consent box

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 – Personal information must be as accurate, complete and up-to-date as possible
regulatoryFindings.description: Application contained inaccurate information (phone number, occupation, income, rent) that customer never provided
violations: Application contained inaccurate information (phone number, occupation, income, rent) that customer never provided
Only driver's licence information was verified as accurate

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4 – Organizations must implement procedures to give effect to privacy principles
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank did not have adequate safeguards to ensure consent was actually obtained
violations: Bank did not have adequate safeguards to ensure consent was actually obtained
No verification mechanism to confirm customer provided application information
Insufficient controls over in-store data collection process

outcome: The bank apologized and cancelled the credit card. The bank requested the credit reporting agency remove the account and inquiry from the complainant's file. The bank discontinued its in-store tablet pilot program for credit applications. The bank committed to implementing future measures requiring demonstration that: (i) the client is given opportunity to read the online application form and privacy communications; and (ii) the client has provided personal information and consented to use/disclosure.
dataType: Driver's licence number, phone number, occupation, annual income, monthly rent, credit report inquiry

companyDescription: An online service company that operates integrated software interfaces to help individuals track personal information held by other organizations.
companyLongDescription: The company operates an online service platform with integrated software interfaces that allows individuals to monitor and manage their personal information across multiple organizations. The platform was designed to connect with partner organizations' systems to provide unified access to personal data. However, a technical glitch in the system architecture caused cross-client data exposure, and the company's customer service and IT support processes proved inadequate to identify and escalate privacy concerns to decision-makers.
caseDescription: A technical glitch in an online service software interface caused one client's personal information to be inadvertently disclosed to another client. The complainant attempted for months to have the issue resolved through customer service and IT support without success. After filing a complaint with the privacy commissioner's office, the company immediately investigated, identified the root cause in the integrated software system, and corrected the technical glitch.
violationSummary: The unintended disclosure of one individual's personal information to another user through a technical glitch represents an exposure of sensitive data due to system failure and inadequate controls.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: A technical glitch in the company's online service software interface caused one client's personal information to be inadvertently disclosed to another client.
whyTheyWereWrong: A person discovered another individual's sensitive personal information visible on their account.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer service and IT support can resolve technical issues affecting personal information access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customer service was unable to resolve the data exposure issue for months despite repeated attempts by the affected individual.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had adequate escalation procedures for privacy concerns raised to customer service.
claimsVsReality.reality: The individual attempted unsuccessfully to escalate privacy concerns to the privacy officer for months, prompting the company to implement new escalation procedures only after regulatory intervention.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 7 – Organizations are responsible for the security of personal information against loss or theft, as well as unauthorized access, disclosure, copying, use or modification
regulatoryFindings.description: Technical glitch in software interface allowed unauthorized access and disclosure of one client's personal information to another client
violations: Technical glitch in software interface allowed unauthorized access and disclosure of one client's personal information to another client
Inadequate monitoring and testing of integrated online service systems to prevent disclosure
Lack of proper escalation procedures for privacy concerns reported by customers

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 1 – Organizations are responsible for personal information in their possession or custody
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to promptly address customer's privacy concerns over several months
violations: Company failed to promptly address customer's privacy concerns over several months
Inadequate staff training on privacy policies and procedures to recognize and escalate privacy issues

outcome: The online company implemented corrective measures including: (1) revised internal policies and procedures with an escalation process to the Chief Privacy Officer for privacy concerns reported to Customer Service; (2) collaborated with the integrated software provider to fix the technical glitch for all users; (3) developed a multi-year contractual agreement with the other organization covering technical issues, enhanced user consent provisions, and mutual compliance obligations. The complainant confirmed resolution to his satisfaction.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified types)

companyDescription: A First Nation band council operating as a federal work, undertaking or business in Canada, providing employment and administrative services to band members.
companyLongDescription: A First Nation band council serves as the governing and administrative body for an Indigenous community in Canada. When operating in core functions such as employment administration, it qualifies as a federal work, undertaking or business (FWUB) under Canadian jurisdiction and is therefore subject to the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA). The band council manages employee relations, leave requests, and related administrative matters.
caseDescription: A First Nation band council lost doctor's notes submitted by an employee in support of leave requests on two separate occasions, then refused to pay the employee's leave without the documentation. The band council was subject to PIPEDA as a federal work, undertaking or business and lacked a privacy policy to govern handling of personal information.
violationSummary: The band council failed to implement adequate safeguards to protect sensitive health information entrusted to it, resulting in the loss of medical documentation. This represents a failure to ensure the security of personal information as required under PIPEDA principles.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: A First Nation band council lost doctor's notes submitted by an employee on two separate occasions to support leave requests, then refused to pay the employee's leave without the documentation.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee was denied payment for legitimate leave and faced financial hardship because the band council lost his personal medical information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The band council maintained proper handling of employee medical documentation submitted in support of leave requests.
claimsVsReality.reality: The band council lost the employee's doctor's notes on two separate occasions, resulting in the employee being denied leave payment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The band council had adequate privacy safeguards and policies in place for managing employee personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The band council lacked any privacy policy to govern the handling of personal information until directed to develop one by the Privacy Commissioner's office.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA applies to all federal works, undertakings and businesses, including First Nation band councils acting in core functions, to protect personal information of employees
regulatoryFindings.description: Band council lost doctor's notes submitted by employee on two separate occasions
violations: Band council lost doctor's notes submitted by employee on two separate occasions
Band council did not implement a privacy policy or safeguards to protect sensitive health information

outcome: The band council agreed to develop and adopt a privacy policy with guidance from the Office of the Privacy Commissioner. The early resolution was considered successful when the band council confirmed adoption of the privacy policy, addressing the underlying privacy governance deficiency. The complainant's employment-related dispute regarding unpaid leave was addressed through a separate Canada Labour Code complaint.
companyNow: The band council adopted a privacy policy following the complaint and has implemented improved privacy practices for handling employee personal information.
dataType: Health data, medical documentation, employment records

companyDescription: A Canadian sports facilities company that operates athletic venues and manages memberships. The company provides facilities for sports activities and tournaments.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian sports facilities operator that manages memberships, suspends accounts for unpaid dues, and hosts sporting tournaments on its premises. The company is affiliated with local sports associations and maintains board member policies including confidentiality requirements. The company provides orientation sessions on privacy policies to new members.
caseDescription: A sports facilities company disclosed a member's outstanding debt information to a related sports association on two occasions without the member's consent. The company claimed the disclosures were in response to direct questions and made under an expectation of privacy, but neither exception is valid under PIPEDA. The disclosure did not qualify for the debt collection exemption under PIPEDA subsection 7(3)(b) because the purpose was to prevent participation in a tournament, not to collect the debt.
violationSummary: The company disclosed sensitive personal information (debt information) about an identifiable individual to a third party without consent and without relying on a valid exemption. This constitutes unauthorized disclosure of personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: The sports facilities company disclosed a member's outstanding debt information to a related sports association on two occasions without the member's consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The member's sensitive debt information was disclosed without authorization, preventing him from participating in a tournament.

claimsVsReality.claim: The disclosure was made in response to a direct question from the association and therefore was exempt from consent requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Being asked a question does not create an exemption from PIPEDA's consent requirement for disclosing personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: There was an expectation of privacy during the discussions, which exempted the company from obtaining consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: An expectation of privacy between the disclosing parties does not substitute for obtaining consent from the individual whose personal information is being disclosed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The disclosure fell under the debt collection exemption in PIPEDA subsection 7(3)(b).
claimsVsReality.reality: The actual purpose was to prevent the member from participating in the tournament, not to collect the debt, so the exemption did not apply.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Knowledge and Consent Requirement
regulatoryFindings.description: Company disclosed personal information (outstanding debt) without the individual's knowledge or consent
violations: Company disclosed personal information (outstanding debt) without the individual's knowledge or consent
Company failed to rely on valid exemptions to the consent requirement

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 7(3)(b) – Debt Collection Exemption
regulatoryFindings.description: Company attempted to rely on the debt collection exemption, but the disclosure purpose was to prevent tournament participation, not to collect the debt
violations: Company attempted to rely on the debt collection exemption, but the disclosure purpose was to prevent tournament participation, not to collect the debt
Exemption does not apply when the purpose of disclosure is unrelated to debt collection

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. The company contravened Principle 4.3 of PIPEDA by disclosing personal information without consent and could not rely on the paragraph 7(3)(b) exemption because the disclosure was not for the purpose of collecting the debt. The company was required to cease such disclosures and implement compliance measures. The company subsequently reviewed its privacy policy with board members and made privacy and confidentiality a standing agenda item for board meetings. The complainant was ultimately permitted to participate in the tournament.
dataType: Financial information (debt/outstanding balance)
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA subsection 7(3)(b) (improper reliance on debt collection exemption)

companyDescription: Veda Advantage is an Australian credit reporting and consumer data management company that provides credit reports, credit scores, and identity verification services to lenders, employers, and consumers.
companyLongDescription: Veda Advantage Information Services and Solutions Ltd is a major Australian credit reporting agency operating under the Privacy Act 1988 and the Privacy (Credit Reporting) Code 2014. The company provides credit reports, credit scores, fraud detection, and identity verification services to financial institutions, employers, and consumers. As a credit reporting body, Veda has statutory obligations to provide consumers with free access to their credit information, while also operating fee-based premium services.
caseDescription: Veda Advantage breached the Privacy Act by making its free credit reporting service less accessible and harder to identify than its fee-based services, and by charging expedited delivery fees to individuals who had not accessed their credit reports in the preceding 12 months. The regulator found that Veda failed to ensure equal availability and ease of access to free credit information across all service channels including phone services.
violationSummary: Veda improperly used individuals' credit reporting information by creating barriers to free access while promoting paid services, constituting unauthorized secondary use and differential treatment in access to personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Veda Advantage made its free credit reporting service significantly less accessible and harder to identify than its fee-based services.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals seeking free credit information were deliberately steered toward paid services, preventing them from easily accessing their own credit reports at no cost.

claimsVsReality.claim: Veda's free credit reporting service is equally available and easy to identify as its fee-based services across all channels including phone.
claimsVsReality.reality: Veda deliberately made the free service less accessible and harder to find than its paid alternatives, particularly through phone services, to encourage consumers to purchase premium reports.

claimsVsReality.claim: Expedited delivery fees are appropriately charged to all users requesting faster service.
claimsVsReality.reality: Veda charged expedited fees to individuals who had not accessed their credit reports in the preceding 12 months, effectively penalizing consumers for using the service and preventing them from obtaining their entitled free information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy (Credit Reporting) Code 2014, paragraphs 19.3(a) and (b) – Free credit reporting information must be as available and easy to identify and access as fee-based services across all service channels
regulatoryFindings.description: Made free credit reporting service less accessible than fee-based services
violations: Made free credit reporting service less accessible than fee-based services
Failed to ensure easy identification of free access option across phone and other service channels
Charged expedited delivery fees to individuals who had not accessed credit reports in preceding 12 months, contrary to requirements

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988, Section 20R(5) and APP 7 – Credit reporting service providers must comply with the Credit Reporting Code
regulatoryFindings.description: Breach of APP 7 through non-compliant credit reporting practices
violations: Breach of APP 7 through non-compliant credit reporting practices

outcome: Veda Advantage was ordered to take action within 6 months to ensure its free credit reporting information service is as available and as easy to identify and access as its fee-based services, including through its phone service. The company was required to refund individuals for expedited delivery charges where those individuals had not sought access to credit reporting information within the preceding 12-month period.
companyNow: Veda Advantage operates as part of the Australian credit reporting infrastructure, providing consumer credit data and reporting services to lenders and other organizations under strict privacy and credit reporting regulations.
dataType: Credit reporting information, financial data

companyDescription: Veda Advantage is an Australian credit reporting agency that compiles and maintains credit information on consumers and businesses.
companyLongDescription: Veda Advantage (now Equifax Australia) is a major credit reporting and identity verification company in Australia, responsible for maintaining credit reports and scores used by lenders, employers, and other organisations. The company collects, stores, and distributes credit data including court judgments, defaults, and payment history. As a credit reporting agency, Veda Advantage is subject to strict Privacy Act obligations regarding accuracy and timeliness of reported information.
caseDescription: Veda Advantage, a credit reporting agency, breached privacy obligations under the Privacy Act by failing to ensure accuracy of court information in its credit reports. The company violated sections 20N, 20P, and 20S of the Privacy Act through inaccurate handling of credit reporting data. The OAIC determined the breach caused non-economic loss to the individual and ordered compensation and procedural review.
violationSummary: The company failed to take reasonable steps to ensure the accuracy and currency of personal information (credit data) in its systems, resulting in inaccurate court information being reported. This constitutes a failure in the secure handling and maintenance of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Veda Advantage failed to ensure accuracy of court information in credit reports, breaching sections 20N, 20P, and 20S of the Privacy Act by maintaining inaccurate credit reporting data.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individual suffered non-economic loss when inaccurate court information on their credit report remained uncorrected, damaging their creditworthiness and financial reputation.

claimsVsReality.claim: Veda Advantage maintained accurate credit reporting data on all consumers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to ensure accuracy of court information in credit reports, leaving inaccurate data on the affected individual's file uncorrected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Court information was properly managed and verified in credit reports.
claimsVsReality.reality: Veda Advantage breached its obligations under sections 20N, 20P, and 20S to maintain accurate, up-to-date, and complete credit reporting information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 20N – Credit provider must take reasonable steps to ensure accuracy of credit information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to ensure accuracy of court information in credit reports
violations: Failed to ensure accuracy of court information in credit reports

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 20P – Credit reporting agency must not disclose inaccurate or misleading credit information
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed inaccurate court information in credit reports
violations: Disclosed inaccurate court information in credit reports

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 20S – Individual has right to request correction of inaccurate credit information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to properly handle correction requests regarding court information accuracy
violations: Failed to properly handle correction requests regarding court information accuracy

outcome: The OAIC found Veda Advantage breached ss 20N(1), 20N(2), 20P, and 20S of the Privacy Act. The company was ordered to: issue an apology to the individual, pay non-economic damages of $10,000, reimburse reasonable expenses of $5,830, and conduct a comprehensive review of procedures to ensure accuracy of court information in future credit reports.
companyNow: Veda Advantage operates as part of the Equifax group following acquisition. The company continues to provide credit reporting and identity verification services in Australia.
dataType: Credit reporting data, financial information

companyDescription: Commonwealth Bank of Australia is the largest retail bank in Australia and one of the country's major financial institutions, providing banking and financial services to millions of customers.
companyLongDescription: Commonwealth Bank of Australia (CBA) is a multinational banking corporation headquartered in Sydney and serves as a primary retail and commercial bank for Australian households and businesses. The bank offers a comprehensive range of financial products including savings accounts, loans, mortgages, credit cards, and investment services. With a history spanning over a century, CBA is one of the 'Big Four' banks in Australia and maintains a significant presence in the Asia-Pacific region.
caseDescription: Commonwealth Bank of Australia breached the National Privacy Principles by mishandling personal information and failing to adequately secure customer data. The bank disclosed personal information without proper authorization and failed to implement adequate data security measures. The complainant was awarded $10,000 in non-economic damages.
violationSummary: The case involved unauthorized use or disclosure of personal information in breach of NPP 2, combined with inadequate data security measures under NPP 4. The primary harm stems from disclosure without proper authorization or consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Commonwealth Bank of Australia disclosed a customer's personal information without proper authorization and failed to implement adequate data security measures to protect sensitive customer data.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's personal financial information was exposed and mishandled, allowing unauthorized disclosure of sensitive data that could enable identity theft, fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: Commonwealth Bank implemented adequate data security measures to protect customer personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank failed to implement adequate data security measures, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of sensitive customer data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Commonwealth Bank properly controlled access to and disclosure of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank disclosed a customer's personal information without proper authorization, breaching privacy obligations.

regulatoryFindings.act: NPP 2 – Use or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Unauthorized use or disclosure of personal information held by the bank
violations: Unauthorized use or disclosure of personal information held by the bank

regulatoryFindings.act: NPP 4 – Data security
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to implement adequate security measures to protect personal information
violations: Failure to implement adequate security measures to protect personal information

False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: ASUS marketed routers with security features but shipped them with authentication bypass vulnerabilities, unencrypted file transfers, weak default credentials.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers compromised thousands of ASUS routers and accessed consumers' USB storage devices containing SSNs, tax returns, and financial information, leading to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: AiCloud is 'your secure space' and 'the most complete, accessible, and secure cloud platform' for private file sharing with 'indefinite storage and increased privacy.'
claimsVsReality.reality: AiCloud had multiple critical vulnerabilities: authentication bypass allowed attackers to access files without credentials; password disclosure vulnerability exposed login credentials in cleartext; thousands of routers were breached and files were indexed by search engines.

claimsVsReality.claim: AiDisk allows consumers to 'safely secure and access your treasured data through your router.'
claimsVsReality.reality: AiDisk used unencrypted FTP protocol, defaulted to unauthenticated internet access to all files, and recommended weak credentials ('Family'/'Family'). Thousands of routers exposed files searchable online; attackers gained unauthorized access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Routers include security features like 'SPI intrusion detection' and 'DoS protection' and can 'protect computers from any unauthorized access, hacking, and virus attacks.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Routers had pervasive vulnerabilities (CSRF, buffer overflow, cross-site scripting) that attackers actively exploited. ASUS didn't test for these well-known vulnerabilities or implement low-cost protections like anti-CSRF tokens, leaving networks at risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: The firmware upgrade tool 'checks the ASUS server for the firmware update' and accurately indicates if your router has the latest version.
claimsVsReality.reality: ASUS repeatedly failed to update its firmware list on the server. The tool inaccurately told consumers their routers were up-to-date when critical security patches were available; this blocked consumers from protecting themselves.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ASUS represented that it took reasonable steps to ensure routers could protect local networks from attack, but failed to implement security architecture reviews, secure protocols (AiDisk used unencrypted FTP), secure defaults, or vulnerability testing.
violations: ASUS represented that it took reasonable steps to ensure routers could protect local networks from attack, but failed to implement security architecture reviews, secure protocols (AiDisk used unencrypted FTP), secure defaults, or vulnerability testing.

ASUS represented AiCloud as a secure means to access personal information, but the application contained authentication bypass and password disclosure vulnerabilities allowing unauthorized access without credentials.
ASUS represented AiDisk as secure, but defaulted to unauthenticated internet access, used unencrypted file transfer, and provided misleading warnings that discouraged security configuration.

ASUS represented the firmware upgrade tool would accurately indicate current firmware status, but failed to maintain its server list, repeatedly notifying consumers their routers were up-to-date when critical security updates were available.

regulatoryFindings.act: Unfair practice standard requires acts causing substantial injury to consumers not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
regulatoryFindings.description: ASUS's failure to implement reasonable security (secure design reviews, code review, penetration testing, low-cost protections like anti-CSRF tokens, secure defaults) caused thousands of routers to be compromised by readily-available attack tools.
violations: ASUS's failure to implement reasonable security (secure design reviews, code review, penetration testing, low-cost protections like anti-CSRF tokens, secure defaults) caused thousands of routers to be compromised by readily-available attack tools.

Consumers had no reasonable way to discover or avoid the risks—vulnerabilities were in default settings and undisclosed to users. A consumer who attempted firmware updates was blocked by the malfunctioning upgrade tool, unable to protect himself despite trying.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging five counts of unfair and deceptive practices (router security misrepresentations, AiCloud security misrepresentations, AiDisk security misrepresentations, firmware upgrade tool misrepresentations, and unfair security practices). The complaint sought to enjoin these practices and require ASUS to implement comprehensive security protections, maintain processes for receiving and addressing vulnerability reports, provide timely notice to consumers of known security risks, and submit to ongoing compliance monitoring.
companyNow: ASUSTeK Computer remains a major global hardware manufacturer specializing in computer components, networking equipment, and consumer electronics. The company has significantly expanded its product lines since 2016 and continues to be a leading router manufacturer.
outcomeSummary: Complaint filed; consent order likely (typical FTC enforcement structure for IoT/security cases)
dataType: Financial information, login credentials, social security numbers, tax returns, medical information, private photos and videos, files on USB storage devices
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – False or Misleading Representations Regarding Security

companyDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is Canada's federal tax and revenue authority, responsible for administering tax laws and managing personal financial information of millions of Canadians.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency is a government institution tasked with collecting taxes, administering benefits and credits, and enforcing tax compliance across Canada. As a custodian of highly sensitive personal and financial information, the CRA manages records for millions of Canadian taxpayers, donors, and businesses. The agency operates under the Privacy Act and must maintain strict safeguards over the personal information entrusted to it. The 2014 incident highlighted systemic vulnerabilities in the CRA's Access to Information and Privacy (ATIP) operations and information handling procedures.
caseDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency inadvertently mailed a consultation package containing personal information of approximately 1,029 individuals to a CBC journalist instead of the intended government department. The package was disclosed without consent and subsequently reported publicly by the CBC, including names and photographs of affected individuals. The CRA failed to implement adequate quality assurance procedures and employee communication protocols in its Access to Information and Privacy directorate.
violationSummary: The CRA disclosed personal information to an unauthorized third party (CBC journalist) without the consent of the individuals involved, violating the fundamental requirement under the Privacy Act that personal information shall not be disclosed without consent except in permitted categories.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The Canada Revenue Agency inadvertently mailed a consultation package containing personal information of 1,029 individuals, including names, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Donors' names, addresses, and sensitive donation information were publicly disclosed by the CBC, exposing individuals' charitable giving patterns.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CRA had adequate quality assurance and employee communication procedures in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigators found gaps in quality assurance procedures and lack of employee communication that allowed a consultation package to be mailed to the wrong recipient, with no one noticing until days later.

claimsVsReality.claim: The mailing error was an isolated incident unlikely to recur.
claimsVsReality.reality: The incident revealed systemic process failures requiring a comprehensive overhaul of ATIP operations, including new mail verification procedures, password protection protocols, and mandatory security training enforcement.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information in the mailed package was adequately protected.
claimsVsReality.reality: Names, addresses, descriptions of donations, fair market values, and donor identities were disclosed without consent to a journalist and subsequently published by the CBC with photographs.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Definition of Personal Information
regulatoryFindings.description: The information disclosed (name, address, donation details, fair market valuations) constitutes personal information as defined under Section 3
violations: The information disclosed (name, address, donation details, fair market valuations) constitutes personal information as defined under Section 3

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 7(a) – Use Without Consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal information was used for a purpose inconsistent with the purpose for which it was obtained (disclosure to media rather than ATIP response)
violations: Personal information was used for a purpose inconsistent with the purpose for which it was obtained (disclosure to media rather than ATIP response)

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Disclosure Without Consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal information was disclosed to a CBC journalist without the consent of the individuals involved
violations: Personal information was disclosed to a CBC journalist without the consent of the individuals involved
The disclosure did not fall within any of the permitted disclosure categories under Section 8(2)

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded. The CRA was not subject to a monetary penalty but was required to implement a comprehensive Action Plan to strengthen privacy protections, including: revised mail-out quality assurance procedures, password protection for consultations, mandatory security training for staff, and an independent third-party review of ATIP's privacy management control framework. The Commissioner will continue monitoring implementation of these remedial measures.
companyNow: The CRA continues to operate as Canada's primary revenue and benefits administration agency. Following this incident, it implemented enhanced quality assurance procedures, password protection for sensitive media, mandatory security training, and commissioned independent third-party reviews of its privacy management framework.
dataType: Name, address, donation information, fair market valuation details

Privacy Act Section 7(a) (use of personal information without consent)

companyDescription: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation (CBC) is Canada's national public broadcaster, providing television, radio, and digital media services.
companyLongDescription: The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a Crown corporation and Canada's primary public media outlet, established to provide broadcasting services across the country. It operates multiple television and radio networks in both English and French, and provides digital content through its website and streaming platforms. The CBC serves as an important news and information source for Canadians.
caseDescription: The CBC received and published personal information of Canadian taxpayers that was inadvertently mailed by the Canada Revenue Agency in response to an Access to Information request. The published article identified several individuals by name and included photographs of six affected individuals. The complaint alleged the CBC violated the Privacy Act by disclosing details of the breach and identifying some individuals in media coverage.
violationSummary: The CBC disclosed personal information (names, addresses, financial details, and photographs) of taxpayers to the public through a published article, which constitutes disclosure of personal information without consent.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The CBC received inadvertently mailed personal information from the Canada Revenue Agency containing taxpayer names, addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: The CBC's publication exposed over 200 Canadian taxpayers' home addresses, tax credit values, and donation details to the public, allowing strangers to identify.

claimsVsReality.claim: The information was obtained legally and the journalist is not bound by the CRA's confidentiality obligations.
claimsVsReality.reality: While legally obtained in error, the publication disclosed sensitive personal information (addresses, tax details, photographs) of 200+ individuals without consent, exposing them to potential targeted harm.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Privacy Act does not apply because this is covered by the journalistic purposes exclusion under section 69.1.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of legal exemptions, the publication of identifiable individuals' tax information and home addresses caused real privacy harm to the affected taxpayers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CBC was considering withholding most details from the list out of respect for privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CBC published names and photographs of six individuals and identified several others by name, making them identifiable alongside their home addresses and tax credit information.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Personal Information Definition
regulatoryFindings.description: Information about identifiable individuals (names, addresses, financial details, photographs) was disclosed
violations: Information about identifiable individuals (names, addresses, financial details, photographs) was disclosed

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 7(a) – Use Restriction
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal information was used for publication purposes without consent of individuals
violations: Personal information was used for publication purposes without consent of individuals

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Disclosure Restriction
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal information was disclosed to the public without consent of individuals
violations: Personal information was disclosed to the public without consent of individuals

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 69.1 – Journalistic Exclusion
regulatoryFindings.description: Exception applied; the Privacy Act does not apply to personal information collected, used, or disclosed for journalistic purposes
violations: Exception applied; the Privacy Act does not apply to personal information collected, used, or disclosed for journalistic purposes

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner concluded that the matter was not well-founded. The CBC's collection, use, and disclosure of the personal information was determined to be for purely journalistic purposes and therefore covered by the exclusion provision under section 69.1 of the Privacy Act. As a result, the Office of the Privacy Commissioner did not have authority over the CBC's handling of the personal information and the complaint was dismissed.
companyNow: The CBC remains Canada's national public broadcaster and primary source of news and cultural programming for millions of Canadians.

Privacy Act Section 7(a) (restriction on use without consent)

companyDescription: Health Canada is the federal department responsible for protecting and promoting the health of Canadians, including administering medical cannabis access programs.
companyLongDescription: Health Canada is a department of the Government of Canada with responsibility for helping Canadians maintain and improve their health. It administers various health programs and services, including the Marihuana Medical Access Program (MMAP), which provided access to medical cannabis for patients with physician support. The department operates under the Privacy Act and is subject to oversight by the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.
caseDescription: Health Canada sent 41,514 windowed envelopes to Marihuana Medical Access Program (MMAP) clients with the full program name visible through the envelope window, thereby disclosing individuals' association with a sensitive medical cannabis program to postal workers and members of the public. The disclosure was found to violate the Privacy Act as it revealed sensitive personal information without proper consent or authorization, exposing individuals to employment, reputational, safety, and health risks.
violationSummary: The disclosure through visible envelope labeling exposed sensitive personal information (program enrollment) to unintended third parties (postal workers, household members, public). The visibility and accessibility of the information to multiple parties beyond the intended recipient constitutes 'Exposure' under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Health Canada mailed 41,514 windowed envelopes to medical cannabis program clients with the full program name visible through the envelope window.
whyTheyWereWrong: The disclosure exposed individuals to job loss, reputational harm, safety risks including violent home invasions.

claimsVsReality.claim: Media coverage and recipients themselves disclosed their MMAP involvement, not Health Canada.
claimsVsReality.reality: Health Canada directly exposed 41,514 individuals' program participation by printing the full program name in visible envelopes; media only covered the incident after the disclosure had already occurred.

claimsVsReality.claim: Mail recipients implicitly consented to disclosure because they had previously corresponded with MMAP and understood mail would be handled by Canada Post.
claimsVsReality.reality: Recipients never consented to having their sensitive medical program enrollment visibly identified on mail; implicit consent to routine postal delivery does not extend to explicit disclosure of program names linking individuals to controlled substances.

claimsVsReality.claim: Disclosure was a consistent use of personal information for correspondence purposes, authorized under the Privacy Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: While corresponding with clients is a consistent use, disclosing their association with a sensitive medical cannabis program to third parties exceeds the scope of necessary communication and violated privacy obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Limiting program name from return addresses would have broad implications on government mail communications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Using generic return addresses or redacted labels is a standard privacy practice that would have prevented 41,514 disclosures without impacting Health Canada's ability to communicate with clients.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Personal information protection
regulatoryFindings.description: Health Canada failed to protect sensitive personal information identifying individuals' association with the MMAP medical cannabis program
violations: Health Canada failed to protect sensitive personal information identifying individuals' association with the MMAP medical cannabis program
The combination of individual's name, address, and program name constituted sensitive personal information requiring protection

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) – Consent requirement for disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Health Canada disclosed personal information without obtaining explicit or valid implied consent from MMAP clients
violations: Health Canada disclosed personal information without obtaining explicit or valid implied consent from MMAP clients
The disclosure was made to Canada Post employees and potentially visible to members of the public and household members

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(2)(a) – Consistent use authorization
regulatoryFindings.description: Health Canada could not establish that disclosing the specific program name in the return address was a consistent use of information collected for program administration
violations: Health Canada could not establish that disclosing the specific program name in the return address was a consistent use of information collected for program administration
The explicit identification of the MMAP on correspondence was not a standard practice and fell outside reasonable expectations of individuals
The program name was not necessary for program administration or envelope return purposes

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada found the complaints well-founded and concluded that Health Canada contravened the Privacy Act. While no monetary penalty was imposed, Health Canada was required to implement enhanced mail-out procedures to protect client personal information. Health Canada established a new Privacy Working Group to assist the Bureau of Medical Cannabis in meeting legal obligations to protect client information and ensure consideration of data sensitivity and stigma in future communications.
companyNow: Health Canada continues to operate as a federal department, now administering medical cannabis access through licensed producers under the Marihuana for Medical Purposes Regulations (MMPR), replacing the earlier MMAP program.
dataType: Health data, medical program enrollment status, personal identity, home address
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) Section 3 – Definition of personal information
Privacy Act (Canada) Section 8(1) – Disclosure without consent
Privacy Act (Canada) Section 8(2)(a) – Consistent use requirement

companyDescription: The Department of National Defence is Canada's federal military and defence department, responsible for the Canadian Armed Forces and national defence operations.
companyLongDescription: The Department of National Defence (DND) is the primary government institution responsible for defending Canada, conducting military operations, and managing the Canadian Armed Forces. It maintains extensive personal information on Canadian Forces members and operates various administrative processes, including Progress Review Boards that make decisions affecting service members' employment and careers. DND is accountable under the Canadian Privacy Act for the retention and protection of personal information used in decision-making processes.
caseDescription: The Department of National Defence prematurely destroyed an audio recording of a Progress Review Board hearing used to decide whether a Canadian Forces member should be terminated from a training program. The department classified the recording as 'transitory' and erased it approximately 10 days after the hearing, despite the complainant's expressed intent to appeal. DND failed to retain the recording for the required two-year minimum period under the Privacy Act, denying the complainant access to evidence and preventing him from verifying the accuracy of the official minutes.
violationSummary: The destruction of personal information (audio recording) used for an administrative decision-making process violated retention requirements. The premature disposal prevented the individual from accessing information used to make a decision directly affecting him (employment termination) and from verifying accuracy, which are core data security and protection obligations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: The Department of National Defence destroyed an audio recording of a Progress Review Board hearing approximately 10 days after it took place.
whyTheyWereWrong: By destroying the recording, DND prevented the complainant from accessing evidence of what was actually said during the hearing that led to his employment termination.

claimsVsReality.claim: The audio recording was a 'transitory' record that could be destroyed once minutes were drafted from it.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Act requires retention of personal information used for administrative purposes for at least two years; the recording's classification as transitory did not override this legal obligation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant's signature on the minutes constituted consent to destroy the audio recording.
claimsVsReality.reality: The signature was merely an acknowledgment that the complainant received the minutes under the heading 'Representations' and did not constitute consent to destruction of the recording.

claimsVsReality.claim: The summary minutes provided an adequate record of the PRB hearing for administrative purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The minutes were only a summary, not a complete transcript, and the complainant contested their accuracy, demonstrating why access to the full audio recording was essential for challenging the decision.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 6(1) requires government institutions to retain personal information used for administrative purposes for a prescribed period to ensure individuals have reasonable opportunity to access it
regulatoryFindings.description: DND destroyed the audio recording approximately 10 days after the PRB hearing, before the two-year retention period expired
violations: DND destroyed the audio recording approximately 10 days after the PRB hearing, before the two-year retention period expired
DND classified the recording as 'transitory' and disposed of it without consent from the complainant
No written policy existed governing retention and disposal of PRB recordings, resulting in inconsistent practices (some recordings retained, others overwritten)

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 6(2) requires government institutions to take all reasonable steps to ensure personal information used for administrative purposes is accurate, up-to-date and complete
regulatoryFindings.description: Destruction of the audio recording prevented the complainant from verifying the accuracy of the PRB minutes, which he contended were incomplete and inaccurate
violations: Destruction of the audio recording prevented the complainant from verifying the accuracy of the PRB minutes, which he contended were incomplete and inaccurate
The complainant was unable to challenge incomplete or inaccurate summaries without access to the original recording

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Regulations Section 4 requires retention of personal information used for administrative purposes for at least two years following last use unless the individual consents to disposal
regulatoryFindings.description: Recording was destroyed within 10 days instead of being retained for two years
violations: Recording was destroyed within 10 days instead of being retained for two years
DND relied on the complainant's signature on minutes as consent to disposal, but the signature only acknowledged receipt of the minutes, not agreement with contents or consent to destruction

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. DND was encouraged to develop and implement a written policy addressing collection, retention, and disposal of audio recordings from PRB hearings, with specific application of Privacy Act Section 6 requirements. In the interim, DND was recommended to retain PRB recordings or verbatim transcriptions for a minimum of two years unless express consent to earlier disposal is obtained from the affected individual. Additionally, it was noted that DND should proactively offer official records created from proceedings to affected individuals and should not refuse disclosure of such records.
companyNow: The Department of National Defence continues to operate as Canada's primary defence institution, now operating under updated privacy policies and procedures for record retention following enforcement actions.
dataType: Employment history, performance evaluations, personal opinions, witness statements, audio recordings of disciplinary proceedings
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 6(1) – retention of personal information used for administrative purposes
Privacy Act Section 6(2) – accuracy and completeness of personal information
Privacy Regulations Section 4 – minimum two-year retention period

companyDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada (VAC) is a federal government department responsible for administering pension and benefits programs for Canadian veterans and eligible members of the Canadian Armed Forces and RCMP.
companyLongDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada is a Crown corporation and federal department that adjudicates and administers disability pensions, health benefits, and compensation programs for Canadian veterans, serving and former members of the Canadian Armed Forces, and eligible RCMP members. In 2002, VAC assumed responsibility for administering disability pension claims for RCMP members under a Memorandum of Understanding. The department operates under the Pension Act and Privacy Act frameworks and maintains multiple personal information banks containing sensitive medical and financial data about beneficiaries.
caseDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada (VAC) disclosed sensitive personal medical and financial information about an RCMP member to the RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre without proper consent or clear legal authorization. The disclosure included medical diagnoses, disability percentages, and detailed financial information about pension awards. This practice was systemic, affecting multiple RCMP employees between 2002 and 2010, continuing even after the RCMP requested VAC limit information sharing in 2005.
violationSummary: VAC disclosed personal medical and financial information to the RCMP without informed consent or adequate legal basis. The disclosure was unauthorized under the Privacy Act because: (1) informed consent could not be established from inadequate privacy notices; (2) the disclosure was not a consistent use as described in the Privacy Act; (3) the RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre had no demonstrated need for the sensitive personal information shared.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Veterans Affairs Canada disclosed sensitive medical diagnoses, disability percentages, and detailed financial information about RCMP members to the RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre.
whyTheyWereWrong: RCMP members' medical diagnoses and financial pension details were exposed to personnel who had no legitimate need for this sensitive information, compromising their privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: VAC claimed the disclosure of personal information to the RCMP was authorized under paragraph 8(2)(a) of the Privacy Act as a use consistent with the purpose for which information was collected.
claimsVsReality.reality: The RCMP did not require detailed medical diagnoses or specific disability percentages to administer pension payments; only total payment amounts were necessary. VAC's own policy change in 2005 confirmed that medical diagnoses should not have been routinely disclosed to the National Compensation Policy Centre.

claimsVsReality.claim: VAC argued that disclosure was necessary because RCMP members are not eligible for provincially insured health services and the RCMP is responsible for medical and dental treatment under the Canadian Health Act and RCMP Regulation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Memorandum of Understanding between VAC and the RCMP allocated health benefit administration to VAC, not to the RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre. Information sharing was not addressed in the MOU, and the RCMP's own 2005 policy directive requested that only summary information (name, regimental number, province, pensioned disability, and percentage) be provided to Health Services Officers, not full medical diagnoses to administrative centres.

claimsVsReality.claim: VAC's disclosure practices were consistent with the stated 'Consistent Uses' in Personal Information Bank VAC/PPU-055, which permitted sharing with government institutions requiring information to determine entitlements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre was not a health services provider and did not require detailed medical information or complete pension decisions to process payments. The description of 'Consistent Uses' did not specifically authorize disclosure to employers or administrative policy centres, and the RCMP itself proactively requested VAC limit and modify the scope of information being shared beginning in 2005.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 & 8(1) - Personal information can only be disclosed with consent or under authorized categories
regulatoryFindings.description: VAC disclosed medical diagnoses, disability assessment percentages, and detailed financial information to the RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre without informed consent from the affected individual
violations: VAC disclosed medical diagnoses, disability assessment percentages, and detailed financial information to the RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre without informed consent from the affected individual
The privacy notices (PEN 923 form declarations) provided to applicants were inadequate to establish informed consent regarding disclosure practices
No explicit consent was obtained for sharing information with the RCMP employer

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Subsection 8(2)(a) - Information may be disclosed for a use consistent with the purpose for which it was collected
regulatoryFindings.description: Information was disclosed to the National Compensation Policy Centre, but no evidence established that this office had a 'need-to-know' for medical diagnoses or financial award details
violations: Information was disclosed to the National Compensation Policy Centre, but no evidence established that this office had a 'need-to-know' for medical diagnoses or financial award details
The Memorandum of Understanding between VAC and RCMP did not justify disclosure of sensitive medical and financial information beyond what was operationally necessary
RCMP's own 2005 request to limit disclosures demonstrated that the original broad disclosures were not consistent with actual operational needs

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act - Proper information management and need-to-know principle
regulatoryFindings.description: Medical information was made accessible to employees not involved in health services provision
violations: Medical information was made accessible to employees not involved in health services provision
Financial information was made accessible to health services personnel who had no need for it
Systemic practice continued for 5 years (2005-2010) after RCMP requested limitation of disclosures
No information management agreement existed between VAC and RCMP to govern proper information flows

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. VAC's disclosure of sensitive personal medical and financial information to the RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre violated the Privacy Act. The investigation revealed this was a systemic issue affecting a significant number of RCMP employees between 2002 and 2010. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner strongly recommended that VAC update the Memorandum of Understanding with the RCMP to provide comprehensive information about proper information flows between the two institutions, including periodic reviews. VAC agreed to update the MOU and the Privacy Commissioner committed to follow-up verification within one year. The Commissioner noted that VAC's later practice (as of 2010 and updated 2013) limiting disclosures to essential information (name, regimental number, province, medical disability description, assessment percentage) and directing it only to divisional health services officers was appropriate.
companyNow: Veterans Affairs Canada continues to operate as a federal department, having since implemented stronger information governance and privacy controls following privacy complaints and regulatory findings regarding inappropriate information disclosure practices.
dataType: Medical diagnosis, psychological evaluation results, disability assessment percentage, financial information (pension amounts, retroactive payments), employment information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act, Section 3 (definition of personal information)
Privacy Act, Subsection 8(2)(a) (authorized disclosures for consistent use)

companyDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's federal law enforcement agency responsible for policing at the national level and providing contract policing services to provinces and territories.
companyLongDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's federal law enforcement agency established in 1873, operating under the RCMP Act. It serves as the national police force and provides contract policing services to Canadian provinces and territories. The RCMP also administers pension and benefits programs for its members, including disability pensions managed through a 2002 memorandum of understanding with Veterans Affairs Canada.
caseDescription: The RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre inappropriately collected sensitive personal medical and financial information from Veterans Affairs Canada regarding an RCMP member's disability pension award. The information, including medical diagnosis and detailed financial payment details, was not necessary for the RCMP's limited administrative role and violated the Privacy Act's requirement that personal information collection relate directly to an operating program or activity.
violationSummary: The RCMP systematically collected sensitive medical diagnoses and financial information beyond what was necessary for their specific administrative functions, treating the information as if they retained responsibility for health services when that had been transferred to VAC. This represents unnecessary and excessive collection of sensitive personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: The RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre collected sensitive medical diagnosis and detailed financial information from Veterans Affairs Canada regarding an RCMP member's disability.
whyTheyWereWrong: The RCMP member's medical diagnosis and financial payment details were exposed to administrative personnel with no legitimate health or benefits administration role.

claimsVsReality.claim: The RCMP needed medical diagnoses from VAC to make recommendations for supplemental health care benefits and establish medical profiles of members.
claimsVsReality.reality: The RCMP's National Compensation Policy Centre—which handles pension and insurance administration, not health services—collected the data; only dedicated health services personnel had legitimate need for such information under RCMP policy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Collection of detailed financial information about disability pension awards was necessary for RCMP operations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under the MOU, VAC assumed direct payment of pensions and administration of health benefits; the RCMP required only the total amount for interdepartmental settlement, not detailed payment information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The collection was authorized under section 4 of the Privacy Act because VAC disclosed it for a consistent use.
claimsVsReality.reality: While VAC may have disclosed for a consistent purpose, the RCMP's collection was neither necessary for its limited administrative role nor consistent with its own internal policies restricting medical information access to health services personnel only.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 - Personal information collected by a government institution must relate directly to an operating program or activity of the institution
regulatoryFindings.description: RCMP collected medical diagnosis and financial information from VAC that did not relate directly to an RCMP operating program, as these responsibilities had been transferred to VAC
violations: RCMP collected medical diagnosis and financial information from VAC that did not relate directly to an RCMP operating program, as these responsibilities had been transferred to VAC
National Compensation Policy Centre collected sensitive medical information outside its scope of human resources administration
Systemic collection of complete disability pension decision letters between 2005-2010 despite identification that the practice was not consistent with RCMP policies

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 - Personal information includes medical, financial, and employment history of identifiable individuals
regulatoryFindings.description: Medical diagnosis from psychological evaluation was unnecessarily collected and stored
violations: Medical diagnosis from psychological evaluation was unnecessarily collected and stored
Detailed financial information including retroactive and future monthly pension payments was collected without business need

regulatoryFindings.act: RCMP Health Service Manual AM II.19 Section D.4, D.5, D.6 - Medical information must be protected by confidentiality and released only to authorized personnel; no medical diagnosis shall be disclosed to management
regulatoryFindings.description: Medical information was made accessible to National Compensation Policy Centre personnel not involved in health service provision
violations: Medical information was made accessible to National Compensation Policy Centre personnel not involved in health service provision
Medical diagnosis was disclosed to non-health services personnel in violation of internal policy

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. The RCMP was directed to update its Memorandum of Understanding with Veterans Affairs Canada to provide comprehensive guidelines for the proper flow of sensitive personal information between institutions. The RCMP agreed to have its Occupational Health and Safety Branch review and update the MOU with VAC input. The office committed to follow-up monitoring within one year to verify implementation. The RCMP declined to implement further amendments to its Health Service Manual access restrictions, which the office deemed insufficient and again urged for reconsideration.
companyNow: The RCMP continues to operate as Canada's federal law enforcement agency, though it faces ongoing scrutiny regarding operational practices, transparency, and internal accountability mechanisms.
dataType: Health data, financial information, medical diagnosis, disability assessment percentage
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 4 (personal information must relate directly to an operating program or activity)
Privacy Act Section 3 (definition of personal information)
Privacy Act Paragraph 8(2)(a) (disclosure for consistent use)

companyDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is the federal law enforcement and border management agency responsible for securing Canada's borders and facilitating legitimate travel and trade.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency operates under the authority of the Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness Act and is responsible for managing over 1,200 ports of entry across Canada. Its frontline officers (BSOs) conduct security screening, inspections, and enforcement activities with members of the public daily. The agency employs thousands of uniformed personnel who interact directly with travellers and goods crossing Canadian borders.
caseDescription: CBSA employees complained that a policy requiring border services officers to wear name tags displaying their surnames instead of badge numbers violated the Privacy Act by disclosing personal information without consent. The Privacy Commissioner found that an employee's surname on a name tag worn in the course of employment relates to their duties and functions, and therefore falls within the statutory exception to 'personal information' under section 3(j) of the Privacy Act. The complaint was dismissed as not well founded.
violationSummary: Complainants alleged improper use and disclosure of personal information (surnames) without consent. However, the Commissioner found this did not constitute a violation because the information fell within the section 3(j) exception for information relating to government employees' position or functions.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: CBSA implemented a policy requiring border services officers to wear name tags displaying their surnames instead of badge numbers while on duty at ports of entry.
whyTheyWereWrong: Officers faced real threats of violence and harassment from disgruntled travellers who could use surnames combined with internet access to locate home addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: Name tags improve public recognition and reinforce officer professionalism and accountability.
claimsVsReality.reality: Officers reported real incidents of harassment and threats from travellers who used their displayed surnames combined with internet access to identify and locate them and their families.

claimsVsReality.claim: Security incidents reported by BSOs relating to name tags were all unfounded.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple incidents between 2010 and 2013 demonstrated that officers had been threatened or harassed by aggrieved travellers, confirming legitimate safety concerns.

claimsVsReality.claim: The policy aligns with best practices of partner agencies with no demonstrated safety risks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Service Canada had withdrawn an identical name tag policy in 2009 after successfully being challenged by the union representing its employees due to documented safety threats to workers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3(j) – Exception to personal information for government employees
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainants alleged surnames displayed on name tags constituted personal information subject to sections 7 and 8 protections. Commissioner found the information fell within the section 3(j) exception as it relates to employees' position/functions (front-line duties) and serves the purpose of holding the CBSA accountable.
violations: Complainants alleged surnames displayed on name tags constituted personal information subject to sections 7 and 8 protections. Commissioner found the information fell within the section 3(j) exception as it relates to employees' position/functions (front-line duties) and serves the purpose of holding the CBSA accountable.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 7 – Prohibition on use of personal information without consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainants alleged CBSA used their surnames without consent. Commissioner found no violation because surnames on name tags relate to position/function and fall within section 3(j) exception.
violations: Complainants alleged CBSA used their surnames without consent. Commissioner found no violation because surnames on name tags relate to position/function and fall within section 3(j) exception.

violations: Complainants alleged CBSA disclosed their surnames without consent. Commissioner found no violation because surnames on name tags relate to position/function and fall within section 3(j) exception.

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner concluded that the complaints were not well founded. The surname of a CBSA border services officer displayed on a name tag worn in the course of employment relates to their duties and functions and therefore falls under the statutory exception in section 3(j) of the Privacy Act. Accordingly, such information is not 'personal information' for the purposes of sections 7 and 8 of the Act, and no violation occurred. The Commissioner noted that while safety concerns were raised, those were more appropriately addressed through the Canada Labour Code complaint process.
companyNow: The CBSA remains Canada's primary border services agency, continuing to operate under the Public Safety portfolio. The name tag policy has remained in effect following the Privacy Commissioner's decision.
