companyDescription: The Public Service Commission of Canada is a federal government agency responsible for conducting investigations into staffing appointment processes under the Public Service Employment Act, including investigations into potential fraud and irregularities.
companyLongDescription: The Public Service Commission of Canada (PSC) is a government institution mandated to investigate staffing appointment processes in the federal public service, including external appointments, internal appointments, and cases involving suspected fraud or political influence. The PSC operates under the Public Service Employment Act and conducts investigations through fact-finding meetings, written submissions, and individual interviews. In this case, the PSC's investigator collected sensitive medical information from a complainant and subsequently shared it with all witnesses in the investigation via a factual report, claiming procedural fairness principles justified the broad disclosure.
caseDescription: The Public Service Commission of Canada disclosed a complainant's detailed medical information (a doctor's letter) to all witnesses in a fraud investigation, sharing it via a factual report without establishing that the witnesses had a need to know this sensitive information. The PSC justified the disclosure under procedural fairness principles, but the Privacy Commissioner found this disclosure was not necessary to meet procedural fairness requirements and violated the Privacy Act's use and disclosure provisions.
violationSummary: The PSC disclosed sensitive medical information to individuals who had no demonstrated need to know it. While procedural fairness may justify some disclosures, an individual would not reasonably expect their medical details to be shared with all investigation participants. The disclosure was excessive and not limited to what was necessary.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Public Service Commission of Canada disclosed a complainant's detailed medical information from a doctor's letter to all witnesses in a fraud investigation via a factual report.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant's medical details were exposed to four witnesses who had no legitimate reason to access them, potentially compromising her privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: All witnesses were 'affected persons' under the Investigator's Guide and thus required the full factual report including the complainant's medical information for procedural fairness
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner found that the PSC had not established a persuasive rationale for why each witness needed access to the complainant's medical details, and that procedural fairness could be achieved through limited disclosure of only necessary information

claimsVsReality.claim: The disclosure was authorized under paragraph 8(2)(a) of the Privacy Act as a use consistent with the purpose for which information was obtained
claimsVsReality.reality: While the Commissioner acknowledged procedural fairness could justify some disclosure, any such disclosure must be limited to only what is necessary to achieve that purpose, and the PSC had not made this determination in this case

claimsVsReality.claim: The PSC's standard practice of sharing full factual reports with all investigation participants was appropriate and necessary
claimsVsReality.reality: The PSC subsequently acknowledged it does not automatically share full factual reports with all participants and committed to enhanced checks, balances, and clearer definitions of 'affected persons' to avoid excessive disclosures

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8(1) - Personal information can only be disclosed with consent or under authorized exceptions
regulatoryFindings.description: PSC disclosed complainant's doctor's letter to all witnesses without consent
violations: PSC disclosed complainant's doctor's letter to all witnesses without consent
Disclosure was not authorized under paragraph 8(2)(a) as it was not necessary for procedural fairness

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 7 - Information shall not be used except for the purpose collected or a consistent use
regulatoryFindings.description: While PSC obtained medical information for fraud investigation purposes, disclosing it to witnesses exceeded what was necessary and what individuals would reasonably expect
violations: While PSC obtained medical information for fraud investigation purposes, disclosing it to witnesses exceeded what was necessary and what individuals would reasonably expect

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 - Collection must relate directly to an operating program or activity
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection of doctor's letter was authorized, but subsequent disclosure to all witnesses was not justified as necessary
violations: Collection of doctor's letter was authorized, but subsequent disclosure to all witnesses was not justified as necessary

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. The PSC contravened subsection 8(1) of the Privacy Act by disclosing the complainant's medical information without authorization. Following the investigation, the PSC committed to implementing enhanced procedures including: (1) training investigators to be careful with medical and sensitive issues; (2) obtaining clearer consent or establishing documented need-to-know before disclosure; (3) revising all factual reports involving medical information before circulation; (4) re-examining the definition of 'affected persons'; and (5) applying principles of limited, proportional disclosure while balancing procedural fairness. The Privacy Commissioner committed to follow-up monitoring within one year to ensure implementation of these changes.
companyNow: The PSC continues to operate as Canada's federal staffing oversight body. Following this case, the PSC implemented enhanced protocols requiring approval for disclosure of sensitive information and reaffirmed its commitment to 'need-to-know' and 'minimal disclosure' principles.
dataType: Health data, medical information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) Section 8(1) - Unauthorized disclosure without consent
Privacy Act (Canada) Paragraph 8(2)(a) - Disclosure not justified as consistent use

companyDescription: Canada Post Corporation is Canada's national postal service provider, operating mail delivery and parcel services across the country.
companyLongDescription: Canada Post Corporation is a Crown corporation established under the Canada Post Corporation Act to provide postal services for the collection, transmission, and delivery of messages, information, funds, and goods within Canada and internationally. The company operates a network of retail postal outlets and delivery services. In 2015, it faced a privacy complaint regarding its electronic signature capture and online display practices for parcel tracking confirmation.
caseDescription: Canada Post collected electronic signatures from mail recipients for delivery confirmation and displayed digitized signature images on its online tracking website without implementing adequate security controls. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found that while the collection and disclosure of signatures for parcel tracking was lawful under the Privacy Act, Canada Post had failed to adequately safeguard the digitized signatures from unauthorized access, use, or disclosure due to weak security protocols and the ability to manipulate tracking numbers to retrieve multiple signature records.
violationSummary: Canada Post failed to implement adequate technical and organizational safeguards to protect digitized signatures displayed online. Specific security failures included absence of HTTPS encryption, ability to copy and manipulate signature images with basic software, and vulnerability to tracking number manipulation allowing unauthorized retrieval of delivery records containing signatures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Canada Post displayed digitized signature images on its online tracking website without implementing adequate security controls such as HTTPS encryption.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' signatures were exposed to unauthorized access and manipulation because the tracking website lacked basic security protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: The label on the electronic signature device clearly informs addressees they can opt-out of having their signature displayed online.
claimsVsReality.reality: The label statement 'I agree my signature may be viewed online' was ambiguous and most addressees assumed signing was mandatory; the label was missing at multiple postal outlets and not consistently applied.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers have other options to decline signature display and these are widely communicated by service representatives.
claimsVsReality.reality: Alternative options (asking delivery agents, contacting customer service, consulting personal information banks) were not clearly communicated and had no evidence of being widely understood or promoted by staff.

claimsVsReality.claim: The current security measures (image degradation, watermarking, signature suppression after 45 days) adequately protect signatures from misuse.
claimsVsReality.reality: Security testing revealed the website lacked HTTPS encryption, degraded JPG images could be copied and manipulated with basic software, and tracking numbers could be easily altered to retrieve multiple delivery records with signatures.

claimsVsReality.claim: The process has been in place since 2003 and has been continuously improved to meet evolving privacy and security needs.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite being in place for over a decade, the tracking website had fundamental security gaps including lack of HTTPS protocol and susceptibility to tracking number manipulation that left customer signatures vulnerable.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 3 – Signatures constitute personal information as they are identifiable to individuals and represent personal calligraphic expression
regulatoryFindings.description: Canada Post collected and disclosed digitized signature images without recognizing them as sensitive personal information requiring enhanced protection
violations: Canada Post collected and disclosed digitized signature images without recognizing them as sensitive personal information requiring enhanced protection

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 4 – Personal information collection must relate directly to an operating program or activity
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection of signatures for proof of delivery met this requirement; however, no finding of violation
violations: Collection of signatures for proof of delivery met this requirement; however, no finding of violation

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8 – Personal information can only be disclosed with consent or under permitted categories; institutions must safeguard information from unauthorized access, use, or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: While disclosure to senders was permitted under Section 8(2)(a), Canada Post failed to implement adequate controls to protect signatures from unauthorized access
violations: While disclosure to senders was permitted under Section 8(2)(a), Canada Post failed to implement adequate controls to protect signatures from unauthorized access
Signatures displayed online without HTTPS encryption
Signature images could be copied and manipulated using basic software
Tracking numbers could be manipulated to retrieve multiple delivery records with signatures
Combination of signature image with identifying information (name, destination city) increased re-identification risk

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner determined that the complaint regarding adequacy of opt-out notice was not well-founded, as Canada Post is not required to obtain consent to disclose signatures for their original purpose. However, the Commissioner found that Canada Post had not adequately safeguarded digitized signatures displayed online and constituted an increased vulnerability for unauthorized disclosure. As Canada Post accepted the Commissioner's recommendations and committed to implementing enhanced security controls (including HTTPS protocol implementation, which was confirmed completed at time of report), the matter was resolved conditionally. Canada Post was required to follow up with the Office in 6 months to confirm implementation of privacy and security controls. The Commissioner also reminded Canada Post to ensure consistency in affixing opt-out labels across all postal outlets and to train staff on signature use and disclosure procedures. The Commissioner further recommended Canada Post reevaluate the necessity of capturing signatures for online parcel tracking, suggesting there may be less privacy-intrusive alternatives.
companyNow: Canada Post continues to operate as Canada's primary postal service provider, delivering mail and parcels nationwide.
dataType: Biometric data (signatures), personal identifiers (name, delivery address)
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) Section 3 – Definition of personal information
Privacy Act (Canada) Section 8(2)(a) – Permitted disclosure for original purpose

companyDescription: A Canadian life insurance company providing pension plan administration and member statement services.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian life insurance company that manages pension plans and issues regular statements to plan members. The company serves as a custodian of sensitive personal and financial information for pension beneficiaries across Canada. In 2015, it discovered a mailing error that inadvertently exposed personal information of 53 pension plan members.
caseDescription: A life insurance company's use of a new window envelope with an enlarged window during mailing inadvertently exposed personal information of 53 pension plan members, including SINs and other sensitive data. The company discovered the risk ten days after mailing and promptly notified affected individuals, offered credit monitoring, and implemented remedial measures to prevent recurrence.
violationSummary: Personal information became visible and potentially accessible to unintended recipients through physical mail exposure due to envelope design failure, constituting an unintended disclosure of sensitive data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The company mailed pension plan statements using a new window envelope with an enlarged window that inadvertently exposed personal information including SINs, dates of birth.
whyTheyWereWrong: Fifty-three pension plan members had their social insurance numbers, dates of birth, spouse names, and beneficiary information exposed through the mail, creating identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company was using best practices in envelope design and mailing procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company switched to a new window envelope design with an enlarged window without adequate testing, resulting in exposure of sensitive personal data during mail transit.

claimsVsReality.claim: The risk was discovered immediately after implementation.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not discover the risk until ten days after the statements had already been mailed to affected members.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.8 – Organizations must protect personal information by using appropriate safeguards against theft, loss, unauthorized access, disclosure, and alteration
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to adequately assess envelope design before deployment for a mailing containing sensitive personal information including SINs
violations: Failure to adequately assess envelope design before deployment for a mailing containing sensitive personal information including SINs
Design flaw in window envelope allowed personal information printed below address lines to become visible if statements shifted during mail transport

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 1.2 – Organizations are responsible for personal information in their possession
regulatoryFindings.description: Insufficient quality control and testing of new envelope design prior to use in mass mailing of sensitive documents
violations: Insufficient quality control and testing of new envelope design prior to use in mass mailing of sensitive documents

outcome: The insurance company notified all 53 affected individuals by letter, explaining the incident, what information may have been compromised, and remedial actions. The company offered one year of free credit monitoring, ceased use of the problematic envelopes, added security alerts to affected accounts, invited members to add security questions for stronger authentication, and explored options to reformat or remove personal information from future statements. The company also notified the Privacy Commissioner's office and demonstrated implementation of best practices in incident response.
dataType: Social Insurance Number (SIN), date of birth, certificate number, spouse's name, named beneficiary information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.7 (Accuracy of Personal Information)
PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.8 (Protection of Personal Information)

companyDescription: An investment brokerage offering self-directed investment accounts where clients execute their own trades without receiving investment advice from the firm.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian investment brokerage that provides self-directed investment account services, allowing retail clients to manage their own investment decisions without suitability advice from the firm. As a securities dealer, the firm is regulated by IIROC (Investment Industry Regulatory Organization of Canada) and subject to provincial securities legislation and anti-money laundering requirements. The firm collects Know Your Client information as required by regulatory obligations, including details about client financial status and family relationships to identify potential conflicts of interest and comply with insider trading and AML regulations.
caseDescription: An individual complained that an investment brokerage was collecting excessive personal information (net worth, marital status, spouse's occupation) as a condition for opening a self-directed investment account. The brokerage justified the collection requirements under IIROC's Know Your Client rules, anti-money laundering obligations under the Proceeds of Crime Act, and provincial securities legislation. The investigation found the collection was justified and necessary for regulatory compliance.
violationSummary: The complainant alleged unnecessary interrogation/collection of personal information beyond what should be needed for a self-directed account. However, the investigation determined the collection was legally required, so no actual violation was found.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: An investment brokerage required applicants to provide personal information including net worth, marital status.
whyTheyWereWrong: The brokerage was not wrong; the information collection was justified by regulatory requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant believed that a self-directed investment account should not require spouse's occupation, marital status, and net worth information because the brokerage would not be determining suitability.
claimsVsReality.reality: IIROC rules, anti-money laundering legislation, and provincial securities laws required the brokerage to collect complete Know Your Client information and identify potential insiders or control persons, regardless of whether the account was suitability-exempt.

claimsVsReality.claim: The brokerage was over-collecting personal information beyond what was necessary for account opening.
claimsVsReality.reality: The brokerage collected only information mandated by IIROC Dealer Member Rules 1300 and 2500, the Proceeds of Crime Act, and provincial securities legislation to identify suspicious transactions, insiders, and control persons.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.3 – Organizations must not require consent to collection of information beyond that required to fulfill explicitly specified and legitimate purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Complainant alleged brokerage was collecting information (net worth, marital status, spouse's occupation) beyond what was necessary for a self-directed account
violations: Complainant alleged brokerage was collecting information (net worth, marital status, spouse's occupation) beyond what was necessary for a self-directed account

regulatoryFindings.act: IIROC Dealer Member Rule 1300 – Dealer Members must use due diligence to learn essential facts relative to every customer
regulatoryFindings.description: Brokerage demonstrated it was collecting information required by IIROC KYC requirements applicable to all account types
violations: Brokerage demonstrated it was collecting information required by IIROC KYC requirements applicable to all account types

violations: Brokerage demonstrated information collection was necessary to meet AML obligations for suspicious transaction monitoring and identification of politically exposed persons

regulatoryFindings.description: Brokerage demonstrated marital status and spouse's occupation were necessary to comply with insider reporting and control position thresholds
violations: Brokerage demonstrated marital status and spouse's occupation were necessary to comply with insider reporting and control position thresholds

outcome: The complaint was found not to be well-founded. The Office determined that the requested personal information (net worth, marital status, spouse's occupation) was required by the brokerage to comply with IIROC's Know Your Client requirements, anti-money laundering requirements under the Proceeds of Crime Act, and provincial securities legislation. The self-directed nature of the account did not eliminate these regulatory obligations. No remediation or penalty was imposed.

companyDescription: Peoples Trust is a federally regulated Canadian trust company headquartered in Vancouver, BC, offering financial services including mortgages, deposits, and secured credit cards through online and physical channels.
companyLongDescription: Peoples Trust is a Canadian financial institution that provides retail banking and credit services to customers across multiple channels including an online application portal, telephone contact centre, and physical branches in Vancouver, Calgary, and Toronto. The company specializes in mortgages, deposit accounts, and secured and prepaid credit card products. As a federally regulated trust company, it is subject to strict privacy and security requirements under Canadian law.
caseDescription: Peoples Trust failed to implement adequate technological and organizational safeguards to protect customer personal information collected through its online application portal. Sensitive data including social insurance numbers and dates of birth were stored unnecessarily, in unencrypted form and duplicate on a vulnerable web server with an obsolete, unpatched web editor, resulting in a breach affecting 12,000 customers. The organization also retained this information far longer than necessary, outside the scope of its retention policies.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement appropriate security safeguards proportionate to the sensitivity of personal information collected, stored unencrypted data indefinitely on vulnerable servers, failed to patch known vulnerabilities, and lacked ongoing monitoring and maintenance systems. This is a classic information security failure resulting in unauthorized access and disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: Peoples Trust stored sensitive customer data including social insurance numbers and dates of birth in unencrypted duplicate form on a vulnerable web server with an unpatched obsolete web editor,.
whyTheyWereWrong: The failure to encrypt or securely segregate customer data resulted in a breach that exposed 12,000 individuals to identity theft risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: Peoples Trust was unaware the obsolete web editor remained on the server and posed a security risk.
claimsVsReality.reality: The old web editor had a widely publicized vulnerability disclosed in February 2013, and Peoples Trust took no steps to patch or remove it despite being on the server since 2005.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer application data needed to be stored on the web server for processing purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Application information was sent to the internal banking system immediately upon submission and did not need to remain stored in unencrypted form on the web server; data stored there dated back to December 2007.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had adequate safeguards in place for a financial institution.
claimsVsReality.reality: Peoples Trust lacked a comprehensive Information Security Policy, performed no security monitoring or vulnerability testing from 2005-2013, and contracted with a third-party web designer with limited financial services experience without stipulating minimum security requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule I Principle 4.7 – Personal information shall be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement adequate technological and organizational safeguards proportionate to the sensitivity of financial and identification data (SINs, DOBs, employment information)
violations: Failed to implement adequate technological and organizational safeguards proportionate to the sensitivity of financial and identification data (SINs, DOBs, employment information)
Stored sensitive customer information in unencrypted format indefinitely on a web server
Maintained an obsolete, vulnerable web editor on the server for 8 years without updates despite known publicized vulnerability as of February 2013
Did not implement ongoing monitoring or maintenance from 2005 to 2013
Did not establish minimum information security requirements in contracts with third-party web developers

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule I Principle 4.5 and 4.5.2 – Personal information shall be retained only as long as necessary to fulfill identified purposes; organizations must develop retention guidelines and procedures
regulatoryFindings.description: Stored customer application information on the web server indefinitely and in duplicate after it had already been transferred to the secure internal banking system
violations: Stored customer application information on the web server indefinitely and in duplicate after it had already been transferred to the secure internal banking system
Retained data from as far back as December 20, 2007 without knowledge or authorization
Retention fell outside the scope of the organization's formal retention policies and schedules
Information was retained unnecessarily beyond what was required for processing applications

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule I Principle 4.1.4(a) – Organizations shall implement procedures to protect personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Lacked comprehensive information security policy addressing systems that collect, use, and disclose personal information
violations: Lacked comprehensive information security policy addressing systems that collect, use, and disclose personal information
Only had generic internal security awareness training document, not a detailed policy for the organization's systems
Did not implement security procedures in the development, implementation, and redesign of the web application portal

outcome: The matter was found to be well-founded and resolved. While no monetary penalty was imposed, Peoples Trust was required to implement comprehensive remedial measures including: (1) complete redesign of the online application web portal with encrypted direct transfer of data to secure internal systems, eliminating unnecessary storage on web servers; (2) implementation of continuous automated monitoring of web servers to identify vulnerabilities; (3) establishment of regular patching and updating schedules; (4) development and implementation of a comprehensive Information Security Policy communicated to all employees; (5) creation of a Privacy Information Security Committee of senior management; (6) notification to all 12,000 affected individuals with tailored letters; (7) placement of six-year credit alerts with Equifax and TransUnion; (8) notification of financial institutions whose EFT data was exposed; and (9) alteration of authentication procedures using information not exposed in the breach. The Commissioner was satisfied that these substantial, timely remedial actions adequately addressed the violations identified.
companyNow: Peoples Trust continues to operate as a federally regulated Canadian financial institution. Following the 2015 breach, the company implemented comprehensive security redesigns and established formal information security governance.
dataType: Names, dates of birth, social insurance numbers, addresses, employment information, contact information, mother's maiden names, banking information

PIPEDA Schedule I Principle 4.5 (retention only as long as necessary)
PIPEDA Schedule I Principle 4.5.2 (retention guidelines and procedures)
PIPEDA Schedule I Principle 4.5.3 (destruction of information no longer required)

companyDescription: A Canadian department store that operated retail locations and used video surveillance systems to monitor customer activity.
companyLongDescription: The department store was a brick-and-mortar retailer operating in Canada during the 2010s. It maintained video surveillance systems throughout its locations to deter and identify suspected shoplifters. The store initially believed it had legal authority to publicly display photographs of suspected shoplifters based on advice from police and legal counsel. However, the store was unaware that PIPEDA's personal information protections applied to such photographs, even when used for loss prevention purposes.
caseDescription: A department store displayed photographs of individuals suspected of shoplifting on a public bulletin board near its entrance without the individuals' consent. The store relied on advice from police and legal counsel that the practice was permissible. The Office found that the photographs constituted personal information under PIPEDA and could not be publicly disclosed without consent.
violationSummary: The store publicly disclosed personal information (photographs) of identifiable individuals without their knowledge or consent, making it a classic case of unauthorized secondary disclosure under the Privacy Taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The department store displayed photographs of individuals suspected of shoplifting on a public bulletin board near its entrance without obtaining their consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: People's photographs were publicly displayed without permission, exposing them to potential harassment, false accusations, and reputational harm when they had not been convicted of any crime.

claimsVsReality.claim: Police and legal counsel advised that the store could post pictures from video surveillance of alleged shoplifters.
claimsVsReality.reality: PIPEDA prohibits such public disclosure of personal information (photographs) without consent, regardless of the purpose or prior advice received.

claimsVsReality.claim: Displaying photographs was an appropriate loss prevention measure.
claimsVsReality.reality: The individuals pictured had not been convicted or proven guilty, and public display exposed them to false accusations and potential harassment.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to obtain meaningful consent before collecting, using or disclosing personal information, and prohibits using personal information for purposes other than those for which it was collected without further consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: The store publicly displayed photographs of individuals without their consent
violations: The store publicly displayed photographs of individuals without their consent
The photographs were used for the purpose of identifying suspected shoplifters, a secondary use not originally consented to by the individuals
The store did not obtain consent from the pictured individuals before posting their images on a public bulletin board

outcome: The store agreed to remove the photographs from the public bulletin board and discontinue the practice of publicly displaying images of suspected shoplifters. The store agreed to handle such matters through the police in the future, rather than through public disclosure.
dataType: Photographs, biometric data (facial features)
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 (Limiting Use, Disclosure and Retention)

companyDescription: A Canadian telecommunications provider offering email and technical support services to residential customers.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian telecom provider that offers email services and remote technical support to help customers troubleshoot connectivity and email configuration issues. The company employs technical support representatives who are authorized to remotely access customer computers with consent to diagnose and resolve service problems. The organization has policies and mandatory procedures designed to govern employee access and conduct during support interactions.
caseDescription: A telecom provider's technical support representative remotely accessed a customer's computer to troubleshoot email issues but inadvertently configured email forwarding without the customer's consent, causing her emails—including one containing a temporary password—to be automatically forwarded to an acquaintance. The representative also failed to follow mandatory troubleshooting procedures and violated the customer's privacy by disclosing her personal information.
violationSummary: The representative disclosed the individual's personal information (emails and temporary password) to a third party (the acquaintance) without the individual's knowledge or consent. The unauthorized configuration of email forwarding settings resulted in an unintended disclosure of sensitive communications.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A technical support representative remotely accessed a customer's computer to fix email issues but inadvertently configured email forwarding to an acquaintance without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's sensitive emails, including a temporary password, were exposed to an unauthorized third party, compromising her account security and privacy without her knowledge or agreement.

claimsVsReality.claim: The telecom provider offered coaching for the first representative, who had a history of non-compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The matter was only brought to the attention of a senior manager, who never responded.

claimsVsReality.claim: The telecom provider implemented progressive disciplinary measures for the first representative.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee citation provided was not signed by anyone in authority and covered a period outside the events in the complaint.

claimsVsReality.claim: The telecom provider terminated the first representative's employment.
claimsVsReality.reality: The representative submitted a letter of resignation; the provider could not prove termination.

claimsVsReality.claim: The telecom provider sent a communiqué to the relevant technical support team about the importance of following mandatory procedures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The telecom provider was unable to prove it had sent any special communiqué about procedures following the incident.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires that the knowledge and consent of the individual are required for the collection, use, or disclosure of personal information, except where inappropriate.
regulatoryFindings.description: The telecom provider disclosed the individual's personal information (emails and temporary password) to an unintended recipient without her knowledge or consent by configuring unauthorized email forwarding
violations: The telecom provider disclosed the individual's personal information (emails and temporary password) to an unintended recipient without her knowledge or consent by configuring unauthorized email forwarding
The technical support representative accessed and modified the customer's email settings beyond the scope of the customer's consent

outcome: The complaint was determined to be well-founded. The telecom provider was required to ensure accurate and complete representations to the Commissioner in future investigations. The organization confirmed existing preventive measures including employee code of conduct requirements, coaching, auditing of compliance with mandatory procedures, and appropriate discipline for misuse. No monetary penalty was imposed, but the provider was encouraged to exercise greater diligence in factual representations to the Office.
dataType: Email communications, password information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (Consent for Collection, Use, or Disclosure)

companyDescription: A local cable television provider offering television services in the Northwest Territories, Canada.
companyLongDescription: The cable provider is a local telecommunications company operating in the Northwest Territories, Canada, providing cable television services to residential and commercial customers. In December 2015, the company adopted a debt collection practice it believed was permissible under privacy law by posting customer account information online. The company later complied with privacy authorities and removed the sensitive information.
caseDescription: A cable television provider posted a list of customers with overdue accounts and their debt amounts on a municipal Facebook page without consent. The provider believed the practice was permissible by analogy to municipal property tax arrears publications. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada determined that while PIPEDA's debt collection exemption allows disclosure to third-party collectors, it does not authorize public dissemination of debtor information without consent.
violationSummary: The cable provider publicly disclosed personal information (names and amounts owed) of customers without consent on social media. While PIPEDA's paragraph 7(3)(b) permits disclosure to third-party debt collectors for collection purposes, it does not extend to public dissemination, making this an unauthorized disclosure of sensitive financial information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A cable television provider posted a list of customers with overdue accounts and their debt amounts on a municipal Facebook page without obtaining consent from the affected customers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' names and debt amounts were publicly exposed online, damaging their reputations and causing potential embarrassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The practice is permissible by analogy to municipal property tax arrears publications, which are public by law.
claimsVsReality.reality: PIPEDA's debt collection exemption permits disclosure only to third-party debt collectors acting as agents, not public dissemination without consent. Property tax publications are required by separate territorial legislation, which does not apply to private debt collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: The debt collection exemption in PIPEDA paragraph 7(3)(b) authorizes public disclosure of debtor information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The exemption permits disclosure to third-party collectors for debt collection purposes only, not public posting on social media platforms without the debtors' knowledge or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA paragraph 7(3)(b) - Debt Collection Exemption
regulatoryFindings.description: Cable provider misapplied the exemption to publicly disclose debtor information on Facebook without consent
violations: Cable provider misapplied the exemption to publicly disclose debtor information on Facebook without consent
The exemption only permits disclosure to third-party debt collectors acting as agents, not public dissemination

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA General Privacy Principles - Consent and Appropriate Disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Posted customer names and debt amounts publicly on social media without obtaining consent
violations: Posted customer names and debt amounts publicly on social media without obtaining consent
Did not limit disclosure to purposes authorized under law or legitimate business practices

outcome: The cable provider agreed to remove the Facebook posting containing customers' personal information. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner provided guidance distinguishing between lawful legislative requirements (such as property tax publication mandates) and unauthorized public disclosure of debtor information. The provider was educated on the proper scope of PIPEDA's debt collection exemption, which permits only disclosure to authorized third-party collectors, not public dissemination.
companyNow: The company continues to operate as a cable television provider in the Northwest Territories following the compliance order.
dataType: Customer names, account status, amounts owed
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA paragraph 7(3)(b) - misapplication of debt collection exemption
PIPEDA principles on consent and appropriate disclosure

companyDescription: A Canadian retail company that operates delivery services to customers' homes.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian retailer that processes customer orders for home delivery. The company collects customer contact information including phone numbers as part of its delivery operations. The retailer employs delivery personnel who are provided with work phones to facilitate customer contact during delivery. The company is subject to PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) regulations in Canada.
caseDescription: A delivery employee transferred a customer's phone number from his work phone to his personal device without authorization and sent inappropriate text messages to the customer. The retailer initially failed to adequately address the customer's complaint but subsequently implemented remedial measures including disciplinary action, mandatory privacy retraining for all employees with access to customer data, and new BYOD policies.
violationSummary: The employee improperly transferred personal information (phone number) to an unauthorized personal device and used it for purposes unrelated to the original collection. This constitutes unauthorized disclosure and secondary use of personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A delivery employee transferred a customer's phone number from his work phone to his personal device without authorization and sent inappropriate text messages to the customer.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's phone number was used without her consent for personal contact, exposing her to unwanted.

claimsVsReality.claim: The retailer disapproves of employees transferring customer information to personal devices.
claimsVsReality.reality: An employee successfully transferred a customer's phone number to his personal phone and used it to contact the customer without authorization, indicating the policy was not adequately communicated or enforced before the incident.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's customer service manager would address the customer's complaint appropriately.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer initially experienced a lack of concern from the assigned manager and felt stonewalled when seeking information to escalate her complaint, requiring intervention by the privacy regulator to achieve resolution.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 1.2 – Organizations are accountable for personal information under their control and must implement policies and practices to give effect to privacy principles
regulatoryFindings.description: Retailer failed to have adequate controls preventing transfer of customer information to personal devices
violations: Retailer failed to have adequate controls preventing transfer of customer information to personal devices
Retailer failed to adequately investigate and respond to initial customer complaint

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 3 – Personal information shall be collected, used, and disclosed only for the purposes for which it was collected
regulatoryFindings.description: Employee transferred customer phone number collected for delivery purposes to personal device
violations: Employee transferred customer phone number collected for delivery purposes to personal device
Employee used phone number for personal communications unrelated to delivery

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 – Personal information shall be used or disclosed for purposes other than those for which it was collected only with consent, or as required by law
regulatoryFindings.description: No consent obtained from customer for transfer of her phone number to employee's personal device or for personal communication
violations: No consent obtained from customer for transfer of her phone number to employee's personal device or for personal communication

outcome: The retailer implemented the following remedial measures: (1) disciplinary action against the employee; (2) mandatory privacy retraining for all employees with access to customer information, completed within one month; (3) new policy requiring delivery employees to immediately return to warehouse when work phone is faulty, preventing unauthorized transfer of customer data to personal devices; (4) company president personally met with affected customer. The customer was satisfied with the remedial actions.
dataType: Phone number, personal contact information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 3 (Collection, Use, and Disclosure Limitation)
PIPEDA Principle 4.2 (Limiting Use, Disclosure, and Retention)

companyDescription: Second Roofer is a roofing company that provides estimation and installation services for residential roof repairs and replacements.
companyLongDescription: Second Roofer is a roofing contractor that engages sub-contracted estimators to provide quotes and facilitate sales for customers seeking roof repair and replacement services. The company collects personal information from customers during the estimation and contracting process, including financial details and contractual history. In 2015, the company faced a privacy enforcement action under PIPEDA after an estimator disclosed customer information to a competitor without authorization.
caseDescription: A roofing company's sub-contracted estimator disclosed a customer's personal financial information and contractual history to a competitor without the customer's knowledge or consent. The disclosure occurred through correspondence between the estimator and the first roofer, where the estimator shared opinions and details about the customer's dealings beyond the scope of the original collection purpose.
violationSummary: The estimator acting as the second roofer's agent disclosed personal information (financial situation and contractual dealings) to a third party (the first roofer) without the individual's knowledge or consent, and in a manner that exceeded the purposes for which the information was originally collected.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A roofing company's sub-contracted estimator disclosed a customer's personal financial information and contractual history to a competitor without the customer's knowledge or consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's personal financial details and dealings with the roofing company were shared with a competitor, exposing the customer to potential business disadvantage.

claimsVsReality.claim: The estimator was merely facilitating a discussion about roof issues with the first roofer by sharing the estimator's name.
claimsVsReality.reality: The estimator disclosed detailed personal financial information, contractual history, and opinions about the customer's motives and financial difficulties to the competitor without any authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: The privacy policy in place was sufficient to govern sub-contractor conduct.
claimsVsReality.reality: The privacy policy existed but had not been formalized in a binding agreement with the sub-contractor, leaving no contractual obligation to comply with privacy commitments.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Organizations must not disclose personal information without knowledge and consent, except in circumstances permitted by subsection 7(3)
regulatoryFindings.description: Estimator disclosed personal financial information and contractual history to first roofer without individual's knowledge or consent
violations: Estimator disclosed personal financial information and contractual history to first roofer without individual's knowledge or consent
Disclosure went beyond purposes for which information was originally collected (roof estimate and warranty claims)

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA – Organizations are responsible for personal information handling practices of sub-contractors acting on their behalf
regulatoryFindings.description: Second roofer failed to ensure sub-contracted estimator adhered to privacy obligations despite having a privacy policy in place
violations: Second roofer failed to ensure sub-contracted estimator adhered to privacy obligations despite having a privacy policy in place

outcome: The second roofer implemented measures to establish formal agreements with sub-contractors requiring them to adhere to the company's privacy policy and to receive training on privacy obligations. The matter was found to be well-founded and resolved based on these remedial measures taken during the investigation.
companyNow: Second Roofer implemented privacy controls including formal sub-contractor agreements requiring adherence to the company's privacy policy and staff training on privacy obligations.
dataType: Personal financial information, contractual history, contact information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA subsection 7(3) (Limitations on Use and Disclosure)

companyDescription: A Canadian pension and benefit provider that administers employment pension plans and insurance benefits for members.
companyLongDescription: This organization manages pension accounts and employment benefits for plan members, handling sensitive personal information including unique identifiers, contact details, and insurance-related documentation. The company processes member requests for address changes and maintains member account records. It is subject to PIPEDA (Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act) requirements for safeguarding personal information.
caseDescription: A pension and benefit provider disclosed a client's unique identifier to an unauthorized third party and failed to maintain accurate contact information after misdirecting five mailings containing sensitive personal information. The provider did not properly authenticate a caller before providing the complainant's ID number, and failed to detect and correct the erroneous address change despite returned mail over several months.
violationSummary: The provider disclosed the complainant's unique identifier to a third party without consent, and subsequently sent multiple mailings containing sensitive personal information to the wrong address due to inadequate authentication and address verification procedures.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The pension and benefit provider disclosed a client's unique identifier to an unauthorized third party without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The client lost insurance coverage and faced financial penalties because misdirected mailings prevented her from receiving time-sensitive forms.

claimsVsReality.claim: The provider's ID number disclosure could not cause harm because a member's ID number alone could not be used to access an account.
claimsVsReality.reality: The ID number was disclosed to an unauthorized third party and combined with her name, creating a privacy breach that exposed the complainant to identity and information security risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: The provider's systems were functioning adequately to protect member information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The provider gave out the complainant's ID number to a caller with an identical name without proper authentication, and failed to detect an address error despite receiving five returned envelopes over several months.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant's insurance cancellation was a natural consequence of her failure to return forms.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant never received the time-sensitive forms because they were misdirected to another person's address due to the provider's errors in authentication and address management.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 — Consent required for disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Provider disclosed the complainant's unique identifier to a third party without her consent
violations: Provider disclosed the complainant's unique identifier to a third party without her consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 and 4.6.1 — Organizations must keep personal information accurate, complete, and up-to-date
regulatoryFindings.description: Provider failed to detect and correct the complainant's erroneous address change despite five returned envelopes over several months
violations: Provider failed to detect and correct the complainant's erroneous address change despite five returned envelopes over several months
Did not suspend mailings or trigger a review when returned mail indicated inaccurate contact information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 and 4.7.1 — Organizations must implement appropriate safeguards to protect personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Provider did not properly authenticate the caller before providing the complainant's ID number
violations: Provider did not properly authenticate the caller before providing the complainant's ID number
Failed to follow established authentication procedures during the address change request

outcome: The provider agreed to remediate by: (i) developing a privacy plan; (ii) reviewing its address change process; (iii) improving forms and training; (iv) improving privacy incident response procedures; and (v) providing associated employee training. All changes were to be implemented by end of 2016. The provider also agreed to undergo a third-party privacy audit by end of Q1 2017 to confirm PIPEDA compliance. The provider updated its mailing processes and reinstated the complainant's cancelled insurance retroactively (subject to reimbursement of unpaid fees). The matter was found to be well-founded and conditionally resolved based on the provider's commitment to implement these changes.
dataType: Unique identifier, address, employment pension information, insurance-related forms, personal account information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (Consent for Collection, Use, and Disclosure)

companyDescription: A debt collection agency that pursued consumers for outstanding debts on behalf of creditors.
companyLongDescription: This collection agency operated in Canada and was responsible for pursuing individuals to recover debts owed to original creditors such as credit card companies. The agency received complaints for maintaining inaccurate personal information, failing to provide individuals with access to supporting documentation, and disclosing sensitive financial information to third parties without proper authorization. The case highlights systemic failures in the agency's record-keeping and verification procedures.
caseDescription: A collection agency pursued an individual for a debt on a credit card account that was not his, resulting in a four-year mistaken debt collection effort and loan denial. The individual was denied access to documentation supporting the debt and had his financial information disclosed to household members. The agency failed to maintain accurate personal information and denied the individual timely access to challenge the accuracy of records held about him.
violationSummary: The collection agency failed to maintain accurate and complete personal information, misidentified the debtor, and denied the individual access to personal information held about him. This resulted in incorrect collection actions and improper disclosure of financial data. The violation fits 'Insecurity' as it reflects inadequate safeguards and procedures for maintaining data accuracy and providing access rights.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A collection agency pursued an individual for four years to collect a debt on a credit card account that was not in his name, disclosed his financial information to household members.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individual was denied a loan based on false debt information on his credit report, suffered years of harassment through unwanted collection calls.

claimsVsReality.claim: The debt was legitimately attributable to the individual and warranted collection action.
claimsVsReality.reality: The credit card account was not in the individual's name; discrepancies on the application indicated possible fraud and the agency ceased collection and corrected the credit report.

claimsVsReality.claim: The individual was provided sufficient access to documentation to challenge the debt.
claimsVsReality.reality: The individual repeatedly requested access to the original credit agreement and authorization documentation but was denied this information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 – Organizations must ensure that personal information is as accurate, complete and up-to-date as possible for the purposes for which it is to be used, especially when action or decisions are made based on that information
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection agency pursued debt collection against incorrect individual based on inaccurate personal information
violations: Collection agency pursued debt collection against incorrect individual based on inaccurate personal information
Debt remained on credit report despite individual's assertions of misidentification

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – Individuals must be able to challenge the accuracy and completeness of personal information held by an organization through timely access
regulatoryFindings.description: Individual requested access to documentation supporting the debt attribution but was not provided access
violations: Individual requested access to documentation supporting the debt attribution but was not provided access
Individual was unable to obtain proof of initial credit agreement or authorization for debt collection

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2.3 – Organizations must limit collection, use and disclosure of personal information to that which is necessary for identified purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Personal financial information was disclosed to other members of the individual's household without authorization
violations: Personal financial information was disclosed to other members of the individual's household without authorization

outcome: The organization investigated upon contact from the regulator and produced the original credit application. Discrepancies were noted on the application, suggesting potential fraud. The organization ceased debt collection pursuit, advised the individual that fraud was possibly involved, and agreed to have the credit report corrected. The individual was notified and satisfied with the outcome.
dataType: Financial data, credit information, personal contact information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 – Accuracy of Personal Information
PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – Access to Personal Information

companyDescription: An office-based call centre company operating as a tenant in a multi-tenant commercial building.
companyLongDescription: A call centre company that rented office space in a shared commercial building and installed video surveillance systems in common areas. The company justified the cameras as security measures following an intrusion incident, claiming they were authorized by building management and required by corporate security standards. However, the installation lacked proper consultation with other tenants and created privacy intrusions that extended beyond the company's own office space.
caseDescription: An office building tenant installed five video surveillance cameras in shared common areas without consent or consultation with other tenants. Two cameras specifically recorded activity between a neighboring tenant's office door and washrooms/elevators. The Privacy Commissioner's Office intervened after complaint, leading to relocation of the two most intrusive cameras from shared areas into the installing company's own offices.
violationSummary: The unauthorized placement of video surveillance cameras in shared common areas constitutes surveillance of individuals without adequate notice or consent, collecting personal information far beyond what was necessary for the stated security purpose.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A call centre tenant installed five video surveillance cameras in shared building hallways and elevator lobbies without consent or consultation with neighboring tenants.
whyTheyWereWrong: The cameras captured personal information about neighboring tenants and their clients entering/leaving offices.

claimsVsReality.claim: Building management authorized the camera installation as long as cameras were discreet
claimsVsReality.reality: Building management had not coordinated with other tenants and cameras were recording shared areas used by neighboring tenants without their knowledge or consent

claimsVsReality.claim: Cameras were necessary for safety reasons following a security incident with an intruder
claimsVsReality.reality: The cameras extended far beyond monitoring the company's own office entrances and instead captured neighboring tenants and their clients moving between their office, washrooms, and elevators

claimsVsReality.claim: Corporate security standards based on ISO and PCI standards required monitoring access to office space
claimsVsReality.reality: Security standards do not justify recording shared common areas used by other building tenants without their consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires meaningful consent before collecting personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Video surveillance cameras installed without consent or consultation with affected tenants
violations: Video surveillance cameras installed without consent or consultation with affected tenants
No notice provided to complainant or his clients that they were being recorded in shared common areas

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Commissioner Guidelines on Video Surveillance require collection of minimum necessary information and reasonable expectations of privacy
regulatoryFindings.description: Cameras positioned to capture activity beyond the company's office entrance, including hallways, elevators, and areas leading to other tenants' offices and washrooms
violations: Cameras positioned to capture activity beyond the company's office entrance, including hallways, elevators, and areas leading to other tenants' offices and washrooms
Excessive scope of surveillance relative to stated security purpose

regulatoryFindings.act: Principle of proportionality and necessity in surveillance deployment
regulatoryFindings.description: Use of five cameras to monitor common areas without demonstrating necessity or proportionality to the identified security incident
violations: Use of five cameras to monitor common areas without demonstrating necessity or proportionality to the identified security incident
Failure to consider less privacy-intrusive alternatives

outcome: Following intervention by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner, the building management and the tenant company agreed to relocate two of the five cameras that most directly violated the complainant's privacy. These cameras were moved from the shared common area hallway and elevator lobby into the company's own office space, limiting their surveillance scope to the company's exclusive premises. The complainant confirmed satisfaction with this resolution.
dataType: Video surveillance footage, movement patterns, biometric data (facial features captured on video)
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Commissioner Guidelines on Overt Video Surveillance in the Private Sector

companyDescription: An anti-virus and computer security service provider operating in Canada, offering virus protection and technical support services to residential customers.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian anti-virus service provider that contracts with customers to provide computer virus protection and technical support. The company failed to implement adequate employee access controls and complaint investigation procedures, resulting in a customer being defrauded through impersonation and unauthorized remote computer access by a third-party marketing company.
caseDescription: An employee of an anti-virus service provider fraudulently accessed a customer's account without legitimate business reason, enabling a third party (marketing company) to impersonate the employee and gain remote computer access. The fraudster convinced the customer to authorize a second credit card charge under false pretenses, resulting in unauthorized billing and financial loss. The service provider failed to investigate customer complaints until regulatory intervention.
violationSummary: The employee's unauthorized access to customer account data and disclosure of the private account number to a third party constitutes breach of confidentiality. The customer's personal financial and account information was disclosed without authorization, enabling fraudulent use.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: An employee fraudulently accessed a customer's account without legitimate business reason, enabling a marketing company to impersonate the employee, gain remote computer access.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer was deceived into authorizing unauthorized credit card charges, suffered financial loss, had their computer remotely accessed by third parties.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company's technicians do not contact customers unsolicited to request remote access.
claimsVsReality.reality: An employee's account credentials were used to impersonate a technician and fraudulently obtain remote computer access by claiming the customer's computer had been hacked.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company maintains secure customer account protections.
claimsVsReality.reality: An employee accessed customer accounts without legitimate business reason, and the company had no auditing system to detect or alert on suspicious access patterns.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer service was responsive to complaints about fraud and impersonation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite multiple attempts by the customer to report the fraud to customer service agents, the company refused to investigate until the Privacy Commissioner's Office intervened.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2.3 – Organizations must protect personal information by implementing security safeguards against unauthorized access, use, or disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Employee was able to access customer account files without legitimate business reason
violations: Employee was able to access customer account files without legitimate business reason
No adequate monitoring system was in place to detect unauthorized account access
Inadequate access controls and employee oversight

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.10.4 – Organizations must investigate all complaints about their handling of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Service provider failed to investigate customer's initial complaints about the fraudulent call and unauthorized access
violations: Service provider failed to investigate customer's initial complaints about the fraudulent call and unauthorized access
Customer had to escalate to regulatory authority before investigation occurred

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 – Collection of personal information must be limited to purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: Employee accessed customer account data without legitimate service or business purpose
violations: Employee accessed customer account data without legitimate service or business purpose

outcome: The service provider was required to conduct an investigation per PIPEDA Principle 4.10.4. The company dismissed the employee responsible, reimbursed the affected customers in full for the unauthorized charges, and implemented structural reforms including: (1) an automated auditing system to flag when employee file access exceeds customer call volume, triggering risk department investigation; (2) a streamlined escalation procedure for privacy concerns to ensure customer complaints reach management attention promptly. The affected individuals were satisfied with the outcome.
dataType: Account number, credit card information, computer access credentials

companyDescription: A credit union that provides financial services to members, including deposit accounts and banking services.
companyLongDescription: A credit union is a member-owned financial cooperative that offers banking services including personal accounts, deposits, and lending products. Credit unions operate under strict regulatory frameworks including PIPEDA in Canada, which govern the handling of member and customer personal information. As a financial institution, credit unions maintain access to sensitive personal financial data and are responsible for protecting member privacy and confidentiality.
caseDescription: A credit union manager accessed an employee's personal bank account without consent or valid business purpose to verify whether the employee was truthful about calling in sick. The manager suspected the employee was out-of-province and reviewed her transaction history. The unauthorized access violated PIPEDA provisions on secondary use of personal information.
violationSummary: The manager accessed the individual's personal financial information for a purpose (verifying truthfulness of sick leave) entirely unrelated to the purpose for which it was collected (banking services). This constitutes improper secondary use of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A credit union manager accessed an employee's personal bank account transaction history without consent or valid business purpose to verify whether the employee was truthful about calling.
whyTheyWereWrong: The employee's financial privacy was violated when her manager reviewed her debit card transactions across provinces to investigate her whereabouts.

claimsVsReality.claim: The manager had a valid business purpose in accessing the employee's personal bank account to verify sick leave claims.
claimsVsReality.reality: No legitimate business purpose existed; the manager was investigating personal suspicions about the employee's location using unauthorized access to her financial transaction data.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employee's personal banking information could be accessed as part of routine employment verification or performance management.
claimsVsReality.reality: The credit union's own policies did not authorize such access, and the employee's personal bank account was not collected for employment verification purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to collect, use, and disclose personal information only for purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate under the circumstances
regulatoryFindings.description: Manager accessed employee's personal bank account without consent or valid business purpose
violations: Manager accessed employee's personal bank account without consent or valid business purpose
Information was used to investigate sick leave claim rather than for banking services purpose
No legitimate authorization existed for the access

regulatoryFindings.act: Organizations must ensure employees understand confidentiality obligations and consequences of unauthorized access
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate employee training or controls to prevent snooping
violations: Inadequate employee training or controls to prevent snooping
Manager accessed personal information without proper authorization despite employment role

outcome: The credit union agreed the manager had accessed the individual's account without valid business purpose. The credit union committed to addressing the manager's conduct, issued a letter of apology to the affected individual, and agreed to implement measures to prevent future unauthorized access. The case was early resolved to the satisfaction of the complainant.
dataType: Financial data, banking transaction history, debit card usage
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA – Unauthorized access without valid business purpose
PIPEDA – Use of personal information for purpose other than which it was collected

companyDescription: Globe24h.com was a Canadian website operator that republished court and tribunal decisions containing personal information without consent.
companyLongDescription: Globe24h.com was a Canadian online service that scraped and republished Canadian court and tribunal decisions containing individuals' personal information without their consent. The operator allowed this sensitive data to be indexed by search engines, making it permanently discoverable online. The company also operated a removal service, charging individuals fees to have their information taken down from the website. This business model exploited publicly available court records to create a searchable database of sensitive personal information.
caseDescription: Globe24h.com collected, republished, and disclosed personal information from Canadian court and tribunal decisions without consent, allowed search engine indexing of this sensitive data, and charged individuals fees to have their information removed. The OPC investigation found the complaints well-founded, and the matter was subsequently pursued in Federal Court, resulting in an order to cease operations and remove all illegally republished content.
violationSummary: Globe24h disclosed personal information from court decisions to the public via its website and search engines without consent, and did so for an improper secondary purpose (generating revenue through removal fees). This constitutes unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Globe24h.com collected and republished Canadian court and tribunal decisions containing personal information without consent, allowed search engines to index this data.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals' sensitive personal information from court records was made permanently searchable online.

claimsVsReality.claim: Globe24h operated a legitimate information republishing service providing access to public court records.
claimsVsReality.reality: The service was republishing personal information from court decisions without consent and charging removal fees, causing real harm to individuals whose private information was searchable online.

claimsVsReality.claim: The removal service provided a fair way for individuals to protect their privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: The removal service charged fees for what should have been a free privacy right, exploiting individuals' need to remove sensitive personal information from searchable web results.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires that personal information be collected, used, and disclosed only with consent and for appropriate purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Globe24h collected and republished personal information from court decisions without consent
violations: Globe24h collected and republished personal information from court decisions without consent
Information was used for an inappropriate secondary purpose (charging removal fees)
Information was disclosed publicly via website and search engine indexing without authorization

outcome: The OPC issued a final report of findings on June 5, 2015 concluding the complaints were well-founded. The matter was subsequently pursued in Federal Court, where on January 30, 2017, the Court confirmed the OPC's findings and ordered Globe24h's operator to remove all Canadian court and tribunal decisions containing personal information from the website, refrain from further republishing such decisions in violation of PIPEDA, and pay nominal damages to the complainant. The website ceased operating shortly after the Court's decision.
companyNow: Globe24h.com ceased operations in early 2017 following the Federal Court decision ordering its shutdown and removal of all republished content.
dataType: Personal information contained in Canadian court and tribunal decisions (names, case details, potentially financial and legal information)

companyDescription: A car dealership that provides vehicle maintenance and loaner car services to customers.
companyLongDescription: A car dealership operating in Canada that offers routine vehicle maintenance and loaner vehicle services to customers. The dealership collects personal information including driver's licenses and credit card details from customers requesting loaner vehicles during service appointments. The organization has documented privacy policies and practices but faced challenges ensuring employee awareness and consistent application of privacy protocols.
caseDescription: A car dealership collected a customer's driver's license and credit card for a loaner vehicle request but employees could not adequately explain why the information was being collected or what safeguards protected it. The dealership failed to respond to the customer's subsequent email inquiry to the privacy officer about data handling practices and retention periods.
violationSummary: The organization failed to provide individuals with access to information about its personal information handling practices and policies, and employees lacked knowledge to answer customer questions about data collection, use, and safeguards.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: A car dealership collected a customer's driver's license and credit card for a loaner vehicle without explaining why the information was needed or what protections existed.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer was left unable to understand how her sensitive financial and identity information would be used or protected.
