companyDescription: TeleCheck Services, Inc. is a financial services company that provides check authorization and verification services to merchants throughout the United States, processing transactions based on consumer identification, check history, and risk assessment factors.
companyLongDescription: TeleCheck Services, Inc. is a financial services company that provides check authorization and verification services to merchants throughout the United States, processing transactions based on consumer identification, check history, and risk assessment factors.
caseDescription: TeleCheck, a check authorization service provider, systematically failed to properly investigate consumer disputes about inaccurate check transaction data, and failed to delete erroneous information from consumer files. The company also restricted reinvestigations in ways prohibited by the FCRA, leaving consumers unable to correct false information that caused merchants to decline their checks. TRS, a TeleCheck affiliate, failed to establish reasonable written policies for data accuracy.
violationSummary: TeleCheck failed to maintain reasonable procedures to ensure accuracy and integrity of consumer credit/transaction information and failed to properly investigate and correct disputed inaccurate information, creating systemic risk of erroneous decision-making by third parties.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: TeleCheck failed to properly reinvestigate consumer disputes, told customers only three reasons for disputes were valid, shifted investigation duties to consumers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers were repeatedly denied the ability to pay by check at thousands of merchants because TeleCheck maintained inaccurate or unverifiable negative records about them.

claimsVsReality.claim: TeleCheck informed consumers that only the transaction amount, date, and whether services were rendered constituted valid dispute reasons under the FCRA.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FCRA permits disputes on any aspect of accuracy or completeness, including authorization, fraudulence, and other grounds beyond those three categories.

claimsVsReality.claim: TeleCheck's dispute procedures required consumers to contact merchants and resolve disputes directly rather than TeleCheck conducting reinvestigations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FCRA obligates TeleCheck as the consumer reporting agency to conduct the reinvestigation itself upon receiving notice of a dispute; the burden cannot be shifted to the consumer.

claimsVsReality.claim: TeleCheck would only investigate and clear fraud-related disputes if the consumer provided a police report identifying the suspect and agreed to participate in prosecution.
claimsVsReality.reality: The FCRA requires TeleCheck to conduct reasonable reinvestigations of all disputes based on information available, without imposing prerequisites such as police reports or prosecution participation.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(b) of the FCRA requires consumer reporting agencies to follow reasonable procedures to assure the maximum possible accuracy of consumer report information.
regulatoryFindings.description: TeleCheck failed to promptly delete or modify inaccurate or unverifiable information from consumer files after conducting reinvestigations, allowing erroneous data to remain and be reported to merchants.
violations: TeleCheck failed to promptly delete or modify inaccurate or unverifiable information from consumer files after conducting reinvestigations, allowing erroneous data to remain and be reported to merchants.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 611(a) of the FCRA requires consumer reporting agencies to conduct reasonable reinvestigations within 30 days (or 45 days if additional information is received) upon receiving a dispute from a consumer.
regulatoryFindings.description: TeleCheck restarted the 30-day dispute timeline when receiving additional consumer information, extended timelines improperly, and failed to complete reinvestigations within required periods.
violations: TeleCheck restarted the 30-day dispute timeline when receiving additional consumer information, extended timelines improperly, and failed to complete reinvestigations within required periods.
TeleCheck incorrectly informed consumers that only transaction amount, date, and service rendered were valid dispute reasons, contrary to FCRA.
TeleCheck shifted the burden of reinvestigation to consumers, instructing them to contact merchants rather than conducting investigations itself.
TeleCheck refused to reinvestigate fraud allegations unless consumers provided police reports and agreed to participate in prosecution.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 611(a) requires specific procedural steps during reinvestigation, including notifying furnishers within 5 business days, notifying consumers of frivolous determinations, deleting/modifying inaccurate information, notifying furnishers of changes, and providing results notice within 5 business days.
regulatoryFindings.description: TeleCheck failed to provide timely dispute notices to furnishers within the 5-business-day requirement.
violations: TeleCheck failed to provide timely dispute notices to furnishers within the 5-business-day requirement.
TeleCheck failed to notify consumers within 5 business days when terminating investigations as frivolous.
TeleCheck failed to promptly delete or modify inaccurate, incomplete, or unverifiable information and failed to notify furnishers of modifications.
TeleCheck failed to maintain procedures preventing reappearance of deleted information, allowing merchants to re-report previously deleted data.
TeleCheck failed to provide results notices or provided incomplete notices lacking the revised consumer report and reinvestigation procedure description.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 623(e)(1) of the FCRA and Furnisher Rule 16 C.F.R. § 660.3(a) require furnishers of consumer information to establish and implement reasonable written policies and procedures regarding accuracy and integrity of information furnished to consumer reporting agencies.
regulatoryFindings.description: TRS failed to consider the guidelines in Appendix E of the Furnisher Rule in its written policies and procedures for ensuring accuracy and integrity of information furnished to TeleCheck.
violations: TRS failed to consider the guidelines in Appendix E of the Furnisher Rule in its written policies and procedures for ensuring accuracy and integrity of information furnished to TeleCheck.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: TeleCheck's systematic failures to reinvestigate, correct, and delete inaccurate consumer transaction data constitute unfair practices affecting consumers' ability to obtain merchant services based on accurate information.
violations: TeleCheck's systematic failures to reinvestigate, correct, and delete inaccurate consumer transaction data constitute unfair practices affecting consumers' ability to obtain merchant services based on accurate information.

outcome: The complaint seeks permanent injunctive relief to prevent continued violations, monetary civil penalties at up to $3,500 per violation for FCRA breaches (with each instance constituting a separate violation), equitable relief including rescission/reformation, restitution and disgorgement, and costs. The court is authorized to issue injunctions against both defendants and award penalties for TeleCheck's knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice.
companyNow: TeleCheck remains a major check authorization and verification service for merchants, though the company has faced significant litigation and regulatory scrutiny over its dispute handling and data accuracy practices.
dataType: Financial transaction data, check history, consumer identification, credit and repayment information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(b) – accuracy obligation
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 611(a) – reinvestigation obligations
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 623(e)(1) / Furnisher Rule 16 C.F.R. § 660.3(a) – written policies for accuracy
FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: TinyCo, Inc. was a mobile gaming developer based in San Francisco that created free-to-play games with in-app purchases, including titles like Tiny Pets, Tiny Zoo, Tiny Village, Tiny Monsters, and Mermaid Resort. The company's games were designed to appeal to children and were marketed across Apple App Store, Google Play, and Amazon Appstore.
companyLongDescription: TinyCo, Inc. was a mobile gaming developer based in San Francisco that created free-to-play games with in-app purchases, including titles like Tiny Pets, Tiny Zoo, Tiny Village, Tiny Monsters, and Mermaid Resort. The company's games were designed to appeal to children and were marketed across Apple App Store, Google Play, and Amazon Appstore.
caseDescription: TinyCo operated mobile gaming apps directed at children under 13 that collected email addresses without parental consent, privacy notices, or disclosure of information practices. The company collected tens of thousands of email addresses from children through incentive-based collection mechanisms, fully aware children were using the apps after receiving parental complaints.
violationSummary: TinyCo systematically collected personal information (email addresses) from children under 13 without lawful basis, transparency, or parental involvement. This constitutes surveillance of minors without proper safeguards.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: TinyCo collected tens of thousands of email addresses from children under 13 through its mobile gaming apps by offering free in-app currency rewards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Tens of thousands of children's personal email addresses were harvested and stored without parental knowledge or authorization, exposing minors to potential unsolicited contact and data misuse.

claimsVsReality.claim: TinyCo apps were games designed for general audiences to enjoy
claimsVsReality.reality: Apps used brightly-colored animated characters, child-oriented language, and fairy-tale themes specifically designed to appeal to children under 13

claimsVsReality.claim: Email collection was optional and transparent
claimsVsReality.reality: TinyCo incentivized collection with free in-app currency, collected tens of thousands of emails, posted no privacy policy, and gave no parental notice

claimsVsReality.claim: TinyCo was unaware children used the apps
claimsVsReality.reality: TinyCo received numerous parental complaints about children using the apps but took no steps to verify age, delete information, or obtain consent

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule § 312.4(b) requires operators to post a privacy policy providing clear, understandable, and complete notice of information collection, use, and disclosure practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: TinyCo failed to post any privacy policy on its kids' apps (Tiny Pets, Tiny Zoo, Tiny Village, Tiny Monsters, Mermaid Resort)
violations: TinyCo failed to post any privacy policy on its kids' apps (Tiny Pets, Tiny Zoo, Tiny Village, Tiny Monsters, Mermaid Resort)

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule § 312.4(c) requires operators to provide clear, understandable, and complete notice of information practices directly to parents.
regulatoryFindings.description: TinyCo provided no direct notice to parents about what information it collected from children or how it used such information
violations: TinyCo provided no direct notice to parents about what information it collected from children or how it used such information

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule § 312.5(a)(1) requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children under 13.
regulatoryFindings.description: TinyCo collected email addresses directly from children without first obtaining or attempting to obtain verifiable parental consent
violations: TinyCo collected email addresses directly from children without first obtaining or attempting to obtain verifiable parental consent

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: COPPA violations constitute unfair/deceptive practices under Section 5; TinyCo's collection without consent or notice was deceptive to both children and parents
violations: COPPA violations constitute unfair/deceptive practices under Section 5; TinyCo's collection without consent or notice was deceptive to both children and parents

outcome: Complaint filed seeking permanent injunction to prevent future COPPA violations, monetary civil penalties of up to $16,000 per violation (each collection, use, or disclosure), and other equitable relief. The complaint alleged multiple separate violations across five child-directed apps with tens of thousands of email collections.
companyNow: TinyCo was acquired by Caesars Entertainment (formerly Eldorado Resorts) in 2019. The company continues to operate mobile gaming titles but with significantly increased regulatory scrutiny following this enforcement action.
dataType: Email addresses, user identifiers
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule § 312.4(b) – Failure to post privacy policy
COPPA Rule § 312.4(c) – Failure to provide direct notice to parents
COPPA Rule § 312.5(a)(1) – Failure to obtain verifiable parental consent

company: PDB Sports, Ltd. (Denver Broncos Football Club)
companyDescription: PDB Sports, Ltd., doing business as the Denver Broncos Football Club, is a professional American football team and member of the National Football League, based in Englewood, Colorado.
companyLongDescription: PDB Sports, Ltd., doing business as the Denver Broncos Football Club, is a professional American football team and member of the National Football League, based in Englewood, Colorado.
caseDescription: The Denver Broncos claimed compliance with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework for handling EU personal data but failed to renew their certification in November 2011. They continued displaying Safe Harbor compliance statements on their website until November 2013, misrepresenting their status as a 'current' participant in the framework. This deceptive practice violated Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.
violationSummary: Company's false Safe Harbor claims created risk of inadequate data protection for EU residents whose personal data was transferred to the U.S., exposing them to reduced privacy safeguards.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The Denver Broncos falsely claimed on their website from November 2008 to November 2013 that they complied with the EU Safe Harbor framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union residents provided personal data to the Broncos believing it would receive Safe Harbor protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: Denver Broncos Football Club complies with the EU Safe Harbor framework as set forth by the Department of Commerce regarding the collection, use, and retention of data from the European Union.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company's self-certification to Safe Harbor was not renewed in November 2011, and Commerce Department updated company's status to 'not current.' Company continued making compliance claims until November 2013.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company represented it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework by displaying compliance statements on its website from November 2008 to November 2013.
violations: Company represented it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework by displaying compliance statements on its website from November 2008 to November 2013.
From November 2011 to November 2013, company's certification status was 'not current' as recorded by Commerce Department, making representations false and misleading.
Company failed to update privacy policy statements after losing Safe Harbor certification, deceiving EU data subjects about protection of their personal data.

outcome: FTC issued complaint against Denver Broncos on June 19, 2014, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint charges the company with falsely claiming Safe Harbor compliance during the two-year period (November 2011–November 2013) when certification status was 'not current.' Enforcement action required company to cease false Safe Harbor claims and comply with applicable privacy laws.
companyNow: The Denver Broncos remain an active NFL franchise, now owned by Walmart CEO Greg Penner as of 2022. The organization continues to operate with updated privacy and data protection policies.
dataType: Personal data from European Union residents

companyDescription: Baker Tilly Virchow Krause, LLP is an Illinois-based accounting and advisory services firm with principal office at 205 North Michigan Avenue, Chicago. The firm provides accounting, tax, and consulting services.
companyLongDescription: Baker Tilly Virchow Krause, LLP is an Illinois-based accounting and advisory services firm with principal office at 205 North Michigan Avenue, Chicago. The firm provides accounting, tax, and consulting services.

claimsVsReality.reality: Mark was used while certification was not current (June 2011–December 2013), violating Commerce Department rules requiring mark use only for organizations with current certification.

company: GeneLink, Inc. (also d/b/a GeneLink Biosciences, Inc.) and foruTM International Corporation (formerly GeneWize Life Sciences, Inc.)
companyDescription: GeneLink, Inc. and foruTM International Corporation (formerly GeneWize Life Sciences, Inc.) developed and sold genetically customized nutritional supplements and skincare products through a multi-level marketing system. The companies used at-home DNA cheek swab kits and third-party laboratory analysis to create purportedly personalized products based on genetic variations, collecting sensitive health and financial data from consumers.
companyLongDescription: GeneLink, Inc. and foruTM International Corporation (formerly GeneWize Life Sciences, Inc.) developed and sold genetically customized nutritional supplements and skincare products through a multi-level marketing system. The companies used at-home DNA cheek swab kits and third-party laboratory analysis to create purportedly personalized products based on genetic variations, collecting sensitive health and financial data from consumers.
caseDescription: GeneLink and foruTM made unsubstantiated health claims about genetically customized nutritional supplements and skincare products, claiming genetic variations could be mitigated through supplementation without scientific proof. The companies also failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect nearly 30,000 consumers' genetic and personal financial data, including Social Security numbers and bank account information, from unauthorized access.
violationSummary: Primary violation involves failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect sensitive personal information (genetic data, SSN, financial data) from unauthorized access. Secondary violations include deceptive health claims lacking scientific basis.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: GeneLink and foruTM marketed genetically customized nutritional supplements and skincare products claiming DNA testing could identify genetic disadvantages that nutritional supplementation would.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 30,000 consumers' genetic profiles, Social Security numbers, bank account details, and credit card information were stored in clear text with inadequate access controls.

claimsVsReality.claim: SNP genetic variations 'predict biochemical processes that are associated with significant physiological disadvantages' and 'negative potential has been scientifically proven to be modulated by nutritional supplementation'
claimsVsReality.reality: Genetic disadvantages identified by the DNA assessments were NOT scientifically proven to be mitigated or compensated for with nutritional supplementation

claimsVsReality.claim: Custom-blended nutritional supplements effectively compensate for genetic disadvantages and reduce individual risk of impaired health or illness
claimsVsReality.reality: No reasonable basis existed for these claims; testimonials claimed treatment of serious diseases (diabetes, cardiac conditions, arthritis) without medical evidence

claimsVsReality.claim: Genetically customized skin repair serum is scientifically proven to reduce appearance of wrinkles and improve skin firmness; clinical study showed 62% reduction in wrinkles after 14 days
claimsVsReality.reality: The serum was not scientifically proven to reduce wrinkles or improve firmness; claims lacked adequate substantiation

claimsVsReality.claim: All information provided is 'kept on a secure server' and personal information is protected with 'appropriate safeguards' through contractually obligated service providers
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information including SSN and bank account numbers was stored in clear text with unrestricted employee access; service providers lacked contractual security obligations; March 2012 vulnerability exposed all customer/affiliate information

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented without substantiation that genetic disadvantages identified by DNA assessments are scientifically proven to be mitigated or compensated for with nutritional supplementation
violations: Represented without substantiation that genetic disadvantages identified by DNA assessments are scientifically proven to be mitigated or compensated for with nutritional supplementation
Represented that custom-blended nutritional supplements effectively compensate for genetic disadvantages and reduce risk of illness without reasonable basis

companyLongDescription: The Receivable Management Services Corporation is a Delaware-based collection agency headquartered in Bethlehem, Pennsylvania, engaged in debt collection and receivables management.
caseDescription: The Receivable Management Services Corporation, a debt collection agency, falsely represented that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework from February 2010 to November 2013, despite having allowed its certification to lapse in February 2010. The company displayed the official Safe Harbor certification mark and made statements on its website claiming Safe Harbor compliance, misleading consumers and data subjects about its privacy protections.
violationSummary: The company distorted the truth about its privacy practices and regulatory compliance status, creating a false impression of legitimacy and data protection through use of an official certification mark it was not entitled to display.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: From February 2010 to November 2013, RMS displayed the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor certification mark and claimed Safe Harbor compliance on its website despite allowing its certification to expire.
whyTheyWereWrong: RMS's false claims deceived European consumers and debtors whose personal financial data the company processed.

claimsVsReality.claim: RMS is registered with the U.S. Department of Commerce's Safe Harbor program and adheres to the U.S. Safe Harbor principles of Notice, Choice, Onward Transfer, Security, Data Integrity, Access, and Enforcement.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company allowed its Safe Harbor self-certification to expire in February 2010 and did not renew it, resulting in a 'not current' status on Commerce's public registry by February 2010. It was not an active Safe Harbor participant during the period from February 2010 to November 2013.

claimsVsReality.claim: Display of the official U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework Certification Mark on the company's website indicated current Safe Harbor compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was not authorized to display the mark after February 2010, as it maintained only 'not current' status and did not re-certify annually as required.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: The company expressly and impliedly represented that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework through website statements and display of the official Safe Harbor certification mark.
violations: The company expressly and impliedly represented that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework through website statements and display of the official Safe Harbor certification mark.

In truth and in fact, from February 2010 until November 2013, the company was not a 'current' participant in the Safe Harbor Framework because it failed to renew its annual self-certification after February 2010, and Commerce updated its status to 'not current' on the public registry.
These false and misleading representations about Safe Harbor participation and compliance constituted deceptive acts or practices affecting commerce.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 19, 2014, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint challenges the company's false Safe Harbor representations and seeks a compliance order requiring truthful disclosure of privacy practices and removal of false certifications. Final resolution and remedial terms are not detailed in this complaint document.

companyDescription: Aaron's, Inc. is a national rent-to-own (RTO) retailer founded in 1955, headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia. It operated over 1,300 company-owned stores and 700 franchised stores across the United States, renting consumer electronics, furniture, and household appliances with purchase options.
companyLongDescription: Aaron's, Inc. is a national rent-to-own (RTO) retailer founded in 1955, headquartered in Atlanta, Georgia. It operated over 1,300 company-owned stores and 700 franchised stores across the United States, renting consumer electronics, furniture, and household appliances with purchase options.
caseDescription: Aaron's, a rent-to-own retailer, allowed franchisees to install surveillance software (PC Rental Agent) on rented computers that secretly monitored consumers via keystrokes, screenshots, and webcams without consent. Aaron's senior management knew about these privacy-invasive practices, provided technical support to enable them, and stored over 100,000 messages containing sensitive consumer data on its corporate servers. The company failed to stop the practice until 13 months after learning of a lawsuit alleging privacy violations.
violationSummary: The core violation is covert surveillance of computer users through keystroke logging, screenshot capture, webcam activation, and location tracking without notice, consent, or transparency. This constitutes unlawful data collection through active monitoring.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Aaron's installed PC Rental Agent spyware on computers rented to consumers, enabling franchisees to secretly log keystrokes, capture screenshots, activate webcams.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers had their homes secretly filmed through webcams, their passwords and financial account credentials captured through keystroke logging.

claimsVsReality.claim: Aaron's policies and training materials prohibit unlawful computer and Internet use and set standards for fair collection practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these stated policies, Aaron's franchisees used spyware to conduct illegal surveillance, and Aaron's provided technical support, network access, and server space to facilitate the unlawful monitoring.

claimsVsReality.claim: Aaron's company-owned stores did not use PC Rental Agent surveillance software.
claimsVsReality.reality: Aaron's senior management actively reviewed the surveillance software's capabilities, reviewed captured images from Detective Mode, and deliberately chose not to install it on corporate stores—indicating full knowledge of its privacy-invasive nature.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. An act is unfair if it causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that cannot be reasonably avoided and is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aaron's permitted and participated in gathering, storing, and processing private and confidential consumer information through covert surveillance software without notice or consent.
violations: Aaron's permitted and participated in gathering, storing, and processing private and confidential consumer information through covert surveillance software without notice or consent.

Aaron's provided technical infrastructure, network access, server space, installation instructions, and franchisee support to enable secret monitoring of consumers' keystrokes, screenshots, webcam feeds, and location data.

Aaron's stored over 100,000 Detective Mode messages containing sensitive personal information (passwords, financial credentials, medical data, Social Security numbers, intimate images) on corporate servers for years without consumer knowledge.

Aaron's senior management knew the surveillance was invasive and privacy-violating, yet continued facilitating franchisee access to the spyware platform and did not revoke access until 13 months after learning of litigation.

Consumers could not detect or uninstall the surveillance software and had no reasonable opportunity to avoid the harm caused by unauthorized monitoring of their homes, devices, and personal communications.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on March 10, 2014, alleging unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The case proceeded to enforcement with a likely settlement requiring Aaron's to cease surveillance practices, comply with privacy protections, and submit to monitoring. No monetary penalty is disclosed in this complaint document; resolution details appear in subsequent settlement orders.
companyNow: Aaron's, Inc. continues to operate as a publicly traded rent-to-own retailer (NASDAQ: AAN) but has eliminated the surveillance practices. The company settled FTC charges and implemented compliance measures to prevent similar privacy violations.
dataType: keystroke logs, passwords, email credentials, financial account information, medical information, Social Security numbers, bank statements, credit card statements, screenshots, webcam images, location data, personal communications
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Apperian, Inc. was a Delaware corporation providing mobile applications management platforms for enterprises, helping companies deploy applications to employees. The company was headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts.
companyLongDescription: Apperian, Inc. was a Delaware corporation providing mobile applications management platforms for enterprises, helping companies deploy applications to employees. The company was headquartered in Boston, Massachusetts.
caseDescription: Apperian made false and misleading claims that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor frameworks for 16 months while its certification status was 'not current.' The company displayed the Safe Harbor certification mark on its website and made explicit statements about Safe Harbor compliance even after its self-certification lapsed in July 2012 until it renewed in November 2013.

claimsVsReality.reality: The mark is only authorized for display by organizations maintaining 'current' self-certification; Apperian displayed the mark while its status was 'not current.'

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Apperian expressly and by implication represented it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Frameworks through website statements and display of the certification mark from July 2010 through at least November 2013.
violations: Apperian expressly and by implication represented it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Frameworks through website statements and display of the certification mark from July 2010 through at least November 2013.

From July 2012 to November 2013, Apperian was not actually a 'current' participant in the Safe Harbor Frameworks because it did not renew its self-certification, making its representations false and misleading.

Apperian's statements and use of the official Safe Harbor certification mark constituted deceptive practices affecting commerce by misleading consumers and regulators about its data protection compliance status.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against Apperian on June 19, 2014, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. companyLongDescription: InfoTrack Information Services, Inc. was an Illinois corporation providing background screening reports to employers nationwide. companyLongDescription: Yelp is a digital platform founded in 2004 that allows users to search for, review, and rate local businesses including restaurants, shops, and services. caseDescription: Yelp failed to implement a functional age-screening mechanism in its mobile app registration feature, allowing children under 13 to register and providing them full access to the service. The company collected personal information from several thousand children without parental consent, proper notice, or adequate privacy disclosures as required by COPPA.
violationSummary: Yelp systematically collected personal information (names, emails, birthdates, GPS location, device IDs) from children under 13 through an online service without proper age verification, parental consent, or notice—classic surveillance of a vulnerable population.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Yelp failed to implement a functional age-screening mechanism in its mobile app registration between 2009 and 2013, allowing thousands of children under age 13 to create accounts.
whyTheyWereWrong: Several thousand children ages 9-13 had their full names, email addresses, photos, and precise locations collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Yelp's privacy policy stated the service was 'intended for general audiences and is not directed to children under 13.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The mobile app had no functional age-screening mechanism and accepted registrations from users indicating ages as young as 9, giving thousands of children full access to collect personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: A third-party privacy review in July 2010 reported that the iOS application prohibited registrations from users under 13.

violations: Yelp failed to disclose its information collection, use, and disclosure practices for children under 13, despite knowing the app accepted registrations from users indicating ages 9-13.

violations: Yelp provided no direct notice to parents before collecting personal information from children ages 9-13 who registered through the mobile app.

regulatoryFindings.description: Yelp obtained no verifiable parental consent prior to collecting or using personal information from thousands of children under 13 via the in-app registration feature.
violations: Yelp obtained no verifiable parental consent prior to collecting or using personal information from thousands of children under 13 via the in-app registration feature.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.

violations: Yelp's privacy policy claimed the service was not directed to children under 13, yet its non-functional age-screen allowed systematic data collection from minors, rendering the policy deceptive.

outcome: This is a Complaint filed by the U.S. Department of Justice on behalf of the FTC on September 16, 2014. caseDescription: Defendants operated as data brokers, collecting hundreds of thousands of consumer payday loan applications containing sensitive personal information and selling 95% of them to non-lenders including fraudsters and telemarketers without consumer consent. At least one buyer, Ideal Financial, used the data to make millions of dollars in unauthorized bank account debits affecting at least 2.2 million consumers. The defendants knew or should have known this fraud was occurring but continued the sales for months after learning of the illegal activity.
violationSummary: Defendants breached consumers' confidentiality by selling sensitive personal financial information collected for legitimate lending purposes to unauthorized third parties who used it for fraud, without any consumer knowledge or consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Collected hundreds of thousands of payday loan applications containing consumers' Social Security numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: At least 2.2 million consumers had millions of dollars fraudulently debited from their bank accounts without authorization after defendants sold their sensitive financial information to illegal.

claimsVsReality.claim: Defendants operated as legitimate data brokers connecting payday loan applicants with lenders.
claimsVsReality.reality: 95% of applications were sold not to lenders but to fraudsters, spammers, and telemarketers who had no legitimate use for Social Security and bank account numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ideal Financial was a legitimate financial services buyer using the data to offer credit products.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ideal Financial was a phony internet merchant that fabricated shell companies and fake websites to deceive payment processors, using the data solely to make unauthorized debits to consumer bank accounts totaling over $47 million.

claimsVsReality.claim: Defendants did not know how their data would be misused.
claimsVsReality.reality: CEO/founder John Ayers was confronted by then-CEO Jeff Petersen on April 25, 2012 about Ideal Financial's illegal use of consumer information; Ayers then hired Brian Jensen (Ideal Financial's VP of Marketing) in May 2012, who informed LeapLab's COO of the fraud practices, yet defendants continued sales to Ideal Financial until October 2012.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants sold payday loan applications containing consumers' Social Security numbers and bank account numbers to non-lenders including telemarketers, spammers, and fraudsters without consumers' knowledge or consent.
violations: Defendants sold payday loan applications containing consumers' Social Security numbers and bank account numbers to non-lenders including telemarketers, spammers, and fraudsters without consumers' knowledge or consent.

Defendants continued selling to Ideal Financial (a fraudster buyer) after learning through newly-hired employee Brian Jensen that Ideal Financial was using the information to make unauthorized bank account debits.
Defendants sold the same consumer applications to multiple non-lender buyers, multiplying fraud risk and violating publisher agreements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(n) of the FTC Act defines unfair acts as those causing substantial injury to consumers that consumers cannot reasonably avoid and that is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: Millions of dollars in unauthorized charges debited from consumer bank accounts using defendants' data.
violations: Millions of dollars in unauthorized charges debited from consumer bank accounts using defendants' data.
At least 16% of Ideal Financial's victims received their information from LeapLab.
Consumers had no reasonable way to avoid this injury; they did not consent to the sale or fraudulent use of their data.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Permanent Injunction and Other Equitable Relief on December 22, 2014, seeking permanent injunctive relief, contract rescission/reformation, restitution, refund of monies paid, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The complaint asserts unfair practices under FTC Act Section 5(a) and seeks to prevent future violations and remedy consumer harm from the defendants' sale of sensitive personal information to fraudsters.
companyNow: Sitesearch Corporation (formerly LeapLab) faced FTC enforcement action in 2014. The company's current operational status is unclear from this document; the action sought structural relief and injunctions.
dataType: Financial account numbers, Social Security numbers, names, addresses, phone numbers, employer information, dates of birth, bank routing numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce
FTC Act Section 5(n) – Definition of unfair acts causing substantial consumer injury

companyDescription: Fandango is a digital movie ticketing service and entertainment platform that allows consumers to purchase movie tickets and access showtimes, trailers, and reviews through its website and mobile applications. As of 2013, the company generated 20% of its ticket sales through iOS mobile applications.
companyLongDescription: Fandango is a digital movie ticketing service and entertainment platform that allows consumers to purchase movie tickets and access showtimes, trailers, and reviews through its website and mobile applications. As of 2013, the company generated 20% of its ticket sales through iOS mobile applications.
caseDescription: Fandango's iOS movie ticketing app failed to validate SSL certificates from March 2009 to March 2013, leaving credit card and authentication data vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks on public Wi-Fi networks. The company made false security claims while testing was inadequate, security audit scope was too narrow, and vulnerability reports were mishandled through automated customer service responses.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect sensitive personal financial and authentication data in transit, allowing potential interception of credit card information and passwords through man-in-the-middle attacks.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Fandango disabled default SSL certificate validation in its iOS app from March 2009 to March 2013, failed to test security for sensitive data transmission.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of consumers unknowingly transmitted unencrypted credit card numbers, security codes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Your information is securely stored on your device and transferred with your approval during each transaction.
claimsVsReality.reality: The app transmitted credit card data and passwords without SSL certificate validation, allowing attackers on public Wi-Fi to intercept, decrypt, and alter all transmitted information.

claimsVsReality.claim: You don't need an account to securely purchase tickets.
claimsVsReality.reality: Purchase transactions were not secure regardless of account status; the SSL certificate validation failure affected all users equally.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Fandango represented that its iOS app provided reasonable and appropriate security for credit card and account information, stating 'Your information is securely stored on your device and transferred with your approval during each transaction' and 'You don't need an account to securely purchase tickets.'
violations: Fandango represented that its iOS app provided reasonable and appropriate security for credit card and account information, stating 'Your information is securely stored on your device and transferred with your approval during each transaction' and 'You don't need an account to securely purchase tickets.'

In reality, the app failed to validate SSL certificates for approximately 4 years, allowing attackers to decrypt, monitor, or alter all communications including credit card numbers, security codes, expiration dates, and passwords through man-in-the-middle attacks.

Fandango's security practices fell short of reasonable standards: it overrode default SSL validation without compensating measures, did not test for SSL certificate validation vulnerabilities, limited security audits to code decompilation threats only (excluding transmission security), and failed to maintain an adequate vulnerability reporting process.

outcome: On August 13, 2014, the FTC issued a complaint against Fandango for violating Section 5(a) of the FTC Act through deceptive security representations and unfair practices. Within three weeks of Commission staff contact, Fandango issued updates to both iOS applications enabling SSL certificate validation by restoring iOS API default settings. The case proceeded to a consent order requiring Fandango to implement reasonable security measures, conduct annual third-party security assessments, maintain a vulnerability disclosure program, and maintain records for 20 years.
companyNow: Fandango remains a major online movie ticketing platform, acquired by Rotten Tomatoes parent company Flixster in 2010 and later acquired by NBCUniversal. The company continues operating as a leading digital ticketing service.
dataType: Credit card information (number, security code, expiration date, billing zip code), email address, password, authentication credentials
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Fantage.com, Inc. developed and operated a massively multiplayer online role-playing game targeted at children ages 6-16, based in Fort Lee, New Jersey.
companyLongDescription: Fantage.com, Inc. developed and operated a massively multiplayer online role-playing game targeted at children ages 6-16, based in Fort Lee, New Jersey.
caseDescription: Fantage.com, a children's online game operator, falsely claimed to comply with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework on its website. The company allowed its Safe Harbor certification to lapse in June 2012 but continued representing itself as a 'current' participant until January 2014. This deceptive conduct violated the FTC Act by misleading consumers and regulators about its data protection compliance status.
violationSummary: Fantage misrepresented its Safe Harbor status through false privacy policy statements, distorting the actual level of data protection available to users and regulators relying on certification claims.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Fantage.com displayed privacy policies claiming compliance with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework on its website while its certification status was not current from June 2012 to January 2014.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children aged 6-16 and their parents in the European Union shared personal data believing Fantage provided Safe Harbor-level data protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Fantage represented on its website that 'When we collect personal information from residents of the European Union, we follow the privacy principles of the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework'
claimsVsReality.reality: From June 2012 to January 2014, Fantage's Safe Harbor certification was not current; Commerce had updated its status to 'not current' on the official Safe Harbor list

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Fantage represented expressly and by implication that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework through privacy policy statements on its website
violations: Fantage represented expressly and by implication that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework through privacy policy statements on its website
From June 2012 to January 2014, Fantage was not a 'current' Safe Harbor participant, making the representation false and misleading
The deceptive representation was disseminated to consumers and affected commerce regarding children's personal data protection

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 19, 2014, against Fantage.com, Inc. for violating Section 5(a) of the FTC Act through deceptive practices regarding Safe Harbor Framework certification claims. The complaint alleges that Fantage's false representations about current Safe Harbor compliance constitute deceptive acts affecting commerce. The complaint did not specify monetary penalties in this initial filing; the resolution would typically include a consent order requiring corrected disclosures and future compliance monitoring.
dataType: Personal data from children ages 6-16, including account information

companyDescription: Credit Karma is a free personal finance and credit monitoring platform that allows consumers to access credit scores, credit reports, and monitor financial status via website and mobile applications. Prior to acquisition, it was a leading fintech company serving millions of users.
companyLongDescription: Credit Karma is a free personal finance and credit monitoring platform that allows consumers to access credit scores, credit reports, and monitor financial status via website and mobile applications. Prior to acquisition, it was a leading fintech company serving millions of users.
caseDescription: Credit Karma's mobile application failed to validate SSL certificates on both iOS and Android platforms, leaving sensitive consumer financial and personal data vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. The company had authorized testing code that disabled SSL validation but failed to remove it before launch, and repeated the same vulnerability in its Android app one month after fixing the iOS version. Despite marketing the app as secure with 'industry-leading security precautions,' Credit Karma did not perform adequate security reviews prior to launch.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect sensitive personal information in transit, specifically by disabling SSL certificate validation without compensatory controls. This exposed consumer data to interception and misuse.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Credit Karma disabled SSL certificate validation in its mobile app for over six months, leaving over 1 million users vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks on public Wi-Fi networks.
whyTheyWereWrong: Attackers could intercept and decrypt users' Social Security numbers, dates of birth, financial account information, passwords, and authentication credentials, enabling identity theft and fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: Credit Karma is committed to protecting users' identity, data, and privacy with 'industry-leading security precautions' (in-app security modal, launch 2012–2013)
claimsVsReality.reality: SSL certificate validation was disabled in both iOS (July 2012–Jan 2013) and Android (Feb–Mar 2013) versions, leaving data vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. The same vulnerability was repeated in Android just one month after being fixed in iOS, indicating inadequate security review and testing.

claimsVsReality.claim: The app transmits sensitive personal information over 'secure SSL connections' (privacy policy, launch 2012–2013)
claimsVsReality.reality: The app failed to validate SSL certificates, meaning connections were not authenticated or protected from spoofing. An attacker on public Wi-Fi could intercept all data, including SSNs, dates of birth, addresses, financial account details, and authentication credentials.

claimsVsReality.claim: We secure your information with 'bank-level VeriSign certified 128-bit SSL encryption' (in-app security modal)
claimsVsReality.reality: While the app may have used SSL encryption protocols, it did not validate the SSL certificates presented to it, defeating the purpose of SSL encryption and making it equivalent to unencrypted HTTP transmission.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Credit Karma represented that it was committed to protecting users' identity, data, and privacy with 'industry-leading security precautions' and that the app transmits sensitive personal information over 'secure SSL connections,' when in fact it failed to validate SSL certificates for 6+ months on iOS and 1+ month on Android, leaving data vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.
violations: Credit Karma represented that it was committed to protecting users' identity, data, and privacy with 'industry-leading security precautions' and that the app transmits sensitive personal information over 'secure SSL connections,' when in fact it failed to validate SSL certificates for 6+ months on iOS and 1+ month on Android, leaving data vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks.

Credit Karma's privacy policy stated 'We enable our servers with Secure Socket Layer (SSL) technology to establish a secure connection,' but the application did not actually perform SSL certificate validation, rendering the connection unencrypted and vulnerable to spoofing attacks.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices. The document is a complaint (not a final order), indicating the case was initiated on August 13, 2014. Based on typical FTC resolutions for similar cases, Credit Karma likely settled via a Consent Order requiring implementation of a comprehensive information security program, regular security assessments, third-party audits, and monitoring for 20 years. The company was required to notify affected users and remediate the vulnerabilities.
companyNow: Credit Karma was acquired by Intuit in 2020 for approximately $100 million and operates as a subsidiary offering free credit monitoring and financial management tools. The company has since implemented enhanced security practices and compliance controls under Intuit's oversight.
dataType: financial data, credit scores, credit reports, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, addresses, phone numbers, authentication credentials, 'out of wallet' identity verification information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Tennessee Football, Inc. is the owner and operator of the Tennessee Titans professional football team, a member of the National Football League (NFL) based in Nashville, Tennessee.
companyLongDescription: Tennessee Football, Inc. is the owner and operator of the Tennessee Titans professional football team, a member of the National Football League (NFL) based in Nashville, Tennessee.
caseDescription: Tennessee Football, Inc. (owner of the Tennessee Titans NFL team) represented on its website that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework for data protection, but failed to renew its certification in August 2009. The company continued making this false claim on its website until November 2013, deceiving consumers and EU data subjects about the level of privacy protection their data received.
violationSummary: The company made a material misrepresentation about its legal status and data protection compliance, causing confidentiality and trust in data handling to be breached. EU residents believed their data was protected under an adequacy framework that the company no longer maintained.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: From August 2005 until November 2013, Tennessee Football, Inc. displayed statements on its website claiming compliance with the EU Safe Harbor framework while failing to renew its required.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union residents and website visitors shared personal data based on false Safe Harbor compliance claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website complies with [the] EU Safe Harbor framework as set forth by the Department of Commerce regarding the collection, use, and retention of data from the European Union.
claimsVsReality.reality: From August 2009 onward, Tennessee Football, Inc. was not a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework because it failed to renew its self-certification. Commerce updated the company's status to 'not current' on the public Safe Harbor list in 2009.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Tennessee Football, Inc. represented that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework when its certification was not current from August 2009 onwards.
violations: Tennessee Football, Inc. represented that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework when its certification was not current from August 2009 onwards.
The company disseminated false and misleading privacy policy statements on its website stating compliance with Safe Harbor requirements despite not maintaining valid certification.
The misrepresentation was made in connection with commerce and the transfer of personal data from EU residents, affecting commerce between the U.S. and EU.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The case documents indicate a complaint was filed on June 19, 2014 (Docket No. C-4473). The complaint alleges deceptive practices and seeks enforcement action to compel the company to cease false Safe Harbor claims and comply with applicable data protection requirements. The company was required to remove false statements from its website and ensure accurate representation of its privacy certification status going forward.
companyNow: Tennessee Football, Inc. continues to operate the Tennessee Titans, an NFL franchise. The company resolved its Safe Harbor compliance issues and updated its privacy practices following the FTC complaint.
dataType: Personal data from European Union residents (collection, use, and retention unspecified but subject to Safe Harbor requirements)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Aaron's, Inc. is one of the two largest rent-to-own companies in the United States, operating approximately 75 stores in California through company-owned and franchised locations. The company rents household merchandise including furniture, appliances, and electronics to consumers under rent-to-own agreements.
companyLongDescription: Aaron's, Inc. is one of the two largest rent-to-own companies in the United States, operating approximately 75 stores in California through company-owned and franchised locations. The company rents household merchandise including furniture, appliances, and electronics to consumers under rent-to-own agreements.
caseDescription: Aaron's, Inc., one of the largest rent-to-own companies in the US, systematically violated California's Karnette Rental-Purchase Act by denying consumer protections through artful contract drafting. The company also permitted and facilitated the secret installation of spyware on rented computers that allowed franchisees to remotely monitor customer activity, capture keystrokes, and access webcams without consent.
violationSummary: Aaron's franchisees secretly installed spyware with Detective Mode capability, allowing remote monitoring of keystrokes, screenshots, and webcam operation. This constitutes unlawful surveillance and covert information collection from unsuspecting customers using rented computers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Aaron's imposed hidden minimum rental terms over 4 months, failed to disclose a mandatory 10% Service Plus fee in advertisements.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers renting computers had their keystrokes, screenshots, and webcam footage secretly captured without consent, exposing sensitive financial data, passwords.

claimsVsReality.claim: Aaron's advertised rental prices such as '$99.99/month' with notation 'Just add tax & Aaron's Service Plus'
claimsVsReality.reality: True monthly cost to consumers was $109.99/month plus tax (10% Service Plus fee), but the primary advertised price misled consumers about actual cost

claimsVsReality.claim: Aaron's used 'Sweepstakes Entry Form' to collect customer personal information including name, address, and phone number
claimsVsReality.reality: No sweepstakes existed; Aaron's used the form solely to collect sales leads and condition customers to provide personal information

claimsVsReality.claim: Aaron's Service Plus program provides benefits such as free delivery and right to reactivate cancelled agreements
claimsVsReality.reality: Many Service Plus benefits are mandated by the Karnette Act to be provided at no charge for all rent-to-own transactions, making the program largely illusory

claimsVsReality.claim: Aaron's rented computers with standard rental agreements and terms
claimsVsReality.reality: Aaron's franchisees installed spyware (PC Rental Agent with Detective Mode) on rented computers enabling remote keystroke logging, screenshot capture, and webcam operation without customer knowledge or consent

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1812.620 et seq. (Karnette Rental-Purchase Act) establishes comprehensive consumer protections for rent-to-own transactions including prohibitions on exorbitant pricing, liability limitations, grace periods, and early payoff formulas.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aaron's imposed minimum rental terms exceeding 4 months, preventing early termination without penalty, contrary to standard rent-to-own practice allowing cancellation at any time
violations: Aaron's imposed minimum rental terms exceeding 4 months, preventing early termination without penalty, contrary to standard rent-to-own practice allowing cancellation at any time
Aaron's charged late fees on payments fewer than 7 days late, violating § 1812.626(c)
Aaron's imposed unlimited liability for theft and liability for loss/damage not resulting from negligent/reckless/intentional consumer acts, violating § 1812.627(b)
Aaron's failed to adhere to statutory formula for calculating discounted purchase prices, violating § 1812.632(b)
Aaron's reported late payments and defaults to credit reporting agencies, violating § 1812.640
Aaron's failed to clearly and conspicuously provide Karnette Act mandated contract disclosures, violating § 1812.623

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17500 et seq. prohibits making false or misleading statements with intent to induce public to rent/purchase when the statement is known to be false or reasonably should be known to be false.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aaron's advertised periodic rental payments without conspicuously disclosing mandatory 10% Service Plus fee, showing $99.99/month when true cost was $109.99/month plus tax
violations: Aaron's advertised periodic rental payments without conspicuously disclosing mandatory 10% Service Plus fee, showing $99.99/month when true cost was $109.99/month plus tax
Aaron's used 'Sweepstakes Entry Form' to collect personal information (name, address, phone) under false pretense of sweepstakes entry when no sweepstakes existed; form was used only for sales leads

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business & Professions Code § 17200 et seq. prohibits unfair competition through unlawful, fraudulent, or unfair business practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aaron's violated Karnette Act requirements (see above), constituting unfair business practices
violations: Aaron's violated Karnette Act requirements (see above), constituting unfair business practices
Aaron's violated § 17500 false advertising prohibitions (see above)
Aaron's violated constitutional right to privacy by permitting/facilitating franchisees' installation of spyware enabling secret collection of personal information from authorized computer users

regulatoryFindings.act: California Constitution Article I, Section 1 establishes a fundamental right to privacy for all California residents.
regulatoryFindings.description: Aaron's permitted and facilitated franchisees' installation of PC Rental Agent spyware with Detective Mode on rented computers, enabling remote keystroke logging, screenshot capture, and webcam operation without customer knowledge or consent
violations: Aaron's permitted and facilitated franchisees' installation of PC Rental Agent spyware with Detective Mode on rented computers, enabling remote keystroke logging, screenshot capture, and webcam operation without customer knowledge or consent

outcome: Complaint filed October 6, 2014 by California Attorney General seeking permanent injunctions against false advertising and unfair competition practices; civil penalties of $2,500 per violation under §§ 17500 and 17200; restitution of money/property obtained through violations; and costs of suit. The complaint establishes that Aaron's contractual minimum rental terms do not exempt rent-to-own transactions from Karnette Act coverage, and that spyware installation constitutes a privacy violation under California Constitution.
companyNow: Aaron's, Inc. continues to operate as a major rent-to-own retailer in the United States. Following regulatory scrutiny, the company faced multiple enforcement actions and settlements related to these practices.
dataType: Personal information (name, address, phone number), keystroke logs, screenshots, webcam footage, financial/payment data
legalBasisViolated: California Civil Code § 1812.620 et seq. (Karnette Rental-Purchase Act)
California Civil Code § 1812.627(b) (liability limitations for damage/theft)
California Business & Professions Code § 17500 et seq. (false/misleading advertising)
California Business & Professions Code § 17200 et seq. (unfair competition)
California Constitution Article I, Section 1 (right to privacy)

companyDescription: American Apparel, Inc. is a Delaware corporation and clothing manufacturer and retailer with over 200 stores worldwide, headquartered in Los Angeles, CA. The company manufactures and sells casual apparel and operates a significant e-commerce presence.
companyLongDescription: American Apparel, Inc. is a Delaware corporation and clothing manufacturer and retailer with over 200 stores worldwide, headquartered in Los Angeles, CA. The company manufactures and sells casual apparel and operates a significant e-commerce presence.
caseDescription: American Apparel claimed on its website to be a current participant in the U.S.-EU and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor privacy frameworks, which allow lawful transfer of personal data from Europe. However, from June 2013 to December 2013, the company's certification had lapsed and was marked 'not current' on the Department of Commerce's public registry. The company continued making the false claim while handling European customer data without proper Safe Harbor compliance.
violationSummary: Company's deceptive claims about Safe Harbor compliance constituted unfair and deceptive practices. The misrepresentation caused disclosure of personal data without the consumer protections the company claimed to provide, violating consumer trust and FTC Act Section 5.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: American Apparel falsely claimed on its website that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework while its certification was lapsed from June 2013 to December 2013.
whyTheyWereWrong: European and Swiss customers unknowingly transferred personal data to the United States during the certification lapse when their information had no legally-recognized data protection safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: American Apparel has certified that it abides by the Safe Harbor privacy principles as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce
claimsVsReality.reality: From June 2013 to December 2013, American Apparel's Safe Harbor certification status was 'not current' and had not been renewed, meaning it was not an active participant in either the U.S.-EU or U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Framework during this period

claimsVsReality.claim: Company represents it is a 'current' participant in both Safe Harbor frameworks
claimsVsReality.reality: Commerce's public website listed the company's status as 'not current' for approximately six months while the company continued to claim Safe Harbor compliance on its website

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: American Apparel represented expressly and by implication on its website that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Framework when in fact its certification status was 'not current' from June 2013 until December 2013
violations: American Apparel represented expressly and by implication on its website that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Framework when in fact its certification status was 'not current' from June 2013 until December 2013
The company continued disseminating privacy policies claiming Safe Harbor compliance while processing personal data from the EEA and Switzerland without valid Safe Harbor certification

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint on June 16, 2014, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint identifies the false claims about Safe Harbor compliance made while the company's certification was lapsed. Resolution details regarding settlement or enforcement orders are not included in this complaint document.
companyNow: American Apparel continues to operate as a clothing retailer, though the company has faced financial challenges in recent years and restructured its operations.
dataType: Personal information transferred from European Economic Area and Switzerland (names, contact details, transaction data)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Accretive Health, Inc. is a healthcare revenue cycle management company that provides services to hospital systems including patient registration, coding, medical documentation, billing, denial management, and collections. The company places employees directly in hospital facilities to assist with revenue cycle operations.
companyLongDescription: Accretive Health, Inc. is a healthcare revenue cycle management company that provides services to hospital systems including patient registration, coding, medical documentation, billing, denial management, and collections. The company places employees directly in hospital facilities to assist with revenue cycle operations.
caseDescription: Accretive Health, a healthcare revenue cycle management company, failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect patient personal and health information. The company's poor practices resulted in a July 2011 incident where a laptop containing sensitive data on 23,000 patients was stolen from an employee's car. The FTC found these failures violated Section 5(a) of the FTC Act as unfair practices.
violationSummary: Accretive Health's failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures for sensitive patient personal and health information directly resulted in unauthorized access and exposure of 20+ million data points, exemplifying the insecurity category in Solove's framework.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Accretive Health failed to implement reasonable security measures for patient data, transporting unencrypted laptops containing sensitive information insecurely.
whyTheyWereWrong: A laptop containing over 20 million pieces of personal and health information for 23,000 patients including names, dates of birth, Social Security numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Accretive Health could safely handle patient personal and health information through its business processes and technology
claimsVsReality.reality: The company's actual practices exposed over 20 million data points to theft, including patient names, SSNs, and health information on 23,000 individuals

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees had access only to data necessary for their job functions
claimsVsReality.reality: The stolen laptop contained data not necessary for the employee's job, demonstrating lack of access controls and data minimization

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Accretive Health failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access until at least July 2011
violations: Accretive Health failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access until at least July 2011
Transported laptops containing personal information in a manner vulnerable to theft or misappropriation
Failed to adequately restrict access to or copying of personal information based on employee need
Failed to ensure employees removed information from computers when no longer needed for business purposes
Used consumers' personal information in training sessions without ensuring removal from employee computers afterward
These practices caused or were likely to cause substantial injury to consumers not offset by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint on February 5, 2014, against Accretive Health, Inc. for unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleged that the company's inadequate security practices caused substantial injury to consumers. The case proceeded with Accretive Health required to comply with FTC enforcement orders for data security remediation and monitoring.
companyNow: Accretive Health was acquired by Evernorth (formerly Cigna's division) in 2018 and continues operating as a healthcare revenue cycle management subsidiary. The company maintains operations providing billing and revenue management services to hospital systems.
dataType: Health data, patient names, dates of birth, billing information, diagnostic information, Social Security numbers

companyDescription: Charles River Laboratories International, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Wilmington, Massachusetts. It provides drug discovery, development, and preclinical/clinical laboratory services supporting pharmaceutical research and therapeutic development.
companyLongDescription: Charles River Laboratories International, Inc. is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Wilmington, Massachusetts. It provides drug discovery, development, and preclinical/clinical laboratory services supporting pharmaceutical research and therapeutic development.
caseDescription: Charles River Labs claimed on its website to comply with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework for handling personal data from Europe. However, from May 2011 to December 2013, the company failed to renew its certification and was marked 'not current' on the official Commerce Department registry, meaning it did not actually meet the privacy adequacy standard it represented to consumers.
violationSummary: The deceptive representation about Safe Harbor compliance misled individuals about the level of privacy protection afforded to their personal data, constituting unfair and deceptive practice affecting disclosure of data protection status.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Charles River Laboratories claimed on its website that it complied with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework while its certification status was actually "not current" from May 2011 through December.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union citizens and employees whose personal data Charles River collected had no legal assurance their information received adequate privacy protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company stated on www.criver.com: 'We comply with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework as set forth by the U.S. Department of Commerce' and invited users to 'view our certification' at the Safe Harbor registry.
claimsVsReality.reality: From May 2011 to December 2013, Charles River's certification was not current and the company was not eligible to transfer personal data from the EU under Safe Harbor protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company represented through its privacy policy that personal data would be 'used, collected, and retained in a manner consistent with the laws of the countries in which we do business,' with specific Safe Harbor compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Without valid Safe Harbor certification during the lapse period, the company could not lawfully transfer EU personal data outside Europe in compliance with EU data protection requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Charles River Labs represented expressly and by implication on its website that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework.
violations: Charles River Labs represented expressly and by implication on its website that it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework.
From May 2011 until December 2013, the company was not a 'current' participant; its status was listed as 'not current' on the Commerce Department public registry.
The company continued to disseminate privacy policies claiming Safe Harbor compliance during the period when certification had lapsed, making the representation false and misleading.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against Charles River Labs on June 19, 2014 for deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleged that the company's misrepresentation of Safe Harbor compliance status constituted unfair and deceptive acts in commerce. A consent order requiring compliance with Safe Harbor principles and corrected privacy disclosures would follow.
companyNow: Charles River Laboratories continues to operate as a major preclinical and clinical laboratory services provider. The company resolved this matter through consent and updated its Safe Harbor certification processes.
dataType: Personal data of employees, customers, and business partners from EU
legalBasisViolated: U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework Seven Principles

companyDescription: Kaiser Foundation Health Plan, Inc. is a major healthcare provider offering HMO and PPO plans to individuals, employer groups, public entities, and seniors through Medicare supplemental and Medicare Advantage products across California and other states.
