companyLongDescription: Kaiser Foundation Health Plan, Inc. is a major healthcare provider offering HMO and PPO plans to individuals, employer groups, public entities, and seniors through Medicare supplemental and Medicare Advantage products across California and other states.
caseDescription: Kaiser failed to encrypt personal information stored on an external hard drive containing data on over 30,000 employees. The drive was lost, purchased at a thrift store, and later recovered. Kaiser delayed notifying affected individuals by nearly three months despite identifying them within weeks of securing the drive.
violationSummary: The unencrypted hard drive containing sensitive personal information was made available to the general public via sale at a thrift store, creating unauthorized disclosure and exposure of personal data.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Kaiser stored over 30,000 Social Security numbers and sensitive employee personal information on an unencrypted external hard drive that was sold at a thrift store.
whyTheyWereWrong: 20,539 California residents had their Social Security numbers, names, dates of birth, and addresses exposed to identity theft and fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: Kaiser could be relied upon to protect sensitive employee personal information
claimsVsReality.reality: Kaiser stored over 30,000 Social Security numbers on an unencrypted external hard drive that was lost and purchased by a member of the public at a thrift store.

claimsVsReality.claim: Kaiser would notify affected individuals of data breaches in the most expedient time possible
claimsVsReality.reality: Kaiser delayed notification for nearly three months despite identifying affected individuals within weeks of securing the recovered drive in December 2011.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.82(a) requires disclosure of a breach of the security of a system containing personal information in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kaiser could have notified individuals as early as December 2011 but did not commence notice until March 19, 2012, a delay of approximately three months.
violations: Kaiser could have notified individuals as early as December 2011 but did not commence notice until March 19, 2012, a delay of approximately three months.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(1) prohibits publicly posting and/or displaying Social Security numbers.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kaiser publicly posted and/or displayed the Social Security numbers of 20,539 Californians on an unencrypted hard drive made available to the general public via sale at a thrift store.
violations: Kaiser publicly posted and/or displayed the Social Security numbers of 20,539 Californians on an unencrypted hard drive made available to the general public via sale at a thrift store.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair competition, including unfair, unlawful, or fraudulent business acts or practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Kaiser engaged in unfair competition through failure to encrypt sensitive personal data and delayed breach notification in violation of California Civil Code sections 1798.82 and 1798.85.
violations: Kaiser engaged in unfair competition through failure to encrypt sensitive personal data and delayed breach notification in violation of California Civil Code sections 1798.82 and 1798.85.

outcome: The complaint seeks permanent injunction against unfair competition practices, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation as determined at trial, and recovery of investigation costs. The case was filed January 23, 2014 in Alameda County Superior Court seeking equitable relief and civil penalties under California law.
companyNow: Kaiser Foundation Health Plan, Inc. remains one of the largest health maintenance organizations in the United States, operating in multiple states and serving millions of members.
dataType: Social Security numbers, employee names, dates of birth, addresses, spouse and children personal information

companyDescription: DataMotion, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing encrypted email and secure file transport systems to businesses, with headquarters in Morristown, New Jersey.
companyLongDescription: DataMotion, Inc. is a Delaware corporation providing encrypted email and secure file transport systems to businesses, with headquarters in Morristown, New Jersey.
caseDescription: DataMotion falsely claimed compliance with the U.S.-EU and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor frameworks by displaying the certification mark on its website and publishing privacy statements, even though its certification lapsed in April 2013 and was not renewed until November 2013. The company made no remedial disclosures during the seven-month period when it was not actually a certified participant, exposing European and Swiss data subjects to unprotected transfers.
violationSummary: The false certification claims exposed EU and Swiss individuals' personal data to unprotected transfers outside their home jurisdictions, contradicting Safe Harbor adequacy protections they were promised.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: DataMotion displayed the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor certification mark and claimed Safe Harbor compliance on its website from April 2012 through November 2013 despite failing to renew its.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union and Swiss customers entrusted DataMotion with sensitive personal data believing their information received legally adequate privacy protections.

claimsVsReality.claim: DataMotion complies with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Framework and has certified adherence to Safe Harbor Privacy Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: From April 2013 to November 2013, DataMotion was not a current participant in either Safe Harbor Framework; its self-certification was not renewed until November 2013.

claimsVsReality.claim: Displayed certification mark on website indicating current Safe Harbor participation (April 2012–present).
claimsVsReality.reality: The certification mark was only authorized for companies maintaining current self-certification; DataMotion's certification lapsed in April 2013 and remained invalid for seven months.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: DataMotion represented it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Frameworks by displaying the certification mark and publishing compliance statements from April 2012.
violations: DataMotion represented it was a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Frameworks by displaying the certification mark and publishing compliance statements from April 2012.
In truth, DataMotion failed to renew its self-certification in April 2013, resulting in 'not current' status from April 2013 to November 2013.
DataMotion continued to display the mark and maintain compliance claims throughout the certification lapse without disclosing that its certification was no longer valid.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against DataMotion alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint was issued on June 19, 2014. The document establishes the factual and legal basis for enforcement action; however, the document is the complaint itself and does not contain the final settlement, consent order, or resolution. Remedial action would be determined in a subsequent administrative proceeding or settlement agreement.
dataType: Personal data of EU and Swiss individuals (unspecified categories, potentially email communications and file transfers)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Reynolds Consumer Products Inc. manufactures and sells food wrapping foil and a variety of household products for cooking, storage, and disposal, with principal operations in Lake Forest, Illinois.
companyLongDescription: Reynolds Consumer Products Inc. manufactures and sells food wrapping foil and a variety of household products for cooking, storage, and disposal, with principal operations in Lake Forest, Illinois.
caseDescription: Reynolds falsely claimed on its website that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework between April 2010 and November 2013, despite failing to renew its certifications. The company continued to represent Safe Harbor compliance to consumers while its status had been marked 'not current' on the Department of Commerce registry.
violationSummary: Reynolds made false statements about its data protection certification status, misleading consumers about the protections applied to their personal data transferred across borders.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Reynolds claimed on its website from April 2009 to November 2013 that it complied with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: European customers and employees transferred their personal data to Reynolds believing it was protected under Safe Harbor, but Reynolds had allowed its certifications to lapse.

claimsVsReality.claim: This Privacy Policy complies with the Safe Harbor Principles as agreed upon by the United States Department of Commerce and the European Commission.
claimsVsReality.reality: Reynolds had not renewed its Safe Harbor certification for customer data since April 2010 and for HR data since April 2011, meaning it was not a 'current' participant in the framework during the period the claim was made.

claimsVsReality.claim: Reynolds was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework (implied by continuous privacy policy statements).
claimsVsReality.reality: Commerce's public registry marked Reynolds' status as 'not current' for customer data from April 2010 and for HR data from April 2011 through November 2013.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Reynolds represented on its website that it was a 'current' Safe Harbor Framework participant when it had failed to renew certifications, making its status 'not current' on Commerce's public registry.
violations: Reynolds represented on its website that it was a 'current' Safe Harbor Framework participant when it had failed to renew certifications, making its status 'not current' on Commerce's public registry.

The company's privacy policy statement claiming Safe Harbor compliance remained published from April 2010 (after customer data certification lapsed) until November 2013, deceiving consumers about data protection standards.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 19, 2014, finding that Reynolds engaged in deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The case alleges systematic misrepresentation of Safe Harbor compliance status. A consent order was expected to require Reynolds to cease the deceptive claims and implement compliance procedures.
companyNow: Reynolds Consumer Products Inc. remains a major manufacturer of household consumer goods including food wrapping foil and storage products, operating under the Alcoa Corp. ownership structure as of recent years.
dataType: Customer data, human resources data (employment records)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: GMR Transcription Services, Inc. was a California-based company that provided digital audio transcription services to customers including universities, corporations, government agencies, and healthcare providers. The company outsourced most of its work to independent typists and third-party service providers.
companyLongDescription: GMR Transcription Services, Inc. was a California-based company that provided digital audio transcription services to customers including universities, corporations, government agencies, and healthcare providers. The company outsourced most of its work to independent typists and third-party service providers.
caseDescription: GMR Transcription Services failed to implement adequate security measures to protect sensitive personal and medical information in audio and transcript files. The company made false claims about HIPAA compliance and security safeguards while automatically routing all medical transcriptions to an India-based subcontractor that left thousands of medical files publicly accessible online through an unsecured FTP server.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information, resulting in widespread public exposure of sensitive data through inadequate third-party oversight.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: GMR Transcription Services failed to implement reasonable security measures and automatically sent medical audio files containing patients' sensitive data to an India-based vendor that stored.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of medical transcript files containing patients' names, birth dates, psychiatric disorder information, medications, children's exam notes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Why GMR Transcription Services? . . . Security Measures to Protect Your Confidentiality. Each transcriptionist within the GMR community is required to sign a Confidentiality Agreement prior to working for us. Materials going through our system are highly secure and are never divulged to anyone.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to verify that its primary medical transcription subcontractor (Fedtrans) implemented any security measures. Fedtrans stored and transmitted files in clear readable text using an unsecured FTP server accessible to anyone online, resulting in thousands of medical files being indexed and publicly accessible via search engines.

claimsVsReality.claim: HIPAA Compliant Medical Transcription Service
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was not HIPAA compliant. It did not require its service providers to implement security measures such as encryption, authentication, or secure file storage. It did not monitor or assess whether Fedtrans employed HIPAA-required safeguards.

claimsVsReality.claim: A good company will make sure that the sensitive information related to patients is handled with great care. From compliance training and secure systems to the confidentiality agreements, Transcription Companies cover all the aspects involved in the HIPAA regulations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company took no measures to ensure secure systems or verify compliance with HIPAA regulations. It did not request or review information about its subcontractor's security practices, audits, or information security program.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents represented expressly and by implication that they implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information in audio and transcript files, when in fact they did not.
violations: Respondents represented expressly and by implication that they implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information in audio and transcript files, when in fact they did not.

Respondents represented that they took reasonable measures to oversee their service providers to ensure they implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures, when in fact they did not adequately verify Fedtrans' security practices or require contractual security obligations.

Respondents failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information, causing substantial consumer injury including exposure of medical records, children's health information, and sensitive psychiatric data.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on August 14, 2014, alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The case alleged three counts: (1) deceptive representations about security measures; (2) deceptive representations about service provider oversight; and (3) unfair practices due to inadequate security. The respondents were required to implement comprehensive information security programs, obtain third-party security assessments, establish contractual security requirements for service providers, and submit compliance certifications to the FTC.
companyNow: Current status of GMR Transcription Services, Inc. is unknown. The company faced significant regulatory action and reputational damage from the public exposure of thousands of medical records.
dataType: Health data, medical records, names, dates of birth, addresses, email addresses, telephone numbers, Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, tax information, psychiatric notes, children's medical information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) - Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) - Deceptive representations regarding security measures
FTC Act Section 5(a) - Deceptive representations regarding service provider oversight

companyDescription: BitTorrent, Inc. is a California-based software company that developed and operated a widely-used peer-to-peer file-sharing protocol for exchanging large files including software, music, movies, and digital books online.
companyLongDescription: BitTorrent, Inc. is a California-based software company that developed and operated a widely-used peer-to-peer file-sharing protocol for exchanging large files including software, music, movies, and digital books online.
caseDescription: BitTorrent, Inc. falsely claimed to be a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework on its website from January 2007 to November 2013, despite failing to renew its self-certification in January 2008. The company continued to represent that it adhered to Safe Harbor principles while its status on the official Commerce Department registry remained 'not current,' deceiving consumers and regulatory bodies about its privacy compliance.
violationSummary: BitTorrent's false representations about Safe Harbor participation constituted deceptive disclosure regarding the legal safeguards protecting personal data transfers, misleading consumers about the jurisdiction and standards governing their personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: BitTorrent falsely claimed on its website from January 2007 until November 2013 that it adhered to the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: European Union users transferred personal data to BitTorrent based on false Safe Harbor claims, leaving their information without the legal protections they believed they had when sharing data.

claimsVsReality.claim: BitTorrent adheres to the European Union Safe Harbor principles as set forth by the United States Department of Commerce regarding the collection, use, and retention of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: BitTorrent did not renew its Safe Harbor self-certification in January 2008 and was listed as 'not current' on the official Commerce Department website (www.export.gov/safeharbor), yet continued making these claims until November 2013.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: BitTorrent represented itself as a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework on its website and privacy policy from January 2007 to November 2013.
violations: BitTorrent represented itself as a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework on its website and privacy policy from January 2007 to November 2013.
BitTorrent's self-certification lapsed in January 2008 and was marked 'not current' on the Commerce Department registry, but the company continued making Safe Harbor compliance claims.
The false representations were material to consumers relying on Safe Harbor protections for their personal data.

outcome: FTC issued a complaint alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The enforcement action charged BitTorrent with falsely claiming Safe Harbor Framework participation for nearly six years after allowing its certification to lapse. The complaint sought to halt the deceptive conduct and enforce compliance with truthful privacy disclosures.
companyNow: BitTorrent, Inc. (formerly Bittorrent Inc.) was acquired by Justin Sun's Tron Foundation in 2018. The company operates as part of the TRON ecosystem focused on decentralized file sharing and blockchain technology.
dataType: Personal data (unspecified categories covered by privacy policy)

companyDescription: TRENDnet, Inc. is a California-based retailer specializing in networking devices including routers, modems, and IP cameras for home users and small to medium-sized businesses. The company had approximately $62–66 million in annual revenue during 2010–2012.
companyLongDescription: TRENDnet, Inc. is a California-based retailer specializing in networking devices including routers, modems, and IP cameras for home users and small to medium-sized businesses. The company had approximately $62–66 million in annual revenue during 2010–2012.
caseDescription: TRENDnet sold IP cameras marketed as 'secure' for home and business monitoring but failed to implement reasonable security measures. Login credentials were transmitted and stored unencrypted, and a critical flaw in the authentication feature allowed hackers to access hundreds of cameras and expose intimate footage from private homes. Nearly 700 cameras were compromised, displaying infants in cribs and families in private settings.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect sensitive personal data (live video feeds) from unauthorized access. Despite marketing the cameras as secure, TRENDnet did not encrypt credentials, did not perform adequate security testing, and failed to monitor vulnerability reports, resulting in a major breach affecting hundreds of cameras.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: TRENDnet marketed IP cameras as secure for home surveillance but transmitted user login credentials in plain text, stored credentials unencrypted on mobile devices.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 700 of the company's cameras were hacked, exposing intimate home video feeds showing sleeping infants, children playing, and private activities, with hackers posting links online.

claimsVsReality.claim: TRENDnet's SecurView IP cameras are 'secure' and suitable for monitoring private areas of homes and businesses.
claimsVsReality.reality: The cameras lacked basic security: credentials transmitted in plain text, stored unencrypted on mobile devices, and a critical flaw allowed unauthorized access to all live feeds regardless of user settings.

claimsVsReality.claim: The DVSA (Direct Video Stream Authentication) setting allows users to control whether login credentials are required.
claimsVsReality.reality: The DVSA setting malfunctioned for 20 camera models from April 2010 to February 2012, failing to honor users' choices and exposing all live feeds publicly without user knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: An authentication feature with login credentials protects access to live feeds.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the feature existed by default, the company transmitted and stored credentials unencrypted, making them easily interceptable and accessible to anyone with basic technical knowledge.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: COUNT 1: Represented that IP cameras and mobile apps were secure means to monitor private areas, but failed to take reasonable security steps (unencrypted transmission/storage of credentials, insufficient testing, no vulnerability monitoring).
violations: COUNT 1: Represented that IP cameras and mobile apps were secure means to monitor private areas, but failed to take reasonable security steps (unencrypted transmission/storage of credentials, insufficient testing, no vulnerability monitoring).
COUNT 2: Represented that users' security settings would be honored, but the DVSA setting failed to function properly and allowed unauthorized access regardless of user settings.

COUNT 3: Failed to provide reasonable security to prevent unauthorized access to live feeds from IP cameras, causing substantial injury to consumers (hundreds of cameras compromised, intimate footage exposed).

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on January 16, 2014, alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint identified three counts: false/misleading security representations, failure to honor user security settings, and unfair practices due to inadequate security. TRENDnet was required to implement reasonable security measures going forward, including encryption of credentials, security testing, vulnerability monitoring, and employee training. The case resulted in a Consent Order requiring ongoing compliance monitoring and remediation.
companyNow: TRENDnet continues to operate as a networking device manufacturer. Following the 2014 FTC action, the company implemented security improvements and remediation measures as required by the consent order.
dataType: Live video and audio feeds, login credentials, location data (inferred from camera IP addresses)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Snapchat is a multimedia messaging application that allows users to send ephemeral photo and video messages. Launched in 2011, it became one of the top free mobile applications with over 350 million daily snaps by 2013.
companyLongDescription: Snapchat is a multimedia messaging application that allows users to send ephemeral photo and video messages. Launched in 2011, it became one of the top free mobile applications with over 350 million daily snaps by 2013.
caseDescription: Snapchat made false claims that messages would 'disappear forever' and that senders would be notified of screenshots, when multiple methods existed to save and view content indefinitely. The company also falsely claimed it did not collect location data while actually transmitting Wi-Fi and cell-based location information, and misrepresented its collection of users' entire address books.
violationSummary: Snapchat's false claims about message permanence and screenshot detection created heightened risk of exposure of sensitive photos and videos. Inadequate security on the Find Friends feature resulted in exposure of 4.6 million usernames and phone numbers.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Snapchat falsely marketed messages as permanently disappearing after timers expired and claimed senders would be notified if recipients took screenshots.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of users shared intimate photos and sensitive personal information based on false promises of disappearance, exposing them to permanent retention by unintended recipients.

claimsVsReality.claim: Messages 'disappear forever' after the timer expires
claimsVsReality.reality: Recipients could save content indefinitely using file browsing tools, third-party applications, and device screenshots

claimsVsReality.claim: Senders will be notified if recipients take a screenshot
claimsVsReality.reality: On iOS versions prior to 7, users could double-press the Home button to bypass screenshot detection without notification

claimsVsReality.claim: We do not ask for, track, or access any location-specific information from your device
claimsVsReality.reality: Android version transmitted Wi-Fi-based and cell-based location information to analytics service from October 2012 to February 2013

claimsVsReality.claim: Only mobile phone number collected for Find Friends feature
claimsVsReality.reality: Application collected names and phone numbers of all contacts in user's address book without notice or consent

claimsVsReality.claim: Employs best security practices to keep your data protected
claimsVsReality.reality: Failed to verify phone numbers until December 2012 and lacked API rate limiting, resulting in 4.6 million usernames and phone numbers being exposed in December 2013

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented that messages would 'disappear forever' when recipients could save content via file browsing tools, third-party apps, and screenshots
violations: Represented that messages would 'disappear forever' when recipients could save content via file browsing tools, third-party apps, and screenshots
Claimed senders would be notified of screenshots when users could easily circumvent detection on iOS prior to version 7
Stated it did not collect location information while transmitting Wi-Fi and cell-based location data on Android
Implied only phone number was collected in Find Friends feature while actually collecting entire address books
Claimed to employ reasonable security measures while failing to verify phone numbers (until Dec 2012) and lacking API rate limiting, allowing compilation of 4.6 million usernames and phone numbers

outcome: FTC issued a complaint against Snapchat on December 23, 2014, alleging six counts of deceptive practices. The case proceeded to a consent order requiring Snapchat to implement reasonable security measures, provide clear disclosures about data collection and retention, and submit to periodic FTC monitoring and audits.
companyNow: Snapchat (now Snap Inc., a public company trading as SNAP) continues operating as a major social media platform. The company implemented privacy improvements and security measures following FTC enforcement.
dataType: Mobile phone numbers, contact information, geolocation data, photos, videos
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Level 3 Communications is a Delaware limited liability company headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado. It is one of the six largest internet service providers globally, providing international communications and data transfer infrastructure services.
companyLongDescription: Level 3 Communications is a Delaware limited liability company headquartered in Broomfield, Colorado. It is one of the six largest internet service providers globally, providing international communications and data transfer infrastructure services.
caseDescription: Level 3 Communications publicly claimed compliance with U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy frameworks on its website from June 2001 through November 2013, despite failing to renew its certification in June 2012. The company's deceptive statements misrepresented its actual Safe Harbor participation status to consumers and regulatory authorities, violating FTC Section 5.
violationSummary: Level 3 misrepresented its Safe Harbor certification status in public privacy disclosures, deceiving consumers and regulators about data transfer protections—a form of deceptive information dissemination.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Level 3 Communications displayed statements on its website claiming compliance with U.S.-EU and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor frameworks from June 2001 until November 2013.
whyTheyWereWrong: European customers and partners transferred personal data to Level 3 based on false Safe Harbor claims, exposing their data to transfer without the legal protections they believed were in place.

claimsVsReality.claim: Level 3 stated: 'Transfers of personally identifiable information made by Level 3 are made in compliance with the Safe Harbor principles to which Level 3 has self-certified its adherence.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Level 3 did not renew its Safe Harbor self-certification in June 2012, making it a 'not current' participant from June 2012 through November 2013, yet continued the misleading claim until November 2013.

claimsVsReality.claim: Level 3 represented itself as a 'current' participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Frameworks.
claimsVsReality.reality: Level 3 was not current with Safe Harbor frameworks during the June 2012–November 2013 period, as evidenced by the Department of Commerce updating its status to 'not current' on the public Safe Harbor website.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Level 3 expressly represented it was a 'current' participant in U.S.-EU Safe Harbor and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Frameworks through privacy policy statements on www.level3.com
violations: Level 3 expressly represented it was a 'current' participant in U.S.-EU Safe Harbor and U.S.-Swiss Safe Harbor Frameworks through privacy policy statements on www.level3.com
From June 2012 to November 2013, Level 3 was not a 'current' participant after failing to renew certification, making the representation false and misleading
The deceptive representations were disseminated to consumers via the company website during the non-compliance period

outcome: FTC issued a complaint on June 19, 2014, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint was filed seeking a compliance order requiring Level 3 to cease false Safe Harbor representations and implement accurate privacy disclosures going forward. No monetary penalty is stated in this complaint document.
companyNow: Level 3 Communications continues to operate as an international communications provider and major internet service provider. The company remains active in telecom and data transfer services with enhanced compliance frameworks.
dataType: Personally identifiable information

company: Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada
companyDescription: Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada (AANDC) is a Canadian federal government department responsible for administering policies and programs related to Indigenous peoples, lands, and resources.
companyLongDescription: AANDC is a federal government entity that manages relationships with Indigenous communities and oversees policies affecting First Nations, Inuit, and Métis peoples. The department administers various programs related to Indian affairs, northern development, and Indigenous governance. In this case, AANDC facilitated the enrollment process for the Qaliqu Mi'kmaq First Nation Band, a newly established First Nation created in 2011 to formally recognize Mi'kmaq people in Newfoundland.
caseDescription: The Qalipu Mi'kmaq First Nation Band published founding members' full names and dates of birth in the publicly available Canada Gazette online as part of an enrollment process. A complainant raised concerns that this disclosure created an identity theft risk. The investigation found the disclosure consistent with Privacy Act provisions but recommended exploring alternatives such as partial date of birth or offline registry linking.
violationSummary: While the disclosure was legally permissible under the Privacy Act, the unrestricted public online disclosure of sensitive personal identifiers (full name and date of birth) created heightened exposure risk in an electronic environment, characteristic of the Exposure category in Solove's taxonomy.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada published the full names and dates of birth of founding members of the Qaliqu Mi'kmaq First Nation Band in the publicly available Canada.
whyTheyWereWrong: Publishing complete personal information including full names and dates of birth online created a real risk of identity theft for band members whose sensitive data became widely accessible.

claimsVsReality.claim: The disclosure of full names and dates of birth was necessary for the identification and recognition of band members.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the disclosure served a legitimate purpose, it created unnecessary identity theft risk that could have been mitigated through partial information or offline registry linking.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – permits disclosure of personal information without consent when disclosure is for the purpose for which information was originally collected
regulatoryFindings.description: AANDC disclosed full name and date of birth of founding band members in publicly available Canada Gazette for identification and recognition purposes, which aligned with original collection purpose but created elevated identity theft risk in online environment
violations: AANDC disclosed full name and date of birth of founding band members in publicly available Canada Gazette for identification and recognition purposes, which aligned with original collection purpose but created elevated identity theft risk in online environment

outcome: Complaint found not well founded; however, the Office recommended that AANDC explore alternative disclosure methods in future to mitigate identity theft risk, including furnishing only partial date of birth or enabling linking through another identifier to an offline registry.
companyNow: AANDC continues to operate as a federal department responsible for Indigenous affairs and northern development in Canada.

caseDescription: Correctional Service of Canada denied a complainant access to a full 10-page report about his treatment and supervision, instead providing only a 3-page abbreviated version claiming it represented the 'gist' of the findings. The abbreviated version was determined to be a misrepresentation of the actual information. After investigation and negotiation, CSC provided the full report with appropriate redactions and committed to staff training on privacy obligations.
violationSummary: The provision of an abbreviated version that misrepresented the full content of the official report constitutes distortion of personal information in the context of access and disclosure obligations.

whyTheyWereWrong: The inmate was deprived of access to his complete personal records regarding his treatment and supervision, receiving a misrepresentation that omitted 11 pages.

claimsVsReality.reality: The full report was 10 pages containing 14 findings; the abbreviated version contained only 2 findings and omitted 11 pages of relevant information about the inmate's treatment and supervision.

claimsVsReality.claim: Withholding the detailed report was justified because it was based on informal interviews.
claimsVsReality.reality: The inmate had a right under the Privacy Act to access his complete personal information held by CSC, regardless of the source or informal nature of the underlying interviews.

companyDescription: Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) is the federal agency responsible for managing penitentiaries and supervising offenders in Canada.
companyLongDescription: Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) is a federal law enforcement and corrections agency operating under the Department of Public Safety. It manages maximum-security and other penitentiaries across Canada, supervises inmate populations, and employs correctional officers. CSC is responsible for implementing security protocols, record retention policies, and complying with privacy legislation including the Privacy Act.
caseDescription: Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) denied an inmate's access requests for 18 video recordings of incidents involving alleged officer misconduct, claiming third-party privacy concerns and institutional security risks. An investigation revealed CSC failed to retrieve or review most requested videos before refusing access, and 16 of the 18 videos were destroyed without proper consideration, with CSC denying access to non-existent records. The denial pattern indicated CSC treated denial as a default approach rather than promoting the openness and accountability intended by the Privacy Act.
violationSummary: CSC's systematic withholding of personal information (video recordings) and denial of legitimate access requests, combined with destruction of records before proper review, constitutes a breach of the duty to handle personal information transparently and accountably as required by the Privacy Act.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
Improper Data Disposal

whyTheyWereWrong: The inmate seeking evidence of officer assaults, hate crimes, and sexual harassment was denied access to videos that could have documented his allegations.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC claimed the 18 videos contained third-party personal information that could not reasonably be severed and that disclosure would be injurious to institutional security.
claimsVsReality.reality: CSC had not retrieved or reviewed most requested videos before refusing access; 16 videos had already been destroyed under standard retention rules without informing the inmate; the two retained use-of-force videos did not contain other inmates as CSC claimed.

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC applied Privacy Act exemptions to justify withholding all 18 video recordings.
claimsVsReality.reality: CSC applied exemptions to 16 recordings that no longer existed when it responded, and did not actually review the two retained recordings before claiming exemptions.

regulatoryFindings.description: CSC denied access to 18 video recordings without retrieving or reviewing them first

CSC applied privacy exemptions (Sections 19 and 21) to records that did not exist at time of refusal

regulatoryFindings.description: CSC's approach treated denial of access as default starting point rather than promoting openness and accountability

CSC failed to implement measures to prevent destruction of records subject to pending Privacy Act requests with short retention periods

outcome: Investigation found 16 complaints concerning destroyed video recordings to be well-founded. Complaints regarding the two remaining use-of-force videos were resolved, as CSC correctly demonstrated that disclosure would be injurious to institutional security. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner recommended that CSC implement appropriate measures to ensure Privacy Act requests reach appropriate officials in time to prevent destruction of records with short retention periods, and to adopt a presumption of openness rather than denial as the starting point for access requests.
companyNow: CSC continues to operate as Canada's federal corrections agency. Following this investigation, it was directed to implement measures ensuring Privacy Act requests reach appropriate officials in time to prevent destruction of records with short retention periods.

National Defence acknowledged the breach and implemented controls, policy updates, and staff training.

company: Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada
companyDescription: Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada (AANDC) is a Canadian federal department responsible for policies and programs affecting First Nations, Inuit and Métis peoples.

caseDescription: Aboriginal Affairs and Northern Development Canada (AANDC) and the Department of Justice Canada systematically collected and monitored personal information from First Nations activist Cindy Blackstock's personal Facebook page and other social media without a direct connection to legitimate government business. The departments argued that publicly available information on Facebook was not subject to privacy protections, but a formal investigation rejected this position. Both departments were ordered to cease collection and destroy previously collected personal information, and to implement policies governing social media collection.
violationSummary: The departments engaged in systematic and deliberate monitoring and collection of personal information from the complainant's social media accounts without legitimate government purpose, constituting surveillance under privacy law.

Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
Improper Data Disposal

whyTheyWereWrong: Blackstock's personal information—her friends, views, skills and residency—was collected and distributed within government without her knowledge.

claimsVsReality.reality: Public availability does not render personal information non-personal under the Privacy Act; restrictions on collection of personal information apply regardless of whether it is publicly available.

claimsVsReality.claim: Information collected from Blackstock's Facebook was relevant to policy development by AANDC and the human rights lawsuit.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation concluded the personal information collected was not obviously relevant to policy development or the litigation, and was collected without legitimate government business justification.

claimsVsReality.reality: The collection was conducted surreptitiously without the complainant's knowledge or consent, and the lack of transparency violated the spirit of the Privacy Act.

outcome: Both AANDC and the Department of Justice Canada accepted all recommendations in full. They were required to: (1) immediately cease accessing personal information on Ms. Blackstock's personal Facebook page and other social media sites unless a direct connection to legitimate government business could be demonstrated; (2) destroy all previously collected personal information without such direct connection; (3) develop and implement internal policies and guidelines governing employee collection of personal information from social media, limiting such collection only to situations with direct connection to operating programs or activities.

companyDescription: SuccessfulMatch Inc. is a dating website operator that runs PositiveSingles.com, a niche dating platform for individuals with sexually transmitted diseases, along with an affiliate marketing network of approximately 60 related dating sites.
companyLongDescription: SuccessfulMatch Inc., incorporated in California with Toronto operations, operates PositiveSingles.com as a specialized online dating service for people with STDs including HIV, Herpes, HPV, and Hepatitis. The company uses an affiliate marketing model where independent entrepreneurs promote PositiveSingles under different domain names (e.g., gaypozdating.com, havehiv.com), but SuccessfulMatch retains complete control of all websites, shared databases, payment processing, and customer support. Members sign up through various affiliate sites but are automatically added to a single unified membership database without understanding the network structure. The company monetizes by paying affiliates commissions for each new profile registered through their domain, creating financial incentives to market to increasingly narrow demographic subsets.
caseDescription: SuccessfulMatch operated PositiveSingles.com, a dating site for people with STDs, and automatically shared user profiles across approximately 60 affiliated dating websites without informed consent. Users' sensitive medical and personal information appeared on unrelated dating sites targeting different demographics, and members could not opt out. The company failed to adequately disclose its network structure and affiliate relationships, and did not maintain sufficient security safeguards to prevent unauthorized access via search engines.
violationSummary: The company used personal information collected for PositiveSingles.com for a secondary purpose (propagating it across an unknown and unlimited network of affiliate sites) without meaningful informed consent. The users' sensitive health information was repurposed across demographically diverse websites without their knowledge or ability to control dissemination.

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. companyLongDescription: A Canadian financial institution operating retail banking services, including credit card issuance and account management. The institution maintains branch networks where customers conduct in-person transactions such as credit card pickup. The bank operates under anti-money laundering compliance obligations under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act.
caseDescription: A bank employee asked a long-standing customer to provide his driver's license number when picking up a replacement credit card, claiming it was required for anti-money laundering compliance. The bank later admitted the explanation provided to the customer was inaccurate and violated the principle requiring employees to properly explain the purposes for collecting personal information.
violationSummary: The bank's employee requested personal information (driver's license number) from the customer without properly explaining the true or necessary purposes for collection. The explanation given (PCMLTFA compliance) was inaccurate, as the customer's existing identification already satisfied regulatory requirements. This represents improper interrogation through misrepresented justification.
