whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's file already contained a birth certificate reference number that satisfied regulatory requirements.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank's customer service unit stated that the request for driver's license information was required under the Proceeds of Crime (Money Laundering) and Terrorist Financing Act (PCMLTFA) and OSFI Guideline B-8.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant's file already contained his birth certificate reference number and place of issue, which fully satisfied the PCMLTF Regulations requirements for identity verification. The bank's ombudsman later admitted the rationale provided to the customer was incorrect.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank's procedures required recording the driver's license number as part of anti-money laundering compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: The PCMLTF Regulations only require that identity be ascertained from an acceptable document (including a birth certificate); they do not require recording of reference numbers when the customer's file already contains compliant identification.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2.5 - Persons collecting personal information should be able to explain to individuals the purposes for which the information is being collected
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank employee provided inaccurate explanation that driver's license was required for PCMLTFA compliance when customer's existing birth certificate reference already satisfied regulatory requirements
violations: Bank employee provided inaccurate explanation that driver's license was required for PCMLTFA compliance when customer's existing birth certificate reference already satisfied regulatory requirements
Employee was unable to properly explain the actual circumstances-specific purposes for requesting identification

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.4 - Collection of personal information shall be limited to that which is necessary for the purposes identified by the organization
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank's procedures required recording full driver's license details despite existing sufficient identification being on file
violations: Bank's procedures required recording full driver's license details despite existing sufficient identification being on file

outcome: The complaint regarding failure to properly identify purposes of collection (Principle 4.2.5) was found to be well-founded and resolved. The bank revised its credit card pickup procedures to limit recording of new identification to only the type and place of issue (rather than full reference numbers) when existing identification meets anti-money laundering requirements. The bank circulated this revised guidance to staff. The complaint regarding collection limitation (Principle 4.4) was found not well-founded because the customer refused to provide the driver's license and no actual collection occurred. The Office recommended the bank remind branches to inform customers of acceptable identification options.
dataType: Driver's license number, birth certificate reference number, identification documents

companyDescription: A legal firm that acted as a legal agent for estate administration matters, providing proxy legal services across provincial jurisdictions.
companyLongDescription: The respondent is a Canadian law firm that operated as a legal agent for another law firm involved in administering estates. The firm had a limited and indirect role in estate administration, specifically handling a land transaction in connection with one estate. The firm served as a service provider rather than direct counsel to the estates or beneficiaries.
caseDescription: A legal firm failed to respond within the required 30-day timeframe to an individual's access requests for personal information relating to estates he was a beneficiary of. The firm initially ignored two access requests before responding only after the Privacy Commissioner intervened. The investigation determined the firm had violated PIPEDA's response obligation, though the firm ultimately conducted a reasonable search and confirmed it held no personal information about the complainant.
violationSummary: The firm's failure to respond to access requests within the statutory 30-day period under PIPEDA constitutes exclusion — denying the individual access to information about themselves and transparency regarding what personal information is held.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The legal firm ignored two written access requests from an individual seeking personal information about estates for which he was a beneficiary.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individual was denied timely access to information he was entitled to under privacy law, forcing him to escalate his complaint to regulators before receiving any response.

claimsVsReality.claim: The legal firm believed it was not required to respond to access requests because it held no personal information about the complainant.
claimsVsReality.reality: Under PIPEDA, organizations must respond within 30 days to access requests even if they hold no responsive information; silence constitutes a deemed refusal.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant was entitled as a beneficiary to access all estate information and general beneficiary entitlements under PIPEDA.
claimsVsReality.reality: PIPEDA only grants individuals access to information that is specifically 'about' them personally; general estate administration documents and statements of accounts do not qualify as the beneficiary's personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 8(3) — Organizations must respond to access requests within 30 days
regulatoryFindings.description: Legal firm failed to respond to two consecutive access requests
violations: Legal firm failed to respond to two consecutive access requests
Firm only responded after Privacy Commissioner intervention

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 & 4.9.1 — Organizations must inform individuals of existence and provide access to their personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Firm initially refused to acknowledge or respond to access requests
violations: Firm initially refused to acknowledge or respond to access requests

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 2(1) — Personal information is information about an identifiable individual
regulatoryFindings.description: Firm's interpretation that it held no personal information about the complainant was reasonable given the information requested was estate administration data, not information specifically 'about' the individual
violations: Firm's interpretation that it held no personal information about the complainant was reasonable given the information requested was estate administration data, not information specifically 'about' the individual

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded and resolved. The firm violated PIPEDA's 30-day response obligation by initially failing to respond to access requests. However, after the Privacy Commissioner's intervention, the firm provided a written response confirming it held no personal information about the complainant. The investigation concluded the firm conducted a reasonable search of its records. The complainant's request for access to personal information has been fulfilled.
dataType: Estate information, financial records, beneficiary entitlements, correspondence, account statements, disbursement receipts

companyDescription: An online dating service that operated in Canada and collected customer profile information, photographs, and email addresses for matching and marketing purposes.
companyLongDescription: This was a Canadian online dating platform that maintained customer profiles, photographs, and contact information to facilitate matchmaking and send marketing communications. The company failed to implement proper data governance practices, including access controls, consent management, and data retention policies. When the company was sold, customer data including the complainant's profile was transferred to the new owner without explicit notification or consent.
caseDescription: An online dating service failed to delete a customer's personal information after he cancelled his membership and requested removal from marketing lists, continuing to send him marketing emails without consent. The organization also denied the customer access to his personal information, including photographs, and failed to maintain adequate privacy safeguards or provide a privacy policy.
violationSummary: The organization continued to use the complainant's email address for marketing purposes after he explicitly withdrew consent, which constitutes unauthorized secondary use of personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Improper Data Disposal
whatTheyDid: The online dating service continued sending marketing emails to a former customer after he cancelled his membership.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer was unable to access his own data or control how it was used after withdrawal, remained targeted by unwanted marketing communications without consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: All of the complainant's personal information had been purged from the service's computer systems and destroyed in a shredder.
claimsVsReality.reality: The original owner had transferred all customer profiles and data to the new owner via the sales agreement, including the complainant's complete profile and email address.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had provided the complainant with his online profile.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant was initially denied access to his personal information and only received partial access months later after the new owner's involvement, and was never provided access to his photographs.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal profile information was not found in any database.
claimsVsReality.reality: The information existed in an active database that was transferred between owners and remained available throughout the complaint investigation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The information was stored safely in inactive files, not on computerized databases.
claimsVsReality.reality: The data was actively maintained in computer systems and transferred between owners as part of a business transaction.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 - Organizations must provide individuals access to their personal information within 30 days
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization denied complainant access to his personal information
violations: Organization denied complainant access to his personal information
Failed to meet the 30-day timeline for providing access
Access was only granted months later after OPC involvement and by new owner

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.8 - Organizations must respect withdrawal of consent for use and disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization continued sending marketing emails after complainant withdrew consent
violations: Organization continued sending marketing emails after complainant withdrew consent
Continued use of email address for marketing purposes despite clear request for removal

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.5.3 - Personal information must be retained only as long as necessary for fulfilling identified purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization retained complainant's information after it was no longer required to deliver dating services
violations: Organization retained complainant's information after it was no longer required to deliver dating services

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4(d) - Organizations must have a privacy policy in place
regulatoryFindings.description: No privacy policy existed at the time of complainant's initial dealings with the organization
violations: No privacy policy existed at the time of complainant's initial dealings with the organization

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7.1 - Organizations must safeguard personal information against unauthorized access and disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization falsely claimed information was not stored in computerized databases
violations: Organization falsely claimed information was not stored in computerized databases
Information was improperly transferred to new owner without adequate safeguards
Photographs were only deleted by new owner when they could not verify content

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 8(8) - Organizations must retain information subject to access requests to allow individuals to exhaust recourse
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization destroyed photographs, limiting complainant's ability to verify completeness of access
violations: Organization destroyed photographs, limiting complainant's ability to verify completeness of access

outcome: The OPC found the complaints well-founded on multiple grounds. The new owner of the dating service subsequently took corrective actions: deleted all of the complainant's personal information, removed his email from marketing lists, developed and posted a comprehensive privacy policy, and implemented documented safeguards for personal information. The complainant received no further communications from the service. All aspects of the complaint were considered either resolved or well-founded and resolved following remediation by the new owner.
dataType: Email address, profile information, photographs, personal profile data
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.8 (Use, Disclosure and Retention of Personal Information)
PIPEDA subsection 8(8) (Retention for Access Request Purposes)

companyDescription: Apple Inc. is a multinational technology company founded in 1976 that designs, manufactures, and sells consumer electronics including iPhones, iPads, and related software and services.
companyLongDescription: Apple Inc. is a major global technology corporation headquartered in Cupertino, California that develops and sells a wide range of consumer electronics, software, and digital services. The company is known for its iPhone, iPad, and Mac product lines, as well as services including iTunes, iCloud, the App Store, and Apple Music. Apple's iOS operating system powers its mobile devices and serves as a platform for third-party application developers. The company maintains strict control over its ecosystem while providing tools for developers to create and distribute applications.
caseDescription: Apple was found to have used and disclosed unique device identifiers (UDID) to third-party app developers for targeted advertising without obtaining meaningful user consent. Although Apple claimed UDID was non-personal information, the regulator found it constituted personal information because Apple could link it to identifiable individuals. Apple subsequently phased out UDID use for advertising and replaced it with Ad ID, implemented user-friendly opt-out mechanisms, and improved transparency in its privacy communications.
violationSummary: Apple disclosed UDID and Ad ID to third-party app developers via APIs without obtaining meaningful prior consent from users, despite having the technical and contractual ability to control such access. The disclosure enabled app developers to build detailed user profiles for targeted advertising purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Apple used and disclosed unique device identifiers (UDIDs) to third-party app developers for targeted advertising without obtaining meaningful user consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Users' detailed browsing and app usage profiles were linked to their UDIDs and sold to advertisers without their knowledge, allowing invasive tracking.

claimsVsReality.claim: UDIDs are non-personal information because they cannot identify a user by themselves
claimsVsReality.reality: Apple could and did link UDIDs to identifiable individuals through Apple ID account details, making them personal information under privacy law

claimsVsReality.claim: Users are adequately informed about UDID use through broad generalized statements in the Privacy Policy
claimsVsReality.reality: Users were not clearly informed that their detailed app usage and browsing profiles were being tracked and sold to advertisers for targeted advertising purposes

claimsVsReality.claim: Users have adequate opt-out mechanisms for UDID-based advertising
claimsVsReality.reality: The opt-out process was buried in device settings and not prominently disclosed at the point where tracking occurred, making true informed consent impossible

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 2(1) and Principle 4.3 require that organizations obtain knowledge and consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information, except where inappropriate.
regulatoryFindings.description: Apple disclosed UDID to app developers without obtaining prior meaningful consent from users
violations: Apple disclosed UDID to app developers without obtaining prior meaningful consent from users
Apple did not adequately disclose to users that UDID would be shared with third-party app developers for advertising purposes
Apple's contractual requirements with app developers were insufficient to ensure users' meaningful consent was actually obtained

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 requires organizations to make reasonable efforts to advise individuals of purposes for which personal information will be used, and purposes must be stated clearly so individuals can reasonably understand the use or disclosure.
regulatoryFindings.description: Apple's Privacy Policy provided only vague, generalized statements about UDID use for 'advertising' without specifically explaining how device identifiers would be used for interest-based profiling and tracking
violations: Apple's Privacy Policy provided only vague, generalized statements about UDID use for 'advertising' without specifically explaining how device identifiers would be used for interest-based profiling and tracking
Apple did not provide clear, prominent notification at the point of disclosure to app developers explaining how UDID or Ad ID would be used
The location of opt-out controls in iOS 6 (buried in device settings under About > General > Advertising) was not intuitive for users

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.5 and 4.3.6 require that consent be appropriate to the sensitivity of the information and reasonable expectations of the individual. Sensitive information requires express consent.
regulatoryFindings.description: UDID, being permanent and enabling comprehensive user profiling across multiple apps and services, constitutes sensitive personal information requiring express consent, but Apple relied on implied consent via Privacy Policy
violations: UDID, being permanent and enabling comprehensive user profiling across multiple apps and services, constitutes sensitive personal information requiring express consent, but Apple relied on implied consent via Privacy Policy
iOS Device users would not reasonably expect that a device identifier assigned by Apple would be made available to third-party app developers without their explicit knowledge
Apple did not implement per-instance consent (at point of disclosure) for sensitive identifier sharing with app developers

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded and resolved. While Apple was not subject to a monetary penalty, the company implemented significant remedial measures including: (1) ceasing use of UDID for advertising by iOS 6 release; (2) phasing out developer access to UDID entirely as of May 1, 2013; (3) introducing Ad ID as a replacement identifier with enhanced user controls; (4) implementing a 'Reset Advertising Identifier' button allowing users to reset Ad ID without factory reset; (5) relocating the 'Limit Ad Tracking' privacy control to a more intuitive location in Privacy settings (iOS 7); (6) providing enhanced explanations in Privacy Policy and device settings about the use of identifiers for advertising; and (7) maintaining contractual controls requiring app developers to obtain user consent before accessing identifiers. Apple was also monitored for ongoing compliance with these obligations.
companyNow: Apple remains one of the world's most valuable companies, continuing to dominate the smartphone market and expanding into wearables, services, and artificial intelligence.
dataType: Unique device identifiers (UDID), advertising identifier (Ad ID), Apple ID account details, user activity data, demographic data, location data, contacts, calendar events, photos
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Section 2(1) – Definition of personal information
PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Knowledge and consent requirement
PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 – Meaningful consent and reasonable notice of purposes
PIPEDA Principle 4.3.5 – Reasonable expectations of the individual
PIPEDA Principle 4.3.6 – Express consent for sensitive information

companyDescription: An unnamed Canadian retailer involved in small claims court litigation with a customer over access to personal information held by the business.
companyLongDescription: The company is a Canadian retailer that became the subject of a privacy complaint when it withheld personal information from an individual involved in ongoing small claims court litigation. The retailer claimed litigation privilege as justification for the access denial. The case was ultimately dismissed by Canada's Privacy Commissioner because provincial court procedures were deemed a more appropriate remedy for the access dispute.
caseDescription: An individual filed a complaint alleging that a retailer unlawfully withheld access to her personal information during ongoing small claims court litigation, citing litigation privilege as justification. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner declined to investigate because provincial court procedures provided a more appropriate and available remedy for the access issue.
violationSummary: The company refused to provide access to personal information held by it, thereby excluding the individual from knowledge and control over her own data. This falls under the Exclusion category, which addresses denial of access to personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A retailer refused to provide an individual with access to her personal information during ongoing small claims court litigation.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individual was unable to access her own personal information needed to support her legal case, preventing her from fully preparing her defense.

claimsVsReality.claim: The retailer claimed litigation privilege justified withholding the personal information from the complainant.
claimsVsReality.reality: Provincial court discovery and cross-examination procedures were available to the individual to obtain the information through proper legal channels, making the blanket withholding unnecessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 8(3) and Principle 4.9 (Schedule 1) require organizations to provide individuals with access to their personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Retailer refused to provide full access to personal information requested by the individual, citing litigation privilege despite some documents already being disclosed in ongoing litigation
violations: Retailer refused to provide full access to personal information requested by the individual, citing litigation privilege despite some documents already being disclosed in ongoing litigation

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner declined to investigate the complaint pursuant to paragraph 12(1)(b) of PIPEDA, determining that provincial court procedures (including cross-examination and discovery mechanisms available during the small claims trial) provided more appropriate means for the complainant to address her access concerns. No enforcement action was taken by the Privacy Commissioner.
dataType: Personal information (unspecified)

companyDescription: A property management company that processes rental applications and maintains tenant records in Canada.
companyLongDescription: The company operates in the residential property rental sector, collecting personal information from prospective tenants through application forms. It outsources application form generation to third-party providers. The company manages tenant screening and verification processes as part of its core business operations.
caseDescription: A property management company was requesting applicants' Social Insurance Numbers, driver's licence numbers, and banking information as mandatory fields on rental application forms, contrary to PIPEDA principles. The company also lacked a privacy policy on its website. The company committed to marking these fields as optional and publishing a privacy policy.
violationSummary: The company was collecting personal information (SIN, driver's licence numbers, banking details) beyond what was necessary or legally required, and without clear disclosure of its policies, constituting excessive information collection and surveillance.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: The property management company requested applicants' Social Insurance Numbers, driver's licence numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Applicants were coerced into disclosing sensitive personal identifiers as a condition of applying for rental housing, exposing them to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: A Social Insurance Number is necessary to obtain a credit report for prospective applicants.
claimsVsReality.reality: Credit reports can be obtained through alternative identity verification methods; SIN collection was not legally required and constituted over-collection of personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company believed the third-party application forms were in compliance with PIPEDA and that providing a SIN was optional.
claimsVsReality.reality: The forms presented SIN, driver's licence number, and banking information as mandatory fields with no indication they were optional, contradicting the company's assertion and violating PIPEDA principles of minimal collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Driver's licence numbers are needed to confirm applicant identity.
claimsVsReality.reality: Only verification of identity through a government-issued card is necessary; the unique identification number on the card is not required for identity confirmation purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.4 — Organizations shall limit the collection of personal information to that which is necessary for the purposes identified by the organization.
regulatoryFindings.description: Requested SIN as mandatory despite it being optional; could have obtained credit reports without it
violations: Requested SIN as mandatory despite it being optional; could have obtained credit reports without it
Requested driver's licence number when only identity confirmation (not unique identifier) was necessary
Requested banking information without established necessity

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 5 — Organizations shall make readily available to individuals specific information about their policies and practices relating to the management of personal information.
regulatoryFindings.description: No privacy policy was available on the company's website
violations: No privacy policy was available on the company's website

outcome: The property management company committed to: (1) marking SIN, driver's licence information, and banking information as optional on rental application forms; (2) publishing a privacy policy on its website once under construction was completed. The Office confirmed these changes were made and the matter was resolved.
dataType: Social Insurance Number, driver's licence information, banking information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.4 (limiting collection to necessary information)
PIPEDA Principle 5 (openness — requirement to make privacy policies readily available)

companyDescription: Equifax Information Services LLC is a subsidiary of Equifax Inc., one of the three major U.S. credit reporting agencies. It assembles and sells consumer reports and prescreened lists containing credit information and financial data to third parties for credit decisions.
companyLongDescription: Equifax Information Services LLC is a subsidiary of Equifax Inc., one of the three major U.S. credit reporting agencies. It assembles and sells consumer reports and prescreened lists containing credit information and financial data to third parties for credit decisions.
caseDescription: Equifax sold prescreened consumer lists containing credit scores and mortgage delinquency data to Direct Lending Source without verifying that recipients had permissible purposes under the Fair Credit Reporting Act. Direct Lending then resold these lists to third parties for marketing to consumers in financial distress, including loan modification and debt relief solicitors. Equifax failed to maintain reasonable procedures to control access or verify end-user identity.
violationSummary: Equifax disclosed sensitive financial data (credit scores, delinquency status) to third parties without permissible purpose under FCRA and without reasonable verification procedures, breaching consumer confidentiality obligations.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Sold prescreened lists containing millions of consumers' credit scores and mortgage delinquency status to Direct Lending from 2008-2010 without verifying the buyer had a permissible purpose.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of financially vulnerable consumers had their sensitive credit data sold to predatory marketers targeting them for exploitative loan modification.

claimsVsReality.claim: Equifax implemented procedures to limit prescreened lists to permissible purposes only.
claimsVsReality.reality: Equifax failed to verify the identity of entities accessing prescreened lists, did not investigate promptly when learning of Direct Lending violations, and continued selling lists despite knowing or should have known lists were being resold without identifying end users.

claimsVsReality.claim: Direct Lending obtained prescreened lists for firm offers of credit.
claimsVsReality.reality: Direct Lending used and sold prescreened lists for marketing products and services to consumers in financial distress, including loan modification, debt relief, and foreclosure relief services—not permissible purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 604(c) of the FCRA prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports to any person other than those they have reason to believe have a specified permissible purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax furnished prescreened lists to Direct Lending without reason to believe Direct Lending had a permissible purpose; Direct Lending used and resold the lists for marketing purposes to consumers in financial distress, which is not a permissible purpose under the FCRA.
violations: Equifax furnished prescreened lists to Direct Lending without reason to believe Direct Lending had a permissible purpose; Direct Lending used and resold the lists for marketing purposes to consumers in financial distress, which is not a permissible purpose under the FCRA.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(a) of the FCRA requires CRAs to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports to permissible purposes, including making reasonable efforts to verify the identity of each new prospective user and the uses certified by each prospective user prior to furnishing such user a consumer report.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax failed to maintain reasonable procedures; did not verify identity of entities accessing prescreened lists through the online portal; failed to investigate promptly or fully when learning Direct Lending was violating internal policies; continued selling to Direct Lending despite knowing or should have known Direct Lending was reselling without identifying end users to Equifax.
violations: Equifax failed to maintain reasonable procedures; did not verify identity of entities accessing prescreened lists through the online portal; failed to investigate promptly or fully when learning Direct Lending was violating internal policies; continued selling to Direct Lending despite knowing or should have known Direct Lending was reselling without identifying end users to Equifax.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Equifax's failure to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to control access to sensitive consumer financial information resulted in substantial consumer injury not reasonably avoidable by consumers and not outweighed by countervailing benefits; prescreened lists were sold to entities ultimately subject to law enforcement actions or warnings.
violations: Equifax's failure to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to control access to sensitive consumer financial information resulted in substantial consumer injury not reasonably avoidable by consumers and not outweighed by countervailing benefits; prescreened lists were sold to entities ultimately subject to law enforcement actions or warnings.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against Equifax on March 5, 2013 alleging violations of the FCRA and FTC Act. The document indicates a complaint was filed; subsequent settlement/consent order details are not included in this document, but Equifax was required to cease the practice and implement compliance measures.
companyNow: Equifax Inc. remains one of the three major credit reporting agencies in the United States and continues to operate as a consumer reporting agency, though subsequent to this enforcement action it has faced additional regulatory scrutiny including the 2017 data breach affecting 147 million consumers.
dataType: Credit scores, mortgage payment status (30/60/90 days late), consumer financial data

companyDescription: Compete was a market research company based in Boston that collected Internet browsing data from consumers through browser toolbars and reward programs, analyzing and selling consumer behavior analytics to business clients.
companyLongDescription: Compete was a market research company based in Boston that collected Internet browsing data from consumers through browser toolbars and reward programs, analyzing and selling consumer behavior analytics to business clients.
caseDescription: Compete, a market research company, collected extensive personal data from consumers through toolbars and reward programs, but misrepresented what it collected and how it protected the data. The company captured sensitive financial and identity information in clear text from secure web pages, including credit card and Social Security numbers, despite claiming it would anonymously strip personal information before transmission.
violationSummary: Compete failed to implement reasonable security safeguards for sensitive consumer data it collected without adequate disclosure, transmitting financial and identity information in clear text despite representations of anonymization and security.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Compete operated data-collection toolbars and consumer reward programs that captured detailed browsing behavior, shopping activity.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 4 million consumers unknowingly had credit card numbers, financial account details, security codes.

claimsVsReality.claim: By joining Community Share, web pages you visit will be anonymously pooled with the Compete community to provide site trust rankings and analytics.
claimsVsReality.reality: Compete captured extensive data including credit card numbers, financial account information, security codes, usernames, passwords, and Social Security numbers in clear readable text.

claimsVsReality.claim: All data is stripped of personally identifiable information before it is transmitted to our servers. Our data collection techniques have been designed to purge personally identifiable information wherever we find it.
claimsVsReality.reality: Consumer-side filters were too narrow and improperly structured; filters only caught limited variations of field names (e.g. 'PIN' but not 'personal ID' or 'security code'); sensitive data was transmitted in clear text before server-side filtering.

claimsVsReality.claim: We take reasonable security measures to protect against unauthorized access to or unauthorized alteration, disclosure or destruction of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Company transmitted sensitive information from secure web pages in unencrypted clear text over the Internet, creating unnecessary risk of interception over unsecured wireless networks in public spaces; failed to implement basic algorithms to screen credit card numbers.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Count 1: Deceptive failure to disclose that products collected extensive Internet behavior data and sensitive information from secure web pages (credit cards, account numbers, SSNs) beyond stated website popularity metrics.
violations: Count 1: Deceptive failure to disclose that products collected extensive Internet behavior data and sensitive information from secure web pages (credit cards, account numbers, SSNs) beyond stated website popularity metrics.

Count 2: Deceptive representation that all personal information was stripped before transmission, when consumer-side filters were too narrow and improperly structured to prevent collection of sensitive data.
Count 3: Deceptive representation about reasonable security measures when company transmitted sensitive data in clear readable text over the Internet without encryption.

Count 4: Unfair practice of failing to employ reasonable safeguards for sensitive consumer data (credit card, financial account, security codes, SSNs) causing substantial injury not offset by consumer benefits and not reasonably avoidable.

outcome: Complaint issued February 20, 2013. Alleged violations of Section 5(a) FTC Act on four counts: deceptive representations regarding data collection scope, false claims about personal information filtering, misrepresentations about data security, and unfair failure to protect sensitive consumer data. After flaws were publicly revealed in January 2010, Compete upgraded filters, added credit card screening algorithms, began encrypting data in transit, stopped distributing Toolbar to new customers, and distributed Consumer Input Panel through third parties.
companyNow: Compete, Inc. ceased independent operations. The company was acquired and its data collection practices were discontinued after the FTC enforcement action and public revelations of security failures in 2010.
dataType: Internet browsing behavior, website URLs, shopping cart activity, credit card numbers, financial account numbers, security codes, usernames, passwords, search terms, Social Security numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Watershed Development Corp. is an Illinois-based rent-to-own franchisor under Aaron's, Inc., operating eight stores in Illinois. It rented computers, furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics with purchase options.
companyLongDescription: Watershed Development Corp. is an Illinois-based rent-to-own franchisor under Aaron's, Inc., operating eight stores in Illinois. It rented computers, furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics with purchase options.
caseDescription: Watershed Development Corp., a rent-to-own computer franchisor, installed PC Rental Agent surveillance software on rented computers that secretly monitored user activities via 'Detective Mode.' The software captured keystroke logs, screenshots, and gathered personal data without user knowledge. Watershed used fake Windows registration popups to deceive consumers into providing contact information, which it then used for debt collection purposes.
violationSummary: Watershed secretly monitored computer users' activities without their knowledge or consent via remotely activated Detective Mode, capturing keystrokes, screenshots, and personal data. This constitutes direct surveillance intrusion into consumers' private digital activities.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Watershed installed spyware called PC Rental Agent and Detective Mode on computers rented to consumers, allowing remote monitoring of keystrokes, screenshots.
whyTheyWereWrong: Renters unknowingly had their passwords, financial account credentials, medical information, and private family details captured.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers are renting computers for legitimate rent-to-own purposes with clear terms.
claimsVsReality.reality: Computers came pre-loaded with secret surveillance software that captured all user activity, credentials, and personal information without disclosure or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pop-up registration windows are from Microsoft Windows and trusted software providers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Windows registration popups were fake—they were generated by Detective Mode to trick users into providing personal information for debt collection targeting.

claimsVsReality.claim: Remote computer disabling via PC Rental Agent serves legitimate debt collection purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Watershed deployed Detective Mode surveillance extensively beyond device recovery, capturing sensitive financial, medical, and personal data with no legitimate business purpose.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondent installed monitoring software on rented computers and gathered sensitive personal information (keystroke logs, passwords, screenshots) without consumer knowledge or consent, causing substantial injury to consumers that cannot be reasonably avoided.

companyDescription: Time Warner Cable was a major American cable and internet service provider offering video, high-speed data, digital telephone, and other telecommunications services to millions of consumers across multiple U.S. markets. At the time of this enforcement action, TWC was one of the largest cable operators in the United States.
companyLongDescription: Time Warner Cable was a major American cable and internet service provider offering video, high-speed data, digital telephone, and other telecommunications services to millions of consumers across multiple U.S. markets. At the time of this enforcement action, TWC was one of the largest cable operators in the United States.
caseDescription: Time Warner Cable failed to provide risk-based pricing notices to consumers who received materially less favorable credit terms based on information from their credit reports between January 2011 and March 2013. When approving cable and internet services, TWC required certain customers to pay deposits or advance payments based on credit information but did not notify them that these unfavorable terms were credit-based, violating the Risk-Based Pricing Rule under the Fair Credit Reporting Act.
violationSummary: TWC used consumer credit reports for a secondary purpose (setting service terms/pricing) without properly notifying consumers, a key transparency and consent violation under privacy frameworks.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Time Warner Cable retrieved consumers' credit reports and imposed deposit or advance payment requirements on some customers based on poor credit history.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers forced to pay deposits or advance payments based on their credit reports were denied transparency about why they faced these financial burdens.

claimsVsReality.claim: TWC used credit reports solely to assess creditworthiness for service eligibility decisions
claimsVsReality.reality: TWC used credit reports to determine differential pricing/terms (deposits vs. no deposits) but failed to disclose this practice to affected consumers as required by law

claimsVsReality.claim: Deposit requirements were applied uniformly based on objective credit criteria
claimsVsReality.reality: Deposits were imposed on some customers based on poor credit while substantial proportion of customers with better credit paid no deposits, yet TWC provided no notice of this differentiation or its basis

regulatoryFindings.act: The Risk-Based Pricing Rule (16 C.F.R. § 640.1 et seq., republished at 12 C.F.R. § 1022.70 et seq.) requires that any person who uses a consumer report in connection with credit decisions and grants credit on materially less favorable terms based on that report must provide a specific risk-based pricing notice containing details about the use of credit reports, terms offered, and consumer rights.
regulatoryFindings.description: TWC used consumer credit reports to determine deposit requirements for cable and internet service applicants, extending credit on materially less favorable terms (deposit/advance payment requirements) to consumers with poor credit histories compared to those with favorable credit.
violations: TWC used consumer credit reports to determine deposit requirements for cable and internet service applicants, extending credit on materially less favorable terms (deposit/advance payment requirements) to consumers with poor credit histories compared to those with favorable credit.

TWC failed to provide the required risk-based pricing notice to affected consumers from January 1, 2011 through at least March 5, 2013, depriving them of information about the basis for their unfavorable terms and their rights regarding credit reports.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: TWC's failure to provide required risk-based pricing notices constituted an unfair practice by withholding material information from consumers about how credit information was being used to set their service terms, preventing informed decision-making and access to free credit reports.
violations: TWC's failure to provide required risk-based pricing notices constituted an unfair practice by withholding material information from consumers about how credit information was being used to set their service terms, preventing informed decision-making and access to free credit reports.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 621 of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. § 1681s) authorizes the FTC to enforce compliance with FCRA requirements by all persons subject to the statute using all FTC Act functions and powers.
regulatoryFindings.description: TWC violated Section 615(h) of the FCRA and the Risk-Based Pricing Rule, making each instance of failure to provide notice a separate FCRA violation subject to civil penalties.
violations: TWC violated Section 615(h) of the FCRA and the Risk-Based Pricing Rule, making each instance of failure to provide notice a separate FCRA violation subject to civil penalties.

outcome: The United States, acting on authorization from the Federal Trade Commission, filed a civil complaint seeking monetary penalties of up to $3,500 per violation (as adjusted under 16 C.F.R. § 1.98(m)), a permanent injunction against future violations, restitution and consumer redress including rescission or reformation of contracts and refunds of deposits improperly charged, and court costs. The complaint alleged that each failure to provide required notice from January 1, 2011 through March 5, 2013 constituted a separate violation, potentially involving hundreds of thousands of instances. The case sought to force TWC to implement compliant risk-based pricing procedures and provide proper disclosures to all affected consumers.
companyNow: Time Warner Cable was acquired by Charter Communications in 2016 and ceased operating as an independent entity. Charter Communications continues to operate under various brand names including Spectrum.
dataType: Credit report information, credit history, credit scores, financial information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act, Section 615(h) (15 U.S.C. § 1681m(h))
Risk-Based Pricing Rule, 16 C.F.R. § 640.1 et seq. and 12 C.F.R. § 1022.70 et seq.

companyDescription: HTC America Inc. is a subsidiary of the Taiwanese multinational HTC Corporation, a mobile device manufacturer specializing in Android and Windows-based smartphones and tablets. Founded in 1997, HTC was a major player in the smartphone market before declining in the 2010s.
companyLongDescription: HTC America Inc. is a subsidiary of the Taiwanese multinational HTC Corporation, a mobile device manufacturer specializing in Android and Windows-based smartphones and tablets. Founded in 1997, HTC was a major player in the smartphone market before declining in the 2010s.
caseDescription: HTC failed to implement reasonable security measures in customizing Android and Windows Mobile devices, introducing multiple critical vulnerabilities that allowed unauthorized third-party applications to access sensitive user information without permission. The company also made deceptive claims about Android's permission system and location data handling in error reporting. Approximately 18.3 million devices were affected by permission re-delegation vulnerabilities, and 12.5 million by insecure logging mechanisms.
violationSummary: HTC's failure to implement reasonable security measures directly enabled unauthorized access to sensitive personal information and device functionality on a massive scale.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: HTC pre-installed custom applications on 18.3 million Android devices with critical security vulnerabilities including permission re-delegation flaws, insecure logging mechanisms.
whyTheyWereWrong: Malware could exploit these vulnerabilities to surreptitiously record phone conversations, track physical location, access text messages and financial data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Android's permission-based security model protects users by requiring applications to request permission before accessing sensitive information.
claimsVsReality.reality: HTC's custom pre-installed applications contained permission re-delegation vulnerabilities that allowed any third-party application to access sensitive information without requesting or obtaining user permission.

claimsVsReality.claim: Location data will not be sent to HTC unless the user checks the 'Add location data' button in the error reporting tool.
claimsVsReality.reality: Active debug code in HTC's CIQ Interface caused GPS-based location data to be written to the system log and transmitted to HTC regardless of whether the user checked the location data option.

claimsVsReality.claim: HTC Loggers was a secure customer support tool accessible only to HTC and authorized network operators after manual user consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Insecure communication mechanisms allowed any third-party application with internet access to communicate with HTC Loggers and extract sensitive data including text message contents, GPS history, contacts, and account credentials without authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: HTC failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security practices in the design and customization of mobile device software, causing substantial consumer injury through unauthorized access to sensitive information and device functionality.
violations: HTC failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security practices in the design and customization of mobile device software, causing substantial consumer injury through unauthorized access to sensitive information and device functionality.

HTC represented in user manuals that Android's permission-based security model would notify users before third-party applications access personal information, but vulnerabilities allowed access without notification or consent.

HTC represented through the Tell HTC error reporting interface that location data would not be sent without user consent via the 'Add location data' checkbox, but debug code caused location data transmission regardless.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 25, 2013 alleging unfair and deceptive practices. HTC was required to comply with a comprehensive security program addressing vulnerability remediation, security testing, staff training, and incident response procedures. The company was subject to ongoing monitoring and required to conduct regular security assessments.
companyNow: HTC continues as a mobile device manufacturer, though its market share has declined significantly. The company faces ongoing pressure from security-conscious consumers and competitors.
dataType: Location data, text message contents, GPS coordinates, contact information, phone numbers, web browsing history, application names, financial account numbers, medical information, email account credentials
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

company: B. Stamper Enterprises, Inc. (d/b/a Premier Rental Purchase)
companyDescription: B. Stamper Enterprises was a rent-to-own franchisee based in Russellville, Kentucky, operating a single store in Indiana that rented furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics to consumers.
companyLongDescription: B. Stamper Enterprises was a rent-to-own franchisee based in Russellville, Kentucky, operating a single store in Indiana that rented furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics to consumers.
caseDescription: B. Stamper Enterprises installed spyware (PC Rental Agent and Detective Mode) on rented computers to secretly monitor consumers' activities, capture sensitive personal information including passwords and financial data, and gather contact information through fake software registration windows. The company used this covertly obtained data to collect debts from renters.
violationSummary: The company engaged in systematic covert surveillance through Detective Mode, which logged keystrokes, captured screenshots and webcam imagery without user knowledge or consent. This constitutes unlawful surveillance under the Solove framework.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: B. Stamper Enterprises installed monitoring software called PC Rental Agent on rented computers that secretly gathered sensitive personal information including keystrokes, screenshots.
whyTheyWereWrong: Renters and other computer users were exposed to covert surveillance that captured usernames, passwords, medical records, Social Security numbers, bank statements.

claimsVsReality.claim: PC Rental Agent was designed to help secure rented equipment and manage payment defaults by remotely disabling non-paying devices.
claimsVsReality.reality: B. Stamper Enterprises used Detective Mode to conduct invasive surveillance capturing passwords, financial data, medical records, and webcam footage without consumer knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pop-up windows appearing on rented computers were legitimate Microsoft Windows registration forms requiring user information to activate software.
claimsVsReality.reality: The registration windows were fake, controlled by Detective Mode, and solely designed to trick consumers into divulging contact information for debt collection purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Unfair gathering of consumers' personal information through hidden monitoring software that caused substantial injury consumers could not reasonably avoid
violations: Unfair gathering of consumers' personal information through hidden monitoring software that caused substantial injury consumers could not reasonably avoid
Unfair collection practices by using improperly obtained confidential data to collect debts with no legitimate business benefit
Deceptive practices by displaying fake software registration windows falsely representing trusted software providers to trick consumers into disclosing contact information

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on April 11, 2013, alleging three counts: Count I (Unfair Gathering of Consumers' Personal Information), Count II (Unfair Collection Practices), and Count III (Deceptive Gathering of Consumers' Personal Information). The complaint did not specify a monetary penalty amount in the document, suggesting a consent order or settlement with monitoring and compliance obligations was the likely resolution.
companyNow: Unknown current status. B. Stamper Enterprises was a franchisee of Premier Rental-Purchase, Inc. operating a single location in Indiana as of 2013.
dataType: Keystroke logs, screenshots, webcam recordings, email credentials, passwords, social media access, financial account access, medical records, Social Security numbers, bank and credit card statements, contact information

companyDescription: DesignerWare, LLC was a Nevada limited liability corporation that developed and licensed PC Rental Agent software to approximately 1,617 rent-to-own stores globally. The software was installed on approximately 420,000 rented computers and provided features enabling remote disablement, location tracking, and surveillance of computer users.
companyLongDescription: DesignerWare, LLC was a Nevada limited liability corporation that developed and licensed PC Rental Agent software to approximately 1,617 rent-to-own stores globally. The software was installed on approximately 420,000 rented computers and provided features enabling remote disablement, location tracking, and surveillance of computer users.
caseDescription: DesignerWare developed and licensed PC Rental Agent software to rent-to-own stores, which installed hidden monitoring software on rented computers. The software enabled surreptitious collection of keystroke logs, screenshots, webcam photos, and geolocation data from approximately 420,000 computers without user knowledge or consent, and disclosed this sensitive personal information to rent-to-own store licensees.
violationSummary: The core violation involves systematic, surreptitious monitoring of computer users' activities including keystrokes, screenshots, and webcam imagery without knowledge or consent. This constitutes intrusive surveillance. Secondary violations include Disclosure (sharing collected data with licensees) and Insecurity (unencrypted transmission of sensitive data).
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: DesignerWare licensed PC Rental Agent software to rent-to-own stores, which was installed on approximately 420,000 rented computers to remotely disable them.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers renting computers had their keystrokes logged revealing financial account passwords and medical records, webcams secretly photographed children and intimate activities.

claimsVsReality.claim: DesignerWare recommended (but did not require) that licensees disclose the presence of PC Rental Agent to consumers at the time they signed rental contracts.
claimsVsReality.reality: In numerous instances, rent-to-own stores did not disclose PC Rental Agent's presence to consumers. DesignerWare took no steps to verify licensee compliance with disclosure recommendations.

claimsVsReality.claim: DesignerWare recommends that Detective Mode be used only to locate and identify persons in possession of lost or stolen computers.
claimsVsReality.reality: In numerous instances, rent-to-own store licensees activated Detective Mode on computers where consumers were merely late on rental payments and where licensees had no reason to believe the computers were criminally stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Detective Mode operates as a protective feature for computer recovery.
claimsVsReality.reality: Detective Mode functioned as spyware/malware that secretly logged keystrokes, captured screenshots and webcam photographs, and transmitted sensitive personal information (financial credentials, medical records, Social Security numbers, intimate imagery) to rent-to-own stores without user knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: Fake registration windows are legitimate software registration prompts.
claimsVsReality.reality: Fake registration windows were deceptive pop-ups designed solely to trick consumers into providing contact information for collection purposes, with no legitimate software registration occurring.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Installed monitoring software on rented computers and gathered sensitive personal, financial, and medical information about consumers without knowledge or consent, then disclosed that information to rent-to-own store licensees.
violations: Installed monitoring software on rented computers and gathered sensitive personal, financial, and medical information about consumers without knowledge or consent, then disclosed that information to rent-to-own store licensees.
Installed geophysical location tracking software on rented computers without consent from renters, tracked computer locations without notice to users, and disclosed location information to licensees.
Furnished rent-to-own stores with software that records keystrokes, captures screenshots, takes webcam photographs, and identifies geophysical location without consumer consent or notice.

Created and deployed fake software registration pop-up windows designed to deceive consumers into providing contact information, falsely representing them as legitimate software provider registration forms.

outcome: This document is the initial FTC Complaint dated April 11, 2013, alleging violations of FTC Act Section 5. The complaint charges DesignerWare, LLC and officers Timothy Kelly and Ronald P. Koller with Count I (Unfair Gathering and Disclosure of Consumers' Personal Information), Count II (Means and Instrumentalities to Engage in Unfairness), and Count III (Deceptive Gathering and Disclosure of Consumers' Personal Information). The document initiates formal enforcement proceedings; final outcomes including consent orders and remedial obligations were determined in subsequent settlements. The complaint alleges substantial consumer harm from unauthorized surveillance, data collection, and disclosure practices.
companyNow: DesignerWare, LLC ceased operations following FTC enforcement action. No current business activity of note.
dataType: Keystroke logs, screenshots, webcam imagery, geolocation data, contact information, email credentials, financial account access, medical records, Social Security numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair acts or practices in or affecting commerce
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: CBR Systems, Inc. is a California-based cord blood and tissue banking company that collects, processes, and stores umbilical cord blood and tissue for potential future medical use. The company operates multiple websites through which consumers and physicians obtain information and services related to cord blood banking.
companyLongDescription: CBR Systems, Inc. is a California-based cord blood and tissue banking company that collects, processes, and stores umbilical cord blood and tissue for potential future medical use. The company operates multiple websites through which consumers and physicians obtain information and services related to cord blood banking.
caseDescription: CBR Systems, a cord blood banking company, collected highly sensitive personal and health data from pregnant women and their families but failed to implement reasonable security safeguards. In December 2010, four unencrypted backup tapes containing data on approximately 298,000 consumers were stolen from an employee's vehicle, exposing names, Social Security numbers, financial account information, and health records. The company's privacy policy falsely promised secure handling of personal information despite inadequate encryption, access controls, and intrusion detection systems.
violationSummary: CBR's failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures for sensitive personal and health data, combined with inadequate encryption and access controls, resulted in exposure of 298,000 consumers' records. This is fundamentally an information processing insecurity issue under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Invasion of Seclusion
whatTheyDid: CBR collected sensitive personal information including Social Security numbers, credit card details, and health records from pregnant women.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 298,000 consumers' complete personal information including Social Security numbers, financial account numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: CBR stated in its privacy policy: 'Whenever CBR handles personal information, regardless of where this occurs, CBR takes steps to ensure that your information is treated securely and in accordance with the relevant Terms of Service and this Privacy Policy.'
claimsVsReality.reality: CBR transported unencrypted backup tapes containing 298,000 consumers' personal information in an unsecured backpack in an employee's vehicle, leading to theft on December 13, 2010. The company lacked basic security controls including encryption, proper access restrictions, and intrusion detection systems.

claimsVsReality.claim: CBR represented: 'Once we receive your transmission, we make our best effort to ensure its security on our systems.'
claimsVsReality.reality: CBR failed to encrypt portable media, maintain secure legacy databases, employ intrusion detection systems, adequately monitor web traffic, or properly retain and review system logs for security threats.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: CBR represented expressly or by implication in its privacy policy (effective March 2006 through October 2011) that it took steps to ensure personal information was treated securely and its transmission security was ensured
violations: CBR represented expressly or by implication in its privacy policy (effective March 2006 through October 2011) that it took steps to ensure personal information was treated securely and its transmission security was ensured

In reality, CBR had not implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect consumers' personal information from unauthorized access, including failing to encrypt backup tapes, failing to restrict database access, failing to adequately supervise service providers, and failing to employ sufficient intrusion detection measures
These misrepresentations in the privacy policy constituted deceptive acts or practices in violation of Section 5(a)

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on April 29, 2013, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleged CBR made false representations about security safeguards while engaging in inadequate data security practices. The resolution typically requires CBR to implement comprehensive information security improvements, undergo regular compliance monitoring, and notify affected consumers. A consent order would mandate reasonable security measures including encryption, access controls, intrusion detection systems, and proper data destruction protocols.
companyNow: CBR Systems remained in operation post-2013 as a private cord blood banking company. The company's current status and operational details are not specified in publicly available enforcement records as of the complaint date.
dataType: Health data, financial data (credit/debit card numbers, checking account numbers), biometric data (blood typing, infectious disease markers), personal identifiers (Social Security numbers, driver's license numbers, dates of birth)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: J.A.G. Rents is a Florida-based franchisee of ColorTyme, Inc., operating two rent-to-own stores in Florida. The company rented furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics including computers to consumers under rental agreements with purchase options.
companyLongDescription: J.A.G. Rents is a Florida-based franchisee of ColorTyme, Inc., operating two rent-to-own stores in Florida. The company rented furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics including computers to consumers under rental agreements with purchase options.
caseDescription: J.A.G. Rents installed hidden monitoring software (Detective Mode) on computers rented to consumers, enabling remote keystroke logging, webcam surveillance, and screenshot capture without consent or knowledge. The company secretly gathered sensitive personal and financial data, including passwords and medical records, and used deceptive fake software registration windows to harvest contact information. This data was used for debt collection purposes.
violationSummary: The installation of hidden Detective Mode software enabling remote monitoring of user activities, keystroke logging, webcam surveillance, and screenshot capture constitutes unlawful surveillance without consent or notice, fitting directly into the Information Collection – Surveillance category.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: J.A.G. Rents installed invisible monitoring software on rented computers that secretly logged keystrokes, captured screenshots, photographed users via webcam.
whyTheyWereWrong: Computer renters were secretly monitored in their homes without consent, exposing passwords to email and financial accounts, medical records, Social Security numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The pop-up registration windows were legitimate software registration notices from trusted software providers such as Microsoft requiring contact information to activate Windows or other software.
claimsVsReality.reality: The pop-up windows were fake registration screens generated by Detective Mode software designed solely to trick consumers into providing contact information for debt collection purposes; no software was actually registered or activated as a result of consumer input.

claimsVsReality.claim: PC Rental Agent served legitimate purposes for remote computer disablement in cases of theft, non-payment, or contract violation.
claimsVsReality.reality: While disablement was a stated function, the software also enabled covert surveillance through Detective Mode, including keystroke logging, webcam monitoring, and screenshot capture that occurred without any disclosure or consumer consent, serving purposes beyond legitimate asset recovery.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Installed monitoring software on rented computers and gathered sensitive personal information including passwords, medical records, financial account access, and Social Security numbers without consumer knowledge, causing substantial injury that consumers could not reasonably avoid because Detective Mode was invisible and uninstallable.
violations: Installed monitoring software on rented computers and gathered sensitive personal information including passwords, medical records, financial account access, and Social Security numbers without consumer knowledge, causing substantial injury that consumers could not reasonably avoid because Detective Mode was invisible and uninstallable.

Used improperly gathered personal information to collect or attempt to collect debts, money, or property pursuant to rental contracts, causing substantial injury through unauthorized surveillance and secondary use of collected data.

Represented to consumers via pop-up windows that they were legitimate software registration notices from trusted providers requiring contact information, when in fact these were deceptive mechanisms designed solely to harvest contact data for debt collection purposes.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against J.A.G. Rents alleging three counts of violation of FTC Act Section 5(a): unfair gathering of personal information, unfair collection practices, and deceptive gathering of personal information. The complaint alleges that J.A.G. Rents' surveillance and data-gathering practices caused substantial injury to consumers that was not outweighed by any countervailing benefits. The complaint was issued on April 11, 2013. Commissioner Joshua D. Wright did not participate in the decision.
dataType: Email credentials, passwords, social media login credentials, financial account access information, medical records, employment applications with Social Security numbers, bank statements, credit card statements, contact information, webcam images, keystroke logs, screen activity
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair acts or practices
FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Showplace, Inc. was an Ohio-based rent-to-own company operating 15 stores across Ohio, renting furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics including computers to consumers.
companyLongDescription: Showplace, Inc. was an Ohio-based rent-to-own company operating 15 stores across Ohio, renting furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics including computers to consumers.
caseDescription: Showplace installed spyware (PC Rental Agent with Detective Mode) on rental computers, enabling covert keystroke logging, webcam monitoring, and personal data harvesting. The software was undetectable and unremovable by users. Showplace used fake software registration windows to deceive consumers into disclosing contact information, then weaponized collected data for debt collection.
violationSummary: Showplace conducted systematic, surreptitious surveillance through Detective Mode, monitoring keystrokes, screenshots, and webcam feeds without consumer awareness or consent. This is quintessential information collection through surveillance.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed invisible, unremovable spyware on rental computers that logged keystrokes, captured screenshots, activated webcams, and harvested passwords.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers renting computers were secretly monitored in their homes, exposing financial account credentials, medical records, emails.

claimsVsReality.claim: PC Rental Agent was merely a remote disabling tool for lost/stolen computers or enforcement of payment defaults.
claimsVsReality.reality: PC Rental Agent secretly enabled Detective Mode, which covertly logged all keystrokes, captured screenshots, photographed users via webcam, and harvested passwords, financial information, medical records, and personal communications.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pop-up windows appearing on rental computers were legitimate software registration prompts from trusted providers like Microsoft Windows.
claimsVsReality.reality: The pop-ups were fake, created by Detective Mode solely to trick consumers into providing contact information that Showplace would use to locate them for debt collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers had transparency and control over the software installed on rental computers.
claimsVsReality.reality: PC Rental Agent and Detective Mode were completely invisible to users, undetectable, and could not be uninstalled by the computer's renter.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Count I: Unfair gathering of consumers' personal information. Respondent installed monitoring software and gathered sensitive personal information (passwords, medical records, financial credentials, webcam footage) without consent. Harm is substantial, unavoidable (software invisible and unremovable), and not outweighed by legitimate benefits.
violations: Count I: Unfair gathering of consumers' personal information. Respondent installed monitoring software and gathered sensitive personal information (passwords, medical records, financial credentials, webcam footage) without consent. Harm is substantial, unavoidable (software invisible and unremovable), and not outweighed by legitimate benefits.

Count II: Unfair collection practices. Respondent used improperly obtained data to collect debts, money, or property. Substantial injury to consumers not offset by countervailing benefits when alternative collection methods existed.

Count III: Deceptive gathering of personal information. Respondent represented that pop-up notices were legitimate software registration windows from trusted providers, when they actually served only to deceive consumers into providing contact information for debt collection purposes.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against Showplace on April 11, 2013, alleging three counts of violations under Section 5 of the FTC Act. The complaint was authorized by the Commission with Commissioner Joshua D. Wright not participating. The outcome indicates initiation of enforcement proceedings requiring Showplace to answer allegations and likely imposing a compliance order and ongoing monitoring obligations.
dataType: Keystrokes, email passwords, financial account credentials, medical records, social media access, employment applications with SSN, bank and credit card statements, webcam images, contact information
