company: Filiquarian Publishing, LLC; Choice Level, LLC
companyDescription: Filiquarian Publishing, LLC and Choice Level, LLC were Minnesota companies operating criminal records mobile applications distributed through iTunes and Google Play. They sold background check apps marketed for employment screening without implementing required Fair Credit Reporting Act compliance safeguards.
companyLongDescription: Filiquarian Publishing, LLC and Choice Level, LLC were Minnesota companies operating criminal records mobile applications distributed through iTunes and Google Play. They sold background check apps marketed for employment screening without implementing required Fair Credit Reporting Act compliance safeguards.
caseDescription: Filiquarian and Choice Level operated mobile apps that provided criminal records for employment screening without complying with Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) requirements. They failed to verify users' permissible purpose, maintain accuracy procedures, or provide required notices, operating unregulated consumer reporting agencies while disclaiming FCRA compliance.
violationSummary: Criminal records were disclosed to unknown third parties without verification of permissible purpose or identity, creating risk of misuse and violation of consumer privacy in sensitive employment decisions.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Operated mobile apps selling criminal record reports to users for $0.99, marketed for employment screening, without verifying user identity, purpose, or legitimate permissible use.
whyTheyWereWrong: Sold thousands of criminal background reports to unvetted buyers with no identity checks, exposing individuals to wrongful employment discrimination, harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Apps include disclaimer: 'products not to be considered screening products for insurance, employment, loans, and credit applications' and 'not compliant with FCRA'; users assume responsibility for FCRA compliance.
claimsVsReality.reality: Apps were actively marketed as 'perfect application for you' when 'hiring somebody and wanting to quickly find out if they have a record.' The disclaimer contradicted the marketing and could not exempt respondents from being a consumer reporting agency under FCRA when operating as such.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users could access 'hundreds of thousands of criminal records' for employment purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: No verification procedures existed to confirm users had a legitimate employment-related permissible purpose, enabling misuse by anyone with $0.99.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 604(a) of the FCRA, 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(a), prohibits a consumer reporting agency from furnishing consumer reports to persons unless the CRA has reason to believe they have a permissible purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents furnished consumer reports via mobile apps to third parties without any procedures to inquire into the purpose for which the user was purchasing the report.
violations: Respondents furnished consumer reports via mobile apps to third parties without any procedures to inquire into the purpose for which the user was purchasing the report.

companyDescription: C.A.L.M. Ventures, Inc. was a Tennessee-based franchisee of Premier Rental-Purchase, Inc., operating a rent-to-own store offering furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics including computers to consumers under rental-purchase agreements.
companyLongDescription: C.A.L.M. Ventures, Inc. was a Tennessee-based franchisee of Premier Rental-Purchase, Inc., operating a rent-to-own store offering furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics including computers to consumers under rental-purchase agreements.
caseDescription: C.A.L.M. Ventures, a rent-to-own computer retailer, installed undetectable spyware called Detective Mode on rented computers that secretly captured consumers' keystroke logs, passwords, screenshots, and webcam photographs without consent. The company also deployed fake software registration windows to deceive consumers into providing personal contact information, then used all improperly gathered data for debt collection and repossession purposes.
violationSummary: The installation of Detective Mode constitutes systematic covert surveillance of computer users through keystroke logging, screenshot capture, and webcam monitoring. This is combined with deceptive collection practices through fake software registration windows, qualifying as surveillance-based information collection under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Installed invisible spyware on rented computers that secretly logged keystrokes, captured screenshots, photographed users via webcams.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers had their financial passwords, email credentials, medical information, and private home photographs secretly captured without consent, exposing them to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: PC Rental Agent software was necessary for legitimate asset recovery and security purposes (disabling stolen/lost computers).
claimsVsReality.reality: The company deployed Detective Mode surveillance features far beyond legitimate security needs, secretly capturing financial credentials, passwords, medical information, and intimate home photographs without consumer consent or disclosure.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pop-up windows displaying 'Windows registration' prompts were legitimate software registration forms from Microsoft or other trusted providers requiring consumer information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The pop-ups were fake deceptive prompts generated by Detective Mode specifically designed to trick consumers into providing contact information for debt collection and repossession purposes, with no actual software registration occurring.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Unfair gathering of personal information: Installed monitoring software on rented computers that secretly captured keystroke logs, screenshots, webcam photographs, and personal financial/medical data without consumer knowledge or consent, causing substantial injury to consumers who could not reasonably avoid this hidden surveillance.
violations: Unfair gathering of personal information: Installed monitoring software on rented computers that secretly captured keystroke logs, screenshots, webcam photographs, and personal financial/medical data without consumer knowledge or consent, causing substantial injury to consumers who could not reasonably avoid this hidden surveillance.

Unfair collection practices: Used improperly gathered information from Detective Mode to collect or attempt to collect debts and repossess computers, causing substantial injury to consumers through unauthorized surveillance-based collection methods.

Deceptive gathering of personal information: Displayed fake software registration windows purporting to be from Microsoft Windows or other trusted providers, deceptively causing consumers to provide contact information believing registration was required, when in fact the sole purpose was to collect data for debt collection and repossession.

outcome: FTC filed complaint on April 11, 2013. The document does not specify the final settlement or remedy beyond the allegations. Based on subsequent public records, C.A.L.M. Ventures agreed to a settlement prohibiting the use of monitoring or surveillance software on rental computers without explicit informed consent, requiring destruction of improperly collected data, and monitoring by FTC for compliance.
companyNow: C.A.L.M. Ventures, Inc. appears to have ceased operations or significantly modified practices following FTC enforcement action in 2013. No current business activity is publicly documented.
dataType: Keystroke logs, passwords, email credentials, financial account access information, social media credentials, medical information, contact information, photographs, webcam footage, home interior images

companyDescription: Citibank, N.A. is a national bank subsidiary of Citigroup, Inc., headquartered in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. It provides retail and commercial banking services including checking, savings, credit card, and debit card accounts to customers nationwide.
companyLongDescription: Citibank, N.A. is a national bank subsidiary of Citigroup, Inc., headquartered in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. It provides retail and commercial banking services including checking, savings, credit card, and debit card accounts to customers nationwide.
caseDescription: Citibank failed to fix a known security vulnerability in its Account Online portal for nearly three years, allowing hackers to access customer data for over 360,000 users including 80,454 Californians. The breach exploited a simple URL parameter manipulation technique and exposed unencrypted personal and financial information. Citibank delayed notifying affected customers by over one month after discovering the breach.
violationSummary: Citibank failed to implement adequate access controls and encryption, allowing unauthorized access to customer data through a preventable exploit. This is a classic insecurity violation where inadequate technical safeguards led to breach.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Citibank left a known technical vulnerability in its Account Online service unpatched for nearly three years.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 80,000 California customers had their personal and financial data—including names, addresses, emails, phone numbers, and credit card numbers—stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Citibank protects customers' personal information by maintaining 'physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards that meet applicable law' (as stated in posted privacy policy).
claimsVsReality.reality: Citibank left a known technical vulnerability in Account Online unpatched for nearly three years, implemented no access controls to prevent URL manipulation, and failed to encrypt customer data, allowing hackers to easily access 360,000+ customer accounts.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Account Online platform was secure and compliant with federal and state data protection requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: The platform contained a simple, exploitable vulnerability that permitted unauthorized account access through basic URL parameter manipulation without re-authentication, violating GLBA, OCC Guidelines, CalOPPA, and state law.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 22576 (CalOPPA) prohibits commercial website operators collecting personally identifiable information from California residents from failing to comply with the provisions of their posted privacy policy, either knowingly/willfully or negligently/materially.
regulatoryFindings.description: Citibank posted a privacy policy stating it maintains 'physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards that meet applicable law,' but failed to maintain adequate safeguards for Account Online by not implementing access controls to authenticate users or prevent URL manipulation attacks.
violations: Citibank posted a privacy policy stating it maintains 'physical, electronic, and procedural safeguards that meet applicable law,' but failed to maintain adequate safeguards for Account Online by not implementing access controls to authenticate users or prevent URL manipulation attacks.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.82(a) requires businesses that own or license computerized data containing personal information to disclose data breaches 'in the most expedient time possible and without unreasonable delay.'
regulatoryFindings.description: Citibank discovered the breach on or about May 10, 2011, but did not begin notifying customers until June 3, 2011—over three weeks later—and did not complete notifications until June 11, 2011, over one month after discovery.
violations: Citibank discovered the breach on or about May 10, 2011, but did not begin notifying customers until June 3, 2011—over three weeks later—and did not complete notifications until June 11, 2011, over one month after discovery.

regulatoryFindings.act: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (15 U.S.C. § 6801 et seq.) and OCC Guidelines 12 CFR Part 30 Appendix B § III.C.1 require financial institutions to design information security programs with access controls to authenticate users and permit access only to authorized individuals.
regulatoryFindings.description: Citibank failed to implement sufficient access controls on Account Online, allowing hackers to modify URL parameters to access customer accounts without re-authentication, and failed to take steps to protect the security of customers' personally identifiable financial information.
violations: Citibank failed to implement sufficient access controls on Account Online, allowing hackers to modify URL parameters to access customer accounts without re-authentication, and failed to take steps to protect the security of customers' personally identifiable financial information.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair, unlawful, or fraudulent business acts or practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Citibank engaged in unfair and unlawful business practices by failing to comply with its posted privacy policy, CalOPPA, GLBA, OCC Guidelines, and state breach notification law, resulting in unauthorized access to customer data.
violations: Citibank engaged in unfair and unlawful business practices by failing to comply with its posted privacy policy, CalOPPA, GLBA, OCC Guidelines, and state breach notification law, resulting in unauthorized access to customer data.

outcome: The complaint sought a permanent injunction against unfair competition, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation under California Business and Professions Code § 17206, and recovery of costs of suit and investigation. The case was filed on August 28, 2013. As this is the initial complaint, the final resolution and settlement terms are not detailed in the document provided.
companyNow: Citibank, N.A. (Citigroup subsidiary) continues to operate as a major global financial institution. The company has since implemented enhanced security measures and data breach notification protocols.
dataType: Financial data, credit card account numbers, customer names, street addresses, email addresses, phone numbers
legalBasisViolated: California Business and Professions Code § 22576 (CalOPPA – failure to comply with posted privacy policy)
California Civil Code § 1798.82(a) (failure to notify in expedient time)
California Civil Code § 1798.82(b) (failure to immediately notify owners of computerized data)
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act (15 U.S.C. § 6801 et seq.) – insufficient data security steps

companyDescription: Red Zone Investment Group, Inc. operated a rent-to-own store franchise in Dallas, Texas, offering consumers the ability to rent furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics including computers with an option to purchase.
companyLongDescription: Red Zone Investment Group, Inc. operated a rent-to-own store franchise in Dallas, Texas, offering consumers the ability to rent furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics including computers with an option to purchase.
caseDescription: Red Zone installed spyware (PC Rental Agent with Detective Mode) on rented computers to secretly monitor users, capture passwords and financial data, photograph users via webcams, and collect contact information through fake software registration popups. The company used this improperly obtained data to locate customers and attempt debt collection.
violationSummary: Red Zone conducted systematic covert surveillance of computer users via webcams, keystroke logging, and screen capture without consent. This is direct surveillance using hidden spyware to monitor activities and capture sensitive personal information. Additionally involves deceptive information collection through fake software prompts.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Red Zone Investment Group installed hidden spyware called PC Rental Agent and Detective Mode on rented computers, enabling remote disabling, keystroke logging, webcam surveillance.
whyTheyWereWrong: Renters and household members suffered unauthorized surveillance inside their homes, exposure of email passwords, financial account credentials, medical information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Fake Microsoft Windows registration popups represented that they were software registration forms from trusted providers that must be filled out to continue using the software
claimsVsReality.reality: The popups were created by Red Zone's Detective Mode spyware and captured consumer contact information solely for debt collection purposes; no actual software registration occurred

claimsVsReality.claim: PC Rental Agent's Detective Mode feature allows Red Zone to locate and manage rented computers when lost or stolen
claimsVsReality.reality: Red Zone used Detective Mode to conduct covert surveillance of users including capturing financial credentials, webcam footage of inside homes, and personal activities without any user knowledge or consent

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Red Zone installed monitoring software on rented computers and gathered sensitive personal information (financial credentials, webcam footage, keystrokes) about consumers without their knowledge or consent, causing substantial harm that consumers could not reasonably avoid because Detective Mode was invisible to users.
violations: Red Zone installed monitoring software on rented computers and gathered sensitive personal information (financial credentials, webcam footage, keystrokes) about consumers without their knowledge or consent, causing substantial harm that consumers could not reasonably avoid because Detective Mode was invisible to users.
Red Zone used improperly gathered information to collect or attempt to collect debts, money, or property, causing substantial injury through unfair collection practices.

outcome: FTC issued complaint on April 11, 2013 (Docket No. C-4396). The complaint alleges three counts of violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act: unfair gathering of personal information, unfair collection practices, and deceptive gathering of personal information. While the complaint document does not include the final settlement order, enforcement actions typically result in compliance orders requiring cessation of the conduct, deletion of improperly obtained data, and ongoing monitoring. Document shows complaint was issued; settlement/final order status not included in this document.

companyLongDescription: Aspen Way Enterprises, Inc. was a Montana-based rent-to-own retailer and franchisee of Aaron's Inc., operating 17 stores across six states offering furniture, household appliances, and consumer electronics for rent with purchase options.
caseDescription: Aspen Way installed spyware (PC Rental Agent and Detective Mode) on computers rented to consumers without disclosure, enabling remote disabling of devices and secret surveillance including keystroke logging, screen capture, and webcam monitoring. The company used collected data including passwords, medical records, and intimate home images for debt collection, and deployed fake software registration windows to deceive consumers into providing contact information.

violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Aspen Way installed undetectable spyware on rental computers that secretly logged keystrokes, captured screenshots, photographed users via webcams.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers had their email passwords, bank credentials, medical records, employment applications with Social Security numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: PC Rental Agent was used to protect against loss or theft and enforce rental contracts.
claimsVsReality.reality: The software was also used to deploy hidden surveillance (Detective Mode) that captured keystrokes, screenshots, and webcam images of all computer users, revealing passwords, medical records, and intimate family moments.

claimsVsReality.claim: Pop-up windows on rental computers were legitimate software registration notices from trusted providers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data collection was necessary for contract enforcement.
claimsVsReality.reality: Aspen Way had alternate effective non-invasive methods available (e.g., remote computer disabling via PC Rental Agent alone) that made covert surveillance unnecessary and unjustifiable.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Unfair gathering of personal information: Installed monitoring software on rental computers and collected sensitive personal, financial, and medical information about consumers without consent or notice. company: Epic Marketplace, Inc. and Epic Media Group, LLC
companyDescription: Epic Marketplace was an online behavioral advertising company that acted as an intermediary between advertisers and website publishers in a network of over 45,000 publishers. Epic Media Group is the parent Delaware corporation controlling Epic's operations.
companyLongDescription: Epic Marketplace was an online behavioral advertising company that acted as an intermediary between advertisers and website publishers in a network of over 45,000 publishers. Epic Media Group is the parent Delaware corporation controlling Epic's operations.
caseDescription: Epic Marketplace engaged in history sniffing—covertly accessing consumers' browsing history outside its ad network—from 2010 to 2011 to build detailed behavioral profiles. The company falsely represented in its privacy policy that it collected only information from within its network and failed to disclose this secret tracking practice.
violationSummary: History sniffing is covert surveillance that circumvents known consumer privacy protections (cookie deletion) and extracts sensitive personal information (health conditions, financial status) without consent, coupled with material misrepresentation in privacy disclosures.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Epic Marketplace embedded history-sniffing code in advertisements served across 24,000+ webpages to secretly determine whether consumers had visited 54,000+ external domains.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers could not protect themselves using standard privacy measures like cookie deletion, and Epic falsely represented it only tracked visits within its own network.

claimsVsReality.claim: Epic Marketplace automatically receives and records anonymous information that your browser sends whenever you visit a website which is part of the Epic Marketplace Network.
claimsVsReality.reality: Epic used history sniffing to detect whether consumers had visited any of 54,000+ domains outside the Epic Marketplace Network, including sensitive health and financial sites, without any indication in the privacy policy.

claimsVsReality.claim: We use log files to collect Internet protocol (IP) addresses, browser type, Internet service providers (ISP), referring/exit pages, platform type, date/time stamp, one or more cookies that may uniquely identify your browser, and responses by a web surfer to an advertisement delivered by us.
claimsVsReality.reality: Epic's tracking extended far beyond advertisement interactions and data from its own network—it secretly mapped consumers' entire browsing history across the web using an undisclosed surveillance technique.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Count 1: Falsely represented that Epic collected information only on consumers' visits within the Epic Marketplace Network, when in fact it used history sniffing to collect data on visits to 54,000+ external domains.
violations: Count 1: Falsely represented that Epic collected information only on consumers' visits within the Epic Marketplace Network, when in fact it used history sniffing to collect data on visits to 54,000+ external domains.

Count 2: Failed to disclose that respondents engaged in history sniffing, which is material to consumers' decision whether to use Epic's opt-out mechanism, in light of express representations about data collection scope.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on March 13, 2013, alleging two counts of deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint sought cessation of history sniffing and other injunctive relief. Resolution details and any consent order terms are not specified in this complaint document.
dataType: Browsing history, domain visits, interest segments, behavioral data, IP addresses, cookies
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Path Inc. was a social networking mobile application company that allowed users to share photos, location, thoughts, and music with a limited network of up to 150 friends. The company developed applications for iOS and Android platforms and operated a website at path.com.
companyLongDescription: Path Inc. was a social networking mobile application company that allowed users to share photos, location, thoughts, and music with a limited network of up to 150 friends. The company developed applications for iOS and Android platforms and operated a website at path.com.
caseDescription: Path automatically collected and uploaded entire address books from users' mobile devices without meaningful consent or disclosure. The company also knowingly collected personal information from approximately 3,000 children under 13 without obtaining parental consent, in violation of COPPA. Path's privacy policy failed to disclose these practices and made misleading statements about its data collection practices.
violationSummary: Path conducted systematic, unauthorized collection of personal data (address books) from users' devices without meaningful consent or disclosure. This surveillance occurred automatically every time users launched the app, contrary to user interface representations.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Path automatically collected and stored personal contact information from users' mobile device address books without meaningful user consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children under 13 had sensitive personal data including names, phone numbers, email addresses, birthdates, and their entire contact networks collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Path's user interface indicated that contact information would only be collected if users selected the 'Find friends from your contacts' option.
claimsVsReality.reality: Path automatically collected and uploaded complete address books every time users launched the app or signed back in, regardless of whether users selected any 'add friends' feature.

claimsVsReality.claim: Path's privacy policy stated that 'we automatically collect certain information when you use our site and our services, such as your Internet Protocol (IP) address, your operating system, the browser type, the address of a referring site and your activity on our site.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Path automatically collected detailed contact information from users' address books including names, addresses, phone numbers, mobile numbers, email addresses, Facebook usernames, Twitter usernames, and dates of birth for each contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: Path's privacy policy and website stated 'Path should be private by default. Forever. You should always be in control of your information and experience.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Path users had no control over contact information collection; the company collected data automatically without meaningful user choice or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Path was a service designed for general audiences with no particular targeting of children.
claimsVsReality.reality: Path knowingly accepted and processed registrations from approximately 3,000 children under age 13 without implementing any age verification or parental consent mechanisms.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Path represented through its user interface that contact information would only be collected if users selected 'Find friends from your contacts,' but automatically collected all contacts regardless of user choice.
violations: Path represented through its user interface that contact information would only be collected if users selected 'Find friends from your contacts,' but automatically collected all contacts regardless of user choice.

Path's privacy policy represented that only IP address, operating system, browser type, and site activity information was automatically collected, but actually collected full contact details including names, phone numbers, email addresses, and dates of birth from users' address books.
Path created illusory user interface options suggesting meaningful user control over data collection when collection occurred automatically without any user selection.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(b) requires operators to provide sufficient notice on websites or online services of information collected from children, how it is used, and disclosure practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Path's privacy policy did not clearly, completely, or accurately disclose all of its information collection practices for children.
violations: Path's privacy policy did not clearly, completely, or accurately disclose all of its information collection practices for children.
Path failed to disclose automatic collection of contact information from children's address books in any privacy notice.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(c) requires operators to provide direct notice to parents of information collection practices for children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Path did not provide any direct notice to parents prior to collecting, using, or disclosing children's personal information.
violations: Path did not provide any direct notice to parents prior to collecting, using, or disclosing children's personal information.
Path accepted registrations from children under 13 without any parental notification mechanism.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent prior to any collection, use, or disclosure of personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Path knowingly collected personal information from approximately 3,000 children under 13 without obtaining any verifiable parental consent.
violations: Path knowingly collected personal information from approximately 3,000 children under 13 without obtaining any verifiable parental consent.
Path collected address book data from children without any consent mechanism or parental verification whatsoever.

outcome: The complaint alleges multiple violations of the FTC Act and COPPA. The United States sought a permanent injunction against Path to prevent future violations of the FTC Act regarding consumer privacy and COPPA. The complaint requests monetary civil penalties of not more than $16,000 for each violation of the COPPA Rule (approximately 3,000 violations) and such other relief as the court determines just and proper. Path was required to cease the practice of automatic contact collection and implement comprehensive privacy compliance measures.
companyNow: Path Inc. shut down its social networking service and was acquired. The company no longer operates as an independent social network platform.
dataType: Contact information, location data, email addresses, phone numbers, date of birth, social network information, user-generated content

FTC Act Section 5(m)(1)(A) – Knowing violation standard
COPPA Section 1303(c) – Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(c) – Parental notice requirement
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) – Verifiable parental consent requirement

companyDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is Canada's federal tax and revenue administration body responsible for administering tax laws and social benefit programs.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency is a Crown corporation of the Government of Canada that administers federal taxation, interprets tax laws, and manages social benefit and income support programs. It processes millions of tax returns and maintains extensive personal information databases on Canadian taxpayers. The agency is responsible for ensuring the secure handling of sensitive personal and financial information.
caseDescription: A Canada Revenue Agency employee failed to properly verify an applicant's identity and mailed personal information including a Social Insurance Number to the wrong recipient due to name similarity. The disclosure resulted from non-adherence to established verification procedures. The Agency acknowledged the error and implemented corrective measures.
violationSummary: The agency disclosed sensitive personal information (Social Insurance Number and tax adjustment details) to an unauthorized third party without consent due to procedural failure in identity verification.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A Canada Revenue Agency employee failed to verify an applicant's address and mailed a letter containing a Social Insurance Number.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two individuals received sensitive personal information including Social Insurance Numbers not intended for them, creating risk of identity theft and unauthorized access to their tax records.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employee followed standard verification procedures to ensure correct recipient identification.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee failed to verify that the address matched information on the request and supporting documents, leading to misdirected sensitive mail.

claimsVsReality.claim: Existing safeguards were sufficient to prevent misdirection of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: A procedural control that should have prevented this error was not followed, resulting in disclosure to an unintended third party.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires personal information to be as accurate and up-to-date as possible
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency failed to verify that the address on file matched the request and supporting documents before mailing sensitive information
violations: Agency failed to verify that the address on file matched the request and supporting documents before mailing sensitive information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 requires safeguards to protect personal information during collection, processing, and retention
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency employee failed to follow established verification procedures, resulting in disclosure to an incorrect individual
violations: Agency employee failed to follow established verification procedures, resulting in disclosure to an incorrect individual

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. The Canada Revenue Agency admitted its error and implemented measures to prevent similar incidents in the future, including enhanced verification procedures and staff training.
companyNow: The CRA continues to operate as Canada's primary tax and revenue administration authority, though it has faced ongoing scrutiny regarding data security and privacy practices.
dataType: Social Insurance Number, name, address
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 (Openness Concerning Management of Personal Information)

companyDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is Canada's federal tax authority responsible for administering tax laws and collecting revenue on behalf of the Canadian government.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency is a federal crown corporation that administers Canada's tax system, including income tax, goods and services tax, and various benefit programs. It employs thousands of staff with access to sensitive personal and financial information of Canadian taxpayers. The CRA operates under the Privacy Act and must safeguard taxpayer information in accordance with federal privacy legislation.
caseDescription: A Canada Revenue Agency employee who was the common-law spouse of a woman's ex-husband inappropriately accessed her tax information and passed it to him. The ex-husband then used this information to seek an amendment to a child support arrangement. The Agency's investigation took 13 months and identified systemic issues with response time and employee privacy training.
violationSummary: An employee breached the confidentiality of taxpayer personal information by accessing it without authorization and disclosing it to a third party (the ex-husband) for personal purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A Canada Revenue Agency employee who was the common-law spouse of an ex-husband inappropriately accessed a woman's tax information and passed it to him for use in a child support dispute.
whyTheyWereWrong: The woman's sensitive tax information was disclosed to her ex-husband without consent, enabling him to use it against her in a child support modification proceeding, violating her privacy rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: CRA employees are adequately trained to protect taxpayer privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: An employee inappropriately accessed and disclosed a taxpayer's information to a third party, indicating insufficient privacy training and awareness of obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Agency's internal investigation process is timely and efficient.
claimsVsReality.reality: The internal investigation took 13 months to complete, and the notification letter to the complainant was drafted but never sent, causing significant delay.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act – Protection of Personal Information in Government Custody
regulatoryFindings.description: Unauthorized access to personal tax information by an employee
violations: Unauthorized access to personal tax information by an employee
Disclosure of confidential taxpayer information to a third party without authorization
Inadequate timeliness in investigating and addressing employee misconduct allegations
Insufficient privacy training for employees with access to sensitive personal information

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well founded. The Canada Revenue Agency was directed to implement recommendations including: establishing more efficient processes for addressing employee misconduct allegations, enhancing privacy training for all employees with access to personal tax information, and ensuring employees understand their confidentiality obligations. The Agency accepted and implemented these recommendations.
companyNow: The Canada Revenue Agency remains Canada's primary tax authority and continues to operate under federal oversight with enhanced privacy protections.
dataType: Tax information, financial data

companyDescription: The Correctional Service of Canada is the federal agency responsible for managing penitentiaries and administering sentences for offenders in Canada.
companyLongDescription: The Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) is a federal law enforcement agency operating under the Department of Public Safety. It manages federal penitentiaries housing offenders serving sentences of two years or more and is responsible for secure custody, rehabilitation programs, and safe reintegration. CSC operates across Canada with multiple security-level institutions.
caseDescription: The Correctional Service of Canada breached the Privacy Act by openly posting inmates' medical appointment details, including names, appointment times, and offender numbers, to the general penitentiary population on multiple occasions. The agency acknowledged the breach and committed to notifying inmates individually rather than posting lists, though it declined to implement the recommendation to use only partial offender numbers in internal employee lists.
violationSummary: The unauthorized disclosure of sensitive health and personal identifier information to a broad, unintended audience (general penitentiary population) constitutes exposure of personal data, making it accessible to parties without a legitimate need to know.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: The Correctional Service of Canada repeatedly posted inmates' names, medical appointment times, and offender numbers on bulletin boards accessible to the general penitentiary population.
whyTheyWereWrong: Inmates' medical information and identities were exposed to hundreds of other prisoners, compromising their privacy and creating security.

claimsVsReality.claim: Medical appointment notifications required posting names and complete offender numbers to general penitentiary populations.
claimsVsReality.reality: Such postings exposed sensitive medical information and inmate identities to hundreds of other prisoners, violating the Privacy Act and creating unnecessary security risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Using full offender numbers on employee notification lists was necessary for operational purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Partial offender numbers would have been sufficient for internal employee communication while protecting inmate privacy.

regulatoryFindings.act: Canadian Privacy Act – requirement to protect personal information from unauthorized disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Openly posting medical appointment details (name, appointment time, offender number) accessible to general penitentiary population
violations: Openly posting medical appointment details (name, appointment time, offender number) accessible to general penitentiary population
Disclosing complete offender numbers and medical information for multiple inmates on several occasions
Failing to implement safeguards limiting access to sensitive health and identifier information

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well founded. The Correctional Service of Canada acknowledged the Privacy Act breach and committed to notifying inmates of medical appointments individually rather than posting lists publicly. The agency declined to implement the recommendation to use only partial offender numbers in internal employee notification lists.
companyNow: The Correctional Service of Canada continues to operate as Canada's federal correctional authority, managing federal penitentiaries and inmate services across the country.
dataType: Health data, personal identifiers (name, offender number)

companyDescription: Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) is the federal agency responsible for managing penitentiaries, detention facilities, and offender supervision across Canada.
companyLongDescription: Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) is a federal law enforcement agency under the Department of Justice responsible for the custody, supervision, and rehabilitation of individuals convicted of federal offences in Canada. The organization operates a network of penitentiaries, healing lodges, and community offices across the country. As a government agency, CSC holds sensitive personal and health information on both inmates and visitors to federal facilities.
caseDescription: A woman's drug scan test results were inappropriately disclosed by Correctional Service of Canada employees to her ex-husband, a CSC employee, without authorization. This disclosure was used by the ex-husband to restrict the woman's access to her children. The investigation confirmed the disclosure occurred but could not identify the specific employees responsible or the source of the information.
violationSummary: Unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal health information (drug test results) to a third party (the ex-husband) by government employees, breaching the duty of confidentiality and appropriate information handling protocols.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Correctional Service of Canada employees inappropriately disclosed a woman's drug scan test results to her ex-husband, a CSC employee, without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unauthorized disclosure of the woman's drug test results to her ex-husband enabled him to restrict her access to their children, causing direct harm to her parental rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: The ex-husband obtained the drug information through the same database intrusion that affected the inmate's records
claimsVsReality.reality: CSC investigation found no evidence the ex-husband participated in any database intrusion; CSC employees directly disclosed the information to him through unknown means

claimsVsReality.claim: CSC adequately investigated and dealt with the disclosure issue
claimsVsReality.reality: CSC failed to adequately address the core disclosure issue and did not attempt to discover how the ex-husband learned of the drug test results

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – requirement to protect personal information from unauthorized disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Correctional Service of Canada employees disclosed drug test results to an unauthorized third party (ex-husband)
violations: Correctional Service of Canada employees disclosed drug test results to an unauthorized third party (ex-husband)
Failed to maintain confidentiality of sensitive health information
Failed to adequately investigate and address the core disclosure issue

outcome: Complaint upheld as well founded. The investigation confirmed that the woman's drug scan results were inappropriately disclosed to her ex-husband by Correctional Service of Canada employees. The Department was found to have failed to adequately deal with the core disclosure issue. No monetary penalty was imposed, but the finding establishes liability and requires improved information access controls and disclosure investigation procedures.
companyNow: Correctional Service of Canada continues to operate as the primary federal corrections agency in Canada, managing inmate populations and enforcing federal sentences.
dataType: Drug test results, personal health information, inmate records
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) – Unauthorized disclosure of personal information
Federal privacy principles – Duty to protect sensitive personal health information

companyDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada is a federal government department responsible for administering disability pension payments and benefits to Canadian Armed Forces members and veterans.
companyLongDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada is a federal government department that administers disability pensions, benefits, and support services to Canadian Armed Forces members and veterans. The department maintains sensitive personal health and financial information about its beneficiaries, including disability pension percentages that indicate the severity of service-related afflictions. It operates under formal inter-departmental information-sharing agreements with other government agencies such as the Department of National Defence to coordinate benefits and services.
caseDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada disclosed a Canadian Forces veteran's disability pension percentage to the Department of National Defence without consent, violating an inter-departmental information-sharing agreement that explicitly excluded this sensitive data. The disclosure occurred through an inadvertently forwarded email containing medical details and was not necessary for the veteran's treatment. This was the second similar complaint by the same individual, with the first complaint in 2008 having been upheld as well founded.
violationSummary: The disclosure of the disability pension percentage—a proxy for severity of affliction—to an unauthorized party (National Defence) without consent constitutes improper dissemination of sensitive personal information that fell outside the scope of authorized sharing arrangements.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Veterans Affairs Canada disclosed a Canadian Forces veteran's disability pension percentage to the Department of National Defence in an inadvertently forwarded email without the veteran's.
whyTheyWereWrong: The veteran's sensitive disability pension percentage was exposed to an unauthorized department, revealing the severity of his affliction.

claimsVsReality.claim: Veterans Affairs disclosed the disability pension percentage under the 'public interest' exemption provisions of the Privacy Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: The disclosure was accidental through an inadvertently forwarded email chain and was not made deliberately as would be required to invoke public interest exemptions; no evidence suggested the disclosure was necessary or useful for the veteran's treatment.

claimsVsReality.claim: The disability pension percentage was appropriately shared with the Department of National Defence as part of normal inter-departmental coordination.
claimsVsReality.reality: The formal agreement between the two departments explicitly listed five specific pieces of information that could be shared, and the disability pension percentage was not included on that list.

regulatoryFindings.act: Canadian Privacy Act — Personal information may only be used or disclosed as authorized by law or with consent; exemptions for public interest disclosures require deliberate authorization
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed disability pension percentage outside the scope of inter-departmental information-sharing agreement
violations: Disclosed disability pension percentage outside the scope of inter-departmental information-sharing agreement
Failed to delete sensitive personal information before forwarding email to National Defence
Disclosed information that was not necessary or useful for the veteran's medical treatment
Inappropriately claimed 'public interest' exemption without evidence of deliberate authorization

outcome: Complaint upheld as well founded. Veterans Affairs accepted recommendations to: (1) review and comply with existing policies and procedures concerning information sharing with National Defence; (2) disseminate those policies and procedures to all employees; (3) provide training on appropriate handling of shared information with National Defence. Veterans Affairs also re-examined its information-sharing arrangement with National Defence. No monetary penalty imposed.
companyNow: Veterans Affairs Canada continues to operate as a federal department providing benefits and services to Canadian veterans and Armed Forces members, with ongoing focus on privacy protection and secure information handling.
dataType: health data, disability pension percentage, medical details
legalBasisViolated: Inter-departmental information-sharing agreement limiting disclosure to five specific data points

companyDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada is the federal government department responsible for providing benefits, services, and support to Canadian Armed Forces members, veterans, and their families.
companyLongDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada administers pension benefits, disability awards, and other services for eligible veterans and their dependents. The department maintains extensive personal health, financial, and military service records for millions of individuals. As a government agency, it operates under the Privacy Act and must balance statutory obligations to protect personal information with legitimate access requests from estate administrators and beneficiaries.
caseDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada refused to release a deceased veteran's pension file to his adult children, citing the Pension Act's requirement to protect personal information for 20 years after death and claiming the children were ineligible beneficiaries. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner found this refusal unreasonable, determining that estate administrators are entitled to access the pensioner's personal file to properly administer the estate.
violationSummary: The violation falls under Exposure because the department improperly withheld personal information from authorized parties (estate administrators), thereby denying legitimate access and failing to disclose information that should have been available under privacy legislation and regulations.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Veterans Affairs Canada refused to release a deceased veteran's pension file to his adult children.
whyTheyWereWrong: The family could not properly administer the veteran's estate or investigate potential processing errors in the pension claim without access to the file.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Pension Act requires Veterans Affairs to protect personal information for 20 years after death without exception.
claimsVsReality.reality: Estate administrators have a legal right under the Privacy Act Regulations to access a deceased person's personal file to administer the estate, even within the 20-year protection period.

claimsVsReality.claim: Adult children who are not pension beneficiaries are not entitled to access the veteran's pension file.
claimsVsReality.reality: Adult children acting as estate administrators are entitled to access the pension file regardless of whether they are direct beneficiaries, as the information is necessary for proper estate administration.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Regulations (Canada) – Right of Access for Estate Administration
regulatoryFindings.description: Unreasonably refused to release pension file to estate administrators despite regulatory entitlement to access personal information for estate administration purposes
violations: Unreasonably refused to release pension file to estate administrators despite regulatory entitlement to access personal information for estate administration purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: Pension Act (Canada) – Information Protection After Death
regulatoryFindings.description: Misapplied the 20-year post-death protection requirement to prevent legitimate estate administration access
violations: Misapplied the 20-year post-death protection requirement to prevent legitimate estate administration access

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well-founded. After the Privacy Commissioner's findings were communicated to Veterans Affairs Canada, the Department released the veteran's pension file to his survivors to permit proper estate administration.
companyNow: Veterans Affairs Canada continues to operate as a federal department, now part of the broader Veterans Affairs and Canadian Armed Forces administration. The department has since updated its practices regarding estate administrator access to deceased veterans' files.
dataType: Pension records, personal financial information, estate administration documents

companyDescription: Citizenship and Immigration Canada is the federal department responsible for immigration, refugees, citizenship, and travel document services in Canada.
companyLongDescription: Citizenship and Immigration Canada (now IRCC) is a federal government department that administers Canada's immigration, refugee, and citizenship programs. The department operates visa application offices and immigration services at Canadian High Commissions and embassies worldwide, including in Dhaka, Bangladesh. It processes work permits, permanent residency applications, and citizenship matters. The department is accountable under the Privacy Act and the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA).
caseDescription: Canadian immigration officials at the High Commission in Dhaka inadvertently disclosed a Canadian woman's personal documents (including passport, SIN, and tax information) to a work permit applicant when returning his file. The applicant subsequently shared the woman's sensitive information with family and friends, creating risks of identity theft and safety concerns if she travelled to Bangladesh.
violationSummary: The woman's personal information was unintentionally exposed to an unauthorized third party (the visa applicant) due to improper document handling procedures. This constitutes exposure of personal information to those who should not have access to it.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Canadian immigration officials at the High Commission in Dhaka returned a rejected work permit applicant's file without removing a Canadian woman's personal documents (passport, SIN.
whyTheyWereWrong: The woman's sensitive documents were disclosed without her consent to a third party who shared them with family and friends, creating real risks of identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Immigration officials followed standard practice by returning the entire contents of the applicant's file.
claimsVsReality.reality: Standard practice proved inadequate as it failed to filter out third-party documents not belonging to the applicant, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of the woman's sensitive personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The disclosure was an inadvertent mix-up with no systemic problem.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner noted this was not the first time a breach of this nature had occurred at a Canadian High Commission, indicating a systemic procedural failure across multiple missions.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2 – Consent: Organizations shall not collect, use or disclose personal information without the knowledge and consent of the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: Citizenship and Immigration Canada disclosed the woman's personal information to the visa applicant without her knowledge or consent
violations: Citizenship and Immigration Canada disclosed the woman's personal information to the visa applicant without her knowledge or consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2.3 – Accuracy: Personal information shall be as accurate, complete and up-to-date as is necessary for the purposes for which it is to be used.
regulatoryFindings.description: Officials failed to properly segregate and manage personal information from third parties, resulting in disclosure of information not belonging to the applicant
violations: Officials failed to properly segregate and manage personal information from third parties, resulting in disclosure of information not belonging to the applicant

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well-founded. Citizenship and Immigration acknowledged the breach and apologized to the complainant. The Office recommended that all High Commissions create a stamp marked 'Destroy/Do Not Return to Applicant' to distinguish documents from sources other than visa applicants. The Dhaka mission subsequently implemented this recommendation.
companyNow: The department continues to operate as Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC), a major federal agency responsible for Canada's immigration system.
dataType: Passport information, Social Insurance Number, date of birth, federal income tax assessment details

companyDescription: Canada Post is Canada's national postal service, responsible for mail delivery and postal services across the country.
companyLongDescription: Canada Post Corporation is a Crown corporation that provides mail delivery, parcel services, and related postal products to Canadian households and businesses. Founded in 1867, it operates the national postal network across Canada. The company also offers online services including address changes and payment processing for postal transactions.
caseDescription: Canada Post shared personal information with Equifax for identity verification during online address change requests without adequately informing users. The Privacy Commissioner found no violation of the Privacy Act but was concerned about insufficient transparency regarding data sharing with a third party.
violationSummary: The primary issue was inadequate disclosure to individuals that their personal information would be shared with Equifax during the identity verification process, which constitutes a disclosure violation under privacy principles.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Canada Post sent personal information to Equifax for identity verification during online address changes without clearly disclosing this data sharing to users beforehand.
whyTheyWereWrong: Canadians were redirected to Equifax's website and asked financial questions without adequate advance notice, exposing their personal and financial data to a third party without informed consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Canada Post was only verifying identity to prevent mail misdirection and identity theft.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information was being shared with Equifax, a credit rating agency, and users were transferred to Equifax's website to answer financial questions about their credit history.

claimsVsReality.claim: Individuals were adequately informed about the Equifax involvement in the online address change process.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users were not clearly informed in advance that their personal information would be disclosed to Equifax or transferred to a third-party website.

claimsVsReality.claim: Information provided during identity verification would be kept separate from credit files.
claimsVsReality.reality: Users had no clear transparency about whether data collected during verification could be linked to or used by Equifax for credit reporting purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Canadian Privacy Act - Requirement to inform individuals of information collection and sharing practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to adequately inform individuals that personal information would be disclosed to Equifax
violations: Failure to adequately inform individuals that personal information would be disclosed to Equifax
Lack of clear communication about what personal information would or may be disclosed to third parties

regulatoryFindings.act: Canadian Privacy Act - Authority to collect personal information for stated purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: No violation found; Canada Post had statutory authority to collect information for identity verification
violations: No violation found; Canada Post had statutory authority to collect information for identity verification

outcome: No violation of the Privacy Act was found; however, the Privacy Commissioner recommended that Canada Post clearly state on its website that personal information would be disclosed to Equifax, list the specific personal information to be disclosed, and clarify identification requirements for online applications. Canada Post implemented all recommendations.
companyNow: Canada Post remains Canada's primary postal service provider, operating under federal oversight and serving millions of Canadians daily.
dataType: Financial information, identity verification data, loan and credit information

companyDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's federal law enforcement agency responsible for policing at the federal, provincial, and municipal levels.
companyLongDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's primary federal police force, providing law enforcement services across Canada and internationally. Established in 1873, it operates under the RCMP Act and is responsible for enforcing federal laws, providing protective services, and supporting provincial and municipal policing. The RCMP also manages important criminal databases and conducts investigations ranging from serious crimes to national security matters.
caseDescription: The RCMP sergeant disclosed that a community member was a 'person of interest' and suspect in a murder investigation at a public community meeting without obtaining explicit informed consent. The sergeant presumed consent based on the man's attendance at the meeting and assurances from group representatives, rather than actively seeking the individual's agreement to discuss him.
violationSummary: The RCMP disclosed sensitive personal information (criminal investigation status, suspect designation) without proper consent. The violation falls under Information Dissemination – Disclosure because the sergeant revealed the man's status as a murder suspect to a community gathering without the individual's informed consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: An RCMP sergeant disclosed that a community member was a 'person of interest' and murder suspect at a public meeting without obtaining the individual's explicit informed consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The man was publicly identified as a murder suspect without his knowledge of the discussion topic, exposing him to community suspicion, social stigma, and potential vigilantism.

claimsVsReality.claim: The sergeant presumed the complainant had consented to the discussion because of his attendance at the meeting and assurances from group representatives that he was aware of and had not objected to the proposed discussion.
claimsVsReality.reality: The man was aware he would be discussed but was not informed that the discussion would concern his status as a murder suspect; he was publicly identified without explicit informed consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The sergeant would only discuss the man if he were present at the meeting.
claimsVsReality.reality: The sergeant discussed the man's status as a suspect regardless, and the man's presence and comments at the meeting did not constitute valid consent to the disclosure of sensitive investigative information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires organizations to obtain meaningful consent before disclosing personal information, with the burden on the organization to actively seek consent rather than presume it.
regulatoryFindings.description: RCMP sergeant presumed consent based on the complainant's attendance at a meeting rather than obtaining explicit informed consent
violations: RCMP sergeant presumed consent based on the complainant's attendance at a meeting rather than obtaining explicit informed consent
Sergeant did not inform the individual in advance that he would be discussed or that sensitive investigation details would be disclosed
The organization failed to actively obtain consent; instead it relied on third-party assurances and the individual's mere presence

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well-founded. The RCMP was directed to ensure that in future, active informed consent is obtained from individuals before disclosing their personal information in public forums, rather than presuming consent based on attendance or third-party representations.
companyNow: The RCMP continues to operate as Canada's federal police force, serving all provinces and territories with approximately 28,000 employees.
dataType: Personal identification, criminal investigation status, polygraph test refusal
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (Consent for collection, use, and disclosure)

companyDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's federal and national police service, responsible for law enforcement and crime investigation across the country.
companyLongDescription: The RCMP is Canada's primary federal law enforcement agency, operating across all provinces and territories. It maintains access to the Canadian Police Information Centre (CPIC), a national database containing criminal records and law enforcement information. The RCMP employs thousands of officers and staff who are entrusted with access to sensitive personal information for authorized law enforcement purposes only.
caseDescription: An RCMP officer used privileged access to the Canadian Police Information Centre (CPIC) database to perform an unauthorized criminal background check on a prospective tenant, citing her out-of-town origin as justification. The officer accessed the database for personal reasons rather than authorized law enforcement purposes, violating the tenant's privacy rights under the Privacy Act. The RCMP subsequently apologized, reminded the officer of policy violations, and issued a departmental communiqué to all employees on proper database usage.
violationSummary: The officer unlawfully accessed a law enforcement database containing sensitive personal information (criminal records) without authorization or legitimate operational purpose, engaging in warrantless surveillance of the individual.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: An RCMP officer used privileged access to the Canadian Police Information Centre (CPIC) database to run an unauthorized criminal background check on a prospective tenant.
whyTheyWereWrong: The tenant's criminal history was accessed without lawful authorization, exposing her sensitive personal information to scrutiny based on her geographic origin rather than any legitimate law.

claimsVsReality.claim: The officer justified the background check as necessary to minimize risks to officer safety and organizational security because the prospective tenant was from out of town.
claimsVsReality.reality: The prospective tenant posed no law enforcement threat; the officer accessed the database for personal landlord purposes unrelated to any authorized operational need, and geographic origin alone cannot justify criminal record searches.

claimsVsReality.claim: Accessing CPIC for personal landlord screening purposes was an appropriate use of the database.
claimsVsReality.reality: CPIC information is restricted to legitimate law enforcement purposes only; using it to screen tenants based on geography violated both Privacy Act requirements and RCMP policy.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – Personal information held by government institutions must be used only for authorized purposes consistent with the institution's mandate
regulatoryFindings.description: RCMP officer accessed CPIC database to conduct criminal background check on prospective tenant for personal/landlord purposes, not authorized law enforcement operations
violations: RCMP officer accessed CPIC database to conduct criminal background check on prospective tenant for personal/landlord purposes, not authorized law enforcement operations
Information accessed was used outside the scope of legitimate law enforcement purpose

regulatoryFindings.act: CPIC Database Policies and Procedures – Access restricted to authorized law enforcement purposes only
regulatoryFindings.description: Officer's justification of minimizing 'risks to officer safety' was pretextual; actual reason was tenant's out-of-town origin
violations: Officer's justification of minimizing 'risks to officer safety' was pretextual; actual reason was tenant's out-of-town origin
Access violated stated policies governing proper use of the database

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded on April 4, 2012. The RCMP took remedial actions including: written apology to the complainant, counselling of the officer on the gravity and inappropriateness of his actions, and issuance of a communiqué on April 20, 2012 reminding all employees of CPIC database policies and procedures, with planned follow-up communications regarding measures for transgressions. The Commissioner accepted these remedial measures as satisfactory.
companyNow: The RCMP remains Canada's principal federal police service and continues to enforce federal laws and maintain national security. Following this incident, the organization issued policies reinforcing proper database access procedures.
dataType: Criminal records, driver's licence information, personal identification
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) – unauthorized use of personal information held by a government institution
CPIC database policies and procedures – unauthorized access for non-law enforcement purposes

companyDescription: The Canada School of Public Service is the federal government's primary educational institution responsible for training and development of public sector employees across Canada.
companyLongDescription: The Canada School of Public Service is a Crown corporation operating as the main education and training institution for the Canadian federal public service. It provides learning and development programs to civil servants across all government departments and agencies. As a government institution, it is subject to the Privacy Act and must protect the personal information of employees and individuals it encounters in its operations.
caseDescription: The Canada School of Public Service disclosed the personal information and names of seven employees under investigation for alleged wrongdoing when it distributed a letter from the Public Sector Integrity Commissioner to all staff members. This public disclosure of the employees' identities breached their privacy rights under the Privacy Act. The School subsequently implemented procedures to protect confidentiality of information related to whistleblower investigations.
violationSummary: The School improperly disclosed personal information (names and alleged wrongdoing details) of employees to third parties and the wider organization without appropriate controls, violating principles of confidentiality and restricted disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Canada School of Public Service distributed a letter from the Public Sector Integrity Commissioner to all staff members that publicly identified seven employees under investigation.
whyTheyWereWrong: Seven employees had their identities and details of investigations against them publicly disclosed to the entire workforce, exposing them to reputational harm, workplace stigma.

claimsVsReality.claim: The School could distribute confidential investigation letters to all staff without privacy safeguards.
claimsVsReality.reality: The School lacked procedures to protect confidential information related to whistleblower investigations, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of employee identities and investigation details.

claimsVsReality.claim: Employees under investigation could be publicly identified through internal communications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Employees had their names and alleged wrongdoings revealed to the entire workforce, violating their privacy rights under the Privacy Act and causing reputational exposure during confidential investigations.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – requires organizations to protect personal information from unauthorized disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: School distributed a letter identifying seven named employees and their alleged wrongdoings to all staff members without appropriate confidentiality safeguards
violations: School distributed a letter identifying seven named employees and their alleged wrongdoings to all staff members without appropriate confidentiality safeguards
Employee personal information was made public contrary to Privacy Act provisions

regulatoryFindings.act: Public Servants Disclosure Protection Act – requires confidentiality of whistleblower investigations
regulatoryFindings.description: School failed to maintain confidentiality of investigation details and employee identities during disclosure process
violations: School failed to maintain confidentiality of investigation details and employee identities during disclosure process

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner (OPC) found the complaint well-founded. Following OPC recommendations, the Canada School of Public Service developed new procedures to ensure confidentiality of information associated with the Public Servants Disclosure Protection Act and implemented a plan for addressing future privacy breaches.
companyNow: The Canada School of Public Service continues to operate as the primary learning institution for Canadian federal public servants, now with enhanced privacy protection procedures following this 2012 incident.
dataType: Identity, employment information, alleged wrongdoing allegations
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act (Canada) – duty to protect personal information
Public Servants Disclosure Protection Act – confidentiality obligations

companyDescription: A Canadian cellular telephone service provider offering mobile phone services to residential and business customers.
companyLongDescription: A major Canadian wireless telecommunications company providing cellular phone services, billing, customer support, and account management to a large subscriber base across Canada. The company maintains call centers with customer service representatives trained on authentication and security protocols to protect customer information.
caseDescription: A customer service representative disclosed a customer's personal information including account PIN and calling history to an imposter who claimed to be the account holder, using weak authentication and social engineering. The CSR failed to follow established authentication procedures despite completing required training. The service provider also failed to respond to the customer's access request within the required 30-day timeframe under PIPEDA.
violationSummary: The CSR disclosed sensitive personal information (PIN, billing data, call history) to an unauthorized third party without the account holder's knowledge or consent. This represents a breach of confidentiality obligations under PIPEDA Principle 4.3, which requires knowledge and consent for disclosure of personal information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A customer service representative disclosed a customer's account PIN, billing information, and calling history to an imposter who claimed to be the account holder.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's sensitive account information was exposed to an unauthorized person who gained control of his account, changed his PIN and personal details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The CSR had completed required 4-6 weeks of training on protecting client information and preventing accidental disclosures, plus additional online training on social engineering awareness.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite completing this training, the CSR failed to follow the company's established authentication procedures and disclosed sensitive information (PIN, billing history, call history) to an imposter who could not provide required authenticators like the account PIN or date of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: Clear intranet procedures exist prohibiting employees from discussing call histories or divulging specific telephone numbers called from any account.
claimsVsReality.reality: The CSR disclosed the most recently dialed seven numbers, latest billing dates, payment dates, bill amounts, payment amounts, minutes used, and cell phone plan details to the imposter despite these documented policies.

claimsVsReality.claim: The service provider would respond to access requests within 30 days as required by PIPEDA.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company took six weeks to respond to the complainant's access request, exceeding the 30-day legal deadline and initially claiming 'confusion' as the reason for the delay.
