regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires knowledge and consent of the individual for disclosure of personal information except where inappropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: CSR disclosed complainant's PIN, billing information, payment dates, call history, and phone numbers to imposter without complainant's consent or knowledge
violations: CSR disclosed complainant's PIN, billing information, payment dates, call history, and phone numbers to imposter without complainant's consent or knowledge

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 and Section 8(3) require organizations to respond to access requests within 30 days of receipt
regulatoryFindings.description: Service provider took six weeks to respond to complainant's access request, exceeding the 30-day statutory deadline
violations: Service provider took six weeks to respond to complainant's access request, exceeding the 30-day statutory deadline

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 8(5) deems a request refused if the organization fails to respond within the time limit without proper extension notice
regulatoryFindings.description: Service provider did not invoke extension procedures under Section 8(4) before exceeding the 30-day response deadline
violations: Service provider did not invoke extension procedures under Section 8(4) before exceeding the 30-day response deadline

outcome: The complaint regarding disclosure of personal information was found well-founded under PIPEDA Principle 4.3. The access matter was found well-founded and resolved under Principle 4.9. The service provider provided coaching to the CSR involved, adjusted the complainant's account balance to zero as a goodwill gesture, and agreed to direct negotiations with the complainant regarding compensation. The Office recommended the service provider consult guidance documents to strengthen its privacy management programs, particularly regarding safeguards and employee training on authentication procedures.
dataType: Account information, billing information, call history, personal identification number (PIN), name, gender, phone numbers dialed
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Section 8(3) (Response Time for Access Requests)
PIPEDA Section 8(5) (Deemed Refusal for Late Response)

companyDescription: A Canadian telecommunications company providing internet and wireless services to residential customers.
companyLongDescription: A major Canadian telecommunications provider offering internet and wireless services. The company maintains call recording and transcription practices, with audio recordings typically retained for six months. The firm processes customer access requests and has defined procedures for handling personal information access requests under PIPEDA, though it failed to execute these procedures consistently in this case.
caseDescription: A telecommunications company failed to provide a customer with access to call transcripts and notes relating to her account dispute within the statutory 30-day timeframe required by PIPEDA. The company's staff mistakenly believed that ongoing settlement negotiations negated the obligation to fulfill the access request, and subsequently deleted the requested audio recordings before the customer could access them. The company also failed to send a notice of extension or properly retain records subject to an access request.
violationSummary: The company breached its confidentiality obligations by failing to provide access to personal information upon request and by deleting records that were subject to a pending access request, thereby preventing the individual from exercising her right to access her own information.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The telecommunications firm failed to provide a customer with access to call transcripts and recordings within the 30-day statutory timeframe, did not send a notice of extension.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer was left unable to obtain evidence of the quoted cancellation fee to dispute her bill, was charged collection fees, had derogatory marks on her credit report.

claimsVsReality.claim: Staff believed ongoing settlement negotiations negated the obligation to fulfill the access request within 30 days.
claimsVsReality.reality: PIPEDA requires access requests to be processed within 30 days regardless of any settlement discussions, and the firm did not even contact the customer within 30 days to begin negotiations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The firm's practice is to provide customers with access to their personal information even during business disputes.
claimsVsReality.reality: This practice was not clearly stated in the Policy or Procedure documents provided to staff, leading to inconsistent application and the customer being denied access.

claimsVsReality.claim: Audio recordings are retained for up to six months as standard practice.
claimsVsReality.reality: Audio recordings that are the subject of an access request must be retained longer, but this critical requirement was only buried in internal procedures and not communicated clearly to staff, resulting in premature deletion.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 8(3) requires organizations to respond to written access requests with due diligence and within 30 days of receipt
regulatoryFindings.description: Telecommunications firm failed to respond to the complainant's March 22, 2010 access request within 30 days
violations: Telecommunications firm failed to respond to the complainant's March 22, 2010 access request within 30 days

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 8(4) requires organizations to send a notice of extension if they cannot meet the 30-day deadline, specifying the new time limit and reasons
regulatoryFindings.description: Firm did not send notice of extension to the complainant, contrary to subsection 8(4)
violations: Firm did not send notice of extension to the complainant, contrary to subsection 8(4)

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 8(5) deems an organization to have refused an access request if it fails to respond within the time limit
regulatoryFindings.description: Firm's failure to respond within 30 days resulted in deemed refusal of the access request
violations: Firm's failure to respond within 30 days resulted in deemed refusal of the access request

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 8(8) requires organizations to retain personal information that is subject to an access request for as long as necessary to allow the individual to exhaust any recourse under the Act
regulatoryFindings.description: Firm deleted audio recordings that were subject to the complainant's access request after their standard six-month retention period expired, without considering the ongoing access request
violations: Firm deleted audio recordings that were subject to the complainant's access request after their standard six-month retention period expired, without considering the ongoing access request

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 requires organizations to provide individuals access to their personal information upon request
regulatoryFindings.description: Firm failed to provide the complainant with access to call transcripts and notes she requested regarding her account dispute
violations: Firm failed to provide the complainant with access to call transcripts and notes she requested regarding her account dispute

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9.4 requires organizations to respond to access requests within a reasonable time and at minimal or no cost
regulatoryFindings.description: Firm did not respond within a reasonable time; staff also suggested it would be too costly to process the complainant's request
violations: Firm did not respond within a reasonable time; staff also suggested it would be too costly to process the complainant's request

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.4(c) requires organizations to implement training and communication of policies to staff
regulatoryFindings.description: Firm's staff deviated from documented access policies and procedures; staff misinterpreted policies to mean access requests need not be fulfilled during settlement negotiations; inadequate training and communication of access obligations to employees
violations: Firm's staff deviated from documented access policies and procedures; staff misinterpreted policies to mean access requests need not be fulfilled during settlement negotiations; inadequate training and communication of access obligations to employees

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded and resolved. The company was required to: (1) amend its access Policy, Procedure, and Flow Chart documents to clarify that access requests must be processed within statutory timelines even during ongoing dispute resolution discussions; (2) amend its Policy to ensure consistency with its Procedure regarding retention of audio recordings for six months after customer receipt; (3) submit revised documents for review; and (4) implement a comprehensive training and communications plan for all employees handling access requests. The firm accepted all recommendations, provided revised policies, issued a memorandum from the Chief Privacy Officer to executives and managers, conducted a presentation on access request compliance, and incorporated access training materials into new employee onboarding.
dataType: Account notes, call recordings, billing information, contact information

companyDescription: A major Canadian telecommunications provider offering telephone, cable, and related services to residential customers.
companyLongDescription: A major Canadian telecommunications provider offering telephone, cable, and related services to residential customers. The company manages customer accounts and billing for multiple service types. In this case, the firm's account management systems failed to properly maintain separate customer accounts when individuals shared the same physical address, leading to unauthorized account merging and disclosure of personal financial information.
caseDescription: A telecommunications firm merged a landlord's account with a new tenant's account without consent, creating a single account in the tenant's name. The firm subsequently disclosed the landlord's personal account and debt information to the tenant during collection calls. The landlord's personal information was disclosed without knowledge or consent.
violationSummary: The firm disclosed personal information (account details, debt information) to a third party (the tenant) without the individual's (landlord's) knowledge or consent, which is a direct breach of confidentiality and unauthorized disclosure.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The telecommunications firm merged a landlord's existing account with a new tenant's account without consent, then disclosed the landlord's personal account.
whyTheyWereWrong: The landlord's sensitive financial and account information was exposed to a third party without his knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The firm's systems properly managed separate customer accounts at the same address.
claimsVsReality.reality: The firm merged two completely separate customer accounts (landlord and tenant) into a single account without consent, creating account management confusion.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer personal information and debt details are disclosed only with proper consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: The firm disclosed the landlord's account information and debt details to the tenant during collection calls without the landlord's knowledge or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 – Personal information shall not be used or disclosed for purposes other than those for which it was collected, except with the knowledge or consent of the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed landlord's account information and debt details to tenant without landlord's consent
violations: Disclosed landlord's account information and debt details to tenant without landlord's consent
Merged two separate individuals' accounts without consent, facilitating unauthorized information sharing

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Organizations shall ensure personal information is accurate and complete.
regulatoryFindings.description: Created incorrect merged account attribution by placing landlord's information under tenant's name
violations: Created incorrect merged account attribution by placing landlord's information under tenant's name

outcome: After being contacted by the privacy office, the firm accepted responsibility, re-created separate accounts for each individual, and made amends with the landlord. The case was resolved early with no further action required.
dataType: Account information, financial/debt information, service subscription details
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 (Limiting Use, Disclosure and Retention)

companyDescription: Veda Advantage is an Australian credit reporting agency that compiles and provides credit information and consumer reports to lenders and financial institutions.
companyLongDescription: Veda Advantage (now Equifax Australia after merger) is a major credit reporting bureau in Australia responsible for maintaining credit files and providing credit reports to assess consumer creditworthiness. The company collects, maintains, and distributes credit history information to banks, lenders, and other financial service providers. As a credit reporting agency, Veda is subject to strict privacy and accuracy requirements under the Privacy Act.
caseDescription: Veda Advantage, a credit reporting agency, breached the Privacy Act by providing misleading and inaccurate credit information about an individual. The credit file contained information that was not accurate, up-to-date, complete, or sufficiently clear to avoid being misleading. The company was required to correct the file, apologize, and compensate the affected individual for non-economic loss.
violationSummary: The violation involved failure to maintain accurate, complete, and non-misleading credit reporting data. This falls under information processing insecurity as the company failed to properly maintain and ensure the quality of personal information in its systems.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Veda Advantage maintained and provided a credit file containing inaccurate, outdated, incomplete information that was misleading about an individual's creditworthiness.
whyTheyWereWrong: The individual suffered non-economic loss and reputational harm when inaccurate credit information was used to assess their creditworthiness.

claimsVsReality.claim: Veda Advantage maintained accurate and up-to-date credit information about the individual.
claimsVsReality.reality: The credit file contained information that was not accurate, not up-to-date, not complete, and was misleading.

claimsVsReality.claim: The credit file was sufficiently clear to not mislead lenders and financial institutions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The file was misleading and would have negatively affected credit assessment decisions based on inaccurate data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 18G(a) - Credit reporting must be accurate, up-to-date, complete and not misleading
regulatoryFindings.description: Veda Advantage maintained inaccurate and misleading credit information in the individual's credit file
violations: Veda Advantage maintained inaccurate and misleading credit information in the individual's credit file
The credit file was not updated with current information
Information in the file was incomplete and misleading

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) s 18R(1) - Prohibition on providing misleading credit reports
regulatoryFindings.description: Veda Advantage provided a misleading credit report to third parties
violations: Veda Advantage provided a misleading credit report to third parties

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found breaches of ss 18G(a) and 18R(1) of the Privacy Act. Veda Advantage was ordered to: (1) provide a written apology to the complainant, (2) amend the credit file to correct inaccurate information, (3) review its processes and conduct staff training to prevent recurrence, and (4) pay compensation of $2,000 for non-economic loss suffered by the individual.
companyNow: Veda Advantage merged with Equifax in 2016 and now operates as part of Equifax Australia, continuing as a major credit reporting agency in Australia.
dataType: Credit reporting data, financial information

companyDescription: L'Oreal Singapore is the Singapore subsidiary of the global cosmetics and beauty company L'Oreal, selling luxury and consumer beauty products through online and retail channels.
companyLongDescription: L'Oreal Singapore operates as a subsidiary of L'Oreal S.A., the world's largest cosmetics manufacturer. The company offers a range of beauty products including skincare, makeup, and haircare under various brands. It maintains an e-commerce website with customer login functionality that allows users to manage accounts, redeem vouchers, and track loyalty points. The company engages third-party vendors for website development and maintenance.
caseDescription: L'Oreal Singapore's website experienced a caching vulnerability in its customer login portal that caused personal data of customers to be disclosed to subsequent users. The organization failed to conduct adequate user acceptance testing that would have identified the issue when code changes were made to improve website loading speed. Seven individuals' personal data was exposed to the risk of unauthorized disclosure.
violationSummary: The organization failed to implement appropriate security measures and testing protocols to protect personal data, resulting in a technical vulnerability that exposed customer information to unauthorized access by other users.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: L'Oreal Singapore failed to adequately test its website login portal after code changes, causing customer personal data including names, emails, and phone numbers to be cached.
whyTheyWereWrong: Seven customers' personal information was exposed to unauthorized disclosure when the caching vulnerability allowed each logged-in user to see the previous user's profile data.

claimsVsReality.claim: L'Oreal claimed it had completed all necessary and appropriate User Acceptance Tests based on the reasonably foreseeable impact of the requested code changes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The UATs were inadequately scoped and only tested a single user logging in, failing to simulate the foreseeable scenario of multiple sequential logins that would expose the caching vulnerability.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website code changes were intended to improve loading speed with appropriate vendor management and testing oversight.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization failed to ensure proper security testing was part of the change management process, resulting in a critical caching vulnerability that exposed customer personal data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PDPA Section 24 requires organizations to make reasonable security arrangements to protect personal data against unauthorized disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to scope User Acceptance Tests to include normal functioning of login and caching functions
violations: Failed to scope User Acceptance Tests to include normal functioning of login and caching functions
Test cases only simulated single user login, failing to test foreseeable scenario of multiple sequential users
Inadequate security arrangements allowed customer personal data to be cached and disclosed to subsequent users

outcome: The Deputy Commissioner for Personal Data Protection found L'Oreal Singapore in breach of section 24 of the Personal Data Protection Act 2012 and issued a warning to the organization. The organization disabled the Customer Login Page upon discovery of the vulnerability and engaged a consultant to conduct investigations and provide recommendations to prevent similar incidents in the future.
companyNow: L'Oreal Singapore continues to operate as a major beauty retailer in Singapore, now with enhanced data protection and security testing protocols following regulatory oversight.
dataType: Name, email address, postal address, mobile number, date of birth

companyDescription: Google is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Mountain View, California, specializing in online search, web-based services (including Gmail), and digital advertising. In 2011, 96% of Google's $36.5 billion revenue came from online advertising.
companyLongDescription: Google is a Delaware corporation headquartered in Mountain View, California, specializing in online search, web-based services (including Gmail), and digital advertising. In 2011, 96% of Google's $36.5 billion revenue came from online advertising.
caseDescription: Google represented to Safari users that their browser's default privacy setting would block DoubleClick tracking cookies and targeted ads. However, Google secretly circumvented Safari's privacy controls by exploiting a form-submission loophole, placing tracking cookies on millions of Safari users without their knowledge or consent.
violationSummary: Google conducted unauthorized surveillance of Safari users' browsing activity through deceptive circumvention of browser privacy controls. The secret placement of tracking cookies enabled persistent identification and monitoring of user behavior across the web.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Google used invisible code to falsely signal form submissions to Safari browsers, causing them to accept DoubleClick tracking cookies despite default privacy settings designed to block.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of Safari users' web browsing activity was collected and tracked without their knowledge.

claimsVsReality.claim: Safari's default setting 'effectively accomplishes the same thing as setting the opt-out cookie' and protects users from DoubleClick tracking.
claimsVsReality.reality: Google's code exploited Safari's form-submission exception to place DoubleClick cookies on Safari browsers with default settings, circumventing the privacy protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: After opting out, 'Google will not collect interest category information and you will not receive interest-based ads.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Google collected interest-category information from Safari users who did not opt out because Google falsely represented that the Safari default setting provided equivalent protection.

claimsVsReality.claim: Google is a member of NAI and adheres to the NAI Code, which requires clear disclosure of data collection practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Google did not disclose its practice of placing DoubleClick cookies on Safari browsers in violation of Safari's privacy controls and users' stated preferences.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(l) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google represented that Safari's default setting would not place DoubleClick cookies or collect interest-category information, but actually placed these cookies on Safari users' browsers
violations: Google represented that Safari's default setting would not place DoubleClick cookies or collect interest-category information, but actually placed these cookies on Safari users' browsers
Google represented that users would not receive targeted advertisements if they did not change Safari's default setting, but served targeted ads based on secretly collected data
Google represented compliance with NAI Code Section III(2)(a) requiring disclosure of data collection practices, but failed to disclose the Safari tracking practices

regulatoryFindings.act: Google Consent Order Part I(A) requires Google not to misrepresent the extent to which consumers may exercise control over collection, use, or disclosure of covered information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Google assured Safari users that the browser's default setting would protect them from DoubleClick tracking, implying consumer control, while secretly circumventing that control
violations: Google assured Safari users that the browser's default setting would protect them from DoubleClick tracking, implying consumer control, while secretly circumventing that control

Google's statements that users could 'opt out' and would then not receive targeted ads applied equally to first-party and third-party cookies, but this protection was illusory for Safari users whose cookies were already placed

outcome: The United States filed a complaint for civil penalties and other relief under FTC Act Sections 5(l) and 16(a) seeking monetary penalties (up to $16,000 per violation based on 2012 penalties inflation adjustment) and permanent injunction from violating the Google Consent Order. The case established that circumventing browser privacy controls through deceptive technical means, combined with false statements about user control and privacy protection, constitutes a material violation of prior FTC settlement obligations. Google was required to cease the conduct and comply with the Consent Order's comprehensive privacy program requirements including biennial third-party assessments.
companyNow: Google (Alphabet Inc.) remains a dominant force in search and digital advertising. As of 2024, Alphabet is one of the world's largest technology companies by market capitalization.
dataType: Browsing activity, IP address, persistent identifiers, interest categories, account ID
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(l) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Google Consent Order (Docket No. C-4336) Part I(A) – Misrepresentation regarding privacy and control over covered information
Google Consent Order Part I(B) – Misrepresentation regarding NAI Code compliance

company: Franklin's Budget Car Sales, Inc., also dba Franklin Toyota/Scion
companyDescription: Franklin's Budget Car Sales, Inc., doing business as Franklin Toyota/Scion, was a Georgia-based franchise automobile dealership that sold new and used vehicles, provided leasing and repair services, and offered consumer financing.
companyLongDescription: Franklin's Budget Car Sales, Inc., doing business as Franklin Toyota/Scion, was a Georgia-based franchise automobile dealership that sold new and used vehicles, provided leasing and repair services, and offered consumer financing.
caseDescription: Franklin Toyota failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect customer personal information, resulting in approximately 95,000 consumers' sensitive data being exposed on peer-to-peer networks. The company made deceptive claims about safeguarding customer information while lacking basic security controls. It also failed to provide required privacy notices and opt-out mechanisms under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures required under the Safeguards Rule, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal information through a P2P network. This represents systemic insecurity in handling customer data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Franklin Toyota collected sensitive personal information from approximately 95,000 customers including names, Social Security numbers, addresses, dates of birth.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 95,000 customers' complete personal identification data became permanently available for download by anyone globally on peer-to-peer networks.

claimsVsReality.claim: We restrict access to non public personal information about you to only those employees who need to know that information to provide products and services to you.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no implemented access controls; a P2P application on a networked computer exposed files to anyone globally.

claimsVsReality.claim: We maintain physical, electronic, and procedural safe guards that comply with federal regulations to guard non public personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked risk assessments, incident response plans, security monitoring, employee training, and any formal information security program.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Franklin Toyota represented that it implements reasonable and appropriate measures to protect consumers' personal information from unauthorized access, but failed to implement any such measures, resulting in data exposure via P2P networks.
violations: Franklin Toyota represented that it implements reasonable and appropriate measures to protect consumers' personal information from unauthorized access, but failed to implement any such measures, resulting in data exposure via P2P networks.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to develop a comprehensive written information security program containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including risk assessment, security design/implementation, testing/monitoring, service provider oversight, and incident response.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to assess risks to consumer personal information collected and stored online
violations: Failed to assess risks to consumer personal information collected and stored online
Failed to adopt policies such as an incident response plan to prevent unauthorized disclosure
Failed to use reasonable methods to prevent, detect, and investigate unauthorized access
Failed to adequately train employees about information security
Failed to employ reasonable measures to respond to unauthorized access or conduct security investigations
Failed to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive written information security program
Failed to designate an employee to coordinate the company's information security program

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) requires financial institutions to provide customers annual privacy notices reflecting their policies and practices, and to provide reasonable means and notices for customers to opt out of information sharing with nonaffiliated third parties.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to send consumers annual privacy notices as required
violations: Failed to send consumers annual privacy notices as required
Failed to provide a clear and conspicuous opt-out notice explaining customers' rights to opt out of sharing nonpublic information with unaffiliated third parties
Did not provide a mechanism by which consumers could opt out of information sharing with nonaffiliated third parties

outcome: FTC issued a complaint on October 3, 2012 alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, the Safeguards Rule, and the Privacy Rule. The complaint alleges unfair and deceptive practices due to false representations about data security, inadequate safeguards resulting in P2P network exposure of 95,000 consumers' records, failure to provide required privacy notices and opt-out mechanisms. The case was initiated requiring Franklin Toyota to implement comprehensive security measures and comply with privacy notification requirements.
companyNow: Unknown. Franklin's Budget Car Sales, Inc. was a franchise automobile dealership operating in Statesboro, Georgia. Current status of operations is not documented in this complaint.
dataType: Names, Social Security numbers, addresses, telephone numbers, dates of birth, drivers' license numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Section 501(b) – Safeguards Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 314
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Section 503 – Privacy Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 313

company: Blue Cross of California (Anthem Blue Cross)
companyDescription: Blue Cross of California, doing business as Anthem Blue Cross, is a California-based health insurance company offering HMO, PPO, and point-of-service health plans to individuals, employer groups, public entities, and seniors through Medicare supplemental and Medicare Advantage products.
companyLongDescription: Blue Cross of California, doing business as Anthem Blue Cross, is a California-based health insurance company offering HMO, PPO, and point-of-service health plans to individuals, employer groups, public entities, and seniors through Medicare supplemental and Medicare Advantage products.
caseDescription: Anthem Blue Cross publicly exposed and printed Social Security numbers of 31,125 Medicare Supplement members on marketing mailers and 2,631 Medicare Part D members on collection letters, with no legal requirement to do so. The Social Security numbers were visible through envelope windows and printed as member identification numbers without adequate safeguards. This violated California privacy law by unnecessarily disclosing sensitive personally identifiable information.
violationSummary: Anthem's exposure of unencrypted Social Security numbers in mailed documents visible through envelope windows and as member IDs on collection letters constitutes information dissemination through exposure—making sensitive personal identifiers accessible to unintended recipients.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Anthem displayed 31,125 Medicare members' Social Security numbers visibly through envelope windows on marketing mailers.
whyTheyWereWrong: 33,756 members faced identity theft and fraud risks when their full Social Security numbers were exposed in mail without legal requirement, allowing theft from postal systems and mail recipients.

claimsVsReality.claim: Anthem represented that it could safely handle sensitive member information and maintain appropriate privacy protections for Social Security numbers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Anthem printed and mailed unencrypted Social Security numbers to tens of thousands of members without legal necessity, exposing them through envelope windows and as identification numbers on collection letters.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(1) prohibits publicly displaying Social Security numbers in a manner that is visible to the public.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem displayed the Social Security numbers of 31,125 members in an area visible through the window of envelopes sent via United States mail service.
violations: Anthem displayed the Social Security numbers of 31,125 members in an area visible through the window of envelopes sent via United States mail service.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(5) prohibits printing Social Security numbers on documents when neither state nor federal law requires such numbers to be on the documents.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem printed the Social Security numbers of 31,125 members on marketing mailer documents mailed to Marketing Mailing Recipients without legal requirement.
violations: Anthem printed the Social Security numbers of 31,125 members on marketing mailer documents mailed to Marketing Mailing Recipients without legal requirement.
Anthem printed the Social Security numbers of 2,631 members on collection letters mailed to Collection Letter Recipients without legal requirement.

regulatoryFindings.act: California Business and Professions Code § 17200 prohibits unfair competition, including any unlawful, unfair, or fraudulent business act or practice.
regulatoryFindings.description: Anthem engaged in unfair competition by violating California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(1) and § 1798.85(a)(5) through the public display and unnecessary printing of Social Security numbers.
violations: Anthem engaged in unfair competition by violating California Civil Code § 1798.85(a)(1) and § 1798.85(a)(5) through the public display and unnecessary printing of Social Security numbers.

outcome: The complaint sought injunctive relief, civil penalties of $2,500 per violation under Business and Professions Code § 17206, and recovery of investigation costs. The case sought to permanently enjoin Anthem and related parties from committing further acts of unfair competition involving Social Security number exposure. No settlement amount was disclosed in the complaint document.
companyNow: Anthem Blue Cross remains in operation as part of Anthem, Inc., a major health insurance provider. The company has since implemented enhanced data protection protocols and privacy safeguards for member information.
dataType: Social Security numbers

companyDescription: MySpace was a social networking website founded in 2003 that allowed users to create customizable profiles and connect with friends. At its peak around 2008, it was one of the world's most visited websites before being overtaken by Facebook. By 2012, the company faced significant user decline and competitive pressure.
companyLongDescription: MySpace was a social networking website founded in 2003 that allowed users to create customizable profiles and connect with friends. At its peak around 2008, it was one of the world's most visited websites before being overtaken by Facebook. By 2012, the company faced significant user decline and competitive pressure.
caseDescription: MySpace shared users' Friend IDs (persistent identifiers linked to full names and profile data) with third-party advertisers without explicit user consent, contradicting its privacy policy. The Friend ID enabled advertisers to access users' basic profile information including full names and to link browsing habits to personal details. MySpace also misrepresented compliance with the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework principles.
violationSummary: MySpace disclosed personally identifiable information (Friend IDs functioning as persistent identifiers) to third parties (advertisers) without user notice or consent, directly contradicting its privacy policy and Safe Harbor certifications. This constitutes unauthorized disclosure and breach of confidentiality.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: From January 2009 through June 2010, MySpace transmitted users' Friend IDs, ages, and genders to third-party advertisers in unencrypted plain text.
whyTheyWereWrong: MySpace's undisclosed sharing of Friend IDs enabled third-party advertisers to identify individual users by name, combine their identities with tracking cookies.

claimsVsReality.claim: MySpace will not share users' personally identifiable information (PII) with third parties unless users have given permission.
claimsVsReality.reality: MySpace shared Friend IDs (which provide access to full names and basic profile information) with numerous third-party advertisers without user notice or consent from January 2009 onward.

claimsVsReality.claim: The information used for ad customization does not provide users' PII or identify users as individuals to third parties.
claimsVsReality.reality: MySpace transmitted Friend IDs to advertisers, which directly enabled identification of users by their full names and linkage to personal profiles for approximately 84% of users.

claimsVsReality.claim: Users' web browsing activity shared with advertisers is anonymized.
claimsVsReality.reality: MySpace provided Friend IDs to advertisers alongside tracking cookies, enabling complete de-anonymization and linkage of browsing history to named individuals' personal profiles.

claimsVsReality.claim: MySpace adheres to the Safe Harbor Privacy Principles of notice and choice.
claimsVsReality.reality: MySpace collected and shared European users' personal data with advertisers without providing notice of this practice or meaningful choice mechanisms, directly violating Safe Harbor requirements.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: MySpace represented it would not share PII with third parties without user permission, but shared Friend IDs (which give access to full names and basic profile information) with advertisers without consent.
violations: MySpace represented it would not share PII with third parties without user permission, but shared Friend IDs (which give access to full names and basic profile information) with advertisers without consent.

MySpace claimed its ad customization process does not allow advertisers to access PII or individually identify users, but transmitted Friend IDs to advertisers enabling identification of 84% of users by full name.

MySpace represented that users' web browsing activity shared with advertisers is anonymized, but linked Friend IDs to tracking cookies, allowing advertisers to correlate browsing history with personal profile information.

regulatoryFindings.act: The U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework requires organizations to provide clear notice of personal data collection and use purposes and to obtain individuals' choice regarding disclosure to third parties before collection or use begins.
regulatoryFindings.description: MySpace certified compliance with Safe Harbor Notice and Choice principles while actively transmitting European users' Friend IDs to third-party advertisers without notice or consent.
violations: MySpace certified compliance with Safe Harbor Notice and Choice principles while actively transmitting European users' Friend IDs to third-party advertisers without notice or consent.
MySpace provided no mechanism for users to opt out of sharing identifiers with advertisers, despite Safe Harbor requiring clear and conspicuous, readily available, and affordable choice mechanisms.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on August 30, 2012, alleging four counts of deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. A consent order was entered requiring MySpace to implement reasonable data security measures, obtain affirmative express consent before using Friend IDs for advertising targeting, restrict future data sharing to purposes disclosed in privacy policy, provide users with transparent privacy controls, conduct biennial privacy audits by an independent third party, and maintain compliance monitoring for 20 years. MySpace was prohibited from misrepresenting its Safe Harbor status.
companyNow: MySpace ceased major operations around 2015 following loss of users to Facebook and other platforms. The brand is now operated under new ownership as a music and entertainment platform with minimal social networking features. The company's user base and revenue are a fraction of historical levels.
dataType: Personal identifiers (name, email, date of birth, gender), profile information (relationship status, sexual orientation, hobbies, interests), Friend ID, location, photos, videos, messages, browsing activity
legalBasisViolated: U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework – Notice Principle
U.S.-EU Safe Harbor Framework – Choice Principle

violationSummary: HireRight failed to implement adequate procedures to ensure accuracy of personal data in consumer reports, resulting in systematic data quality failures that exposed individuals to misidentification and employment discrimination.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies

whyTheyWereWrong: Job applicants were wrongfully denied employment or other employment benefits based on false criminal history information attributed to them in background reports.

claimsVsReality.reality: Reports included expunged records, duplicate entries, and records from other individuals; company failed to implement procedures to ensure accuracy or currency

violations: Closed dispute reinvestigations without providing written notice of results to affected consumers

Failed to maintain strict procedures to ensure public record information was complete and up to date

violations: Engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by furnishing inaccurate consumer reports that harmed employment prospects of individuals who were denied employment or employment-related benefits

companyDescription: EPN, Inc. (also operating as Checknet, Inc.) is a Utah-based debt collection agency that collects debts on behalf of clients in commercial credit, retail, and healthcare sectors. companyLongDescription: EPN, Inc. (also operating as Checknet, Inc.) is a Utah-based debt collection agency that collects debts on behalf of clients in commercial credit, retail, and healthcare sectors. The company processes and stores sensitive consumer personal information as part of its core business operations.
caseDescription: EPN, a debt collection agency, failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive consumer personal information stored on its computer networks. A peer-to-peer file-sharing application installed by an executive exposed approximately 3,800 consumers' highly sensitive data—including Social Security numbers, health insurance information, and diagnosis codes—to public P2P networks. The files remained accessible indefinitely once shared.
violationSummary: The company's pervasive failure to implement reasonable and appropriate information security measures—including lack of incident response plan, employee training, network monitoring, and P2P application detection—directly resulted in unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal information to the internet.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: EPN failed to implement reasonable security measures including no incident response plan, inadequate employee training, no network scanning for unauthorized applications.
whyTheyWereWrong: Personal information for approximately 3,800 consumers including Social Security numbers, health insurance numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: EPN handled clients' sensitive consumer data as part of routine debt collection.
claimsVsReality.reality: EPN had no meaningful security infrastructure to protect this data; a P2P application installed without authorization exposed files to public networks indefinitely.

claimsVsReality.claim: EPN's systems were secure and appropriately managed.
claimsVsReality.reality: EPN lacked an incident response plan, did not assess security risks, provided inadequate employee training, did not scan for unauthorized applications, and had no monitoring of outgoing data transmissions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: EPN failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information, causing substantial injury to approximately 3,800 consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
violations: EPN failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access to personal information, causing substantial injury to approximately 3,800 consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

outcome: FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document is the formal complaint issued October 3, 2012. company: W3 Innovations, LLC (doing business as Broken Thumbs Apps)
companyDescription: W3 Innovations, LLC, doing business as Broken Thumbs Apps, was a software development company based in Cupertino, California that developed and distributed approximately 40 mobile applications for iPhone and iPod touch through Apple's App Store, with several apps specifically targeted at children under 13.
companyLongDescription: W3 Innovations, LLC, doing business as Broken Thumbs Apps, was a software development company based in Cupertino, California that developed and distributed approximately 40 mobile applications for iPhone and iPod touch through Apple's App Store, with several apps specifically targeted at children under 13.
caseDescription: W3 Innovations developed and distributed mobile apps directed to children under 13 that collected over 30,000 email addresses and personal information without parental consent or adequate privacy notices. The company operated online services (Emily's Girl World and Emily Dress-up apps) with built-in features that encouraged children to submit personal information through blogs and direct email to a fictional character 'Emily', but failed to obtain verifiable parental consent or post required privacy policies.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected personal information from children through multiple mechanisms (blogs, email submissions, comment forms) without notice or consent, constituting surveillance of a vulnerable population.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: W3 Innovations operated mobile apps including Emily's Girl World and Emily's Dress Up targeted at children, collecting over 30,000 email addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Over 30,000 children under age 13 had their email addresses and personal information collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Emily's Girl World app marketing stated: 'a fun story-telling app with charming graphics ... which we thought that younger girls and nostalgic adults in particular might enjoy' and 'Best of all, as if all of that wasn't enough, you can also send an email directly to Emily to say hi! As other fans will tell you, Emily listens and reads all of your emails.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The app actively collected personal information from children including email addresses, names, personal stories, photographs, and embarrassing personal details through multiple submission mechanisms, yet the company maintained no privacy policy, provided no parental notice, and obtained no parental consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: The apps were interactive and encouraged user engagement and sharing.
claimsVsReality.reality: The interactive features (blogs, comment forms, direct email) functioned as personal information collection mechanisms that harvested over 30,000 email addresses from children without safeguards, parental awareness, or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b) requires operators of online services directed to children to post a clear privacy policy on their website or online service.
regulatoryFindings.description: W3 Innovations failed to maintain or link to any online notice of their information collection, use, and disclosure practices for the Emily's Girl World app and Emily Dress-up apps.
violations: W3 Innovations failed to maintain or link to any online notice of their information collection, use, and disclosure practices for the Emily's Girl World app and Emily Dress-up apps.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(c) requires operators to provide clear, understandable, and complete notice directly to parents of information practices and required disclosures.
regulatoryFindings.description: W3 Innovations did not provide any direct notice to parents regarding collection, use, or disclosure of children's personal information.
violations: W3 Innovations did not provide any direct notice to parents regarding collection, use, or disclosure of children's personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.5(a)(1) requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent prior to collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: W3 Innovations collected over 30,000 email addresses and personal information from children without obtaining any verifiable parental consent before collection.
violations: W3 Innovations collected over 30,000 email addresses and personal information from children without obtaining any verifiable parental consent before collection.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: A violation of the COPPA Rule constitutes an unfair or deceptive act or practice under Section 5(a)(1) of the FTC Act. W3 Innovations' collection of children's personal information without consent and without required privacy notices was inherently deceptive and unfair.
violations: A violation of the COPPA Rule constitutes an unfair or deceptive act or practice under Section 5(a)(1) of the FTC Act. W3 Innovations' collection of children's personal information without consent and without required privacy notices was inherently deceptive and unfair.

outcome: The United States sought permanent injunction, monetary civil penalties of up to $16,000 per violation (with violations calculated per collection/use/disclosure instance), and other equitable relief. The complaint alleges over 30,000 separate violations based on individual collections of email addresses and personal information. A permanent injunction would prevent future COPPA violations. The company was required to implement comprehensive compliance measures including privacy policy posting, parental notice, and verifiable consent mechanisms.
companyNow: Unknown. The complaint was filed in 2012 by the U.S. Department of Justice on behalf of the FTC. The current operational status of W3 Innovations, LLC and its app distribution status is not specified in the document.

FTC Act Section 5(a)(1), 15 U.S.C. § 45(a)(1) – unfair and deceptive practices

companyDescription: Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) is the federal agency responsible for managing penitentiaries and supervising offenders in Canada. It operates correctional institutions across the country.
companyLongDescription: Correctional Service of Canada is a federal law enforcement agency under the Department of Public Safety that operates and maintains penitentiaries for inmates serving sentences of two years or more. The agency is responsible for the custody, care, supervision, and rehabilitation of federal offenders in Canada. CSC operates institutions ranging from minimum to maximum security facilities across multiple provinces and territories.
caseDescription: A contract worker at Grande Cache Institution printed a report containing the names, dates of birth, and personal information of all serving inmates. The report was given to a welding instructor who kept it in his office and referred to it frequently. The report later turned up among a discharged inmate's belongings, resulting in an unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal information.
violationSummary: The inmate report containing sensitive personal data was exposed to unauthorized individuals and ultimately found among a prisoner's belongings. This represents an unintended disclosure and loss of control over sensitive information.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: A contract worker printed a report listing names, dates of birth, and personal information of all inmates at Grande Cache Institution.
whyTheyWereWrong: Two inmates had their sensitive personal information, including names and dates of birth, exposed to unauthorized individuals due to inadequate safeguards, creating privacy risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: The report was securely managed and restricted to authorized personnel only.
claimsVsReality.reality: A contract worker printed the full inmate list, gave it to a welding instructor who kept it in an office, and it ended up in an inmate's possession.

claimsVsReality.claim: Staff understood the importance of safeguarding personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Both the contractor and welding instructor had received training but failed to follow proper procedures, demonstrating inadequate implementation of privacy protocols.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to protect personal information against unauthorized access, use, disclosure, modification, or destruction
regulatoryFindings.description: Contract worker printed sensitive inmate report without proper controls
violations: Contract worker printed sensitive inmate report without proper controls
Report was stored in an unsecured location (welding shop office) with frequent public access
Report was not properly accounted for or secured, leading to loss and unauthorized possession by inmate
Both contractor and instructor had received privacy training but procedures were inadequate to prevent breach

outcome: The Correctional Service of Canada formally acknowledged the privacy breach and upheld the complaints as well-founded. Corrective measures were implemented: the sensitive report can no longer be printed and must only be viewed on computer screens; enhanced procedures were established to ensure staff and external contractors understand the need to safeguard personal information and protect it from unauthorized disclosure. No additional action was called for due to the corrective measures already underway.
companyNow: Correctional Service of Canada continues to operate as Canada's federal correctional agency, managing penitentiaries and community supervision of federal offenders.
dataType: Names, dates of birth, inmate personal information

companyDescription: Correctional Service of Canada (CSC) is the federal agency responsible for managing penitentiaries and overseeing incarcerated individuals in Canada.
companyLongDescription: The Correctional Service of Canada operates federal prisons and detention facilities across the country, including maximum-security institutions like Kent Institution near Agassiz, British Columbia. CSC is responsible for managing inmate records, parole decisions, and sensitive personal information about offenses and criminal history. The organization must comply with the Privacy Act in handling confidential documents and inmate communications.
caseDescription: A 10-page National Parole Board decision containing sensitive information about an inmate's offence was not placed in a sealed envelope at Kent Institution maximum-security prison. The document was intercepted, photocopied, and circulated among fellow inmates without the complainant's consent. An investigation confirmed the disclosure violated the Privacy Act.
violationSummary: The confidential parole board decision was mishandled during mail processing (not sealed), allowing unauthorized access and circulation among other inmates, constituting a clear breach of confidentiality and failure to maintain safeguards over sensitive personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A 10-page National Parole Board decision containing graphic details of an inmate's offense was not placed in a sealed envelope at Kent Institution, allowing it to be intercepted.
whyTheyWereWrong: An inmate's sensitive personal information about his offense was exposed to dozens of other prisoners, causing embarrassment, potential safety risks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Confidential parole board decisions would be securely delivered to inmates through internal mail systems.
claimsVsReality.reality: A 10-page parole decision was not placed in an envelope, was intercepted, photocopied, and circulated among multiple inmates without authorization or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sensitive inmate documents were handled with appropriate security measures.
claimsVsReality.reality: The document was simply folded, stapled, and had the inmate's name written on the outside, making it vulnerable to interception and copying by other prisoners.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – Protection of personal information held by federal institutions
regulatoryFindings.description: Failure to maintain adequate safeguards (sealed envelopes) for confidential documents during mail delivery
violations: Failure to maintain adequate safeguards (sealed envelopes) for confidential documents during mail delivery
Unauthorized access and circulation of sensitive parole board decision to multiple inmates
Inadequate security measures in document handling procedures

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well founded. Following the incident, the warden of Kent Institution implemented corrective measures: confidential documents are now placed in sealed envelopes before delivery through internal mail. The prison also acknowledged the privacy breach and informed the inmate of his right to complain to the Office of the Privacy Commissioner.
companyNow: CSC continues to operate Canada's federal prison system and remains subject to Privacy Act requirements and oversight by the Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada.

companyDescription: The Canadian Wheat Board was a federal Crown corporation that marketed wheat and barley on behalf of Western Canadian grain producers.
companyLongDescription: The Canadian Wheat Board was a federal marketing agency responsible for the export and domestic sales of wheat and barley produced by farmers in Western Canada. It operated under a single-desk marketing system and maintained records including farmers' personal information such as Social Insurance Numbers. The organization implemented data protection protocols and shared information with government agencies including the Canada Revenue Agency in compliance with legal requirements.
caseDescription: The Minister of Agriculture filed a privacy complaint against the Canadian Wheat Board based on media reports suggesting the agency had improperly disclosed farmers' Social Insurance Numbers to third parties including grain handlers and the Canada Revenue Agency. An investigation found the wheat board had appropriate protocols in place, did not disclose SINs to unauthorized third parties, and only shared data with tax authorities when legally required.
violationSummary: The complaint alleged improper disclosure of sensitive personal information (SINs) to third parties, which falls under the Information Dissemination – Disclosure category, though the investigation found no actual violation occurred.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The Canadian Wheat Board maintained protocols for handling farmers' Social Insurance Numbers and shared personal data with tax authorities only when legally required.
whyTheyWereWrong: No actual wrongdoing occurred; the investigation found the wheat board had appropriate safeguards in place.

claimsVsReality.claim: Media reports suggested the Canadian Wheat Board had improperly disclosed farmers' Social Insurance Numbers to unauthorized third parties including grain handlers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation found the wheat board does not disclose SINs to third parties and only shares personal data with tax authorities when legally required; appropriate protocols and safeguards were in place.

claimsVsReality.claim: An internal audit highlighted potential privacy weaknesses in the handling of the Permit Book process and farmer personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The wheat board had appropriate protocols, procedures and agreements in place to ensure personal information was collected, used, safeguarded and shared with care.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to collect, use, and disclose personal information responsibly and only as permitted by law or with consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Allegation of improper disclosure of SINs to third parties — investigation found no actual violation; wheat board had appropriate protocols and only disclosed data to CRA when legally required
violations: Allegation of improper disclosure of SINs to third parties — investigation found no actual violation; wheat board had appropriate protocols and only disclosed data to CRA when legally required

outcome: The privacy complaint was dismissed as not well founded. The investigation confirmed that the Canadian Wheat Board had appropriate protocols, procedures and agreements in place to ensure personal information was collected, used, safeguarded and shared properly. The wheat board was commended for its good information-management practices.
companyNow: The Canadian Wheat Board's single-desk marketing powers were eliminated in 2012, ending its monopoly on wheat and barley sales.
dataType: Social Insurance Numbers (SINs), farmer personal information, grain sales records

company: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada
companyDescription: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada (HRSDC) is a federal government department responsible for managing employment insurance programs and related social services.
companyLongDescription: HRSDC is a Canadian federal department that administers employment insurance benefits and conducts mandatory information sessions for EI claimants to validate their identities. As the custodian of Social Insurance Numbers, the Department is responsible for protecting this critically important personal identifier. The Department holds information sessions primarily for claimants who apply for benefits online without face-to-face contact.
caseDescription: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada lost an attendance sheet containing the names, telephone numbers, and Social Insurance Numbers of 32 employment insurance claimants at an information session. The Department failed to properly safeguard this sensitive personal information, particularly the SINs which are critical identifiers vulnerable to identity theft. The Department subsequently notified affected individuals, implemented corrective measures including redacting SINs from future attendance sheets, and took steps to mitigate consequences.
violationSummary: The Department failed to implement adequate physical and organizational safeguards to protect highly sensitive personal information (SINs, names, contact details) in its custody, resulting in the loss of a document containing this data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada lost an attendance sheet containing names, telephone numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: The 32 claimants' Social Insurance Numbers were exposed to potential identity theft and misuse because the Department failed to safeguard this critically important personal identifier that is.

claimsVsReality.claim: HRSDC properly safeguarded personal information at information sessions.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Department failed to properly safeguard an attendance sheet containing 32 claimants' names, phone numbers, and Social Insurance Numbers, which was lost at an information session.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Department took reasonable steps to protect sensitive data.
claimsVsReality.reality: SINs were printed on attendance sheets and left unsecured, creating vulnerability to identity theft by the very department responsible for issuing and managing SIN use.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.7 requires organizations to protect personal information with safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information.
regulatoryFindings.description: HRSDC failed to implement adequate physical safeguards to prevent loss of attendance sheets containing highly sensitive SINs
violations: HRSDC failed to implement adequate physical safeguards to prevent loss of attendance sheets containing highly sensitive SINs
Sensitive personal information was printed and left unprotected at information sessions

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well-founded. HRSDC implemented corrective measures including: notifying all 32 affected individuals; directing officials to fully black out SINs on attendance sheets before use at future EI claimant information sessions; implementing this practice nationally; and taking steps to mitigate consequences of the breach. Officials in the affected region were credited with taking reasonable steps to prevent recurrence.
companyNow: HRSDC continues to operate as a federal government department, later reorganized as Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC) in 2013.
dataType: Social Insurance Numbers (SINs), names, telephone numbers

companyDescription: Keele Community Correctional Centre is a halfway house in Toronto operated by the Correctional Service of Canada, providing transitional housing for 40 men released from federal institutions.
companyLongDescription: Keele Community Correctional Centre is a correctional facility operated by the Correctional Service of Canada in Toronto that functions as a halfway house for approximately 40 men transitioning from federal institutions under statutory release provisions. caseDescription: A psychiatric nurse employed by Keele Community Correctional Centre left an envelope containing a former inmate's treatment notes on public transit. violationSummary: The unintended exposure of sensitive psychiatric treatment notes on public transit constitutes information dissemination through exposure, where personal information became accessible to the public without authorization.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation

whyTheyWereWrong: A former inmate's confidential psychiatric treatment notes were exposed to the public on a bus, allowing anyone to access his private medical history and sensitive personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Patient files could be safely transported between locations without special precautions.
claimsVsReality.reality: Unencrypted patient files transported via public transit were lost and exposed to the public.

claimsVsReality.claim: Standard staff protocols were sufficient to protect sensitive patient information during transport.
claimsVsReality.reality: A nurse failed to secure confidential psychiatric treatment notes, resulting in exposure of a vulnerable former inmate's private medical records.

violations: Nurse transported patient treatment files on public transit without encryption
Inadequate safeguards for sensitive psychiatric health information
Loss of confidential patient records due to lack of proper security procedures

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well founded. The facility acknowledged the privacy breach and implemented corrective measures including reminding the nurse of his duty to safeguard patient information, prohibiting transport of unencrypted patient files from the office, and conducting an internal investigation. companyNow: Keele Community Correctional Centre continues to operate as a transitional housing facility for the Correctional Service of Canada in Toronto.

companyDescription: Health Canada is the federal department responsible for protecting and promoting the health of Canadians, including occupational health and safety programs.
companyLongDescription: Health Canada is a department of the Canadian federal government tasked with protecting public health, managing drug approvals, overseeing food safety, and administering occupational health and safety programs. The department operates fitness-for-work evaluations and health assessments for federal employees. caseDescription: Health Canada improperly withheld personal information from an individual who sought access to records collected during a workplace fitness-for-work evaluation. violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Health Canada withheld personal information from a workplace fitness-for-work evaluation, claiming section 28 of the Privacy Act allowed it to protect health-related sensitive records.
whyTheyWereWrong: The withheld information was not exclusively health-related sensitive records, so the employee was wrongly denied access to his own personal information and evaluation records.

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well-founded. Health Canada undertook to release the requested personal information to the complainant. The file was resolved following the Department's commitment to provide access.

companyDescription: The Public Service Commission of Canada is a federal agency responsible for recruitment, staffing, and human resources management for the Canadian public service.
companyLongDescription: The Public Service Commission of Canada is a Crown corporation and independent agency of the Government of Canada that manages recruitment and staffing for the federal public service.
