It administers special programs including priority hiring initiatives for veterans and former military personnel.
caseDescription: An individual complained that the Public Service Commission of Canada improperly collected and disclosed his medical release information from the Canadian Forces without authorization. The information was used in a priority hiring program for former military personnel. Investigation found the agency had obtained written consent for collection and disclosure, and all procedures complied with the Privacy Act.
violationSummary: No violation found. The complaint was dismissed as not well founded because the complainant had provided written consent to the collection and disclosure of his medical release record.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The Public Service Commission of Canada collected and disclosed an individual's medical release information from the Canadian Forces for use in a priority hiring program for former military.
whyTheyWereWrong: No wrongdoing occurred; the individual had provided written consent for collection and disclosure, and all procedures fully complied with the Privacy Act.

claimsVsReality.claim: The individual complained that the Public Service Commission improperly collected and disclosed his medical information without authorization.
claimsVsReality.reality: The individual had provided written consent for collection and disclosure, and the agency fully complied with the Privacy Act in all procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act (Canada) – lawful collection and disclosure of personal information with individual consent

outcome: Complaint dismissed as not well founded. Investigation determined that the Public Service Commission of Canada had complied fully with the Privacy Act. The complainant had provided written consent for the collection and disclosure of his medical release record for use in the ex-military hiring priority program.
companyNow: The Public Service Commission of Canada remains an active federal agency overseeing public service recruitment and staffing, now operating under evolving federal employment frameworks.
dataType: Medical/Health data, Military service records

companyDescription: Canada Post is Canada's national postal service and primary mail delivery provider, delivering mail and parcels to residential and business addresses across the country.
companyLongDescription: Canada Post is a Crown corporation and the primary postal service operator in Canada, responsible for delivering mail, parcels, and express shipping services to all Canadian addresses. The organization employs letter carriers, supervisors, and administrative staff across hundreds of facilities nationwide. As a large public employer, Canada Post handles sensitive employee information including disability insurance claims and medical documentation.
caseDescription: A Canada Post supervisor unauthorized accessed and read a medical form submitted by an employee for a disability insurance claim, which had been provided in a sealed envelope with the understanding it would be forwarded unopened. The supervisor used the health information contained in the form to contradict other medical documentation supplied by the employee without authorization. The privacy authority upheld the complaint as well-founded, finding the secondary use of personal health information violated applicable privacy principles.
violationSummary: The supervisor used health information collected for the purpose of processing a disability insurance claim for a different, unauthorized purpose: to challenge the validity of other medical documentation. This is a clear secondary use of personal data without the individual's permission.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A Canada Post supervisor accessed and read a medical form submitted by an employee for a disability insurance claim.
whyTheyWereWrong: The supervisor used the employee's confidential health information from the form to contradict other medical documentation without authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: The supervisor would not have opened a sealed envelope containing the medical form.
claimsVsReality.reality: The supervisor admitted she may have read the form and definitively used the health information from it to contradict the employee's other medical documentation, regardless of whether the envelope was sealed.

claimsVsReality.claim: The disability insurance claim form was submitted with the understanding it would be forwarded unopened to the insurer.
claimsVsReality.reality: The supervisor accessed the medical information, read it, and weaponized it against the employee by using it to challenge their medical claims without authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2.1 requires organizations to identify the purposes for which personal information is collected before or at the time of collection
regulatoryFindings.description: Health information was collected for disability insurance claim processing but was subsequently used by the supervisor to contradict other medical documentation without authorization or notification of this secondary purpose
violations: Health information was collected for disability insurance claim processing but was subsequently used by the supervisor to contradict other medical documentation without authorization or notification of this secondary purpose

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 requires that personal information not be used or disclosed for purposes other than those for which it was collected, except with consent
regulatoryFindings.description: The supervisor used health information from the medical form for the unauthorized secondary purpose of challenging the validity of other medical documentation without the employee's permission
violations: The supervisor used health information from the medical form for the unauthorized secondary purpose of challenging the validity of other medical documentation without the employee's permission

outcome: The privacy authority upheld the complaint as well-founded. Canada Post was directed to implement corrective measures: remind all staff to submit insurance claim forms directly to the insurer rather than through supervisors, and instruct managers to refuse to accept such forms on behalf of employees. The authority found the breach to be isolated and acknowledged that Canada Post maintains clear practices for managing disability claims.
companyNow: Canada Post continues to operate as Canada's national postal service, though it has faced ongoing financial challenges in the digital age and restructuring discussions in recent years.
dataType: Health data, medical information, disability insurance claim details
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 (Limiting Use, Disclosure, and Retention)

companyDescription: Canada Post is Canada's national postal service, responsible for delivering mail and providing postal services across the country.
companyLongDescription: Canada Post Corporation is a Crown corporation that operates Canada's postal system, providing mail delivery, parcels, and related services to millions of Canadian households and businesses. Founded as the successor to the Post Office Department, it maintains a widespread network of postal outlets and delivery infrastructure. The organization is subject to Canadian privacy law (PIPEDA) and has statutory obligations to maintain secure postal operations while protecting customer information.
caseDescription: An individual complained that Canada Post required him to provide his driver's licence number to terminate his postal box rental. Canada Post justified the requirement as necessary to prevent fraudulent use and investigate illegal activities. The privacy commissioner found the collection reasonable and dismissed the complaint.
violationSummary: The complainant objected to collection of identification data (driver's licence number) for postal box termination, which constitutes surveillance-based information collection, though the regulator ultimately found it justified.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Canada Post required an individual to provide his driver's licence number to terminate his postal box rental, collecting personal identification from all box renters.
whyTheyWereWrong: The requirement exposed individuals' driver's licence numbers to collection and retention without demonstrating that this specific identifier was necessary.

claimsVsReality.claim: Collection of driver's licence numbers is necessary to prevent fraudulent use and closure of postal boxes and to investigate illegal activities.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Privacy Commissioner found the collection reasonable based on Canada Post's statutory mandate for secure postal service, but the necessity of collecting the full driver's licence number (rather than other forms of ID) was not independently validated.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires that personal information collection be reasonable and for purposes consistent with the organization's statutory mandate

outcome: Complaint dismissed as not well founded. Canada Post's collection of driver's licence and other identification numbers was found to be reasonable given the organization's statutory obligation to provide a secure postal service and its legitimate need to prevent fraudulent use and investigate illegal activities.
companyNow: Canada Post continues to operate as Canada's national postal service, though it has faced modernization challenges as mail volumes decline in the digital era.
dataType: Driver's licence number, personal identification
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.4 (Use, Disclosure and Retention of Personal Information)

companyDescription: Canada Post is Canada's national postal service and Crown corporation responsible for mail delivery and related services across the country.
companyLongDescription: Canada Post is a Crown corporation and wholly-owned subsidiary of the Government of Canada that operates the national postal service. It provides mail delivery, parcel services, and related telecommunications services to all Canadian addresses. The organization employs thousands of workers and processes millions of pieces of mail and parcels annually. As a large public sector employer, Canada Post administers various employee benefits including special paid leave programs.
caseDescription: Canada Post collected excessive personal information from employees applying for special paid leave to care for ill relatives, including health details about the patient and information about third-party caregivers and other employees. The regulator found the collection exceeded what was necessary to determine leave eligibility and upheld the complaint, though Canada Post only partially implemented recommended privacy safeguards.
violationSummary: Canada Post engaged in unnecessary collection and retention of detailed personal and health information beyond what was required for the stated purpose of administering leave requests. The surveillance extended to third parties and other employees, creating an overly broad data collection practice.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Canada Post required employees applying for special paid leave to care for ill relatives to submit excessive personal information, including health details about patients.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees were forced to disclose sensitive health and family information about others without their consent, exposing personal data of patients.

claimsVsReality.claim: Collecting extensive personal information about patients and third parties is necessary to fairly administer the special leave program and prevent fraud.
claimsVsReality.reality: The regulator found that the information collected exceeded what was necessary to determine leave eligibility, and Canada Post could not demonstrate extensive abuse to justify collecting data on other family members working for the organization.

claimsVsReality.claim: The detailed application form is only a guide for supervisors to use at their discretion.
claimsVsReality.reality: In practice, supervisors erroneously distributed the complete form directly to employees to fill out, resulting in systematic over-collection of personal data from thousands of applicants.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 requires organizations to identify purposes before collecting personal information and Principle 4.4 requires that personal information be only as accurate, complete and current as necessary
regulatoryFindings.description: Canada Post collected personal health information about patients without establishing it was necessary for leave administration
violations: Canada Post collected personal health information about patients without establishing it was necessary for leave administration
Collected names and information about third-party caregivers beyond what was required to assess leave entitlement
Continued collecting information about other family members employed at Canada Post despite lack of evidence of widespread abuse

outcome: The complaint was upheld as well-founded. Canada Post agreed to collect only absolutely necessary personal information, remove requirements for third-party names, and update procedural guidelines to restrict data collection to required information only. However, Canada Post maintained collection of information about other family members employed there to prevent benefit abuse. The regulator expressed ongoing reservations about this practice and encouraged Canada Post to find less privacy-intrusive methods to address fraud concerns.
companyNow: Canada Post continues to operate as Canada's national postal service, though it has faced ongoing challenges with declining mail volumes and financial sustainability in the digital age.
dataType: Personal health information, family relationship data, employee identification, care provider information
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.4 (Accuracy, Completeness and Currency of Personal Information)
PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.3 (Consent for Collection, Use and Disclosure)

companyDescription: An online market research panel that surveys Canadian members on various topics and collects demographic and profiling information to target appropriate participant groups for client research projects.
companyLongDescription: The company operates as a voluntary membership panel offering free participation in surveys on diverse topics. Members complete initial profiling questionnaires and receive monthly supplemental profiling surveys designed to build detailed demographic profiles for research targeting purposes. The firm provides clients with aggregated, anonymized survey responses while maintaining individual member profiles containing personally identifiable information linked to survey responses. The panel's business model depends on accurate and detailed profiling data to identify and target appropriate demographic groups.
caseDescription: An online market research firm collected and requested confirmation of survey respondents' full dates of birth unnecessarily, including in a profiling survey that also collected sensitive financial information. The firm failed to adequately inform respondents that survey responses would be linked to their personal profiles containing identifying information, and refused to limit date of birth collection to only month and year as recommended.
violationSummary: The organization collected date of birth for primary purposes (demographic targeting) but used it secondarily for other purposes (fraud detection, data quality checking, birthday greetings) without adequately disclosing these secondary uses or obtaining meaningful consent from respondents.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The online market research firm collected and repeatedly requested survey respondents' full dates of birth unnecessarily.
whyTheyWereWrong: By collecting full birth dates alongside detailed financial information (banking habits, account types, household assets), the firm created an identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Full date of birth is necessary for demographic purposes and reliable market research, and collecting only month and year would be insufficiently accurate.
claimsVsReality.reality: The regulator found that full date of birth collection was unnecessary and that truncating to month and year would satisfy the organization's legitimate research needs while reducing identity theft risk.

claimsVsReality.claim: Members are sufficiently informed that survey responses will be linked to their personal profiles because they are told a profile is built to determine survey invitations.
claimsVsReality.reality: The complainant was not fully aware that her responses to the profiling survey would be linked to identifying information in her profile, indicating consent was not meaningful and purposes were not clearly disclosed.

claimsVsReality.claim: Confirming date of birth in surveys is necessary to detect fraudulent responses and verify information accuracy.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company acknowledged that fraud detection was not the actual reason for requesting date of birth in the specific survey at issue, and the regulator found such collection unnecessary even for legitimate verification purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 requires organizations to identify the purposes for collecting personal information at or before the time of collection
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization did not explicitly inform the complainant that her survey responses would be linked to her profile containing her name and date of birth
violations: The organization did not explicitly inform the complainant that her survey responses would be linked to her profile containing her name and date of birth
The email invitation language was insufficiently clear about the linkage of survey responses to personal identifying information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 requires meaningful knowledge and consent, with purposes stated so individuals can reasonably understand how their information will be used
regulatoryFindings.description: The complainant misunderstood the purpose of the profiling survey, believing her data was being collected for a client company rather than the Respondent itself
violations: The complainant misunderstood the purpose of the profiling survey, believing her data was being collected for a client company rather than the Respondent itself
The wording of the survey invitation could lead participants to misunderstand that responses would be added to and linked with their profiles

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.4 requires that collection of personal information be limited to that which is necessary for identified purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: The organization collected and confirmed all three elements of date of birth (day, month, year) when month and year would be sufficient for demographic targeting purposes
violations: The organization collected and confirmed all three elements of date of birth (day, month, year) when month and year would be sufficient for demographic targeting purposes
The organization continued collecting full birth dates despite being unable to demonstrate necessity for the additional day element

outcome: The Office found the complaint well-founded but partially unresolved. The respondent agreed to: (1) delete the complainant's personal information from its records; (2) revise consent language in profiling surveys to explicitly inform members that responses will be linked to their profiles. However, the respondent refused to implement the Office's recommendations to delete the day element from existing birth dates and cease collecting the full date of birth in future registrations and profiling surveys, arguing such granular data was necessary for data quality and fraud detection. The Office concluded these refusals were not justified under PIPEDA's collection-limitation principle and indicated it would explore further options for enforcement.
dataType: Date of birth, financial information, demographic data, banking habits, personal characteristics and opinions

companyDescription: Wentworthville Leagues Club is a social and entertainment venue in New South Wales, Australia, operating as a registered club providing dining, gaming, and recreational facilities to members and the public.
companyLongDescription: Wentworthville Leagues Club is a hospitality venue located in Wentworthville, New South Wales, Australia. The club operates as a registered members' club providing dining, entertainment, gaming, and social facilities. As a hospitality establishment, the club collects and maintains personal information about members and patrons, including contact details and other identifying information used for membership and service delivery purposes.
caseDescription: Wentworthville Leagues Club breached the National Privacy Principles by disclosing personal information of an individual without consent or authorization. The unauthorized disclosure caused non-economic loss to the affected individual. The club was ordered to provide an apology, implement staff training, and pay compensation of $7,500.
violationSummary: The club disclosed personal information without proper authorization or consent, violating the confidentiality obligations required under NPP 2.1(g), which protects against unauthorized disclosure of personal information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Wentworthville Leagues Club disclosed an individual's personal information without their consent or authorization, breaching the National Privacy Principles.
whyTheyWereWrong: The unauthorized disclosure caused non-economic loss to the affected individual, exposing their private information and violating their reasonable expectation of confidentiality.

regulatoryFindings.act: NPP 2.1(g) – Privacy Act 1988 (CTH)
regulatoryFindings.description: Unauthorized disclosure of personal information without consent or authorization
violations: Unauthorized disclosure of personal information without consent or authorization
Failure to protect personal information from being disclosed to third parties

outcome: The OAIC determined a breach of NPP 2.1(g) and ordered the Wentworthville Leagues Club to provide a written apology, implement staff training on privacy obligations, and pay compensation of $7,500 to the affected individual to address non-economic loss. Aggravated and pecuniary damages were not awarded.
dataType: Personal information subject to disclosure

companyDescription: Ceridian Corporation is a Delaware-based service provider that offers payroll processing, payroll-related tax filing, benefits administration, and other human resource services to business customers, operating the Powerpay web-based platform for small businesses.
companyLongDescription: Ceridian Corporation is a Delaware-based service provider that offers payroll processing, payroll-related tax filing, benefits administration, and other human resource services to business customers, operating the Powerpay web-based platform for small businesses.
caseDescription: Ceridian operated Powerpay, a web-based payroll service, while making false claims about security. The company stored sensitive employee data in plain text, failed to fix known SQL injection vulnerabilities, and in December 2009 attackers exploited these failures to steal personal information of over 27,600 employees including Social Security numbers and bank account details.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect personal data, resulting in a data breach of sensitive payroll information. This reflects the Solove category of Insecurity, which concerns inadequate safeguards against unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Ceridian stored employee personal data in plain text, failed to assess web application vulnerabilities to SQL injection attacks, did not implement readily available defenses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited these failures to steal personal information of at least 27,673 employees, including Social Security numbers, bank account numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ceridian's comprehensive security program is designed in accordance with ISO 27000 series standards, industry best practices and federal, state and local regulatory requirements.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ceridian stored sensitive personal information in plain text, failed to assess vulnerability to SQL injection attacks, did not implement available defenses, and failed to detect unauthorized access until data was stolen.

claimsVsReality.claim: Ceridian shall use the same degree of care as it uses to protect its own confidential information of like nature, but no less than a reasonable degree of care, to maintain in confidence customer information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Ceridian failed to employ reasonable and appropriate measures to prevent unauthorized access, resulting in the theft of 27,673 individuals' sensitive financial and personal data through an easily-exploitable SQL injection vulnerability.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Ceridian represented that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures compliant with ISO 27000 standards and used reasonable care, but in fact stored data in plain text, failed to patch known vulnerabilities, and did not detect unauthorized access.
violations: Ceridian represented that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures compliant with ISO 27000 standards and used reasonable care, but in fact stored data in plain text, failed to patch known vulnerabilities, and did not detect unauthorized access.

Ceridian's failure to implement reasonable security measures caused substantial injury to consumers when hackers exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to export 27,673 individuals' sensitive personal information.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 8, 2011, alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint resulted in a consent order requiring Ceridian to implement comprehensive information security improvements, including establishing a security program, conducting regular risk assessments, implementing authentication and encryption, maintaining reasonable logging and monitoring, and submitting to ongoing independent security audits for 20 years.
companyNow: Ceridian is now part of Dayforce (formerly HighGround Inc./Dayforce), a leading Human Capital Management platform, following acquisitions and restructurings. The company continues to provide payroll, benefits, and HR services globally.
dataType: Name, address, email, phone number, Social Security number, date of birth, direct deposit account numbers, bank account numbers

companyDescription: Frostwire LLC was a Florida-based software company that designed and distributed file-sharing applications compatible with peer-to-peer networks, particularly the Gnutella network. The company operated from at least 2007 through 2011, offering free downloads of both desktop and mobile file-sharing applications.
companyLongDescription: Frostwire LLC was a Florida-based software company that designed and distributed file-sharing applications compatible with peer-to-peer networks, particularly the Gnutella network. The company operated from at least 2007 through 2011, offering free downloads of both desktop and mobile file-sharing applications.
caseDescription: Frostwire designed and distributed file-sharing applications (FrostWire Desktop and FrostWire for Android) that misled consumers about file-sharing settings and caused them to unwittingly share personal files publicly. The desktop version misrepresented which downloaded files would be shared, while the Android app defaulted to sharing all pre-existing files across multiple categories without adequate consumer disclosure or control.
violationSummary: The application's default configurations and misleading UI exposed consumers' personal files to public access and download on P2P networks without adequate consent or disclosure. This falls squarely within the exposure category of information dissemination—making private information broadly accessible to unknown parties.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Distributed FrostWire Desktop and FrostWire for Android applications with deceptive installation interfaces.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers unwittingly exposed intimate personal files including photographs, voice recordings, and documents to millions of anonymous users worldwide for download.

claimsVsReality.claim: Files downloaded and stored in the 'Save' folder will not be shared with the file-sharing network
claimsVsReality.reality: Downloaded files were automatically designated as 'Individually shared' files and were actively shared on the Gnutella network regardless of folder placement

claimsVsReality.claim: Users can control what's shared through the installation setup screen's checkbox options
claimsVsReality.reality: Pre-checked boxes defaulted to sharing all files in multiple categories (Pictures, Video, Audio/Music, Applications, Documents, Ringtones) with no adequate disclosure; users had to manually unshare individual files one at a time after installation

claimsVsReality.claim: If you uncheck 'Share Finished Downloads' in Options-Sharing, downloads will not be shared
claimsVsReality.reality: Previously downloaded files continued to be shared as 'Individually shared' files even after unchecking the setting; the UI did not disclose this persistent sharing of existing downloads

claimsVsReality.claim: FrostWire for Android provides '[c]ontrol what's shared'
claimsVsReality.reality: The application provided no meaningful control mechanism; it automatically shared broad file categories by default and required tedious one-by-one unsharing of individual files without clear UI instructions

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Misrepresented through the 'Save Folder and Shared Folders' dialog box that files downloaded to the 'Save' folder would not be shared with the Gnutella network, when in fact they were automatically shared as 'Individually shared' files
violations: Misrepresented through the 'Save Folder and Shared Folders' dialog box that files downloaded to the 'Save' folder would not be shared with the Gnutella network, when in fact they were automatically shared as 'Individually shared' files
Failed to disclose that FrostWire Desktop, by default, publicly shared files consumers downloaded from the Gnutella network even when stored in 'unshared' folders

Designed FrostWire for Android with default settings that automatically designated pre-existing files in multiple categories (Pictures, Video, Audio/Music, Applications, Documents, Ringtones) for public sharing immediately upon installation, without adequate consumer notice or ability to control which files would be shared

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(n) of the FTC Act defines an unfair practice as one that causes or is likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that is not reasonably avoidable and is not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
regulatoryFindings.description: FrostWire for Android's design caused substantial injury by enabling unwitting public sharing of personal files (photographs, documents, voice recordings) with little or no notice to consumers
violations: FrostWire for Android's design caused substantial injury by enabling unwitting public sharing of personal files (photographs, documents, voice recordings) with little or no notice to consumers

Consumers could not reasonably avoid this injury given the default installation process, lack of adequate disclosure, and burdensome unsharing procedures (requiring manual unsharing of files one at a time)
The unfair practice provided no countervailing benefits to consumers, as standard file-sharing applications (including Frostwire Desktop itself) do not share user-originated files by default

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint seeking permanent injunctive relief under Section 13(b) of the FTC Act and other equitable remedies to halt violations and redress consumer injury. The complaint alleges three counts: (1) false representations about file-sharing in FrostWire Desktop, (2) failure to disclose material information about download sharing in FrostWire Desktop, and (3) unfair design of FrostWire for Android. As this is the original complaint document filed on 10/07/2011, the final resolution and specific remedies are not detailed in this filing. The FTC sought permanent injunction, consumer redress, and case costs.
companyNow: Frostwire ceased active development of its desktop and mobile file-sharing applications following regulatory pressure and has largely faded from public prominence. The company's current operational status is unknown.
dataType: Personal files stored on mobile devices and computers including pictures, videos, documents, audio files, applications, and user-originated content
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce

companyDescription: ScanScout was a video advertising network that acted as an intermediary between website publishers and advertisers, specializing in online behavioral advertising and targeted video ad placement.
companyLongDescription: ScanScout was a video advertising network that acted as an intermediary between website publishers and advertisers, specializing in online behavioral advertising and targeted video ad placement.
caseDescription: ScanScout used Flash cookies to track user online behavior for targeted video advertising from April 2007 to September 2009. The company's privacy policy falsely claimed users could prevent tracking by changing browser settings to block cookies, but Flash cookies operated outside browser controls and could not be disabled this way. This deceptive practice violated FTC Act Section 5(a).
violationSummary: ScanScout engaged in systematic collection and storage of users' online activities through Flash cookies to enable behavioral targeting, while deceiving users about their ability to control this surveillance.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: ScanScout used Flash cookies to collect and store user online activity data for targeted video advertising while falsely telling users they could prevent tracking by changing browser cookie.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of users could not actually stop ScanScout's data collection because Flash cookies operated outside browser controls, allowing the company to profile.

claimsVsReality.claim: You can opt out of receiving a cookie by changing your browser settings to prevent the receipt of cookies
claimsVsReality.reality: ScanScout used Flash cookies that were not controlled through browser settings; changing browser privacy settings did not prevent Flash cookie tracking

claimsVsReality.claim: General user data is automatically collected through the use of cookies and users can control this via browser settings
claimsVsReality.reality: Flash cookies could not be deleted or blocked through browser settings, making user control claims false for the actual tracking mechanism in use

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ScanScout represented in its privacy policy that consumers could prevent data collection by changing browser settings to block cookies
violations: ScanScout represented in its privacy policy that consumers could prevent data collection by changing browser settings to block cookies
This representation was false or misleading because Flash cookies were not controlled through browser settings and remained active even when HTTP cookies were blocked
Consumers had no actual ability to opt out of ScanScout's tracking by the means suggested in the privacy policy

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on December 14, 2011, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleged that ScanScout's representations about cookie opt-out methods were false and misleading because Flash cookies operated independently of browser controls. This initiated formal enforcement proceedings against the respondent.
dataType: Online behavioral activity, browsing history, IP address, operating system, browser type

companyDescription: SettlementOne Credit Corporation was a consumer credit reporting company that compiled and sold trimerge reports—consolidated credit data from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion—to mortgage brokers and other lenders to assess consumer creditworthiness.
companyLongDescription: SettlementOne Credit Corporation was a consumer credit reporting company that compiled and sold trimerge reports—consolidated credit data from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion—to mortgage brokers and other lenders to assess consumer creditworthiness.
caseDescription: SettlementOne failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive consumer credit reports it compiled and distributed to mortgage brokers. Between February and June 2008, hackers exploited vulnerabilities in end-user client networks and accessed at least 784 consumer reports without authorization. The company did not assess client security risks, implement monitoring systems, or take corrective action after breaches were discovered.
violationSummary: SettlementOne's comprehensive failure to implement, monitor, or maintain reasonable security controls directly led to unauthorized access to sensitive consumer financial data, exemplifying the insecurity category of privacy harm.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: SettlementOne failed to develop information security policies, assess client security risks, or require basic security measures like firewalls.
whyTheyWereWrong: At least 784 consumers had their highly sensitive financial data including Social Security numbers, addresses, dates of birth.

claimsVsReality.claim: SettlementOne issued credentials (username/password) to authorized clients to access consumer reports through a secure online portal.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company did not verify the security of client computer networks and allowed clients without basic security measures (firewalls, updated antivirus software) to access highly sensitive consumer data, enabling hackers to exploit vulnerabilities in client networks.

claimsVsReality.claim: SettlementOne operated a controlled system for distributing consumer reports to legitimate business users.
claimsVsReality.reality: Between February and June 2008, hackers exploited multiple vulnerabilities in end-user client networks and accessed at least 784 consumer reports. Hackers could also view any report pulled by the client in the previous 90 days, indicating systemic lack of access controls and monitoring.

claimsVsReality.claim: SettlementOne responded appropriately to security breaches.
claimsVsReality.reality: After discovering breaches, the company terminated some affected end users but did nothing in other cases. In one instance, SettlementOne restored access to an end user whose credentials had been stolen, despite the client providing no documentation that their systems were virus-free or properly secured.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. §§ 314.3, 314.4) requires financial institutions to protect customer information by developing comprehensive written security programs containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards, including risk assessment, implementation of controls, monitoring effectiveness, and adjustment in light of identified risks.
regulatoryFindings.description: SettlementOne failed to develop and disseminate information security policies for itself and end-user clients.
violations: SettlementOne failed to develop and disseminate information security policies for itself and end-user clients.
SettlementOne failed to assess risks of allowing end users with unverified or inadequate security to access consumer reports.
SettlementOne failed to implement reasonable steps to address identified risks, such as evaluating end-user computer network security or requiring appropriate security measures.
SettlementOne failed to maintain an effective system of monitoring access to consumer reports and detecting suspicious activity.
SettlementOne failed to take corrective action after discovering breaches, and in one instance restored access to an end user despite stolen credentials and lack of documentation of proper security.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604 (15 U.S.C. § 1681b) prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports except for specified permissible purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: SettlementOne furnished consumer reports to unauthorized hackers who had no permissible purpose to obtain such reports.
violations: SettlementOne furnished consumer reports to unauthorized hackers who had no permissible purpose to obtain such reports.

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(a) (15 U.S.C. § 1681e(a)) requires consumer reporting agencies to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports to permissible purposes and prohibits furnishing reports to any person if the agency has reasonable grounds for believing the report will not be used for a permissible purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: SettlementOne failed to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports when it allowed clients without adequate security safeguards to access them.
violations: SettlementOne failed to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports when it allowed clients without adequate security safeguards to access them.

SettlementOne furnished consumer reports under circumstances where it had reasonable grounds for believing the reports would not be used for permissible purposes, as evidenced by the multiple breaches.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SettlementOne engaged in unfair practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect consumers' personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
violations: SettlementOne engaged in unfair practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect consumers' personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers.

outcome: This is a Complaint issued on August 17, 2011. The document indicates the FTC had reason to believe violations occurred and alleged unfair and deceptive practices. The case would proceed to settlement or adjudication. Typical FTC outcomes for such cases include Consent Orders requiring comprehensive information security program implementation, regular compliance monitoring and reporting, third-party security audits, and corrective measures.
dataType: financial data, credit reports, Social Security numbers, addresses, employer history, account numbers

Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 607(a), 15 U.S.C. § 1681e(a)

company: Playdom, Inc. (subsidiary of Disney Enterprises, Inc.)
companyDescription: Playdom was an online game developer and operator. It was formed as successor to Acclaim Games, Inc. (dissolved), acquiring Acclaim's online virtual world platforms in May 2010. Disney acquired Playdom as a subsidiary on August 27, 2010, consolidating online gaming properties.
companyLongDescription: Playdom was an online game developer and operator. It was formed as successor to Acclaim Games, Inc. (dissolved), acquiring Acclaim's online virtual world platforms in May 2010. Disney acquired Playdom as a subsidiary on August 27, 2010, consolidating online gaming properties.
caseDescription: Playdom (formerly Acclaim Games) operated approximately 20 online games, including Pony Stars directed at children, and collected personal information from approximately 1.224 million children without proper parental consent. The company failed to provide adequate notice to parents, obtain verifiable parental consent before data collection, and falsely represented in its privacy policy that children could not disclose personal information online when in fact the platform enabled such disclosure through user profiles and forums.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected personal information from children across multiple platforms without proper parental consent mechanisms. COPPA surveillance violations occurred through registration systems and profile data collection.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Playdom operated approximately 20 online games that collected personal information from approximately 1.224 million children under 13 without obtaining verifiable parental consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 1.224 million children were exposed to contact and safety risks because their real names, locations, email addresses, and instant messenger IDs were collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: When a child under 13 years of age signs up we not [sic] collect the Email address without the permission of the Parent or Legal Guardian and we will collect the other items listed above. We do not collect anything else.
claimsVsReality.reality: Defendants collected children's email addresses, usernames, passwords, birth years, gender, and enabled children to publicly post real names, locations, website URLs, email addresses, and instant messenger IDs through personal profile pages and community forums.

claimsVsReality.claim: If a child under 13 years of age wants to post information on our website or chat with other players, we will require that they do not disclose any personal information such as the real name, address, phone number and anything that can be used to contact the child.
claimsVsReality.reality: The platform design and personal profile pages included fields for children to enter and publicly disclose real name, location, website, email, and various instant messenger IDs. Children could create profiles, post comments in forums, and upload personal information visible to other users.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Section 312.4(b) requires operators to post a clear, understandable, and complete privacy policy on their website describing what information they collect from children online, how they use it, and their disclosure practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants' privacy policy falsely stated they would prohibit children from posting personal information such as real names, addresses, phone numbers, and contact information, when in fact the personal profile pages and community forums allowed children to enter and publicly post such information.
violations: Defendants' privacy policy falsely stated they would prohibit children from posting personal information such as real names, addresses, phone numbers, and contact information, when in fact the personal profile pages and community forums allowed children to enter and publicly post such information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Section 312.4(c) requires operators to provide direct notice to parents of their information collection, use, and disclosure practices for children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants failed to provide parents with direct notice of information practices prior to collecting, using, or disclosing children's personal information.
violations: Defendants failed to provide parents with direct notice of information practices prior to collecting, using, or disclosing children's personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Section 312.5(a)(1) requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent prior to any collection, use, or disclosure of personal information from children under 13.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants collected children's personal information (email, user ID, password, birth year, gender, instant messenger IDs) without obtaining verifiable parental consent. Sending a welcome email to a parent-provided address and automatically granting full account access does not constitute verifiable consent.
violations: Defendants collected children's personal information (email, user ID, password, birth year, gender, instant messenger IDs) without obtaining verifiable parental consent. Sending a welcome email to a parent-provided address and automatically granting full account access does not constitute verifiable consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants made false and misleading representations in their privacy policy that they would prohibit children from disclosing personal information online, while the platform design and features actually enabled and facilitated such disclosures.
violations: Defendants made false and misleading representations in their privacy policy that they would prohibit children from disclosing personal information online, while the platform design and features actually enabled and facilitated such disclosures.

outcome: The United States filed a civil complaint seeking monetary penalties, permanent injunction, and other equitable relief. Each of approximately 1,224,000 instances of COPPA violations constitutes a separate violation subject to civil penalties of up to $11,000 per violation (pre-February 10, 2009) or $16,000 per violation (post-February 10, 2009). The complaint requested injunctive relief to prevent future violations and required compliance with COPPA Rule provisions.
companyNow: Playdom became a subsidiary of Disney Enterprises, Inc. in August 2010. By August 26, 2010, Playdom had permanently shut down most of the online virtual worlds formerly operated by Acclaim Games, though some games were transferred to non-U.S. operators (e.g., Feerik Ltd.). The company remains under Disney ownership.
dataType: Email addresses, usernames, birth year, gender, location data, instant messenger IDs, user activity logs, forum posts
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.4(c) – insufficient parental notice
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. § 312.5(a)(1) – lack of verifiable parental consent
FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) – unfair or deceptive acts
FTC Act Section 5(m)(1)(A) – civil penalties authority

companyDescription: ACRAnet, Inc. was a consumer reporting agency based in Spokane, Washington that assembled and sold trimerge reports (merged credit reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) to mortgage brokers and other entities for credit determination purposes.
companyLongDescription: ACRAnet, Inc. was a consumer reporting agency based in Spokane, Washington that assembled and sold trimerge reports (merged credit reports from Equifax, Experian, and TransUnion) to mortgage brokers and other entities for credit determination purposes.
caseDescription: ACRAnet, a consumer reporting agency, failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect highly sensitive consumer financial data. Between December 2007 and November 2008, hackers exploited vulnerabilities in end-user client networks, accessing at least 694 consumer reports without authorization. The company allowed clients without basic security protections to access trimerge reports containing unverified credentials.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security controls resulted in unauthorized disclosure of consumer reports containing sensitive personal and financial information to third parties (hackers). This constitutes a breach of confidentiality of information in the company's custody.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: ACRAnet failed to implement information security safeguards, allowed clients without firewalls or antivirus software to access sensitive consumer credit reports.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited vulnerabilities in end-user networks and accessed at least 694 consumer reports containing Social Security numbers, account numbers, addresses.

claimsVsReality.claim: ACRAnet issued credentials to authorized end-user clients for secure access to sensitive consumer reports
claimsVsReality.reality: ACRAnet allowed clients with no verified security measures (no firewalls, outdated antivirus) to access reports, and did not evaluate or monitor client network security

claimsVsReality.claim: ACRAnet implemented reasonable safeguards to protect consumer information
claimsVsReality.reality: ACRAnet had no comprehensive written security policies, did not assess risks, did not monitor access patterns, and did not correct known vulnerabilities after multiple breaches

claimsVsReality.claim: ACRAnet protected consumer reports from unauthorized access
claimsVsReality.reality: Hackers accessed at least 694 consumer reports and had ability to view any report pulled by end users in the previous 90 days

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information by developing a comprehensive written information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACRAnet failed to design and implement information safeguards to control risks to customer information
violations: ACRAnet failed to design and implement information safeguards to control risks to customer information
Failed to regularly test or monitor the effectiveness of existing controls and procedures
Failed to evaluate and adjust the information security program in light of known or identified risks
Failed to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive information security program

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 604 of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. § 1681b) prohibits a consumer reporting agency from furnishing a consumer report except for specified permissible purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACRAnet furnished consumer reports to hackers who did not have a permissible purpose to obtain a consumer report
violations: ACRAnet furnished consumer reports to hackers who did not have a permissible purpose to obtain a consumer report

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(a) of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. § 1681e(a)) requires every consumer reporting agency to maintain reasonable procedures to limit the furnishing of consumer reports to specified purposes and prohibits furnishing reports if the agency has reasonable grounds for believing the report will not be used for a permissible purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACRAnet failed to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports to permissible purposes
violations: ACRAnet failed to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports to permissible purposes
ACRAnet furnished consumer reports under circumstances where it had reasonable grounds for believing the reports would not be used for permissible purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ACRAnet's failure to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures caused or was likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers
violations: ACRAnet's failure to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures caused or was likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers

outcome: FTC issued a formal complaint on August 17, 2011, alleging violations of the Safeguards Rule, FCRA, and FTC Act. The complaint was the basis for enforcement action requiring ACRAnet to implement comprehensive information security improvements and comply with ongoing monitoring and compliance obligations.
dataType: financial data, full name, addresses, Social Security numbers, date of birth, employment history, account numbers
legalBasisViolated: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act § 501(b) / Safeguards Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 314

companyDescription: Chitika was an online behavioral advertising company operating from Massachusetts that acted as an intermediary between website publishers and advertisers, using cookies to track consumer browsing and serve targeted ads.
companyLongDescription: Chitika was an online behavioral advertising company operating from Massachusetts that acted as an intermediary between website publishers and advertisers, using cookies to track consumer browsing and serve targeted ads.
caseDescription: Chitika, an online behavioral advertising company, represented to consumers that they could opt out of targeted advertising for a reasonable period. However, the opt-out cookies expired after only 10 days, automatically resuming tracking without consumer knowledge. After FTC contact, Chitika extended the expiration to 10 years but only for future opt-outs, leaving prior opt-outs unprotected.
violationSummary: Chitika misrepresented the duration of consumer opt-out protections, then resumed tracking and secondary use of consumer data (behavioral targeting) without renewed consent after opt-out cookies expired.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Chitika set opt-out cookies that expired after only 10 days (May 2008–February 2010), automatically resuming behavioral tracking.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of consumers who clicked Chitika's opt-out button believed their tracking preferences would persist for a reasonable period.

claimsVsReality.claim: You can opt-out of receiving Chitika cookies, and this opt-out will last for a reasonable period of time. Chitika encourages business practices that protect user privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Opt-out cookies expired after only 10 days (until March 2010), causing automatic resumption of tracking and behavioral targeting without consumer knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Chitika uses cookies to store anonymous activity data.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cookies contained unique identification numbers and were linked to specific consumer browsing activities including search terms, enabling persistent identification and tracking.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Chitika represented that opt-out would last for a reasonable period of time, but opt-out cookies actually expired after 10 days, resuming tracking without consumer knowledge
violations: Chitika represented that opt-out would last for a reasonable period of time, but opt-out cookies actually expired after 10 days, resuming tracking without consumer knowledge
Consumers were not informed that opt-out cookies would expire after 10 days, deceiving them about the duration of privacy protection
After opting out, consumers' browsing activities were tracked and used for targeted advertising once the opt-out cookie expired, violating their explicit privacy choice

outcome: Complaint issued June 7, 2011 alleging deceptive practices under FTC Act Section 5(a). Chitika modified opt-out cookie expiration to 10 years after FTC staff contact (March 1, 2010), but modification applied only to future opt-outs. Complaint challenged the deceptive representations regarding opt-out duration and effectiveness. Document represents initial complaint filing; final settlement terms not provided in this document.
companyNow: Chitika operated as a significant online advertising intermediary in the late 2000s and early 2010s. The company's current operational status is unknown from available information.
dataType: Search terms, web browsing activity, online activity tracking data
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive acts or practices in commerce

companyDescription: Teletrack, Inc. was a Georgia-based consumer reporting agency that compiled and sold consumer credit reports and marketing lists to non-traditional credit providers including payday lenders, rental purchase stores, and non-prime auto lenders.
companyLongDescription: Teletrack, Inc. was a Georgia-based consumer reporting agency that compiled and sold consumer credit reports and marketing lists to non-traditional credit providers including payday lenders, rental purchase stores, and non-prime auto lenders.
caseDescription: Teletrack, a consumer reporting agency, furnished marketing lists containing consumer names and addresses to third parties without permissible purposes under the Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA). The company compiled these lists from credit inquiry data without obtaining proper consent, violating FCRA section 604 which restricts the purposes for which consumer reports may be furnished. This constituted knowing violations forming a pattern or practice of FCRA breaches.
violationSummary: Teletrack disclosed consumer personal information and derived marketing lists to third parties (purchasers of mailing lists) without permissible purpose or consumer consent, constituting unauthorized disclosure in violation of FCRA section 604.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Teletrack sold marketing lists containing consumers' names, addresses, and personal details derived from credit inquiries to third parties for marketing purposes without proper legal.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' sensitive personal information was disclosed to marketers without their knowledge or consent, enabling unwanted solicitations and exposing them to identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Teletrack was operating as a compliant consumer reporting agency furnishing reports only for permissible purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Teletrack was furnishing marketing lists derived from credit inquiry data to third parties for marketing purposes, violating FCRA section 604 which permits furnishing consumer reports only for specific enumerated purposes, not general marketing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumer data was being used only for the original purpose of credit decisioning.
claimsVsReality.reality: Teletrack added consumer names, addresses, phone numbers, dates of birth, employer information, and credit inquiry flags to marketing databases and sold these lists to third parties for direct marketing campaigns.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 604 of the FCRA (15 U.S.C. § 1681b) prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports to third parties except for certain enumerated permissible purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: Teletrack furnished consumer reports (marketing lists) to third parties for marketing purposes, which is not a permissible purpose under section 604 of the FCRA.
violations: Teletrack furnished consumer reports (marketing lists) to third parties for marketing purposes, which is not a permissible purpose under section 604 of the FCRA.
Since at least 2007, Teletrack engaged in multiple instances of furnishing consumer reports to persons without permissible purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 621(a)(1) of the FCRA authorizes the FTC to enforce compliance with the FCRA using all FTC Act functions and powers.
regulatoryFindings.description: Teletrack's violations of FCRA section 604 constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices in violation of FTC Act section 5(a).
violations: Teletrack's violations of FCRA section 604 constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices in violation of FTC Act section 5(a).

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair and deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Teletrack's practice of furnishing marketing lists derived from credit inquiries without permissible purposes constitutes unfair and deceptive acts or practices affecting commerce.
violations: Teletrack's practice of furnishing marketing lists derived from credit inquiries without permissible purposes constitutes unfair and deceptive acts or practices affecting commerce.

outcome: The complaint sought preliminary and permanent injunctive relief, monetary civil penalties of $2,500 per violation (pre-February 2009) and $3,500 per violation (post-February 2009), judgment on each count, and costs of litigation. The complaint alleged knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice. The government requested equitable remedies to halt ongoing violations and prevent future breaches.
companyNow: Teletrack, Inc. (now operating as Clarity Services or similar subsidiary under parent company ownership) continues as a consumer reporting agency serving alternative finance and specialty lending sectors.
outcomeSummary: Complaint filed seeking penalties and injunction
dataType: Name, address, Social Security number, phone number, employer information, date of birth, email address, driver's license number

companyDescription: Lookout Services, Inc. was a Texas-based company providing the I-9 Solution, a web-based platform designed to help employers comply with federal employment eligibility verification requirements by collecting and storing employee identity documents and Social Security numbers.
companyLongDescription: Lookout Services, Inc. was a Texas-based company providing the I-9 Solution, a web-based platform designed to help employers comply with federal employment eligibility verification requirements by collecting and storing employee identity documents and Social Security numbers.
caseDescription: Lookout Services operated the I-9 Solution, a web-based platform storing highly sensitive employment verification data for over 37,000 consumers. Despite marketing claims of secure data protection and perimeter defense, the company failed to implement basic security measures, allowing unauthorized access through weak credentials (including the guessable 'test/test' login) and URL manipulation vulnerabilities. Two separate breaches in October and December 2009 exposed this sensitive personal information.
violationSummary: The company failed to provide reasonable and appropriate security measures for highly sensitive personal information, including weak authentication, lack of intrusion detection, and password storage in clear text. The insecurity directly enabled unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Lookout Services marketed its I-9 Solution as secure while storing passwords in clear text, allowing weak passwords identical to usernames.
whyTheyWereWrong: An employee of a customer company gained unauthorized access to personal information of over 37,000 consumers including Social Security numbers, passport numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Secure Your Data – data will be encoded and transmitted over secured lines and the FTP interface will protect your data from interception and unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lookout stored passwords in clear text, allowed weak credentials like 'test/test', did not require password changes, and allowed URL manipulation to bypass authentication entirely.

claimsVsReality.claim: Perimeter Defense – servers continuously monitor attempted network attacks on a 24x7 basis using sophisticated software tools.
claimsVsReality.reality: Lookout did not deploy an intrusion detection system until October 2009, after the initial breach; inadequate system log monitoring until December 2009; two separate breaches occurred exposing over 37,000 consumers' data.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lookout represented, expressly and by implication, that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access, when in fact it failed to establish password complexity requirements, enforce credential changes, deploy intrusion detection systems, or prevent URL-based authentication bypass.
violations: Lookout represented, expressly and by implication, that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access, when in fact it failed to establish password complexity requirements, enforce credential changes, deploy intrusion detection systems, or prevent URL-based authentication bypass.

Lookout engaged in unfair practices by failing to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to prevent unauthorized access to sensitive personal information, causing substantial injury to consumers through identity theft risk that was not reasonably avoidable.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on June 15, 2011 alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint does not specify final settlement terms in the provided document, but enforcement action was initiated requiring Lookout to address security deficiencies and comply with FTC orders regarding reasonable data security practices.
companyNow: Unknown – the company may have been acquired, dissolved, or reformed after the 2009 breaches and FTC enforcement action.
dataType: Social Security numbers, passport numbers, alien registration numbers, driver's license numbers, military identification numbers, names, addresses, dates of birth
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

company: US Search, Inc. and US Search, LLC
companyDescription: US Search, Inc. is a data broker that operates www.ussearch.com, providing online search services to the public that aggregate publicly available personal information. The company offers reverse lookup services and consumer information reports derived from public records and partner sources.
companyLongDescription: US Search, Inc. is a data broker that operates www.ussearch.com, providing online search services to the public that aggregate publicly available personal information. The company offers reverse lookup services and consumer information reports derived from public records and partner sources.
caseDescription: US Search, Inc. and its subsidiary charged consumers $10 for a 'PrivacyLock' service that purported to remove their personal information from search results and affiliated websites. However, the service failed to block information appearing in reverse searches, address-based real estate searches, associate searches, and newly generated records—making the core promise deceptive.
violationSummary: The company made misleading representations about a privacy removal service, implying comprehensive blocking of personal information when the service failed to prevent disclosure across multiple search types and record categories.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Charged consumers $10 for a 'PrivacyLock' service that was marketed as preventing their names and addresses from appearing in US Search's website, advertisements, and search results.
whyTheyWereWrong: The PrivacyLock service failed to prevent personal information from appearing in reverse phone/address searches, real estate records, associate listings.

claimsVsReality.claim: PrivacyLock will prevent your name and address from appearing on the US Search website, US Search advertisements, and US Search reports, guaranteed for 1 year.
claimsVsReality.reality: PrivacyLock did not block information from appearing in reverse searches by phone number or address, in real estate record searches, or when the consumer's name appeared as an associate in searches for other people.

claimsVsReality.claim: Your information will be suppressed from affiliate and advertiser websites as well, backed by our 1 year promise.
claimsVsReality.reality: The service failed to suppress information from all relevant search types and record categories, leaving personal data accessible through multiple search pathways.

claimsVsReality.claim: When consumers change addresses, new records would remain subject to PrivacyLock protection.
claimsVsReality.reality: When consumers changed addresses, new records were generated that were not subject to the PrivacyLock restriction.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Made false or misleading representations that the PrivacyLock service would prevent a consumer's name from appearing on the company's website, advertisements, and search results when in fact the service failed to block reverse searches, real estate record searches, associate searches, and newly generated records.
violations: Made false or misleading representations that the PrivacyLock service would prevent a consumer's name from appearing on the company's website, advertisements, and search results when in fact the service failed to block reverse searches, real estate record searches, associate searches, and newly generated records.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on March 14, 2011, alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The company was required to cease the deceptive representations and implement a compliance program. Details of any monetary settlement or additional remediation are not specified in this complaint document.
companyNow: US Search merged with BeenVerified (owned by Blackstone). The data broker service continues to operate under different ownership and regulatory scrutiny has remained a persistent issue for the industry.
dataType: Name, age, address, phone number, aliases, maiden name, death records, address history, relatives, neighbors, marriage/divorce records, associates, property information, bankruptcy, tax liens, civil judgments, criminal records, email address, online profiles

companyDescription: Skid-e-kids was a social networking website marketed as the 'Facebook and MySpace for kids,' targeting children ages 7-14 and their parents, allowing profile creation, photo/video uploads, messaging, and friend connections.
companyLongDescription: Skid-e-kids was a social networking website marketed as the 'Facebook and MySpace for kids,' targeting children ages 7-14 and their parents, allowing profile creation, photo/video uploads, messaging, and friend connections.
caseDescription: Skid-e-kids, a social networking site marketed to children ages 7-14, collected personal information from approximately 5,600 children without obtaining verifiable parental consent. The operator's privacy policy falsely claimed to collect parent email addresses and notify parents before account activation, but in reality never requested parental contact information and automatically registered children without any parental involvement or notification.
violationSummary: The operator systematically collected personal information from children through mandatory registration and profile creation without implementing required parental consent mechanisms, enabling ongoing surveillance-like data collection.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Operated Skid-e-kids, a social network marketed to children ages 7-14, that collected personal information including names, birth dates, email addresses, locations, photos.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 5,600 children's personal information was collected and made publicly accessible through user profiles.

claimsVsReality.claim: The privacy policy stated that the Skid-e-kids.com website requires child users to provide a parent's valid email address in order to register, and that parental email would be used to activate the account and notify parents of privacy practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The registration process never requested a parent's email address, accounts were automatically activated immediately upon child registration, and parents were never notified or provided any opportunity to consent before their children's personal information was collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Website marketed as 'the social networking alternative for kids ages 7 to 14' where 'parents are in charge.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Parents had no actual involvement, notification, or control over their children's account creation or data collection; children could independently register and publicly share personal information without parental knowledge or consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA prohibits operators of commercial websites or online services directed to children from collecting personal information from children without verifiable parental consent and without providing clear notice of information practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children
violations: Failed to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children
Failed to provide clear, understandable notice on the website of what information is collected from children and how it is used
Failed to provide direct notice to parents of information collection practices before collecting data
Misrepresented in privacy policy that parent email addresses would be collected and parents would be notified, when in fact no parent contact was ever requested or attempted

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Made false and misleading representations in privacy policy claiming parental email collection and notification procedures that were never implemented
violations: Made false and misleading representations in privacy policy claiming parental email collection and notification procedures that were never implemented
Deceived parents and guardians about the information collection practices and parental involvement in account activation

outcome: This is a complaint filing seeking permanent injunction, monetary civil penalties of up to $16,000 per violation (approximately 5,600 instances of personal information collection without consent), and other equitable relief. The complaint alleges violations of COPPA and FTC Act Section 5. Resolution and final penalty amount not specified in this complaint document.
companyNow: The current status of Skid-e-kids and Jones O. Godwin is unknown from this complaint filing dated 2011. The case sought permanent injunction to prevent future violations.
