dataType: Children's personal information including name, birth date, gender, email address, location, profile information, photos, videos

companyDescription: Twitter, Inc. operates www.twitter.com, a social networking platform that enables users to post brief messages ('tweets') of 140 characters or less to followers via web, email, and mobile devices. Founded in 2006, Twitter facilitates communication among individuals, media outlets, businesses, and government entities.
companyLongDescription: Twitter, Inc. operates www.twitter.com, a social networking platform that enables users to post brief messages ('tweets') of 140 characters or less to followers via web, email, and mobile devices. Founded in 2006, Twitter facilitates communication among individuals, media outlets, businesses, and government entities.
caseDescription: Twitter failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect nonpublic user information and honor user privacy choices despite making explicit privacy commitments. Between January and May 2009, intruders exploited weak administrative password policies to gain unauthorized access to sensitive user data and send fraudulent tweets from high-profile accounts.
violationSummary: Twitter's inadequate security practices failed to protect nonpublic user information from unauthorized access and compromised the integrity of user privacy controls despite explicit representations regarding security safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Twitter granted nearly all employees unrestricted administrative access to the system, stored admin passwords on public login webpages, failed to enforce strong passwords.
whyTheyWereWrong: Intruders exploited these failures to access millions of users' nonpublic tweets and personal information, reset passwords.

claimsVsReality.claim: Twitter is very concerned about safeguarding the confidentiality of personally identifiable information and employs administrative, physical, and electronic measures designed to protect information from unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Twitter granted nearly all employees unrestricted administrative access without password policies, required weak passwords that could be guessed, stored credentials in plain text in personal email accounts, and lacked basic security controls like password expiration or separate admin login pages.

claimsVsReality.claim: Direct messages are not public; only author and recipient can view direct messages.
claimsVsReality.reality: Intruders exploited administrative access failures to view any user's direct messages, and Twitter employees could access direct messages of any user through inadequately secured administrative credentials.

claimsVsReality.claim: Protected tweet accounts keep updates private and only approved followers are able to see the profile and tweets.
claimsVsReality.reality: Intruders gained unauthorized administrative control allowing them to view protected tweets of any user, and employees could access protected tweets without adequate access restrictions.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Twitter represented in its privacy policy that it employed 'administrative, physical, and electronic measures designed to protect your information from unauthorized access' when in fact it failed to establish basic password security policies, enforce periodic password changes, restrict administrative access, or provide a separate administrative login page.
violations: Twitter represented in its privacy policy that it employed 'administrative, physical, and electronic measures designed to protect your information from unauthorized access' when in fact it failed to establish basic password security policies, enforce periodic password changes, restrict administrative access, or provide a separate administrative login page.

Twitter represented that direct messages were private and viewable 'only by author and recipient' and that protected tweets could be viewed 'only by approved followers', while simultaneously failing to prevent unauthorized administrative access that could expose these messages to intruders.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document is the complaint initiating proceedings; final settlement terms are not included in this document, but FTC enforcement actions against Twitter typically resulted in consent orders requiring implementation of comprehensive information security improvements, regular third-party audits, and ongoing compliance monitoring.
companyNow: Twitter was acquired by Elon Musk in October 2022 and rebranded as X in 2023. The platform continues operating as a major social media service with billions of users, though under different ownership and management.
dataType: Email addresses, IP addresses, mobile phone numbers, direct messages, protected tweets, user account credentials, personal identifiable information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: The Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) is Canada's federal law enforcement agency responsible for policing, national security, and administration of programs including the Canadian Firearms Program.
companyLongDescription: The RCMP is a federal law enforcement organization that serves as Canada's national police force and operates under the Ministry of Public Safety Canada. It administers multiple programs including the Canadian Firearms Program (CFP), which oversees firearms licensing and regulation. The RCMP manages a database of over 1.9 million licensed firearms owners and is responsible for enforcing firearms laws and regulations across Canada. The organization operates under the Privacy Act and must comply with federal privacy and data protection requirements.
caseDescription: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada investigated whether the RCMP improperly disclosed personal information about firearms licensees to EKOS Research Associates for conducting a client-satisfaction survey. The investigation found that the RCMP appropriately used and disclosed the information under contract, with proper safeguards in place, and that the use was consistent with the original purpose of collection.
violationSummary: No violation was found. The complaint was determined to be not well-founded.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The RCMP disclosed personal information about 37,495 firearms licensees to EKOS Research Associates to conduct a client-satisfaction survey without prior public notice of this specific use.
whyTheyWereWrong: Licensees were not transparently informed that their personal data could be used for surveys beyond the original firearms licensing purpose.

claimsVsReality.claim: The RCMP's disclosure of licensee information to EKOS was a proper use of personal information collected for firearms licensing purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the Privacy Commissioner found the disclosure legally compliant, the CFP had not clearly communicated to licensees that their information could be used for satisfaction surveys, limiting transparency about secondary uses of their data.

claimsVsReality.claim: EKOS properly safeguarded the personal information and took privacy seriously.
claimsVsReality.reality: While the investigation confirmed EKOS met contractual security requirements and deleted personal identifiers, the initial disclosure of unredacted data to EKOS created exposure risk before anonymization occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 7 - Use of Personal Information
Privacy Act Section 8 - Disclosure of Personal Information
Privacy Act Section 4 - Collection Authority

outcome: The complaint was found to be not well-founded. The RCMP's disclosure of personal information to EKOS under contract was lawful and appropriate. The Commissioner noted that EKOS properly safeguarded information, stripped personal identifiers from survey responses, and adhered to confidentiality and security provisions. The RCMP committed to improving transparency regarding personal information use by updating the Personal Information Bank description, revising website communications, and considering future Privacy Impact Assessments.
companyNow: The RCMP continues to operate as Canada's primary federal law enforcement agency, managing national security, policing, and regulatory programs including firearms administration.
dataType: Firearms license holder information, demographic data, firearms status information

companyDescription: The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) is a federal law enforcement and border management agency responsible for securing Canada's borders and enforcing customs and immigration laws.
companyLongDescription: CBSA is a department of the Government of Canada tasked with protecting Canada's borders, collecting duties and taxes, and enforcing customs and immigration legislation. The agency operates ports of entry, conducts security investigations, and manages the movement of goods and people across Canadian borders. As a government agency, CBSA is subject to the Privacy Act and PIPEDA in its handling of personal information.
caseDescription: An individual filed complaints alleging that the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) improperly collected personal data from his publicly posted blog after his term position ended. Investigation revealed that CBSA employees accessed the blog in a personal capacity using government workstations, consistent with the government's Acceptable Use Policy. No evidence of unauthorized personal data collection was found.
violationSummary: The complainant alleged surveillance and tracking of his online activity through government access logs, though the investigation found no actual collection of personal information occurred.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: CBSA employees accessed the complainant's publicly posted blog using government workstations after his term position ended.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant believed his personal data was being improperly collected by the government agency, causing him concern about his privacy and surveillance.

claimsVsReality.claim: The complainant alleged that CBSA improperly collected personal data from his blog.
claimsVsReality.reality: CBSA employees viewed the publicly posted blog in a personal capacity using government workstations, consistent with the government's Acceptable Use Policy, with no evidence of unauthorized data collection by the agency.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to limit collection, use and disclosure of personal information to purposes that a reasonable person would consider appropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: Alleged improper collection of personal data from public blog content accessed via government computers
violations: Alleged improper collection of personal data from public blog content accessed via government computers

outcome: Complaints were determined to be not well founded. The investigation concluded that viewing a publicly posted blog from a government workstation does not constitute collection of personal information when employees act in a personal capacity consistent with the Acceptable Use Policy. No remediation or penalties were imposed.
companyNow: CBSA continues to operate as Canada's primary border services agency, managing border security, customs enforcement, and immigration compliance.
dataType: Blog content, online activity logs
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 (Limiting Use, Disclosure and Retention)

company: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada
companyDescription: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada is a Canadian federal department responsible for administering employment insurance, labour programs, and skills development initiatives.
companyLongDescription: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada (HRSDC, now Service Canada) is a department of the Government of Canada that administers employment insurance benefits, manages labour-related programs, and oversees skills development and training initiatives. The department processes claims and appeals from employment insurance claimants across Canada, handling sensitive personal and financial information. It operates regional offices across the country, including the Quebec regional office where this breach occurred.
caseDescription: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada inadvertently disclosed personal information of 191 employment insurance claimants to an individual appealing a claim denial. The disclosure included names, dates of birth, employee identification numbers, Social Insurance Numbers, and employment status. The department quickly retrieved the data, notified affected parties, and implemented measures to prevent recurrence.
violationSummary: The unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal data (including SINs) to unintended recipients through accidental inclusion in an appeal package constitutes an exposure of personal information. The data became accessible to someone who had no legitimate need for it.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada accidentally included the personal information of 191 employment insurance claimants in an appeal package sent to one individual.
whyTheyWereWrong: The disclosure exposed 191 people's most sensitive identifiers to an unknown individual, creating a direct risk of identity theft and fraud when their Social Insurance Numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The department handled appeal dockets securely and protected personal information during the EI Board of Referees process.
claimsVsReality.reality: The department's Quebec regional office failed to segregate sensitive information and accidentally included 191 claimants' complete personal records in a single appeal package.

claimsVsReality.claim: Proper procedures were in place to prevent unauthorized disclosure of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The breach occurred because existing procedures were not followed, requiring the department to re-remind officials of proper data protection practices after the incident.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 1.2 – Organizations are responsible for personal information in their custody and must implement safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement adequate controls when preparing and packaging appeal dockets, resulting in accidental inclusion of sensitive personal information of 191 unrelated individuals
violations: Failed to implement adequate controls when preparing and packaging appeal dockets, resulting in accidental inclusion of sensitive personal information of 191 unrelated individuals

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.8 – Personal information shall be protected by security safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the information
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate procedures for handling and reviewing documents containing sensitive data such as Social Insurance Numbers before dispatch to appellants
violations: Inadequate procedures for handling and reviewing documents containing sensitive data such as Social Insurance Numbers before dispatch to appellants

outcome: The investigation confirmed that 79 of 82 complaints were well-founded. Human Resources and Skills Development Canada moved quickly to retrieve the improperly disclosed data, notified all 191 affected individuals, advised them on identity theft risk reduction, provided a contact person at the department, and flagged the Social Insurance Numbers with the Social Insurance Registration Office for fraud monitoring. The department also reminded Quebec regional office officials of proper procedures for protecting personal information when processing EI Board of Referees appeals to prevent similar incidents.
companyNow: The department continues to operate as Service Canada and Employment and Social Development Canada (ESDC), maintaining responsibility for employment insurance and related social programs.
dataType: names, dates of birth, employee identification numbers, Social Insurance Numbers, employment and leave status
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.8 (Protection of Personal Information)

companyDescription: EKOS Research Associates is a Canadian public opinion research and polling firm that conducts surveys and market research for government and private clients.
companyLongDescription: EKOS Research Associates Inc. is a Canada-based polling and market research company specializing in public opinion surveys, customer satisfaction studies, and social research. The firm conducts research for government agencies, corporations, and non-profit organizations. EKOS is known for electoral polling, policy research, and program evaluation surveys across Canada.
caseDescription: The RCMP shared contact information for 1,270 gun licence holders with polling firm EKOS Research Associates to conduct a client-satisfaction survey about the Firearms Program. EKOS collected demographic and firearm ownership data during interviews. The investigation found no Privacy Act violation, as the secondary use was consistent with the original collection purpose and EKOS maintained appropriate security and confidentiality protections.
violationSummary: The complaint centered on whether using personal information collected under the Firearms Act for a client-satisfaction survey constituted an unauthorized secondary use. The investigation concluded the secondary use was consistent with the original purpose, but the Solove category applies because secondary use (even compliant secondary use) was the core issue.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The RCMP shared contact information for 1,270 gun licence holders with polling firm EKOS Research Associates to conduct a client-satisfaction survey about the Firearms Program.
whyTheyWereWrong: Gun owners' contact details and firearm ownership information were disclosed to a private company without explicit prior notice that their data would be used for polling purposes beyond program.

claimsVsReality.claim: The secondary use of firearms licensee data for customer-satisfaction surveying was consistent with the original collection purpose under the Privacy Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: Gun owners were not explicitly informed at the time of licensing that their contact information and firearm ownership details would be shared with private polling firms for survey purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: EKOS met all contractual requirements for secure and confidential handling of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Although EKOS met contractual obligations, the RCMP's initial disclosure of the data to a private company without clearer public communication about potential uses created privacy concerns that triggered an official investigation.

regulatoryFindings.act: Canadian Privacy Act – authorized collection and secondary use
Canadian Privacy Act – confidentiality and security of personal information when shared with contractors

outcome: The complaint was determined to be not well founded. EKOS and the RCMP were found compliant with the Privacy Act. The RCMP had proper authority to collect the information, the secondary use for a client-satisfaction survey was consistent with the original collection purpose, and EKOS met all contractual requirements for secure and confidential handling. The Office recommended that the Canada Firearms Centre clarify public information on actual and potential uses of collected data and conduct Privacy Impact Assessments before launching similar projects.
companyNow: EKOS Research Associates continues to operate as a polling and research firm in Canada, though it has faced scrutiny over data handling practices in subsequent years.
dataType: Contact information, demographic data (age, gender), firearm ownership information
legalBasisViolated: Canadian Privacy Act – secondary use provisions

companyDescription: The Toronto Port Authority is a Canadian federal crown corporation responsible for the management and operation of the Port of Toronto, a major maritime transportation hub.
companyLongDescription: The Toronto Port Authority is a federal agency that operates and manages port facilities and maritime infrastructure in Toronto, Ontario. As a crown corporation, it oversees cargo handling, vessel traffic, and port operations for the Greater Toronto Area. The organization maintains databases of stakeholder and employee information for legitimate business purposes. In 2010, the organization faced a privacy violation when an employee misused internal personal information for unauthorized political purposes.
caseDescription: A Toronto Port Authority employee improperly accessed and used the organization's email database containing approximately 60 individuals' personal email and home addresses to solicit donations and attendance at a political fundraising event. The employee falsely represented the solicitation as authorized by the Port Authority by using the organization's name in the email signature. The Port Authority had not authorized this use and the activity was unrelated to legitimate business purposes.
violationSummary: The employee disclosed personal information (email addresses and home addresses) from the Port Authority's database to third parties without authorization or knowledge of the data subjects. This constitutes unauthorized secondary use and disclosure of personal information held by a public institution.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: A Toronto Port Authority employee used the organization's email database containing approximately 60 personal email and home addresses to solicit donations.
whyTheyWereWrong: Sixty individuals received unsolicited political fundraising solicitations to their personal home addresses that they had not provided for that purpose.

claimsVsReality.claim: The employee was authorized to use the Port Authority's database for this fundraising purpose.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Port Authority had not authorized the employee to use its personal information database for any political fundraising activity.

claimsVsReality.claim: The email signature conveyed that this was an official Port Authority communication.
claimsVsReality.reality: The employee falsely represented the solicitation as authorized by improperly using the organization's name in the email signature for an unauthorized personal political activity.

claimsVsReality.claim: The personal addresses were collected for general communication purposes.
claimsVsReality.reality: The personal home addresses in the database were confidential records collected by the Port Authority for legitimate business purposes, not for political solicitation.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 4.3 – Personal information collected by an organization shall not be used or disclosed for any purpose other than that for which it was collected, except with the consent of the individual or as required by law.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employee used personal email addresses and home addresses from Port Authority business card database to solicit political fundraising donations without authorization
violations: Employee used personal email addresses and home addresses from Port Authority business card database to solicit political fundraising donations without authorization
Use was unrelated to Port Authority business activities
No consent obtained from individuals whose personal information was disclosed

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act – Public institution employees have responsibilities regarding acceptable use of information under institutional control.
regulatoryFindings.description: Employee misused personal information under Port Authority's control
violations: Employee misused personal information under Port Authority's control
Employee represented unauthorized solicitation as sanctioned by the Port Authority through use of organizational affiliation in email signature

outcome: The Toronto Port Authority acknowledged the complaint was well-founded. The organization took corrective measures including: (1) reminding all employees of their responsibilities for acceptable use of information under institutional control; (2) pledging to provide Privacy Act training to workers; and (3) implementing measures to prevent recurrence. The investigating authority was satisfied with these remedial actions and made no further recommendations.
companyNow: The Toronto Port Authority continues to operate as a federal crown corporation managing the Port of Toronto, having implemented enhanced privacy training and information governance protocols following the 2010 incident.
dataType: Email addresses, business contact information, personal addresses
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Section 4.3 (personal information shall not be used or disclosed for purposes other than those for which it was collected)
Privacy Act Section 19 (unauthorized use of personal information by public institution employees)

companyDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) is Canada's federal tax administration responsible for administering tax laws, managing taxpayer records, and collecting revenue for the Canadian government.
companyLongDescription: The Canada Revenue Agency is a federal agency mandated to administer tax legislation, collect taxes, and manage sensitive taxpayer information for millions of Canadians. As a government body, it maintains extensive databases of personal and financial information protected under the Privacy Act. The CRA employs thousands of workers across multiple tax centres with access to confidential tax records, making information security and employee conduct critical to public trust.
caseDescription: Multiple Canada Revenue Agency employees inappropriately accessed the personal tax information of high-profile sports figures without authorization and for purposes unrelated to their duties. One former employee posted some of this personal tax data to an Internet chat group. The investigation confirmed unauthorized access constituted a breach of the Privacy Act.
violationSummary: Employees accessed confidential tax information without authorization and outside the scope of their job duties, breaching the confidentiality obligation under the Privacy Act. The former employee's posting of this information to a public Internet chat group further compounds the breach of confidentiality.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: CRA employees inappropriately accessed personal tax information of high-profile sports figures without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: High-profile individuals had their confidential tax records exposed publicly on the Internet and accessed by multiple employees out of curiosity, violating their privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: CRA employees accessed tax information only in the course of their official duties.
claimsVsReality.reality: Multiple employees accessed tax information of high-profile sports figures out of curiosity, unrelated to any legitimate job function.

claimsVsReality.claim: CRA systems adequately protect taxpayer confidentiality from internal breaches.
claimsVsReality.reality: A former employee was able to extract and post personal tax data to an Internet chat group, and multiple current employees accessed the same records without detection or authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act – Protection of personal information from unauthorized access
regulatoryFindings.description: CRA employees accessed personal tax information without authorization
violations: CRA employees accessed personal tax information without authorization
Access occurred for purposes unrelated to employees' duties
One former employee posted tax information to a public Internet chat group

outcome: The CRA suspended one employee who accessed personal tax data without authorization and terminated two others. The agency implemented corrective measures including modernization of the National Audit Trail system to improve monitoring of employee access to taxpayer information systems.
companyNow: The CRA continues to operate as Canada's primary tax administration authority. Following this incident, it implemented enhanced monitoring systems and employee conduct protocols to prevent unauthorized access to taxpayer information.
dataType: Tax records, personal financial information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act – unauthorized access to personal information
Privacy Act – use of personal information for purposes unrelated to duties

companyDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada is the federal department responsible for providing services and benefits to Canadian military veterans and their families.
companyLongDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada (now Veterans Affairs and Associate Minister of National Defence) is the primary federal institution delivering benefits, pensions, healthcare, and support services to Canadian Armed Forces veterans, retirees, and their dependents. The department administers various programs including disability benefits, healthcare coverage, rehabilitation services, and housing support. It operates veterans' hospitals and rehabilitation facilities across Canada and manages sensitive personal and medical information on hundreds of thousands of veterans.
caseDescription: Veterans Affairs Canada improperly included excessively detailed and sensitive medical information in briefing notes to the Minister without limiting access on a need-to-know basis, and transferred a veteran's medical file to a hospital without obtaining required consent. The department's widespread sharing of sensitive personal information among officials who had no operational need for it violated the Privacy Act.
violationSummary: The department re-used and disseminated the veteran's personal information (medical data collected for benefits applications) for purposes beyond the original collection purpose (ministerial briefings) and to unrelated internal departments and external entities without consent or necessity.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Veterans Affairs Canada included excessively detailed medical information in briefing notes to the Minister without need-to-know access controls.
whyTheyWereWrong: A veteran's sensitive medical information, diagnosis, symptoms, and treatment details were widely shared among departmental officials who had no operational need for it.

claimsVsReality.claim: Veterans Affairs transferred the veteran's medical information to the hospital to establish suitability for a treatment program and stated departmental guidelines required consent via a Release of Information Form.
claimsVsReality.reality: The department transferred large volumes of the veteran's personal and medical information to the hospital without obtaining the required Release of Information Form consent, violating its own policies and the Privacy Act.

claimsVsReality.claim: The sensitive medical information in briefing notes to the Minister was necessary for the stated purpose of informing the Minister about the veteran's participation in a Parliament Hill press conference.
claimsVsReality.reality: The briefing notes contained excessive detail including diagnosis, symptoms, prognosis, treatment plans, and financial benefit amounts that went far beyond what was necessary for briefing the Minister on the veteran's advocacy activities.

claimsVsReality.claim: Multiple departmental branches including Communications and Media Relations needed access to the veteran's detailed medical information to contribute to briefing notes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Officials from Communications, Media Relations, and Program Policy branches had full access to sensitive medical information but had no operational need to know any medical details to fulfill their duties on the briefing notes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 7 — Personal information under government department control shall not, without an individual's consent, be used by the department except for the purpose for which the information was obtained or compiled, or for a use consistent with that purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: Included excessively detailed and sensitive medical information in briefing notes to the Minister beyond what was necessary for stated purpose
violations: Included excessively detailed and sensitive medical information in briefing notes to the Minister beyond what was necessary for stated purpose
Re-used and updated detailed medical briefing notes for unrelated ministerial purposes
Shared sensitive medical information with departmental officials across multiple branches (Program Policy, Communications, Media Relations) who had no operational need for the information
Transferred veteran's medical file and personal information to a hospital without obtaining required written consent via Release of Information Form

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner issued formal recommendations requiring Veterans Affairs Canada to: (1) develop an enhanced privacy policy framework with adequate protections and controls for accessing personal information; (2) revise information-management practices to implement need-to-know basis sharing only; (3) provide employee training on appropriate personal information handling; and (4) review procedures to ensure consent is obtained before transferring information to veterans' hospitals. The Office also determined to conduct a systemic audit of the department's handling of veterans' personal information to ensure federal privacy law compliance.
companyNow: Veterans Affairs Canada continues to operate as a federal department, now integrated with the portfolio of the Associate Minister of National Defence, delivering services to over 600,000 veterans and their families.
dataType: Medical information, health diagnosis, symptoms, prognosis, financial benefits, treatment plans, appointment frequency
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 7 (use limitation — personal information shall not be used without consent except for the purpose for which obtained or a consistent use)

companyDescription: A Canadian dental benefit plan administrator that manages group dental coverage and online access to benefit information for plan members and their dependents.
companyLongDescription: The organization administers group dental benefit plans for Canadian employers and members. It provides online portals for members to access dental coverage information, claims history, and benefit details. The company processes personal health information for plan members and their dependents, including minors. The case involved their policy requiring explicit consent from individuals aged 16 and older before parents could access dependent children's benefit information online.
caseDescription: Parents of a 17-year-old dependent were unable to access their daughter's online dental benefit information from their group dental plan administrator, despite being plan members and paying for her expenses. The administrator required the minor's consent before disclosing her personal information to parents. The administrator's policy was based on the Ontario Health Care Consent Act, which permits individuals aged 16 and older to provide health-related consent independently.
violationSummary: The administrator's withholding of personal information from parents who had legitimate access rights and financial responsibility represents exclusion under the Solove taxonomy — the failure to provide individuals with information about themselves or allow others to access information, limiting parental oversight despite dependent status.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: The dental plan administrator required a 17-year-old dependent to provide explicit consent before parents who were plan members.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents were unable to manage their dependent daughter's healthcare costs and coverage despite being financially responsible.

claimsVsReality.claim: The administrator required consent from anyone 16 years or older before another plan member could access their information, based on the Ontario Health Care Consent Act.
claimsVsReality.reality: Parents who were plan members and financially responsible for their dependent daughter's dental care were unable to access basic benefit information necessary to manage her healthcare and expenses.

claimsVsReality.claim: The policy was reasonable and defensible under PIPEDA because an individual's knowledge and consent are required for disclosure of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The policy created a practical burden for parents managing dependent minors' healthcare by requiring the child to provide passwords or explicit consent rather than allowing parental access to coverage and claims information.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 4.3 requires knowledge and consent for disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Administrator required consent from 17-year-old before parents could access dependent's dental benefit information, even though parents were plan members and financially responsible
violations: Administrator required consent from 17-year-old before parents could access dependent's dental benefit information, even though parents were plan members and financially responsible

outcome: The administrator's policy was defended and upheld as reasonable based on the Ontario Health Care Consent Act, which allows individuals aged 16 and older to provide health-related consent. The parent was satisfied with the explanation and understood that consent could be provided by sharing account credentials with parents.
dataType: Health data, dental benefit information

companyDescription: Directors Desk LLC provided a secure online platform allowing corporate board members to access board meeting materials, minutes, and related documents. The company marketed compliance with U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework to attract corporate clients.
companyLongDescription: Directors Desk LLC provided a secure online platform allowing corporate board members to access board meeting materials, minutes, and related documents. The company marketed compliance with U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework to attract corporate clients.
caseDescription: Directors Desk LLC claimed to be a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework but failed to renew its certification. From February 2008 to August 2009, the company maintained false statements on its website representing current Safe Harbor participation when it had 'not current' status. The FTC charged this as deceptive practice under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.
violationSummary: The company materially misrepresented its compliance status with an international privacy framework, distorting consumer understanding of data protection commitments through false claims on its privacy policy.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Directors Desk claimed on its website to be a current Safe Harbor participant while its certification lapsed for 18 months from February 2008 to August 2009.
whyTheyWereWrong: Corporate board members using Directors Desk transferred sensitive board meeting materials and personal data across borders relying on false Safe Harbor claims.

claimsVsReality.claim: Directors Desk is a participant in the Safe Harbor program developed by the U.S. Department of Commerce and the European Union. We have certified that we adhere to the Safe Harbor Privacy Principles.
claimsVsReality.reality: From February 2008 to August 2009, Directors Desk did not renew its Safe Harbor certification and held 'not current' status on the Department of Commerce's public registry.

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy policy effective since June 2004 with current Safe Harbor compliance
claimsVsReality.reality: Policy was never renewed after February 2007 self-certification, and certification lapsed in February 2008 without renewal for 18 months

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company represented expressly and by implication that it was a current Safe Harbor participant when it had not renewed certification and held 'not current' status
violations: Company represented expressly and by implication that it was a current Safe Harbor participant when it had not renewed certification and held 'not current' status
False and misleading privacy policy statements were disseminated on company website to consumers and business partners
Company failed to notify Department of Commerce that its Safe Harbor representation was no longer valid, as required by Safe Harbor rules

outcome: Complaint issued January 12, 2010. Directors Desk was ordered to cease deceptive practices and comply with the Safe Harbor framework if claiming participation. Company required to maintain accurate representations of privacy certification status on all platforms.
companyNow: Unknown. Directors Desk LLC appears to have ceased major operations; website and Safe Harbor certification status are no longer current as of available public records.
dataType: Corporate board member personal data, board meeting materials, board minutes, documents
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: First Advantage SafeRent, Inc. is a consumer reporting agency founded in 2005 that assembles and sells tenant screening reports, including eviction records, payment history, and criminal background information, to multi-family housing businesses for leasing decisions.
companyLongDescription: First Advantage SafeRent, Inc. is a consumer reporting agency founded in 2005 that assembles and sells tenant screening reports, including eviction records, payment history, and criminal background information, to multi-family housing businesses for leasing decisions.
caseDescription: SafeRent, a consumer reporting agency serving the multi-family housing industry, systematically rejected consumer requests for file disclosures and dispute reinvestigations submitted by facsimile, requiring consumers to use mail instead. This violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act's mandatory disclosure and reinvestigation requirements.
violationSummary: SafeRent's rejection of non-mail requests prevented consumers from exercising their statutory right to access and dispute their consumer files, effectively excluding them from FCRA protections.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: SafeRent rejected consumer requests for file disclosures and dispute reinvestigations submitted by facsimile, requiring consumers to submit written requests by U.S.
whyTheyWereWrong: Prospective renters were locked out of accessing their own consumer reports and correcting false eviction records, causing delays in clearing their names.

claimsVsReality.claim: SafeRent could limit file disclosure and reinvestigation requests to written mail submissions only
claimsVsReality.reality: The FCRA requires consumer reporting agencies to disclose and reinvestigate upon consumer request without imposing unreasonable procedural barriers such as refusing facsimile submissions

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 609(a)(1) requires all consumer reporting agencies to disclose to consumers, upon request, all information maintained in their consumer files.
regulatoryFindings.description: SafeRent rejected multiple file disclosure requests submitted by facsimile and required consumers to submit written requests through U.S. mail instead
violations: SafeRent rejected multiple file disclosure requests submitted by facsimile and required consumers to submit written requests through U.S. mail instead

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 611(a)(1)(A) requires all consumer reporting agencies to reinvestigate the completeness or accuracy of items in a consumer's file upon receipt of a dispute notice from the consumer.
regulatoryFindings.description: SafeRent did not conduct reinvestigations of disputed items when consumers submitted requests by facsimile, instead requiring written reinvestigation requests via U.S. mail
violations: SafeRent did not conduct reinvestigations of disputed items when consumers submitted requests by facsimile, instead requiring written reinvestigation requests via U.S. mail

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: SafeRent's systematic rejection of facsimile requests constituted unfair and deceptive practices in violation of Section 5(a)
violations: SafeRent's systematic rejection of facsimile requests constituted unfair and deceptive practices in violation of Section 5(a)

outcome: SafeRent agreed to a Stipulated Final Judgment and Order requiring payment of $100,000 civil penalty. The company was permanently enjoined from failing to disclose consumer file contents upon request and from failing to maintain reasonable procedures to ensure reinvestigation compliance. SafeRent must comply with ongoing monitoring, reporting, and record-keeping requirements for five to eight years, including notification of business changes, annual compliance reports, and distribution of the Order to all relevant personnel.
companyNow: First Advantage SafeRent, Inc. remains a consumer reporting agency in the multi-family housing sector. The 2010 settlement required sustained compliance monitoring through at least 2015-2018.
dataType: Tenant eviction records, lease and payment information, criminal history records, consumer files

companyDescription: Dave & Buster's, Inc. is a Missouri-based corporation operating 53 restaurant/entertainment complexes across the United States under the brands Dave & Buster's, Dave & Buster's Grand Sports Café, and Jillian's. The company accepts payment cards and cash for consumer purchases and operates interconnected networks for transaction processing.
companyLongDescription: Dave & Buster's, Inc. is a Missouri-based corporation operating 53 restaurant/entertainment complexes across the United States under the brands Dave & Buster's, Dave & Buster's Grand Sports Café, and Jillian's. The company accepts payment cards and cash for consumer purchases and operates interconnected networks for transaction processing.
caseDescription: Dave & Buster's failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive payment card data collected from 53 restaurant/entertainment locations. An intruder exploited multiple security vulnerabilities between April and August 2007, compromising approximately 130,000 payment cards and resulting in hundreds of thousands of dollars in fraudulent charges.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures for sensitive personal financial information falls squarely within the Solove category of insecurity — the handling of personal information in a manner that creates substantial risk of unauthorized access or disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Dave & Buster's collected sensitive payment card data including account numbers, expiration dates.

companyLongDescription: LifeLock, Inc. is an identity theft protection and monitoring company founded in 2005 based in Tempe, Arizona. The company provides fraud alerts, credit monitoring, and identity restoration services to consumers and has enrolled over one million customers.
caseDescription: LifeLock advertised an identity theft prevention service that claimed to provide complete protection against identity theft and secure customer data with encryption and access controls. claimsVsReality.reality: LifeLock did not provide ongoing monitoring or review of customers' credit files

companyDescription: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada (HRSDC) is the federal government department responsible for employment, social development, and skills programs. It processes applications and benefits for programs like the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
companyLongDescription: Human Resources and Skills Development Canada is a federal government department tasked with administering major employment and social benefit programs for Canadian citizens. HRSDC manages large-scale mailings of sensitive personal information to millions of applicants and beneficiaries. The department is responsible for protecting personal data under the Privacy Act and implementing robust quality-control procedures.
caseDescription: In March 2009, a mechanical malfunction in the Quebec processing centre's mail-sorting equipment, compounded by human error, caused 11,900 forms containing personal information to be incorrectly distributed to applicants. Forty-four cases of mix-ups were reported, with recipients receiving forms destined for other individuals containing names, addresses, and encoded SINs. A technician failed to report the initial duplications and did not utilize duplicate detection mechanisms, allowing the error to persist.
violationSummary: Personal information (names, addresses, SINs) was unintentionally exposed to unauthorized recipients due to mechanical failure and inadequate human oversight and error detection protocols.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: A mechanical malfunction in mail-sorting equipment, combined with a technician's failure to report duplications or use duplicate detection mechanisms.
whyTheyWereWrong: Recipients received forms destined for other individuals containing names, addresses, and encoded Social Insurance Numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: The technician recalibrated equipment and allowed the job to continue
claimsVsReality.reality: The technician did not use available duplicate detection mechanisms or notify management, allowing the error to propagate to 11,900 forms and 44 confirmed cases of unauthorized disclosure

outcome: The complaint was determined to be well-founded. Human Resources and Skills Development Canada undertook corrective measures including improvements to mailing equipment functioning, review and strengthening of quality-control procedures, and mandatory updates to employee training on Privacy Act obligations and related policies. companyLongDescription: Facebook, founded in 2004, is the world's largest social media platform with over 200 million users worldwide and approximately 12 million in Canada as of 2009. The platform enables users to create profiles, share content, and communicate with friends and family. Facebook's business model relies on collecting user data to enable targeted advertising. The platform's explosive growth raised significant questions about how personal information should be protected in the social media context.
caseDescription: Facebook was found to contravene PIPEDA in multiple areas including insufficient transparency about collection and use of date of birth, problematic default privacy settings that did not align with user expectations, inadequate disclosure of advertising practices, and inadequate safeguards for third-party application access to personal information. While some allegations were resolved through corrective measures, significant unresolved issues remained regarding third-party applications and non-user data.
violationSummary: Facebook's primary violations involved the secondary use of personal information for advertising, targeted marketing to third-party developers, and uses not clearly disclosed to users at time of collection. The company used profile data for purposes (advertising, application access) beyond the primary purpose of enabling social networking.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Facebook collected users' dates of birth without adequate explanation, set overly permissive default privacy settings that exposed personal information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Canadian Facebook users had no meaningful control over their personal information because Facebook's opaque practices meant they could not understand what data was collected.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook provides users with sufficient transparency about why date of birth is required and how it will be used.
claimsVsReality.reality: Facebook's explanation via a pop-up link was inadequate; users lacked clear information about data collection purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook's default privacy settings align with user expectations about who can see their information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Default settings were overly permissive and exposed personal information in ways users did not anticipate or understand.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook clearly discloses its advertising practices and how user data enables targeted ads.
claimsVsReality.reality: Facebook failed to adequately explain how personal information was collected and used for advertising targeting purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Facebook has adequate safeguards to protect user data when third-party developers access it through applications.
claimsVsReality.reality: Facebook did not have sufficient safeguards in place and failed to ensure meaningful consent was obtained before developers accessed user and friend data.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2.3 - Purposes must be specified at or before time of collection
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to clearly explain purposes for collecting date of birth; used vague language like 'preserving integrity of site'
violations: Failed to clearly explain purposes for collecting date of birth; used vague language like 'preserving integrity of site'
Did not specify at time of collection that DOB would be used for targeted advertising
Did not clearly define what 'profile information' means or clarify that hidden DOB could still be used for ads

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 - Organizations must make reasonable effort to advise individuals of purposes and ensure consent is meaningful
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide clear explanation of all purposes for DOB collection in registration pop-up
violations: Failed to provide clear explanation of all purposes for DOB collection in registration pop-up
Did not adequately explain differences between Facebook Ads and Social Ads
Did not provide sufficient time-of-collection notification about advertising purposes
Failed to inform users that hiding DOB from profile does not exempt it from advertising use

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.5 - Reasonable expectations of individuals are relevant in obtaining consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Default privacy settings for photo albums set to 'Everyone' did not align with user reasonable expectations
violations: Default privacy settings for photo albums set to 'Everyone' did not align with user reasonable expectations
Default public search listing exposed user information beyond what users would reasonably expect
Users not directed to privacy settings at registration, impeding informed choice

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.3 - Cannot require consent to collection, use, or disclosure beyond that necessary to fulfill explicitly specified purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Required users to consent to Facebook Ads as condition of service without clear explanation of necessity
violations: Required users to consent to Facebook Ads as condition of service without clear explanation of necessity
Required users to consent to disclosure of information to third-party developers beyond what was necessary for application function

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 - Organizations must protect personal information with appropriate safeguards
regulatoryFindings.description: Did not adequately monitor or screen third-party application developers for legitimate purposes
violations: Did not adequately monitor or screen third-party application developers for legitimate purposes
Relied on user reporting rather than systematic audit of developer compliance
Did not provide technological barriers to prevent developer misuse of user data
Provided access to user information beyond what was necessary for application operation

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.1.3 - Organizations remain responsible for personal information transferred to third parties for processing
regulatoryFindings.description: Attempted to disclaim responsibility for third-party developer activities
violations: Attempted to disclaim responsibility for third-party developer activities
Failed to implement adequate contractual and technical safeguards against misuse

outcome: The Assistant Privacy Commissioner issued a Report of Findings on July 16, 2009, concluding that Facebook contravened PIPEDA in multiple respects. With respect to date of birth collection, advertising practices, and default privacy settings, the allegations were deemed well-founded but resolved based on Facebook's agreement to implement corrective measures including: revising language in pop-ups to clarify purposes, expanding the Privacy Policy to explain advertising practices, implementing a Privacy Wizard tool, introducing per-object privacy controls, and improving notification at registration. Facebook agreed to follow a 'notice and comment period' with users before implementing language changes. With respect to third-party applications, account deactivation/deletion, deceased user accounts, and non-user personal information, the allegations were deemed well-founded but remained unresolved, as Facebook had not agreed to fully implement all recommendations. The Commissioner requested follow-up verification of implementation within 30 days.
companyNow: Meta Platforms (formerly Facebook) remains the dominant social networking company globally, though it now operates multiple platforms including Instagram and WhatsApp. The company faces ongoing regulatory scrutiny regarding privacy practices, data handling, and algorithmic transparency.
dataType: Profile information (name, email, date of birth, gender, photos, location, interests, relationship status, education, work history, network affiliations, friend lists, activity logs, wall posts, dating preferences, political views)

companyDescription: Accusearch Inc., operating as Abika.com, was a U.S.-based online people-search service that compiled and sold personal information about individuals, including non-public telephone records and psychological profiles.
companyLongDescription: Accusearch Inc. (doing business as Abika.com) operated as a virtual person-to-person internet search engine connecting customers with information brokers, private investigators, and data aggregators to conduct searches on individuals. The company offered services including telephone record lookups and psychological profile generation based on data mining public and private databases, consumer records, and social media activity. Abika marketed psychological profiling services as tools for dating screening, hiring decisions, and litigation strategy. The company operated without meaningful consent mechanisms for individuals being searched, claiming paid searches required no consent while its free search consent process was easily circumvented.
caseDescription: Accusearch (operating as Abika.com) collected, used, and disclosed personal information of Canadian individuals without their knowledge or consent through its online search services. The company obtained sensitive non-public telephone records and other personal data from customers and vendors without screening for appropriateness of purposes, including requests to investigate current or former romantic partners. The company also compiled and sold psychological profiles based on data mining techniques without proper factual basis or consent.
violationSummary: Accusearch systematically disclosed non-public personal information (telephone records, addresses, call histories) to third parties without the knowledge or consent of the individuals whose data was being sold, and failed to screen requests to prevent disclosure for inappropriate purposes such as relationship investigations.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Accusearch operated Abika.com, which collected and sold personal information including telephone records.
whyTheyWereWrong: Canadians had their phone records and personal data sold to people investigating romantic partners and conducting surveillance, exposing them to stalking, harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Abika is a person-to-person search engine like Google and Yahoo that connects people seeking information to those who have it.
claimsVsReality.reality: Abika systematically collected, compiled, and sold non-public personal information including telephone records and psychological profiles without subjects' knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Only free searches require consent; paid searches are completely private and confidential.
claimsVsReality.reality: Paid searches routinely involved disclosure of personal information about non-consenting individuals, including phone records sold to requestors investigating romantic partners and conducting unauthorized surveillance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Psychological profiles are literary and artistic opinions created based on information provided by the requestor.
claimsVsReality.reality: Psychological profiles were compiled from data mining public and private databases, behavioral records, consumer activities, and social media without subjects' knowledge, generating false and inaccurate psychological assessments used to evaluate and screen individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company does not collect or maintain databases on people.
claimsVsReality.reality: Abika maintained extensive databases of personal information obtained from customers and vendors, including home addresses, telephone numbers, telephone records, and compiled profiles on hundreds of Canadians.

claimsVsReality.claim: There is no private or personal information collected or disclosed through Accusearch services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Canadian paralegal firms used Abika to obtain home addresses, telephone numbers, and telephone records on individuals, which were then forwarded to private investigation companies and their U.S. clients without the knowledge or consent of the subjects.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Knowledge and consent of the individual are required for collection, use, or disclosure of personal information except where inappropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: Collected and disclosed telephone records and personal information of Canadians without their knowledge or consent
violations: Collected and disclosed telephone records and personal information of Canadians without their knowledge or consent
Made more than 100 requests to vendors for telephone records of persons living in Canada between February 2005 and April 2006
Processed 668 orders from Canadian customers between October 2002 and July 2006 resulting in collection of personal information without subjects' knowledge or consent
Failed to implement adequate consent mechanisms; free search consent process could be circumvented by entering any email address

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 – Personal information shall be as accurate, complete, and up-to-date as necessary for purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Compiled and disclosed psychological profiles with unverified and questionable accuracy; complaint not well-founded due to lack of objective verifiable evidence of inaccuracy
violations: Compiled and disclosed psychological profiles with unverified and questionable accuracy; complaint not well-founded due to lack of objective verifiable evidence of inaccuracy

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA subsection 5(3) – Organization may collect, use, or disclose personal information only for purposes a reasonable person would consider appropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: Accepted and fulfilled requests without screening for appropriateness of purposes
violations: Accepted and fulfilled requests without screening for appropriateness of purposes
Knowingly collected and disclosed personal information for highly inappropriate purposes including investigating current or former romantic partners
Failed to establish policies or practices to screen requests according to appropriateness of requestor's purposes
Disregarded consumer safety and well-being concerns

outcome: Privacy Commissioner found that complaints relating to knowledge/consent and appropriateness of purposes were well-founded. Commissioner recommended that Abika cease collecting, using, and disclosing personal information of Canadians without their knowledge and consent. Abika was directed to respond within 30 days with implementation plan. Abika requested extensions and ultimately advised it would seek Canadian legal counsel but did not provide substantive compliance response within extended timeframe. No monetary penalty was imposed by the Privacy Commissioner; however, Abika had previously been subject to a December 2007 U.S. Federal District Court permanent injunction and ordered to disgorge $199,692.71, with compliance requirements for five years. The U.S. Court of Appeals affirmed this judgment in June 2009.
companyNow: Abika.com was permanently shut down by court order in 2007 following an FTC injunction. Accusearch Inc. and its owner were subject to strict compliance measures and financial penalties in the U.S., and the company ceased operations thereafter.
dataType: Telephone records, call history, home addresses, phone numbers, personal background information, psychological profiles

companyDescription: A Canadian bank providing mortgage and financial services to customers holding personal and joint accounts.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian financial institution offering mortgage lending and banking services to retail customers. The bank employs mortgage specialists who meet with customers to process joint mortgage applications. The bank maintains practices for handling sensitive financial information disclosure in joint application scenarios.
caseDescription: A bank mortgage specialist disclosed a customer's financial information to his wife without meaningful consent during a joint mortgage application meeting. The bank failed to adequately inform the couple about the purposes and scope of financial information disclosure before proceeding with the meeting.
violationSummary: The bank disclosed personal financial information without obtaining meaningful consent from the individual. Although the bank argued for implied consent, the disclosure occurred without proper knowledge-based notification to the complainant, and the circumstances (wife's clear distress and unawareness) should have signaled that implied consent was inappropriate.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A bank mortgage specialist disclosed a customer's financial information, including credit reports.
whyTheyWereWrong: The husband was unaware his financial details would be shared with his wife, causing her distress when she discovered debt information she did not expect.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank maintained that the mortgage specialist had the husband's implicit consent to disclose his information to his wife, given that the purpose of the meeting was to discuss a joint mortgage.
claimsVsReality.reality: The husband was unaware that his financial information would be disclosed to his wife, and the bank's mortgage specialist did not follow the bank's own standard practice of informing joint applicants about the disclosure of assets and liabilities beforehand.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank argued that its usual practice was to have an initial discussion with joint applicants to inform them that a discussion of their assets and liabilities would be necessary, and that if neither party raises an objection, implied consent could be presumed.
claimsVsReality.reality: In this case, the mortgage specialist did not follow the bank's usual practice of informing the couple about the need to discuss their financial information, and the wife's clear distress upon learning of undisclosed accounts should have signaled that the presumption of implied consent was no longer reasonable.

claimsVsReality.claim: The mortgage specialist did not recall disclosing information to the wife about the complainant's line of credit or credit card account, and maintained she would not have done so because the balances were too insignificant to mention.
claimsVsReality.reality: The Assistant Commissioner found it more probable than not that the mortgage specialist did display the complainant's line-of-credit information and credit card balance on her laptop to reassure the wife after the initial mistaken disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Meaningful Consent: Organizations must obtain knowledge-based consent before disclosing personal information, with clear understanding of purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank failed to make reasonable effort to inform the couple of purposes for financial information disclosure to one another
violations: Bank failed to make reasonable effort to inform the couple of purposes for financial information disclosure to one another
Bank did not follow its own stated practice of informing joint applicants about asset and liability discussions before proceeding
Disclosure occurred without establishing reasonable knowledge basis for inferring the complainant's consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 – Knowledge Requirement: Individuals must have knowledge of purposes before consent is meaningful
regulatoryFindings.description: Mortgage specialist did not inform the complainant about the scope of financial information that would be discussed with his spouse
violations: Mortgage specialist did not inform the complainant about the scope of financial information that would be discussed with his spouse

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.5 – Spousal Disclosure Standard: Personal information must not be disclosed to spouses without explicit consent, requiring high standard of notification
regulatoryFindings.description: Financial information was disclosed to spouse without adequate prior notice or explicit consent from the account holder
violations: Financial information was disclosed to spouse without adequate prior notice or explicit consent from the account holder

outcome: The complaint was found to be well-founded. The Assistant Commissioner concluded that the bank did not have meaningful consent for the disclosure of the complainant's financial information to his wife. However, because the incident resulted from a one-time employee error and the bank responded appropriately and had adopted reasonable practices with respect to protecting joint mortgage applicant information, no monetary penalty was imposed. The bank was required to ensure compliance with consent requirements going forward.
dataType: Financial information, credit reports, line of credit information, credit card balances, debt information

companyDescription: Genica Corporation and its wholly-owned subsidiary Compgeeks.com operated an e-commerce business selling computer systems, peripherals, and consumer electronics online through the www.geeks.com website, collecting sensitive customer payment information during transactions.
companyLongDescription: Genica Corporation and its wholly-owned subsidiary Compgeeks.com operated an e-commerce business selling computer systems, peripherals, and consumer electronics online through the www.geeks.com website, collecting sensitive customer payment information during transactions.
caseDescription: Genica and Compgeeks.com collected sensitive financial information from customers purchasing computer equipment online but failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect it. From January to June 2007, hackers exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to access and export personal data including credit card information of hundreds of customers. The company's privacy policies promised strong security protections that were never actually implemented.
violationSummary: The core violation is the failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access, combined with the storage of sensitive data in unencrypted, plain-text format vulnerable to SQL injection attacks.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Genica Corporation and Compgeeks.com collected sensitive customer credit card information through www.geeks.com but stored it in plain text.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited these preventable security failures between January and June 2007, stealing hundreds of customers' complete credit card numbers, expiration dates.

claimsVsReality.claim: We use secure technology, privacy protection controls and restrictions on employee access to safeguard your personal information
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information was stored in clear, readable text on a network accessible through the website with no encryption

claimsVsReality.claim: We use state of the art technology (e.g., Secure Socket Layer, or SSL) encryption to keep customer personal information as secure as possible
claimsVsReality.reality: Information was not encrypted in storage and was vulnerable to SQL injection attacks that went undetected and unpatched for months

claimsVsReality.claim: We have put in place privacy protection control systems designed to ensure that personal Customer data remains safe and private
claimsVsReality.reality: No adequate network monitoring, intrusion detection, access controls, or vulnerability assessment mechanisms were implemented

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents made express and implied representations that they implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access through privacy policies stating they use 'state of the art technology' and 'privacy protection control systems' to keep customer data 'safe and private'
violations: Respondents made express and implied representations that they implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information against unauthorized access through privacy policies stating they use 'state of the art technology' and 'privacy protection control systems' to keep customer data 'safe and private'

In truth, respondents did not implement reasonable and appropriate security measures: they stored personal information in clear, readable text; failed to assess vulnerability to SQL injection attacks; did not implement defenses; lacked network monitoring and access controls; and failed to employ intrusion detection systems
These false or misleading representations regarding data security constituted deceptive acts affecting commerce

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on March 16, 2009 against Genica Corporation and Compgeeks.com alleging deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act for misrepresentations regarding data security. The case proceeded to enforcement, with respondents required to implement comprehensive information security improvements and ongoing monitoring/compliance obligations.
dataType: Financial data (credit card numbers, expiration dates, security codes), contact information (name, address, email, phone)

companyDescription: ExpatEdge Partners, LLC was a Minnesota-based software and consulting services company providing expatriate payroll and tax management solutions to businesses with international employees.
companyLongDescription: ExpatEdge Partners, LLC was a Minnesota-based software and consulting services company providing expatriate payroll and tax management solutions to businesses with international employees.
caseDescription: ExpatEdge Partners claimed on its website from 2002 to 2009 that it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework. However, the company failed to renew its Safe Harbor self-certification in November 2006 and never renewed it thereafter, while continuing to make false claims of current Safe Harbor compliance on its privacy policies.
violationSummary: The company made false public claims about its participation in a privacy framework designed to protect personal data transfers from the EU. This misrepresentation undermined trust in data protection commitments and breached the confidentiality framework consumers relied upon.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: ExpatEdge Partners disseminated privacy policies from December 2002 through July 2009 falsely claiming it was a current participant in the U.S.-EU Safe Harbor privacy framework.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers and business partners who relied on ExpatEdge's false Safe Harbor claims believed their personal data received EU-standard protections when in fact the company had no valid compliance.

claimsVsReality.claim: ExpatEdge self-certifies the Policy to the U.S. Department of Commerce's Safe Harbor Privacy Program (stated in privacy policies Dec 2002–Jul 2009).
claimsVsReality.reality: ExpatEdge did not renew its Safe Harbor self-certification in November 2006 and remained in 'not current' status on the Commerce Department's public website from that date forward.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ExpatEdge represented expressly and by implication that it was a current participant in the Safe Harbor framework by stating 'ExpatEdge self-certifies the Policy to the U.S. Department of Commerce's Safe Harbor Privacy Program' in privacy policies posted from December 2002 until July 2009.
violations: ExpatEdge represented expressly and by implication that it was a current participant in the Safe Harbor framework by stating 'ExpatEdge self-certifies the Policy to the U.S. Department of Commerce's Safe Harbor Privacy Program' in privacy policies posted from December 2002 until July 2009.

Since November 2006, ExpatEdge was not a current participant in the Safe Harbor, as it failed to renew its self-certification and remained listed with 'not current' status on the Commerce Department's public Safe Harbor list.
The representations were false or misleading because they misled consumers and business partners about the company's actual privacy compliance status and data protection commitments.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on November 9, 2009, alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The company was required to cease making false Safe Harbor claims and comply with FTC orders regarding accurate privacy representations.
