The children subsequently received credit card marketing materials, and the program was slow to rectify the situation despite updating account profiles.
violationSummary: The loyalty program disclosed personal information (names and addresses) of minors to third parties for marketing purposes without proper age verification or consent, violating the principle that personal information should not be disclosed to third parties without appropriate safeguards or consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: The loyalty program failed to record date of birth during telephone registration, causing children members' names.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children received unsolicited credit card marketing materials intended for adults, and the program delayed correcting the problem for six to eight weeks despite updating account profiles.

claimsVsReality.claim: The program does not market to members under 18 and does not provide partner companies with such information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Due to missing date of birth data, children's names and addresses were provided to partner credit card companies, resulting in minors receiving credit card marketing materials.

claimsVsReality.claim: The program would quickly rectify the situation once notified.
claimsVsReality.reality: The program took six to eight weeks to stop sending marketing materials to the children, even after updating account profiles, because marketing lists were generated weeks in advance.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2 requires that personal information be as accurate, complete, and up-to-date as necessary
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to collect date of birth during account registration, preventing identification of minors
violations: Failed to collect date of birth during account registration, preventing identification of minors
Did not maintain accurate age information in member profiles

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 3 requires obtaining meaningful consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed children's names and addresses to partner credit card companies without age-appropriate consent
violations: Disclosed children's names and addresses to partner credit card companies without age-appropriate consent
Did not obtain parental consent for disclosure to third parties

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 limits use and disclosure of personal information and requires retention policies aligned with legal and business purposes
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed personal information of minors to marketing partners contrary to stated policy of not marketing to members under 18
violations: Disclosed personal information of minors to marketing partners contrary to stated policy of not marketing to members under 18
Continued sending marketing materials to children even after account profiles were updated

outcome: The loyalty program acknowledged the breach and sent an apology letter to the complainant. The program confirmed it does not market to members under 18 and does not provide such information to partner companies. Children's names and addresses were deleted from the marketing system and mailings ceased. The program acknowledged the delay in rectifying the situation was excessive. The complaint was settled.
dataType: Names, addresses, age/date of birth
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 3 (Consent for collection, use, and disclosure)
PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (Limiting use, disclosure, and retention)

companyDescription: A condominium corporation responsible for managing a residential complex and enforcing by-laws among unit owners.
companyLongDescription: A condominium corporation is a legal entity that manages a multi-unit residential property and is responsible for enforcing by-laws, collecting fees, and making decisions affecting all unit owners. This corporation became the subject of a privacy complaint when it disclosed details of a dispute with a resident to other owners. The case illustrates how organizations may misunderstand what constitutes protected personal information under privacy law.
caseDescription: A condominium corporation disclosed a letter about a dispute with a resident to all condominium owners without consent, posting it on bulletin boards and including it in board meeting minutes. The corporation initially believed only publicly available contact information was at issue, but the regulator clarified that the sensitive fact of the dispute involvement itself constituted protected personal information requiring consent.
violationSummary: The corporation disclosed personal information (the fact that the complainant was involved in a dispute) to multiple parties without consent, treating it as publicly available when in fact the sensitive nature of the dispute information required protection.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The condominium corporation disclosed a letter about a resident's dispute with the corporation to all owners by posting it on bulletin boards.
whyTheyWereWrong: The corporation exposed the resident's involvement in a private dispute to all condominium owners without permission, damaging her reputation and privacy within her residential community.

claimsVsReality.claim: The personal information at issue consisted only of the resident's name, address, and telephone number, which were publicly available.
claimsVsReality.reality: The sensitive personal information was the fact of the resident's involvement in a dispute with the corporation, which was not public and required consent to disclose.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Personal information should not be disclosed without consent unless authorized by law
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed sensitive personal information (dispute involvement) to all condominium owners without consent
violations: Disclosed sensitive personal information (dispute involvement) to all condominium owners without consent
Posted the letter on bulletin boards making it accessible to multiple parties
Included the dispute information in official Board meeting Minutes

outcome: The condominium corporation was advised that the fact of the complainant's dispute with the corporation constituted protected personal information requiring consent for disclosure. The corporation sent a letter of apology to the complainant, and the matter was settled without monetary penalty.
dataType: Personal information regarding legal dispute involvement, name, address, telephone number
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (Consent for Collection, Use and Disclosure)

companyDescription: Accusearch, Inc., operating under the domain Abika.com, was a data brokerage service that advertised the ability to obtain and sell confidential telephone call detail records from telecommunications carriers to paying clients worldwide, including records for prepaid calling cards and internet-based phone services.
companyLongDescription: Accusearch, Inc., operating under the domain Abika.com, was a data brokerage service that advertised the ability to obtain and sell confidential telephone call detail records from telecommunications carriers to paying clients worldwide, including records for prepaid calling cards and internet-based phone services.
caseDescription: Accusearch obtained and sold confidential telephone call detail records from telecommunications carriers without customer authorization, using false pretenses and fraudulent statements. The company posed as telecommunications customers to induce carrier employees to disclose private phone records, which were then sold to third parties. This practice violated Section 5(a) of the FTC Act by engaging in unfair practices causing substantial consumer injury.
violationSummary: The core violation was unauthorized acquisition and sale of confidential customer proprietary network information held by telecommunications carriers. This constitutes a breach of the confidentiality relationship between carriers and customers, with information disseminated to third parties without consent.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Accusearch obtained and sold confidential customer phone records from telecommunications carriers without authorization by using false pretenses, fraudulent statements.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' telephone call detail records were sold to third parties without knowledge or consent, exposing them to privacy invasion, identity theft, stalking, harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: Accusearch advertised that it could legally obtain 'Details of incoming or outgoing calls from any phone number, prepaid calling card or Internet Phone' with 'Phone searches available for every country of the world.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Accusearch obtained records through fraudulent means — false pretenses, fraudulent statements, stolen documents, and impersonation of telecommunications customers — without any customer authorization, violating federal law.

claimsVsReality.claim: Accusearch presented itself as a legitimate service providing accessible phone record information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Accusearch's business model depended entirely on deceiving telecommunications carriers and violating consumer privacy rights; the practices were 'entirely invisible' to consumers who could not avoid or consent to the disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Accusearch obtained and sold customer proprietary network information (phone records) without knowledge or authorization, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
violations: Accusearch obtained and sold customer proprietary network information (phone records) without knowledge or authorization, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits.

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(1), provides that telecommunications carriers shall only use, disclose, or permit access to customer proprietary network information except as required by law or with customer approval.
regulatoryFindings.description: Accusearch induced carrier employees to disclose confidential customer phone records through false pretenses and fraudulent statements without customer knowledge or written authorization.
violations: Accusearch induced carrier employees to disclose confidential customer phone records through false pretenses and fraudulent statements without customer knowledge or written authorization.

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(2), provides that customer phone records may only be disclosed upon affirmative written customer request to a customer-designated person.
regulatoryFindings.description: Accusearch obtained customer phone records without any customer authorization and sold them to third parties without designation by the customer.
violations: Accusearch obtained customer phone records without any customer authorization and sold them to third parties without designation by the customer.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Injunctive and Other Equitable Relief in the U.S. District Court for the District of Wyoming on April 31, 2006, seeking permanent injunction against FTC Act violations, rescission of contracts, restitution to injured consumers, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The complaint alleges unfair practices in obtaining and selling confidential customer phone records without authorization.
companyNow: Accusearch, Inc. (operating as Abika.com) was the subject of FTC enforcement action in 2006. The current operational status of the company is unknown; historical records indicate it was a phone records data broker service.
dataType: Telephone call detail records (customer proprietary network information), phone numbers, call patterns, telecommunications usage data
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices
Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(1) – prohibition on unauthorized disclosure of customer proprietary network information
Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(2) – requirement for affirmative written customer request to disclose records

companyDescription: Information Search, Inc. was a data broker or information services company engaged in the collection and handling of customer phone records and related personal data.
companyLongDescription: Information Search, Inc. was a data broker or information services company engaged in the collection and handling of customer phone records and related personal data.
caseDescription: Information Search, Inc. was sued by the FTC for unauthorized access to and disclosure of customer phone records. The defendants admitted to obtaining and handling phone records but disputed whether those records were confidential. The case involved allegations of improper data handling practices.
violationSummary: The defendants admitted to handling customer phone records but disputed confidentiality status. The core issue involves unauthorized access to and handling of personal phone records, which constitutes a breach of confidentiality obligations.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Information Search, Inc. obtained and sold customer phone records without proper authorization or confidentiality protections to unauthorized third parties.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers' telephone numbers and personal contact information were exposed to data brokers and other commercial entities without consent, enabling unsolicited marketing calls.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customer phone records were not confidential
claimsVsReality.reality: The FTC and legal standards treat personal phone records as confidential consumer data requiring protective measures

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Information Search, Inc. obtained and handled customer phone records without appropriate confidentiality safeguards and authorized access controls
violations: Information Search, Inc. obtained and handled customer phone records without appropriate confidentiality safeguards and authorized access controls

outcome: Second Amended Answer filed by defendants on June 29, 2006. Defendants denied allegations in paragraphs 1, 11-16, and 17, admitted allegations in paragraphs 2-7, and specifically denied that customer phone records were confidential while admitting to paragraphs 9-10. The case proceeded through litigation with both sides presenting competing claims regarding the nature and confidentiality status of the data.
dataType: Customer phone records, personal telephone data

companyDescription: CEO Group, Inc., operating under the name Check Em Out, was a data broker that obtained and sold confidential telecommunications customer records to clients via their website. The company charged fees for access to customer phone records, including detailed call history and billing information.
companyLongDescription: CEO Group, Inc., operating under the name Check Em Out, was a data broker that obtained and sold confidential telecommunications customer records to clients via their website. The company charged fees for access to customer phone records, including detailed call history and billing information.
caseDescription: CEO Group, Inc. and its founder Scott Joseph obtained and sold confidential customer telephone records from telecommunications carriers without customer authorization. They used false pretenses, fraudulent statements, and deceptive practices—including posing as customers—to induce carrier employees to disclose protected customer proprietary network information. The company then sold these records to third parties for profit.
violationSummary: The defendants obtained protected customer proprietary network information (CPNI) through deceptive means and sold it to third parties without customer consent, directly breaching confidentiality obligations under the Telecommunications Act.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: CEO Group, Inc. and founder Scott Joseph obtained confidential customer phone records from telecommunications carriers using false pretenses, fraudulent statements.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' private telephone call records, billing names, addresses, and toll call histories were sold to unknown third parties without consent, enabling stalking, harassment.

claimsVsReality.claim: CEO Group advertised: 'Give us any residential, cellular or business telephone number and we will research the billing name and billing address, a record of toll calls made from that number and other valuable information.'
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no authorization from customers to access or provide this information; it obtained records through deception and fraud by posing as customers or using false pretenses with carrier employees.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company offered to obtain phone records as a legitimate business service for customers with a valid need.
claimsVsReality.reality: Account holders never authorized the company to obtain access to or sell their confidential records; the practices were entirely invisible to affected consumers who could not reasonably avoid the harm.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants deceptively obtained customer proprietary network information by using false pretenses, fraudulent statements, and misrepresentations to telecommunications carrier employees
violations: Defendants deceptively obtained customer proprietary network information by using false pretenses, fraudulent statements, and misrepresentations to telecommunications carrier employees
Defendants sold confidential customer phone records to third parties without customer knowledge or authorization
Defendants advertised on their website that they could obtain customer phone records and toll call histories for a fee, inducing customer harm

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(1) requires that telecommunications carriers may only use, disclose, or permit access to customer proprietary network information as permitted by law or with customer approval for specific purposes related to the service.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants caused telecommunications carrier employees to disclose protected customer proprietary network information in violation of carrier obligations
violations: Defendants caused telecommunications carrier employees to disclose protected customer proprietary network information in violation of carrier obligations
The disclosure was obtained through deception and misrepresentation, not through lawful means or customer authorization

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(2) restricts disclosure of customer phone records to affirmative written request by the customer only.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants obtained customer phone records without affirmative written customer request or authorization
violations: Defendants obtained customer phone records without affirmative written customer request or authorization
Defendants used false pretenses to induce carrier officers, employees, or agents to disclose records in violation of this restriction

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Injunction and Other Equitable Relief seeking permanent injunctive relief, rescission of contracts, restitution, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains, and other equitable remedies. The complaint alleged violations of FTC Act Section 5(a) for surreptiously obtaining and selling confidential customer phone records without customer knowledge or authorization. The Court was requested to: (a) permanently enjoin Defendants from violating the FTC Act; (b) award equitable relief including rescission of contracts, restitution, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains; and (c) award the FTC costs of bringing the action and other equitable relief.
dataType: Telephone call records, billing information, toll call history

companyDescription: ChoicePoint was a leading provider of credentialing information and consumer data, operating thousands of databases containing billions of personal records on consumers. It furnished consumer reports and public record information to over 50,000 subscribers including insurance companies, landlords, banks, private investigators, and debt collectors.
companyLongDescription: ChoicePoint was a leading provider of credentialing information and consumer data, operating thousands of databases containing billions of personal records on consumers. It furnished consumer reports and public record information to over 50,000 subscribers including insurance companies, landlords, banks, private investigators, and debt collectors.
caseDescription: ChoicePoint, a major data broker with billions of consumer records, failed to implement reasonable procedures to verify subscriber identities before furnishing sensitive consumer reports. Fraudsters obtained unauthorized access to 163,000 consumers' personal information including SSNs and credit reports, resulting in at least 800 confirmed identity theft cases. The company made false public claims about its rigorous credentialing and monitoring practices.
violationSummary: ChoicePoint failed to maintain reasonable security procedures and practices to verify subscriber identities and monitor for unauthorized activity, resulting in unauthorized disclosure of sensitive consumer information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: ChoicePoint sold consumer reports containing Social Security numbers, dates of birth, and financial data to applicants with false credentials.
whyTheyWereWrong: 163,000 consumers had their sensitive personal information exposed to identity thieves, resulting in at least 800 confirmed cases of identity theft and financial fraud against real people.

claimsVsReality.claim: ChoicePoint uses administrative, technical, personnel, and physical safeguards to protect the confidentiality and security of personally identifiable consumer information
claimsVsReality.reality: ChoicePoint failed to implement reasonable verification procedures and approved accounts with fraudulent credentials, resulting in 163,000 consumers' data being exposed

claimsVsReality.claim: Every ChoicePoint customer must successfully complete a rigorous credentialing process
claimsVsReality.reality: ChoicePoint approved subscriber applications containing obvious red flags including commercial mail drops, contradictory business addresses, suspended businesses, and suspicious patterns without further investigation

claimsVsReality.claim: ChoicePoint monitors the use of its public record information to ensure appropriate use
claimsVsReality.reality: ChoicePoint failed to monitor subscribers for unauthorized activity despite receiving multiple law enforcement subpoenas between 2001 and 2005 alerting it to fraudulent accounts

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 604(a) prohibits consumer reporting agencies from furnishing consumer reports except for specified permissible purposes.
regulatoryFindings.description: ChoicePoint furnished consumer reports to subscribers who did not have a permissible purpose to obtain such reports
violations: ChoicePoint furnished consumer reports to subscribers who did not have a permissible purpose to obtain such reports

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 607(a) requires consumer reporting agencies to maintain reasonable procedures to limit furnishing of consumer reports and to make reasonable efforts to verify the identity of each new prospective user and the uses certified by such users prior to furnishing such user a consumer report.
regulatoryFindings.description: ChoicePoint failed to utilize readily available business verification products to identify commercial mail drops
violations: ChoicePoint failed to utilize readily available business verification products to identify commercial mail drops
ChoicePoint accepted contradictory or illogical application information without further inquiry
ChoicePoint approved applications with blank critical information such as business license numbers
ChoicePoint failed to examine or audit subscribers to ensure permissible use
ChoicePoint failed to monitor subscribers for unauthorized activity despite receiving law enforcement subpoenas

regulatoryFindings.act: FCRA Section 607(a) also prohibits furnishing a consumer report to any person if the agency has reasonable grounds for believing that the consumer report will not be used for a permissible purpose.
regulatoryFindings.description: ChoicePoint furnished consumer reports under circumstances where it had reasonable grounds for believing the reports would not be used for permissible purposes
violations: ChoicePoint furnished consumer reports under circumstances where it had reasonable grounds for believing the reports would not be used for permissible purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: ChoicePoint made false and misleading representations about implementing reasonable and appropriate security measures and a rigorous credentialing process for subscribers
violations: ChoicePoint made false and misleading representations about implementing reasonable and appropriate security measures and a rigorous credentialing process for subscribers
ChoicePoint failed to employ reasonable security measures to protect consumers' personal information

outcome: The complaint seeks permanent injunction, consumer redress, disgorgement, monetary civil penalties up to $2,500 per violation of the FCRA, and other equitable relief. The case was filed on January 30, 2006 in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Georgia.
companyNow: ChoicePoint was acquired by Experian in 2008 and ceased to exist as an independent entity. Today it operates as part of Experian's consumer reporting and data services division.
dataType: Names, Social Security numbers, dates of birth, bank account numbers, credit card account numbers, credit histories, public records
legalBasisViolated: FCRA Section 604(a) – furnishing consumer reports without permissible purpose
FCRA Section 607(a) – failure to maintain reasonable procedures to verify identity of prospective users
FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FCRA Section 621(a) – pattern or practice of knowing violations

companyDescription: CardSystems Solutions, Inc. was a Delaware corporation based in Tucson, Arizona that provided authorization processing services for credit and debit card purchases. The company processed card purchases totaling at least $15 billion annually for approximately 119,000 merchants.
companyLongDescription: CardSystems Solutions, Inc. was a Delaware corporation based in Tucson, Arizona that provided authorization processing services for credit and debit card purchases. The company processed card purchases totaling at least $15 billion annually for approximately 119,000 merchants.
caseDescription: CardSystems Solutions failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect sensitive payment card data stored on its systems. A hacker exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to steal magnetic stripe data for tens of millions of credit and debit cards, resulting in millions of dollars in fraudulent purchases and widespread card cancellations affecting consumers.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures directly resulted in a data breach exposing millions of payment card records, demonstrating inadequate information security practices.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: CardSystems Solutions stored credit and debit card magnetic stripe data in vulnerable formats for up to 30 days, failed to assess SQL injection vulnerabilities.
whyTheyWereWrong: A hacker exploited these failures to steal magnetic stripe data for tens of millions of cards, enabling fraudulent purchases that forced banks to cancel.

claimsVsReality.claim: CardSystems provided secure payment authorization processing services to merchants.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company stored sensitive payment card data in vulnerable formats, failed to implement basic security controls, and was compromised by a hacker who exploited SQL injection vulnerabilities to exfiltrate tens of millions of payment card records over several months.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: CardSystems failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information it stored, causing substantial injury to consumers through data breach exposing tens of millions of payment card records with complete magnetic stripe data, security codes, and cardholder information.
violations: CardSystems failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information it stored, causing substantial injury to consumers through data breach exposing tens of millions of payment card records with complete magnetic stripe data, security codes, and cardholder information.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint against CardSystems on September 5, 2006, alleging violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act for failing to provide reasonable security for personal information. The complaint initiated an enforcement proceeding to address the company's inadequate security practices that led to the massive payment card data breach.
companyNow: CardSystems Solutions was acquired by Global Payments Inc. in 2007, following the breach and regulatory action. The breach became one of the largest payment card data breaches at that time.
dataType: Financial data, credit and debit card information, magnetic stripe data, customer names, card numbers, expiration dates, security codes

company: Nations Title Agency, Inc. (NTA) / Nations Holding Company (NHC)
companyDescription: Nations Title Agency, Inc. was a Kansas-based financial services company specializing in real estate settlement services, residential closings, title abstracts, title commitments, appraisals, foreclosure management, and asset disposition. The company routinely handled sensitive consumer financial information including Social Security numbers, bank accounts, mortgage data, and credit histories.
companyLongDescription: Nations Title Agency, Inc. was a Kansas-based financial services company specializing in real estate settlement services, residential closings, title abstracts, title commitments, appraisals, foreclosure management, and asset disposition. The company routinely handled sensitive consumer financial information including Social Security numbers, bank accounts, mortgage data, and credit histories.
caseDescription: Nations Title Agency and its parent company failed to implement reasonable security safeguards for sensitive consumer financial information, resulting in a 2004 hacker breach and the discovery of discarded documents containing personal data in an unsecured dumpster in 2005. The company made false claims about its security measures while maintaining inadequate policies for data protection, employee screening, access controls, and service provider oversight.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards required by the Safeguards Rule, resulting in actual unauthorized access and exposure of customer information through both network breaches and physical carelessness.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Nations Title Agency failed to implement reasonable security measures for consumer data, including risk assessments, access controls, employee training, secure document disposal.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited these failures to access thousands of customers' Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and mortgage information in April 2004.

claimsVsReality.claim: NTA maintains physical, electronic and procedural safeguards in compliance with federal standards to protect the information and strives to maintain the confidentiality and integrity of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: NTA failed to assess security risks, implement reasonable access controls (like strong passwords), conduct employee screening and training, securely handle and dispose of documents, detect unauthorized access, or conduct security investigations. A hacker gained access to the network in April 2004, and sensitive documents were found discarded in an unsecured dumpster in February 2005.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 501(b) of the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act requires financial institutions to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information by developing a comprehensive written information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information security
violations: Failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information security
Failed to design and implement information safeguards to control identified risks and failed to regularly test and monitor them
Failed to investigate, evaluate, and adjust the information security program in light of known or identified risks
Failed to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive written information security program
Failed to oversee service providers or require them by contract to implement safeguards

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Disseminated false or misleading privacy policy representations claiming to maintain reasonable safeguards and protect customer information from unauthorized access
violations: Disseminated false or misleading privacy policy representations claiming to maintain reasonable safeguards and protect customer information from unauthorized access
Did not implement the reasonable and appropriate security measures claimed in privacy policy despite obtaining and storing highly sensitive consumer financial data

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Privacy of Customer Financial Information Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) requires financial institutions to provide customers with clear and conspicuous notices that accurately reflect their privacy and security policies and practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Disseminated privacy policy that did not accurately reflect actual security policies and practices
violations: Disseminated privacy policy that did not accurately reflect actual security policies and practices
Privacy policy contained false or misleading statements regarding measures implemented to protect consumer personal information

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging violations of the Safeguards Rule, Privacy Rule, and FTC Act Section 5(a) against Nations Title Agency, Nations Holding Company, and Christopher M. Likens. The complaint, issued June 19, 2006, sought a compliance order requiring the respondents to develop and implement a comprehensive information security program, conduct regular risk assessments, implement reasonable safeguards, oversee service providers, and maintain accurate privacy policies. The outcome indicates enforcement action via consent order requiring ongoing monitoring and compliance with data security standards.
companyNow: Nations Title Agency and Nations Holding Company operated as part of a real estate title and settlement services business with 57 wholly-owned subsidiaries across twenty states. Current operational status is unknown; the company may have been subject to court-ordered remediation or restructuring following the 2006 enforcement action.
dataType: Financial data, Social Security numbers, bank and credit card account numbers, mortgage information, loan applications, purchase contracts, income histories, credit histories
legalBasisViolated: FTC Standards for Safeguarding Customer Information Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 314
FTC Privacy of Customer Financial Information Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 313

companyDescription: DSW Inc. is a major footwear retailer operating approximately 190 stores across 32 U.S. states as of 2005-2006, selling men's and women's shoes through physical retail locations. The company processes payment card and check information at point-of-sale terminals across its nationwide store network.
companyLongDescription: DSW Inc. is a major footwear retailer operating approximately 190 stores across 32 U.S. states as of 2005-2006, selling men's and women's shoes through physical retail locations. The company processes payment card and check information at point-of-sale terminals across its nationwide store network.
caseDescription: DSW Inc. stored sensitive payment card and checking account data in unencrypted files on inadequately secured computer networks across 190 stores. The company failed to implement basic security measures such as encryption, access controls, and unauthorized access detection. This resulted in a breach compromising approximately 1.44 million credit/debit cards and 96,000 checking accounts, causing fraudulent charges and financial losses to customers.
companyWorth: Unknown (as private subsidiary of Caleres Inc.; Caleres Inc. market cap approximately $1.5B as of recent data)
violationSummary: The core violation was inadequate security controls over personal financial data. DSW failed to implement readily available technical safeguards (encryption, access restrictions, monitoring) that would have prevented unauthorized access, directly resulting in a large-scale data breach affecting millions of payment cards and banking credentials.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: DSW stored sensitive payment and banking information including credit card numbers, debit card security codes.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers exploited these security failures to steal data from approximately 1.44 million credit and debit cards.

claimsVsReality.claim: DSW was operating normal retail payment processing systems to authorize credit cards, debit cards, and checks at point-of-sale.
claimsVsReality.reality: DSW's systems stored sensitive payment data in unencrypted files on unsecured networks, allowing hackers to access and steal data from multiple store locations through inadequately protected wireless access points.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: DSW failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information, specifically: storing sensitive data in multiple files without business justification; failing to use encryption or access controls on wireless networks; storing unencrypted files accessible via commonly known credentials; insufficient network segmentation; and inadequate unauthorized access detection; resulting in compromise of 1.44 million credit/debit cards and 96,385 checking accounts
violations: DSW failed to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal information, specifically: storing sensitive data in multiple files without business justification; failing to use encryption or access controls on wireless networks; storing unencrypted files accessible via commonly known credentials; insufficient network segmentation; and inadequate unauthorized access detection; resulting in compromise of 1.44 million credit/debit cards and 96,385 checking accounts

outcome: The FTC issued a Complaint on March 7, 2006, alleging unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document indicates the initiation of an enforcement proceeding against DSW. Resolution would typically include a Consent Order requiring DSW to implement comprehensive information security measures, maintain reasonable safeguards for personal information, conduct regular security assessments, and submit to monitoring and compliance reporting.
companyNow: DSW Inc. (now operating as Designer Shoe Warehouse) remains in operation as a subsidiary of Caleres Inc. The company continues retail footwear operations and has since implemented enhanced data security protocols in response to this enforcement action and industry standards evolution.
dataType: Financial data (credit card numbers, debit card numbers, expiration dates, security codes, checking account numbers, routing numbers, account numbers), identification data (driver's license numbers and state)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: 77 Investigations, Inc. was a California-based company offering to obtain confidential customer phone records and other personal information. The company advertised services to locate unlisted cell phone numbers and obtain phone bills through websites, operating from multiple addresses across California, Florida, Colorado, and Tennessee.
companyLongDescription: 77 Investigations, Inc. was a California-based company offering to obtain confidential customer phone records and other personal information. The company advertised services to locate unlisted cell phone numbers and obtain phone bills through websites, operating from multiple addresses across California, Florida, Colorado, and Tennessee.
caseDescription: 77 Investigations and its president Reginald Kimbro obtained and sold confidential customer phone records from telecommunications carriers without customer authorization. They used false pretenses, fraudulent statements, and impersonation to induce carrier employees to disclose the records, then resold them to clients for a fee.
violationSummary: Defendants obtained confidential customer proprietary network information through fraudulent means and disclosed it to unauthorized third parties without customer knowledge or consent, breaching the confidentiality of telecommunications data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: 77 Investigations obtained confidential customer phone records from telecommunications carriers without authorization using false pretenses, fraudulent documents.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers had their detailed phone records exposed without knowledge or consent, revealing sensitive calling patterns.

claimsVsReality.claim: We can obtain phone bills and call detail records for you if you provide a name and address.
claimsVsReality.reality: Records were obtained by fraudulently impersonating customers to carrier employees and using false pretenses and stolen documents, without actual customer authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: Our services help you find unlisted cell phone numbers and obtain billing information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company was illegally accessing confidential customer proprietary network information protected by the Telecommunications Act and reselling it to unauthorized third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants engaged in unfair practices by obtaining and selling confidential customer phone records without customer knowledge or consent, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits.
violations: Defendants engaged in unfair practices by obtaining and selling confidential customer phone records without customer knowledge or consent, causing substantial injury to consumers that was not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits.

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(1) provides that except as required by law or with customer approval, telecommunications carriers receiving customer proprietary network information shall only use or disclose it in provision of the telecommunications service or related services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants, without authorization from customers, obtained customer proprietary network information (phone records) through false pretenses and impersonation of customers to carrier employees, then sold the information to third parties.
violations: Defendants, without authorization from customers, obtained customer proprietary network information (phone records) through false pretenses and impersonation of customers to carrier employees, then sold the information to third parties.

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(2) requires customer phone records be disclosed only upon affirmative written request by the customer to a person designated by the customer.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants disclosed customer phone records to third-party clients without any affirmative written request from or designation by the actual customers whose records were involved.
violations: Defendants disclosed customer phone records to third-party clients without any affirmative written request from or designation by the actual customers whose records were involved.

outcome: The FTC filed a complaint seeking permanent injunctive relief, rescission of contracts, restitution, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The complaint alleged unfair practices under FTC Act Section 5(a) in connection with surreptitiously obtaining and selling confidential customer phone records.
dataType: Telephone call detail records, billing information, customer phone records
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Far West Credit, Inc. was a Utah-based consumer reporting agency that assembled and evaluated consumer credit information for the mortgage industry, creating reports by merging data from nationwide credit bureaus with supplemental documentation from mortgage brokers.
companyLongDescription: Far West Credit, Inc. was a Utah-based consumer reporting agency that assembled and evaluated consumer credit information for the mortgage industry, creating reports by merging data from nationwide credit bureaus with supplemental documentation from mortgage brokers.
caseDescription: Far West Credit, a consumer reporting agency, failed to follow reasonable procedures to verify consumer credit information before including it in reports used for mortgage approvals. The company accepted false documentation from mortgage brokers with financial interests in loan completion, resulting in fraudulent reports used for FHA-insured mortgages that subsequently defaulted, causing losses to taxpayers.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of consumer reports, compromising the security and reliability of critical financial information used in lending decisions.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Far West Credit accepted and incorporated unverified credit account documentation from mortgage brokers into consumer reports without adequate review.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers received fraudulent credit reports containing fabricated trade lines, causing them to qualify for mortgages they should not have received.

claimsVsReality.claim: Far West Credit would accept consumer-provided or broker-provided documentation to supplement insufficient credit histories from nationwide bureaus.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company added false and fabricated account information to reports without adequate verification, including accounts from utility and cable companies that did not service the consumers' geographic areas, and reused the same fraudulent documents for multiple unrelated individuals.

claimsVsReality.claim: The documentation provided by Keystone showed legitimate sources of credit and credit status.
claimsVsReality.reality: Much of the documentation was false, presented information that warranted careful review or inquiry, and contained verifiable red flags that should have triggered additional verification procedures.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 607(b) of the FCRA requires consumer reporting agencies to follow reasonable procedures to assure maximum possible accuracy of information contained in consumer reports that they disseminate.
regulatoryFindings.description: Far West Credit failed to adequately review and verify credit information provided by Keystone Mortgage before adding it to consumer reports.
violations: Far West Credit failed to adequately review and verify credit information provided by Keystone Mortgage before adding it to consumer reports.

Documentation provided by Keystone contained false information and red flags indicating accounts with utility and cable companies that did not service the consumers' areas, and the same documents were used to create records for multiple individuals.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: By failing to follow reasonable procedures under FCRA Section 607(b), Far West Credit engaged in unfair or deceptive practices in creating and disseminating consumer reports with inaccurate information.
violations: By failing to follow reasonable procedures under FCRA Section 607(b), Far West Credit engaged in unfair or deceptive practices in creating and disseminating consumer reports with inaccurate information.

outcome: The United States filed a civil complaint seeking monetary civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation, permanent injunctive relief prohibiting future violations of Section 607 of the FCRA, and such other relief as the court deems just and proper. The case seeks judgment against Far West Credit for knowing violations constituting a pattern or practice.
companyNow: Unknown. The company's current status is not indicated in this January 2006 complaint filing.
dataType: Consumer credit information, financial data, credit history

companyDescription: Integrity Security & Investigation Services, Inc. was a Virginia-based company that advertised online services to obtain confidential customer phone records and financial information from telecommunications carriers and financial institutions for resale to clients.
companyLongDescription: Integrity Security & Investigation Services, Inc. was a Virginia-based company that advertised online services to obtain confidential customer phone records and financial information from telecommunications carriers and financial institutions for resale to clients.
caseDescription: Integrity Security & Investigation Services obtained and sold confidential customer phone records and financial information without customer knowledge or authorization. The company advertised these services online and used false pretenses and fraudulent statements to induce telecommunications carriers and financial institutions to disclose customer data. Defendants resold this sensitive information to third parties for profit.
violationSummary: The company systematically breached the confidentiality of customer proprietary network information and financial data by obtaining it through deception and selling it without authorization, violating the trust relationship between carriers/institutions and customers.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Integrity Security & Investigation Services advertised and sold confidential customer phone records and financial institution data obtained through false pretenses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers had their private phone call records and bank account information disclosed without knowledge or consent, exposing them to privacy invasion, identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Company advertised ability to obtain 'Residential Toll Calls – Local Long Distance', 'Residential Toll Calls – Long Distance', and 'Private Cellular Toll Calls' as legitimate services
claimsVsReality.reality: These records were obtained using false pretenses, fraudulent statements, and misrepresentations to induce carrier employees to disclose confidential customer information, and were sold without customer authorization

claimsVsReality.claim: Company offered to obtain individual account numbers, bank account balances, and credit card transactions from financial institutions
claimsVsReality.reality: These services were provided using false pretenses including impersonating customers, without actual customer authorization or knowledge

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), provides that unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce are declared unlawful.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants obtained and sold confidential customer phone records without customer knowledge or authorization, using false pretenses and fraudulent statements to induce carrier employees to disclose the information.
violations: Defendants obtained and sold confidential customer phone records without customer knowledge or authorization, using false pretenses and fraudulent statements to induce carrier employees to disclose the information.
Defendants obtained and sold customer financial information from financial institutions without authorization, using false pretenses including posing as customers of those institutions.
Defendants' practices caused substantial injury to consumers that was not reasonably avoidable and was not outweighed by countervailing benefits.

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(1) requires that customer proprietary network information may only be used, disclosed, or accessed by telecommunications carriers in provision of the service or related necessary services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendants obtained customer proprietary network information from telecommunications carriers through fraudulent means and without customer approval.
violations: Defendants obtained customer proprietary network information from telecommunications carriers through fraudulent means and without customer approval.
Defendants sold this confidential information to third parties, violating the restriction that such information be used only by the carrier for service provision.

regulatoryFindings.act: Telecommunications Act 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(2) requires that customer phone records may only be disclosed upon affirmative written request by the customer to any person designated by the customer.
regulatoryFindings.description: Customers never provided affirmative written requests for disclosure of their phone records.
violations: Customers never provided affirmative written requests for disclosure of their phone records.
Customers never designated Defendants or their clients as recipients of their confidential phone records.

outcome: The FTC sought permanent injunctive relief, rescission of contracts, restitution, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains, and other equitable relief under Section 13(b) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleges violations of Section 5(a) for unfair practices involving surreptitious obtaining and selling of confidential customer phone records and financial information without knowledge or authorization. Case filed in U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia, Newport News Division, May 1, 2006.
dataType: Customer phone records, financial information, bank account numbers, bank account balances, bank account activity statements
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices
Telecommunications Act 47 U.S.C. § 222(c)(1) – Customer Proprietary Network Information Protection

companyDescription: CIBC is a major Canadian financial services company offering banking, investment, and insurance products to retail and commercial customers.
companyLongDescription: Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce (CIBC) is one of Canada's largest financial institutions, providing a wide range of banking, investment management, and insurance services to millions of customers across North America. Founded in 1961 through the merger of the Imperial Bank of Canada and the Canadian Bank of Commerce, CIBC serves retail, commercial, and institutional clients. The bank operates through multiple business divisions and maintains a significant presence in personal banking, business banking, and wealth management.
caseDescription: CIBC's privacy practices failed when customer personal information was repeatedly misdirected via facsimile to unauthorized recipients in the United States and Quebec over a 3-year period from 2001 to 2004. The bank's employees failed to recognize these incidents as privacy breaches, did not notify most affected customers until after the matter became public, and took ineffective measures to recover the misdirected documents.
violationSummary: Customer personal information was exposed to unauthorized third parties through misdirected faxes, representing unintended disclosure and loss of control over sensitive data to external recipients.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: CIBC misdirected customer faxes containing personal information to unauthorized recipients in the United States.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' private banking information was exposed to strangers and businesses without their knowledge, their trust was breached.

claimsVsReality.claim: CIBC had privacy policies and procedures in place to protect customer personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Employees failed to recognize misdirected faxes as privacy breaches, privacy officials were not informed, and the policies had critical gaps that allowed incidents to occur unaddressed for years.

claimsVsReality.claim: CIBC took measures to recover misdirected personal information and ensure it was destroyed.
claimsVsReality.reality: The bank asked recipients to shred documents but took no other recovery measures; in 2004 it learned a U.S. company had not destroyed documents requested for shredding in 2002.

claimsVsReality.claim: CIBC promptly notified customers when their personal information was compromised.
claimsVsReality.reality: Except for one individual, affected customers were not notified until after the matter became public in 2004, years after misdirection incidents occurred.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act – Safeguards Principle
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to implement effective policies and procedures to protect personal information
violations: Failed to implement effective policies and procedures to protect personal information
Employees were not adequately trained on privacy policies
Privacy officials were not informed of the misdirected fax incidents
Ineffective response mechanisms when privacy breaches were reported

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act – Accountability Principle
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to notify affected customers promptly (except one individual)
violations: Failed to notify affected customers promptly (except one individual)
Did not take adequate measures to recover misdirected personal information
Relied on unverified assurances from third parties to destroy sensitive documents

outcome: CIBC implemented comprehensive remedial measures including: immediate ban on branch faxing across Canada with transition to secure alternative mediums; review and prioritization of all fax processes; implementation of secure fax dialing systems; restructuring of risk assessment and privacy escalation procedures; development of Privacy Issue Escalation Procedures with defined roles and responsibilities; identification and training of privacy contacts in all business areas; launch of privacy intranet site; and development of customer notification protocols. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner recommended full implementation of these safeguards, establishment of immediate notification mechanisms for future breaches, and ongoing reporting to the Assistant Privacy Commissioner. The Audit and Review Branch is verifying compliance and assessing additional communication risks.
companyNow: CIBC remains one of Canada's Big Five banks and continues to provide financial services across retail, commercial, and investment banking sectors.
dataType: Customer personal information, financial data
legalBasisViolated: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) – Principle of fair information practices
PIPEDA – Safeguards principle (failure to implement adequate policies and procedures)

companyDescription: A Canadian bank that provides retail banking services including account management and deposit processing.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian financial institution offering traditional banking services to consumers and businesses. The bank maintains branch locations where customers can conduct deposits, withdrawals, and account inquiries. The institution implements privacy policies and employee training programs to protect customer financial information.
caseDescription: A bank employee disclosed a customer's account balance to the customer's estranged husband without authorization when he came to deposit a support payment. The disclosure caused financial hardship to the customer when the husband withheld the next support payment based on the revealed balance. The bank acknowledged the violation of privacy principles and settled the complaint.
violationSummary: The employee disclosed personal financial information (account balance) to an unauthorized third party without the individual's knowledge or consent, constituting an improper information dissemination.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A bank teller disclosed a customer's account balance to her estranged husband without authorization when he came to deposit a support payment.
whyTheyWereWrong: The disclosure caused the husband to withhold the next support payment, placing the customer in financial hardship because her account funds were already committed to other bill payments.

claimsVsReality.claim: The teller had no recollection of disclosing the account balance and stated it was not her practice to provide balances verbally due to disclosure risks.
claimsVsReality.reality: The estranged husband reported that the teller revealed the account balance to him during his deposit visit, which he then used to justify withholding support payments.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank had adequate privacy policies, procedures, and employee training in place to safeguard customer information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite these measures, an employee disclosed confidential financial information without knowledge or consent, violating PIPEDA Principle 4.3.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Knowledge and consent of the individual are required for the collection, use, or disclosure of personal information, except where inappropriate
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank employee disclosed customer's account balance to the estranged husband without the customer's knowledge or consent
violations: Bank employee disclosed customer's account balance to the estranged husband without the customer's knowledge or consent

outcome: The bank apologized to the complainant. The bank and complainant privately agreed to settle the matter of compensation. No systemic issues were found; the bank had adequate privacy policies, procedures, and employee training in place. The matter was considered settled by the Assistant Privacy Commissioner and the complainant.
dataType: Financial data (bank account balance)

companyDescription: A retail store that processes in-store credit applications for customers making purchases.
companyLongDescription: The retail store operated a point-of-sale credit application system where salespeople collected customer personal information for credit application purposes. The store was responsible for obtaining proper authorization before submitting applicant data to financial institutions for credit adjudication. In this case, the store failed to follow its own procedures by allowing a salesperson to enter customer information and submit an application without first securing the customer's written consent.
caseDescription: A retail store salesperson entered a customer's personal information into the computer system and submitted a credit application without obtaining the customer's signature first. The financial institution issued a credit card based on the unapproved application, and the customer continued receiving unwanted correspondence despite requesting removal. Both the store and financial institution failed to prevent unauthorized use of personal data.
violationSummary: The salesperson processed personal information for credit application purposes without proper authorization (unsigned consent), and the financial institution used the information to establish an account and issue a credit card without valid consent from the individual.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A retail store salesperson entered a customer's personal information into the computer system.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's personal data was used to open a credit account without her consent, and she continued receiving unwanted financial correspondence despite requesting removal.

claimsVsReality.claim: The customer authorized the credit application and submission to the financial institution.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer explicitly rejected the application by tearing up the contract and leaving the store before signing anything.

claimsVsReality.claim: The customer would not receive further correspondence from the financial institution.
claimsVsReality.reality: The customer continued to receive unwanted correspondence from the financial institution despite being told removal would occur.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 3 requires organizations to obtain meaningful consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Salesperson entered personal information into computer system before obtaining complainant's signature
violations: Salesperson entered personal information into computer system before obtaining complainant's signature
Financial institution established credit account and issued card without valid signed consent from the individual
Financial institution continued to send correspondence despite customer's request to stop

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 1 requires organizations to be accountable for personal information in their custody
regulatoryFindings.description: Retail store failed to implement controls to ensure signatures were obtained before data entry
violations: Retail store failed to implement controls to ensure signatures were obtained before data entry
Financial institution failed to verify authorization before processing the application

outcome: Both the retail store and financial institution took corrective action. The store implemented procedures requiring salesperson to obtain the applicant's signature before entering personal information into the computer system. The financial institution removed the inquiry and trade line from the complainant's credit file, purged all information relating to the transaction, and apologized. The complainant and the Privacy Office were satisfied with the remedial actions taken.
dataType: Personal information, credit application data, financial information

companyDescription: Bank 1 and Bank 2 are Canadian financial institutions that provide retail banking services including mortgages and credit products.
companyLongDescription: Bank 1 and Bank 2 are Canadian banks operating in the retail and commercial banking sector. Bank 1 offers mortgage lending services through a centralized mortgage centre, while Bank 2 provides credit products and loan services. Both institutions serve customers across multiple branches in Canada. These were established financial institutions with significant customer bases at the time of the 2005 investigation.
caseDescription: Two Canadian banks misdirected faxes containing personal information to unrelated recipients over multiple years (1998–2003 and 1997–2001 respectively). Bank 1 sent over 100 faxes with mortgage data to a Montreal resident; Bank 2 sent faxes containing credit applications and social insurance numbers of approximately 24 customers to another individual. Both banks failed to respond effectively when recipients reported the errors, and privacy issues only became apparent after media coverage.
violationSummary: Personal information was unintentionally exposed to third parties due to misdirected faxes. The banks failed to implement adequate safeguards to prevent disclosure and did not respond promptly when recipients reported errors. This represents exposure of sensitive personal data (names, addresses, social insurance numbers) to unintended recipients.
violations: Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Bank 1 misdirected over 100 faxes containing mortgage data to a Montreal resident between 1998–2003, and Bank 2 sent faxes with credit applications.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' mortgage details, names, addresses, and social insurance numbers were exposed to unrelated strangers for years, creating identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank 1 employees treated misdirected faxes as isolated keying errors requiring no escalation.
claimsVsReality.reality: Over 100 faxes were misdirected across multiple branches to the same recipient over 5+ years, indicating a systemic fax routing issue, not isolated errors.

claimsVsReality.claim: Bank 2 branch employees were responsive to error notifications from the fax recipient.
claimsVsReality.reality: The recipient's calls reporting misdirected faxes were not returned, and the bank only acted after media coverage forced intervention.

claimsVsReality.claim: Banks had effective privacy policies in place to prevent disclosure of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Privacy policies existed only on paper; employees were unaware of them, no one escalated breaches internally, and management only learned of problems after public reporting.

regulatoryFindings.act: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act – Safeguarding Principle
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank 1 failed to implement adequate controls to prevent misdirected faxes containing mortgage loan information; faxes sent without cover pages; similar fax numbers not pre-programmed to prevent keying errors
violations: Bank 1 failed to implement adequate controls to prevent misdirected faxes containing mortgage loan information; faxes sent without cover pages; similar fax numbers not pre-programmed to prevent keying errors
Bank 2 failed to prevent transmission of credit applications and social insurance numbers to wrong recipient; fax number differed by only one digit from loan centre and no safeguards were in place

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA – Implementation of Policies and Procedures
regulatoryFindings.description: Neither bank had effective internal processes to ensure employees understood privacy implications and proper faxing procedures
violations: Neither bank had effective internal processes to ensure employees understood privacy implications and proper faxing procedures
Employees failed to escalate misdirected fax incidents to management; issues only addressed after public media coverage
Banks did not have adequate complaint processes or breach notification procedures in place initially

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner of Canada found that both banks failed to safeguard personal information and implement adequate privacy policies. Both banks were required to and subsequently implemented the following remedial measures: (1) fully implement planned measures to improve internal communication of privacy breaches; (2) commit to notifying all affected customers of privacy breaches; (3) examine and improve processes for confirming correct fax transmission; (4) implement measures to recover erroneously transmitted customer information; (5) revise privacy policies and procedures to incorporate faxing guidelines; (6) establish pre-programmed fax numbers to minimize keying errors; (7) conduct staff training on faxing guidelines; (8) change vulnerable fax numbers; and (9) implement regular review checklists for branch compliance. Both banks fully implemented all recommendations by the time of the final report (2007).
companyNow: Both banks implemented comprehensive privacy reforms following the 2005 investigation, including enhanced fax protocols, customer notification procedures, and staff training on privacy safeguards.
dataType: Names, addresses, social insurance numbers, mortgage loan information, credit application data
legalBasisViolated: Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) – Principle 1: Accountability

companyDescription: Petco Animal Supplies, Inc. is a major pet supplies and services retailer operating over 636 stores across the United States and a website at PETCO.com. The company sells pet food, supplies, and veterinary services to consumers.
companyLongDescription: Petco Animal Supplies, Inc. is a major pet supplies and services retailer operating over 636 stores across the United States and a website at PETCO.com. The company sells pet food, supplies, and veterinary services to consumers.
caseDescription: Petco made misleading claims that consumer credit card information was encrypted and secure on its website, but failed to implement reasonable security measures. An SQL injection attack in June 2003 exposed credit card numbers in plain text. The company had ignored well-known vulnerabilities that security experts had warned about since 1997.
violationSummary: Petco failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect sensitive personal financial information stored in its database. Data was maintained in unencrypted form despite representations claiming encryption and protection from unauthorized access.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Petco falsely promised customers that their credit card numbers were fully encrypted and secure, but stored the data in plain readable text in its database where attackers could access it using.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers who trusted Petco's security guarantees had their credit card numbers and personal information exposed to unauthorized access by third parties who exploited the unprotected database.

claimsVsReality.claim: Your information is secure. Customers' data is strictly protected against any unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: Credit card numbers were stored in plain readable text in the database and could be accessed by attackers using SQL injection attacks.

claimsVsReality.claim: Entering your credit card number via our secure server is completely safe. The server encrypts all of your information; no one except you can access it.
claimsVsReality.reality: Data was only encrypted during transmission. Once it reached the server, it was decrypted and stored in plain text, accessible to anyone exploiting the SQL injection vulnerability.

claimsVsReality.claim: 100% Safeguard Your Shopping Experience Guarantee means you never have to worry about the safety of your credit card information.
claimsVsReality.reality: An actual SQL injection attack in June 2003 exposed credit card numbers in clear text, directly violating this guarantee.

claimsVsReality.claim: Protecting your information is our number one priority, and your personal data is strictly shielded from unauthorized access.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company failed to implement basic security procedures to detect application vulnerabilities or prevent exploitation, despite industry warnings since 1997.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Petco represented that personal information was maintained in encrypted format and inaccessible to unauthorized persons, but stored credit card data in plain text in the database
violations: Petco represented that personal information was maintained in encrypted format and inaccessible to unauthorized persons, but stored credit card data in plain text in the database

Petco represented that it implemented reasonable and appropriate security measures, but failed to implement simple, readily available defenses against SQL injection attacks despite industry knowledge of the vulnerability since 1997

outcome: FTC issued a complaint on March 4, 2005, alleging unfair or deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The case alleged false claims regarding data security and encryption. Resolution likely included compliance orders requiring implementation of reasonable security measures, regular monitoring, and structural reforms to data protection practices.
companyNow: Petco Animal Supplies was acquired by BC Partners in 2017 and went private. The company continues to operate as a major pet supply retailer with both physical stores and e-commerce operations, having presumably implemented enhanced security practices following the FTC enforcement action.
dataType: Credit card numbers, expiration dates, names, addresses
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Superior Mortgage Corporation was a New Jersey-based residential mortgage lender operating 40 branch offices across 10 states and six websites, collecting sensitive customer financial data during loan applications.
companyLongDescription: Superior Mortgage Corporation was a New Jersey-based residential mortgage lender operating 40 branch offices across 10 states and six websites, collecting sensitive customer financial data during loan applications.
caseDescription: Superior Mortgage Corporation failed to implement reasonable security safeguards required under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act's Safeguards Rule. The company delayed risk assessments, lacked password policies, failed to encrypt sensitive customer information in transit, and misrepresented encryption protection to consumers on its website. Customer data collected through mortgage applications remained unprotected for over two years.
violationSummary: Company failed to implement and maintain reasonable technical and administrative safeguards for customer financial data, leaving it vulnerable to unauthorized access and disclosure.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
