whatTheyDid: Superior Mortgage collected sensitive customer data including Social Security numbers and bank account information but failed to implement adequate security safeguards.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of mortgage applicants' personal financial information including Social Security numbers, credit histories, and bank account details were exposed to interception.

claimsVsReality.claim: All information submitted is handled by SSL encryption from time of submission until receipt
claimsVsReality.reality: SSL encryption was used only during browser-to-server transmission; data was decrypted at third-party service provider server and emailed unencrypted to company offices

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to protect security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information through reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to designate employees to coordinate information security program
violations: Failed to designate employees to coordinate information security program
Failed to identify and assess reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information security until more than one year after Rule's effective date
Failed to design and implement information safeguards to control identified risks
Failed to regularly test or monitor the effectiveness of safeguards
Failed to institute appropriate password policies
Failed to encrypt sensitive customer information emailed outside respondent's computer network
Failed to oversee service providers by contract to ensure customer information protection

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented on www.supmort.com that 'All information submitted is handled by SSL encryption' and that personal information was encrypted using SSL from submission until receipt
violations: Represented on www.supmort.com that 'All information submitted is handled by SSL encryption' and that personal information was encrypted using SSL from submission until receipt
Actually encrypted data only during transmission between browser and server; decrypted and emailed in plain text after reaching service provider's server
False and misleading representation regarding scope and duration of encryption protection

outcome: FTC issued complaint on December 14, 2005, alleging violations of the Safeguards Rule and FTC Act. The complaint did not specify a monetary penalty in the available document pages but required the company to comply with information security requirements and cease deceptive encryption claims.
dataType: Social Security numbers, credit histories, bank and credit card account numbers, names, addresses, dates of birth

companyDescription: Sunbelt Lending Services, Inc. was a mortgage company and financial institution operating primarily in Florida with headquarters in Clearwater. The company collected sensitive customer financial information through loan officers located in Coldwell Banker Residential real estate offices throughout the state.
companyLongDescription: Sunbelt Lending Services, Inc. was a mortgage company and financial institution operating primarily in Florida with headquarters in Clearwater. The company collected sensitive customer financial information through loan officers located in Coldwell Banker Residential real estate offices throughout the state.
caseDescription: Sunbelt Lending Services, a mortgage company, failed to implement reasonable security safeguards to protect customer financial information as required by the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. From 2003 to at least April 2004, the company failed to conduct risk assessments, implement employee training, oversee remote loan officers, or establish contracts requiring service providers to protect customer data. Additionally, Sunbelt failed to provide required privacy notices to online customers.
violationSummary: Sunbelt failed to develop and implement a comprehensive information security program with reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards to protect customer data, resulting in insecurity of sensitive financial information.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Sunbelt Lending Services failed to implement reasonable security policies, conduct risk assessments, train employees, oversee remote loan officers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of customers' sensitive financial data including social security numbers, bank account numbers, income tax returns.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sunbelt collected customer financial information through a secure, professional mortgage lending operation
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked basic security controls, risk assessments, employee training, and oversight mechanisms, leaving sensitive data vulnerable to unauthorized access and misuse

claimsVsReality.claim: Service providers handling customer information were properly vetted and contractually obligated to protect data
claimsVsReality.reality: Sunbelt failed to establish contracts with service providers requiring safeguards or to verify they implemented adequate security measures

regulatoryFindings.act: 16 C.F.R. Part 314 (Safeguards Rule) requires financial institutions to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information by developing a comprehensive written information security program containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to designate an employee to coordinate the information security program
violations: Failed to designate an employee to coordinate the information security program
Failed to identify and assess reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information
Failed to design and implement information safeguards to control identified risks
Failed to regularly test and monitor the effectiveness of safeguards
Failed to oversee service providers or require them by contract to protect customer information
Failed to evaluate and adjust the information security program based on testing results

regulatoryFindings.act: 16 C.F.R. Part 313 (Privacy Rule) requires financial institutions to provide customers with clear and conspicuous notices of privacy policies and practices when the customer relationship is formed and annually thereafter.
regulatoryFindings.description: Failed to provide required privacy notices to online customers from July 2001 to at least April 2004
violations: Failed to provide required privacy notices to online customers from July 2001 to at least April 2004

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act, Section 5(a)(1) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Violations of the Safeguards Rule and Privacy Rule constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices
violations: Violations of the Safeguards Rule and Privacy Rule constitute unfair or deceptive acts or practices

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint against Sunbelt Lending Services, Inc. on January 3, 2005, alleging violations of the Safeguards Rule and Privacy Rule under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. The complaint seeks a consent order requiring Sunbelt to implement a comprehensive information security program, conduct risk assessments, provide employee training, oversee service providers, provide required privacy notices, and submit to ongoing monitoring and compliance verification. No monetary penalty is specified in the complaint document.
companyNow: Sunbelt Lending Services, Inc. was a wholly-owned subsidiary of Cendant Mortgage Corporation, which operated through loan officers at Coldwell Banker Residential offices in Florida. Current status and operations are unknown.

Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act, Section 502 (Privacy Rule, 16 C.F.R. Part 313)

companyDescription: Consumerinfo.com offered free credit reports online and bundled credit monitoring services. The company operated under multiple trade names including Experian Consumer Direct, QSpace Inc., and iPlace Inc., and was based in Irvine, California.
companyLongDescription: Consumerinfo.com offered free credit reports online and bundled credit monitoring services. The company operated under multiple trade names including Experian Consumer Direct, QSpace Inc., and iPlace Inc., and was based in Irvine, California.
caseDescription: Consumerinfo.com advertised free credit reports but automatically enrolled consumers in a paid credit monitoring service without adequate disclosure of the $79.95 annual fee. Consumers were charged without express informed consent after a 30-day trial period, with fees automatically renewing and charges appearing on credit cards as 'Credit Report Fee'. The company further misrepresented its free reports as equivalent to statutory free reports required under the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act.
companyWorth: Unknown (subsidiary of Experian plc, valued at approximately $6.5B as of 2005)
violationSummary: The company failed to adequately disclose material terms (automatic charging, annual fees, auto-renewal) despite collecting sensitive financial and identity data. This constitutes inadequate disclosure of information practices affecting how personal data (especially credit card numbers) would be used.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Consumerinfo.com advertised free credit reports with a 30-day free trial membership while concealing an automatic $79.95 annual charge that renewed without explicit consumer consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers were charged hundreds of millions in aggregate fees without understanding their credit card obligations.

claimsVsReality.claim: FREE credit report with 30-day FREE trial membership at no obligation, no commitment
claimsVsReality.reality: Automatic enrollment in paid $79.95/year (or $12/month after 2004) credit monitoring service with fees charged if consumer did not actively cancel within 30 days

claimsVsReality.claim: Valid credit card information required only to establish your account; card will not be charged during free trial
claimsVsReality.reality: Credit cards were charged automatically after 30 days without express informed consent, and charges renewed annually without contemporaneous notice

claimsVsReality.claim: Your credit rating will NOT be affected when we pull your free credit report
claimsVsReality.reality: Truthful, but materially misleading when combined with undisclosed paid service enrollment and charges

claimsVsReality.claim: Free reports available through our websites are equivalent to statutory free reports under the Fair and Accurate Credit Transactions Act
claimsVsReality.reality: The free reports offered through consumerinfo.com and freecreditreport.com were commercial promotions requiring enrollment in a paid service, not the statutory free annual reports available through www.annualcreditreport.com established by the FACT Act

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Represented consumers could obtain free credit reports and free trial memberships at no obligation while failing to disclose the $79.95 annual fee unless they cancelled within 30 days
violations: Represented consumers could obtain free credit reports and free trial memberships at no obligation while failing to disclose the $79.95 annual fee unless they cancelled within 30 days
Failed to disclose adequately that automatic charges would be assessed to consumers' credit cards without express informed consent
Placed material fee disclosure only in small text in a 'Privacy Policy Notice' section rather than prominently in advertising or payment information sections
Auto-renewed annual memberships by charging credit cards without contemporaneous notice or consumer action required
Advertised free reports as equivalent to FACT Act statutory free reports without disclosing these were commercial promotions requiring paid monitoring service enrollment

outcome: The FTC sought permanent injunction, consumer redress including rescission of contracts, refunds of monies paid, and disgorgement of ill-gotten gains. The complaint was filed August 15, 2005, seeking relief for deceptive marketing and unfair billing practices. The case established precedent for requiring clear, conspicuous disclosure of material terms (especially automatic renewal and fees) before charging consumers for purportedly 'free' services.
companyNow: Consumerinfo.com (operating as Experian Consumer Direct and related entities) continues as a subsidiary of Experian, one of the three major U.S. credit bureaus. The company has been subject to ongoing regulatory scrutiny regarding credit monitoring services and billing practices.
dataType: Credit report data, personal identity information, financial data, credit card numbers
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FTC Act Section 13(b) – Authority to seek injunctive relief

companyDescription: BJ's Wholesale Club, Inc. is a membership-based warehouse retailer operating approximately 150 stores across 16 eastern U.S. states, serving approximately 8 million members with branded merchandise including food, electronics, office supplies, and other general goods. Members pay for purchases with credit and debit cards via in-store and online transactions.
companyLongDescription: BJ's Wholesale Club, Inc. is a membership-based warehouse retailer operating approximately 150 stores across 16 eastern U.S. states, serving approximately 8 million members with branded merchandise including food, electronics, office supplies, and other general goods. Members pay for purchases with credit and debit cards via in-store and online transactions.
caseDescription: BJ's Wholesale Club failed to implement reasonable security measures to protect payment card data collected from customers at 150 stores across 16 eastern states. From November 2003 to February 2004, the company stored sensitive cardholder information without encryption, used default credentials for system access, and lacked wireless access point controls. This insecurity enabled hackers to access the network and steal personal information that was used to create counterfeit cards, resulting in millions of dollars in fraudulent purchases and thousands of cancelled cards.
companyWorth: Unknown (subsidiary of Berkshire Hathaway; parent company market cap ~$850B as of 2024)
violationSummary: The company's inadequate security measures for personal financial information at rest and in transit directly enabled unauthorized access and data theft, exemplifying the insecurity category under Solove's taxonomy.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: BJ's Wholesale Club stored unencrypted credit and debit card data on in-store networks with default login credentials, unsecured wireless access points.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hackers accessed the unencrypted personal information and created counterfeit cards that generated millions of dollars in fraudulent purchases.

claimsVsReality.claim: BJ's systems were secure enough to protect payment card data during processing and storage.
claimsVsReality.reality: Cardholder data was stored unencrypted on in-store networks accessible via default credentials and unsecured wireless access points, enabling attackers to steal information used for counterfeit cards and millions in fraudulent charges.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: BJ's Wholesale Club's failure to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal financial information caused or was likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers, constituting an unfair practice in violation of Section 5(a).
violations: BJ's Wholesale Club's failure to employ reasonable and appropriate security measures to protect personal financial information caused or was likely to cause substantial injury to consumers that was not offset by countervailing benefits and was not reasonably avoidable by consumers, constituting an unfair practice in violation of Section 5(a).

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint on September 20, 2005, alleging unfair practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint detailed security failures including lack of encryption, default credential access, inadequate wireless controls, and insufficient breach detection. The resolution required BJ's Wholesale Club to implement comprehensive information security measures, maintain adequate safeguards, monitor and test security effectiveness, and comply with ongoing FTC monitoring and reporting requirements. No monetary fine was disclosed in the complaint document.
companyNow: BJ's Wholesale Club, Inc. continues to operate as a membership-based warehouse retailer with approximately 220 clubs across the United States. The company is a subsidiary of Berkshire Hathaway (acquired majority stake in 2011) and remains a major competitor in the warehouse club sector.
dataType: Financial data (credit card numbers, debit card numbers, cardholder names, card expiration dates)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

company: Vision I Properties, LLC (d/b/a CartManager International)
companyDescription: Vision I Properties, LLC (doing business as CartManager International) was a Utah-based software company that licensed shopping cart and checkout page software to thousands of small online retailers. The software collected consumer purchase and contact information during checkout but resided on the company's servers while appearing to be part of merchants' websites.
companyLongDescription: Vision I Properties, LLC (doing business as CartManager International) was a Utah-based software company that licensed shopping cart and checkout page software to thousands of small online retailers. The software collected consumer purchase and contact information during checkout but resided on the company's servers while appearing to be part of merchants' websites.
caseDescription: Vision I Properties operated shopping cart software for online retailers but secretly rented nearly one million consumers' personal information to third parties for marketing purposes starting January 2003. The company neither disclosed this practice to consumers nor adequately informed merchants, despite merchants' privacy policies explicitly promising not to sell or share customer data. Consumers had no reasonable way to know their checkout information would be used for direct mail and telemarketing.
violationSummary: Company collected personal information under implied confidentiality (merchants' privacy policies stated data would not be sold/rented) but then disclosed it to third parties for marketing, breaching that confidentiality. Also involves secondary use of data contrary to stated privacy commitments.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Vision I Properties rented personal information including names, addresses, phone numbers, and purchase history of nearly 1 million consumers to third parties for direct mail.
whyTheyWereWrong: Nearly 1 million consumers' financial and contact data was shared with third-party marketers without their knowledge or consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: CartManager's online license agreement stated 'CartManager shall retain full ownership of all data submitted by either Merchant or Purchaser through the CartManager Shopping Cart.'
claimsVsReality.reality: This statement was buried in the middle of the agreement and did not explain that consumer data would be rented to third parties for marketing purposes in violation of merchants' public privacy policies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Merchants' privacy policies stated they do not sell, trade, rent, or lend customer information to third parties and protect customer privacy.
claimsVsReality.reality: Merchant customer information was systematically rented to third parties for direct mail and telemarketing starting January 2003, contradicting these policies.

claimsVsReality.claim: Shopping cart checkout pages appeared to be part of merchants' websites, displaying merchant names and logos and implying they were covered by merchants' privacy policies.
claimsVsReality.reality: The pages did not disclose that collected information was not subject to merchant privacy policies or would be shared with third parties, deceiving consumers about data handling.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company collected personal information from consumers through shopping cart pages designed to appear part of merchants' websites, implying coverage by merchants' privacy policies that explicitly forbade sale or rental of customer data.
violations: Company collected personal information from consumers through shopping cart pages designed to appear part of merchants' websites, implying coverage by merchants' privacy policies that explicitly forbade sale or rental of customer data.
Company rented nearly 1 million consumers' names, addresses, phone numbers, and purchase histories to third parties for marketing purposes without disclosing this practice to consumers.

Company failed to adequately inform merchants that it intended to use customer information contrary to their privacy policies or share it with third parties, burying data ownership claims in the middle of online license agreements.

Consumers suffered substantial injury (exposure to unwanted direct mail and telemarketing) not offset by countervailing benefits, and the injury was not reasonably avoidable because practices were not adequately disclosed.

outcome: Complaint issued by Federal Trade Commission on April 19, 2005 alleging violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint alleges unfair and deceptive practices in collection and secondary use of consumer personal information without adequate disclosure. Outcome of final settlement/consent order not specified in this complaint document.
companyNow: Unknown current status. CartManager/Vision I Properties was subject to FTC enforcement in 2005 for deceptive privacy practices involving shopping cart software.
dataType: Name, billing and shipping addresses, phone number, email address, credit card information, purchase history
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: A collection agency that failed to maintain accurate debt records and update credit reporting agencies, causing credit damage to borrowers.
companyLongDescription: This collection agency was responsible for collecting debts and reporting payment status to credit bureaux. The agency maintained inaccurate records and did not properly report when debts were paid off, resulting in credit file damage for consumers. The case highlighted failures in the agency's record-keeping and communication processes with credit reporting bodies.
caseDescription: A collection agency failed to update credit bureaux with accurate information about a paid-off debt, leaving the complainant's credit file inaccurate and damaging his creditworthiness. After complaints to the agency and intervention by the privacy office, the agency corrected its records and notified credit bureaux to amend the complainant's credit files.
violationSummary: The agency maintained inaccurate financial information and failed to correct or update it despite multiple requests, resulting in harm to the complainant's ability to access credit.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: A collection agency failed to update credit bureaux with accurate information after a debt was paid off, leaving the complainant's credit file marked as outstanding.
whyTheyWereWrong: The complainant was unable to obtain new credit because the agency did not report the paid debt, directly damaging his creditworthiness.

claimsVsReality.claim: The collection agency had no record of the lawyer's letters requesting debt correction.
claimsVsReality.reality: The letters were sent but the agency failed to maintain proper records or communication systems to track and act on such requests.

claimsVsReality.claim: The debt remained outstanding in the agency's system and credit bureau reports.
claimsVsReality.reality: The debt had actually been paid off years earlier; the agency's failure to update records created a false status that damaged the complainant's credit.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.6 requires that personal information be as accurate, complete, and up-to-date as necessary for the purposes for which it is to be used.
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection agency maintained inaccurate information (unpaid debt status) in the complainant's file despite the debt having been paid off years earlier
violations: Collection agency maintained inaccurate information (unpaid debt status) in the complainant's file despite the debt having been paid off years earlier
Agency failed to update credit bureaux with corrected information despite multiple written requests from the complainant's lawyer

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 requires organizations to protect personal information against loss, theft, and unauthorized access.
regulatoryFindings.description: Agency's inadequate record-keeping and filing systems resulted in loss of documentation of the complainant's payment and subsequent correction requests
violations: Agency's inadequate record-keeping and filing systems resulted in loss of documentation of the complainant's payment and subsequent correction requests

outcome: The collection agency corrected its records after receiving notice from the privacy office and updated credit bureaux accordingly. The complainant's credit files were amended to reflect the accurate status of the paid-off debt. The complaint was settled in November 2004.
dataType: Financial data, credit history, debt payment status
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.6 (Accuracy of Personal Information)

companyDescription: A federally regulated transportation company that processed employee severance packages and maintained personnel records.
companyLongDescription: A federally regulated Canadian transportation company that managed employee severance benefits and maintained detailed employee records including identification, seniority, and social insurance numbers. The company worked with union representatives regarding severance package approvals and employee communications. The incident revealed inadequate controls over the collection and disclosure of sensitive personal information in automated employee records.
caseDescription: A transportation company disclosed an employee list containing personal information including names, ID numbers, seniority numbers, and social insurance numbers to union representatives without employee knowledge or consent. The disclosure occurred in two instances: once when a manager shared a spreadsheet with a union representative, and again when management provided employee data to facilitate best wishes cards. The company settled by removing the SIN requirement from severance applications and implementing a consent requirement for future disclosures.
violationSummary: The company disclosed sensitive personal information (names, identification numbers, SINs) to third parties (union representatives) without employee knowledge or consent, constituting unauthorized disclosure of personal data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: A transportation company disclosed employee lists containing names, ID numbers, seniority numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees had their sensitive personal information, including social insurance numbers, exposed to third parties without permission, creating risk of identity theft and financial fraud.

claimsVsReality.claim: The SIN was included on the spreadsheet in a column that was hidden but not password protected.
claimsVsReality.reality: One union representative stated there was no SIN on the spreadsheet they received, indicating either the claim was false or the data handling was inconsistent and uncontrolled.

claimsVsReality.claim: It was not immediately apparent to either the manager or the union representative that the SIN was included.
claimsVsReality.reality: Regardless of whether the disclosure was obvious, the company had no consent from employees and no documented process to obtain consent before sharing personal information with union representatives.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2.1 – Consent: An organization shall only collect, use or disclose personal information with knowledge and consent of the individual.
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed employee personal information to union representatives without employee knowledge or consent in two separate instances
violations: Disclosed employee personal information to union representatives without employee knowledge or consent in two separate instances

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 – Limiting Use, Disclosure and Retention: Personal information shall not be used or disclosed for purposes other than those for which it was collected.
regulatoryFindings.description: Shared employee severance application data with union without employees' prior consent for such disclosure
violations: Shared employee severance application data with union without employees' prior consent for such disclosure

outcome: The company admitted the error and implemented remedial measures: (1) eliminated the requirement for severance applicants to provide their SINs, and (2) amended the severance application form to include a consent statement explicitly requesting employee authorization before releasing personal information to the union. The complaint was settled during investigation in November 2004.
dataType: Names, identification numbers, seniority numbers, social insurance numbers (SIN)
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 2.3 (Accuracy – personal information must be accurate and up-to-date)
PIPEDA Principle 4.2 (Limiting use, disclosure and retention – personal information cannot be used or disclosed without consent)

companyDescription: A Canadian bank that offers personal deposit accounts and credit products to retail customers.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian financial institution providing banking services including personal deposit accounts and credit products. The bank processes applications through both online and in-person channels and has relationships with credit bureaux for credit reporting and risk assessment.
caseDescription: A bank inappropriately required consent to a credit check for applicants seeking a no-fee personal deposit account and collected unnecessary personal information including length of employment and social insurance numbers without clear disclosure. The bank's application form language describing information exchange with credit bureaux was unclear and did not adequately explain when credit reports would be obtained.
violationSummary: The bank collected personal information (credit checks, employment history, SIN) that was unnecessary for the stated purpose (opening a no-fee deposit account) and without clear consent or transparent disclosure of how and when this information would be used.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The bank required consent to a credit check for applicants seeking a no-fee personal deposit account and collected unnecessary personal information including length of employment.
whyTheyWereWrong: Applicants seeking a basic deposit account had their credit reports pulled without clear consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: Credit check consent is required to open a no-fee personal deposit account.
claimsVsReality.reality: A credit check is not necessary for a basic deposit account; applicants should be able to open accounts in person without credit bureau inquiries.

claimsVsReality.claim: Length of employment and social insurance numbers are standard required information for deposit account applications.
claimsVsReality.reality: These data points are only relevant for credit applications, not deposit accounts, and SIN provision should be optional.

claimsVsReality.claim: The application form clearly explains when credit reports will be exchanged with credit bureaux.
claimsVsReality.reality: The language was unclear and failed to adequately disclose the conditions under which credit reports would be obtained.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.2 - Organizations shall obtain consent for the collection of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Bank required credit checks without clear explanation that this was optional for deposit account applicants
violations: Bank required credit checks without clear explanation that this was optional for deposit account applicants
Bank collected employment history and SIN without adequately explaining necessity or obtaining proper consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 5.2 - Collection of personal information shall be limited to what is necessary
regulatoryFindings.description: Credit check collection was not necessary for a no-fee personal deposit account
violations: Credit check collection was not necessary for a no-fee personal deposit account
Employment length was collected from all applicants rather than only those applying for credit

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 6.2 - Accuracy, completeness, and currency of information disclosed to individuals
regulatoryFindings.description: Application form language describing information exchange with credit bureaux and timing was unclear
violations: Application form language describing information exchange with credit bureaux and timing was unclear

outcome: The bank agreed to modify its online account application forms to: (1) inform applicants they can apply for a deposit account in person if they do not want a credit check; (2) require length of employment information only from applicants applying for credit; (3) make SIN provision optional; and (4) review and improve language describing information exchange with credit bureaux. The bank confirmed the complainant's credit rating was not affected by the deposit account application.
dataType: Financial data, employment history, social insurance number (SIN), credit report information

companyDescription: A Canadian pharmacy chain that dispenses prescription and over-the-counter medications to customers.
companyLongDescription: A pharmacy chain operating in Canada that provides prescription fulfillment and pharmaceutical services to patients. The chain had implemented a consent form practice requiring customers to authorize broad disclosure of their personal health information as a prerequisite for obtaining medications, including regular prescriptions. The pharmacy serves a broad patient population dependent on consistent medication access.
caseDescription: A pharmacy required customers to sign an overly broad consent form authorizing disclosure of personal information for marketing purposes as a condition of obtaining medication. The complainant feared coercion due to dependence on medications. The pharmacy clarified it does not disclose customer data for marketing, simplified its consent form, and implemented a verbal consent alternative.
violationSummary: The pharmacy's consent form language created the appearance of unauthorized secondary use and disclosure of personal information for marketing purposes, causing distress through misleading disclosure practices and apparent coercion.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The pharmacy required customers to sign an overly broad consent form authorizing disclosure of personal information for marketing purposes as a condition of receiving medication.
whyTheyWereWrong: Patients dependent on medications faced coercion to consent to their health data being shared for marketing, creating fear of losing access to essential treatments if they refused.

claimsVsReality.claim: The consent form accurately and transparently described the pharmacy's data disclosure practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The consent form was overly broad and did not clearly reflect that the pharmacy does not actually disclose customer data for marketing purposes; customers received multiple complaints about the confusing language.

claimsVsReality.claim: Signing the consent form was the only way customers could obtain their medications.
claimsVsReality.reality: The pharmacy implemented a verbal consent alternative, demonstrating that a signature was not technically necessary to dispense medication.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 3 requires that organizations obtain meaningful, informed consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent form was overly broad and failed to clearly communicate what disclosure practices would occur
violations: Consent form was overly broad and failed to clearly communicate what disclosure practices would occur
Customers were coerced into signing through threat of medication denial

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 requires that personal information be collected, used, and disclosed in a form that is accurate, complete, and understandable
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent form language was unclear and misleading about intended use of personal information for marketing
violations: Consent form language was unclear and misleading about intended use of personal information for marketing

outcome: The pharmacy clarified that it does not disclose customer personal information to third parties for marketing purposes. The company simplified and clarified its consent form language. The pharmacy implemented a new policy allowing customers to provide verbal consent to privacy practices as explained by the pharmacist, rather than requiring written consent as a condition of service. The complainant was satisfied with the resolution.
dataType: health data, personal information for marketing purposes

companyDescription: Two unnamed Canadian banks that processed retirement savings transfers and dormant account notices for customers.
companyLongDescription: These were Canadian financial institutions handling registered retirement savings plan transfers and account management services. Both banks failed to implement adequate safeguards to prevent sensitive customer information from being exposed during mail transmission. The banks served individual customers with retirement accounts and dormant accounts requiring periodic notifications.
caseDescription: Two Canadian banks improperly exposed sensitive personal information through envelope windows and address fields. In the first case, social insurance numbers and account numbers were visible through the envelope window on registered retirement savings plan transfer documents. In the second case, a bank disclosed bankruptcy information in the address field of a dormant account notice.
violationSummary: The banks failed to adequately protect personal information by making it visible or accessible to third parties through physical envelope windows and address fields. This constitutes exposure of sensitive data (SINs, account numbers, bankruptcy status) to unintended recipients.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Two banks exposed sensitive personal information through envelope windows and address fields on customer documents, including social insurance numbers, account numbers, and bankruptcy status.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' financial and legal information was visible to mail handlers and others who could see through envelope windows or read address fields, compromising privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: The banks' document formatting and mailing practices adequately protected customer personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: Social insurance numbers, account numbers, and bankruptcy status were visible through envelope windows and in address fields, exposing customers to identity theft and privacy breaches.

claimsVsReality.claim: Information in address fields was properly managed and would not inadvertently disclose sensitive client details.
claimsVsReality.reality: Bankruptcy status was being entered as free-form text in address fields and printed on external envelopes visible to mail handlers and recipients.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 requires organizations to safeguard personal information with appropriate security measures
regulatoryFindings.description: First bank failed to protect SINs and account numbers by allowing visibility through envelope window
violations: First bank failed to protect SINs and account numbers by allowing visibility through envelope window
Second bank disclosed bankruptcy status information in address field visible to postal workers and others

outcome: Both banks implemented remedial measures. The first bank removed SINs and account numbers from the window-visible portion of envelopes and relocated them to non-visible areas. The second bank modified its client profile process to code bankruptcy information automatically rather than entering free-form text that could be added to address fields. Both complainants confirmed satisfaction with the outcomes.
dataType: Social insurance numbers (SINs), account numbers, bankruptcy status, name, address

companyDescription: An unnamed Canadian insurance company offering life insurance products to consumers.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian-based insurance provider specializing in life insurance coverage. The company collects personal and health information from applicants as part of the underwriting process. During the period in question, the company was reviewing its consent language in application forms to improve clarity and compliance with privacy principles.
caseDescription: An insurance company was complained against for requiring overly broad consent to collection, use, and disclosure of personal data in life insurance applications. The Office confirmed the company's actual practices were compliant, but found the consent language lacked precision and clarity. The company agreed to revise its consent language and collaborate with the Office on further improvements.
violationSummary: The complaint centered on overly broad consent requests in data collection, which relates to interrogation — excessive or unclear requests for information during the collection phase.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: The insurance company used consent language in life insurance application forms that was unclear and lacked precision regarding the scope of personal data collection, use, and disclosure.
whyTheyWereWrong: Applicants could not clearly understand what they were consenting to, leaving them uncertain about how their sensitive personal and health information would be used or shared by the insurer.

claimsVsReality.claim: Consent language clearly communicated the scope of data collection, use, and disclosure to applicants.
claimsVsReality.reality: The consent language lacked precision and clarity, leaving applicants uncertain about how their personal information would be handled.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to obtain meaningful, informed consent for the collection, use, and disclosure of personal information with clear, precise language
regulatoryFindings.description: Consent language in application forms was overly broad and lacked precision and clarity
violations: Consent language in application forms was overly broad and lacked precision and clarity

outcome: The complaint was settled in June 2004. The insurance company agreed to revise its consent language in application forms to improve precision and clarity, and committed to collaborating informally with the Office during the review process. The company also agreed to share the revised consent language with the complainant and consider any further feedback.
dataType: Personal information related to life insurance applications

companyDescription: A small, family-owned interprovincial trucking company operating in Canada that transports goods across provincial borders.
companyLongDescription: This is a small, family-owned trucking business engaged in interprovincial transportation services in Canada. The company had minimal formal administrative infrastructure, particularly regarding privacy and data protection processes. At the time of the complaint in 2004, it had not established written privacy policies or designated privacy responsibilities, which was typical for small businesses of that era but left employee information vulnerable.
caseDescription: A former employee alleged his personal information was disclosed to a creditor without consent. Investigation found no evidence supporting the allegation, as the complainant had provided some information to the creditor himself. The trucking company, lacking formalized privacy processes, implemented a written privacy policy and appointed an Information Officer as a result.
violationSummary: The alleged unauthorized disclosure of personal information to a third party without consent falls under the Information Dissemination – Disclosure category, though investigation found the allegation unfounded.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A small family-owned interprovincial trucking company lacked formalized privacy processes and record-keeping systems for handling employee personal information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Without documented privacy policies and procedures, the company had no safeguards to prevent unauthorized disclosure of employee personal information to third parties like creditors.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company disclosed the complainant's personal information to a creditor without consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Investigation found no evidence supporting this allegation; the complainant had actually provided some of the information to the creditor himself.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to obtain consent before disclosing personal information and to have proper information handling practices in place
regulatoryFindings.description: Alleged disclosure of employee personal information without consent (allegation unsubstantiated)
violations: Alleged disclosure of employee personal information without consent (allegation unsubstantiated)
Lack of formalized privacy reporting and record-keeping processes

outcome: The complaint was settled. The trucking company implemented a written privacy policy, appointed an Information Officer, and reviewed employee information practices. The company took steps to ensure employees are aware of fair information handling practices. Both the complainant and the privacy office were satisfied with the resolution.
companyNow: Unknown; the company implemented privacy reforms following this 2004 case but its current operational status is not documented.
dataType: Employee personal information

companyDescription: A Canadian electronics retailer that sells and repairs computers and electronic devices across multiple store locations.
companyLongDescription: A major Canadian electronics retailer operating physical stores across the country, offering sales, repairs, and support services for computers and consumer electronics. The company serves retail customers seeking computer repair, warranty support, and device replacement. Following this incident, the company became a leader in data wiping practices for returned electronics in the Canadian retail sector.
caseDescription: An employee sold a returned laptop without wiping the customer's personal data from the hard drive, resulting in the complainant's information being disclosed to the purchaser. The company retrieved the device and implemented comprehensive data wiping procedures across all Canadian stores to prevent future incidents.
violationSummary: The company's failure to remove personal information from returned electronics before resale resulted in unintended exposure of the complainant's data to a third party, exemplifying the Solove category of exposure through lack of safeguards.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: An employee sold a returned laptop without wiping the customer's personal data from the hard drive, causing the customer's sensitive information to be disclosed to the purchaser.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's personal information remained on the laptop and was exposed to an unknown third party who purchased the device, creating risk of identity theft and privacy violation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company safely handles returned electronic devices and customer personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: An employee sold a returned laptop containing the customer's personal data without any wiping or verification process, exposing the information to an unknown buyer.

claimsVsReality.claim: Returned devices are processed according to company policy before resale.
claimsVsReality.reality: The returned laptop was placed for sale without examination or data removal, indicating no enforcement of data handling procedures at the point of resale.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 requires organizations to retain personal information only as long as necessary and dispose of it securely
regulatoryFindings.description: Company failed to wipe personal information from returned laptop before resale
violations: Company failed to wipe personal information from returned laptop before resale
Employee did not follow any procedure to safeguard customer data on returned electronics

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 1 requires organizations to be accountable for personal information in their possession
regulatoryFindings.description: Lack of safeguards and documentation procedures for handling returned electronic devices containing personal data
violations: Lack of safeguards and documentation procedures for handling returned electronic devices containing personal data

outcome: The company retrieved the laptop from the purchaser and returned it to the complainant. The company implemented mandatory data wiping procedures for all computers returned to its stores across Canada, requiring employee documentation of the process. Similar safeguarding procedures were extended to other electronic devices sold by the company.
dataType: Personal information stored on computer hard drives
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.7 (Retention and Disposal of Personal Information)

companyDescription: A trucking company that engaged in unauthorized disclosure of employee personal information to competitors.
companyLongDescription: A transportation company that operated without formal privacy safeguards. Following a complaint from a former employee regarding unauthorized sharing of personal data with competitor firms, the company was found to lack basic privacy infrastructure including documented policies, procedures, and designated privacy oversight. The case led to the company implementing comprehensive privacy governance.
caseDescription: A trucking company disclosed personal information about a former employee to competing trucking firms without authorization. The company lacked privacy policies, procedures, and a designated privacy officer. The complaint was settled with the company agreeing to implement comprehensive privacy policies and appoint a privacy officer.
violationSummary: The company disclosed the former employee's personal information to third parties (other trucking firms) without consent or lawful basis, constituting improper disclosure under privacy principles.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: The trucking company disclosed personal information about a former employee to competing trucking firms without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: The former employee's personal information was shared with competitors without consent, exposing him to potential recruitment solicitation, competitive targeting.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company operated standard business practices by sharing employee information with industry peers.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company disclosed personal information without authorization, violating the former employee's privacy rights.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company had adequate privacy safeguards in place.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked any formal privacy policies, procedures, or designated privacy officer to govern personal information handling.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy principles requiring proper handling of personal information and organizational accountability
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosure of personal information to third parties without authorization
violations: Disclosure of personal information to third parties without authorization
Absence of privacy policies and procedures
No designated privacy officer or representative

outcome: The complaint was settled in June 2004. The trucking company agreed to develop and implement comprehensive privacy policies and procedures, and forwarded copies to the Office for confirmation. The company also designated a privacy officer to oversee compliance.
dataType: Personal information (employment records, identity information)

companyDescription: A Canadian lending institution that provided loans to consumers.
companyLongDescription: A Canadian lending institution that provided consumer loans. The organization operated without formal privacy governance structures, policies, or documented practices to protect customer personal information. During debt recovery operations, the company failed to maintain adequate safeguards over sensitive financial data.
caseDescription: A lending institution disclosed a customer's delinquent account information to her uncle without consent. During investigation, the organization was found to lack any privacy policies or practices. The institution agreed to remediate by implementing privacy governance, employee training, and stricter disclosure protocols.
violationSummary: The institution disclosed personal financial information to an unauthorized third party without the individual's consent, violating the principle of limited disclosure and lack of consent-based processing.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A lending institution disclosed a customer's delinquent account information to her uncle without her consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer's private financial information was shared with a family member, exposing her financial difficulties and debt status without her knowledge or permission.

claimsVsReality.claim: The institution operated with appropriate handling of customer financial information during debt recovery.
claimsVsReality.reality: The institution disclosed a customer's delinquent account details to a third party without consent and had implemented no privacy policies or practices.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to obtain consent before disclosing personal information to third parties
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed account delinquency information to uncle without complainant's consent
violations: Disclosed account delinquency information to uncle without complainant's consent

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to implement privacy policies and practices
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization had no privacy policies or practices in place
violations: Organization had no privacy policies or practices in place

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to limit disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Staff did not limit information disclosed during debt recovery process
violations: Staff did not limit information disclosed during debt recovery process

outcome: The lending institution agreed to send a letter of apology to the complainant, adjusted her outstanding loan balance, struck a privacy committee, instituted mandatory privacy training for all employees, and implemented protocols to limit information disclosure during debt recovery activities. The case was settled in June 2004 with both the complainant and the Privacy Commissioner satisfied with the remedial actions.
dataType: Account information, delinquency status, financial records
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 (Limiting Use, Disclosure and Retention)

companyDescription: A national transportation company operating crew management systems for employee scheduling and payroll management.
companyLongDescription: A major Canadian transportation company that operates automated systems for managing crew schedules, payroll, and employee records. The company's crew management platform was designed to coordinate personnel across transportation operations but contained excessive personal information fields accessible to non-HR personnel. The system stored sensitive employee data including government identification numbers and health information without adequate access controls.
caseDescription: An employee raised concerns that unauthorized personnel, including union representatives, could access sensitive personal information such as social insurance numbers, dates of birth, and health information in an automated crew management system. The company agreed to restrict system access by removing the display of SINs, birth dates, and health information from employee screens, addressing the security vulnerability.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement adequate access controls and data minimization in its automated crew management system, allowing unauthorized personnel to potentially access sensitive employee personal information including SINs and health data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: The company stored sensitive employee personal information including social insurance numbers, dates of birth.
whyTheyWereWrong: Employees' social insurance numbers, dates of birth, and health information were exposed to unauthorized access, putting workers at risk of identity theft, fraud, and privacy violations.

claimsVsReality.claim: Union representatives and other unauthorized personnel could not access certain sensitive employee information in the crew management system.
claimsVsReality.reality: The system was configured to display social insurance numbers, birth dates, and health information on employee screens accessible to unauthorized personnel, creating an actual security vulnerability regardless of whether all data was technically retrievable.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 requires organizations to protect personal information against unauthorized access and use
regulatoryFindings.description: Inadequate access controls in crew management system allowing unauthorized personnel to view sensitive employee data
violations: Inadequate access controls in crew management system allowing unauthorized personnel to view sensitive employee data
Failure to implement data minimization by displaying SINs, birth dates, and health information unnecessarily

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2 requires organizations to be accountable for personal information in their possession
regulatoryFindings.description: Lack of proper system configuration to restrict access to sensitive employee information by unauthorized parties
violations: Lack of proper system configuration to restrict access to sensitive employee information by unauthorized parties

outcome: The company agreed to adjust its automated crew management system to eliminate the display of social insurance numbers, birth dates, and health information from employee screens. The system was modified to restrict unauthorized access to sensitive personal data. The complainant's concerns were addressed and the case was settled in February 2004.
dataType: Social insurance number, date of birth, wage rates, vacation eligibility, health information

companyDescription: A Canadian professional organization that hosts conferences and conducts talks on matters of professional interest to its members.
companyLongDescription: A professional association or regulatory body in Canada that organizes conferences where members present talks on topics relevant to their profession. The organization was subject to the Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) and had obligations to respond to access requests from individuals regarding their personal information.
caseDescription: A doctor submitted an access request to a professional organization for personal information that would have been presented at a conference. The organization failed to respond to the access request; however, investigation revealed the presentation was never given and no personal information was actually held by the organization.
violationSummary: The organization failed to respond to a subject access request, violating the individual's right to access their own personal information. Although no actual data existed, the failure to respond to the request itself constitutes a violation of access rights obligations.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: A professional organization failed to respond to a doctor's access request for personal information that was supposed to be presented at a conference.
whyTheyWereWrong: The doctor was denied a timely response to his legal right to access his own personal information, leaving him uncertain about what information the organization held about him.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization held personal information about the doctor that would be presented at a conference.
claimsVsReality.reality: The presentation was never given and the organization did not actually hold any personal information relating to the doctor.

claimsVsReality.claim: The organization would respond to the doctor's access request.
claimsVsReality.reality: The organization did not respond to the access request at all; investigation confirmed no one had acted on it.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to respond to access requests for personal information held about individuals
regulatoryFindings.description: Organization failed to respond to the doctor's access request
violations: Organization failed to respond to the doctor's access request
No acknowledgment or action taken on the subject access request

outcome: The organization was required to acknowledge that it failed to respond to the access request. Investigation confirmed no personal information existed as the presentation was not held. The complainant accepted early resolution with no further action required.
dataType: Professional information, conference-related personal data

companyDescription: Dynacare is a Canadian medical laboratory and diagnostic services company operating across Canada.
companyLongDescription: Dynacare is a Canadian medical laboratory operator that processes patient test samples and provides diagnostic results. As a healthcare company handling sensitive patient information, it is subject to PIPEDA and provincial health information legislation. The company manages multiple locations and employees with access to confidential patient records.
caseDescription: Dynacare sent a facsimile transmission containing sensitive patient health information (name, age, medical test results, diagnosis) to the wrong recipient in January 2004 due to manual misdiraling. The company failed to notify the affected individual and was unable to identify which of five employees was responsible for the error. The incident violated PIPEDA's prohibition on disclosure of personal information without consent.
violationSummary: Sensitive health information was inadvertently exposed to unintended third parties (apartment managers) due to a facsimile misdial error. This constitutes unauthorized disclosure of personal information to parties outside the intended recipients.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Dynacare sent a facsimile containing a patient's name, age, height, smoking habits, patient number, diagnosis.
whyTheyWereWrong: A patient's sensitive health information was exposed to an unauthorized third party, compromising their medical privacy.

claimsVsReality.claim: Dynacare indicated it would consider notifying the affected individual of the privacy breach.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had not notified the patient whose personal information was disclosed at the time of the investigation.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company required all employees to sign confidentiality oaths and was aware of the need to protect medical records.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite confidentiality agreements, a manual facsimile transmission error still occurred, and the company could only narrow responsibility to one of five employees, demonstrating inadequate controls and oversight.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA – Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act
regulatoryFindings.description: Disclosed personal health information without consent to unauthorized third parties
violations: Disclosed personal health information without consent to unauthorized third parties
Failed to implement adequate controls to prevent misdirected facsimiles
Failed to notify the affected individual of the privacy breach
Did not maintain current confidentiality agreements with employees

outcome: The Assistant Privacy Commissioner concluded that Dynacare contravened PIPEDA by disclosing personal information without consent. Dynacare was directed to: implement electronic auto-fax verification systems; provide employee instructions for confirming fax number accuracy before transmission; develop and have employees annually review and sign updated confidentiality agreements; revise policies and procedures for full PIPEDA compliance; notify the affected individual; and follow OPC recommendations for facsimile transmission of personal information.
companyNow: Dynacare continues to operate as a major medical laboratory and diagnostic services provider in Canada, now part of larger healthcare networks.
dataType: Health data, medical records, patient test results, diagnosis, personal medical history
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA – Disclosure of personal information without consent

companyDescription: A major Canadian department store with credit card operations and affiliated brand companies.
companyLongDescription: A large Canadian retail department store operating credit card accounts and managing multiple affiliated brand companies. The store uses opt-out consent mechanisms for disclosures to its own affiliates and claims not to share personal information with unaffiliated third parties without express consent. The case involved a mail solicitation process that lacked transparent communication about the store's intermediary role.
caseDescription: A customer complained that a department store disclosed his personal information to a third-party credit monitoring company without consent. Investigation found no actual disclosure occurred; the store had sent the mail-out on behalf of the third party without clearly indicating this relationship. The store agreed to improve transparency and review its opt-out policies.
violationSummary: The primary concern was potential unauthorized disclosure of personal information to non-affiliated third parties. Although investigation found no actual disclosure in this case, the violation type reflects the nature of the complaint regarding lack of transparency and unclear communication about information sharing.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: A department store sent a credit monitoring company's mail solicitation to a customer on behalf of the third party without clearly disclosing that the store was acting as an intermediary rather.
whyTheyWereWrong: The customer had previously requested no third-party sharing and received mail that appeared to be a direct store disclosure, causing confusion.

claimsVsReality.claim: The department store disclosed the complainant's personal information to a credit monitoring company.
claimsVsReality.reality: No personal information was actually disclosed; the store merely mailed out solicitations on behalf of the third party.

claimsVsReality.claim: The mail solicitation clearly indicated the department store was acting on behalf of the credit monitoring company.
claimsVsReality.reality: The mail-out was unclear about the store's intermediary role, appearing to the customer as a direct store endorsement or disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 2.3 – Organizations shall obtain consent before disclosing personal information to third parties
regulatoryFindings.description: Lack of clear disclosure that the store was acting on behalf of the third party in the mail solicitation
violations: Lack of clear disclosure that the store was acting on behalf of the third party in the mail solicitation
Failure to clearly communicate the source and purpose of the mail-out to the customer

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.9 – Organizations shall protect personal information by appropriate safeguards
regulatoryFindings.description: Insufficient clarity in opt-out mechanisms and consent processes regarding disclosure to affiliated and non-affiliated entities
violations: Insufficient clarity in opt-out mechanisms and consent processes regarding disclosure to affiliated and non-affiliated entities

outcome: The store clarified that no personal information was actually disclosed to the non-affiliated credit monitoring company. The store apologized and agreed to: (1) ensure future mail-outs clearly indicate when the store is acting on a third party's behalf; (2) review its account application policies to provide new customers the opportunity to opt out of information sharing with affiliated brand companies at the time of enrollment; and (3) review and improve suppression mechanisms across its various affiliated companies to ensure efficient opt-out processing.
dataType: Personal information, credit card account details
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Principle 2.3 (Consent for collection, use, and disclosure)

companyDescription: Gateway Learning Corporation marketed educational products for children learning math and reading under the 'Hooked on Phonics' brand, selling primarily to parents and teachers through its website www.hop.com since at least 2000.
companyLongDescription: Gateway Learning Corporation marketed educational products for children learning math and reading under the 'Hooked on Phonics' brand, selling primarily to parents and teachers through its website www.hop.com since at least 2000.
caseDescription: Gateway Learning Corporation collected personal information from parents under a privacy policy promising not to share data without consent. In April 2003, the company began renting customer data including children's age ranges and gender to third-party marketers without consent. The company failed to notify customers of material privacy policy changes before applying them retroactively to previously collected data.
violationSummary: Company breached explicit confidentiality commitments made in published privacy policies by renting customer personal information and children's data to third parties without consent, violating the trust relationship established through clear privacy promises.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Gateway Learning rented personal information from online customers to third parties without consent, including parent names, addresses, phone numbers, and children's ages.
whyTheyWereWrong: Parents provided their personal and children's data under a privacy policy promising no sharing without explicit consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: We do not sell, rent or loan any personally identifiable information regarding our consumers with any third party unless we receive a customer's explicit consent.
claimsVsReality.reality: Beginning April 2003, Gateway rented customer personal information and children's data to third-party marketers without seeking or receiving consumer consent.

claimsVsReality.claim: We do not provide any personally identifiable information about children under 13 years of age to any third party for any purpose whatsoever.
claimsVsReality.reality: Gateway provided children's age ranges (0-5, 2-5, 6-10 years old) and gender to third-party marketers as part of data rental arrangements.

claimsVsReality.claim: If at some future time there is a material change to our information usage practices that affect your personally identifiable information, we will notify you of the relevant changes on this Site or by email.
claimsVsReality.reality: When Gateway posted a revised privacy policy on June 20, 2003 permitting third-party data sharing, it took no steps to alert existing customers of this material change, and continued renting data collected under the original policy.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company made express representations in published privacy policy that it would not 'sell, rent or loan' personal information without explicit consumer consent, then rented customer data to third parties without consent beginning April 2003
violations: Company made express representations in published privacy policy that it would not 'sell, rent or loan' personal information without explicit consumer consent, then rented customer data to third parties without consent beginning April 2003
Company represented it would not provide personal information about children under 13 to third parties for any purpose, then rented age ranges and gender of children to third-party marketers

Company represented it would notify consumers of material changes to privacy practices, then posted revised privacy policy permitting data sharing without alerting existing customers of the material change

regulatoryFindings.act: Unfair practices under FTC Act Section 5 must cause or be likely to cause substantial injury to consumers not outweighed by countervailing benefits and not reasonably avoidable by consumers.
regulatoryFindings.description: Retroactive application of revised privacy policy to data collected under original no-sharing promise caused substantial injury by exposing customers to unsolicited marketing contacts based on information they provided under different terms
violations: Retroactive application of revised privacy policy to data collected under original no-sharing promise caused substantial injury by exposing customers to unsolicited marketing contacts based on information they provided under different terms

outcome: FTC issued complaint on September 10, 2004 alleging unfair and deceptive practices. The document is the complaint itself, initiating formal enforcement proceedings. Gateway Learning was required to cease the unauthorised data rental practices and implement compliance measures. The company temporarily suspended data rental on July 1, 2003, and posted revised privacy policies acknowledging the practices.
companyNow: Unknown; the company operated the 'Hooked on Phonics' educational products brand. Current operational status not disclosed in this 2004 complaint document.
dataType: Parent names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, billing/shipping addresses, purchase history, child age and gender
legalBasisViolated: Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) – implied through children's data protection claims

companyDescription: Bonzi Software, Inc. was a privately held software company based in San Luis Obispo, California, founded by Joe Bonzi and Jay Bonzi. The company developed and distributed software products including InternetALERT, marketed as computer security software.
companyLongDescription: Bonzi Software, Inc. was a privately held software company based in San Luis Obispo, California, founded by Joe Bonzi and Jay Bonzi. The company developed and distributed software products including InternetALERT, marketed as computer security software.
caseDescription: Bonzi Software marketed InternetALERT security software with exaggerated claims about its ability to protect computers from unauthorized access. The software actually provided only limited protection by monitoring a small number of communications ports and failed to include standard security features like virus protection or data leakage prevention. The company's advertising misrepresented the software's effectiveness to consumers.
violationSummary: The software's inadequate security features and failure to protect the promised monitoring capabilities constitutes a fundamental insecurity in data protection mechanisms.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Bonzi Software advertised InternetALERT security software through banner, button, and pop-up ads claiming it would protect computers from Internet attackers.
whyTheyWereWrong: The software provided only limited port monitoring and lacked essential security features like virus protection or data theft prevention.

claimsVsReality.claim: InternetALERT is an absolute 'MUST' for anyone connecting to the Internet and will protect your computer against malicious attackers by notifying you of break-in attempts and stopping them.
claimsVsReality.reality: The software monitored only 11-21 of hundreds of available communications ports. It did not monitor ports already open at installation time and lacked essential security features like virus protection or data leakage prevention.

claimsVsReality.claim: Your computer's data is at risk and InternetALERT will prevent attackers from stealing credit card information, reading email, planting viruses, stealing banking credentials, and deleting files.
claimsVsReality.reality: InternetALERT's limited port monitoring capability did not prevent these threats. It offered no protection against actual attack vectors for the described harms.

claimsVsReality.claim: Make Your Computer Safe & Secure In 5 Minutes with InternetALERT.
claimsVsReality.reality: The software provided partial monitoring only and could actually create security vulnerabilities by opening closed ports without consumer awareness of the implications.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Bonzi Software represented through advertising that InternetALERT significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized access and data theft, when in fact the software provided only limited intrusion monitoring on a small subset of communications ports.
