violations: Bonzi Software represented through advertising that InternetALERT significantly reduces the risk of unauthorized access and data theft, when in fact the software provided only limited intrusion monitoring on a small subset of communications ports.

The software failed to include security features necessary to significantly reduce data protection risks, such as virus protection or features to prevent unauthorized transmission of personally identifiable information.

Marketing materials used alarming language and explicit threats (credit card theft, email reading, virus infection, banking fraud) to induce purchase, but the actual product's limited port monitoring did not match these representations.

outcome: The Federal Trade Commission issued a complaint on October 7, 2004, alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The case resulted in a consent order requiring Bonzi Software to cease making unsubstantiated claims about InternetALERT's security capabilities and to include clear, substantiated disclosures about the software's actual protective scope. Ongoing monitoring and compliance requirements were imposed.
companyNow: Bonzi Software is no longer active in the software market. The company and its flagship BonziBuddy adware became notorious in internet culture and the company ceased operations in the early 2000s.
dataType: IP addresses, computer system information
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: AT&T Corp. is a major United States telecommunications company providing local and long-distance telephone service, as well as wireless and broadband services to consumers and businesses.
companyLongDescription: AT&T Corp. is a major United States telecommunications company providing local and long-distance telephone service, as well as wireless and broadband services to consumers and businesses.
caseDescription: AT&T violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act by taking adverse action against consumers (denying or limiting telephone service based on credit reports) without providing required notices and disclosures. The company failed to inform consumers of the reporting agencies consulted, their rights to dispute inaccurate information, and how to obtain free credit reports. This systematic non-compliance affected numerous telephone service applicants.
violationSummary: AT&T disclosed adverse information from consumer reports to make service decisions but failed to disclose required information back to consumers about those decisions, their sources, and remedial rights—a failure to provide transparent notice of information use in decision-making affecting consumer rights.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: AT&T denied or restricted telephone service to consumers based on credit reports, then sent notices that failed to identify which consumer reporting agencies provided the damaging information.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers could not challenge inaccurate credit data or obtain free copies of their reports to correct errors.

claimsVsReality.claim: AT&T conducted credit reviews to determine eligibility for service and provided appropriate customer notices of adverse decisions
claimsVsReality.reality: AT&T made adverse service decisions based on credit reports but systematically failed to provide required notices identifying the reporting agencies, consumer rights to dispute, or how to obtain free credit reports

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 615(a) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act requires any person taking adverse action based on information in a consumer report to provide specified notices including: the fact of adverse action taken; the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer reporting agency; a statement that the agency did not make the decision; notice of the right to obtain a free copy of the consumer report within 60 days; and notice of the right to dispute the accuracy of information in the report.
regulatoryFindings.description: AT&T took adverse action by limiting service charges and denying service based on consumer reports but failed to disclose the names, addresses, and telephone numbers of the consumer reporting agencies consulted
violations: AT&T took adverse action by limiting service charges and denying service based on consumer reports but failed to disclose the names, addresses, and telephone numbers of the consumer reporting agencies consulted
AT&T failed to notify consumers of their right to obtain a free copy of their credit report from the reporting agency within 60 days
AT&T failed to inform consumers of their right to dispute the accuracy or completeness of information in the consumer reports used

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: AT&T's pattern of taking adverse action without full FCRA-required disclosures constitutes unfair or deceptive practice under FTC Act Section 5(a)
violations: AT&T's pattern of taking adverse action without full FCRA-required disclosures constitutes unfair or deceptive practice under FTC Act Section 5(a)

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 621(a)(1) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act establishes that violations constitute unfair or deceptive acts in violation of FTC Act Section 5(a) and authorizes civil penalties.
regulatoryFindings.description: AT&T's systematic failures to comply with FCRA adverse action notice requirements demonstrate a pattern of knowing violations under Section 621(a)(2)(A)
violations: AT&T's systematic failures to comply with FCRA adverse action notice requirements demonstrate a pattern of knowing violations under Section 621(a)(2)(A)

outcome: The United States District Court for the District of New Jersey was authorized to issue judgment and equitable relief against AT&T. The Court was empowered to enjoin AT&T from violating FCRA provisions, award monetary civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation, and issue additional relief as deemed just and proper. The complaint sought permanent injunction preventing future violations and compliance with all FCRA adverse action notice requirements.
companyNow: AT&T Corp. (now AT&T Inc.) remains one of the largest telecommunications providers in the United States, serving millions of customers with wireless, broadband, and other services.
dataType: Financial data, consumer credit information, personal identifiers (name, address, telephone number)
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 615(a), 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a)

companyDescription: UMG Recordings, Inc. is a major music recording and entertainment company headquartered in Santa Monica, California, owned by Vivendi. The company markets and promotes numerous musical recording artists and labels worldwide, including through internet platforms.
companyLongDescription: UMG Recordings, Inc. is a major music recording and entertainment company headquartered in Santa Monica, California, owned by Vivendi. The company markets and promotes numerous musical recording artists and labels worldwide, including through internet platforms.
caseDescription: UMG Recordings operated hundreds of websites that collected personal information from children under 13 without obtaining verifiable parental consent beforehand. The company collected tens of thousands of children's personal details including addresses and phone numbers, then asked parents for consent only after collection. UMG failed to provide adequate privacy notices and gave parents no way to review or delete collected information.
violationSummary: UMG systematically collected personal information from children without proper consent mechanisms, employing surveillance-like practices on a large scale across hundreds of websites targeting or knowingly collecting from minors.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: UMG Recordings collected personal information from tens of thousands of children under 13, including names, home addresses, phone numbers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Tens of thousands of children's home addresses, phone numbers, and detailed personal information were exposed to unauthorized collection.

claimsVsReality.claim: UMG's consent process sought parental approval for children's participation in named activities
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal information was collected from children before any parental notification or consent was sought; consent emails were incomplete and failed to disclose what data had already been collected

claimsVsReality.claim: UMG maintained privacy policies on its websites
claimsVsReality.reality: Privacy policies, where posted, did not clearly, understandably, or completely disclose information collection, use, and disclosure practices required by COPPA

claimsVsReality.claim: Parent consent verification was implemented
claimsVsReality.reality: No steps were taken to verify that the person providing consent was actually the child's parent; a simple hyperlink click or 'Submit' button was the only verification

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b) requires operators to post a privacy policy on their website providing clear, understandable, and complete notice of information collection, use, and disclosure practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: UMG failed to provide sufficient notice on its websites of what information it collected from children, how it used such information, and its disclosure practices
violations: UMG failed to provide sufficient notice on its websites of what information it collected from children, how it used such information, and its disclosure practices

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(c) requires operators to provide direct notice to parents of information practices before collection.
regulatoryFindings.description: UMG sent parent consent emails only after collecting child personal information, without disclosing what data had already been collected or the full scope of collection
violations: UMG sent parent consent emails only after collecting child personal information, without disclosing what data had already been collected or the full scope of collection

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.5 requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent before any collection, use, or disclosure of personal information from children under 13.
regulatoryFindings.description: UMG collected tens of thousands of children's personal details (name, address, phone, email, interests) without first obtaining verifiable parental consent; consent was requested only after collection
violations: UMG collected tens of thousands of children's personal details (name, address, phone, email, interests) without first obtaining verifiable parental consent; consent was requested only after collection

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.6 requires operators to provide a reasonable means for parents to review personal information collected from their children and to refuse further use or maintenance.
regulatoryFindings.description: UMG provided no mechanism for parents to review or delete information collected from their children
violations: UMG provided no mechanism for parents to review or delete information collected from their children

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: UMG's practices of collecting children's data without prior parental notice and consent constituted unfair and deceptive practices under the FTC Act, as violations of COPPA Rule are per se unfair under 15 U.S.C. § 57a(d)(3)
violations: UMG's practices of collecting children's data without prior parental notice and consent constituted unfair and deceptive practices under the FTC Act, as violations of COPPA Rule are per se unfair under 15 U.S.C. § 57a(d)(3)

outcome: This is a civil complaint filed by the United States on behalf of the FTC seeking monetary civil penalties of up to $11,000 per violation, a permanent injunction against future COPPA violations, and other equitable relief. The complaint alleges hundreds of separate violations (one for each collection, use, or disclosure of a child's personal information from April 21, 2000 through the filing date). The ultimate resolution is not shown in this complaint document alone.
companyNow: UMG Recordings is a major music recording company and subsidiary of Vivendi, one of the world's largest media conglomerates. The company continues to operate as a leading music label and rights holder.
dataType: Children's personal information including date of birth, name, home address, telephone number, email address, gender, interests, and preferences

company: Imperial Palace, Inc. (Imperial Palace Casino) and Imperial Palace of Mississippi, Inc.
companyDescription: Imperial Palace, Inc. operated the Imperial Palace Casino in Las Vegas, Nevada, and Imperial Palace of Mississippi, Inc. operated a property in Biloxi, Mississippi. Both entities engaged in gaming and hospitality operations with multiple employment screening practices.
companyLongDescription: Imperial Palace, Inc. operated the Imperial Palace Casino in Las Vegas, Nevada, and Imperial Palace of Mississippi, Inc. operated a property in Biloxi, Mississippi. Both entities engaged in gaming and hospitality operations with multiple employment screening practices.
caseDescription: Imperial Palace obtained consumer credit reports on employment applicants but failed to provide required notices before taking adverse employment decisions based on those reports. The company violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act by not disclosing that credit information was used in hiring decisions and not providing applicants with copies of reports and their rights under the FCRA.
violationSummary: The company failed to implement required procedural safeguards (notice and disclosure) when using sensitive consumer data (credit reports) to make adverse decisions affecting individuals' employment opportunities.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Imperial Palace obtained consumer credit reports on job applicants for employment screening and denied employment based on credit information without providing applicants with required legal.
whyTheyWereWrong: Job applicants were rejected for employment based on credit information without knowing the real reason for denial.

claimsVsReality.claim: Imperial Palace's contracts with consumer reporting agencies specified that the company was responsible for complying with the FCRA and providing required applicant notices.
claimsVsReality.reality: Despite contractual obligations and actual use of credit reports in employment decisions, the company systematically failed to provide any required FCRA notices to applicants denied employment based on credit information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The Background Form was used merely to record and internally rate applicant information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The form was actively used to rate creditworthiness and make employment recommendations (Favorable/Unfavorable) that directly resulted in hiring decisions, constituting adverse action based on credit reports without disclosure.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 604(b)(3) of the FCRA requires that before taking adverse action against an applicant based on information in a consumer report, an employer must provide the applicant a copy of the consumer report and a copy of the applicant's rights under the FCRA.
regulatoryFindings.description: Imperial Palace took adverse employment actions based on applicant credit reports but failed to provide applicants with copies of their consumer reports and notices of their rights under the FCRA.
violations: Imperial Palace took adverse employment actions based on applicant credit reports but failed to provide applicants with copies of their consumer reports and notices of their rights under the FCRA.
The company's Background Form recorded credit ratings and recommendations (Poor/Fair/Good, Favorable/Unfavorable) based on consumer reports but never disclosed this information to applicants.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 615(a) of the FCRA requires any person taking adverse action with respect to a consumer based on information in a consumer report to provide notice including: (1) notice of the adverse action; (2) the name, address, and telephone number of the consumer reporting agency; (3) notice that the agency did not make the adverse decision; (4) notice of the right to obtain a free copy of the report within 60 days; and (5) notice of the right to dispute accuracy or completeness.
regulatoryFindings.description: Imperial Palace failed to provide applicants denied employment based on credit reports with any of the required Section 615(a) notices, leaving applicants unaware why their applications were rejected or how to challenge inaccurate information.
violations: Imperial Palace failed to provide applicants denied employment based on credit reports with any of the required Section 615(a) notices, leaving applicants unaware why their applications were rejected or how to challenge inaccurate information.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: The FCRA violations constituted unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) by using applicants' credit information in employment decisions without disclosure or transparency.
violations: The FCRA violations constituted unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) by using applicants' credit information in employment decisions without disclosure or transparency.

outcome: This is a complaint filed seeking permanent injunction and monetary civil penalties. The document does not contain a final judgment or settlement order. Imperial Palace was ordered to cease violations of the FCRA, with potential civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation. The case sought injunctive relief and monetary damages, with the court authorized to award appropriate equitable and monetary relief.
companyNow: Imperial Palace Casino operated as a major Las Vegas casino property but faced significant regulatory pressure from this FTC enforcement action regarding employment screening practices.
dataType: Consumer credit reports, employment screening data, personal financial information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 604(b)(3), 15 U.S.C. § 1681b(b)(3)
Fair Credit Reporting Act Section 615(a), 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a)

company: MTS, Inc. d/b/a Tower Records/Books/Video and Tower Direct, LLC d/b/a TowerRecords.com
companyDescription: Tower Records was a major retailer of music and video recordings, books, and entertainment products with physical stores and a significant e-commerce presence at TowerRecords.com since 1996. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2004 and ultimately ceased operations in 2006.
companyLongDescription: Tower Records was a major retailer of music and video recordings, books, and entertainment products with physical stores and a significant e-commerce presence at TowerRecords.com since 1996. The company filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy in February 2004 and ultimately ceased operations in 2006.
caseDescription: Tower Records failed to implement adequate security measures on its e-commerce website, allowing unauthorized users to access customer personal information including purchase history, addresses, and phone numbers. A vulnerability in the Order Status application persisted for eight days in December 2002, exposing data for approximately 5,225 consumers. The company had promised in its privacy policy to use state-of-the-art technology to safeguard customer information, but failed to implement standard industry practices for detecting and preventing known vulnerabilities.
violationSummary: Tower Records failed to implement reasonable and appropriate security procedures to protect personal data from unauthorized access. The broken account and session management vulnerability was a known, preventable risk in the information technology industry, yet Tower Records created this vulnerability through inadequate code review and security testing procedures.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Tower Records redesigned its Order Status application in November-December 2002 and failed to include authentication code.
whyTheyWereWrong: Approximately 5,225 customers' billing addresses, shipping addresses, email addresses, phone numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tower Records stated: 'Your privacy is important to us. TowerRecords.com is committed to safeguarding your privacy online. We will never share your personal information with anyone for any reason without your explicit permission.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Tower Records failed to safeguard customer information. Due to missing authentication controls, approximately 5,225 customers' personal information including names, addresses, email, phone numbers, and full purchase histories were accessible to any visitor who entered a valid order number.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tower Records claimed: 'We use state-of-the-art technology to safeguard your personal information' and 'You and only you have access to this information.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Tower Records did not implement basic, publicly available security measures that had been standard industry practice since 2000. The Order Status application lacked even elementary authentication code to verify user identity, allowing complete strangers to view other customers' complete purchase and contact information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Tower Records stated: 'TowerRecords.com takes steps to ensure that your information is treated securely and in accordance with the relevant Terms of Service and this Privacy Policy.'
claimsVsReality.reality: Tower Records failed to implement appropriate checks and controls on the code-writing process, did not adopt security testing policies or procedures, and did not provide employee training on web application vulnerabilities – fundamental security practices that were widely known and publicly available.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Tower Records represented through its published privacy policy that it implemented measures 'reasonable and appropriate under the circumstances' to maintain and protect privacy and confidentiality of personal information, using 'state-of-the-art technology' and ensuring customers have exclusive access to their account information.
violations: Tower Records represented through its published privacy policy that it implemented measures 'reasonable and appropriate under the circumstances' to maintain and protect privacy and confidentiality of personal information, using 'state-of-the-art technology' and ensuring customers have exclusive access to their account information.

In truth and in fact, Tower Records failed to implement procedures that were reasonable and appropriate to detect and prevent vulnerabilities, failed to implement appropriate checks and controls on code writing/revision, failed to adopt security testing policies, and failed to provide employee training on web application security – all standard industry practices since at least 2000.

outcome: FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint was filed on May 28, 2004, during Tower Records' Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings (filed February 9, 2004). The company remained in possession of its business and property as debtor-in-possession. The complaint sought remedial action to address the security failures and protect consumers going forward.
companyNow: Tower Records ceased operations in 2006, liquidating its remaining stores after filing for bankruptcy. The company no longer operates as a going concern.
dataType: name, billing address, shipping address, email address, telephone number, purchase history
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

companyDescription: Sprint Corporation was a major U.S. telecommunications company providing local, long distance, and wireless telephone services. As a creditor under ECOA, Sprint extended credit to consumers by providing telephone services on a credit basis, billing after service delivery.
companyLongDescription: Sprint Corporation was a major U.S. telecommunications company providing local, long distance, and wireless telephone services. As a creditor under ECOA, Sprint extended credit to consumers by providing telephone services on a credit basis, billing after service delivery.
caseDescription: Sprint failed to provide legally required disclosures when taking adverse action against telephone service applicants based on credit reports. The company denied service or required deposits based on credit information but failed to inform consumers of their rights to obtain free copies of their credit reports or dispute inaccuracies, in violation of the Fair Credit Reporting Act and Equal Credit Opportunity Act.
violationSummary: Sprint excluded consumers from telephone services based on credit information without providing legally mandated disclosures, preventing consumers from exercising their rights to access and dispute credit reports.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Failure to Honor Consumer Rights
whatTheyDid: Sprint conducted credit reviews for telephone service applicants and denied service or required advance deposits based on consumer reports.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers were denied phone service or forced to pay deposits without being told they could get their credit report for free or challenge inaccurate information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Sprint provided required adverse action notices to consumers denied service or required to pay deposits
claimsVsReality.reality: Sprint's notices lacked statutory disclosures including consumer rights to obtain free credit reports within 60 days and dispute accuracy, in violation of FCRA Section 615(a)

claimsVsReality.claim: Sprint complied with ECOA disclosure requirements when taking adverse action
claimsVsReality.reality: Sprint's notices failed to include the ECOA non-discrimination statement and identify the federal agency administering ECOA compliance, violating Regulation B Section 202.9(a)

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 615(a) of the FCRA requires that when adverse action is taken based on information in a consumer report, the person must provide notice including: (1) notice of adverse action; (2) name, address, and phone of the reporting agency; (3) statement that the agency did not make the decision; (4) specific reasons for adverse action; and (5) notice of right to obtain free copy of report within 60 days and right to dispute accuracy.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sprint took adverse action (denying service or requiring deposits) based on consumer reports but failed to provide required disclosures about consumer rights
violations: Sprint took adverse action (denying service or requiring deposits) based on consumer reports but failed to provide required disclosures about consumer rights
Sprint gave notices lacking information about the right to obtain a free copy of the consumer report within 60 days
Sprint gave notices lacking information about the right to dispute accuracy or completeness of the consumer report

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 202.9(a) of Regulation B requires creditors taking adverse action to provide notice within 30 days containing specific statements including the ECOA non-discrimination statement and identity of the federal agency administering ECOA compliance.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sprint failed to provide required ECOA Section 701(a) statement in adverse action notices
violations: Sprint failed to provide required ECOA Section 701(a) statement in adverse action notices
Sprint failed to identify the federal agency that administers ECOA compliance in notices to applicants

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Sprint's violations of FCRA and ECOA disclosure requirements constitute unfair or deceptive acts in violation of Section 5(a)
violations: Sprint's violations of FCRA and ECOA disclosure requirements constitute unfair or deceptive acts in violation of Section 5(a)

outcome: The complaint seeks permanent injunction against violations of FCRA and ECOA, monetary civil penalties for each violation under FCRA (up to $2,500 per violation) and ECOA (up to $11,000 per violation), and such additional relief as the court deems just and proper. The case was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of Florida.
companyNow: Sprint merged with T-Mobile in 2020 to form T-Mobile US, Inc., which continues as a major wireless carrier. The original Sprint Corporation no longer exists as an independent entity.
dataType: Consumer credit information, consumer reports, financial information
legalBasisViolated: Fair Credit Reporting Act (FCRA) Section 615(a), 15 U.S.C. § 1681m(a)
Equal Credit Opportunity Act (ECOA) Section 701(d), 15 U.S.C. § 1691(d)

companyDescription: Nationwide Mortgage Group was a mortgage broker based in Fairfax, Virginia that processed residential mortgage loans and collected sensitive customer financial information in the course of loan processing, underwriting, and closing.
companyLongDescription: Nationwide Mortgage Group was a mortgage broker based in Fairfax, Virginia that processed residential mortgage loans and collected sensitive customer financial information in the course of loan processing, underwriting, and closing.
caseDescription: Nationwide Mortgage Group failed to implement adequate security safeguards for sensitive customer financial information, storing data on an Internet-connected network without monitoring for vulnerabilities or assessing security risks. The company also failed to provide customers with required privacy notices about how their personal information would be handled.
violationSummary: The company's failure to implement reasonable security measures, conduct risk assessments, monitor networks, and test safeguards resulted in customer financial data being vulnerable to unauthorized access, breach, and theft.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Nationwide Mortgage Group stored customers' Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, credit histories.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers' highly sensitive financial and identity information was exposed to theft, fraud, and misuse because the company failed to implement basic security safeguards despite handling data.

regulatoryFindings.act: The Safeguards Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 314) requires financial institutions to protect the security, confidentiality, and integrity of customer information by developing a comprehensive written information security program containing reasonable administrative, technical, and physical safeguards.
regulatoryFindings.description: Nationwide failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information security
violations: Nationwide failed to identify reasonably foreseeable internal and external risks to customer information security
Nationwide failed to implement information safeguards to control identified risks and failed to regularly test or monitor them
Nationwide failed to develop, implement, and maintain a comprehensive written information security program
Nationwide failed to designate one or more employees to coordinate the information security program

regulatoryFindings.act: The Privacy Rule (16 C.F.R. Part 313) requires financial institutions to provide customers with clear and conspicuous privacy notices when the customer relationship is formed and annually.
regulatoryFindings.description: Nationwide failed to provide customers with required privacy notices reflecting its information practices
violations: Nationwide failed to provide customers with required privacy notices reflecting its information practices

outcome: The FTC issued a cease and desist order requiring Nationwide to comply with the Safeguards Rule and Privacy Rule. The company must obtain biennial independent security assessments from a qualified CISSP, CISA, or GIAC professional for 10 years, implement a comprehensive written information security program, designate a security coordinator, conduct risk assessments, implement technical and physical safeguards, monitor network effectiveness, and provide the FTC with compliance reports within 180 days. John D. Eubank must notify the FTC of any business changes for 10 years. The order terminates after 20 years from issuance (November 9, 2024) or 20 years from any subsequent FTC complaint, whichever is later.
dataType: Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, credit histories, income tax returns, customer names

FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

companyDescription: Guess?, Inc. is an American fashion retailer founded in 1981 that designs, produces, and sells branded clothing and accessories globally through retail stores and e-commerce platforms including www.guess.com.
companyLongDescription: Guess?, Inc. is an American fashion retailer founded in 1981 that designs, produces, and sells branded clothing and accessories globally through retail stores and e-commerce platforms including www.guess.com.
caseDescription: Guess? operated an e-commerce website that collected sensitive customer financial data but failed to implement adequate security measures. The company represented that personal information was encrypted and stored securely, but in reality, an attacker could easily access unencrypted credit card numbers through known SQL injection vulnerabilities. A breach occurred in February 2002 exposing customer credit card data.
violationSummary: The core violation was inadequate security controls allowing unauthorized access to stored payment card data. The company made explicit representations about encryption and security that proved false due to failure to implement reasonable safeguards.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Guess collected customers' credit card numbers and personal information through www.guess.com but stored them in unencrypted.
whyTheyWereWrong: A visitor successfully used an SQL injection attack in February 2002 to read customers' credit card numbers.

claimsVsReality.claim: All personal information including credit card information is stored in an unreadable, encrypted format at all times.
claimsVsReality.reality: Credit card numbers were stored in clear text accessible to attackers using SQL injection attacks through the web application.

claimsVsReality.claim: This site has security measures in place to protect the loss, misuse and alteration of information; all orders transmitted over secure connections using SSL encryption.
claimsVsReality.reality: No reasonable security procedures were implemented to detect or prevent access to database tables; SQL injection vulnerabilities existed since at least October 2000 and were exploited in February 2002.

claimsVsReality.claim: The GUESS? Online Store uses Cybersource SSL technology—the industry standard for encryption—to create a secure transaction environment.
claimsVsReality.reality: While SSL was used for transmission, the application layer had critical flaws allowing database-level access without authentication.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents represented that personal information was stored in unreadable, encrypted format at all times using SSL encryption and multi-layer firewall protection, but this was false.
violations: Respondents represented that personal information was stored in unreadable, encrypted format at all times using SSL encryption and multi-layer firewall protection, but this was false.

Respondents represented they implemented reasonable and appropriate measures to protect personal information against loss, misuse, or alteration, but they failed to implement basic vulnerability testing or prevention measures.
Respondents failed to adopt adequate policies and procedures to protect sensitive consumer information.
Respondents failed to test or assess the website application for known vulnerabilities.
Respondents left the website vulnerable to SQL injection attacks that were publicly known since at least 1997 and preventable with publicly available measures.

outcome: FTC issued complaint in July 2003 alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a). The complaint alleged two deceptive misrepresentations: (1) that personal information was stored in unreadable encrypted format when it was actually accessible in clear text, and (2) that reasonable security measures had been implemented when they had not. Resolution typically resulted in a consent order requiring implementation of comprehensive information security program, regular security assessments, third-party audits, and consumer notification.
companyNow: Guess?, Inc. remains an active international fashion retailer and now implements compliance with data protection regulations including GDPR and CCPA. The company has modernized its security infrastructure following the 2003 enforcement action.
dataType: Financial data (credit card numbers, expiration dates), names, addresses
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) - Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce

company: Educational Research Center of America, Inc. (ERCA) and Student Marketing Group, Inc. (SMG)
companyDescription: ERCA was a Pennsylvania corporation claiming to be a non-profit conducting voluntary surveys of high school and middle/junior high school students. SMG, a New York corporation doing business as College Bound Selection Service, funded survey creation and distribution and compiled student lists for sale to commercial entities.
companyLongDescription: ERCA was a Pennsylvania corporation claiming to be a non-profit conducting voluntary surveys of high school and middle/junior high school students. SMG, a New York corporation doing business as College Bound Selection Service, funded survey creation and distribution and compiled student lists for sale to commercial entities.
caseDescription: ERCA and SMG collected personal information from millions of high school and over 300,000 middle/junior high school students through surveys. They represented the data would be shared only with educational institutions, but actually sold student lists to commercial entities including banks, insurance companies, and consumer goods providers for marketing purposes. The deceptive practices violated the FTC Act by misrepresenting how sensitive personal information from minors would be used.
violationSummary: The company disclosed sensitive personal information of minors to commercial entities (banks, insurance companies, list brokers) for marketing purposes, contrary to representations that data would be shared only with educational institutions. This is a core disclosure violation involving unauthorized secondary use of children's data.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: ERCA and SMG collected personal information from millions of high school students and over 300,000 middle/junior high students through surveys distributed by schools.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hundreds of thousands of minors had their sensitive personal data—including religious affiliation, race, ethnicity, grades, birth dates.

claimsVsReality.claim: ERCA is a non-profit corporation conducting a voluntary survey designed to help students further their education and enable colleges to identify potential students.
claimsVsReality.reality: SMG used the survey data primarily to compile and sell student lists to commercial entities including banks, insurance companies, consumer goods providers, and list brokers for marketing purposes, not educational purposes.

claimsVsReality.claim: Information collected from high school students through the Surveys is shared only with colleges, universities, and other entities providing education-related services.
claimsVsReality.reality: Information was shared with commercial entities for marketing purposes, not limited to education-related entities.

claimsVsReality.claim: Information collected from middle and junior high school students is compiled into survey reports shared with colleges and universities.
claimsVsReality.reality: Little if any information from younger students was compiled into reports; the data was primarily shared with commercial entities for marketing purposes.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Respondents represented through marketing materials and privacy statements that information collected from high school students would be shared only with colleges, universities, and education-related entities, but actually sold student data to commercial entities including banks, insurance companies, and list brokers for marketing purposes.
violations: Respondents represented through marketing materials and privacy statements that information collected from high school students would be shared only with colleges, universities, and education-related entities, but actually sold student data to commercial entities including banks, insurance companies, and list brokers for marketing purposes.

Respondents represented that information from middle and junior high school students would be compiled into survey reports shared with colleges and universities, but actually shared little to no information in reports; instead sold the data primarily to commercial entities for marketing purposes.
Misrepresentations were made to both students/parents and to educators regarding the scope and purpose of data use, concealing the commercial marketing purpose of the data collection.

outcome: Complaint issued by the FTC on May 6, 2003 alleging violation of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act through deceptive practices regarding the use and disclosure of personal information collected from students. The complaint alleges unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce involving misrepresentations about how student survey data would be used and shared.
companyNow: Unknown current status. The complaint document does not indicate whether a settlement was reached or the current operational status of ERCA or SMG.

companyDescription: Zachary Keith Hill operated phishing and fraud schemes impersonating major internet service providers and payment processors to steal consumer financial information.
companyLongDescription: Zachary Keith Hill operated phishing and fraud schemes impersonating major internet service providers and payment processors to steal consumer financial information.
caseDescription: Zachary Keith Hill conducted phishing attacks impersonating AOL and PayPal, sending deceptive spam emails that tricked consumers into submitting sensitive financial and personal information via fraudulent web pages. The defendant collected this data without encryption or authorization and used it to make unauthorized purchases, establish fraudulent accounts, and access consumers' accounts without permission.
violationSummary: Defendant fraudulently obtained consumer financial information through impersonation and deceptive web pages, then breached confidentiality by accessing and misusing that information for unauthorized transactions and account takeovers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Zachary Keith Hill sent phishing emails impersonating AOL and PayPal, directing consumers to fake billing pages that harvested credit card numbers, bank account details.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers who submitted their financial information had unauthorized charges made to their accounts, lost access to legitimate services, and became victims of identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Emails and web pages were from AOL's Billing Center or PayPal's authorization systems
claimsVsReality.reality: Emails were sent by Zachary Keith Hill from unauthorized servers; web pages were hosted by Hill on unauthorized domains and designed to deceive consumers

claimsVsReality.reality: Data was sent directly to Hill's email accounts for his unauthorized access and misuse

violations: Hill falsely represented that spam emails and web pages were sent by AOL and PayPal
Hill falsely represented that consumers needed to provide billing information or risk account termination
Hill failed to disclose that submitted data would not be encrypted or transmitted securely as claimed

violations: Hill obtained credit card numbers, bank account information, and other financial data through false pretenses impersonating AOL and PayPal

companyNow: Individual defendant; status unknown. Case filed December 2003 in U.S. District Court, Southern District of Texas.

Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Section 521 – Obtaining customer information of financial institutions by false pretenses

companyDescription: Canada Post is Canada's national postal service, providing mail delivery and related services to residents and businesses across the country. It also operates ancillary services including the National Change of Address program.
companyLongDescription: Canada Post is a Crown corporation responsible for providing postal services throughout Canada. Beyond standard mail delivery, it offers services such as the National Change of Address (NCOA) program, which allows individuals relocating to redirect their mail to new addresses. The company also engages in direct mail marketing services and address disclosure programs. As a public utility, Canada Post operates under the Canadian Privacy Act and federal oversight.
caseDescription: Canada Post's National Change of Address (NCOA) service collected individuals' new addresses ostensibly for mail redirection but disclosed this information to mass mailers, direct marketers, and list brokers without obtaining clear, informed consent. The company used 'negative consent' (opt-out) rather than affirmative consent, and failed to transparently disclose that personal information was being sold to third parties for commercial purposes.
violationSummary: Canada Post disclosed personal information (new addresses) to third parties (mass mailers, direct marketers, list brokers) without obtaining individuals' informed consent. The disclosure was not clearly communicated, and individuals had no reasonable expectation that their data would be sold for commercial purposes.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Canada Post collected individuals' new addresses through its National Change of Address service and disclosed them to mass mailers, direct marketers.
whyTheyWereWrong: Individuals' address information was sold to third parties for commercial purposes without their knowledge or meaningful choice, exposing them to unsolicited marketing.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers are informed that their new address may be provided to mailers if they request it.
claimsVsReality.reality: This critical disclosure appeared only in fine print on the back of the form, not in marketing materials or on the website, leaving most customers unaware of the practice.

claimsVsReality.claim: Providing new addresses to mailers is a free service to customers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Canada Post actually received fees from the mailers (list brokers, direct marketers, and mass mailers) for selling customer address information, profiting from the disclosure.

claimsVsReality.claim: A safeguard exists because mailers must already have the customer's name and old address before receiving the new address.
claimsVsReality.reality: This safeguard was inadequate because mailers routinely buy, sell, and trade mailing lists with each other without original consent from the individuals whose data appears on those lists.

claimsVsReality.claim: Customers can opt out by contacting Canada Post if they do not want their address shared.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customers had to actively write a letter within seven days to opt out—a deliberately burdensome process that few would discover or complete, constituting negative rather than affirmative consent.

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 5(2) – requirement to inform individuals of the purpose for collection with plain and full identification
regulatoryFindings.description: Canada Post failed to specify to NCOA applicants its intention to disclose new addresses to mass mailers and direct marketers for commercial purposes
violations: Canada Post failed to specify to NCOA applicants its intention to disclose new addresses to mass mailers and direct marketers for commercial purposes
The authorization form did not clearly identify that personal information would be sold to third parties

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy Act Section 8 – requirement to obtain consent for disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Canada Post disclosed individuals' new addresses to mass mailers and direct marketers without obtaining informed consent
violations: Canada Post disclosed individuals' new addresses to mass mailers and direct marketers without obtaining informed consent
The company used 'negative consent' (opt-out) rather than affirmative consent
None of the exceptions under Section 8(2) applied to justify disclosure without consent

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded. Canada Post was found to be in contravention of Sections 5(2) and 8 of the Privacy Act. The Commissioner recommended that Canada Post: (1) clearly indicate in its brochure and literature that the selling of individuals' new addresses to organizations including list brokers, mass mailers, and direct marketers is a feature of the NCOA service, and (2) add a check-off box on the NCOA form to obtain informed consent for such disclosure. Canada Post agreed to the first recommendation but refused to implement the second recommendation regarding affirmative consent. The Commissioner determined that Canada Post continues to violate the privacy rights of all NCOA subscribers until the process is changed.
companyNow: Canada Post continues to operate as Canada's primary postal service, though it faces ongoing financial pressures from declining mail volumes and competition from digital communication. The organization remains subject to privacy law compliance requirements.
dataType: Name, address, mail forwarding information
legalBasisViolated: Privacy Act Section 5(2) – failure to clearly identify purpose of collection
Privacy Act Section 8 – disclosure without consent

companyDescription: A Canadian federal financial institution that collected, used, and shared customer personal information with affiliated organizations for marketing purposes.
companyLongDescription: The bank operated as a federal work, undertaking, or business under Canadian jurisdiction and maintained relationships with multiple subsidiary and affiliate organizations. It engaged in secondary marketing practices involving the sharing of customer personal information across its corporate family. The bank maintained privacy-related documents and processes intended to inform customers of these practices, though the adequacy and accessibility of these communications became the subject of regulatory review.
caseDescription: A customer complained that a bank disclosed personal information to affiliates for secondary marketing purposes without obtaining explicit consent and without adequately informing customers of their opt-out rights. The bank's privacy materials and processes were investigated to determine whether they met PIPEDA's knowledge and consent requirements.
violationSummary: The allegation centered on unauthorized disclosure of personal information to affiliates for secondary marketing without proper knowledge and consent mechanisms, which falls under information dissemination violations.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: A bank disclosed customer personal information to affiliates for secondary marketing purposes without clearly communicating opt-out procedures.
whyTheyWereWrong: Customers were not adequately informed about which affiliates would receive their data or given easily accessible ways to opt out.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank's privacy materials and processes constitute sufficient effort to ensure customers understand secondary marketing purposes and have reasonable opt-out mechanisms.
claimsVsReality.reality: Customers were not adequately informed of the specific affiliates receiving their data, and opt-out procedures were not clearly presented or easily executable, making informed consent difficult.

claimsVsReality.claim: The bank provides clear information about the extent and purpose of data sharing through its privacy documents and codes.
claimsVsReality.reality: Privacy materials did not list specific affiliates and buried important information in lengthy documents with unclear language, making it difficult for ordinary customers to understand actual data-sharing practices.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3 – Knowledge and consent of the individual are required for collection, use or disclosure of personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Allegation that bank failed to obtain consent for disclosure to affiliates for secondary marketing purposes
violations: Allegation that bank failed to obtain consent for disclosure to affiliates for secondary marketing purposes

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.2 – Organizations must make reasonable effort to ensure individual is advised of purposes and consent must be meaningful through clear understanding
regulatoryFindings.description: Alleged failure to clearly inform customers of secondary uses and sharing practices
violations: Alleged failure to clearly inform customers of secondary uses and sharing practices
Alleged reliance on fine print and buried information

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4.3.5 – Reasonable expectations of the individual are relevant when obtaining consent
regulatoryFindings.description: Alleged failure to provide adequate opt-out procedures and clear disclosure of sharing practices
violations: Alleged failure to provide adequate opt-out procedures and clear disclosure of sharing practices

outcome: The Commissioner found the complaint was not well-founded. The bank's privacy-related materials and processes were determined to constitute a reasonable effort to ensure individuals were advised of secondary purposes and provided opportunity to refuse or withdraw consent. The Commissioner commended the bank's policy of personally presenting optional secondary purposes to customers and guiding them through an opt-out procedure, noting it was exemplary and akin to opt-in consent if consistently applied.
dataType: Personal information for marketing purposes, customer identifiers

companyDescription: American Pop Corn Company, based in Sioux City, Iowa, is a popcorn manufacturer and marketer operating the Jolly Time brand. The company sells popcorn products throughout the United States and operates commercial websites for marketing.
companyLongDescription: American Pop Corn Company, based in Sioux City, Iowa, is a popcorn manufacturer and marketer operating the Jolly Time brand. The company sells popcorn products throughout the United States and operates commercial websites for marketing.
caseDescription: American Pop Corn Company operated a 'Kids Club' section on its website that collected personal information from children without obtaining verifiable parental consent. The company falsely claimed in its privacy policy that it would notify parents and allow them to invalidate registrations, but never actually did so. The company collected more personal information than necessary to participate in club activities.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected personal information from children through a directed website section without proper legal safeguards, constituting surveillance of minors.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: American Pop Corn Company operated the Jolly Time website's Kids Club section, collecting approximately 500 children's full names, physical addresses, email addresses.
whyTheyWereWrong: Hundreds of children's sensitive personal information including home addresses was collected and stored without parents' knowledge or approval, creating exposure to unsolicited marketing.

claimsVsReality.claim: When a guest under age 18 registers in the Kids Club, parents/guardians will receive an email informing them of registration and may elect to invalidate it.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company never collected parent email addresses, never sent notification emails, and never provided any opportunity for parents to invalidate registrations.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website instructions told children to 'check with your parents first' before providing personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: No verifiable parental consent was obtained; the suggestion to check with parents was purely advisory with no enforcement mechanism or notification system.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA and the Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule require website operators directed to children to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.

violations: Company collected first name, last name, physical address, email, and birth date from approximately 500 children without any verifiable parental consent.
Company failed to obtain parental consent before collecting personal information from children.

regulatoryFindings.description: Company's privacy policy did not clearly disclose all information collection, use, and disclosure practices.
violations: Company's privacy policy did not clearly disclose all information collection, use, and disclosure practices.
Company failed to provide direct notice to parents of its information practices.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA requires operators to give parents reasonable means to review collected information and refuse its further use or maintenance.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company provided no means for parents to review or delete information collected from their children.
violations: Company provided no means for parents to review or delete information collected from their children.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA prohibits conditioning children's participation in activities on disclosure of more personal information than reasonably necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company required collection of first name, last name, address, email, and birth date to participate in games and receive prizes, more than reasonably necessary.
violations: Company required collection of first name, last name, address, email, and birth date to participate in games and receive prizes, more than reasonably necessary.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in commerce. A violation of COPPA constitutes an unfair or deceptive act.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company made false and misleading statements in its privacy policy claiming it would collect parent email addresses, notify parents, and allow them to invalidate registrations, when it actually did none of these.
violations: Company made false and misleading statements in its privacy policy claiming it would collect parent email addresses, notify parents, and allow them to invalidate registrations, when it actually did none of these.
Company represented it would obtain parental consent while actively collecting children's data without consent.

outcome: Complaint filed seeking monetary civil penalties of up to $11,000 per violation (approximately 500 violations estimated), permanent injunction against operating websites directed to children in violation of COPPA, and other equitable relief. Court authorized to issue injunction and award civil penalties under FTC Act Section 13(b) and COPPA enforcement provisions.
companyNow: American Pop Corn Company (now known as Snack Time Foods) continues to operate in the popcorn market. Following this enforcement action, the company was required to implement comprehensive COPPA compliance measures and privacy safeguards.
dataType: Children's personal information: name, address, email, date of birth

companyLongDescription: Discreet Data Systems was an unincorporated entity operating over the telephone and internet that purported to provide asset location and information search services. companyDescription: Eli Lilly and Company is a major multinational pharmaceutical corporation founded in 1876, specializing in medications for depression, diabetes, immunology, and oncology.
companyLongDescription: Eli Lilly and Company is a major multinational pharmaceutical corporation founded in 1876, specializing in medications for depression, diabetes, immunology, and oncology.
caseDescription: Eli Lilly operated a Medi-messenger email reminder service through Prozac.com that promised to protect subscriber privacy. On June 27, 2001, an employee sent a termination notice that inadvertently disclosed all 669 subscribers' email addresses to each other due to failure to implement adequate security procedures and employee training.
violationSummary: The company breached its own privacy policy by failing to maintain appropriate safeguards for personal information (email addresses) voluntarily provided by consumers for a sensitive health-related service.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Eli Lilly sent a termination email to Medi-messenger subscribers with all 669 recipient email addresses visible in the 'To:' line.
whyTheyWereWrong: 669 depression medication users had their sensitive personal email addresses exposed to strangers due to Eli Lilly's failure to provide employee training, oversight.

claimsVsReality.claim: Eli Lilly respects privacy and has developed a privacy code with security measures including SSL encryption to protect confidentiality of personal information.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company lacked basic operational safeguards: no employee training on privacy/security, inadequate oversight of the employee creating the email program, no program review by experienced personnel, and no internal testing before sending the disclosure email.

claimsVsReality.claim: Personal information will only be used as described in the privacy statement and all uses comply with applicable laws.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal email addresses were disclosed to 669 strangers due to failure to implement controls and proper procedures, violating the company's own privacy commitments.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Company represented through privacy policies that it employed measures appropriate under the circumstances to maintain and protect the privacy and confidentiality of personal information.
violations: Company represented through privacy policies that it employed measures appropriate under the circumstances to maintain and protect the privacy and confidentiality of personal information.
In fact, the company failed to provide appropriate employee training, oversight, checks and controls, and did not test the computer program before sending the disclosure email.
The June 27, 2001 email disclosed all subscribers' email addresses, causing unintentional but preventable disclosure of personal information due to inadequate internal security measures.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint alleging unfair and deceptive practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The document indicates the case was filed in 2002. Based on the complaint structure, Eli Lilly was likely subject to a consent order requiring implementation of comprehensive information security safeguards, employee training, and third-party auditing to ensure compliance with privacy policies and appropriate data protection measures going forward.
companyNow: Eli Lilly and Company remains one of the world's largest pharmaceutical manufacturers, headquartered in Indianapolis, Indiana, with significant R&D operations and global pharmaceutical sales.

whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of consumers stored credit card numbers, billing addresses, and personal identity information in Passport Wallet believing it was secure, exposing them to data theft.
