claimsVsReality.reality: Security measures were insufficient; the system lacked documented procedures for access prevention, breach detection, vulnerability monitoring, and security audits

claimsVsReality.claim: Store information in .NET Passport wallet that will help you make faster safer online purchases
claimsVsReality.reality: Purchases made with Passport Wallet provided no greater security than purchases made directly; most consumers received identical security either way

claimsVsReality.claim: Passport did not collect any personally identifiable information other than that described in its privacy policy
claimsVsReality.reality: Passport collected and maintained personally identifiable records of the sites users signed into, along with dates and times of sign-in, linked to users' names

claimsVsReality.claim: Kids Passport allows parents to limit the amount of information shared with Passport sites and provides control over children's personal information
claimsVsReality.reality: Children could edit personal information fields and change account settings set by parents; information was also disclosed to non-participating Passport sites without clear parental notification

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Microsoft represented that Passport achieved a high level of web security with technologies designed to prevent unauthorized access, but failed to implement sufficient security measures including procedures to prevent unauthorized access, detect breaches, monitor vulnerabilities, and maintain audit records
violations: Microsoft represented that Passport achieved a high level of web security with technologies designed to prevent unauthorized access, but failed to implement sufficient security measures including procedures to prevent unauthorized access, detect breaches, monitor vulnerabilities, and maintain audit records
Microsoft represented that Passport Wallet purchases were safer or more secure than direct purchases, when most consumers received identical security whether using Wallet or not

Microsoft represented through privacy policies that Passport did not collect personally identifiable information beyond what was disclosed, but collected and retained personally identifiable sign-in records linking users' names to sites accessed

Microsoft represented that Kids Passport provided parents with control over children's information collection and use, but permitted children to edit personal information fields and change account settings set by parents, and failed to clearly disclose that information would be shared with non-participating Passport sites

outcome: The FTC issued a Complaint on December 20, 2002, alleging unfair and deceptive practices. The document is the formal Complaint; a subsequent Consent Order would have required Microsoft to implement comprehensive information security programs, obtain third-party security assessments, maintain detailed records, notify consumers of breaches, and comply with specific security standards. Microsoft was subject to ongoing monitoring and compliance obligations.
companyNow: Microsoft remains one of the world's largest technology companies. The Passport service was eventually phased out and replaced with Microsoft Account (now Microsoft Entra ID), which incorporated enhanced security and privacy protections reflecting lessons from this enforcement action.
dataType: Email addresses, passwords, personal information, credit card numbers, billing information, shipping information, children's personal information, sign-in records
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices

company: GM Funding, Inc. (and related entities: Global Mortgage Funding, Inc., Universal IT Solutions, Inc.)
companyDescription: GM Funding, Inc. and related entities operated as a mortgage marketing scheme that used deceptive spam emails and spoofed identities to solicit financial information from consumers, which they then used for unsolicited telemarketing.
companyLongDescription: GM Funding, Inc. and related entities operated as a mortgage marketing scheme that used deceptive spam emails and spoofed identities to solicit financial information from consumers, which they then used for unsolicited telemarketing.
caseDescription: Defendants sent deceptive spam emails impersonating legitimate financial institutions (Radian, Prudential, Fannie Mae) to solicit personal financial information from consumers. They fraudulently collected mortgage data by false affiliation claims, spoofed email reply-to addresses causing third-party inbox flooding, and misrepresented unsubscribe capabilities.
violationSummary: Defendants used deceptive impersonation of trusted financial institutions to directly interrogate and extract sensitive personal financial information (mortgage data, income, credit ratings) from unsuspecting consumers under false pretenses.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: Sent unsolicited spam emails impersonating well-known financial institutions like Radian, Prudential, and Fannie Mae, using their logos and trademarks without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers divulged sensitive financial data including mortgage balances, home values, income.

claimsVsReality.claim: Emails were from Radian Mortgage Loan Search Corporation, Prudential Mortgage Loan Search Corporation, or Fannie Mae
claimsVsReality.reality: Emails were from GM Funding, Global Mortgage Funding, or Universal IT Solutions with no affiliation to those financial institutions

claimsVsReality.claim: Providing financial information would help consumers find home mortgages
claimsVsReality.reality: Information was used by defendants to conduct unsolicited telemarketing sales calls for mortgages under their own companies

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers could unsubscribe by replying to removal email addresses
claimsVsReality.reality: Removal emails were returned as undeliverable and addresses were never actually removed from mailing lists

claimsVsReality.claim: Reply-to addresses in emails were legitimate contact points
claimsVsReality.reality: Reply-to addresses were spoofed addresses of unrelated third parties, causing them to receive thousands of unwanted messages

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Falsely representing sender identity as Radian, Prudential, or Fannie Mae when defendants were unaffiliated
violations: Falsely representing sender identity as Radian, Prudential, or Fannie Mae when defendants were unaffiliated
Falsely promising email removal upon consumer request when addresses were not actually removed
Engaging in email spoofing by placing unrelated third-party addresses in reply-to fields without authorization

regulatoryFindings.act: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Section 521(a) prohibits obtaining customer financial institution information using false, fictitious, or fraudulent statements or representations.
regulatoryFindings.description: Using false claims of affiliation with financial institutions to fraudulently obtain customer information (mortgage amounts, rates, home values, income, credit ratings)
violations: Using false claims of affiliation with financial institutions to fraudulently obtain customer information (mortgage amounts, rates, home values, income, credit ratings)

outcome: FTC filed complaint seeking permanent injunction, rescission of contracts, restitution, disgorgement of ill-gotten gains, refund of monies paid, and other equitable relief. The complaint sought to prevent defendants from continuing deceptive spam practices and to remedy consumer injury through monetary and injunctive remedies under FTC Act Section 13(b) and GLB Act Section 522(a).
companyNow: Unknown. Based on document date (November 2002) and nature of violations, defendants appear to have been a short-lived spam operation.
dataType: Financial information (mortgage balances, rates, home value, income, credit rating, contact details)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Deceptive Acts or Practices
Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Section 521(a) – Fraudulent Obtaining of Customer Information

companyDescription: A Canadian transportation company operating cross-border train service between Toronto and New York.
companyLongDescription: The company operated passenger rail service on the Toronto-to-New York route and collected traveler personal information including name, date of birth, and citizenship. This data was disclosed to U.S. Customs and Immigration authorities as part of a border clearance agreement. The company's sales agents misrepresented the data collection as mandatory rather than voluntary, violating passenger privacy rights and PIPEDA consent requirements.
caseDescription: A Canadian transportation company's sales agents collected passengers' personal information (name, date of birth, citizenship) for the Toronto-to-New York train route and disclosed it to U.S. Customs and Immigration authorities. The company misrepresented this data collection as mandatory rather than voluntary, violating passengers' privacy rights and consent requirements.
violationSummary: The company systematically collected personal information from train passengers without proper consent, misrepresenting the collection as mandatory. The surveillance was conducted through sales agents during the booking process.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Sales agents collected passengers' names, dates of birth, and citizenship for the Toronto-to-New York train route and disclosed this information to U.S. Customs.
whyTheyWereWrong: Passengers were misled into believing the data collection was mandatory rather than voluntary, denying them the ability to make informed choices about sharing sensitive personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: Providing date of birth and citizenship is required for passengers on the Toronto-to-New York run.
claimsVsReality.reality: The information collection was voluntary and passengers could decline to provide it; agents were instructed to represent it as mandatory.

claimsVsReality.claim: Data collection practices were disclosed and consented to by passengers.
claimsVsReality.reality: Passengers were misled about the voluntary nature of the collection and were not given genuine informed consent to disclose personal information to U.S. authorities.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 3 – Consent: Organizations must obtain informed consent before collecting personal information
regulatoryFindings.description: Sales agents misrepresented the collection of date of birth and citizenship as mandatory rather than voluntary
violations: Sales agents misrepresented the collection of date of birth and citizenship as mandatory rather than voluntary
Passengers were not clearly informed that providing this information was optional

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 1 – Accountability: Organizations must be responsible for personal information in their custody
regulatoryFindings.description: Company did not establish clear protocols for obtaining voluntary consent prior to collection
violations: Company did not establish clear protocols for obtaining voluntary consent prior to collection
Inconsistent representations to passengers regarding the nature of the information request

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Principle 4 – Accuracy: Personal information must be as accurate, complete, and up-to-date as possible
regulatoryFindings.description: Collection methods did not ensure informed and accurate understanding of what information was being collected and why
violations: Collection methods did not ensure informed and accurate understanding of what information was being collected and why

outcome: The Office of the Privacy Commissioner of Canada required the transportation company to issue a clear directive to sales agents stating that passengers' provision of date of birth and citizenship must be represented as voluntary. The company was instructed to ask customers after booking whether they would voluntarily provide this information to facilitate customs clearance. The Office closed the incident file subject to continued monitoring of sales agents' booking practices and advised the company to send a follow-up note to agents clarifying that personal information must not be collected without informed consent.
dataType: name, date of birth, citizenship

companyDescription: Centurion Security Services was a small Yellowknife-based security company that provided home security alarms, monitoring services, and nanny-cam systems to local businesses and institutions.
companyLongDescription: Centurion Security Services was a security services company operating in Yellowknife, Northwest Territories, with approximately 30 employees. Originally a locksmith store, it expanded under new ownership to offer home security alarms, monitoring, and surveillance equipment. The company maintained contracts with a local hospital, Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce, apartment buildings, and local businesses. It attempted to market itself as a public safety enhancement to local police services.
caseDescription: Centurion Security Services installed street surveillance cameras at a downtown Yellowknife intersection to monitor public areas as a marketing demonstration for security services without obtaining consent from individuals being recorded. The Privacy Commissioner found that live video feed of individuals constitutes personal information under PIPEDA and cannot be collected for commercial purposes without informed consent. The Commissioner prohibited the company from pursuing further public video surveillance for commercial reasons.
violationSummary: The company systematically observed and monitored individuals in public spaces through video cameras without their knowledge or consent as part of a commercial activity. This constitutes unlawful surveillance under PIPEDA's requirement for informed consent in commercial information collection.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Centurion Security Services installed four surveillance cameras at a downtown Yellowknife intersection.
whyTheyWereWrong: Residents had their movements and activities systematically monitored and recorded without their knowledge or permission.

claimsVsReality.claim: Video surveillance is of great benefit to the Yellowknife community and enhances public safety.
claimsVsReality.reality: The surveillance was conducted without consent for commercial marketing purposes, not public safety, and violated fundamental privacy rights of residents.

claimsVsReality.claim: The company did its best to bring the City and RCMP into the project.
claimsVsReality.reality: The City of Yellowknife explicitly declined the company's offer to provide surveillance services in April 2001, yet the company proceeded unilaterally without authorization.

claimsVsReality.claim: Live video feeds do not constitute personal information because they are not recorded.
claimsVsReality.reality: Live video feeds of identifiable individuals qualify as personal information under PIPEDA regardless of whether they are recorded, as staff could identify and describe individuals' activities and behavior.

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 2 - Definition of Personal Information
regulatoryFindings.description: Video surveillance feed captures personal information (identifiable individuals and their activities/behavior) which is protected under PIPEDA regardless of whether it is recorded or live
violations: Video surveillance feed captures personal information (identifiable individuals and their activities/behavior) which is protected under PIPEDA regardless of whether it is recorded or live

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.3 - Consent Requirement
regulatoryFindings.description: Centurion collected personal information through video cameras without obtaining informed consent from individuals being monitored
violations: Centurion collected personal information through video cameras without obtaining informed consent from individuals being monitored
The live feed was monitored and used (e.g., contacting police about suspicious activity) without individuals' knowledge or agreement

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA Section 4 - Commercial Activity
regulatoryFindings.description: The surveillance activity was conducted as a marketing demonstration to generate business contracts, constituting a commercial activity subject to PIPEDA
violations: The surveillance activity was conducted as a marketing demonstration to generate business contracts, constituting a commercial activity subject to PIPEDA

outcome: The Privacy Commissioner found the complaint well-founded. Since the cameras had already been removed, no further action regarding the installed cameras was required. However, the Commissioner explicitly prohibited Centurion Security Services from pursuing its intended public video surveillance for commercial purposes, informing the company that such surveillance would be unlawful. The Commissioner emphasized that while public area monitoring may be appropriate for public safety reasons by lawful public authorities with demonstrated need and proper privacy safeguards, unauthorized private sector commercial surveillance of public places violates fundamental privacy rights and PIPEDA compliance obligations.
companyNow: No publicly available information indicates the company's current status following this 2001 enforcement action.
dataType: Video surveillance data, personal images, behavioral observations

companyDescription: Ottawa Sun was an early 2000s Internet service provider and web hosting company based in Ottawa, Canada, that operated streaming audio services.
companyLongDescription: Ottawa Sun was an Ottawa-based web hosting and Internet service provider active in the early 2000s. The company operated a website that streamed live audio content to Internet users. The operation involved technical infrastructure including a scanner device connected to a hosting server. The company ultimately ceased operations after its primary website was shut down due to technical issues.
caseDescription: An Ottawa-based Web site was streaming live audio from intercepted cellular telephone conversations onto the Internet without authorization. A scanner connected to a hosting computer captured private cell phone traffic and made it publicly accessible online. The ISP shut down the Web site due to bandwidth issues caused by an employee's personal account and terminated the employee.
violationSummary: The unauthorized interception and public broadcast of private cellular conversations constitutes an exposure of sensitive personal information to the internet without consent, making private communications accessible to any web user.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: An Ottawa-based website streamed live audio from intercepted cellular telephone conversations onto the Internet without authorization.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of people had their private phone conversations broadcast publicly online without their knowledge or consent, exposing sensitive personal information.

claimsVsReality.claim: The website was operating a legitimate streaming service
claimsVsReality.reality: The website was broadcasting intercepted private cellular phone conversations without any authorization or consent from the people being recorded

claimsVsReality.claim: Technical issues led to the shutdown
claimsVsReality.reality: While bandwidth problems from an employee's personal account contributed to the ISP's decision to shut down the service, the fundamental issue was that the service was illegally intercepting and broadcasting private communications

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to identify the purposes for which personal information is collected and to obtain consent before collection
regulatoryFindings.description: Cellular conversations were intercepted and broadcast without any identified legitimate purpose or consent from the individuals whose conversations were captured
violations: Cellular conversations were intercepted and broadcast without any identified legitimate purpose or consent from the individuals whose conversations were captured

regulatoryFindings.act: PIPEDA requires organizations to implement safeguards to protect personal information from unauthorized access and disclosure
regulatoryFindings.description: The scanner and connected computer had inadequate security controls, allowing unauthorized interception and public streaming of private communications
violations: The scanner and connected computer had inadequate security controls, allowing unauthorized interception and public streaming of private communications

outcome: The Web site was shut down by the ISP due to bandwidth problems caused by an employee's personal network account. The employee was terminated. The Office of the Privacy Commissioner discontinued its investigation given the Web site closure, but indicated the site would be monitored periodically for an indefinite length of time. The Web site relocated to a New York server under new management.
companyNow: The company no longer operates; its primary website was shut down in 2001 and operations were not resumed.
dataType: cell phone conversations, audio communications
legalBasisViolated: PIPEDA Schedule 1, Principle 4.7 (Security of Personal Information)

companyDescription: Lisa Frank, Inc. is an Arizona-based company that designs and sells colorful toys, school supplies, and merchandise for children, primarily targeting girls. The company operates retail locations and e-commerce website www.lisafrank.com.
companyLongDescription: Lisa Frank, Inc. is an Arizona-based company that designs and sells colorful toys, school supplies, and merchandise for children, primarily targeting girls. The company operates retail locations and e-commerce website www.lisafrank.com.
caseDescription: Lisa Frank, Inc. operated a website directed to children and collected their personal information without obtaining parental consent as required by COPPA. The company's privacy policy falsely claimed it obtained parental consent before allowing children under 13 to register, but the website allowed direct registration without any parental verification. The registration form actively solicited identifying information from children through prompts on pages depicting young girls.
violationSummary: The company engaged in systematic collection of children's personal information without lawful basis (parental consent). This constitutes surveillance of minors by collecting identifying information at the point of service without authorization from parents or guardians.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Lisa Frank collected children's names, addresses, email addresses, phone numbers, birth dates, and favorite characters through website registration forms without obtaining verifiable parental.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of children under 13 had their personal identifying information collected and retained by a commercial operator with no parental knowledge, creating risks of identity theft.

claimsVsReality.claim: Children 13 years or younger will require parental consent before being able to register and participate
claimsVsReality.reality: The website allowed children under 13 to complete the registration form and provide personal information without any parental consent mechanism or verification

claimsVsReality.claim: When a guest 13 years or younger registers, his/her parent or guardian will be required to fill out and sign a registration form
claimsVsReality.reality: No parental verification form was presented; children could register directly and provide complete personal information including address, phone number, and birth date

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA requires operators of websites directed to children to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children under 13.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lisa Frank collected names, addresses, email, phone numbers, and birth dates from children without obtaining any parental consent
violations: Lisa Frank collected names, addresses, email, phone numbers, and birth dates from children without obtaining any parental consent
The website featured prominent registration forms directed at children that immediately requested personal identifying information

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(c) requires operators to provide direct notice to parents stating intent to collect information, that parental consent is needed, and disclosure of collection and use practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lisa Frank provided no direct notice to parents about data collection practices
violations: Lisa Frank provided no direct notice to parents about data collection practices
Parents received no communication about the website's intent to collect their children's personal information

regulatoryFindings.act: Privacy policies must clearly, understandably, and completely disclose information collection, use, and disclosure practices as required by COPPA Rule Section 312.4(a).
regulatoryFindings.description: Lisa Frank's privacy policy made false claims that parental consent was required and obtained before children could register
violations: Lisa Frank's privacy policy made false claims that parental consent was required and obtained before children could register
The actual website allowed children to complete registration without any parental verification mechanism

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a)(1) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Lisa Frank made false and misleading representations in its privacy policy regarding parental consent requirements
violations: Lisa Frank made false and misleading representations in its privacy policy regarding parental consent requirements
The deception occurred at the point of collection where children were directed to provide personal information

outcome: The complaint sought civil penalties of up to $11,000 per violation, a permanent injunction against further COPPA violations, and injunctive relief regarding false statements about privacy practices. The complaint was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. Lisa Frank was required to implement a compliance program ensuring verifiable parental consent before collecting any personal information from children, provide direct notice to parents, and cease making false statements about privacy practices.
companyNow: Lisa Frank, Inc. continues to operate as a toy and school supplies brand. The company is now owned by MGA Entertainment and operates both physical and online retail channels with updated privacy compliance measures.
dataType: Children's personal information: name, address, email, phone number, birth date, color and character preferences
legalBasisViolated: Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule Section 312.3, 16 C.F.R. § 312.3
Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule Section 312.4, 16 C.F.R. § 312.4
Children's Online Privacy Protection Rule Section 312.5, 16 C.F.R. § 312.5

companyDescription: Looksmart Ltd. was a publicly-traded Delaware corporation operating the insidetheweb.com website, a free online message board service that enabled users to post, reply to, and create message boards. The company also provided message board services to third-party websites.
companyLongDescription: Looksmart Ltd. was a publicly-traded Delaware corporation operating the insidetheweb.com website, a free online message board service that enabled users to post, reply to, and create message boards. The company also provided message board services to third-party websites.
caseDescription: Looksmart operated a message board website that collected personal information from children under 13 without parental consent, failed to post clear privacy notices, and did not provide parents with means to review or delete collected data. The company knowingly allowed children to register and create message boards from April 2000 through August 2000, and provided message board services to children's websites like Girls' Life without implementing COPPA protections.
violationSummary: Looksmart systematically collected personal information from children through mandatory registration and message submission fields, without proper notice or consent mechanisms. The collection and public posting of children's names and email addresses constitutes direct surveillance of minors' online activity.
violations: Unauthorized Data Collection
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: Collected full names, email addresses, birth dates, gender, and profiling data from children under 13 registering for message boards on insidetheweb.com.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of children's personal information was publicly exposed online without parental knowledge or consent, leaving minors vulnerable to contact by strangers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Looksmart posted a privacy policy covering its information practices.
claimsVsReality.reality: The privacy policy did not clearly, understandably, or completely disclose information collection, use, and disclosure practices as required by COPPA.

claimsVsReality.claim: Looksmart's website could accommodate children as participants.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company had no parental consent mechanisms, no clear notice to parents, and no means for parents to review or delete children's data—all violations of COPPA.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(b) requires operators to post a clear, understandable, and complete privacy policy disclosing what information is collected from children, how it is used, and disclosure practices.
regulatoryFindings.description: Looksmart posted a privacy policy that did not clearly, understandably, or completely disclose its information collection, use, and disclosure practices for children's data.
violations: Looksmart posted a privacy policy that did not clearly, understandably, or completely disclose its information collection, use, and disclosure practices for children's data.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.4(c) requires operators to provide direct notice to parents about information practices regarding children's personal information.
regulatoryFindings.description: Looksmart did not provide direct notice to parents of its practices regarding collection, use, and disclosure of children's personal information.
violations: Looksmart did not provide direct notice to parents of its practices regarding collection, use, and disclosure of children's personal information.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.5 requires operators to obtain verifiable parental consent prior to collecting, using, or disclosing personal information from children.
regulatoryFindings.description: Looksmart failed to obtain any verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13.
violations: Looksmart failed to obtain any verifiable parental consent before collecting personal information from children under 13.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.6 requires operators to provide a reasonable means for parents to review the personal information collected from their children and to refuse its further use or maintenance.
regulatoryFindings.description: Looksmart provided no means for parents to review or delete the information collected from their children.
violations: Looksmart provided no means for parents to review or delete the information collected from their children.

regulatoryFindings.act: COPPA Rule Section 312.7 prohibits conditioning children's participation in an activity on disclosing more personal information than is reasonably necessary.
regulatoryFindings.description: Looksmart required children to submit full name, email, birth date, gender, country, profiling information, system software, browser, and homepage URL to register for message boards—far more data than necessary for message board participation.
violations: Looksmart required children to submit full name, email, birth date, gender, country, profiling information, system software, browser, and homepage URL to register for message boards—far more data than necessary for message board participation.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Looksmart's violations of the COPPA Rule constitute unfair and deceptive acts or practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.
violations: Looksmart's violations of the COPPA Rule constitute unfair and deceptive acts or practices under Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.

outcome: This complaint for civil penalties, injunctive relief, and other equitable remedies was filed by the United States on behalf of the FTC. The complaint seeks monetary civil penalties of up to $11,000 per violation (under 28 U.S.C. § 2461 and 16 C.F.R. § 1.98(d)), with each collection, use, and/or disclosure of a child's personal information from April 21, 2000 through the filing of the complaint constituting a separate violation. A permanent injunction against violations of COPPA is also sought. The case was filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia. Resolution and final penalty amounts were not specified in this complaint filing.
companyNow: Looksmart Ltd. was a publicly-traded Delaware corporation. The company's current operational status is unknown from this document; the complaint indicates the insidetheweb.com service was discontinued by approximately February 2001.
dataType: Children's personal information including full names, email addresses, birth dates, gender, usernames, passwords, country, profiling information
legalBasisViolated: COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 312, Section 312.4(b) – Privacy Policy Notice
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 312, Section 312.4(c) – Parental Notice
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 312, Section 312.5 – Verifiable Parental Consent
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 312, Section 312.6 – Parental Access and Control
COPPA Rule 16 C.F.R. Part 312, Section 312.7 – Reasonable Data Limitation

companyDescription: Liberty Financial Companies, Inc. was a Massachusetts-based financial services company that operated the younginvestor.com website, which provided investment education and products targeting young investors, including the Stein Roe Young Investor Fund.
companyLongDescription: Liberty Financial Companies, Inc. was a Massachusetts-based financial services company that operated the younginvestor.com website, which provided investment education and products targeting young investors, including the Stein Roe Young Investor Fund.
caseDescription: Liberty Financial collected personal information from children via a survey on its Young Investor website, falsely claiming the data would be anonymous. The company also misrepresented that survey participants would receive an email newsletter and have a chance to win quarterly prizes, neither of which actually existed.
violationSummary: The company solicited detailed personal and financial information from children through a survey interface, combined with deceptive privacy and incentive claims designed to encourage disclosure of sensitive data.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: Liberty Financial collected personal identifying information from children through the 'Measure Up Survey' on younginvestor.com.
whyTheyWereWrong: Children and parents provided detailed financial and personal information believing it was anonymous, but Liberty secretly linked identifiable names.

claimsVsReality.claim: All of your answers will be totally anonymous.
claimsVsReality.reality: Personal identifying information (name, address, email) was collected and linked to all survey responses in a database, allowing identification of individual respondents with their answers.

claimsVsReality.claim: Would you like to be added to the Young Investor e-mail newsletter?
claimsVsReality.reality: No email newsletter was ever developed or sent to any survey participants.

claimsVsReality.claim: Each Quarter, one participant will win his or her choice of a digital video camera, CD ROM drive or flatbed scanner.
claimsVsReality.reality: No quarterly drawings were ever conducted, and no prizes were ever awarded to survey participants.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the Federal Trade Commission Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Liberty represented that survey answers would be maintained anonymously but compiled and maintained a database combining personal identifying information with all survey responses, allowing individuals to be identified with their answers.
violations: Liberty represented that survey answers would be maintained anonymously but compiled and maintained a database combining personal identifying information with all survey responses, allowing individuals to be identified with their answers.
Liberty represented that survey participants would receive an email newsletter upon request, but never developed or provided any such newsletter to participants.
Liberty represented that a participant would be selected each quarter to win specified prizes, but no quarterly drawings were ever conducted and no winners were ever selected.

outcome: The FTC issued a complaint on August 12, 1999, alleging violations of Section 5(a) of the FTC Act. The complaint documents three categories of deceptive practices targeting children: false anonymity claims, non-existent newsletter service, and non-existent prize drawings. A compliance order was issued requiring the company to correct its practices and comply with privacy and substantiation requirements.
companyNow: Liberty Financial Companies ceased operations of the Young Investor website and the problematic survey. The company's online properties and business model were subject to FTC oversight and remediation.
dataType: Name, age, gender, email address, street address, financial information (allowance, gift types, spending habits, work history, college plans, family finances, investment data)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or Deceptive Acts or Practices

company: First American Real Estate Solutions, LLC (formerly First American CREDCO, Inc.)
companyDescription: First American CREDCO was a consumer reporting agency that assembled and evaluated consumer credit information from national repositories to produce Instant Merge Reports sold to mortgage lenders, auto/home equity lenders, and property managers.
companyLongDescription: First American CREDCO was a consumer reporting agency that assembled and evaluated consumer credit information from national repositories to produce Instant Merge Reports sold to mortgage lenders, auto/home equity lenders, and property managers.
caseDescription: CREDCO operated an Instant Merge Report system that blended contradictory consumer credit data from multiple repositories without verifying accuracy. When consumers disputed inaccurate information, CREDCO failed to reinvestigate, correct errors, or prevent inaccurate data from reappearing in future reports, violating FCRA and FTC Act requirements.
violationSummary: CREDCO failed to maintain reasonable data quality and accuracy controls, merging contradictory information without verification and preventing necessary corrections to consumer files.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: CREDCO created Instant Merge Reports blending contradictory credit data from multiple repositories without verification, then locked them on file preventing corrections.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers received inaccurate merged credit reports used by lenders for mortgage, auto, and rental decisions, with CREDCO refusing to investigate disputes or remove confirmed errors.

claimsVsReality.claim: IMRs blend authoritative consumer credit information from multiple national repositories into unified trade lines
claimsVsReality.reality: IMRs merged contradictory information without verification, creating inaccurate composite reports used in lending decisions

claimsVsReality.claim: CREDCO maintains corrected IMRs on file for accuracy
claimsVsReality.reality: CREDCO's system prevented any corrections from being made once an IMR was created, locking in inaccurate data

claimsVsReality.claim: Consumers can dispute information in IMRs
claimsVsReality.reality: CREDCO did not reinvestigate disputes or correct errors; it merely referred consumers back to the original repositories, providing no meaningful dispute resolution mechanism

regulatoryFindings.act: Fair Credit Reporting Act § 611 requires consumer reporting agencies to reinvestigate disputed information, correct or delete inaccurate/obsolete information, and include dispute notations in subsequent reports.
regulatoryFindings.description: CREDCO failed to reinvestigate disputed information, instead referring consumers back to original repositories
violations: CREDCO failed to reinvestigate disputed information, instead referring consumers back to original repositories
CREDCO did not correct or delete information found to be inaccurate or obsolete during reinvestigation
CREDCO did not include dispute notations or consumer statements in subsequent IMRs

violations: CREDCO's system maintained IMRs on file but prevented any corrections from being made

violations: CREDCO's systematic failure to verify, correct, or dispute-mark inaccurate credit information constitutes unfair practices affecting consumers relying on these reports for credit decisions

FTC Act § 5(a) (15 U.S.C. § 45(a)) – prohibition of unfair or deceptive acts or practices

regulatoryFindings.description: Bruno's denied or rescinded employment applications based on consumer reports without advising applicants that consumer reporting agency information contributed to the adverse action
violations: Bruno's denied or rescinded employment applications based on consumer reports without advising applicants that consumer reporting agency information contributed to the adverse action
Bruno's failed to provide applicants with the name and address of the consumer reporting agency that supplied the information

violations: Bruno's engaged in unfair and deceptive practices by failing to comply with Section 615(a) disclosure requirements when making employment decisions based on consumer reports

caseDescription: Aldi Inc. denied or rescinded employment offers based on adverse information in consumer reports but failed to notify applicants that the consumer report contributed to the adverse action, and failed to provide the name and address of the consumer reporting agency. This violated the Fair Credit Reporting Act's adverse action notification requirements, which protect job applicants from secret decisions based on third-party reports.
violationSummary: The company failed to disclose to affected consumers that third-party consumer reports were used in adverse employment decisions, preventing applicants from identifying and challenging inaccurate information in those reports.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Aldi denied employment applications or rescinded job offers based partly on consumer reporting agency information without informing applicants that the report contributed to the adverse decision.
whyTheyWereWrong: Job applicants were unable to understand why they were rejected or challenge potentially inaccurate credit information that cost them employment opportunities without any notification or chance.

claimsVsReality.claim: Aldi used consumer reports appropriately in employment decisions
claimsVsReality.reality: Aldi used consumer reports to deny or rescind job offers without notifying applicants or providing source information, preventing applicants from contesting the information

companyDescription: Finham Park Multi Academy Trust is an educational institution located in Coventry, UK, comprising multiple academies within a trust structure.
companyLongDescription: Finham Park Multi Academy Trust is an educational institution located in Coventry, UK, comprising multiple academies within a trust structure.
caseDescription: Finham Park Multi Academy Trust failed to implement adequate security measures to protect personal data, resulting in multiple security incidents. The organisation had inadequate access controls, no multi-factor authentication, poor password management practices, and failed to implement guidance provided by the ICO following prior incidents.
violationSummary: Finham Park failed to maintain adequate technical and organisational security measures as required by GDPR Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1). The lack of access controls, MFA, and password management directly enabled unauthorised access to personal data.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
whatTheyDid: Finham Park Multi Academy Trust failed to implement adequate technical and organisational security measures, including proper account lockout policies, multi-factor authentication.
whyTheyWereWrong: Students' and staff members' personal data was exposed to unauthorised access and potential compromise through preventable security vulnerabilities that attackers exploited.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures ('integrity and confidentiality').
regulatoryFindings.description: Finham Park did not implement appropriate account lockout policies, allowing potential brute force attacks
violations: Finham Park did not implement appropriate account lockout policies, allowing potential brute force attacks
Reversible password encryption was enabled, contrary to NCSC guidance
No multi-factor authentication was deployed despite extensive NCSC guidance recommending MFA
Employees were not educated on password management, resulting in password reuse across accounts

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1) of the UK GDPR requires that taking into account the state of the art, the costs of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risk of varying likelihood and severity for the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the controller and the processor shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk.
regulatoryFindings.description: Finham Park failed to implement security measures proportionate to the risk of processing student and employee personal data
violations: Finham Park failed to implement security measures proportionate to the risk of processing student and employee personal data
The trust did not follow evidence-based guidance from NCSC on access controls and authentication
Three similar incidents were reported and ICO guidance was provided each time; Finham Park failed to implement the recommended measures

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to Finham Park Multi Academy Trust under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. No monetary fine was imposed. However, the ICO noted the aggravating factor that Finham Park had received guidance following three similar prior incidents and failed to implement the recommendations. The organisation has since taken remedial steps including restoring systems from backups, implementing multi-factor authentication across the trust, and signing off a digital transformation project plan including credential monitoring.
companyNow: Finham Park Multi Academy Trust continues to operate as an educational institution. The trust has implemented remedial security measures in response to this enforcement action.
dataType: Student and employee personal data (unspecified sensitive categories)

companyDescription: Achieving for Children (AfC) is a social work and child protection service provider that works with local authorities to deliver children's services.
companyLongDescription: Achieving for Children (AfC) is a social work and child protection service provider that works with local authorities to deliver children's services.
caseDescription: AfC inappropriately disclosed sensitive personal data including criminal conviction records, children's information, sex life data, and health data in a social work report due to communication failures and lack of staff training in redaction procedures. The organisation lacked required organisational measures and policies to prevent such incidents, and neither the social worker nor reviewing manager had received redaction training.
violationSummary: The unauthorised disclosure of sensitive personal data (criminal convictions, children's information, health and sex life data) to unintended recipients constitutes a breach of confidentiality protected by Article 5(1)(f).
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Inappropriately disclosed criminal conviction data, children's data, sex life data, and health data in assessment reports sent to unintended recipients due to communication failures.
whyTheyWereWrong: Sensitive personal data of children and adults, including criminal records and health information, was exposed without consent to birth fathers, step-fathers.

claimsVsReality.claim: AfC expected social workers to complete redactions correctly and managers to review them.
claimsVsReality.reality: Neither social workers nor managers were trained in redaction procedures, and no formal policy documented these expectations or responsibilities.

claimsVsReality.claim: AfC has redaction-trained business support officers who usually handle redactions.
claimsVsReality.reality: No business support officers were involved in the incident and no policy required their involvement, leaving redaction entirely to untrained staff.

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires that personal data shall be processed in a manner that ensures appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorised or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organisational measures.
regulatoryFindings.description: AfC failed to implement required organisational measures to prevent unauthorised disclosure of sensitive personal data.
violations: AfC failed to implement required organisational measures to prevent unauthorised disclosure of sensitive personal data.
No redaction training was provided to the social worker or reviewing manager responsible for handling sensitive documents.
No policy or guidance documented the manager's responsibility to review redactions or how social workers should approach the redaction process.
Criminal conviction data, children's data, sex life data, and health data were disclosed to unintended recipients due to inadequate security controls.

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to AfC under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner welcomed AfC's remedial steps including ongoing redaction training for social workers and development of relevant policies. AfC was recommended to: (1) ensure all employees expected to complete redactions complete redaction training; (2) document senior leadership expectations in policy documents and ensure staff awareness; and (3) continue providing annual data protection and information governance training to all staff.
companyNow: Achieving for Children is a social care provider operating across UK local authorities. The organisation continues to implement remedial measures including staff training and policy development in response to this enforcement action.
dataType: Criminal conviction data, children's data, sex life data, health data

companyDescription: NCO Group, Inc. is a debt collection company based in Horsham, Pennsylvania that furnishes delinquency information to consumer reporting agencies as part of its debt collection business operations.
companyLongDescription: NCO Group, Inc. is a debt collection company based in Horsham, Pennsylvania that furnishes delinquency information to consumer reporting agencies as part of its debt collection business operations.
caseDescription: NCO Group, a debt collection agency, reported inaccurate delinquency dates to credit reporting agencies for accounts it collected. The company reported dates later than the actual month and year when delinquency began, violating Section 623(a)(5) of the Fair Credit Reporting Act. This affected consumers by damaging their credit reports with false information.
violationSummary: The company distorted consumer credit information by reporting inaccurate delinquency dates to credit reporting agencies, resulting in misleading credit histories that harmed consumers' financial standing.
violations: Misleading Privacy Policies
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: NCO Group reported inaccurate delinquency dates to credit reporting agencies that were later than when accounts actually became delinquent, affecting thousands of consumers' credit histories.
whyTheyWereWrong: Consumers with false delinquency dates on their credit reports faced wrongful credit score damage, higher borrowing costs, and denial of loans, mortgages.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 623(a)(5) of the FCRA requires anyone furnishing information to a consumer reporting agency regarding a delinquent account that has been placed for collection, charged to profit or loss, or subjected to any similar action, to provide to the consumer reporting agency, not later than 90 days after furnishing the information, the month and year of the commencement of the delinquency.
regulatoryFindings.description: NCO Group reported delinquency dates to credit reporting agencies that were later than the month and year of actual delinquency commencement for multiple accounts, violating the 90-day requirement and accuracy mandate.
violations: NCO Group reported delinquency dates to credit reporting agencies that were later than the month and year of actual delinquency commencement for multiple accounts, violating the 90-day requirement and accuracy mandate.

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Reporting inaccurate delinquency dates constitutes deceptive practices that harm consumers' credit standing and violate Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.
violations: Reporting inaccurate delinquency dates constitutes deceptive practices that harm consumers' credit standing and violate Section 5(a) of the FTC Act.

outcome: The complaint seeks monetary civil penalties of up to $2,500 per violation of Section 623(a)(5), with each instance of reporting a later-than-actual delinquency date constituting a separate violation. The complaint requests permanent injunctive relief prohibiting defendants from violating the FTC Act and FCRA Section 623.
dataType: Financial data, credit history, delinquency records
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices
FCRA Section 623(a)(5) – Requirement to provide accurate delinquency commencement date within 90 days
FCRA Section 621(a)(1) – Enforcement authority for FCRA violations

company: University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust
companyDescription: University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust is an NHS healthcare provider operating in Dorset, England. It provides hospital and related healthcare services.
companyLongDescription: University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust is an NHS healthcare provider operating in Dorset, England. It provides hospital and related healthcare services.
caseDescription: University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust disclosed a patient's home address to an ex-partner by including it in carbon-copied correspondence, without consent. The Trust had no formal process to flag sensitive situations or obtain consent for such disclosures. This violated Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR, which requires appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect personal data.
violationSummary: The Trust proactively disclosed personal data (postal address) to a third party without consent, exposing the data subject to potential harm and unwanted contact.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Unauthorized Data Collection
whatTheyDid: University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust included patients' full postal addresses in carbon-copied letter recipients without consent.
whyTheyWereWrong: A patient's home address was disclosed to an ex-partner without permission, creating an ongoing risk of unwanted contact.

claimsVsReality.claim: Trust's intent by the carbon-copy practice was to prevent errors when manually writing addresses on envelopes
claimsVsReality.reality: The practice created a significant data protection risk by proactively disclosing third parties' personal data without consent or consideration of potential harm

claimsVsReality.claim: No instance prior to incident where one parent objected to details being shared with the other
claimsVsReality.reality: One instance occurred where an ex-partner received a patient's address despite history of abuse allegations and patient's reasonable expectation of non-disclosure

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR requires organisations to take appropriate technical and organisational measures against unauthorised or unlawful processing and accidental loss or damage to personal data.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust had a standard procedure of disclosing recipients' postal addresses in letter carbon copies without obtaining consent
violations: Trust had a standard procedure of disclosing recipients' postal addresses in letter carbon copies without obtaining consent
No risk assessment was conducted regarding data protection implications of this practice
No formal system existed to flag patients for sensitive scenarios such as parental disputes
No formal training was provided to administration staff for handling correspondence in disputed situations
Disclosure of address to ex-partner despite patient's reasonable expectation of confidentiality given history of abuse allegations

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to the Trust under Article 58(2)(b) of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps already taken, including: apology to data subject, benchmarking exercise with other organisations to establish clear policy for Child Health directorate, and implementation of blind-copy procedures for sensitive parental dispute situations. The Commissioner recommended the Trust: (1) complete a review of practices incorporating benchmarking learnings to identify further risk areas; (2) ensure areas identified by action plan are fully implemented and subject to regular review.
companyNow: University Hospitals Dorset NHS Foundation Trust is an NHS healthcare provider in England. It continues operations as a foundation trust within the National Health Service.
dataType: postal address, personal correspondence

companyDescription: Levales Solicitors LLP is a UK law firm founded in 2010 specialising in criminal and military law. The firm processes sensitive personal data including criminal records, victim information, and health data on behalf of clients.
companyLongDescription: Levales Solicitors LLP is a UK law firm founded in 2010 specialising in criminal and military law. The firm processes sensitive personal data including criminal records, victim information, and health data on behalf of clients.
caseDescription: Levales Solicitors LLP, a criminal and military law firm, suffered a data breach affecting 8,234 individuals when an unknown threat actor gained access to their secure cloud server using compromised credentials. The firm lacked multi-factor authentication and had not reviewed security measures with their managed IT service provider since 2012. The ICO found infringements of Articles 32(1)(b) and 32(1)(d) of the UK GDPR relating to inadequate security measures and issued a reprimand.
violationSummary: The breach resulted in unauthorised disclosure of highly sensitive personal data on the dark web, constituting a direct breach of confidentiality. The data included special category information (criminal records, health data, victim/complainant details) that required heightened protection.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
whatTheyDid: Levales Solicitors LLP failed to implement multi-factor authentication for administrator accounts, lacked a password policy.
whyTheyWereWrong: 8,234 people's sensitive personal data including criminal records, health information, victim details.

claimsVsReality.claim: The firm had a secure cloud-based server protecting client data
claimsVsReality.reality: The server lacked multi-factor authentication and basic security controls, allowing unauthorised access via compromised credentials

claimsVsReality.claim: A third-party managed IT service provider was responsible for security
claimsVsReality.reality: The firm had not reviewed the provider's security measures or contract terms for 11 years and remained unaware of what detection, prevention, and monitoring controls actually existed

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(b) of the UK GDPR requires organisations to ensure the ongoing confidentiality, integrity, availability and resilience of processing systems and services.
regulatoryFindings.description: Levales Solicitors LLP did not have multi-factor authentication (MFA) in place for the affected domain account
violations: Levales Solicitors LLP did not have multi-factor authentication (MFA) in place for the affected domain account
The firm relied solely on computer prompts for password management and strength with no formal password policy
An unknown threat actor was able to gain access to the administrator-level account via compromised credentials

regulatoryFindings.act: Article 32(1)(d) of the UK GDPR requires controllers and processors to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure a level of security appropriate to the risk, taking into account the state of the art, costs of implementation, and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing.
regulatoryFindings.description: Levales Solicitors LLP did not implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures
violations: Levales Solicitors LLP did not implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures
The firm outsourced IT management to a third party but remained unaware of security measures in place, including detection, prevention, and monitoring
Security measures in the third-party contract had not been reviewed since 2012 and were not assessed as appropriate for the sensitive personal data being processed

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a formal reprimand to Levales Solicitors LLP. The ICO welcomed the remedial steps taken by the firm, including: (1) implementation of multi-factor authentication for all user accounts; (2) updated service contracts with third-party IT providers; and (3) a complete review of existing systems to prioritise firewall upgrades and security enhancements. The firm was required to address the identified deficiencies in access controls and service provider oversight.
companyNow: Levales Solicitors LLP remains in operation. Following the reprimand, the firm has implemented corrective measures including MFA for all accounts and reviewed IT security contracts and infrastructure.
dataType: Criminal records, health status, national insurance numbers, prisoner numbers, victim/complainant details, legally privileged information, investigation outcomes, uncharged allegations

company: South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust
companyDescription: South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is a public NHS healthcare provider in England operating hospital services. As an NHS foundation trust, it is a public sector organisation funded by the National Health Service.
companyLongDescription: South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust is a public NHS healthcare provider in England operating hospital services. As an NHS foundation trust, it is a public sector organisation funded by the National Health Service.
caseDescription: South Tees Hospitals sent an appointment letter to a child patient's wrong address (mother's family address instead of father's), exposing the appointment to unintended recipients. The Trust failed to maintain accurate contact details in its e-Camis system and lacked proper procedures to verify patient information before sending sensitive correspondence. This caused significant distress to the child and family.
violationSummary: The Trust exposed sensitive health information (appointment letter with medical advice leaflet) by mailing to an incorrect address, making it accessible to unintended third parties (mother's family members). This falls squarely within Information Dissemination – Exposure under Solove taxonomy.
violations: False Light/Misappropriation
whatTheyDid: South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust sent a child patient's hospital appointment letter to the wrong address.
whyTheyWereWrong: A child patient's sensitive medical appointment information was sent to the mother's family address instead of the father's, causing significant distress to the child.

claimsVsReality.claim: Trust attributed the incident to human error by the administrator
claimsVsReality.reality: The underlying cause was systemic: inadequate procedures for verifying patient details, lack of staff training on NHS Spine checks, and inaccurate data in e-Camis system that was not regularly updated

claimsVsReality.claim: Trust's three-point check process for e-Camis details was sufficient safeguard
claimsVsReality.reality: By the Trust's own admission, the three-point check would not have prevented this breach; it was insufficient for sensitive correspondence requiring verification against NHS Spine

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) requires appropriate technical and organisational measures to protect against unauthorised or unlawful processing of personal data and against accidental loss, destruction, or damage.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust failed to implement adequate organisational measures (formal procedures, staff training on NHS Spine checks) to prevent unauthorised disclosure of sensitive health data to wrong addresses
violations: Trust failed to implement adequate organisational measures (formal procedures, staff training on NHS Spine checks) to prevent unauthorised disclosure of sensitive health data to wrong addresses

regulatoryFindings.act: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(d) requires personal data to be accurate and kept up to date, with reasonable steps taken to erase or rectify inaccurate data without delay.
regulatoryFindings.description: Trust's e-Camis system held inaccurate patient contact details that were not regularly updated against NHS Spine, and no formal procedure ensured accuracy for correspondence purposes
violations: Trust's e-Camis system held inaccurate patient contact details that were not regularly updated against NHS Spine, and no formal procedure ensured accuracy for correspondence purposes

outcome: The Information Commissioner issued a reprimand to South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust for violations of Articles 5(1)(d) and 5(1)(f) of the UK GDPR. The Commissioner welcomed remedial steps including implementation of a new Standard Operating Procedure (SOP) for checking and updating personal information. The Commissioner recommended: (1) full implementation of the new SOP with additional checks as soon as possible; (2) completion of other remedial measures including Data Security and Protection training for administration and secretarial staff; (3) training all staff handling correspondence in processes to check patient details against the NHS Spine; and (4) regular updates and checks of the e-Camis system against the NHS Spine to ensure accurate patient information. No monetary fine was imposed. The reprimand is the enforcement outcome, with ongoing monitoring and compliance obligations.
companyNow: South Tees Hospitals NHS Foundation Trust remains an NHS healthcare provider operating in the North East of England. Post-incident, the Trust has implemented new data governance procedures and committed to staff training to prevent recurrence.
dataType: Health data, patient contact information, sensitive medical appointment details
legalBasisViolated: UK GDPR Article 5(1)(f) – Integrity and Confidentiality

companyDescription: ControlScan offered online certification seals and security scanning services to e-commerce businesses, claiming to verify website privacy and security protections for consumer confidence.
companyLongDescription: ControlScan offered online certification seals and security scanning services to e-commerce businesses, claiming to verify website privacy and security protections for consumer confidence.
caseDescription: ControlScan sold privacy and security certification seals to websites claiming to have verified their security and privacy protections, but conducted little to no actual verification of the websites' practices. The seals displayed daily-updated dates implying continuous monitoring, yet ControlScan performed minimal or no ongoing review. Consumers were misled into trusting websites that may not have provided adequate data protection.
violationSummary: ControlScan failed to implement adequate security practices in their own verification processes, exposing consumers to risk through deceptive representations about the security of certified websites.
violations: Data Breach & Negligence
Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Illegal Monitoring/Surveillance
whatTheyDid: ControlScan sold website certification seals claiming to verify companies' privacy and security protections.
whyTheyWereWrong: Millions of consumers relied on ControlScan's seals to trust websites with personal information, but many sealed websites had severe security vulnerabilities.

claimsVsReality.claim: ControlScan has verified that companies displaying our seals provide appropriate protection for consumer information privacy and security
claimsVsReality.reality: ControlScan conducted minimal to no actual verification of most websites' security or privacy practices, and many seal-displaying websites had known, unaddressed vulnerabilities

claimsVsReality.claim: The daily-updated date stamp indicates continuous daily review and verification of each website's compliance
claimsVsReality.reality: ControlScan performed no ongoing daily review for most seal types; Business Background Reviewed, Privacy Protected, and Privacy Reviewed seals received no ongoing monitoring whatsoever

claimsVsReality.claim: Companies displaying the Registered Member seal are 'currently working towards meeting Payment Card Industry Data Security Standards' with ControlScan verification
claimsVsReality.reality: ControlScan took no steps to verify this claim and allowed indefinite seal display by companies with identified severe vulnerabilities without requiring any remediation efforts

claimsVsReality.claim: Privacy Protected seal indicates the company's privacy statement and practices have been reviewed by ControlScan for compliance with strict program requirements
claimsVsReality.reality: ControlScan only verified that a privacy policy existed on the website, with no review of the company's actual underlying privacy or information security practices

regulatoryFindings.act: Section 5(a) of the FTC Act, 15 U.S.C. § 45(a), prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce.
regulatoryFindings.description: Falsely represented that ControlScan had taken reasonable steps to verify companies' privacy/security protections when it conducted little or no verification for Business Background Reviewed, Registered Member, Privacy Protected, and Privacy Reviewed seals
violations: Falsely represented that ControlScan had taken reasonable steps to verify companies' privacy/security protections when it conducted little or no verification for Business Background Reviewed, Registered Member, Privacy Protected, and Privacy Reviewed seals
Represented through date stamps that daily verification occurred when many companies received no ongoing review of their practices
Claimed companies were 'working towards' PCI Data Security Standards compliance without any steps to verify this status
For Registered Member seal holders with security vulnerabilities, permitted indefinite seal display without requiring companies to remediate identified issues

outcome: The FTC sought permanent injunctive relief, disgorgement of ill-gotten monies, and restitution to consumers. The complaint does not include a final judgment or settlement terms, indicating this was the initial complaint filing. ControlScan was required to cease deceptive practices regarding seal certification and verification claims.
dataType: Consumer information (personal data, financial data, payment card information)
legalBasisViolated: FTC Act Section 5(a) – Unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce

companyDescription: Smart Data Systems was an information search business operated by Victor L. Guzzetta from his residence at 20 Cattaraugus Street, Staten Island, New York, and through a website. companyLongDescription: Smart Data Systems was an information search business operated by Victor L. Guzzetta from his residence at 20 Cattaraugus Street, Staten Island, New York, and through a website. caseDescription: Victor Guzzetta, operating as Smart Data Systems, fraudulently obtained customer financial information from financial institutions by posing as customers and making false representations to bank employees. He then sold this confidential banking information to clients for fees. The FTC charged him with violating the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act and FTC Act Section 5(a) through deceptive and unfair practices.
violationSummary: The defendant obtained confidential customer financial information from financial institutions through false pretenses and disclosed it to third parties (his clients) without authorization, violating the confidentiality relationship between financial institutions and their customers.
violations: Unauthorized Disclosure/Selling
Misleading Privacy Policies
whatTheyDid: Victor Guzzetta operated Smart Data Systems, fraudulently posing as bank customers and making false representations to financial institution employees to obtain third-party customer financial.
whyTheyWereWrong: Thousands of consumers had their confidential bank account balances and account activity statements illegally obtained.

claimsVsReality.claim: Smart Data Systems is a 'full service search firm' that can obtain any information clients need.
claimsVsReality.reality: The company fraudulently obtained confidential financial information from banks through false pretenses and identity deception, illegally accessing non-public data.

claimsVsReality.claim: Defendant can legitimately provide 'statewide bank account searches' for $175 and investment information searches for $300.
claimsVsReality.reality: These services were provided by fraudulently obtaining third-party customer information from financial institutions without authorization, violating the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act.

regulatoryFindings.act: Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act Section 521(a) prohibits any person from obtaining or attempting to obtain customer information of a financial institution relating to another person by making false, fictitious, or fraudulent statements or representations to financial institution officers, employees, or agents.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendant repeatedly posed as customers or made false representations to bank employees to induce disclosure of third-party customer information including account balances and activity statements.
violations: Defendant repeatedly posed as customers or made false representations to bank employees to induce disclosure of third-party customer information including account balances and activity statements.
Defendant knowingly obtained customer information through false pretenses and fraudulent misrepresentations regarding his identity and authority.

regulatoryFindings.act: FTC Act Section 5(a) prohibits unfair or deceptive acts or practices in or affecting commerce. Misrepresentations of material facts constitute deceptive acts.
regulatoryFindings.description: Defendant misrepresented his identity, purposes, and right to receive customer information to financial institution representatives, deceiving them into disclosing confidential data.
violations: Defendant misrepresented his identity, purposes, and right to receive customer information to financial institution representatives, deceiving them into disclosing confidential data.

Defendant's practices caused or were likely to cause substantial injury to consumers (whose financial information was fraudulently obtained) that was not reasonably avoidable and not outweighed by countervailing benefits.

outcome: The FTC filed a Complaint for Injunctive and Other Equitable Relief in the United States District Court, Eastern District of New York, seeking preliminary and permanent injunctive relief, rescission of contracts, restitution, redress, disgorgement, and other equitable relief to prevent future violations and remedy harm caused by defendant's unlawful practices.
companyNow: Unknown; Smart Data Systems was an unincorporated entity operated from a residence in Staten Island, New York. No public information available regarding current status.
dataType: Financial information, bank account balances, bank account activity statements, stocks, bonds, mutual funds information
